en: Oṃ. The Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, together with the commentary composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya.

The Introductory Section (Upodghāta-prakaraṇam) Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. I bow to that elephant-faced Lord (Gaṇeśa), whom the wise, headed by Vāgīśa (Bṛhaspati), salute at the commencement of all undertakings, so that they may achieve their purpose. (1) I praise that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas, and who created the entire universe from the Vedas. (2) By his glance, King Vikrama assumed that very form [of Vidyātīrtha] and commanded Mādhavācārya to illuminate the meaning of the Vedas. (3) Having provided concise commentaries on the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsās, the compassionate Mādhavācārya is now prepared to declare the meaning of the Vedas. (4) Since the *Ādhvaryava* (the duties of the Adhvaryu priest) holds primacy among sacrifices, the Yajurveda will first be explained; thereafter, the Ṛgveda will be expounded for the sake of the *Hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest). (5) In this regard, the first chapter must be studied according to the traditional lineage (*saṃpradāya*). By means of that alone, an intelligent person who has attained proficiency will be able to understand everything. (6)
Regarding this, some say:

since the *Ṛgveda* is known everywhere as being first, its commentary is appropriate at the beginning according to the maxim "that which is more venerable comes first. Its priority is stated in the *Puruṣasūkta*: "From that sacrifice, from which everything was offered, the *Ṛks* and the *Sāmans* were born."
"From him the meters were born; from him the Yajus was born" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.90.9).

Therefore, from that Supreme Lord—who has been described as "the thousand-headed Puruṣa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.90.1)—who is the sacrifice, who is worthy of sacrifice, who is worthy of worship, and who is the "all-oblation" (sarvahuta) being offered by all;
for although Indra and others are offered in various places, there is no contradiction, because the Supreme Lord himself exists in the form of Indra and the other deities.
And thus says a Vedic mantra: "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
The sages speak of the One Being as many—calling him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.164.46).

And the Vājasaneyins declare: "As for what people say, 'Sacrifice to that one,' 'Sacrifice to that one'—each individual deity is but an emanation of this very [Brahman], for he alone is all the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6).
Therefore, by all [beings], it is indeed the Supreme Lord who is offered as an oblation.
Not only is the recitation of the Ṛgvedic verses more highly esteemed, but it is also so because they serve as the cause for the excellence of the sacrifice.

1. By the *ṭa-ṭha* manuscript, [it is read as] *taktākṣeṇa*. 2. By the *ṭa-ṭha* manuscript, [it is read as] *sāyaṇācāryam*. 3. By the *ṭa-ṭha* manuscript, [it is read as] *sāyaṇācāryau*. 4. By the *va-pha* manuscript, [it is read as] *prathamādhyāyaḥ*. By the *ca-ta-pha* manuscripts, [the following two verses are seen as additional after the third verse]: "4. *sa prāha nṛpatiṃ rājan sāyaṇāyāṃ mamānujaḥ | sarvaṃ vettyeṣa vedānāṃ vyākhyātṛtvena yujyatām || ityukte mādhavācāryeṇa vīrabukamahīpatiḥ | anvagāt sāyaṇācāryaṃ vedārthasya prakāśane ||*" [In these verses: 5. By the *ṭa-ṭha* manuscript, "'atra'" does not exist. 6. By the *ta-tha* manuscript, "'tasmāt'" does not exist. 7. By the *ca-cha-ja* manuscript, "'yajñāt'" does not exist. 8. By the *ṭha* manuscript, "'pūjanīyāt'" does not exist. 9. By the *ṭha* manuscript, [it is read as] *parameśvarasya*. 10. By the *ṭa-ṭha* manuscript, [it is read as] *prāthamyamātreṇa*.

Furthermore, the Taittirīyas recite in the Ṛgveda: "Whatever part of the sacrifice is performed with the Sāman or the Yajus is indeed loose; that which is performed with the Ṛk is firm" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.10.3).

And likewise, in order to strengthen the conviction regarding the matter of the Lord’s benefit, the Brāhmaṇas found in all the Vedas cite examples from the Ṛgveda, saying, "This very thing has been declared."

Even in the section on mantras within the Yajurveda, many ṛks intended for recitation by the Adhvaryu priest at various points are well-known. As for the Sāmans, it is well established that they all rest upon the Ṛgveda. Furthermore, the followers of the Atharvaveda also study them extensively within their own Saṃhitā.
Therefore, its superiority over all other Vedas is well-established by their own words.

Furthermore, the Chandogas record these words of Nārada addressed to Sanatkumāra regarding primacy: "O Venerable One, I have studied the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaṇa as the fourth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.2).
Likewise, it is recited in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5).

In the *Tāpanīya Upaniṣad* as well, the study of the mantras, the *Ājapa*, and so forth, is prescribed in a specific sequence: "The four Vedas—Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharvan—together with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and branches (*śākhā*), constitute the four feet" (*Nṛsiṃha-tāpanīya Upaniṣad* 1.2).
This should be cited as an example everywhere else.
Therefore, since the *Ṛgveda* is the most venerable, it is appropriate to explain it first; thus, for the sake of those [students], it is said:

Regarding this, although the *Ṛgveda* holds primacy among all Vedas in terms of study, recitation, completion, and the *brahmayajña*, since the knowledge of meaning is for the sake of performing sacrifices (*yajñānuṣṭhāna*), and because the *Yajurveda* is primary in that regard, it is more appropriate to begin with its explanation. Furthermore, a certain verse from the *Ṛgveda* itself supports this: "One [priest] sits nourishing the essence of the *ṛcs*; another sings the *gāyatra* song upon the *śakvarīs*."
"Brahmā, being self-luminous, speaks the knowledge born [of realization]; he indeed measures out the measure of the sacrifice" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.71.11).
The author of the Nirukta, Yāska, briefly demonstrates the purport of this ṛc: "Thus, he explains the application [of the verses] according to their sequence.
Furthermore, he himself explains the first quarter-verse: "One, having become a Hotṛ, sits at the nourishment with a verse, praising as one worthy of praise" (Nirukta 1.8).
This is its meaning:
the word *vaś* is a synonym for *eka* (one) and serves as an epithet for the *hotṛ*.
A single officiating priest named *hotṛ* prays at the time of the sacrifice for the nourishment of the *ṛc*s contained within his own Veda.

In the sections concerning the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*), having gathered together the collections of *ṛc* verses that were previously unknown, one completes them by declaring, "This much is recited";
this is *puṣṭi*.
The word *ṛk* denotes the sense of that which is worthy of worship (*arcanīya*).

The etymology of the word *ṛc* is as follows: it is that by which a particular deity, a particular ritual action, or a particular means for accomplishing it is honored (*arcyate*) or praised (*praśasyate*).
Now, he explains the second quarter [of the verse]: "One sings the *gāyatra*; the *udgātṛ* sings the *śakvarīs*.

The *gāyatra* is derived from the root *gai*, meaning 'to praise. The *śakvarīs* are so called because they are capable (*śaknoti*) [of praising]; it is understood that their nature as *śakvarīs* is due to the fact that they were able (*aśaknuvan*) to overcome Vṛtra."
This is its meaning:
one officiating priest named Udgātṛ sings a hymn designated by the word *gāyatra* upon verses designated by the word *śakvarī*.
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *gāyatra* is stated to be the form of the root *gāyati*, which signifies the act of praising.
Regarding the word *śakvarī*, it is derived from the verbal root *śak* (to be able) with the suffix *itya*.

Its etymological derivation is "those verses (*ṛc*) by which one is able to slay Vṛtra, the enemy," as is known from the Brāhmaṇa text concerning Karṣi. Now, he explains the third quarter [of the verse]: "In every birth of Brahman, he speaks knowledge."
"Brahmā is all-knowing; he ought to know everything.
This is its meaning:

there is one officiating priest named Brahmā who, at each and every sacrifice when the ritual is commenced, gives his permission for the acts such as the fetching of water. Being thus addressed, "O Brahmā, shall I fetch the water?", he grants permission by saying, "Oṃ, fetch it."
And that Brahman is one who is conversant with all rites prescribed in the three Vedas;
therefore, having observed the fitness [of others], he is capable of knowing what each person does not know and of correcting them in the event of negligence.

The Chāndogas record this capability: "This indeed is the sacrifice; its two paths are mind and speech. By means of the mind, the Brahman priest perfects one of these two paths, while by means of speech, the Hotṛ and the Udgātṛ perfect the other" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.16.1–2).
The entire sacrifice must be performed correctly with a mind free from negligence, and the mantras prescribed in the three Vedas must be recited with speech.
In that regard, the three officiants beginning with the Hotṛ, acting together, purify the sacrificial path of the Ṛgveda;
the Brahmā, however, alone purifies the entire sacrificial path of the Manas (Mind).
Therefore, it possesses this capacity.
Now, the fourth quarter [of the verse]:

1. *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *ṇa*, and *ya* are mentioned; *nābhidhīyante*. 2. *ṭa* and *ṭha* are absent because they are "struck by the Vedas" (*vedairāhatatvāt*). 3. *ca*, *cha*, *jha*, *pha*, and *śa* are absent because they are "unestablished" (*aprasiddham*). 4. Among the *amreḍita*s (repeated words), those excluding *ṭa* and *ṭha*; however, the *Chandogas* [include them]. 5. Among the *amreḍita*s, excluding *ṭa*, [it occurs] primarily (*prāthamyena*). 6. Because it is devoid of *ṭa* and *ṭha*, it is at the beginning (*tasya ādau*). 7. It is called thus: *ṭha*; it is replied to as *ṭha*. 8. *ṭa* and *ṭha* certainly exist. 9. *ṭa* and *ṭha* are at the beginning of the *brahmavāda*; *ṭha* is at the beginning of the *brahmaja*. 10. *ṭha*: the word "but" (*tu*) is absent. 11. *ṭha*: of that (*tasya*). 12. *ṭa* and *ṭha*: and (*ca*). 13. *ṭa*: predominance (*prādhānyam*). 14. A combination (*saṃghātam*) of *gha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *pa*, *pha*, and *śa*. 15. *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *pha*, and *śa* are due to etymological derivation (*vyutpatteriti*). 16. *ṭha*: the *Sāman*. 17. *ca*, *ta*, and *pa*: the word "this" (*ayam*) is absent. 18. *ṭa* and *ṭha*: the word "enemy" (*śatrum*) is absent. 19. *ṭa* and *ṭha*: the phrase "in each birth" (*jāte jāte*) is absent. 20. *ṭa* and *ṭha*: the word "sacrifice" (*yajñe*) is absent. 21. *ṭa*: the root *tud*... to strike (*saṃbhātum*). 22. *gha*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, and *ya* constitute the sentence (*vākyam*).
The first chapter (Prathamollāsa) 2.
Viṣṇu says: "One [priest] measures out the measure of the sacrifice; he is the Adhvaryu, the leader of every sacrifice.
This is its meaning.

One officiating priest named Adhvaryu specifically measures—that is, constructs—the *mātrā*, which means the form or nature, of the sacrifice. That he is the one who brings it about is understood from the etymological derivation of the name "Adhvaryu. (The term *mātrā* is derived from the roots *mīyate* or *nirmīyate*, meaning "it is measured" or "it is constructed.")
In the word "adhvaryuḥ," one should restore the elided vowel *a* according to the grammatical process of *andhasyā* and thus form the name "adhvarayuḥ.
Its etymological meaning is "one who yokes the sacrifice" (*adhvaram yunakti*), and its intended sense is "the leader of the sacrifice" (*adhvarasya netā*).

Intending this very point, Yāska provides an etymological definition (*nirvacana*) that illustrates how the *Adhvaryu-veda* effects the accomplishment of the sacrifice: "The *mantras* are so called from 'thinking' (*manana*), the *chandas* from 'covering' (*chādana*), the *stoma* from 'praising' (*stavana*), and the *yajus* from 'joining' (*yunakti*)" (*Nirukta* 7.12).

This being the case, since the body of the sacrifice is accomplished within the *Yajurveda* associated with the *Adhvaryu*, and the two remaining parts—the *stotra* and *śastra*—required by it are fulfilled by the other two Vedas, it is logical to explain the *Yajurveda*, as the basis (*upajīvya*) upon which they depend, first of all.
Since the Sāmans are based upon the Ṛks, it is appropriate that the explanation of the Ṛk be presented first among both; therefore, the Ṛgveda is now being explained.
But surely, the Veda itself does not even exist; how then can there be its specific subdivision, the Ṛgveda?
For instance, what is this thing called "Veda"?
For in that case, there is neither a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) nor a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Nor is anything established apart from these two;
for it is the opinion of those who know the principles of logic that "the establishment of a real entity occurs by means of both its defining characteristic and its means of valid cognition."
If it is argued that its definition is "the last among the specific means of valid cognition, namely perception, inference, and scripture," we say no;
for this would over-extend to the Smṛtis of Manu and others.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the definition of scripture— namely, "that which establishes a correct experience of what is beyond the senses"— is present in those [Vedic texts] as well by virtue of their power of convention (*samaya*),
and that this is so because of the qualification "provided they are not of human origin" (*apauruṣeyatve sati*),
we say: no.
[If it is argued that] even the Veda is of human origin because it was created by the Supreme Lord—
if you claim that "being of human origin" means being created by a person possessing a body—
that is not so.
If it is argued that because the Lord also possesses a body— as evidenced by Vedic texts such as "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.90.1)—
the intended meaning of "not of human origin" (apauruṣeya) is merely the absence of being created by a living soul who bears a body that is the fruit of karma, we say:
no.
Because the Vedas were produced by the Ādityas through the intention of specific living beings— as stated in the Śruti:
"The Ṛgveda was first born from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vāyu, and the Sāmaveda from Āditya" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 5.32)—
the Lord's status as creator should be understood as being through His role as the impeller of Agni and the others.
If it is argued that the Veda is the collection of sounds consisting of the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, we say no;
for there is no definitive determination of what constitutes such a Mantra and what constitutes such a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, there is no definition whatsoever of the Veda.
Nor do we perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence.

If it is argued that such statements as, "O Venerable One, I study the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda as the fourth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.2), constitute the means of valid cognition, we say no.
For that statement as well, since it falls within the scope of the Vedānta, there would follow the consequence of its being dependent upon an initial undertaking;
indeed, even one who is skillful is not able to climb onto his own shoulder.
If it is argued that the scriptural statement, "The Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good for the twice-born" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.40), serves as the authority,
we say no;
for that too has been refuted because it lacks a foundation in direct revelation (śruti).
Perception and the other means of knowledge, moreover, are incapable even of apprehending [the Veda's] capacity [to convey meaning].
Furthermore, the worldly consensus regarding the subject matter of the Veda, though universal, is erroneous—like the common notion that "the sky is blue.
Therefore, the existence of the Veda, being devoid of both defining characteristics and means of valid cognition, cannot be accepted; such is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
Now it is said: first of all, the definition consisting of being composed of mantra and brāhmaṇa is faulty.
For this very reason, Āpastamba stated in the *Yajñaparibhāṣā*: "The name 'Veda' applies to both mantra and brāhmaṇa" (*Āpa.Pari.* 1.33).
As for the essential nature of these two, it will be determined later; furthermore, the specific kind of "non-human authorship" that we intend to mean will become clear in what follows.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of the Veda should also be understood as consisting of the aforementioned scripture (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), and worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*).

This is just as, for example, although substances such as jars and cloths lack self-luminosity, the sun, the moon, and so forth do possess it. (Note: 1. In manuscript *Ṭa*, the word "one" (*ekaḥ*) is absent.)
2. In the manuscript labeled Ṭa-Ṭha, the word "svarūpam" is missing.
3. In the manuscript labeled Ya, it reads "dakyotanam"; in the manuscript labeled Ta, it reads "dakyotakam". 4. In the manuscript labeled Ṭha, it says "sidhyati".
5. In the manuscript ṭa, "in the specific means of valid cognition" (pramāṇaviśeṣeṣu) is not present.

6. In the manuscripts ca, pha, it reads "due to the absence of being created by a body-bearing living person" (dhārijīvapuruṣanirmitatvābhāvāt); in the manuscripts ka, kha, ga, na, pa, it reads "created by a body-bearing living being" (śarīradhārijīvanirmitam).
7. In the manuscript ṭa, it says "because of the scriptural mention of having a body" (śarīradhāritvaśravaṇāt).

8. In the *ca-pa-pha* recension, the reading is "bearing a body that is the fruit of karma" (*karmaphalaśarīrarūpadhārī*); in place of the *ṭa-ṭha* recension’s "if it is argued that the form of the fruit of karma is not intended [to be expressed]," the reading is "if it is argued that the state of bearing a body is not intended [to be expressed], [we say] no.
9. In place of the *ṭa-ṭha* recension’s "because that sentence also [would entail] the same consequence," the reading is "for its authority is not observed in its own statement.
10. *Ṭa*: "even a clever boy"; *ṭha*: "even a clever actor-boy."
11. The sounds *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *pa*, and *pha* do not have the suffix *tu*. 12. *Ṭa* and *ṭha* are not accepted.
13. *Ca*, *cha*, *pa*, and *pha* also [do not have] *tvam*.
14. Among the others, excluding *ṭa* and *ta*, due to the absence of self-luminosity;
[this concerns] the *Ṛgveda*.

Self-luminosity is not contradictory; likewise, even though humans and others cannot grasp their own shoulders or their own days and nights, let the Veda—whose power remains unimpeded—possess self-referential capacity just as it possesses the capacity to convey other objects.

For this very reason, those who know the tradition demonstrate the unimpeded power of the Veda: "For an injunction (*codanā*) is capable of making known such things as what has been, what is being, and what will be, as well as the subtle, the concealed, and the remote" (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.2).

This being the case, it is impossible for anyone—such as a Cārvāka or others—to deny the authority of the Veda, which is established by both definition and means of valid cognition; for then the authority of Smṛti, which is rooted in the Veda, and of worldly consensus, which is rooted in both, would be unavoidable.
Therefore, it is settled that the Veda, established through its defining characteristics and its means of proof, cannot be rejected by anyone.
Granted, there may indeed be some category of object that constitutes the meaning of the Veda;
nevertheless, it does not deserve to be explained, because it is useless due to its lack of authoritative status.

The Veda is not indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its defining characteristic cannot be established therein. For instance, some state the definition as: "A means of valid cognition is that which brings about correct experience."
Others, however, declare that "a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which makes known an object not previously apprehended.
But neither of these two definitions is possible in the case of the Veda.
For the Veda consists of the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas.
Among those, some mantras are unintelligible.
One mantra is: "O Indra, that spear of yours is unfailing" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.169.3);
another is: "That which was placed in the mouth, the seer found it in the waters" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.44.8).
Another [example] is: "spṛṣveva jarbharī turpharītū" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.106.6).
In this same way, passages such as "āpāntamanyustupalaprabharmā" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.89.5) and others are to be cited.
For indeed, no meaning whatsoever is understood from these mantras.
When there is no experience whatsoever regarding these [objects], then their validity and their status as means to that [validity] are far removed.

Even though the mantra "Was it below? Was it above? (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.129.5) possesses the capacity to inform, it lacks authority because it conveys a doubtful meaning, like a sentence such as "Is it a post or a person?
The mantra "O herb, protect him" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.1.1) refers to *darbha* grass (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.17.8).
"O *svadhiti*, do not harm him" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.2.1.1)—this refers to the razor (*kṣura*) [according to the *Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* 1.17.9].
"Listen, O pressing-stones" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.3.13.1)—this refers to the stones (*pāṣāṇa*).
In these instances, the address of insentient objects—the *darbha* grass, the razor, and the stones—is heard as if they were sentient beings.
Therefore, like the sentence "two moons," it lacks authority because it conveys a contradictory meaning.

Furthermore, the two mantras, "Rudra is only one; he did not stand for a second" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.6.1) and "The thousands upon thousands of Rudras who are upon the earth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.11.1), lack authority because they convey a contradiction, similar to the statement "I shall remain silent for as long as I live.
The mantra "Let the waters flow forth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.1.1) prescribes the moistening of the head with water at the time of the sacrificer's shaving.

The mantra, "O *śubhikā*, ascend my head, beautifying my face," spoken at the time of marriage for the purpose of an auspicious rite, declares the placement of the *śubhikā*—a wreath made of flowers—upon the heads of the bridegroom and the bride.
Since these two mantras merely restate meanings already well-known in the world, they do not possess the quality of conveying an unknown object.
Therefore, the portion consisting of mantras is not a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
To this it is replied: The meaning of the *ṛg* and other mantras has been elucidated by Yāska in his work, the *Nirukta*.
The failure to understand them on the part of those lacking familiarity with that work does not constitute a fault in the mantras themselves.
For this very reason, they cite here a worldly maxim: "It is not the fault of the wooden post that the blind man does not see it; rather, that is the fault of the person" (*Nirukta* 1.16).
Furthermore, the mantra "Was there, perhaps, below? (RV 10.129.5) is not intended to provoke doubt;
rather, it is directed solely toward ascertaining the extreme profundity of the Supreme Reality, which is the cause of the universe.

For that very purpose, its difficulty of comprehension—due to the weight of tradition, the scriptures, and the lineage—is presented through this particular mode of expression: "Was there, perhaps, below? (adhaḥ svid).
This very intention is made explicit in the subsequent mantras beginning with "Who indeed knows? (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.129.6).
Even in the mantras concerning herbs and other entities, it is the conscious presiding deities who are addressed by those respective names.
And these deities were indicated by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa in the sūtra: "But there is designation based on the presiding deities" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.5).

Since even a single Rudra assumes a thousand forms by his own majesty, there is no mutual contradiction. Although the moistening of the head with substances such as water is well known in the world, the grace of the presiding deity thereof is not so known; therefore, because it makes known a matter previously unknown, the portion consisting of the mantra possesses authority, as the defining characteristic [of a valid means of knowledge] is present.

1. In all [manuscripts] except for Ṭa and Ta, there is self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). 2. In Ṭa and Tha, the proof (*siddhi*) is characterized by [the presence of] *lakṣaṇa*. 3. In Ga, Gha, Ca, Cha, Ṇa, Ta, Tha, Pa, Ya, and Śa, it is possible (*śakyaḥ*). 4. However, in the case of these two, Ta and Tha; or rather, in the two sentences beginning with Ṭha. 5. In Ṭa, the word "of the head" (*śirasaḥ*) is absent. In Ṭha, the phrase "by water, of the head" (*jalena śirasaḥ*) is absent. 6. In Ca, Ṭa, and Ṭha, there is no understanding of the names (*nāmabodhaḥ*). 7. In Ṭa, Ta, and Tha, it is for the purpose of making known the doubt (*sandehabodhanāya*). 8. In Ka, Jha, and Śa, there is the state of being difficult to understand (*durbodhatvam*). 9. In Ṭa, by means of the substance of water (*jaladravyeṇa*). 10. In Ta, despite its being established in the world (*lokasiddhatvepi*); in Ṭa, the word "also" (*api*) is absent. Chapter One, Verse 5.
Intending this very point, the venerable Jaimini established in the section on mantras (Mantrādhikaraṇa) that mantras have their intended meanings (vivakṣitārthatva) [Jai.
Sū. 1.2.31–45]. We shall explain those sūtras by citing them in order.
Therein, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) in the sūtra: "Because of the scriptural injunctions regarding their purpose" (tadarthaśāstrāt).
That very meaning which a mantra is capable of expressing is the subject matter of that scripture or Brāhmaṇa passage; such a passage is a "scriptural statement of its meaning" (*tadarthaśāstra*).
From such a scripture, it is understood that the mantra does not intend to convey its own literal meaning.
For instance, by the mantra "Spread yourself wide" (*uru prathasva*; Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.8; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 1.22), the spreading out of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is enjoined.
The Brāhmaṇa passage, “He spreads out the sacrificial cake” (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.8.4; Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.2.8), expresses that very same thing.

Since that [act] is already understood through the mantra itself, the Brāhmaṇa—which would have been intended to convey its meaning—would be redundant. However, if the meaning of the mantra were not intended to be expressed, then the Brāhmaṇa is useful for conveying the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra.
Therefore, mantras assist in the performance solely through their being uttered.

Now, one might object: "If the purpose were merely recitation, an unseen (adṛṣṭa) result would have to be postulated; however, if they express meaning, a seen (dṛṣṭa) result is obtained. Therefore, even while accepting that the Brāhmaṇa is explanatory (anuvādaka), the mantra must indeed be expressive. Anticipating this objection, the author provides the following sūtra as a reply:
Regarding the phrase "because of the restriction of the sentence":
in the mantra, a restriction is observed such that the sentence must be recited exactly as "agnimūrdhā divaḥ kakut" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.44.16).
However, the comprehension of the meaning occurs even if the order is reversed, such as "mūrdhābhiḥ" and so forth.
Therefore, for the sake of ensuring the efficacy of the fixed order of recitation, the very purpose of a mantra is its utterance.

Now, one might object that even if the fixed order of recitation serves only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the recitation of the mantra must still be for the sake of understanding its meaning. Anticipating this, the Sūtra states another defect:
"Because of the teaching of what is already known" (*buddhaśāstrāt*).
For instance, the injunction-mantra (*praiṣamantra*) "Agnim īḷe... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.1.2) is recited at the time of the ritual performance.
Furthermore, that [duty] such as carrying the fire and so forth was already understood by the Āhitāgni as his own obligation at the very time of study;
for it to be taught again through the recitation of a mantra regarding a matter already understood would be purposeless.
Indeed, one does not put on shoes again when they are already on one's feet.

One might object: "Even for one who has already understood the meaning, let there be recollection by means of a mantra in order to avoid forgetfulness due to negligence. Anticipating this objection, the author sets forth another fault in the aphorism:
"Because of the statement of what is non-existent.
A mantra is recorded in the Veda: "Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, seven are his hands" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.58.3).
Indeed, there exists no sacrificial implement whatsoever endowed with four horns and so forth that could be recollected through the recitation of mantras.
Anticipating the objection that there might be some such deity [as the object of address], the author sets forth another flaw in the aphorism:
"Because of the binding of meaning to the insentient" (*acetane 'rthabandhanāt*).

In such instances as "O herb, protect him! (*oṣadhe trāyasvainam*) and "Listen, O pressing-stones! (*śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ*), one binds the intended meaning to an insentient substance by means of attributes appropriate only for a sentient being.
And because it is not logical.

Now, one might object that since the *Vaiyāsika-śāstra* (the Brahma-sūtras) indicates in the aphorism "designation by means of the presiding deities" (*abhimānivyapadeśa*), the intention is to refer to the presiding deities of herbs and so forth; having raised this doubt, he states another defect in the sūtra:
"Because of contradiction in meaning" (*arthavipratiṣedhāt*).
The mantra is recorded in the scripture: "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space... (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.89.10).
The claim that "the sky is the same as the intermediate space" is a contradictory meaning.

In the same way, passages such as "Rudra is indeed one" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.6.1) and "those Rudras who are thousands upon thousands" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.11.1) should also be cited as examples.
Now, one might object: just as in passages such as "You alone are the mother and you alone are the father," Aditi is praised by way of being the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and so forth;
likewise, let there be for the single Rudra, through the power of yoga, the assumption of many forms. Therefore, there is no contradiction in meaning.
Anticipating this objection, the Sūtra states another fault: "Because [the mantra] is not recited like the Vedic study (svādhyāya).
A certain woman named Pūrṇikā performs the threshing of grain.

In his vicinity, a young student sometimes recites the *avaghāta* mantra for the purpose of learning its textual form (*svādhyāya*). He has no intention of expressing its meaning, as that mantra is repeated with every stroke of the pestle; he practices that mantra and other mantras solely for the sake of grasping the syllables.

In that case, just as the mantra for threshing, even when recited at the time of Vedic study, does not express its own meaning to Pūrṇikā, so too it will not express its own meaning at the time of the ritual performance.
Is it not so, young man, in that case?

1. Ṭa-ṭha: *masūyat*. 2. Ṭa-ṭha: the word *śāstrasya* does not exist. 3. Ṭa-ṭha: *tathāpi*. 4. Ca-Ṭa: the statement of the Brāhmaṇa is meaningless (*anarthakam*). 5. Ṭa-Ṭha: a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭaṃ prayojanam*) is obtained. 6. Ta: *vādatvam*. 7. Ca-Cha-Pa-Pha: for the sake of the recitation (*pāṭhārtham*). 8. Jha-Ṇa-Na-Śa: of the meaning of the Buddha (*buddhārthasya*). 9. Ṭa-Ṭha: *icchanti*; Ga-Gha-Pha: *pratimuñcanti*. 10. Ca-Cha-Ṭa-Pa-Pha: *°syārthasya*. 11. Ta: another fault (*anyadoṣam*). 12. Ga-Gha-Ca-Cha-Ta-Ṇa-Pa-Pha-Ya: it is remembered (*anusmaryate*). 13. Ta: *°citaṃ rakṣaṇam*. 14. Tha: *°taccāyuktam*. 15. Ṭha: *pratipādyatā*. 16. Ca-Cha-Tha-Pa-Pha: the word ‘*evam*’ does not exist. 17. Ṭa-Ṭha: there is no contradiction (*nāsti virodhaḥ*).
Karma:
For whose sake is there no intention to speak?
Pūrṇikā, too, is incapable of understanding.

Anticipating the objection that there exists a desire to express meaning even regarding an unintelligible action (*avyavahārya*), and that understanding is indeed possible, he sets forth another defect in the Sūtra: "Because [the meaning] is unknowable" (*avijñeyāt*).
The meaning of certain mantras cannot be known.
For example: “O Indra, our seer has drunk of thee” is one mantra;
“Like two sickles, he moves swiftly and trembles” is another mantra.

One might object: "Was it not for the sake of understanding the meaning of such mantras that the *Nirukta*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and *Nigama* were composed? Anticipating this, the author states another flaw in the aphorism: "The mantras would be purposeless due to connection with non-eternal things. In the mantra, "What do they do among the Kīkaṭas? (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 3.53.14), a region named Kīkaṭa is mentioned;
likewise, a city named Naicāśākha and a king named Pramaganda are mentioned. These objects are recorded as being non-eternal.
This being the case, it is understood that prior to the authoritative instruction (*pramāṇa*), this mantra did not previously exist for that purpose.

Thus, by these reasons—beginning with the scriptural statement regarding its purpose—it follows that mantras do not have the function of conveying meaning; rather, their purpose is solely the visible act of recitation. This is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Therein, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta) in the aphorism: “But the meaning of the sentence is not different” (*aviśiṣṭas tu vākyārthaḥ*). By the word “but” (*tu*), he excludes the view that the purpose of mantras is mere recitation.
The meaning of a sentence, which is understood through the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasambandha*), is no different in the world and in the Veda.
This being the case, just as in the world a sentence is uttered solely for the purpose of communicating meaning, so too should it be understood in the performance of Vedic sacrifices.
For a meaning revealed by a mantra can be executed, whereas that which is not revealed by itself cannot.
Therefore, the visible purpose of uttering a mantra is precisely the revelation of its meaning.

Now, an objection may be raised: beginning with “Thou art Agni, thou art Nārī,” and ending with “I take thee with the Triṣṭubh metre” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.1.1.3–4), a mantra is traditionally recited.

Since the taking up of the fire-wood is already understood through that very mantra, why is it further enjoined in the Brāhmaṇa passage, “He takes it up with four [verses]” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.1.4)?
Fearing that this injunction would be redundant, the author provides the answer in the Sūtra: “Because of a subordinate quality, there is a restatement.”
The further hearing of a matter already understood through the mantra by the Brāhmaṇa serves the purpose of enjoining the quality of the number four;
for in the absence of this injunction, one might satisfy [the fire] with any one of the four mantras.

Now, one might object: in the passage, “With the mantra ‘They have grasped this rein of immortality,’ he takes up the horse’s bridle” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.2.1), the act of taking up the rein is already established by the inherent power (*sāmarthya*) of the mantra itself; why then is a Brāhmaṇa statement recorded as its further applicatory injunction (*viniyojaka*)?
Fearing that this would be redundant according to your own view, the author provides the answer in the Sūtra: “Exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).
The prohibition, namely “He does not take up the donkey’s bridle,” constitutes the exclusion.
For that purpose, this statement from the Brāhmaṇa is given.
But surely, in the case of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), three defects would ensue:
the word "takes" (*ādatte*) would abandon its own primary meaning, which is the taking of the rope;
and a secondary meaning, characterized as a prohibition, would have to be assumed for this word.
[Objection: "Because of the commonality of the term *raśanā* (rope), the taking up of the donkey-ropes obtained by [the rule] is sublated; thus there are three defects.
[Response: Not so, because the donkey-ropes have not been [previously] obtained.
To explain: in your view, because the recitation within the context would otherwise be inexplicable, the sentence "one should perform the taking with this mantra" is inferred.

Once the relationship between the mantra and the act of taking is established by that sentence, and subsequently, when the inquiry arises as to whether the taking is of the horse's or the donkey's bridle, one must first accept the taking of the bridle in general on the basis of its indicative power (*liṅga*), and only then can the application to the donkey's bridle be stated.
And that [taking] is delayed.

By the sentence "the horse's halter," since there is no connection between the mantra and the act of taking established by direct perception, the taking—which would otherwise apply to any halter due to the indicative power (*liṅga*)—is restricted to the specific object upon hearing the word "horse's halter.
Consequently, because the mantra has no further expectancy and because the donkey's halter is not applicable, there is no sublation of what has already been obtained.
Therefore, the meaning of a prohibition is not postulated,
nor is the meaning of an injunction abandoned;
in that case, how could there be the threefold fault?
Intending this very non-attainment [of the donkey's tether] as the exclusion [of other objects], it was aphorized as "parisaṃkhyā" (exclusive specification).

One might object: "Is not the Brāhmaṇa statement, 'He spreads it with the words, "O wide one, spread yourself! still as useless as before? Anticipating this, the author provides the following Sūtra: "Or it is an explanatory praise (arthavāda). The word "or" (vā) excludes the charge of uselessness. This is its explanatory praise: "It thereby causes the master of the sacrifice to expand."
Therefore, a rule connected with that explanatory passage (arthavāda) is recited in the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, one might object: since the injunctive word "prathayati" (he causes to expand) itself must be praised by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with "the patron of the sacrifice indeed," why is that very act of expanding (*prathana*) not already established? Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the following answer in a sūtra:

1. The intention to express that meaning (*tad-artha-vivakṣā*). 2. The *niṣaṇṭha* [sections] beginning with *ca*, *pa*, and *pha*. 3. The letters *ṭa* and *ṭha* do not exist in *ca*. 4. The state of being merely *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 5. The sentence (*vākya*) is employed with *ṭha*. 6. In the Vedic sacrifice (*yāga*), there is *ta*. 7. In the *Brāhmaṇa*, there are *ca*, *ta*, and *pha*. 8. In *ka*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ḍa*, and *śa*, the word "sound" (*śabda*) does not exist. 9. In *ṭa* and *ṭha*, there is "taking" (*ādāna*). 10. In *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ta*, *tha*, and *ta*, there is "here" (*atra*). 11. In *ka*, *jha*, *na*, and *śa*, it does not exist when established (*siddhe*). 12. In *ṭa*, there is the "object" (*viṣaya*). 13. In *ṭa* and *ṭha*, when it is established (*siddhe sati*). 14. In *ṭa*, it is "established" (*avasthāpyate*). 15. In *ṭha*, by this (*tyanena*). The First Chapter of the Ṛgveda.
"Also because of the observation of non-eternality" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.28)—this is another reason stated in the Sūtra.

Its meaning is as follows: "Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.10.2). Because of the observation of non-eternal entities such as Babara and others, and because they did not exist prior to that [statement], the Veda must be of human origin. To this, the following answer is given: "But it is merely a similarity of sound" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.31).
This is its meaning:
that which is the designation "Kaṭhaka" and so forth is based on the act of speaking;
whereas the further observation of "Babarān" and so forth is merely a commonality of sound.
But in that context, no impermanent person named Babara is intended to be expressed;
rather, "Babara" is an imitation of a sound.
This being the case, it is the wind that is denoted as making the sound "bebara."
And that Prāvāhaṇi is one whose nature is to carry [the breath] forth preeminently;
in this manner, it should be inferred in other cases as well.
Thus, since no defect whatsoever is possible, the mantras must be employed solely for the manifestation of their intended meaning.
An objection might be raised: "Is this not merely a logical argument, since a visible purpose is obtained when there is the manifestation of meaning?

We do not see any Vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*) that supports this. Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the following sūtra as a reply: "And the instruction by means of an indicative mark is for that purpose" (*liṅgopadeśaśca tadarthavat*).
It is heard in scripture: "One should worship the Āgnīdhra altar with a verse addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*)."
This is its meaning:
that *ṛc* whose deity is Agni is "āgneyī";
with that [verse], one should worship the station of the Āgnīdhra.

In this context, while instructing the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), the *Brāhmaṇa* does not teach by reciting the opening of the mantra—“One should attend with the verse ‘O Agni, lead us’” (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.189.1)—but rather teaches by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*).
When Agni is primarily propounded in that *ṛc*, then that *ṛc* has Agni as its deity (*devatā*).
This being the case, the designation “addressed to Agni” (*āgneyī*), which ends in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) expressing the deity, becomes logically consistent.
Therefore, this instruction makes it known that the mantra sentence possesses meaning.
Consequently, because its meaning is intended to be expressed, the mantra is recited at the time of performance for the sake of bringing about the comprehension of that meaning.
Regarding this very fact of the meaning being intended to be expressed, he provides another indicative mark in the Sūtra: "Modification (ūha)."
*Ūha* is the recitation of a mantra prescribed for the archetype (*prakṛti*) by substituting other words appropriate to it, so that its meaning remains applicable to the modified form (*vikṛti*).
For example, the archetypal mantra concerning an animal sacrifice is: "May the mother approve him, may the father approve him, may the brother approve him" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 3.6.6.1).
When there are two animals in the modified form, the *ūha* of that mantra becomes: "May the mother approve both of them."
When there is a plurality of animals, the modification (ūha) "may the mother acknowledge them one by one" must be performed.
To explain this mantra, the Brāhmaṇa is traditionally handed down as follows: "The mother does not increase, nor does the father.
In this regard, the following must be considered.
In this context, is it the growth of the body that is being negated, or rather the growth of the word?
The use of the word *mātṛ* ending in the singular as *mātarau* (dual) or *mātaraḥ* (plural) constitutes the "growth of the word.
Among these, the growth of the body cannot possibly be negated, because such growth is directly perceived in accordance with the stages of life, such as childhood, youth, and old age.

Therefore, the prohibition of the *vṛddhi* [augment] for the word-forms "mātṛ" and "pitṛ" alone remains as the residue. By prohibiting the *vṛddhi* in these specific forms, it is indicated that for the other word, namely "enam," the *vṛddhi* follows the meaning.
In that regard, if the meaning were not intended to be expressed, how could the dual number be applied when there are two animals, or the plural number when there are many animals?
Therefore, mantras have intended meanings.
Regarding that very point, he provides another indicative mark (liṅga) in the Sūtra: "And because of the word of injunction" (vidhiśabdācca).
A word found in the Brāhmaṇa that takes the form of an explanation of a mantra is called a "word of injunction" (vidhiśabda).
And this is thus handed down in the tradition: "He says this: 'May we live for a hundred winters, for a hundred years.
In that context, "a hundred winters" (*śataṃ himāḥ*) is the opening phrase (*pratīka*) of the mantra to be explained;
the remainder, however, is the explanation of its intended meaning (*tātparya*).
If, however, the meaning of a mantra were not intended to be expressed, what purpose could possibly be explained for the mantra?
Therefore, mantras have intended meanings and must be recited at the time of ritual performance in order to manifest their own meaning.
Regarding this, there are two summary verses: "Are mantras such as 'uru prathasva' causes of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)?"
In the sacrifice, they are the illuminators of the spreading of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and other such rites.
1. "ta-babara" (thus). 2. "ca-cha-pa-pha" (follow this). 3. "ṭha" (he stands).

4. In place of "ca-pa-pha-prakṛtapaḥ; ta-tha-prakṛtapaḥ; ṭha-'prākṛta... when there are two animals," [it should be read as] "the mantra concerning the model animal (prakṛtapaśu) when there are two animals in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti). 5. Ṭa: the mantra.
6. Ṭa: here this.

7. In the manuscripts designated Ga, Gha, Ca, Cha, Ṇa, Na, Pa, Pha, and Ya, the word "vā" does not exist. 8. In the manuscripts designated Ga, Cha, Ṇa, Na, Pa, Pha, and Ya, it is explained [as follows].
First Chapter.
Even for a Brahmin, mantras are causes of merit only because of his knowledge of them;
since that knowledge is visible, the invisible [result] is not superior.
(Ja. Nyā. 1.2.4). Thus [it is said].
Granted that the portion consisting of the mantras possesses authority;
however, it is not appropriate for the portion consisting of the brāhmaṇas to do so. For instance:

The Brāhmaṇa is of two kinds: injunction (*vidhi*) and explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "The Brāhmaṇas are the injunctions for ritual action; the explanatory passages are the supplements to the Brāhmaṇas" (Āp. Pariśiṣṭa 34–35).
Injunction (*vidhi*) is also of two kinds: that which impels one to act who has not yet acted, and that which makes known what was previously unknown.

Injunctions found in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, such as "They offer the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni as the *Dīkṣaṇīya* sacrifice" (*Ai. Brā.* 1.1), are those that impel one to act who has not yet acted.
Those found in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*, such as "In the beginning, this [world] was indeed the Self alone" (*Ai. Ā.* 2.4.1), are those that make known what was previously unknown.

In that regard, there is no authoritative validity for the injunctions contained in the *karmakāṇḍa*, such as "One should offer oblations of groats of wild sesame (*jatilayavāgvā*) or groats of wild millet (*vīdhukayavāgvā*)" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.4.3.2), because they enjoin substances unfit for engagement [in ritual action]. [The *Ṛgveda* is] the correct experience.

Having rejected the reading of another recensional branch (*śākhā*), the Taittirīyas cite an alternative reading: "If one were to say, 'May she be easy to approach and easy to settle upon,' the sacrificer would be likely to die" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.1.9.6); this is the rejection.
"One should rather say, 'May she be easy to serve and easy to rule over,'" this is the instruction regarding the alternative reading.
In that case, the application is determined by the difference between the individuals who perform the rite.
The same should be understood regarding injunctions (*vidhi*).
However, your criticism of the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup and so forth is appropriate only for someone like you who is unacquainted with the history of Mīmāṃsā.
In the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, the option (*vikalpa*) between taking and not taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup was determined in the eighth quarter of the tenth chapter (Jaimini Sūtra 10.8.6).
In the first pāda of the second chapter, the *apūrva* was determined for the sake of establishing a result that occurs at a later time (*kālāntarabhāvi*) (Jai. Sū. 2.1.5).

Similarly, in the Uttara-mīmāṃsā, in the fourth pāda of the first chapter, under the sūtra "And because of the designation [of Brahman] as the cause in the case of ether and so forth, according to how it is taught" (Bra. Sū. 1.4.14), the contradictions among the Śruti texts regarding the Supreme Self as the cause of the world were refuted.

In the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* of the first pāda of the second chapter, however, the sūtra "If it be argued that [the world] does not [arise from Brahman] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no, because [the word 'non-existent'] refers to another state, as is clear from the remainder of the passage" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.17) determines that the word *asat* occurring in the Taittirīya passage does not refer to emptiness (*śūnya*), but rather to the unmanifest state (*avyaktāvasthā*).

Similarly, Jaimini, having asserted in the *Codanāsūtra* that an injunctive statement is the means of valid knowledge regarding Dharma, established its authority in the *Autpattikasūtra* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.2; 5).

Vyāsa as well, having asserted the authority of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman in the aphorism "Because [Brahman] has the scriptures as its source" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.3), established this through subsequent aphorisms such as "On account of the harmony of those [scriptural texts]" (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.4).
Therefore, for you who are not a Mīmāṃsaka, the aforementioned logical sequence of pervasion is unavoidable. Consequently, the authority of the injunctive portion [of the Veda] is firmly established.
Jaimini established the authority of the explanatory (*arthavāda*) portions with great effort;
his aphorisms (*sūtras*) are now being explained (*jai. sū. 1.2.1–18*).

Therein, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in a sūtra: "Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that [action] as their purpose are useless; therefore, [the Veda] is said to be eternal."

Since the entirety of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is directed toward the exposition of ritual action (*kriyā*), those portions of the Veda that do not expound ritual action have no intended meaning of their own.

These are merely *arthavādas* (explanatory passages), which are handed down as follows: "He wept; because he wept, that is the origin of the name Rudra" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.5.1.1); "He cut out his own omentum" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.1.1.4); "The gods, having settled upon the sacrificial ground, did not know the directions" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 6.1.5.1).
Since such a statement possesses no intended meaning whatsoever, it is therefore called "non-eternal" (*anitya*).

Although, due to its beginninglessness, it lacks non-eternality in terms of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), nevertheless, because it lacks its specific function—namely, the communication of dharma—and because it is similar to transient poetic chatter, the meaning is that it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

Now, one might object: "Even if the cited *arthavādas* lack authority regarding the duty to be performed (*anuṣṭheya-dharma*), let them possess authority with respect to their own literal meaning; for since they are cognizers of that [meaning], their inherent authority cannot be set aside. Anticipating this objection, [the author] notes that since some other *arthavādas* are seen to contradict other means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*), they are non-authoritative; and on the basis of that example, intending to establish the non-authority of all *arthavādas*, he formulates the sūtra: "And because of contradiction with scripture and what is perceived" (*śāstradṛṣṭavirodhācca*).

Three kinds of contradiction are observed in the *arthavādas*: contradiction with scripture (*śāstra-virodha*), contradiction with perception (*dṛṣṭa-virodha*), and contradiction with both scripture and perception (*śāstra-dṛṣṭa-virodha*).
For instance, in the passage "The mind is a thief; speech is a liar," the mental theft and verbal falsehood mentioned there contradict the prohibitory scriptures.
In the passage, "Therefore, the gods saw the sun in the day and did not perceive smoke; they saw the sun in the night and did not perceive smoke," there is a contradiction with perception.
Likewise, in the passage, "And we do not know this: whether we are Brahmins or non-Brahmins," there is also a contradiction with perception.
And: "For who knows whether [a person] exists in that other world or does not exist? (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.1.1).

1. Having rejected the reading "ṭha". 2. The teaching of the reading "ṭha". 3. Regarding the rules for *ca*, *pha*, and *ta*; [the rule] regarding *pa* and *ta* is as prescribed. 4. Just so, the subsequent [reading] is "ṭa-ṭha-tathaiva". 5. The reading "ṭa-ṭha-'tadvat'" does not exist; among the others, excluding *ta* and *tha*, it follows that. 6. Because of the hearing of *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *ya*. 7. Of the second chapter, "ṭa". 8. Among the others, excluding "ṭa", [the reading] is "'ārambhārtham'". 9. In the sūtra on "non-origination" (*ayonitva*), [the readings] are *ka*, *kha*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *na*. 10. By the sūtras beginning with "anyādādibhiḥ", [the readings] are *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 11. For *ka*, *kha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *na*, it is difficult to avoid [the fault]. 12. It is established, [the readings being] *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 13. Through effort, [the readings being] *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 14. They are explained, [the readings being] *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 15. Because of the activity, [the readings being] *ca*, *cha*, *pa*, and *pha*. 16. The reading "'arthavādānām'" does not exist in *ṭa*. 17. The meaning is "ṭa"; the meaning is "ṭha". 18. The intended meaning is "ṭa-ṭha". 19. The reading "'api'" does not exist in *ṭha*. 20. Upon seeing the lack of authority due to contradiction, [the reading is] *ṭa*. 21. The reading "'iti'" does not exist in *ca*, *cha*, *pa*, and *pha*. 22. False speech, [the readings being] *ṭa* and *ṭha*.
In this first chapter, verse 11, there is a contradiction with the scriptures;
for in such scriptural injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," a fruit pertaining to the next world is observed.
Therefore, because of these contradictions, the doctrines [of the opponents] lack authority.

One might object: "Even though [passages] such as 'He wept' are purposeless, and [passages] such as 'The mind is a thief' are unauthoritative due to contradiction, let there nonetheless be authoritativeness for the *arthavādas* that set forth results, since they differ from both of those cases. Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the following sūtra: "In that case, because of the absence of a result. Just as the matter stated by the *arthavādas* contradicts other means of knowledge, so too the result is stated by them even though it does not exist.
For instance, with reference to the Garga-trirātra sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "The face of one who knows this shines" (Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa 20.16.6).
With reference to the touching of the deities in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard: "In the progeny of one who knows this, a champion is born" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.4.6).
Yet we do not perceive such a fruit for those who possess this knowledge.

Now, one might object: "Even if those passages concerning results in this life lack authority due to inconsistency, let those passages concerning results in the hereafter possess authority. Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the following sūtra:
"And the remaining portion is not intended for practical application;
therefore, since there is no contradiction with the scripture merely by stating the literal meaning of the words, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is indeed justified."

Now, an objection is raised: what was stated [in the *Tantravārttika*], namely "by *suyajña*, there would be injunctions of the ritual rules," is incorrect because of a lack of grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

In the passage, "'With a branch of the *vetasa* and with *avakā* plants one should offer; for water is peaceful'" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.4.4.3), the *vetasa* and *avakā* are enjoined while the waters are praised; thus, there is a lack of coordination. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But let there be [the status of] a quality (*guṇavāda*). The word "but" (*tu*) excludes the fault of lack of coordination.
For here, a statement of quality (*guṇavāda*) is intended.

Just as in the world, when Devadatta is a native of Kaśmīra, he considers himself praised when the regions of Kaśmīra are being praised; so too here, when the reeds (*vetasa*) and the cane (*avaka*) growing in the waters are praised, these two become praised themselves.

Because they have grown from the waters which are [now] pacified, the reed and the cane, being themselves pacified, pacify whatever is undesirable for the sacrificer—such a statement of quality is what is intended here.

In the passage "He wept" (*so'rodīt*) as well, because silver has the nature of fallen tears, there would be the undesirable consequence of weeping even in one's own home upon giving silver; therefore, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction "Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyam*), by means of that prohibition.
In this context, the quality intended is the absence of weeping resulting from the absence of giving silver.
And by means of that quality, the injunction consisting of the prohibition of giving silver is praised.
Although the fact that silver originates from tears is absolutely non-existent, nevertheless, according to the method described, the praise of the injunction is accomplished.
The injunction, "He who desires offspring and cattle should sacrifice this hornless goat dedicated to Prajāpati" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1.4–5), is praised by way of its being nourished by Prajāpati.

Since Prajāpati, having offered even his own nourishment (*svapoṣa*) into the fire, then sacrificed a hornless goat (*tūpara*) born from that [offering] for his own sake and thereby obtained offspring and cattle, this hornless goat is thus the producer of offspring and so forth; therefore, the praise here intended is for the quality of being hornless.
The injunction "The sun is the *prāyaṇīya* oblation" is praised by means of the disorientation regarding the directions expressed in the passage "the quarters did not know."

That is to say, when the deity Aditi removes even the confusion regarding the directions and makes known the specific direction, then it goes without saying that she removes the error concerning the performance of the Soma sacrifice, which consists of a collection of many kinds of ritual acts; thus, it is this quality residing in the deity Aditi that is intended to be praised here.

Whether or not there remains any fear of confusion regarding the directions due merely to her own assumption of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), we who accept that the passage is intent upon praise do not lose anything at all.
For in the world, praise is seen even with reference to an object that does not exist, as in the verse: "Your crest is growing; you wear [the garment] on your private parts; drink with faith."

Now, the opponent has cited the passage, "Theft is the mind; falsehood is speech," in order to demonstrate a contradiction with the scriptures. To this, the author provides the answer in the Sūtra: "Because it is due to its form" (*rūpāt*).
This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stated for the purpose of praising the injunction: "When gold is in his hand, then he takes [it]."

Just as in the world, when it is said that "Devadatta alone is to be honored by Akimapi," indifference is mentioned even falsely merely to praise Devadatta’s honor, but not to establish that [Akimapi] is himself worthy of honor; so too here, in order to praise the taking of gold in the hand, the mind's nature as a thief and speech's nature as a liar are mentioned.
In that case, the meaning of the words must be construed through figurative description (*guṇavāda*).
Just as thieves are of a hidden nature, so too is the mind; thus, its hidden nature is the quality (*guṇa*) intended here.
Since speech generally speaks falsehood, its general nature (*prāyikatva*) is considered a merit in that context;
however, the hand is neither concealed nor does it speak falsehood.
Therefore, the holding of gold in the hand is praised as being commendable.

As for that which was cited as contradicting perception—namely, "The gods saw smoke alone from the fire," and so forth—the author provides the answer in the Sūtra: "Because of its distance and abundance.

This explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intended to praise the two injunctions: "One offers the Agnihotra in the evening with the mantra 'Light is light, svāhā! and "In the morning with 'Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!'".
Since the flame is not seen during the day, therefore the Sūrya-mantra alone should be employed in the morning.

Since smoke is seen only at night, the mantra for fire should be employed at night; such is the praise of those two mantras. As for the mention of the non-perception of smoke and flame, it is caused by the qualities of distance and abundance.
For when things are distant and abundant, even trees and the like on a mountain peak are not clearly seen; rather, there is merely an appearance of seeing them, resembling blades of grass.

1. The words *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *tha*, *pa*, and *pha* have the meaning of "theft" (*steya*); the word *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *ya*, and *sta* have the meaning of "thief" (*stena*). 2. [The letters] *ga*, *gha*, *tra*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *pa*, *pha*, and *kāśmīra* [are used].
3. *Ta*: the word "only" (*eva*) is absent; for the phrase "stute eva," there is instead "te eva stute."
4. According to the rule "jha-na-śa-'n":
5. [The rule] "ca-ṇa-pa-pha-'api'" does not exist.
6. In the *Gha* recension: *yatheya*; in the *Ṭa* recension: *yadeya*.
7. ka, ta, tha, pa, pha likewise; 8. ṭa, ṭha, jha, śa, [he] grasps;
9. gha, ya, cha, ṇa, ta, pa, pha, even in the world.
10. The *sūryamantra* should be employed with the letters *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *pa*, and *pha* during the day; thus [ends] the first section (*aṣṭaka*). 13.
It is the same in this case as well.

As for the other instance cited as contradicting what was seen by others—namely, "O Lord, we do not know whether we are Brahmins or non-Brahmins"—the author provides the answer in the Sūtra: "On account of the fault of the speaker, and because sons are seen [to be of different castes].
This explanatory passage (arthavāda) is intended to praise the injunction: "While the axle-pin is being inserted, one should say, 'O Gods, O Ancestors... etc.

If the sacrificer were to follow the *pravara* invocation with the mantra beginning, "The gods are the fathers" (*tai. brā.* 3.7.5.4), then even one who is not a Brahmin would become a Brahmin; this is a praise of the invocation.
The statement, "And this is not difficult to discern," is employed there as a description of its quality of being difficult to know.
For where there is an offense on the part of the woman, a son is seen belonging to the progenitor, even though he is the biological offspring of the husband.

Therefore, because sons are seen to belong to both the husband and the paramour, it is difficult to determine what one's own birth-status truly is. With this intention, he employed the name; however, there is no contradiction with what is observed therein.
For it is not possible to deny one's own Brāhmaṇahood, which is clearly perceived there, by saying "nor am I this."
If it is argued that only contradictions with scriptural philosophy have been cited—such as, "For who knows whether he exists in the other world or not?"—the author provides the answer in the Sūtra:
"The desire for what is not yet present" (*ākālikepsā*).
Furthermore, the injunction regarding the door of the *prācīnavaṃśa* hall is: "He makes it resemble the universe."
The remainder of that [passage] is: "For who indeed knows that?

By means of the visible result consisting in the avoidance of calamities such as smoke and the like, the injunction regarding the door is praised. However, the result in the form of attaining heaven is not immediate (*ākālika*).

"Occurring at the wrong time" (*ākālika*) means belonging to a remote period, that is to say, not existing at present. The desire for that—namely, the wish to know—is the cause for the statement of uncertainty: "For who indeed knows that? (*ko hi tad veda*).

Just as the events concerning one's grandsons, great-grandsons, and so forth, occurring in the future, cannot be determined with certainty, so too the attainment of heaven and the presentation of arguments regarding the possession of [certain] qualities [are uncertain].
The intention is that the avoidance of smoke and the like, however, is certain because it is perceptible.
As for the other examples cited, such as the contradiction with what has been seen elsewhere—"His face shines, he who knows thus"—the Sūtra provides the answer:
"It is a praise of knowledge" (vidyāpraśaṃsā).
This is a supplement to the injunction regarding the Garmatrirātra sacrifice.
Even the experience [of the knowledge] having that as its object is a cause for the beauty of the face, let alone its actual practice; thus it is praised.
Just as the face becomes beautiful through ear-ornaments and the like, so too the face of the knower, blossoming through very great effort, appears as if beautified when seen by the disciples.
Therefore, because of its association with the quality of similarity to beauty, it is said to "beautify" (*śobhate*).

Furthermore, as for other examples of contradiction and the like that have been cited, such as "In the offspring of one who knows this, a champion is born," that too is a supplementary portion (śeṣa) of the injunction regarding the consecratory formula (anumantraṇa) of the Veda.
Here, too, the praise is to be understood through the logic of "how much more so" (kaimutikanyāya), and should be applied in the same manner as previously explained.
The son of a knower becomes himself learned through his father’s instruction; furthermore, he acquires knowledge through formal reception [of the Veda].
Therefore, with such a quality in mind, it is said: "He is born as a vigorous one."

Regarding the argument that other [scriptural passages] would be rendered meaningless, such as the example cited: “By the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one obtains all desires,” the author provides the answer in the Sūtra: “All this is subordinate to the qualified person (*adhikārika*).
This is a supplementary statement to the injunction: “One should offer the final oblation.”

The *pūrṇāhuti* is praised as "an excellent oblation" because it is the cause for the attainment of all desires. Just as in the expression "all Brahmins are to be fed," the term "all" refers specifically to those Brahmins who have arrived at one's own house, so too here, the "all-ness" should be understood as referring only to that fruit which is possible within the context of the qualification—that is, the fruit resulting from the completion of the ritual through the *pūrṇāhuti*. In the absence of the *pūrṇāhuti*, the rite of fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) becomes deficient in its constituent parts.
And that deficiency is remedied by the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); this is one desire.
When that has been restored, the fires such as the *āhavanīya* become fit for rituals such as the *agnihotra*; this is an internal desire.
And through those rituals, their fruit is attained; this is another desire.
If it is argued that such attainment of all desires is accomplished even by means of other oblations (*āhuti*), let it be so;
what loss is there to us?
Indeed, this does not detract from the praise of the *pūrṇāhuti*.
1. The [phonemes] *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pa*, and *pha* do not exist as "also" (*api*).
2. The [phonemes] *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *tha*, *pa*, and *pha* attain that [state].
3. The account of sons and grandsons for *ṭha*; the account of cooked food, sons, grandsons, and so forth for *ca* and *cha*; and the account of grandsons and so forth for *pa*.
4. Ṭa-ṭha is determined.
5. Ṭa-ṭha is its mouth.
6. In the [reading] ga-ṭa-ṭha-ya, the word "eva" (indeed) is not present.

7. The letters *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *pha*, and *ya* result in the completion of one's actions (*karmasāṅgatva*). Whatever has been performed, such as the completion of actions, [is achieved through] *ṭha*. 8. *Ga*, *gha*, *pa*, *pha*, and *ya* result in the deficiency of limbs (*aṅgavikala*); *cha* and *ṇa* result in the limbs being fruitless (*viphalam*). 9. *Ca*, *cha*, *pa*, and *pha* result in the attainment of all desires (*sarvakāmaprāpti*).
10. Between the oblations of *ṭa* and *ṭha*, there is some deficiency.

Now, one might object: since the *pūrṇāhuti* is a subsidiary (*aṅga*), let its mention of a fruit be merely a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) intended for praise, because it has been determined by the sūtra, "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, the mention of a fruit is an *arthavāda*, because they exist for the sake of another" (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.1). However, since the sentence concerning the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is an injunction of a primary rite (*karma-vidhi*), and since the conquest of all worlds is its principal fruit, its lack of purpose (*anarthakya*) is unavoidable. Anticipating this objection, he provides the following answer in a sūtra: "The fruit resides in the ritual; among those [subsidiaries], there may be a distinction of fruit according to their magnitude or quality, as is seen in the world."
The fruit produced by the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) consists of the conquest of one of the worlds—earth, intermediate space, or heaven.
Furthermore, through other rituals, these fruits such as earth and the others attain a greater measure or superior quality.
Therefore, since there would be a distinction in the fruits, this [sacrifice] is not purposeless.
"Like the world" (*lokavat*) is an illustration for the point already stated.
Just as in the world, when one sells *khārī*-measures of rice for a *niṣka* and then buys it again for another *niṣka*, there is an increase in quantity;
or just as for a *niṣka* one obtains what is about to be described, but for two *niṣkas* one obtains fine silk (*dukūla*), which is the essence.
Likewise, the superiority of enjoyment or the essential nature of enjoyment should be understood through other [scriptural] actions;

for even the mental commission of the murder of a Brahmin is crossed over merely by knowledge, whereas the physical commission of that great sin is [crossed over] by the Aśvamedha sacrifice—thus, there is no pointlessness in this [teaching].

As for the example of a prohibition of what is not applicable, namely "Neither in the intermediate space nor in heaven," and likewise the example of a connection with the non-eternal, namely "Babara Prāvāhaṇi," he provides the answer to both of these in the Sūtra:
"In the case of the other two, as previously stated.
In the case of these two examples, the answer should be understood to be exactly as stated before.

The explanatory passage (arthavāda) consisting of the censure of piling [the fire-altar] in the intermediate space and so forth is a supplement to the injunction "one should pile [the altar] after placing gold [beneath].
Therefore, the answer already stated—namely, "they [the arthavādas] exist for the purpose of praising the injunctions"—remains valid here as well.
Since there is no occasion for piling in the intermediate space, let that censure be a constant restatement (nityānuvāda).
By that [statement] as well, an injunction can be praised;

for by restating an eternally established fact—that the wind is the swiftest—the injunction regarding the animal sacrifice is praised. Regarding the passage, "Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired," it has been stated in the final section of the first chapter that a certain human being named Babara is not intended to be expressed; rather, what is intended to be expressed is the eternally established entity in the state of worldly usage: the wind, which possesses the sound "babara" and has the nature of blowing forth (prāvahaṇa).

Therefore, because the possible defects have been avoided, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) possess authority. Regarding this, there are summary verses: "The authoritative status of an explanatory passage such as 'Vāyu indeed... does not reside in the duty (*dharma*) that is to be enjoined; rather, what is it that exists therein?"

Since the mutual dependence among injunctive, explanatory (arthavāda), and descriptive words is exhausted [in their respective functions], there can be no syntactic unity (ekavākyatā) with them; how, then, could they possess authority regarding dharma?
The injunction and the explanatory passage (arthavāda) are mutually expectant regarding the praiseworthy human goals;
therefore, they form a single syntactical unit, and thus the arthavādas possess authority as a means of knowing dharma.
(Jaina Nyāya 1.2.1). Thus [it is said].

Thus, since there is no cause for invalidity regarding the three parts existing in the Veda—namely the mantra, injunction (vidhi), and explanatory passage (arthavāda)—and since the intrinsic validity of those which convey meaning is accepted, the authority of the entire Veda is established.
But even so, since the Veda would be of human origin, its lack of authority would follow, like the words of a deceiver.

And Jaimini set forth the fact of its being of human origin as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the first chapter of his *Sūtras* (Jai. Sū. 1.1.27–32): "And the Vedas, being designated by the name of persons, are [the result of] close contact.
Certain disputants maintain that there is a close contact regarding the Vedas with respect to persons.
The word "and" (ca) serves to collect together the works such as the *Raghuvaṃśa* composed by Kālidāsa and others;
for these are cited here as examples.
Just as the *Raghuvaṃśa* and other such works do not exist now [in their original form], so too are the Vedas.
The Vedas, however, are not beginningless;
for this very reason, persons are mentioned as their authors.

Just as Vyāsa and others are mentioned as the authors of the *Mahābhārata*—as in "the *Bhārata* of Vyāsa" or "the *Rāmāyaṇa* of Vālmīki"—so too, because Kaṭha and others are mentioned as the authors of specific regional recensions (śākhās), such as the *Kāṭhaka*, the *Kauthuma*, and the *Taittirīya*, [it follows that] the Vedas...

1. Excluding *ṭa* and *ṭha*, because of the absence of the *śg* [suffix] in the others. 2. In the sūtra concerning *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 3. *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ta*, *tha*, and *pha* are produced. 4. *ta* and *tha* scatter. 5. In *ṭa* and *ṭha*, the word "dukūla" does not exist. 6. In *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *ja*, *pa*, *pha*, and *pya*, there is no lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*). 7. In these two examples, *ca*, *cha*, *sa*, *pa*, and *pha*. Veda-bhāṣya, First Adhyāya.
Derived from Puruṣa.

Now, one might object: "Since the Vedas are indeed eternal, their designations such as 'Kāṭhaka' and so forth could simply arise from the fact that they were the originators of the tradition, like a teacher. Anticipating this doubt, the author provides another reason in the Sūtra: "And because of the observation of non-eternal things" (*anityadarśanācca*). Persons such as Babara, who are non-eternal—that is, subject to birth and death—are heard of in the Veda: "Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired," and "Kusurubinda Auḍulaki desired" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.2.2.1). This being the case, since the Vedas did not exist prior to Babara and the others, the Vedas are non-eternal.

The word "and" (ca) is intended to aggregate the following inferences: "The Vedic statement under dispute is of human origin, because it is a statement, like the statements of Kālidāsa and others. Etc.
He states the established conclusion (siddhānta) in the aphorism: “But the priority of the word has been stated” (*uktaṃ tu śabdapūrvatvam*).
The word “but” (*tu*) excludes the non-eternality of the Vedas.
It has already been stated in a previous aphorism that the word, in the form of the Veda, has priority over persons such as Kaṭha and others—that is, it is beginningless (*anāditva*).

In the sūtra "But the relation of a word with its meaning is innate" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.5), by the term *autpattika* ("innate"), the author establishes that all words—the Vedas included—possess this [eternal] designation; thus, their status as sentences resulting from human composition is refuted.
Since they are not perceived [to have been composed] therein, they must therefore be of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
(Ja. Nyā. 1.1.8). Thus [it is said].
But has not the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa stated in his Sūtras that the Veda is an effect of Brahman—in the aphorism: “Because it has its source in the Scripture” (*śāstrayonitvāt*)?
The meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman is the knower of the meaning [of the Veda], because it is the cause of the syllables of the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas. Certainly so.
It does not become a product of human authorship (*pauruṣeya*) merely by this much, because it lacks being created by a human being.

Intending this very non-human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*), Bādarāyaṇa himself has established its eternity in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* within the context of conventional usage, as if it were like space and so forth, in the Sūtra: "And for this very reason, there is eternity" (*ata eva ca nityatvam*, BS 1.3.29).
There are also Śruti and Smṛti texts on this point.
"By eternal speech, O Virūpa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.75.6) is the Śruti;
"Speech, without beginning or end, eternal, was emitted by the Self-existent One" (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 232.23) is the Smṛti.
Therefore, since no suspicion of a defect in the author arises, the faultless authority of the Veda, consisting of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, is established.
Now, it might be argued that it is not logical for the Veda to consist of both mantra and brāhmaṇa, because the essential nature of those two cannot be determined.
This is not so;
for [that nature] has not been determined in the seventh section (adhikaraṇa) of the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter.
The seventh section formulates [the following]: "O serpent, understand the mantra; 'sa' (that) is the definition of a mantra.
This is not so, for it does not apply to *vāyu* (wind) and other such things, since there is no exclusion of them.
The definition of mantras given by the ritualists is free from defects;
they apply the term "mantra" to those [Vedic texts] that serve as reminders for the performance of rituals and so forth.
(Jaṃbūdvīpaprajñapti-sūtra, Nyāyāvatāra 2.1.7) ||
