In the context of the *ādhāna* (the ritual of establishing the sacred fires), this is recited: "O Ahi Budhnya, protect my mantra" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.2.1.26).
In that regard, there is no definition of a *mantra*.
To say that it is "the determination of meaning through supplying ellipses" is not a definition.

If it is said that "a mantra is that which expresses a prescribed meaning," then the mantra "He sacrifices the kapiñjala birds for the Vasanta season" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 24.20) would fall under this definition because it possesses the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*).
If it is said that "a mantra is the cause of reflection (*manana*)," then there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the Brāhmaṇas as well.
If it is argued that there is mutual non-pervasion (avyāpti) among the definitions such as "a mantra is one that speaks thus" or "a mantra is one ending with the word *uttamapuruṣa*," it is not so;
for the designation (*samākhyāna*) of those skilled in ritual (*yājñika*) constitutes a faultless definition.
And that designation establishes the status of mantras for those things which remind one of the performance [of rituals] and so forth.
Mantras such as "uru prathasva" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.8.1) serve as reminders for performance;
those such as "agnim īḷe purohitam" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.1.1) consist of praise;
and those such as "iṣe tvā" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.1.1) end with the word "svāhā."
“O Agni, come for the feast” (*agna ā yāhi vītaye*; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.5.2.1) and so forth are those accompanied by address.
“O Agnīdh, carry forward the fires” (*agnīdagnīn vi hara*; Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.1.2) and so forth are in the form of commands.
“Was it below, indeed, that it was? Was it above, indeed, that it was? (*adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīt*; Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.129.5) and so forth are in the form of inquiry.
“O Ambā, O Ambālī, O Ambikā, no one leads me away” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.4.16.1)—such passages are of the nature of lamentation.
“I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.4.16.2)—such passages are of the nature of answers.
In this manner, other examples may also be cited.

In this very way, among things of such a kind, there exists no other common property (*anugata-dharma*) apart from conventional designation (*samākhyāna*) that could be stated as their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the utility of a defining characteristic was demonstrated by the ancient teachers: "Even seers do not reach the end of individual objects when considered separately;
however, through a defining characteristic, the wise reach the end of established doctrines."
Thus,
therefore, the definition [of a mantra] is the designation by those who are proficient that "this is a mantra."
The eighth section formulates [the argument]: "Is this Brahminhood not a discernible characteristic, or rather is it?
It does not exist, because there is no established rule that the portions of the Veda are finite."
The Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa—these are the two parts; therefore, by virtue of the Mantra, that which is other than it is called the Brāhmaṇa.
This is the definition of a Vedic Brāhmaṇa.
(Jaina Nyāya 2.1.8)
1. The over-extension [of the rule] regarding *ṭha* and *mati*. 2. *ca*, *cha*, *pha*, *pha*—therein.
This is the first group of eight (aṣṭaka). 17.
In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, this is recorded: "These five oblations are for the Brāhmaṇa alone" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.7.1.1).
In that context, there is no definition of a Brāhmaṇa.
Why?

Because it is impossible to refine the definitions [of mantra and brāhmaṇa] by determining the exact extent of the Vedic portions—due to the defects of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in some parts of the *brāhmaṇas* and over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in other parts—the previously mentioned *mantra* portion constitutes one category. Furthermore, certain other categories have been collected as cited by the ancients: reason (*hetu*), etymological derivation (*nirvacana*), censure (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and injunction (*vidhi*).
The performance by another, a prior tradition, and the assumption of a restrictive rule.
Thus:
"For by that food is made" is the reason (*hetu*); "That curdled milk becomes curds" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.3.4) is the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*).
"Beans are indeed impure" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.8.1) is a censure.
"Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.1.1) is a praise. "I am deliberating whether I should offer this oblation or not" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.9.1) is a doubt.
"The Audumbarī post is equal in height to the sacrificer" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.10.3) is an injunction (*vidhi*).

"They cook beans for the Mahat [sacrifice]" is a traditional account of another's action (*parakṛti*). "In former times, the Brāhmaṇas used to eat [beans]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.7.5) is a past event (*purākalpa*).

"One should offer [oblations] with *tuṣapāla* cakes for as many [enemies] as have been seized from the *vāruṇa* [sacrifice]" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.3.12.1)—this is an instance of the postulation of a restrictive determination (*viśeṣāvadhāraṇakalpanā*).
Other examples may likewise be cited.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the definition of a Brāhmaṇa is "that which contains reasons (*hetu*) and so forth," because reasons and the like also exist within the mantras.

‘...for indeed with hands and arms’ (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.2.4)—this is the *hetu* (reason). ‘They brought forth the great [waters]; therefore it is called water’ (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.1.2; Atharvaveda 2.13.4)—this is the *nirvacana* (etymological derivation).
‘The thoughtless man finds food in vain’ (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.117.6)—this is the *nindā* (censure).
"He is the head of the earth, the summit of heaven" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.44.16) is praise.
"Is he below? Is he above? is doubt.
"In spring, one should sacrifice kapiñjala birds" is an injunction.
‘A thousand have been offered’ (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.21.18) is a *parakṛti* (an account of another’s action);
‘By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice’ (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.164.50) is a *purākalpa* (a report of the past).
If it is argued that the Brāhmaṇa consists largely of such [grammatical] formations, we say no.

[The definition fails] because it overextends (*ativyāpti*) to the mantra to be chanted in this Brāhmaṇa passage: "‘Thus you gave,’ ‘thus you sacrificed,’ ‘thus you cooked’—thus should the Brāhmaṇa sing" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.9.14.3).
If it is argued that a Brāhmaṇa is that which is composed of a sentence containing the phrase "thus he said" (*ityāha*), [the answer is] no;

for it would overextend to these two mantras: "‘May this king partake of fortune,’ thus he says" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.41.2) and "‘Whoever calls me a sorcerer, or whoever, being a demon, says “I am pure”’" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.104.16).

If it is argued that the definition of a Brāhmaṇa is "that which has the form of a narrative (ākhyāyikā)," we say no; for this would over-extend to such texts as the *Yama-Yamī Saṃvāda Sūkta* and others. Therefore, since it follows that there is no definition for a Brāhmaṇa, we reply: [The definition is: A Brāhmaṇa is a text consisting of prose passages (*vākya*) that explain the meaning of mantras and rituals (*vidhi*), and which do not have the form of a dialogue (*saṃvāda*). This excludes works such as the *Mahābhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and the *Purāṇas*. Furthermore, it excludes the *Ārṣeya* and *Upaniṣad* sections of the Brāhmaṇas themselves, as well as the *Brāhmaṇa-kalpa-sūtra* and the *Śulba-sūtra*. Among these, the *Brāhmaṇa-kalpa-sūtra* consists of prose passages that explain the ritual procedures (*kalpa*) for the performance of sacrifices. The *Śulba-sūtra* consists of prose passages that explain the measurements (*māna*) of the sacrificial altars (*agni*). Thus, the definition is established.

Since it is accepted that the Veda consists of only two parts—the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa—and since the definition of the Mantra has already been stated, the remaining portion of the Veda will naturally have the definition of being the Brāhmaṇa. Jaimini formulated these two definitions in his Sūtras: "Among those two, the name 'Mantra' applies to the Ṛks [and similar verses]," and "The term 'Brāhmaṇa' applies to the remainder" (Jai. Sū. 2.1.32–33). Thus, among those two, the designation "Mantra" is applied by tradition to the Ṛks or to those sentences that express them, as seen in the expression: "We study the Mantras."
The meaning is that the term "Brāhmaṇa" is used by them for the portion other than the mantra.

But is it not the case that in the section concerning the *brahmayajña*, portions other than the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*—namely the *itihāsas* and so forth—are traditionally taught, as in: "The *brāhmaṇas*, the *itihāsas*, the *upapurāṇas*, the *gāthās*, and the *nārāśaṃsīs*" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 2.9)?
Not so;

for, according to the maxim of the Brahmin and the wandering mendicant (*vipraparivrājaka*), the *itihāsas* and other such categories are mentioned separately only because they are sub-divisions of the *brāhmaṇas* and the like.
The *itihāsas* are such [passages] as "The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.3.11.1).

The *purāṇa* consists of the collection of statements that, beginning with the prior state of the world such as "In the beginning, indeed, this was nothing at all" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 2.2.9.1), set forth the process of creation (*sarga*).
The *kalpa*, however, is recited in the section concerning the piling of the *āruṇaketuka* fire-altar: "Thus are the mantras."
"From this point forward, it is a ritual period (*kalpa*)," as stated in *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 1.31.2: "If one should offer the oblation (*bali*).

Furthermore, in the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), specific mantras are prescribed by the rule: "He sings around [the altar] with these *yamagāthās*" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.1.8.2).
1. ṭa—pacati;
2. ṭha—evam prāpte; 3. ga gha ca cha ṭa u ṇa tha pa pha ya—in certain explanatory [commentaries] on that Veda.
Ka. 1: Verses (gāthās).
The ṛcs that set forth accounts of human events are the nārāśaṃsyas.

Therefore, since there is no portion distinct from the mantra and brāhmaṇa, and because the nature of the mantra and brāhmaṇa has been defined, the fact that the Veda consists of both of these is well-established.

Furthermore, a specific internal distinction regarding mantras has been examined in that very same chapter (*pāda*) as follows: "When it is suspected that there is no defining characteristic for the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus because of their intermixture, [the answer is] that the *pāda*, the chant (*gīti*), and the prescribed recitation (*praśiṣṭapāṭha*) constitute their non-intermixture" (Jaimini Nyāya Mālāvistara 2.1.10).
This is recorded in scripture: "O Ahi Budhnya, protect for me the mantra which the seers who know the three Vedas know—the Ṛks, the Sāmans, and the Yajus" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.9.1.26).
Those who know the three Vedas are called *trividaḥ*.
The "threefold ones" (traividāḥ) are those who know the three Vedas; they are so called because they are the transmitters of that which belongs to the three Vedas.
The construction is: "Protect that portion of the mantra which they describe as threefold, in the form of the Ṛk and so forth.
In this regard, there is no fixed definition for the threefold Ṛk, Sāman, and Yajus.
Why?
Because the resulting confusion is difficult to avoid.
One must state the definition as: "A mantra is that which is recited among the Vedas and other texts well-known to teachers."
And that [classification] is confused.
This mantra, "May Savitṛ the god impel you with a flawless purifier, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.5.1), is recited in the Yajurveda among the Ṛks and Yajus;
yet it does not possess the nature of a *yajus*, because in its Brāhmaṇa it is treated as an *ṛc* in the passage, "with the Sāvitrī *ṛc*" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.5.3).
Having made the declaration, "Sing this Sāman for me" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 9.10.5), a certain Sāman is sung in the Yajurveda.
Furthermore, three Yajus formulas—"Thou art imperishable, thou art unshakable, thou art sharpened by breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.17.6)—are recorded in the Sāmaveda.
Likewise, the Ṛks that serve as the substratum for the Sāman being sung are also recorded in the Sāmaveda.

If it is argued that, therefore, there is no defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), we say no; for the feet and so forth possess non-overlapping characteristics. Mantras endowed with feet and meaning and composed in meter are *ṛcs*; mantras in the form of song are *sāmans*; and mantras recited as instructed, being devoid of meter and song, are *yajus*. Thus stated, there is no confusion whatsoever. This threefold classification was defined by Jaimini in three sūtras: "Among those [mantras], that in which there is a division into feet according to the sense is *ṛc*"; "The designation *sāman* applies to songs"; and "The term *yajus* applies to the remainder" (Jai.Sū. 2.1.35–37).
Depending precisely upon this internal distinction among mantras, the Vedas came to possess a threefold division: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda.
And among all those Vedas, or at least one of them, study must be performed by the initiated student according to his own capacity.
Thus Yājñavalkya records: "Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order.

With the intention that, in the case of studying a single Veda, the Veda obtained through the lineage of one's father, grandfather, and so forth, is what should be studied, the word *sva* ("one's own") is prescribed in the injunction: "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15).
Furthermore, that study is not something to be performed [only occasionally], but is obligatory (*nitya*).

For this very reason, it is aphorized in the *Puruṣārthānuśāsana*: "The study of the Veda [is obligatory], because there is a fall from the path in the case of non-study. And its necessity is indeed recorded in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*): "The Vedic study is free from evil; it is a divine purifier. He who abandons it becomes one who has no share in the world of truth, nor a share in the heavenly realm (*nāka*). Thus it is said of them: 'He who abandons it, though he was once a friend-finder and a companion, has no share even in speech.'"
"If he hears this, he hears enough; he does not need to know the path of good action" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15). Therefore, one's own Veda should be studied.
Because it protects the person who studies it like a friend by recognizing his efforts, it is called the *sakhividveda* (the friend-like Veda).
The accomplishment, through mere study, of the fruit of sacrifices—which are otherwise to be achieved through great effort and many materials—is the protection of that [Veda].
This is also declared in scripture: "Whatever sacrifice one studies, by that very one it becomes as if performed; indeed, one attains union with Aditi" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15).

Although this is the fruit of the *brahmayajña* (study of the Veda for its own sake), nevertheless, since the *brahmayajña* is impossible without the study undertaken for mastery (*grahaṇādhyayana*), its fruit is also thereby accomplished.
For that man who, having studied such a friend in the form of the Veda—consisting of the three Vedas—yet abandons it, there is no fortune even in his speech;
what need is there to mention that he has no fortune regarding the fruit?

For one who, after disparaging this Veda—which establishes that all deities possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman—proclaims everywhere worldly talk as the cause for a dispute over falsehood, the absence of fortune in his speech is indeed manifest.
For this very reason, it is traditionally taught: "One should not meditate on many Vedic hymns, for that is a weariness of speech" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21).

1. Those beginning with *ṭa* are the *pādakas*. 2. Those beginning with *ṭa-ṛbhubhyaḥ* and so forth are the *nāras*. 3. The mantras recited as *ṭa* are the *mantras*. 4. Among those excluding *ṭa* and *u*, they are generally agreed upon as belonging to the *yajus*. 5. In the *gāyana*, [the letters] *ca, cha, ṇa, pa, pha*. 6. Those prescribed as *ca, cha, ta, tha, pa, pha*. 7. By the meaning of *sa, cha, tha, pa, pha*, and by the meaning of *ṭa* and *u*. 8. *U* is both *apagutha*. 9. *Ṭa* and *ṭha* are all defects. Thus ends the first chapter (*ullāsa*). 19.

Even though he may listen to poetry, drama, and the like, that listening is nonetheless entirely useless; the meaning is that it is because of his lack of knowledge regarding the path of meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*). Smṛti also states: "The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself in other matters..."
"He, along with his progeny, quickly attains the status of a Śūdra even while still alive" (Manu Smṛti 2.168).
In this manner, many other such passages should also be cited here.

If it is argued that there is a circularity—since knowledge of the object to be enjoined by the injunction to study arises only after the Veda has been studied, yet the engagement in study occurs only when such knowledge exists—the answer is: certainly so.
For this very reason, those who follow the system of the Guru (Prabhākara) laboriously establish the engagement in a student’s study through the teaching performed by a teacher.

However, those who follow other systems describe the knowledge of the injunction to study as having existed even before the initial study, like the knowledge of the injunction for the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and so forth, which is obtained from one's father or others.

Whether it be the application of the injunction for teaching or the application of the injunction for oneself, in any case, the Veda must indeed be studied by those who have been initiated (upanīta). Furthermore, that study has a visible purpose and consists in the grasping of the syllables; this has been set forth in aphorisms within the *Puruṣārthānuśāsana*.
We shall cite those aphorisms and their commentary.
He presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to establish that study has a visible purpose: "But study has an invisible purpose, because it is enjoined.
Since injunctions are not observed in the case of eating and other such activities which have visible results, it must be understood that the enjoined study has an invisible purpose.
If it is argued that no specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) is heard [in the text], he says in response: "The extension (*atideśa*) of the streams of ghee and so forth, or heaven as a substitute.

Having extended the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the streams of ghee and so forth from the *brahmayajña* recitation to the obligatory study (*nityādhyayana*), that which occurs therein—the streams of ghee and so forth—should be conceived as the fruit according to the logic of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice.
For those who do not accept the extension of the explanatory passage, heaven should be conceived as the fruit according to the logic of the *viśvajit* sacrifice.

To the question, "Since the manifestation of impressions (*saṃskāra*) and attainment (*prāpti*) have visible results, how can there be the postulation of invisible [results]?", he says: "The manifestation of impressions and attainment are untenable."
The meaning is that since no application (*viniyoga*) of the study of the *saṃskṛta* [Veda] is observed anywhere, its attainment is for its own sake and not for the sake of another.

Having raised the objection that the attainment of the *svādhyāya* is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because it is the cause for understanding the meaning, he states—"That which is a subordinate part of something else does not convey the meaning"—referring to the fact that sentences such as those concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which are enjoined as parts of the recitation (*adhyayana*) like mantras employed for acts such as the removal of poison, lack authority regarding their own literal meaning.
This is because the sentence enjoining the study itself is considered a subordinate part only of the study it prescribes.
He states that it is a means of valid cognition with respect to its own meaning: "The sentence of study is a subordinate member of another."

[Objection: But if this is so—that the purpose is not seen (adṛṣṭārthatva)—then since there would be no fruit residing in the *svādhyāya* which serves as the object (*karma-kāraka*), the suffix *-tavya*, which denotes the object, would be contradicted by the injunction "it should be studied" (*adhyetavya*). To this, he says: "There is a transformation into an instrument (*karaṇa-pariṇāma*), like [the case of] barley-meal (*saktu*). In the sentence "He offers the barley-meal" (*saktūñ juhoti*), although the injunction appears to prescribe the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of offering with respect to the barley-meal—which is the primary element as the object—the transformation into an instrument is made, namely, "he offers with the barley-meal" (*saktubhir juhoti*). This is because, once the barley-meal has been reduced to ashes through the purificatory rite of offering, there is no further application (*viniyoga*) for those ashes; therefore, setting aside the primacy of the object, the transformation into an instrument is effected.

In this case as well, since it is impossible for the *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) and the *prāpti* (attainment) to pertain to the two actions, one must effect a modification of the sentence to read: "by means of the recitation, [one purifies] the rice grains."
Now, he establishes the final position that when a visible result exists, an invisible result should not be postulated: "But when there is a visible [result], there is no invisible [one]."
What is that visible fruit? To this he says: "In the case of direct perception, there are acquisition and latent impression."
He states that the attainment of the syllable (akṣara) constitutes a human goal through a traditional succession: "the understanding of the meaning of attainment.
The word "is born" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Nor should it be suspected that the injunction is redundant because its efficacy is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), as is the case with eating and similar acts; for, as in the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and other such rites, the injunction is justified for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus he says: "This is an injunction."

Regarding the objection that there can be no purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) because no application (*viniyoga*) for the Veda as a refined object (*saṃskṛta*) is observed, he replies: "The establishment of the purificatory rite follows from the employment [of the Veda] in the injunctions for sacrifices and study.
For the injunctions regarding sacrifices, requiring an understanding of their subject matter, employ the Veda as a means to that understanding.
And the injunction for study indicates that the Veda is to be refined through the act of study, rather than by means of reading from a written text and so forth.
Therefore, because both are accepted, that [existence] is established.
Now, is it not the case that what is called *saṃskāra* is a specific unseen potency (*adṛṣṭātiśaya*),
and that [potency] does not...

1. Knowledge of the meaning of the injunctions regarding *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 2. The engagement in the procedure of [the study of] *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 3. The application and reasoning regarding *gha*, *ca*, *pha*; [according to the reading of *ta* and *tha*: the application]. 4. Regarding that (*ṭha*). 5. The purpose of the instruction (*ṭa* and *ṭha*). 6. In that sense (*te*). 7. The visible fruit (*ṭa* and *ṭha*). 8. Regarding this, he says (*ṭa* and *ṭha*). 9. The word "thus" (*iti*) is not present in *ṭa* and *ṭha*. 10. Of the determination (*ca*, *cha*, *pa*, *pha*). 11. The phrase "of the private recitation" (*svādhyāyasya*) is not present in *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *pa*, *pha*, and *ya*. 12. The word "for" (*hi*) is not present in *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *tha*, *pa*, and *pha*. 13. Study free from distractions (*ca*, *pa*, *pha*).

[The word] *svādhyāya* is included [in the compound]. Since it is mentioned first, as indicated by the suffix *-tavya*, it refers to the study (*adhyayana*) which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root of its own base.
To the question, "In that case, how can the Veda (*svādhyāya*) be something consecrated (*saṃskṛta*)?", he says: "The suffix *-tavya* expresses the object of the action (*karman*)."

In this context, because the suffix *tavya* denotes the object (*karman*), it functions as the objective factor (*kāraka*). Since the suffix *tavya* is more closely related to the object denoted by the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*)—namely, study—than to anything else, the suffix *tavya* expresses the transcendental result (*apūrva*) residing specifically in the Veda (*svādhyāya*). The sense is that even though the restriction regarding the transcendental result is produced by the meaning of the verbal root, it is nonetheless a restriction [of the result] because it is delimited by that [study]. As it has been said: "A mantra does not independently establish a meaning," that is incorrect; for such a status is appropriate for those mantras which have independent unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*) as their purpose.
In this case, however, there is an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) based on the private recitation (*svādhyāya*).

Since its fruit is the comprehension of the meaning established by the power of the syllables contained within that recitation, it is impossible to postulate any other fruit; therefore, the unseen merit merely reinforces the authority [of the text] and does not obstruct it. Thus he says: "The cognition of its own meaning is not obstructed when the unseen merit is an independent subsidiary. One might object: "By the logic of the *saktu* (barley-meal), since the predominance of the objective factor (*karmakāraka*) has been abandoned, here too there would be an independent unseen merit. To this he replies: "Because it is consistent with what is heard in the text, the logic of the *saktu* does not apply here."

The meaning is this: while one might abandon what is heard in the case of roasted barley flour (*saktu*) and assume what is not heard because there is no possibility of [the flour] moving, such [an assumption] is not appropriate here, as has already been demonstrated. Having thus established that the injunction for study has a visible purpose, he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) to refute the position that it extends up to the comprehension of the meaning: “The determination of the meaning [arises] from the Veda according to Bhaṭṭa and Guru, because the injunction terminates in the human goal.”

Since there is a rule that every injunction must ultimately culminate in human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), Bhaṭṭa and Guru maintain that here too, the ascertainment of the meaning—which is a fruit constituting a human purpose—is prompted by the injunction to study.

Anticipating the objection that "certainly, neither from a single recitation nor even from one accompanied by repetition is the ascertainment of the meaning observed," he says, "it would imply inquiry," meaning that if that were the case, the injunction for study, in order to achieve that [ascertainment], would necessitate inquiry as the means for the ascertainment of the meaning.

Is it not the case that there is a universal rule that an injunction (vidhi) is the motivator only for that which is itself enjoined and for that which assists it? If so, how can the injunction to study imply such a thing [as the comprehension of meaning]? To this he says: "The implication of what is not enjoined and does not assist is like the repetition of threshing," as in the case of "One threshes the rice-grains. In this instance, only the act of threshing is enjoined, not its repetition.
Furthermore, because that [threshing] has already been accomplished,
it cannot be an auxiliary to the enjoined act;
for threshing is established by a single blow of the pestle even without the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Nevertheless, just as that [agent] would imply a performance of the ritual procedure for the sake of achieving the result of producing rice, so too should it be understood in the present case.

One might object: "Even if comprehension of the meaning does not arise from the mere study of the Veda, since such comprehension does arise for one who studies the Veda in the company of a grammarian, the injunction would not require him to undertake inquiry. Anticipating this objection, he states that inquiry is indeed necessary to remove obstacles to the understanding of the meaning: "When that knowledge [of the meaning] arises from direct study, inquiry serves to dispel contradictions."
He establishes the conclusion: "But because attainment, like [the acquisition of] cows and so forth, is a human goal due to its being a desired existence.

Just as cows and other means are sought after by persons even though they are merely causes for results such as milk, so too, since the attainment of syllables—which is the cause for understanding the meaning that possesses the result—is itself a human goal, it must be understood that the injunction to study terminates in the attainment of syllables.

Now, if it is argued that the status of the attainment of the syllable (*akṣara*) as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is contingent upon the comprehension of the meaningful content which bears fruit, then—since that comprehension itself would be the primary human goal—why should the injunction not terminate with that comprehension? To this, he says: "In this way, the form of study [is established] even when the result ends with comprehension. For the result of comprehension is indeed the performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*).
If that were the case, then for a Brāhmaṇa or others who possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for this [study] because of their status as such, that study would become mandatory.

But there is no study of the injunctions for the Rājasūya and other such sacrifices, because in those cases there is an absence of results such as engagement [in performance]. He states that this fault does not apply to his own position: "The acquisition of the hand is for the purpose of recitation."

Nor can it be argued that if [the Veda] were not a source of knowledge (*abodhaka*), the comprehension of meaning would simply not be established; for it is the very nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to bring about the cognition of its object (*prameya*).
This is because we observe that even in the case of worldly statements, they produce cognition even without an injunction (*vidhi*). Thus he says: "1. By virtue of expressing the action (*karma*)."
2. [The section on] the suffix -tavya belonging to the recitation of the Ṭa and Ṭha [sections]. 3. [The section on] the explanatory statement regarding the base meaning of the Ṭha [section].
4. [The section on] the non-existence of another unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) in the Ga, Gha, Ba, Cha, Ṇa, Pa, and Pha [sections].
5. [The letters] ga, gha, ca, cha, ṇa, pa, pha, ya—such as these.
6. ga, gha, ca, cha, ṇa, ta, pa, pha, ya—[these] dispel contradictions in meaning.
7. ca, cha, pa, pha—[these belong to] that which makes it known.

8. [The section on] the sentences of the *Rājasūya* and other [rituals], beginning with the letters gha, ca, cha, ṇa, tha, pa, pha. 9. [The section on] the letters ṭa, ṭha; since an injunction (*vidhi*) does not terminate in mere cognition, there is the comprehension of the meaning.
First Chapter: 21.
"Cognition occurs as in the world."

Now, one might object: "If awakening were of the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), then since it could be enjoined for one desiring awakening, a person who finds pleasure [in it] would be the qualified candidate (*adhikārī*). Anticipating this, and considering that even in the case of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), a person who desires the opposite [of what is prohibited]—such as a *varṣabrāhmaṇa* mentioned in the *Uktha*—is easily available as a qualified candidate here, the author refutes the desirability of awakening (*bodhasya kāmyatvam*) by stating, simply for the sake of clarity: "He was previously indifferent toward both the objects of knowledge and their non-appearance. (So'kāmyaḥ prāgbodhyānābhānayoḥ).

Regarding the understanding of the meaning of the Veda— characterized by the Agnihotra and other rites— which occurs prior to formal study through the instruction of a father or others, just like the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), that comprehension of the meaning is not something to be desired (*kāmya*), precisely because it is already established. If it were not [already] present, it could not be desired,
since desire necessarily arises only toward an object already known.

One might object: “Surely, when something is known in a general way, a desire to know it in its specific details arises; or rather, even when it has been understood in detail through the instruction of one’s father or others, it is entirely appropriate to desire further knowledge in order to determine the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that instructional cognition. Anticipating this objection, he states: “Because such a specification is impossible,” meaning that even so, the injunction to study for the purpose of attaining an understanding of the meaning is not possible. For it is not possible to specify the various cognitions of specific matters such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice all at once under a single conceptual form, because they are infinite in number.
If the subject were indicated by way of a general form, then only the universal would be the result of the injunction, and not a specific cognition;
therefore, such an indication is not tenable.

Now, one might object: "If there is no utterance of the Veda with the aim of understanding its meaning, it would lack *tātparya* (intentionality) regarding its own subject matter. Anticipating this doubt, he states—"*Tātparya* [is known] from the word"—meaning that *tātparya*, which is apprehended through indicators such as the opening context (*upakrama*) and so forth, is established by the very power of the words themselves.

If it is argued that the utterance of a word in common usage would be useless with respect to the knowledge of its meaning, we say no; for it serves to remove the slight obstruction caused by defects arising from human agency. Thus he says: "The utterance for the sake of indication [removes] the defect in common usage."

One might object: "If the injunction for study does not culminate in comprehension (*bodha*), then the science of inquiry (*vicāra-śāstra*) would not proceed due to a lack of a motivating cause. Anticipating this, he says: "Inquiry is justified as being conjoined with a subsequent injunction. The injunctions for performing sacrifices, having been provisionally understood through the study of the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-veda*), are unable to impel one to performance without a firm, determinative knowledge established by resolving contradictions; therefore, they motivate the inquiry into sacrifices for the sake of such determination. However, the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) directly enjoins the inquiry into Brahman.

This being the case, it is all the more logical that the injunction for hearing (śravaṇa) possesses the quality of being the motivator (*prayojaka*) for its own enjoined object, and that the ritual injunctions (*kratu-vidhi*) possess the quality of being the motivators for that which assists their enjoined objects.

However, on the alternative view that [the study of the Veda] is motivated by the injunction for formal study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), since that injunction culminates in the attainment of heaven through the medium of the rituals, the performance of the rituals would also be motivated by it; consequently, the ritual injunctions themselves would fall into redundancy.

If it is argued that since the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) is restricted solely to those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), then upon its application, the inquiry [into ritual] would also be obtained by them and not otherwise; [we reply: the establishment of the necessity (*nityatva*) of the inquiry into rituals (*ṛtu-vicāra*) applies to all three castes, or else that of the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-vicāra*). Of these, the first is equal even in our own view; thus he says: "Therefore, the inquiry into rituals is necessary for all three castes. The meaning is: because it is heard in scripture that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) from non-performance, the rituals are obligatory (*nitya*) for the three castes; therefore [the inquiry is also necessary].
The second [point] states that it is not so: "Furthermore, the inquiry into Brahman belongs only to the Paramahaṃsa";
the word "eternal" (nitya) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
[Objection: According to the aforementioned principle, since the study [of the Veda] consists merely in the grasping of syllables, the knowledge of its meaning would likewise not be enjoined. [Reply:
Not so;
for that is enjoined by another scriptural passage.
"The Veda, with its six limbs, is to be studied and known by a Brahmin as a duty without motive (*niṣkāraṇa*); this is the injunction regarding that.

In this context, by the word "without motive," the fact that study and knowledge are prompted by desire (*kāmyatva*) is excluded. Regarding the understanding of the meaning, the author of the *Nirukta*, Yāska himself, cited two statements found within the scriptures that incite a person toward such understanding: “Furthermore, there is praise of knowledge and censure of ignorance: ‘This man is like a pillar, a mere carrier of burdens—he who, having studied the Veda, does not know its meaning.’”
He who knows the meaning thus enjoys all prosperity; with his sins shaken off by knowledge, he goes to the heavenly realm.
"That which is grasped but not understood, and is merely recited as a verbal formula,
never blazes at all— like dry fuel in a place without fire" (Nirukta 1.18).
In these two mantras, by the phrase "he who knows the meaning," knowledge of the meaning of the Veda is praised;
by the other phrase, the absence of such knowledge is censured.
He who knows the meaning of the Veda attains all that is auspicious in this world.
Likewise, when his evil is destroyed by that knowledge, he dies.

1. *va-pha*: of that injunction, namely the knowledge of the meaning; 2. *ṭa-yadhadhītam*: that which has been studied; 3. *ṭa-ṭha*: by means of this meaning; 4. *ṭa*: the absence of the knowledge of the meaning; 5. *pha*: by this. 22. The First Aṣṭaka. 23.
Because it is the meaning of the mantra:

"To that person who has set out to purify both the literal meaning of his own words and the intended significance (*tātparya*) through investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) by means of those who know the meaning of grammar, the Veda reveals its own body with full confidence.
The phrase beginning with "its own" (*svām*) is an explanation of the word *svakīyām*.

The passage beginning with "knowledge" (*jñānam*) is an explanation of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). It means that the mantra speaks through this third quarter as a form of speech capable of illuminating the meaning of the Veda. He shows the intended meaning of the fourth quarter: "With the highest speech, like a wife desiring [her husband] for her husband at the proper times, well-dressed—meaning, wearing beautiful clothes—and desiring him at the proper times; just as he sees her, so does he hear her: this is a praise of one who knows the meaning."
This is its meaning: by means of the "highest" speech, which consists of the fourth quarter, an analogy for the meaning of the third quarter is expressed. The word *uśatī* is explained as "desiring."
Although she wears soiled garments during the day at the time of household chores, she nevertheless wears beautiful garments during the times of sexual union.
The reason for this is:
"desiring [him] during the fertile periods."

Just as a husband looks upon this wife with complete devotion and listens to her words with a mind intent on her welfare, so too does this man—who has abandoned the study of the fourteen branches of knowledge—correctly perceive the secret meaning of the Vedas and, with a mind intent on his own welfare, embrace the truth concerning Dharma and Brahman as declared by the Vedas.
This is the praise spoken for one who is proficient in the meaning of the Vedas.
Furthermore, Yāska cited another Ṛgvedic verse (Nirukta 1.20): “The next [verse] is for a more extensive etymological explanation:
‘They say that you alone are one whose friendship is firmly drunk; they do not urge him on even in contests for prizes.
He moves by means of a non-cow, as if by mere illusion—having heard speech that is without fruit and without flower’” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.71.5).
This is the meaning:
immediately following the verse previously cited beginning with "uta tvaḥ paśyan," there occurs a certain verse that serves as a further explanation of the meaning of the aforementioned mantra;
it is capable of establishing that meaning with even greater clarity.
If it is asked how this is so, it is explained as follows:

Furthermore, they say—those who are experts (*abhiśāḥ*) declare—that a man skilled in the fourteen branches of knowledge, standing in friendship with speech in the form of the Veda, is one united with the drinking of the nectar taught in the Veda;
thus, in the mantra "the friend-finding friend" (*sakhividam sakhāyam*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15), the friendship of the Veda is illustrated.
Or rather, they say that even among those who have drunk the nectar of immortality to an excess while dwelling in friendship with the gods in the heavenly world—
those who are masters of speech, bold in assemblies, or swift as horses—
they do not urge this man, who is so skilled in the meaning of the Vedas, to speak.
No one attains [the goal],
because they are unable to debate with him.
But another, who is intent merely on recitation, hears speech that is devoid of flowers and fruit.
The knowledge of *dharma* as taught in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) is the flower;
the knowledge of *brahman* as taught in the later section (*uttarakāṇḍa*) is the fruit.

Just as in the world a flower produces a fruit, so too the knowledge of the *dharma* consisting of Vedic recitation and other rites, through its performance, generates the desire for the knowledge of *brahman*, which is the fruit itself.

This is according to the Vedic scripture: "The Brahmins seek Him through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
And just as the fruit [of action] is the cause of satisfaction, so the knowledge of Brahman is the cause of having accomplished all that is to be done.
This is according to the scripture: "When there is the singular realization of the Full, one becomes one who has accomplished all that is to be done by thinking, 'I am That Brahman.'"

This man, a reciter of the Veda devoid of such flowers and fruits, moves together with a deceptive illusion that is not a cow (*adhenu*). A cow that has recently calved and yields milk is called a *dhenu* based on the etymological derivation from the root *dhinoti* (to satisfy), because she is a cause of joy. For one who is intent merely upon the recitation [of the text], the speech in the form of the Veda does not yield the milk that consists of the knowledge of its meaning; thus, it is a non-cow (*adhenu*).
For this very reason, they are "illusory" (māyayā), meaning they possess deceptive forms like those of cows created by a magician;
the sense is that one who moves about with such illusion does not attain the supreme human goal.

Since Yāska has thus boldly provided an illustration for the praise of knowledge and the censure of ignorance, the injunction regarding the meaning [of the Veda] must be accepted just as there is an injunction regarding its study, according to the maxim: "That which is praised is [simultaneously] censured."

Furthermore, in the Nakṣatreṣṭi section, the statement regarding the fruit of the rite is recorded as being identical for both the sacrifice and the knowledge thereof: "Just as Agni is the eater of food among the gods, even so does he become the eater of food among men who sacrifices with this oblation and who knows it thus" (Taittirīya Gṛhyasūtra 3.1.4.1).
Therefore, like the sacrifice, the knowledge of it is also enjoined for the sake of the fruit.
By this principle, injunctions for knowledge are to be seen in all the Brāhmaṇas as well.
If it is argued that in the sūtra *vidyāpraśaṃsā* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.15), Jaimini has stated that the fruits of knowledge are of the nature of praise, let it be so;
for it is possible to praise by means of a fruit even when it is not yet present.

When there is an omission of the Darśa or Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Vaiśvānara-iṣṭi is enjoined as an expiation, and its praise is performed precisely by means of the already existing fruit of heaven.

1. The meaning of the word *ṭa*. 2. *Ṭha*: they say that [he] has drunk nectar to an exceeding degree (*atiśayena*). 3. *Ṭa-ṭha*: the word ‘or’ (*vā*) is not present. 4. *Ṭha*: to be known (*veditum*). 5. *Ṭha*: by this (*anena*). 6. *Ṭha*: like a conjurer’s cow (*aindrajālikago*). 7. *Ṭha*: “*yat*. [As it is said:
“For the sake of the heavenly world (*suvarga-loka*), the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are performed” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.5.4).

This was cited by the Teachers (*ācāryaiḥ*) in order to show that even a statement regarding the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna-phala-vākya*) has its own literal sense (*svārthe*) as its intended meaning (*tātparya*), because the status of being an explanatory passage (*arthavādatva*) belongs only to speech that is subordinate to another purpose.
And because it expresses things as they actually are, it possesses the quality of being a statement of reality.
Just as the New and Full Moon sacrifices are performed for the sake of the heavenly world, so too [is this case];
nor is there the status of being a mere statement of fact, as in the scriptural passage concerning "evil reputation" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Vārttika 127–128).
Thus it is said.

Nor should it be suspected that the performance of rites is rendered useless because the fruit is attained through mere knowledge alone; for this objection has already been refuted by the fact that the fruit is more abundant [when combined with action].

And on this point, the Sūtra of Jaimini has been cited: "Since the fruit arises from the completion of the ritual acts, there shall be a distinction in the fruit according to their magnitude or intensity, as is seen in the world" (Jai.Sū. 1.2.17).

This has been explained by us through the example: "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice and he who knows this thus, both cross over the murder of a Brahmin" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.12.2). Furthermore, the Chandogas declare that there is a superior result from performance accompanied by knowledge compared to performance alone: "Both perform it—the one who knows this thus and the one who does not know it.
But knowledge and ignorance are indeed different."
"Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).

Although, in that context, the word "knowledge" (vidyā) is intended to refer specifically to the knowledge connected with the auxiliary rites (aṅga), nevertheless, this principle is the same for all forms of knowledge.
If it is asked, "Whence comes such devotion of yours toward this [Veda]?",
then whence comes such excessive hostility from you?
As for praise, we have already shown it to be even greater.
We do not find any censure at all.
Furthermore, just as the *apūrva* produced by ritual action (*karman*) accompanies the individual soul after death, so too does the *apūrva* produced by knowledge (*vidyā*) accompany it.
Thus the Vājasaneyins declare: “Knowledge and action take hold of him, as does his prior experience” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).
Therefore, since the knowledge of the meaning, like the study itself, is enjoined, the Veda must be explained for the sake of understanding its meaning.

Since there is no inclination on the part of the listener to engage [with a work] without first knowing its subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), relationship (*sambandha*), and intended audience (*adhikārī*), these elements are now defined.
For this commentary, the Veda is the subject matter;
the knowledge of its meaning is the purpose.
The relationship [between this work and the Veda] is that of the commentary and the text to be commented upon;
the qualified person is one who seeks knowledge.
Although this much is well known, nevertheless, if the Veda were devoid of subject matter and so forth, the commentary would likewise lack its ultimate subject matter and other such elements.
Therefore, the true nature of the Veda is stated:
in the Veda, dharma and brahman are respectively the subjects of the Pūrva-kāṇḍa and the Uttara-kāṇḍa, because these two are not obtainable through other means.
Accordingly, it is aphorized in the *Puruṣārthānuśāsana*: “Dharma and brahman are the subject matter of the Vedic corpus.”

In the second sūtra of the Jaiminīya [Mīmāṃsā], those who know the tradition have stated two restrictive rules: "Only *codanā* is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma*" and "*Codanā* alone is the means of valid knowledge. To establish this point—that it is *codanā* alone—the fourth sūtra refutes that *dharma* is an object of perception: "Perception is not the cause [for knowing *dharma*], because it apprehends only what is presently existing" (Jai. Sū. 1.1.4). This is because *dharma*, which manifests itself after its performance, did not exist previously; therefore, it lacks the fitness to be perceived.

Even at a later time, because it is devoid of form and other qualities, it is not apprehended by the sense organs; for this very reason, it is designated as "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) by all. Furthermore, due to the absence of any inferential mark (liṅga), it does not fall within the scope of inference either.
If it is argued that "the Veda is the indicator (liṅga) of dharma and adharma," then certainly so;
this relationship between indicator and indicated is also understood through the Veda. Therefore, the Veda alone is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding dharma.

In the second interpretation of the third sūtra of the *Traiyāsika* [section], the authors of the Commentary have explained that even Brahman, as an already established reality (*siddhavastu*), is the exclusive subject matter of scripture: "The intention is that Brahman, the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, is understood solely from scripture as the means of valid knowledge" (*Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkara-bhāṣya* 1.1.3). And there is a scriptural passage: "One does not think of that Great One without the Veda" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 3.12.1.7).

Regarding this, the previous teachers have stated the following concerning its establishment: "And because it is devoid of form, marks, and so forth, there is the fitness for [the suffix] *mān* [to denote the means of knowledge]" (*Vedāntanyāyabhūṣaṇa* 1.1.3.18).
Therefore, since they cannot be obtained by any other means, both Dharma and Brahman are the objects of the Veda.
Knowledge of both of these is the direct purpose of the Veda.

Nor should it be suspected that this knowledge culminates in something that is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), like the cognitions "the earth consists of seven islands" or "that king is going," because it results in a human goal endowed with merit (*dharma*). For it is said: "Dharma is the foundation of the entire world; in this world, subjects flock to one who is most virtuous; by dharma one dispels evil; everything is established in dharma; therefore, they call dharma supreme" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.63).
This is because a king who wields the rod of punishment acts as a restrainer.

1. By the example beginning with "ṭa"; 2. by "ca," "cha," "tha," "pha," "ta," and "veśca"; 3. by "ṭa" and "kica"; 4. "ca," "cha," "ṭa," and "pha" are understood; "ṭha" can be understood; 5. even though "ṭa" and "cha" are established in the mind; 6. because "ṭa" is being heard. Chapter One, Verse 25:
Furthermore, just as even a weak person may achieve victory between two contending men through the assistance of a king, *dharma* is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

And thus the Vājasaneyins record in the context of the creation: "He created Dharma as a form superior to that [the Kṣatra]; this Dharma is the sovereign power (kṣatra) of the sovereign power (kṣatra). Therefore, there is nothing higher than Dharma; moreover, the weaker man appeals to the stronger by means of Dharma, just as one does to a king" (Gṛhyopaniṣad 1.4.14).

In such scriptural passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.2), "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9), and "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3), the human goal resulting from the knowledge of Brahman is well-established.
One who seeks the knowledge of both [the ritual and the spiritual] is qualified for the Veda;
and that person belongs to one of the three higher castes.

In the case of the *brāhmaṇa*, *kṣatriya*, and *vaiśya* castes (*brīhyādayaḥ*), however, even though there is a requirement for knowledge, their eligibility regarding the Veda is obstructed because, due to the absence of initiation (*upanayana*), they lack the right to study it.
Knowledge of Dharma and Brahman, on the other hand, is obtained through the medium of the Purāṇas and similar texts.
Therefore, the eligibility of men of the three higher castes to know the meaning [of the Veda] is through the Veda itself.

As for the connection of the Veda with *dharma* and *brahman*: [the first view] is not tenable because mantras such as "saṃbandhas tu vedasya... (ŚB 1.1.1) and others are employed in certain contexts within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Nor is the second [view] correct, because in the passage "They offer the cake for Agni-Viṣṇu, the eleven-potherd cake pertaining to the consecration" (AiB 1.1), the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice has already been introduced within the Brāhmaṇa section.
To this it is replied: the section on mantras proceeds by way of the *brahmayajña* and so forth, not by way of the sequence of sacrificial performance.
And the *brahmayajña* is enjoined as follows:
"He who studies even a single verse of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, or Sāmaveda—that is the *brahmayajña*" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.10).
This very *brahmayajña* (Vedic study sacrifice) is to be performed according to the sequence of the traditional recension (*āmnāya*), beginning with "I praise Agni" (*agnim īḷe*).
Likewise, it is enjoined: "One recites all the *ṛc*s, all the *yajus* formulas, and all the *sāman* chants as the *pāriplava* at the *vācastoma*.
Similarly, it is enjoined: "While the *āśvina* śastra is being recited, one should recite all the ten maṇḍalas of the Rigveda, even if the sun should not rise."

Likewise, a recitation of the entire Veda as an expiation is prescribed in such passages as: "He who officiates at a sacrifice, or accepts a gift, becomes as if emptied or indeed utterly depleted; having officiated or accepted a gift, he should recite his own Vedic study three times without eating" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.16).
In all such applications of the entire section of mantras, the sequence transmitted through the traditional lineage must be respected.

However, regarding the specific application of particular mantras, Āśvalāyana demonstrates that one must rely on the means of valid knowledge—namely, direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and so forth.
Therefore, there is no contradiction even in the absence of a sequential order for the sections on mantras.

As for the mantras beginning with "iṣe tvā," since they are recited according to the sequence of the performance of the ritual acts, Āpastamba and others proceeded to compose their Sūtras according to that very same order.
Precisely because they have been so handed down, that same sequence applies even to the silent recitations (japa) and other such acts.

Although the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* is introduced in the Brāhmaṇa, nevertheless, because that sacrifice is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and thus depends upon it, Āśvalāyana appropriately provides its exposition at the beginning.
Therefore, the Kalpasūtra assists by teaching the performance of the ritual through the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantras.
Consequently, Āśvalāyana has prescribed the application of the *sāmidhenī* verses, such as "pra vo vājā" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.27.1), right here [at the start].
If it is asked, "From where are [the mantras] such as 'namaḥ pravaktre' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.2), which are recited in other recensions, applied? there is no fault in this.

For, according to the principle of the "inclusion of subordinate elements" (guṇopasaṃhāra), the application established in another Brāhmaṇa of those [mantras] recited in another recension must be stated here.
As the experts of logic say: "A single ritual action is recognized across all recensions."
Therefore, even a ritual procedure (kalpa) is required, just like the training (śikṣā).

Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is also useful for determining the nature of words and their meanings by means of the instruction regarding roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*). Thus, it is recited in the *Aindravāyava-graha-brāhmaṇa*: "Speech, indeed, was turned away and unmanifested. The gods said to Indra, 'Make this speech of ours manifest. He chose Atharvāṅgiras, saying, 'Let him take [the draught] for me and for Vāc together. Therefore, the Aindravāyava draught is taken together."
"Indra, having entered into its midst, articulated it;
therefore this articulated speech is uttered" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.4.7.3).

In former times, speech—beginning with "I praise Agni, the domestic priest" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.1.1)—was unarticulated (*avyākṛtā*), existing as a single essence like the roar of the ocean, devoid of any treatise that effects the division into *prakṛti*, *pratyaya*, *pada*, or *vākya*.

At that time, Indra, being entreated by the gods, was pleased by the boon of receiving the Soma juice in a single vessel for both himself and Vāyu; he then divided that unbroken speech in the middle, making the distinction between base and suffix everywhere. Therefore, the meaning is that even now this speech, having been analyzed (*vyākṛtā*) by great seers such as Pāṇini and others, is studied by all.
The specific purpose of this very grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) has been shown by Vararuci in the *Vārttika*: "Preservation, addition, brevity, and absence of doubt are its purposes."
These purposes, beginning with protection (*rakṣā*), as well as other purposes, have been clarified by Patañjali in the *Mahābhāṣya*:
"Grammar should be studied for the protection of the Vedas;

for one who knows [the rules regarding] elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), and the modification of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*) will properly preserve the Vedas and determine the meaning of the Vedas."

Furthermore, there is indeed *ūha* (modification). Those mantras which have been recited with all [their original] gender markers and all case endings must necessarily be modified according to the requirements of the sacrifice.
A person who is not a grammarian is not able to perform such modification.
Therefore, grammar should be studied.

Furthermore, there is the traditional authority (*āgama*) which states: "The Veda, along with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), must be studied and understood by a Brahmin as a duty without [extraneous] motive.
And among the six auxiliary limbs, grammar is the most important.
Furthermore, effort directed toward the primary subject becomes fruitful;
moreover, grammar is to be studied as something that has already attained its purpose.
Bṛhaspati taught Indra the complete study of words (*śabdapārāyaṇa*) consisting of words explained word-for-word for a thousand celestial years, yet he did not reach the end.
Bṛhaspati was the teacher;
Indra was the student;
and the period of study lasted for a thousand divine years.
And he did not reach the end.
But today, even if his lifespan were at its maximum, he would live for only a hundred years;
therein, how could there be a step-by-step [attainment]?
1. Devoid of the letters *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, and *grantha*;

A corrupt word:

one should study grammar so as not to employ corrupted words.

"But he who employs words correctly at the time of linguistic usage, being skilled in their distinctions— he attains infinite victory in the hereafter and does not stumble through the use of corrupt words."

For corrupt words (*apaśabda*) are more numerous than correct words (*śabda*).

Now, as for the learned one who knows the yoga of speech, that is his refuge. This is a difficult proposition; it cannot be that ignorance serves as a refuge.
For indeed, even one who might kill a Brahmin or drink liquor while being unaware [of their status]— I consider him too to be fallen.
If that is so, then who [is not]?
Only one who knows the yoga of speech [is liberated]; however, for one who knows the yoga of speech, knowledge is his refuge.

Those who are wise—

Indeed, one person, though seeing, does not see;

*Saktu* is so called because it is crushed (*sakta*) or because it is scattered (*saktu*). Or it may derive from the root *kas*, in its reversed form, meaning it is expanded (*vikasita*). *Titau* is a winnowing fan; it is so called either because it is stretched (*tatavat*) or because it is struck (*tujavat*).
The steadfast ones, possessing meditation, have fashioned speech with their mind through wisdom; they have fashioned speech.
Here, those who are like heroes recognize their friendships;
here, friends recognize their friendships; they recognize their states of union.
Who is this difficult path, accessible by a single way and beyond the scope of speech?
And who, moreover, are they? They are the grammarians.
Whence is this?
"This auspicious fortune is deposited in speech.
Indeed, for them, auspicious fortune is deposited in their speech.
Fortune increases through the dwelling of auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the *Sārasvatī* [offering], ritualists recite: "One who has established the sacred fires and employs an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) should perform the expiatory *Sārasvatī* sacrifice."
"One should study grammar so that one does not become subject to expiatory rites.

The work was composed in twelve chapters;
it is also called the Nirukta.
This is because of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "in this [work], the possible constituent meanings of each individual word are stated exhaustively.

For there, having first proposed the thesis—"There are four classes of words: nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*)"—and having defined the nature of particles by stating that "they fall upon various high and low meanings," it is illustrated as follows: "'*na*' is used in the common language (*bhāṣā*) for the purpose of negation, as in *nendraṃ devamamaṃsata* ('they did not consider Indra a god'), where it serves the purpose of negation"; and "'*durmadāsaḥ na surāyām*' ('like those intoxicated by wine') is used for the purpose of comparison" (Nirukta 1.1; 4).

Furthermore, it is understood from this treatise that while in common usage the negative particle *na* serves solely for negation, in the Veda it functions as an illustration of both meanings: negation and comparison.
Thus, the specific etymological explanations (*nirvacana*) of various words stated by the author will be cited by us precisely at the occasion of explaining their respective mantras.
Nor should it be suspected that these etymologies are without foundation.
It is for the very purpose of such etymological derivation that certain word-explanations have been stated in the Brāhmaṇas; thus,
[we have] the Ṛgveda.
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He might strike me."
Thus it is also recorded elsewhere.

The accounts of Hariścandra, Anāciketa, and others, as well as the statements concerning Dharma and Brahman associated with Yoga, which are declared in the *Aitareya*, *Taittirīya*, *Kāṭhaka*, and other recensions (*śākhās*), have been made explicit in various historical works (*itihāsa*).
Furthermore, the creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth, declared in the Upaniṣads, have been clarified by the Brāhmaṇas and others in the Vādas and Purāṇas.
Cosmic creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manvantaras,
and the history of the dynasties— thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics.

Thus, since it is understood that the *Smṛtis* and other such texts are expounded by the *Purāṇas*, and because the sixteen categories—such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the objects of cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), and illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*)—are defined in the *Nyāyaśāstra*, one is able to reach a definitive conclusion according to those principles: "This sentence is authoritative regarding this matter, and not that one. Furthermore, the utility of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* and *Uttaramīmāṃsā* for the purpose of the Vedic meaning is indeed extremely clear.
In the *smṛtis* proclaimed by Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, and others, the procedures for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and other rites as taught in the Vedas are elaborated.

For instance, the rule for twilight worship begins with: "Now, indeed, these exponents of Brahman, facing east during the twilight, scatter upwards the waters consecrated by the *gāyatrī*" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.2).
Likewise, the rule for the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) begins with: "These five great sacrifices are continuously extended" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.10).
In this manner, other categories of knowledge should be understood.

Since the Purāṇas and other such works serve as aids for understanding the meaning of the Vedas according to the method described, it is appropriate that they constitute branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*).
Regarding the acquisition of knowledge enriched by these fourteen branches of learning, including the Purāṇas and others, there is a specific qualification for the seeker.
He has been illustrated by four mantras found in other treatises;
and Yāska cited those mantras (Nirukta 2.4).
Among them, this is the first mantra:
Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: "Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is envious, nor to one who is lacking in self-control, nor to one who is dull-witted; thus shall I be full of power."
Thus [it is said].
The deity presiding over knowledge approached the Brāhmaṇa teacher who was her instructor;
having arrived, she made this request:
"O Brāhmaṇa, protect me by not teaching me to one who is unqualified."
I am the cause of the human goals (puruṣārtha) for you, like a hidden treasure.
Whoever feels malice toward me, who am such [a source], or toward you, who are my teacher;
or whoever does not practice knowledge with sincerity—[for them, this is fruitless].
Do not speak of me to such pseudo-disciples who are not disciplined in the observances of bathing, sipping water, and other such customs;
for only by so doing shall I abide within your heart and bestow the fruit [of my teaching].
Now the second mantra:

"He who, by means of his unfailing [instruction], fills one's ears and bestows immortality while removing suffering—he should be regarded as both father and mother; one should not speak falsely or deceitfully to him."
Thus [it is said].

Having stated the rule for the teacher in the preceding mantra, the rule for the student is stated in this mantra. "False" refers to worldly speech that is untrue, devoid of the goals of human life, or unbeneficial; its opposite is "truth," namely the Vedic statement which is unfailing.

The teacher who pierces the ears of the disciple with such speech—that is, who completely fills them—is one who always causes [the student] to hear the Veda; for, by virtue of the prefix and the context, the root *tṛd* functions in a different sense. This is the meaning.
Doing what? Causing no suffering.
Causing the boy of dull intelligence—who is unable to grasp even half of the friendliness at first—to grasp a quarter or a portion of a quarter, in such a way that no suffering arises.
Furthermore, "bestowing the nectar" (amṛta):
the meaning of the Veda is called "nectar" because it brings about immortality—whether that be birth among the gods or liberation (mokṣa). He is one who performs the bestowal of that [meaning].
A good disciple should regard such a teacher as his primary father and mother.
While the parents who preceded him are indeed primary because they provided this inferior human body,
one must not commit even a single act of malice toward that teacher who is the very embodiment of one's primary father and mother.

Now the third mantra: 1. From the understanding of *ga*, *gha*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ya*, and *tvā*. 2. *Ṭa*: the Vedic statement. 3. *Ṭa*: *go* is indeed clear. 4. *Ca*, *cha*, *tha*, *pha*: thus. 5. *Ṭa*: at the very beginning. 6. *Cha*: of the immortal (*amṛtasya*). 7. *Ṭa*, *ṭha*, *tha*: the human body (*manuṣyaśarīra*). First Aṣṭaka, 31.
Those Brahmins who, having been taught by their teacher, do not respect him in word, thought, or deed—
just as they are not worthy of being fed by the teacher, even so does that sacred learning consume them.
Thus [it is said].

However, those base Brahmins who, though instructed by their teacher, do not honor him through humility, concern for his welfare, or service—being devoid of respect, these pseudo-disciples are not to be fed by the teacher; they are not fit to receive his grace. Indeed, the teacher does not bestow compassion upon them.

Just as they are not to be protected by the teacher, so too that Vedic statement, which was heard and taught by the teacher, does not protect those inferior disciples; the meaning is that it does not yield its fruit.
Now follows the fourth mantra:
"O Brahman, teach me to that man whom you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with the practice of celibacy;
to one who would never deceive you in this world—to such a guardian of the treasure, O Brahman, speak."
Thus [it is said].
O Teacher, you should impart this knowledge to that very principal disciple whom you know to be endowed with qualities such as purity;
moreover, to that principal disciple who would never at any time bear malice toward you— that guardian of your treasure— O Brahman, you should declare me, who am of the nature of the Veda.
Since the deity of knowledge has been thus entreated, the teacher must impart the Vedic knowledge to his principal disciple.
For that purpose, the Ṛgveda is being commented upon by us in accordance with its six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Since the Brāhmaṇa portion of the Veda—composed of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa—is useful for the explanation of the Mantras, the Brāhmaṇa, together with the Āraṇyaka section, has first been explained.
Now, by means of citations from the Brāhmaṇa found here and there, the Saṃhitā text, which consists of Mantras, is to be explained.

And that [Veda], beginning with "agnim īḷe" and ending with "yathā vaḥ susahāsati," consists of eight books (*kāṇḍa*) and ten *maṇḍalas*, comprising four or five chapters (*adhyāya*), eighty-five sections (*anuvāka*), slightly more than a thousand hymns (*sūkta*), slightly more than two thousand verses (*varga*), and slightly more than eight thousand *ṛc* verses.

The general application (*viniyoga*) of this entire work, according to the traditional order of recitation (*āmnāta-krama*), such as for the *brahmayajña* and silent recitation (*japa*), has already been stated previously.
However, the specific application (*viśeṣa-viniyoga*) in various sacrifices has been demonstrated by the author of the *Sūtras*.
And that application is threefold: the application of the hymn (*sūkta*), the application of the [hymn] beginning with "tat," and the application of each individual verse (*ṛc*).
In that context, the hymn beginning with "agnim īḷe" is prescribed for the Prātaranuvāka in the Agni sacrifice.
This application was formulated by Āśvalāyana in the thirteenth section of the fourth chapter: "avā no agne... [and] 'agnim īḷe'gnim dūtam'.
For in that case, the determination of the hymn is made by the mention of fewer than four quarters (pādas).
This is because it is defined by the technical rule: "The term *sūkta* [is used] at the beginning of a *sūkta*, even when a foot [of a verse] is missing" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 1.1).
In that *sūkta*, the second verse of the first *ṛc* is enjoined as the *yājyā* for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in the Pavamāna sacrifice.
This is formulated in the first section of the second chapter: "The two *saṃyājyā* verses are 'sāhāgnidhvā abhiyujaḥ' and 'agnim īḷe purohitam'."

In that context, because the entire foot is recited, it is understood to be an *ṛc*, since there is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): “The term *ṛc* [is used] when a foot is being recited” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.1). Similarly, when it is said, “the two *saṃyājyās*,” it is understood to refer to those belonging to Sviṣṭakṛt, because of the technical rule: “[When] ‘the two *saṃyājyās*’ are mentioned, they should be understood as those pertaining to Sviṣṭakṛt” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.1). Thus, there is a determination of their connection with Sviṣṭakṛt.
In that case as well, because it is cited as being the second mantra, it possesses the status of a *yājyā*.

Although the preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the recollection of the deity is already accomplished by this very *puronuvākyā* ending with "svāhā," nevertheless, the combination (*samuccaya*) of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* was deliberated upon in the fourth quarter of the twelfth chapter of the Mīmāṃsā: "Is the *yājyā* an alternative to the *puronuvākyā*, or are they combined?
It is an alternative, because the deity is manifested by either one alone."
There is a combination [of the two] because of the commonality of the *puronuvākyā* verses and because of the [scriptural] injunction;

for the function of manifesting the deity is one and the same. If it is argued that just as there is an option (*vikalpa*) between two pairs, so too there should be an option between the two [verses] contained within each pair, we say: not so.
This is because the designation "puronuvākyā" (invitatory verse) is unintelligible without a subsequent *yājyā* (offering verse).

Furthermore, by the direct scriptural statement, "Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, he offers with the *yājyā*," their concomitance (*sāhitya*) is enjoined, preceded by a mention of the distinction between the functions of indicating the deity and the offering of the oblation.
Therefore, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).

This hymn beginning with *abhí tvā śūra nonumaḥ* consists of nine verses, as stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*: "Agniṃ na yaḥ; Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra.
Since Madhucchandas, the son of Viśvāmitra, is the seer (*ṛṣi*) who perceived this hymn, he is its *ṛṣi*.

In former times, they attained these through austerity, having been authorized by the Self-born One himself.
Thus [it is said].

The traditional law (smṛti) records a transgression for the absence of knowledge regarding the seers and so forth: "He who teaches or even recites [the Veda] without knowing the seer, the meter, the deity, and the application— indeed, he becomes a sinner."
One who employs a mantra without knowing its seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), deity (daivata), the meaning of the Brāhmaṇa, as well as its accents and so forth, is called a "thorn in the mantra."
Thus.
And the method for understanding [mantras] is recorded in tradition: "The accent, the phoneme, the syllable, the prosodic measure, the application, and the meaning—
these must be understood step by step by one who desires to know the mantra."
Thus [it is said].
Although the meter of the *agnim īḷe* hymn and others is not mentioned here in the *Chandonukramaṇikā*, it is stated thus in the *Paribhāṣā*:
"In the beginning, before Hiraṇyastūpa, [the meter] is Gāyatrī" (*Anuvāka* 12.14).
This means that since Hiraṇyastūpa will be named as the seer (*ṛṣi*) of these mantras, the general meter for the mantras preceding him is Gāyatrī.
It is called *chandas* because it covers (*chādana*) the person, shielding them from connection with evil;
this is recorded in the *Āraṇyakakāṇḍa*: "The *chandases* indeed cover him from evil action" (*Ai. Ā. 2.5*).
Alternatively, it is called *chandas* because it covers the fire being piled (*cīyamāna*).

And the Taittirīyas record this: "Prajāpati piled the fire-altar; having become a horse, he stood still. The gods, being afraid, did not approach him. Desiring to cover themselves with the *chandases*, they [covered themselves]; that is the *chandastva* of the *chandases*" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.6.1).
Alternatively, it is called *chandaḥ* because it covers (*ācchādayati*) the one who is in the waters (*apsu*).

This is also recorded in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The gods, indeed, entered into the thoughts that were fleeing from death; they concealed themselves by means of the *chandases*; because they concealed themselves by these, that is the *chandastva* of the *chandases*" (Chānd. Up. 1.4.2).

Likewise, it is taught that the word *deva* is derived from the verbal root *div*, meaning "to shine": "'It has become light for us,' they said; that is the *devatva* of the gods. Therefore, one who shines is a *deva*.
The meaning is that it shines by means of the mantra.
Because it contains the word *styūman* [in the sense of "shining"], this hymn (*sūkta*) has two deities.
Thus it is stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*: "From *maṇḍala* onwards, it belongs to Agni and Indra" (Anu. 12.12).

2. [In other versions] the reading is "manujñātān."

3. The consonantal syllables *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *ya*. 4. *Ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *vā*. 5. *Ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *tha*, and *pha* prior to the *Hiraṇyastūpa* [sūtra]. 6. *Ga*, *ca*, *pha* belong to the *Hiraṇyastūpa*; *tha* belongs to the *Hiraṇyastūpa*s.

7. The syllables *na-cha-ya-pha* do not exist as "iti. 8. *Ta-agni naya madhucchandā vaiśvāmitra* was the beginning; thus ends the first book (*maṇḍala*), the first chapter (*anuvāka*), the first hymn (*sūkta*), and the twenty-third [verse] of the first *aṣṭaka*.

Oṃ. I praise Agni, the domestic priest, the divine ministrant of the sacrifice, the invoker who bestows the most abundant treasures. (1) Oṃ. Agni. I praise. The domestic priest. Of the sacrifice. The divine one. The ministrant. The invoker. The bestower of the most abundant treasures. (1)
I praise—that is, I laud—the deity named Agni.
The verbal root is *īḍ* (in the sense of "to praise");
