In the word *indra*, there is the acute accent on the first syllable due to its being a vocative (*āmantrita*).
In the word *ā*, there is the acute accent on the first syllable because it is a particle (*nipāta*).
[The word] *citrabhāno*.
Following the word *padāt*, there is the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the suppression of the accent of the vocative).
In the sense of "desiring for oneself," the suffix *kyac* is added to the word *yuṣmad* by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8).
Then, by the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.98), the substitution of *tvad* occurs for the portion ending in *map*.
The suffix *u* is added after the root ending in *kyac* by Pāṇini’s rule 3.2.170 (*kyāc chandasi*).

When *svayave* is obtained, although the rule 7.2.86 (*yuṣmadasmador anādeśe*) prescribes *āvaṃ* only before case-endings, here by way of irregularity (*vyatyayena*), *āvaṃ* is applied even before a consonant-initial suffix.
The vowel *u* is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the accent of the suffix.
The word *aṇu* denotes subtlety (*saukṣmya*). Through association with that quality, it is applied here to the fingers.
Although the suffix *ṅīp* would have been expected by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.44), the suffix *ṅīn* is used instead by way of a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).
The particle *niṣ* is udātta at the beginning.
This particle *tanā* is always used in the sense of "necessarily" (*nityam*), and because it is a particle, it is udātta at the beginning. [The word] *putāsaḥ*.
The suffix *isuk* is applied [to the word *adya*] by the rule *āja-serasuka* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.50).

1. *ṭha*—the cause for the substitution of *irāman*. 2. *ta*—the juice of *somavalī*. 3. *ṭha*—and that. 4. *ca-cha-ta-tha-pha*—the acute accent (*udāttatva*). 5. *gha-ca-kṣa-ta-tha-tva* occurs here; *cha-ṇa-ya-tva* occurs in *yava*.

**indra ā yāhi dhiyeṣito viprajūtaḥ sutāvata upa brahmāṇi vāghataḥ || 5 ||** O Indra, come hither, impelled by our prayer, urged by the wise, to the sacred hymns of the worshipper who has pressed the Soma. || 5 ||
O Indra, come to yourself; come to this ritual action.
For what purpose? To approach the *brahmāṇi*—the Vedic hymns in the form of the Vedas—of the *vāghataḥ*, the officiating priests.
Of what nature is he?
He is impelled—that is, attained—by our intellect, meaning he is urged by our wisdom (*asmadyakṣyā*). He is driven forward by inspired thought (*viprajūtaḥ*).
Just as he was impelled by the devotion of the sacrificer, so too was he impelled by other wise brahmins, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Of what sort was the *vāghat*?
He was "possessing the pressed juice" (*sutāvat*), meaning he was provided with the soma that had been pressed out.
Among the eleven names for wisdom beginning with *kena*, the term *dhīḥ* is listed (Nirukta 3.9.7).
Among the twenty-four names for the wise, the terms *vipraḥ* and *dhīraḥ* are listed (Nirukta 3.15.1).
Among the eight names for officiating priests beginning with *bharatāḥ*, the term *vāghataḥ* is listed (Nirukta 3.18.3).

In the word *iṣita*, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *iṣ* in the sense of "going," and there is no insertion of the augment *iṭ*. Since the augment *iṭ* is unaccented according to the rule "augments are unaccented" (*āgamā anudāttāḥ*), the accent of the suffix *kvip* remains. [The word is] *viprajūtaḥ*.

The word *vipra* is derived from the verbal root *ḍuvap* in the sense of "sowing a seed" (*bījasaṃtāne*). It is formed with the suffix *ran*, according to the rule *ṛtendrāgravatravipra* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.166) and others, and is thus established as a *nipātana* (irregularly formed word).
Due to the prefix *ni*, the vowel *i* of the root *vap* is substituted, and there is an absence of the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
Because of the prefix *ni*, the word is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable).
Driven by them, he arrived.
The root *ju* (or *jū*) is a Vedic (sautra) root used here according to its literal meaning (Pāṇini 3.2.150).
The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "śrukaḥ kiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.11).
By the rule "The third [case-ending] is used for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.2), there is the accentuation of the preceding word as in *abrahmahatyā*.
In *sutāvataḥ*,
the lengthening is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Because the suffix *mat* is unaccented (*anudātta*), the accent of the suffix *kap* alone remains.
In the word *brahmāṇi*, the initial syllable is udātta according to the rule "nabviṣayasthānisantasya" (Phiṭ-sūtra 26).
*vāghachanda* is listed among the names of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
it bears the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).

O Indra, come swiftly; O Lord of the Bay Horses, approach our sacred prayers. Bestow upon us favor at the pressing of the juice. 6. O Indra, come! Swiftly! Toward our sacred hymns! O Lord of the Bay Steeds! At the pressed soma, grant us your pleasure! 6.

The word *hari* is the name of Indra’s two horses, because it is recited among his names in the passage: "The two bay steeds (*harī*) belong to Indra; the ruddy ones (*rohita*) to Agni" (Nirukta 1.15.1).
O *harivaḥ*, Indra associated with the horses, come here to approach our sacred prayers (*brahmāṇi*). Of what nature are you?
You are the one who repeatedly impels the path of the voice.

And having come here, at this rite involving the pressing of Soma performed by our son, accept—hold and take for yourself—our *canas*, that is, our food characterized as the oblation (*havis*). This is the meaning.

*tūtujān*: This is the substitute *kānac* for the *liṭ* [perfect] tense of the root *tuj*, according to Pāṇini 3.2.106 (*liṭaḥ kānaj vā*). The lengthening of the reduplicated syllable occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.7 (*tujādīnāṃ dīrgho'bhyāsasya*).
The word *harivaḥ* has its initial syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*) by Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.189, *abhyastānām ādiḥ*.

In the form *harivaḥ*, the suffix *matup* is applied in the sense of "one who possesses these [bay horses]," and the *m* of *matup* is changed to *v* by Pāṇini’s rule 8.2.15, *chandasi iraḥ*. In the vocative case, the augment *num* is added by Pāṇini’s rule 7.1.70, *ugidacām*.

In the elision of the final consonant of a *saṃyoga* (Pāṇini 8.2.23), the *nakāra* undergoes the substitution of *ru* by the rule "the *ru* [is substituted] for *mat* and *vas* in the vocative in the Veda" (Pāṇini 8.3.1). There is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) according to the eighth book [of Pāṇini].

Because there is no semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) between *brahmāṇi* and *harivaḥ*, the restriction "a grammatical operation concerning words applies only when they are semantically connected" (Pāṇini 2.1.1) precludes the application of the rule for the *parāṅgvadbhāva* of a vocative following a vocative; consequently, since the *nighāta* of the vocative does not apply, the word retains its initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*), and thus the vowel *a* in *upa* becomes more depressed (*sannatara*).
1. In manuscript Ṭha, "vedarūpāṇi" is absent.
2. In manuscript Ca, it reads "tathā tairapi". 3. In manuscript Ṭha, it reads "jihvāyā iḍā".
4. *ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pha-ya-mantrita-parāṅvadvā*; *ya-mantrita* [is] optionally treated as *parāṅvat*. In the form *dadhiṣva*, there is the suffix *thās* in the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *dhā*.
[By Pāṇini 3.4.80: *thāsaḥ se*.

By the rule *savābhyāṃ vāmau* (Pāṇini 3.4.91), the substitution of *v* for the vowel *e* occurs. Since both [the suffixes] are designated as *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), there is the addition of the suffix *śap* because they are *sārvadhātuka* (Pāṇini 3.1.68), followed by reduplication (*dvirbhāva*) because of the *luṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.10), and the augment *iṭ* because they are *ārdhadhātuka* (Pāṇini 7.2.35).
Finally, the elision of the long *ā* occurs by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64).

The word *canaḥ* is derived from the root *cāy* with the suffix *asun*, according to the rule *cāyateśca hrasvaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.639). Due to the letter *ca* [in the sūtra], there is the augment *nuṭ* and the elision of the *ya*.
O protectors of men, you All-Gods who uphold the people, come hither;
you who give, come to the pressed juice of the giver.
O protectors, upholders of the people, all you gods, come hither to the pressed juice of the donor who gives. 7.
O Viśvedevas—those specific deities so named—come hither, come toward the pressed Soma of the *dāśvāṃs*, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation.
And those gods are *omāsaḥ*, protectors; *carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ*, sustainers of men; and *dāśvāṃsaḥ*, givers of the fruit [of sacrifice].
The word *carṣaṇi* is listed among the twenty-five names for "men" in the *Nighaṇṭu* (2.3.8).
Among the twenty-nine names of specific deities beginning with "Aśvinau," the term "Viśvedevas" and "Sādhyas" is recited [in Nirukta 5.6.27].

Regarding this mantra, he (Yāska) has explained it as follows: "Whether they be protectors or those worthy of being protected, all the gods bestowed by men, come here; [the gods] have given [the gift] to the one who gave. Thus, this very same *vaiśvadeva* triplet in the *gāyatrī* meter is found among the *daśatīyas*. Whatever [verse] has many deities (*bahudaivata*) is employed in the place of the *vaiśvadevas*, provided it possesses the characteristic of "all" (*viśva*). This is the opinion of Śākapūṇi. In this context, Yāska’s view is that the word *viśva* is a synonym for the word *sarva* ("all").
According to the opinion of Śākapūṇi, this is the unique characteristic mark of a particular class of gods.

The word *omāsaḥ* refers to the gods (*devāḥ*) because they protect (*avanti*). Following the recurrence of the root *man*, the suffix *man* is applied according to the rule: “The suffix *man* is added after the roots *avi*, *si*, and *vi* with the augment *bhu* [and is *kit*]” (Uṇādi-sūtra 1.141).

The substitution *ūṭ* occurs by the rule *jvaratvarastrivimavām upadhāyāś ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.20). Although the suffix *man* is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*), *guṇa* substitution takes place due to its being included among the *bahulaka* (irregular) cases. The augment *asuk* is added to *jas* by the rule *ājaserasuk* (Pāṇini 7.1.50).
The word *āmantrita* (vocative) has an acute accent on its first syllable. *Carṣaṇīyaḥ* means humans;
the gods are called *carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ* because they sustain them through the granting of rain and other such favors.

Regarding the preceding vocative in the general sense, because of the prohibition [of the rule] *avidyamānavat* by the sūtra *vibhāṣitaṃ viśeṣavacane bahuvacanam* (Pāṇini 8.1.74), there is *nighāta* (anudātta accentuation) due to its not being at the beginning of a *pāda*. If it is objected: "But since it is indeed present [as a word], then by the rule *subāmantrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), it would behave like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavat*), resulting in the absence of a single *pada*; how then can there be *nighāta* on the grounds of being followed by another *pada*? The answer is: No.
Because of the statement *vaskaraṇaṃ svāśrayam api yathā syāt* (Pāṇinian Mahābhāṣya on 8.1.72), the *nighāta* conditioned by the distinction of *pada*s is also established.

Even if there were a single word (*aikapadya*) with an initial acute accent, the grave accent (*nighāta*) would certainly apply by the rule "a word [consisting of more than one syllable] has all its syllables grave except for one" (Pāṇini 6.1.158).

If it is argued that in this very case, in the phrase *dravatpāṇī śubhravatī*, the subsequent part [of the compound] would likewise incur the grave accent as a remainder (*śeṣanighāta*) because it behaves like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavat*), we say no; for in that instance, the status of behaving like a subordinate member is overridden by the subsequent rule "a preceding vocative is treated as non-existent" (Pāṇini 8.1.72), which renders it as if non-existent.

In this case, however, because the rule "the plural is used for a specific mention when [the singular] has been optionally stated" (*vibhāṣitaṃ viśeṣavacane bahuvacanam*) prohibits the treatment as non-existent (*avidyamānavatva*), the preceding vocative is also considered existent; thus, its status as a subordinate element (*parāṅgavatva*) is accepted, which constitutes a difference [from the previous case]. *viśve*.
The word *viśve* is udātta on its first syllable because it begins with a vowel (*pādādi*).

Furthermore, the word *viśva* here denotes the deities of the *gaṇas*; it is not a synonym for the word *sarva*. Because it functions as a general term intended to qualify [the following], it does not stand in apposition with *omāsaḥ*.

For if there were apposition, then since the preceding *pāda* would be treated as a subordinate member (*parāṅgavat*), the rule regarding the initial accentuation of a vocative (*āmantritāyudāttatā*)—as seen in examples such as *mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhau*—would not apply here either.
Furthermore, the word *devāsaḥ* is a qualifier of *ke it*.
They are called *devāḥ* because they shine (*dīvyanti*), meaning they possess luminosity.

Now, one might object: "Since the conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the etymological meaning of its parts" (Paribhāṣā 98), the conventional (*rūḍha*) sense of the word *deva* should be accepted, not its etymological (*yaugika*) sense.
1. In the *ṭha* manuscript, the word "ca" is absent. 2. In the *cha*, *ta*, and *tha* manuscripts, it reads "dekamiva.
For if [the term] were used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), the comprehension would be hindered by the mediation of reflecting upon the meanings of the individual parts.

If it is argued that there is no deviation [from the rule] when the word is established as a conventional whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*), we say no. For if the word *deva* were established as a conventional whole, it would refer to the general class and thus lack the status of a specific term (*viśeṣavacana*). Consequently, because it would not be designated by the rule "the plural is optionally used for a specific term" (*vibhāṣitam viśeṣavacanam bahuvacanam*), the word *devāsaḥ*—just like the word *śubhaspatī*—would necessarily have its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) due to the absence of the specific [plural] designation. Furthermore, following the requirements of accentuation, it is indeed appropriate to accept the etymological derivation (*yoga*) of the word *deva*, even at the expense of abandoning its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).
"Come! Come hither!
When the *śap* affix is elided by Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.73 (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), the elision of the letter *m* occurs according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.37 (*anudāttaupadeśa...*) and so forth.
Because the prefix *āṅ* follows a word (*padāt*), the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) applies.

*dāśvāṃsaḥ*: From the root *dāś* in the sense of "to give," the form *dāśvān* is derived by means of the suffix *kvasu*. Due to the specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*) at Pāṇini 6.1.12—“*dāśvān*, *sāhvān*, *mīḍhvāṃsaḥ*”—the augment *iṭ* required by the general rule for roots beginning with *krī* (Pāṇini 7.2.13) does not occur, nor does reduplication. By the accent of the suffix, the *kvasu* itself bears the udātta accent.
In the word *dāśuṣaḥ*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.131, *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*.
Thereafter, by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.108, *saṃprasāraṇācca*, the single substitute for the preceding and following vowels (*pūrvarūpa*) is applied.
Finally, the substitution of *ṣ* is applied by Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.59, *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*.
May all the gods, the swift crossers of waters, come quickly to the pressed juice, as oxen go to their stalls.
O gods, swift crossers of the waters, come quickly to the pressed juice, as oxen go to their stalls. 8.
May the Viśvedevas—specific deities who are a group bearing that name—come quickly to the pressed Soma.
Of what nature are they? They are *apturas*, meaning those who bestow rain at the appropriate times.
"Swift," meaning they are yoked for the sake of heaven and are free from the impurity of sloth toward favoring the sacrificer.
Regarding the arrival of all the gods toward the Soma, there is the illustration beginning with "oxen" (*ustrā*):
just as the "oxen"—that is, the rays of the sun—arrive day by day without sloth, so too [do the gods].
Among the fifteen names of the rays beginning with *khedayaḥ*, the term *ustrā vasavaḥ* is recited (Nirukta 1.5.9).
Among the twelve names of the days beginning with *vastoḥ*, the term *svasarāṇi dhraṃsaḥ gharmaḥ* is recited (Nirukta 1.9.5).
And that word has been explained by Yāska: "The *svasarāṇi* are the days, for they move of their own accord (*svayaṃ-sārīṇi*); or else, *svar* is the sun, and he causes them to move."
"There is also a Vedic verse [Nirukta 5.4]: 'Like camels [going] to their pastures.'"
*Devāsaḥ*: formed by adding the suffix *ac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134), it is anudātta because of its *cittva* status. *Apturaḥ*: from the root *tura* meaning "to sound," with the *ślu* vikaraṇa.
The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of "they sound forth" by the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76).
The original accent of the final member of the compound is maintained by the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139).
[O ye gods,] come hither!
The form *āgacchantu* is used here with the middle voice plural ending (*madhyamapuruṣabahuvacana*) by way of grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*) in the sense of “let them come.
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.73), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.

For that [suffix], by the rule *tasan-asan-athanāś-ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.45), the substitution of *ta* occurs; however, because of the prohibition [of the substitution of *ṅit*] by the rule *apit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), and since [the substitute] is not *ṅit*, there is no elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*).
The word *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* [in the previous rule] indicates the *nighāta* (non-accentuation).
From the root *tvar* in the sense of "haste" (*saṃbhrame*), those who sound forth are called *tūrṇyaḥ*.
Following the recurrence of the prefix *niḥ*, the suffix *nip* is applied according to the Unādi Sūtra 4.491: *vahi-śri-vraśc-ud-glahā-vāra-vāribhyo nit*.
It is accented on the first syllable by the rule *nittvād ādyudāttaḥ*.

In the phrase *ustrā iva*, there is no elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktyalopa*) and the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*) because of the rule *ivena* (Pāṇini 2.1.4–5); thus, in this compound, the original accent of the preceding member is obligatory.
That which moves (*sarati*) is *saraḥ*, namely the sun (*sūrya*).
[The suffix] *ac* is applied after [the root] *pac* and others.
Those days (*ahāni*) in which there is a *svas* (light/sun) are called *svasarāṇi*.
According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.2.1, "In a *bahuvrīhi*, the preceding member retains its original accent," the word *sva-* is acute-accented on its first syllable.

1. By means of the connection with *ṭha*. 2. *ta*, *sa*, and *etannāma* [are used]. 3. In *cha* and *pha*, "coming ones, let them come. 4. In *ṭha*, "the *amuras* are those who hasten the waters. 5. In *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, and *pha*, there is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) with the particle *iva*:
"May all the gods, the unerring ones, possessing the power of illusion (*ehimāyās*), free from malice (*adruhas*), the bearers (*vahnis*), enjoy the sacrifice (*medham juṣanta*)."
May all the gods, who are unfailing, whose powers are infallible, and who are free from malice—may these bearers of the oblation enjoy the sacrifice. 9.
May the Viśvedevas—specific deities of that name—enjoy and partake of this *medha*, the sacrificial oblation connected with the sacrifice.
Of what nature are they?
They are *vasavaḥ*, meaning those who are free from decay or free from exhaustion.
*Ehimāyāsaḥ*: those whose wisdom (*prajñā*) pervades everywhere.
Alternatively, when they said to Saucīka as he was entering the waters, "Come! Do not go!", this designation of the gods as *ehimāyāsaḥ* is based on the imitation of that [utterance].
*vadruhaḥ*: free from malice; *vahnayaḥ*: carriers, those who bring wealth;
*astridhaḥ*:
[the negative particle] *nañ* with the suffix *kvip* (Pāṇini 3.3.108.9) applied to *stridh*, which signifies either destruction (*kṣaya*) or drying up (*śoṣaṇa*), used in the plural.
The word is oxytone due to the rule that the final syllable of a *kṛt*-derived compound retains its original accent (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).

Alternatively, in the sense of "he purifies" (*punāti*), the absence of the short vowel *i* and the oxytonic accent in the form ending in the suffix *ṇu*— according to Pāṇini 7.3.44, which prescribes *i* for the vowel preceding *k* when followed by a suffix beginning with *āp* and not being a *sup*— should be understood as a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
The word *saraḥ* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it ends in the suffix *-as*.
Due to the accentuation rules for the suffixes *matup* and *ḍīp*, which are marked with *p*, they are unaccented.
[The word] *vājebhiḥ*.
The word *vāja* is accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group (Pāṇini 6.1.203);
for it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* since it is not etymologically derived [by specific suffixes].
Thus, "actions possessing food" (*vājinyaḥ kriyāḥ*) means actions in which there is food (*anna*).
The suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *ata iniṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.2.115).
That Sarasvatī who possesses those actions (*kriyā*) is called *vājinīvatī*. The substitution of *va* for the *matup* suffix is according to the rule *chandasīraḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.15).
Because the *matup* and *piḍīp* suffixes are *anudātta* (unaccented), the initial *udātta* (acute) accent of the suffix *ina* alone remains.
[The word] *yajñam*: the suffix *naṅ* is applied by the rule “*yajayāca*” (Pāṇini 3.3.90).
It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (pratyayasvara).
*Vadhū*: from the root *vaś* in the sense of "desire."
*Kāntiḥ* means longing (*abhilāṣaḥ*).
By the rule *adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.72), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*; consequently, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent).
*Dhiyāvasuḥ*:
she from whose presence wealth (*vasu*) arises through wisdom (*dhī*) and ritual action (*karman*) is *dhiyāvasuḥ*.
According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.168, *māvekācaḥ*, the case ending is udātta.
By the rule "in a bahuvrīhi compound, the first member retains its original accent" (Pāṇini 6.2.1), the accent of the case-ending alone remains;
there is no elision (luk) of the third case-ending due to Vedic usage.
Inciting true words, awakening wise thoughts,
Sarasvatī has established the sacrifice.
Inciting words of truth, perceiving auspicious thoughts, Sarasvatī has established the sacrifice. 11.
That Sarasvatī has upheld (dhāre) this sacrifice—
what kind of goddess?
She is the impeller (codayitrī), the one who urges on pleasant and truthful words.
"Sumatīnām" means of those practitioners endowed with excellent intelligence; "cetantī" means making known that which is to be performed by them.
Codayitrī:
from the root *cuda* in the sense of "impelling," with the suffix *tṛc* added to the causative (*pyantāt*).
Because it ends in the suffix *cvi*, it is udātta on its final syllable.
By the rule *ṛtvebhyo ḍīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5), the feminine suffix *ḍīp* is applied;
its [final vowel] becomes udātta by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.174).
Regarding *sūnṛtānām*:

from the root *ūn* in the sense of "diminution" (*parihāṇe*), by the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76), the suffix *kvip* is applied. Thus, that which "completely diminishes" (*sutarām ūnayati*) what is unpleasant is called *sūna*, meaning "the pleasant. Since that [pleasant thing] is also "true" (*satya*), it is *sūnṛta*.
The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member [of the compound] is due to Pāṇini’s rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam* (6.2.199).
[The form] *cetantī* [is derived from] the root *citī* in the sense of “perceiving” (*saṃjñāne*).
In this case, because the suffixes *śap* and *ḍīp* are marked with *pi*, they are unaccented;
likewise, because the suffix *śatṛ* follows a root taught with a short *a*, it is unaccented by the accent rule for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes.
Thus, the accent of the verbal root alone remains.
In the word *sumati*, because the suffix *matup* contains a short vowel, the case ending receives the udātta accent according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.177: *nāminyatarasyām*.
A great flood is Sarasvatī; she makes herself known by her banner. She illumines all sacred thoughts.
The great flood, Sarasvatī, awakens with her signal; she illumines all our thoughts and shines forth everywhere. 12.
For Sarasvatī is of two kinds: as a corporeal deity and in the form of a river.
Of these, the former was established by the previous two verses;
by this [verse], however, she is established in the form of a river.
Such Sarasvatī, by her banner—that is, by her activity in the form of a flowing current—makes known, or brings to light, the great flood, that is, the abundant water.
Furthermore, in her own purposeful form as a deity, she shines forth, or specifically illumines, all *dhiyaḥ*—that is, all the insights of those who perform the rites;
the meaning is that she provides all the cognitions regarding the objects of ritual performance.
Yāska demonstrates the dual nature of Sarasvatī: "In this regard, there are Vedic citations for the word *sarasvatī* both as a river and as a deity" (Nirukta 2.23).
Among the one hundred and one names for water, it is listed as "arṇaḥ kṣodaḥ" (Ni. 1.12.1).

Yāska explains this Ṛgvedic verse: "The great flood (*arṇaḥ*), Sarasvatī, makes known and causes to understand by means of a signal—either through action or through wisdom—and all these various cognitions..."

"rājati" (Nirukta 11.270). *Maho arṇaḥ*: "mahaḥ" [is derived from] "mahat," where the letter *t* is replaced by *s* through metathesis (*vyatyaya*). Its short vowel is subject to *guṇa*. It is oxytone (*antodātta*) by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). When the rule "eṅaḥ padāntādati" (Pāṇini 6.1.109) would have required the formation of a single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*), the rule "prakṛtyāntaḥpādampare" (Pāṇini 6.1.115) causes the original form to remain (*prakṛtibhāva*). The meaning is "he flows. [The word *arṇaḥ* is formed] with the suffix *asun* and the augment *nuṭ*, according to the rule "udake juṭ ca" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.636). *Ketunā*: oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem. *Viśvāḥ*: the word *viśva-* ends in the suffix *kan* and is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). || 6 || || 1 ||
In the first maṇḍala, in the second anuvāka, there are four hymns.
Among them, this first hymn beginning with "surūpa" consists of ten verses, as indicated by the statement: "'surūpakṛtnum,' ten [verses].
Following the previous [rules], the recurrence of Madhucchandas and the Gāyatrī meter applies; thus, those two remain the seer and the meter.
Because of the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the fourth ṛc, "Ask Indra," Indra is the deity.

In the morning pressing of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin during the Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, when there is an increase in the stoma, there are six hymns for insertion (*āvāpa*), beginning with "surūpakṛtnum utaye. This is stated in the section titled "The days of the Abhiplava-Pṛṣṭha" in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra: "For the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the six hymns beginning with 'surūpakṛtnum utaye' [are to be recited]. (Āśva. Śr. S. 7.5).
The first three hymns are to be recited at the Mahāvrata sacrifice during the Niṣkevalya Śastra, in the Auṣṇiha and Cārṣāta meters.
And it has been stated by Śaunaka: "The three [hymns] beginning with *surūpakṛtnumūtaye* and the hymn *indra sānasiṃ rayim*" (AiĀ 5.2.5).
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), the verse *surūpakṛtnumūtaye* is the optional *stotriya* triplet for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
This is because it is prescribed in the *khaṇḍa* on the *hotrakas* in the rule: "For at every exhilaration you are our giver, O maker of beautiful forms, for our aid" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.4);

and because in the *vaiśvadeva-śastra* of the *agniṣṭoma*, the verse beginning with "for our aid, the maker of beautiful forms" is to be recited in a continuous stream, as prescribed by the rule: "They fashioned the chariot for our aid, the maker of beautiful forms" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.18).

For our protection, we offer oblations at dawn to the one who creates beautiful forms, as one calls a good milch-cow for the sake of the milker. 1. To the creator of beautiful forms, for our aid; as to a cow that yields milk well, for the milker; we offer oblations at the vigorous dawn. 1.
We invoke Indra—the performer of beautiful deeds, the maker of forms endowed with splendor—for our protection, day by day, at every dawn.
As for the illustration of this invocation:
we call him as one calls a well-milking cow for the sake of a milker.
Just as in the world, a cowherd calls the cow that is to be milked for his own sake by means of a loud call, so it is here;
among the twelve names of days beginning with "vastoḥ," the word "gharṣivadyavi" is recited (Nirukta 1.9.12).
*Surūpakṛtnum*:
"Kṛtnu" means one who performs (*karoti*).
[The suffix] *kanu* is applied after the roots *kṛ* and *han* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.310).
Due to its being a *kit*, there is an absence of *guṇa*. The addition of the letter *t* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
It is accented on the final syllable due to being a compound (*samāsa*).
For the sake of protection (*ūtaye*).
Following the rule "the [suffix] is udātta" (*udāttaḥ*), the suffix *kin* is prescribed as an udātta nipātana by Pāṇini 3.3.97: "*ūti-yūti-sāti-heti-kṛti-yañ ca*".
[The word is] *sudughām*.

"She who yields well" is *sudughā*. According to Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.2.70 (*duhaḥ kaśca*), there is the suffix *kap*, and the letter *h* is replaced by *gh*. Because the suffix is marked with the *k*-indicator (*kit*), there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
Because the suffix *kap* is treated as having a liquid (*pittva*), it is acutely accented on its final syllable; thus, by the accentual rule for verbal roots (*dhātusvara*), the vowel *u* is acute.
In a *gati*-compound with the word *su*, that same accent remains by the rule of the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).
In an *iva*-compound, according to the rule "In an *iva*-compound, there is no elision of case-endings and the first member retains its original accent," that same accent likewise remains.
One who milks the cow is a *godhuk* (cow-milker). The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *sṛghasṛ...* (Pāṇini 3.2.61),
and the accentuation follows the rule for the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
We sacrifice (*juhumasi*). In the first person plural of the root *hve*, the substitution of *śru* for *śap* occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.76).

Furthermore, by the rule *abhyastasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.33), the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the root *hve*—which is the cause of its being termed "repeated" (*abhyasta*)—occurs prior to the reduplication.
By the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), there is substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*).
By the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), there is lengthening.
Then, by the rule *ślau* (Pāṇini 6.1.10), there is reduplication.
By *abhyāsasya hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.59), [the reduplication] becomes short; by *suvajabhve* (Pāṇini 7.4.62; 8.4.53).
By *idanto misaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.46), there is the augment *i*. By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the *m*-sound—
1. When the *uṣṇih* meter consists of the ganas *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ya*, it is called *ārṣī*.
(Kārikā 8.58)
Ṛgveda:
the state of being udātta;
gha-vidya-vi.
The word *śas* is oxytone by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
There is reduplication according to Pāṇini 8.1.4: *nityavīpsayoḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 8.1.2: *tasya param āgreḍitam*, and 8.1.3: *anudāttaṃ ca*, the second member [of the reduplicated form] is unaccented (*anudātta*).
Come to our libations; O drinker of Soma, drink of the Soma!
For this exhilaration bestows cattle upon us.
Come to our libations; O drinker of Soma, drink of the Soma! For you, the giver of cattle, the exhilaration is indeed rich in wealth. 2.
O Soma-drinker, O Indra, drinker of Soma, come near to our three libations—the three pressings—to drink the Soma;
and having arrived, drink the Soma.
May your exhilaration, O wealthy one, be the giver of cattle.
The meaning is that when you are pleased, we obtain the cattle.
*Upa*: because it is a particle (*nipāta*), it is accented on the first syllable.
*Savanā*.
"Savanāni" refers to the pressings [of Soma], derived from the root *sū* in the sense "Soma is pressed for these.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.117; the case-ending (*sup*) is replaced by *ḍā*, and there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
By the rule *liti* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.193), the vowel preceding the suffix is acute. [The form] *gahi*:
from the root *gam*, there is elision of the *śap* suffix by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.73).
Because it occurs twice, there is the elision of the letter *m* by the rule “*anudāttaupadeśa°*” (Pāṇini 6.4.37).

Regarding the application of the rule “*ato heḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.4.105), which prescribes the elision [of the suffix *hi*], the elision of *m* prescribed by the rules concerning the *ābha* suffixes becomes as if non-existent (*asiddhavat*) according to the rule “*asiddhavadatrā bhāt*” (Pāṇini 6.4.22). Thus, one obtains *somapāḥ*.
The *nighāta* (anudātta accent) is applied by the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19).
Even though that [vocative] is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), the *nighāta* of *pibati* occurs by virtue of its dependence on what precedes it, according to the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.

Nor does the preceding word also become non-existent due to the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) with respect to what follows, because such a status is absent here due to a lack of syntactic connection (*asāmarthya*).
"Godāḥ" means "one who gives a cow.

Although the suffix *kvip* [would normally apply] by the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76), the suffix *vic* is applied instead by the rule *āto maninkanibvanipaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.74), because it is a *pratipadavidhi* (a rule prescribing a suffix immediately after a specific word).
For if *kvip* were used, the vowel *ā* of the root would be changed to *ī* by the rule *dhumāsthā°* (Pāṇini 6.4.66) and others.
*Revān*:

This is formed with the possessive suffix *matup*, meaning "one who has wealth (*rayi*)"; according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.176, "The *matup* [suffix] is acute after a word ending in a short vowel or the augment *nuṭ*. Thus, the *matup* is accented on its first syllable.
The substitution of *v* [for *m*] occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.15 (*chandasi iraḥ*).
By Pāṇini 6.1.37.6 (*rayimantau bahulaṃ chandasi*), there is *saṃprasāraṇa*, the substitution of the subsequent vowel for the preceding one, and *guṇa*. [Thus we have] *madaḥ*.
By the rule *‘mado’nupasarge’* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.67), the suffix *ap* is applied; [the resulting form] is unaccented (*anudātta*) because it begins with a prefix (*piba-*).
Now, of those most intimate thoughts of yours, which have three abodes—do not overlook us; come hither!
Now, O you who dwell in the three abodes of our most intimate thoughts, do not overlook us; come hither! 3.
Now, after the drinking of Soma—O Indra, standing among those most intimate, most proximate, and excellent-minded persons endowed with noble wisdom, may we know you as the threefold abode.
[The word] *brahma* [is used here].
The phrase "for the sake of obtaining" (*lābhārtham*) is to be supplied, meaning for the sake of attaining the *sumatīnām*—those of noble intellect—pertaining to the performance of ritual acts.
The meaning is: "I shall remember you for the sake of attaining wisdom.
You too, do not speak excessively of us (*ati mā khyaḥ*); do not describe our true nature to others. Rather, come (*ā gahi*)—come to us alone.
The particle *atha* is udātta on its first syllable; this is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.136, *nipātasya ca*. [Note: 1.
The term *sarūpam* does not exist in the Ṭha commentary.]
2. Ṭha—‘Revataḥ’;
3. Ṭha—‘śobhanaprajñānām’ is absent.
Thus [is] the lengthening of the vowel.
Regarding *antamānām*:

[the suffix] *tamap* is used in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyane*), according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.55. By Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.149, there is the elision of the *tādi* [portion] in the case of *tama*, resulting in the form *tama*. Thus, it means "those who are exceedingly near" (*atiśayenāntikāḥ*).

That which has an end (*anta*) is *antika*, meaning "near. The suffix *ṭhan* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.2.115 (*ata iniṭhanau*). Because it is a *nivādi* suffix, it is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

For there is no end to excellence in terms of distance; however, regarding excellence in terms of proximity, whatever is near to something is its very limit. Because of this principle, "near" (*samīpa*) is called "limit" (*antika*).
It exists.

In the potential mood (*vetteḷiṅ*), the suffix *yāsuṭ* is acute-accented and marked with the *ṅit* indicator, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.103: "In the Parasmaipada, *yāsuṭ* is acute and *ṅit*. Because it occurs at the beginning of a metrical foot (*pādādi*), it does not undergo elision of accent (*nighāta*) by the rule *tiṅatiṅaḥ*. [The word is] *sumatīnām*.

Even though the word *mati* ends in the suffix *kin*, the vowel *i* is udātta by the rule *mantrē vr̥ṣēpacamanavidabhūvīrā udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.96). In the compound *sumatayaḥ* ("those whose thoughts are excellent"), because it is a *bahuvrīhi* and follows the rule for the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakr̥tisvaratva*), the *e* [of *su*] is udātta. Thus: "Let them not speak ill of us from any other side, even from afar... [RV 10.37.12].
Bestowing their service upon Indra alone.
Or let our revilers say: "Withdraw from elsewhere, offering worship only to Indra. (5)

"Of us"—that is, of our own—referring to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), as is understood from the context; let them speak, let them praise Indra. Furthermore, O revilers, you who are censurers, depart, go out from this place.
From another place—that is, even from a different location—[they come] going forth.
Of what sort are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)? They are those who offer, that is, perform, service (*duvas*) unto Indra.
The word "iccha" (let them) is used for emphasis;
the meaning is: "Let them remain performing service at all times."
They are called *nidaḥ* because they revile; [the root] *ṇidi* means "to revile. The suffix *krip* is Vedic, as it lacks the *tumun* suffix.

Because the *sup* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*), the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains. Even though it is in the vocative case (*āmantrita*), because it belongs to a separate sentence, it does not undergo the *nighāta* (elision of accent) since it follows a word within its own sentence; thus, it retains its initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*). [The word] *anyataḥ*.
In the word *liti*, the vowel is acute by virtue of the suffix *pratyaya*.
The particle *cit* has the sense of the word *api* (also/even).
By this, it is understood that not only from here, but having gone out from here, they also go out from elsewhere.

This very relationship between the two verbal roots is expressed by the *luṅ* suffix in the word "ārata," for that suffix is prescribed under the governing rule concerning the connection of roots (*dhātusambandha*). Thus: "They have ceased."

Regarding *ataiḥ*: by the rule "In the Veda, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [are used] for the sense of the *loṭ*" (Pāṇini 3.4.6), the *luṅ* is used in the sense of the *loṭ*. The substitution of *ta* occurs for the second person plural. By the rule "And after the roots *as*, *śās*, and *yat*" (Pāṇini 3.1.56), the suffix *ciṇ* is substituted [for the *aṅ*].
By the rule *ṛd-śo'ṅi guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.16), there is guṇa substitution; the augment *āṭ* is added;
[the form is] *dadhānāḥ*.

The suffix *śānac* would have been *udātta* at the end by virtue of being *cit*, but this is superseded by the subsequent rule, "the first syllable of reduplicated forms" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.189), which assigns the *udātta* accent to the initial syllable. In the word *duvas*,
the initial syllable is *udātta* by the rule "not after *nadī*, *vapā*, *payas*, or a stem ending in *ni*" (*nadīvapayasyānisantasya*, Phiṭ-sūtra 26).
And may the people, O wondrous one, call us fortunate and free from enemies; may we abide in the protection of Indra.
And may the people, O Wondrous One, call us fortunate; may we indeed abide in the protection of Indra.

O Indra, the destroyer of enemies, through your favor, may even our foes call us "subhaga"—that is, endowed with excellent wealth. What need is there to mention that the common people (kṛṣṭayaḥ) will say we have become lowly? [Rather, they will praise us. Therefore, may we remain in the protection (śarmaṇi) of Indra—that is, in the happiness obtained through Indra's grace—endowed with riches.
Among the twenty-five names for wealth beginning with *magha*, the word *rayiḥ* is listed as "sovereignty, power, fortune" (*ni.
2.10.10*). Among the twenty-five names for humans beginning with *manuṣyāḥ*, the word *kṛṣṭayaḥ* is listed (*ni. 2.3.7*).
Furthermore,
[the word] *subhagān* is udātta on the final syllable according to the rule *evamādīnām antaḥ* (Pāṇinian Sūtra Phiṭ-sūtra 82).

Because the word *bhaga* is listed among the *kravadi* group [of words], its having the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member—which would otherwise be overridden by Pāṇini 6.2.102 (*nañsubhyām*)—is instead governed by Pāṇini 6.2.118 (*kravādayaśca*), resulting in the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member.
In the *saṃhitā*, the *nakāra* becomes *ru* (the letter *r*) according to Pāṇini 8.3.9 (*dīrghādaṭi samānapāde*).
Then, by Pāṇini 8.3.17 (*bho-bhago-...*), it undergoes *yatva* (becoming *ya*).
The elision of *y* occurs by the rule "lopaḥ śākalyasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.19). Because that [elision] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), no further sandhi operation takes place.
By the rule "āto 'ṭi nityam" (Pāṇini 8.3.3), the vowel *ā* becomes nasalized.
The word *ariḥ* [is derived as follows]: there is a transposition of the case endings (*vacanavyatyaya*). It ends in the suffix *i*, according to the rule *aca haḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.578).
It has an acute accent on the final syllable due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya*). [Examples:
*voceyuḥ*, *uccyāsuḥ*.

From the root *vac* in the sense of "speaking," in the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*) with the substitution of *jus* for *si* (Pāṇini 3.4.108), the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.86); then, the augment *um* is added by the rule *vaca um* (Pāṇini 7.4.20). 1.
Ṭha—udātta.
The suffix *guṇa* [is applied].
By the rule *kidāśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.4.104), the suffix *yāsuṭ* is added.

Since the substitute for the *liṅ* is treated as *sārvadhātuka* by the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), there is the elision of the *sakāra* by the rule *liṅaḥ salopo'nanyasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.79).
[The form is derived as follows: By Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.80, *ato yeyaḥ* [the *yā* of *liṅ* is replaced by *īya*];
by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.87, *āḍuṇaḥ* [the augment *āṭ* is added].
Since the root ends in *a*, the *liṅ* suffix is unaccented by the accent rule for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following a root taught with an initial vowel (*adupadeśāt*).
Only the accent of the *aṅ* suffix remains;
with that, there is *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *i*.
By the rule “*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*” (Pāṇini 8.2.5), it becomes udātta.

*Dasma*: from the root *dasu* in the sense of "to destroy" (*upakṣaye*), with the causative meaning (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) understood, [the suffix] *mak* is applied according to *Uṇādi Sūtra* 1.142: *ipidhṛnīdhadisyādhūsūbhyo mak*.
Because it follows a word (*padāt paratvāt*), it receives the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the enclitic accentuation of a vocative).

The word *kṛtyaḥ* [is derived as follows]: by the rule *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.2.104), the suffix *ktic* is applied; because it is followed by *manuṣyānmanvāt*, the suffix *citaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.163) applies, making it udātta on the final syllable. [The form] *syāma*.
‘ama bhuvi’;
‘asoralopaḥ’ (Pāṇini 6.4.111);
the *yāsuṭ* [augment] is acute-accented (*udātta*).
There is no *nighāta* because it begins with a *pāda*. Regarding *śarmaṇi*:
[the root] *śṛ* means "to injure."
It is called *śarma* because it destroys (*hinasti*) suffering; the suffix *manin* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.75 (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*),
and the augment *iṭ* is prohibited by Pāṇini 7.2.8 (*neḍvaśi kṛti*).
The first syllable of *nivāda* is udātta.
Bring hither, O swift one, this swift [Soma], which is the glory of the sacrifice, the delight of men,
the lord, the exhilarating, the impetuous.
Bring hither the swift one for the sake of speed, him who is the glory of the sacrifice, the delighter of men, the lord, and the exhilarating impeller.
The particle *īm* occurs in the sense of the word *idam* (this).
O sacrificer, bring—*ā bhara*—this Soma for Indra, who is swift (*āśave*) and engaged in the entirety of the Soma sacrifice.
Of what kind is this Soma?

The swift one, pervading the three pressings, the glory of the sacrifice— the very embodiment of the sacrifice’s success— delighting men, being the cause of joy for the officiating priests and the sacrificers, reaching toward his goal as he attains the ritual acts, he who exhilarates the pressing:
this Soma is a friend to that Indra who gladdens and delights the sacrificers,
because he is the cause of their satisfaction or the cause of their satiation.
Āśu: [The suffix] uṇ [is applied] by the rule *kṛvāpājimisvadisādhyaśūnya uṇ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.1). It has the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*).
To the swift one;
as before;
the glory of the sacrifice.
By the rule *samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223), the final syllable is udātta.
It is called *mādana* because one becomes intoxicated by means of it;
the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayoś-ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.117).

Because of its elision (*lup*), the preceding vowel *ā* is acute (*udātta*). By the rule "A *kṛt* suffix following a motion-word, an agentive word, or a subordinate word retains its accent" (Pāṇini 6.2.139), that very accent remains.
Thus, *patyayat*.
The causative suffix *ṇic* is applied to the root *patera-* according to Pāṇini 3.1.25 (*caurādibhyaś ca*).
By Pāṇini 6.4.48 (*ato lopaḥ*), the final *a* is elided.
Due to the status of that [elision] as *sthānivat* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel (Pāṇini 7.2.116).
The *laṭ* [present tense suffix] undergoes the substitution of *śatṛ*.

Because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), this [substituted form] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* [suffix]; consequently, since the condition for the acute accent on the root (*adupadeśāt*, Pāṇini 6.1.186) does not apply, the suffix itself retains its original udātta accent. Furthermore, even though it is an *ārdhadhātuka*, by the maxim *sarve vidhayaśchandasi vikalpyante* (Paribhāṣā 35), the elision of the *ṇi* [causative marker] prescribed by *ṇeraniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51) does not take place.

By the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *am*. Because of the prohibition of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations based on a suffix) by the rule *na lumatā* (Pāṇini 1.1.63), the augment *num* does not apply by the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70). Thus, the word *mandrayā* is udātta (accented) on its final syllable.
The word *mandayati* is a compound with *indre* based on the rule of *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) in Pāṇini 2.1.40, which states "the locative case [is compounded].

According to Pāṇini 6.2.2, "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when preceded by a word meaning 'equal to' (*tulyārtha*), etc.," there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, which here is the locative case.
1. Regarding the *ṭha*-operation:

Having drunk of this, O Śatakratu, you became the slayer of the Vṛtras; you protected the strong steed in the contests for booty. 8. *asya* (of this), *pītvā* (having drunk), *śatakrato* (O Śatakratu), *ghnaḥ* (slayer), *vṛtrāṇām* (of the Vṛtras), *abhavaḥ* (you became), *pra* (forth), *āvaḥ* (you protected), *vājeṣu* (in the contests for booty), *vājinam* (the strong steed). 8.
O Śatakratu, O Indra, performer of many deeds, having drunk a portion of this soma, you became the slayer—indeed, the destroyer—of the Vṛtras, the enemies headed by the asura named Vṛtra.
Thereafter, in battles (*vājeṣu*), you protected with your own form your devotee, the possessor of strength (*vājinam*) amidst the contests.
By the word *asya*, Soma situated in the space directly in front at the time of the ritual performance is indicated; however, the previously mentioned Soma is not being referred back.

Therefore, because this is not a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), the substitution of *aś* for *idam*—as prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule 2.4.32 (*idamo 'nvādeśe 'nudāttaḥ tṛtīyādau*)—does not apply here.

Therefore, there is not a universal anudātta (low-pitched) accent; rather, after the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* etc. (Pāṇini 7.2.102) and the elision of the consonant (Pāṇini 7.2.113), the vowel *a* is udātta by virtue of the nominal stem accent (*prātipadika-svara*). Thus, with the word "from an udātta ending" (*antodāttāt*) being understood [from a previous rule], the case-ending becomes udātta by Pāṇini 6.1.171: "After *aḍ*, *idam*, *adas*, and those beginning with *upajña*. In the form *pītvā*: from the root *pibati* with the suffix *ktvā*, it is udātta at the end by the accent of the suffix according to Pāṇini 6.4.66: "By *ghu*, *mā*, *sthā*, etc. (the *kṛt* suffix *ktvā* is treated as having an udātta accent).
Due to a lack of capacity, there is no status as a member of a compound with another vocative.
*Ghnaḥ*.
By the rule *mūrtī ghnaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.77), the suffix *na* is applied to the root *han* in the sense of solidity (*kāṭhinya*).

The word *arśas* ending in *ac* is formed from the sense "he has that" (*tad asyāsti*) according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.2.127, which belongs to the *arśa-ādi* group; it is accented on the final syllable because it is marked with the *cit* indicator. [It occurs] in the context of *vājeṣu*.
[The word] *vṛṣan* is ādyudātta because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group.
[The word] *vājinam*: the accent is that of the suffix *-in*.

As such, O Lord of a hundred powers, we strengthen you, the prize-winner, in the contests for booty, O Indra, so that you may win riches. 9. Him | thee | in the contests | the prize-winner | we strengthen | O thou of a hundred powers | of riches | O Indra | for the winning. 9.

O Śatakratu, you who are endowed with many deeds or endowed with great wisdom, O Indra—for the sake of winning (*sātaye*) wealth or for the sake of enjoying it—we invoke you, the powerful one (*vājin*), in battles (*vājeṣu*). We make you possessed of food (*vājayāmaḥ*).
Among the forty-six names of battle, beginning with *raṇaḥ*, it is recited: "In manly strength, in the great prize, in battle, they went" (*ni.
2. 17. 42*). Among the twenty-eight names of food, it is recited: "Soma-juice (*andhaḥ*), food (*vājaḥ*), vigor (*pājaḥ*)" (*ni. 2. 7. 2*).
In the twelve names for "much," beginning with *uru* and *tuvi*, *śatam sahasram* is recited (Nirukta 3.1.9).
In the fifteen names for "action" (*karman*), beginning with *apaḥ* and *apanaḥ*, *śakama kratuḥ* is recited (Nirukta 2.1.11).
In the eleven names for "wisdom" (*prajñāna*), beginning with *ketaḥ* and *ketuḥ*, *kratuḥ asuḥ* is recited (Nirukta 3.9.5).
In the word *tvā*, the substitute *tvā* occurs by the rule *tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.23), with the continuation of the rule *anudāttaṃ sarvam* (Pāṇini 8.1.18). [The word is] *vājeṣu*.
The root *vaj* (or *vraj*) means "to go.
That by which one causes the body's sustenance to proceed is called *vāja*, meaning strength or food;
it is derived from the root with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

In this regard, although the rule *karṣātvato ghaño 'nta udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.159) would result in an udātta accent on the final syllable as an exception to the *ñitsvara*, that too is further set aside by the rule *vṛṣādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.203), which prescribes an udātta accent on the first syllable.
[Thus we have] *vājayāmaḥ*.
One who possesses *vāja* is *vājavān*.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "one who performs that" according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.1.26 (*tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe*).

Because of the status as if it were already desired (*iṣṭavadbhāva*) when that suffix follows, by the rule 6.4.155 (*iṣṭavanne prātipadikasya*), there is the elision of the suffix *matup* according to 5.3.65 (*vinmator luk*).
Then, by 6.4.155 (*ṭeḥ*), there is the elision of the final vowel *a*.
The *ṇic* suffix [causes] the udātta accent on the final syllable;
the *śap* suffix [is] anudātta due to being *piṭ*;
[and finally,] by the rule for the accent of *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes—

[In the verse] *ma. 1. a. 2 sū. 5*, although [the word *dhanānām*] is part of a compound (*samāsa*), it retains its non-acute (*anudātta*) accent. Because it begins a quarter-verse (*pādādi*), there is no elision of accent (*nighāta*) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. In *śatakrato*, there is the elision of accent (*nighāta*) due to being a vocative (*āmantrita*). In *dhanānām*, the initial syllable is acute (*udātta*) according to the Paribhāṣā-sūtra *nadīviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 26). In *sātaye*, while the term *udāttaḥ* is understood from the previous rule, the suffix *ktin* is acute by Pāṇini 3.3.97: *uti-yūti-jūti-sāti-heti-kīrtayaś ca*.

To him who is a great river of wealth, easy to cross, the friend of the one who presses the soma—to that Indra, sing! 10. To him who is a great river of wealth, easy to cross, the friend of the one who presses the soma—to that Indra, sing! 10.
To that Indra who is the stream, protector, or master of wealth—that is, of riches—sing! O officiating priests, offer praise for his sake.
Of what nature is Indra?

He is great, preeminent in virtues; he is a good ferryman, one who excellently brings the ritual work to completion; and he is the friend, as dear as a kinsman, of the sacrificer who presses the soma.
*rāyaḥ*:
The acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending is due to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.101, *uḍidampadādvyubhyo yat*.
*Avaniḥ*.

From the root *ava*—which signifies protection, going, affection, satisfaction, understanding, entering, hearing, lordship, requesting, action, desire, effort, pervasion, embracing, injury, giving, state of being, and increase—and by the rule *atisṛṣṭayammayaśyavitṛbhyo'vaniḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.259), the form *avaniḥ* is derived.
[The suffix] has the udātta accent on its initial syllable.
[The word] *supāraḥ*.

From the root *pṛ*, meaning "to protect" and "to fill," with the suffix *jiti* (indicating the present participle), the rule "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) being carried over, the suffix *pacādyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134) is applied.
By the rule "that which has the *cit* marker" (Pāṇini 6.1.163), it is accented on the final syllable.
[Thus derived is] *sunvataḥ*.
The case-ending is udātta by the rule *śataranumo nadyajādī* (Pāṇini 6.1.173).
*Sakhā* ends in the suffix *iṇ* by the rule *samāne hyaścodhataḥ* (Uṇādi-sūtra 4.576).

By virtue of that [suffix], there is the elision of *ya*; and the word *sa-* becomes udātta. Because it is marked with *ḍ*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the first vowel); [thus formed is] *tasmai*.

With the word "ādiḥ" understood from the previous context, the suffix *adi* is applied to the root *tan* by the rule "tyajita-ni-tanibhyo ḍit" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.129). Because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, there is elision of the final phoneme (*ṭilopa*). By the accent of the suffix, the word *tat* is udātta.
[The form *tad*] undergoes the substitution of *yat* for the initial vowel.

The [final vowel] is udātta by the rule "ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.5). When the accentuation of the case-ending would have been udātta by the rule "sāvekācastṛtīyādivibhaktiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.168), there is a prohibition for the nominative singular because it begins with an *a*-vowel, according to the rule "na go-han-sāv-avarṇa" (Pāṇini 6.1.182). Thus: *indrāya*.

The word *indra* is a nipātana (irregularly formed) derivative ending in the suffix *rūpa*. By virtue of being a nipātana, it is udātta on its first syllable. According to the rule "that which one intends as the goal by means of an action is the *saṃpradāna*" (Pāṇini 1.4.32), the statement "the mention of the action must be included" (Pāṇinian Mahābhāṣya on 1.4.32) applies; therefore, because he is to be reached through the act of singing (*gāna*), the fourth case is used in the sense of the *saṃpradāna*.
The second hymn, consisting of ten verses, begins with "ā tu.
Following the recurring phrase "surūpakṛtnuṃ daśa," he has thus enumerated [the hymn] as beginning with "ā tu yuñjanti.
The seer, meter, deity, and ritual application are as before.
As for its specific application: this triplet is the *stotriya* for the *maitrāvaruṇa* recitation during the third round (*paryāya*) of the *atirātra* sacrifice;

for it is stated in the section beginning "Of the rounds of the *atirātra*" (*Atirātre paryāyāṇām*) that [the verse] "Come hither, sit down" (*ā tvetā ni pīdata*; Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4) [is to be used].
Come hither, sit down; sing forth unto Indra, O friends who bring hymns of praise! 1. Come! Indeed! Come! Sit down! Sing forth unto Indra, O friends who bring hymns of praise! 1.

The particle *tu* is an indeclinable used in the sense of "quickly. The word *inaśabdaḥ* (the sound *ina*) is to be repeated with two prefixes, *ā* and *ni*. O friends, the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), come, come quickly to this ritual! The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. Having arrived, sit down; having sat down, sing forth to Indra—praise him thoroughly and excellently. Of what sort are these friends? They are "bearers of the *stoma*," meaning they bring or convey the *stomas* such as the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* into this ritual.
*ā tu ā*:
these are acute on the first syllable because they are particles (*nipāta*).
*ita*.
The root *i* means "to go. According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.2.135 (*vyor upajave tiṅi*), there is lengthening in the *saṃhitā* [text] before a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). [Thus we have] *ni*.
Because it is a particle (*nipāta*), it is accented on the first syllable.
[The form] *sīdata* [is derived from the root] *sad*; by the rule "pāghrādhmāsthānādāṇṇahaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.78), etc., there is the substitution of *sīda* for *sad*.
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs in the *saṃhitā* by the rule "sadiprateḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.66). Regarding *abhi*:
by the statement "and the prefixes, except for *abhi*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 81), it has the udātta accent on the final syllable of the nominal stem.
*Stomavāhasaḥ*:

According to the *Uṇādisūtra* (1.137), "The suffix *man* is applied after the roots *ati*, *stṛ*, *su*, *hṛ*, *kṣubh*, *rā*, *yā*, *vā*, *didyut*, and *yakṣ*," the word *stoma* ends in the suffix *man* derived from the root *stu* ("to praise") and is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) by virtue of being a *nitya*-formation.
Those who carry (*vahanti*) the *stoma* are called *stomavāhasaḥ*.
‘vahihādhāmyaścchandasi’ (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.660).
May he indeed come to us for our spiritual attainment, for wealth, and for inspired wisdom;
may he come to us with riches.
May he come to us for our union; may he come for wealth; may he come for inspired wisdom; may he come to us with spoils of war. 3.
The particle *gha* is a nipāta used for emphasis;
it is connected with all those words [beginning with *sa*].

That very *sa*—that same Indra, distinguished by the qualities previously mentioned in the mantra—*ā bhuvat*: may he come to be present for our *yoga*, that is, for our connection with the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) not previously attained.
The meaning is: "May he accomplish the purpose of man.
May he alone be present for wealth (*rāya*), for the sake of riches;
may he alone be present with the wise woman (*puraṃdhi*).
Or rather:
regarding the word *puraṃdhī*, Yāska [states] that it means "one who has become present in manifold cognition" (*bahuvidhāyāṃ buddhau ā bhuvat*) and "a female supporter" (*udhrīḥ*). (Nirukta 6.13)
May he himself come to us, together with strengths consisting of gifts and foods. May he approach.

*Gha*: By Pāṇini 8.1.71, *cādayaḥ* are unaccented (*anudātta*). It is a suffix (*pratyaya*). Because it is marked with *ṇi*, it has the udātta accent on its first syllable. *Sametsu*: From the root *ad* preceded by *sam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied. *Śatravaḥ*: The root *śati* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "to injure. By Uṇādi Sūtra 4.543, the suffix *kun* is added after *ru* and *śati*. Because it is marked with *ṇi*, it has the udātta accent on its first syllable. *Tasmai*: By Pāṇini 6.1.168, the case ending (*vibhakti*) would have been udātta; however, by the prohibition in Pāṇini 6.1.182, "not in the case of *go*, *śvan*, or a word ending in *s* followed by *a-varṇa*," the original accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*) remains.
Pressed for the drinker, these pure Soma juices, mixed with curd, go forth for the feast. 5. Pressed for the drinker; pressed; these; pure; go; for the feast; Soma juices; mixed with curd. 5.
These are the Soma juices prepared for this ritual;
[they are] for the drinker of the pressed [juice], the one who drinks the Soma that has been pressed— the dative case used in the sense of the genitive.
Regarding the root *vṛdh* in the sense of "to grow":
because the augment *iṭ* is optional after the suffix *ktvā* by Pāṇini 7.2.56 (*udito vā*), there is a prohibition of *iṭ* in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffix by Pāṇini 7.2.15 (*yasya vibhāṣā*).
It is accented acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
For preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhyāya*):
*jyaiṣṭhya* is the state of being the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*).
The suffix *vyañ* is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 5.1.124, “*guvacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ karmaṇi ca*.
The word *jihvā* has its acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable.
O Indra, lover of songs, may the swift Soma juices enter you;
may they be a blessing for you, the wise one.
O Indra, lover of songs, let the swift Soma juices enter you; may they be for your well-being, for you who are preeminent in wisdom. 7.
O Indra, may these Soma juices enter you; may they enter you directly.
Of what nature are these Soma juices?
They are swift, pervading the three pressings or both the primary and modified sacrifices.
Of what kind is Indra?

*Girvaṇas*: a particular deity who is to be honored with songs—that is, with hymns of praise. Yāska states: "The god is *girvaṇas* because they win him over (*vanayanti*) by means of songs" (Nirukta 6.14).
O such Indra, may the Soma juices, which are of the nature of bliss (*śam*), be for you, the highly wise (*pracetase*).
O lover of hymns (*girvaṇas*): "hymns" (*giraḥ*) are praises, so called because they are sung.
From the root *gṛ* in the sense of "sound," with the suffix *krip*, there is shortening and substitution by *r* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.100 (*ṛta iddhātoḥ*). Thus,
they are called *girvaṇas*, meaning those who are praised or served by means of songs (*gīrbhiḥ*).
The root *vana* (or *saṇa*) means "to enjoy" (*saṃbhakti*). Enjoyment here signifies service (*sevā*).
The suffix *asun* is applied according to the rule *sarvadhātubhyo 'sun* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.628).
For *pracetasa*, when it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) of the first member.
The hymns have magnified you; the recitations [have magnified] you, O Lord of a hundred powers;
may our songs magnify you.
The hymns have magnified you; O Śatakratu, may our songs of praise magnify you. || 8 ||
O Śatakratu, O performer of many deeds, O possessor of great knowledge, O Indra, the *stomas*—the hymns of the chanters of the *Sāmans*—have magnified you;
likewise, the many *ukthas*—the ritual recitations (*śastras*)—have magnified you.
Since this was so in the past, therefore now also may our songs of praise magnify you, strengthen you, and bring you to full exaltation.
The *stoma*s;
*mā* with *niṣṭhā* is udātta;
they have increased.
Regarding the root *vṛdh* in the sense of "to grow": after the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* augment (Pāṇini 3.1.48),
the rule *urṛt* (Pāṇini 7.4.7)— which prescribes the substitution of *ṛ* for the penultimate vowel *ṛ* of the root *vṛdh*— overrides even the internal *guṇa* substitution.

The rules [to be applied here] are: reduplication (*dvirbhāva*; Pāṇini 6.1.11), the substitution of the remaining initial sound (*halādiśeṣa*; Pāṇini 7.4.60), the treatment as *sa*-present (*sanvadbhāva*; Pāṇini 7.4.93), the shortening of the vowel (*itva*; Pāṇini 7.4.79), the lengthening of the vowel (*dīrghatva*; Pāṇini 7.4.94), and the augment *aṭ* (*aḍāgama*; Pāṇini 6.4.71). Thus we have *ukthā ukthāni*.
The suffix *thak* is added to the root *vac* according to the rule *pātṛtudicaricisicibhyasthak* (Uṇādisūtra 2.164).
Because it has the *kit* designation, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
By the rule “In the Veda, the remainder [is variously treated]” (Pāṇini 6.1.70), there is elision of the suffix *śi* and elision of the nasal *n*. It is oxytone due to the accent of the suffix.

Because it lacks the capacity [to function as a governing factor], even that which follows an *āmantrita* does not undergo the treatment of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*); thus, there is no unaccented status (*anudāttatva*).
"Vardhantu": from the root *vṛdh*, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
1. They have attained the pervasiveness of *ṭha*. 2. They increase *ṭha*. 3. *ṭha* is short. 4. *ṭha* is a storm. 5. *ṭha* is not udātta.

Indra, whose protection is inexhaustible, has bestowed upon us this thousandfold strength, in which all manly powers reside. (9) [In the pada-pāṭha: *akṣita'ūtiḥ* | *sanot* | *imam* | *vājam* | *indraḥ* | *sahasriṇam* | *yasmin* | *viśvāni* | *pausyā* ||9||
"Indra shall win"—that is, he shall fully enjoy—"this food," namely the *vāja* in the form of Soma.
Of what nature is Indra?
He is "one whose protection is imperishable," meaning his preservation is most extensive.
The meaning is that she never abandons her protection at any time.
Of what kind is the prize (*vāja*)?
It is "thousandfold" (*sahasriṇam*), meaning it possesses the number one thousand because it operates both in the primary forms (*prakṛti*) and the modified forms (*vikṛti*).

The connection with the preceding is as follows: "In which *vāja* all (*aviśvāni*)—that is, every (*sarvāṇi*)—manly powers (*pausyāni*), meaning manly strengths (*puṃsvāni balāni*), exist; such is the *vāja*."
"Of unimpaired life.

Now, is it not the case that this verbal root *kṣi*, meaning "to perish," is intransitive? And since it lacks an object, the suffix *ka* ought to be applied to it in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), an abstract state (*bhāva*), or an agent (*kartṛ*).

Therefore, in this context, if [the root *kṣi*] were used in the sense of either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), then since the suffix *kyap* is not prescribed for those two, and with the continuation of the rule "after *kṣi*" (Pāṇini 6.4.59), the rule "in the case of a *niṣṭhā* suffix, when it does not have the sense of the past" (Pāṇini 6.4.60) would require a long vowel.
Consequently, by the rule "for *kṣi* after a long vowel" (Pāṇini 8.2.46), there would be the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *niṣṭhā*, resulting in *akṣīṇa*, and not *akṣita*.
Alternatively, if the word *kṣita* is taken as denoting a state (*bhāva*) according to the rule "the suffix *kta* is used in the neuter sense of a state" (Pāṇini 3.3.114).

In that case, because it would not have another referent (*anyārtha*), the prohibition by the rule *aṇyadarthe* would apply; consequently, due to the absence of the two long vowels (*dīrghatva*), the form *kṣitam* would be established.
However, since a *nañ-tatpuruṣa* is not applicable here, one must instead have a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which no destruction exists.
And thus, by the rule *nañ-subhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172), there would be the udātta accent on the final syllable of the second member.

Furthermore, if the word *ūti* were used in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that same accent would be established by the rule regarding the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*), and thus the intended initial acute (*ādyudātta*) would not be achieved.
True;
for this very reason, the root *kṣi* is taken here as having the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it.
Because that [root] is transitive (*sakarmaka*), this past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed with respect to the object (*karman*).
Consequently, due to the prohibition "when the sense is other than that of *aṇ*" (*aṇyadarthe*), neither the lengthening of the vowel nor the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *niṣṭhā* will occur.
Thus, in a negative *tatpuruṣa*, the meaning is "not destroyed," "unwasted," or "indestructible" (*akṣitā*, *akṣayitā*).
In that case, by virtue of the rule regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of an indeclinable preceding a compound member, the negative particle *nañ* bears the acute accent (*udātta*).
Furthermore, when a *bahuvrīhi* is formed with the word *ūti*, that same accent will apply; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

[The form *kṣitā*] is either derived from the root *kṣi* (as in *ri*, *kṣi*, *ciri*, *jiri*, *dāśa*, *dṛ*) in the sense of "desire to harm," or it is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the objective sense (*karman*) of the root *kṣi* meaning "to injure."
And likewise, in the sense of "he should not be harmed" (*ahiṃsita*), the vowel is established by the aforementioned sequence; thus there is no fault.
[The form] *sanet* [is derived from] the roots *vana* and *paṇa*, meaning "to share" (*saṃbhakti*).
It belongs to the *bhū* class (*bhauvādika*).
The word *vāja* is acutely accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group.
Indra; *ranaḥ* is acute-accented on the first syllable due to the suffix *ni*;
*sahasriṇam*.
He possesses a thousand;
[the suffix] *ini* or *ṭan* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.115 (*ata iniṭanau*). It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
*Viśvāni*: by *viśeḥ kan* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.149), it is ādyudātta due to the suffix *kan*. *Pauṃsyāni*: the deeds of a man (*puṃsaḥ*).
Since *bāhyaga*, etc., belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended groups), the suffix *pyañ* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.124: *guṇavacanabrāhmaṇādibhyaḥ karmaṇi ca*.

Because the suffix has a *ji*-marker, the word is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). For the nominative plural ending, the substitute *ḍā* is applied by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.39: *supāṃ suluk...* and so forth.

But surely, since the suffix *nan* is prescribed for the meanings beginning with "originating from" (*bhavana*) by the rule *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nanstanau bhavanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.87), which extends up to the rule *dhānyānāṃ bhavane kṣetre khañ* (Pāṇini 5.2.1)—just as one says *pauṃsaḥ* for "the offspring of a man" (*puṃso'patyam*) or *pauṃsaḥ* for "come from a man" (*puṃsa āgataḥ*), and so forth—in the same way, when the meaning is "the state or action of a man" (*puṃso bhāvaḥ karma vā*), the suffix *pyañ* should be set aside [by *nan*], and the form should necessarily be *pausnāni*. How then can it be said that they are *pausyāni*?

It is said: because the limit is indicated by the word "tvāt" in the rule *ā ca tvāt* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.120), there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the suffixes *tva* and *tal* with the suffixes beginning with *imanij*, up to and including *brahmaṇastva* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.136).
Likewise, in that very same rule, due to the word "ca," there is likewise a co-occurrence of *nañ* and *stan* with *vyat* and the others; there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*).

1. [The suffix] *ṭha* is used in the sense of "is released. 2. [The suffixes] *ca*, *cha*, and *pha* occur in the sense of the present tense. 3. [The suffixes] *ga*, *gha*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *ya*, and *pauṣya* denote masculines. 4. [The suffix] *ṭha* is used in the sense of "will be. O Indra, lover of songs, may mortals not harm us; as the lord, ward off the weapon. (10)
O Indra, lover of songs, let not mortal men do harm to our bodies; as the sovereign lord, ward off the weapon of death from us. 10.

O Indra, lover of hymns (*girvaṇas*), may the mortal men who oppose us not inflict injury upon our bodies; let them not commit harm against us from every side. O Lord, you who are capable, ward off from us the slaughter being wrought by our enemies. Among the twenty-five names for humans listed [in the Nighaṇṭu], "mortals" (*martāḥ*) and "winds" (*vātāḥ*) are recited together (Nirukta 2.3.13).
*Martāḥ*: [The suffix] *tan* is applied by the rule *asihasimṛpriṇvāmidamilūpadhūvibhyastan* (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.366).
Because it is *niṣ* (a kṛt suffix), it is udātta on the first syllable.
*abhi*:
[The suffix *kvi* is applied] after words such as these (PŚ 82).
*duhan*.
The root *druh* is used in the sense of "desire to harm.
According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.4.7, *liḍarthe leṭ*, the *leṭ* suffix is employed in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*).
From this [suffix] comes *jhi*.

By Pāṇini’s rule *jho‘ntaḥ* (7.1.3), [the substitute] *antaḥ* is applied for *jh*. Then, by the rule *itaśca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (3.4.97), the *i*-vowel is elided. Thereafter, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

By the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), the *tiṅ*-suffixes are designated as *apit*; by the rule *jhalāṃ jaś jhaśi* (Pāṇini 8.4.53) and others, there is the substitution of *jaś*-sounds for *jhal*-sounds. [Thus we have] *tanūnām*.
Furthermore, due to a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*), there is no application of the rule regarding "behaving like a subsequent member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*).
O Indra, lover of songs!
Come!
Thou art the sovereign lord.

Because the verbal root (*dhātu*) is unaccented (*anudātta*), when the suffix *śap* is elided, and only the *l*-suffixes remain as part of the verbal root which is also unaccented, the accent of the root alone remains.
[Thus we have] *yavaya*.

In the case of the root *yu*, with the addition of *ṇic*, the *vṛddhi* substitution is not applied on the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not necessarily permanent" (*Paribhāṣā* 93.1).
Alternatively, it is called *yava* because it unites (*yauti*); this is derived from the root with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134.
In the sense of "he makes [something] into barley," the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.26–27: "In the sense of 'he does that' or 'he describes that,' [the suffix is added]."
By the rule "the elision of the *ṭi* occurs as in the case of the *iṣṭan* suffix" (Pāṇini 6.4.155), there is the elision of the *ṭi*.
Due to the status of that [elided element] as a *sthānivadbhāva* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. Thus: *vadham*.
In the rule *hanaśca vadhaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.76), the suffix *ap* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).

By virtue of being taught in conjunction with that [suffix], the substitute *vadha* is treated as if it were the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) and is thus accented on the final syllable. Consequently, by the accent rule known as *udāttanivṛttisvara*, the suffix *ap* itself becomes accented.

Regarding the word-hymns (*padasūkta*) beginning with “*surūpa*,” the number of mantras, the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), the deity (*devatā*), and the application (*viniyoga*) of the third hymn, “*yuñjanti*,” are to be understood as before.
That hymn consists of ten verses; among them, four—the first three and the last one—are dedicated to Indra (*aindra*).
Beginning with this fourth verse, “ādaha,” there are six verses addressed to the Maruts (*mārutyaḥ*).
Among them, these two verses, “vīḷu cit” and “indreṇa,” although addressed to the Maruts, are also addressed to Indra.

All of this is stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*: “*Surūpakṛtnum* [is] ten [verses] addressed to Indra; however, those beginning with ‘yujam,’ ‘ādaha,’ and so on, are six addressed to the Maruts, as well as the two [beginning with] ‘vīḷu cit’ and ‘indreṇa’.”
In this hymn, the triplet beginning with “yuñjanti” serves as the *anurūpa* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin at the third *paryāya* of the night.
Accordingly, in the section titled “The *Paryāyas* of the Atirātra,” it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘yoge-yoge tavastaram,’ ‘yuñjanti bradhnam aruṣam’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
They harness the ruddy, radiant one who moves around those who stand still; the luminous realms shine in heaven. 1.
They harness the ruddy, glowing one as he moves; those who stand around him behold the luminous realms shining in heaven.

For Indra is endowed with supreme sovereignty (*parameśvaryam*). And this supreme sovereignty is established because he exists in the form of the sun, the stars, and so forth. [The verse says: "They harness" (*yuñjanti*) Indra—who is "bradhna," existing in the form of the sun; "aruṣa," existing in a form free from harm; and "caranta," spreading everywhere in the form of the wind—"while they stand around him" (*pari tasthuṣaḥ*), that is, living beings situated all around establish a connection with him as their deity for their own ritual actions.
The specific manifestations of that very Indra, namely the *rocanāni* (shining ones), the stars, “shine” (*rocante*) or manifest in the sky (*divi*), in the celestial world.
The fact that this mantra expresses the aforementioned meaning is explained in another Brāhmaṇa: “He says, ‘They yoke the ruddy one’;
for yonder sun is indeed [the ruddy one]...”

1. In the case of *ṭha*, it is oxytone (*antodātta*) by virtue of its connection with *tatsaṃniyoga*; in the case of *ca* and *pha*, it is oxytone by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva* as taught in connection with *tatsaṃniyoga*; in the case of *ta*, it is oxytone by virtue of its connection with *tatsaṃniyoga* as taught in connection with *tatsaṃniyoga*. 2. In the case of *ṭha*, the word ‘nakṣatra’ does not exist. 3. In the case of *ṭha*, [the reading] is *ahiṃsakāmi*.
"The radiant one.
He thereby yokes the sun for him. "The day-maker," he says.
Agni, indeed, is formless;
he thus yokes Agni for him.
"Go forth," he says.
"Vāyu indeed moves.
He thus yokes Vāyu for him.
"Those who stand around," he says.
"These worlds indeed stand around.
He thus yokes these very worlds for him.
"The luminous realms in heaven hold fast," he says.
"The constellations (*nakṣatra*) are indeed the lights in the sky;
he makes the constellations shine for him" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.9.4.1–2).
Among the twenty-five names for the great (*mahan*), "the great *bradhna*" is recited (Nirukta 3.3.2).
