The sun is also called *bradhna* precisely because of its greatness.
They harness [the chariot].
By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the word *antaḥ* has the acute accent on its first syllable.
*Bradhnam*.
The final syllable of the nominal stem (prātipadika) is udātta.
*Arūpam*. [The roots] *upa*, *rūpa*, and *riṣ* have the meaning of "injury" (*hiṃsā*).

They are called *rupas* because they injure (*ropati*); the suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.135 (*igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*). By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it is udātta.

He for whom there are no forms (*rūpa*) is "formless" (*arūpa*). According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.2.102 (*nañbhyām*), the final syllable of the compound has the udātta accent. When the form *arūpaḥ* is followed by the nominative singular ending *am*, the rule Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.107 (*ami pūrvaḥ*) applies, resulting in the single substitute (*pūrvarūpa*). By Pāṇini’s Sūtra 8.2.5 (*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*), this single substitute retains the udātta accent.
In *carantam*,
the *dāp* suffix is unaccented by virtue of being anudātta;
furthermore, by the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix, the accent of the verbal root alone remains.

*tasthuṣaḥ*: This is the *kasu* substitute for the root *sthā* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.107. Although the augment *iṭ* is antaranga by virtue of Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.67 (*vasvekājādghasām*), it is superseded by the rule "vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is stronger than that which follows from vocalization" (Pāṇini Mahābhāṣya 6.1.17.2). Consequently, because the suffix *śas* causes the stem to be treated as a nominal base (*bha*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.18, the vocalization of the *vasu* suffix applies by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.131 (*vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*).
The state of being preceded by another [vowel] applies. By the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
The vowel of the suffix *vasu* is acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accentual rule for suffixes.
They are pronounced with the acute accent (*rocante*).
By the rule that *tiṅ* suffixes belonging to the *lasārvadhātuka* class are unaccented,
and by the rule that the *śap* augment is unaccented when it follows a *pit* suffix, [the verb form is unaccented].
The accent is that of the verbal root itself.

[The word] *rocanā* [is formed with] the suffix *yuc*, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.149: "And [the suffix *yuc* is applied after a root] beginning with a consonant and having an *anudātta* vowel as its penultimate."
The substitution of *an* [for the final vowel] occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.1 (*yugoranākau*).
The acute accent on the final syllable is prescribed by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.163 (*citaḥ*). [Thus we have] *divi*.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is applied by the rule *ūḍidam* (Pāṇini 6.1.171), and so forth.
They harness his two beloved bay horses to the chariot, on opposite sides— red, bold, and swift-drawing steeds.
They yoke his two beloved bay horses, with separate sides to the chariot—red, bold, and swift to carry him.

They yoke to the chariot of this Indra—who is designated by words such as *bradhna* and who dwells here and there, distinct from the physical forms of Āditya and others—the two horses named *hari*, acting as his charioteers.
That the two horses belonging to Indra bear the name *hari* is stated in the *Nirukta*: "The two *hari* belong to Indra; the two *rohita* belong to Agni" (1.15.1).
Of what nature are these two *hari*?
*Kāmyā* means those who are to be desired.
*Vipakṣasau* refers to two horses whose two flanks (*pakṣasī*, i.e., sides) are diverse.
They belong to the chariot on both sides, like the two victorious [horses] of Indra.
The two red-colored, courageous, and bold steeds are the carriers of men—of humans led by Indra’s charioteer Mātali.
Regarding this [word] *asya*, which refers back to that which was called *bradhnam* by the rule "idamo 'nvādeśe 'ś anudāttaḥ tṛtīyādau" (Pāṇini 2.4.32), the substitute *aś* is applied.
Because it is marked with the indicator *ś* (Pāṇini 1.1.55), it is an all-substitute (*sarvādeśa*) and is unaccented (*anudātta*).
The rule "the case-ending is exclusively anudātta" results in the entire word being anudātta. *Kāmyā*: from the root *kam*, meaning "to desire."
[The suffix] *ka* is applied by Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.30 (*kamerṇiṅ*).
From the root *kāmayati*, [the suffix] *yat* is applied by Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.97 (*aco yat*).
By virtue of being an exception to the rule regarding three svarita accents, the initial udātta accent is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.213 (*yato 'nāvaḥ*).
The dual ending is replaced by *ḍā* according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk*).
[The word] *harī* [is derived from the root] *hṛ*, meaning "they carry the chariot";
the suffix *in* is applied according to Uṇādi Sūtra 4.558 (*hapiṣi*, etc.).
The word *nisvāda* has an udātta accent on its first syllable.
[The form] *vipakṣasā* is derived from the roots *pac* and *vac* by the rule *pacivacibhyāṃ suṭ ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.659), which prescribes the suffix *asun* along with the augment *suṭ*.
Those two whose sides (*pārśva*) have different wings (*pakṣa*);
the word *vi-* is acute-accented (*udātta*) because it is a particle (*nipāta*).
By the rule regarding the original accent of the first member of a compound (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*), that same accent remains.
The dual ending is replaced by *ḍā*.
*Rathe*:
it is called a chariot (*ratha*) because people delight (*ramante*) in it.

[The suffix] *kvan* is applied [to the root *ras*] in the sense of "sport" (*krīḍā*), according to the rule: “*kvan* is added after *hani*, *kupī*, *ni*, *rām*, and *kāśi*” (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.109). Because it is marked with the *kit* designation, [the rule] “*anudātta-upadeśa-*... [applies].

1. A suffix beginning with *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, or *pha* is udātta when it ends in a vowel. 2. Also, [the suffixes] after verbal roots ending in *ka*, *jha*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ya*, *śā*, *si*, *vi*, *si*, and *ghas* are udātta.

By the rule *pā. sū. 6.4.37* and others, there is the elision of the letter *m*. By the *nis-svara* (the accent of the negative particle), the first syllable is udātta. *Śoṇā*: from the root *śoṇu* in the sense of "color" or "motion"; since it functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied. It is udātta on the first syllable, like *jihvā*. The substitution of *ḍā* is by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). *Dhṛṣṇū*: from the root *jighṛṣā* in the sense of "boldness. By the rule *trasigṛdhṛdhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.140), the suffix *knu* is applied. Due to its being *kit*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *Nuvāhasā*: [meaning] "they two carry constantly" (*nūn vahataḥ*). From the root *vah*, the suffix *asun* is applied by the rule *vahihābhyāṃ chandasi* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.660). Because the term *ṇit* is understood from Uṇādi Sūtra 4.657, there is *vṛddhi*. Being *nivāt* (by the rule *nityādir nityam*), it is udātta on the first syllable. By the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), that same accent remains.
Making a banner for him who has no banner, and a form for him who is formless, O men—
you were born together with the dawns.
Making light for the lightless, O men, creating beauty for the formless, you were born together with the dawns. 3.
"O mortals, O men, look upon this support"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
What is this support? It is said:
this Indra, whose form is the sun, was born—that is, he arose—having come together with the burning rays (upabdhi) or with the dawns (upaḥ-kāla) every day.
Alternatively, by metaphorically attributing death to the setting sun itself, the plural number is used through a grammatical transposition (vyatyaya) to form an address.
It should be construed as: "O mortal, every day you are born.
What are you doing?
To the living being who is without consciousness—overcome by sleep and thus devoid of discernment—he makes a sign, providing discernment in the morning;
to the object that is without form—unmanifest due to being enveloped in darkness during the night—he brings forth form, making its beauty manifest by dispelling the darkness at dawn.
Regarding this, Yāska states: "Peśas is a name for form, derived from the root piṃśati."
The words ‘aketave’ and ‘apeśase’ should be understood as being in the dative case with the sense of the ablative.
*ketum*: the accent is that of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). *kṛṇvan*.
The root *kṛv* is used in the senses of "injuring" and "doing.
There is the substitution of *śatṛ* for the present tense marker (*laṭ*).
By the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58), the augment *num* is added.

When the suffix *śap* would otherwise apply in the agentive (*kartṛ*) sense, the suffix *um* is applied by the rule *adhnvimṛṇvyośca* (Pāṇini 3.1.80); simultaneously with that, the vowel *v* is replaced by *a*. By the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the *a* is elided.

Due to the status of that [elision] as *sthānivadbhāva*, the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not take place by the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.86).
The vowel *a* [in *aketa*] is acute by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
In *aketave*, because it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final syllable of the second member is acute according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.172: *nañsubhyām*.
*peśaḥ*: [The first syllable is] udātta by the rule *indivapayasthānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 26).
*maryāḥ*.

In such cases as *chandasi nihrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.123), the term is derived from the irregular form (*nipāta*) of the root *mī*. There is the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the low accentuation of a vocative) according to Pāṇini 6.1.198.
Due to a lack of syntactic connection (*asāmarthya*), the preceding element does not undergo the treatment of being like a member of a compound (*parāṅgavadbhāva*).
*apeśase*: by the rule *nañsubhyām*, the final syllable of the compound is udātta. *sam*.
The particle is udātta on its first syllable. *Upadhmāna* [is derived from] the root *upa-plu-p* in the sense of "burning."
By means of blazing rays.
Regarding the form *laṭaḥ*, when the substitute *śatṛ* is applied, the suffix *śap* would normally be expected; however, by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *śa* is used instead.
Because of the rule "sārvadhātukamapit" (Pāṇini 1.2.4), this [suffix] is marked with the *ṅit* designation, and consequently, the *guṇa* strengthening of the penultimate light vowel does not occur.
The suffix *śas* is acute by virtue of being a pratyaya-svara.
Because it follows a verbal root (*dhātu*) that is taught with the suffix *śatṛ*, the *sārvadhātuka* affix is unaccented.
By the rule "an ekādeśa [replacing a preceding acute and a following grave] is acute" (Pāṇini 8.2.5), the resulting single substitute is acute.
"Thou wast born.
[This is used] in the sense of "he was born," with the substitution of the masculine gender (puruṣavyatyaya) and the application of the nighāta accent.
Burn him according to your own nature; they have brought him back again to the state of an embryo, assuming a name worthy of sacrifice.
Then, indeed, they have brought him back again to the state of an embryo, following his own inherent nature, as they assume a name worthy of sacrifice.
Herein is the specific application:

on the twenty-fourth day, at the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin there are two verses beginning with "ādaha svadhāmanu," and one verse beginning with "indreṇa saṃ hi dakṣase."
This triplet is known as the *palahastoniya*;
thus it is stated in the Sūtra:
"1. *pa*-nipātitaḥ."
2. Transposition of the Case Endings (*tadpuruṣavyatyaya*).

In the section beginning with "In the twenty-fourth [year], the Hotṛ was born" (*caturviṃśe hotājaniṣṭa*), it says: "For with Indra, through skill, from then on, according to their own nature, one and two" (*indreṇa saṃ hi dakṣasa ādaha svadhāmanvyekā dve ca*; Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.2).
Although this is a hymn addressed to Indra (*aindra-sūkta*), nevertheless, in the six words beginning with "from then on" (*ādaha*), the Maruts are described.
This is because it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "The Maruts are generally [associated] with Indra" (Anu. 2.22).
The particle *āt* is a nipāta used in the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*). The word *aha* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).

"Immediately after the two have rained," [the text says]. "In accordance with their own nature": looking toward the food or water that is to be produced hereafter, the Maruts, the gods, "impelled the state of being an embryo"—they sent forth the form of an embryo of water within the cloud.
They have impelled Parjanya, the maker of rain.
The word "again" (punaḥ) is employed to show that they act in this manner every year.
Of what nature are the Maruts? They are "sacrificial" (*yajñiya*), meaning worthy of sacrifice, and are called "those who uphold their own strength" (*svadhānāḥ*).
In the *Gaṇapāṭha* of the Maruts, names suitable for sacrifice such as "īdṛṅcāmyādṛṅc" and others are recorded elsewhere.
Among the twenty-eight food-names beginning with "andhas," "ūrka, rasaḥ, svadhā" (Nirukta 2.7.17) is recited.
Among the one hundred water-names beginning with "arṇas," "tejaḥ, svadhā, akṣaram" (Nirukta 1.12.17) is recited.
The two particles *ā* and *adha* are accented on their initial syllable.
Regarding *svadhām*: it is called *svadhā* because it sustains (*dadhāti*) or nourishes (*puṣṇāti*) one’s own world (*svam lokam*).
By the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), the suffix *ka* is applied. The word has the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the compound, as it is a *kṛt*-derivative.
The particles *anu* and *punaḥ* are both acute-accented (*ādyudātta*) at their beginning.
The state of being an embryo is *garbhatva*. It has the accent of a secondary derivative (*pratyayasvara*).
[The root] *īr* [becomes] *ir*.

From the root *īr* ("to go"), which is anudātta and has its causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the substitution of *irec* for the *jha* of the *liṭ* affix occurs according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.81. It is antodātta because of its *cit* designation.

According to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.1.4, "saha supā," there is a separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) by the word "sup"; thus, even when a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is compounded with *āṅ*, the final syllable is antodātta by virtue of Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.223, "samāsasya."

The suffix *ām* does not occur [after the root *dhā*] because of the rule "ijādeśca gurumato'nṛccaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.36), due to its being a mantra. There is an absence of *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because of its connection with the word *aha*, owing to the prohibition in "tupyapaśyatāheḥ pūjāyām" (Pāṇini 8.1.39).
[The form is] *dadhānāḥ*.

Regarding *jñāna*, since the final syllable would otherwise be udātta, the rule "for words ending in *abhi* and others, the first syllable is udātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.189) applies, resulting in initial udātta.
*Yajñiya* means "worthy of sacrifice"; the suffix *gha* is applied according to the rule "after *yajña* and *iṣṭi*, the suffixes *gha* and *khañ* [are added]" (Pāṇini 5.1.71).
The substitution of *iy* [for the final vowel and following consonant] is applied by the rule *āyaneyīnīyiyaḥ phaḍhakhachāṃ pratyayādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.2).
By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the vowel *i* is acute (*udātta*).

Even the firm [fortress], O Indra, you shattered with your breaking powers; even from the cave, with your carriers, you found the cattle along [the way]. 5. Even the firm, O Indra, you shattered with those who break; even from the cave, with your leaders, you found the cattle along [the path]. 5.
There is a certain legend:
the cows were carried off from the world of the gods by the Paṇis and cast into darkness;
and Indra, with the Maruts as his helpers, [recovered] them—so it is said.

And this is indicated in the Anukramaṇikā: "The five Asuras, seeking to recover the cows hidden [by them], spoke with uneven numbers to Saramā, the divine dog sent by Indra, as they sought to form an alliance with the Paṇis" (Anuvāka 10.108).
Furthermore, it is indicated as an illustration in another mantra: "The waters were obstructed like the cows by the Paṇi" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.32.11).
It is with reference to this very narrative that the following is said.

O Indra, together with the Maruts—who are breakers, bearers, and capable of carrying [the chariot] elsewhere—you shattered even that which is ‘vīḷu’, even a firm and inaccessible place. Even ‘guhā’, those cows (‘ustriyāḥ’) placed within a cave, you ‘anu avindaḥ’, having searched for them, you found them.
In the list of twenty-eight names for strength beginning with ‘ojaḥ pājaḥ’, it is read: ‘dakṣaḥ vīḷu cyautnam’ (Nirukta 2.9.14).
In the *Navagavyaka* section of the *Gonāmāni*, it is recited: "Ahalyā, Uṣṇā, Ustriyā" (*Nirukta* 2.11.3).
*vīḷu*:
the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*); *cit*.
The group beginning with *ca* is unaccented (*anudātta*). [Example: *āruktubhiḥ*.
[Derivation: The suffix *kan* is applied to the root *ruj* in the sense of "breaking" according to the *uṇādi* rules.
Due to the presence of the *kit* suffix, there is an absence of the *guṇa* vowel substitute.
Due to the presence of the *cit* suffix, the word is oxytone (accented on the final syllable).
In a compound, it takes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the subsequent member, which is a *kṛt*-derived word.
1. For the sake of the meaning of non-difference from that;
2. and it is formulated as a sūtra with the letter *ca*.

*guhā*: [This is] the substitution of *ḍā* for the locative case-ending (*saptamī*). It is acute-accented on the first syllable by the rule *grāmādīnāṃ ca* (Phiṭ-sūtra 38). *vahnibhiḥ*: The suffix *nip* is added to the root *vah* by the rule *vahniścyudulhāhāvaribhyo nit* (Uṇādi-sūtra 4.491). Because it has the marker *n*, it is acute-accented on the first syllable. *avindaḥ*: By the rule *kṣe mucādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.59), the augment *num* is inserted. By the rule *luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣvaḍudāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.71), the augment *aṭ* is acute-accented. *utsiyāḥ*: Those who dwell [there] are called *utsiyāḥ*. The suffix *riyak* is added to the root *vas* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The absence of the *ṣatva* change (of *s* to *ṣ*) is to be understood through the principle of diversity (*bāhulakāt*). For it is said: "The specific meaning of the sacrificial word arises from the suffix, the base, and its modification" (Pāṇini 3.3.1.2). The vowel *i* is acute-accented by the accent of the suffix itself. || 11 ||
Seeking the gods, they have directed their songs toward the one who bestows wealth, the great and renowned one, according to their thought.
Seeking the gods, they have raised their voices toward the great one, the finder of wealth, who is renowned according to his wisdom. 6.

Desiring the gods known as the Maruts, the singers—the officiating priests—have praised with hymns in order to reach the great and mature host of Maruts. Of what sort is that host of Maruts? It is "vidadvasu," endowed with riches that make themselves known by proclaiming their own majesty; it is "śruta," renowned and celebrated.
The analogy is that of the host of Maruts. "As [is] the thought" means: just as they praise Indra, the thinker, so [should one praise him].

*Devayantaḥ*: desiring the gods for themselves (*devān ātmana icchantaḥ*). [This is derived] by *Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.1.8 (*supa ātmanaḥ kyac*) and *Pāṇini Sūtra* 7.4.33 (*kyaci ca*), which prescribes the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel; however, the lengthening [of that *ī*] prescribed by *Pāṇini Sūtra* 7.4.25 (*akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ*) does not occur. This is because of *Pāṇini Sūtra* 7.4.35 (*na cchandasyaputrasya*), which prohibits all such instances of *ītva* or lengthening that would otherwise apply before the suffix *kyac* in Vedic usage.

Although it is *ītva* alone that is under discussion here, nevertheless, it is understood that this prohibition applies even to the lengthening (*dīrghatva*) that is separated [from the context]. This is appropriate because in forms such as *aśyāyantaḥ*, the initial [vowel] is prescribed by the rule *aśvādyasyāt* (Pāṇini 7.4.37).
The suffix *śatṛ* is added to the base ending in *kyac*;
and because *kyac* is marked with the *cit* designation, the final syllable is udātta according to the rule *citaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.163).

Since the suffix *śap* is treated as *pit*, and the *śatṛ* suffix is unaccented by the rule regarding the accent of *lasārvadhātuka* affixes, the resulting single substitute (*ekādeśa*) becomes udātta according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 8.2.5: “A single substitute for [an] udātta [and another vowel] is udātta.
For example:
“The suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing manner” (Pāṇini 5.3.23).
By the rule *lini* (Pāṇini 6.1.193), the syllable preceding the suffix is acute. In *matim*,
the suffix *kin* is acute by the rule *mantrē vṛṣēdhapacamana* (Pāṇini 3.3.96).

Although the word *mati* primarily denotes knowledge (*jñāna*), it is used figuratively for Indra as the possessor of that knowledge. Alternatively, since no other substantive is provided in the compound, this is a name (*saṃjñā*) of Indra.
Consequently, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *man* in the sense of the agent, according to Pāṇini’s rule *kvica saṃjñāyām* (3.3.104).

In its case, because the suffix *upadeśa* is *anudātta*, there is a prohibition of the *it*-augment (Pāṇini 7.2.10). Due to the *cit* designation, it has the *udātta* accent on the final syllable. *Accha*.

Because it is connected with the sense of "going" (*gacchati*) as an intensifier (*adhyāhata*), the term *accha* receives the designation of a *gati* by Pāṇini 1.4.69, *accha gatyarthavedeṣu*. Since there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designation of *nipāta* [by Pāṇini 1.4.57–60] along with the designation of *gati*, it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable) according to the Phiṭ-sūtra 80, *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ*. Regarding *vidadvasum*: from the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāne*), with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied. Thus, *vidadvasuḥ* refers to one who, because of possessing an excellence of generosity (*audāryātiśaya*), makes known (*vidanti* = *jñāpayanti*) riches (*vasūni* = *dhanāni*). He is the one who possesses such wealth.

In the case of the root *vid* with the suffix *śatṛ*, by the rule "after [roots] beginning with *ad*, there is elision of *śap*" (Pāṇini 2.4.72), *śap* is elided; thus, by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the *śatṛ* becomes udātta.
In the bahuvrīhi compound, that same accent remains by virtue of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*).
They praise or extol, thus they are called *giraḥ*.

From the root *guṇāti* with the suffix *kvip*, there is the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* by Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.1.100 (*ṛta iddhātoḥ*), followed by the replacement of that *i* with *ra*. It is accented acute (*udātta*) by the accent of the verbal root. *Mahām* means "the great one" (*mahāntam*).
There is the elision of the letters *na*, *ta*, and *ka*;
this is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
The word is accented on its first syllable by the accentuation rule for nominal stems (*prātipadika-svara*).
*anūṣata*: [from] the root *ṇu* in the sense of "to praise";
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
In the *luṅ* [aorist] tense, there is the substitution of *ad* for *jha* (Pāṇini 7.1.5).
Due to the status of being *ḍit*—because it begins with *ku*—there is an absence of *guṇa* (Pāṇini 1.1.5). The absence of *iṭ* and the lengthening of the vowel *u* are Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The elision (nighāta);
the word "śrutam"; the accent of the suffix (pratyayasvara).
1. [The vowels] ṭha, devān, and ātmanaḥ are *icchantaḥ*. 2. [The consonants] ga, pha, ya, and am are *anudātta*. 3. [The consonants] ca, cha, ta, pha, and śa belong to Indra alone.
O Ṛbhus,
for you have united with Indra, who is undaunted, so that you may act with skill; you are both joyful and equal in splendor.
For you have come together with Indra for skillful power, meeting with him who is fearless; both of you are joyful, possessing equal splendor.
O Marudgaṇa, you, uniting—that is, coming together—with Indra, will surely see him clearly;
the meaning is that he must certainly be seen by us.
With what kind of Indra?
By one who was fearless, that is, devoid of fear.
Of what nature were Indra and the host of Maruts?
They were *mandū*, meaning eternally joyful.
"Of equal splendor" means possessing identical radiance.
Once in the past, during the period of the slaying of Vṛtra, all the gods who were Indra’s companions were driven away by the fear of Vṛtra.
At that time, Indra met with the Maruts for the purpose of conquering the entire army belonging to Vṛtra.

This very meaning is summarized in the mantra, “From the snorting of Vṛtra” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.96.7), and is elaborated upon in the Brāhmaṇa, “Indra, indeed, being about to slay Vṛtra” (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 3.20).
The word *indra* denotes either the host of Maruts endowed with supreme sovereignty, or [the individual Indra];
in that case, the address to Indra must be supplied from outside the text.

And thus it has been explained by Yāska: “For you are seen by Indra, coming together with a fearless host; you two are ‘mandū,’ meaning exhilarated, or rather, it may mean ‘with that exhilarating one,’ and this [phrase] is explained as ‘having equal splendor’” (Nirukta 4.12).
"You shall see him; you shall perceive him. The Ātmanepada ending is used according to *Kātyāyana-vārttika* 1.3.29, which states that the root *dṛś* takes this ending when preceded by *sam*.
Regarding the root *dṛś*, the suffix *leṭ* is employed in the sense of a benediction (*prārthanā*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.7, which prescribes *leṭ* in the sense of the *liṅ* (optative).
‘thāsaḥ se’ (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.80);
the augment *aṭ* is added by ‘leṭo’ḍāṭau’ (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.94);
and the suffix *sip* is applied by ‘sibbahula leṭ’ (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.34).
The absence of *guṇa* [substitution] occurs because of the rule “An operation conditioned by a specific designation (*saṃjñā*) is not obligatory” (Paribhāṣā 93).
The substitution of *pa* [for *ta*] occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.36 (*aśnotyādibhyaḥ*).
The substitution of *ka* [for *ṭa*] occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.41 (*paṭhoḥ kaḥ si*).
By the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59), there is the substitution of *p* for the *s* of the suffix *sip*.
Due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously"), the suffix *śap* also occurs after *sip* (Pāṇini 2.4.73).
Because of the intervention by *sip*, the substitution of *paśya* does not take place (Pāṇini 7.3.78).
The root *śap* is unaccented because it is marked with the *pittva* indicator;
the subsequent *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is also unaccented;
thus, the accent of the verbal root alone remains.

Due to the connection with the word *hi*, the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) prescribed by Pāṇini 8.1.28 (*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*) does not occur, because of the prohibition stated in 8.1.34 (*hi ca*). [The form] *saṃjagmānaḥ*:
from the root *gam* preceded by *sam*, the suffix *liṭ* is applied in the sense of the present tense according to Pāṇini 3.4.6 (*chandasi luṅliṭ*).
The suffix *liṭ* is applied because the rule *samogamyucchibhyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.29) prescribes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
The substitution of *kānac* occurs according to Pāṇini 3.2.106,
and the doubling of the consonant [of the reduplicated syllable] occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.8.
The substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following sounds occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.60;
the change of the semivowel to a vowel in the reduplicated syllable occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.62;
and the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.98.
And *kānaca* [suffixes] express the state of being high-pitched (*udāttatva*). In a *gati*-compound, there is the original accent of the final member when it is a *kṛt*-derivative.
[The word is] *abibhyuṣā*.

‘Jibhī bhaye’: the *liṭ* suffix is applied as before; the *parasmaipada* ending is used according to Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.78: “The *parasmaipada* is used for the remaining [roots] when denoting the agent (*kartṛ*).”
By the rule *kasuśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.107), the *liṭ* suffix is replaced by *kasu*.
Due to its *kit* status, there is no *guṇa* strengthening;
furthermore, there is the substitution of *dvirbhāva* (doubling).
In the absence of the short vowel resulting from reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the augment *iṭ*—
which would otherwise be required by the rule *krādiniyamāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.13)— is precluded by the restrictive rule *vasvekājādghasām* (Pāṇini 7.2.67).
In the third person singular of the negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), the vowel *u* replaces the *va* by the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), because of the presence of the suffix *bhāva*.
By the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), there is the substitution of the preceding form (*pūrvarūpatva*). By the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ*.
The substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule *eranekāco’saṃyogapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.82) takes precedence over the substitution of *iṭ*.
The initial member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).

When this is joined with the preceding word in *saṃhitā*, the rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), which would require the substitution of the following vowel (*parapūrvatva*), is superseded by the rule *prakṛtyāntaḥpādamanyapare* (Pāṇini 6.1.115), whereby the original form is maintained (*prakṛtibhāva*). Thus: *mandū*.
In the rule *madistutimodamadasvapnakāntigatiṣu* (Dhātupāṭha 2.2), the augment *num* is applied by the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58).
Following the recurrence of the word *kuḥ*, [the forms] *kharu*, *śaṅku*, *pīyu*, *nīlaṅgu*, and *ligu* are derived from the root *lup* with the suffixes *ca*, *pha*, and *jha*.

In this regard, because of the mention [of the suffix] without a case-ending in (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.36), it is stated that *ku* occurs even after other verbal roots, just as in the case of *hiṅgu* from the root *hiṃ*.
It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
The dual ending is *au* (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.1.2).
By the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), [the vowel is replaced by] the preceding homogeneous vowel.
And in the third case singular, by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39) and others, there is the lengthening of the preceding homogeneous vowel. Thus: *samānavarcasā*.
The term *samānavarcas* is either a *dvandva* compound meaning "those two whose splendor is equal" or a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "whose [splendor] is equal.
In the dual number, the replacement by the vowel *ā* occurs according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* and so forth. The final syllable of the stem *samāna-* is udātta.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by virtue of the original accent of the first member, that very accent alone remains.
With blameless,
radiant, and victorious qualities, he worships with the desirable attributes of Indra.
With blameless, heaven-reaching qualities, the powerful sacrifice praises Indra with his desirable attributes. 8.

This sacrifice, proceeding with *makhas*—those who are blameless (*vanavadyaiḥ*), free from defects, and who have ascended to the heavenly world (*vabhidyubhiḥ*)—shines forth (*varcati*) together with the hosts of Maruts (*guṇaiḥ*), who are desirable (*kāmyaiḥ*) because they bestow fruits, so as to honor Indra (*indrasya indram*) with power (*sahasvat*). The meaning is that this sacrifice exceedingly pleases both the Maruts and Indra.
Among the fifteen names of sacrifice beginning with "yajñaḥ," the word "makhaḥ" is listed [in the *Nighaṇṭu*] as a name for Viṣṇu (Ni. 3.17.11).
In the forty-fourth *arcanīka* section, it is recited: "He worships; he sings" (*arceti gāyati*, *Nirukta* 3.14.1).
Those for whom no fault exists are "faultless" (*anavadya*);
the final syllable of the compound is accented according to Pāṇini 6.2.172 (*nañsubhyām*). Those who have reached heaven are "heaven-attainers" (*abhidyavaḥ*).
By those [words] *abhidyubhiḥ*.
The word *abhi* is oxytone by virtue of the accent of its nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that same accent remains by virtue of the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*).
*Makha*:
[This is] the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
*Sahasvat*: [It means] that which possesses strength (*saha*) in this sacrificial action (*aśvamedha-karman*).
Because the technical designation *bha*—by the rule *tasau matvarthe* (Pāṇini 1.4.19)—supersedes the designation *pada*, there is no substitution of *ru* for the *s*.
Furthermore, by the rule *mādupadhāyāśca matorvo'yavādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.9), the *ma* of the suffix *matup* is replaced by *va*.
The word *sahasvat* has its first syllable udātta according to the Phiṭ-sūtra: *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ-sūtra 26).
Because the suffix *matup* is grave (*pit*), it alone remains [by the rule of the remaining accent].
[The suffix *kāmya* is derived] from the root *kam* by [the addition of] *ṇiṅ*, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.30: *kamerṇiṅ*.

By the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), there is vṛddhi [of the penultimate vowel]. Since the root belongs to the class of roots ending in *am*—as per the rule *janījṛṣkṣvidisvidimidikhidichidikīrtibhyaśca* (Bhvādi-gaṇa-sūtra)—the *mit* designation would normally apply; however, because of the prohibition *na kyamicamām* (Bhvādi-gaṇa-sūtra), the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatvam*) prescribed by *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.92) does not occur.
From this causative form (*ṇyantāt*), the suffix *yat* is applied according to *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97).
There is elision of *ṇi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51).
When [the rule] "the suffix *ti* is circumflex" (Pāṇini 6.1.185) would have applied, the initial udātta accent is applied by the rule "in a word ending in *yat*, except for *anāva*" (Pāṇini 6.1.213).
Therefore, O dweller of the house, from the surrounding region or from the luminous realm of heaven,
may our songs be fashioned for you here.
Therefore, from all sides, come hither; either from heaven or from the realm of light. Toward him, our songs of praise are directed. 9.
O Marut, wind that pervades all around, come from this intermediate space which is the abode of the Maruts; come to this ritual act.
Or come from the sky, the heavenly world;
or come from the radiant orb of the sun.
The meaning is: "Come from every place where you may be at the time of our ritual. As for the purpose of this coming, it is stated:
while engaged in that ritual, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) thoroughly prepares (*saṃvṛñjate*), that is, perfectly accomplishes, the *viraḥ*, which are the hymns of praise.
"Ṛñjati means 'the act of adorning' (Nighaṇṭu 6.21)," says Yāska.
The meaning is: "Come to hear these hymns of praise.

Although, because the mantra is being employed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), one would expect the verb to be in the first person from the root *ṛt* (to perform a rite), nevertheless, the use of the third person occurs here due to the employment of the remote (impersonal) construction.

And regarding the definition of those [verses] composed in absentia (*parokṣakṛta*), Yāska says: "Those *ṛc*s are of three kinds: composed in absentia, composed in presence (*pratyakṣakṛta*), and spiritual (*ādhyātmika*).
Among them, those composed in absentia are joined with all nominal case-endings and with the third person of the verb" (*Nirukta* 7.1).
Therefore:
"pañcamyāsas til" (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.7);
"etadoś" (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.5);
"śivāt sarvādeśaḥ" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.55).
By the rule *'liti' (Pāṇini 6.1.193), the syllable preceding the suffix is acute. [The word] *parijana* [is derived from the root] *aja*, meaning "to go" or "to throw."
The suffix *manin* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.75, *anyebhyo’pi dṛśyante*.
The elision of the vowel *a* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
There is the *nighāta* accentuation due to the vocative case.
*gahī*: From the root *gam*, there is the elision of the *śap* suffix by Pāṇini 2.4.73 (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
By Pāṇini 3.4.87 (*herdhi vā*), and by the rule beginning with Pāṇini 6.4.37 (*anudāttopadeśa...*), there is the elision of *m*.

Therefore, by the rule *ato heḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.105), the elision of *hi* does not occur; for when that [elision] is to be applied, the elision of *m* is considered *asiddha* by the rule *asiddhavadatrā bhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22), and thus [the stem] does not end in *a*. [The form] *divaḥ*:
by the rule *udidam* (Pāṇini 6.1.171) and others, the case-ending receives the udātta accent.
Or:
[the particle] *vā* is unaccented by the rule "The particles beginning with *ca* are unaccented" (Phiṭ-sūtra 84).
From *rocanāt*.
The root *ruc* means "to shine.
By the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149), the suffix *yuc* is applied. By the rule *yuvo ranāko* (Pāṇini 7.1.1), the substitution of *ran* for *yu* occurs.
The word *cit* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

Regarding *adhi*: by the rule "adhi and pari are meaningless" (Pāṇini 1.4.93), since there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the designation of a *karmapravacanīya* with the designation of a particle (*nipāta*), it is an initial-accented (*ādyudātta*) word according to the rule "particles beginning with *ni* and *gā* have their first syllable accented" (Phitsūtra 80).

In this [context], because it is a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) to that which was already designated by "parijana" and so forth, the *aś* [substitute] is anudātta according to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.32: "The anudātta *aś* is used for *idam* in a subsequent reference when followed by the third case ending and so on.
By the rule of Śiva, it is a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*).

The case ending (*vibhakti*) is entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*) because of the rule *anudāttau suppitau* (Pāṇini 3.1.4), which prescribes that case endings (*sup*) and verbal suffixes beginning with *p* (*pit*) are unaccented. Thus:
*ṛjate*.
The roots *ṛji* and *bhṛjī* mean "to fry.
Because of its connection with the prefix *sam*, [the root] here functions in the sense of "preparing" or "adorned.
There is a *nighāta* (elision of accent).
In the case of *giraḥ*,
the accent is that of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
Either from here we summon him, or from heaven, or from the earth,
or Indra from the great mid-air.
From here, or from heaven, or from the earth, we implore Indra for bounty; or from the great intermediate space. 10.
We pray most earnestly for the winning of wealth from the god Indra. From which world? That is now stated:

either from this very earth being split asunder, or from the earthly world (*pārthiva*), or from heaven (*divaḥ*), the celestial world, or from the great (*mahaḥ*) and expansive (*praudāt*) *rajas*, that is, from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa-loka*) which colors the quarters of the sky and so forth.
The meaning is: "May this Indra, having brought wealth from wherever it may be, bestow it upon us.
Among the twenty-seven acts of supplication, the words "īmahe" and "yāmi" are recited [in Nirukta 3.19.1].
From this [word]: from the word *idam*, the suffix *tasil* is applied in the ablative case.
By the rule "idama iś" (Pāṇini 5.3.3), *iś* is substituted [for *idam*].

From Śiva [the rule] "sarvādeśaḥ" [applies]. Here, the scope of Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.171, *udidam*, is exemplified by *ābhyām* and *ṇbhiḥ*; the scope of sūtra 6.1.193, *liti*, is exemplified by *pacanam* and *pācakaḥ*.

Both [the suffix *l* and the suffix *tas*] are permanent (*nitya*). In that case, because of its subsequent position, the rule "In a conflict, the subsequent operation prevails" (Pāṇini 1.4.2) applies; thus, by the rule "when *li* follows" (Pāṇini 6.1.193), the vowel *i* becomes acute.

Subsequently, because *tas* is designated as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) by the rule "A nominal stem and a case-ending" (Pāṇini 1.4.14), the acute accent prescribed for case-endings other than those called *asarvanāmasthāna* by the rule "that which begins with *u*" (Pāṇini 6.1.171) takes effect.

If it is argued that, according to the maxim *sakṛdgatau vipratiṣedhe yadbādhitaṃ tadbādhitaṃ eva* (Paribhāṣā 40), "when there is a conflict between two rules, that which is once superseded is superseded for good," and thus the rule *udidam* (Pāṇini 6.1.171) does not apply again, we say: no. For it is accepted that, in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*), there is the principle of *punaḥprasaṅga-vijñāna* (Paribhāṣā 39)—that is, a rule may apply again if its conditions are met. If it is further objected: "In that case, even in words like *yataḥ* and *tataḥ*, although the accent of the suffix *tasil* has been superseded by the subsequent *liṅ-svara* (the acute accent of the finite verb), the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168) would still cause the *tasil* to be acute," we say: no.
This reading follows the *Kāśikā* regarding the fact that the words *yat* and *tat* end in the vowel *sāva*.
1. By virtue of ending in the vowel *sāva*.
This is because of the prohibition [stated] in Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.182: *na godhnasāvavarja*.

Nor can it be argued that there is a principle of "reapplication" (*prasaṅga-vijñāna*); for while such a principle might apply universally, it is here adopted only in specific instances according to the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*).
This is the conclusion.
In the sense of "giving" (*dāna*), [the root *paṇ* takes the suffix *kvip*].
By the rule *ghāvādeḥ paḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64), the *pa* is changed to *sa*.
The suffix *kvip* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).

In the word *janamanvanam* [from *jana-manvan*], the substitution of *ā* for *n* occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.42 (*janasanakhanām sanjhaloḥ*). The augment *iṭ* does not apply because of the prohibition in Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.9 (*titutratathasisusarakaseṣu ca*).

When the rule regarding the accent of the suffix *ni* would have applied, the term *udāttaḥ* is understood from the previous context; thus, by Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.97 (*ūtiyūtijūtimātihetītītyaiyaśca*), the word is treated as a particle (*nipāta*) and receives an acute accent (*udātta*) on its final syllable.
We implore (*īmahe*). [The root] *īṅ* means "to go.
Even though it takes the suffix *iyan*, there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*, Pāṇini 2.4.73).

Because this verbal root has the marker *ṅ*, by the rule *tāsyanudāttenṅidupadeśāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the *laṭ*-affixes following a root taught with an *anudātta* marker become *anudātta*; thus, only the accent of the root itself remains. Nor does the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* apply to cause the suppression (*nighāta*) of that accent, because of the prohibition in the rule *cavāyoge prathamā* (Pāṇini 8.1.59).

For in the two subsequent sentences as well, since they contain the word *vā*, the sentence would otherwise remain incomplete; therefore, a finite verb must necessarily be supplied, and in relation to that, this [first] finite verb is considered the "first" (*prathamā*).
From *divaḥ*: the acute accent (*udātta*) of the case ending is due to the rule beginning with “*uḍidam*”. From *pāthivāt*.
The root *prath* means "to become manifest.

[The earth] is called *pṛthivī* because it expands (*prathate*). According to the Uṇādi Sūtra 1.148, "From *prath*, the suffix *pivan* and vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) [occur]," the suffix *pivan* is applied.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *‘pittaurādiśca’* (Pāṇini 4.1.41). It is acute (*udātta*) by the accent of the suffix;
by the principle of the remainder being unaccented (*śeṣanighāta*), the word *pṛthivī* has its first syllable unaccented (*anudātta*).

In the sense of "a modification of the earth" (*pṛthivyā vikāraḥ*), the suffix *orañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.139) applies; under the continued influence of that rule, the suffix *añ* is added by Pāṇini 4.3.140 (*anudāttādeś*).
By Pāṇini 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*), there is the elision of the vowel *ī*.
Then, by Pāṇini 7.2.117 (*naḍādīnāṃ ca*), there is the vṛddhi substitution for the first vowel among the vowels.
The status of being a *svarita* [accent] is established by Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.51.
By the rule *antodāttādiniyam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.97), it is *udātta* at the beginning.
*Adhi*.
Being a particle (*nipāta*), it is accented on the first syllable.
*Indram*: ending in the suffix *ran*, it is accented on the first syllable.
*mahaḥ*: [The form] *mahataḥ* [is used]; the elision of the letters *a* and *ka* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
In *rajasaḥ*,
[the vowel] is udātta by the rule “*nadvipayasyānisantasya*” (Pāṇini 6.1.213).
The hymn consisting of ten verses beginning with "indram" is the fourth among those starting with "surūpakṛtnum. The seer, meter, deity, and general application are as before;
however, the specific application is now stated.
In the *Mahāvrata* and the *Nikēvalya-śastra*, there is the hymn beginning with "Indramid gāthinaḥ.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: "The head is the *Gāyatra*; 'Indramid gāthinaḥ'... (Ai. Ā. 5.2.1).
Likewise, on the twenty-fourth day, in the *śastra* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, there is the triplet of *paryāsa-stotriyas* beginning with "Indramid gāthinaḥ."

Beginning with “A Hotṛ was born in the twenty-fourth [year],” and continuing until “Come hither, for thy strength is excellent; Indra indeed, the singers sing aloud” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.2), this very triplet serves as the *anurūpa* in the first *paryāya* of the *atirātra* sacrifice during the recitation of the Acchāvāka.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “For Indra, the exhilarating one, the pressed juice; Indra indeed, the singers sing aloud” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
To Indra indeed the singers have sung the lofty hymn; to Indra the chanters with their songs; to Indra the voices have cried out. 1.
To Indra alone have the singers raised their lofty song; to Indra with hymns the chanters; to Indra the voices have cried out. 1.

The *gāthins*—the chanters (*udgātṛs*) associated with the songs (*gīta*) of the *sāmans*—praised Indra alone with the *brahman*-named *sāman* based on the verse "tvāmiddhi havāmahe" (Ṛgveda 6.46.1). The *arkiṇas*—the *hotṛ* priests endowed with hymns (*ṛc*) as the means of praise—praised Indra alone with *arkas*, that is, with the *ṛc* mantras.
Those remaining, the *adhvaryus*, praised Indra in this same way with *vāṇīs*, that is, with the words in the form of *yajus*.
Yāska has stated that the word *arka* refers to a mantra: "The *arka* is a mantra. [In some versions: 1. it is recited as a specific *gāyatrī*;
2. in others, a *tṛca* is prescribed; in others, a *tṛca* is determined.
3. "The [group] beginning with *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *indra*.
As it is said: "That by which they utter" (*Nirukta* 5.4).
Furthermore, among the fifty-seven names of speech beginning with "śloka," the term "vāśī" or "vāṇī" is recited (*Nirukta* 1.11.12).

*gāthinaḥ*: the suffix *than* is applied to the root *gā* by the rule "after *upa*, *kṛp*, and *gā*, the suffix *than*" (*uṇādi-sūtra* 2.161). It is udātta on the first syllable because it belongs to the *ni* class.
Those who possess these *gāthās* are called *gāthinaḥ*.
The suffix *ini* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *vrīhyādibhyaśca* (5.2.116).
By the accentuation of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the vowel *i* is acute (*udātta*).
And that is taught by the *Mati* [grammar]:
"bṛhat" [is used] for "bṛhatā";
the singular locative ending is elided by the rule "supāṃ suluk".
The word *pṛṣat* is prescribed as a final-accented (*antodātta*) nipāta by the rule *pṛṣadhanmahajjagacchatruvac* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.241).
Regarding *arkebiḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *arc*, meaning "to worship."
The word *arka* refers to mantras, derived from the sense "that by which one is honored" (*arcyate ebhiḥ*).
The suffix *gha* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.3.118, "In the masculine, when forming a name, *gha* is generally used.
The substitution of *k* for the original consonant (*kutva*) occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule 7.3.52, "The substitution of *k* occurs for *c* and *j* before the suffixes *ghi* and *ṇyat*."
The final syllable is udātta by virtue of the accentual rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*).

The substitution of *ais* for *bhis* does not occur because of the rule "in the Veda, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*, Pāṇini 7.1.10). They are called *arkas* because they possess hymns (*mantras*) that serve as the means for praise.

The word *vāṇīḥ* has its first syllable acute by the rule *vṛṣādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.20). The lengthening of the vowel occurs because the prohibition of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) by the rule *dīrghāj jasi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.105) is made optional in the Vedic language by the rule *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.106).
The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
[He] praised; from the root *ṇu*, meaning "to praise."
The substitution of *n* for *m* is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.65 (*ṇo naḥ*).
In the *luṅ* tense, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
For the suffix *jha*, there is the substitution of *at* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.5).

The absence of the augment *iṭ* and the lengthening of the vowel *u* are Vedic (*chāndasa*). Due to the root beginning with a guttural (*kutādi*), the suffix *sic* is treated as having the *ḍit* designation (Pāṇini 1.2.1), which results in the absence of *guṇa* substitution (Pāṇini 1.1.5).
Indra indeed is with the two bay steeds, mingled with them, yoked by a word;
Indra is the wielder of the thunderbolt, the golden one.
Indra indeed, joined with his two bay steeds, has come together with the word-yoked [horses]; Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, is golden-hued. 2.

"Indra"—that is, Indra himself—is "with" (sacā) the two "bay horses" (haryoḥ), namely the horses named Hari, "simultaneously" (yugapat) and "thoroughly joined" (ā-sammiśraḥ), meaning he is perfectly united with them on all sides.
Of what sort are the two bay horses?
They are "yoked by word" (vacoyujā), meaning they are harnessed to the chariot by Indra's mere command; that is to say, they are well-trained.
This one is "Indra," the "Vajrī," meaning endowed with the thunderbolt; he is "Hiraṇyaya," meaning golden, that is to say, adorned with all ornaments.
Of the two bay horses;
"harataḥ" (they carry) thus "harī" (the two bays); [ending] *in*.
The word *niśvāda* is udātta at its beginning.
It has been stated [in Nirukta 5.5] that *sacā* means "together. Thus, it means "mixed."
*Misraṇam* means *miśraḥ*.
[The suffix] *vañ* is applied to the root *miśrayati* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.18).
One whose [components] are thoroughly mixed (*samyaṅ miśrau*) is *saṃmiśraḥ*.
The form *latvam* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). It means "he thoroughly mixes. In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accentuation is that of the original form of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
*vacoyujā*: that which is yoked by speech is *vacoyuj* (speech-yoked). For the genitive dual of these two, the substitution of *ā* occurs according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

The word *yuja* is acutely accented on the final syllable by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). By the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), that same accent remains. Thus: *vajrī*.
He possesses a vajra;
by the rule *ata iniṭhanau* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.115), the suffix has the accent. Thus: *hiraṇyayaḥ*.
By the rule *ṛhyavāśvayavāstvamāśvīhiraṇyayāni chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.175), the elision of the letter *m* in the word *hiraṇyaya* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
The vowel *a* is acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix;
together with the preceding grave (*anudātta*) vowel, it becomes acute according to the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*.
Indra raised the sun high in heaven for far-reaching vision;
he split apart the mountain with his rays.
Indra raised the sun high in heaven so that it might be seen from afar; he split the mountain asunder with his rays.
1. *ca*, *cha* are praised (*arcante*); *ta*, *pha*, *śa* are being praised (*arcyante*). 2. *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *ya*, *śa* consist of gold (*hiraṇyamayaḥ*).
3. [The letters] *ca* [occur] in the word "consisting of gold" (*hiraṇyamaya*); *cha*, *pha* [occur] in the word "consisting of gold" (*hiraṇyamaya*).
This Indra raised the sun into the sky, in the celestial realm, for long-lasting, mature, and uninterrupted vision— that is,

for the purpose of enabling living beings to see by dispelling that darkness which had previously overwhelmed the world through the demon Vṛtra. And that sun, with his rays (gobhiḥ), has set all the world in motion— meaning he has specially impelled and illuminated it, from the mountains and principal peaks down to the entire universe— for the sake of being seen.
Alternatively, Indra himself, by means of the *gobhiḥ*—that is, the waters acting as the instrumental cause—thoroughly impelled (*vyairayat*) the mountain, the cloud.
Among the fifteen names for rays, it is read in the *Nighaṇṭu* (1.5.3): "The rays are *gāvaḥ*.
Among the thirty names for clouds, it is read in the *Nighaṇṭu* (1.10.1): "*adriḥ* is a cloud (*gāvā*)."
*dīrghāya* is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). *Cakṣase*.
The suffix *asun* is applied to the root *cakṣ* by the rule "asun after all roots" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.628).
Due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously"), there is no substitution of *ṇya* or other such replacements.
Because it is marked with the *ni*-sign, the first syllable is udātta-accented.

Although the word *sūryam* is listed among the names for battle (*saṃgrāma*) in the sense that "it impels or drives forth," it is not accepted here [as such], because if it were a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "great wealth (*mahat dhana*) in this battle," its final syllable would fail to be accented acute (*antodātta*).
In *mahādhane*:
since that wealth (*dhana*) is great, it is accented on the final syllable by the rule *samāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.223). [The word] *abhe*.
By the rule *atigṛbhyāṃ bhan* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.432), the suffix *bhan* is applied; it is udātta by virtue of being part of the *nistvādādi* group. [Thus we form] *havāmahe*.
The root *heñ* is used in the sense of "striving" (*spardhā*) and "sound" (*śabda*).
Because it is trivalent (*triśvāt*), the Ātmanepada ending is applied when the action benefits the agent, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.72.
In place of the present tense marker *laṭ*, the ending *mahiṅ* is substituted, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.78.
By the rule *ṭita ātmanepadānām* (Pāṇini 3.4.79), the suffix *ṭi* [is replaced by *e*].
Then, by *kartari śap* (Pāṇini 3.1.68), the *śap* affix is added.

Following the continued application of *haḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.32), the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.34) applies, whereby the semivowel *va* undergoes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) to become *u*.
The state of having another [vowel] preceding;
the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel; and the lengthening according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.101: "A long vowel is substituted for *a* before a suffix beginning with *yañ*."
The *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies by the rule "tiṅṅatiṅaḥ.
Regarding *yujam*: [it is derived] from the root *yuja* in the sense of "concentration" (*samādhi*) with the suffix *kvip*.

The augment *num* does not occur [in *yuj*] by virtue of the rule *yujerasamāse* (Pāṇini 7.1.71). For that rule, based on the specific mention of *yujeḥ*, does not apply to the form devoid of the vowel *i*. Alternatively, according to the maxim *anityam āgamaśāsanam* (Paribhāṣā 93), the *num* augment does not occur even for the root *yujir* in the sense of "joining."
Regarding the word *vṛtreṣu*:
from the root *vṛt* meaning "to turn" (*vartane*),
those which exist in a hostile manner (*pratikūlatayā vartante*) are called *vṛtrāṇi*, that is, enemy clans.
The suffix *rak* is applied by the rule "sphāyitañci" (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.170).
Due to its *kit* status, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Vṛtra-han. The suffix *ini* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.115 (*ata iniṭhanau*). It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
O ever-conquering one, ward off Vṛtra and the narrow pass for us; be our protector, unopposed by any foe.
O you who grant gifts at all times, drive away that Vṛtra, that Curu, from us; for us, you are irresistible. 6.
O giver of all desired fruits together from the sacrifice, O showerer of rain, Indra, for the sake of producing rice and other grains, release this visible moving cloud of waters for our benefit.
Likewise, for us, be unopposed—
uttering no word of "no" in response to whatever we request.
Therefore, he has never stumbled in our domain.
With this very intention, Yāska said: "Apratiṣkuta means 'unopposed,' 'unrefuted,' or 'unstumbling'" (Nirukta 6.16).
*vṛtram*: the vocative accent (*āmantrita-nighāta*). *amum*.
It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (prātipadika-svara).
*Curu*: he moves, thus "curu."
The suffix *u* is applied by the rule "bhṛ-mṛ-śī-tṛ-car-i-sa-ri-tan-dhi-ni-mā-sji-my-a-uḥ" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.7). It is udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
[Thus it forms] *satrādāvan*.
The word *satra* has the sense of "together" (*saha*).
Because it gives the entire collection of desired fruits together, it is called *satrādā*. The suffix *vanip* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.74: *āto maninkvanivvanipaśca*.
The initial acute accent (*udātta*) is applied by Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.198 (*āmantritasya ca*),
and there is no suppression of accent (*nighāta*) because it occurs at the beginning of a *pāda*.
*Apa*.
The long vowel [in *vṛddhi*] is by Pāṇini’s rule 6.2.136, *nipātasya ca*.
A particle (*nipāta*) is udātta on its first syllable. *Vṛddhi*.
The root *vṛñ* is used in the sense of "choosing.
From the imperative (*loṭ*) mood, the suffix *sip* is applied;
for that [suffix], *hi* is substituted by the rule *serhyapicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87).
[The suffix] *inu* [is applied] after roots beginning with *śvi* (Pāṇini 3.1.73).
Its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule "frequently in the Veda" (Pāṇini 2.4.73).
Furthermore, the substitution of *hy* [for *hi*] occurs by the rule "after *śru*, *śṛṇu*, and *prakṛ*, in the Veda" (Pāṇini 6.4.102).
Because that [suffix] is marked with ḍ, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the preceding vowel;
it receives the *nighāta* accent;
[the form is] *asmabhyam*.
From the word *asmad*, the substitution of *bhyam* for *bhyas* occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.30.
Then, by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.90, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letter *d*.
However, the substitution of *e* [for the final vowel] by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.103 does not take place because it is a plural form ending in a *jhal* consonant.
It has been stated [in Pāṇini’s Mahābhāṣya]: "When there is a further application [of a rule] after an operation on a constituent part, there is no prescription for what has already been established.
By the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the vowel *a* in *sma* is udātta.

According to the rule "bhyaso bhyam," the substitute *abhyam* takes the place of *bhyas*; with respect to this substitution, by the rule "elision of the remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*), there is elision of the portion of the word *adas* ending in *m*.
Then, by the accent of the cessation of the acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*),
there is an acute accent for the initial *a* (Pāṇini 6.1.161).
[The word is] *apratiṣkutaḥ*.
It is not established by anything.
[The root] *kuḍ* means "to sound.
By the rule *niṣṭhā* (Pāṇini 3.2.102), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object.
The separation occurs before *prati*.
Because *pāraskara* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa*, the augment *suṭ* is applied (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.157).
Because *supāmā* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa*, the substitution of *pañcam* is applied (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.98).
In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*) of the first member, which is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), is retained.
One after another, the hymns of Indra are ever more exalted;
I find no end to his perfect praise.
Impetuous, impetuous, those higher hymns of Indra—I find no crookedness in him; I seek his fair praise. (7)

"Whatever hymns (*stoma*)—specific types of praise—are more excellent (*uttara*), that is, superior, among other gods who bestow their respective fruits, with all those hymns I do not find a worthy, beautiful praise (*suṣṭuti*) for this wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), Indra. The meaning is that because of Indra’s extreme abundance of qualities and his renown as the most excellent even among other gods, even those hymns well-known for their excellence are not sufficient.
Yāska explains this *ṛc* as follows: "This [word] *tuñje-tuñje* refers to this action of the ritual."
"In every gift, the praises of Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, increase; yet I find no end to his flowing bounty" (Nirukta 6.17–18).

*Tujjetujje*. It has been stated that *tujjati* means "the act of giving. Therefore, the suffix *ac* is applied after the root [in the sense] of the agent, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).
By the rule *citaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.163), the word [ending in *cita*] has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
By the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4), there is reduplication (*dvirbhāva*).
By the rule *tasya paramāmreḍitam* (Pāṇini 8.1.2), the second member receives the technical designation *āmreḍita*.
By the rule *anudāttaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.3), it is unaccented (*anudātta*). In the sense of "giving," the meaning is "he gives";
however, in the *Nirukta*, it is explained according to its meaning as "in every act of giving."
Regarding the latter [term]: the root *tṛ* is used in the senses of "floating" and "crossing.
In the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), the suffix *ap* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.57 (*ṛdorap*).
The word *ut* expresses excellence (*atiśaya*).

The term *uttara* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has excellence as its quality. According to the rule "the particles beginning with *ut* are udātta on their first syllable" (Phiṭ-sūtra 80), the word *ut* is udātta on its initial vowel.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member prevails.
As for *stomāḥ*: by the rule beginning with "atistumu" (Uṇādisūtra 1.137), the word *stoma*, being formed with the suffix *man*, is derived from a root and is thus udātta on its initial syllable.
*vindhe* [is derived from] the root *vidl* in the sense of "obtaining," in the present tense (*laṭ*).
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used because of the *svarita* accent;
this is the first person singular (Pāṇini 3.4.78);
[the suffix] *śa* is applied according to "śa after *tud* and others" (Pāṇini 3.1.77).
The augment *num* is applied by the rule *śe mucādīnām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.59).
By transposition (*vyatyaya*), the letter *d* becomes *dh*. Of this...
Because it refers back to the subject at hand, Indra, the form *idam* takes the substitute *aś* by Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.4.32 (*idamaḥ aś*);
due to its being marked with the *śit* designation, this substitution is a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*) and is unaccented.
[The word is] *suṣṭutim*.
The root is *ṭuj* in the sense of "praising.
By the rule *dhātvādeḥ paḥ saḥ*, the *p* is changed to *s*. By the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94), the suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
The prefix *su-* forms a *prādi-samāsa* with the upasarga [root] by Pāṇini 2.2.18.

By the rule "upasargātsunoti" (Pāṇini 8.3.65), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Here, although the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of *su-* would be obtained by the rule regarding the original accent of the first member of an indeclinable compound (*avyayapūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*), that is set aside; and when the acute accent of the verbal root (*dhātu*) would be obtained by the rule "gatikārakopapadātkṛta" (Pāṇini 6.2.139) concerning the original accent of the final member, that too is superseded. Consequently, by the rule "tādau ca niti kṛtyatau" (Pāṇini 6.2.50), the acute accent must belong specifically to *su-*, which is the immediately preceding member designated as a *gati*.

However, that [rule] is overridden by the rule *manuktin-vyākhyāna-śayana-sthāna-sthānaja-kādi-kītāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.151), which prescribes that the final syllable of the second member of the compound is udātta.

Thus, they say that in examples such as *suhavāṃ suṣṭutī huve* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.32.4), *vṛṇe codasva suṣṭutim* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.75.6), and *yāste rāke sumatayaḥ* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.32.5), there is udāttatva on the final syllable.
Nevertheless, it appears that this does not hold true exactly as stated in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule *manuktin* and so forth.

For in that context, because the term "from a kāraka" (*kārakāt*) is understood from the rule *kārakāddhṛtaśrutayorevāśiṣi* (Pāṇini 6.2.148), it is stated that the rule *manaḥ-kvin* and so forth applies only in cases such as *pāṇinikṛtiḥ*. Furthermore,
the rule *prakṛti-prahṛti* (Kātantra 6.2.151) is cited as a counter-example to this.
It might be argued as follows: "That by which one praises is praise" (*stutiḥ*); thus, by means of the suffix *ktin*, the *ṛc* verse, functioning as the instrument (*karaṇa*), is denoted.
And by the word *su-*, it is precisely the instrument that is qualified, not the meaning of the verbal root.
And thus, in the case of *suṣṭutiḥ*, the word *su-* will indeed be restricted to denoting a kāraka;
whereas in cases such as *prakṛtiḥ* and *prahatiḥ*, the prefix *pra-* is merely a qualifier of the root meaning (*dhātvartha*). Therefore, that [argument] is also an invalid example. No.

This being the case, since the word *su* lacks connection with a verbal action (*kriyā*), the designation of "preposition" (*upasarga*)—stated in Pāṇini’s Sūtra 1.4.59, "Prepositions [are so called] when there is a connection with a verbal action"—would not apply.

1. [The reading] *ca-cha-tha-pha-śa* explains this. 2. [The reading] *ta* [explains it] by virtue of its having the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). 3. [The readings] *ga-gha-ca-cha-ṇa-ya-śa* [explain it] as an exception (*apavāda*) to that. 4. [The readings] *ga-gha-ca-cha-ṇa-ta-pha-ya* [explain it] by virtue of its being accented acute (*udātta*). 5. [The readings] *cha-ṇa-ya* [state] that likewise, "it does not exist. 6. [The reading] *ta* [states that it is] a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). [In the commentary on] verse 11, it would not be [so].
And in that case, by the rule "upasargād anunāsikasya" (Pāṇini 8.4.14), the substitution of *p* for *n* would not occur.
[Objection: But surely the instrument (*karaṇa*) is denoted by the suffix *ktin*;
and the instrument is that which effects an action.
And thus, since the prefix *su-*—which qualifies the instrument (*karaṇa*)—is connected with the action included within that instrument, it will possess the status of a preverb (*upasarga*).
This is not so;

for if that were the case, according to the rule "those [words] which are connected with an action are designated as preverbs in relation to that [action]" (Pāṇini 1.4.60), its status as a preverb would apply only in relation to the meaning of the root *kṛ* ("to do"), and not in relation to the meaning of the root *stu* ("to praise"). Consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* (the *patva* change) would simply not occur.
But surely, by way of the meaning of the verbal root *stu* itself, the word *su-* will be an adjective qualifying its instrument;

for that which is a beautiful praise, its instrument must also be beautiful. And thus, through its connection with the meaning of the root *stu*, it will also possess the status of a prefix (*upasarga*) in relation to it, thereby retaining its *p*-sound.

Since it is a qualifier of the instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of that [suffix], the word *su* will also be a term denoting a *kāraka*; thus, without contradicting the rule for *vṛddhi*, the word *suṣṭhu* will be the scope of the sūtra *man-kthin-ādi*. As for the statement that *prahṛtiḥ* is cited as an example for the suffix *kin* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), that is not so.
In that context, the word *karaṇa* (instrument) is intended in its primary sense.

Even in the example provided for the suffix *ktin*, it is intended that the word qualifies the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) alone, and not that it qualifies the meaning of the suffix itself by way of the root; thus, the counter-example is logically justified.

However, in the case of *suṣṭutiḥ*, the operation of the word *su-* extends as far as the instrument denoted by the suffix *ktin*; therefore, this is indeed a primary example (*udāharaṇa*) and not a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
No.

In this case, does the word *su* intend to qualify both the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) by its own direct denotation (*śruti*), or does it qualify one by direct denotation and the other by implication (*artha*)?
Even if it intends to qualify both, is it done simultaneously or successively?

In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the word expressing the qualifier must recur for every individual object qualified. In the second case, there would be the occurrence of a cessation of activity;
yet, neither is a cessation of activity observed nor is it accepted in the case of words, elders, or actions.

Therefore, there is no dual purport based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Now, if the purport lies in one instance by way of direct scriptural statement and in the other by way of implication (*artha*),
then, since the connection with the meaning of the verbal root would be merely implied, the *ṣatva* substitution would not be established.

If the connection between the suffix-meaning and the object were merely implied (*ārthika*), then the accentuation rules in forms such as *manktin* would not be established. Furthermore, if one were to claim that even an implied connection with the *kāraka* serves as an example [of a word-meaning], then counter-examples such as *prakṛteḥ prahṛtiḥ* would be impossible;

for since the connection with the mere meaning of the verbal root is directly expressed by the word itself (*śruti*), who could prevent its connection with the instrument (*karaṇa*)? This is the general direction of the argument.

Therefore, if one accepts here that the rule is intended merely to establish the connection with the meaning of the suffix, let the accent be established; however, the substitution of *pat* [for *su*] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively, let it be a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is beautiful praise" (*śobhanā stutiḥ yasyām*).
And in this way, by the rule *nañsubhyām*, it will have an udātta accent on the final syllable.
Alternatively, the word *suṣṭutayaḥ* means "those which praise well";
thus, by the rule *kticktau ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.104), when the suffix *ktic* is applied, the resulting form is oxytone because it belongs to the *cvi*-class.
Nor should it be asked how verses (*ṛcaḥ*), which function as instruments, can be denoted by the suffix *ktic*, which expresses an agent.
Just as in the expression "the wood cooks," it is appropriate for those [faculties] to be considered instruments when one intends to emphasize their own primary activity.
Like a bull among the herds, I am the lord of the peoples by my own might, irresistible and unopposed.
Like a bull, a leader of the herd, he drives the people with his might—the sovereign, whom none can resist. 8.
Indra, the bull who has increased through desire,
reaches— that is, approaches— the people, that is, human beings, with his own vigor and strength in order to favor them.
Of what sort is Indra?
Īśāna is the capable one;
*apratiṣkuta* means free from opposition,
meaning he does not refuse when entreated.
The example is that of Indra. *Vaṃsagaḥ* means a bull whose movement is desirable; he reaches [his goal] just as one reaches herds of cattle.

*Vṛṣā*: The suffix *kanin* is applied to the root *vṛṣ* by the rule "The suffixes *kanin*, *vṛṣan*, *pitṛ*, *aśvan*, *dhanvin*, *rājin*, *dyu*, and *pratidiv* [are added after various roots]" (*Uṇādisūtra* 1.154). Due to the *k*-marker, there is an absence of *guṇa* strengthening.
The word *yūtha* is accented on the first syllable by the rule *nistvādādyudāttaḥ*. Like herds (*yūthāni*):
they are called *yūthāni* because young animals (*yuvan*) mingle (*miśribhavanti*) therein.
The root *yu* is used in the sense of "mixing" and "not mixing.
The word [yūtha] is derived with the suffix *thak*, as prescribed by the rule *tithapṛṣṭhathyūthaprothāḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.169).
The lengthening of the vowel occurs due to this specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*).
The vowel *ā* is acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accentual rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*).
There is elision (*luk*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.70: *śe chandasi bahulam*.
Furthermore, even in the compound, that same [accent] applies according to Pāṇini 2.1.4.2: *ivena vibhaktyalopaḥ pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvaṃ ca vaktavyam*.

1. And this being so; 2. because of the connection with the meaning of the verbal roots *ṣa*, *ṇa*, *ya*, and *dha*; 3. not another [meaning] in substance; 4. the consequence of the occurrence of *ca*, *cha*, *tha*, *pha*, and *śa*; 5. somehow [the occurrence of] *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *pha*, and *śa*; 6. the connection of the instruments (*karaṇa*) with *na*, *cha*, *ṇa*, and *pha*; 7. *ca* and *pha* [denote] one who is begging.

*Svaraḥ* (sound). *Vaṃsagaḥ* (bull): the desired form and accent are established by virtue of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group (Pāṇini 6.3.109). *Kṛṣṭayaḥ* (ploughers): from the root *kṛṣ* "to plough," the suffix *kvic* is applied according to the rule *kviccakau ca saṃjñāyām*. It is accented on the final syllable because it belongs to the *cchivādi* class. *Iyarti* (he moves): from the roots *ṛ* or *sṛ* "to go. The suffix *tip*; the elision (*ślu*) of *śap*; doubling (*dvirbhāva*) by the rule *ślau* (Pāṇini 6.1.10); the substitution of *u*, *r*, and *at* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rules *uradapara-* and *halādiśeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.66; 60); the substitution of *i* for the vowel *a* by the rule *atipiparyastyaśca* (Pāṇini 7.4.77); the substitution of *iyaṅ* for the reduplicated syllable by the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78); the *guṇa* strengthening of the stem, followed by the replacement of *r* (*raparatvam*). *Ojasā* (by strength): from the root *ujj*, the suffix *asun* is added with the elision of *b* by the *ujjerbalopaśca* (Uṇādisūtra 4.631); the *guṇa* of the light penultimate vowel (Pāṇini 7.3.86); it is accented on the first syllable because it is a *nvi*-derived word. *Īśānaḥ* (ruler): from the root *īś* "to rule. The present participle suffix *śānac*; the elision of *śap* by the rule *adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.72). The accent of the root remains, as the *anudātta* nature of the *l* suffix (which would otherwise be accented on the final by the rule *citaḥ*) prevails over that. *Apratipukanaḥ*: not being called out; from the root *ku* "to sound" in the sense of an object (*karman*), the suffix *ka* is applied. The augment *suṭ* is added by the *pāraskarādi* group (Pāṇini 6.1.157); the substitution of *pavam* occurs by the rule *supāmādi-pavam* (Pāṇini 8.3.98). This is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*); it retains the original accent of the first member, which is an indeclinable (*avyaya-pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratvam*).
He who alone rules over the peoples, over the Vasus—Indra, over the five tribes. 9. He who alone rules over the peoples, over the Vasus—Indra, over the five tribes. 9.

That Indra who himself alone rules—that is, exercises sovereignty—over the *carṣaṇīs*, meaning human beings, and likewise rules over the *vasūs*, meaning riches; that Indra favors the five *kṣitis*, meaning the five classes of people worthy of habitation, with the Nipādas as the fifth—this is the sense of the remainder [of the verse].
One [derivation]: from the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going. By the rule *iṇ-bhī-kā-pā-śalya-timarcibhyaḥ kan* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.323), the suffix *kan* is applied.
The absence of the *kal* suffix occurs by virtue of the rule of general application (*bāhulaka*). [The word] *niś* has its first syllable accented.
[The term is] *carṣaṇīnām*.
It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

With the phrase "from that which is accented on the final syllable" (*antodāttāt*) being understood [from the previous rule], the case ending receives the acute accent by *Pāṇini Sūtra* 6.1.177: *nāmantyatarasyām*.
Thus: *vasūnām*.

With the word "ni" understood from the previous context, the suffix *u* is applied by Uṇādi Sūtra 1.10: "After the roots śṛ, as, sthā, hita, vasi, vas, saha, ni, kvi, di, bandhi, and mani, [the suffix u is added].
Because it is a *nivāt* suffix, it is udātta on its first syllable. [Thus: *irajyati*.

In the list beginning with *kaṇva*, there is the root *iraj* in the sense of "envy"; here, however, it has the meaning of "sovereignty. [The suffix] *yak* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.27: *kaṇvādibhyo yak*.
The accent is udātta by virtue of the suffix.
*Pañca*. [The root] *paci* is used in the sense of "making manifest."
‘Peṃceśca’: [the suffix] *kan* is applied; by virtue of the *nivādi* rule, it is udātta on the first syllable. [The word is] *kṣitīnām*.
It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (prātipadika-svara).
The case-ending is optionally acute according to the rule "nāmantyatarasyām."
When about to recite the *āśvina* [śastra], one should offer the oblation with the verse, "Indraṃ vo viśvataspari.

This is prescribed in the section beginning with "Upon the completion [of the sacrifice], they press for the *āśvina*" (*āśva. śrau. sū.* 6.5), which states: "With the two verses beginning 'baṇ mahām asi sūrya' and 'indraṃ vo viśvataspari'...
On the twenty-fourth day, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin has "indraṃ vo viśvataspari" as his introductory verse (*ārambhaṇīyā*).
Beginning with "In the twenty-fourth," it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "O Varuṇa, [lead us] by a straight path... Indra for you from every side" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.2).

We invoke Indra for you from all sides, away from other people; may he belong to us alone. 10. Indra | for you | from every side | around | we call | from among the peoples | ours | let him be | exclusive. 10.
We, the officiating priests and the sacrificers, invoke for your sake Indra, who stands above and beyond all people from every side;
therefore, may that Indra be ours alone, his own, and superior even to others. (Note: The variants *cha*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha* refer to five specific manuscript traditions.)
