The meaning is: "May he grant [favor] to us. *Indram*: ending in the suffix *ran*, it is acute-accented on the first syllable by virtue of being a *niś* (a word class beginning with a prefix). *Vaḥ*: while the rule "everything is unaccented" (*anudāttaṃ sarvam*) is in force, the form *vas* is substituted for the plural by Pāṇini 8.1.21: *bahuvacanasya vasnasau*. *Viśvataḥ*: by Pāṇini 6.1.193: *liti*, the syllable preceding the suffix is acute-accented. *Pari*: being a particle (*nipāta*), it is acute-accented on the first syllable. In the *saṃhitā* (continuous text), the *visarjanīya* becomes *satvam* (the sound *s*) by Pāṇini 8.3.41: *pañcamyāḥ parāvadhyarthe*. *Havāmahe*: from the root *hve* (to call), with the suffix *śap*; by Pāṇini 6.1.34: *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) and the subsequent single-substitute (*parapūrvatva*). Then the *guṇa* and *avādeśa* substitutions occur. *Janāḥ*: they are produced, thus "people" (*jana*). From the root *jan* (to produce), the suffix *ghañ* is added in the sense of the object (*karman*). By Pāṇini 7.3.35: *janivadhyośca*, there is no *vṛddhi* of the penultimate vowel. It is acute-accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *jri* class. *Asmākam*: the word *asmad* is acute-accented on the final syllable. In the alternative where the final syllable is elided by Pāṇini 7.2.90: *śeṣe lopaḥ*, the eleventh vowel (the *ā* in *ākam*) is acute by Pāṇini 7.1.33: *sāma ākam*. In the alternative where the *ṭi* (the final syllable) is elided, the vowel *ā* is acute by the "acute-accented on the substitute" rule (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). *Kevalaḥ*: because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group, which is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, it is acute-accented on the first syllable. 14 || 2 ||
In the third section (anuvāka), there are four hymns (sūktas).

Among them, the first is the ten-verse hymn beginning with "endra sānasim"; the fifth is the six-verse hymn beginning with "surūpakṛtnum. As for the seers (ṛṣis) and other details, they are as before.
As for the specific application: in the *mahāvrata* and the *niṣkevalya*, there are two hymns beginning with "o indra sānasim rayim" in the eighty triplets of the *auṣṇiha* [meter].

In the fifth *āraṇyaka*, in the section titled "The eighty *auṣṇiha* triplets," Śaunaka has prescribed: "'Surūpakṛtnumūtaye'—these three [hymns], and the two hymns beginning with 'o indra sānasim rayim'" (*AiA* 5.2.5).
In the *atirātra* sacrifice, during the first round, the hymn "o indra sānasim" is used in the *acchāvāka-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Indram id rāthino bṛhat indra sānasim" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
In the Darśa sacrifice, the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) for the Sāṃnāyya offering by one who sacrifices to Indra is "endra sānasiṃ rayim.
In this section titled "The Deities Have Been Stated," it is sūtrited: "endra sānasiṃ rayiṃ pra samāhipe puruhūta śatrūn" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.6).
Bring for our protection Indra’s wealth, which wins booty, conquers all, ever victorious,
and most exalted.
O Indra, bring for our protection wealth that wins the prize, that is easily conquered, ever-conquering, and most exalted. 1.
O Indra, for our protection, bring hither—bring forth—wealth, riches. What kind of wealth? That which is *sānasi*, worthy of being shared by all.
Having conquered, he possesses the nature of victory over equal enemies;
for by providing wealth to his servants, enemies are indeed overcome. He is ever-conquering, meaning he is always the cause of the subjugation of his foes.
*Varṣiṣṭham* means most extensive, that is to say, exceedingly great or abundant.

*Sānasi*: From the root *vana* in the sense of "to distribute" (*saṃbhaktau*), the suffix *asip* is applied; there is vṛddhi [of the vowel], and the word is oxytone (*antodātta*) by the rule *sānasidharṇasi* (Uṇādisūtra 4.547). *Rayim*.
It is acutely accented on the final syllable by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*).
*Sajitvānam*:
one whose habit is to conquer enemies together.
The suffix *kanip* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.75, "It is seen after other [roots] as well. This forms a compound with an upapada.
By Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.3.84, "In the Vedic language, the substitution of *samāva-* for *samāna-* occurs before the words *mūrdhan*, *prabhṛti*, and *udaka*," the word *samāna* is replaced by *samāva*.
By the rule regarding the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of a compound, the accent of the verbal root alone remains. *Varṣiṣṭham*:
from the word *vṛddha*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.55, *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau*.
By the rule *priyasthira-* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.157), the word *vṛddha* undergoes the substitution of *varṣa*. Because the suffix *iṣṭhan* has the marker *n*, it is udātta on its first syllable.
[The word is] *ūtaye*.
With the word "udāttaḥ" (acute-accented) understood from the previous context, [the suffix] *kin* is prescribed as acute-accented by the rule beginning with "uti-yūti-jūti-sāti...
[Pāṇini 3.3.97]. [In the word] *bhara*, the substitution of *bha* for *ha* occurs by the rule "hy-ahor bhaś chandasi" (Pāṇini 8.2.32).

Regarding the prefix *āṅ*, which is to be employed before a verbal root according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.4.80 (*te prāgdhātoḥ*), its separated usage in the Vedic language is permitted by the rule 1.4.82 (*vyavahitāśca*).

May we, aided by you, hold back the Vṛtras with the blow of the fist, and with the swift steed. 2. With which [aid] we may hold back the Vṛtras with the blow of the fist, being protected by you, with the swift steed. 2.

"By means of that wealth with which we have equipped our warriors, may we utterly restrain (ni-ruṇadhāmahai)—that is, hold back—the Vṛtras, the enemies, by means of a crushing blow of the fist (ni-muṣṭi-hatyayā); bring us such wealth," is the meaning.
"Protected by you (tvotāsaḥ), guarded by you, may we restrain them by means of our own swift horse (arbatā)"; the phrase "may we restrain" is to be supplied here.
The sense is: "May we destroy the enemies through both infantry combat and cavalry combat."

In the word *muṣṭihatyayā*, the suffix *kyap* is applied when a word ending in *su* is an *upapada*, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.108 (*hanasta ca*). By virtue of that rule, the letter *n* is replaced by *t*. Although the original accent of the second member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) would normally apply, the word has an udātta accent on the final syllable because the term *bahulam* in Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.199 (*parādiśchandasi bahulam*) indicates that words such as *tricakra* have the udātta on the final syllable in the Vedic language. (See commentary on Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.199.1.)
Even for the preposition *ni*, which has a connection with a verb, there is a usage with an intervening word according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.4.82, *vyavahitāśca*.
[The form is] *vṛtrā*.
The elision of the *ś* [in *naḥ*] occurs by the rule *śeṣchandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.1.70).
There is the elision of the *n*.
[Thus we have] *ruṇadhāmahai*.
Because [the suffix] has the marker *ṅit* due to its initial conjunction (*ādisaṃyoga*), the elision of the vowel *a* does not occur by Pāṇini’s rule 6.4.111, *kṣmor halopaḥ*.
Precisely because it has the marker *ṅit*, the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accentuation of the *vikaraṇa* suffix *śram* alone remains.
But surely, the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* would require the subsequent verb to be unaccented (*nighāta*)?
No;
for there are two verbal suffixes here:
one is explicitly heard in the phrase "nibiḍayā muṣṭyā niruṇadhāmahe."
In the phrase *arbatā niruṇadhāmahai*, the second [verb] is elided;
the particle *ca*, which serves to conjoin the two, is also dropped.
Consequently, by the rule *cādilope vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.1.63), this first verbal ending (*tiṅvibhakti*) is not subject to elision (*nihata*).

For instance, in the passage, "He does not satisfy himself, nor does he give to another" (*Tai. Saṃ. 2.5.4.3*), because the particle *ca* expressing conjunction has been elided, the first verbal suffix in *tṛpyati* is not suppressed, whereas the second in *dadāti* is indeed suppressed.
Now, one might object: in that case two verbal suffixes are heard, but here only one is heard.
Since that very [first case] is permitted later on and no other is heard, one might ask: "In the absence of a second, how can this be called the first?
No;
for we observe the prohibition of *nighāta* (elision of accent) based on the status of being "first," even with respect to a second that has not been perceived.

For in the passages, “He places the *puroḍāśa* cake on the fire and [places] the clarified butter” (*Tai. Saṃ.* 1.6.9.3–4) and “He brings forward the sprinkling waters and the clarified butter” (*Tai. Saṃ.* 1.6.9.4), since the verbal roots *adhiśrayati* and *āsādayati* are heard in the first two sentences, their status as primary is accepted precisely by virtue of their requiring *anvaya* (supplying) into the subsequent two sentences; thus, the prohibition of *nighāta* (tonal depression) by the rule “*ca-vā-yoge prathamā*” (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 8.1.59) is observed.
[The word *tvotāsaḥ* means] those protected, guarded, or aided by you.

By the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.98), there is the substitution of *tvā* for the form ending in *map*, and the elision of the letter *d* is Vedic; furthermore, there is the absence of the augment *iṭ* after the root *ava* in its past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) form.
By the rule *jvaravarasrivimavāmupadhāyāśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.20), the vowel *ūṭ* is substituted. The absence of *vṛddhi* by the rule *edhyedhyatūsu* (Pāṇini 6.1.89) is also Vedic.
By the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 6.2.48), the vowel of the first member [of the compound] retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), and thus the vowel *ā* is acute (*udātta*).
By the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is acute; thus the syllable *oṃ* is acute. [The word is] *arvatā*.

It is called *arvā* because it goes (*gacchati*) like a steed (*arvatā*); [the root] *arva* means "to go. The suffix *vanip* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.75: "The suffix *vanip* is seen after other roots as well."
By the rule *nedvāśi kṛti* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.8), there is a prohibition of the substitution of *it*.
By the rule *lopo vyorvali* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.66), there is the elision of the letter *v*.
By the rule *arvaṇastasāvanañaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.127), the letter *t* is substituted [for the final *n*].
In *vanip*, because it is a *pit* suffix, the accent remains that of the verbal root itself.

O Indra, protected by you, may we take up the thunderbolt as a weapon; may we utterly conquer our rivals in battle. 3. O Indra, protected by you, may we take up the thunderbolt as a weapon; may we utterly conquer our rivals in battle. 3.
1. *Ca-ph-mukhyā śrutikā*:

"O Indra, we who are protected by you (*tvotāsaḥ*)—sustained by you—take up (*ā dadīmahi*), that is, accept as our own, the thunderbolt (*vajram*), the weapon that is exceedingly heart-piercing for the striking of enemies.
And with that thunderbolt, may we completely conquer (*saṃ jayema*), thoroughly defeat, the contending enemies (*stṛdhaḥ*) in battle (*yudhi*)."
"Protected by you.
This has been stated.
"The thunderbolt."
The root *vaj* (in the sense of "to go") forms a word ending in the suffix *ran* by virtue of the rule *ṛjendrāgra-* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.186), etc.; thus it is a nipāta [irregular formation].
It means "dense."

*Ghana* means hardness. The suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.2.127 because it belongs to the *arśas*-class of words. It is accented on the final syllable due to its derivation from *citra*.
The substitution of *ḍā* [for the case ending] is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
[Thus we have] *dadīmahi*.
[The root] *ḍudāñ* means "to give."
The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśīr-nāman*).
Since the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed; thus, by the rule *svaritajitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.72), the third person plural ending *mahiṅ* is used.
Furthermore, because the root belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is *ślau* (reduplication) of the *śap* affix by the rule *juhotyādibhyaḥ śluḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.75).
By the rule *śnāṃ* (Pāṇini 6.1.10), there is reduplication.
By the rule *liṅaḥ salopo’nantyasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.79), there is the elision of the *s*. By the rule *śnābhyastayorātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112), there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.
*jayema*.
Because *śap* is a *pit* suffix, it bears an acute accent (*udātta*).
Furthermore, among the accents of the *tiṅ* (verbal endings) belonging to the *lasārvadhātuka* class, only the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
The word *yudhi* follows the rule *chandasi pare’pi* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.81), which permits the use of the form with the suffix *sam*. [The root] *yudh* means "to fight."
The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because the word belongs to the *saṃpadādi* group (Pāṇini 3.3.108).
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. They vie with one another; thus they are called *stṛdhaḥ*.
The root *spardh* means "in rivalry.
By the rule *kvip* (Pāṇini 3.2.76), the suffix *kvip* is applied. According to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *r*, resulting in the vowel *ṛ*.
And there is the elision of the vowel *a*.
O Indra, with you as our ally, may we, through heroic archers, overcome those who extend their attacks against us.
O Indra, with you as our ally, we—brave and archers—shall overcome those who attack us. 4.

"We are the performers of ritual actions; may we be joined with these heroes—those endowed with valor who hurl weapons. This is the implied sense. O Indra, together with you as our ally (*yujā*), may we utterly overcome (*sāsahāma*) those enemies who seek to extend their armies against us.
*Śūrebhiḥ*:
[derived from] the roots *śu* and *śru*, meaning "to go.
Following the recurrence of the rule *ṛn* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.182), the suffix *ṛn* is applied by the rule *śū-si-ci-mīnāṃ dīrghaś-ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.183).
Due to the presence of the *kit* suffix, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
Due to the presence of the *nit* suffix, there is the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*).
Because the substitution of *ais* is prohibited by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” (Pāṇini 7.1.10), the form is thus derived by the rule “*bahuvacane jhalyet*” (Pāṇini 7.3.103).

By the force of the rule *sahayoge tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.19), because of the employment of the word *vayam* (we), it is understood that "we shall unite. It is logical [to accept this] even without the word *saha*, due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule *vṛddho yūnā* (Pāṇini 1.2.65). [The term] *astraiḥ* refers to those whose nature is to discharge missiles and weapons, or to those who perform such actions well (*tatsādhukāribhiḥ*).

In the sense of "throwing" (*asu kṣepaṇe*), the suffix *tṛn* is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.2.135 (*tṛn*) in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlyadiṣu*). Because it is marked with the *niṭ* indicator, it is acutely accented on the first syllable (*ādyudāttaḥ*).

Because of the rule "and after *ṛdh* and others" (*radhādibhyaśca*, Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.45), which prescribes an option, there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* in this case [of the instrumental singular].
[The form] *tvayā* [is derived from the base *tva*].
[The suffix] *madik* [is applied] by the rule "from *yuṣ* and *as*, *madik*" (*yuṣma-sibhyāṃ madik*, Uṇādi Sūtra 1.136).
Due to the presence of the *kit* suffix, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
In the word *yuṣmad*, the vowel *a* is acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix.
The third-person singular case ending is *ṭā* (Pāṇini 4.1.2).

By the rule *tvamāvekavacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.97), there is the substitution of *sva* for everything up to the final *m*. By the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*). By the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, this single substitute is acute (*udātta*).
In the word *yujā*, the suffix *kvin* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.59 (*ancu-yuji-kuñcāṃ ca*).
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to Pāṇini 6.1.168 (*sāvekācaḥ*).
We endure it intensely, again and again; we shall endure it.
[The root] *sah* means "to endure" (*marṣaṇe*).
[By the rule] *dhātvādeḥ paḥ saḥ*, the *pa* at the beginning of the verbal root is changed to *sa*.

1. The suffix *ṭhan* is prescribed after a single-vowel root beginning with a consonant. 2. In the *ta* manuscript, the form *mahiṅ* does not exist. 3. In the *ta* manuscript, [the reading] is *jayema*; the root *ji* means "to conquer. 4. In the *ṭha* manuscript, they are accompanied by such a reproach. 5. In the *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *pha*, and *śa* manuscripts, [there is the rule regarding] the roots *śṛ*, *pṛ*, *cam*, and *mī*. 6. In the *ṭha* manuscript, [the text reads]: "from this, up to 'samabhi'... 7. In the *ca*, *ta*, and *pha* manuscripts, immediately after the phrase "absence of *iṭ*" (*iḍabhāvaḥ*), there is the following: "In reality, however, because [the root] is absent from the *rudh*-class and others, the *tṛn* suffix is *aniṭ* according to the rule *śaṃsikṣādibhyaḥ*. The suffix *yaṅ* is applied in the sense of frequent repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhivāra*) [Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.22].
There is elision [of the suffix] by Pāṇini 2.4.74: *yaṅo'ci ca*.
There is reduplication by Pāṇini 6.1.9: *sanyaṅoḥ*.
Then there is the application of *halādiśeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.60).
The vowel lengthening [is applied] by the rule *'dīrgho 'kitaḥ'* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.83).
The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*).

According to the principle that "the *carkarīta* [intensive] is to be regarded as having the *parasmaipada* endings and as belonging to the *adādi* class," the suffix *mas* is employed as the third person plural *parasmaipada*.
In the active voice (*kartari*), there is the *śap* suffix;
due to its being treated like the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*).
By the rule "nityaṃ ṅitaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.99), the final *s* is elided.
The augment *yāsuṭ* is applied by the rule "yāsuṭ parasmaipadodātto ṅicca" (Pāṇini 3.4.103).
The elision of the *sakāra* occurs by the rule "liṅaḥ salopo'nantyasya" (Pāṇini 7.2.79).
Because it is taught later [in the sequence of rules], the acute accent (*udāttatva*) remains attached specifically to *yāsuṭ*.
There is no *nighāta* because it begins with the word *pāda*.
[This was done] with effort by one desiring to extend himself for battle.

Thus, by virtue of being the most similar [to the original vowel], the *vṛddhi* substitute becomes exclusively acute (*udātta*). In the forms *prathinā* and *prathimanā*, the suffix *imanic* is applied in the sense of "the state of being *pṛthu*" according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.1.122: *apṛthvādibhya imanic vā*.
By the rule *ra ṛto halāderlaghoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.161), the substitution of *ra* occurs for the vowel *ṛ*.
Following the continued application of *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu* (Pāṇini 6.4.154), the elision of the final syllable (*ṭilopa*) is applied by the rule *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.145).
The word *prathiman* is anudātta (unaccented) because of its designation as having the *cittva* property.
In the third case singular, due to the existence [of the form] *bhavat*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.134 (*allopo’naḥ*).
The elision of the letter *m* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending follows from Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.161 (*anudāttasya ca yatrodāttalopaḥ*).
*Śavaḥ*:
[The word] has its first syllable accented because of the rule *nabviṣayasyānisantasya* (Phiṭ Sūtra 26).
Or those men who have sought refuge in non-delusion for the sake of winning a small portion [of wealth], or those who, seeking wisdom, are divided in their thoughts.
Thus ends the section on the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
[In the word] *pivante*,
[the root is] *piva* in the sense of "to sprinkle."
The augment *num* is added by the rule "idito num dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.58). Because the suffix *śap* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*).
Furthermore, by the accentual rule for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) alone remains.
*urvīḥ*.

The word *uru* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.44: "The suffix *ṅīp* is added after a word denoting a quality that ends in *u*."
There is the substitution of *yaṇ*.
By the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.174), the vowel *ī* is acute (*udātta*).
Together with the suffix *jas*, by the rule "ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ," the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is acute.
*Āpaḥ*: the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). *Kākudaḥ*.
It is accented on the final syllable by the accentuation rule of the nominal stem (prātipadika).

In the Ukthya sacrifices characterized by the *abhilava* and *paḍaha* sequences, at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* priest has the *anurūpa* and *stotriya* verses beginning with "evā hyasya sunṛtā.
In the section beginning with "evā hyasya mṛḷāni te" and starting with "atha brāhmaṇācchaṃsinaḥ," there is the phrase "evā hyasi vīrayuḥ" and "evā hyasya sunṛtā.

By the rule "bham" (Pāṇini 1.4.18), the designation *bha* is applied; then, by the rule "vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam" (Pāṇini 6.4.131), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *va*, which becomes *u*.
The state of having something preceding it [is indicated].
By the rule "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca" (Pāṇini 8.3.60), this is a pada. By the accent of the suffix, the vowel *u* is udātta.
For such indeed are thy powers and aids, O Indra,
that they are instantly present for the sake of a donor like me.
For indeed, O Indra, these manifestations and aids of yours are instantly available for the sake of a donor like me. ||9||
"O Indra," [these] "vibhūtayaḥ" are your specific manifestations of sovereignty;
"evā hi" means they are indeed of such a nature. As to what kind they are, that is now stated:
"Immediate aids"— meaning protections in the form of your own guardianship— exist "even at once" for "one like me," that is, for the sacrificer who has offered the oblation (*dāśuṣe*).
That is to say,
they become manifest at the very moment the ritual action is performed.

*māvate* means "to one like me. The suffix *vatup* is added to the word *asmad* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.39.1: "In the section on *vatup*, there is an addition [to the rule] for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the Vedic language when expressing similarity.
By the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.98), the substitution of *mā* occurs for the portion of *asmad* ending in *map*.
In conjunction with the word *ada*, there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.97 (*ato guṇe*).
Following the recurrence of the rule "in the case of *hrasva*, *vat*, and *uṣ*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.89), the letter *d* is replaced by *ā* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.91 (*ā sarvanāmnaḥ*).
This results in a long vowel through the rule of homogeneous vowel lengthening (*savarṇadīrghatva*).
In the case of *vatup*, when it follows a word ending in *paśu*, the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone remains. Thus, *sadyaḥ*.
It is an irregularly formed word (*nipātita*) by the rule "sadyaḥ-parasparā-aiṣamaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.3.22), in the sense of "on the same day" (*samāne ahani*).
The final syllable is udātta by virtue of the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyaya-svara*).
The word *cit* is anudātta according to the rule "Particles beginning with *ca* are anudātta" (*Cādayo'nudāttāḥ*, Pāṇini 8.1.58).
The forms *santi* and *asmi* occur; in the sense of "on earth" (*bhuvi*), *jhi* is substituted for the *laṭ* [present tense] suffix.
By the rule *'jho 'ntaḥ'* (Pāṇini 7.1.3), [the final *t* of the suffix is replaced by *an*].
By the rule *'adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ'* (Pāṇini 2.4.72), there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. The first syllable of the *tiṅ* suffix is acute (*udātta*).

By relying on the letter *ś* [in the suffix *dāśuṣe*], the rule "when a suffix is elided, the operations conditioned by that suffix still take place" (Pāṇini 1.1.62) does not apply to the unaccented nature of the *la-sārvadhātuka*.
This is because of the prohibition: "there is no application of the rule regarding suffixes when the operation depends upon a specific phoneme" (Paribhāṣā 21).
Thus, [the form] is *dāśuṣe*.
The mantra has gone; it is gone.
For thus indeed are his desirable [hymns] to be recited— the stoma and the uktha—
for Indra, for the drinking of the soma.
For indeed, his desired hymn of praise and recitation are to be chanted for Indra, so that he may drink the Soma. 10.

"The *stoma* of this Indra—the hymn (*stotra*) accomplished by means of the *sāman*—and the *uktha*—the recitation (*śastra*) accomplished by means of the *ṛc*—are indeed both of such a nature. Of what nature? That is stated:
they are 'desirable' (*kāmyā*), meaning they are to be desired, and 'praiseworthy' (*śaṃsyā*), meaning they are to be praised by the officiating priests."
For what purpose is the recitation? That is stated: "For Indra, for the drinking of Soma"—that is, for the sake of Indra’s drinking of Soma.
For thus it is for him.
It has been explained in the section on the *vyavahita* mantra. [Now follow] the optional rites (*kāmyā*).
From the denominative (*kamerṇiṅantāt*) [root *kam*] with the suffix *ṇiṅ*, the suffix *yat* is applied by Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.97 (*aco yat*).
By Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.51 (*geraniṭī*), there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi*.

When the circumflex accent (*svarita*) would have been obtained by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.185 (*tisvaritam*), the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatvam*) is applied instead by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.213 (*yato’nāvaḥ*).
The substitution of *ḍā* for *su* [is applied].
*Stomaḥ*: by the rule "astistusu" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.137), the suffix *man* is added.
*Uktha*: [derived from] the root *vac*, meaning "to speak. By the rule *pā-tu-divaci-rici-sici-sibhyas-thak* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.164), the suffix *thak* is applied.
Because it is a kit, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*);
[then] the substitution of the preceding vowel and the absence of *guṇa*.
[The form is] *śaṃsyā*.
The root *śaṃs* means "to praise.
From this, by the rule *aco yat*, the suffix *yat* is applied.
By the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, the word is accented on its first syllable.
The substitution of *ḍā* for *sup* [the nominal suffix] occurs.
In "soma-pītiḥ" (the drinking of Soma),

although the original accentuation of the final member of a compound formed with a *kṛt*-suffix would apply, there is instead an initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively, Indra is "the drinker of Soma" (*somapīti*), meaning that Indra for whom there is the drinking of Soma.
According to Pāṇini’s rule 6.2.1, *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*, the first member of the compound retains its original accent.
The hymn consisting of ten verses beginning with “*indrehi*” is recited in the [hymns] beginning with “*surūpakṛtnum*. Its seer and other details are as before.
The distinction, however, is that in the second round (*paryāya*) of the *atirātra* sacrifice, the verse “*indrehi*” is used for the *acchāvāka* chant.

In the section titled "At the Atirātra, of the Paryāyas," it is prescribed [in the sūtra]: "O Vasu, this pressed soma is ready; come, O Indra, and exhilarate yourself with the soma" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
O Indra, exhilarate yourself with the soma-juice through all the Soma-offerings;
you are great, reaching across the mid-air with your aid.
O Indra, come hither; exhilarate yourself with the soma-juice at all the Soma-pressings;
may you be our protector.
By means of vital energy.
O Indra, come; come to this ritual act.
Having arrived, exhilarate yourself with all the Soma-juices—by means of the *andhas* (soma-essences) which are the forms of the Soma-flowers—and be joyful.
Thereafter, becoming possessed of *ojas* (vital power) and *bala* (strength), be the *abhiṣṭi*, that is, the overcomer of enemies; this is the sense of the remainder.

Among the twenty-eight names for strength, there is "Ojaḥ pājaḥ" (Ni. 2.27). [Regarding the ritual formula: "O cup-bearers of the *hotṛ*s, come hither toward the bright [Soma] with your power and resolve" (ĀpŚS 12.23.4). Of what nature is he?
And for what reason is he gladdened? He is one whose nature is to perform deeds well. For what kind of Indra?
For Mandin, who is possessed of joy, and who has performed—that is, accomplished—all deeds.
The meaning is "having the nature of accomplishing all actions.

Regarding the word *īm*, Yāska states that its purpose is to fill out the meter: "Now, those particles which occur in prose or in metrical texts of measured syllables for the sake of completing a sentence are called *padapūraṇas*; in metrical texts, they are meaningless, such as *kam*, *īm*, *id*, and so forth" (Nirukta 1.9).
This is the meaning of that passage.

When the intended meaning has been completed by other words alone, those words such as *īm* and so forth that are employed should be understood as serving to fill out the sentence in Brāhmaṇa passages and the like, which lack meter and thus have no fixed number of syllables (*amitākṣara*).
In texts characterized by meter (*mitākṣara*), they serve to fill out the verse-quarter (*pāda*).
And these [words] are *kam*, *īm*, and so forth.
To demonstrate the meaninglessness of this word *īm*, he cited this verse: "Em enaṃ sṛjatā sute;
āsujainam sute" (Nirukta 1.10).
*enam*:

In the second case of *idam*, the substitute *enad* is applied by Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.4.34 (*dvitīyāṭaussvenaḥ*). Because the term *anudāttaḥ* from sūtra 2.4.32 is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), this [substitute] is entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*).
[The verb is] *sṛjata*.
In the *Saṃhitā*, there is a lengthening [of the vowel] according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.3.137: *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*.
*Mandi* means a cause of joy;
[it is derived from] the root *madi*, which [is used] in the senses of praise, joy, intoxication, sleep, beauty, and motion.

The augment *num* is applied by the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58). In the sense of "he employs one who is being pleased" (*mandamānam prayuṅkte*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is added by the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26).
Since the root ending in *ṇic* ends in a vowel (*ajanta*), the suffix *ik* is added by the rule *aca iḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.508).
There is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix by Pāṇini’s rule *ṇeraniṭi* (6.4.51). The final syllable is udātta by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
[The form is] *mandine*.
The forms *mandebhyaḥ* and so forth are as before.
In the dative plural, by the rule *caturthyekavacane 'napuṃsakasyāpi vā num āgamaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.73), there is optionally the addition of the augment *num*. Thus: *cakribhyām*.
The root *ḍukṛñ* is used in the sense of "making.

According to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.101, *āhagamahanajanaḥ kikinau liṭ ca*, the suffixes *kikin* are applied like the *liṭ* (perfect) after the roots *āp*, *han*, *gam*, and *jan*, when the agent possesses that habit, that nature, or performs that action skillfully.
Because this suffix is marked with *k* (kit), there is an absence of *guṇa* (vowel strengthening).
There is the substitution of *yaṇ*. Because it is a substitute for a semi-vowel (*liṅdvātvāt*), there is reduplication.
Due to the status of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the *yaṇ* substitution according to Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.59 (*dvivaṃcane'ci*), the form *kṛśan* is reduplicated.

In *abhyāsasya*, there is the substitution of *ur*, followed by *ra* and *paratva*, and the replacement of the remaining consonant (*halādiśeṣa*). Because the *kin* suffix is *nit*, it is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). [The word] *viśvāni*.

The suffix *kan* is applied to the root *viś*. It is accented on the first syllable because it is marked with the *ṅit* designation. Although there is a connection with the word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix (*asya cakraḥ*), the genitive case prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule 2.3.65 (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*) does not occur here.

Because of the rule "kikinau liṭ ca," the *kin* suffix is treated as having the nature of the *liṅ* (optative) suffix; consequently, due to the prohibition stated in Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.69—"na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām"—[the sixth case ending is not applied].
Rejoice, O fair-jawed one, with our exhilarating hymns, O you who pervade all people; be present at these libations.
Rejoice, O you of beautiful jaws, with our gladdening hymns, O lord of all people; come together with us to these libations.
O Suśipra— O you of beautiful jaws or beautiful nose,
for Yāska has stated, "Śipra means the jaws or the nostrils" (Nirukta 6.17)—
O such Indra, rejoice and become exhilarated by the *mandibhiḥ*, that is, by the hymns and praises which are the causes of joy.

O Viśvacarṣaṇi—one who is joined with all men, meaning one worthy of worship by all sacrificers—such as you, O Indra, come together with the other gods to these three *savana*s (pressings) occurring during the sacrifice; this is the sense of the ellipsis.

In the case of the root *mad* in the imperative (*loṭ*) form of the word *madi-stuti*, the augment *num* does not occur because of the maxim "the teaching of augments is not permanent" (*anityam āgamāśāsanam*, Paribhāṣā 93). Furthermore, by the rule "the *num* is added to a root that ends in an *it*-letter" (*idito num dhātoḥ*, Pāṇini 7.1.58), *num* is not applied here. Since the root is *anudātta* (unaccented), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix receives the acute accent (*udātta*) according to the rule "that which is taught as *anudātta* or ends in an *it* is unaccented, except for the first person endings" (*tāsyanudāttedidadupadeśāt*, Pāṇini 6.1.186);
thus, the accent remains that of the root itself.
In the *saṃhitā*, there is lengthening according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.3.135, *aco ’tastiṅaḥ*.
There is the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) for *suśipra* as it is in the vocative case (*āmantrita*).
[The word] *mandibhiḥ* [is treated similarly].
The rest has been explained.
Regarding *stomairbhiḥ*:
because it belongs to the *mantra* category, it is accented on the first syllable.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 7.1.10), the substitution of *ais* for the case-ending *bhis* does not occur.
[The form is] *viśvacarṣaṇe*.
There is *nighāta* (elision of the accent).
Sacā | It has been said: "In these."
By the rule beginning with "uḍiḍam," the case ending is udātta (acute-accented).
1. With the ṭha-ta stomas:
"O Indra, our songs have been released; they have risen up toward you, the unappeased bull, the lord."
The songs have been released for you, O Indra; they have risen up toward you, the unappeased bull, the lord. ||4||

O Indra, I have released (*asṛgram*) these songs (*giraḥ*), your praises; they have risen up and reached you who are established in heaven. You have enjoyed (*ajoṣaḥ*) such songs. Of what sort are you? A bull (*vṛṣabham*), a showerer of desires, a lord, a drinker of Soma, or a protector of the sacrificers—since Yāska has stated, "He is either a drinker (*pātā*) or a protector (*pālayitā*)" (Nirukta 4.26). *Asṛgram*: from the root *sṛj* (to release), in the *laṅ* tense, first person singular (*mip*). By Pāṇini 3.1.77, the suffix *śa* is added; by 7.1.8, the augment *ruṭ* is added to the suffix; the *j* becomes *g*; and by 6.4.71, the augment *aṭ* is added, which is acute (*udātta*) because it is taught later and thus remains. The accent of *giraḥ* is that of the nominal stem. *Ahāsata*: from the root *ohāṅ* (to go), in the *luṅ* tense. The root is replaced by *ah*; the suffix *sic* is added; the augment *aṭ* and the grave (*anudātta*) accent are applied. *Ajoṣaḥ*: from the root *jupī* (to enjoy or serve), in the *laṅ* tense, second person singular (*thās*). The suffix *śa* is added; since it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix in Vedic by 3.4.117, the *ḍit* designation does not apply, so the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the light penultimate vowel. The loss of the *th* in *thās* is a Vedic feature; the *savarna-dīrgha* (long vowel) is formed, followed by the acute *aṭ* augment, which remains due to its later application. *Vṛṣabham*: from the roots *pṛp*, *vṛp*, or *mṛp* (to sprinkle), with the suffix *abhuc* (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.402); the suffix *kit* is added by 3.403, causing the absence of *guṇa*. It is acute on the final syllable because of the *ciṭ* designation. *Patim*: from the root *pā* (to protect), with the suffix *ḍati* (Uṇādi-sūtra 4.417). The *ḍit* designation causes the elision of the suffix marker; the suffix is acute on its first syllable.
O Indra, bestow upon us that wonderful, desirable, and excellent gift;
may it be present for you as all-pervading and sovereign power.
O Indra, bestow wonderful and desirable wealth upon us; for yours indeed shall be that abundant and sovereign power.

O Indra, impel and properly direct toward us that most excellent, desirable wealth (*rādhaḥ*)—wealth that is manifold, appearing in the form of gems, pearls, and so forth—so that it may come hither, toward us. That which is sufficient for enjoyment is called by the word *vibhu* (all-pervading); that which exceeds even this is called by the word *prabhu* (lord). Such wealth belongs to you alone; therefore, the meaning is: "Grant it to us. In the list of twenty-eight names for wealth beginning with *magham*, "rāyaḥ" and "rādhaḥ" are recited (Nirukta 2.10.17). **codaya**: From the root *cuda* (to impel), with the causative suffix (*pyantāt*), in the imperative (*loṭ*). The accentual suppression (*nighāta*) occurs according to Pāṇini 8.1.28 (*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*). **rādhaḥ**: Wealth is that by which they prosper (*rādhnuvanti*). Derived from all roots with the suffix *asun* (Uṇādisūtra 4.628). Being a *niv* [type of formation], it has the acute accent on the first syllable. **vareṇyam**: From the root *vṛj* with the suffix *eṇya*. It has the acute accent on the first syllable because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* class. **asad**: From the root *as* (to exist/be). In the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, third person singular. The *ikāra* is elided by Pāṇini 3.4.97 (*itaśca lopaḥ*). The augment *aṭ* is added by Pāṇini 3.4.94 (*leṭoḍāṭau*). The suffix *śap* is elided by Pāṇini 2.4.72 (*adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ*). Since the augment *aṭ* is unaccented (Pāṇinian Paribhāṣā 3.1.3.7), the accent of the verbal root itself remains. **vibhu**: That which pervades (*vibhavati*) is *vibhu*. With the root *bhū* still in force, the suffix *ḍ* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.180 (*viprasabhyo ḍsaṃjñāyām*). Because the suffix is marked with *ḍ*, the penultimate vowel is elided (*ṭilopaḥ*). By the accent of the suffix, the *ukāra* becomes acute; by the rule of the original accent of the second member of a compound (*kuduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), that same accent remains. The same applies to *prabhu*. 17. Translation complete.
O Indra, impel us toward that sacred law for the sake of wealth— us who are zealous,
O you of many glories, and full of renown.
O Indra, impel us well toward that wealth—impetuous and glorious, O you of abundant splendor! 6.

O Indra, possessed of abundant power and vast wealth, impel us practitioners well toward that ritual act for the sake of attaining riches—impel us effectively. Of what sort are we? Zealous, that is, full of exertion; and glorious, that is, possessing fame. In the word *tatra*: from the pronoun *tat*, the suffix *tra* is added by Pāṇini 5.3.10 (*matvarthe ṣṭran*), and by 6.1.193 (*liti*), the vowel preceding the suffix is acute. *Indra*: as a vocative, it is acute on the first syllable; furthermore, because it occurs at the beginning of a *pāda*, there is no suppression of accent (*nighāta*). *Rāye*: the case-ending is acute according to the rule beginning with "uḍidam" (Pāṇini 6.1.171). *Rabhasvataḥ*: from the root *rabh* meaning "to begin"; "beginning" refers to the commencement of an undertaking. The suffix *asun* is added to all roots (Uṇādi-sūtra 4.628); being a *niv* suffix, it is acute on the first syllable. *Maṃturaḥ*: [the suffix] *pirat* results in the first syllable being acute.

Bestow upon us great renown, splendor, and the winning of thousands; O Indra, those nourishments borne on chariots. 8. Bestow upon us—bestow—renown, great splendor, and the winning of thousands, O Indra; those [nourishments] borne on chariots. 8.
O Indra, bestow upon us great renown; grant us vast fame.
Likewise, bestow upon us that splendor consisting of wealth which is preeminent in granting thousands.
And likewise, bestow upon us those foods—well-known in the form of rice, barley, and so forth—which are "possessing chariots," meaning they are accompanied by many chariots.
*asme*: the substitution of *śe* is according to the rule "supāṃ suluk... and so forth. *dhehi*.
By the rule "ghasor id vābhyāsalopaśca" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.119), there is the substitution of *i* for the root vowel and the elision of the reduplication.
Thus, from the root *bhū*, we have *śravaḥ*.
By virtue of the affix *asun* being *niṣ* (having an indicatory letter *ṇ*), it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable).
He is called *sahasrasāḥ* because he wins or gives a thousand;
[the root] *paṇ* is used in the sense of "giving.
[The suffix] *viṭ* is applied by Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.67: "After the roots *jan*, *san*, *khan*, *kram*, and *gam*, the suffix *viṭ* is added."

By the rule "vidvanoranunāsikasyāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.41), there is the substitution of the vowel *ā*. It is initially udātta on the final syllable by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*); subsequently, that same accent remains by the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).
In the word *rathinī*, the suffix *ya* is udātta because it follows the rule "the [suffix] after [a stem ending in] *ratha* is udātta.
Then, by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added; and that [suffix] is anudātta because it is marked with the letter *p*.

In the case of *iṣas*, if it is used etymologically (*yaugika*), it has the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*); if it is used as a conventional term (*rūḍha*), it has the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadikasvara*).

Praising with songs Indra, the lord of wealth, the master of riches, the one worthy of praise, who comes to the sacrifice for our protection—[we praise him]. 9. O Vasu, [praising] Indra, the lord of wealth, with hymns, [praising] the one worthy of praise, the one who comes to the oblation for our aid. 9.
For the sake of protection—that is, for the preservation of our wealth and riches—we invoke Indra with oblations. What are we doing?
Praising and extolling him with songs of praise.
What kind of Indra?
The lord of wealth (vasupati), the protector of riches; the one worthy of hymns (ṛgmiya), the progenitor of the Ṛg-verses; the one who goes, whose nature is to go to the place of sacrifice.
Regarding *vasoḥ*: [the root] *vas* means "to dwell. The suffix *up* is applied according to the rule beginning with *śrustusihi* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.10).
Because of the recurrence of the term "nit," [the word] is udātta on its first syllable due to being a *niś* [ending].

Regarding *vasupatim*: although the rule for the udātta accent on the final syllable of a compound would normally apply, the rule *apatyāvaiśvarye* (Pāṇini 6.2.18) prescribes that the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound is maintained.
With hymns (*gīrbhiḥ*):
the acute accent of the case-ending is due to Pāṇini’s rule *sāvekācaḥ* (6.1.168).
Singing (*gṛṇantaḥ*).
The root *gṛ* means "to sound.
From the present tense marker (*laṭ*), the suffix *śatṛ* is applied;
then, by the rule *ṛdha-tvi-kyaḥ kṣā* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.81), the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *kṣ*.
Because the suffix *śatṛ* is treated as having the marker *ṅ* by the rule *sārvadhātukamapit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), there is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule *śvābhyastayorātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112).
The vowel *a* of the suffix *śatṛ* receives the udātta accent by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
[The word] *ṛgmiyam*.
One who measures the *ṛc*s is an *ṛgmī*; that which belongs to him is *magmya*. [The root] *māṅ* is used in the senses of "measuring" and "sound.
[The suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.76).
The substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule "ghumāsthā" (Pāṇini 6.4.66).
For the letter *c*, the substitution of *k* occurs by "coḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30),
and the substitution of *g* occurs by "jhalāṃ jaśonte" (Pāṇini 8.2.39).

In the second case singular, the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs by the rule "aci śnu-dhātu-" (Pāṇini 6.4.77). However, the substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule "eranekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.82) does not take place, because of the paribhāṣā: "All rules are optional in the Veda" (Paribhāṣā 35).
By the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*), the vowel *i* is udātta.
We call upon Homa; [the root] *heñ* means "to compete" and "to sound. [The suffix] *laṭ*.
Although we (asmad) is in the plural here, *mip* is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The vowel *i* is replaced by *a* by way of transposition.
The suffix *śap* is elided according to the rule "there is diversely (*bahulam*) elision in the Veda" (*chandasi*).
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.34), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *ha*, substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*), and *guṇa*.
By the rule *dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.162), the vowel *o* is acute (*udātta*).
The *mip* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*) by the accent of the *pit* markers.
"Gantāram" [is derived from] the root "gam-lṛ," meaning "to go" (in the sense of moving). The suffix "tṛn" is applied in the sense of habitual action (tācchīlya).
The word *niśvāda* has its first syllable accented (*udātta*).
In the word *ūtaye*,
the suffix *kin* is prescribed as having an acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule "ūti-ūti" (Pāṇini 3.3.97).
1. *ṭha-dhehi*: [The suffix] *loṭ* [is applied]. 2. *ṭha-prakṛtisvaraḥ*: [The accent is] the original accent of the base (*prakṛtisvara*). 3. *ṭha-ṛgbhiḥ stutam*: "Praised with verses.

*Sute-sute nyokase bṛhad-bṛhat ediriḥ | indrāya śuṣmam arcati || 10 ||* At every pressing, the one who dwells within [the sacrifice], the expansive one, the noble, praises the strength for Indra. (10) *In each pressing, to him who has his dwelling within, the great, the great, indeed, the noble one, praises the vigor for Indra.* (10)
The syllables *ā* and *i* are used for the purpose of filling out the meter;
or alternatively,
the syllable *ā* signifies pervasiveness (*vyāpti*).
According to the lexicographical definition, "The word *ādi* is used in the sense of 'slight' (*īṣat*) and 'pervasion' (*abhivyāpti*)," the particle *api* also signifies 'slightness.
Thus, one who "moves toward" (*iyarti*), that is, proceeds toward or attains the ritual action to be performed, is an *ariyajamāna*.
Every sacrificer, being an *ediri*, praises—that is, extols—the *śuṣma*, the strength, at each pressing of the Soma for Indra;
that is to say, he lauds the prowess of Indra. Of what kind is this *śuṣma*?
"Bṛhat" means great or mature.
To what kind of Indra?
"Nyokase" means to him who has a fixed dwelling place; to the great and mature one.
*sute-sute* | [The root] *puṣ* [in the sense of] ‘pressing’ takes the suffix *kta*; by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), it is udātta.
The reduplication [of the word] occurs due to the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4) for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
According to the rule *tasya paramāmreḍitam* (Pāṇini 8.1.2), the second member is designated as *āmreḍita*, and by the rule *anudāttaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.3), it receives the anudātta accent.
[The form is] *nyokase*.

In the word *niyatamoka*, the syllable *ni* is udātta according to the rule "the indeclinables beginning with *ni* are udātta" (Phiṭ-sūtra 80). When its *i* undergoes the *yaṇ*-substitution (*niyamoka*), the vowel *o* becomes svarita according to the rule "after an udātta or a svarita, the following non-udātta *yaṇ*-vowel is svarita" (Pāṇini 8.2.4). Thus, the *o*-kāra is svarita.
*bṛhate*: According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.173, "The enumeration of forms for *brahma-hata*," there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending beginning with *a*, such as the dative. *Ariḥ*.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.
By the rule *aca iḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.578), the suffix *i* is applied. Following the rule for *guṇa*, the vowel is changed to *ar*. Thus, it becomes *ari*.
By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the vowel *i* is acute (*udātta*).
In *indrāya*,
by the rule "ṛji-ndra" (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.186) and others, the suffix *ran* is applied, and the vowel *i* is acute.
*śuṣmam*: the accent is that of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). *arcati*.
The *nighāta* accent.
The number of mantras and the specific meter of the hymn beginning with "gāyanti" are enumerated thus: "gāyanti dvādaśānuṣṭubhaṃ tu.

Since the word "tu" is defined in the technical rule (paribhāṣā) starting with "tuhi havai" (Anuvāka 12.3) as indicating the nature of a hymn, it should be understood that both this hymn and the one to be mentioned next are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
The seer and the deity are as before.
In the Uktha-stotras of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) of the Abhilava-ṣaḍaha, the *stotriya* triplet for the Acchāvāka priest is "They sing (*gāyanti*).
This is prescribed in the section beginning with "Ehū ṣu" as: "They sing thee, the Gāyatrins; songs [go] to thee like a charioteer" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.8).
"They sing thee, the Gāyatrins; those possessing *ṛks* praise the *ṛk*."
The Brahmins, O performer of a hundred sacrifices, have raised you up as if a sacrificial post.
The singers of the Gāyatrī chant thee; the reciters of hymns sing the song of praise. O Śatakratu, the priests have raised thee up like a pole. 1.
O Śatakratu, O performer of many deeds, O possessor of great wisdom, Indra, the Gāyatrins—the Udgātṛ priests—sing praises to you.

The Arkins—the Hotṛ priests endowed with hymns for the purpose of worship—worship Indra, the one worthy of praise, extolling him with the mantras of the Śastra recitations. The Brahmans—the Brāhmaṇas beginning with the Brahman priest—raise you up, bringing you to exaltation.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a bamboo flute.
Just as craftsmen dancing upon a bamboo flute make the mature bamboo rise upward.
Or rather, it is just as those who abide on the true path cause their own lineage to rise high;

Yāska explains this ṛc as follows: "The singers sing thee; the chanters of the *arkas* praise thy *arka*; O Śatakratu, the Brāhmaṇas have raised thee up like a bamboo pole (*vaṃśa*). A bamboo pole is so called because it lies in the forest (*vanaśaya*), or because it is felled (*śyata*) from the forest" (Nirukta 5.5).
1. For what kind [of person]? 2. To whom: *ga*, *gha*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ya*.

3. After the rule "the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*) applies to *ca*, *cha*, and *pha*," there is an addition: "'In the twenty-eight names of strength (*balanāman*), *śuṣ*, *saha* (which becomes *ho*), and *yaha* are recited.'"

4. Having established [the meaning] as "you" (*tvām*), he explains the word *arka* in many ways: "It is a god called *arka* because they honor him (*arcanti*); it is a mantra called *arka* because they honor with it (*anena*); it is an *arka*-mantra because it honors (*arcati*) all beings; it is the *arka* tree because it is covered (*vṛtaḥ*) with bitterness. (Nirukta 5.4).
They sing.
Because the suffixes *śas* and *siṅ* follow [the root] and because they are marked with the *l* indicatory letter (*las*), they are unaccented (*anudātta*);
the verbal root (*dhātu*) is accented (*udātta*).
Those who possess the *gāyatra* *sāman* as their final udātta [accent] are called *gāyatrinaḥ*. [This is formed] by the rule "ata iniṭhanau."
By the accent of the suffix, the vowel *i* is acute (*udātta*).
They worship (*arcanti*). [The root] *arca* is used in the sense of worship.
It belongs to the *bhū* class (*bhauvādika*).
The suffixes *śas* and *ṅi* are unaccented (*anudātta*);
thus, the accent remains that of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) alone.
There is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because it begins with a word (*pādādi*).
"Arka":
those by which one praises are *arkas*, namely the mantras.
Indra, who consists of that [light], is also called *arka* by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because he is worthy of worship by them.

The suffix *gha* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.3.118: “The suffix *gha* is generally used after a verbal root when a masculine technical name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed.
By Pāṇini’s rule 7.3.52: “*ku* is substituted for *c* and *j* before the suffixes *ghi* and *ṇat*,” the letter *c* undergoes the change to *k*, resulting in the form *arka*.

[The word *ejat*] ends in the suffix *ni*, according to the rule *pratyayasvareṇānto 'sṛpibhyāṃ kit* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.489). There is no absence of the suffix *kvip* and so forth. It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [In the form] *ejati*: the root is *ej* in the sense of "moving. The elision of the verb-ending is governed by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.
Having yoked your two powerful, bay stallions that fill out the girth-bands,
O Indra, drinker of Soma, come to hear our songs for our sake.
Having yoked the two bay steeds, the powerful ones that fill the girths, come, O Indra, drinker of Soma, to the hearing of our songs for our sake. 3.
O *Indra*, drinker of Soma (*somapā*), having yoked your two bay horses (*harī*), harness them in every way.
Then, immediately thereafter, for the sake of hearing our songs of praise (*girāṃ upaśrutim*) nearby, come to our region.
Of what sort are the two bay horses?

"Keśinau" means possessing long hair hanging down from the region of the shoulders; "vṛṣaṇau" means two young bulls capable of impregnation. "Kakṣyaprā" refers to those who fill out the *kakṣyā*—the girth-rope used for binding an elephant's belly—the meaning being that their limbs are well-developed.
O Indra, you who are the cause for the pouring of the vessel, come to this ritual action;

having arrived, respond to the *stomas*—the hymns employed by the *udgātṛ*—uttering a sound in the form of a response (*praśa*). Likewise, directed toward the duties of the *adhvaryu*, utter a sound in praise (*gṛṇīhi*).
Likewise, making the sounds of the *śastra* recitations employed by the *hotṛ* priest indistinct, produce a roar;
by this satisfaction, the human sacrificer will praise you—this is the meaning.
Thereafter, increase along with us (*sacā*) our *brahma*, our food, our sacrifice, and the ritual action being performed.
By providing all the necessary components, increase the sacrifice and cause its fruit and the food [resulting from it] to flourish.
Among the twenty-eight names of the sacrifice beginning with "anyaḥ," the term "brahma varcaḥ" is recited (Nirukta 2.7.25).
Here,
from the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going," [the suffix] *si* becomes *hi*.
Because it has the marker ṅ due to being treated as *herapita*, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
There is *nighāta* (elision of accent).
With *āṭ*, there is *guṇa*.
"An *ekādeśa* [substitute] for a vowel preceded by an *udātta* is itself *udātta*. Thus,
there is an *udātta* accent in "stomān."
The suffix *man* is applied by [the rule] *'artitusu'* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.137), etc.; because of its being included in the *nvi*-group, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.
*Vardhana*.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.3.117 (*karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca*).
By the rule "when a suffix marked with *l* follows," the vowel preceding the suffix receives the acute accent (*udātta*).
To the one who has crushed many enemies in the city;
from the root *pidh* in the sense of "going," [with the rule] "for roots beginning with *dh*, *p* becomes *s*."
Here, the prefix *nir-*—which has the same meaning as the word *niḥ*—is placed first.
By the rule "and *kvip*," the suffix *kvip* is applied;
there is the elision of *kvip* that removes the entire suffix.
The compound is formed according to Pāṇini’s rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (2.2.18).

Because of the intervention of the letter *i* between the *s* of *nis-* and the root *iṇ*, the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the verbal root—prescribed by the rule *upasargātsunoti* (8.3.65) and others—is not applied here due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatvāt*).
However, the *s* of *nisaḥ* [becomes ṣ] by the rule *puṃsi punaḥ* (8.4.41).

The compound is formed with the word *puruṣa* ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) as the object of the action. In *pi-dha*, the initial vowel has the acute accent (*udātta*) by virtue of the root accent (*dhātusvara*).
In *niṣpidhe*, because it is a *prādi*-compound, the original accent of the final member of the *kṛt*-derivative (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) applies.
Because the term *kudrahaṇa* includes even that which is preceded by a verbal root (*gati*) or a kāraka, the same accent applies even in the case of a *kāraka-samāsa*.
[Thus] *śakraḥ* is derived from the sense "he is able" (*śaknoti*),
with the suffix *rak* according to the rule *sphāyitañcivañciśaki* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.170), etc.
The conditional accent (*pratyayasvara*). For example:
"The suffix *thāl* is used in the sense of expressing a manner" (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.23).
In *suteṣu*,
the vowel *a* preceding the suffix *kta* is acute by virtue of the accent of the suffix itself.

Salutation to the letter *na*. In the *saṃhitā* [text], there is the substitution of *ṇa* according to Pāṇini’s rule 8.4.27: *naśca dhātusthorupabhyaḥ*. Thus, it becomes *rāraṅgan*. The root *raṇ* has the meaning "to sound."

The suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule "dhātor ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.22). Elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule "yaṅo 'ci ca" (Pāṇini 2.4.74). Reduplication takes place by virtue of the technical designation of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), according to the rule "dvirvacane 'ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59). Thus, by the rule "sanvallaghuni caṅpare 'naglope" (Pāṇini 7.4.93), the form becomes *jāgarti*. This is the meaning of the word *jāgrat*. The term *jāgrat* is used here as a synonym for *sākṣin* (the witness). The sense is that the Self is the witness of all states, such as waking and dreaming. It is not the case that the Self is subject to these states; rather, it is the witness of them. Therefore, the Self is eternal. The phrase "He who knows this" means one who knows the Self as described above. "Becomes immortal" means he attains immortality. "In this very world"—that is, while still alive—he attains immortality. He does not wait for death to reach liberation. This is the meaning. The statement "he becomes immortal" is made with reference to the attainment of the state of Brahman, which is free from the cycle of rebirth. It does not mean that he becomes identical with the Absolute Brahman, for that is impossible for one who is still embodied. Furthermore, the scripture says: "Having attained the state of Brahman, he does not return again. This indicates that the attainment of the state of Brahman is the final goal. Moreover, the scripture says: "When all desires dwelling within the heart are cast away, then a mortal becomes immortal; even here he attains Brahman. This shows that immortality is achieved through the cessation of desire. Therefore, the meaning is that one who knows the Self as described becomes immortal in this very life. Thus, the Upanishad concludes its teaching on the knowledge of the Self. This is the end of the first section of the second chapter. The second chapter is concluded. The third chapter begins. Now, the scripture describes the meditation on the five fires, which is a means to attain the knowledge of the Self. The purpose of this meditation is to purify the mind so that it may become fit for the realization of the Self. The text says: "Now, those who know this [five-fire meditation] and those who worship in the forest with faith... and so forth. This meditation is intended for those who are unable to practice the yoga of the Self directly. By means of this meditation, one gradually attains purification of the mind and eventually reaches the knowledge of the Self. Therefore, the scripture teaches this meditation as a preparatory stage for the ultimate goal of self-realization. Thus ends the third chapter. The fourth chapter begins. Now, the scripture describes the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāna*). The purpose of this description is to show the two distinct paths taken by those who possess knowledge and those who perform ritual actions. Those who know the Self and those who practice the five-fire meditation proceed by the path of the gods to the world of Brahman. Those who perform sacrifices and good deeds proceed by the path of the fathers to the world of the moon and return again to this world. The scripture says: "Those who know this and those who worship in the forest with faith go by the path of the gods to the world of light, from there to the sun, from the sun to the region of lightning; then a person consisting of mind comes and leads them to the worlds of Brahman. In those worlds of Brahman they dwell for long ages. They do not return again. This describes the path of the gods. On the other hand, the scripture says: "Those who perform sacrifices and good deeds go by the path of the fathers to the smoke, from smoke to night, from night to the dark fortnight, from the dark fortnight to the six months of the southern solstice, from there to the world of the fathers, and from the world of the fathers to the moon. Reaching the moon, they become food. There the gods feed upon them as they would on Soma. When their merit is exhausted, they return by the same path by which they went, passing through the ether and the air, and reaching this world, they are born again as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans. This describes the path of the fathers. Thus, the scripture teaches the distinction between the two paths to illustrate the fruits of knowledge and action. The ultimate goal remains the attainment of the Self through knowledge. Therefore, the scripture concludes: "But those who live in villages and perform works, they return again to this world. This emphasizes that the cycle of rebirth continues for those who lack knowledge of the Self. Hence, the seeker of liberation must strive for the knowledge of the Self. This is the end of the fourth chapter. The fifth chapter begins. Now, the scripture describes the meditation on the small space (*dahara-vidyā*) within the heart. The purpose of this meditation is to lead the mind toward the realization of the Supreme Self. The text says: "There is a small lotus-like palace in the city of Brahman, and within it is a small space. That is what you should seek to understand, that is what you should desire to know. This small space within the heart is not the physical space, but the Supreme Self. The scripture explains that within this small space reside all things—earth, fire, water, air, heaven, earth, mountains, and all beings. This demonstrates that the Supreme Self is the substratum of all existence. The scripture further says: "As the spokes are fixed in the hub of a wheel, so all this is fixed in the Self. This illustrates the omnipresence and supportiveness of the Self. The seeker should meditate on the Self as being within the heart, as pure consciousness, and as the source of all. Through this meditation, the mind becomes concentrated and attains the vision of the Self. The scripture concludes: "He who knows this, having shaken off all evil, like the husk from grain, and having made himself transparent like the water of a well, reaches the world of Brahman and becomes immortal. This describes the result of the meditation. Thus, the scripture teaches the meditation on the small space as a means to attain immortality. This is the end of the fifth chapter. The sixth chapter begins. Now, the scripture describes the meditation on the Self as the eater (*attā*). The purpose of this meditation is to remove the misconception that the Self is merely a consumer of objects. The text says: "O Gārgī, the knower of Brahman said: 'That which eats the food, that which wears the clothing, and that which performs actions—that is the Self. This identifies the Self as the true agent and enjoyer, yet distinct from the body and senses. The scripture further clarifies that the Self is not subject to hunger or thirst, but is the witness of these states. The seeker should realize that the Self is the inner controller, the source of all activity, and the ultimate reality. The scripture concludes: "He who knows this, having overcome all difficulties, reaches the world of Brahman and becomes immortal. This emphasizes that the realization of the Self as the transcendent witness leads to liberation. Thus, the scripture teaches the meditation on the Self as the eater to establish the identity of the individual self with the Supreme Self. This is the end of the sixth chapter. The seventh chapter begins. Now, the scripture describes the meditation on the Self as the light within the heart. The purpose of this meditation is to dispel the darkness of ignorance and reveal the luminous nature of the Self. The text says: "There is a person within the heart, shining like gold, having a golden beard and hair, golden in every limb. His name is 'Ut' (the Exalted). This describes the Self as a radiant being of pure light. The scripture explains that this light is not produced by external sources, but is innate to the Self. The seeker should contemplate this light as the source of all illumination and the dispeller of all darkness. The scripture concludes: "He who knows this, having shaken off all evil, like the husk from grain, and having made himself transparent like the water of a well, reaches the world of Brahman and becomes immortal. This reiterates the result of the meditation. Thus, the scripture teaches the meditation on the Self as the light to reveal the self-luminous nature of the Supreme Reality. This is the end of the seventh chapter. The eighth chapter begins. Now, the scripture describes the meditation on the Self as the breath (*prāṇa*). The purpose of this meditation is to show that the Self is the vital force sustaining all life. The text says: "The breath is indeed the oldest and the best among the vital functions. Therefore, one should honor the breath. This identifies the Self with the supreme vital energy. The scripture explains that the breath is not merely the physical function of respiration, but the conscious principle that animates the body. The seeker should realize that the Self is the source of all vitality and the sustainer of all beings. The scripture concludes: "He who knows this, having shaken off all evil, like the husk from grain,
The substitution of the *hal* [consonant] remains (*halādiśeṣaḥ*).

A long vowel is substituted by the rule "a long vowel for a non-kit root" (*dīrgho'kitaḥ*, Pāṇini 7.4.83). By the principle of "characterization by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇena*), the verbal designation (*dhātusaṃjñā*) applies via the rule "those ending in *san* etc. are roots" (*sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, Pāṇini 3.1.32). Consequently, in the sense of the *liṅ* [optative], the *leṭ* [subjunctive] is used according to the rule "the *leṭ* occurs in the sense of the *liṅ*" (*liṅarthe leṭ*, Pāṇini 3.4.7), specifically in the sense of the *liṅ* defined as the relation between cause and effect (*hetuhetumadbhāva*, Pāṇini 3.3.156).
For here, Indra’s act of rejoicing is the reason for the necessity of performing the instruction of the *uvatha*.
[The suffix] is the *leṭ* in the form of *tip*.
By the rule "itaścalopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.97), there is the elision of the vowel *i*.
By the rule *leṭo ’ḍāṭau* (Pāṇini 3.4.94), the augment *aṭ* is applied.

The suffix *śap* occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. Regarding this [root], it should be regarded as having the *carikṛta* (reduplication) formation, being parasmaipada and treated like the *adādi* class; thus, although the elision (*luk*) of *śap* would normally apply by the rule *adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ*, it is prohibited by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
Because the *śap* affix is unaccented (*anudātta*), the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu*) alone remains as the final acute (*antodātta*).

Due to the intervention of *śap* between the root and the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix, the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) prescribed for reduplicated roots (*abhyasta*) by Pāṇini 6.1.189 does not apply there.
Nor is there elision by the rule "a *tiṅ* [is unaccented] after a non-*tiṅ*" (*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*).
In this case, because of the connection with the word *yathā*, the prohibition [of accentuation] applies according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 8.1.36: *yāvadyathābhyām*.
Alternatively, there will be no *nighāta* (elision of accent) here by virtue of the rule *cavāyoge prathamā*.

Here, in the subsequent sentence, this first-person finite verb ending (*tiṅvibhakti*) is used in relation to the previously mentioned case-ending in the word *sabhyeṣu* (and among the members of the assembly), as indicated by the particle *ca*.
Regarding the word *sabhyeṣu*: [it means] "in the sacrificial works," which are the "sacrificial grains" (*sasya*).
Following the recurrence of the rule *karmaṇi ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.124), the suffix *ya* is applied to the word *sabhā* by the rule *sabhāyā yaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.126).

In that case, regarding the *bhaṃ* [stem] in knowledge (*jñā*), there is the elision of the vowel *i* by the rule "yasyeti ca" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.148). It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
We beg him for friendship, him for wealth, him for heroic might; may that Śakra, the powerful Indra, bestowing desirable riches upon us, be our protector.
Him indeed we seek for friendship; him for song; him for great heroic power. He is the mighty one, and may that Indra, bestowing desirable wealth upon us, be powerful for us.
When friendship has become the cause, we seek—that very Indra;
likewise, for the sake of wealth (*rāye*), we seek him;
and likewise, for the sake of excellent heroic power (*suvīryai*), that is, for the purpose of noble capability, we seek him.
Moreover, Śakra—the powerful Indra—bestowing *vasu*, wealth, upon us, was capable (*śakan*) in protecting us.
(Seventeen)

In the ritual acts of petitioning (*yāccākarma*), the forms "īmahe" and "yāmi" are recited (Nirukta 3.19.1). In accordance with that, it should be explained as "we petition Indra. *Sadhryagbhāvaḥ* means friendship (*sakhitvam*). The suffix *tva* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.1.119: *tasya bhāvastvatalau*. It is accented on the first syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *Īmahe*: from the root *īṅ* (to go). Because it has the marker *ṅ*, the Ātmanepada is used (Pāṇini 1.3.12). The suffix *śyan* is added according to the rule *divādibhyaḥ śyan*. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śyan*. The *nighāta* (suppression of accent) occurs by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. *Rāye*: the vowel of the case-ending is accented by the rule *aḍiḍam*. *Suvīrye*: one whose valor (*vīrya*) is excellent (*śobhana*) is *suvīryaḥ*. By this word, which denotes the possessor (*bhavitṛvācin*), the state (*bhāva*) is indicated; thus the meaning is "in the state of possessing excellent valor" (*suvīryatve*). The acute accent on the first syllable of the final member is applied by the rule *vīravīryau ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.120), which follows the governing rule *bahuvrīhau* (6.2.106). *Śakraḥ*: he who is capable (*śaknoti*) is *śakraḥ*. [This is derived] from the roots *sphāyi*, *tañci*, *vañci*, and *śaki*... [etc., as per the relevant grammatical rules].
There is no such extensive rule as "parādiś chandasi bahulam" (in the Vedic language, the accentuation often applies to the beginning of the following word).
For if that were the case, in the word *suvivṛtam*, the latter member would simply be *vivṛtam*, and thus only the initial vowel *i* of that member would have to be accented.

Even though in the compound *vivṛtam* the vowel *ṛ* becomes the beginning of the word, nevertheless, because the compound *suvivṛtam* is stronger due to being the "remaining remainder" (*satiśiṣṭa*), the accentuation must occur on the very first vowel of the latter member of that compound, which is the vowel *i*.

It is said that in the rule *agatiranantaraḥ*, when the term *ṛc* is mentioned, the *kṛd-grahaṇa-paribhāṣā* (the metarule regarding the mention of *kṛt*-suffixes) is not resorted to. If that were resorted to, then even when there is an intervening *gati*, since the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) would apply, the mention of "immediate" (*anantara*) would be purposeless.

It is precisely with this intention that the example *abhyudgatam* is cited as a counter-example for the purpose of the mention of "immediate," so that the intervening word *abhi* does not [receive the accent].
Therefore, it is well-established that the vowel *ṛ* alone is the acute (*udātta*); thus,
[the word] *sunirajaṃ* means "to be attained without effort and without fault."

The root *aja* means "to go" and "to throw. The prefixes *su* and *ni* are placed before it. [The suffix] *khal* is applied after a verb when preceded by the adverbs *īṣat*, *asu*, or *kṛcchra* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.126).
And in this context, it cannot be maintained that the word *su-* is separated from the suffix *ni* by [the intervention of] *padma*.

For the word *su-* has as its cause the fact that it ends in a *sup*-affix and ends in a vowel (*svanta*), not mere immediate contiguity (*ānantarya*). For this very reason, there are such usages as *sugahvaraṃ* and *durgahvaraṃ*.
As before, in the compound *gati-samāsa*, by the rule *aliti* (Pāṇini 6.2.49), the syllable preceding the suffix is acute; thus, the vowel of the root (*dhātu*) is acute.
In the compound with *nis*, by the rule *kṛd-uttara-pada-prakṛti-svara* (the accent of the first member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix remains), that same [root vowel] is retained as acute.

Furthermore, in the compound with the word *su*, by the paribhāṣā *kṛd-grahaṇe gati-kāraka-pūrvasyāpi grahaṇam* (Paribhāṣā 28)—which states that when a *kṛt*-suffix is mentioned, it includes a *kṛt*-form preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*—by the rule *kṛd-uttara-pada-prakṛti-svara*, that same [root vowel] is again retained as acute.
"Tvādāttam" means made clear by its own purification;
[the root] "daip" is used in the sense of "purifying."
The substitution of *ā* for *e* occurs by the rule "ādeca upadeśe’śiti" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.45).
For even though the letter *p* is present as an *anubandha*, this [root] ends in *ej* according to the paribhāṣā "anānubandhakṛtamanekāj-tvam" (Paribhāṣā 7).
And [the suffix *a*] is added in the sense of the object by the rule "ṇicaśca" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.102).

In the rule *'dādhā ghvadāp'* (Pāṇini 1.1.20), because the designation *ghu* does not apply due to the prohibition *adāp*, the substitution of *dad* [for *dā*] as prescribed by *'do dadhoḥ'* (Pāṇini 7.4.46) does not take place. If it is argued: "The prohibition *adāp* in that rule applies only to the root *dāp* 'to cut' which is taught as a *pratipadokta* (directly stated) term, and not to the root *daip* 'to purify' which is *lākṣaṇika* (derived through a grammatical definition). This is because of the restrictive principle (Paribhāṣā 105): 'Between a term taught as a *pratipadokta* and one that is *lākṣaṇika*, the *pratipadokta* is to be understood, not the *lākṣaṇika*,'" we say: No.
This is due to the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) stated in the *Paribhāṣā* 106: "In the inclusion of [stems] beginning with *gām*, there is no distinction.
From the word *yuṣmad*, the third-person singular case ending receives the substitute *ḍā* by *Pāṇini Sūtra* 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk...*);
then, by *Pāṇini Sūtra* 7.2.97 (*tvamāvekavacane*), the portion up to the final *m* of the stem is replaced by *tvā*.
By the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), there is substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*).

When the designation *bha* applies, by the rule *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.143), the final vowel of that which ends in *at* is elided. By the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*, the long *ā* becomes acute (*udātta*).
The third-case compound is formed by Pāṇini’s rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (2.1.32).
Furthermore, the non-elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending is justified by *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (6.3.14).
When the original accent of the final member of the *kṛdanta* compound would otherwise apply, the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (6.2.48) prescribes that the initial member retains its original accent.
*Yaśas*:
[derived from] the root *aś* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*).
[The form is derived] by the rule *aśeryud ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.6.30), which prescribes the suffix *amun*.
Therefore, by rule, the augment *yuṭ* is added to the verbal root;
due to the prefix *ni*, the word is udātta-accented on its first syllable: *nigavvām*.

The accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*) applies. Although the acute accent of the case-ending would have been required by the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168), it is prohibited by the rule *na gośvasāvarṇa* (Pāṇini 6.1.182). [Thus,] *vṛdhi*.
The root *vṛñ* means "to choose.
By the rule *śruśṛpṛkṛbhyaśchandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.102), the substitution of *dhi* for the suffix *hi* occurs.
Furthermore, by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is also the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śa*.

The elision [of the final vowel] occurs. [In the word] *kṛṇuṣva*, [the suffix] *num* is added [after the root vowel] because of the rule "ito num" (Pāṇini 7.1.58), applied to the root *kṛvī*, which means "to injure" and "to act."
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition;
[the substitution of] *s* for the final *tha* of the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.78; and [the substitution of] *se* for *thās* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.80.
Regarding the rule *savābhyāṃ vāmau* (Pāṇini 3.4.91):
although the suffix *śap* would have applied by *kartari śap* (Pāṇini 3.1.68), the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *adhinivṛṇvyora ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.80).
By virtue of its co-occurrence (*tatsaṃniyogena*), the letter *v* is replaced by the letter *a*.
In this case, there is elision [of the *a*] according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.4.48 (*ato lopaḥ*).

Due to the status of the elided *a* as *sthānivat* (acting as if it were still present) by virtue of Pāṇini’s Sūtra 1.1.57 (*atra parasmin pūrvavidhau*), neither the substitution of *laT* nor the *guṇa* of the penultimate vowel occurs.

Here, although the accent of the *vikaraṇa* is later applied, it is set aside by the rule "the accent of that which remains is stronger, except in the case of *vikaraṇas*," and thus the *tiṅ*-suffix itself receives the udātta accent on its first syllable.

1. The suffix *ṭha* itself is the means of liberation (*nistāra*). 2. Because of the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, and *ya* here. 3.
