One who prepares the oblation is called haviṣkṛt.
[The suffix] krip is applied, and there is the augment tuk after a short vowel.
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.45: "In a compound, [the *s* of] a word ending in *ni* becomes *ṣ* when it does not stand as a final member.
The accentuation follows the rule for the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound.
O praised one, bring the gods hither on your most pleasant chariot;
you are the Hotṛ-priest appointed by Manu.
At the head, on the most comfortable chariot, being praised, bring the gods hither; you are the Hotṛ appointed by Manu. 4.

O you who are denoted by the word *ida*, being praised (*īḷita*) and lauded (*snuta*) by us, having placed the gods upon your most comfortable (*sukhatama*)—that is, the supreme cause of happiness—chariot (*ratha*), bring them hither (*ā vaha*) to the field of action (*karmabhūmi*). The epithet "praised" (*īḷita*) is used here to indicate that you are denoted by the word *ida*. You are the one established here by Manu—that is, by the mantra or by Manu himself in the form of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and others—as the Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods.
*Sukhatama*:
[This is derived from] *sukha* with the suffix *matup*, meaning "that which has happiness in it.
In this case, there is elision (*luk*) according to the rule: "The elision of *matup* should be stated after words expressing a quality" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 5.2.94.3).

*Atiśayena sukhaḥ* means "most pleasant" (*sukhatamaḥ*). Because the suffix *tamap* is unaccented (*anudātta*), the word retains the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*). [The word is] *rathe*.
The root *ram* is used in the sense of playing (*krīḍā*). A *ratha* is that in which they delight (*ramante’smin*).
[The suffix] *kthan* is applied according to the rule: “After the roots *han*, *kṛp*, *ni*, *mī*, and *kāś*, [the suffix] *kthan* [is added]. (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.159).
The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is by the rule *ekāca upadeśe’nudāttāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.10).
The elision of the letter *m* is by the rule *anudāttopadeśa* (Pāṇini 6.4.37), etc.
[The word] has the acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable because it is *nityādi*.
*Īḷitaḥ*: [from] *īḍ* in the sense of "praising"; the suffix *kta* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.102 (*niṣṭhā*).
The augment *iṭ* is added; according to the rule “augments are unaccented” (*āgamā anudāttāḥ*),
it is unaccented by virtue of its connection with that [root].

Thus [the word *devān*] is unaccented; it bears the accent of the suffix. Regarding the word *devān*, in the *saṃhitā* stage, the substitution of *r* for the final *n* occurs by the rule *dīrghādaṭi samānapāde* (Pāṇini 8.3.9).
By the rule *ānaṭi nityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.3), the vowel *ā* becomes nasalized.
By the rule *bhomago* (Pāṇini 8.3.17) and others, the *r* of *roḥ* is changed to *y*.
That *y* is then elided by the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.19).
Because that [condition] is unestablished, the rule "ādugah" does not apply. The word "ā" is acutely accented on its first syllable because it is a particle (nipāta).
*asi*. [From the root] *as*, meaning "to exist" (*bhuvi*). Present tense (*laṭ*); second person singular suffix (*sip*).
By the rule *‘adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ’* (Pāṇini 2.4.72), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
By the rule *‘tāsastyor lopeḥ’* (Pāṇini 7.4.50), there is elision of the letter *s*. [Thus,] *hotā*.
The suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).
After this suffix, by the rule *sau ‘ṛtuśana* (Pāṇini 7.1.94), the substitution *anaṅ* occurs; because the suffix is marked with *ṅ*, it undergoes substitution at the end of the stem.

By the rule *apnan* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.11), there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*). By the rule *halḍyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.68), there is the elision of the case-ending. Being a *nis* compound, it is udātta on the first syllable.
Manu is so called because he reflects; thus, *manuḥ*. [The root] *man* [is used] in the sense of "knowing."

The suffix *u* is applied by the rule *śṛ-vi-sahi-tapi-yasi-vasi-hani-kṣi-dhi-vandhi-mani-bhyaś-ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.10). Since the term *nit* is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into that rule, [the suffix] is udātta on its first syllable. Thus, *hitaḥ*.
In the word *manu-hita*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *niṣṭhā*.
By the rule *dadhāter hiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.42), the substitution of *hi* for the root *dhā* occurs.
In the compound *manunā hitaḥ*, the form *su* is substituted in place of the third-case ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), and so forth.
Its *r* becomes *ṛ*. The absence of elision (*luk*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.2.48, *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.
O wise ones, strew the sacrificial grass, its back anointed with ghee,
where the vision of immortality is found.
Strew the sacrificial grass continuously, O wise ones, with its back anointed with ghee, where the vision of immortality is found. 5.
O wise ones, O intelligent officiating priests, spread the *barhis*—the *darbha* grass—upon the altar (*vedi*).
Here too, the fire named *barhis* is indicated.
Of what kind is the *barhis* to be spread?

"Ānuṣak" means connected in succession, mutually bound together. "Ghṛtapṛṣṭham" refers to that sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon which ghee is on the back—that is, the upper surface—because the ladles filled with ghee have been placed upon it. On that sacrificial grass, there occurs the "cakṣaṇa"—the sight or manifestation—of "amṛtasya," meaning of the ghee which is like nectar.
Or else: [it may be interpreted as follows...]
The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "Whose sacrificial grass (barhis), belonging to the immortal god, becomes visible first? Spread that sacrificial grass."
*stṛṇīta*:
from the root *stṛñ* meaning "to cover," this is the second person plural imperative with the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix.
‘The *loṭ* [suffixes] are treated like the *laṅ* [suffixes]’ (Pāṇini 3.4.85).

By the rule ‘[the substitutes] *ta*, *tha*, *tha*, and *mi* [are applied]’ (Pāṇini 3.4.101), there is the substitution of *ta* for *tha*. [Then] ‘*śnu* [is added] after roots beginning with *ṛ*’ [applies].
The substitution of *ī* is by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.113 (*ī halyaghoḥ*).
The substitution of *ṇ* is by the rule "it should be stated that [the substitution applies] after a vowel of the *ṛ*-class" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.4.1).
The shortening of the verbal root is by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.60 (*pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*).
When there is a conflict, the accent of the suffix (*svaravalīyastva*) prevails, except in the case of *vikaraṇas*.
Therefore, in *tiṅ* forms, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) belongs to the suffix itself. As in *barhiḥ*.
By the rule *bṛṃhelaupaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.266), the suffix *i* is applied and the nasal is elided; the accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *Ānuṣak*.
It is called *ānuṣak* because it follows (*anu-pajati*) from all sides (*ā-samantāt*).
The root is *paj* in the sense of "clinging" (*saṅga*), and according to the rule *dhātvādeḥ paḥ saḥ*, the *p* at the beginning of the root is changed to *s*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76). The elision [of the root vowel] occurs by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24).
The prefixes *āṅ* and *ava* are placed before [the verbal root].
Regarding the word *vāci*:
the verbal root denoting the manifestation of speech (*vāg-ābhivyakti*) here indicates manifestation in general.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.3.115: *lyuṭ ca*.
There is no substitution [of *khyāñ* for *cakṣiṅ*].

Since that [suffix] is an *ārdhadhātuka*, the substitution of *khyāñ* prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.4.54 (*cakṣiṅaḥ khyāñ*) would otherwise apply; however, there is a prohibition of this by the rule "asanayośca" (Pāṇini 2.4.54, vārttika 10).
May the divine doors, which increase the cosmic order and are unobstructed,
swing wide today and now for the sacrifice.
May the divine doors, increasers of Truth, wide and unobstructed, be opened today and now for the sacrifice.

"Let the doors—the gates of the sacrificial hall—be opened; let them be thrown open by the lifting of their panels. Of what nature are they? They are 'ṛtāvṛdhaḥ' (increasers of *ṛta*), that is, increasers of truth or of sacrifice; 'devīḥ' (divine), meaning radiant; and 'asaśrataḥ' (unwearied), meaning unwearied by the opening, being free from the crowding of men who enter."
Alternatively:

let these specific forms of Agni, named after the doors and presiding over them, enter—that is, attend—to the sacrificial halls which are *asaśrataḥ*, meaning devoid of men who would enter, for the sake of admitting those men. As to what purpose is served by attending the doors or by the entry of men therein, that is now stated:
"Today, on this very day," "certainly," "indeed" (avaśyam); "to sacrifice" (yaṣṭave) means "in order to sacrifice.
Because of the word "ca" (and), it should be understood that [the sacrifice may also take place] on another day.

*Ṛtāvṛdhaḥ*: In the sense of "those who cause *ṛta* to increase," the suffix *kip* is applied to the root *vṛdh* with the causative (*ṇic*) meaning internalized, according to the rule *'kip ca'*. This forms an *upapada-samāsa*.
The lengthening of the first member [of the compound] occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137).
The root *vṛdh* is udātta by virtue of its verbal accent (*dhātusvara*).
In the compound, that same accent remains by the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived word (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
*Devīḥ*: By the rule *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.4.66), there is the long vowel of the same class as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*).
From the word *deva*, ending in the suffix *ac* (added by the rule *pacādyac*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *puṃyogādākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48).
The vowel [of the suffix] is acute by virtue of its being a *pratyaya-svara*.

Together with the case-ending (*vibhakti*), it becomes acute by the rule "an *ekādeśa* [substituted] for [a preceding grave vowel and] an acute [vowel] is acute" (Pāṇini 8.2.5). Thus, *amaśrataḥ* [is acute].
The root *gluñcu* [is used] in the sense of "going. The letter *j* is replaced by *c* through metathesis (*vyatyaya*).
The suffix *laṭ* is substituted by *śatṛ*.
In the absence of doors, those [structures] such as the *prāgvaṃśa* hall and others, in which people do not move about while moving along, are called *amaśrataḥ*.
This is a word ending in the suffix *cap*, formed by the rule "sadyaḥ-parūt" (Pāṇini 5.3.22) and others. It is thus a conventional form (*nipātita*).
Because it is designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38), there is elision (*luk*) of the subsequent case-ending.
It is accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
In the *saṃhitā*, the lengthening occurs according to the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*.
Surely;
by the rule "the end of words such as these [is udātta]" (Phiṭ-sūtra 82), there is the udātta accent on the final syllable.
[The form] *yaṣṭave* [is derived accordingly].
The suffix *taven* is applied to the root *yaj* by the rule *tum-arthe sese-na* (Pāṇini 3.4.9) and so forth.
The change to *ph* occurs by the rule beginning with *vaś-ādi*. It is udātta-accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *niv*-class.
I invoke Night and Dawn, the well-adorned ones, at the sacrifice;
may they sit upon this sacred grass of ours.
I invoke Night and Dawn, the well-adorned ones, at this sacrifice; may they sit upon this sacred grass of ours. 7.
In common usage, the words *nakta* and *uṣas* denote specific times;
however, here they are employed for the two forms of Agni who preside over those times.
"Nakta and Uṣas"—the two forms of Agni named Nakta and Uṣas—"I invoke" (*upahvaye*), that is, I call upon them, while this sacrificial rite is being performed.
For what purpose?

"Naḥ" means "our. "Idam" refers to this "barhis," that is, the *darbha* grass, which is placed upon the altar (*vedyām*). [The purpose is] for them to sit—that is, to reach—the seat. Of what sort are they?
"Supeśasā" means "endowed with beautiful form."

*Naktaṃ* and *uṣāḥ* form the compound *naktopāsā*. The long vowel *ā* in the dual case-ending is substituted according to Pāṇini’s rule *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39). The elision of the *m* and the lengthening of the penultimate vowel are Vedic (*chāndasa*) features.
By the rule "devatādvandve ca" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.141), both the preceding and following members of the compound simultaneously take their original accent (prakṛtisvara). *Supeśas*:
those two whose *peśas*—that is, form—is beautiful.
The form is as before.
The word *peśas* is ādyudātta because its suffix belongs to the *naḍ*-class.
In a *bahuvrīhi*, by the rule "after *nañ* and *su*" (Pāṇini 6.2.172), the udātta falls on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*).
1. Regarding the person who has entered the *tara-śa* [state]:

because this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of final acute accent (*antodāttatva*), there is acute accent on the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) by the rule "In the Veda, [the first syllable of a compound] is acute" (Pāṇini 6.2.119).
In this [case].
The case ending is udātta by the rule *aḍidam* (Pāṇini 6.1.171) and others. In *āsande*,
[the root] *sad* [is used] in the senses of falling apart, going, and sinking.
‘The *pa* at the beginning of a verbal root is replaced by *sa*.
From this [root] preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.108.1;
this forms a *prādi*-compound.
The original accent of the final member of a compound ending in a *kṛt* suffix [retains its position].
Those two divine Hotṛs, the sages with beautiful tongues, do come hither;
may they perform this sacrifice of ours.
Those two with beautiful tongues, the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the sages—come hither! May they perform this sacrifice for us. 8.
The word *tat* here, being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), denotes a well-known object.
*Nā*: those two; *tau*: the two fires well-known among the ritualists (*yājñika*);
*upa huye*: I invoke; *naḥ*: our; *imam yajñam*: this sacrifice; *yakṣatām*: may those two worship; that is, may both perform [the rite].
Of what nature are they? They are "sujihvā," meaning endowed with beautiful tongues, speaking pleasant words, or possessing splendid flames;
they are "hotārā," performers of the oblation; and "daivyā," divine, belonging to the gods.
Therefore, these two fires are named the divine Hotṛs, the two sages (kavī) who are possessed of wisdom.
Those two [words]. Here, the dual ending of the second case is replaced by the vowel *ā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
It is accented acute (*udātta*) by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*.
*Sujihvau*:
those two whose tongues are beautiful. In the word *nammuṣyās*, the final syllable of the second member [of the compound] is udātta (accented).
As before, there is a single substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*). In *saṃhitā*, there is the substitution of *āv*.
Then, by the rule "the elision of *va* and *ma* [is optional] according to Śākalya" (*vamya lope śākalyasya*, Pāṇini 6.1.127), there is elision.
*Hotārā*: from the root *hu*, with the suffix *tan*; in the dual, there is *guṇa* substitution by Pāṇini’s rule 7.3.110, *ṛto ṅi*.
In the word *asan*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghaḥ*).
The vowel *ā* is substituted as before.
Because it has the marker *ṅit*, it is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudāttaḥ*).
*daivyā*: [this is] for the gods (*devānām*);

[the suffix] *yaj* is applied by the rule *devāyatana-ādy-aco ñyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). *imam*: [this is] for this one. *devāyatanau*: [this is] for the two abodes of the gods; [the suffix] *ñya* is applied by the rule *devāyatana-ādy-aco ñyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). *iti yaj*: thus [is] the suffix *yaj*.
The elision of the vowel *a* is according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.4.148, *yasyeti ca*.
The initial vowel is udātta according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.197, *jinyādir nityam*.
The long vowel *ā* is as in the previous case.
*yakṣatām* and *yajatām*:

after the suffix *śap* in the *loṭ* [imperative] mood, the suffix *sip* occurs due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* in Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.34 (*mibbahulaṃ leṭi*). Then, the substitutions for *k*, *c*, and *ṇ* take place.
Iḷā, Sarasvatī, and Mahī— may these three goddesses,
who bring delight, sit upon the sacrificial grass, free from harm.
Iḷā, Sarasvatī, Mahī—the three goddesses who bring happiness—let them sit upon the sacrificial grass, they who are unfailing. 9.

Here, the word *mahī* denotes Bhāratī as endowed with the quality of greatness (*mahattva*), because in other similar Āprī hymns, *Iḷā*, *Sarasvatī*, and *Bhāratī* are traditionally recited together. These three goddesses (*tisro devīḥ*), who are radiant (*dīpyamānāḥ*) and whose forms are the sacrificial ladles (*vahni-mūrtayaḥ*), denoted by words such as *Iḷā* and the rest, should sit—that is, they should take their place—upon the *barhis*, the grass strewn upon the altar. Of what nature are they?
May they be *mayobhuvaḥ*, meaning producers of happiness, and *asridhaḥ*, meaning free from exhaustion or decay.
*Ilā*: [derived from] the root *īḍ* meaning "to praise";
the shortening [of the vowel] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The accent of the verbal root [remains].
The suffix *ṭāp* is applied according to the rule: “*ṭāp* is also applied to those ending in a consonant, as in *vācā*, *diśā*, *niśā*” (Kaiyaṭa on Pāṇini 2.4.82). Thus, *ṭāp* is added.

*Sarasvatī*: [The word] *saras* is derived from the root *as* with the suffix *un*, and it is accented on the first syllable (*udātta*) because it is a *nivādādi*. The feminine suffix *matup* is added in the sense of "she who possesses that."

The substitution of *v* occurs because the word has *adupadha* (a short vowel in the penultimate position). Since the status of being a *pada* is sublated by the rule *tasau matvarthe* (Pāṇini 1.4.19), there is an absence of the substitution of *r* and so forth. Furthermore, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6).
The suffixes *matup* and *īp* are unaccented because they are marked with *p*.
In the word *mahī*, there is the elision of the letter *ṭ* in the word *mahīta*.
This is a Vedic form (*chāndasa*).
The elision of the vowel *a* occurs by Pāṇini’s rule 6.4.148, *yasyeti ca*.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the suffix *ṅīp* is established by the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*.
In the case of *tisraḥ*,
when the suffix *jas* follows, the substitute *tistra-* is applied by the rule *tricaturor striyāṃ tisṛcatasṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.99).
Then, the substitution of *r* for the vowel *ṛ* is applied by the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.100).
The *jasa* [ending] is acute by virtue of the rule *tisṛbhyo jasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.166). *Devīḥ*:
the wives of the gods are goddesses (*devyaḥ*).

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *puṃyogādākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.48). The elision of the vowel *a* occurs by the rule *yasyeti ca*. By the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), the *ṅīp* becomes udātta.
In the case of *jasi*, the lengthening that was prohibited by the rule *adīrghāj jasi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.105) is optionally permitted by the rule *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.106),
as in *mayobhuvaḥ*.
The root *mīñ* means "to injure.
That which injures suffering is *mayaḥ*, meaning happiness.
Those who bring that [happiness] into being are *mayobhuvaḥ*.

From the root *bhū* with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *kvip* is applied; the accentuation follows the rule for the natural accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*). Thus:
*barhiḥ*.
By the rule *bṛṃhanelopaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.266), the suffix *isi* is applied; it bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [The form] is *sīdantu*.
The root *pad* is used in the sense of "falling" (*viśaraṇa*) and so forth. By the rule *pāghrā* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.78), the substitute *sīda* is applied.
[The word is] *astridhaḥ*.

From the root *midh*, meaning "to injure" or "to dry up," the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) after the suffixes *saṃpad* and others; then, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with the negative particle *nañ*.

This results in the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapadāntodāttatva*), by the rule "nañsubhyām," which overrides the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*).
The *puronuvākyā* for Tvaṣṭṛ at the *pātnīvata* sacrifice is "iha tvaṣṭāramagriyam" (here [we invoke] Tvaṣṭṛ, the foremost).

Regarding the *maṇḍa*, it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "śaṃ yuvākāya saṃrepitaḥ" (hail to the one addressed by both; he has been sent forth), as in: "saṃ te payāṃsi samu yantu vājā iha tvaṣṭāramagriyam" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.10).
Here I invoke Tvaṣṭṛ, the omniformed one who was once unfriendly;
may he belong exclusively to us.
Here, I summon Tvaṣṭṛ, the foremost, the omniform; may he be ours alone. 10.
I invoke here, for this ritual act, Tvaṣṭṛ— the fire named Tvaṣṭṛ—
of what kind? Foremost, most excellent, and possessing manifold forms.
"May he be 'ours alone,' that is, unique and not shared with others;
the meaning is: may he bestow grace even more abundantly than upon other sacrificers."
Tvaṣṭṛ.
[The root] *takṣu* / *tvakṣu* is used in the sense of "making thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*). [The suffix] *tṛn*.

By the rule *svaratisūtisūyatidhūtūñdito vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), there is an option for the absence of the augment *iṭ*. In the case of its absence, by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogadhorante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), there is the elision of the letter *k*. Then there is the substitution of *ch*. In the second singular [case], by the rule *ṛto ṅisarvanāmasthānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), there is *guṇa*, and by the rule *atvasantasya cādhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14), there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel.
Because the suffix *tṛn* is marked with *ṇi*, it has an udātta accent on its first syllable. *Agriyam*:
following the rule *agrāt* (Pāṇini 4.4.116), the suffix *ghac* is applied by the rule *ghacchau ca* (Pāṇini 4.4.117).
By the rule *āyaneyī* (Pāṇini 7.1.2), the substitution of *iy* for the phoneme *dh* occurs. Then, by the rule *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant].

According to the maxim *āyanādiṣūpadeśivadvacanaṃ svarasiddhyartham* (Pāṇini 7.1.2), because of the treatment as if it were the original form (*upadeśivadbhāva*), the suffix is udātta by virtue of being the first member of the affix; however, due to the presence of *ghu*, *ci*, and *śu*, it becomes antodātta.
"Viśvarūpa":
he whose forms are all forms, by virtue of being Tvaṣṭṛ.
For the Śruti states: "Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of animals in their pairs" (Tai. Saṃ. 6.1.8.5).

Since the word *viśva* has an udātta accent on its first syllable, it would normally retain its original stem accent (*prakṛtisvara*) in a bahuvrīhi compound; however, by the rule "In a bahuvrīhi, when it is a name, *viśva* [takes the accent on the final syllable]" (Pāṇini 6.2.106), the final syllable of the first member becomes udātta.
*Asmākam*:
from the root *asu* in the sense of "throwing."
By the rule *yupya-sibhyāṃ madik* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.136),
[the suffix] is udātta on the first syllable by the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*).
The sixth case plural ending is *ām*.

In this context, even though the rule *yo ḍaci* (Pāṇini 7.2.89) would otherwise apply, it is superseded by the substitution of *āṅ* for *akam* (Pāṇini 7.1.33), because the latter is both obligatory (*nitya*) and a rule prescribed by a specific mention (*pratipadavidhi*). Consequently, due to the prohibition in *anādeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.86), the substitution of *y* does not occur. Thus, when the *dakāra* is elided by *śeṣe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90), the suffix *suṭ*—which would have applied subsequently because the stem ends in an *akāra*—is precluded by the fact that its original locus (*sthānin*) has been removed, as indicated by the mention of the form *sāma*. Indeed, the specific mention of *sāma* in the rule is intended precisely for this purpose. [The word] *kevalaḥ* [is used].
Because *vṛṣan* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa*, it is udātta on the first syllable.
O Vanaspati, release the oblation to the gods;
let the consciousness of the giver be directed forward.
O Vanaspati, release the oblation for the gods; let the consciousness of the giver be directed toward the divine. 11.
1. By the rule *ta-śa-yasyeti ca*, there is elision of the vowel (*alopa*). 2. When *ākam* is substituted for the genitive plural endings *tāsām*, *phāsām*, and *śāsām*.

O Vanaspati, O divine one, release—that is, present—our oblation to these gods who are the recipients of the offering. By your grace, let there be spiritual discernment (*cetana*) regarding the world beyond for the sacrificer, the *dhātu*. *Vanaspati*: The vocative accent (*āmantrita-nighāta*). *Devā*: No accent due to being at the beginning of a *pāda*; optionally, the first syllable of the vocative is acute (*āmantritādyudātta*). *Haviḥ*: The suffix accent (*pratyayasvara*) of the root *hvi*. *Dhātuḥ*: From the root *dā*, with the suffix *tṛc*. It is oxytone by the rule *citaḥ*. In the genitive singular (*ḍasi*), the vowel *u* replaces *ṛ* according to Pāṇini 6.1.111, followed by the substitution of *r* (*raparatva*). The *s* is elided by Pāṇini 8.2.24. The *u* is acute by the accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*). *Cetanam*: From the root *citī* (to perceive). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). The *y* is replaced by *an*, and the penultimate vowel undergoes *guṇa*. The syllable preceding the suffix is acute by Pāṇini 6.1.193.
Svāhā! He performs the sacrifice for Indra in the house of the sacrificer;
there I summon the gods.
Svāhā! Perform the sacrifice for Indra in the house of the sacrificer; there, summon the gods hither. 12.
The word *svāhā*, signifying the offering of oblations, indicates this specific oblation by that name.
Perform, O priests, the sacrifice accomplished through that [oblation] for Indra—that is, for the sake of Indra’s satisfaction—in the house of the sacrificer;
and therein, at that sacrifice, I summon the gods.
*kṛṇotana*. [The root] *kṛvi* is used in the senses of "harming" (*hiṃsā*) and "making" (*karaṇa*). Because it begins with the vowel *i*, the augment *num* is applied.
In the case of the middle voice plural ending *lopa*, there is the substitution of *na* by the rule *tasthasthamipām* (Pāṇini 3.4.101).
Then, by the rule *tasanasanathanāśca* (Pāṇini 7.1.45), there is the substitution of *tanap*.

When the suffix *śap* would otherwise apply, the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.80); furthermore, by connection with that suffix, the letter *v* is replaced by the vowel *a*.

In that case, there is elision by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48). Because of the status as a *sthānivadbhāva* for that [elided element] by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the *guṇa* substitution of the short vowel in the penultimate position (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not occur for the *ṛ*-vowel. However, because the suffix *tanap* is marked with *p*, it is not *ñit*; consequently, there is *guṇa* substitution for the *u*-vowel.
For Indra:
by the rule "ṛtendra" (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.186), the suffix *ran* is applied; because it is marked with *ṇi*, it is udātta on the first syllable.
The word *yajvanaḥ* [is derived as follows]:
regarding the sense of "worshiping the gods, associating,
and giving," the rule *suyajo ḍvinip* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.103) applies.

When the designation *bha* applies, the elision [of the final syllable] would otherwise occur; however, there is a prohibition by the rule "not after a conjunct consonant ending in *v* or *m*" (Pāṇini 6.4.137).
Because the suffix *vanip* is marked with *p*, the accent of the verbal root alone remains.
[Thus we have] *gṛhe*.
The root *grah* means "to seize" (*upādāna*). The suffix *kap* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.1.144, *gehe kaḥ*.
Substitution by semivowels (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.16, *ahijyā*, and so forth.
The state of having another [word] preceding it; the accent of the suffix; therein.
By the rule *‘liti’* (Pāṇini 6.1.193), the syllable preceding the suffix is acute.
In the *saṃhitā* reading of *‘devā~ upa’*, the *n* becomes *r* by the rule *‘dīrghādi’* (Pāṇini 8.3.9).

By the rule *āto ’ṭi nityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.3), there is a substitution of a nasal for the vowel *ā*. By the rule *bho-bhago-...* (Pāṇini 8.3.17), there is the substitution of *y*. This *y* is then elided by the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.19).
Regarding the third hymn consisting of twelve verses beginning with “aibhir agne,” the seer and the meter are as before.
That hymn is addressed to many deities;
for this very reason, it is enumerated as: “aibhir agne devam.”

As for the application (*viniyoga*): at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) of the first *Chandoma* day of the expanded twelve-day sacrifice (*vyūḍha-dvādaśāha*), the hymn "With these, O Agni, [accept] the services and the songs" (*aibhir agne duvo giraḥ*) is used for the *Vaiśvadeva* Śastra.

Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: beginning with "Now the *Chandomas*: 'From the ocean... (*samudrād bhiḥ*), it says, "'With these, O Agni, [accept] the services and the songs' is the *Vaiśvadeva* [Śastra]" (*āśva. śrau. 8.9*).
O Agni, with all these gods, come to our service and our songs for the drinking of Soma, and perform the sacrifice.
O Agni, come with all these gods for the drinking of Soma, to our service and our songs; and perform the sacrifice. 1.

O Agni, come hither with all these gods who have been honored at this sacrifice, for the sake of drinking the Soma— come for the purpose of the sacrificial rite involving the Soma-drink— and attend to our service (*duvas*) and our songs of praise (*giras*);
having arrived, perform the sacrifice (*yakṣi*).

By these [words]. Because of the reference to the gods previously mentioned by means of *idam*, the substitute *aś* is applied as anudātta according to the rule "In the subsequent mention (*anvādeśa*) of *idam*, *aś* is anudātta when followed by a case ending from the third case onwards.
By the power of Śiva, this is a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*).
By the rule *nedamadasorakoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.11), there is no substitution of *ṇa* for the case-ending *bhis*.
The case-ending is simply unaccented (*anudātta*).
Nor does the rule *uḍidampadādyappumraidyubhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.171) cause the case-ending to be accented; for in that context, the governing rule *antodāttāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.169) applies.
*duvaḥ*: By the rule "the word *duvas-* [is] udātta when followed by a suffix beginning with *n* and not having *ni*" (Phiṭ-sūtra 26), it has the acute accent on the first syllable. *viśvebhiḥ*.

The word *viśva* ends in the suffix *kvip*; it is oxytone because it begins with the negative particle *ni*. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.10), the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* does not occur.
By the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet* (Pāṇini 7.3.103), the substitution of *e* occurs.
For the drinking of Soma.
The word *soma* is derived with the suffix *man* according to the rule *arti-stu-sū-...* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.137), and being [a word] ending in *man*, it is udātta on its first syllable.
*Somapītiḥ* refers to that sacrifice (*yāga*) in which there is the drinking (*pīti*) of Soma.
To him;
the dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of.
By the gods.
In the word *yakṣa*, there is no substitution of *ais* for the case-ending *bhis* according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*;
rather, there is the substitution of *e* according to the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet*. Thus: *yakṣa*.
The suffix *sip* is substituted for the *loṭ* [imperative] ending of the root *yaj*.
By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” (Pāṇini 2.4.73), there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix;
here, by the word “*ādi*,” the substitution of *patra* is indicated.
The substitution of *k* for *s* occurs by Pāṇini’s rule 8.2.41 (*paṭhoḥ kaḥ si*).
The replacement of *si* with *hi* does not take place because of the archaic nature of the Vedic text (*chāndasatvāt*).
Since *sip* is marked as *pit*, it is unaccented; therefore, the accent remains that of the verbal root alone.
The Kaṇvas have invoked you; they, the inspired poets, sing your hymns.
O God, come hither with the gods!
The Kaṇvas have called upon you; they praise your inspired thoughts, O Sage. O Agni, come hither with the gods! 2.
O wise Agni, the wise Kaṇvas, the officiating priests, have summoned you—the accomplisher of the sacrifice.
Thus they praise and proclaim your deeds.
Therefore, O Agni, come hither together with the gods.
Among the twenty-four names for the wise man beginning with ‘vipraḥ,’ the word ‘kaṇvaḥ’ is listed as a synonym for ‘ṛbhuḥ’ in Nirukta 3.15.7.
*tvā*: The substitution *tvā* [for *tvām*] occurs by the rule "tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.23); it is entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*). *Kaṇvāḥ*.

The word *kaṇa* has the meaning "sound. The suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *aśri-prapilaṭikaṇviṣaṭi* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.149), etc.; because of its inherent [nisan] status, it is udātta on the first syllable.
*ahūpata*. [The root] *hve* is used in the sense of rivalry and sound.
Since the rule *“chandasi luṅliṭ”* (Pāṇini 3.4.6) is in effect, the *luṅ* suffix is applied.
After the root *jīv*, the *ātmanepada* affixes are used in place of *jhi*.
By the rule "ātmanepadeṣvanataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.5), there is the substitution of *at* for the final vowel.
For the *cli* suffix, *sic* is substituted.
By the rule *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10), there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*).
By the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), there is lengthening (*dīrghatva*).
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.59).
Due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *ū*. Thus, [the form is] *aḍḍāmaḥ*.
They proclaim;
from the root *gṛ* in the sense of "sound," in the present tense (*laṭ*).
*jhi* | *‘jho ’ntaḥ’* | *‘kryādibhyaḥ śnā’* |
The shortening of the root vowel occurs by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.80). The elision of the long *ā* occurs by the rule *śnābhyastayorātaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.112).
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs according to the statement *ṛvarṇācceti vaktavyam* (Kāśikā 8.4.1.1).
Only the accent of the finite verb (tiṅ) remains;
[for example,] *vipra*,
where the vocative is subject to the rule of enclitic depression (*āmantritanighāta*).

In the case of *te*, since the term *anudātta* is understood from the previous rule, the sixth-case ending is replaced by *te* according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 8.1.22, which states: "For the singular [ending], *te* and *me* [are substituted].
Thus, *devebhiḥ*.
The substitution of *ai* for *e* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly.
[The imperative] *gahi* [is derived from] the root *gam-lṛ* (to go).
The *sip* suffix follows the imperative (*loṭ*). [By the rule] *serhyapicca*, it is replaced by *hi*. [By the rule] *kartari śap*, the *śap* suffix is added.
In this case, there is elision [of the suffix] by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73).
The letter *m* is dropped by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa... (Pāṇini 6.4.37).

Because that [elision of *m*] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "amidvadvad vā bhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), the elision of the imperative suffix *hi* by the rule "ano heḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.105) does not occur.
1. [The rule] *ta.śa-jhasya* [applies].
Indra-Vāyu, Bṛhaspati, Mitra-Agni, Pūṣan, Bhaga, the Ādityas, the Māruta group. (3) "Indra-Vāyu," etc.; "Bṛhaspati"; "Mitra-"; "Agni"; "Pūṣan"; "Bhaga"; "the Ādityas"; "the Māruta"; "group. (3)
O Agni, worship Indra and the other gods, as well as the host belonging to the Maruts, the winds; the two words "and" (ca) and "worship" (yakṣa) carry over from the preceding context.

*Indraśca vāyuśca* becomes *indravāyū*. Regarding the form *indravāyū*, the substitution of *ānaṅ* (for the final vowel and following consonant of the first member) prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule *devatādvandve ca* (6.3.26) is prohibited by the Vārttika: *ubhayatra vāyoḥ pratiṣedho vaktavyaḥ* (6.3.26.1).
Furthermore, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of both members, which would have applied by the rule *devatādvandve ca* (6.2.141), is barred by the prohibition *nottarapade'nudāttādau* (6.2.142).
The accent is simply that of the final member of the compound.

In *bṛhaspatim*, there is elision of the suffix *tal* and the addition of the augment *suṭ*, according to the rule: "In the case of *kara* and *patya* following *tad* and *bahu* respectively, when *śrotra* and *devatā* are to be expressed as the meanings, *tal* is elided and *suṭ* is added" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.157).
Some, such as Vāmana, describe the word *bṛhat* as having its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*). [The root] *pā* means "to protect. One who protects is a *pati*.
Regarding *pāterdatiḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.497),
it is acutely accented on the first syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
In the compound, by the rule *ubhe vanaspatyādiṣu yugapat* (Pāṇini 6.2.140), both members of the compound retain their original accents (*ubhayapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
*Mitrā*: [This is] the second case. By the rule "supāṃ suluk" (Pāṇini 7.1.39) and others, there is the substitution of *āj* for the case-ending.
The Ādityas:
the sons of Aditi are the Ādityas. [This is derived] by Pāṇini’s Sūtra 4.1.85: "The suffix *ṇya* is applied after *aditi*, *āditya*, and words where *āditya* or *apatya* form the final member."
The accent of the derivative suffix;
[the word] *māruta* means "a modification of the Maruts."
The suffix *añ* is applied by Pāṇini Sūtra 4.3.140, "anudāttādeśa";
because it has the marker *j*, it is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

May your exhilarating drops flow forth, O Indus, which cause intoxication—drops of honey, resting in the vessels. 4. May your exhilarating drops flow forth, O Indus, which cause intoxication—drops of honey, resting in the vessels. 4.
O Indra and other gods, for your sake these drops of Soma are being prepared—that is, they are being produced in abundance.
Of what nature are they?
They are exhilarating, providing satisfaction.
"Matsara is Soma, from the root *mad*, which means 'to satisfy'," says Yāska (Nirukta 2.5). "Mādayiṣṇavaḥ" means causes of exhilaration. "Drapsāḥ" means those in the form of drops.
The *madhvaḥ* are the sweet [Soma juices];
the *camuṣadaḥ* are those situated in the *camū* vessels, that is, in the cups (*camasa*) and other such drinking vessels.
The use of the separated form [pra] is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.82, *avyavahitāśca*.
They perish.
In the case of *bhaj*, there is the substitution of *riṅ* by Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.4.28 (*riṅ-śayagliṅkṣu*). Alternatively, for *haj*,
there is the substitution of *bh* for *h* by Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.2.32 (*hyagrahor bha-c-chandasi*).
*Indavas*:
from the root *undī*, meaning "to moisten";
they are so called because they moisten the vessels.
With the word "niṭ" understood from the previous rule, the suffix *up* is applied by Uṇādisūtra 1.12, "undericcādeḥ," and the initial vowel is replaced by *i*.
Because it is marked as *nitt*, the word is udātta on its first syllable.
[Thus we have] *matsarāḥ*.
In the sense of "intoxication" (*mada*) and "satisfaction" (*tṛpti*),
with the word *cit* understood from the previous context, the suffix *sap* is applied by the rule *kṛmadibhyaḥ kit* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.353).
The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *titutrathasimasarakaseṣu ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.9).
Because it has a penultimate *c* vowel,
it is udātta on the final syllable. [The word] *mādayiṣṇavaḥ* [is derived from the root] *madī*, meaning "to exhilarate" or "to smear."
The suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied by the rule *ṇecchandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.137).

When the elision of the *ṇi*-affix would have occurred by the rule *ṇeraniṭī* (Pāṇini 6.4.51), the substitution of *ay* is applied by the rule *ayāmantālvāyyetnviṣṇuṣu* (Pāṇini 6.4.55). Because it has the marker *c*, it is accented on the final syllable (*āntodātta*).
Regarding *madhvaḥ*:
it has been stated that the word *madhu* is udātta on its first syllable;
the masculine gender of the word *madhu* is due to a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).

Because of the rule "A grammatical operation conditioned by a specific designation (*saṃjñā*) is not invariably obligatory," the *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *ava*] does not occur by Pāṇini’s Sūtra 7.3.109, *jami ca*.
Thus, we have *camūpadaḥ*.
[The roots] *camu*, *amu*, *jamu*, and *jhamu* mean "to eat."
Those vessels (*camasa*) in which things are drunk (*camyate*) or consumed (*bhakṣyate*) are called *camvaḥ*.
The suffix *ū* is applied according to the rule "kṛpicami" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.81).
Those who sit (*sīdanti*) therein are called *camūpadaḥ*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "satsūdviṣa" (Pāṇini 3.2.61) and others.
The substitution of *pat* for *sup* occurs because the group beginning with *sup* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
The accentuation follows the original accent of the final member (*uttarapada-prakṛtisvara*).
Seeking your aid, the Kaṇvas, having spread the sacrificial grass, praise you, bearing oblations and having prepared them well.
Seeking aid, the Kaṇvas, having trimmed the sacrificial grass, possessing oblations, and having prepared them well, praise you. || 5 ||

O Agni, the *ṛtvij*s (priests) praise you; they laud you. Of what sort are they? They are *avasyavaḥ*: desiring the gods who are the cause of *avana*, which means protection. They are *kaṇvāsaḥ*: wise ones. They are *vṛktabarhiṣaḥ*: those who have cut the *darbha* grass for the purpose of spreading it [on the altar]. They are *haviṣmantaḥ*: possessed of sacrificial oblations (*havis*). They are *araṃkṛtaḥ*: those who have made themselves ready or adorned. Regarding the word *īḷate*: the root *īḍ* means "to praise. Because it is *anudātta-it* (having an *anudātta* vowel as its *it*), the suffix *jha* is substituted for the present tense marker (*laṭ*). By the rule "after roots beginning with *ad* etc., there is elision of *śap*," there is elision of *śap*. The *jha* is replaced by *at*. The final *ṭi* is changed to *e*. Since the *l-sārvadhātuka* suffix is *anudātta* by the rule "that which is marked with *anudātta* or *anubandha* *t* is *anudātta*" (Pāṇini 6.1.186), the accent of the verbal root alone remains. Regarding *avasyavaḥ*: those who protect (*avanti*) are *avāḥ*, namely the gods. They desire them intensely. [The derivation is: from a noun ending in a case-suffix, the suffix *kyac* is added when expressing one's own desire (Pāṇini 3.1.8). By the rule "in *kyac* also" (Pāṇini 7.4.33), the change to *ī* does not occur, because of the prohibition "not in the Veda, except for *putra*" (Pāṇini 7.4.35). By the rule "the suffix *suk* is to be stated after all nominal stems in the sense of longing" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 7.1.51), *suk* is added. Then the suffix *up* is added by the rule "in the Veda, after a stem ending in *kyac*" (Pāṇini 3.2.170). There is elision of the *a*. The final syllable is *udātta* by the accent of the suffix. Regarding *kaṇvāsaḥ*: the root *kaṇ* has the meaning "to sound. Those who sound—that is, chant—intensely through hymns and the like are *kaṇva*s, the priests. The suffix *kan* is added by the rule "also after *aśi*" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.149). Being a *nis* (root-based) formation, it is *udātta* on the first syllable. By the rule "for *ājas* there is *amuk*" (Pāṇini 7.1.50), *amuk* is added. Regarding *vṛktabarhiṣaḥ*: *vṛkta* means "cut. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member prevails. Regarding *haviṣmantaḥ*: those to whom *havis* belongs are *haviṣmant*s. Because of the rule "when *t* or *as* follow, it is treated as a *bha* stem in the sense of possessive suffixes" (Pāṇini 1.4.19), it is a *bha* stem; thus, since it is not a *pada*, the change to *r* (sandhi) does not occur. Regarding *araṃkṛtaḥ*: those who adorn themselves are *araṃkṛtaḥ*. The suffix *kvip* is added by the rule "and *kvip*" (Pāṇini 3.2.76). There is the augment *tuk* after the short vowel. By the rule "in names and in the Veda, the *l* of *kapilaka* etc. optionally becomes *r*" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 8.2.18), the letter *l* is replaced by *r*.
May the steeds who carry thee— the swift ones with backs of ghee, impelled by thought—
bring the gods hither for the drinking of Soma.
Those who carry you, whose backs are sprinkled with ghee, who are yoked by thought—those bearers, bring the gods here for the drinking of the Soma.
O Agni, those horses which carry you on the chariot—
of what sort are they? They have glistening backs (*ghṛtapṛṣṭhāḥ*), meaning their backs are radiant by virtue of their physical form.
"Yoked by the mind," meaning harnessed to the chariot by the mere act of mental resolve; "carriers," meaning the draft-horses— with those horses,
[O Agni,] bring the gods for the drinking of Soma, that is, for the sake of the sacrifice which has the drinking of Soma as its purpose— this is the ellipsis.
*Ghṛtapṛṣṭhāḥ*:
[The root] *ghṛ* means "to flow" and "to shine.
Those whose backs (*pṛṣṭha*) are shining (*ghṛta*) are *ghṛtapṛṣṭhāḥ*.
The word *ghṛta* is oxytone by virtue of the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the preservation of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
[The term] *manoyujaḥ* means "those who are yoked by the mind."
The suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvigadadhṛk* (Pāṇini 3.2.59).
The accentuation follows the rule for the natural accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
[The form is] *tvā*.
In the case of *tvām*, the substitute *tvā* is unaccented by the rule "tvāmau dvitīyāyāḥ.
[In *vahanti*],
because the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is unaccented, the accent falls on the root.
Just as there is an absence of elision (*nighāta*) due to its connection with that [suffix], so too in *vahniyaḥ*:

following the recurrence of the rule "niḥ" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.488), the suffix *nip* is applied by the rule "from *vahi*, *śra*, *śru*, *du*, *gal*, *āh*, and *atvari*, [the suffix] *nip*" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.411).
Its [the prefix *ni-*] accentuation is *nisvāda-ādyudātta* (acute on the first syllable). Regarding *somapītaye*,
it has been explained.

When followed by the letter *sakāra* (*s*), the augment *ṣuk* is applied to the nasal *nakāra* (*n*) in *saṃhitā* according to Pāṇini’s rule 8.3.30 (*naśca*). Then, the substitution of the retroflex *ṭavarga* (*carvam*) occurs according to 8.4.55 (*khari ca*).
Finally, the second *sakāra* is changed to *ṣakāra* according to 8.4.46.3 (*cayo dvitīyāḥ śari pauṣkarasādeḥ*).
1. Let your horses bring them hither—those invincible ones who increase the cosmic order; O Agni, make them accompanied by their wives.
O fair-tongued one, make him drink the honeyed draught.
O Agni of the beautiful tongue, make those worshipful ones, who increase the cosmic order, accompanied by their wives; cause them to drink of the honeyed draught.
O Agni, make those gods, Indra and the others, worthy of sacrifice, adorable, increasers of truth (or of the sacrifice), and accompanied by their wives.
O you of beautiful tongue, cause the gods to drink their portion of the sweet soma.

The word *yajatrān* [is derived from] the root *yaj* with the suffix *atran*, according to the rule *aminakṣiyajibandhipatibhyo'tran* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.385). [The word] *ṛtāvṛdhaḥ* [means those who increase the cosmic order].
The root *vṛdh* means "to grow. From this root, with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.76 (*kvip ca*).
The lengthening of the vowel in the first member of the compound is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.137 (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*).
The vowel of the root *vṛdh* has the udātta accent.
In a compound, the initial syllable of the final member, being a *kṛt*-derivative, retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
*Agne*.
Because it begins with a *pāda*, there is no *nāmantrita-nighāta*; rather, there is the optional *ādyudātta* accentuation.

In the sense of "shining": the suffix *yuc* is applied in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.2.149 (*anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*). By the rule *citaḥ*, the final syllable has the udātta accent. *Viśvān*: *viśva-* with the suffix *kan* is ādyudātta by virtue of being listed among the *nivāt* words. *Uparbudhaḥ*: "Those who wake up nearby" (*uparbudhyante*) are called *uparbudhaḥ*. The suffix *kip* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.76 (*kip ca*). The vowel *u* is udātta by the accent of the verbal root. In the compound, the original accent of the final member (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*) applies. *Citraḥ*: The suffix *ran* is applied according to the Uṇādi Sūtra 2.186 (*kajindra...*). It is ādyudātta because it is a *nivāt* word. *Hotā*: From the root *hū* ("to sacrifice"), the suffix *van* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). The semi-vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*; this is followed by the replacement of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatvam*) and the formation of *guṇa*. It is ādyudātta because it is a *nivāt* word. *Iha*: The suffix *ha* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.11 (*idamo haḥ*). The substitution of *iś* for *idam* occurs according to Pāṇini 5.3.3 (*idama iś*). Because it is a substitute for a whole word (*sarvādeśa*), it takes the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvaraḥ*). *Vakṣati*: From the root *vah* ("to carry"), the suffix *leṭ* is used in the sense of the optative (*liṅarthe*) for a request. For that [suffix], *tip* is applied. In the sense of the agent, the suffix *śap* is added.
By the rule *pā. sū. 7. 4. 42*, there is the substitution of *hi* for *ha*.
Thus, *manunā hitaḥ* becomes *manuhitaḥ*.
The compound is formed by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (*pā. sū. 2. 1. 32*).

By way of an exception to the *kṛtsvara* accent, the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 6.2.48) applies, resulting in the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound. [The word] *sīdasi*: [the root] *sad* [is used] in the senses of “falling apart,” “going,” and “settling.”
The suffix *laṭ*:
[the third person singular] *sip*.
By the rule *pāghrādhmā* (Pāṇini 7.3.78) and others, there is the substitution of *sīd* for *sip*.
Nighāta:
In the case of *sam*, where there is elision of the *s* in the *saṃhitā* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.134 (*so 'ci lope cet pādapūraṇam*), the *guṇa* [substitution] occurs.
[The word is] *adhvaram*.
That in which *dhvara*—meaning violence or injury—is not present is *adhvara*.
According to Pāṇini’s rule *nañsubhyām* (6.2.172), the final syllable of the second member of the compound is udātta.

In the case of *no adhvaraṃ*, where the sandhi rule *eṅaḥ padāntādati* (6.1.109) would have required the formation of a single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*), this is prevented by the rule *prakṛtyāntaḥpādamanyapare* (6.1.115), which maintains the original form of the word within the foot of a verse when followed by a different vowel.
Yoke, O God, the ruddy, tawny, and red horses to your chariot;
with them, bring the gods here.
Yoke, O God, the tawny ones to your chariot, the bay steeds, the ruddy ones; with them, bring the gods here. 12.

O divine Agni, *rohitaḥ*—the mares designated by the word *rohit*—are his female horses. *Yuñjva*: yoke them to the chariot. The particle *hi* is for the purpose of filling out the meter. Of what sort are they? *Arupīḥ*: swift-moving. *Haritaḥ*: capable of carrying away—that is, of leading—the men mounted on the chariot. With those mares, *iha*—in this ritual act—bring the gods hither. *Yuñjva*: from the root *yujir* (to join). The imperative (*loṭ*). Because it is *svarita*-accented, it takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). By the rule *thāsaḥ se*, *se* replaces *thās*. By *savābhyāṃ vāmau*, *va* replaces *m*. By *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam*, the suffix *śnam* is added; its elision occurs due to the diversity of usage (*bāhulaka*). There is the accent of the *kṛt* suffix and the substitution of *pa* for *va*. By the accent of the suffix, it is oxytone (*antodātta*). In *saṃhitā*, there is lengthening by Pāṇini 6.3.135 (*vyaco'tasmin*). *Arupīḥ*: from the root *ṛ* (to go). They go quickly, thus they are *aruṣyaḥ*, the mares. By Uṇādi-sūtra 4.513 (*ṛhannibhyāmupan*), the suffix *upan* is added. There is guṇa of the root and *rapara* substitution. Being *nighāta*, the word *aruṣ* is ādyudātta. From that, in the feminine, the Vedic suffix *ḍīp* is applied. In the nominative plural (*śas*), there is lengthening by Pāṇini 6.1.102 (*prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*). *Rathe*: from the root *ram*, with the Uṇādi suffix *kyan*; being *nighāta*, it is ādyudātta. *Haritaḥ*: by Uṇādi-sūtra 1.97 (*hasruhiyubhibhya itiḥ*), the suffix *iti* is added to *hṛ*. The vowel *i* is udātta by the accent of the suffix. *Rohitaḥ*: from the root *ruh*, by the same rule, the suffix *iti* is added. The vowel *i* is udātta by the accent of the suffix. *Tābhiḥ*: the potential udātta of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) by Pāṇini 6.1.168 (*sāvekācaḥ*) is prohibited by 6.1.182 (*sāvavarṇa*). In *devān*, as before, there is the substitution of *ṛt* and the *anunāsika*. 27. Translation complete.

Regarding this fourth hymn consisting of twelve verses beginning with “indra somam,” the seer and the meter are as previously stated. Although this entire hymn has the Seasons (*ṛtu*) as its deity, nevertheless, various other deities such as Indra are combined in each verse. Accordingly, it is enumerated: “*indra somam*; [the verses] are addressed to the Seasons; therein [the first] is for Indra, the second for the Maruts, the third for Tvaṣṭṛ, the fourth for Agni, the fifth for Indra, the sixth for Mitra-Varuṇa, four [verses] for Draviṇodas, one for the Aśvins, one for Agni, and the remaining verses have the Seasons as their deities throughout.”
But the application (viniyoga) should be understood as being based on the Smṛti.
O Indra, drink the Soma according to the season; let the exhilarating drops, whose home is there, enter into you.
O Indra, drink the Soma according to the season; let the exhilarating drops, which have their home therein, enter into you. 1.

O Indra, drink the Soma together with the *ṛtu*. Let the drops—the Somas being drunk—enter you. Of what sort? Intoxicating (*matsarāsaḥ*), causing exhilaration; having that as their abode (*tadaukasah*), meaning they always reside within your belly. O Indra! [The accentuation of] the vocative is acute on the first syllable according to the rule for words beginning with *pāṣṭhika*. [Regarding] *somam*: the suffix *man* is applied by the rule "after *arti*, etc. (*Uṇādi-sūtra* 1.137); it is acute on the first syllable because it begins with *ni*. [Regarding] *piba*: this has been explained in the verse "pibā mitrasya" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.14.10). [Regarding] *ā... viśantu*: let them enter you.
Thus, the particle *ca*, which has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), is elided along with the sense of the pronoun *asya* contained in the subsequent sentence.

Consequently, by the rule *cādilope vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.1.63), this first-person verbal ending (*tiṅvibhakti*) is not dropped. However, although the elision of *ca* is the same in the case of *viśan vai*, the second-person ending is indeed dropped because it is a second-person form.

In the *Saṃhitā*, regarding the vowel *guṇa* that would otherwise occur in the word *āhunaḥ*, its non-occurrence is due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the opinion of Śākalya, by the rule *ṛtyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.128).
[The examples] *indavaḥ* and *pra vo mriyante* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.14.4) have been explained therein.
They are stingy.
Regarding this, it is stated in that very same [work]:
"The augment *asuk* is applied by the rule *ājseresuk* (Pāṇini 7.1.50)."
*Tadokasaḥ*:
those for whom that very thing is their *okaḥ*, meaning their dwelling place (*sthānam*); they are thus described.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is retained].
O Maruts, drink [the soma] according to the seasons; as the *potr* priests, purify the sacrifice, for you are indeed the bounteous givers.
O Maruts, drink from the *potrī* cup of the seasons; purify the sacrifice! For you indeed are the givers of good gifts (*sudānas*).

By means of the word "you" (*yūyam*), referring back to the Maruts through their well-known preeminence of power, the particle *hi* expresses that they are the cause for the purification in this prayer, "purify [it]! (*punītana*).
Accept our sacrifice; O Neṣṭṛ, drink with the Ṛtu-cup, for you are the bestower of treasures.
Favor our sacrifice; O Grāvastut, drink with the Ṛtu-cup, O Neṣṭṛ, for you are the bestower of treasures. ||3||
The word *grā* denotes a woman.
Thus Yāska says: "Menā means women; they honor them (*mānayanti*), they know them (*jānanti*), they go toward them" (Nirukta 3.21).
One who possesses these [women] is *grāvān*.
The word *neṣṭar* here refers to the god Tvaṣṭṛ, because he served as the *neṣṭṛ* priest at a certain sacrificial session of the gods.
O Neṣṭṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, who art accompanied by the wives [of the gods], O Grāvans, praise our sacrifice on all sides—that is, sing it in the presence of the gods.
Together with the *ṛtu*, drink the Soma.
For since you are a "ratnadhāḥ"—that is, a giver of jewels—you are one who bestows them; therefore, the meaning is that you ought to drink the Soma.
Regarding *abhi*: because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) stated in the *Phiṭ-sūtra* 81, "And [the prepositions] excluding *abhi*," the word *ami* has its final syllable udātta. [Thus:
*gṛṇīhi*.
The root *gṛ* means "to sound. In the imperative (*loṭ*), the suffix *sip* is replaced by *hi*.
By the rule *kyādibhyaḥ śnā*, the suffix *śnā* is applied.
Because it is marked with the *ṅ* (indicating it is *ṅit*), the vowel is shortened by the rule "ī halyaghoḥ.
Due to the *ṅ* marker of the suffix *śrā*, there is an absence of *guṇa*. Furthermore, by the rule "pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ," the vowel is shortened.
The word *tiṅaṅatiṅaḥ* receives the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
The suffix *matup* is used in the sense of "he who possesses these" (*grā asya santi*).
The substitution of *va* for *ma* occurs by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

In *saṃbuddhau*, by the rule "amatuv-aso ruḥ," there is the substitution of *ru*; this becomes a *visarga*. Since it occurs at the beginning of a *pāda*, the *āmantrita* (vocative) elision does not apply, and thus the *āmantrita-udātta* accentuation applies optionally.

Since *grāva* functions as a qualifier and is thus a specific term (*viśeṣavacana*), the prohibition "an *āmantrita* [is not unaccented] when followed by a word in grammatical apposition" (*nāmantritaṃ samānādhikaraṇe*) does not apply; consequently, because the subsequent word *iṣṭa* is treated as if non-existent (*avidyamānavat*), its initial vowel optionally receives the acute accent (*ādyudātta*).
[In the word] *piba*, because the suffix *śap* is marked with *p*, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
Because the two preceding [words] are unaccented (*amantrita*), they are treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*); thus, there is no *nivāta* [sandhi].
[The term] *ratnadhāḥ* means "one who holds jewels" (*ratnāni dadhāti*). The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *kvip ca*.

The accent of the *dhātu* (verbal root) remains; in a compound, by virtue of the rule that the original accent of the final member ending in a *kṛt* suffix is preserved, that very accent alone is retained.
Thus, *asi*.
Because *sip* is a *pit* [suffix], it bears the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*).
The elision (*nivāta*) prescribed by the rule "a *tiṅ* after a *tiṅ*" does not occur here, due to the prohibition contained in the rule "also when *hi* follows."
O Agni, bring the gods here; seat them in the three wombs; attend to them and drink according to the season.
O Agni, bring the gods here; seat them in the three wombs; attend to them all around; drink according to the season. ||4||

O Agni, bring the gods here to this ritual act; then, seat the gods in their three places of origin, that is, at the three *savana*s; thereafter, honor them—that is, adorn them—and drink the Soma together with the *ṛtu*. The line "O Agni, the gods" has been explained. Regarding *yoniṣu*: the root *yu* means "to mix. The suffix *nip* is applied according to *Uṇādisūtra* 4.491 (*vahitri*), etc.; it is accented on the first syllable because it is a *niṣṭhā*-type formation. Regarding *triṣu*: the case-ending is accented according to Pāṇini 6.1.179 (*paṭṭricaturbhyo halādiḥ*). Regarding *bhūṣa*: the root *bhūṣ* means "to adorn. The *nighāta* accent applies by the rule *tiṅaṅatiṅaḥ*. Regarding *piba ṛtunā*: [this has already] been explained.
O Indra, drink the Soma from the Brahmin’s gift according to the seasons;
for with you alone is the friendship established.
O Indra, drink the Soma from the Brahmin’s gift according to the seasons; for your friendship alone is invincible. ||5||
O Indra, drink the Soma from the vessel that is the sacrificial gift (*rādhas*) belonging to the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* priest, who is connected to the *brāhmaṇa*.
Having done what? Having followed the seasons, that is, the seasonal deities (*ṛtu-devas*).
The meaning is: "Let even the seasons drink.
For since this friendship of yours is *astṛta*—that is, unobstructed and uninterrupted by name—it is therefore fitting that you drink together with the seasons.
Regarding "brāhmaṇāt":

here, by the word *brahman*, the second member of the *brahmavarga*—namely *brāhmaṇa* on the eighth [day]—is being referred to. And that [word], being masculine, has its first syllable unaccented (*anudātta*) due to the *śeṣanighāta* rule.
The word *camasa* is related to that [Brāhmaṇa];
and since it is restricted to him alone, just like his limbs, when there is a desire to express it as a limb, the rule *anudāttāderyañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.44) applies.
Therefore, in this context, the word *brāhmaṇa* ending in *camasa* is udātta on its first syllable (*jihvā*).
Rāghava says: [The suffix] *asun* is applied after all verbal roots.
Because it is marked with *ṇ*, the word is udātta on its first syllable.
"Drink!
[In this form,] there is the udātta accent on the first syllable (pā-).
There is lengthening by the rule "vyaco 'ḍatamiṅaḥ."
In the word *kartrāranu*, the *n* undergoes the substitution of *r* by the rule *dīrghādaṭi samānapāde*.
Then, by the rule *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā* (Pāṇini 8.3.2), the *u* may optionally become nasalized.
Thus: *tava*.
‘*yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso’ś*’ (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.27).
Because it is marked with *ś*, it is a substitute for the whole [case-ending].
In the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, which is the archetype (*prakṛti*), as well as in the modified forms (*vikṛti*) such as the Ukthya and others, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) praise this divine Agni.
What are the officiating priests like?
They are *vdraviṇasaḥ*, possessors of wealth; *vgrāvahamnāsaḥ*, those who hold in their hands the pressing-stones which are the means for the extraction [of soma].
What is the god like?
*Draviṇodāḥ* means the giver of wealth; or alternatively, it refers to Agni, the bestower of wealth—the sense being that he should drink the *soma*. This is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Yāska explains this mantra as follows: "Regarding *draviṇodāḥ*: why is wealth (*draviṇa*) called *draviṇa*? Because they run toward it, or because strength is *draviṇa*, since they run by means of it; the giver of that is *draviṇodāḥ*. Of him, there is this [verse]: *draviṇodā draviṇasaḥ*," and so forth.
This is the detailed etymological exposition (*nirvacana-prapañca*) stated by Yāska.
This should be understood from that very same work.
Regarding *draviṇodāḥ*:
[it is derived] by [the rule] *dru kṣibhyām iman* (Uṇādi-sūtra 2.208).
The word *draviṇa* is acutely accented on its first syllable (*nivādādyudātta*).
One who gives that [wealth] is *draviṇodāḥ*. The suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule "and *kip*."
The addition of the letter *s* to the first member of the compound is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) phenomenon. [Following this,] the substitution of *r* and then *u* occurs.
The accentuation follows the rule that the final syllable of the second member of a *kṛt*-derived compound retains its original tone (*prakṛtisvara*).
In the view that there is a single syntactic unit (ekavākyatā) with "devaviśeṣaṇatvena," the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) undergoes the substitution *svā* [for *am*].
Alternatively, they desire wealth for themselves (*draviṇam ātmana icchanti*), hence "they seek wealth" (*draviṇasyanti*).
[This is derived] by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*.

The augment *suk* is added when the suffix *kyac* follows, according to the rule: "The suffix *suk* should be stated after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*) in the sense of longing" (Pāṇini-mañjarī 7.1.51.2).

From the verbal root *draviṇasyati*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because it belongs to the *saṃpad-ādi* group; then, by the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*), the final vowel is dropped.
Because of the prohibition of its being treated as a *sthānin* (original element) by the rule "that which is elided is not like the original" (*pā. ma. 1.1.58.2*), there is the elision of the *ya*.
Thus, the word *draviṇa* signifies the desire for wealth.

In the sense that it "destroys" (*dasyati*) the desire for wealth—that is, it exhausts it by the granting of fuel and riches—from the root *dasu* meaning "to destroy," with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule "and *kip*" (*kip ca*).
Thus, the word *draviṇodaḥ* ends in the letter *s*.
Accordingly, the usage of the Nirukta, "The proclamations [beginning with] *draviṇodas* occur" (Nirukta 8.2), is justified.

Therefore, when occurring in a separate sentence (*bhinnavākyatva*), the word *draviṇodaḥ* is in the nominative case in its own sense; however, when occurring in a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), it takes the meaning of the accusative by way of grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).

In the case of *draviṇasaḥ* as well, according to the view that there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the meaning is "of the Soma [called] *draviṇas*"; here, the addition of the letter *s* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Its initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*), however, remains established by rule.
But according to the view that there is a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) because it has attained the designation of a priest (*ṛtvij*), it is derived from a *kyac*-stem with the suffix *kvip*.
Therefore, elision and so forth are as before.

However, in this view, since the suffix *kyac* is treated as having the *cit* designation, it would normally be oxytone; by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*), it is instead ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable).
Those whose hands are joined with pressing-stones are called *grāvahastāsaḥ*.

By the rule *ājaserasuk*, the word *grāvan* is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) because it belongs to the *vṛṣan*-class. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratvam*) prevails.
In the word *adhvare*: that in which *dhvara*—meaning violence (*hiṃsā*)—is not found.
By the rule *nanmumyām*, there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of the second member of the compound.
He praises (*īḍate*).
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because the root is marked with the *anudātta* accent. By the rule "after roots beginning with *ad-*, etc.," there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
The substitute for this [root] is *adā*.
May Draviṇodas grant us those riches which are renowned among the gods; those we seek to win.
May the giver of wealth grant us riches which are renowned among the gods; those we seek to win. 8.
May the god Draviṇodas grant us riches and treasures—those treasures which are renowned for their excellence in the sacrificial offering.
All those riches we claim for ourselves among the gods as our cause;
that is to say, we appropriate them in order to worship the gods with wealth.
The giver of wealth. Explained. Riches.

The suffix *up* is applied by the rule "śṛ-snu-s-nāhi" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.10). Because the term "nit" is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), it is acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). [Thus:
*śṛṇivare*.
The root *śru* is used in the sense of "hearing.
Since the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ* ("in Vedic [usage], the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [tenses may be used for all times]") is in force, the *liṭ* suffix is applied.
Then, by *jha irec* (Pāṇini 3.4.81), the *jha* portion of the *liṭ* is replaced by *irec*.

In accordance with the rule *chandasyubhayathā* ("in Vedic usage, [the suffixes] are optionally [treated as both ārdhadhātuka and sārvadhātuka]"), because it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, there is the substitution of *śru* by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*), and through its connection with that, the absence of the augment *śap*.
When the substitution of *uvaṅ* would otherwise apply, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs by the rule *hubhuvoḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.87).
By the marker *cit*, the word is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
The prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies by the rule "yadvṛttānnityam. [In the word] *tā*, the elision of the *śe*-suffix occurs by the rule "śe-chandasi bahulam."
The elision of the *n* is according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 8.2.7, *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*.
[Thus we have] *vanāmahe*.
The root *vana* (with *paṇ*) means "to share" or "to enjoy."
The middle voice is used here by way of substitution.
The giver of wealth desires to drink; offer the oblation and step forward!
Let it be sought from the office of the Neṣṭṛ priest by the officiating priests.
O giver of wealth! He desires to drink; offer the oblation! Step forward! Let it be sent forth from the office of the Neṣṭṛ by the priests. ||9||
The god Draviṇodas, together with the seasons, desires to drink the *sobha* from the vessel belonging to the Neṣṭṛ priest;
therefore, O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), go to the place of sacrifice where it is desired,
and having gone, offer the oblation.
Having offered the oblation, establish yourselves and also proceed from the place of sacrifice to another location.
The giver of wealth.
Explained.
He desires to drink.
The root *pā* means "to drink. [The form] *pipāsati* is derived by adding the desiderative suffix (*san*) to express "he wishes to drink";
the long vowel *ī* is a Vedic (archaic) feature.
"tiṅḍatiṅaḥ" is a prohibition [of the designation *nighāta*].
"juhota": this is the second person plural of the imperative (*loṭ*).
Because there is no *laṅ* suffix for that [verb], there is the substitution of *ta*. For that, by the rule "of that, *tasa*, *nasa*, *natha*, and *na*," there is the substitution of *tab*.
For that, by the rule "after *pi*, *ru*, etc., there is *uṇ*," there is the suffix *uṇ*.

With the phrase "the first of those that have been repeated" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*) continuing [from the previous rule], when the acute accent on the initial syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) would otherwise apply by Pāṇini 6.1.190 (*anudātte ca*), the vowel *o* becomes acute by Pāṇini 6.1.192 (*bhīhībhṛhumadajanadhanadaridrājāgarāṃ pratyayātpūrve piti*).
[The form is] *tiṣṭhata*.
[The root] *sthā* [is used] in the sense of stopping motion (*gatinivṛtti*).
Because there is no *laṅ* for that [root] which has the middle plural ending *-loṇ*, there is the substitution of *t*.
Following the rule *pā-ghrā-dhmā-* etc., there is the substitution of *tiṣṭha*.

The Ātmanepada [ending] does not apply by the rule *sam-ava-pra-vibhyaḥ sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.22); for in that rule, the term *nirdiṣṭa* (as specified), which is carried over [from the previous sūtra], is intended to mean immediate proximity (*ānantarya*), and here there is an intervention by the word *ca*.

In the case of *te prāghnātaḥ*, although the word *pra* is prescribed to be used before [the verb] by the rule *upasargeṇa* (Pāṇini 1.4.80), its usage as separated [from the verb] is permitted in Vedic by the rule *vyavahitāśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.82). Here, the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the preceding [verb] *juhota*, but not with the subsequent *ipyate*. Consequently, because there is no application of the prohibition stated in *aprathamavān cavāyoge prathamā* (Pāṇini 8.1.59), the elision (*nivāta*) applies according to *tiṅḍatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28).
"O Neṣṭar, O Potar, purify the sacrifice" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.15.2). What has been stated regarding the word *potrā* in this passage should be understood here as well.
*Ipyana*.
The root *i* means "to go";
this is the third person plural middle voice form of the present indicative.
And that fourth [portion] which we worship with the seasons, O Giver of Wealth—
be thou a granter of half to us.
Since we worship you, the giver of wealth, with the fourth season according to the cosmic rhythms, therefore, O Giver, become a bestower of riches upon us. 10.
O God, Draviṇodas, because we worship you together with the seasonal offerings (ṛtubhiḥ), for that reason—
*adha* being a particle meaning "therefore"— be a giver (*dadiḥ*) of wealth to us; indeed, you must certainly become so.
The fourth is that which completes the four.
*Turīyam*: [The suffix] *cha* is applied according to *Pāṇini Sūtra* 5.2.51.1 (*caturaśchayatāv ādyakṣaralopaś ca*), which prescribes the elision of the first syllable.
Before the acute accent (*udātta*) of that suffix, the substitution of *īya* is applied by *Pāṇini Sūtra* 7.1.2 (*āyaneyī...*).

According to the rule *āyanādīnām upadeśivacanaṃ svarasiddhyartham* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.2.1), once the substitution has been made, the vowel *i* becomes acute (*udātta*) by virtue of the accent of the suffix. Thus, *draviṇodaḥ*.
This has been explained.
In *pādādi* (the beginning of a verse-quarter) and so forth, there is the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative.
In *yajāmahe*,
because the suffix *śap* is marked with *p*, and because the *tiṅ* suffixes have the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*, the accent remains on the root alone.
Because the preceding vocative is non-existent, or because of its connection with *yad-vṛtta*, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent).
It has been stated that this prohibition applies even when there is a separation [by other words].
*Adha*.
The letter *dh* is Vedic;
[the particle] *sma*; [the group beginning with] *ca* is unaccented (*anudātta*).
In the *saṃhitā* [text], there is a long vowel according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.3.136, *nipātasya ca*. [Thus] *dadiḥ*.
[The root] *ḍudāñ* means "to give."
The suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *ātaśca upasarge* (Pāṇini 3.2.171), which prescribes the suffixes *kikin* and *liṅ*.
Because it is of the *liṅ* class, reduplication and other such operations apply.
Then, the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64).
The accent of the conditional suffix.
O Aśvins, you who possess long reins and pure ordinances, who bring the sacrifice at the proper seasons, drink the honeyed mead.
O Aśvins, drink the honey; you of long-reaching power, of pure vows, the bearers of the sacrifice through the seasons. 11.
O Aśvins, drink the *madhu*—the Soma that has been made sweet. Of what nature are you? [The following describes them:]... [End of fragment]

Possessing radiant splendor, they are engaged with the shining Āhavanīya and other fires; pure in their rites (śucitratā), they are accompanied by Ṛtu, the deity of the season; and as bearers of the sacrifice (yajñavāhasā), they are the executors of the sacrifice.
"Aśvinā": the form *ākāra* (ā) is substituted for the dual vocative ending by the rule "supāṃ suluk... [Pāṇini 7.1.39];
it is accented on the first syllable as an *āmantrita* (vocative).
In *pibatam*, the root accent is preserved because the suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*);
furthermore, by the rule regarding the accent of *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root itself remains.
The suffix *u* is applied by the rule "madhu-phala-pāṭi" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.18).
Because the word "jin" is understood as a governing term [from a previous rule], it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) due to its being a *nivādi*.

*Dīyabhī*: [derived from] the root *div* in the sense of "playing" (*krīḍā*) and so forth; the suffix *vic* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.75: "It is seen [that the suffix *vic* is applied] after other roots as well."
Because the elision of a *val* (consonant) is stronger than the elision of an affix (*veṣṭalopāt valilopo balīyān*), there is the elision of the first *v* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.66–67).

For if the affix were elided first, the elision of the *val* would not occur due to the prohibition: "In a rule dependent on a phoneme (*varṇāśrayavidhi*), there is no application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle" (Paribhāṣā 21).
The dual number is Vedic (*chāndasam*).

Due to the rule beginning with *tujādi* (Pāṇini 7.1.102), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Alternatively, because of the *yaṅ-luk* formation, by the maxim "a rule not preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not mandatory" (Paribhāṣā 93), there is an absence of *guṇa* in the reduplicated syllable. Thus, from the root *dī*, one obtains *dīdī-* before the suffixes *abhi* and *yat*, resulting in *dīdy-abhi*.
The initial syllable of "āmantrita" (vocative) has the udātta accent;
because it occurs at the beginning of a pāda, there is no nighāta (anudātta).
[The word is] *śucitratā*.
Those two whose vows are pure; the form *tau* is derived from the dual ending *bhyām* by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

Since the word *dīdyadbhyām* is a general term (not a proper name), the prohibition regarding the treatment as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) by the rule *nāmantritam* applies, and thus it retains its eighth-case (anudātta) accentuation.
Because the preceding [element] functions as a subordinate part (*parāṅgavat*), there is monotony (*aikasvarya*).
[The word is] *yajñavāhasā*. [The root] *vah* [is used] in the sense of "carrying" (*prāpaṇe*).
"Yajñavāhasau" means "the two who carry the sacrifice.
The suffix *asun* is applied according to the rule "vahi-śādhy-abhya-chandasi" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.660).
For it is stated there that by the rule "gatikārakayor api pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvaṃ ca" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.666), [the suffix] occurs even when accompanied by an upapada.
Due to the recurrence of the term "giṇ," there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk" and so forth, the case ending is replaced by the vowel "ā.
There is the suppression of accent (nighāta) for the vocative.
Due to the lack of capacity in the preceding element, it does not undergo the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) of the subsequent one.
