Regarding the second [day], it is prescribed in the section beginning with "agnim vo devam" in the *Sūtra*: "The two triplets 'mahī dyauḥ pṛthivī ca naḥ' and 'yuvānā pitarā punaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.10).

The youthful parents again, with true mantras, acting uprightly—the Ṛbhus performed their work. 4. The youthful parents again, possessing true mantras, acting with rectitude—the Ṛbhus performed their tasks. 4.
The Ṛbhus, the gods of that name, made their own parents—their mother and father—though they were previously old, young again; that is, they made them youthful.
Of what nature were they?
They were possessed of the power of unfailing mantras (*satyamantra*).

Because the mantras have been perfected through the performance of *puraścaraṇa* and other rites, whatever fruit is aimed for when the mantras are employed, that very fruit is accomplished exactly so.
Therefore, the meaning is that they are capable of restoring youth to their aged parents.
*Ṛjūyavaḥ*: desiring straightness for themselves; that is, being free from deceit.

For this very reason, the mantras performed by these [practitioners] succeed. By means of the *vidyā* called *vyāptivatī*, "possessing pervasion"— wherein "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) refers here to the unimpeded power of their mantra in all ritual activities.

Yāska explains the word *ṛbhu* in this way: "The *ṛbhavaḥ* are so called because they shine widely (*uru bhānti*), or because they shine by means of their activity (*vartena bhānti*), or because they come into being by means of their activity (*vartena bhavanti*)" (Nirukta 11.15).

*Yuvānā*: The word *yuvan* ends in the suffix *kanin* derived from the root *yu*, and is accented on the first syllable according to the rule beginning with *niśca*. The vowel *ā* replaces the case-ending by the rule beginning with *supāṃ suluk*.
The two *pitarā* mantras; their form is as before;
they are mantras of truth.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member prevails.
The word *ṛju* here refers to the state [of being straight];
they desire straightness for themselves.
The vowel lengthening occurs by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25).
The suffix *u* is added by the rule *kyācchandasi* (Pāṇini 3.2.170).
The accent is that of the suffix (pratyayasvara).
[The root is] *viṣṭī*,
from the root *viṣ* meaning "pervasion" (*vyāptau*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvinkau ca saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.174). The augment *iṭ* is prohibited by the rule *tinutra* etc.
(Pāṇini 7.2.9). From that [base], the substitution of *ī* for the *jas* ending occurs by the rule *iyādiyājīkārāṇām upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
And that [substitution] occurs for the *sakāra* by the rule "alo 'ntyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52).
Then, when the *guṇa* is applied by "ād guṇaḥ," the long vowel of the same class as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is applied by "prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.102).
If it is argued that this should be set aside and the *guṇa* of the short vowel should take effect instead by "jami ca" (Pāṇini 7.3.109) because it is a subsequent rule, we say no.
Because a grammatical operation preceded by a specific technical designation (saṃjñā) is not invariably obligatory; thus,
*akṛta* [is formed] from the root *kṛ* with the suffix *luṅ*.
This is the ātmanepada [ending]. There is the substitution of *ad* for *jha*.
Furthermore, by the rule "mantre ghasaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.80) and others, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix.
The substitution of *yaṇ* [for *i*];
the augment *aṭ*;
and the *nighāta* accent.
May your exhilarations come together with Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and with the Ādityas, the kings. || 5 ||

Those exhilarating Soma juices belonging to you, O Ṛbhus—which cause intoxication—have come together with Indra and with the Ādityas; they have met. The drinking of Soma by the Ṛbhus along with Indra and the Ādityas takes place at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).

For this very reason, the *āvāhana-nigada* (invocation formula) has been recited by Āśvalāyana as follows: "Bring hither Indra, accompanied by the Ādityas, full of sweetness, possessed of power, possessed of vigor, accompanied by Bṛhaspati, and accompanied by all the gods" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.3).

By what kind of Indra? By one "accompanied by the Maruts" (*marutvatā*), that is, joined with the Maruts. For this very reason, another mantra is thus recorded in the tradition: "O Indra, let there be friendship between you and the Maruts" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 8.96.7).
By what kind of Ādityas?
By kings who were blazing.
*Madāḥ*:
"Those by which they become intoxicated" are the *soma* juices;
[the suffix] *ap* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.67: *mado 'nupasarge*.
Because it is a *pit* [suffix], it is unaccented (*anudātta*);
thus, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) alone remains.
By the rule "ājaserasuk," the augment *asuk* is added to the suffix *jas*.
*Agmata*:
from the root *gam* with the prefix *sam*, in the *luṅ* tense; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule "samo gamyucchi... (Pāṇini 1.3.29), etc.
The substitution of *ad* for *jha* occurs; the suffix *cli* is elided by the rule "mantre ghasa... (Pāṇini 2.4.80);
and the penultimate vowel is elided by the rule "gamahana... (Pāṇini 6.4.98).

The term "and even when separated" (*vyavahitāśca*) indicates that the *sam-* [prefix] may be used with an intervening word; this is a case of *nighāta* (elision of accent). [The example is] *marutvatā*.

The term *marutvān* means "one who possesses Maruts. According to Pāṇini’s rule *tasau matvarthe* (1.4.19), the designation *bha* supersedes the designation *pada*; consequently, there is no application of the *jaś*-rule (i.e., the change of *t* to *d*). Furthermore, by the rule *jhayaḥ* (8.2.10), the *m* of the suffix *matup* is changed to *v*.

In *ādityaiḥ*, by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.10), there is no substitution of *ais* for the case-ending *bhis*; instead, by the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet*, the substitution of *e* occurs. Thus:
*rājabhiḥ*.
Because the word *rājan* ends in the suffix *kanin*, it has the udātta accent on its initial syllable according to the rule *nivādādyudāttaḥ*.

And that new cup of Tvaṣṭṛ, the god, which was fashioned—out of it, they made four again from the *arka*. 6. And that new cup of Tvaṣṭṛ, the god, which was fashioned—out of it, they made four again from the *arka*. 6.

Moreover, Tvaṣṭṛ—the deity of that name—performed the act of carving; he fashioned "navam," meaning new, "tyam," that very "camasam," a specific wooden vessel capable of holding Soma, "niṣkṛtam," meaning he brought it to completion with perfect finish—this is the sense.

The Ṛbhus, who were the disciples of Tvaṣṭṛ, skilled in the art of carving, further made that single cup which had been constructed by him "caturaḥ," meaning they fashioned it into four for our sake (using the dative case).
This meaning, consisting of the fourfold making of one, is also clearly evident in another mantra: "Make the single chalice into four" (Ṛgveda Maṇḍala 1, Sūkta 161, Verse 2).
"New" (*nava*): from the root *ṇu*, meaning "to praise. It is called "new" because it is praised (*nūyate*).
The suffix *apratyaya* occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*). For it is everywhere found in grammatical treatises as an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ghañ*.

And the suffix *ghañ* occurs everywhere in the sense of any *kāraka* other than the agent (*kartṛ*), according to the rule "in the sense of a *kāraka* other than the agent, when it is a name" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.3.19).

Although it was stated there that this applies "in the case of a technical term" (*saṃjñā*), nevertheless, because the particle *ca* serves the purpose of avoiding the restriction to technical terms, it certainly occurs even when not a technical term.
That which is connected is a "connection" (*saṃbandha*). It has been stated that the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
*Tvaṣṭṛ*:
[derived from] the root *takṣū* or *tvakṣū* in the sense of "making thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*),
with the suffix *tṛn* according to the *Uṇādi* rules.
Due to the rule *uditot* (Pāṇini 7.2.44), there is the absence of the augment *iṭ*.
By the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), the letter *k* is elided. Thus, *niṣkṛtam*.

The suffix *kta* is applied after the root *kṛ* when it is not preceded by a prefix (*nirupasarga*), in the sense of the object (*karmani*). Regarding the change to the letter *ṣ*, the rule "in a *prādi*-compound, the substitution is optional when [the suffix] does not stand at the end of a subsequent member" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 6.3.34) applies. Here, although the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would have been required by the rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.65), it is prohibited by the rule "not with *loka*, indeclinables, etc. (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.69). Nevertheless, because the agent is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*), the genitive is applied as a residual case (*śaiṣikī ṣaṣṭhī*) rather than by the rule "the third case for the agent and the instrument" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.18).
Just as when the object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed as a residual factor (*śeṣatvena*), [the suffix] *māp* is applied; for example: 1. *māyate* (he measures);
2. *somādhāralakṣaṇam* (characterized by the support of Soma).

6. *ga-cha-jha-ṇa-ra-tasya tvaṣṭuḥ*. Thus: by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the suffix *ni* is udātta. *akṛte akṛpata*: from the root *kṛ*, in the *luṅ* tense, there is the substitution of *t* for *jha* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). By the rule *mantra ghasa* etc., there is the elision (*luk*) of *cl*. Because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the *tiṅ* suffix is treated as *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, due to the absence of the *ṅit* designation, *guṇa* occurs. *caturaḥ*: by the rule *caturaḥ śasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.167), the vowel *u* is udātta. *punaḥ*: this is listed among the *svarādi* group as being udātta on its first syllable.
In the third *chandoma*, during the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra*, there are two *ṛc*s to be inserted (*āmantraṇa*) beginning with "te no ratnāni dhattana.

This is prescribed in the section [of the *Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra*] beginning with "tṛtīyasyāganma maha" as follows: "indra iṣe dadātu naḥ... te no ratnāni dhattana—this one [verse] and two [others]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.11).

Bestow upon us treasures—threefold sets of seven—for the one who presses the soma, each one by one, through our excellent praises. 7. You; for us; treasures; bestow; threefold; indeed; sets of seven; for the presser; one by one; with beautiful hymns. 7.

O *Ṛbhus*, who were previously established among the *pūrvās* (the eastern quarters), being joined with our excellent praises (*suśastibhiḥ*), grant—each one by one in succession—to us, our kin, and to the sacrificer who presses the *soma*, delightful treasures (*ratnāni*) such as gold, gems, pearls, and other riches.
The phrase "each one" (*ekamekam*) is used with the intention of expressing that for each individual substance among the gold and so forth, as much as is required, [should be given].
Of what nature are these treasures?
"Tris" means three times repeated;

thus, there is a triple repetition of the jewels as "superior," "middling," and "inferior. Furthermore, "sāptāni" refers to those consisting of groups numbering seven; perform and accomplish these ritual acts.
What are the seven?
They are repeated three times, i.e., threefold.
One group consists of the seven havis-sacrifices, beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) and the new- and full-moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa).

The second group consists of the seven *pākayajñas*, beginning with the *aupāsanahoma* and the *vaiśvadeva*. The third group consists of the seven *somasaṃsthās*, beginning with the *agniṣṭoma* and the *iṣṭoma*.
*ratnāni*.

[The root] *ram* is used in the sense of "sporting. With the word *nit* being understood from the previous rule, the suffix *nap* is applied by the rule *ramesta ca* (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.294); by virtue of that [suffix], the letter *m* is replaced by *t*.
The root *nisvad* is udātta.
[In the imperative] *dhattana*, [the form] is *dhatta*;
by the rule "tasanasanathanāśca," the suffix *ta* is replaced by *tan*.

The group of seven is called *sāptam*. The suffix *an* is applied to form the word for a "group" according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.1.61, *sasanoraj chandasi*; furthermore, the elision of the final vowel (*ṭi-lopa*) occurs according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.4.144, *nastaddhite*.
By virtue of the rule *jittvādādivṛddhiḥ*, there is initial *vṛddhi* and the accentuation of the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*).

Here, by this term "class" (*varga*), the members of the class (*vargin*) are indicated; therefore, the plural number is used. Otherwise, since only a single member of the class would be repeated, the singular number alone would have been appropriate.
For the one who presses [the soma],
[the word] "śataranumaḥ" has an udātta accent on the case ending. One by one.
In the rule *‘niṣṭhāvīpsayoḥ’*, the word is doubled due to distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
The first occurrence of the word *eka* ends in the suffix *kan* derived from the root *iṇ*; being a *niṣṭhā* [term], it is udātta on its initial syllable.

Regarding the second occurrence of the word *eka*, since it receives the designation of *āmreḍita* by the rule *‘tasya paramābhreḍitam’*, it becomes anudātta according to the rule *‘anudāttaṃ ca’* (Pāṇini 8.1.3).
By means of excellent recitations (*suśastibhiḥ*). They are called *śastayaḥ* because they are recited (*śasyante*) by these; that is, the *ṛc*s.
The root *śaṃs* means "to praise.
The suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). Because this suffix is marked with *k*, there is elision [of the *n*].

In the *prādi* compound *śobhanāḥ śastayaḥ*, although by the rule that a word ending in *ktin* is *ādyudātta* (the acute accent falls on the first syllable), and by the rule that a *kṛt*-formed compound retains the original accent of its final member (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*), that same [initial accent] would have been obtained; however, it is superseded by the subsequent rule *man-ktin-yāpye-ṇya-anīyaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.151), which prescribes that the final syllable of the final member is *udātta*.

The bearers [of the sacrifice] have maintained [the rite]; they have anointed themselves with skillful action, [securing] a portion worthy of sacrifice among the gods. 8. They have maintained; the bearers; they have anointed themselves; with skillful action; the portion; among the gods; worthy of sacrifice. 8.

The *Ṛbhus*, who are the bearers of the sacrifice by means of accomplishing the ladles (*camasa*) and other implements, maintained their vital breaths; although they were previously subject to death as human beings, they sustained their lives through the attainment of immortality.
And thus another mantra declares: "Being mortals... [and so forth].
"Having attained immortality" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.110.4).

Furthermore, through their "good deed"—that is, by means of the excellent activity consisting in the procurement of materials for the sacrifice—they stood among the gods and partook of, that is, consumed, the sacrificial portion worthy of sacrifice, characterized as the oblation (havis).
This meaning is made clear in another mantra, such as: "Possessing the means [of sacrifice], they attained the sacrificial portion" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.60.1).
In the Brāhmaṇa as well, the narrative beginning with "The Ṛbhus indeed won the Soma-drink among the gods through austerity" (Ai. Brā. 3.30) is quite explicit.
The word *vahyaḥ* [is derived as follows]: with the word *nit* continuing [from the previous rule], the suffix *nip* is applied by the rule "vahiśca" and so forth. [The form] *abhajanta*.
There is no *nighāta* because it begins with a *pādādi* word.
In the term *sukṛtayā*, the suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *kṛ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.120: *vibhāṣā kṛvapoḥ*.
That act of worship whose performance is beautiful is "well-performed" (*sukṛtā*).

In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) is set aside by the rule *nañ-subhyām*, which prescribes that the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is acute.

Now, one might object: since the suffix *kyap* in the word *kṛtya* is marked with the *pi*-diacritic, it is unaccented; therefore, by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), the initial syllable should be acute.
Consequently, by the rule *ādyudāttaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.2.119), the word must be udātta on its first syllable.
For it has been stated that, by this preceding exception (*purastādapavāda*), even the final-udātta accent of the subsequent member prescribed by *nañsubhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172) is superseded.
If that is so, then the word *kṛtyā* is formed with the suffix *kyap* in the feminine sense of abstract action (bhāva) according to the rule *kṛñaḥ śa ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.100).
Although *kyapa* is prescribed after a root ending in *pī*, it takes the acute accent (*ādattatva*) by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
In a *prādi*-compound, that same accent remains by virtue of the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative (*kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*).
[The word is] *bhāgam*.
The word *karpāsa-vanaḥ* is oxytone according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.159.
Regarding *yajñiyam*:
in the sense of "fit for sacrifice" (*yajñamarhati*), the suffix *gha* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.71, which prescribes *vakhaj* after the words *yajña* and *stṛ*.
Its accentuation is that of the horse-instruction;
it has the accent of the suffix.

The fourth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "ihendrāgnī," has its seer and meter as previously stated. Its deity, however, is specified as follows: "In this [hymn], Indra and Agni are the deities."
As for the application (*viniyoga*): in the *acchāvāka-śastra* of the *agniṣṭoma*, the hymn "O Indra and Agni, I call you hither" (*ihendrāgnī upa haye*) is used.

This is because it is prescribed in the section beginning with "The stotra [is] before the śastra, O Agni" (*stotramagne śastrāt*) as follows: "In the *acchāvāka-śastra*, 'O Indra and Agni, I have come to you with this thought' (*ihendrāgnī upeyaṃ vāmasya manmanaḥ*), nine [verses]" (*āśvalāyana-śrautasūtra* 5.10).
Likewise, during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) of the six-day period (*abhiplava-ṣaḍaha*), this same hymn is used in the *acchāvāka-śastra* for the purpose of reciting the *stomātiśaṃsana*.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra, beginning with "The Abhiplava, Pṛṣṭha, and Grāha [chapters]," followed by: "O Indra and Agni, O Indra and Agni, come hither" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).
Hither, O Indra and Agni, I call you; we desire this hymn of praise for you two, you who are the foremost drinkers of Soma.
Here, O Indra and Agni, we approach; indeed, we desire their hymn of praise. They two, the greatest drinkers of Soma, [desire] the Soma. 1.
"In this rite, I invoke the two gods Indra and Agni; we desire—that is, we long for—the hymn of praise belonging to these very two, Indra and Agni.
May those two gods, who are most capable of drinking Soma, drink the Soma. (This is the completion of the sense.)
*Indrāgnī*.
Even here, although it is a *devatā-dvandva* (a copulative compound of deities), the substitution of *ānaṅ* for the final vowel of the first member does not occur.

For, while the term *dvandve* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*) from the previous sūtra, the explicit mention of *dvandva* again in this sūtra (Pāṇini 6.3.26) indicates that *ānaṅ* applies only in a *dvandva* consisting of those [deities] who are well-known in common usage to be associated together (*āhacarya*).
Therefore, in this *avagraha*, the word *indra* is short;
by the rule "of a compound" (*samāsasya*), it has the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*).
However, the rule "also in a dual divinity compound" (*devatādvandve ca*) does not apply to provide the original accent for both members of the compound.
Because of the prohibition [contained in] Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.142, "not when the second member begins with an anudātta vowel," due to the fact that the word *agni* has an anudātta as its first vowel.
*Uśmasi*:
[from the root] *vaś* "to desire."

The suffix *mas* [is substituted] for the *laṭ* [present tense marker]. By the rule "the *i* in *masi* is elided" (Pāṇini 7.1.46), the vowel *i* is dropped. Due to the root belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* [suffix].

In *maserdvisvān*, there is a vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule beginning with "agrahajyā-". The forms *tā* and *somapātāmā* both have the vowel *ā* substituted [for the case-ending] by the rule "supāṃ suluk-".
Praise those two, Indra and Agni, at the sacrifices, O radiant men;
sing of them in *gāyatra* hymns.
Praise them at the sacrifices, O men: Indra and Agni, the radiant ones! Sing of them in *gāyatrī* verses. ||2||
Those men—the officiating priests—should praise those two previously mentioned, Indra and Agni, during the sacrifices through the performance of rituals with words;
likewise, they should adorn them with various kinds of ornaments so that they appear radiant;
and furthermore, they should sing praises to those two previously mentioned, Indra and Agni, in the form of Sāmans within the Gāyatra mantras, which are composed in the Gāyatrī meter.
In that case, by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the vowel *ā* [is substituted]; thus, *śubhratā*.
In this Saṃhitā, the vowel lengthening occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.3.137: "It is also seen in other cases."
We invoke Mitra for his praises, and Indra and Agni,
the Soma-drinkers, for the drinking of the Soma.
Those two, Indra and Agni, the drinkers of Soma, we invoke for the praise of Mitra and for the drinking of Soma. 3.
The ellipsis is: "May those two aforementioned gods become [present] for the glorification of me, a friend, who am the object of affection and the performer [of the rite].
Or alternatively:
"We desire to praise those two, Indra and Agni, who are related to me, a friend"; this is the ellipsis.
O Soma and Agni,
by that truth, be watchful at this forward-facing station;
O Indra and Agni, grant us protection.
By that truth, O Indra and Agni, watch over us with foreknowledge; grant us protection at every step. 6.

O Indra and Agni, by that truth which consists in the unfailing bestowal of fruits, through this rite performed by us, remain wide awake with great vigilance in the place—the world of heaven and so forth—which clearly indicates the enjoyment of the fruit.
Then, grant us *śarma*—meaning happiness or a home;
for among the twenty-two names for "home" beginning with *gayaḥ kṛdaraḥ*, we find *śarma varma* (Nirukta 3.4.21).

Those two who possess excellent chariots, who are the best of charioteers, the two gods who touch the heavens—those Aśvins we invoke. 2. Those who possess excellent chariots, who are the best of charioteers, both gods who touch the heavens—those Aśvins we invoke. 2.

Those two Aśvins, both gods, those two Aśvins who are possessed of beautiful chariots, the best of chariot-warriors among all charioteers, who touch the heavens and dwell in the celestial realm—those two we invoke; we call them hither.

In the words beginning with *yā* and ending with *apsu*, the vowel *ā* is the substitute for the dual case-ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *Surathā*: those two who possess a beautiful chariot (*suratha*) are called *surathau*.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the rule *anañsubhyām*—which prescribes that the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta, thereby setting aside both the general rule for the udātta of the final syllable of a compound and the specific rule for the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member—is superseded by the rule *ādyudāttaṃ chandasi*, which prescribes that the first syllable of the second member is udātta in the Vedic language. Thus, in *rathītama*, the first syllable of the second member becomes udātta.
Furthermore, according to Pāṇini’s rule *anyenām api dṛśyate* (6.3.137), the vowel *i* is lengthened to *ī* in the *saṃhitā* (continuous text).

*Madhumatī*: Among the one hundred and one names for water listed in [Nighaṇṭu] such as "arṇaḥ" and "kṣodaḥ," the term "madhu" is read as a synonym for "purīṣa" (Ni. 1.12.11).
Therefore, it means "possessing water."
The meaning is that this whip becomes moistened by the sweat-water that flows from the horse due to its swift gait.
*Sūnṛtāvatī* means endowed with pleasant and truthful speech.

Both the sound produced by the striking of the sharp whip and the cry uttered by the horse while shedding tears at the time of being struck are dear to the sacrificer, as they serve as the cause for swift movement.
Alternatively,
among the fifty-seven names of speech beginning with "śloka" and "dhārā," the term "kaśā" is listed as "adhiṣaṇā" (Nirukta 1.11.43).
This refers to the honeyed speech (*madhumatī*) of the Aśvins— one endowed with sweetness, free from harshness, and full of pleasant truths— meaning it is concerned with the bestowing of rewards.
It should be construed as: "With that speech, [the two] joined together the sacrifice."
*Kaśā*:

[The suffix] *pacādyac* [is applied].

[The word] *sūnṛtāvatī*. [The root] *ūna* [is used] in the sense of "diminution."

That speech in which such *ṛtam* (righteousness) or truth (*satyam*) exists is *sūnṛtā*.

She who possesses that [rope] is "Kaśā"; thus, "sūnṛtāvatī" is a name for the rope (kaśā).

At that time, during a certain sacrifice, the Adhvaryu priests offered a portion of the sacrificial cake called the *prāśitra* to Savitṛ, the Brahman priest. While being held in his hand, that *prāśitra* cut off his hand.
Thereupon, the Adhvaryu priests who had given the *prāśitra* fashioned a golden hand for him and restored it.

This matter is concluded in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa: "While he was handing over the *prāśitra* portion to Savitṛ, his hand was severed; they gave him two golden ones in its place; therefore he is praised as Hiraṇyapāṇi (the Golden-handed).

Regarding the words *hiraṇya* and *pāṇi*, Yāska explains them thus: "'Hiraṇya': from what [root]? It is so called because it is being drawn out (*āyamyamāna*), or because it is taken from person to person (*hiyate janājjanam*), or because it is most delightful (*hitaramaṇa*), or because it is delightful to the heart (*hṛdayaramaṇa*), or it may be derived from the root *haryati*, which has the sense of desiring. (Nirukta 2.10).
Likewise, [it is said]: "The word *pāṇi* is derived from the root *paṇ*, which has the sense of honoring" (Nirukta 2.26).
The word *hiraṇya* is acute on the first syllable because it is the object of the negative particle (*nañ*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the preceding member prevails.

*Napātam*: [The root] *pā* is used in the sense of "to protect. The word *pāt* is the form of this [root] ending in the suffix *śatṛ*.

The author of the Vṛtti [on Pāṇini] maintains that in the compound with the negative particle *nañ*, there is a prohibition of the elision of the *n* by the rule "anabhrānnapāt... and so forth. [He explains:
"Agni" is that which does not protect (*na pāti*), because it dries up [things].

If it is asked: "In that case, how is the genitive in *apām* justified, given that the genitive in the sense of the object is prohibited by the rule 'na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalartha... (Pāṇini 2.3.69)?"—then let this [genitive] be characterized as a "residual" (*śeṣa*) genitive.

Fire and the sun are related to water by way of being its causes, according to the Vedic revelation: "From fire, water [arises]" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.2), and the Smṛti: "From the sun, rain is born" (Manusmṛti 3.76).
In this view, it should be understood that the absence of the *num* augment—prescribed by the rule "ugidacām"—is also due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*).

The substitution of *tuK* for the root *pāti*, which ends in the suffix *kriP*, should be understood as a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). Alternatively, it is *napāt* because he does not cause to fall (*na pātayati*);
this is derived from the root *pat* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *yaN* followed by *kvip*.
The two [words] beginning with *agni* do not bring about water, but rather dry it up;
they possess the accentuation of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable preceding member.
For the sake of protection (*avase*).

We invoke Savitṛ—the illuminator of men (*nucakṣasam*), the distributor (*vibhaktāram*) of manifold wealth (*rādhasaḥ*) consisting of gold, silver, and other forms, for the sake of providing a dwelling (*avasauḥ nivāsahetoḥ*). It is appropriate that he should grant this much wealth to this sacrificer; thus we call upon him who apportions it. The Kauṣītakins, in their Brāhmaṇa which serves as an exposition of this ṛc, declare his very nature as a distributor: "That wonderful wealth (*vasoś citraṃ rādhaḥ*) which exists, Savitṛ alone distributes it among the various creatures.
Thus, he is the distributor.
The word *nucakṣas* is oxytone because it is a bahuvrīhi compound;
that same accent remains by virtue of the rule that the final member of a compound retains its original accent (*kruduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
[We] invoke (*havāmahe*).

Because it is a *dhātu* (verbal root) [ending in] *anartha* (meaningless), there is no substitution of *ray* for *ya*.
The accentuation follows the rule for a compound where the final member is *krud* (an angry person).

In the sense of "speaking," the suffix *iṇ* is applied according to the rule "samāne rayaścodāttaḥ" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.576); by virtue of its connection with that suffix, it is marked with *ḍit*, and there is the elision of *ya*.
Because it is marked as *ḍit*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.

And there is the substitution of *ā* [for *i*]. In *ni ṣīdata*, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.66: *sadiraprateḥ*.

In the Agniṣṭoma, at the morning pressing, "O Agni, bring the wives here" (*agne patnīrihā vaha*) is the standing *yājyā* of the Neṣṭṛ.

The wives— the word *pati* ending in *ṅī* (i.e.,

*patnī*)— the goddesses (*devī*), the divine ones (*devyaḥ*), the wives of the gods (*devapatnyaḥ*), with protection (*avasā*) and with great (*mahaḥ*) shelter (*śarmaṇā*) and happiness (*sukhena*), may they attend (*abhi sacantām*) to us (*naḥ*), that is, may they serve us with favor.
What kind of goddesses are they? They are "wives of kings," meaning protectors of men; they are "with unsevered wings," meaning with unclipped feathers.
For indeed, the wings of the wives of the gods who are in the form of birds are not severed by anyone.

The word *devī* ends in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 4.1.48 (*puṃyogādākhyāyām*). By the accentuation rule for suffixes (*pratyayasvara*), it is udātta on the final syllable.

*Acchinnapatrāḥ*:
"not cut" means *na chinnāni* (not cut). There is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) which forms the first member of the compound.

Those whose leaves are uncut—[in this bahuvrīhi compound, the first member retains its original accent]—I invoke here Indra’s consort for well-being, and Varuṇa’s consort, the foremost, for the drinking of Soma. 12. Here: Indra’s consort; I invoke; Varuṇa’s consort; for well-being; the foremost; for the drinking of Soma. 12.
In this rite, for our well-being— that is, for our preservation— and for the drinking of Soma, I invoke the wives of Indra, Varuṇa, and Agni:
Indrāṇī, Agnāyī, and Varuṇāṇī.

By the rule *indravaruṇa* etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.49), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the augment *ānuk* are applied in the sense of connection with a masculine [referent]. The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [Thus:
*agnāyīm*.

By the rule *vṛṣākapyagnisitasitakusidānām udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.37), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied; through its connection, the vowel *i* becomes the udātta diphthong *ai*. [The word] *somapītaye* has been explained previously more than once.

In the second *chandoma*, within the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra*, the triplet beginning with "Great are heaven and earth for us" (*mahī dyauḥ pṛthivī ca naḥ*) is the insertion-verse (*nividdhānīya*) for Heaven and Earth. This is prescribed in the section beginning with "The second [is] 'O Agni'" (*dvitīyasyāgni vaḥ*) in the Sūtra: "Great are heaven and earth for us; you two, the youthful parents again" (*mahī dyauḥ pṛthivī ca no yuvānā pitarā punaḥ*; Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.10). In the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, this same verse "Great are heaven... is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the single-pot-sherd offering to Heaven and Earth.
In the section [dealing with] the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice for rice and *śyāmāka* millet, it is sūtra-ed: “*ye ke ca umā mahino ahimāyā mahī dyauḥ pṛthivī ca naḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.9).
This same verse is also employed in the fire-churning (*agnimanyana*).
In the section [dealing with] the morning *vaiśvadeva* offering, it is sūtra-ed: “*abhi tvā deva savitarmahī dyauḥ pṛthivī ca naḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.16).
If the *sāṃnāyya* spills, one should pour it out at the place of the *āhavanīya* fire with this very [verse].

In the section titled "In the event of a failure" (*vidhyaparādhe*), it is likewise prescribed in the sūtra: "If it spills, they should pour it out within the space of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the verse beginning 'The great heaven and earth... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.10).

This [verse] is also prescribed in the *āśvina* recitation in the section titled "When the [other rites] have been concluded, for the *āśvina*" as follows: "'The great heaven and earth... for you are heaven and earth, the source of all blessings... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.5).

May the great Heaven and Earth sprinkle this sacrifice for us; may they nourish us with provisions. 13. Great Heaven and Earth: may they both sprinkle this sacrifice for us; may they fill us with provisions. 13.

May the vast *dyauḥ*, the deity of the heavenly world, and *pṛthivī*, the deity of the earth, sprinkle (*mimikṣatām*) this sacrifice of ours with their own essential essence; that is, may they desire to sprinkle it.
Likewise, with their sustainments (*bharībhiḥ*) and nourishments, [may they] [favour] us.
1. *ḍha*: I invoke.

"May both goddesses fill [us]. *Mahī*: From the word *mahat*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.6 (*ugitaśca*). The elision of the *ac* portion is due to Vedic usage (*chandasaḥ*). According to the supplementary rule for *brahman* and *mahat* (Pāṇini 6.1.173.1), the *ṅīp* is acute. *Dyauḥ*: The stem *div* is oxytone by its own nominal accent (*prātipadika-svara*). By the rule "after *go*, [the case-ending] is treated as having the *ṇit* augment" (Pāṇini 7.1.90), the following *su* becomes *ṅit*; thus, even though the *vṛddhi* occurs, it remains acute by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāvena*). *Pṛthivī*: From the root *prath* in the sense of "making known. The suffix *pivan* is added with the substitution of *śi* according to Uṇādi Sūtra 1.148 (*pratheḥ śivansaṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*). The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.41 (*vidvorādiśyaśca*). It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*). *Mimiksatām*: From the root *miha* in the sense of "to sprinkle. In the desiderative (*san*), there is reduplication and the application of the *halādiśeṣa* rule; then the changes of *ha* to *t*, *ka* to *k*, and *pa* to *t*. *Piptatām*: From the root *pṛ* in the senses of "protecting" and "filling. Some say the vowel is short. There is *ślu* for the *śap* suffix. By the rule "and for *ati* and *piparti*" (Pāṇini 7.4.77), the *a* of the reduplicated syllable becomes *i*. It bears the accent of the *tiṅ* suffix. *Marīmabhiḥ*: From the root *ḍubhṛñ* in the senses of "supporting" and "nourishing. The suffix *īman* is added according to Daśapādī Pāṇini 6 (*hustṛbhṛstṛsṛbhya īman*). Because it begins with *ni*, it is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudāttaḥ*).

The wise ones lick with their prayers the butter-like milk of those two, at the fixed station of the Gandharva. (14) Of those two, the wise ones lick the butter-like milk with their prayers, at the fixed station of the Gandharva. (14)
The firm station of the Gandharva is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
And thus it is recited in the Tāpanīya branch: "The intermediate space, frequented by hosts of Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases" (Nṛsiṃha Tāpanīya 1.2).

In the ether characterized by that intermediate space, there exists the connection between those two, heaven and earth; their "milk"—that is, water—is "like ghee," resembling clarified butter. "The wise ones"—intelligent living beings—"lick with their thoughts," that is, they lick [it] through their ritual acts.
Or alternatively:
they lick that which is endowed with *ghṛtavat*, that is, *ghṛtam* (ghee), namely Māra.
By the transposition of letters, the *repha* [the letter *r*] is placed first.
[The word] *gandharva* [is derived from the root] *ghṛñ* in the sense of "holding."
By the rule "ga-iti-gan-ghṛño vaiḥ," the suffix *vap* is applied; through its connection, the word *go* undergoes the substitution of *gan*.
The verse "syonā pṛthivi" is prescribed for touching the earth during the Mahānāmnī recitation.
It is sūtra-ed in the section beginning with "etadvidam brahmacāriṇam" as follows: "'syonā pṛthivi bhava' [is used] until the end" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.14).
Furthermore, this verse is to be muttered during the Smārta rite of descending from the high bed (*pratyavarohaṇa*) in the winter season.

In the section titled "The Descent on the Full Moon of Mārgaśīrṣa," it is sūtra-ed: "Having sat down upon that [seat] and having muttered the mantra, 'O Earth, be pleasant'... (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.3.6).

O Earth, be pleasant, free from thorns, and a place of rest for us; grant us wide-extending shelter. 15. O Earth, be pleasant, free from thorns, and a place of rest for us; grant us wide-extending shelter. 15.
"O Earth, become pleasant and so forth, endowed with a pair [of qualities].
The word *syona* signifies "extensive.

Thus, in the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa, having cited a certain mantra containing the word *syona*, it is explained: "'Enter Indra's lap, O pleasant one; [be] pleasant,' by this he says 'the extensive, the extensive.'"
Alternatively,
the word *syona* denotes happiness (*sukha*) (Nirukta 3.6.15);
accordingly, a statement by Yāska will be cited.

"O Earth, grant us—that is, give to us—a dwelling place (*niveśanī*) that is free from thorns (*anṛkṣarā*), a refuge (*śarma*) that is expansive (*asaprathaḥ*). Having cited this verse, Yāska explains it as follows: "O Earth, be pleasant to us, free from thorns, providing a dwelling place. A 'thorn' (*kaṇṭaka*) is so called because it causes pain (*ṛcchati*); it may also be derived from *kantapa*, *kuntati*, or *kaṇṭi*. It is the most elevated among actions. Grant us a refuge (*śarma*) that is all-pervading and wide. (Nirukta 9.32).

*Syonā*. According to some, [the variant] *avibu* occurs when *cha*, *ta*, *śa*, or *ṣa* follows. The third person plural ending *loṭ* becomes *tām*. According to others, there is the *ḍha-sāraḥ*. When *ta*, *ṣa*, or *ga* follow *ghṛñ*, *gam* is substituted. *Cha*, *cha*, *ta*, *pha*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *ṛ* are to be recited (*japya*). According to others, *syonā* is joined with a pair beginning with *syonatva*. *Cha*, *ḍha*, *ra*, and *ha* constitute the place of residence.

In *tantusantāne*, the suffix *na* is applied by Uṇādi Sūtra 3.289 (*asiveṣṭyonaṃ ca*). The *ya* is substituted for the final *ṭ*. It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). In the two words *syonā* and *pṛthivi*, there is a connection only with the verb *bhava* ("be"), and not with each other. Therefore, due to a lack of syntactic capacity (*asāmarthya*), the condition for being treated like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) does not apply; consequently, the vowel *o* in *syonā* does not receive the acute accent of the vocative (*āmantritādyudāttatvam*). Regarding *anukṣarā*: the root *ṛ* means "to go. That which goes within [the body] is an *akṣara*, namely a thorn. It is derived from the roots *tan* and *ṛṣi* with the suffix *kasaran* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.355). The change to *ka* occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.41 (*paṭhoḥ kaḥ si*). The change to *ṣ* occurs by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*. A Bahuvrīhi compound is formed with the negative particle *nañ*. The augment *nuṭ* is added by Pāṇini 6.3.74 (*tasmānḍuci*). The final syllable of the latter member receives the acute accent by the rule *nañmubhyām*. Regarding *niveśanī*: it is that in which things enter (*niviśanti*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied by Pāṇini 3.3.117 (*karaṇādhikaraṇayośca*). By the rule *liti*, the syllable preceding the suffix receives the acute accent. Regarding *yaccha*: the root *dāṇ* means "to give. The substitution of *yaccha* occurs according to the group beginning with *pātrā* (Pāṇini 7.3.78). The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *vyo'tastiṅaḥ*. Regarding *satrathaḥ*: the root *gratha* means "to bind" or "to weave. The suffix *asun* is applied. The compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.2.28 (*tena saheti tulyayoge*) meaning "that which exists together with *prathas*. The *samāsānta* suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied by Pāṇini 6.3.82 (*vopasarjanasya*). It bears the accent of the first member (*pūrvapadasvara*). 6. End of section.
At the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), when there is an excess of *soma*, one recitation (*śastra*) is to be chanted.

Here, the five verses beginning with "From here, O gods" (*ato devāḥ*) are used. Regarding the phrase "when there is an excess of *soma*," it is stated in the section [of the *Śrautasūtra*]: "With verses addressed to Indra and to Viṣṇu—namely, 'Great is Indra by his vigor' (*mahān indro ya ojasā*) and 'From here, O gods, may they protect us' (*ato devā avantu naḥ*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.7).
In the *atiryāma* sacrifice, even when there is an *atiriktoktha*, these five verses serve as the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*.

Accordingly, it is stated in the section beginning with "yasya paśavaḥ" in the Sūtra: "'ato devā avantu naḥ' are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 9.11). Furthermore, these two are also employed in the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the *dati* and *argha* [errors].

Similarly, it is prescribed in the section "This [portion] for the wife" (*vedaṃ patnyai*) in the sūtra: "With the two verses beginning 'From here may the gods protect us' (*ato devā avantu naḥ*) and with the *vyāhṛtis*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.11).
Between the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, if there is ordinary speech, this [verse] 'From here may the gods protect us' is the *japa*.
For it is prescribed: "One should mutter [the verse] 'From here may the gods protect us'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.7).
Therefore may the gods protect us from where Viṣṇu strode forth by the seven supports of the earth.
Therefore, may the gods protect us from that place where Viṣṇu strode across the seven regions of the earth. 16.
Viṣṇu is the Supreme Lord.

By means of the seven abodes—that is, by means of the seven meters beginning with the Gāyatrī which serve as instruments—he strode forth in various ways from the earth, from that place; therefore, may the gods protect us from this region of the earth.

The followers of the Taittirīya recension record in their texts that Viṣṇu, by means of the *chandas* as instruments, [conquered] the worlds beginning with the earth: "The gods, having Viṣṇu as their leader, conquered these worlds by means of the *chandas*" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.1.1).

In Viṣṇu’s incarnation as Trivikrama, the earth was the starting point for his three strides. The momentary occupation of a portion of the earth is the warding off of sin for those residing in the world of mortals (*bhūrloka*).
Therefore, from this word *etad*, the suffix *tasil* is applied by the rule *pañcamyāstasil* (Pāṇini 5.3.7),
and the substitution of *aś* is applied by the rule *etadoś* (Pāṇini 5.3.5).
In the word *lisavarega*, the vowel *a* is udātta;
for [the suffix] *tasil* [is applied].
By the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.1), the designation *vibhakti* is applied; thus, the substitution of *yat* for the words beginning with *tyad* occurs: *liṅgāvaraḥ*, *viṣṇuḥ*.
By the rule *vidheḥ kicca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.319), the suffix *nuc* is applied. Because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution.
Due to the continued application of the term *nit*, the word is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable).
He strode forth.
By means of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "sup," there is a compound with *viśva*;
it has the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
Because of its connection with the preceding word, there is no *nighāta* (elision of accent).
*Sapta*:
by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *-bhis*.
In *dhāmabhiḥ*,
the suffix *manin* is applied to the root *dadhāti* by Pāṇini’s rule 3.2.74 (*āto manin-kvanib-vanipaś ca*).
It bears the accent of the *nit* suffix.
The verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" is the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*) for the Vaiṣṇava Upāṃśuyāja.
This is stated in the section "The deities have been mentioned" (*uktā devatāḥ*) in the Sūtra: "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame tredhā... eṣa enām" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.6).
[This occurs] between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires. Ṛgveda 22.
In the event of a transgression, one should scatter ashes upon the dog's tracks with this very [verse].

This is formulated in the section on "Errors in the Performance" (*vidhyaparādhe*) as follows: "One should strew ashes over the dog's footprint with [the verse] 'Viṣṇu strode through this' (*idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame*)," according to the *Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 3.10.
In the *Ātithyā* sacrifice, this same verse serves as the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*) for the principal oblation.
In the section titled "Now, the Atithya [offering]," it is sūtra-ed: "This Viṣṇu strode out; may we attain that beloved path of his" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.5).
This very verse is the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*) for the Upasad [rite] dedicated to Viṣṇu.
In the section titled "Now, the Upasad," it is sūtra-ed: "Increasing the dwelling, driving away disease; this Viṣṇu strode out" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.8).
Vishnu strode across this [universe]; in three places he planted his step; in the dust he gathered it all together.
Viṣṇu strode across this; he established his station in three places; he planted his foot firmly in the dust. 17.
Viṣṇu, assuming the Trivikrama incarnation, strode across (vi-cakrame) this entire perceived world of sight;
he took his steps (padaṃ ni-dadhe) in three ways (tredhā), that is, in three places.
In the dust (pāṃsure) of this Viṣṇu’s footprint, this entire world is firmly rooted (samūḷaham), being perfectly contained within it.

This very Ṛgveda verse has been explained by Yāska himself: “Viṣṇu [is so called] from the root *viś* (to enter) or from *vyabh* (to pervade); he strides over whatever exists here; Viṣṇu places his foot in three ways for a threefold existence: on the earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven—so says Śākapūṇi. On the Samārohaṇa mountain, at Viṣṇupada, on Gayaśiras, Aurnavābha says: ‘His footprint is firmly established in the dust (*pāṃsura*), in the swelling intermediate space; the foot is not seen. Or rather, it may be used in a figurative sense: ‘Like dust, the foot is not seen. As for *pāṃsavaḥ*, they are so called because they are produced (*sūyante*) by feet, or because they lie down (*śerate*) having fallen (*pannāḥ*), or because they are worthy of praise (*pansanīyāḥ*). (Nirukta 12.18–19).
"Tredhā. The suffix *edhāc* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.46 (*edhācca*). The word *citaḥ* is udātta on the final syllable.
*Samūḷham*. [The root] *vah* means "to carry. By the rule "the *niṣṭhā* suffixes," the suffix *kta* (which becomes *ka*) is applied.
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *vacisvapi-* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) and so forth;
then there is the substitution of *ḍha*, the substitution of *dha*, the substitution of *ḍha* again, the elision of *ḍh*, and the lengthening of the vowel.
By the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the preceding prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

In the word *asya*, the substitute *aś* (for *idam*) is anudātta according to the rule “*idamo 'nvādeśe*,” and the suffix is also [anudātta] by the accent of the nominal endings (*sup-svara*). In *pāṃsure*:
The suffix *ra* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) according to the rule *‘nagapāṃsupāṇḍubhyaśca’* (Pāṇini 5.2.107). It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Regarding the *upasat*, this verse beginning with *‘trīṇi padā’* serves as the *yājyā* at the morning sacrifice and the *anuvākyā* at the evening sacrifice for the Vaiṣṇava offering.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The three steps [of Viṣṇu] he strode out; thus, the Sviṣṭakṛt and subsequent rites are omitted when [the sacrifice] has been interrupted" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.8).
Viṣṇu, the infallible guardian, strode forth his three steps,
thereby upholding the sacred laws.
Viṣṇu, the guardian who cannot be deceived, has strode forth his three steps; from there, he maintains the sacred laws. 18.

Viṣṇu—the one who cannot be harmed by anyone (*adābhya*), the protector (*gopā*) of the entire world—strided out his three steps (*trīṇi padāni vi cakrame*) across these locations, beginning with the earth.
What was he doing?
Sustaining and nourishing the sacred laws (*dharmāṇi*), such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and others.
Regarding *padā*: by the rule “*supāṃ suluk*,” etc., the case ending (*vibhakti*) is replaced by *ḍā*.
Since that [substitute] would normally be unaccented (*anudātta*) by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, it becomes accented (*udātta*) by the accent known as *udāttanivṛttisvara*.
The Gopas; this is mentioned in the verse "gopāsṛtasya" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.1.8).
Adābhya.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124).
This forms a *nañ*-compound (*nañ-samāsa*). The original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member remains.

[The suffix] *dhārayan* [is derived from *dhṛ*]; because it is a root ending in a short vowel (*pit*), it is unaccented (*anudātta*). Furthermore, by the rule regarding the accent of *la-sārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) alone remains.
1. "In the places of *ca*, *cha*, *pha*, *śa*, and *ha*, [the substitution occurs] due to the exhaustion of the *sila* [rule]; the twenty-first is the *pratiṣṭhā*.
Because the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "due to the confusion of the sages" (Anuvāka 12.2) continues to apply, Medhātithi Kāṇva is the seer (*ṛṣi*).

The verse beginning with "apasvantaḥ" is a Purauṣṇih, because it possesses the characteristic of a Purauṣṇih where the first pāda consists of twelve syllables, according to the rule: "If the first [pāda] has twelve [syllables], it is a Purauṣṇih" (Anuvāka 5.2). The verse beginning with "apsu me somaḥ" is an Anuṣṭubh.
The first three verses beginning with "idamāpaḥ" are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
the remaining nineteen verses are in the *gāyatrī* meter.
Because of the metrical rule stating "at the beginning [of a section], it is in *gāyatrī*" (Anuvāka 12.14), the first verse has Vāyu as its deity.
Then follow two verses having Indra and Vāyu as their deities;
then one verse having Mitra and Varuṇa as its deity;
then, in the subsequent [verse], Indra distinguished by the host of Maruts is the deity.
Then there is one verse addressed to the Viśvedevas;
immediately following that is one addressed to Pūṣan;
and the remaining verses have the year as their deity.
The verse beginning with "payasvān me" is joined with the following half-verse; however, the verse beginning with "saṃ māgne" has Agni as its deity.
The application of the hymn (sūkta) is to be understood from its indicative mark (liṅga), specifically in the second [day] of the Abhilaṣa-ṣaḍaha.
The original accentuation (prakṛtisvaratva) applies:
"indravāyū.
This is a dvandva compound meaning "Indra and Vāyu."
Regarding the phrase "the prohibition of *ānaṅ* must be stated for both cases" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.26.1), there is a prohibition of *ānaṅ*.

Furthermore, because the rule "not when the second member begins with an unaccented vowel" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.142) prohibits the application of the original accent of both members—which would otherwise apply by the rule "also in a dual divinity compound" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.141)—only the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound remains.
[We] invoke.
The root *han* is used in the sense of "striving" (*spardhā*) and "sound" (*śabda*).
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
By the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca*, the preceding vowel takes the place of both [the semivowel and the following vowel].
The substitution of *guṇa* and the replacement [of the root] occur. Because *śap* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*).

Since the *tiṅ* suffix would otherwise be subject to the acute accent on the first syllable of the word by virtue of the accentuation rules for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the suppression of the accent (*nighāta*) is applied according to the rule *tiṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28).
For the word *asya*, the acute accent on the genitive case ending is applied by the rule *uḍidampadādyappumraidyubhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.171).

For the purpose of drinking; from the root *pā* in the sense of "drinking," the suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.95: *khyāgāpāpacaḥ*.
In the word *ghumāsthā*, there is the substitution of *ī* [for *a*];
the final acute accent is due to transposition (*vyatyaya*).

The word *jajñānā* is derived from the root *jan* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*). According to Pāṇini 3.2.105, the *liṭ* suffix is used in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). For that *liṭ*, by Pāṇini 3.2.106, the substitute *kānac* is optionally applied. By the rule beginning with *gamahana* (Pāṇini 6.4.98), there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopaḥ*). Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the word *jana* undergoes reduplication (*dvirvacanam*). By the rule *stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40), the letter *n* is replaced by *j*. The acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatvam*) is due to the *cit* suffix. The long *ā* is as before. The word *pūtadakṣaḥ*: the root is *pū* in the sense of "purification" (*pavane*). The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *niṣṭhā*. There is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11). Thus, *pūta* means "purified. Those two [the Aśvins] whose *dakṣas* (powers/abilities) are purified are *pūtadakṣau*. By the rule *bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā* (Pāṇini 6.2.1), the original accent of the first member of the compound is retained.
Those two who increase through Truth (*ṛta*), who are the lords of the light of Truth—
those Mitra and Varuṇa I invoke.
By means of Truth, those two who increase Truth, the lords of the light of Truth—those Mitra and Varuṇa I invoke. 5.
May Mitra and Varuṇa, who by the cosmic order (ṛta) and truth have slain Vṛtra, together with the bounteous Indra as their ally—
may no evil-minded one have power over us.
O bounteous ones, you have slain Vṛtra with Indra as your powerful ally; let not the malevolent one prevail over us. 9.

O bounteous ones (*sudānavaḥ*), you hosts of Maruts, endowed with beautiful giving, destroy—meaning annihilate—the enemy Vṛtra together with Indra as your powerful ally (*yujā*). Let Vṛtra, who is possessed of evil reputation (*duḥśaṃsaḥ*) due to his wicked renown, have no power over us (*naḥ*); let him not be capable [of harming us]. **Grammatical Analysis:** * **Hata**: From the root *han* (to strike/to go), in the imperative (*loṭ*) second person plural. The suffix *tha* is replaced by *ta*. By the rule *adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ*, the *śap* augment is elided. By the rule *anudāttopadeśa...* (Pāṇini 6.1.37), the nasal (*n*) is dropped. * **Sudānavaḥ**: From the root *dāñ* (to give). The *auṇādika* suffix *nu* is added according to *dābhyāṃ nuḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.312). In the *prādisamāsa* compound, there is the *āmantritanighāta* (the vocative accent). * **Yujā**: From the root *yujir* (to join). The suffix *kin* is applied according to *ṛtvig...* (Pāṇini 3.2.59). By the rule *sāvekācaḥ*, the third case singular ending receives the acute accent (*udātta*). * **Duḥśaṃsaḥ**: The suffix *khal* is applied according to *īṣadduḥsupu...* (Pāṇini 3.3.126). By the rule *liti*, the syllable preceding the suffix receives the acute accent. * **Īśata**: From the root *īś* (to rule). Although the *luṅ* tense would normally apply after the prohibitive particle *māṅ*, by the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*, there is a substitution (*vyatyaya*) for the *laṅ* tense. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, the *śap* augment is elided. Due to the connection with *māṅ*, by the rule *na māṅyoge*, the *āṭ* augment is absent. There is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.
We invoke all the gods and the Maruts to drink the Soma;
for they, the sons of Pṛśni, are formidable.
We invoke all the gods, the Maruts, for the drinking of the Soma; for they are mighty, the sons of Pṛśni. 10.
We invoke all the gods known as the Maruts for the drinking of Soma; that is, we call them for the purpose of consuming the Soma.
And those Maruts are fierce, possessing a strength unbearable to enemies, and are the sons of Pṛśni—the earth endowed with various colors.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) signifies well-known fact.
And that well-known fact is to be understood from another mantra: "The sons of Pṛśni" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.58.5).
"Pṛśnimātaraḥ" means those whose mother is Pṛśni. The word *pṛśni* is listed as an initial-accented (*ādyudātta*) nipātana in the Uṇādi-sūtras (4.412) under the rule *ghṛṇipṛśni*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is maintained].
Like conquerors, the thundering roar of the Maruts comes forth boldly when you go toward that which is auspicious,
O heroes.
The thundering roar of the Maruts goes forth boldly, as it were, like conquerors, when you go forth in splendor, O heroes. 11.

The thunder—the sound—of the Maruts, the gods, goes forth endowed with boldness (*dhṛṣṇuyā*). Of whom is it like? It is like that of victorious, conquering heroes and warriors. O leaders, O Maruts, when (*yat*) you go toward what is auspicious and beautiful through the sacrifice to the gods, then your sound goes forth; such is the connection with the preceding [verse]. *Taṇyatuḥ*: from the root *tanu* in the sense of "extension. The suffix *yan* is applied according to the rule *ṛtanyañji-* etc. (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.442). *Dhṛṣṇuyā*: from the root *dhṛṣ* in the sense of "boldness. The suffix *knu* is applied by Pāṇini 3.2.140 (*trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipaḥ knuḥ*). By the rule *supāṃ suluk-* etc., the case-ending *s* is replaced by *yā*. Because of its *cit*-nature, it is udātta-accented on the final syllable. *Yāthana*: the ending *than* is substituted for *tha* by the rule *tasanasanathanāśca*. Due to its connection with the word *yat*, there is no *nighāta* (elision of accent).

1. Those fierce ones, terrible in battle and the like, whose sounds are *ta*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *u*. 2. From *śa* and *go*. 3. To the region where the gods dwell. 4. *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *tha*, *pa*, *ku*: thus [it is] *ku*.

Born from the laughing lightning, may they protect us; may the Maruts cleanse us. 12. Born from the laughing (*has-kāra*) lightning (*vi-dyutaḥ*), from that (*ataḥ*) [place], may they protect us (*avantu naḥ*). May the Maruts (*marutaḥ*) cleanse us (*maḷayantu naḥ*). 12.
May the Maruts, born from that [place]—from the laughing, illuminating lightning that shines intensely within the atmosphere—protect us on all sides;
may those same Maruts gladden us and grant us happiness.
From the root *has* (as in *hase hasane*,
"to laugh");
however, here it functions in the sense of mere manifestation.
From this [root], the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule for words such as *saṃpad*.
When this word is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *aṇ* is added to the root *ḍukṛñ* in the sense of "making," by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1).

Although the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* etc. would have required the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member, the rule *gatikāraka-* etc. instead prescribes the original accent of the *kṛt*-derived second member.
The substitution of *s* for the visarga is applied by the rule "ataḥ kṛkami0" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.46), etc.
O glowing Pūṣan, bring hither the one with variegated sacrificial grass, the supporter of heaven,
like a man who has driven out his lost cattle.
O Pūṣan, O glowing one, bring hither the one with the variegated sacrificial grass, the supporter of heaven; drive him here like an unbound animal. 13.
O Pūṣan, bring from heaven— the remainder of the sentence being "bring"— the Soma that is possessed of variegated sacrificial grass (citrabarhiṣam), which is the support (dharuṇam) of the sacrifice.
Pūṣan is further qualified as "O Āghṛṇi," one endowed with approaching splendor.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
O *aja* (O you who are ever-moving), just as in the world someone, having searched for a lost animal in a great forest or similar place, brings it back; so it is here.
O *āghṛṇe* (O radiant one)!

From the root *ghṛ* in the sense of "flowing" or "shining," the suffix *ni* is applied according to the rule *ghṛṇi-ghṛbhi*. The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule *ṛvarṇācceti vaktavyam*.
This is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with a prefix).
The vocative is accented on the first syllable.
*Dharuṇam*:
from the root *dhṛñ* in the sense of "supporting."
From this root ending in *py*, the suffix *un* is applied according to the rule "dhāreṇilucca" (Dhātupāṭha 5);
due to metathesis (*vyatyaya*), in the absence of the [initial] accent, the suffix-accent (*pratyayasvara*) prevails.
[The form is] *divaḥ*.
In the word *‘uḍidam’* and so forth, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is acute (*udātta*).
[The root] *aja*: “*aja* [is used] in the senses of going and throwing.”
The glowing Pūṣan found the king who was hidden, concealed in a secret place,
resting upon variegated sacrificial grass.
Pūṣan, the radiant one, found the king who was hidden, concealed in a secret place, he whose sacrificial grass is brilliant. || 14 ||

The glowing Pūṣan found—that is, obtained—King Soma. Of what kind? Hidden away, extremely concealed. The reason for this is that he was situated in the world of heaven, which is like a cave (*guhā*) and difficult of access, and thus *citrabarhiṣam* [possessing variegated grass]. Regarding *apagūḷaham*: from the root *gū* "to conceal," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini 3.2.102 (*niṣṭhā*). By Pāṇini 8.2.31 (*ho ḍhaḥ*), the *h* becomes *ḍh*. By Pāṇini 8.2.40 (*jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*), the *t* becomes *dh*. Then the substitution of *it*, the elision of *ḍh*, and the lengthening of the vowel take place. In the compound, by Pāṇini 6.2.49 (*gatiranantaraḥ*), the preceding member retains its original accent. Regarding *guhā*: the locative case ending is elided by Pāṇini 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk...*). Regarding *hitam*: in the formation of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*), the root *dhā* is replaced by *hi*.
Moreover, may he, with his drops, further impel the six yoked ones for me;
may he plow up barley with the cows as it were.
Thus he has sent me six yoked [steeds] along with drops; he has ploughed up barley for me as if with cattle. 15.
1. Ḍha-anvivya; ra-anveṣya | Kārikā 23:

"Moreover (uta), that Pūṣan, for the sake of the sacrificer, with the drops (indubhiḥ)—that is, with the Soma as the cause of sacrifice—'anuseṣidhat' means he proceeds by following in sequence through the six seasons, beginning with spring, repeatedly moving along them; this is the sense."
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"They did not care for the barley with cows and oxen.
Here, the word *na* has the sense of comparison (*upamārtha*).
Just as one directs [the plough] toward barley and repeatedly plows the ground year after year, so it is in that case.
The acute accent on the first syllable [of *mahām*] is due to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.212, *mahām | 'ḍayi ca*.
[The word *indubhiḥ* follows.]
In the root *undī* [meaning] "to moisten," the suffix *up* is applied by the rule *undericcādeḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.12), with the substitution of *i* for the letter *u*;
because the term *nit* is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), the word is udātta-accented on its first syllable.
By the rule "dīrghādaṭi samānapāde," the *n* becomes short in the *saṃhitā*;
by the rule "āto'ṭi nityam," the vowel *ā* becomes nasalized (*sānunāsika*). Thus:
*anuseṣidhat*.

From the root *piñj*, the suffix *yaṅ* is applied by the rule *dhātor ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.22). Then, its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *yaṅo 'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74). Thus, [the form] *piñjūyate* is derived.
By the characteristic of the *pratyaya* [suffix], there is reduplication according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.9 (*asanyaṅoḥ*). There is elision of the initial consonant (*halādiśeṣaḥ*).
According to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.82 (*guṇo yaṅlukoḥ*), there is *guṇa* substitution for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by Pāṇini 8.3.57 (*iṇkoḥ*).
Since it belongs to the class beginning with *san*, it receives the designation "root" (*dhātu*); consequently, the suffix *śatṛ* replaces *laṭ*, and *śap* is added for the agent (*kartṛ*).
By the rule "and like *adādi*," there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix].
There is a prohibition of the augment *num* by the rule "not after a reduplicated stem" (*nābhyastāc chatuḥ*, Pāṇini 7.1.78).
When the accent of the suffix would otherwise apply, the initial syllable becomes udātta by the rule "the beginning of reduplicated stems" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.189).
Regarding *gobhiḥ*: although the rule *sāvekācaḥ* would have required the acute accent (*udātta*) on the *bhisa* ending, there is a prohibition by the rule *na gośvan*. [The form] is *carkṛpat*.
The root *kṛp* is used in the sense of "scratching. When the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), there is reduplication,
the substitution of *halādi-śeṣa*, and by the rule *rimriko ca luki* (Pāṇini 7.4.91), the augment *ruk* is added to the reduplicated syllable.

From this root ending in the *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive without *yaṅ*), there is the *leṭ* suffix *tip*. By the rule "elision after *i*," the *i* is dropped; by the rule "the augment *aṭ* or *āṭ* for *leṭ*," the augment *aṭ* is applied.

By the rule "adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ," there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. When the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel would have applied, it is prohibited by the rule "nābhyastasyāci piti" (Pāṇini 7.3.87). The *nighāta* (anudātta accent) is applied by the rule "tiṅatiṅaḥ."
When the *ekadhanā* vessels have been brought in the third turn, he should follow them himself and recite the two verses beginning with "anvayaḥ.
At the third turn, with the verse "apo devīḥ," he should enter the *havirdhāna* shed along with the *ekadhanā* vessels as they enter.
Thus it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "With the verse 'ambayo yantyadhvabhiḥ,' he should go after the three [turns] at the end" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.1).
The dappled mares go to the sacrifice, the swift ones of those performing the rite,
sprinkling the milk with honey.
The sisters, moving along their paths for those who perform the sacrifice, go with the speckled milk mixed with honey. 16.
"Of us who desire the *adhvara*—the sacrifice—for ourselves, the *ambayaḥ*—the waters standing in the place of mothers—are [present].
And thus it is recited in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa: 'The *ambayaḥ* go by their paths; the *ambayaḥ* are indeed the waters.
Those waters 'go'—that is, they proceed—'by their paths,' meaning by the routes leading to the sacrificial ground."
Of what nature are the waters?

They are "kinswomen" (*jāmayaḥ*), meaning beneficial relatives; likewise, they are "joining with honey," that is, endowing the milk with a sweet flavor; and they are "making things spotted," meaning they provide the coloring for cows and other animals.

Regarding *ambayaḥ*: from the root *ravi* (or *labi*) in the sense of "sound," the suffix *i* is applied by virtue of the term *bāhulaka* ("by way of diversity") within the section beginning with *aca haḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.578).
The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
[In the word] *adhvabhiḥ*,
the suffix *kan* is applied by the rule "after the root *ad*, [the suffix *kan* is added] and [the final consonant] *gh* is substituted" (*Uṇādisūtra* 4.555).
Since the suffix [ya] is unaccented after the causative suffix (ṇic), the accent of the verbal root remains;
thus, *jāmayaḥ*.
[The root is] *jamu* "to eat."

The suffix *i* is applied by virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*). [The form] *adhvarīyatām* is derived from the word *adhvara* with the suffix *kyac*, according to the rule "after a word ending in a case-suffix, *kyac* is added when one wishes for oneself" (*supa ātmanaḥ kyac*).
The substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule "kyaci ca.

According to the statement "it should be stated that [the prohibition applies] to words other than *aputra*" (Pāṇini Mañjarī 7.4.35), there is no prohibition of the *ī*-substitution by the rule "not in the Veda for *aputra*" (Pāṇini 7.4.35). Furthermore, because of the principle "all rules are optional in the Veda," even the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "of *kavi*, *adhvara*, and *patana*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.39) does not take place.

From a verbal root ending in the *kyac* suffix: [the substitution of] *śatṛ* for *laṭ*. Due to being marked with *p*, the *śap* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*). And because *śatṛ* is a *lasārvadhātuka* affix, it is also unaccented; thus, by the rule of monophthongization (*ekādeśa*), there is a single replacement for these two along with the *kyac* suffix.

When the final syllable is udātta by the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, there is the udātta accent on the fifth vowel (the *u*) by the rule *śaturanumo nadīyājādī*. *Pṛcchantīḥ*: from the root *pṛcī* in the sense of "contact," with the suffix *śatṛ* for the present tense (*laṭ*), *śnam* after roots beginning with *rudh*, elision of the vowel *a* by *aśoralopaḥ*, and the substitution of *anusvāra* and its subsequent *parasavarṇa*. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by *ugitaśca*; the lengthening of the preceding vowel to its homogeneous long form (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) occurs optionally in the Vedic language (*vā chandasi*). The udātta accent of the *ṅīp* is established by the rule *śataranumaḥ*.
Those waters which are near the sun, or those with which the sun is joined—may they speed our sacrifice forward. 17.
Those [waters] which are near the sun, or those which are together with the sun—may they impel our sacrifice. 17.
Those waters which are situated near the sun—
as another Vedic scripture states, "The waters are contained within the sun" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.8.1)—
or else, those waters with which the sun exists together.
The distinction is that in the former case water is predominant, while in the latter case the sun is;
such waters as those may they further our sacrifice— that is, may they please our ritual—
by means of which [waters].
The prohibition of the acute accent on the case-ending by the rule *na gośvansāvavarṇa* applies here, superseding the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
The remaining grammatical derivation is clear.
I invoke the divine Waters where our cattle drink; to the rivers be this oblation! (18)
The Waters: O Goddess, come hither! Where our cows drink from the rivers, there let there be an oblation for you. 18.
I call upon those divine waters in which our cows drink—that is, perform their drinking.
We must offer the oblation (*havis*) to the *sindhavaḥ*, the flowing waters, who are deities.
[The word] *apaḥ* [is used].
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the suffix *śas* is established by the rule "ūḍidam" and so forth.
They drink;
here, the substitution of *piba* occurs by the rule "pāghrā" and so forth.

The root *śap* is unaccented because it is marked with the *pittva* designation. The root *ni* is acutely accented on its first syllable by the rule regarding the accent of verbal roots (*dhātusvara*) when followed by the suffix *lasārvadhātuka*.
There is no suppression of accent (*nighāta*) due to the rule beginning with "in the presence of particles such as *yat*, *yadi*, etc. (Pāṇini 8.1.30).
The root is *ḍukuñ* in the sense of "making. According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.4.14, *kṛyārthe tavaikenyenya-tvanaḥ*, the suffix *tvana* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).

Guga: [The word *gugā* has its first syllable udātta due to the absence of a svarita accent. "Within the waters is nectar, within the waters is healing medicine; and for the praise of immortality, O gods, become swift victors. (19)
Within the waters is immortality; within the waters is healing. And for the praise of the waters, O gods, become possessors of strength. 19.
Within the waters—that is, in the midst of them—there exists the nectar (*amṛta*), the *pīyūṣa*;
for it is non-dual (*advikāra*).
This is also supported by another scriptural passage: "The waters, indeed, are nectar" (*amṛtaṃ vā āpaḥ*) (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.2.1–2).

In the same way, medicine and healing herbs exist within the waters, because the collyrium that wards off hunger and disease is produced from them. Moreover, for the sake of praising such divine waters— for the purpose of glorification— O gods, the priests and other Brahmins [should offer].
"Indeed, these Brahmins are the gods manifest," according to another Vedic text (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.3.1).
"O *vājinaḥ*, be swift;
that is to say, perform the praise quickly."
In the word *apsu*, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the locative case ending is established by the rule *ūḍidam* etc.;
in the *saṃhitā* (continuous text), the circumflex accent (*svarita*) is applied by the rule *udāttasvaritayorṇaḥ svaritaḥ*.
*Amṛtam*. By the rule *naño jaramaramitramṛtāḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.116), the first syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*) is acute-accented.
[The word] *praśastaye*.

And because of the rule "tādau ca niti" (Pāṇini 6.2.50), which states that [a word] followed by *n* and beginning with *t* [retains its accent], the root-vowel of the prefix (*gati*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*).

Let it be so. Because of the rule "the vocative [word] preceding [another] is as if non-existent," the preceding vocative is treated as non-existent; consequently, since it occurs at the beginning of the quarter-verse (pāda), there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent).
In the *Kārīrī* sacrifice, for the northern *ājyabhāga*, the verse "ap su me" serves as the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*).
This is prescribed in the section on the "Sacrifice for those desiring rain" in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (2.13): "apsvame sadhiṣṭvāpsu me somo abravīt."
Soma has told me that within the waters are all healing remedies, as well as Agni, the source of universal welfare, and the waters themselves, which possess every medicine.
Within the waters, Soma has told me that all healing medicines reside, as well as Agni, the source of universal well-being, and the waters themselves, which possess every remedy. 20.
Soma, the god, told me—the great seer who perceives the sacred hymns—that within the waters, in their midst, all healing medicines exist.
Likewise, Soma spoke of Agni, named Viśvaśambhuva, the bringer of happiness to the entire world, as abiding in the waters.
Thus, the followers of the Taittirīya recension record his entry into the waters in the section beginning "Greater than the Agra-s," stating: "He entered the waters" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.6.1).
It is well known that medicinal plants such as creepers, shrubs, and tree roots exist in water because they are produced by rain;
he also spoke of those waters which are "all-healing," meaning those in which all medicines reside.
*bheṣajā*: the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the dual ending] by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *viśvaśambhuvam*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *bhū* with an internal causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*).
By means of transposition (*vyatyaya*), the original accent of the first member of the compound is maintained.
Alternatively:

He for whom all activities whatsoever are conducive to happiness; [in this compound] the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member is according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.2.106: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the word *viśva* [is acute on the final syllable] when it forms a name. [The following word is] *āpaḥ*.
When the accusative plural suffix *śas* would have been expected, *jas* is substituted by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
By the rule "asnū" (Pāṇini 6.4.11), there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-dīrgha*),
resulting in *viśvabheṣajīḥ*.
It is like the expression *viśvaśambhuvam*.
O Waters, bestow healing medicine as a protection for my body, so that I may long behold the sun.
O Waters, bestow healing medicine as a protection for my body, so that I may long behold the sun. 21.

O Waters, grant me—for the sake of my body—a protective shield, a remedy, and medicine that wards off disease. Furthermore, may we be able to see the sun for a long time, remaining free from illness; this is the implied sense.
*Pṛṇīta*.
[The root] *pṛ* [is used] in the senses of "protecting" (*pālan*) and "filling" (*pūraṇa*). [This is] the imperative, middle voice, third person plural; [the suffix] *tha*.
For that [suffix], there is the substitution of *ta* by the rule "atasthasthamipām";
then the suffix *ṣva* is added by the rule "ṛyādibhyaḥ ṣvā";
and finally, the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule "pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ."
The substitution of *ī* occurs by the rule "ī halyaghoraḥ";
the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule "ṛvarṇācca";
and the accent of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) prevails by the principle "the accent of that which remains after the application of other rules is stronger, except in the case of *vikaraṇa* suffixes."
It remains:
*āpaḥ*.

Since this [word] is treated as non-existent according to the rule "an *āmantrita* preceding [another] is as if non-existent," there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because it begins the quarter-verse (*pāda*).
*Varūtham*.
[Derived from] the root *vṛṣ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*).
[The suffix] *ūyathan* is applied by [Uṇādi Sūtra 2.163]: *jṛvṛbhyāmūyathan*.
The word *nisvādā* is udātta at its beginning.
In the form *tanve*, the designation *nadī* is optional according to Pāṇini’s rule 1.4.6 (*ḍiti hrasvaśca*), and thus there is an absence of the augment *āṭ*.
When the acute accent on the case-ending would otherwise apply by the rule "udāttayaṇo halūpāt," [the following exceptions apply]:
1. ḍha-na-vābhrim;
2. ca-pha-śa-pa-oṣadhīnām; ḍha-auṣadhīnām.

3. As in the case of *viśvaśambhu*, [the substitution occurs] after *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *pha*, *śa*, and *pa*. By transposition, according to the rule "of the acute and circumflex," there is circumflex (*svarita*) accentuation. [The form is] *dṛśe*.
