By the rule *sanniyogena* (Pāṇini 7.3.57), there is the substitution of *k* for the following consonant after the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Thus:
*nānadadbhiḥ*.
The root *ṇad* means "inarticulate sound.
As in the previous cases, when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*), the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is lengthened by the rule "dīrgho 'kitaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.63).
The acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable remains as before.
By those breathing;
[the root] *śvas* means "to breathe.
Everything else is as before.
"Hiraṇyaratham": by the rule "samāsasya," it has an udātta accent on the final syllable. He gave.
In the word *agātisthāḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*. [The term] *daṃsanāvān* contains the word *daṃsas*.
The word *damsaḥ* is listed among the names for ritual action (*karman*) in [the list] beginning with *apraḥ damsaḥ veṣaḥ* (Tribhāṣyaratna 2.1.3).
*Damsanā* is simply *damsa*;
the suffix *matup* is added according to the rule "that which belongs to this" (*tad asyāsti*).
*Daṃsanā* is that by which one displays [power];
it refers to the triplet beginning with *āśvināvaśvāvatyā*, occurring in the *prātaranuvāka* during the *āśvina* ritual period in the *gāyatrī* meter.
This is prescribed in the section titled "Now the *āśvina*" (*athāśvinaḥ*) in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (4.15): "The *āśvina* [verses] are *yajvarīr apaḥ* and *āśvināvaśvāvatyā*."

O Aśvins, come with food accompanied by horses, with powerful vigor; O destroyers of enemies, come with wealth of cattle and gold. 17. O Aśvins, come with food accompanied by horses, with powerful vigor; O destroyers of enemies, come with wealth of cattle and gold. 17.
Impelled by Indra, Śunaḥśepa praised the Aśvins.
Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Indra said to him, 'Praise the Aśvins now; they desire your hymn. He then praised the Aśvins with the following triplet" (AiB 7.16).
O Aśvins, come hither to this ritual together with food (*iṣ*) that is "rich in horses" (*aśvāvatyā*), meaning provided with many horses, and that is "impelled" (*śarvīrayā*). Come!
"O Aśvins, destroyers of enemies, by your grace, may our house be *gomat*—endowed with many cows—and *hiraṇyavat*—furnished with much gold; this is the ellipsis.

[The word] *aśvāvatyā*: the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.3.131, which states: 'In a mantra, the final vowel of soma, aśva, indriya, and viśvadeva is lengthened before the suffix -mat.'"
*iṣā*: the third case ending receives the acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. *yātam*.
The root *yā* is used in the sense of "attaining. In the imperative (*loṭ*), the suffixes *tas* and *tam* are applied;
due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

[The word] *śarvīrā* [is derived from the root] *śu* "to go. The suffix *īran* occurs after this root as well, by virtue of the term "variously" (*bahulavacanāt*) in the rule *kṛṣpṛkaṭīpaṭiśoṭībhya īran* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.470).
The word *nitya* has the udātta accent on its first syllable.

For your chariot, O Dastras, is of equal yoking, immortal; it is urged forth upon the ocean, O Aśvins. (18) *Samānayojanaḥ* | *hi* | *vām* | *rathaḥ* | *dastrā* | *amartyaḥ* | *samudre* | *aśvinau* | *īryete* || 18 ||

O Aśvins, destroyers of enemies, your chariot is "of equal harnessing," meaning it is yoked equally for both of you because you two mount a single chariot; it is harnessed for the sake of both at once. That chariot is "immortal," meaning it is free from destruction, its course being unimpeded.
For this very reason, O Aśvins, it "moves" or travels within the "ocean," that is, in the intermediate space (antarikṣa).

Regarding the word *samudra*, which is recited among the names of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), Yāska explained it thus: "Why *samudra*? Because from it the waters flow forth (*samudravanti*); the waters rush toward it (*samabhidravanti*); beings rejoice (*saṃmodante*) in it. [This occurs] among the names of the intermediate space, as in the passage: "Sagara is the ocean (*samudra*). [Note: The various manuscript readings cited (ga-cha-jha-ṇa-dha-na-ra-śa-ṣa-sa-ha) and (pha-śa) refer to specific textual variants found in different recensions of the Nirukta.]

"Samudgaḥ" means "it swells" (*samunatti*) [Nirukta 2.10]. It has the same etymological derivation (*samānayojana*). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. "Amartyaḥ": here, there is the original accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) as the first member. "Īyate": from the root *īṅ* in the sense of "motion. Since it is taught with a short vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the *sārvadhātuka* suffix receives the *anudātta* accent; however, because the suffix *śyan* has the marker *n*, it receives the *udātta* accent on its first syllable. By the rule "hi ca," there is no prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent).
You two have fixed the wheel of the chariot upon the summit of the navel;
one wheel revolves around the sky.
Having placed the wheel of the chariot upon his head, you two have guided it; one [wheel] moves around the sky.
O Aśvins, you two fixed one wheel of your chariot upon the summit—that is, on top—of the firm mountain which was impossible to strike or destroy;
the other wheel moves around the sky, traversing the world of heaven.
Having superimposed [it].
From *ahan* (day), [we derive] *ahnaḥ*. "The application of the suffix *ka* in the sense of the *ghañ* suffix occurs in the case of *sthā*, *nau*, *āpi*, *adhi*, *han*, and *yu*."
For we have indeed thought of you from afar,
like a wonderful, ruddy mare.
For we have meditated upon you from the near end and from the far end, like a dappled, ruddy mare. 21.

O you whose nature is all-pervasive, O wonderful and worthy of praise, O shining one, O deity presiding over the time of dawn—our humans do not perceive (*na amanmahi*) your true form either from the near (*vantāt*) or from the far distance (*parākāt*).
The word *hi* indicates what is well-known;
the meaning is that it is well known among us that we are unable to know the extent of the deity’s majesty at both the near and the far boundaries.
We thought (*amanmahi*).
[The root] *man* means "to know.
Due to the rule "in the Vedic language there is great diversity" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), the suffix *śyan* is elided by virtue of that expression "great diversity."
‘Luṅ-luṅ-lṛṅ-vad-adātaḥ’; by the rule ‘hi ca’, there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent. [The word is] *aśve*.
The root *aś* means "to pervade.
The suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule beginning with *aśipruṣi*. There is the acute accent on the first syllable because it is a vocative (*āmantrita*).
Come hither with these strengths, O Daughter of Heaven;
O Agni, bestow wealth upon us.
Come hither with these strengths, O Daughter of Heaven; bestow wealth upon us. 22.
O daughter of Heaven, O goddess Uṣas, daughter of the gods, come hither with these strengths and those [powers];
bestow upon us abundant wealth and firmly establish riches among us.
By these [rules]: according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage, diversely), there is no substitution of *ais* for the *bhisa* ending after the word *tyad*. [Thus,] *gahi*.
This has been stated more than once:
*duhitardivaḥ*.

Even in the case of *divaḥ* [in the compound] *parasyāpi divaḥ*, when there is the coreferential connection (*anvaya*) with *divo duhitaḥ*, because it is preceded [by another vocative], the entire group of vocatives becomes entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*) by virtue of the rule *subāmantrite parāṅgavat svareṇa* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), which treats the preceding element as if it were part of the subsequent one.
Alternatively,

according to the principle that "technical rules and *paribhāṣās* apply at the time [the operation they govern is to take place]" (*kāryakālaṃ hi saṃjñāparibhāṣam*, Paribhāṣā 3), when the rule *suvāmantritam* forms a single syntactic unit with the eighth-book rule *āmantritasya ca*, the former— being subsequent— undergoes the treatment of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), resulting in all syllables being unaccented (*sarvānudāttatvam*). Subsequently, after the two vocatives have received their respective accents, the irregular application (*vyatyaya*) expressed by the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* occurs.
In *asme*,
the form *śe* is a substitute for the locative case according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
In the seventh section, there are five hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, beginning with "tvam agne prathamaḥ," consists of eighteen verses;
its seer is Hiraṇyastūpa of the Aṅgiras lineage.
The first eight verses consist of *aṣṭīpada* (eight-footed) *triṣṭubh*s.
The remaining verses are *jagatī*s, according to the technical rule regarding those ending in *triṣṭubh*.
The deity is Agni. Thus says the Anukramaṇikā: “*tvamagne yūnā*: Hiraṇyastūpa [composed] an Āgneya hymn; it is in Triṣṭubh, with the last two verses being Aṣṭi.
This hymn, beginning with “*tvamagne prathamaḥ*,” is used in the Prātaranuvāka during the Āgneya sacrifice and in the Āśvina Śastra.

In the section beginning with “Now, of this night,” it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “O Agni, you are the first Aṅgiras, the seer; born of great power, the immortal one pierces [the darkness]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
This hymn is to be used as the insertion for the Jātavedas Nivid at the Āgnimāruta Śastra on the third day of the Abhiplava sacrifice.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the section beginning with “The third day of this [period]”: “The Āgnimāruta [Śastra] begins with ‘O Agni, you are the first Aṅgiras’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, at the Āgnimāruta-śastra, this Jātavedasya hymn is to be inserted as the *nivid*; for it has been stated [in the Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.1]: "The third pressing is recited with the third *abhilāvika* [hymn]. Thus, because of that [rule], it is already established.
O Agni, you were the first Aṅgiras, the seer and god; you became the auspicious friend of the gods. Under your law, the Maruts were born—all skillful workers, unwearied and vigorous.
O Agni, you were the first Aṅgiras, the seer and god; you became the auspicious friend of the gods. Under your ordinance, the Maruts were born—all-performing and skillful artisans. || 1 ||
O Agni, you are the first and primordial among all the Aṅgirasas because of being their progenitor;
such a one became the Ṛṣi named Aṅgiras. And thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Those who were the embers became the Aṅgirasas" (AiB 3.34).
Thus, having yourself become a god (*deva*), you became the auspicious (*śiva*) friend of other gods.

In your service (*vrata*), your ritual action, the Maruts—wise sages (*kavayaḥ*), those of noble deeds (*vipranāpasaḥ*), those who have pervaded all with knowledge or whose deeds are known, and those of shining vision (*bhrājadṛṣṭayaḥ*) with blazing weapons—were born as the deities known by that name.
"Vipra-nāpasaḥ": [the root] *vid* means "to know"; thus, a *vipra* is one who possesses knowledge (*vedana*).

Due to the inclusion of the word *bahula*, the suffix *map* is applied according to the *uṇādi* rules. Then, by the rule *pāmādibhyo naḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.100), the suffix *na* is added in the sense of "that which belongs to this. The final syllable is udātta due to the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Those whose deeds are wise are "vipranāpasaḥ.
Due to the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* in the rule "anyeṣām api dṛśyate," the lengthening of the vowel occurs even at the time of the *avagraha*.
They were born.

The root *jan* is used in the sense of manifestation (*prādurbhāva*). In its [derivative] form *janya*, there is the substitution of *ja* by [Pāṇini’s rule] *jñā-naji-jāḥ* (Pā. Sū. 7.3.79). [Thus, the term is] *ājadṛṣṭayaḥ*.
"ājū dīsau":
[the suffix] śat is used by way of transposition (vyatyaya);
since it is a *lasārvadhātuka*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
The word *ṛṣi* is derived from the root *ṛṣ* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *ki*, according to the rule *kic-ka-tau ca saṃjñāyām*.
Consequently, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is retained.
O Agni, you are the first, the best of the Aṅgirases; as a seer, you encompass the sacred law of the gods.
All-pervading, wise for the entire world, son of two mothers, you who lie down—how many times have you helped us?
O Agni, you, the first, the most excellent Aṅgiras, the seer, encompass the sacred law of the gods.
Threefold, wise for the sake of every world, son of two mothers, you lie in many places for the sake of man. 2.

O Agni, you, being the first, the primordial, and the most excellent of the Aṅgirasas—having become preeminently an Aṅgiras—and being a *kavi*, a wise seer, you adorn (*paribhūṣasi*) the *vratam*, the ritual action, of the other gods on all sides.
Of what nature are you? You are *vibhu*, manifold, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the entire world (*viśvasmai bhuvanāya*).
The meaning is that he assumes many forms, such as the Āhavanīya fire and others. "Medhiraḥ" means wise; "dvimātā" means born from two [pieces of] fire-wood (araṇi).
Or alternatively:
The creator of the two worlds;
for the sake of humanity, O Vāyu, in how many ways—by how many modes—are you everywhere *śayuḥ*, i.e., lying down?
The meaning is that no one knows how many such modes there are for you as you abide in the various houses of men.
You adorn (*bhūṣasi*). The root *bhūṣ* [in the sense of] "adornment" belongs to the *bhūvādi* class.
Vibhuḥ: By the rule *viprasaṃbhyo dvasaṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.180), the suffix *ḍa* is added to the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *vi*.
The accentuation follows the rule for the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
For *bhuvana*: the suffix *kyun* is applied according to *uṇādisūtra* 2.238, *bhū-asū-bhṛ-sji-bhyaś chandasi*.

In the case of *yoḥ*, there is no substitution [of the final vowel], and it is acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the rule regarding the accent of the negative particle (*nisvara*).
*Medhiraḥ*:
[The root] *medha* means "to congeal" (*saṃga*).
From this, the suffix *iran* is applied by way of general rule (*bāhulaka*).
Nisvara; dvimātṛ:
he whose two mothers exist is "dvimātṛ."

The suffix *kap* [prescribed] by the rule *nadyataśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.153) does not apply here, because *mātṛ* and *mātṛkā* are mentioned separately; thus, it is stated that the optional application of *kap* under the rule *nadyataśca* is contingent upon the word *mātṛ*.
Due to its inclusion in the *tricakrādi* group, the word has udātta accent on the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*).
Alternatively:
The mother of two is *dvimātā*; by the rule "of a compound," it has an udātta accent on the final syllable. *Śayuḥ*.
From the root *śīṅ* in the sense of "sleeping," the suffix *up* is applied according to the rule *bhṛmṛśī* (Uṇādi-sūtra 1.7), etc., resulting in the word *svapna*.
[The word] *katidhā* [is formed similarly].

For the word *kiṃ* ending in *-tya*, there is the designation of "number" (*saṃkhyā*) by the rule *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.23). Then, by the rule *saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā* (Pāṇini 5.3.42), the suffix *dhā* is applied. [The form] *āyave*:
the suffix *uṇ* is applied by the rule *chandasīnaḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.2).
1. Because it is stated that [the result] is contingent upon conditions (*jha-pākṣikatva*):
"O Agni, you were the first to be manifested by Mātariśvan through the desire for good wisdom for Vivasvat.
Both heaven and earth trembled at the choosing of the Hotṛ; O Vasu, you have bestowed great wealth upon us, O worthy of sacrifice."

O Agni, you are the first for Mātariśvan; manifest yourself through your excellent wisdom for Vivasvat. The two worlds, heaven and earth, trembled at your election as the Hotṛ-priest. O Vasu, you have assumed the burden of the great sacrifice. 3.
O Agni, you exist as the first—that is, the foremost—for Mātariśvan;
for, in accordance with the statement "Agni, Vāyu, Āditya" (Nirukta 7.7), your preeminence is understood everywhere.
As such, through *sukratūyā*—the desire for excellent action—manifest yourself, become visible, for Vivasvat, the sacrificer who serves [you].
Having seen your power, heaven and earth (rodasī) trembled and shook;
for Yāska states: "The roots *abhyas* and *rej* signify fear and trembling" (Nirukta 3.21).
At the *hotṛvūrya*, that is, at the choosing of the Hotṛ priest.
O Vāyu, you have roared toward the sky for the sake of showing favor to Manu;
you have proclaimed that the heavenly world is to be attained through meritorious deeds.
For the sake of Purūravas—the king of that name who was performing service to you—you became exceedingly gracious, resulting in most auspicious fruits and actions.
When you are released— that is, produced— by the friction of the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) through rapid churning,
then they first led you from the eastern region (*vedaḥ*) to establish you as the *āhavanīya* fire;
afterwards, they led you to the western region to bring you forth in the form of the *gārhapatya* fire.
The meaning is that after the performance of the *āhavanīya* rite, they maintained [the fire] in the form of the *gārhapatya*.
The root *vāś* means "to sound.
[It is used] for Purūravas.
*Purūravas* means "he who cries out much" (*puru rauti*).

From the root *ru* in the sense of "sound," with the *uṇādi* suffix *asun*, the lengthening of the first member of the compound is prescribed by the rule: "And in *puras*, [there is] *purūravas*" (*uṇādi-sūtra* 4.671).
Regarding *sukṛte*: the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *sukarmapāpamantrapuṇyeṣu kṛñaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.89),
and from that, the augment *tuk* is added.
In *pitroḥ*, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending is due to the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt.
[In *mucyase*, the suffix is acute.]

Because it is taught as having an initial vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented. Although, according to the rule "the accent of that which remains is stronger, except in the case of *vikaraṇas*," the accent of the *vikaraṇa*—even though it is subsequently prescribed (*satiśiṣṭa*)—does not override the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*, nevertheless, it certainly overrides the accent of the verbal root (*dhātu*), because it has been stated that "the accent of the *bhā* [suffixes] overrides the accent of the root. Therefore, when the accent of the *yak* itself would have been expected, there is instead an initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatvam*) by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
O Agni, you are the bull who increases prosperity; you become worthy of renown for the one who is free from impurity.
You who know the offering that brings rain, you alone, O Agni, win over the people.

O Agni, you are the bull, the increaser of prosperity; you become worthy of renown for the one who is pure and free from sin. O Agni, sole life-force, you who know the oblation and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, you cause the people to prosper. ||5||

O Vṛṣabha, you are the showerer of desires and the increaser of prosperity, the cause of the increase of wealth and nourishment for the sacrificer. For the sake of favoring the sacrificer—who is endowed with a pure ladle (*sruca*) raised upward—you are *śravāyya*, one to be heard through the sacred mantras.
That sacrificer who thoroughly knows (*pariveda*), that is, offers, the oblation accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ* call.
Vekāyu: O foremost Agni, you, as the leader, enter that first sacrificer; you illuminate—that is, you cause to shine forth from all sides—the subjects who are favorable to him.
*Puṣṭivardhana*:
[derived from] the root *vṛdh* in the sense of "to increase";
from this causative (*ṇijanta*) form, the suffix *lyu* is applied because it belongs to the *nandy-ādi* group.
By the rule *ltisvareṇa*, the first syllable of the final member [of the compound] becomes udātta;
by the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*, that very accent remains. [This applies to the word] *urgatasuce*.
The root *yam* means "to cease.

From this root, preceded by the prefix *ut*, the suffix *kta* (called *niṣṭhā*) is applied; then, by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa," there is the elision of the nasal. By the rule "gatiranantaraḥ," the preceding prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *ugratā-sukyenā*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
Regarding the word *veda*: in the *saṃhitā* text, the lengthening occurs according to the rule “*vyaco 'tastikaḥ*.”
O Agni, you who are all-seeing, you deliver the man who follows crooked paths through his deeds at the assembly;
he who, in the clash for heroes where booty is to be seized, slays the many even when they have encountered only a few.

O Agni, you deliver the man who follows a crooked path through his deeds at the assembly, O far-seeing one; for when the heroes strive together for wealth in the clash of battle, even with few men you strike down many in the encounter.
1. *ca-pha-mukhyāyu*:

O *vicaṣaṇa*, endowed with distinguished knowledge, O *agni*, you protect, preserve, or fulfill at the *vidatha*—the ritual action worthy of being joined (*sacana*)—the man who walks in crooked ways, who has strayed from the path, and who is devoid of good conduct.
The meaning is: "You perform that which is joined with the execution of good deeds.

"You, who [are present] in the *paritakmyā*—that is, in the battle which must be traversed on all sides, which is like wealth (*dhana*), most dear to the arrows, and which is to be sought after by means of arrows (*śarasātā*)—[you are there] even among those few (*adabhra*) men who are devoid of valor.
Regarding this, Yāska says: "'*Dabhra*' and '*arbha*' mean 'small' (*alpa*). (Nirukta 3.20).
When the spear is properly hurled to fight, for the sake of favoring that [spear], you strike—that is, you kill—the many powerful opposing enemies;
such is the meaning of your greatness.
*vṛjinavartinam*:
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *vṛjinā vartinyā*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) of the first member. *sakaman*.
The root *vac* means "to assemble. The suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well.
The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "not before *iva*, *śi*, or a *kṛt* suffix."
The substitution of *k* for *p* occurs by virtue of the rule *nyaṅkv-āditvāt* (Pāṇini 7.3.53).
The locative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). [Thus: *piparṣi*.
The root *pṛ* is used in the senses of protecting and filling.
In the case of the suffix *sip*, there is the augment *śrau*, reduplication, the substitution of *ha* for *hasva*, the replacement of *at* by *ava*, and the retention of the initial consonant;
furthermore, by the rule "atipipyośca," the vowel of the reduplicated syllable is changed to *i*.

Regarding *śarasātā*: from the root *śu* in the sense of "to go" (*gatau*), the word *śara* ends in the suffix *ran* and is accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*) according to the Unādi Sūtra 2.183: *śuṣicimīnāṃ dīrghaśca*.
The word *sāti* is derived from the root *ṣaṇ* (meaning "to share" or "to enjoy") with the suffix *ktin*. The substitution of *ā* for *a* occurs by the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ*.
In this *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that in which there is a sharing (*sāti*) of arrows"—the accent of the first member remains as its original form.
In the expression "supāṃ suluk," the suffix *ḍā* is substituted for the locative case ending. [The word] *paritakmye* [is derived from] the root *taka*, meaning "to laugh."
From this [root], the suffix *mak* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the *Uṇādi* rules.
The suffix *ya* is applied by the rule "and in the Vedic language" (*chandasi ca*, Pāṇini 5.1.67), as in the sense "one who goes there.

In the compound, by the rule "prepositions [are compounded] with a word in the nominative when meaning 'gone' and so forth" (*prādayo gatādyarthe prathamayā*, Pāṇini-mahābhāṣya 2.2.18.4), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) which is the prior member is maintained.
*dabhrebhiḥ*:
from the root *dabh* (in the sense of "to deceive"),
the suffix *rak* is applied according to the rule beginning with *sphāyitañci*.
In the word *samṛtā*, there is no substitution of *ais* for the case-ending *bhis*, because of the rule "this [substitution] occurs frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). Regarding the accent,
the preceding particle *gati* retains its original pitch (*prakṛtisvaratvam*) according to the rule "a *gati* that is not separated by another word [retains its accent]."
The form is as before. [In the word] *haṃsi*, there is an anusvāra by the rule "naścāpadāntasya jhali" (Pāṇini 8.3.24) applied to the suffix *sip* of the root *han*.
Just as there is no blow [to the self] through union with that;

[the word] *bhūyasaḥ* [is derived as follows]: by the rule "The *ī* of *īyasun* following *bahu* is elided, and *bahu* becomes *bhū*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.158), there is the elision of the *ī* of the suffix *īyasun* after the word *bahu*, and the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu*.
By virtue of being a *niti*, it has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
O Agni, you bestow immortality in the highest state upon the mortal for the sake of glory day by day—
you who, being thirsty, provide nourishment for both races and bring the sun to the mortal man.

O Agni, you establish that mortal in supreme immortality for the sake of glory day by day—you, who, being thirsty, provide nourishment to both classes of beings, like a youth, and bring them toward the light of the sun. 7.
O Agni, you place—that is, you sustain—such a person who serves you day by day for the sake of renown (*śravase*) in the highest immortality (*amṛtatve*), the supreme state free from death.

That sacrificer who, desiring both kinds of progeny—for the sake of obtaining the two types of offspring, namely bipeds and quadrupeds—becomes intensely yearning (*tatṛṣāṇaḥ*), for that sacrificer, who possesses true knowledge (*sūrye abhijñāya*), you provide *mayaḥ*, which is happiness; for according to another Vedic text, "that which is happiness is indeed *mayaḥ*."
And you also bring forth food from all sides; you produce it everywhere.
*tṛṣāṇaḥ*:
[derived from] *tṛp* in the sense of thirsting;
the suffix *kānac* is applied after the root in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
Because it contains a *cit* vowel, the first syllable is udātta.
In the *saṃhitā*, the long vowel is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) irregularity.
[The form] is *kṛṇoṣi*.
The root *kṛvi* belongs to the meaning of "injuring" and "doing.
The suffix *up* is applied according to the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca*.
There is an optional prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule *cādi-lope vibhāṣā*.
1. [The letters *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *pha* are not present.
O Agni, being praised, make us a glorious singer for the winning of riches.
May we succeed through our new and skillful work; O divine Heaven and Earth, protect us!

O Agni, being praised, make us glorious and the singer [of hymns] successful in the winning of riches. May we prosper in our work with new ritual action. O Heaven and Earth, together with the gods, protect us! 8.
Arising from the distant place while being praised, do you, at the time for giving us wealth, make for us a son—a maker of deeds, endowed with glory, and a performer of action.
Through a new, obtained, and enduring son, may we increase our ritual acts, such as sacrifices and offerings.
O Heaven and Earth, both deities, together with the other gods, protect us excellently!
*Yaśasam*:
the suffix *ac* is applied because it belongs to the *arśas-ādi* group;
by virtue of this suffix, the preceding vowel receives the udātta accent.

Alternatively, by the rule “*kvip* should be prescribed after all nominal stems” (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kvivaktavyaḥ*, Pāṇini-mahābhāṣya 3.1.11.3), the suffix *kvip* is added to the word *yaśas*. Since that [form] ending in a suffix belongs to the class beginning with *san* and ending with *añc*, it receives the designation of a verbal root (*dhātu*). Consequently, because the suffix *kvip* is applied last (being *satiśiṣṭa*) among those ending in *kvip*, the final syllable of the verbal root is udātta by the rule “*dhātoḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.1.162).

"Kṛṇuhi. [In this form,] there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *hi* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.106, which states: "And after [a verbal root ending in] *u*, the elision of *hi* is optional in Vedic verse. [The form] is *stavānaḥ*.

By the rule "samyañc stuvaḥ" (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.246), the suffix *ānac* is applied even to the root *stu* alone due to the frequentative usage (*bahulavacanāt*). Because it belongs to the *vṛṣan*-class, it has the acute accent on the first syllable.
[May we] prosper (*ṛdhyāma*).
The root *ṛdh* means "to increase.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
The augment *yāsuṭ* is acute-accented (*udātta*).
*dyāvāpṛthivī*:
the substitution *dyāvā* occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.3.29 (*divo dyāvā*). It bears the anudātta accent as an *āmantrita* (vocative).

O Agni, you are in the lap of our fathers, a shining one among the gods, O blameless and watchful one. Be a protector of the body and a providence for the singer; O auspicious one, you bestow all wealth.

O Agni, you, the blameless god who is ever-watchful among the gods, have been born in the lap of your parents; be the creator of our bodies and the provident guardian for the singer. O auspicious one, you have gathered all wealth within yourself.

O blameless one, free from fault, you who are watchful among all the gods, being present in the lap—that is, in the vicinity—of the two parents, Heaven and Earth, become a maker of our bodies, that is, a creator of our forms as sons; be aware of us, meaning, show us favor. Likewise, for the singer, the performer of the rite—the sacrificer—be possessed of supreme wisdom in the form of grace; this is the sense.
O Agni, you who are the embodiment of auspiciousness and blessing, you pour forth (*vpiṣe*) all wealth (*viśvaṃ vasu*), that is, every kind of treasure, for the sake of the sacrificer.
[The word] *upasthe* [is formed from the root] *sthā* with the suffix *ka* by the rule *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4).

The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*. The acute accent on the final syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is applied according to the Vedic extension [of Pāṇini’s rule] *marudvṛdhādīnāṃ chandasy upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 6.2.106, vārttika 2). [Thus we have] *jāgṛviḥ*.

The root *jāgṛ* means "to wake" (*nidrākṣaye*). According to the rule *gṛdhastajāgṛbhyaḥ kin* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.414), the suffix *kin* is applied. Due to the *niṭ* designation of the suffix, the word is accented on the first syllable.
*Bodhi*: from the root *budh* in the sense of "understanding" (*avagamane*). By the rule "in the Veda [the suffix] is frequently elided," there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), because the absence of *pit*-status for the suffix *hi* is optional according to the rule "vā chandasi" (Pāṇini 6.4.76), it possesses *pit*-status; consequently, since the verbal stem (*aṅ*) is not marked with *ṅ*, the elision (*luk*) of *hi* occurs by the rule "aṅitaśca" (Pāṇini 6.4.103). Thereafter, the *guṇa* substitution of the light penultimate vowel takes place, followed by the elision of the final letter of the root.

1. [The forms] *na-pitṛ-rūpayoḥ*. 2. The suffix *ḍha-ka* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). [The word] *pramatiḥ*: from the root *man* (to know), with the suffix *ktin*; by the rule "anudāttapadam," etc., there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*). In the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose intellect (*mati*) is excellent (*prakṛṣṭā*)," the accent remains on the original form of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*). [The form] *upiṣe*: from the root *ḍu-vap* (to sow/secrete). In the Vedic *liṭ* [perfect], *thās* becomes *se*. By the rule "vacisvapi," etc., there is *saṃprasāraṇa* followed by the substitution of the preceding vowel. There is reduplication and the application of the *hlādiśeṣa* rule. By the restriction of the *krādiniyama*, there is the augment *iṭ*.
O Agni, you are our providence; you are our father; you are the creator of our strength. We are your kinsmen.
Hundreds and thousands of riches, along with noble heroes, come together unto you, O protector of the sacred law, O invincible one.

O Agni, you are our providence; you are our father; you are the maker of our strength. We are your kinsmen. O undeceivable guardian of the sacred law, hundreds and thousands of riches, accompanied by heroic sons, come together unto you who keep your vow.
O Agni, you are our *pramati*, endowed with a preeminent intellect characterized by grace toward us;
likewise, you are our father, our protector.
Likewise, you are the maker of vitality and the bestower of long life.
We, the performers of rites, are your *jāmi*s—your kinsmen.

O *adābhya*, O Agni who cannot be harmed by anyone, hundreds of riches (*rāyas*)—possessing the number one hundred—fully attain you, who are endowed with noble heroes (*suvīra*) and who protect the sacred observance (*vratapā*) of ritual action.
Likewise, thousands— that is, things numbering a thousand— of riches (*rāyaḥ*) come together [to him] who possesses good heroes (*suvīram*).

Although, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the rule “*nañsubhyām*” would require the final syllable of the second member to be accented, the rule “*vīravīryau ca*” (Pāṇini 6.2.120) prescribes that the first syllable of the second member is accented.
Regarding *adābhya*:

some say that *dabh* exists as a separate verbal root; [the form] is derived with the suffix *ṇyat* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.124.3, which states: "It should be stated [that the suffix applies] after *dabh*."
The gods made you, O Agni, the first living breath for the sake of Āyu, the lord of the clans of Huṣa.
They made Iḍā the ruler over the progeny of Manu; thus a son is born to me from my father.

The gods made you, O Agni, the first living being for the sake of living man, the lord of the clans of Nahuṣa; they made Iḷā the instructor of Manu’s progeny—when a son is born to me, whose father shall he be? 11.

O Agni, in ancient times the gods made you the first for Āyu—for the sake of Āyu, the specific descendant of Nahuṣa in human form; they made you Āyu, the lord of the people (*viśaspati*), the commander of the army.

Likewise, they made Iḷā, the daughter of Manu, known by that name, the instructor and the teacher of Dharma. Thus it is stated in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*: “Iḷā, indeed, was the daughter of Manu, desiring knowledge of sacrifice” (TB 1.1.4.4).

The Vājasaneyins also record this: "She said, 'Place me in the midst of the *anuyāja* offerings; through me, you shall obtain all desires. She [the earth] instructed Manu. This means: when a son is born to my father Aṅgiras—who is related to me, Hiraṇyastūpa—then at that time, O Agni, you yourself are the *āsīr* (benediction) in the form of a son; such is the ellipsis.
For Āyu.
The dative case is used here according to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.62.1, which states that the dative may be employed in the sense of "for the sake of" (yadarthe).
[This refers to] Nahuṣa.
The root *ṇah* means "to bind.
According to the Unādi Sūtra 4.515, *ṇah-ki-li-han-yati-lasi-bhya ucc*, the suffix *ucc* is applied;
due to its inclusion in the *vṛṣādi* group, it bears the udātta accent on the first syllable.
*Viśaspatim*: The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member [of the compound] is due to the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam*. *Manuṣasya*.
The word *manernin* is formed with the suffix *uṇ*; it has the udātta accent on the first syllable because it begins with a particle (*nipāta*). [The form] *śāsanīm*.

1. Regarding *jha-sa*, [the rule] "after *ś* [the suffix] *yat* is not applied" does not apply here. The root *ḍhā* means "to bind. From that [root], [the suffix *ana* is added]. 2. Regarding *ca-cha-jha-na-pha-śa-ṣa-ha*, by virtue of the diversity of grammatical usage (*bāhulaka*), there is the doubling of the consonant. The first syllable of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is accented acute (*udātta*).

That by which something is taught is called *śāsanī*; for it is derived with the suffix *hyuṅ* (i.e., *ana*) according to the rule "and after roots ending in *kṛt* [or those denoting instrument or location]."
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), etc.;
its initial syllable is acute (*udātta*) by the accent of the *liṅga*.
[The word *mama* means] "of whom am I"?

In the sense of "this is mine" (*mamedaṃ*), by the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), the suffix *aṇ* is applied; then, by the rule *tavakamamakāvekavacane* (Pāṇini 4.3.3), the word *asmad* is replaced by *mamaka*. There is no application of *vṛddhi* because of the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not necessarily permanent.
By means of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*), the word is udātta-accented on the first syllable.
O Agni, O God worthy of praise, protect us two, the liberal patrons, with your protections, O Turvaśa.
You are the savior of our offspring and progeny, and of our cattle, guarding them without blinking in accordance with your sacred law.

O Agni, with your protections, O God, guard us—the liberal patrons and Turvaśa—worthy of praise. You are the protector of our offspring and descendants, and of our cattle; you watch over us without blinking, remaining ever-vigilant within your sacred law. 12.
O Agni, O God worthy of praise, do you protect us, the wealthy ones, with your own protections;
likewise, protect even the bodies of our sons, Turvaśa and Yadu.
Our son’s offspring—the grandson and those following him—remain ever vigilant and attentive within your service; you are the protector of the cattle belonging to those who dwell therein.
The meaning is: for one such as you, what need is there to mention [your willingness] to protect us?
From *maghavan*, in the *śas* [nominative plural] case, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.133: *śrayuvamaghonām atkvite*.
From *tanu*.
By the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti*, the suffix *śas* is replaced by *jas*.
There is a prohibition of the long vowel resulting from the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* substitution by the rule *dīrghājjasi ca*.
By the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*, the *svarita* accent is applied.
For in the case of *śasi*, the accentuation of the case-ending would apply by the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt."
O Agni, you are kindled as the four-eyed guardian for the sacrificer who is vigilant;
you, who are maintained as one free from hostility by him who offers oblations, accept with your mind even the prayer of the poor man.

O Agni, you are kindled as the closest protector for the one who sacrifices, for the one who does not falter, you who possess four eyes; you who are maintained by him who offers oblations so that he may be free from harm—you accept even the prayer of the poor man with your mind. 13.

O Agni, you, the worshipful one, being the protector and guardian of the sacrificer who is worthy of worship, and being present as his intimate companion, are kindled—that is, you shine forth—with four eyes, meaning endowed with flames that serve as the seat of the senses in all four directions, for the sake of the sacrifice which is unassailable by demons.

O you who are free from predatory beasts, non-violent, and a nourisher—unto you, that sacrificer who has offered oblations, you grant with your own mind the mantra connected to him, which belongs to the singer (the praiser) himself; that is, you accept and solicit the hymn in the form of your own praise through your own consciousness.
For the sake of sacrifice (*yajyave*). The suffix *yu* is applied to the root *yaj* by the rule "yajimanisundhi" (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.300), etc., resulting in *pāyuḥ*.
The suffix *uṇ* is applied by the rule *kṛvāpājī* etc.; the augment *yuk* is added by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33). [Thus:
*aniṣaṅgāya*.
The root *sañj* means "to cling.
In the bahuvrīhi compound *anipajña*, because of the rule *nañsubhyām*, the final syllable of the subsequent member (*nipajña*) is udātta.
Thus: *caturakṣaḥ*.
He who possesses four unimpaired eyes is "four-eyed" (*caturakṣa*).
The suffix *ṣac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule *bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.113).
By the rule *citaḥ*, the word has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
For the sake of nourishment (*dhāyase*).

[The suffix] *yat* is applied after the verbal root √vah (1), after words ending in *ca*, *pha*, or *tas* (2), and after the word *yajvan* (3). The suffix *yat* is treated as having the *yu* designation; because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group, it is udātta-accented on its first syllable.

The suffix *asun* is applied by the rule *hābhābhyaśchandasi*. Because the term *ṇit* is understood from the previous context, the augment *yuk* is added by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*. [Thus we have] *kīreḥ*. [The root] *kṛt* means "to cut. From this causative (*ṇyanta*) form, the suffix *i* is applied by the rule *aca iḥ*; the *ṇi* is elided, and the elision of the other [part of the] root is Vedic. [The word] *mantram*: [the root] *matri* means "to speak secretly. By adding the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), it is acutely accented on the first syllable due to its inclusion in the *vṛṣādi* group. [The verb] *vanoṣi*: [the root] *vanu* means "to beg. The suffix *u* is added by the rule *tanādikṛbhya uḥ*. The accent belongs to the suffix.

Thou art the first to grant wide renown to the singer who seeks thy favor; that supreme wealth which thou winnest for him, thou art called the father even of the ignorant, providing him with providence. Thou instructest the simple, being more wise than those who know, as thou ordainest the two directions of space.

O Agni, that which you win as supreme wealth for the widely-praised worshipper—that you call your own; even for the lowly, you are called their guardian and father. You instruct the simple one, you who are more knowledgeable, directing him toward the two worlds. 14.

O Agni, for the sake of the priest—the *vāghat*—who possesses wide renown (*uruśaṃsa*) and is worthy of praise by many, you desire that he, the performer of the rite, may obtain that most excellent and desirable wealth (*rekṇas*). Likewise, you are called by the wise the "Father," the protector endowed with supreme intelligence, even for the weak sacrificer who must be supported and nourished from all sides. Thus, as one of superior knowledge, you [protect] the simple-minded child.
This is because of the lexicographical definition: "Infant (*potaḥ*), child (*pākaḥ*), boy (*arbhakaḥ*), and *ḍimbhaḥ*" (Amara-kośa 2.5.38).

Yāska also says the same: "A child (*pākaḥ*) is one who is to be nurtured (*paktavyaḥ*)" (Nirukta 3.12). You "instruct" (*praśāssi*) such a sacrificer—that is, you thoroughly provide him with instruction.
Likewise, you "govern" the directions, such as the East and so forth;
for in the absence of your command, there would be confusion among those who perform their duties.
Thus it is heard in scripture: "The gods, having settled upon the sacrificial ground, did not know the directions."
That [path] which goes toward the southern direction is turned back by Agni.

This too is recorded in that very [text]: "Going on the path for well-being, they discerned the eastern direction by means of her; [they discerned] the southern by means of Agni" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.5.1–2).
The Aitareyins have likewise recorded it: "Then he chose this boon: 'By me alone may you discern the eastern direction; by Agni, the southern'" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 1.7).
"Uruśaṃsāya":
[the root] *śaṃs* means "to praise. That which is praised is a *śaṃsa*.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an object (*karman*).
By the rule regarding the accent of the prefix *ni*, the word is initially udātta;
however, by the rule that the original accent of the final member of a compound is retained (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*), that very [initial] accent remains.
*Spāham*. [The compound] *spṛhā-sambandha*.
[The suffix] *aṇ* [is applied] by [the rule] "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*).
*Rekṇas*:
from the root *ric*, meaning "to emit" or "to leave.
By the rule *ricerdhane ghica* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.638), the suffix *asun* is applied.
By the word *ca*, the augment *nuṭ* is added.
By the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52),
there is the substitution of *k* for [the *j* of] *ādhasya*.
The root *ghrā* is used in the sense of "satiety.
By the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), the substitution of *ā* for *i* occurs.
Then, by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136), the suffix *ka* is applied.
*Śāssi*. [The root] *śās* [is used] in the sense of "instructing" (*anuśiṣṭi*).
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
Since *sip* is unaccented (*anudātta*) after [the prefix] *pra*, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
In the phrase "you govern the ripening and you govern the quarters," the sense of "and" (*ca*) is understood;
therefore, by the rule "optionally when there is elision of *ca* and so forth" (*cādilope vibhāṣā*), the first finite verb ending (*tiṅvibhakti*) is not dropped.
*Viduṣṭaraḥ*:

From the word *vidut* with the suffix *tarap*, the designation *bha* is applied by the rule *ayasmādīni chandasi* (Pāṇini 1.4.20). Consequently, by the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and substitution of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*). Finally, the change to *ṣ* is applied by the rule *śāsivasi*.
Since *tarap* is marked with the *pittva* indicatory letter, it is *anudātta*; therefore, by the accent of the suffix *vasu*, the vowel *u* is *udātta*.
1. Va-pha: there is wealth in cattle. 2. Ḍha: delusion regarding the directions; na: absence of delusion.
3. Jha-ḍha: from the southern direction.
O Agni, you are not turned back; like a well-sewn coat of mail, you protect the man who offers the sacrificial fee from every side.
He who provides sweet food in the dwelling, who makes it pleasant, and who performs the sacrifice—such a one is equal to heaven itself.

O Agni, you protect on every side the man who offers the sacrificial fee, like well-sewn armor. He who provides sweet food, who makes his dwelling pleasant during the winter, and who performs the sacrifice for life—he indeed reaches the height of heaven. 15.

O Agni, you protect—that is, you thoroughly guard—from all sides the man, the sacrificer, by whom the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been bestowed upon the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Therein lies the illustration: just as armor (*varman*), well-fashioned and made seamless with needles, protects one in battle, so it is.

"O Earth, sweet and pleasant, dwelling in your home during the spring season, you who make the guests comfortable—whatever sacrificer performs the *jīvayāja*, a sacrifice accompanied by living beings or one accomplished through living, that sacrificer becomes a likeness, a model, of heaven (*divaḥ*).
The meaning is: just as heaven brings happiness to those who practice [virtue], so do you bring happiness to the officiating priests and others."
"Sewn" (*syūtam*):
[from the root] *pī*, "to weave" (*tantusaṃtāne*),
with the suffix *kta* according to the rule for the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*).
By the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
By the rule "chvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.19), the substitute *ūḍ* is applied for the letter *v*.
Thus, one who eats (*kṣadati*) sweet things (*svādūn*) is called *svādukṣmā*.
The root *kṣad* has the sense of eating (*atti*).

The suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen [to be used] after other roots as well. Since it begins with a nasal (*nit*), it is accented on the first syllable; this results in the accentuation of the original form of the second member of the compound (*kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svara*).
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, however, there is a reversal [of the usual gender]. *Jīvayāja*:
"the sacrifice in which living priests (*jīva-ṛtvij*) are sacrificed to"—that is, honored with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)—here the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
The absence of the *kutva* change is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively,
*jīvayāja* refers to the sacrificing with living beings, that is, with animals.

The suffix *dhañ* is added to the root *yājayati*. Due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the elision of the *ṇi*-affix—by the rule *ṇeraniṭi*—the substitution of *k* for *j* (as prescribed by *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*) does not occur.
By the accentuation rule for *thāthādi* compounds, the final syllable of the second member bears the udātta accent.
This is an illustration.

In the *saṃhitā* [text], the elision of the nominative suffix *su-* occurs according to the rule: “The suffix *su-* is elided before a vowel, provided that the elision completes the metrical foot. Thus:
*divaḥ*.
By the rule "ūḍidam," the case ending is acute-accented.
Having performed the office of a priest (*ārtvijya*), one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) should offer his own oblation with this verse, "O Agni, this [prayer]...

In the section beginning with "He chooses the priests," it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "In this manner, one who has not maintained the fires [offers] at home with [the verse], 'O Agni, forgive this transgression of ours' (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.23.23)."
O Agni, forgive this our transgression; forgive the path we have traveled from afar.
You are the friend, the father, and the guardian of those who offer Soma; you are the ground that makes mortals into seers.

O Agni, forgive this our transgression; forgive this path which we have traveled from afar. You are a kinsman, a father, and the wise protector of those who offer Soma; you are the ground that makes seers of mortal men. 16.
O Agni, forgive (*mīmṛṣaḥ*) this injury (*śaraṇi*)—in the form of a breach of our vows—which now pertains to us and has been committed by us;
likewise, forgive that path (*imadhvānam*) along which we have gone, having departed from afar to a distant place, abandoning the service of you in the form of the *agnihotra* and other rites.
You [are the protector] of the mortals who are worthy of Soma and perform its rituals.
1. [This is] for the purpose of reaching a distant place.
You are endowed with qualities such as fluidity (*āpya*) and so forth.

*Āpiḥ* means one who is to be reached; *pitā* means protector; *pramatiḥ* means possessed of excellent intelligence; *bhramiḥ* means *āmakaḥ*, which signifies the one who carries out the ritual action.
"Made by the seers" (ṛṣikṛta) means one who makes [them] visible; the sense is that he becomes manifest out of a desire to favor them. "Refuge" (śaraṇa).
From the root *śṛ* in the sense of "to injure," the *an* suffix is added according to the *uṇādi* rules; thus, *mīmṛṣaḥ*. From the root *sṛ* in the sense of "endurance" (*titikṣā*).

From this [root], when the suffix *ṇic* is added and *guṇa* is about to occur, the substitution of *ṛ* for the penultimate vowel is applied by the rule *nityaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.4.8). Then follow the elision of *ṇi*, reduplication, the retention of the first part (*lādiśeṣa*), the substitution of *o* for *ra*, the addition of *sa*, the elision of *nu*, and the lengthening of the single vowel. Finally, the *nighāta* accent is applied by the rule *tiṅatiṅaḥ*.
*Agāma*:
from the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going. The substitution of *gā* occurs by the rule *iṇo gā luṅi* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.45).
In the word *agātisthāḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*; the augment *aṭ* is acute (*udātta*). [The form] *bhramiḥ*.
In the word *amuna*,
the suffix *in* is applied by the rule *ameḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.560).
Following the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*), the preceding vowel takes the form of the subsequent one (*parapūrvatva*).
Because the term *kit* is understood from the rule *igupadhātkit*, there is a prohibition of *guṇa* due to its being *kit*;
and because it is *nit*, it has the acute accent on the first syllable.
O Agni, like Manu, O Aṅgiras, like Aṅgiras, like Yayāti, and like the ancients, sit upon this seat, O Pure One!
Come hither, bring the divine folk, and seat them upon the sacrificial grass; and sacrifice to that which is dear.

O Agni, like Manu, like Aṅgiras, O Aṅgiras, like Yayāti, come to our dwelling as in former times, O Pure One! Approach and bring hither the divine folk; seat them upon the sacred grass and sacrifice to the Beloved. 17.

O pure one, O you endowed with purity, O Aṅgiras, whose nature is to pervade, O Agni, whose nature is to go here and there for the purpose of receiving the oblation, come toward this place—go with directness to the seat, the site of sacrifice.
Regarding that, there are four illustrations:
as Manu goes to the place of performance; as Aṅgiras goes; as King Yayāti by name goes; and as other ancient ancestors went in former times.
Just as Manu and others go to the sacrifice,
or just as you yourself go to the sacrifice of Manu and others—
having gone there, bring hither the divine host, the assembly of deities, to this ritual act.
Having brought them, seat those gods upon the sacrificial grass spread with darbha blades;
having seated them, sacrifice the beloved and desired oblation and give it.

As in the case of *manuvat*: the suffix *vati* is used either in the sense of the nominative case according to Pāṇini 5.1.115 (*tena tulyam*)—meaning "equal to that"—or in the sense of the genitive case according to Pāṇini 5.1.116 (*tatra tasyeva*).
Due to the presence of the *ayas* [suffix] and so forth, there is an absence of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*.
The accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*):
thus in *aṅgirasvat* and so forth; [the same applies to] *vaha*.
In the *saṃhitā*, there is a long vowel according to the rule "aco 'stiṅaḥ.
[The form] *yakṣi* is derived from the imperative (*loṭ*), with the elision of the suffix *śap* by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi."
In the word *serhyapicca*, the absence of the suffix *hi* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*);
[the resulting forms] undergo the changes to *ṣa* and *ka*.

In the *sāmidhenī* season, at the *ukhāsaṃbharaṇīya* sacrifice, the *puronuvākyā* for Agni accompanied by the *brahman* is this verse: "O Agni, by this *brahman*... This is prescribed in the section on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (4.1): "Having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices... 'O Agni, grow strong by this *brahman*; and let there be *brahman* and homage for you, O Jātavedas'."

O Agni, grow strong by this sacred prayer (brahman), whether we have performed it for you with skill or with knowledge. And lead us toward greater prosperity through our leaders; release us into your benevolence that is rich in strength.

By this prayer, O Agni, grow strong, whether we have performed it for you with skill or with knowledge. And lead us forward toward greater wealth; unite us with a benevolent favor that brings abundance. 18.
1. O Agni, in this rite, be strengthened by this *brahman*—the mantra employed by us;
and by our power (*śakti*) or our knowledge (*vid*), that hymn (*stotra*) which we have fashioned for you.

The phrase "by this prayer" (etena brahmaṇā) connects with what precedes. Furthermore, "lead us," that is, us who perform the rites, "to better fortune"—meaning to the excellence characterized by the attainment of greater wealth. "Unite us" with "benevolent thought directed toward the performance [of the rite]," that is, with a beautiful intellect accompanied by the power of the invocation. Join us together with it.
*vadhrava*: from the root *vṛdh* in the sense of “to grow”; the augment *aṭ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood.

By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is elision (luk) of the suffix śap; then the doubling [of the root], the substitution of the remaining initial consonant (halādiśeṣa), and the change of the vowel to 'a' (uratva). In the continuous text (saṃhitā), the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is due to Vedic usage.
In the word *śaktī*, by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the substitution of the third case ending (*-bhyām*) with a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one; furthermore,
because the suffix *ktin* has the marker *n*, it is accented on its first syllable.
vidā | By the rule *sāvekācaḥ*, the third case ending receives the udātta accent. nepi |
The root *ṇīj* is used in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*).
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
By the rule *upasargādasamāse ṇaḥ*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs.

By *sumatyā*, [the rule] beginning with *mankkin* establishes the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable of the subsequent member; this has been explained in detail in the first chapter (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.7.7).
The acute accent of the case-ending follows from the rule *udāttayaṇo hali*.
The second hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "indrasya nu vīryāṇi," has Hiraṇyastūpa Āṅgirasa as the seer and Triṣṭubh as the meter.
Indra is the deity;
this is according to the Anukramaṇikā, which states, "Of Indra, [the hymns] are five less.
In the Agniṣṭoma, at the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina-savana), during the Niṣkevalya Śastra, the hymn beginning with "indrasya nu vīryāṇi" is the Nividdhānīya Sūkta.

In the section titled "Of the Exclusive [Hymn]," it is stated: "One should insert the *nivid* addressed to Indra in this [hymn], 'Now, the heroic deeds of Indra' (*indrasya nu vīryāṇi*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.15).
This is also prescribed for that same *śastra* at the Viṣuvat day;

it is sūtra-ed in the section titled "The Viṣuvat is to be proclaimed by day": "Having recited the *nivid* addressed to Indra in this [hymn], 'Now, the heroic deeds of Indra'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.6).
This very same [application] is also enjoined for the Mahāvrata and the Nikevalya:
in the section beginning “The Rathantara is the right wing,” it says, “He makes the four Satīs into six Bṛhatīs: ‘I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra’” (Ai. Ā. 5.2.2).

Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra, those which the wielder of the thunderbolt performed in the beginning: he slew the dragon, released the waters, and shattered the obstructors, cleaving asunder the mountains.

Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra, those which the wielder of the thunderbolt performed in the beginning: he slew the serpent, he released the waters, and he shattered the trees and the ridges of the mountains. 1.

Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), endowed with the *vajra*, performed those deeds characterized by valor and prowess which were primary, ancient, and already established; I shall now quickly proclaim those exploits of that Indra. As for what those exploits were, it is said:
he slew *ahi*, the cloud.
This is his first heroic deed (*vīrya*).
Furthermore, he "pierced" (*tatarda*) the waters—that is, he struck them down upon the earth;
this is his second heroic deed.
He split apart the flowing rivers belonging to the mountains—that is, he caused them to flow by dragging both banks;
this is his third heroic deed.
The same should be understood for the subsequent cases as well.

The word *vīryāṇi* [is derived as follows]: from the root *śūra-vīra-vikrāntau* (meaning "to be brave" or "to exert valor"), with the suffix *ṇi*, and then by the rule *aco yat* (*Pāṇini* 3.1.97), the suffix *yat* is applied.

By the rule *ṇer aniṭi*, there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi*. By the rule *tisr udāttā*, the word *tisraḥ* bears the *svarita* accent. By the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, the initial acute (*ādyudātta*) accent does not apply.

For if the word were *ādyudātta* (having the acute accent on the first syllable), then in a *bahuvrīhi* compound with *suṣāda*, the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member would already be established by the rule “*ādyudāttaṃ chandasi*” (in the Vedic language, [the first syllable of the second member] is acute); consequently, the further prescription in the rule “*vīravīryau ca*” would be redundant.
Therefore, it is understood that the *ādyudātta* accentuation prescribed by the rule “*yato 'nāvaḥ*” does not apply to the word *vīra*. 1. *Śa-vasumattara* signifies the characteristic of strength.
2. "I shall speak quickly.
3. "What are the energies? And what are those energies? (Ṛgveda 10.119.30)

Thus [it is said]. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the suffix itself is *svarita* according to the rule "that which ends in *ti* is *svarita*" (*titsvaritam*). [In the form] *vocaṃ*: the substitution of *aṅ* for *ciṅ* occurs by the rule "for *as*, *vac*, and *khyā*, there is *aṅ*" (*asyativaktikhyātibhyo'ṅ*). The absence of the augment *aṭ* occurs by the rule "in the Veda, it is frequent even when not joined with *mā*" (*bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge'pi*). [In the form] *cakāra*: by the accent of the *liṭ*-suffix, the syllable preceding the suffix is acute (*udātta*). Because of its connection with the particle *yat*, it does not lose its accent (*anighāta*). [In the form] *ahan*: in the *laṅ* tense, after the elision of the *i* by the rule "and after [a root ending in] *i*" (*itaśca*), the *t* is elided by the rule "after [stems ending in] consonants, *ṅī*, or *ā*" (*halaṅyābhyaḥ*). [In the form] *aham*: from the root *han* preceded by *āṅ*, the suffix *im* is applied by the rule "after *āṅ*, *śri* and *han*, there is *im* and shortening" (*āṅi śrihanibhyāṃ hrasvaśca*; Uṇādisūtra 4.577); there is also the shortening of *āṅ*. By the word *ca* [in the rule], the fact that the suffix is *ḍit* and the acute accent on the first member of the compound are drawn over from the rule "after *veñ*, there is *ḍit*; the first member has the acute accent" (*veño ḍit, samāne rayaśrodāttaḥ*). Then, upon the elision of the *ṭi*, the first member retains its acute accent. [In the form] *tatadam*: from the root *uñdi* meaning "to injure" or "to disregard. It loses its accent by the rule "a finite verb loses its accent after another finite verb" (*tiṅatiṅaḥ*). [In the form] *vakṣaṇāḥ*: from the root *vakṣ* meaning "anger. The suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule "after *kuṣ*, *maṇḍ*, etc. (*kuṣamaṇḍādibhyaśca*; Pāṇini 3.2.151). The accent of the suffix overrides the *cit*-accent by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).

He slew the dragon resting upon the mountain; Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for him the thunderbolt that roars like heaven. Like lowing cows, the waters, flowing swiftly, have gone straight down to the ocean. He slew the dragon resting upon the mountain; Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for him the thunderbolt that roars like heaven. Like lowing cows, the waters, flowing swiftly, have gone straight down to the ocean.
He struck—that is, he slew—the serpent (ahi) who had taken refuge upon the mountain;
for this Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, the architect of the universe, fashioned the thunderbolt (vajra), which was well-projected or, alternatively, worthy of being proclaimed through praise.
When the cloud was split by that thunderbolt, the waters, flowing forth with their currents, went straight down into the ocean.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like cows lowing with cries toward their calves.
Just as cows go suddenly to the calves' dwelling, so it is here.
"Śiśriyāṇam":
[derived from] the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" (*sevāyām*),
with the suffix *kānac* of the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The rules for reduplication, *bahula*, *ādiśeṣa*, and the substitution of *yaṅ* apply.
By the rule "the suffixally marked (*cit*) is udātta," there is high-pitched accent (*svarita*) at the end.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.

From this root, preceded by the prefix *su*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *ṛhaloṇyat*. Due to the principle that "a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not obligatory," the *vṛddhi* substitution does not take place.
Alternatively,
from the root *sū* in the sense of "to sound" or "to torment," with the suffix *ṇyat*, there is no *vṛddhi* as before;
by the rule *titsvaritam*, it bears the *svarita* accent.
They are called *vāśrāḥ* because they low (*vāśanti*).
[The root] *vāśr* means "to sound. The suffix *rak* is applied according to the rule beginning with *sphāyitañci*.
They went.
By the rule "usi gamahana0," there is elision of the penultimate vowel.

Acting like a bull, he chose the Soma; at the Trikadruka rites, he drank of the pressed juice. Maghavan took up his missile, the thunderbolt; with it, he struck down him who was the first-born of the serpents. vṛṣāyamāṇaḥ (acting like a bull), avṛṇīta (chose), somam (the Soma), trikadrukeṣu (at the Trikadruka rites), apibat (drank), sutasya (of the pressed juice). ā (onward/up), sāyakam (missile), maghavā (Maghavan), adatta (took up), vajram (the thunderbolt), ahan (struck), enam (him), prathamajām (first-born), ahīnām (of the serpents).
Acting like a bull, behaving as a bull, Indra chose, that is, selected, the Soma.
The three sacrifices named Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus are called the Trikadrukās. Among those, he drank—that is, he consumed—a portion of the pressed-out Soma.
Maghavan, the wealthy Indra, took up his shaft— the binding thunderbolt—
and with that thunderbolt he struck the first-born cloud among the clouds.

*vṛṣāyamāṇaḥ*: acting like a bull (*vṛṣa*). The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.11 (*kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*), and the vowel is lengthened by Pāṇini 7.4.25 (*akitsārvadhātukayoḥ*). Since the root begins with a short vowel (*adupadeśāt*), it is udātta at its end; thus, the suffix *kyaṅ* also results in an udātta at the end of the verbal base. *sāyakam*: from the root *biñ* in the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*). It is called *sāyaka* because it binds (*sinoti*). The suffix *ṇvul* is added, and by the accent rule for *lit* (Pāṇini 6.1.193), it is udātta on the first syllable. *prathamajām*: born first (*prathamaṃ jāyate*). The suffix *vid* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.67 (*janasanakhanakramagamavidviśibhyaḥ kvan*). By Pāṇini 6.4.41 (*vidnoḥ*), the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel occurs.
O Indra, when you, with the Ahi, struck down the first-born illusions of the great deceivers,
and thereby generated the sun, the sky, and the dawn— since then, indeed, you have found no enemy.

When you, O Indra, struck down the first-born of the serpents, and then, with your piercing power, destroyed the wiles of the sorcerers; when you brought forth the sun, the sky, and the dawn—since that time, indeed, you have found no enemy at all.
Moreover, O Indra, when you struck down the first-born cloud among the many clouds, and thereafter utterly destroyed the illusions belonging to the deceitful Asuras,
you then existed generating the sun, the dawn, and the sky, illuminating them by removing the obscuring clouds.
At that time, because of the absence of obscuring darkness, you indeed did not find—nor, it is said, did you obtain—an enemy, a slayer, or a foe.
*ahan*. In the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *han*, there is elision of the suffix *si* by the rule "hanty-ādy-aḥ";
the augment *aṭ* is acute (*udātta*).
Just as there is no destruction through union with that [state],
so it is for those possessed of *māyā*.
Since the word *māyā* is listed among the *vrīhy-ādi* group, the possessive suffix *ini* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.2.116 (*vrīhy-ādibhyaś-ca*).
*Amīnaḥ*: from the root *mīñ* in the sense of "to injure," belonging to the *kryādika* (curādi) class.

The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *mīnāter nigame* (Pāṇini 7.3.81). *Tādītnā* is derived from *tadānīm*, where there is a transposition of letters (*varṇaviparyaya*) due to its inclusion in the *pr̥ṣodarādi* group.
It is said that the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "nipātasya"; thus,
*vivitse*.
In the root *vid* meaning "to find," the augment *iṭ*,
which would have been required by the rule governing roots beginning with *krī*, does not occur due to an irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
Indra struck Vṛtra, the great obstructor, across the shoulder with his massive thunderbolt, his deadly weapon;
like tree trunks hewn down by an axe, the serpent lies prostrate upon the earth.
Indra slew Vṛtra, the worst of Vṛtras, Vyansa—with his great bolt, his mighty weapon. Like tree trunks hewn down by an axe, the serpent lies prostrate, pressed close against the earth. || 5 ||
This Indra, having prepared his thunderbolt—that great weapon—with that thunderbolt he struck Vṛtra, the one who excessively obstructed the worlds in the form of darkness;
or rather, he who overcomes all enemies through obstructions (vṛtras). He struck that Asura named Vṛtra so that his shoulders were separated, as it were, with severed arms.
There is an illustration regarding the cutting of the shoulder:
"by the vajra" means by an axe; "vivṛkṇa" means specifically severed limbs;
"skandhān iva" means just as the trunks of trees are cut, so it is in that manner.
That being so, Vṛtra lies outside the earth, closely joined (*upapṛk*) with it; he makes his bed, meaning he falls to the ground like a split log.
*vṛtrataram*: from the root *vṛ* (or *vṛt*) in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*). The word *vṛtra* ends in the suffix *rak*, according to the rule beginning with *sphāyitañci*.

One crosses over everything by means of *vṛtra*, which is an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*). 1. By the rule for roots taught with a final *jha* vowel (Pāṇini 6.1.197), the root is udātta on its final syllable. 2. By the rule for suffixes taught with a final *ḍha* vowel (Pāṇini 6.1.163), it is immediately followed by that [udātta]. 3. By the rule for the suffix *ḍha* (Pāṇini 4.4.80). 4. By the rule for the suffix *ḍha* (Pāṇini 4.4.80), it means "that which covers" (*āvāraka*). Thus, it is *vṛttataraḥ*.
The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *tṛ* according to the rule *pacādyac*.

By the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam*, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the initial syllable of the second member of the compound; however, in the case of the suffix *tarap*, the accentuation is shifted by means of metrical license (*vyatyaya*).

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member applies, there is the circumflex accent (*svarita*) according to the rule "of a *yaṇ* resulting from an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel.

[The word] *vadhena*: by the rule "and *vadha* from *han*," the suffix *ap* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*); simultaneously with that, the root *han* undergoes the substitution *vadh*.
And that [suffix] has its acute accent on the final syllable.

There is elision of the final *a* by the rule "elision of *at*" (*ato lopaḥ*). By the rule regarding the accent of the disappearance of an acute accent (*udāttanivṛttisvara*), the suffix becomes acute.
*Vivṛkṇā*: [derived from] the root *vṛj* with the prefix *vi-*, meaning "to cut. The suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
By the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.

By the rule *oditaśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.45), the status of being a *niṣṭhā* [perfective participle] applies because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. Then, when the substitution of *pa* [for *na*] would be applicable by the rule *vaścaśraja*, the status of *natva* is established by the principle: "The substitute of a *niṣṭhā* is established before suffixes that have a different vowel as their initial sound, except in the case of rules concerning the augment *it*. Because *natva* is thus established, there is no *atva* [of the *niṣṭhā* ending], and consequently, the substitution of *pa* does not occur.
In the case of the verbal root *kṛ* when it is to be applied [as a suffix], there is the substitution of *ku* for *cu* according to Pāṇini’s rule *coḥ kuḥ* (8.2.30), resulting in *kurve*;
the elision of the *ś* suffix is according to *śeś chandasi bahulam* (6.1.70);
and the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratvam*) of the prefix (*gati*) is maintained according to *gatiranantaraḥ* (6.2.49).
It lies down.
The absence of the suffix *śap* is due to the rule "in the Veda, [the substitution] is frequent.
Of the earth.
The acute accent (udātta) of the case-ending is due to the rule: “udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt.”

Like one who fights, the intoxicated [foe] indeed challenged the great hero, the fierce crusher of the *ṛjīṣa*. He did not escape the onset of his weapons; shattered, the one whose enemy was Indra fell apart.

Like one who fights without arms, the one difficult to intoxicate has indeed challenged the great hero, the mighty oppressor, the drinker of the dregs. He has not escaped the onset of his weapons; shattered, he whose enemy was Indra has been mangled.
Vṛtra, intoxicated by evil pride and filled with arrogance, challenged Indra—just as one who is unfit for battle challenges a warrior. Indeed, he called upon him.
What kind of Indra?

A great hero, exalted by his virtues, having become great, impelled by valor, a mighty oppressor (*tuvibādha*) who afflicts many, and a consumer of the *ṛjīṣa* (the residue of the Soma) who drives away enemies.
The aforementioned Durmada was unable to cross—that is, he was unable to overcome—the gathering or encounter with the weapons of those enemies belonging to such an Indra.

Vṛtra, whose enemy was Indra (or for whom Indra was the slayer of his foe), being slain by Indra, fell into the rivers; thus, "rujānāḥ" (breaking), he thoroughly crushed the rivers. The meaning is that by the fall of Vṛtra’s body, which covered all the worlds, the banks of the rivers and the stones therein were completely pulverized.
Like "ayoddhā" (one who has no warrior).

In the *bahuvrīhi* compound "na vidyate yoddhā asya" (he for whom no warrior exists), the final syllable of the second member is udātta according to the rule "nabhsubhyām. Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the application of compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*), there is an absence of the suffix *kap* by the rule "nadyutaśca" (Pāṇini 5.4.153).
He sacrificed (*juhve*). [The root] *duh* is used in the sense of hating, competing, and making sound. The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *abhyastasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.33).
The absence of *uvaṅ* substitution is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

Alternatively, because the designation *sārvadhātuka* applies by the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*), the *yaṇ* substitution occurs according to Pāṇini 6.4.77: *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke*.
In this matter, the paribhāṣā regarding "that which is taught by its specific definition" (Pari. 105) is adopted in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*).
Otherwise, the *yaṇ* substitution would not occur in forms such as *ājuhvānaḥ*.

Nor should it be argued that if this were the case, the same [substitution] would also apply in instances such as *sātaye huve vām* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.60.13), because [in that case] there is an absence of multiple vowels (*anekāctva*).
For the term "anekāc" (having more than one vowel) applies there. [The word] has its final syllable accented acute by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
By the rule "hi ca," the prohibition of the *nivāta* [accent] is applied.
Mahāvīra:
he who is both great (*mahat*) and a hero (*vīra*) is Mahāvīra. The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel [of *mahat*] is applied by the rule *ānmahataḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.46).
*tuvibādham*: [the root] *bādh* means "to agitate. He agitates many (*tuvīn*) things; thus, he is *tuvibādha*.
The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *pac*. In the word *samṛtim*, by the rule “*tādau ca*,” the verbal root retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
*Rujānāḥ*:
from the root *ruj* meaning "to break. They are called *rujānāḥ* because they break the banks; thus, they are rivers.
‘The rivers become *rujānāḥ*; they break (*rujanti*).
[The reading] ‘of such a kind’ does not exist in the Ca-pha-śa-ṣa [recensions].
[In the Ca-ḍha-pha [recensions],] it has been omitted.

3. The substitution of *ca*, *pha*, and *yaṇ*. Regarding the word *kūlāni* (Nirukta 6.4), Yāska [provides this]. [The suffix] *śānac* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). [The root] *piṣ* takes the suffix *śa* according to the rule "after *tud* and others, *śa*. The absence of *num* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Since the root is taught with a short *a* (*adupadeśa*), when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented, the accent falls on the *vikaraṇa* suffix. [Thus we have] *pipiye*. [The root] *piṣ* means "to crush. [The form] *indraśatruḥ* is formed by transposition of the *liṭ* suffix. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*) applies.
Footless and handless, he rushed at Indra; Indra hurled his thunderbolt at him and struck him on the ridge.
Vṛtra, seeking to become a match for the bull, lay there scattered in many places like a eunuch.
Footless and handless, he struck out; he smote Indra’s thunderbolt upon his back. Seeking to become a match for the bull, the emasculated Vṛtra lay scattered in many places. || 7 ||

Because his feet were severed by the thunderbolt, Vṛtra was footless; because he was handless, he was without hands. Directed toward Indra, he *aptanyat*—he desired battle, he sought combat. Previously, while Vṛtra was alive, the waters held within the clouds, being obstructed by him, did not fall as rain upon the earth; at that time, the minds of men were distressed. But when Vṛtra was dead, the waters, free from obstruction, flowed forth, surmounting the body of Vṛtra.
The meaning is that men are satisfied by the appearance of rain at that time;
this is clarified by the second half of the verse:

"Vṛtra, while in his living state, by his own greatness (*mahinā*), surrounded and obstructed those very waters situated within the clouds; the serpent Vṛtra became one who lay beneath the feet (*pasṛtaśīr*) of those waters."
Although Añji has no foot, nevertheless, because he is marked by Vṛtra, his lying beneath the foot is logically consistent.
It is split.
By the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhāto naḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.42), the dental *t* is replaced by *n*. Thus:
*amuyā*.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39], the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is replaced by *yāj*. Thus, *śayānam*.
[The form *śayānam* is derived from the root *śī*] by the rule *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.21].
Because the root [dhātu] has the marker ḍit, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the root remains.
*Rahāṇāḥ*: [from] the root *raha*, meaning "in the production of seed" or "manifestation."
The suffix *śānac* is used by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).

Since the suffix *śap* would normally apply in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), *śa* is used instead by way of irregularity. Furthermore, according to the statement "the rules regarding augments are not restrictive," the substitution of *suk* occurs.
