Because it is taught as having an initial vowel (adupadeśāt), when the suffixal accent (vikaraṇasvara) would normally apply due to the anudātta nature of the *lasārvadhātuka* affix, the accent of the root (*dhātusvara*) prevails by way of exception (*vyatyayena*). Thus, *mahimā*.
[The root] *maha* is used in the sense of "worship" (*pūjāyām*).
The suffix *in* is applied according to the rule "after all roots.
The acute accent of the case ending is due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Or else:

*Mahimā*, *mahimnau*. Since the word *maha-* is listed among the *pṛthv-ādi* group, the suffix *imanij* is applied in the sense of "the state of that" (*tasya bhāvaḥ*) by the rule *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā* (Pāṇini 5.1.122). By the rule *ṭeḥ*, there is the elision of the final vowel (*ṭi*).
The word *citaḥ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

In the third case singular, when the suffixal vowel is elided, that [final syllable] becomes accented by the rule regarding the accentuation of the substitute for an acute vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*).
The elision of the letter *m* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
*Pasṛtaśīḥ*: one who sleeps on the ground. [The compound is] *pādasyādhaḥ śete* ("he sleeps beneath the feet"). The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "kvip ca."
By the rule *tasi 'pahna* etc., the word *pāda* is replaced by *pada*.

The word *prabhṛti* in the phrase *śaraprabhṛtiṣu* expresses a class or type (*prakāra*). This is because it has been stated [in Kātantra 6.1.63] that even in the case of *śalādoṣaṇī*, the replacement of *doṣan* occurs.
The addition of the word *su* in the middle is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

Alternatively, when the word *pāda* is in the locative plural and undergoes the substitution *pada*, the suffix *tasil* is applied in the sense of the locative according to Pāṇini’s rule *itarābhyo ’pi dṛśyante* (Pā. Sū. 5.3.14).
The absence of the augment *iṭ* is Vedic.
Her offspring became lowly, O son of Ṛta; Indra has cast off her burden.
The son was the higher, the light-bearer; Ānu lies like a cow with her calf.
Her limbs were cast down; she became the mother of Vṛtra. Indra struck her down from there. The mother was above, the son was below. Dānu lies there like a cow with her calf. || 9 ||

"Vṛtraputrā" means that mother whose son was Vṛtra; she, the mother, "anīcāvayāḥ"—one who had not reached a low state—fell down across [her son] (tiraścī) over the body of her son in order to protect him from the blow, meaning she lay herself across him. At that time, this "Indra" took up ("jabhāra") his "vadhah," the weapon used for slaying, and struck it below ("ava") this mother, upon Vṛtra.
At that moment, the "sūḥ," the mother, remained "uttarā," situated above.
But the son remained situated in the lower part.
And that Dānu, the Dānavī, the mother of Vṛtra, lay dead, having made her bed. In this regard, there is an illustrative example.
A "cow" (dhenu) is a well-known ox; "together with her calf" means that just as she does not lie down while accompanied by her calf, so it is here.
*Nīcāvayāḥ*:
"Vayas" means the arm, derived from the root *vi* (to eat) with the suffix *-as* (such as in *aṇ* etc.). Thus, it refers to one whose arms are low.
She whose limbs (*vayas*) are bent (*nyaṅgī*) is "one with lowly limbs" (*nīcāvayāḥ*).

From the word *nyañc*, the third-case singular ending is substituted for the following case-ending according to the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti*. Following the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *acaḥ*, lengthening occurs by the rule *cau*.

Regarding the rule *añceśchāndasaḥ sarvanāmasthānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.170): 1. According to the reading *jha-sa-vṛṣṭyābhena*, however. 2. Because it is transgressed in the readings *ca-cha-jha*; because it is surpassed in the reading *pa*. 3. In the readings *ca-cha-pha-ba*, the word "mahimnā" is absent. 4. In the reading *jha*, [the word] is "sahasā"; in the reading *ḍha*, the word "hatā" is absent. 5. In the readings *ga-ṇa-ra-ha*, "adharaḥ" means situated in the lower part. *dāsapatnīḥ*: *Dāsa* is Vṛtra, the cause of the destruction of the universe; he is the *patiḥ* (lord/master) of those waters, hence they are called *dāsapatnīḥ*.
For this very reason, they are called *ahigopāḥ*. Those for whom the serpent *ahi*—that is, Vṛtra—is the protector (*gopā*) or guardian;
"protection" (*gopana*) means the restraint such that they do not flow according to their own will.
This very point is clarified:
"The waters stood still, being restrained.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Like cows [by] Paṇi:
the meaning is that just as when an Asura named Paṇi, having carried off the cows and placed them in a cave, blocked the entrance of the cave and held them confined;

so too, Indra, having struck Vṛtra—that cave which was the outlet for the flowing waters and had been closed and obstructed by Vṛtra—opened it up (*apavavāra*), he removed the obstruction of the waters caused by Vṛtra.

Regarding this, Yāska says: "Dāsapatnī means 'having the Dāsa as lord' or 'having the Dāsa as master. A Dāsa is so called from the root *das*, because he destroys actions. The serpent-guardians stood there, hidden and protected. Ahi (serpent) is so called from moving (*ayana*) in the intermediate space; this other [meaning] also comes from the same root, with the prefix removed: it strikes (*āhanti*). The waters were obstructed, like cows by a Paṇi."

*Paṇi* is derived from *paṇ*; the merchant (*paṇin*) deals with merchandise (*paṇya*). Regarding the phrase "the opening of the waters which was covered": *bila* becomes *bhara*, for it supports (*bibharti*) Vṛtra after he has been slain; or else, it is so called because it covered (*vṛṇoti*), or because it rolled away (*vartate*), or because it increased (*vardhate*).

"It is known that because he covered (*avṛṇot*), that is the *vṛtra*-ness of Vṛtra; because he rolled forward (*avartata*), that is the *vṛtra*-ness of Vṛtra; because he grew (*avardhata*), that is the *vṛtra*-ness of Vṛtra" (Nirukta 2.17).
Dāsapatnī:
[The root] *dasu* means "to destroy. He who causes destruction (*dāsayati*) is the Dāsa, namely Vṛtra.
The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *pacādyac*.
By the rule *citaḥ*, there is an udātta accent on the final syllable.
[The compound means] those for whom a Dāsa is the husband.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 4.1.34); through that conjunction, the letter *i* is replaced by *n*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member prevails.
Alternatively:
The protectors of the servant:
[the compound] *pālayitrī* has its first member retaining its original accent according to the rule *patyāvaiśvarye*.
[The word] *ahigopāḥ*.
The root *gup* is used in the sense of "to protect. One who protects is a *gopā*.
The suffix *āya* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.1.31: *āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā*.
From that [suffix], the *kip* affix is applied. Then, by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the *a* is elided.
According to the principle *verapṛktalopādhali lope balīyān* (Pāṇini 1.1.51–52), the elision of the *yakāra* (*y*) occurs first.

Furthermore, the status as a *sthānivat* for the elision (*lopa*) resulting from the rule "after *ac*, before a subsequent [element]" is prohibited by the rule "not in the case of a word-final [element] or reduplication. [The example is:
*ahigopā yāsām*. The accentuation is as previously described.
*Niruddhā*:
[derived from] the root *rudh* in the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*).
By Pāṇini’s rule 8.2.40, *jhapastathordho'dhaḥ*, the dental *t* of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is replaced by *dh*.
In the word *gatiranantaraḥ*, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*).
In *jaghanvān*,
the suffix *kasu* is applied to the root *han* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
By the rule *abhyāsācca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.55), there is the substitution of *k* for the *h* following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Since the augment *iṭ* is obtained by the rule *krādiniyama*, its optional application is prescribed by the rule *vibhāṣā gamahana* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.68), and thus [the form] arises.
In *saṃhitā*, the *r*-substitution and the nasalization (*anunāsika*) of the *n* have been stated.

You became a horse's foal, O Indra, when you were a child; for you alone, O god, all the others contended against you. You won the cattle, O hero, you won the Soma, and you released the seven rivers to flow.
The horse’s tail became your banner, O Indra. When you struck him, O God, you alone conquered the cattle and won the Soma, O Hero; you released the seven rivers to flow. 12.
O Suke Vajra! Because the term *vajra* is listed among the names of the thunderbolt in the passage "Śakaḥ Cakraḥ" (Nirukta 2.20.6), [you are called] so.

O Deva, you who shine and are skilled in all weapons, being unique and without a second, when Vṛtra struck you with hostility, at that time you became the horse’s tail-hair (*vāra*) belonging to a horse.

Just as a horse’s mane effortlessly wards off flies and the like, so too did he repel Vṛtra without regard for him; this is the meaning. Furthermore, you conquered the cows that had been carried away by Paṇi;
O heroic Indra, endowed with valor, you conquered Soma.
And likewise, the Taittirīyas recite in this narrative: "Tvaṣṭṛ, the son of the Hand" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.9.1)—[variants:

*kṣa* = cause of the destruction of the universe; *na* = cause of the non-destruction of the universe; *ḍha* = cause of calamity for the universe]—"having caused the ruin of the sacrifice, he forcibly drank the Soma" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.12.1).

In the verse “*sasā sindhūn*, *imaṃ me Gaṅge*” (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.75.5), the knower [of the truth] understands that you, O Gaṅgā, “did release” (*avāsṛjaḥ*)—that is, made manifest—the rivers whose number is six for the sake of flowing (*satave*), meaning to move in the form of a current.
The sense is that you removed the obstruction of the flow caused by Vṛtra.
From these [words],
*aśnebhavaḥ* is formed; the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "in Vedic [usage], after *bhū*, [the suffix *yat* is added] when meaning 'occurring in'."
The word *anāvaḥ* has its initial syllable udātta according to the rule beginning with “*yato ’nāvaḥ*.
It is called *vāraḥ* because it wards off (*vārayati*) gadflies and mosquitoes; it is derived from the root *vṛ* with the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* group).

[The suffix -a] is applied after words beginning with *kapilaka* by virtue of the rule *lāghavikebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.137). Because it belongs to the *vṛṣan* group, it has an udātta accent on the first syllable.
[The word is formed as] *pratyaham*.
In the phrase *yadvṛttānnityam*, there is no prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent).
In the phrase *tiṣṭhe codāttavati*, the *gati* (preverb) is unaccented (*anudātta*). [The form is] *ajayaḥ*.

Because the word *gāḥ* occurs within another sentence, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) does not apply to the word *tiṣṭhati* in relation to it, according to the rule: "The *nighāta*, the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, and so forth, must be stated as occurring within the same sentence" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.18.5).
In *satave*, the suffix *taven* is used in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*), according to the rule: "The suffix *taven* is used in the sense of *tumun*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.9).
By virtue of being a *niti*, it has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
Neither lightning nor thunderbolt could check him, nor the mist which he scattered, nor the hail and the rain;
when Indra and Ahi fought as warriors, Maghavan emerged victorious over the fortified cities.
Not for him did the lightning or the thunderbolt prevail; nor did the mist that he scattered, nor the hail. When Indra and Ahi fought, the bounteous Indra emerged victorious for all future times.
All those illusions, such as lightning and others, which Vṛtra created by his *māyā* in order to obstruct Indra were unable to restrain him.
This very meaning is expressed by this mantra:
“The lightning (*vidyut*) created for the sake of this [Vṛtra] (*asmai*), for the sake of Indra (*indrārtham*), did not (*na*) obstruct (*siṣedha*), that is, it did not reach Indra.”
Likewise, that "thundering" roar and that "mihā" (rain)—the shower of rain which Vṛtra had scattered—he did not ward off;
nor did he ward off the "hāduni," the thunderbolt which Vṛtra had hurled.
And when both Indra and Ahi—Indra and Vṛtra—both fought, engaged in battle.
The connection with the preceding clause is that at that time, lightning and the other [weapons] had not yet arrived.
Furthermore, ‘Maghavan,’ the wealthy Indra, ‘vi jigye,’ specifically conquered, ‘aparībhyaḥ,’ from the others—that is, from the other illusions created by Vṛtra as well.
He prohibited it. [The root] *piñ* means "to protect. *Miham*.
In the sense of “to sprinkle” (√mih),
the word *mih* refers to rain because it sprinkles abundantly;
the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule “*kip ca*.”
He scattered [it].
[The root] *kṛ* [is used] in the sense of "scattering.
[The suffix] *śa* [is applied] after roots such as *tud*.
In the word *ṛtéd dhātoḥ*, the substitution of *i* for *e* occurs;
the augment *aṭ* is acute (*udātta*),
while the subsequent elision (*nighāta*) occurs due to its connection with a following *yad*-form.
They fought (*yuyudhāte*).
[The root] *yudh* means "to strike together.
In the *liṭ* [perfect tense], the accent belongs to the suffix.
It is conjugated as *jigye*.
By the rule *sanalliāṭojeḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.57), there is the substitution of *k* for the *j* following the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
O Indra, behold the karma that brings one across; let fear of the mortal who harms you enter his heart.
Like a hawk in flight, you have fearlessly traversed the regions, crossing the nine and ninety flowing rivers.

Whom did you see as your pursuer, O Indra, when fear seized your heart from the one who had struck you? And when you, like a frightened hawk, crossed the ninety-nine flowing rivers and the regions of space? || 14 ||

O Indra, if fear had entered your heart—that is, your mind—when you had slain Vṛtra, thinking "I have not killed him," then whom did you see as the "slayer" (yātāram)—that is, the killer—of the serpent Vṛtra? Who other than yourself was the person you had slain?
1. Ḍha: *secanakām*. Ka. 31.

The meaning is: "Let there be no fear for you, because of the absence of such another person. For this reason—that you, having reached the ninety-nine flowing rivers, have crossed over the *rajāṃsi*, that is, the waters therein—the following illustration is given.
"Not a hawk.
This means that, just as there was fear for you because of the long journey of a powerful bird named a hawk, may such fear not exist for us; this is the intended meaning.
And that journey to a distant place is recorded in the Brāhmaṇa: "Indra, having slain Vṛtra, thinking 'I have not released [the waters],' went to the furthest distances" (AiB 3.15).
The Taittirīyas also record: "Indra, having slain Vṛtra, went to the furthest distance, thinking 'I have committed a sin'" (TS 2.5.3.6).
In the word *hṛdi*, the substitution of *hṛd* for the word *hṛdaya* occurs by the rule beginning with "pad-n" (Pāṇini 6.1.63).
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending occurs by the rule beginning with "aḍiḍam" (Pāṇini 6.1.171).
"Of one who has gone. [This is] the *kasu* suffix after the root *han* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
In the singular of the fifth case, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel in *avas*.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the third chapter begins.
In the seventh section, beginning with "śvasme prathamaḥ," there are five hymns.
Among them, the third hymn, beginning with "etāyāma," consists of fifteen verses.
By the technical rule (paribhāṣā), "the seer [is inferred] from another," the seer is Hiraṇyastūpa Āṅgirasa.
Since it is not explicitly stated, Indra is the deity;
Triṣṭubh is the meter.
The word "eta" refers to the index. For the *gosava* and *vīvadha* sacrifices, when there is no option [regarding the deity], the hymn beginning with "etāyāma" is prescribed.

This is likewise stated in the section beginning with "one who is about to sacrifice with the *atimūrtti* [sacrifice]" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 9.8): "In the *gosava* and *vīvadha*, for one desiring cattle, the midday [pressing] consists of the verse 'indra somametāyāma'."
May Indra, who desires cattle, increase this our excellent providence;
for he, who is never deaf to us, surely brings near the highest thought of this wealth of cattle.
Come here! Seeking cattle, we approach Indra; may he increase our excellent providence.
Will he not, being unassailable, surely turn toward us the supreme desire for his wealth of cattle? 1.
The gods spoke thus among themselves:
"O gods, come here! Desiring to recover our cows that have been carried off by the Asura named Paṇi, you must come.
Together with you, we shall find Indra, who is capable of bringing back the cattle."
And that Indra, being free from harm (*vanābhṛṇa*), having gladdened the supreme wisdom (*pramati*) of us gods by means of the acquisition of cattle, shall increase it well (*su vavṛdhāti*).
Immediately thereafter, may that Indra abundantly bestow upon us the supreme knowledge (*paraṃ ketaṃ*) concerning wealth (*vasya vrāyaḥ*) and the nature of cattle (*gavām*).
Thus: from the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going.
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
This [form] is derived from the root *i* in the first person plural of the *laṅ* (imperfect). By the rule "āḍ-uttamasya pi ca," there is the augment *āṭ*.
Because it is marked as *pi*, the *guṇa* substitution characteristic of *sārvadhātuka* suffixes applies, resulting in the replacement by *āy*.

Nor does the substitution of *yaṇ* [for *i*] by the rule "iṇo yaṇ" (Pāṇini 6.4.81) apply here; for according to the metarule "Exceptions set aside preceding rules" (Paribhāṣā 60), that [rule] is an exception to the substitution of *iyaṅ*.
Therefore, due to its higher status in the order of application, the *yaṇ* substitution sets aside the *guṇa* [substitution].
Since the suffix *kyac* is known to be unaccented (*anudātta*), the word is initially accented on the first syllable by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*).
*Gavyantaḥ*:
desiring cows for themselves.
By the rule "supa ātmanaḥ kyac," the suffix *kyac* is added to the word *go* as the object;
by the rule "vānto yi pratyaye" (Pāṇini 6.1.79), *av* is substituted for *au*;
and from the verbal root ending in that suffix, the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle marker) is applied.
Because this [root] is taught with an initial *a*, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
In the word *pramatiṃ*, there is the elision of the nasal (anunāsika) by the rule "anudāttopadeśa... etc., following the suffix *ktin* after the root *man*.
By the rule *tādau ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.50), the verbal prefix (*gati*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*).
[Thus we have] *vavṛdhāti*. The root *vṛdh* means "to grow."
The augment *āṬ* is added [to the root].
By the rule "in the Veda, diversely," there is the elision (*ślau*) of the suffix *śap*.
In the *saṃhitā*, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
*Anābhṛṇaḥ*.
[The root] *mṛṇ* means "to injure. Those who injure or cause harm are called *mṛṇāḥ*.
The suffix *ka* is applied by virtue of the rule for suffixes following a verbal root with an *iṭ*-augment or a penultimate *u*.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one who has no debts" (*anaṛṇaḥ*), the final syllable of the second member is udātta according to the rule *nañsubhyām*.
[This refers to] "of this wealth" (*asya rāyaḥ*).
In both instances of "aṅiḍam," the case ending is udātta.
Regarding "gavām," there is a prohibition by the rule "na gośvasāvarṇa" against the udātta accent of the case ending that would otherwise be required by the rule "sāvekācaḥ."
*Keta*:
[derived from] the root *kit* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāne*),
ending in the suffix *ghañ*, and accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
He inclines (*āvarjate*).
[The root] *vṛj* is used in the sense of "bending" or "inclining.

Since it belongs to the *adādi* class, the elision of the suffix *śap* would normally apply; however, by the rule "it occurs diversely in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), that elision does not take place here.
The suffix *śap* is unaccented because it is marked with the *pit* indicator;
and since the *tiṅ* suffixes are *lasārvadhātuka*, they take the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*).
By the rule *tiṅi codāttavati* (Pāṇini 8.1.71), the verb of motion (*gati*) is unaccented.
Due to its separation from the particle *ku*, there is a prohibition of the non-accentuation [of the verb] by the rule *nipātairyadyadihantakuvinnecceccaṇkaccidyatrayuktam* (Pāṇini 8.1.30).

Like a hawk swooping down upon its cherished nest, I fly toward Upedaha, who is unassailable and richly endowed; I come paying homage to Indra with incomparable deeds, for he is to be invoked by our hymns at the sacrifice.
I fly toward the giver of wealth, the irresistible one, like a falcon to its beloved nest—worshiping Indra with humble hymns, he who is to be invoked by his praisers on his journey. 2.

Indra is to be invoked by you—the singers and those who perform the rites—for the sake of favoring the singers during the journey when a battle has commenced with his enemies; he is to be summoned by them. To that Indra, I, the performer of the rite, go forth; I approach him indeed.
Doing what?
Honoring and worshiping him with these most excellent hymns of praise (*arkas*), which stand as the highest of comparisons.
What kind of Indra? A giver of wealth (*dhanada*), one who bestows riches; "unassailable" (*apratīta*), meaning not overcome by those possessing strength.
This is an illustration for the attainment of Indra.
Just as a hawk—a swift bird named *śyena*—rushes with devotion toward its own place, so do I hasten to reach Indra, my own dwelling-place, a home cherished by the ancients and frequented by them.
Dhanadā:
she is called Dhanadā because she gives wealth (dhana). The suffix *vic* is applied according to the rule "āto manin-kvanib-vanip-śa ca."
*Apratītam* means not encountered by enemies, nor returned. It has the accent of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*) due to the indeclinable being the first member of the compound. *Juṣṭām*.

The root *juṣ* is used in the senses of "pleasure" and "service. According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 7.2.14 (*śrīdito niṣṭhāyām*), there is a prohibition of the substitution of *i* for the final vowel in the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). By Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.210 (*nityaṃ mantre*), the word bears an udātta accent on its first syllable.
I fall [prostrate].
The augment *āṭ* is added to the root *li*.
Paying homage.
From the word *namaḥ*, the suffix *kyac* is applied in the sense of worship according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.1.19 (*namovarivaścitraṅaḥ kyac*). The accent belongs to the affix (*pratyayasvara*).

Because it is taught as beginning with a short vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented; thus, by the rule for a single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*), the resulting syllable is accented acute (*udātta*).
These are called *upamās* because things are compared (*upamīyante*) by means of them. [The root] *māṅ* is used in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*).
The suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.3.58: "The application of *ka* is prescribed in the sense of the *ghañ* suffix."
In accordance with the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is no substitution of *ais* for the instrumental ending.
There is the accentuation of the original form of the final member of the compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*). [The word is] *havyaḥ*.
The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule "hej bahulaṃ chandasi"; the suffix *yat* is added by the rule "aco yat," and *guṇa* substitution takes place.
The substitution of *ava* [for *ava*] is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.80: *dhātostannimittasyaiva*.
By the rule *yato'nāvaḥ*, the word is udātta-accented on the first syllable. [Thus: *yāman*.
The root *yā* is used in the sense of "attaining.
The suffix *manin* results in the acute accent on the first syllable of the *niṣṭhā* [past participle].
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending.
With all his hosts, unattached to quivers, he drives away the cattle at will;
O Indra, though much is being said against you, do not be angry with us, O most exalted one.

With all his might, the noble one has fastened on his two quivers; he drives the cattle wherever he desires. O Indra, being praised, grant us much of your wealth; do not diminish it, for you have grown great from us. 3.
Sarvasena fought against Kṛṣṇasena.
He unfastened the quivers—the containers of arrows—and fastened the quiver upon his back.
Indra, the noble Lord, desires to release the cows that were seized by the Asura; he drives those cows together and brings them safely to the home of that god.
O Indra, you who are expanded by greatness, bestowing upon us abundant wealth in the form of cattle while seeking to give it, do not become a *paṇi* toward us; do not be a robber.
The meaning is: do not demand a price for the cows.
Sarvasena: [The word] *senā* means "that which exists together with *ina*" (the leader). The substitution of *sa* for *saṃ* occurs by the rule *bopasajanasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.82).
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *sarvāsaraṇaśīlā senā yasya* ("he whose army has the habit of fleeing everywhere"), the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratvam*) applies.

According to the rule "this accent is also maintained by means of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa*" (Kātyāyana-vārttika 6.1.191), the word *sarva-* is acute on its first syllable by the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule *sarvasya supi* (Pāṇini 6.1.191).
[The form is] *iṣudhīn*.
They are called *iṣudhi* because arrows (*iṣu*) are placed (*dhīyante*) within them.
The suffix *ki* is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.2.93, *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca*.
In the *saṃhitā*, the *n* is shortened by the rule beginning with *dīrghād aṭi* (Pāṇini 8.2.86).
By the rule "atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā" (Pāṇini 8.3.2), the preceding vowel becomes nasalized. Thus: *asakta*.

*Upaśākebhiḥ*: "Those who make [something] capable" are *upaśākāḥ*. From the root *śaklṛ* ("to be able"), with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *ac* is added by the rule *pacādyac*. The acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the final syllable of the second member by the rule *thāthādisvara*. *Viṣun*: From the prefix *viṣu* and the root *nañ*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule for *saṃpadādi* formations. The substitution of *ku* for *naś* occurs by the rule *naśervā* (Pāṇini 6.2.63). Alternatively, there is the augment *luṅ* after the root *añjati* preceded by *viṣu*. *Sanakāḥ*: This is a name of the Asuras. From the root *paṇu* ("to give"), those who give or bestow are *sanāḥ* (givers); the suffix *ac* is added by *pacādyac*. Those who cry out or sound from eternity (*sanāt*) are *sanakāḥ*. The suffix *ka* is added by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*. The vowel *ā* is elided by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*. The accent follows the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*. *Pretim*: By the rule *tādau ca niti*, the original accent of the prefix *pra* is maintained. *Īyuḥ*: From the root *eti*, because *us* follows, the substitution *yaṇ* for *iṇ* applies. Due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci*, the letter *i* is reduplicated. The lengthening of the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.4.69).
Their heads were shattered; they, the non-sacrificers who vied with the sacrificers, turned away from Indra.
When you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, the self-radiant and fierce one, blew them away from heaven and earth, you cast down those devoid of holy rites.

Even their heads were turned back, O Indra, those non-sacrificers who contended with the sacrificers. When you, O fierce Lord of the Bay Steeds, self-born from heaven, blew away the lawless ones from both worlds.
"O Indra, those followers of Vṛtra, being themselves devoid of sacrifice (*ayajvānaḥ*), yet competing with those who perform sacrifices (*yajvabhiḥ*), turned their own heads away and fled.
How were they?
They were devoid of sacrifice themselves, while simultaneously contending with those who performed the sacrificial rites.

O *harivaḥ*, possessor of bay horses; O you who are joined with horses; O you who are established in stability; O *ugra*, fierce one endowed with heroism, O Indra—*yat* when, from *divaḥ*, the intermediate space, and from *rodasyoḥ*, heaven and earth, you *niḥ prādhamaḥ*, blew away completely the *avrataḥ*, those who violate their vows, the followers of Vṛtra; then, being impelled by the wind of your mouth, they turned back—this is the connection with what precedes.
*Śīrṣā*: the elision of the *śi* suffix occurs by the rule *śe chandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.1.70). *Vavṛjuḥ*.

The root *vṛj* means "to avoid. According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 1.2.5, "liṭ [affixes] following a non-conjunct [root] are *kit*," there is an absence of *guṇa* due to its being a *kit*. Thus, [the form] is *ayajvānaḥ*.

From the root *yaj*, by the rule *suyajor ḍun* (Pāṇini 3.2.103), the suffix *ḍun* is applied in the sense of the past; because this suffix is marked with *p*, it is anudātta, and thus the word retains its original udātta accent on the first syllable by virtue of the root accent (*dhātusvara*).
In the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the original accent of the initial member, being an indeclinable (*avyaya*), prevails.
[The word] *divaḥ*.
In the word *uḍidam*, the vowel *i* is udātta because it is part of a case ending (*vibhaktyudātta*). Regarding *harivaḥ*: he who possesses two bay horses (*harī*) is called *harivān*.
In the word *chandasīraḥ*, the substitution of *v* for *matup* occurs according to the rule *chandasīraḥ*.
In the vocative singular, the substitution of *r* for *mat* and *vas* occurs according to the rule *matuvasoḥ*.
[The form is] *avratān*.
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final syllable of the second member is udātta by the rule "anansunyām.
By the rule "dīrghād iṭi," the *nakāra* becomes *ru* (repha) in the *saṃhitā* reading.
By the rule "āto 'ṭi nityam," the vowel *ā* becomes nasalized (*sānunāsika*).

*Adhamaḥ*: [The root] *dham* is used in the sense of "sound" and "blowing. In the *laṅ* tense, with the suffix *sip* and the *śap* affix, there is the substitution of *dham* for [the root *dhmā*] according to the rule beginning with “*pāghrā*” (Pāṇini 7.3.78).
The peoples dwelling in the nine regions sent forth their armies against Arya Utsanavavr̥dha.
Like castrated bulls with virile weapons, they were utterly defeated; pursued by the shouting [foes], they fled, taking note even of Indra.

The noble Utsas, whose army was undecaying, marched forth; the people dwelling in the nine regions, like eunuchs with virile weapons, were cast out. Taking heed of Indra, they departed with their leaders. 6.
The followers of Vṛtra desired to fight against the army of Indra, who is blameless and free from reproachable faults.
At that time, the Navagvas—those whose movements are ever-new, or whose conduct is worthy of praise—[acted].
Or rather:
Among the Aṅgirases who were performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), those who rose after nine months without having achieved the fruit [of the sacrifice] received the name *Navagvas*,
because they are so addressed in such passages as, "The Navagvas, having pressed the Soma, [invoked] Indra" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.29.12).
The *kṣitayas* are human beings, such as the Aṅgirases and others.
This is because the term is listed among its names in the Nirukta (2.3.6): “*kṣitayaḥ kṛṣṭayaḥ*.
*Ayātayanta*: they incited Indra with various kinds of mantras for the sake of battle.

When Indra had gone forth to fight, the followers of Vṛtra, driven out and rejected by that Indra, became conscious of their own powerlessness; making it known, they fled from Indra’s presence by excellent, well-prepared paths for escape, having gone far away.
Therein lies the illustration:
like those fighting with a hero who is a bull, endowed with virility and capable of impregnation.
Like eunuchs who are like impotent men;
for they are so used in Smṛti texts such as "The *vadhri* is one who is naturally impotent" (*nisargapaṇḍa*).
Just as they are driven far away by a powerful man, so it is in this case.

They desired to fight (*ayuyutsan*). In the root *yudh* meaning "in combat," there is an absence of *guṇa* due to the *kit* status of the suffix *san*, according to Pāṇini’s rule 1.2.10: *sani halantācca*.
The prohibition of the substitution of *it* is applied by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.10).
The *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). [Thus we have] *senām*.
An *senā* is that which exists together (*saha vartate*) with this [army]. By the rule *vopasarjanasya*, the word *saha* undergoes the substitution of *sa-*;
in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member is maintained.
They exerted themselves. [The root] *yat* means "to strive.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "and when there is a causal agent" (*hetumati ca*).
*Kṣitayaḥ*. [The root] *kṣi* means "to dwell" and "to go. Those who dwell and move are *kṣitayaḥ*, namely human beings.
The suffix *kit* is applied by the rule “*kit kau ca saṃjñāyām*” (Pāṇini 6.1.27). Thus, *navagvāḥ*.
They are called *navagvāḥ* because they go (*gacchanti*) with nine steps (*navabhir mānaiḥ*).
The suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* according to the *auṇādika* rules;

or alternatively, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, the nasal is elided by Pāṇini’s rule 6.4.40 (*gamaḥ kau*), and the vowel *a* is changed to *ū* by the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) 6.4.40.2, which states: “It should be stated that for the roots *gam* and others, [the *a*] becomes *ū*.”
In the word *vṛṣāyudhaḥ*, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule *jasi ‘oḥ supi* (6.4.83); the lengthening [of the vowel] is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Thus, it becomes *vṛṣāyudhaḥ*.

In the word *‘kip ca’*, the suffix is *kip*. Regarding this *‘kip ca’*, since it is stated [in the Kātantra] that “it occurs after both words with an upapada and those without an upapada” (Kā. 3.2.76), here it occurs after words with an upapada.
By the rule “it is also seen after other [roots] as well,” there is lengthening of the first member in the *saṃhitā* form.
*Niraṣṭāḥ*. [The root] *aśrū* means "to pervade.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
By the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15), there is a prohibition of the substitution of *it*.
By the rule beginning with *vaśra*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for *p*.
And in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.
Alternatively,
the substitution of *s* with *ṣ* (*patva*) in the word *nirastāḥ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

In that case, since *niṣṭhā* [the suffix -ta] is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), the preceding prefix *gati-* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) according to the rule "a non-intervening *gati* [retains its accent]."
By those who speak: [the root] *vana-paṇa* means "to enjoy"; from this, with the prefix *pra-* and the suffix *kvip*, [the form *pravan* is derived].
By the rule "it should be stated that [the final vowel] of *gama* and so forth [is elided]" (Pāṇini 6.4.40.1), the nasal is elided;
then the *tuk* augment is applied,
and the word retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) because the suffix begins with a *ku*-class consonant.
*citayantaḥ*:
from the root *cit* in the sense of "perceiving" (*saṃjñāne*),
with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the present participle suffix *śatṛ* (replacing *laṭ*).
Śap:
By the rule "the teaching regarding augments is not mandatory," there is an absence of the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
O Indra, you fought these who were choosing and feasting at the far edge of the mid-world;
from heaven you burned down the Dasyu on high, and you protected the prayer of those who press the juice and strike down their foes.

You, O Indra, fought against these who were both weeping and laughing at the farthest limit of the mid-air; you burned down the Dasyu from on high from heaven, and you protected the prayer of those who press the juice and offer praise. ||7||

O Indra, you [subdued] these two kinds of followers of Vṛtra—the weeping ones, who were crying out, and the laughing ones, who were eating or laughing—beyond the *rajas*, that is, in the farthest part of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
The word *rajas* denotes the intermediate space, as it is said: "The worlds are called *rajaṃsi*.
(Note: In some recensions, such as Cha, Ṇa, Ta, Dha, Na, Pha, Śa, and Sa, there is the variant reading *navanītagatayaḥ*.)
2. To protect from the six, the nine, the ten, and the non-existent;
3. Because of the traditional recollection [of the rule] "ḍha" (Nighaṇṭu 4.19), as it has been stated.
*Ayodhaya*: you fought; the meaning is that you slew him by means of battle.

*Dasyum*: the destroyer, Vṛtra. Having brought him from *divaḥ*—from the heavenly world—you *uccā avādahaḥ*: you utterly burnt him down. Destroy Vṛtra along with his retinue. Thereafter, you *pra āvaḥ*: you excellently protected the *śaṃsam*, the praise, of the sacrificer who *sunvataḥ*—performs the pressing of Soma—and *stuvataḥ*—performs the hymn of praise.
*Rudataḥ*:
from the root *rudir* in the sense of "shedding tears," with the suffix *laṭ* replaced by *śatṛ*.
Due to its inclusion in the *adādi* group, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. By the accent of the suffix, it is oxytone (*antodātta*).
By the rule “*śataranumaḥ*,” the *śas* case-ending is acute (*udātta*).
*Jakṣataḥ*.
[The root] *jakṣ* [is used] in the senses of eating and laughing.
As before, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

By the rule "jakṣyādayaḥ ṣaṭ" (Pāṇini 6.1.6), [the six roots beginning with *jakṣ*] receive the designation *abhyasta*. Consequently, by the rule "abhyastānām ādiḥ," the first syllable is udātta-accented. [Thus, the accent of] *sunvataḥ* [is established].
In the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the root *śru*, the substitution of *bhu* for the root applies according to the rule "svādibhyaḥ bhuḥ.
Then, by the rule "husuvoḥ... and so forth, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.
Finally, the acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is applied by the rule "śataranumaḥ..."
From the root *stu*,
meaning "to praise" (*stauti*).
Because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
The substitution is *uvaḍ*;
the accent is as before.
Fashioning a girdle for the earth, adorning themselves with golden jewels, they sped forth like swift horses;
their touch placed Indra around the sun.
Fashioning a girdle for the earth, being adorned with gold and jewels, they did not bypass Indra as they sped along; their touch encompassed him together with the sun.

Those followers of Vṛtra who, having fashioned for themselves a covering—an all-pervading mantle—of the earth, the ground; who are shining, adorned with gold and with necklaces and other ornaments made of gold; and who exist increasing and advancing—they, such followers of Vṛtra, fought Indra in battle but did not overcome him; they were not capable of conquering him.
Then that Indra, as the sense of touch (*sparśa*), surrounded the obstructing followers of Vṛtra with the sun, the Āditya; he made them enclosed and separated [from him].
And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "The Āditya, from afar, strikes away the demons who seek to harm" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.6.3).

Regarding *cakrāṇāsaḥ*: from the root *kṛ*, while the rule "in the Veda, the *liṭ* [perfect tense suffix] is used" is in force, the *kānac* suffix is applied for the *liṭ*; thereafter, the augment *asuk* is added.
The word *citaḥ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). *Pariṇaham*:
the act of wrapping around is *parīṇat*.

From the root *nah* preceded by *pari*, the suffix *krip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*); by the rule *na-hi-vṛti-* (Pāṇini 6.3.116), the first member of the compound takes its long vowel. Regarding *pṛthivyāḥ*:
the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *udāttayaṇaḥ*.
*hinvānāsaḥ*: [The root] *hi* means "to go" and "to increase.
The suffix *cānaś* expresses habitual action (*tācchīlika*).
*titiruḥ*. The root *tṛ* (tirati) has the sense of "going."
When you, O Indra, encompassed both heaven and earth on all sides with your greatness,
you blew away the Dasyu with the Brahmins— those who were not thinking [of him] by means of those who were mindful of him, O Indra.

O Indra, when you have overwhelmed both heaven and earth with your greatness on every side, you have, by means of the prayers of those who possess self-awareness, struck down the Dasyu among those who lack it, O Indra. 9.

O Indra, when you, by your own greatness, had encompassed both worlds—heaven and earth—on all sides and had consumed them entirely, at that time you [regarded] those who did not think [of you], who were unable to follow the meaning of the mantras, and who were merely desirous [of their own ends], as sacrificers whom you considered thus: "These sacrificers of ours are to be protected.
1. *ḍha-sa-upakṣayitāram* | 2. *ḍha-yuddhāyodhatam* |
3. Even those who are unable to deliberate upon or meditate on the meaning of the *ṅa*-mantra;

"By those who harbor such pride," [it is said]. "With *brahma* mantras," [you] "did drive out (*niḥ-adhamaḥ*)"—that is, you expelled—the thief, the Asura in the form of Vṛtra and others. Yāska states: "'The root *dhmā* means to go' (Nirukta 6.2). "You did not enjoy (*abubhojīḥ*). [The root] *bhuja* is used in the senses of "protecting" and "eating. In the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *sip*, the *bhlu* substitution for the *vikaraṇa* occurs by Pāṇini 2.4.76 (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). The augment *īṭ* is added by Pāṇini 7.1.97 (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), resulting in *adubhojīḥ*. Due to its connection with *yadvat*, it does not lose its accent (*anighāta*). "By greatness (*mahinā*)" means by majesty (*mahimnā*). From the word *mahat*, the suffix *imanij* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *pṛṣvādi* words. By the rule "*ṭeḥ*" (*Pāṇini 6.4.155*), the final syllable is elided. In the singular instrumental case, when the *alopa* occurs, the vowel becomes acute (*udātta*) by the rule regarding the restoration of the original accent (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). The elision of the *m* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). "Those who do not think (*amanyamānān*). Those who think, i.e., know, are *manyamānāḥ*. The root *man* is used in the sense of "knowing. The suffix *śyan* is added by the rule *divādibhyaḥ śyan*. Because *śyan* is *niś*, the word is acutely accented on the first syllable. In the compound, the original accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) prefix prevails. In the *saṃhitā* text, the short vowel and the nasalization (*anunāsika*) are indicated as prescribed.

They who did not reach the limit of heaven and earth, nor surpassed the Danus with their magic powers—Indra, the bull, made the thunderbolt his ally; with his own light, he milked the cows from the darkness.

No; those who reached the limits of heaven and earth did not overcome the Giver of Wealth with their magic powers. Indra, the Bull, made the thunderbolt his ally; with light, he milked the cows out from the darkness. 10.
The specific waters from heaven, the celestial realm, did not reach the end, the place of the earth,
because they were obstructed by Vṛtra who had assumed the form of a cloud.

Precisely because of this lack of contact with the earth, they did not encompass— that is, they did not pervade— the earth which bestows wealth, through their illusory powers consisting of activities such as providing assistance for crops.
The meaning is that they did not provide assistance, such as by increasing the growth of water-drinking plants.
At that time, this Indra took up the *vajra*—the weapon for splitting the clouds—in his own hand;
then, with that *vajra* shining with light, he milked out—that is, he completely extracted—the *gāḥ*, the waters characterized by movement, from the *tamas*, the cloud in the form of darkness.
The meaning is that he rained water after piercing the cloud.
Regarding the word *divaḥ*: by the rule "ūḍidam," the genitive case ending is acute-accented (*udātta*).
They reached. [The root] *ā-plṛ* means "to pervade";
this is the form in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the second person singular ending (*ḍasi*).

Just as there is no *nighāta* (tonal suppression) due to its connection with *yat*, so too in the case of *paryabhūvan*, because the word *yat* is not supplied (*anupajñāt*), there is an absence of *nighāta*.
*yujam* [is derived from] the root *yujir* in the sense of "joining" (*yoge*). By the rule beginning with *ṛtvig-*, etc., the suffix *kin* is applied.
Due to the statement "the teaching of grammatical tradition is non-eternal," there is an absence of the augment *num*. [The form] *adukṣat* [is derived from] the root *duh*, meaning "to milk."
In the *Laghu-śabdenduśekhara*, the substitution of *ksa* for *kl* is prescribed by the rule "luṅi śala igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.45).
Then, the change to *gh* occurs by the rule "dāderdhātorghaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.32),
and the substitution of *bh* follows from the rule beginning with "ekāco baśaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.37).
In the *saṃhitā*, the absence of the *bha*-sound is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) phenomenon.
Following his own nature, the waters flowed; he grew great in the midst of the navigable rivers.
With a focused mind and with his most powerful impetus, Indra struck down the youthful [Vr̥tra]. The waters flowed according to their own nature; he grew great in the midst of the navigable rivers.

With a focused mind and with his most powerful impetus, Indra struck down the youthful one. 11. According to his own nature, the waters flowed; he grew great in the midst of the navigable rivers. With a focused mind and with his most powerful impetus, Indra struck down the youthful one. 11.
The waters, flowing toward the food (*vasu-dhā*) of that Indra—namely the grain and other crops—became rain from the clouds.
Then this Indra grew on all sides in the midst of many navigable waters, those suitable for crossing by boat.
[This was done] by those possessing the pride [of being his own].
*Prāsa*.
Although existing in abundant water, he did not sink, but rather grew even more.

Then Indra, with his mind directed toward Vṛtra as he moved along with him, struck him with his most powerful (*ojiṣṭhena*) weapon, the thunderbolt (*vajra*), which serves as the instrument of slaughter. He slew him during certain days (*abhi cyugū ahan*), having recognized that even though Vṛtra had fallen into the midst of the waters, his mind followed after Indra wherever he stood; it is in this sense that he struck him down.
They moved across. The root *kṣar* means "to move.
[This refers to] those who are not others, those who are not to be ferried by boat.

The suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *nau-vayo-dharma-...* (Pāṇini 4.4.91). By the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* (Pāṇini 6.1.79), the *au* of *nau* is replaced by *āv*, resulting in *nāvya*. Due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by the rule *anāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), the suffix-accent is applied as *tisvarita* (i.e., the suffix receives the svarita accent).
By *satrīcīnena*. That which goes together is *sadyaṅ*.
[The form] *sadhyā* is derived by the substitution of *sadhi* for *saha*, according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.95.
By the rule *vibhāṣāñjeradikstriyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.8), the suffix *kha* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
By the rule *tasya āyan* etc., the substitute *īn* is applied for this suffix.
Then, by the rule *acaḥ*, the vowel *a* is elided, and by the rule *cau*, lengthening occurs.
By the rule stating that a substitute behaves like its original (upadeśivad-vacana), the vowel *ī* is acute (*udātta*).
[The word] *ojiṣṭhena*: one who possesses vigor (*ojas*) is "vigorous" (*ojasvin*).

The suffix *vini* is applied by Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.121 (*asāyāmedhā*). From that, the comparative suffix *iṣṭhan* is added. Then, by Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.65 (*vinmatorluk*), there is the elision (*luk*) of *vini*.
By the rule *teḥ*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix; by the rule *nic-cād-ādy-udāttatvam*, it is accented on the first syllable. [The form is] *hanmanā*.
*Hanma* means "that by which one strikes" (*hanyate 'nena iti hanma*).
By the rule *amyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*, the suffix *manin* is applied even in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), due to the inclusion of the word *raśi*.
Because it ends in a *nic* suffix, it has the acute accent (*ādyudātta*) on its first syllable.
In the third case singular, although elision (*lopa*) would otherwise apply, there is a prohibition by the rule *na saṃyogād vamantāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.137).
Indra pierced the firm fortifications of Ilībiśa and split Śuṣṇa limb from limb;
O Maghavan, as much as was your power and vigor, with the thunderbolt you slew the enemy Pṛtyu.

He pierced him; Indra shattered the firm stronghold of Ilībiśa and split Śuṣṇa asunder. O Maghavan, according to your speed and according to your might, you slew the enemies with your thunderbolt—Pṛtyu. 12.
These belong to Vṛtra, who lay in the hole of the earth—the *ilā* of Ilībiśa;
as Yāska says: "belonging to him who lay in the *ilā*-hole" (*Nirukta* 6.19).
Indra pierced through those firm, firmly established, and abundant waters that had been obstructed by the Asura. He pierced them thoroughly.
Or rather:
he utterly pierced the firm and powerful armies;

then he shattered—that is, struck him in various ways—Śuṣṇa, the "dryer" (śoṣaka) of the world, who was Vṛtra, equipped with weapons such as the horns of cattle, buffaloes, and other animals, which were like high-horned [missiles].

O Maghavan, O Indra, endowed with wealth, with whatever speed you possess, whatever impetus, whatever vigor, and whatever strength exists—endowed with all that, you slew Vṛtra, the enemy who desired battle, with your thunderbolt.
He pierced.
The root *vyadh* means "to strike.
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule beginning with *iyani grahajyā*.
In the word *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*, due to the rule of *nighāta* (enclitic accent), and by the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ* in *saṃhitā*, the augment *aṭ* becomes *svarita*. In *ilībiśasya*,
the desired form and accent are established because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
*dṛlhā*: It is derived as an irregular form (*nipātana*) according to Pāṇini’s rule 7.2.20, *daṃhiḥ nihnyāyāṃ dṛḍhaḥ sthūlabalayoḥ*.
The elision of the suffix *śa* occurs by virtue of the rule *śe chandasi bahulam*.
He split. The root *bhid* means "to tear apart.
In the *laṅ* [aorist] tense, *śnam* is added after roots such as *rudh*.
By the rule *itaśca* (Pāṇini 3.4.100), the letter *i* is elided; then, by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ*, the suffix *ṭi* is elided. Thus: *śuṣṇam*.
[The root] *śuṣ* means "to dry."
He who dries up is *śuṣṇaḥ*.

The suffix *na* is applied according to the rule *tṛṣi-śuṣi-parisebhyaḥ kicca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.392). Because the term *nit* is understood from the previous context, the word is udātta-accented on its first syllable.
*avadhīḥ*: by the rule *laṅi ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.43), there is the substitution of *vadha* for the root *han*.
[The word is] *pṛtyum*.
From the word *pṛtanā*, by the rule *kvaci kabhyaccarapṛtanasya*, there is the elision of the final syllable;
then, by the rule *kyācchandasī*, the suffix *u* is added.
1. The letters *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *dha*, *na*, *pha*, and *sa* do not exist [in this context].
2. *Ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*, *ra*, *śa*, *sa*—as far as there is fire (*tejas*).
O Abhisidhma, with your sharp weapon, strike down the enemies of Ajikāda; shatter their fortresses.
Indra, displaying his own wisdom, struck the thunderbolt with the vajra, cleaving it asunder.

From the side of the goat, he struck down his enemies; with his sharp weapon, he shattered their strongholds. Indra struck Vṛtra with his thunderbolt and, scattering [the foe], he furthered his own purposeful thought. 13.

That *vajra* of Indra, the *sidhma*, the accomplisher, went forth against the enemies, specifically targeting the foes of Indra. The root *gāti* means "to go," as it is listed among the verbs of motion in the *Nighaṇṭu* (2.14.113): "gāti, jigāti. And that Indra, with that *vajra*—sharp (*tigmena*), piercing (*vṛṣeṣaṇa*), the most excellent weapon—shattered (*vy abheta*) in various ways the fortresses (*purah*) of Vṛtra. Then that Indra, having joined Vṛtra together with his own *vajra*, and striking Vṛtra while being "gladdening" (*śāśadānaḥ*), greatly increased (*prāvatirat*) his own mind—that is, his own joyful intellect. [Grammatical Notes: *Sidhma*: From the root *vidhu* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃrāddhau*). The suffix *mak* is added according to the *Uṇādi* rules; due to its *kit* nature, there is no *guṇa*. It bears the accent of the suffix. *Ajikāt*: From the root *gā* in the sense of "praise" (*stutau*), but here it has the sense of "motion. The suffix *ślu* is applied because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class. In the case of the reduplication (*dvirbhāve*), the substitution of *hvam* for the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. *Tigmena*: By the rule "yuji-rucitijāṃ kuśca" (*Uṇādi Sūtra* 1.143), the suffix *mak* is added and *kṛt* status is assigned. *Vṛṣeṣaṇa*: By the rule "kṛpivṛbhyāṃ kin" (*Uṇādi Sūtra* 3.403), the suffix *abhac* is added. *Abheta*: From the root *bhidir* in the sense of "cleaving. The suffix *śap* is used irregularly (*vyatyayena*) in the *bhrami-prāsa* sense. Its elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. There is elision of the penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇe*) and then the elision of the *hal* and *ṅy* etc. Alternatively, the elision occurs in the *luṅ* tense. *Prāvatirat*: The prefix *pra-* combined with *tirati* has the sense of "increasing. Alternatively, the suffix *śa* is used irregularly for the root *tarati*. By the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ," the substitution of *it* occurs. *Śāśadānaḥ*: From the root *śad* in the sense of "falling" or "perishing" (*śatane*). From this, the suffix *yaṅ* is added, followed by *śānac*. Because it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix in the Vedic language by the rule "chandasyubhayathā," there is the elision of the *at* and the *yalopa*. Because it is a *sārvadhātuka* suffix, the initial vowel is acute by the rule "abhyastānāmādiḥ" (*Pāṇini* 6.1.189).
They brought Kutsa to Aindra, in whom he took delight—the bull who fights with brilliant splendor.
The dust raised by his hooves reached the sky; the son of Śvitra stood for the sake of the one who conquers men.

They helped Kutsa, O Indra, in whom you took delight; you protected Darśadyu, the bull, as he fought. The dust raised by his hooves reached the sky; Śvaitreya stood up for the sake of conquering men. 14.
O Indra, you protected (vāvaḥ) that Kutsa—namely, the ṛṣi who founded the Gotra of that name;
you abide (vākan) in this Kutsa, desiring his praise (stuti).
"That Kutsa" is the connection with the preceding clause.
Likewise, you protected with preeminent care this one named Vadarśadyu, whose form shines throughout the ten directions;
how was he? A bull, the most excellent, engaged in battle, fighting against his own enemies.
The dust (*vraṇu*) fallen from the hoof of your horse reached (*nakṣata*) the sky, the world of heaven.

Śvaitreya, the son of a woman with white skin (*śvitri*), who had previously been submerged in enemy waters, by your grace rose up (*ut tasthau*) from the water for the sake of *nṛsāha*, that which is to be endured by men.
*cākan*. [The root] *caka* means "to be satisfied. From this, with the suffix *pya*, the form *śatṛ* [is applied].

By the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, because it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, there is elision of the *ṇi* affix and the substitution of *śap*. It has an udātta accent on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Alternatively:
1. There is elision of the *ṇ*, *t*, *n*, *l*, *ś*, and *s* [when followed by a consonant].

From the root *kan* with the suffix *yaṅ-luk*, in the *laṅ* tense, second person singular (*sip*), the absence of the augment *nuk* in the reduplication is Vedic. The lengthening [of the vowel] is by the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ*. Upon the elision of *si*, the *m* of the suffix becomes *n* by the rule *mo no dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.64). It bears the accent of the verbal root; its non-suppression (*anighāta*) is due to its connection with *yadvat*. *yudhyantam*: The active voice (*parasmaipada*) is used by transposition. *daśayum*: From the root *div* meaning "to shine," the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *sampad* (Pāṇini 3.3.94). By the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19), *uṭ* is substituted. That which has its burden (*dhūḥ*) in the ten directions (*daśasu dikṣu*) is *daśayuḥ*. The shortening [of the vowel] is Vedic. Alternatively, the word *śu* is listed among the names for "day" (Nirukta 1.9.2); by this, light—which is the cause of its activity—is indicated. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent of the first member remains as the original. *śaphacyutaḥ*: "Fallen by the hoof" (*śaphena cyutaḥ*). The accent of the first member remains as the original by the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 6.2.48). *nakṣata*: From the root *nakṣ* meaning "to go. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by transposition. *śvetreyaḥ*: "The offspring of Śvitri. The suffix *ṅak* is applied by the rule *krībhyo ṅak* (Pāṇini 4.1.120). *nṛsahāya*: "One who endures men. The suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the object by the rule *śakisahośca* (Pāṇini 3.1.99). The acute accent on the first syllable is by the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213). In the compound, the accent of the final member as a *kṛt*-derivative prevails. The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] is by the rule *pūrvapadāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.106). The long vowel in the *saṃhitā* is Vedic.
You protected the bull in the battles, O Maghavan; you won the field, the cattle, and the shelter.
Even those who stood there for a long time were made to falter; you brought low the possessions of those who acted as enemies.

You protected the bull for shelter in the battles; O Maghavan, you [won] the white cow in the contest for the field. Even though they had stood there for a long time, they made the wealth of those acting as enemies low; you have brought it down.
O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, you protected—that is, you guarded—the previously mentioned man, the son of Śvitri, who was Śvitrya.
For what purpose? For the sake of winning the field (*kṣetrajeṣe*), that is, at the time of battle with the enemies for the purpose of obtaining the territory.

Of what kind? It is a state of well-being (*śarma*)—meaning peace—attained by abandoning mental agitation through your protection; it is a bull preeminent in virtues, who has gone into the waters (*gāṃ jaleṣu gataṃ*), that is, into the fourth state (*turyāsu*), for the sake of the mind (*manmathyarthaḥ*).
This is because the word *buburam* is listed among the names for water in the *Nirukta* (1.12.21).
In this battle against us, those enemies who stood for a long time—even for a very long duration—and acted as adversaries, committing hostilities;
of them, who desire to act as enemies (*śatrūyatām*), you have made their pain low—that is, you have inflicted inferior sufferings upon them.
The word *tuṣra* refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
In this context, the word *bhavat* means "beloved" (*priya*). The suffix *ghan* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 4.4.115 (*tu-prād-dhan*), and for that [suffix], the substitution of *iy* occurs.
The elision of the vowel *i* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
Due to the suffix being marked with *n*, the word is accented on the first syllable.
[The term is] *kṣetrajeṣe*.

In the root *jeṣ* (from *ji*, meaning "to go" or "to move"), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *saṃpad*. Thus, *kṣetra-jed* means "the movement within the field."
The compound has the udātta accent on its final syllable.
By the rule "antodāttād uttarapadāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.199) and others, the case-ending receives the udātta accent. Thus:
*śvitryam*.
The word *śvaitrya* means "born of a *śvitri* woman.
The suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *bhave chandasi* ("in the sense of 'born' in the Vedic language").
Its initial syllable is acute-accented by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*.
*tasthivāṃsaḥ*. [This is derived from] the root *tiṣṭhati* with the suffix *kasu*. The augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *vasvekājādghasām*.
They performed [the rite]. From the root *kṛ*, in the *laṅ* tense, the suffix *cli* is elided by the rule "In mantras, [the suffixes of the aorist] are elided after *ghas* etc. [Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.80].
[The form is] *śatrūyatām*.
"Those who desire enemies for themselves" are *śatrūyantaḥ*. [The suffix] *kyac* is applied according to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*; from that which ends in *kyac*, the suffix *śatṛ* is added.
In *tasya*, because the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*), the monophthongic accent (*ekādeśasvara*) applies, resulting in an acute accent (*udātta*).

Since it has been stated that "the substitution [of the monophthong] is not considered as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes" (Pāṇini 6.1.86), the acute accent of the stem ending in the present participle suffix *-śatṛ* remains; thus, by the rule "after *śatṛ* ending in *anu*, the case endings beginning with *nadi* and vowels are acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.173), the case ending is acute.
In the phrase *adharā vedanāḥ*, the elision of the suffix *śe* occurs according to the rule "in the Vedic language, the suffix *śe* is frequently elided" (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
*akaḥ*: In the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *kṛ*, there is elision of the suffix *cli* by the rule “*mantre ghasa*” etc.;
[then] *guṇa* [substitution occurs].
1. *ca-pha-śa* is *barburam*.
2. *cha-ṇa-na-la-yuphe* means "in battle"; *ca-pha-yupha-yuddhe*; *sa-yuphe*. 3. *śa-kṛtavāmasi*.

The fourth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "triścid dhy adya," has Hiraṇyastūpa Āṅgirasa as its seer (ṛṣi), according to the rule "ṛṣiś ca śrāmyasmāheḥ. The deities (devatā) are the Aśvins.
The ninth verse, “ka trī cakā,” and the twelfth, “ā no aśvinā,” are *triṣṭubh*s;
the remaining verses are *jagatī*s according to the rule concerning those ending in *triṣṭubh*.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: “The *Aśvina* hymn consists of three sets of three and twelve [verses]; the ninth and the others are *triṣṭubh*s.”

This hymn belongs to the *prātaranuvāka* at the *āśvina* sacrifice, in the *jagatī* metre. It is prescribed in the section beginning with "Now the *āśvina*" in the Sūtra: "The *jagatī* [hymn] is 'triścid dhi tvā,' 'ayele,' and 'dyāvāpṛthivī'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.15).
This same hymn is also used for the *āśvina* cup, because it is extended by the rule: "According to the method of the *prātaranuvāka*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.5).

May you two, O possessors of triple knowledge, be present today with your wisdom; may your journey and your gift be impartial, O Aśvins. For your restraint is like that of a garment in winter; may you be worthy of being approached by the wise.

Even thrice today, O you who are mindful, be present for us. Vast is your journey and your bounty, O Aśvins. For you are like the fastening of a garment in winter; may you be drawn near by those possessed of wisdom.
O Aśvins, the two wise gods, you who are *navedasā*—

the word *navedasā* being a name for the wise, as it is listed among their names in the passage, "The sage is *navedāḥ*, the thinker" (*Ṛgveda* 3.15.9)— such as you two, come three times (*triścit*) even today to this ritual for our sake; that is, come hither for us.

In this context, the expression "thrice" refers to the three *savana*s (pressings), or it is intended to indicate an excess of reverence, as another scriptural passage states: "For by means of the triad, the gods [attained their goal]" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 3.2.3.8). Your chariot, which is the means for your movement, is *vibhu*: pervasive.
Moreover, the "vratam" (vow) refers to the "giving" (dānam), as the word "vibhuḥ" (the pervasive one) is understood to be the remainder [of the compound].
Indeed, between you two, both of you, there exists a specific relationship characterized by mutual restraint; this is certainly the case.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like the day, which is clothed in the rays of the sun, with the night, which is possessed of frost—
as the connection between day and night never departs even for a moment—
so too are you both [united] by the wise, the intelligent officiating priests.
*Manīṣī* is a name for the wise, as it is listed among their names in *Nirukta* 3.15.11: "The wise one, Mandhātṛ.
O you two who are to be invoked and to be honored, by virtue of your favor, become subject to him and dependent upon him.
Now.
In the *saṃhitā* [text], there is a long vowel according to the rule “*nipātasya ca*” (Pāṇini 6.3.136).
Regarding *navedasā*:
they do not know [it] in a contrary way, thus they are *navedasau*.
From the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing," the suffix *asun* is added according to the *Uṇādi* rules.
In the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the original form of the letter *n* is maintained by the rule *nañaḥ śiśīlāpoḥ*, etc. By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the case-ending is replaced by the vowel *ā*.
The vocative is unaccented.
*Yāmaḥ*: that by which one goes, or by which one is made to go, is a *yāma*, namely a chariot.
By [the rule] beginning with “*atitusu*,” the suffix *man* is applied. Because it ends in *niṣ*, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.
Alternatively:
From the root *yam* in the sense of "restraint," the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the passive sense (*karman*).
Due to its inclusion in the *vṛṣādi* group, it has an acute accent on the first syllable. [The word] *rātiḥ*.
From the root *rā* in the sense of "giving," the suffix *ktin* is applied to form the abstract noun;
its acute accent is established by the rule beginning with *mantre vṛṣa*.
[The word is] *yuvoḥ*.
According to the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti*, the genitive dual ending is replaced by another genitive dual ending.
Consequently, because it is a subject of this substitution, the change to *y* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 7.2.89, *yo'ci*) does not occur.
Then, by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ*, the *ṭi* portion is elided; subsequently, the case-ending becomes acute according to the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*.
But according to the view that the final [vowel] is elided, it is by means of the accent of the single-substitute (ekādeśasvara):
"like the Himyā.
*Himā* is a name for night, because it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (1.7.22) with the words, "The *ūdhas*, *pathas*, and *himā* [are feminine]."
The suffix *mak* is applied by the rule *‘hanarhi ca’* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.144).
[Thus] *hima* means that which destroys (*hanti*) lotuses (*padma*). The suffix *yac* is applied by the rule *‘arśa-ādibhyo’c’*.
The word *himā* is the feminine form of *hima*.
Then, for the third case singular of the following [word], the substitution of *ṅī* occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
Subsequently, upon the elision of the *ṭi*-suffix, its vowel becomes acute by the rule regarding the accentuation of the disappearance of an acute vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*).
Regarding "vāsasaḥ":
from the root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*).
It is called the "garment of the day" (*aharvāsaḥ*) because it causes [the world] to dwell [in light] and covers it by means of illumination.
*Abhyāyaṃsenyā*:
from the root *yama* in the sense of "ceasing" (*uparame*), preceded by the two prefixes *abhi* and *ā*, the *senya* suffix is added according to the *uṇādi* rules;
the form *ā* [for the case-ending] is substituted by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
1. Ḍha: The two Aśvins. 2. Ca-cha-na: Come hither! Sa: You have come!
All three know all things according to the longing for Soma on the honey-bearing chariot.
Three supports have been firmly established for me to grasp; thrice by night and thrice by day you come with your strength.
Three are the steeds on the honey-bearing chariot; all indeed know the longing for Soma. Three are the pillars set up for support; thrice by night you travel, O Aśvins, and thrice by day.
In the honey-bearing chariot of the Aśvins, which is equipped for carrying various kinds of sweet substances and foods, there are three strong wheel-components as firm as thunderbolts;
these three, numbering three, exist in this manner.
Thus, all the gods (viśve devāḥ) know this mode of existence of the three wheels regarding the journey toward Soma’s lovely wife, Vena.
The meaning is that all the gods know: "When Soma marries Vena, at that time the Aśvins shall go, having mounted a grand chariot equipped with three wheels and provided with various kinds of food.
Upon that chariot, three specific supports (*skambhas*), three in number, have been fixed (*skabhitāsas*).
For what purpose?
To "begin" means to mount or to grasp.

When one travels with the speed of a chariot, at that time there are pillars serving as hand-rails for the purpose of removing the fear of falling; this is the meaning. O Aśvins, you two travel three times—meaning you go thrice—by such a chariot during the night.
Likewise, you go three times even during the day;
the meaning is that you mount the chariot again and again both by night and by day for the sake of sport.
Regarding *madhuvāhana*:
it is called *madhuvāhana* because it carries honey (*madhu*);
the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
They know (*viduḥ*). By the rule "vido laṭo vā" (*Pāṇini 3.4.83*), the substitution of *us* for *jhi* occurs after the root *vid* in the present tense (*laṭ*). [The form] *skambhāsaḥ*.
‘In the sense of obstructing movement.
They are called *skambhāḥ* because they obstruct—that is, they become impediments.
[The suffix] *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).

*Skabhitāsaḥ*: *skambh* is a root belonging to the *sautra* class. From this root, when the suffix *niṣṭhā* (kta) is applied, although the prohibition of *iṭ* would normally apply by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, the elision of *iṭ* is established as an irregularity (*nipātita*) by the rule *grasitaskambhitastimitāḥ*.
Regarding *ārabhe*:
from the root *rabh* in the sense of "rashness" (*rābhasya*),
the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) by virtue of its inclusion in the *saṃpad-ādi* group, preceded by the prefix *ā*.
The word-final accentuation of the base applies when a *kvip* suffix is present.
On the same day, within the secret enclosure, sprinkle the sacrifice thrice with honey;
O Aśvins, thrice pour forth for us food accompanied by strength at evening and at dawn.

On the same day, thrice in the place of concealment, thrice today, sprinkle the sacrifice with honey. O Aśvins, you two, thrice, pour forth for us food rich in strength during the evenings and at the dawns.
O Aśvins, you two gods, on this day of performance, may you both be the ones who provide a threefold concealment—that is, the covering of the faults occurring during the threefold performance.

On this very day, sprinkle the sacrifice—the oblation contained within the sacrifice—with honey, with sweet juice, three times. Furthermore, throughout the nights and the days—meaning continuously during the nights and the days—make for us the food-offerings rich in vigor (*vājavatīḥ*), which produce strength; that is to say, pour them forth and bestow them upon us.
I have killed.
The elision of the locative case ending occurs by the rule "supāṃ suluk," resulting in *avagohanā*.
The root *guhū* means "to conceal. [The term] *guhayitārau* refers to the two who conceal that which is spoken; the suffix *lyu* is applied because it belongs to the *anudāttet* class.
The absence of the *ū*-vowel substitution—which would otherwise apply by the rule *udupadhāyā gohaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.89)—is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
[The form is] *mimikṣatam*. [The root] *miha* means "to sprinkle."
In the case of *san*, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt" (Pāṇini 7.2.10).

Because *san* has the property of being *kit* according to the rule "halantācca" (Pāṇini 1.2.10), there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*). Then follow reduplication and the replacement of the remaining consonants (*halādiśeṣa*). [The forms] *ṭharvakasvaptvāni* and *vājavatīḥ* are derived; in the latter, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ugitaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.6). In *pinvatam*, the root *pivi*, *mivi*, and *ṇivi* mean "to sprinkle"; because it is marked with *it*, the augment *num* is added, and the suffix *śap* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
Moving in threefold course for the people who follow the threefold vow, bestow your aid thrice upon the one worthy of protection;
O Aśvins, bring him the threefold wealth, and thrice nourish his strengths like inexhaustible streams.

Three times come to our dwelling; three times to the people who follow your law; three times to the one who presses the Soma well. Bestow your aid in three ways, as it were. O Aśvins, you two carry no other [as your vehicle]; three times pour forth nourishments for this man like flowing streams.
O Aśvins, you two come to our house—the means for our journey—three times; that is, reach it thrice.
Likewise, [come] to the person who is *anuvrata*, endowed with activities favorable to us;
for that word is listed among the names of deities in the Nirukta (3.17.10) as "the sacrifice at the gathering of the gods" (*devatātā makhaḥ*).

In the word *liti*, the initial syllable is acute (*udātta*) because it precedes a suffix marked with *L*. The locative case ending is replaced by *ḍā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Thus, *tridham*.
He stands in the three wheels (*cakra*), thus he is *tridaḥ*. The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4).
The change of *sa* to *ṣa* is effected by the rule *ambāmba* (Pāṇini 8.3.97), etc.
In the word *sūra*, [the root] *pū* is used in the sense of "impelling. The suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule *susudhāgṛdhibhyaḥ kan* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.182).
The word *niruccā* has its first syllable accented (*ādyaudātta*).
There is a transposition of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*). [He] ascended.
By the rule *kṛmṛduruhibhyaśchandasi* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.59), the suffix *ślī* is replaced by the augment *aṅ*.
O Aśvins, thrice bestow celestial remedies, thrice those from the earth, and thrice grant us gifts.
O Lords of Splendor, bring threefold protection and auspicious peace for my son, carrying a triple-layered refuge.

O Aśvins, grant us threefold divine medicines; grant us threefold earthly ones, and threefold from the waters. O Lords of Splendor, bring protection and well-being to my son, and bestow triple-layered shelter. 6.
O Aśvins, grant us three times the divine medicines— that is, the herbs existing in the heavenly realm— and likewise grant us three times the earthly medicines produced upon the earth;
and may the fires also grant us three times the medicines from the intermediate space.

*Āpaḥ* is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), because it is listed among its names in [the Nirukta]: “*Āpaḥ*, *pṛthivī*, *bhūḥ*” (Nirukta 1.3.8). *Śaṃyoḥ* is the name of the son of Bṛhaspati;
this is known from another Brāhmaṇa text: “They heard Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.10.1).

Its connection is as follows: "The protection (*omāna*), that is, a particular kind of happiness, has been given by you to my son, my own child. O Lords of Beauty (*śubhaspatī*), you two who are the guardians of the auspicious medicinal plants, bring—that is, cause to attain—the happiness which has as its object the pacification of the three humors (*dhātu*), namely wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*)."
The suffix *ya* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.66 (*daṇḍādimyo yaḥ*).
[Thus we have] *bheṣajā*.

The suffix *gha* is applied [to the root] *bhṛ* in the sense of medical treatment (*cikitsā*) and when forming a masculine designation (*saṃjñā*), according to the rule "in the masculine, when it is a name. [Thus:
*śaṃyuḥ*.
The root *śam* is derived from the sense of “to pacify” (*upaśame*) with the suffix *kip*. Thus: *śam*.
The root *yu* means "to mix.
From this [root], the suffix *vic* is applied.
By the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaraḥ*, the original accent of the final member of the compound is retained.
The three realms (*tridhātu*). [The suffix] *tun* is applied after the roots *si*, *tan*, *gam*, *mā*, *mi*, *sās*, *vī*, *dhā*, *sṛ*, and *kṛṣ*.
[The suffix] *añc* is applied after [the root] *añj*.
In the word *aḍitam* and so forth, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is udātta. Regarding *omānam*:
from the root *av*, the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule “it is seen after other roots as well.”

By the rule *jvaratvara* etc., the substitution of *ūṭ* occurs for the vowels *a* and *va*. Then, the *guṇa* substitution, characterized by the rules for *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* affixes, takes place.

If, in the rule *jvaratvara*, the phrase *anunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19) were not carried over [by *anuvṛtti*], then the substitution of *ūṭ* for the letter *v* would still occur by the preceding rule alone.
*Śubhaspatī*: [The root] *śubh* means "to shine. The suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule for *saṃpad* and other formations.
In the *saṃhitā* text, the *visarjanīya* of "paṣṭrāḥ" becomes *s* (satva) according to the rule "pati-putra.

Because of the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) by the rule "sub-āmantrita," the entire compound consisting of "paṣṭrāḥ" and the vocative (*āmantrita*) receives the universal low accent (*sarvānudātta*) according to the eighth [chapter] of the *Pāṇinīya Śikṣā*.
O Aśvins, worthy of worship, day after day you have traversed the threefold earth;
O Nāsatyas, lords of the chariot, you have gone around the three distant regions as the wind goes to its sister winds like its own self.

Three times, O Aśvins, worthy of sacrifice, day after day, you have traversed the threefold earth. O Nāsatyas, as chariot-borne riders from afar, come to our dwellings like the wind to its own resting places. 7.
1. *Ca-pha-śamana-viṣayaṃ śarma sukham* [Ma. 1. Aṃ. 7. Sū. 34]:
"Three are the wheels of the threefold chariot; who knows the three seats that are co-dwelling?"
When will the yoking of the vigorous donkey take place, by which you two Nāsatyas come to the sacrifice?

Who [made] the three wheels of the triple chariot? Who [made] the three seats which are joined together? When is the yoking of the vigorous donkey, by which you two, O Nāsatyas, come to the sacrifice? || 9 ||
O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, the two shafts of your threefold chariot—which is endowed with three horses—are joined together at the front;
