this constitutes one yoke-pole.
At the rear, they are separated.
In that case, two corners are formed.
Regarding such a chariot, we do not see where its three wheels— three wheels— are situated.
Those specific pieces of wood which are of the same lineage—
the *nīla* being like a house—
O Nāsatyas, come here with the thirty-three gods for the drinking of the honey-sweet draught, O Aśvins.
Prolong our lifespan, wipe away our sins, drive off our enemies, and be our companions.
O Nāsatyas, come hither with the thirty-three gods, O Aśvins, to the drinking of the honey-sweet draught. Prolong our life-span; wipe away our sins; drive off our enemies; be our companions. 11.

O Nāsatyas, you two Aśvins, who are free from falsehood and untruth, come hither to this place of divine sacrifice together with the thirty-three gods—those deities belonging to the three groups of eleven, as set forth in such mantras as "The gods who are eleven in heaven" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.139.11)—for the sake of the drinking of *madhu*, that sweet substance consisting of Soma;
and may you extend our lifespan, increasing our vitality.
Wipe away our misdeeds, our sins, cleansing them entirely;
drive away hatred, ward off those who harbor it;
remain ever with us, dwelling together in companionship.
With three [syllables].
The case ending is acute according to the rule *pañcatricaturbhyaḥ*.
With eleven [syllables].
[The suffix] *id* is applied by [Pāṇini’s rule] *tasya pūraṇe* (Pā. Sū. 5.2.48) to form the ordinal numbers for the eleven. *Madhupeya*.
In the word *pāna*,
the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the object by the rule *aco yat*.
By the rule *īdyati* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.65), the vowel *ā* is replaced by the vowel *ī*.

In the phrase "yato'nāvaḥ" and so forth, there is the udātta accent. In the compound "madhu ca tapeyam," there is the original accent of the final member of the *kṛt*-derived word. [The form] is "tāriṣṭam."
The root *tṛ* means "to float" and "to cross.
In this Vedic (chāndasa) usage, the *luṅ* suffix is employed for the sense of a request (*prārthanā*); the *leḥ* is replaced by *sic*, and the augment *iṭ* is added.
The prohibition of the lengthening of the *it* vowel—which would otherwise apply by Pāṇini 7.2.38 (*vṛto vā*)—is established by Pāṇini 7.2.40 (*sici ca parasmaipadeṣu*).
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge’pi*” (the augment *aṭ* is optionally absent in the Vedic language even when not preceded by *mā*).

Here, because the particle *ca* is not employed despite its meaning being understood from the words *tāriṣṭam* and *mṛkṣatam*, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent applies according to the rule “*cādi-lope vibhāṣā*” (the *nighāta* is optional when particles such as *ca* are elided).
The initial acute accent is applied by the rule *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.187). [The form] *mṛkṣatam* [is derived from] the root *mṛś* in the sense of touching.
In the Vedic language, the *luṅ* suffix is used in the sense of the *loṭ* (imperative), according to the rule *chandasi luṅliṭaḥ*.
The substitution of *kas* for [the root] is according to *śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.45). The prohibition of the *iṭ* augment is by the rule *ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt*.
In *paśvakuruve*,
as before, there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*.
[The form] *sedhatam* [is derived similarly].
The root *iḍ* is used in the sense of "going" (*gati*).
Here, even though it is used alone, the suffix *vidhi* (the injunctive) functions in the sense of the prefix *prati*.
The *loṭ* (imperative) is used in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*).

The word *śapaḥ* is unaccented because it is a prefix (*pūrva*). The accent of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is the same as that of the root, due to the rule regarding the accent of *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes. There is no elision of accent (*nighāta*) because the word begins the quarter-verse (*pādādi*) and because it follows another verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
Hatred (*dveṣaḥ*).
[The suffix] *vic* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule “*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*.
It is the imperative form of the root *bhū*.

Because the word *dveṣaḥ* is contained within this same sentence, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) does not apply to this [word *sacābhuvā*] in relation to it, according to the rule: "The *nighāta*, as well as the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, must be stated to occur within a single sentence" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.18.5). As for *sacā*: this particle has the same meaning as the word *saha*.
And thus Yāska says: “*Sacā* has the sense of *saha* (together)” (Nirukta 5.5).
[The term] *sacābhuvau* means "those who exist together" (*sacā bhavataḥ*).
[This is formed with] the suffix *kip*.
The substitution of *yaṇ* [for the vowel] by the rule *oḥ supi* (Pāṇini 6.4.83) is prohibited by the rule *na bhū-sudhiyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.85).
The long vowel *ā* for the case-ending is substituted by the rule *supāṃ suluk-pūrvasavarṇ-ācch-e-yāḍ-āḍ-yā-ya-āḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
O Aśvins, come to us on your three-wheeled chariot, bringing horses and wealth accompanied by heroic sons.
Hearing me, I invoke you both for protection; be our strengtheners in the winning of the prize.

O Aśvins, on your three-wheeled chariot, bring hither to us wealth consisting of horses and heroic sons. Hearing me, I call upon you for protection; be present for our increase and for the winning of booty. 12.
4. Drinking honey-spirituous liquor.
The Rigveda.

O Aśvins, with your threefold chariot—which, because its course is unimpeded, traverses the three worlds—bring hither to us wealth consisting of excellent heroes, accompanied by noble sons, servants, and the like; having brought it, bestow it upon us.
Hearing our hymn of praise, I repeatedly invoke you both for our protection.
[Do this] for us in the battle for booty.

Because [the term] is listed among the names for battle in the passage, “In the winning of booty, in the great contest” (Nirukta 2.17.36), [it means] "for growth" (*vṛdhe*) and for increasing (*vardhanāya*). And may you two be so.
*Suvīram*: "One whose heroes (*vīra*) are excellent"—in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule *vīravīryau ca*, the first syllable of the final member is acute. *Śṛṇvantā*.

The root *śru* means "to hear. In the present participle (*śatṛ*), by Pāṇini 3.1.74, *śruvaḥ śru ca*, there is the substitution of *śru* and the change to the form *śru*. Then, by the rule *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke*, there is the application of the *yaṇ* substitute.
The vowel *ā* [in *johavīmīti*] is by virtue of the rule *supāṃ suluk*. [The word] *johavīmi* [is derived from the root *hu*]. [The root] *dviṣ* [is used] in the sense of rivalry and sound.

In the case of the elision of *yaṅ* (*yaṅluk*), from this root which has undergone vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.33, the augment *īṭ* is applied in the first person singular of the *laṅ* by Pāṇini 7.3.94:
*vṛdhe*. From the root *vṛdh* in the sense of "growth" (*vṛddhau*), the suffix *kvip* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpadādi* compounds.
In the word *vājasātau*: [the root] *paṇ* means "to give. By the rule beginning with *titutra*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.

The substitution of *ā* [for *a*] occurs by the rule beginning with "janasana"; furthermore, because the word means "that in which there is a winning (*sāti*) of spoils (*vāja*"), the original accent of the first member of the compound is retained.
‘Hy ābhy agnim’: this is the fifth hymn, consisting of eleven verses.
Hiraṇyastūpa is the seer (ṛṣi). The first and the ninth verses are in the Jagatī meter.
The remaining verses are *triṣṭubh*s.
Savitṛ is the deity for the entire hymn.
For the first verse, “hyābhyagnim,” the deities are Agni, Mitra-Varuṇa, Rātri, and Citra, as indicated by their respective characteristic marks (*liṅga*).
And thus it is enumerated: “Two [verses] for Agni, eleven for Savitṛ, nine Jagatī verses, and three pādas whose deities are indicated by their marks.
This hymn, dedicated to Savitṛ, serves as the insertion (nivid) in the Vaiśvadeva Śastra on the fourth day of the Abhiplava Ṣaḍaha.
It is prescribed in the section beginning with “The third day’s third round” in the Sūtra: “‘hyābhy agnim’, ‘asya me’, and ‘dyāvāpṛthivī’—these three” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).
I call Agni first for our well-being; I call Mitra and Varuna here for protection;
I call Night, who brings rest to the world; I call the god Savitar for aid.
I invoke Agni first for well-being; I invoke Mitra and Varuṇa here for protection; I invoke Night, who brings rest to the moving world; I invoke the god Savitṛ for aid. || 1 ||
For our well-being—that is, for our non-destruction;
Yāska states, “*Svasti* is a name for non-destruction” (Nirukta 3.21).
First, at the outset, I invoke Agni.
In this rite, for our protection, I invoke Mitra and Varuṇa.
I invoke Night, the deity of night, who is the cause of the settling—the resting place—for all that moves, the realm of living beings;
for it is well known that all mobile creatures, having performed their respective activities during the day, settle in their own homes at night.
I invoke the god Savitṛ for protection, that is, for the sake of our preservation.
*Mitrāvaruṇau*: By the rule *devatādvandve ca*, the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs for the first member;
by the same rule *devatādvandve ca*, both members retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
*rātrīm*:
[the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *rātrerāñjamau* (Pāṇini 4.1.31). *niveśanīm*.
It is called *niveśanī* because "they settle within it" (*niviśanty asyām*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca*;
the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* and so forth.
For the sake of protection (*ūtaye*). From the root *av* with the suffix *ktin*, by the rule "jvaratvara" etc., there is the substitution of *ū* for the semivowel *v* and for the penultimate vowel.
By the rule "ūti-yūti" etc., the suffix *ktin* is acute-accented.
Advancing through the dark expanse, establishing both the immortal and the mortal,
the god Savitṛ journeys upon his golden chariot, beholding all beings.
Advancing with his dark radiance, settling both the immortal and the mortal, the god Savitṛ comes on his golden chariot, beholding all beings. 2.

Savitṛ, the Sun, [travels] through the black space (*rajas*), that is, through the world of black color. Regarding this, Yāska states: "The word *kṛṣṇa* is derived from the root *kṛṣ*, meaning 'black' is the color" (*Nirukta* 2.20), and also: "The worlds are called *rajāṃsi*" (*Nirukta* 4.19).
For the intermediate world (antarikṣaloka) becomes black in color prior to the arrival of the sun.
Moving along that path of the intermediate space, returning again and again, he establishes the immortal god and the mortal man each in their own respective place.
Or alternatively:

Bestowing the immortal life-force (*amṛta*) which is free from death, and the mortal body (*martya*) which is subject to death; likewise, in the *Āraṇyakakāṇḍa*, in the form of a Brāhmaṇa explaining this portion of the mantra, "The immortal one [is] of common origin with the mortal" (*amartyo martyena sayoniḥ*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.164.38), there is the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent). [The word] *uddātā*: the root *ud-√ve* follows the same formation as before. *Yajataḥ*: by the rule *bhṛmṛdṛśi...* (Uṇādisūtra 3.390) and so forth, the suffix *atac* is added to the root *yaj* in the sense of the object. *Viśvā duritā*: in both instances, the elision of the *ś* occurs according to the rule *śecchandasī bahulam*.
Enveloped in pearls, possessing every form, with golden pins, great and worthy of worship—
Savitṛ, of wondrous luster, has mounted his chariot, assuming his power through the dark realms.
Enveloped in pearls, multiform, with golden pins, the worshipful Savitar, of wondrous luster, has mounted his lofty chariot, assuming power over the dark realms. 4.
Savitṛ has mounted the chariot; "has mounted" means he has ascended. Of what kind? Enveloped on all sides (*abhīvṛtam*), meaning existing all around it.
Likewise, it is multiform through *kṛśanas* and multicolored through gold;
for *kṛśana* is listed among the names for gold in the Nirukta (1.2.7).
In some places there is a row of elephants made of gold, in some a row of horses, and in others a row of men—thus its manifold nature.
*Hiraṇyaśamyam*:
*Śamyās* are pegs that are thrown onto the shoulders of the horses at the time of yoking the chariot to restrain them;
these are made of gold and are present on the chariot.
"Great" means mature.
Of what nature is Savitṛ? "Worthy of sacrifice," meaning he who is to be worshipped.
Citrabhānu, endowed with various rays,

assuming his own power (*taviṣī*)— which is of the nature of light— for the sake of dispelling darkness, directed toward the worlds that are black (*kṛṣṇa*), meaning dark-colored due to being possessed of gloom (*rajāṃsi*).
*Abhīvṛtam*: it revolves all around (*abhitaḥ*), thus it is *abhīvṛta*. [The root] *vṛtu* means "to revolve."
The lengthening of the vowel in the first member of the compound is according to the rule *kapi naḥivṛti0* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.116).
*Viśvarūpa*:
he whose forms (*rūpāṇi*) are all-encompassing (*viśvāni*) is *viśvarūpa*.

In the case of *hiraṇyaśamyam*, although it is not a proper name (*asaṃjñā*), the final syllable of the first member is accented by the transference of the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when it is a proper name, *viśva* [is antodātta]"; thus, even when it is not a proper name, the first member has its final syllable accented.
[The root] *harya* means "to go" and "to be beautiful."
By the rule *haryateḥ kanyan hara ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 5.722), the suffix *kanyan* is applied and the verbal root undergoes the substitution *hira*;
because it ends in *nit*, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) prevails.
He stood. [The form] *tiṣṭhate* [is derived from the root] *sthā* with the suffix *luṅ*; by the rule "gātisthā0," there is the elision (*luk*) of *m*. [The word] *kṛṣṇā*.
The suffix *na* is applied by the rule *kṛṣervarṇe* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.284). The elision of the suffix *śa* occurs by the rule *śecchandasi bahulam*.
[Thus we have] *taviṣīm*.
The root *tavi* is a Vedic (sautra) root.
By the rule *tavaterdiṅgā* (Uṇādisūtra 1.48), the suffix *ṭi* is added.
Since the suffix ends in *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* etc. (Pāṇini 4.1.15).
The initial udātta accent should be understood as occurring by way of transposition (vyatyaya) because [the word] belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group.
In the case of *dadhānaḥ*,
the initial udātta accent is due to the rule "the beginning of reduplicated forms" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*) when the suffix *śānac* is present.
The dark steeds with white-footed hooves have looked down upon the people as they carry the chariot with its golden fore-shaft;
all the worlds abide in the lap of the divine Savitṛ, throughout the quarters of space.

The dark-hued ones with white-footed hooves have looked upon the people, drawing the chariot with its golden fore-shaft; constantly, all the worlds abide within the lap of the divine Savitṛ, facing every direction. 5.
*Śyāva*s: these are the horses of the Sun, so named. This is because it is stated in the *Nighaṇṭu*: "The *śyāvas* belong to Savitṛ" (1.15.8).
And they were *śitipādaḥ*, endowed with white feet.
*Hiraṇyaprauga*:
the front of the chariot—the tip of the poles and the place where the yoke is fastened—is called the *prauga*.
And that [chariot] here was made of gold;
carrying it, the people—meaning living beings—beheld it with particular clarity.
(The root *yaj* is used here.)
2. *Ḍha-bahuham*:
the meaning is that they have made manifest.
*Śaśvat* means always; *viśvāḥ prajāḥ* (all creatures) stood in the lap—that is, in the vicinity—of the divine *savitṛ*, the impeller, the Sun, who is distinct from other gods.
Not only the subjects, but indeed all beings and all the worlds stood near the sun for the sake of light.
*Śitipādaḥ*: those whose feet (*pādāḥ*) are *śitayaḥ*, i.e., white-colored, are *śitipādāḥ*. The substitution of *su* for the case-ending *jas* is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
Alternatively: *śiti* means white-colored, such as crystal and the like; those whose feet are like that are [called] *śitipāt*.
By the rule *pādasya lopo'hastyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.138), there is elision of the final syllable of the word *pāda* when it serves as the final member of a compound;
for the word *upamānāt* is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) into that rule.
Furthermore, by virtue of belonging to the *vṛṣādi* group, the word *pāda* has its first syllable accented acute (*ādyudātta*).
In the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound *tasya*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member applies according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.2.138: *aśitairnibhyābahvajbahuvrīhāvabhasat*.
Regarding *ahyan*: in the *luṅ* tense of the root *syāti*, the substitution of *aṭ* for *cli* occurs according to the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ*.
*hiraṇyaprada-āgam*:
in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is retained;
[the word] *vahantaḥ*.

The word *śapaḥ* is unaccented because it is marked with the *pittva* designation. In *śatrum*, the accent of the verbal root prevails due to the elision (*lup*) of the suffix, according to the rule regarding the accent of the verbal root. [The word] *daivyasya*.

In the sense of "belonging to him" (*tasyedam*), the suffix *yañ* is applied after the word *deva* by the rule *devādyañño* (Pāṇini 4.1.85). The initial vowel is subject to *vṛddhi* strengthening by the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117).
By the rule *bhityādirnityam*, the word is necessarily udātta-accented on its first syllable.
In *upasthe*: the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge*;
the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*.
The acute accent on the final syllable of the first member [of the compound] is due to its inclusion in the *marudvṛdhādi* group.
Three heavens are within the lap of Savitṛ; one is in the world of Yama, where heroes prevail.
They stand upon the immortal [realm] like the linchpin of a chariot; let him who understands this declare it here.
Three are the heavens of Savitṛ; two are his lap; one is in the realm of Yama, the hero-conquering. Like a chariot-rim, the immortals have stood upon it. Let him who knows it declare it here. 6.
The heavens—characterized by the celestial realm—are the three shining worlds, numbering three in total.

Among them, two worlds abide in the vicinity of Savitṛ, the Sun; for both the heavenly world and the earthly world are illuminated by the Sun. One is the middle ground, the intermediate world (antarikṣaloka).
In the realm of Yama, in the abode of the Lord of the Fathers, the conqueror of heroes (*virāṣāṭ*) overcomes those who go to the *virās*.
This means that the deceased persons (*pretāḥ puruṣāḥ*) travel by way of the intermediate space (*antarikṣamārgeṇa*) to the world of Yama.
The immortals (*amṛtāḥ*), namely the lights such as the moon and the stars, or the waters, have taken their stand upon the immortal ones; having approached Savitṛ, they remain there.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
the *āṇi* is a specific wedge inserted into the hole of the axle of a chariot or similar vehicle; it is called *āṇi*.
Just as a chariot remains stable by means of reaching the *āṇi* associated with the chariot, so it is here.
But that person who understands—that is, knows—"That Savitṛ"—let that person speak, let him declare it here in this matter;
the meaning is that the greatness of Savitṛ cannot be described by anyone.
*tisraḥ*: by the rule *tisṛbhyo jasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.166), the case ending (*jas*) is acute. *dvau*.

In the *saṃhitā*, there is the substitution of *ā* [for *u*] and the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule "ālopaḥ śākalyasya"; thus, there is the elision of the letter *v*. [The form] is *upasthā*.
According to the supplementary rule (*vārttika*) "āṅyājādyārāṃ copasaṃkhyānam" (Pāṇini 7.1.39.1), there is the substitution of *āṭ* for the locative case ending.
The absence of *prakṛtibhāva* [in the case of *virāṣāṭ*] is due to the rule *āṅo'nunāsikaśchandasī* (Pāṇini 6.1.126).
[The root is] *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*).
The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.58 (*ghañarthe kavidhānam*).
The substitution of *i* for *ī* occurs according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.103 (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
This being so, the term *virāṭ* is explained as that which "is chosen" (*vṛyante*).
He who endures them is *virāṣāt*.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied to the root *sah* by Pāṇini’s rule *chandasi sahaḥ* (3.2.63).
The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* is effected by the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ* (8.3.56).
The long vowel of the preceding member [of the compound] is also seen in these cases; for example, *rathyam*. This belongs to a chariot (*ratha*), thus it is *rathyam*.

Regarding *'rathādyat'* (Pāṇini 4.1.78), after the rule *'dhātusvaraḥ'* [which states that the accent of the verbal root remains], there is an additional point: "By virtue of the rule *'kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvena'*, that very same [root-accent] is preserved. 2. *Ḍha* refers to a specific type of wood.

Regarding the word *yat*: by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, it has the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable. *Amṛtā*: the elision of the *śi* suffix occurs by the rule *śeṣ chandasi bahulam*. *Ciketad*: from the root *kit* in the sense of “knowing. In the *leṭ* mood, the augment *aṭ* is added; the *ikāra* is elided by the rule *itaśca lopaḥ*; and because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is reduplication (*ṛju*). There is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*). By the rule *anudātte ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.190), the beginning of the reduplicated form (*abhyasta*) receives the acute accent. Due to its connection with a word beginning with *yad*, it does not undergo the grave accent (*anighāta*). || 6 ||

The fair-winged one has surveyed the intermediate spaces, the deep-quivering Asura, the excellent leader. When now does the Sun appear? Who has perceived it? To which heaven has his ray extended? vi suparṇo antarikṣāṇy akhyad gabhīravepā asuraḥ sunīthaḥ | kadānīṃ sūryaḥ kaściketa katamāṃ dyāṃ raśmir asyā tatāna || 7 || The fair-winged one has surveyed the intermediate spaces, the deep-quivering Asura, the excellent leader. When now does the Sun appear? Who has perceived it? To which heaven has his ray extended?

"Suparṇaḥ" means one of beautiful flight, a ray of the Sun. This is because it is listed among its names in the *Nirukta*: "The names of the fifteen rays are [listed], beginning with 'Suparṇaḥ'" (*Nirukta* 1.5.15). "Antarikṣāṇi" refers to the three worlds situated in the intermediate space, characterized by the atmosphere; he has "Vi-akhyat," that is, he has made them known or illuminated in every way. What kind of ray? "Gabhīravepāḥ," meaning deep-vibrating; the sense is that the trembling or movement of the ray cannot be perceived by anyone. "Asuraḥ," the giver of life to all. Thus it is recited elsewhere: "He rises, taking up the breaths of all beings" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 1.14.1). "Sunīthaḥ," meaning well-guiding or providing excellent guidance; the sense is that by illuminating the path, he causes one to reach the desired destination. Where now, during this night, does the Sun possessing such a ray abide? Who knows this secret? The meaning is: no one at all. Which heaven has the ray of this Sun pervaded during the night? Who knows even this? **Grammatical Notes:** * **Suparṇaḥ**: By the rule "nañ-subhyām" (*Pāṇini* 6.2.172), the final syllable of the second member is udātta. * **Gabhīravepāḥ**: From the root *vep* (in the sense of trembling). With the suffix *asun*, we get *vepa*. That whose trembling is deep is *gabhīravepāḥ*. The accent follows the natural accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*). * **Asuraḥ**: From the root *as* (in the sense of throwing). He throws away his enemies, thus he is *asuraḥ*. The suffix *uran* is added by *Uṇādi-sūtra* 1.42. Due to the *nit*-suffix, the initial syllable is udātta. Alternatively, he gives (*rāti*) the vital breaths (*asūn*), thus he is *asuraḥ*. The suffix *ka* is added by the rule "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (*Pāṇini* 3.2.3). * **Sunīthaḥ**: From the root *ṇī* (in the sense of leading). The suffix *kyan* is added by the rule "hani-kuṣi-nī-ra-mi-kāśibhyaḥ kyan" (*Uṇādi-sūtra* 2.159). In the *prādi*-compound, the final syllable of the second member is udātta by the rule "thā-thādinā" (*Pāṇini* 6.2.144). * **Idānīm**: From the word *idam*, the suffix *dānīm* is added in the sense of the locative case by "dānīṃ ca" (*Pāṇini* 5.3.18). By "idam iś" (*Pāṇini* 5.3.3), *idam* is replaced by *iś*. The suffix is udātta. * **Sūryaḥ**: From the root *sū* (in the sense of impelling). He impels, thus he is *sūryaḥ*. The suffix *kyap* along with the augment *ruṭ* is prescribed by the rule "rājasūya-sūrya... (*Pāṇini* 3.1.114). When the suffix is udātta, the root-accent remains udātta. * **Ciketa**: From the root *kit* (in the sense of knowing). Perfect tense (*liṭ*). * **Katamām**: Of which kind? From the interrogative *kim*, the suffix *ḍatamac* is added by "vā bahūnāṃ jātiparipraśne ḍatamac" (*Pāṇini* 5.3.93). Due to the *ḍit*-suffix, there is elision of the final *a*. By the rule "citaḥ" (*Pāṇini* 6.1.163), the final syllable is udātta.

He has revealed the eight regions of the earth, the three desert wastes, the yojanas, and the seven rivers. The golden-eyed god Savitṛ has come, bestowing precious treasures upon the donor. He has revealed the eight regions of the earth, the three desert wastes, the yojanas, and the seven rivers. The golden-eyed god Savitṛ has come, bestowing precious treasures upon the donor.
1. *Ḍha* means "suparṇa" (eagle), because it is listed among the names for the rays.

2. *Ḍha* means "trembling. Savitṛ has "spread out," that is, illuminated, the eight *kakubhas* belonging to the earth—the four cardinal directions beginning with the east and the four intermediate directions beginning with the southeast—thus making eight directions in total.

Likewise, Savitṛ—the golden-eyed one, whose eyes are endowed with what is beneficial, or whose eyes are made of gold—has come here; he has spread out the three worlds, namely earth and the others, characterized by the intermediate space (*dhana*), as well as the seven rivers such as the Gaṅgā and the oceans, thereby uniting living beings with their respective enjoyments. May that divine Savitṛ come hither.
Doing what?
Bestowing—that is, granting—to the donor, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation, desirable treasures that are worthy of being chosen.
*asyat*: from the root *syati* (to throw), in the *laṅ* tense, the *cli* suffix is replaced by *ad* according to the rule "asyativakti-" and so forth. *trī*.
The elision of the *śi* suffix occurs by the rule "śeṣchandasi bahulam.
[The word is] *dhanva*.
[The roots] *riv*, *rav*, and *dhav* have the sense of moving.

The augment *num* is applied by the rule "idito num dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.58). From this [root], the suffix *kanin* is applied by the rule "kaninyuvṛṣitaśirādhiganvipratidivaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.97). The case-ending is elided by the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
There is elision of the *n*.
Due to the *nit* status of the suffix, the first syllable is udātta. This is the construction.

They are called *yojanas* because living beings are joined (*yojayanti*) with them for the purpose of enjoyment; the suffix *lyu* (i.e., *ana*) is used here according to the rule beginning with *nam-pādi*, and the suffix *ṇi* is elided by the rule *ger aniṭī*.
As before, there is the elision of the *ś* sound. *Hiraṇyākṣaḥ*:
he whose eyes (*akṣīṇi*) are made of gold (*hiraṇyamaya*) is *Hiraṇyākṣaḥ*.
The suffix *ṣac* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) by the rule "bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.113). [In the form] *agāt*,
the substitute *gā* is applied for the root *iṇ* in the *luṅ* tense by the rule "iṇo gā luṅi" (Pāṇini 2.4.45).
In the form *gatisthā*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*. In *dadhat*,
because it ends in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*, the augment *num* is prohibited by the rule *nābhyastāc chatuḥ*.
There is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "bhābhyastayorātaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.120).
There is acute accent on the first syllable by the rule "abhyastānāmādiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.189).
[The word is] *dāśuṣe*.
The word [vasu] is derived as a base ending in the *kasu* suffix by the rule "dāśvānsāhvān... etc.

In the singular dative case, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam," followed by the substitution of the preceding vowel for the two sounds (*parapūrvatva*).
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca.
[The word is] *vāryāṇi*.
[The root] *vṛh* [is used] in the sense of "to collect" (*saṃbhaktau*).
By the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*,
and by the rule *īdavanda* etc., the word has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
Savitar, the golden-handed, the all-beholding, moves between both heaven and earth;
he drives away disease and impels the sun; through the dark realm, he reaches the sky.
The golden-handed Savitṛ, the observer of the people, moves between both heaven and earth. He drives away disease; he impels the sun and reaches toward the sky through the dark expanse. ||9||
"Hiraṇyapāṇiḥ" means one who possesses hands made of gold; or alternatively,
one who held gold in his hand in order to bestow it upon the sacrificers.
*Vicarṣaṇiḥ*: endowed with various modes of seeing.
*Vicarṣaṇiḥ* has the sense of "one who sees. This is because it is listed among the names [of Agni] in the *Nirukta* (3.11.6): "vicarṣaṇiḥ, viśvacarṣaṇiḥ."
The god Savitṛ moves between both heaven and earth, that is, he travels in the midst of both worlds;
he drives away, that is, he completely dispels, affliction such as disease and the like;
likewise, he goes forth.
Although Savitṛ and Sūrya are one and the same deity, there still exists the relationship of the goer and the destination due to the distinction between their forms.

With "black" (kṛṣṇa), meaning that which draws away or dispels darkness, and with "rajas," meaning brilliance, he "reaches toward" (abhi ṛṇoti) the "heaven" (dyām), that is, the sky, pervading it on all sides.

*dyāvāpṛthivī*: By the rule *divaśca pṛthivyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.30), because of the word *ca*, the substitution *dyāvā* occurs for the word *div*. In the case of a *devatā-dvandva* (dual compound of deities), there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*) of both members.
There is no prohibition by the rule *nottarapade'nudāttādau* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.142), because [the word *īśvara*] is excluded by the specific exception *apṛthivīrudrapūṣamanviṣu*. Thus it is said:
*īyate*.
The root *īṅ* means "to go. [In the phrase *bādhate īṅ gatau*,] there is the *nighāta* accent according to the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*. [He] obstructs.

And because the meaning of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is understood from the word "or" (*veti*), even though the word *ca* is not employed, there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent according to the rule "when *ca* and other particles are elided, it is optional.
Regarding *veti*: the root *vī* is used in the senses of motion, procreation, beauty, eating, and devouring.
Because it begins with *adādi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
Since *tip* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
Even though this...
1. By means of the nature of the letter *ḍha*.
2. The world is blinded by the night of ignorance, [which is] *ḍha*. (Ka.

In the second case as well, because it follows a *tiṅ* suffix, there is an absence of *nivāta*. [The form] is *ṛgnoti*. [This is derived from] the root *ṛguganau*. Because it belongs to the *tanādi* class, the suffix *u* is applied. According to the opinion of Āpiśali, there is an absence of *guṇa*, on the grounds that within the *tanādi* group, *guṇa* applies only to the root *kṛ*, and not to others.
The golden-handed Asura, the good leader, the gracious one, the flowing stream, the protector of travelers— he, the god,
being praised at every evening, drives away the Rakṣases and the Yātudhānas.

The golden-handed Asura, the good leader, the gracious one, the flowing streams—may he come hitherward; driving away the Rakṣasas and the sorcerers, the God has taken his stand, being praised at the approach of evening. 10.
The golden-handed, the bestower of wealth, the giver of life, the good leader—that is, the one who is highly praised;
for he is listed among the names for wisdom in the Nirukta (3.8.7) as "Sunīthaḥ pākaḥ.
He is the one who brings excellent happiness, the possessor of flowing wealth, who comes forward, moving toward the place of action.
Or rather, why has this god remained standing, being praised and lauded at every doṣā, that is, every night?
What was he doing?

And speak before the gods with your superior power. *panyāḥ*: by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the case-ending *jas* is replaced by *su*; by the rule *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne*, the first syllable receives the acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*). *pūryāṃsaḥ*: those made by the ancients (*pūrva*) are *pūryāḥ*. By the rule *pūrvaiḥ kṛtaminiyau ca* (Pāṇini 4.4.133), the suffix *ya* is applied; the accent belongs to the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), and the augment *asun* is added. *areṇavaḥ*: by the rule *nañsubhyām*, the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) receives the acute accent. *sukṛtāḥ*: the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense (*karmani*); by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the preceding preposition (*gati*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*). *sugebhiḥ*: they go well upon these, thus they are *sugāḥ*. By the rule *suduroradhikaraṇe* (Pāṇini 3.2.48), the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam*; the accent belongs to the original form of the second member (*kuduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*). *rakṣa*: in the *saṃhitā* text, the vowel is lengthened according to the rule *vyo'tastiṅaḥ*. 7 || 7 ||
In the eighth section (anuvāka), there are eight hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of twenty verses, begins with "pra vo yahvam.
Its seer (ṛṣi) is Kaṇva, the son of Ghora.
The odd-numbered *brahmī* verses consist of twelve syllables in their third quarter;
the even-numbered *sato-bṛhatī* verses consist of twelve syllables in their first and third quarters.
Their deity is Agni.
The verses beginning with “ūrdhva ū ṣu” are dedicated to the sacrificial post (yūpa).
This is indicated in the Anukramaṇī: “Pra vo viṃśatiḥ; Kaṇva Ghaura [composed] the [hymn] for Agni; the [verses] beginning with ‘prāgāt’ and ‘ūrdhva ū ṣu’ are for the sacrificial post.
Now, one might object: since these two [verses] beginning with “ūrdhva ū ṣu” are not excluded from the Āgneya sacrifice, they ought to have Agni as their deity as well.

For instance, because the Sūtra employs only the opening lines—“enā vo agnim” and “pra vo yahvam” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13)—it is understood that the entire hymn is dedicated to Agni. Had these two been addressed to other deities, the Sūtra would have prescribed an extraction, as it does elsewhere: “one should omit the last verse of the hymn beginning with ‘vasiṣvā hi’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13). But it does not so prescribe.
Therefore, how can they be called "pertaining to the sacrificial post" (*yaupya*)?
This is not a fault.

Since the fire that has the sacrificial post as its substrate is being praised, these two are also considered to have Agni as their deity; thus, in the *Āgneya* sacrifice, no separate extraction (*uddhāra*) is made for them.
With the intention of emphasizing the predominance of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), even the statement that [the two verses] are "made of wood" (*yaupya*) is not contradictory.
In the *Prātaranuvāka* of the *Āgneya* sacrifice, within the *Bārhata* meter, there is the hymn beginning with “*pra vo yahvam*.
This is prescribed in the section beginning with “Now, at the time of the dawning of this night,” in the Sūtra: “*enā vo agnim pra vo yahvam*.”
We entreat with well-spoken words and hymns the mighty Agni, who belongs to many tribes of the god-seeking people, and whom the kindling-sticks attend and praise.
We implore with well-spoken words and hymns Agni, the vigorous one, for you—the divine-seeking clans of many peoples—him whom indeed others also praise. 1.

Being officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), for the sake of your favor—of you who are great (*yahvam*)—we earnestly entreat Agni with hymns (*sūktebhiḥ vacobhiḥ*), that is, with words in the form of hymns. [He is great] "for the many (*purūṇām*) people (*viśām*), who are desirous of the gods (*devayatīnām*)," as it is said in the list of names for the "Great" (*mahat-nāmasu*): "The Great One has grown" (*yahvaḥ vavakṣita*, Nirukta 3.3.13). We pray to him most intensely.
Because it is recited among the rites of supplication in the *Nighaṇṭu* (3.19.1), "We implore; we go," [the word *īmahe* means "we implore"].
"Others" means that other sages as well "praise"—that is, they laud—that Agni "on all sides. "Him, Agni"—this connects with what precedes.
Of the many:
the word *nāman* has an acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule "nāmanpatarasyām. Of the people (*viśām*).
The acute accent on the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. Regarding *devayatīnām*:
those who desire the gods for themselves are called *devayantyaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* and the prohibition *na cchandasyaputrasya*, there is a prohibition of both the short and long *ī*-vowel substitution. This is because of the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of the subsequent prescription of the *ā*-vowel substitution in the rule *aśvāghasyāt*.
After a root ending in *kyac*, the suffix *laṭ* is replaced by *śatṛ*.
In the sense of the agent (*kartari*), the suffix *śap* is added.
Because *śap* is marked with *p*, it is *anudātta* (unaccented).

In the formation of the *ekādeśa* (single substitute) of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) with the *kyac* suffix by means of the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka* [suffix], the *śatṛ* becomes acute according to the rule “*ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*” (a single substitute for an acute vowel is acute).
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule “*ugitaśca*”.
Due to the statement “the prescription of augments is not permanent,” there is an absence of the *num* augment.

Because of the rule stating that the substitution of a single vowel (*ekādeśasvara*) is not considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to what precedes it (Pāṇini 8.2.1), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the suffix *śatṛ* is already established; thus, by the rule "śataranumaḥ," the feminine stem ending in *nadi* receives the acute accent.
[Examples: *sūktebhiḥ*.
In *vakteḥ*, the suffix *kta* is applied by the rule *sikttau ca saṃjñāyām*; the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member is due to the rule *thāthādinā*. 268.

The gods—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman—kindle you, the ancient messenger. O Agni, that mortal who offers oblations to you conquers all wealth through you as his ally. O Agni, Varuṇa and the other gods kindle you, the ancient messenger. That mortal sacrificer who has offered oblations to you, with you as his helper, wins all wealth. *Aryamā*: He measures out what belongs to the noble ones (*arya*); formed with the suffix *kanin* according to the rule beginning with *śṛṇuṣva*. *Indhate*: From the root *indhī*, meaning "to kindle"; in the present tense (*laṭ*), after the substitution of *ad* for *jha*, the *bh* is substituted; then by *ābhalopaḥ* and *bhasoralopaḥ*, the vowel *a* is elided. *Dadāśa*: From the root *dāśva*, meaning "to give"; in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *nal*, the vowel preceding the suffix becomes acute by the accent of the suffix (*lisvara*), and there is no suppression of the accent due to its connection with *yadvṛtta*.

Thou art the delightful Hotṛ, the lord of the house, and the messenger of the people, O Agni. In thee all the firm ordinances have come together, which the gods have established. O Agni, thou art the *mandra*—the source of joy—the *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods, the *gṛhapati*, the protector of the home of the *viśaḥ* (the people in the form of sacrificers), and the *dūtaḥ*, the messenger of the gods. In *tve* (in thee), *viśvā vratā* (all the ordinances)—all ritual acts—have *saṃgatāni* (come together). The word *vrata* is listed among the names for action in the Nirukta (2.1.7): "Vrata means *karvara* (act). The *devāḥ* (gods), such as Earth and the others, *akṛṇvata* (performed) those *dhruvā* (firm/steadfast) acts. [The connection with the preceding verse is: "Earth supports, Parjanya rains, and Sūrya shines"—these very acts have come together in thee. Grammatical notes: *gṛhapatiḥ*: By the rule *patyāvaiśvarye*, the first member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). By *supāṃ suluk*, the case-ending *sas* (genitive singular) is replaced by *śeṣa*. By *tvamāvekavacane*, *maparyantasya* is replaced by *tvā*. In the alternative where the *ṭi* is elided, the case-ending becomes acute by the *udāttanivṛttisvara*; in the other case of elision, it is by the accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*). *saṃgatāni*: From the root *gam* with the suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle). There is a prohibition of *iṭ* by *ekācaḥ*. The nasal is elided by *anudāttopadeśa...*. The prefix *gati* retains its original accent by *gatiranantaraḥ*. *vratā dhruvā*: In both cases, there is elision of the *śi* (nominal suffix). *akṛṇvata*: From the root *kṛvi* (meaning to injure or to do). The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by *vyatyaya* (irregularity). *Num* is added because it is marked with *it*. O Agni, most youthful and youngest, in you alone—who are auspicious and endowed with good fortune—all the oblation (*havis*) is offered and cast from every side.

Therefore, being well-disposed and gracious toward us, worship the gods endowed with excellent power on this day, and furthermore tomorrow, and on all subsequent times, continuously at every moment. O auspicious one!
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *śobhano bhago yasya*, there is initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*).
By the rule *yacchandasī*, there is acute accent on the first syllable of the final member. [The vocative] *yaviṣṭha*.
From the word *yuvan*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied.
By the rule beginning with *sthūladūra*, there is elision of everything following the *yaṇ* (the *u*) and the preceding vowel undergoes *guṇa*.
The addition of the letter *y* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
O Yakṣi; [the suffix] śap is elided by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi";
[the form] suvīryā.
Those whose vigor (*vīrya*) is excellent;
the acute accent on the first syllable of the compound is due to the rule *vīravīryau ca*.
The substitution of the vowel *ā* for the case-ending is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

In the evening *abhiṣṭava* (recitation), this verse, “*taṃ ghemithā namasvinaḥ*,” is prescribed in the subsequent chapter. It is stated in the section beginning with “*athottaram*” in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (4.7): “The *prāgāthī* [verse] in the forenoon; the *kāṇvī* in the afternoon. “*Taṃ ghemithā namasvina upa svarāja̭māsate*... [They, the reverent ones, sit near him, the self-ruling one...]
With oblations, men kindle Agni with their hymns, having crossed over all difficulties.
To him, the self-ruling one, the reverent ones sit down in this manner; with oblations, men kindle Agni, having crossed over all difficulties. 7.

O Agni, those sacrificers who are *namasvin*—either having yoked themselves with homage or being endowed with reverence—the word *namaḥ* signifying food because of its inclusion among the names for food in the Nirukta (2.7.22): "Homage is life, truth, and pleasant speech. Such sacrificers sit near you, the self-ruling one (*svarāj*), shining by your own power, that very one characterized by all the previously mentioned qualities, in this manner, through the offering of oblations and so forth.

"Manuṣaḥ" means human beings who are sacrificers, by means of the seven *hotrā*s—that is, the seven officiating priests who utter the *vaṣaṭ* call; for another Śruti states: "The seven *hotrā*s offer the *vaṣaṭ* call facing eastward" (*Tai. Brā.* 2.3.6.4). They kindle you, O Agni—they thoroughly inflame you.
What kind of men are they?
They are those who have overcome their enemies, crossing over them with preeminence; they are those who offer homage.
In the word *asāyāmedhā*, the suffix *vini* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). [The term] *svarāj*: he shines by his own light; thus, he is *svarāj*.
In the word *satsṛdvipa*, the suffix *kip* is applied;
it takes the original accent of the final member of the compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
They sit.
The root *ās* means "to sit.
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. [Thus we have] *titivārṃsaḥ*.
The root *plu* means "to float" or "to cross.
According to the rule *chandasi liṭ*, the *liṭ* suffix is used for the present tense;
for that, the suffix *kasu* is applied by the rule *kruśca*.
The absence of the augment *iṭ* follows from the rule "vasvekājād dvam" (Pāṇini 7.2.67).
The substitution of *it* for *ṛ* follows from the rule "ṛta iddhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.100).
The *guṇa* substitution follows from the rule "ṛcchatyṛtām" (Pāṇini 7.4.11).

Furthermore, the lengthening [of the vowel] prescribed by the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77) does not occur, because both of those rules are non-obligatory (*anitya*) on the principle that "a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical name is non-obligatory.
Alternatively,
one should regard *tirati* as a different verbal root altogether.
*Sīrthaḥ*: [derived from] the root *sṛdh* in the sense of "drying up" (*śoṣaṇe*);
the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule *'kip ca'*.
Slaying Vṛtra, they crossed over heaven and earth; they made the waters wide for their dwelling.
When invoked with oblations, the Bull became manifest in glory to Kaṇva; he roared at the sacrifices for the sake of the Gavi.

Slaying Vṛtra, they crossed over heaven and earth and the waters; they have made wide room for their dwelling. May the bull, resplendent when invoked, be present for Kaṇva. Let him roar, the one half [of the sacrifice], in the quests for cattle. 8.
1. Ha!
O Agni, as you were slaying Vṛtra, the other gods, striking from their own side, crossed over—that is, they traversed it.

Immediately thereafter, you made the two worlds, heaven and earth, and the waters—the intermediate space—for the dwelling, that is, for the habitation of living beings, so that they might become wide and expansive.
The word *āp* denotes the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), as it is listed among its names in [Nirukta] 1.3.8: "The waters are the earth.

May you, however, O Kaṇva—Kaṇva by name, the great sage—be a bull (*vṛṣan*) who showers down desires, be glorious (*dyumnin*) and wealthy, and be one to whom oblations are offered from all sides (*āhuta*). May you thus come to be.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a horse, "neighing"—that is, making a sound—in battles "for cows," meaning those involving the desire for cattle, brings about what is desired; such is the implied sense.

Apa: | The word "udidam" has an udātta accent due to the suffix śas. Kṣayāya.
The roots *kṣi* [mean] "dwelling" and "going.
That in which they dwell—that is, reside—is a *kṣaya*, meaning a place of residence.
The suffix *gha* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *gha* is generally used in the masculine when forming a name."
The word *bhuvanam* has its initial syllable udātta according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.201, *kṣayo nivāse*.
It is derived from the root *bhū* in the leṭ tense with the augment *aṭ*.
The elision of the vowel *i* occurs by the rule "there is also elision from here" (*itaśca lopa:*);
the elision of the suffix *śap* occurs by the rule "it is frequent in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*);
and the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution occurs by the rule "in the case of *bhū* and *su*, [the augment] *tiṣ* is applied" (*bhūsuvostiṣṭhi*).
When the augment *aṭ* is unaccented, the accent of the verbal root prevails. Thus, *āhutaḥ*;
[it is derived as] *āhūyate* (he is called), hence *āhutaḥ*.

He cried out; [the root] *kadi*, *kradi*, or *kudi* is used in the sense of "calling.
The absence of the augment *num* in the present participle (*śatṛ*) is a Vedic anomaly.
Because it is taught as having an initial vowel (*adupadeśāt*), when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
[This occurs in the word] *gaviṣṭheṣu*.
[The root] *iṣu* [is used] in the sense of "desiring" (*icchāyām*).

O Agni, sit down; settle upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). You are great; you are pre-eminent in qualities. Being most desirous of the gods (*devavītamaḥ*), shine forth; blaze up. O *miyedhya*—worthy of sacrifice, praised, and excellent—O Agni, emit (*visaja*) your smoke, which is of the nature of movement (*aruṣam*), visible (*darśitam*), and beautiful to behold. *Sīdasva*: from the root *sad* (to dissolve, go, or sink), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by transposition; in the imperative (*loṭ*) used for a request, the substitution of *sīd* for *sad* occurs according to the rule *pāghrā*. *Mahān*: in the *saṃhitā*, the vowel *a* and the letter *n* are said to become *hrasva* and nasalized. *Śocasva*: from the root *śuc* (to shine). Since it is taught with a short *u* (*adupadeśa*), the accent of the verbal suffix (*lasārvadhātuka*) is unaccented, leaving the accent of the root. Due to its position after a finite verb (*tiṅ*), there is no suppression of the accent (*nighāta*). *Devavītamaḥ*: from the root *vī* (to go, procreate, desire, eat, or consume). One who knows or goes to the gods is *devavīḥ*; the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvip ca*. *Devavītamaḥ* means "most desirous of the gods. Since the suffix *tamap* is *pit*, it is unaccented, and the original accent of the final member of the compound remains. *Aruṣam*: not causing harm (*a-ropaṇam*). From the root *rip* (to injure) with the suffix *ka* added in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāve*) according to the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam*. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound "that which has no harm," the final syllable of the second member is accented by the rule *nañsubhyām*. *Miyedhya*: the suffix *ya* is applied in the Vedic sense of "worthy of" (*arha*) by the rule *chandasi ca*. The intervening *m* and the augment *iy* are Vedic (*chāndasa*). *Visaja*: from the root *sṛj* (to emit). The suffix *śa* is applied because it belongs to the *tudādi* class. The accent of the verbal derivative (*vikaraṇa-svara*) applies. Because it begins a quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no suppression of the accent. *Darśitam*: the suffix *atac* is applied to the root *dṛś* in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *mṛdaśa*.

O Agni, carrier of oblations (*havyavāhana*), for the sake of Manu—that is, for the favor of Manu—all the gods (*devāsaḥ*) placed you here in this region inhabited by the divine folk (*devajana*), you who are most worthy of sacrifice (*yajiṣṭham*), most excellent in worship, or most fit to be honored.

Medhyātithi—the great seer named Kaṇva, so called because he was accompanied by guests who were seekers of wisdom (*medhā*)—placed you there; the ellipsis being that he did so having made you one who delights in wealth (*dhanaspṛtam*). Likewise, Indra (*vṛṣā*), the showerer of benefits, placed you there.
Likewise, another praiser, the sacrificer who has placed you—himself being thus praised—he, you, should sit down together; such is the connection with what precedes.
