The root *cara* has the sense of "going.
According to Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.3.115 (*lyuṭ ca*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
By the accent rule for the *liṭ*-suffixes, the syllable preceding the suffix is acute (*udātta*).
The original accent of the final member of the compound [is retained].
*dadhire*. [From the root] *dhṛ* "to stand firm."

Because the *liṭ* affix is marked with *k*, there is an absence of *guṇa*, and consequently, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. Due to its being marked with *c*, it has the udātta accent on the final syllable.
Because of its connection with the word *yat*, it does not undergo *anighāta*.
*Śravasyavaḥ*:
*śravaḥ* means "wealth," derived from the root *śru* ("to be heard") with the suffix *asun*.
"Desiring that for themselves" means *śravasyavaḥ*.
[The suffix] *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*;
then, by the rule *kyācchandasī*, the suffix *u* is added.

1. Ḍha-uṣaḥ: in the sense of "inciting" (upodevane). 2. Ḍha-priyahitāḥ: words that are dear and beneficial. 3. Ta-pha-codaya; La-sa-codaya. 4. Ḍha-purastāt. 5. Ḍha-karotītyarthaḥ: meaning "he performs. 6. Ḍha-na iva.
O Dawn, those who yoke their minds for the sake of giving during your journeys—among them, Kaṇva, the best of the Kaṇvas, here proclaims the name of these men, as does Sūrya.
O Uṣas, those who harness their minds for your journeys to bestow gifts—here indeed Kaṇva, the most Kaṇva-like among these men, praises the name of Sūrya. 4.
When your journeys, O Dawn, have begun, the wise ones—those who understand giving—direct their own minds toward the act of giving, for the sake of bestowing wealth and other riches.

This means that noble and generous lords desire to give at the break of day. Regarding those who thus desire to give, the most highly intelligent Kaṇva, the great seer, proclaims here at this very time of dawn that world-renowned name of theirs associated with generosity; he recites it aloud.
Both he who desires to give and he who praises the giver by mentioning his name perform this very act at the time of dawn; thus is the praise of the dawns.
He utters. The root *gṛ* is used in the sense of "sound"; it belongs to the *kaiyādi* (adādi) class.
The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule “*pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*” (Pāṇini 7.3.80).
In *nṛṇām*,
there is a prohibition of the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] by the rule “*nṛ ca*” (Pāṇini 6.4.6), which applies when a case-ending beginning with *nām* follows.
The acute accent on the case-ending is due to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.184: *nṛ cānyatarasyām*.
Like a young woman, she comes forth like a daughter, bestowing enjoyment;
wearing out the dwelling, the footed one stirs up the winged birds.
Like a maiden, like a mother toward her son, Dawn approaches, bestowing gifts. Wearing away the strength of all that has feet, she moves; she causes the birds to fly up. || 5 ||
The goddess Uṣas, the nourisher, who protects all with excellence or pervades all, indeed arrives day after day.
Herein is an illustration:
like a *sūnarī*, a woman who is a skilled leader of household duties, she is like a mistress of the house.
What kind of Dawn is she?
She is one who causes the *vṛjana*—the moving, wandering multitude of living beings—to grow old, bringing them to decay;
for when the non-greatness [of life] has returned, living beings become worn out through the loss of their vitality.

Furthermore, at the time of dawn, the multitude of living beings endowed with feet rises from sleep and goes forth for their respective duties. Moreover, this Dawn causes the birds to fly up; the birds, having risen at the time of dawn, go here and there.
In the *saṃhitā* [text], the long vowel is applied by the rule "ṛci tunugha" and so forth.
She is called *sūnarī* because she leads well (*suṣṭhu nayati*).
In the word *nṛnaya*, the suffix *i* is applied by the rule *acaḥ haḥ*.

In this *gati-samāsa*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *kṛdikārād aktinaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.45, Gaṇasūtra), based on the metarule (*paribhāṣā* 28): "When there is a mention of a *kṛt*-derived form, that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included."
The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member [of the compound] is due to the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam*;
the lengthening of the vowel in the first member is due to the rule *nipātasya ca*;
thus: *prabhuñjatī*.
The root *bhuja* is used in the senses of "protecting" and "eating. From it, the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is applied; because it belongs to the *rudhādi* class, the augment *bha* is inserted.
By the rule "aśoralopaḥ," there is elision of the vowel *a*;
by the rule "ugitaśca," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied;
and by the rule "śataranamaḥ," the syllable *naś* receives the udātta accent.
*Vṛjanam*: from the root *vṛjī*, meaning "to exclude" or "to ward off. That which is excluded is *vṛjana*, namely the multitude of living beings (*prāṇijāta*).
The suffix *kyu* is applied by the rule *kṛpvṛjimandinidhābhyaḥ kyuḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.239). Because it is marked with *k*, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light vowel.
When *y* and *o* are replaced by *an*, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) applies.
*Padvat*: *pad* means "foot"; that which possesses this [foot] is *padvat*. By the rule "after a *jhay* [consonant], the *m* of *matup* becomes *v*," the *m* of *matup* is replaced by *v*.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the suffix *matup* occurs by way of transposition.
Nor does the rule “in the application of accent rules, a consonant is as if non-existent” (Paribhāṣā 79) apply here,
because of the specific function of the *ṭha*.
It must be stated that when [the suffix] is as if non-existent, the *matup* suffix receives the acute accent according to the rule "after a short vowel and *nuṭ*, *matup*" (Pāṇini 6.1.176).

Since this would already be established by the rule "after a short vowel" (*hrasvāt*) alone, the fact that *nuṭ* is mentioned again indicates that this *paribhāṣā* is not to be applied; thus it is stated in the *Vṛtti*.
Otherwise, in the case of *marutvān* as well, the *matup* would receive the acute accent.
She who drives apart the assembly and the seekers of wealth, knowing not their station;
at her dawning, O possessor of riches, those who desire food sit waiting for you as for a bird.
She who brings forth the sacrificial food, she knows the station of those who seek it; bestowing strength, at her dawning, none who desire her remain sitting still, O possessor of abundant wealth. 6.
"The deity who impels—that is, urges forward—the man who possesses *asamarna*, meaning one whose actions are harmonious and appropriate;
it is well known that the time of dawn (*uṣaḥkāla*) rouses from sleep those men skilled in the activities of the household, garden, and so forth, and impels them toward their respective duties.
Furthermore, Dawn impels the *arthinaḥ*, the seekers or supplicants."
For they too, at the time of dawn, [gathered] together...

He goes forth, moving preeminently toward the human beings with chariots, specifically with chariots joined in numbers of hundreds. [The form] *ayukta* is the root-aorist (*luṅ*) of the root *yuj*; the suffix *sic* is elided by Pāṇini 8.2.26 (*jhalo jhali*). *Udayanam*: "from rising" or "where he rises"; derived from the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *lyuṭ* used in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇe*). The accentuation follows the rule for the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*). *Subhagā*: "she whose fortune (*bhaga*) is beautiful. The first syllable of the second member has the acute accent according to the rule *āyudāttaṃ chandasi*. *Mānuṣān*: "human beings," meaning the sons of Manu. The suffix *añ* is applied with the augment *puk* by the rule *manojātavantyatī puka ca*; because the suffix is marked with *ji*, the first syllable has the acute accent.
The daughter of heaven, the bountiful Dawn, the noble lady, makes the world visible for all to behold; she creates light for the living and drives away hostilities, revealing the path to success.
The whole world bows down before her gaze; the noble daughter of heaven makes light appear. The wealthy Dawn, the daughter of heaven, shines away all enmity and drives away our adversaries. 8.

The entire (*viśvam*) moving (*jagat*) world, the multitude of living beings, bows down (*nanāma*) for the sake of the light (*cakṣase*) of this Dawn (*asyāḥ uṣasaḥ*). The meaning is that all people, submerged in the darkness of night, having found the Dawn who dispels it, offer their salutations. Why? [Because...]
Since this *sunarī*, the excellent leader who brings about the attainment of desired fruits, the Dawn (*uṣas*), creates light— that is, she illuminates everything—

moreover, the wealthy (*maghonī*), the possessor of riches, the Daughter of Heaven (*divaḥ duhitā*) born from the light of the celestial realm, the Dawn (*uṣas*), drives away (*apa ucchat*) those who hate (*dveṣaḥ*); likewise,
she drives away (*apa ucchat*) those who parch (*sidhaḥ*).
Therefore, the meaning is that the entire world pays homage to the deity who is the cause of attaining what is desired and avoiding what is undesired.
For this [word *asyāḥ*]:

by the rule “*idamo 'nvādeśe*” (Pāṇini 2.4.32), there is the substitution of *aś*, which is anudātta; and since the case-ending is also anudātta due to being called *suhava*, the word is entirely udātta.
[The verb] *nanāma*.

In the *Saṃhitā*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable according to the rule "it is also seen in other cases as well. For if it were among the *tujādi* group, the long vowel would be heard even at the time of the *pada-pāṭha*, as in *tutujānaḥ* and similar forms.
*Jyotiḥ*.

With the continuation of the rule *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ*, the rule *isusoḥ sāmarthye* (Pāṇini 8.3.44) prescribes the substitution of *visarjanīya* by *ṣ*. [Thus we have] *dveṣaḥ*. [The root] *dvipa* [means] "to be hostile."
By the rule "it is also seen after other [roots]," the suffix *vic* is applied; the penultimate vowel undergoes *guṇa* substitution due to being light (*laghu*);
thus, *maghonī*.
She is called *maghonī* because she desires (*vanati*) and bestows (*saṃbhajate*) wealth (*magham*).
The word *maghavan* is derived with the suffix *kanin* according to the rule beginning with “*śrudhakṣan*.
The feminine suffix *dīp* is applied by the rule “*ṛjebhyo dīp*.”
In the word *bhas*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule “*śru-yava-maghonām at-taddhite*” [Pāṇini 6.4.133].
[The root] *ucchi* means “to shine” (*vivāse*).
In the sense of separation, there is avoidance [of the augment].
While the rule "luṅ-laṅ-liṭaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.6) is in effect, the suffix *laṅ* is used.
Due to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasy amādyoge 'pi," there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.
*Sidhaḥ* [is derived from the root] *sidhu* in the sense of "drying up" (*śoṣaṇe*). The suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *kip ca*.
O Dawn, daughter of heaven, shine upon us with thy radiant and gleaming light;
bringing us abundant fortune, dawn thou upon our sacrifices.
O Dawn, daughter of heaven, shine upon us with thy radiant and gleaming light; bringing us abundant prosperity, dawn thou brightly for our sacrifices. 9.
O Daughter of Heaven, O Goddess Uṣas, shine forth everywhere with your radiant, gladdening light!
What are you doing?
Bestowing abundant prosperity upon us during the days of our divine worship.
1. In manuscript ḍha, the phrase "with chariots yoked with horses" is absent.
2. In manuscript ḍha, the meaning is "they perform a bowing.
3. In manuscript ḍha, [it is] "by that which causes delight to all."
Bringing [wealth] to us, accomplishing it;
likewise, shining forth, driving away the darkness.
upa: | The vocative accent (āmantritā-śuddhāttatva) is optional. duhitardivaḥ |

Furthermore, by the rule *param api chandasi*, when the subsequent word *divaḥ* ending in a case-suffix (*padam*) is treated as if it were part of the preceding vocative member, the entire vocative compound becomes entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*) according to the eighth [chapter of Pāṇini].
[The word] *āvahantī*:
the feminine suffix *ḍīṣ* and the primary suffix *ap* are unaccented because they are marked with *p*.
Because [the root] *śat* is taught with an initial low vowel (*adupadeśa*), the suffix belonging to the *lasārvadhātuka* category is unaccented by virtue of its own accent;
therefore, the accent of the verbal root remains.
In the compound, the original accent of the final member ending in a *kṛt* suffix prevails.
*Bhūri*: It is called *bhūri* because it prevails and does not perish. The suffix *kin* is applied according to the rule: *adi-śada-bhṛ-śu-bhyaḥ kin* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.505).
The initial vowel is acute by virtue of being a *nittva* [suffix].
*Saubhāgyam* is the state of being fortunate (*subhaga*).
The suffix *an* is applied because [the word] *subhaga* is listed among those beginning with acute-accented words in the rule "subhagānmantra" (Pāṇini 5.1.128).

Regarding the form *nyucchantī*: although the rule *“hragasindhvante pūrvapadasya ca”* (Pāṇini 7.3.19) would require the vṛddhi strengthening of both members of the compound, it is stated in the *Vṛtti* that, by virtue of the maxim *“sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante”* (all rules are optional in Vedic usage), here the vṛddhi occurs only in the second member. [The root] *uccha* means “to shine forth.”
The root *vṛj* belongs to the Taudādika (the sixth class).
Because it is taught with a short vowel (*adupadeśa*), when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the accent falls on the *vikaraṇa*.

Regarding the term *diviṣṭeṣu*: by the word *div*, the sun (*āditya*) who dwells in heaven (*diviṣṭa*) is indicated. Those days on which his *iṣṭayaḥ*—his desires, seekings, or movements—occur are called *diviṣṭayaḥ*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is maintained].
For you alone are the breath and the life of the universe when you shine forth, O noble lady;
as such, O radiant one, hear us with your great chariot and grant us wondrous wealth.

For the breathing and the life of the entire universe depend on you alone, O noble lady, when you shine forth three times. As such, O radiant one, hear our call with your great chariot, O you of wondrous wealth! 10.
O goddess Dawn, O daughter of the Sun, for the breathing, the consciousness, the living, and the maintenance of life of every class of living beings indeed reside in you alone;
since you drive away the darkness,
O radiant one endowed with distinguished light, may you come toward us by a great and noble path— this is the ellipsis.
Likewise, O Goddess Uṣas, you who possess wonderful wealth, hear—listen to—our invocation.
"Breathing" (*prāṇana*). [The root] *ana* is used in the sense of "motion.
By the rule *lyuṭ ca*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs as follows: in a compound, by the rule *aniteḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.19), the letter *n* following the cause—a letter *r* situated in a prefix—undergoes the change to *ṇ*.
Now, one might object: since the term *aniteḥ* refers specifically to the root *iṭ* (the causative marker), how can there be the change to *ṇ* in the case of the root *ana* meaning "motion"?
In that case, because "life" (*jīvana*) is mentioned separately, activity is indicated by that very element (*dhātu*).
In the compound, there is the accent of the original form of the final member (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara*).
In the *saṃhitā*, the monophthongized substitute (*ekādeśa*) is acute due to the accent of the single substitute.
In the word *tve*, the suffix *ṅ* (the genitive ending) of the seventh case is replaced by *e* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Thus, it becomes *ucchasi*.
In *uccha vivāse*,
[the root] belongs to the *tud* class;
because the suffix *sip* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented, and thus the accent falls on the *vikaraṇa* (conjugational suffix).
By the rule "nipātair yadyadihanta," there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent. *Sūnari*:
she who leads well (*suṣṭhu nayati*) is called *sūnari*.

From the root *nṛ* (to lead), the *ip* suffix is applied according to the *uṇādi* rule *aca iḥ*. Since this is a *gati-samāsa*, the rule *kṛdgrahaṇe gatikārakapūrvasyāpi grahaṇāt* applies; thus, by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added.
Furthermore, by the rule *nipātasya ca*, the initial vowel of the first member (*nṛ*) is lengthened.

In accordance with the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam*, which prescribes that the first syllable of the second member [of a compound] is udātta, the rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19) applies, resulting in the *nighāta* (suppression of accent) for the vocative.
*Vibhāvari*:
she whose light (*bhā*) is distinguished (*viśiṣṭā*).
The suffix *vanip* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.2.109, *chandasīvanipau*.
By the rule *vano ra ca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added, and simultaneously, the *n* of the suffix is replaced by *r*. [Thus, the form is *śruṣṭī*];
hear! (*śrudhi*).
In the phrase *śṛṇuprukruvebhyaśchandasi*, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs;

by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*); and because *hi* is not marked with *pittva*, it is oxytone (*antodātta*) by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
There is no elision (nighāta) because it begins with a pada-initial.
*Magha* is a name for wealth.
She whose wonderful wealth (*magha*) is manifold is *citramaghā*.
‘The suffix *ḍha* is also seen after other [roots]’: 1. *uṣodevatā*.

[The substitution of *au* for *ava* occurs] after a cause (the letter *a*) situated in a prefix consisting of *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *pha*, *la*, *śa*, or *sa*; that is, after a cause situated in a prefix [ending in those letters].
In *saṃhitā*, the final vowel of the preceding word becomes long. [Example: *havam*.
The root *dviṣ* is used in the sense of rivalry and sound.
By the rule "bhāve 'nupasargasya," the suffix *ap* is applied; by virtue of that application, there is also vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

Win for us indeed the prize that is wondrous among the human folk; with that, bring hither the well-performed sacrifices, [bringing] those many [offerings] which they who praise you present. 11. Win for us indeed the prize that is wondrous among the human folk; with that, bring hither the well-performed sacrifices, [bringing] those many [offerings] which they who praise you present. 11.
O Uṣas, "win"—that is, beg for or take possession of—"vāja," which is food characterized by the oblation, as is well known in the Śrutis.

That "vāja" which is "citra," meaning wonderful or praiseworthy, and which exists among the "mānuṣe jane," that is, among the human beings who have been born as sacrificers—to that vāja, the connection with the preceding words is thus:
"by means of that [vāja], bring hither, that is, cause to reach, the 'adhvarān,' the sacrifices free from injury, belonging to the 'sukṛtaḥ,' those sacrificers who have performed [the rites] well."
"Those many sacrificers who perform the sacrifice praise you"—this connects with the preceding phrase "those who have performed good deeds.
What is meant is this:
having accepted the oblation offered by the sacrificers, you again bring their sacrifice to completion.
*vājam*:
[derived from] the root *vaja-bhaja* meaning "to go"; the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).

In the rule *ajivyajyośca* (Pāṇini 7.3.60), because the word *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārthatva*), and because the *Vṛtti* states that there is an absence of the *kṛtva*-suffix even in the case of *vāja* and *vājam*, there is an absence of the *kṛtva*-suffix here as well.
When the rule *karṇāvataḥ* would have prescribed an udātta accent on the final syllable, the initial syllable is instead udātta due to its inclusion in the *vṛṣādi* group.
[The form is] *vaṃsva*.
The root *van* means "to beg.
Here, by means of this verbal root signifying begging, the subsequent acceptance [of the gift] is indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
By the rule "optionally in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).

Because it has an anudātta vowel as its final phoneme, the suffix *lasārvadhātuka* is anudātta, and thus the accent of the root remains. By the rule "hi ca," there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent).
[The word is] *sukṛtaḥ*.
In the expression "sukarmapāpa" and so forth, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *kṛ* in the sense of a completed action (*bhūtārtha*). There is the addition of the augment *tug*.
The accentuation follows the rule for the natural accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).

Regarding *adhvarān*: since *dhvara* means violence (*hiṃsā*), the term *adhvara*—meaning "that in which there is no violence"—is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By the rule *nam-subhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172), the final syllable of the latter member of the compound is acute-accented.

As for the word *adhvarān*, because it denotes that which is most desired by the agent (*karturīpsitatamam*, Pāṇini 1.4.49), it receives the designation of *karman* (object). However, as for the word *sukṛtaḥ*, it receives this designation by the rule *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51); furthermore, because *vahati* is specifically enumerated among the roots that govern two objects in the rule *nīvahoraṃteśca* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.51).
In the word *adhvarān*, the *n* becomes *m* in saṃhitā by the rule "dīrghād aṭi" (Pāṇini 8.3.9).
By the rule "āto 'ṭi nityam" (Pāṇini 8.3.3), the preceding vowel *ā* becomes nasalized (*sānunāsika*).
They chant.
From the root *gṛ* in the sense of "sound," [the suffix] *śnā* is applied according to the rule *śryādibhyaḥ śnā*; then, by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*, the shortening of the vowel occurs.

In the phrase "bhāvyastayorātaḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *ā*; it bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*), and because of its connection with a *yad*-clause, it is not subject to the rule of non-accentuation (*anighāta*).

Bring all the gods from the mid-air for the drinking of Soma, O Dawn! May you bestow upon us wealth consisting of cattle and horses, praiseworthy strength, and heroic vigor, O Dawn! 12. Bring all the gods; for the drinking of Soma; from the mid-air; O Dawn; you; may she; bestow upon us; consisting of cattle; possessing horses; praiseworthy; O Dawn; strength; heroic vigor. 12.
O Uṣas, you—come from the intermediate space, from the world of the atmosphere, and bring hither all the gods for the drinking of Soma; cause them to reach our place of sacrifice.
O Uṣas, may you, being such, bestow upon us food that is rich in cattle, possessed of many cows, endowed with horses, praiseworthy, and accompanied by excellent heroic power.

*Nidhehi* means "place" or "establish. *Dhāḥ*: from the root *dhā*, the *luṅ* (aorist) is used in the sense of a benediction according to the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*. By the rule *gatisthā*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge’pi*, there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*. *Gomat* and *aśvāvat*: in the mantra, by the rule *somāśvendriya*, there is lengthening before the suffix *matup*. In both cases, the case-ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *Ukthyam*: *uktha* is a hymn of praise (*stotra*). That which exists therein is *ukthya*. The suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *bhave chandasi*. Since "all rules are optional in the Veda," the rule *yato’nāvaḥ* (which would have made the first syllable udātta) does not apply; instead, by the rule *tisrvaritam*, the word has the *svarita* accent. *Uṣaḥ*: as a vocative, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable. Because it begins the quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no suppression (*nighāta*) of the accent. *Suvīryam*: that whose heroism (*vīrya*) is excellent. By the rule *vīravīryaṃ ca*, the first syllable of the second member of the compound is udātta.
May she whose radiant, auspicious beams have shone forth bestow upon us wealth containing all desirable things, well-fashioned and rich in cattle— Uṣas.
O radiant one,
O great and worshipful goddess Upā, those ancient seers (ṛṣis)— the visionaries of the mantras— who are indeed well-known, [approached] thee for protection.
*Avas* is a name for food.
"For protection (*avas*) and for food (*annāya*), they have sacrificed (*juhure*)"—the meaning is that they have invoked her and praised her with hymns in the form of mantras.

O *Uṣas*, you who are such, being characterized by *rādhas*—wealth in the form of oblations offered by us—and by *śukla*—brilliant *śocis*, a luster capable of dispelling darkness—just as [you did] for those seers, so for us (*naḥ*), look toward our *stomas*, our praises, and *guṇīhi*: proclaim that we have praised well.
The meaning is: "Be satisfied with our hymns of praise.

Regarding the word *ūtaye*: from the root *av* (to protect), with the suffix *ktin*, the semivowel *v* and the penultimate vowel are changed to *j* according to the rule *jvaratvara* etc. (Pāṇini 6.4.20).
By the rule "utiyūti" etc., the suffix *kin* is prescribed as having an udātta accent.
[The form] *juhure* [is derived from] the root *heñ*, meaning "in rivalry" and "in sound."
In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), due to the rule "and [the reduplication] of the reduplicated stem" (*abhyastasya ca*), there is reduplication of *didī* and *devan*.
The suffix *isi* is applied according to the rule "from *añcu*, *ci*, *hu*, *sṛp*, *chā*, and so forth, the suffix *isi*" (Uṇādisūtra 2.265).
The light penultimate syllable receives the accent;
this is the accent of the suffix.
Sprinkle us with great wealth, adorned with all beauties; sprinkle us with refreshments, with splendor that pervades all, and with strengths, O thou who art rich in booty!
O Dawn, bestow upon us great wealth of every form; sprinkle us with refreshing nourishments, with splendor that overcomes all, and with mighty strengths, O thou rich in booty! 16.
O Uṣas, "pour out" (sam-mimikṣva)—that is, sprinkle upon or bestow—"wealth" (rāyā), that is, riches, "upon us" (naḥ).
With what kind of wealth?
With "abundant" (bṛhatā) and "all-adorned" (viśvapeśā) wealth.
*Peśas* is a name for form;
by means of its possession of manifold forms.
Likewise, "with *iḷās* and with cows, sprinkle us thoroughly."
*Ilā* is a name for a cow, because it is listed among its names in [Nirukta] 2.11.7: "The *ilā* is the *jagatī*.
The vowel *ā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), because it occurs at the end of a word.
And it is said: "In this very sense, the letter *ā* comes from the gods and the ancestors" (Nirukta 1.4). Furthermore:
"O Great One, O Worshipful Goddess Upā, be thoroughly mixed with *dyumna*, that is, glory.
Yāska states: "*Dyumna* is derived from the root *dyut* [to shine]; it means either glory or food" (Nirukta 5.5).
With what kind of splendor? With that which is "all-conquering" (viśvatūrā), meaning destructive toward all enemies;
likewise, O "possessor of nourishment" (avājinīvati)—you who are endowed with the activity that serves as the means for obtaining food—sprinkle us thoroughly with "vājas," that is, with foods.
For there is another scriptural passage stating, "Food indeed is strength" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 9.3.4.1).
The King: [In the phrase] "uḍidam" and so forth, the case ending is udātta (accented). [The word] "bṛhatā".
In the rule "The [final syllable] of *bṛhat* and *mahat* becomes acute when followed by a short vowel," the case ending is acute.
*Viśvapeśāḥ*:
he whose forms (*peśāṃsi*) are all-encompassing (*viśvāni*) is *viśvapeśāḥ*.

In the case of *bahuvrīhi*, by the rule "when *viśva* [is a member], [the final syllable is acute] in a name," there is an irregularity (*vyatyaya*) whereby the final syllable of the first member is acute even when it is not a name.
Alternatively,
it belongs to the class beginning with *maruddvṛdha*, which is a *dvandva*.
*mimikṣva* [is derived from] *√mih*, "to sprinkle. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
In the imperative (*loṭ*), by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," the suffix *śap* is replaced by *kṣu*. Then, reduplication and the elision of the remaining initial consonant (*halādi-śeṣa*) apply.
Finally, the substitutions for *ch*, *k*, and *p* take place.
Because the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) is more specifically prescribed (*satiśiṣṭatva*), that alone remains.

Since the preceding word does not reside within the same sentence (*asamānavākyasthatva*), the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) does not apply for the suppression of accent (*nighāta*), according to the statement: "The suppression of accent, the substitutes for *asmad*, and so forth, must be stated as occurring only within the same sentence. Thus: *viśvaturā*.
The word *tuḥ* is derived from the root *turv*, which means "to injure. According to the rule "krip ca," the suffix *krip* is applied.
By the rule "rālopaḥ," there is the elision of the *v*. Thus, from *viśvapām tūḥ* comes *viśvatuḥ*. By the rule "samāsasya," the final syllable is udātta.
"O possessor of vigor (vājinīvati)! 'Vigor' (vāja) means food; that which possesses this is 'vigorous' (vājinī), namely, action.
She who possesses such action is thus described."
The sixth hymn consists of four verses beginning with "upa bhadrebhiḥ. Regarding this, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Upaśrutka is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The seer (ṛṣi) is Praskaṇva, the son of Kaṇva.
By the technical rule beginning with *tu* (Pāṇini 1.2.37), this subsequent [verse] is also in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.

Since it was stated previously that "the *upastha* [is the seat]," this hymn (*sūkta*) is also the *upastha*. This hymn belongs to the *anuṣṭubh* metre in the *ṛtu* of the *prātaranuvāka* performed at the *upastha*.
For it is prescribed: "One should approach with the auspicious [verses] according to the *anuṣṭubh* meter" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.14).
This hymn is also used in the *āśvina* recitation, because of the extended application (*atideśa*) stated as: "According to the rule for the *prātaranuvāka*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.5).

O Uṣas, come with auspicious things from the very light of heaven. Let those who possess the reddish-white steeds bring you to the house of the Soma-presser, O Uṣas. 1. O Uṣas! With auspicious things, come! Even from the luminous realm of heaven! Let those possessing the reddish-white horses carry you to the house of the one who offers Soma, O Uṣas! 1.

O Goddess Uṣas, come hither from the sky— the intermediate region— from the luminous, shining realm, by means of auspicious, praiseworthy, and beautiful paths; "from above" (adhi) signifies from the upper part.
From that which exists above; *cit* has the sense of "honored" (2). Come, come hither from such a honored intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*).

O Uṣas, may those red-hued cows, possessing the color of dawn, bring you—red-footed—to the house of the Soma-offerer, the sacrificer endowed with Soma, that is, to the sacrificial hall which is the place of divine worship. May they convey you there.
*gahi*: By the rule *gameloṭi bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
Since the suffix *hi* is treated as having an indicatory letter *ṭ* (by the rule *herapittvena*), there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) by the rule beginning with *anudāttopadeśa...*.

Therefore, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *he* does not occur, because the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "that which is [treated as] non-existent here is as if it had not taken effect" (*asiddhavad atrābhāt*). [The form] *rocanāt* [is derived from] the root *ruc* in the sense of shining.
The suffix *yuc* is applied by the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*.
With the substitution of *yan* for *ya*, the final syllable is udātta by the rule *citaḥ*. Thus, [the word] is *aruṇapsāḥ*.
The root *psā* means "to eat. They eat, they consume, they suckle at the breast; thus, *psavaḥ* refers to calves.
The suffix *ku* is derived from the *uṇādi* list.
The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*. Those whose calves (*psavaḥ*) are ruddy (*aruṇāḥ*) are "those having ruddy calves" (*aruṇapsavaḥ*).
Here, because the redness of the calves is established, it is understood that the mothers likewise possess that same quality.
"Dice follow the father;
cows follow the mother," says Gonardīya (Pāṇini Mahābhāṣya 1.3.21.5).
And their status as "approachers" (*upavāhana*) is stated in the *Nighaṇṭu*: "The ruddy cows of the dawns" (Ni. 1.15.7).
The word *aruṇa* ends in the suffix *-una*, according to *arteśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 5.685).

Because the word *cit* is understood from the rule *tṛṇākhyāyāṃ cit* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.339), it is oxytone (*antodātta*). That same accent remains when it occurs in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by virtue of the rule that the first member retains its original accent (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).

O Uṣas, daughter of heaven, with that well-adorned, sweet-sounding chariot which you have mounted today, protect the people of noble fame. *supeśasam* (well-adorned), *sukharan* (sweet-sounding), *ratham* (chariot), *yam* (which), *adhyasthāḥ* (you have mounted), *uṣaḥ* (O Uṣas), *tvam* (you), *tena* (with that), *suśravasam* (of noble fame), *janam* (people), *pra ava* (protect), *adya* (today), *duhitaḥ* (daughter), *divaḥ* (of heaven). || 2 ||

O Uṣas, that chariot which you have mounted, upon which you now stand—what kind of chariot is it? It is *supeśasam*: beautiful in its parts, or endowed with a beautiful form. Yāska states that *peśas* is a name for form (*Nirukta* 8.11). Alternatively, it means "endowed with beautiful gold," because *peśas* is listed among the names for gold in *Nirukta* 1.2.6. Or, it means "possessing a beautiful *kha*" (space), that is, spacious. Or, it is the cause of happiness. Or again, *sukham* is an adverb; the meaning is "in such a way as to be pleasant. O Daughter of Heaven, O Goddess Uṣas born from the celestial world, with that chariot, come today—at this time—to the person, the sacrificer, who possesses *suśravasam*, i.e., who is endowed with excellent oblations. Regarding *supeśasam*: from the root *piś* (to form parts), the suffix *asun* is added. Because it is a *nit* (having *n* as an indicatory letter), it is accented on the first syllable. This is the word *peśas*. That which has beautiful *peśas* is *supeśas*. [The compound] is accented on the first syllable.
1. To be honored by the ḍha-group;
2. worthy of worship by the ḍha-group; 3. protect, O ḍha.
In the word *yacchandasi*, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the first syllable of the second member of the compound.

Regarding *adhyasthāḥ*: from the root *sthā*, since the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ* (Vedic usage permits the aorist, imperfect, and perfect) is in force, the aorist (*luṅ*) suffix is used; by the rule *gatisthā* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), there is the elision (*luk*) of the *sic* augment.

The augment *aṭ* is udātta. Because it is connected with a word that has a specific metrical cadence (*yadvṛtta*), it does not undergo elision (*anighāta*). Furthermore, by the rule "tiṅi codāttavati," the verb following the particle *gati* becomes anudātta.
By that [rule], "it is also seen in other cases," there is a long vowel in the *saṃhitā* [text]:
*suśravasam*.
‘Śrava’ is a name for food, as Yāska [states] in Nirukta 10.3: ‘It is so considered because it is heard.
In the word *supeśasam*, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the first syllable of the second member of the compound.
*Ava*.
Since the root *ava* is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as meaning "protection," "motion," "pleasure," and "praise," here it has the sense of "going.

Regarding the phrase *duhitardivaḥ*: because of the rule *paramapi chandasi*, when there is the status of being a member of a prior compound for that which ends in the genitive case, the entire initial syllable of the two-word aggregate becomes entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*).
O Arjuna, you who possess the two-footed and four-footed, the birds of the air,
and the seasons— O Dawn, bring them forth from the ends of heaven.
Even the winged birds, the bipeds and quadrupeds, O bright Uṣas, have awakened according to their seasons from the ends of heaven. 3.

O Arjuna, O you of radiant white color, O Dawn, at your dawning, directed toward your arrivals (*ṛtūn*), bipeds such as humans and quadrupeds such as cattle, as well as winged birds—those possessing feathers and wings—even from the ends of the sky, from the very limits of the atmosphere, they move forth with vigor. The meaning is that all living beings, who during the night were overwhelmed by darkness, become active immediately upon your arrival.
"Patriṇaḥ" [means those having wings]. From the root "pat," meaning "to go"; that by which one flies is a "patra" (wing).
The suffix *anna* is applied by [Uṇādi Sūtra] 3.385, *aminakṣi*, etc.; from that, the possessive suffix *ini* is added. Thus, *dvipat*.

In the expression *dvipada* ("having two feet"), the final syllable of the word *pāda* is elided by Pāṇini’s rule 5.4.140, *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya*. This is a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). Because the word is treated as a *bha*-stem due to its inclusion in the *ayasmayādi* group, the substitution of *pat* for *pāda* occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.4.130, *pādaḥ pat*.
The final syllable of the second member [of the compound] is udātta by the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pādamūrdhasu bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.197).
*Catuṣpāt*:
he who has four feet (*catvāraḥ pādā asya*).
That which is distinct from the vowel is as previously described.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member prevails.
Following the rule "iṇaḥ ṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.3.39), and with the continuation of the rule "idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.41), the *visarjanīya* is changed to *ṣ*.

Nor should one suspect that the substitution of *upadhmānīya* [for *p*]—as prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule *kupvoḥ kaḥ pau ca* (8.3.37)—should apply here because this [substitution of *visarga*] is not established as being subsequent; for, according to the maxim *yena nāprāpte*, that [rule for *upadhmānīya*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to it.
As stated in the *Vṛtti*: "An exception indeed subverts even what is subsequent.
*Āran*.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.

While the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ* (Vedic usage permits the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* suffixes) is in force, the *luṅ* suffix is applied; by the rule *satiśāsayatibhyaśca*, the suffix *ciṇ* is replaced by *aṭ*. Then, by the rule *ṛdṛśo’ṅi guṇaḥ*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs.
The augment *aṭ* is added. [The word] *ṛtūn* [is derived from] the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go."
From this [root], the suffix *ku* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) according to the *auṇādika* rules.
Regarding *anu*: by the rule *anurlakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.4.84), *anu* functions as a *karmapravacanīya*.
The accusative case ending is applied by the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.8).
In the *saṃhitā*, the *n* is changed to *r* by the rule *dīrghādaṭi samānapāde*.
Then, by the rule *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvamya tu vā*, the preceding sound of the *r* optionally becomes nasalized.
From *divaḥ*: by the rule "uḍidam," the case ending is udātta. From *antebhyaḥ*.
By the rule "pañcamyāḥ parāvadhyarthe," the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s*.
Shining forth indeed with your rays, you illuminate the entire radiant realm;
as such, O Dawn, the Kaṇvas have invoked you with their songs, seeking to win your favor.
Shining forth indeed with your rays, you illuminate the entire radiant realm. You, O Uṣas, the Kaṇvas have invoked with their songs, desiring wealth. 4.

O Uṣas, shining forth and dispelling the darkness, you illuminate the entire multitude of living beings with your own rays—that is, with your splendors—so that everything becomes radiant and possessed of light;

for since this is so, the Kaṇvas—the wise officiating priests desiring wealth, or the great seers born of the Kaṇva lineage—have invoked you, such as you are, with their songs, meaning they have praised you with words characterized by hymns of praise.
*Kaṇva* is a name for the wise, as it is listed among those names in the statement: "Kaṇva, Ṛbhu" (Nirukta 3.15.7).
It is derived from the root *bhā*, meaning "to shine.
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* (second) class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
Because *sip* is a *pit* suffix, it takes the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). By the rule "and after *hi*," there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of accent).
By the rule "also when *tik* is accented," the *gati* prefix becomes unaccented.
*rocanam*: [derived from] the root *ruc* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*). The suffix *yuc* is applied according to the rule *anudāttettaśca halādeḥ*.
The word *citaḥ* has its final syllable udātta. *Vasūyavaḥ*:
desiring wealth (*vasu*) for themselves.
The suffix *kyac* is applied after a verbal root ending in *su* (the word for "well") when used reflexively (*ātman*).
The vowel lengthening occurs by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ. The suffix *u* is added by the rule "kyācchandasī."
With songs; the accentuation of the case-ending is due to the rule "sāvekācaḥ. Kaṇvas.
The word *kaṇa* signifies sound.
The suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule "aśipubhilaṭikaṇi" and so forth;
because it is marked with the *ni*-diacritic, it bears the udātta accent on its first syllable.
*ahūpata*.
In the *luṅ* tense, following the rule "the *ha* [of *hi*] undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa*," the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs by the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
When the preceding vowel [from the *saṃprasāraṇa*] has been substituted, lengthening occurs by the rule "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*).
The suffix *sic* follows the root *vi*.
By the rule "ekācaḥ," there is a prohibition of *it*.
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is an absence of *guṇa* [vṛddhi].
The seventh hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "udu tyam," is the seerly composition of Praskaṇva and has Sūrya as its deity.

It is stated that the first nine verses are Gāyatrīs and the remaining four are Anuṣṭubhs. Thus it is enumerated: "udu tyaṃ; [the seer is] Sasonā; it is addressed to Sūrya; the first nine are Gāyatrīs."

In the Saura sacrifice called the Ābhīna, nine verses beginning with "udu tyam" are to be recited. This is prescribed in the section on the Ābhīna sacrifices in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (6.5): "When the [rites] have been completed, for the Ābhīna: 'sūryo no divaḥ', 'udu tyaṃ jātavedasam'—these nine."
Those rays carry up that god Jātavedas, the Sun, so that everyone may behold him. ud | ūm iti | tyam | jātavedasam | devam | vahanti | ketavaḥ | dṛśe | viśvāya | sūryam || 1 ||

The *ketavaḥ*—the indicators, the horses of the Sun, or rather the rays of the Sun—*ud vahanti*, they carry upward, the *sūryam*, the Sun, the impeller of all. The particle *u* is for filling the metrical foot;
as it is said: "In verses of measured syllables, [particles such as] *kam*, *īm*, *it*, and *hi* are meaningless" (Nirukta 1.9).
For what purpose? "For all," that is, for the entire world, "to see"—
meaning they carry him upward so that all people may behold the sun.
What kind of Sun?
That well-known *jātavedas*, the knower of all beings that have been born—or one whose wisdom is born, or whose wealth is born—the radiant *deva*.
Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "The horses, the banners, or the rays carry up that *jātavedas*, the god Sūrya, for the seeing of all beings" (*Nirukta* 12.15).
*Jātavedasam*.
He is called *jātavedas* because he knows (*vetti*) all that is born (*jātāni*).

According to the rule "the original accent of the first member is retained even when [a suffix] follows a verbal root or a kāraka," the suffix *asun* is applied, and the original accent of the first member is preserved.
*dṛśe*:
This is an indeclinable used in the sense of the infinitive suffix *tum*, according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.4.11 (*dṛśe viśve ca*).
[It means] "to see" the Sun.

In the word *rājasūyasūrya*, derived from the root *pū* in the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*) with the suffix *kyap* and the addition of the augment *ruḍ*, the word is thus formed as an irregularity (*nipātita*). Consequently, because the suffix is marked with *p* (indicating it is *pit*), it is unaccented; therefore, by the accent of the verbal root, the word is udātta on its first syllable.
Away go those stars like thieves through the nights, before the sun who beholds all. 2. *apa* | *tye* | *tāyavaḥ* | *yathā* | *nakṣatrā* | *yanti* | *aktubhiḥ* | *sūryāya* | *viśvacakṣase* || 2 ||
1. *Ḍha*: They invoked; they called upon;
they praised. (Ṛgveda 44)

"Those who are harmful, acting contrary to what is established, like thieves; the *nakṣatras* are the *nakṣatras*, the abodes of the gods—for it is stated in another Śruti: 'The *nakṣatras* are indeed the abodes of the gods' (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.5.2.6).
Or else:
In this world, those who attain heaven after performing ritual actions are seen in the form of stars.
Thus it is heard in scripture: "He who sacrifices here reaches that world; therefore, this is the 'star-nature' (nakṣatra-tva) of the stars" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.5.2.5).
Or alternatively:

The luminaries of those who have performed meritorious deeds are called the *nakṣatras*, according to the Vedic tradition: "These *nakṣatras* are indeed the luminaries of those who have performed meritorious deeds" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.4.1.3).
Yāska, however, says: "'Nakṣatras'—they are so called because of their movement toward their task; and the Brāhmaṇa states that they are not [mere] powers (*kṣatrāṇi*)" (*Nirukta* 3.20).
Such *nakṣatras* "go away," that is, depart, "with the nights" (*akubhiḥ*).
"O Viśvacakṣas, the illuminator of all— having seen the arrival of the Sun, the Asura; like a thief, O Sūrya,
you are the one who enables crossing, the all-seeing, and the maker of light."
You illuminate the entire radiant realm.
O Sūrya, you are the deliverer, visible to all, the maker of light; you illumine the entire radiant realm. 4.
O Sūrya, you are the *taraṇi*, the traverser; you are the one who goes the great distance that cannot be traveled by any other.
And so it is remembered in the Smṛti: "Salutations to you, who traverse two thousand, two hundred, and two more *yojanas* in half a *nimiṣa*!"
Or rather:
you shall be the savior of your devotees from disease,
according to the traditional teaching that "one should seek health from the Sun."
Likewise, he is "visible to the universe" (*viśva-darśataḥ*), meaning he is worthy of being seen by all living beings;
for the sight of the Sun is the cause of removing the sin produced by seeing outcastes and others.
And thus says Āpastamba: "Upon seeing [him], there is the sight of the luminaries."
Alternatively:
he by whom the entire universe—the totality of created beings—is "darśata," meaning visible or to be manifested, is so described;
likewise, he is the "jyotiṣkṛt," the maker of light, that is, the creator of illumination.
The meaning is "the illuminator of every object.
Alternatively,
it means "the illuminator of the moon and other [luminaries] at night."

In the two words *pūjanī* and *ṛtvij*: the suffix *kin* is applied by the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā kin*. By the rule *aniditām*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the nasal (*n*). By the rule *ugidacām*, the augment *num* is added. Then, the rules for the elision of *hal* and *ṅī* (i.e., *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*), and the elision of the final consonant of a cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) apply. Because the elision of the final consonant of the cluster is considered "asiddha" (not yet established) for the purposes of the preceding rules, there is no lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrgha*) nor the absence of the nasal elision. By the rule *kinpratyayasya kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.62), the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *g*) occurs. By the rule *aniganto'ñcatau* (Pāṇini 6.2.52), since the word ends in a vowel other than *i* (i.e., *aniganta*), the exclusion applies; thus, when the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) does not occur, the original accent of the second member (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) prevails. Regarding *eṣi*: from the root *iṇ* meaning "to go. In the second person singular (*sip*), due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. By the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Regarding *svaḥ*: from the prefix *su-* and the root *ati*. The suffix *vic* is applied. After the *guṇa* substitution, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs. By the rule *nyaṅstvarau svaritau ca*, the word has a *svarita* accent. Regarding *dṛśe*: from the root *dṛśir* meaning "to see," the form is prescribed as an indeclinable (*nipātita*) in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*) by the rule *dṛśe vīpsye ca*. || 7 ||
O Purifier, with that eye wherewith you behold the people as they stir about, O Varuṇa, [look upon us].
O Pāvaka, with that eye wherewith you, O Varuṇa, look upon the bustling people.

O Purifier, O Drier of all, O Varuṇa, O Warder-off of the undesirable, O Sūrya—you who behold this world with that eye, with that light, as it sustains, supports, or nourishes the living beings born of men; we praise that light. (This is the ellipsis.
Or rather, the connection is with the following verse.
"By that eye he trembled.
And thus it has been stated by Yāska: "Or rather, the completion of the sentence is also found in the subsequent [verse], 'We praise that of yours,' and by that he trembled" (Nirukta 12.22).
*Bhuraṇyantam*:
[The root] *bhuraṇ* is used in the sense of "supporting" and "nourishing.
Because it belongs to the *kaṇḍv-ādi* group, the suffix *yak* is applied.

Then, by the rule *śatṛ* [Pāṇini 3.2.124], the suffix *śap* is applied; because it is taught with an initial *a*, the *lakāra* and the verbal suffix (*dhātu*) are unaccented, so that the accent of the *yak* alone remains. *Varuṇa*.
The root *vṛj* means "to choose" (*varaṇe*).
From this root, with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *unan* is applied according to the rule *kṛdāribhya unan* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.333).
Here, by the word *varuṇa*, the Sun (*āditya*) alone is intended.
And thus it is declared elsewhere: "From him were born Mitra and Varuṇa" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.9.2), and also:
"Mitra, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, and Aryaman" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.13.3).
You traverse the wide expanse of the sky, measuring out the days with your rays,
O Sūrya, beholding all living beings.
O Sūrya, you rise toward the sky, traversing the broad mid-region, measuring out the days with your rays and beholding all living beings.
"O Sūrya, you [traverse] the *pṛthu*—that is, the wide and expansive—*rajas*, the world.
For Yāska says: 'The worlds (*lokāḥ*) are called *rajāṃsi*' (Nirukta 4.19). Which world?"
"You go forth—indeed, you proceed specifically—to the sky, to the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*).
Doing what?
Measuring out—that is, producing—the days together with the nights."
Because the division of day and night is dependent upon the movement of the sun;
likewise, "beholding"—that is, illuminating—the various classes of beings that possess birth.
In the word *rajaspṛthu*, the substitution of *s* for the visarga is according to Pāṇini’s rule 8.3.49: *chandasi vāpnātreditayoḥ*.
In *ahā*, the elision of the case-ending *śe* occurs according to the rule *śecchandasi bahulam*.
*mimānaḥ* [is derived from] *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring";
it belongs to the *jauhotyādi* (third) class.
In the case of *śānaci* with *ślau*, after the reduplication (*dvirbhāva*), the short vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is applied by the rule "abhajāmit.
Then, the elision of the long *ā* is applied by the rule "abhyastayorātaḥ.
Finally, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the reduplicated form is applied by the rule "abhyastanāmādiḥ."
Births (*janmāni*). [The root] *janī* [is used] in the sense of manifestation (*prādurbhāve*).
The suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule: "It is seen [to be applied] after other roots as well."
Because it ends in *n*, it has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
Seven bay horses carry you in your chariot, O divine Sūrya,
you of flaming hair, the far-seeing one.
Seven bay horses carry you in your chariot, O divine Sūrya, you of radiant locks and far-seeing vision. 8.
1. The nature of *ca* and *pha* is light (*prakāśa*). 2. *Ca* and *pha* are the elements.

O *Sūrya*, O *Devā*, O *Dyotamāna*, O *Vicakṣaṇa*, O illuminator of *Sarvasya*, the *Sapta*, meaning those numbering seven, the *Haritaḥ*, meaning the rays whose nature is the essence of nectar, or indeed the rays themselves, carry you, bring you, to this place.
"What is it like?
"It is 'seated upon the chariot'—this is the ellipsis.
Likewise, 'with hair of flame'."
"He in whom rays are seen like flames or like hair" is how he is described; "him"—referring to that [chariot].
"Haritaḥ" is a name for the horses of the Sun (Āditya), because it is stated in the *Nighaṇṭu*: "Haritaḥ is [a name] of Āditya" (*Ni.* 1.15.3).
‘Śociṣkeśam’:
[the word] ‘śuci’ is used in the sense of ‘to shine’;
by [the rule] ‘arcí-śuci-’ etc., it ends in the suffix ‘dṛs’.

"The word *antaudāttaḥ* [means] that very [word] which, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, remains [with its accent] by virtue of the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvena*). According to the rule *nityaṃ samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *visarjanīya*."

The Sun has yoked the seven pure ones, the daughters of the chariot; with them, his own yoke-mates, he goes. 9. He has yoked the seven, the pure ones, the daughters of the Sun's chariot; with them, who are his own yoke-mates, he goes. 9.
The Hero—the Sun, the impeller of all—has yoked to his own chariot seven such mares as these, the purifiers, the female horses.
Of what nature are they? They are the granddaughters of the chariot (*rathasya naptyaḥ*), meaning those who do not cause it to fall;
the sense is that with them yoked, the chariot moves without falling.
With those horse-women who have become thus—being harnessed to the chariot by their own efforts and through their own application—he goes, that is, he returns to the sacrificial hall;
therefore, an oblation must be offered to him—this is the remainder of the statement.

It is incorrect [to use the active voice], because the root *yuj* (in the sense of "joining") is marked with the *svarita* accent; therefore, when the action benefits the agent, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is required.
In the case of *luṅ*, there is *liṭ* and *sic*.
By the rule "ekācaḥ," there is a prohibition of *it*.

Because of the rule "liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu" (Pāṇini 1.2.11), *sic* has the *kit* designation; consequently, there is an absence of the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghupadhaguṇa*).
By the rule *jhalo jhali*, there is the elision of the *s* of *sic*;
by the rule *coḥ kuḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for *c*. [Thus we have] *śundhyuvaḥ*.
The root *śundh* means "to purify. The suffix *yu* is applied according to the rule *yajimani śundhisajinabhyo yuḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.300).
In the nominative plural (*śasu*), the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs according to the rule *tanvādīnāṃ chandasi bahulam upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.77.1).
*Sūraḥ*: [derived from] the root *pū* in the sense of "impelling. The suffix *kran* is applied according to the rule *susūdhāgṛdhibhyaḥ kran* (Uṇādisūtra 2.182).
The initial udātta accent is due to the *nittva* [of the suffix].
Regarding *naptyaḥ*: the word *naptṛ* is derived among the *uṇādi* suffixes by the rule *naptṛ-neṣṭṛ* etc. (Uṇādisūtra 2.252), in the sense of "one who does not cause to fall" (*na pātayati*).
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *ṛnebhyo ṅīp*.
The substitution of *yaṇ* [for *i*] results in the acute accent (*udātta*) for the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by the rule "the *yaṇ* following an acute vowel preceded by a consonant.
By the rule "substitutes for case-endings are themselves case-endings," the substitution of *jas* for *śas* occurs;
thereafter, the substitution of *yaṇ* [for *s*] results in the circumflex accent (*svarita*) by the rule "the *yaṇ* following an acute or circumflex vowel."
The substitution of *repha* is Vedic;
and it has been stated: “There are two others as well: modification and elision of phonemes” (Kātantra 6.3.109).
However, in another recension (*śākhā*), it is read simply as “*naptyaḥ*.”

By their own reasonings (*svayuktibhiḥ*): those whose reasonings (*yuktayaḥ*)—that is, their own arrangements (*yojanāni*)—are connected with the sun. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is maintained.
At the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice, during the ritual sprinkling with water, the *hotraka* priests should recite the mantra beginning with "Out from the darkness" (*uddyaṃ tamasas pari*).
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the section on the *patnīsaṃyāja* in the Sūtra: "Out from the darkness... he rises up" (*āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.13).
Beholding the light rising above the darkness,
we have reached the god Sūrya among the gods, the supreme light.
Upward from the darkness, beholding the light, we have gone up to the higher one—the god among gods, Sūrya—to the highest light. 10.

1. What is the ḍha-like state? "We are the performers [of the sacrifice], situated beyond darkness—that is, above darkness, or above the night; or rather, existing above darkness, meaning free from sin.
Thus it is declared in the scripture: "He rises up beyond darkness; for darkness is indeed evil; having reached the very evil, he slays it" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.8.6).

"Beholding the light"—the radiant one, the highest, the most exalted, or the most excellent—"among the gods," that is, among the deities, "the god," endowed with qualities such as generosity, "Sūrya," while worshipping him with hymns and praises, we have "gone to," that is, attained, the "supreme," most excellent, "light" in the form of Sūrya.
Thus it is heard in the Śruti: "'We have gone to the supreme light,' he says; for the sun indeed is the supreme light; he attains union with the sun itself" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.8.6).
And this is logical, because of another scriptural passage: "In whatever way they meditate upon Him, that very thing they become."
"From out of darkness.
The *visarjanīya* becomes *s* according to the rule "after the fifth [case-ending], when the sense is 'beyond' (*parāvadhi*). "Beholding the light."

By the rule "isusoḥ sāmarthye" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.44), the *visarjanīya* is changed to *ṣ*. In this context, *sāmarthya* (semantic connection) is accepted as being of the nature of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). Thus: *devatrā*.
The suffix *trā* is applied in the sense of the locative case according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.4.56: *devamanuṣyapuruṣapurum̐hūtavyebhyo dvitīyāsamyor bahulam*.
It bears the accent of a suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
[The verb form is] *aganma*.

According to the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*, the *laṅ* suffix is used for the sense of a request (*prārthanā*). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix. According to *svośva* (Pāṇini 8.2.65), the *m* of the root is changed to *n*. The augment *aṭ* is acute (*udātta*).
There is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent) because it begins with a *pāda*. Regarding *uttama*:

although the suffix *tamap* would normally result in an *anudātta* (unaccented) vowel by rule, the phrase "both *uttama* and *śreṣṭha* are [acute] everywhere" prescribes that they have an acute accent on the final syllable of the *pāda* according to the *uṇchādi* list.
This triplet beginning with "udyan" is for the purpose of pacifying disease.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "The final triplet [is] for the affliction of disease.
And this is appropriate.

Since Praskaṇva praised the Sun with this triplet of verses for the sake of pacifying his own ailments, the Sun, being thus praised by that triplet, expelled the disease from him. Therefore, even now, the Sun should be worshipped with this triplet for the pacification of disease.

As it has been said by Śaunaka: "This mantra beginning with 'udyantam' is dedicated to the Sun; it destroys sin, cures disease, neutralizes poison, and bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation."

Rising today, O Sun of friendly luster, ascending to the highest heaven, destroy my heart-disease and my jaundice. 11. Rising; today; O you whose splendor is friendship; ascending; to the higher; heaven; heart-disease; mine; O Sūrya; and; jaundice; destroy. 11.

O Sūrya, the impeller of all, possessed of a favorable radiance for everyone, rising at this very time, ascending to the higher heaven—the intermediate space—or rather, ascending to the higher heaven with excellence, you reach it directly.
Or else:
ascending to the higher heaven, the intermediate space, you attain it with preeminence.

Being such as you are, [you are capable of removing] my "heart-disease"— the internal disease residing in the heart— and "harimāṇam"— the external disease characterized by the removal of bodily luster;
or else, it means the yellowness of the body, a discoloration resulting from illness.
Destroy both of these; the meaning is that you liberate me, your praiser, from this twofold disease.
*Mitramahaḥ*: he whose *mahaḥ* (splendor) is *mitra* (favorable). This is an example of the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the enclitic accentuation of a vocative).
Regarding *uttarām*: by means of the prefix *ud*, the Atharvaveda, which is in contact with it, is indicated;
therefore, the comparative suffix *tara* is applied.

In the first alternative (*pakṣa*), because *antarikṣa* functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the substance (*dravya*), there is no application of the suffix *ām*, since it conveys excellence (*prakarṣa*) of the substance.

In the second [alternative], excellence of the action of ascending (*ārohaṇa-kriyā*) is understood; thus, by the rule *kim-etis-taddhita-ādy-adravya-prakarṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.11), the suffix *ām* is applied.

In the first alternative, since the suffixes *ṭā* and *asarap* are marked with the indicator *p* (*pit*), they are unaccented (*anudātta*); consequently, only the accent of the preverb (*upasarga-svara*) remains.
In the second [view], however, since the suffix *ām* is prescribed later, its accent would prevail; therefore, by way of exception (*vyatyaya*), the word has the udātta accent on the first syllable.
Alternatively, it should be regarded as belonging to the *vṛṣādi* group, for that is indeed an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
Hṛdroga.
[The substitution of *a* for *o* occurs] optionally before the words *śoka*, *pya*, and *mogeṣu* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.51).
1. *ca-cha-na-pha-rogaṃ ca* (and the substitution of *roga* for *ra*).
2. *ca-cha-ta-na-pha-śa-sa-ām* (of the vowels *ā* and *ī* following *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *na*, *pha*, *śa*, and *sa*).
Thus, there is the substitution of *had* for the word *hṛdaya*.
*mama*: by the rule *yuṣmadasmador ṅasi*, the first syllable is udātta (accented).
*harimāṇam*.
The root *han* means "to take away.
The suffix *imanin* is added according to the Uṇādi Sūtra 4.588 (*jani-habhyām imanin*).
By means of metathesis (*vyatyaya*), the word bears the udātta accent on the final syllable.
Alternatively,
since the word *hari* signifies a class (*varga*), the suffix *imanin* is applied by virtue of the particle *ca* in the rule *varṇadṛḍhādibhyaḥ pyaṅ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.123).
Following the recurrence of the phrase *iṣṭhemeyaḥsu*, there is the elision of the final *ṭi* by the rule *ṭeḥ*.
We place my yellowness upon the parrots, we place it upon the female parrots;
indeed, we deposit my yellowness within the yellow-winged birds.
We transfer my yellowness onto the parrots, onto the female parrots; and indeed, we deposit my yellowness within the yellow-woodpeckers. 12.

We place my yellowness—the state of being yellow residing in the body—upon the parrots, those birds who desire such a color, and likewise upon the *ropaṇākās*, a species of female parrot; and furthermore, we deposit my yellowness within the *hāridravas*, the yellow trees that possess such a hue. May that yellowness remain there in comfort and not afflict us.
We place [it].
By the rule "idanto masi," there is the augment *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) after the suffix *mas*.
The sun has risen with all-powerful force;
may he subject my enemy to me, and may I not be subject to the enemy.
Up has risen this Āditya together with all his conquering power, subjecting my enemy to me; may I not be subject to the enemy. 13.
This Aditya, the son of Aditi, the Sun, has risen with all his power and might.
What is he doing?
Subduing—that is, harming—the one who hates me, the one who causes me affliction; furthermore, may I not do harm to the hater, to the disease that works evil against me.
The meaning is: "May the Sun himself destroy the disease that causes us harm.
[He] went (*agāt*).
In the *luṅ* tense of the root *i*, there is the substitution of *gā* by the rule *iṇo gā luṅi*.

In the word *ādityaḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic* by the rule *'gātisthā0'*. The suffix *ṇya*, which belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, is applied in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) by the rule *'dityādityādiṣya0'*.

*randhayan*. [The root] *radh* [is used] in the senses of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*) and "cooking/completing" (*saṃrāddhi*). [This form is derived] from the causative (*pyantāt*) [of the root], with the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) applied to the present tense marker (*laṭ*).
By the rule *radhijabhor aci* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.61), the augment *num* is added to the root before the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
The particle *mā* is a combination of two particles, *mā* and *u*, used in the sense of "do not" (*maiva*).

Because of the rule *'ot' (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.15)*, the vowel *o* is a *pragṛhya*; consequently, by the rule *'pluta-pragṛhyā aci...* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.125), there is *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form).
[In the word] *dviṣate*, the case ending is acute according to the rule *'śaturanumaḥ...'*.
Regarding *radham*: in the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *radh*, by virtue of its belonging to the *puṣādi* class, there is the substitution of *aṭ* for *ṅi*;
furthermore, by the rule "after *ravi* and *jabh*, [the augment] *num* [is added] before a vowel," the augment *num* is applied to the root.
By the rule "aniditām0," there is the elision of the nasal;
by the rule "na māḍyoge," there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*.

1. By destroying the disease that causes affliction through the letters *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *dha*, *na*, *pha*, and *śa*; by destroying the disease that causes affliction through *la* and *ma*; by destroying the disease that causes affliction through *sa* and *ma*. In the tenth section (*anuvāka*), there are seven hymns (*sūkta*).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fifteen verses, begins with "abhi tyam."
Regarding this, they relate the following ancient legend: Aṅgiras, desiring for himself a son equal to Indra, worshipped the deities.
To him, Indra himself was born as a son in the form of Savya, so that there might be no one in the world his equal.
That Savya Āṅgirasa is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this hymn.
The fourteenth and fifteenth verses are *triṣṭubh*s;
according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "of this hymn ending in *triṣṭubh*, the remaining verses are *jagatī*s," the remaining thirteen verses are *jagatī*s.
Indra is the deity.

All of this has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "The hymn beginning with *abhi tyam* consists of five verses less [than ten]; Savya, desiring a son equal to Indra, approached [the sacrifice] with the *irā* verse ending in two *triṣṭubh*s; for him, Indra himself was born as his son.
This hymn is to be recited by the Hotṛ priest in the first round (*paryāya*) of the night during the Atirātra sacrifice.
It is prescribed in the section titled "The Rounds of the Atirātra" in the Sūtra: "'O Adhvaryus, bring that ram; [bring] Soma for Indra'—this is the *yājyā*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
This hymn is also to be recited in the *niṣkevalya* litany during the *viṣuvat*, which constitutes the midpoint of the *gavāmayana* sacrifice.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Having recited the Aindra *nivid* in this [hymn]—namely, *yastigmaśṛṅgaḥ*, *abhi tyaṃ meṣam*, and *indrasya nu vīryāṇi*... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.6).
Exalt with songs that ram, Indra, who is invoked by many and worthy of praise, the surging ocean of wealth;
he whose divine powers traverse the heavens as men do not, the most bountiful one—worship this inspired sage for our enjoyment.

Exalt with songs that ram, invoked by many, worthy of praise, Indra, the surging ocean of wealth; him whose celestial powers do not waver like the heavens among men—him, the most liberal, the inspired sage, worship for our enjoyment! 1.
Indra came in the form of a ram and drank the soma of that well-known ram who was contending with his enemies;
or else,
he came as a ram and drank the soma of Medhātithi, the son of Kaṇva, who was performing the sacrifice.
That seer said to him, "A ram.
Therefore, even now, Indra is addressed as "O Ram" (*meṣa*).

A Brāhmaṇa passage, which serves as an explanation for a portion of the Subrahmaṇyā mantra—"O ram of Medhātithi"—is handed down thus: "For the ram, having become [a ram], carried off Medhātithi, the descendant of Kaṇva."
The meaning is that he (Indra) struck down Soma after it had arrived.
"Puruhūtam" means invoked by many sacrificers; "ṛgmiyam" means being modified or praised by the *ṛc* verses—the meaning is that a deity is indeed modified through praise.
Alternatively,
he is called *ṛgmī* because he is measured or expressed by means of the *ṛc*s;
[the text refers to] him.
O singers, gladden—that is, bring joy to—the face of Indra with your songs (gīrbhiḥ), who is a flood of wealth, a dwelling place for riches, and distinguished by such qualities.
The deeds of this Indra proceed specifically for the benefit of human beings (mānuṣā).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as the rays of the sun are beneficial to all,
so too praise and honor that most bountiful, ever-increasing, and wise Indra for the sake of enjoyment.
*Meṣa*:
[derived from] the root *miṣ* in the sense of "rivalry" (*spardhā*).

Although the suffix *ka* would have been expected by virtue of the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhalakṣaṇe ke*), the suffix *ac* is applied according to the statement: "Words such as *devasama* and *meṣa* are to be seen among the *pacādi* group."
‘Ṛgmiyam’:

in the sense of ‘its modification’ (*tasya vikāraḥ*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to *Kātyāyana-vārttika* 4.3.144, which states, ‘they desire the suffix *mayaṭ* invariably after a word consisting of a single vowel.
The change of the letter *a* to *i* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The vowel of the suffix;
or else,
from the root *māṅ*, meaning "to measure" and "to sound."

One who is measured by *ṛc*s is called *ṛgmīḥ*. In the formation of this word with the suffix *kip*, the substitution of *ī* according to the rule "ghumāsthā" (Pāṇini 6.4.66) occurs first— due to its higher priority over the elision of the *y* (*yalopa*)— and then the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs according to the rule "aci śnudhātu" (Pāṇini 6.4.77).
The word *madata* has the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the compound due to the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*. [The root] *mad* [is used] in the sense of "joy."
The suffix *ṇic* is applied when there is a cause [for the action].

Since the root *madī* is listed among the *ghaṭādi* roots in the sense of "joy" and "speaking," when it occurs in the sense of joy, the *mit* designation applies by the rule "the *ghaṭādi* roots are *mit*. Consequently, shortening occurs by the rule "there is shortening for *mit* roots" (Pāṇini 6.4.92).

When the *śap* suffix is added in the second person plural middle voice (*madhyamapuruṣabahuvacana*), because the context is Vedic—as indicated by the rule "in the Veda, both ways"—the *ṇi* is elided by the rule "after a *ger*, [the *ṇi*] is elided before a suffix marked with *ṅ* that lacks *iṭ*" (Pāṇini 6.4.51).
Because the suffix *ta* is marked with the *ṅit* designation by the rule "sārvadhātukamapit," there is lengthening of the vowel by the rule "ṛci tudhamaśrutkutrotruyāṇām.
[The form is] *vasvaḥ*.
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this teaching regarding augments (*āgama*), there is an absence of the *num* augment.

Because of the rule "In the Vedic language, there is optionally [the substitution] in *jas* and so forth" (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.109.1), [the form] "tam" does not exist in the versions of Ta, Dha, Śa, and Sa. 1. In the version of Ḍha, it says "Indra is the ram. 2. In the versions of Cha, Na, La, Śa, and Sa, it says "Kāṇvāyani. 3. In the versions of Ḍha, Na, and Śa, it is praised. 353.

By the rule *gher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111), there is an absence of *guṇa*, and thus the *yaṇ* substitution [of *ar* for *ṛ*] occurs. *Arṇavam*: that which has water (*arṇas*) in it is *arṇavaḥ*, meaning the ocean. By the rule *arṇaso lopaś ca* (Kāśikā 5.2.109.2), the suffix *vapu* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), and there is the elision of the suffixal *s*. By means of that word, which denotes a reservoir of water, the mere locus is indicated. It bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). *Vicaranti*: the root *car* means "to move. Because it is taught with a short *a* (*adupadeśāt*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are *anudātta*; thus, the accent of the verbal root remains. By the rule *tiṅi codāttavati* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), the prefix (*gati*) is *anudātta*. However, due to its connection with *yadvṛtta*, it does not undergo elision of accent (*anighāta*). *Mānuṣā*: by the rule *śeṣa chandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.1.70), there is the elision of the case-ending *śe*. *Bhuje*: from the root *bhuja* in the sense of "protecting" or "eating. The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the rule *saṃpadādi-lakṣaṇaḥ*. By the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168), the case-ending receives the acute accent (*udātta*). *Maṃheṣṭham*: from the roots *mahi* and *vahi* in the sense of "growth. That which is most increased (*maṃhitā*) is *maṃheṣṭhaḥ*. By the rule *tuchandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.59), the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added. By the rule *turiṣṭhemayaḥsu* (Pāṇini 6.4.154), the suffixal *t* is elided. Due to the *nit* designation, it has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). *Arcata*: from the root *arc*. *(Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the portion available.)*

Thus, the root *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). *Dakṣāsaḥ*: from the root *dakṣa* in the sense of "to increase" (*vṛddhau*). They are called *dakṣāḥ* because they cause things to increase (*dakṣante ebhiḥ*). The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). Due to the presence of the *ji*-class marker, the first syllable is udātta. By the rule *ājaserasuk*, the form becomes *dakṣāsaḥ*. *Madacyutam*: from the root *cyuṅ* in the sense of "motion" (*gatau*). From this root, with the causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *kip ca*. By the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*, the augment *tuk* is added. *Śatam ṛtavo yasya*: in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*) prevails. *Javanī*: *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* etc. By the accent of the *lit* suffix, the syllable following the letter *ja* is udātta. *Aruhat*: from the root *ruh* in the *laṅ* tense. By the rule *kramṛharuhibhyaśchandasi*, the substitute *aṭ* is applied for the *cli* augment.
You chose the lineage for the Aṅgirases; you were the deliverer for Atri among the Śatadru rivers, finding the way.
Even with his army, you brought wealth to Vimada; you made the mountain dance for Ājāvasvāvasāna as he won the prize.

You chose the lineage away from the Aṅgirases; you were the finder of the path for Atri among the hundred-doored [fortresses]. Even with the Sasa, you brought wealth to Vimada in the contest, making the rock dance for him as he strove.

O Indra, you opened up—that is, you performed the opening—of the *gotra*, which possesses the word "overseer" (*adhyakṣa*), namely the cloud that obstructs the water, for the sake of the Aṅgirases, that is, for the benefit of the descendants of Aṅgiras. The meaning is that you struck down with your thunderbolt the cloud that was the obstructor of Vṛtra and made it manifest.
Or alternatively:
The herd of cattle (*gotra*) stolen by the Panis and hidden in caves, you disclosed to the seers, the Angirases; by opening the doors of the cave, you made it manifest.
And furthermore, for the great seer Atri—of what sort was he? [The answer follows: He who was... [end of fragment].

Upon the machines with a hundred distances and a hundred gates, which had been cast by the Asuras for the purpose of inflicting pain, you became the "finder of the way" (gātuvit)—the one who provides the path.
Likewise, even for the great seer named Vimada, you brought wealth (vasu) accompanied by an army (sasena), though he was unaware of it.

Similarly, in battle (ājau) for the sake of victory, for another worshipper who was dwelling (vavasānasya), you performed protection by making the mountain (adri)—that is, the thunderbolt (vajra)—dance; this is the sense remaining [in the verse].
Therefore, the sense is: by whom can your greatness be described?
*Gotra*:
[derived from] the root *guḍ*, meaning "inarticulate sound";
the suffix *tra* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
Alternatively,
with the word “*khala-gorathāt*” understood from the previous rule, the suffix *tra* is applied in the sense of a collection according to Pāṇini 4.2.51 (*iniñ-kvaci-chaś-ca*),
as in the case of “*śatadureṣu*.”
They have a hundred doors; "du" means two or one. They are called "doors" (durāḥ) because they are closed (driyante) or shut (saṃdriyante).
The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam*.

The vowel-vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of the preceding letter (*parapūrvatva*) are Vedic (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, that which occurs in place of both [sounds] may be designated by either one; thus, by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51), it becomes followed by *ra* (*rapara*).
Or rather,
the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the word *dvāra* should be regarded as Vedic;
[the term is] *gātuvit*.
The root *gā* means "to go.
From this root, the suffix *tu* is applied according to the rule *kabhimanijanibhāgāpātrāhibhyaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.72). One who causes that [path] to be known or obtained is a *gātuvit*.
