In the root *vidl* meaning "to obtain," the suffix *kip* is applied after the root has incorporated the causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*). The accentuation follows the rule for the natural accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
"Sasena. "Sasa" is a name for food, because it is listed among those names in [the Nirukta] with the words: "Sasa is called 'life' (āyus)" (Nirukta 2.7.21).
*Āji* is a name for battle,
as it is listed there [in the Nighaṇṭu] with the words *āhave ājau* (Nirukta 2.17.8).
*Adrim*.
It is called *adrivajra* because it devours (*atti*) or consumes (*bhakṣayati*) the enemy;
the suffix *krin* is applied according to the rule “*adaśādibhya uśubhimyaḥ krin*.
Due to the *nit*-designation [of the suffix], the word is accented on its first syllable.

Yāska, however, explained the word *adri* in this way: “It may be derived from the root *dṛ*, in the sense of ‘shattering mountains,’ or it may be from the root *at* [in the sense of ‘reaching’]” (Nirukta 4.4).
Regarding *vavasānasya*: the root *ghas* is used in the sense of ‘dwelling.’
The suffix *cānaś* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) with the meaning of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” the *śap* is replaced by *śru*;
then the reduplication and the *halādiśeṣa* [rules] apply.
Because it contains the letter *c*, there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable.
1. Ḍha: the covering of the waters of Vṛtra; 2. Ḍha: the covering of the enemies of Vṛtra;
3. Sa: causing to dance, impelling.

You opened the coverings of the waters; you caused the water-bearing wealth to flow down upon the mountain. When, O Indra, you slew Vṛtra with your might—the serpent—you then caused the sun to ascend to heaven for all to behold. tvam | apām | apidhānā | avṛṇoḥ | apa | adhārayaḥ | parvate | dānumat | vasu | vṛtram | yat | indra | śavasā | avadhīḥ | ahim | āt | it | sūryam | divi | ā | arohayaḥ | darśe || 4 ||
O Indra, you opened—the word *apidhānā* being repeated for emphasis—the coverings, that is, the clouds which conceal the waters; you threw them open.
Likewise, upon the mountain—that is, in your own dwelling place characterized by regions to be filled—you [overcame] the one possessed of *dānu*, meaning the one endowed with violence (*hiṃsā*).
Or else:
Danu is the mother of the Asuras; she is indeed Dānu.
You have held the wealth (*vasu*)—the riches—of such beings as Vṛtra and others who possess her [nature].
The meaning is that, having conquered the enemies and seized their wealth, you deposited it in your own house. Alternatively, *dānumat* is an adjective qualifying *vasu* (wealth).
The meaning is that it is endowed with beautiful giving.
O Indra, when (*yat*)—that is, at which time—with might (*śavasā*), by strength, you [slew] Vṛtra, the one who enclosed the three worlds.
And so it is recorded in another scripture: “Because he enclosed these worlds, that is the essence of Vṛtra’s name” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.12.2).

"Āhi" means one who strikes from all sides (*samantāt*). Thus the Vājasaneyins recite: "He became the slayer of all; he became all speech, all fame, all food, and all prosperity. Because he became all this, he is called *ahi*.
You have slain—that is, brought to destruction—such an Asura.
Immediately thereafter, you caused the sun to ascend in the sky, in the heavenly world, so that it might be seen;
the meaning is that you liberated the sun, which had been obstructed by Vṛtra, from that Vṛtra.
Of the waters. By the rule beginning with "uḍidaṃ," the case ending is acute. Apidhānā.
*Apidhānāni* means those by which something is covered or concealed;
the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
According to the rule “*liti*,” the vowel preceding the suffix is acute (*udātta*), as it is the final vowel of the verbal root.
That [vowel] is a single-substitute vowel (*ekādeśasvara*).
There is the original accent of the final member of the compound (*kuduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous combination (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) with the preceding vowel of the case-ending.
*adhārayaḥ*: there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because it begins with a *pāda*. *parvate*.
Parvata possesses mountains;
Yāska [states] that "parva" [is derived] from the root *pṛṇāti* or *prīṇāti* (Nirukta 1.20).
[He is] possessed of gifts (*dānumat*).

The suffix *nu* is derived from either the root *do* in the sense of "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍane*) or the root *dāṇ* in the sense of "giving" (*dāne*), according to the rule *dābhyāṃ nuḥ* in the *auṇādika* [section].
When used as an adjective qualifying *asura*, the genitive case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

With your wondrous powers, you cast down the sorcerers; with your own inherent strengths, you struck down those who poured oblations upon the heated cauldron. O you whose mind is set on man, you protected Pipru and shattered his fortresses; you aided R̥jiśvan in the slaying of the Dasyus. 5. With your wondrous powers, you cast down the sorcerers; with your own inherent strengths, you struck down those who poured oblations upon the heated cauldron. O you whose mind is set on man, you protected Pipru and shattered his fortresses; you aided R̥jiśvan in the slaying of the Dasyus. 5.
O Indra, you [conquer] by means of *māyās*—that is, by means of the knowledge of the methods of victory;
for *māyā* is a name for knowledge, as it is listed among its synonyms in the passage "Śacī, Māyā" (Nirukta 3.9.9).
Or else:

By means of *māyās*—deceptions well-known in the world—the *māyins*, those possessed of the characteristic *māyā* known as *utkalakṣaṇa*, [obscure] that which covers the three worlds. (1. ḍha-lokatrayāvārakam)
"You have driven away—the *dhmāti* root meaning 'to go' according to Yāska (*Nirukta* 6.2)—the Asuras, Vṛtra and the others.

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "Those Asuras who, by means of *svadhā*—that is, food characterized by oblations—offered [it] into their own mouths while they were 'sleeping' (*śuptau*), that is, while shining (*adhi-śobhamāne*). These are the Asuras referred to.

And thus it is recorded by the Kauṣītakins: "The Asuras, indeed, offered oblations into their own selves when the fire had been kindled; they were defeated. It is also recorded by the Vājasaneyins: "The gods and the Asuras contended. Then the Asuras, out of arrogance, thinking 'We shall not offer to anyone,' moved about offering oblations into their own selves; they were defeated."
Likewise, O *anṛmaṇas*— you who possess a mind of grace toward the *nṛs*, the sacrificers who are to be protected— you shattered, you destroyed, the *puras*, the fortified dwellings,

of that Asura named *Pipru*. Having done so, [you rescued] the singer named *Ṛjiṣvān*, whose movement is straight, in battles joined for the slaying of the *Dasyus*— those who cause harm— or, alternatively, [in battles] against those who have been slain by the *Dasyus*.
When the slaying of the Dasyus was the occasion, you protected [them] excellently; you guarded them with preeminence.
*Māyinaḥ*:
Since the word *māyā* is listed among the *vrīhyādi* group, the possessive suffix *ini* is applied according to the rule *vrīhyādibhyaś ca*.
[The roots] *śuptau* and *śubha dīptau* [are used].

The suffix *ktin* is used here in the sense of the object (*karmani*). The prohibition of the *ip* augment is according to the rule "tinutrapaḥ," etc. The absence of the substitution of *dha* for *tha* (as prescribed by "jhapastathoḥ") is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
The substitution of *c* for *j* occurs by the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55).
[Thus we have] *ajuhvata*;
this is the *ātmanepada* form of the root *hu* in the *laṅ* tense, by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
By the rule *adabhyastāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.4), there is the substitution of *at* for *jha*.
By the rule *huśnuvoḥ sārvadhātuke*, there is the substitution of *yaṇ*.
[The root] *piproḥ* is from *pṛ*, meaning "to protect" and "to fill."
The suffix *ku* is applied by the rule "pṛ-mṛ-dṛ-bhṛ-stṛ-cari-tani-rāji-bhyaḥ kuḥ" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.23).
Regarding the absence of the substitution of *u* [for the final vowel] in the rule "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya," it is because it has been stated that "it occurs diversely in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
The dual number is a Vedic usage (*chāndasam*).

By the rule *ur aṭ* [Pāṇini 7.1.50], the substitution of *u* for the reduplication occurs; by *halādiśeṣaḥ* [Pāṇini 7.4.60], all other consonants of the reduplication are elided. By the rule *arti-pipatyośca, bahulaṃ chandasi* [Pāṇini 7.4.77], the substitution of *i* for the reduplication occurs.
Then, the *yaṇ* substitution [of *i* for *y*] takes place.
*nṛmaṇas*: one whose mind (*manas*) is directed toward men (*nṛ*). The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *chandasyudavagrahāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.26).
*arujaḥ*:
[derived from] *rujo* in the sense of "breaking.
Due to the doubling of the root, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
*Ṛjiṣvānam*:
"Ṛjiṣvan" is so called because he moves (*aśnute*) or reaches straight forward (*ṛju*).
It belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular formations].

In the word *dasyuhateṣu*: [the root] *han* [is used in the sense of] "injury" and "going. According to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.108, *hana-sta-ca*, the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*).

The letter *takāra* is a substitute for the final [letter]. In those battles where there is the slaying (*hatyā*) of Dasyus, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the beginning of the second member of the compound, according to the rule: "In Vedic usage, the initial of the following member is frequently [accented]."
But in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member preceded by *ku*.
[The form] is *āvitha*,
from the root *ava* in the sense of "to protect."

You protected Kutsa in the slayings of Śuṣṇa; you delivered Śambara over to Atithigva. You trampled even the great Arbuda with your foot; like a true son of Sūnṛtā, you were born for the slaying of the Dasyus.

You protected Kutsa in the slayings of Śuṣṇa; you delivered Śambara over to Atithigva. You trampled even the great Arbuda with your foot. Indeed, from the very beginning, you were born for the slaying of the Dasyus.
O Indra, you protected Kutsa—the seer named Kutsa—during the Śuṣṇahatyas;
that is, in battles involving the slaying of Śuṣṇa, the "Drier-up," an Asura of that name. You guarded him.

Likewise, for Divodāsa—who was to be approached by guests—you subjected the Asura named Śambara to injury; you caused him harm. Similarly, you completely overcame even the great and highly increased Asura Arbuda with your foot; you trampled him down. Because this is so, from time immemorial, you have been born for the slaying of the Dasyus—that is, for the destruction of those who cause affliction.
The meaning is that you are always habitually inclined toward the slaying of robbers.
*arandhayaḥ*.
[The root] *radh* [is used] in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*) and "attaining" (*āpti*).
By the rule *radhijabhor aci* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.61), the augment *num* is applied to the root.
For *atithigva*: the suffix *du* is added to the root *gam* according to the *auṇādika* rules;
[the form] is *kramīḥ*.
The root *kram* means "to step.

There is a prohibition of the *vṛddhi* substitution by the rule *hayantakṣaṇa* (Pāṇini 7.2.5). The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāyoge’pi* ("the augment *aṭ* is frequently absent in the Vedic language even when there is no conjunction with a negative particle").
Or, by the rule "sāvekācaḥ," [the udātta accent applies] optionally. 1.
This is the connection (anvaya) according to the manuscript marked Ḍha.
Alternatively, the vowel of the case-ending is acute according to the rule "uḍiḍampadādi.
[The form] *jajñiṣe* [is derived from] the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation."
In the case of the perfect tense (liṭ), there is elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule "gamahana," etc.
In you all powers are gathered together; your bounty rejoices at the drinking of Soma.
Your thunderbolt, placed in your arm, is renowned; cut down all the manly strengths of the enemy.

In you indeed all powers are united together. Your bounty rejoices at the drinking of Soma; your thunderbolt, placed within your arms, is renowned. Rend asunder the enemy and strike down all his manly strengths.
O Indra, in you all power—every strength—is placed together, directed toward a single goal, and not turned away.
Likewise, your mind rejoices at the gift for the drinking of Soma;
furthermore, the thunderbolt resting in your two arms is perceived by us.
Therefore, cut down—perform the severing of—all the *vṛṣṇyāni*, all the heroic powers, of the enemy, the one who strikes down and is an adversary.
It goes together, thus *sadhryak*.
From the root *añc*, the suffix *kvin* is applied according to the rule beginning with "ṛtvik" etc.;
the elision of the nasal is by the rule "aniditām".
In the compound, by the rule *sahasya sadhiḥ*, the word *saha* undergoes the substitution *sadhi*.

By the rule *coḥ kuḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for the palatal (*c*). Although the natural accent of the first member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix would normally apply, the rule *adisadhyorantodāttatvanipātanaṃ kṛtsvaranivṛttyartham* (Pāṇini 6.2.114) prescribes that the substitution *sadhi* is specifically accented on the final syllable in order to prevent the application of the *kṛt*-accent. Thus, *sadhi* is udātta on its final syllable.
When *yaṇ* is substituted for it, the following unaccented vowel becomes *svarita* by the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ.
[The word is] *rādhaḥ*.
One prospers (*rājhoti*) by means of this.
In this context, *rādhaḥ* refers to the mind (*manas*). By virtue of the suffix *asun*, it is accented on the first syllable. [The term is used] for the sake of drinking Soma (*somapīthāya*).
The root *pā* means "to drink.
By the rule *pātutṭadivaci*, etc., the suffix *thak* is applied. By the rule *ghumāsthā*, the substitution of *ī* occurs.

It is conjugated as *haṣate*. Since the root *hapa* is prescribed in the sense of "satisfaction" (*tuṣṭau*), the form is obtained by the transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the *śap* affix and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
He perceived (*cikite*). [The root] *kit* means "to know.
Since the rule "in the Veda, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [tenses may be used for all times]" is in effect, the *liṭ* (perfect) is used here in the passive sense.
In the word *bāhvoḥ*, the case ending is acute by the rule “*udāttayaṇaḥ*”. [The root] *vṛśca*.
The root *ovrasc* is used in the sense of cutting; it belongs to the *tud*-class (the sixth class). By the rule *grahijyādinā saṃprasāraṇam*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
The accent is that of the suffix (vikaraṇasvara).
In the *saṃhitā*, there is lengthening according to the rule "aco 'ntyādi ṭi" [Pāṇini 1.1.64].
[The form is] *vṛṣṇyā*.
The root *vṛṣ* means "to sprinkle.
The suffix *nak* is added according to the Uṇādi rules. Those things which exist therein are called *vṛṣṇyāni*.
The form ‘bhave’ is derived from the rule *bhave chandasi*;
the acute accent on the first syllable is due to the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*;
and the elision of the suffix *śe* is according to the rule *śeṣaś chandasi*.
Distinguish between the noble ones and the other Dasyus; subject those who follow no sacred law to the one who spreads the sacrificial grass, as you punish them.
Be a powerful helper and an instigator for the sacrificer; I delight in all these deeds of yours during the shared rejoicings.

Know them! And those who are plunderers, subject them to the one who spreads the sacrificial grass; punishing the lawless, become the powerful instigator for the sacrificer. All these [deeds] of yours have been pleasing to me at the joyful feasts. 8.
O Indra, you must distinguish the Aryas—the wise who perform their duties—knowing them specifically.
And as for those Dasyus, the enemies who destroy those performers of duty, you must likewise distinguish them; this is the sense of the remainder.

Having known them, [act] for the sake of the sacrificer who possesses the *barhis* (the sacrificial grass), that is, who is endowed with sacrifice; [and act against] those without vows (*avrata*), where "vow" (*vrata*) is a name for ritual action.
Subdue those bandits who oppose our ritual action; that is, cause them to suffer injury. Or rather, bring them under the control of the sacrificer.
Regarding this, Yāska states: "The root *radh* signifies coming under one's power" (Nirukta 6.32).
Doing what?
Governing—that is, exercising the instruction and restraint of the wicked.
Therefore, you are Śākī, endowed with power, the impeller and instigator of the sacrificer.
O Bhava, the sense is: having repelled the Asuras who obstruct the sacrifice, cause the sacrificers to properly perform their sacrifices.

I too, as your praiser, desire (cākana) to praise all those various deeds of yours previously mentioned in every way (viśvat) during the sacrifices (yajñeṣu) which are accompanied by communal rejoicing (sadhamādeṣu).
Know [it].
The root *jñā* is used in the sense of "understanding";
it belongs to the *kaiyādika* (curādigaṇa) class.
By the rule *jñā-janor-jā*, there is the substitution of *jā*.

Here, according to the view of those for whom the grammarian’s statement *ṣlī gatau vṛta* is intended solely for the completion of the *lvādi* group and not for the completion of the *ṣvādi* group, the shortening [of the vowel] would have to occur by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*.
But this is not so.
This is because of the force of the long-vowel pronunciation in the rule *jñā-janor jā*.

However, in the case of the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation," the long vowel is established even without its explicit long-vowel pronunciation by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* (Pāṇini 7.3.101).
Therefore, since the explicit long-vowel pronunciation would otherwise be rendered purposeless, it is established that the short vowel does not occur here.
For *barhiṣmat* [the suffix -mat is applied];
because of the rule "tasau matvarthe" (Pāṇini 1.4.19), there is the absence of *sva* and *vajraśvi*.
[The form] *randhaya*.
*ratha-hiṃsā-sarā-dravyoḥ* | *śāsana* | *śāsu* means "to instruct."

In the case of *śatṛ*, there is elision (*luk*) of *śap* because [the root] belongs to the *adādi* class. By the rule “*jakṣity-ādayaḥ ṣaṭ*” (Pāṇini 6.1.6), the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) is applied; consequently, by the rule “*nābhyastāc chatuḥ*,” the prohibition of the augment *num* applies.
Furthermore, by the rule “*abhyastānām ādiḥ*,” the initial syllable receives the acute accent (*udātta*).
Śākī:
[derived from] the root *śak* in the sense of "to be able";
the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
From that [root], the suffix *ini* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
The acute accent on the first syllable occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Or else:
*Vṛṣādi* is to be understood [as the governing rule]. Regarding *viśvā tā*:
in both instances, there is the elision of the case-ending (*śelopa*) by the rule "the remainder [is retained] in the Veda" (*śeṣacchandasi*).
Regarding the word *sadhamādeṣu*: they indeed rejoice together (*saha mādyanti*) [in them], thus they are called *sadhamādāḥ*, which refers to sacrifices (*yajñāḥ*).
The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
Now, one might object: "In the rule *mado’nupasarge*, the suffix *ap* ought to apply. Do not say so.

For although it would have sufficed to state simply *mada* in the rule *vyadhajaporanupasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.61), the fact that *mado’nupasarge* is mentioned separately indicates that the suffix *ghañ* should also optionally apply. This was stated by the author of the Nyāsa regarding the continuation of the term *pratyayādīnām* [from the previous rule].
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the word *saha* undergoes the substitution *sadhā* according to the rule *sadhamādasthayoś chandasi*.
[The form] *cākana* [is derived from] the root *kana*, meaning "to shine," "to be beautiful," or "to go."
In this context, the sense is that of "shining. The suffix *liṭ* is applied while the rule “*chandasi luṅ-laṅ-liṭaḥ*” is in force.
Due to the optionality of the *ṇit*-character prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.1.91 (*ṇaluttamo vā*), there is an absence of *vṛddhi*.
Due to its inclusion in the *tuja*-class, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable.
Making the mountains subject to him who followed his vows, Indra, with his firm foundations, loosened those things that were unsteady;
though he was already grown great, he increased further as he reached toward heaven, and being praised, he struck down Vṛtra and utterly destroyed him.

For the one who follows his vows, Indra, making the lawless ones subject, brought them low; rending those who do not endure, he struck down Vṛtra—who, though grown great and seeking to reach the very heavens, was swelling with pride—along with his gathered hosts. || 9 ||

Indra, who subdues—meaning he harms or brings under his control—the *apavrataḥ*, those of departed rites (the non-sacrificers), for the sake of the *anuvrataḥ*, the sacrificer of favorable deeds; likewise, the *ābhūmayaḥ*:
those who come forward (*ā-bhū*) are the *ābhūvaḥ*, namely the praisers.

With those [missiles], he exists as one who loosens—that is, destroys—the *anābhavas*, which are the opposite of that. Praising (*stavānaḥ*)—that is, performing praise—the seer named Vṛtra, whose nature is to utter praise, struck down (*vijaghāna*) the well-heaped anthills (*saṃdihaḥ*).
Having had his obstacles removed by Indra, he took away the essence of the earth, characterized by the anthills, for the sake of the sacrificial materials; such is the meaning.
And so it is recorded in another scripture: "In that there is a collection of anthills, one secures for oneself the very sap and vigor of the earth" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.3.4).
For *anuvrata*: that whose ghee (*ghṛta*) is favorable (*anukūla*). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.

*Śrathayan*: [The root] *śratha* is used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*). With the addition of the causative suffix *ṇic*, because it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, the suffix *ṇiC* is applied; then, by the rule "the short vowel for roots marked with *mit*," there is shortening of the vowel.
They increase;
the *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition;
they desire to reach.

1. The meaning is "ḍha. 2. [The suffix *kvin* occurs] after [roots ending in] *ca*, *cha*, *pha*, *la*, *śa*, *sa*, and those associated with *sadhamāda*. 3. [The suffix *kvip* occurs] after *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *pha* when referring to asuras. 4. [The suffix *kvip* occurs] after *na* and *sa* when they have attained [the state].

The root *nakṣ* means "to go. The addition of the vowel *i* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, *inakṣati* has the meaning "to go," and another verbal root must be sought. Regarding *stavānaḥ*: by the rule "the suffix *ānac* is added to *stu*" (Uṇādisūtra 2.246), the suffix *ānac* is applied to the root *stu* even when preceded by a prefix, due to the frequentative usage (*bahulavacana*). The acute accent on the first syllable occurs by metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*). Regarding *jaghāna*: by the rule "and after a reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsācca*), the *ha* of the root *han* following the reduplication undergoes the change to *gha* (*kutva*). Regarding *saṃdihaḥ*: the root *diha* means "to increase. By the rule "the kṛt and lyuṭ suffixes are used diversely" (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*), the suffix *kip* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). The accentuation follows the rule for the original accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).

When Uśanas fashioned for you power with might, your impetuous force pushed apart the two worlds (Heaven and Earth) by its greatness. O hero-minded one, the mind-yoked steeds of the Wind bore you toward glory as you were being filled [with strength]. takṣat | yat | te | uśanā | sahasā | sahaḥ | vi | rodasī iti | majmanā | bādhate | śarvaḥ | ā | tvā | vātasya | nṛmaṇaḥ | manaḥyujaḥ | ā | pūryamāṇam | avahan | abhi | śravaḥ || 10 ||
O Indra, when Uśanas Kāvya by his own power (sahasā) fashioned (takṣat)—
that is, thoroughly sharpened—
your power (te sahaḥ), your own might (śavaḥ), then by that majesty (majmanā), which purifies all, it forced apart the two worlds, heaven and earth (rodasī).
They are terrified; that is the meaning.
And so it is stated elsewhere in an unknown [text]: "At whose roar the two worlds trembled" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.12.1).
Or else:
The meaning is that he oppresses him from whom the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), are afraid—namely Vṛtra and the like.

O Indra, *nṛmaṇas*, you who possess a mind intent on favoring men—that is, the sacrificers who are to be protected—[we invoke] you, who are being filled from all sides with the aforementioned strength. [We invoke] those yoked by the mind (*manoyujaḥ*), meaning those who move with the same speed as Vāta, the wind, through the mere operation of thought.
May such horses as these bring [us] hither, toward the glory—that is, toward the food characterized by the oblation.

*takṣat* | [The root] *takṣū*, *tvakṣū* [is used] in the sense of "making thin. In the *laṅ* [tense], there is the absence of the augment *aṭ* according to the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the augment is] optional even when not joined with *māṅ*."

Since the suffix *śap* is *pittvāt* (marked with *p*), it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains. *Uśanā*: from the root *vaś* "to desire," [the suffix] *kanas* is added by the rule "*vaśeḥ kanasiḥ*" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.678).
By the rule *'grahijyā'* and so forth, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
By the rule *'ṛdupadhasya purudaṃso 'nehasāṃ ca'* (Pāṇini 7.1.94), there is the substitution of *anaṅ*.
By the rule *'sarvanāmasthāne ca'* (Pāṇini 6.4.8), there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghatva*).
The elision of the *dal* (the second member) occurs after words such as *hal*. [The form] *majmanā* [is derived from the root] *majj*,
meaning "to purify."
The suffix *man* is derived according to the *uṇādi* rules.
[Thus we have] *nṛmaṇas*. The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by the rule "in the Veda, after a word ending in *a*, when there is no *avagraha*."
They brought [it].
The *laṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of a prayer (*prārthanā*) according to the rule "In Vedic, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [suffixes may be used for all tenses]."

When Indra rejoiced with Uśanas Kāvya, he mounted his two swift, most swift-moving steeds. Fierce, he released the flowing waters by their current; he shattered the strongholds and cast down the fortresses of Śuṣṇa. mandiṣṭa | yat | uśane | kāvye | sacā | indraḥ | vaṅkū iti | vaṅkutarā | adhi | tiṣṭhati | ugraḥ | yayim | niḥ | apaḥ | srotasā | asṛjat | vi | śuṣṇasya | daṃhitāḥ | airayat | puraḥ || 11 ||
Whenever Indra, being praised, rejoiced together with the desiring Kāvya Uśanas, at that time he mounts the two *vaṅkū*—the horses that move most crookedly;
that is to say, having yoked them to the chariot, he ascends it. Or else:
"Vaṅkutara" means that which goes exceedingly crookedly; one should connect this with "having yoked the two horses (vaṅkū) on the chariot, which are by nature prone to moving crookedly.
"Ugra" means full of water; "tāraśaḥ" [is derived from] *tṛ*.

Indra released the waters with a stream—that is, in the form of a flow—from the *yayi*, the moving cloud; he caused the waters to go forth. Likewise, he shattered and drove apart the *purah*, the fortified cities or dwellings, of *śuṣṇa*, the Asura who dries up everything. [Grammatical notes: *mandiṣṭa*: From the root *mad* (in the sense of praise, joy, intoxication, sleep, beauty, or motion). In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the augment (*aṭ*) is absent according to the rule "there is much [irregularity] in the Veda even when there is no connection with *mā*" (*bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅ-yoge’pi*). *uśane*: From the root *vaś* (to desire), with the *kyu* suffix added by the *uṇādi* rules. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the *prahijyādi* group, and the substitution of *y* for the two vowels (*yoḥ*). *sacā*: From the root *pac* (in the sense of union). The *kvip* suffix is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the *saṃpadādi* class. The substitution of *āṭ* for the case-ending is prescribed by the rule "the addition of *āṭ* is also to be stated for *āṅ*, *yā*, and *jā*" (*āḍyājayārāṃ copasaṃkhyānam*). In the *saṃhitā*, the nasalization of that vowel occurs by the rule "*āṭ* becomes nasalized in the Veda" (*āḍo’nunāsikaśchandasi*). *vaṅkū*: From the root *vaṅgu* (in the sense of motion), with the *upa* suffix added by the *uṇādi* rules. Due to the word "much" (*bahula*), there is the change to *k* (*kutvam*). *vaṅkutarā*: "More crooked" (*vaṅkū* + comparative suffix). The case-ending is replaced by *ā* according to the rule "for case-endings, *su*, *luk*, etc. (*supāṃ suluk*). Here, a specific kind of motion is indicated by a general term for motion. *yayim*: From the root *yā* (in the sense of reaching). The *kip* suffix is applied according to the rule "after the roots *āp*, *gam*, *han*, and *jan*" (*ādyagamahanajanah*). Because it is a *liṅga* (neuter), there is reduplication and shortening. The *ā* is elided by the rule "*ā* is elided before an *iṭ* suffix and elsewhere" (*āto lopa iṭi ca*). The accent is that of the suffix. The ablative case ending is replaced by *am* according to the rule "case-endings may be substituted for case-endings" (*supāṃ supo bhavanti*). *haṃhitāḥ*: From the root *hahi* (in the sense of growth). Because it is marked with *idit*, the *num* augment is added. *airayat*: From the root *īr* (in the sense of impelling), belonging to the *curādi* (tenth) class. In the *luṅ* tense, the augment *āṭ* is prefixed. The *vṛddhi* strengthening occurs by the rule "*āṭ* and [the preceding vowel]" (*āṭaśca*).
You mount this chariot for the sake of those who drink the strong draught, in which you take delight when the offerings of Śaryāta are presented.
O Indra, just as you have taken pleasure in those who press the Soma, you ascend to heaven the far-reaching song of praise.

O Indra, you mount your chariot among those who drink the strong draught; you take delight in the offerings presented by Śaryāta, as you did among those who press the Soma. You ascend to heaven the far-reaching song of praise.

Regarding this, the Kaupītakins relate an ancient legend: at the sacrifice of the royal sage named Śaryāta, the great seer Cyavana, born of the Bhṛgu lineage, took possession of the sacrificial vessel as an obstacle.
Seeing him, Indra became enraged;
[the priests] appeased that Indra and gave the Soma back to him.
This meaning is established in this [verse]:
O Indra, you [are present] "among the drinkers of the bull" (*vṛṣapāṇeṣu*). "Drinkers of the bull" (*vṛṣapāṇāni*) refers to the drinks of Soma, which is capable of pouring forth (seeding).
When those [Soma vessels] have become the instrumental cause, you "mount the chariot"—that is, you mount the chariot yourself and proceed;
the sense is that no one else impels it.

And this being so, those Somas in which you "rejoice," that is, attain exhilaration, are such Somas as were "prepared" (prabhṛtāḥ), meaning excellently produced, belonging to the royal seer named Śaryāta.
The meaning is that they have been consecrated by the preparatory rites such as pressing and so forth.

Therefore, "just as you have delighted (*cākanaḥ*)—that is, just as you desire—in the *suta-soma* sacrifices, namely in the sacrifices belonging to others which involve the pressed Soma, so too do you desire the Somas of this Śaryāta.
This being so, "you ascend to (*ā rohaṣe*) the *śloka*—meaning either fame characterized by hymns of praise or glory—which is *anarvāṇam*, unassailable and stable, in the *divi*, the heavenly world."
Or rather:
you cause this sacrificer to attain glory, characterized as described above, in the sky, in the heavenly world— so it is said.
The lengthening [of the vowel] is by the rule "nipātasya ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.136).
In the word *vṛṣapāṇeṣu*,
[the root] is *pā* in the sense of "drinking."
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
According to Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.4.10, "vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ," there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the word *pāna* when it follows a cause situated in the preceding member of a compound.
[Thus we have] *prabhṛtāḥ*.
The root *bhṛ* is used in the sense of "bearing" (*bharaṇe*).

The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*). By the rule "the immediately preceding prefix [retains its] original accent" (*gatiranantaraḥ*), the prefix retains its natural accent (*prakṛtisvaratvam*).
You are slow.
[The root] *mad* is used in the senses of praise, joy, sleep, beauty, and gait.
Because it has an initial vowel (*adupadeśa*), the suffix *lasārvadhātuka* is unaccented, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
*cākana*:
from the root *kana*, meaning "to shine," "be beautiful," or "move";
here it has the sense of "shining" or "beauty."
*Kānti* means desire.
In the case of *leṭ* with the suffix *sip*, there is the augment *aṭ*;
this is indicated by the rule "in the Veda, [it occurs] diversely."
*bhluḥ*.
Due to its inclusion in the *tujādi* group, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

According to the rule "all rules are optional in the Veda" (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*), since the acute accent on the first syllable of the reduplicated form (*abhyasta*) does not apply here, the acute accent falls on the other part of the verbal root (*dhātu*) by the rule "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*).

*Anarvāṇam*: [The form is derived] either from the root *at-* with the suffix *vanip*— on the basis of the rule "it is seen after other roots as well" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*) which includes the mention of the word *dṛśi*—

or, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the negative particle *nañ*, when followed by the accusative singular ending *am*, there is an absence of the substitute [of *an* for *arvan*] because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) stated in the rule "*arvaṇas tṛ maghonaś ca na śiṣyaḥ sau"* (Pāṇini 6.4.127).

In the word *ślokam*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghatva*) by the rule *sarvanāmasthāne ca*. There is acute accent on the final syllable of the second member of the compound by the rule *nañsubhyām*. Regarding *ślokam*: the root *ślok* means "to collect" (*saṃghāta*). It is called *śloka* because it is collected (*ślokyate*); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and due to the presence of the letter *j* [as an it-letter], there is acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*). Regarding *rohase*: this is the Ātmanepada form of the root *ruh* by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyayena*).
For the sake of great Kakṣīvat, who desires eloquence, O Indra, I shall subdue the Vṛcis for you as he presses the soma.
You became the beloved of Vṛṣaṇaśva, O wise one; all these deeds of yours are to be proclaimed at every libation.

O Indra, you became the beloved wife of Vṛṣaṇaśva for the sake of the great Kakṣīvat, who was eloquent and pressing the Soma—O you of noble wisdom! All these deeds of yours are indeed to be proclaimed at every libation. 13.
On this point, there is the following narrative: One day, the King of Aṅga was sporting in the waters of the Gaṅgā with his women.

At that time, an ascetic named Dīrghatamas, because he was so infirm that he was unable to do anything by himself, was thrown into the middle of the Gaṅgā out of malice by his wife, sons, servants, and others.
That seer arrived at the pleasure grounds of the King of Aṅga by means of a certain raft.
Having learned that the seer was omniscient, the king spoke thus to him as if to a river deity:
"O Blessed One, I have no son; let this queen bear me a son."
He replied, "It is true.

The queen, however, having told the king that it was true, thought, "This elder man is loathsome and not suitable for me," and with this thought she sent her own maidservant named Uṣik. When she was sprinkled with water purified by mantras by that omniscient seer, she became the wife of the seer.
From her was born the seer Kakṣīvān;
he himself became the king's son,
and he performed the Rājasūya and other sacrifices in many ways.

Indra, being well-pleased by the sacrifices performed by that king, bestowed upon him a woman named Vṛcayā who was capable of crossing over [difficulties]. This meaning is set forth in the first half-verse: O Indra, you [gave] to the great, to the one desiring speech—meaning to the one who desires for himself speech characterized by hymns of praise—to Kakṣīvat, the king of this name, who was pressing Soma in sacrifices dedicated to you, [the woman] Vṛcayā, known as Vṛcayā, who was small (alpām).

The meaning is "a young woman. You granted such prosperity. Likewise, O Indra, you who are well-performing of good deeds (*sukṛtaḥ*)—meaning one of beautiful actions or beautiful wisdom—you became *Menā*, a maiden named Menā, for the king named Vṛṣaṇaśva.

And likewise, a Brāhmaṇa passage in the form of an explanation of a portion of the *Subrahmaṇyā* invocation is thus handed down by the Jñātāyanins: “‘Vṛṣaṇaśvasya menā’—having become Vṛṣaṇaśva’s Menā, Maghavat dwelt in his family.
And Indra himself desired her when she had reached the bloom of youth.
Thus it is also handed down by the Tāṇḍins: “Vṛṣaṇaśva had a daughter named Menā.”
"Indra desired him.
Therefore, those deeds of such a nature as were performed by you—those which are yours—all of them indeed must be proclaimed at the *savanas*, that is, at the sacrifices;
the meaning is that they are to be extolled with hymns of praise.
To the great one.
The acute accent on the case-ending is due to the rule “*bṛhanmahatopasaṃkhyānam*” (the addition of *bṛhat* and *mahat* to this rule).
To the one who possesses eloquence.
By the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, the suffix *kyac* is applied; then, by the rule *kyāc chandasi*, the suffix *u* is added [to form *kāmya*]. Thus: *kakṣīvate*.
The cords for tethering horses are *kakṣyās*.
Yāska states: “*Kakṣīvān* means ‘possessing a girth-cord’” (*Nirukta* 6.10).

Furthermore, by the rule *āsandīvadaṣṭhīvaccakrīvatkakṣīvat* (Pāṇini 8.2.12), the vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the replacement of the suffix *matup* with *vat* are prescribed as irregular forms (*nipātana*) when used as proper names.
*Menā* is a name for a woman; this is because of the reading in the *Nirukta* (3.21), “*menā* means those who know,” from the verbal root *man*,
"to know."
She is called Menā because she thinks and knows household duties; the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *pacādyac*.
The form *menā* is derived thus by the rule: “The substitution of *e* for the vowel of the roots *naś* and *man* should be stated before the *liṭ* affix” (Pāṇini 6.4.120, vārttika 5).
It should be viewed as beginning with *vṛṣan*.
Yāska [states]: “*Menāḥ* means those who honor her” (*Nirukta* 3.21).
[The word occurs] in the contexts of the *savanas*.

"Savana" is a name for sacrifice (*yajña*). It is derived from the sense "it is pressed (*sūyate*)" or "it is extracted (*abhiṣūyate*)," with the suffix *lyuṭ* used in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇe*). [It is] to be proclaimed (*pravācyā*).

The root *vac* is used in the sense of speaking. With the suffix *ṇyat*, [the form is *vācyam*]. [Regarding the rule] "after *yaj*, *yāc*, *ḍha-kabhāp*": 2. In the *ḍha*-manuscript, the phrase "having said 'it is true' to the king" is not present. 3. In the *ḍha*-manuscript, [the word] "thinking" (*matvā*) is present. 4. In the *ḍha*-manuscript, it is of the nature of an explanation of a portion of the *Subrahmaṇyomita* mantra. 5. In the *ḍha*-manuscript, [the reading] "for of Vṛṣaṇaśva" (*sa-vṛṣaṇaśvasya hi*) is present. Page 46.

By the rule *pravacaśca* (Pāṇini 7.3.66), there is an absence of *kutva*. Although a circumflex (*svarita*) accent would have been expected, there is instead an initial acute (*udātta*) by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*). Alternatively, [the word *pravacana*] is derived from the root *vac* with the suffix *yat* according to *aco yat*; its initial acute is established by *yato ’nāvaḥ*, and it takes the natural accent of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).
Indra has been established in the solitude of the pious, like a sacrificial post at the rites; he is the pillar of the dwelling.
Seeking pastures, seeking chariots, and seeking wealth, Indra, the lord of power, rules as the bestower of gifts.

Indra has been established in the exclusive possession of the pious; at the sacrifices, the hymn of praise is like a pillar fixed in the dwelling. Seeking horses, seeking cattle, seeking chariots, and seeking wealth—Indra alone rules over riches as their bestower. 14.

Indra, the god, when poverty (*nir-eka*) became the cause [of distress] for the sacrificers who were of good intellect (*sudhyaḥ*)—meaning those of beautiful actions or beautiful wisdom—resorted to them (*aśrāyi*) to protect them;
for among the Aṅgirases, *pajñeṣu* is a designation for the patrons (*patra*). And thus says the Śākhā: [...]
This speech, characterized by praise, directed toward you, O Indra—present before us—has been uttered and offered by us to you.
To what kind of one? To the bull (*vṛṣabha*), who is of a raining nature; to the self-ruling king (*svarāj*), who shines by his own splendor; to the one of true vigor (*satyaśuṣma*).
*Śuṣmam* is a name for strength, because it withers enemies;
[the term] *avitathabalāya* means "to him who possesses unfailing strength"; *vītave* means "to him who has increased exceedingly."
Since this is so, therefore, in that *vrajana*— that is, in that battle characterized by the act of striking— we are accompanied by all *vīras*,
meaning warriors who especially drive away enemies;
we are thus endowed with all such soldiers.
The particle *sma* has the sense of the word *su* (well/excellent).
In *tava sma śarman*, meaning "in the beautiful house granted by you," [the sense is] "may we be with the wise ones (*sūribhiḥ*)—that is, with sons and others—we shall abide; this is the meaning.
Or alternatively:
May we be together with the wise—the learned officiating priests—in your auspicious sacrificial hall;
for *śarman* is a name for a house, as it is listed [in the Nighaṇṭu] alongside *varman* in the passage "śarma varma" (Nirukta 3.4.21).
In *svarāje*:
[the root] *rāj* means "to shine";
[the suffix] *kvip* is applied according to the rule *sasṛdvipa*.
To Satyaśuṣma. He whose vigor (śuṣma) is real (satya). In this bahuvrīhi compound, the accentuation follows the natural accent of the first member.
*Tavase*:
*tavi* is a root found in the *sūtra*;
from this, the *as* suffix is added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
In the sense of "avoiding" (*vrajane*), from the root *vṛjī* meaning "to avoid" (*varjane*), the suffix *kyu* is applied according to the rule *kṛpavṛjimandinidhābhyaḥ kyuḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.239).
In *śarman*, the locative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
The prohibition of the elision of the final *n* is applied by the rule *na ḍisaṃbuddhayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.8).
[The form] *syāma* [is derived as follows]:
by the rule *naśca* (Pāṇini 8.3.30), the augment *ṣuṭ* is added to the *s* in *saṃhitā*; then, by the rule *khari ca*, the *ṣ* undergoes *carv*-substitution (becoming *s*).
By the rule *‘cayo dvitīyāḥ śari pauṣkarasādeḥ’* (Pāṇini 8.4.48), the letter *t* is replaced by *th*.
The second hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "tyaṃ su meṣam," belongs to Savya; it is addressed to the Aśvins and Indra.
The thirteenth and fifteenth verses are Triṣṭubhs, while the remaining ones are Jagatīs.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "In 'tyaṃ su' there are two Triṣṭubhs at the end."
This hymn is used in the Marutvatīya śastra on the central day of the Gavāmayana, known as the Viṣuvat.
It is prescribed in the section titled “The Viṣuvat is the Divākīrtya” in the sūtra: “‘Tyaṃ su meṣam’ and ‘Kayā śubhā’ constitute the Marutvatīya” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.6).

I would turn hither with my well-fashioned hymns that ram, the finder of light through his greatness, whose hundred strong ones rush forth together; like a prize-winning steed or a chariot, I would bring Indra hither for our protection.

Hitherward, with my well-fashioned hymns, may I turn Indra hither for protection—to that ram who finds the light of heaven, from whom a hundred well-being-bestowing powers issue forth together, like a prize-winning steed or a chariot swift to the call. ||1||
That famous ram, who contends with his enemies, the finder of heaven—
*svar* meaning the sun or the heavenly world;
its knower or attainer.
Or alternatively:
"Svaḥ" means excellent wealth; [Indra is] the one who causes that to be obtained.
O Adhvaryu, worship Indra, who is distinguished by such qualities, properly for me.
A hundred— numbering one hundred— excellent (*subhvaḥ*) singers proceed together, simultaneously, in the praise of Indra; or rather,
a hundred excellent horses go together, simultaneously, to draw Indra’s chariot.
I have chosen that Indra for our protection with well-fashioned hymns and excellent praises; I turn back his chariot, as one would turn a wagon, so that he may hasten toward us.
What kind of chariot?
One that speeds toward the invocation—the calling or the sacrifice—with great velocity.
There is an illustration regarding movement with speed:
like a horse (*vājī*), which is the means for swift motion.
*Mahya*:
[derived from] *maha* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*),
belonging to the *curādi* class and ending in *-ā*.
In the *Saṃhitā*, there is lengthening according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well. *Subhvaḥ*: those who become well, that is, the praisers (*stotāraḥ*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvip ca*. There is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member due to the suffix *kvu*.
In the nominative plural (*jasi*), the substitution of *yaṇ* (by the rule *oḥ supi*) is prohibited by the rule *na bhusudhiyoḥ*.
1. The suffixes *ca*, *na*, *pha*, and *sa* are *kypatyayas*.

2. [The vowels] *cha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*, the thirteenth (*ta*), and the fifteenth (*la*, *śa*, *sa*)—since the prohibition [of *yaṇ* substitution] would otherwise apply, by the rule "in Vedic usage, both ways," there is the occurrence of both, and thus the *yaṇ* substitution takes place.
By the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ," the following *jas* (nominative plural) becomes *svarita* because it follows a *yaṇ* that precedes both an *udātta* and a *svarita*. [Thus we have] *īrate*.
[The root] *īr* [is used] in the senses of "going" and "trembling."
Because it belongs to the *ad-ādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix;
for the *jha* [augment], there is the substitution of *at*;
and likewise for the final vowel (*ṭi*).
Because the [suffix] has an anudātta indicatory letter (*anudāttettva*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes become anudātta; thus, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
Due to its connection with *yad*, there is no suppression of the accent (*anighāta*).

For in that case, it has been stated that even when there is a mention of the ablative case (*pañcamīnirdeśa*), the grammatical operation is desired to apply even across an intervening element (Kāśikā 8.1.66).
Atya; "atya" is a name for a horse, according to the reading "atyaḥ hayaḥ" (Nirukta 1.14.1).
Vājam.
It is called *vāja* because by means of it one is impelled (*vājyate*) or goes (*gamyate*).
[The root] *vaja-vraja* means "to go.
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).

Regarding the rule *ajivrajyośca* (Pāṇini 7.3.60), because the word *ca* has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned (*anuktasamuccayārthatvāt*), it is stated that there is also the absence of the *kṛt* suffix in *vājaḥ* and *vājyam*. [The form] *havanasyadam* [is derived from the root] *syand*, meaning "to flow."
The word *syada* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) noun ending in the suffix *ghañ*, as prescribed by the rule *syado jave* (Pāṇini 6.4.28), when speed is being expressed.
For this very reason, there is both the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) and the absence of *vṛddhi*.
Nor does the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 1.1.4) prohibit the *vṛddhi* [in this case].

For it is an irregular (illakṣaṇā) increase (vṛddhi) that is prohibited here, and this [increase] is not irregular. Because the suffix *ghañ* has the marker *j*, the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is udātta.
By virtue of the rule that the original accent of the final member of a compound is retained (*kuduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvena*), that very [accent] remains.
*Vadhutvām*.
[The root is] *vṛtu* in the sense of "turning."

In the optative (*liṅ*), the *parasmaipada* ending is used because of the rule "the suffix *dhyāyī*" [is applied]. By the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), there is the substitution of *ślu* for *śap*.
This results in reduplication and so forth.
Because *yāsuṭ* is marked with the *ḍi*-sign, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel;
furthermore, the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) applies by the rule "tiṅaṅatiṅaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.28).

That mountain was not shaken from its foundations; he of a thousandfold protection increased in his powers when Indra, exulting in the soma-juice, slew Vṛtra who had encompassed the rivers, and released the waters into the ocean.

He, like a mountain, immovable in his foundations, Indra, possessing a thousandfold aid, has grown mighty in his powers when he slew Vṛtra who obstructed the rivers; he roared as he crushed the floods in the ocean, exhilarated by the soma-juice.

Exceedingly rejoicing (*jahraṣāṇaḥ*) through the *andhas*—the food characterized by Soma—Indra, when he slew Vṛtra, the Asura who obstructed the three worlds; how was Vṛtra? "River-obstructing" (*nadīvṛtam*): from the root *nad*, "rivers" are the waters; [Vṛtra was] the one who obstructed them. What was Indra doing? "Ubjan," pushing down the waters (*arṇaḥ-arṇasi*) into the depths. At that time, that Indra, like a mountain (*parvataḥ na*)—a mass of rocks possessing many joints—stood immovable (*acyutaḥ*) for lack of motion among the *dhuruṇeṣu*, the supporting bases that sustain all; he, possessing a thousand protections (*sahasramūtiḥ*), grew strong (*vavṛdhe*) in his powers (*taviṣīṣu*). Regarding the words: *dhuruṇeṣu*: From the root *dhṛ* with the suffix *ṇuk* (Pāṇini 3.2.171); the accent is that of the suffix. *sahasramūtiḥ*: He whose protections (*ūtayaḥ*) are a thousand; the absence of the elision [of the *t*] is Vedic. *vavṛdhe*: In the *saṃhitā*, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.7. *nadīvṛtam*: He who obstructs the river (*nadīm vṛṇoti*); formed with the suffix *kvip* and the augment *tug*. *ubjan*: From the root *ubj* meaning "straightness"; the accent is that of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa-svara*). *arṇārṇasi*: By Uṇādi-sūtra 4.636, the suffix *asun* is added to *arṇ* with the augment *nuṭ*; due to its being *nit*, it is acute-accented on the first syllable. *jahraṣāṇaḥ*: From the root *hṛṣ* meaning "joy"; the suffix *jñānac* is applied after the *yaṅ*-intensive form. The initial accent follows Pāṇini 6.1.189. Alternatively, from the *yaṅ*-intensive itself, the suffix *śānac* is used; by the rule "often in the Veda" (*bahulam chandasi*), there is elision of *śap*; by "in the Veda both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*), the suffix *śānac* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, resulting in the elision of *at* and *y*. Due to its being a *sārvadhātuka*, the initial accent of the reduplicated form applies. *andhasā*: That which is eaten (*adyate*) is *andhas*; by Uṇādi-sūtra 4.645, the suffix *asun* is added to *ad* with the augment *num* and the substitution of *dh* for the final letter. Being *nit*, it is acute-accented on the first syllable.
1. Like Mount Ḍha;
2. he grew like Ḍha.
For he, the slayer of Vṛtra, has increased in the doors, in the waters, and in the udder; he is the moon-like wise one, made strong by exhilaration through the inspired poets.
I honor that Indra with a well-crafted prayer, for he is the most liberal giver; indeed, he is the fulfiller of the draught of soma.

For he is far-reaching among those who are far; Vṛtra is in the udder. He is wise as the moon, increased by exhilaration through the inspired thoughts of the sages. With a well-fashioned prayer, I honor that Indra, the most bountiful giver; for he is the one who pours forth the soma-juice. 3.
That Indra, distinguished by the previously mentioned qualities, is indeed the preeminent protector (*āvarītṛ*) against the enemies who obstruct;
that is to say, he is one whose nature is the conquest of foes.
For he dwells pervading (*vavaḥ*) the firmament (*ūdhani*), which possesses rising waters, acting as a sustainer (*maṃbhaka*).

For this very reason, the Moon-Buddha (Candrabudha) is the root of delight for all living beings, because the atmosphere is the source of all delight. He is "increased by intoxication" (madavṛddha): "intoxications" (madāḥ) are Soma juices, as they are that by which [beings] become intoxicated; he is increased by them.
Indra who has become thus— the most generous giver, whose wealth increases or whose gifts increase—

him whom those who spread the entire sacrificial grass fill in heaven, like well-being-seeking rivers flow into the ocean; him, the slayer of Vṛtra, his aids and his unassailable powers have followed, he who wins the light in the heatless waters.

Him whom they satisfy in heaven with all sacrificial grass, like well-being-seeking waves toward the ocean—him, Indra, his aids followed in the slaying of Vṛtra; his unassailable powers, whose waters are unexhausted.

Those *soma* juices—whose dwelling place, station, and sacrificial grass (*barhis*) are indicated by the term [the sacrifice itself]—completely fill (*āpṛṇanti*) that Indra who resides in heaven, in the world of *svarga*.
Therein lies the illustration:
they are like rivers (*nadyaḥ*), which are "well-being" (*subhvaḥ*), filling the ocean.
The meaning is that it is just as rivers fill the ocean.
What kind of rivers?
"Their own," meaning those belonging to the ocean itself.

And thus it is handed down in scripture: "Homage to the ocean, the one who knows the way, the lord of the rivers" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.6.2.6). "The *abhiṣṭayaḥ*—those who move forward toward [the battle]—the *ūtayaḥ*, the protectors, the Maruts, when the slaying of Vṛtra had become the occasion, stood following after that Indra; they remained with him as their aim.
Of what sort were the Maruts?"
"Śuṣmāḥ" means those who dry up the enemies. "Avātāḥ":
"vātāḥ" refers to enemies who move in a contrary direction; [the term] means being devoid of such.
"Ahutapsvaḥ": meaning not crooked in form, that is, having beautiful limbs.
They satisfy. The root *pṛ* is used in the senses of "protecting" and "filling.
It belongs to the *krayādi* (the sixth class).

The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ" (the roots beginning with pū take a short vowel). The elision of the long *ā* occurs by the rule "ābhyastayorātaḥ" (the *ā* of the reduplicated stem is elided). This is the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
Because of its connection with the *vṛt* class [of roots], there is no *nighāta* (elision of accent). *Saṃbarhiṣaḥ*.
[The root] *ṣaṭ* [is used] in the senses of "falling apart," "going," and "exhaustion."
It is called *sañ* because things sink (*sīdanti*) in it;
the suffix *manin* is applied in the sense of a locus according to the *Uṇādi* rules.
Due to its being marked with *ṅ* (the *nit* designation), it has the acute accent on the first syllable.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that [accent] alone remains by virtue of the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*). Thus:
*subhvaḥ*. [The word *bhū* is derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule "kvip ca."]
The first member of the compound retains its original accent (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).

Regarding the *jas* ending, although the substitution of *yaṇ* by the rule "oḥ supi" would normally be prohibited by the rule "na bhūsudhiyoḥ," the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs here because of the rule "chandasyubhayathā.
Consequently, by the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ," the *jas* ending, being followed by a *yaṇ* substitute for an acute-accented vowel, becomes circumflex-accented (*svarita*).
*Abhiṣṭayaḥ* and *ithya eṣaṇāni*: according to the rule "and [the word] *abhi*, except when it is a prefix," the word *abhi* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that [accent] alone remains by virtue of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*).
Because it begins with *e*, there is substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpatva*).
[Thus we have] *vṛtrahatye*.

In the case of *hantaśca*, the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *han* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), and there is a substitution of the final letter with *t*. Since the suffix is marked with *p* (denoting it as *pit*), it is unaccented (*anudātta*); thus, the accent of the verbal root remains. [The resulting form is] *ahantapsvaḥ*.

The root *hū* is used in the sense of crookedness (*kauṭilye*). From this [root], by means of the suffix *niś*, there is the substitution of *hu* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.31: *hu harer chandasi*. From the root *psā* in the sense of eating (*bhakṣaṇe*), the suffix *ḍa* is added as an *auṇādika* formation.
*na hutapsvaḥ*: *ahutapsvaḥ*.
[This is an example of] the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) which serves as the prior member (*pūrvapada*).
Toward his own rain, as he fights in the exhilaration of this [Soma], his aids have flowed forth like waters down a slope;
when Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, emboldened by the plant-juice, shattered the enclosures of Vala as Trita did.

Toward his own rain, as he fights in the exhilaration of this [Soma], his aids have flowed forth like waters down a slope; when Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, boldly drinking the plant, shattered the enclosures of Vala as Trita did. ||5||

When the Maruts were exhilarated by the drinking of Soma for their aid, they rushed toward Vṛtra— the possessor of his own rain— who was fighting in front of this Indra as he battled with him; they went forth like waters rushing down a slope,
just as water, by its very nature, flows toward a low-lying place.
Whenever [he was] with the *andhas*— that is, the soma characterized by the [letter] *ḍha* or *na*— it was like [pouring it] into the ocean.

Having drunk the yellow [Soma], Indra—the bold one, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*)—shattered, that is, tore apart and slew, the Asura named Vala who was obstructing [the waters]. Herein is the illustration: "like Trita the enclosing-sticks" (*paridhīn*). Three persons were born from Agni into the waters: Ekata, Dvita, and Trita, for the purpose of removing the sacrificial oblation and its smearings from the gods. Thus it is recorded by the Taittirīyas: "He [Agni] fell upon the waters with his flame. From that, Ekata was born. He fell upon them a second time. From that, Dvita was born. He fell upon them a third time. From that, Trita was born" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.8.10-11). There, when Trita had fallen into a well while attempting to drink water, the Asuras placed "enclosing-sticks"—that is, obstructors or covers—to block him. Just as he shattered those, so did he [Indra] shatter Vala. *svavṛṣṭim*: In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent remains on the first member according to the rule of *prakṛtisvara*. *yudhyataḥ*: From the root *yudh* meaning "to fight," belonging to the *divādi* class. By transposition (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *śatṛ* is used. Since the root is taught with a short *u*, the *l-sārvadhātuka* suffixes are *anudātta*; however, because the suffix *iy* has the marker *n*, it is *ādyudātta*. *raghvīḥ*: The root *radh* means "to go. The suffix *up* is added according to Uṇādi Sūtra 1.29: *radhijabhorrnalopaśca*. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to Pāṇini 4.1.44: *voto guṇavacanāt*. In the nominative plural (*jas*), the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* is optionally applied in the Veda (Pāṇini 6.1.107). The accent of the *ṅīp* suffix remains. *dhapamāṇaḥ*: From the root *dhipṣā* meaning "boldness. Although the suffix *śap* would normally be expected, *śa* is used by transposition (*vyatyaya*), and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is also employed. Since the root is taught with a short *a*, the *l-sārvadhātuka* suffixes are *anudātta*, and thus the accent of the *vikaraṇa* suffix remains. *bhinat*: In the *laṅ* tense, the augment *aṭ* is absent due to the rule: *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge'pi*. The accent belongs to the *vikaraṇa* suffix. It does not receive the *anighāta* (non-suppression) because of its connection with *yad-vṛtta* (the relative pronoun *yat*). *valasya*: From the root *val* meaning "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*). That which covers everything is *vala*. The suffix *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*). Because the action is considered the object, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the fourth (*caturthī*) by the rule: *kriyāgrahaṇaṃ kartavyam*. *paridhīn*: They are called *paridhayaḥ* because they are "placed around" (*paridhīyante*). The suffix *ki* is added to the root *dhā* preceded by a prefix according to Pāṇini 3.3.92: *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*. The vowel *ā* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.64: *āto lopa iṭi ca*. The accent remains on the first member of the *kṛdanta* compound. 12. Translation complete.

He moves about with fervor; you have displayed your power. Having encompassed the waters, you lay low the source of the mid-world. When, O Indra, you struck Vṛtra—who was difficult to seize—on his slope, you brought down the thunderbolt between his jaws. pari īm ghṛṇā carati tittiṣe śavaḥ apaḥ vṛttvī rajasaḥ budham ā aśayat vṛtrasya yat pravaṇe durgṛbhbhranaḥ nijaghantha hanvor indra tanyatum || 6 || He moves all around with heat; you have manifested your might. Having enclosed the waters, you reached the source of the atmospheric realm. When, on the slope of Vṛtra—who was hard to grasp—you struck him down, O Indra, you cast the thunderbolt between his two jaws.

Vṛtra, who, having obstructed the waters—that is, having blocked the floods—lay resting upon *rajas*, the upper region of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), for that Vṛtra, who dwells in the *pravaṇa*—the intensely desirable intermediate space—and who is *durgṛbhraṇaḥ*, difficult to seize or restrain; for his pervasion cannot be grasped by anyone, according to the Śruti: "He enveloped these worlds."

O Indra, when you struck down— that is, thoroughly smote— Vṛtra who had become thus, with the *tanyatu*, the thunderbolt (the accusative used in the sense of the instrumental) which spreads its blow across the jaws— the sides of the mouth— or rather, which produces sound; at that time, O Indra, *ghṛṇā*— the brilliance characterized by the conquest of enemies— surrounded and pervaded you.
Thy own *śavas*, or strength, has stood firm in the light.
*tittiṣe*.
[The root] *tvip* means "to shine.
In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, the accent falls on the suffix.
The absence of affliction for living beings.
Having acted (*vṛttvī*).
[From] the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*).
By the rule *snābhyādyaśca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.49), because of the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the letter *ī* is substituted for the suffix *ktvā*.
[The form] *rajasaḥ* [is derived from the root] *rañj*, meaning "to color" or "to dye."
"In this night, the Gandharvas and others [dwell].
Here, *rajaḥ* means the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
In the case of the suffix *-asun*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*) according to the rule: "The addition of *rajaka*, *rajana*, and *rajas* is prescribed" (Kāśikā 6.4.24.4).
The initial udātta accent is due to the *nittva* [of the suffix].
He lay down (*aśayat*).
The verb *śīṅ* takes the *parasmaipada* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
In accordance with the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.4.73), there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. [The word] *durgṛbhītaḥ*:

from the roots *grah* (in the sense of "taking") and *aś* (in the sense of "pervading"), when the prefix *dur-* is used as an attendant word (*upapada*), the desired form and accent are established by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
nijaghantha | ‘hana 1.
[of the third letter] fallen after ḍha, sa, and pa.
2. In this [root] *rañj*,
which belongs to the classes meaning "to injure" and "to go," the augment *iṭ*—

which would otherwise be required by the rule for roots beginning with *krī* (Pāṇini 7.2.13)— is prohibited in the case of the *thala* suffix of the *liṭ* [perfect tense] by the rule "upadeśe 'cataḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.62).
Regarding the phrase "and from repetition" (*abhyāsācca*): due to the repetition, the following *h* becomes *gh*.
By the rule "in the *liṭ* [perfect]," the vowel preceding the suffix is udātta. By the rule "also when a *tiṅ* ending is udātta," there is the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) of the *gati* prefix.
Due to its connection with the suffix *vṛt*, there is an absence of *nighāta* (anudātta accent).
[The form] is *tanyatu*.
[The root is] *tanu* in the sense of "expansion."

From this [root], the suffix *yatuc* is applied by the rule *ṛtanyañji* (Uṇādi-sūtra 4.442). Alternatively, from the root *stan* in the sense of "sound," the suffix *yatuc* is applied due to the presence of the term *bahula*, resulting in the elision of the letter *s*.
The waves do not overwhelm you, for you are the one who knows the sacred word (*brahman*), O Indra; those hymns of yours are your means of strengthening.
Even Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for you a companion, Śarva; he wrought the thunderbolt of overwhelming power.

The waves do not overwhelm you, O Indra, for those sacred hymns (*brahmāṇi*) are your means of strengthening. Even Tvaṣṭṛ increased your allied power; he fashioned the thunderbolt of surpassing might.

O Indra, those collections of mantras in the form of *brahmans*—namely the *stotras* and *śastras*—which are your strengtheners (*vardhanā*), truly reach you (*nyupanti*) most completely. Therein is an illustration: like waves (*ūrmayaḥ*), that is, currents of water, reaching a lake (*hradam na*). Furthermore, the divine Tvaṣṭṛ, by means of a bride, increased (*vavṛdhe*) your fitting strength (*yujyam śavaḥ*). Moreover, he fashioned (*tatakṣa*) the thunderbolt (*vajram*), which possesses overwhelming power (*abhibhūtyojasam*), sharpening it with the force capable of overcoming enemies. Regarding the word *nyupanti*: the root *kṛpī* means "to go"; it belongs to the *taudādika* class. Because it is taught with a short vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the suffixes of the present tense (*lasārvadhātuka*) are unaccented, and thus the accent falls on the *vikaraṇa* suffix. By the rule *hi ca*, there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (the general accentual suppression). Regarding *ūrmayaḥ*: the root *ṛ* means "to go. They are called *ūrmayaḥ* because they "go" (*ṛcchanti*) or move. By the *Uṇādi Sūtra* (4.634), the suffix *mi* is added after the root *ṛ*. When the *guṇa* substitution occurs, the vowel *a* is replaced by *u*. The accent is that of the suffix. Regarding *vardhanā*: the root *vṛdh* means "to grow. They are called *vardhanā* because "one grows by means of them" (*vartate ebhiḥ*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an instrument. By the rule *śeś chandasi*, the final *ś* is elided. Regarding *tatakṣa*: the roots *takṣū* and *tvakṣū* mean "to make thin" or "to fashion. In the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *nal*, by the accent of the *lis* suffix, the preceding syllable is acute. Since it begins the quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no *nighāta*. Regarding *abhibhūtyojasam*: that by which one is overcome is *abhibhūti*; the suffix *kin* is used in the instrumental sense. By the rule *tādau ca niti...*, the original accent of the prefix (*gati*) is retained. That whose power (*ojas*) is such an overcoming is *abhibhūtyojas*. In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member is maintained.
Having struck with your bay steeds, O Indra of gathered power, you opened a path for man by releasing the waters;
you cast the iron thunderbolt from your arms and established the celestial sun so that it might be seen.

Having struck Vṛtra with your bay steeds, O Indra of gathered wisdom, you set the waters free for man to flow. You held the iron thunderbolt in your arms; you placed the sun in heaven so that it might be seen. 8.

O Indra, you whose power is accumulated, who accomplishes the rite, and who knows how to bring it to completion—for the sake of human beings, desiring a path (*gātu*) as a way, you, yoked with your bay horses (*haribhiḥ*), indeed struck down Vṛtra, the Asura who obstructs the worlds.
Immediately thereafter, [you] set loose the waters, the rain-waters—this is to be supplied. From your two arms, your hands, you took up the iron (*āyasa*) thunderbolt.
The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
And the sun in the sky, in the heavenly world, is for us all to see—that is, for our vision.
1. Na-cha-ta-pha-śa is Tvaṣṭṛ, the god; dha-tvaṣṭā is indeed Tvaṣṭṛ, and he is the god; na-sa is Tvaṣṭṛ, indeed Tvaṣṭṛ himself. You have supported them; you have established them.
*jaghanvān*:
[This is derived from] the root *han* with the suffix *kasu* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the statement of its optionality in Pāṇini’s Sūtra 7.2.68: *vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām*.

"You desire a way. [The suffix] *kyac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.8.2 (*chandasi parecchāyām api*). The prohibition of the long vowel [in the penultimate syllable] applies according to the rule *na chandasyaputrasya*.

When the suffix *śatṛ* follows a root ending in *kyac*, since the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented (*anudātta*) due to the rule regarding roots taught with an initial vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the accent of *kyac* alone remains. In the case of [the forms] *bāhyaḥ* and so on, the case-ending receives the acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule "after a vowel that is acute (*udāttayaṇ*) and preceded by a consonant (*halpūrvāt*)."
They made for themselves a great, bright, moon-like, swelling, and praiseworthy ascent to heaven out of fear;
when the Maruts, seeking the light and rejoicing in their aid, gladdened Indra as he won the human battle.

Vast, self-luminous, and full of power—when they performed that which was worthy of praise, the ascent of heaven out of fear; when the Maruts, who have the human race as their foremost concern and who accompany the sun, rejoiced in support of Indra for his aid. ||9||
O singers and sacrificers, when you, out of fear—that is, out of dread of Vṛtra—made the Bṛhat-sāman worthy of praise (ukthya), that is, fit for hymns;
what kind of Bṛhat-sāman?
One endowed with its own shining, gladdening splendor, and powerful.
*Amati* means "he conquers enemies"; thus, *ama* is strength. That [strength] is possessed by it. It is the "ascent" (*rohaṇam*)—that is, the cause of ascending—to *divaḥ*, meaning heaven.
With such a hymn of praise, they praised Indra for his victory over Vṛtra.
Regarding the term *pradhana*:
according to the etymological derivation of the Nairukta school, "that in which wealth (*dhana*) is scattered (*pra-kīrṇa*) is *pradhana*"; thus, *pradhana* is a name for battle.

The "aids" (ūtayaḥ), who engage in battle for the benefit of humanity, being the protectors of heaven (svaḥ) and the great guardians of men (nṛpācaḥ)—that is, serving as breath within men—they likewise gladdened even Indra (indram anu amadan) with joy in succession.
At that time, it is implied, Indra became intent upon the slaying of Vṛtra.
*Svaścandram*: one whose own moon (*svakīya-candra*) belongs to him.
The augment *suṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.151: "The augment *suṭ* occurs before a word beginning with *candra* when it follows a short vowel in a mantra."
The letter *śa* [is substituted] by the *śruva* suffix.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member. [The word] *bhiyasā*.
In the third case singular of the word *bhīs*, there is the Vedic augment *asuk* and its udātta accentuation.
[The term] *nṛpācaḥ* [is derived from] the root *pac* in the sense of "to assemble."
Yāska [states] that this [root] has the meaning of "serving.
Furthermore, because the word *ca* in the rule *vahaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.64) serves to include what is not explicitly mentioned, the suffix *ṇvuc* is also applied after that [root]. Thus: *amadan*.

Regarding the root *mad* in the sense of "joy": because it is listed among the *ghaṭādi* group in the rule "madī harṣalapanayoḥ," it possesses the *mit* designation; consequently, by the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ," its vowel is shortened.
In the *laṭ* (present) tense, because the suffix *śap* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule "chandasyubhayathā," the *ṇi* is elided by the rule "ṇeraniṭī."

Even the heaven trembled before the might of this serpent; with his vigor, O Indra, he hurled the thunderbolt at you. When, in the exhilaration of the pressed juice, you shattered the head of Vṛtra—the great one—with your power, the two worlds (Heaven and Earth) were rent asunder.

Even the heaven itself, though mighty, trembled in fear from the hole of this serpent as you, O Indra, hurled the thunderbolt. When, in the exhilaration of the pressed soma, you shattered with your power the head of Vṛtra—the great one—between the two worlds, heaven and earth.
Even the mighty heaven—the celestial world itself—trembled excessively, being separated [from its place] out of fear of the roar, the sound, of this serpent Vṛtra;
that is to say, it shook.
O Indra, of your pressed [Soma]...

2. Regarding the heaven-world (*svargaloka*). When exhilaration and joy arose from drinking the *soma*—which had been consecrated by means of the pressing and other rites—your thunderbolt (*vajra*) shattered and severed the head of Vṛtra, who was habitually oppressive to the many, by means of his might (*śavas*), that is, his strength, against both *rodasī*, heaven and earth.
At that time, the heavenly world became motionless due to the absence of fear; this is the implied meaning.

*ayodhavīt*. From the root *yu*, meaning "to mix" or "to mingle," in its form with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅ-luganta*), the augment *īṭ* is applied to the unaccented (*apṛkta*) suffix in the present tense (*laṭ*) by the rule *yaṅo vā* (Pāṇini 7.3.14).
The augment *aṭ* is udātta.
[The form] *baddhānasya* [is derived from] the root *vādhu*,
meaning "to stir" (*viloḍane*).
In the case of the suffix *anaś* used in the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*), there is elision (*bhlu*) of the *śap* affix according to the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” (Pāṇini 2.4.73).
Due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), the remaining initial consonant of the root (*halādiśeṣa*) and the shortening of the vowel of the root also occur.
By the rule “*citaḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.1.163), the word bears an udātta accent on its final syllable.
When heaven and earth, tenfold in extent, and all the days stretched out for the people,
then, O Maghavan, your all-encompassing might became equal to the sky in strength and greatness.
When, O Indra, the tenfold earth and all the days had spread out across the peoples, even then, O Maghavan, your triple-famed power became equal to heaven in its might and its vastness.
If indeed the earth were to become tenfold—ten times its size—or if all the *kṛṣṭayaḥ*, all human beings, were to traverse and measure all the days;
O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, even in those aforementioned places, times, and agents, your *sahaḥ*—your strength for the slaying of Vṛtra and other deeds—is *viśrutaḥ*, renowned and celebrated.
By your own power (*śavasā*), the *barhaṇā*—the action consisting of the destruction of Vṛtra and others—prevails throughout the heavens.
Just as the sky is vast, so too is the laughter you directed at Vṛtra and others great; such is the meaning.
*Tatāna*:
from the root *tanu* in the sense of "expansion";
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used because it is marked with the *svarita* accent.

In place of the *liṅ* (optative) sense, the *laṭ* (present) occurs; where *u* would have been the suffix, by transposition (*vyatyaya*) *śap* is used. The doubling [of the root] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively:

Regarding the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage [the suffix] is frequently [omitted]), when the suffix *u* is present, there is again, by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *śap*. Because *śap* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*). And by the accentual rule for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasyamādyoge’pi*” (the augment *aṭ* is not added frequently in the Veda even when joined with *ām*).
Because of its connection with the word *yat*, there is no *anighāta*.
It is fully revealed (*viśvṛtam*).
The root *śru* means "to hear.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
By the rule "the preceding [element] is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) when it is immediately followed by a verb," the preceding member retains its original accent.
*Barhaṇā*: [derived] from the root *vṛh* (in the sense of addressing,
harming, or covering),
with the *kyu* suffix added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
Regarding the distinction between *ba* and *va*, there is the substitution of *va* for *va*. It has the accent of a suffix (*pratyayasvara*),
and it is also listed among the words denoting acts of killing in the passage "nibrahyati" (Nirukta 2.19.30).
*bhuvat* [is derived from] *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (*sattāyām*). The augment *aṭ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood.
The elision of the vowel *i* occurs by the rule "inaśca lopaḥ.
The elision of the suffix *śap* occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. Since the prohibition of *guṇa* applies by the rule "bhūsuvostiṅi," the substitution *uvaṅ* takes place.
You, O bold one, whose power is self-manifesting, have encompassed the sky and the firmament for our protection;
you have made the earth the measure of your might, and as the one who surpasses all, you have pervaded the waters, the sun, and the heavens.

On the far side of this space, of the wide expanse, you, whose power is light, O bold-minded one, have made the earth a measure for your might, for the sake of protection; you encompass the waters, the sun, and heaven, and you reach unto the sky. 12.

1. The subjects are those drawn by *ca* and *pha*; not those drawn by *na* and *sa*.
