The lengthening of the vowel occurs due to the exclusion [of this case] by the rule *na ṇyadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.4.60).

For this very reason, by the rule "kṣiyo dīrghāt," there is an absence of the substitution of *n* for the final letter of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). That which has been excessively worn away is "prakṣitam" (worn out); that which is not worn out is "aprakṣitam" (unworn).
The initial member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
*Bibharṣi* [is derived from] the root *ḍubhṛñ*, meaning "to support" or "to nourish."
In the *laṭ* [present tense] with the suffix *sip*, there is *ślu*-elision of *śap*. By the rule "of *bhṛj* etc., *it*," there is shortening of the reduplication. Thus: *apāḍham*.

From the root *abhi-sah* in the sense of "overpowering," when the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows with an initial *t*-sound, the augment *iṭ* is applied by Pāṇini’s rule *atīṣasaha* (7.2.48). However, because the application of *iṭ* is optional, the prohibition of *iṭ* applies by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*.

When the rules for changing *dh* to *ṣ*, *ṣ* to *ṭ*, and the elision of *ṭ* have been applied, the substitution of *o* for the vowel *a* of the roots *sah* and *vah* would be required by the rule *sahivahorodavarṇasya*; however, by the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) *sāḍhyai sāḍhvā sāḍheti nigame* (6.3.113), the substitution of *ā* occurs instead.
What was stated as "sāḍhā" is to be understood as an illustration of that which ends in the suffix *tu*.

In the word *tanvi*, because of the rule "In the Vedic language, there is optionally [the absence of] the statement regarding *jas* and so forth," the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs instead of the absence of *at* and *atva* prescribed by "acca gheḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.119).
By the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ," the case-ending (vibhakti) becomes svarita;
however, by the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt," it would otherwise have been udātta, but this does not apply here due to its being Vedic (chāndasa).
It has been stated that the sixth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "eṣa pra pūrvīḥ," belongs to Sanu, is addressed to Indra, and is composed in the Jagatī meter.
It is also listed in the Anukramaṇī as "eṣa pra ṣaṭ.
This hymn is to be recited during the Niṣkevalya litany on the Viṣuvat day.
In the section titled "The Equinox and the Divākīrya," it is sūtra-ed: "'eṣa pra pūrvīrvāmadaḥ pra maṃhiṣṭhāya'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.6).

He has shattered many ancient things; like a horse, he has stirred up the maiden in his impetuous rush. He causes the skillful one to drink from the golden vessel, having turned his chariot yoked with bay horses toward the Ṛbhus.

He has pushed back his many enemies; like a steed, he has cast off his weariness. The impetuous one has yoked his golden chariot, drawn by tawny steeds, and turned it toward the Ribhus, so that they may drink the powerful draught for his great benefit.

Indra, the eater of food, the lord of the earth, the sky, and the mid-region, has brought forth for that sacrificer many abundant refreshments—refreshments characterized by Soma, placed within the *camū* vessels and the *camasa* cups. He draws them out with excellence for the sake of drinking.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like one who gathers the heat.

Just as a horse approaches a mare for sport, so Indra— having turned and stationed his golden, sun-bright chariot yoked with bay horses, and having halted it for the great task consisting of the slaying of Vṛtra and other deeds— [approaches] Dakṣa, the lord and protector of the extensive *vidatha* (sacrifice), the powerful and mighty Indra. With splendor, that is, with a hymn that illuminates the deity, "ascend quickly"— that is to say, praise him immediately.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Like lovely women [climbing] a mountain"— just as beautiful women ascend a mountain for the sake of gathering their desired flowers.
*Gūrtyaḥ*:
from the root *gṛ*, meaning "to sound";
they are called *gūrtyaḥ* because they praise (*guṇanti*).

And regarding *kiccakau*: the suffix *ki* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the substitution of *u* for *i*. By the rule *hali ca*, there is lengthening.
The word *citaḥ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*).

In *nemañcipaḥ*, [the root] *gam* in the sense of "bending" takes the suffix *śatṛ*; by transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is the substitution of *e* for the vowel, and the letter *t* is replaced by *n*.
The *nema-cipaḥ* are those who, bowing down, kindle [the fire] and reach Indra;
[this is derived] from the root *iṣ* (to go) with the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *kvip ca*.
The accentuation follows the rule for the original accent of the final member of a compound (*krud-uttarapada-prakṛtisvaratvam*).
Alternatively,
from the root *ṇīñ* in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*), the suffix *man* is applied according to the rule *arti-tu-su-ityādinā*;
due to the statement of "generally" (*bahulavacanāt*), the letter *n* does not receive the designation *it*.
Those whose arrows have been brought forth and bestowed;
the acute accent on the first syllable of the final member [of the compound] is due to the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam*.
[The word is] *parīṇasaḥ*.
The verbal root *ṇas*, meaning "crookedness," has the sense of "going" because all roots share a single fundamental meaning.
[The word] *parīṇasaḥ* means "those that go around" (*parito nasanti gacchanti*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *kvip ca*.
The lengthening of the first member of the compound is by the rule *nipātasya ca*; the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* is by the rule *upasargādasamāse 'pi*;
and the acute accent on the initial syllable occurs by metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively,
the root *naś* signifies "going.
From this, as before, by means of the *kvip* suffix, the letter *ś* becomes *s*.
*Saniṣyacaḥ*: From the root *paṇ* in the sense of "giving," the suffix *in* is applied in the sense of the object according to the rule *hanṛtaḥ ktaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.102).

Then, by adding the suffix *kyac* in the sense of "desiring for oneself" (*ātmanecchā*) according to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.8), and subsequently applying the augment *suk* according to the rule *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kvip vā lālasāyām sukvau ca vaktavyau* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 7.1.51), the form *saniṣyacaḥ* is derived.
The suffix *u* is applied by the rule *kyāc chandasi*; [the form] *nu* [is derived from *nanu*];
and the lengthening of the vowel is a *sāṃhitika* (euphonic) change according to the rule *ṛci tanughaḥ*.
The suffix *sahaḥ*;
there is a Vedic elision (*luk*) of the *matup* suffix following this [term].
He, the great and four-colored one, free from dust, through his manly power, drives forth his strength with impetuous force like a peak from a mountain;
by which, in the exhilaration of the Soma, he, the iron-strong one, bound the guileful Śuṣṇa fast in bonds for the sake of the Ābhūs.

He, the bright-shining, the great, the dustless, like the peak of a mountain, displays his power with impetuous force for manly deeds; by which [power], in the exhilaration of the iron [draught], he cast down the guileful Śuṣṇa and bound him fast in fetters among those who were present.
That Indra is *turviṇi*, meaning the destroyer of enemies or one who acts swiftly; Yāska states that *turviṇi* means *tūrṇavaniḥ* (Nirukta 6.14), which signifies "one who quickly bestows.
Its meaning is "one who quickly grants."
He becomes great and fully grown.

The strength (*bala*) and manly power (*pauṣya*) of that Indra, which is to be performed by heroes—by men—is in battle dustless, blameless, and truly a destroyer of enemies; it shines forth with impetuosity.
Therein lies an illustration:

Like the peak of a mountain—that is, like the summit of a hill—so too was it given as described. Indra, whose body is like iron (āyasaḥ), meaning one whose form is joined with an accumulation of iron, and who is a sustainer (dudhaḥ)—the supporter and establisher of the wicked enemies—when exhilarated by the intoxication of drinking soma, by that strength caused the sorcerer (māyinaḥ) Śuṣṇa, the witherer of all, to be confined in prisons (ābhuṣu), in bonds (dāmani), and in fetters (nigaḍe). Thus he caused him to dwell there.
The phrase "therefore, enough" is to be construed with what precedes.
*turviṇiḥ*: *turv* has the sense of "to injure. From this root, the suffix *ani* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
*Areṇu*. Because it covers like dust (*reṇu*), the word *reṇu* denotes something blameworthy (*avadya*).
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule *nañ-suv-ām*, the final syllable of the latter member is accented.
*Tujā* [is derived from the root] *tuj*, meaning "to injure. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*.
The vowel *ā* is the substitution for the case-ending according to the rule *supām suluk*.
[The word] *dudhaḥ*:
he who holds or establishes the wicked is *dudhaḥ*.
From the root *dhṛ* in the sense of "staying" (*avasthāna*), with the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) internalized, the suffix *ka* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.5.2 (*mūlavibhujāditvāt*).
There is a substitution of *yaṇ*,
and the elision of the letter *r* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
He causes delight.
Because it ends in a nasal (amantatvāt), it is designated as having the *mit* marker; consequently, by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*, there is shortening of the vowel.
The lengthening in the *saṃhitā* is Vedic (*chāndasaḥ*).
1. *ca-cha-ṇa-da-na-pha-la-sa* denote "they succeed" or "they attain. (Ka.

50) If the goddess, the strengthening power that increases thee, attends upon Indra for aid as the sun attends the dawn—he who with bold might drives away the enemy—that steed of golden hue stirs up the dust in great abundance. If the goddess, the strengthening power that increases thee, attends upon Indra for aid as the sun attends the dawn—he who with bold might drives away the enemy—that steed of golden hue stirs up the dust in great abundance. (4)

When the goddess *Taviṣī*— splendid power— attends to, or unites with, that *Indra* who, by means of his bold and terrifying strength, drives away and destroys the darkness, that is, the demon Vṛtra and others, for the sake of protection; when she serves him, as Yāska says (*Nirukta* 3.21),
just as the sun always attends to and remains ever connected with the goddess *Uṣas*, so too does she attend to him.

At that time, Indra— the one who causes sound by producing agitation among the *ahardayaḥ*, enemies who go about seizing [their prey]— drives away (*iryati*) the vast (*bṛhat*) dust (*reṇu*), which is a scattering (*repana*) or injury, causing it to reach the enemies.
*Svāvṛt* means "one who increases by you" (*tvayā vardhate*). The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *kvip ca*.
By the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*, there is the substitution of *sva* for everything up to the final *m*.
The change of *d* to *ā* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the second case ending is replaced by *ā*.
He follows (*siṣakti*).
[The root] *pac* means "to join together.
By the rule "in the Veda [the suffixes are applied] diversely," there is the substitution of *plu* for the *śap* [suffix].
By the rule "vahula chandasi," there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable:
*iryati*. [The roots] *ṛ* and *sṛ* mean "to go."
It belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class.
From this root, with the *ṇic* suffix included within it, the present tense (*laṭ*) affix is applied;
then, by the elision of *śap* and the subsequent substitution of *v* for *u*, followed by the *halādi-śeṣa* rule, [the form is derived].
By the rule "atipipartyośca," the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) receives the vowel *i*.
By the rule "abhyāsasyāsavarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.4.78), the substitute *iyaṅ* is applied. By the rule "anudātta ca," the reduplicated syllable becomes udātta (accented).
Because the preceding word is part of a compound sentence, it does not follow immediately after a word [in the same sentence], and thus there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent). [The word] *reṇum*:
from the root *rī*, meaning "to go" or "to impel."
From this [root], the *nup* suffix is applied according to the *uṇādi* rules;
the vowel *ṛ* is lengthened;
and the suffix *artih* is added.
The suffix *vic* is also seen after other [roots], according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*.
Thus, those who go to the spokes (*arān*) and are tawny (*harayaḥ*) are called *haryaḥ*; he is the one who causes them to sound.
The root *syam* is used in the sense of sound, noise, or word.

From this root, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the *in* affix is added according to the *uṇādi* rules; the *ṇi* is elided by the rule "the *ṇi* is dropped before an affix beginning with a vowel that does not take *iṭ*."
Because it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, the suffix *mit* applies; consequently, by the rule "there is shortening for those marked with *mit*," there is shortening [of the vowel].
Furthermore, the accentuation follows the rule for the original accent of the final member of a compound ending in a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛd-uttara-pada-prakṛti-svara*).

Likewise, when, in the battle called *svarmīlaha*—

where *mīlaha* is a name for wealth, meaning that battle in which there is well-attained (*suḥ*) wealth to be won— and while you were exhilarated (*made*) by the drinking of Soma, you slew Vṛtra, the obstructing Asura, with your joyful (*haryā*) power (*śaktyā*).
At that time, he [pierced] the ocean of waters, the cloud;

To the most generous—Yāska states that *maṃhati* is the act of giving (*Nirukta* 1.7)—to the giver;

to the great one, exalted by his qualities; to the one of vast wealth; to the one of true vigor, possessing exceedingly real strength; to the powerful one, increased in form—to Indra, distinguished by such attributes, I offer forth with excellence my *mati*, that is, my hymn worthy of reflection.
The strength of that Indra is difficult to withstand, meaning it cannot be held back by others.
Therein lies the illustration:
like waters on a slope, that is, in a low-lying place.

Just as the force of waters cannot be halted by anyone, so it is with him. Thus, for the sake of the strength of the praisers—O Śarva—he by whom wealth (radhas) is made "uncovered" (apāvṛta), that is, freed from obstruction, pervading all things throughout the entire life of the world; the connection with this Indra is as stated previously.

*Viśvāyu*:

[This is] for Indra, the beloved one, who desires the slaughter of his enemies.
Yāska states: "The root *haryati* has the sense of desiring" (*Nirukta* 7.17).

Or rather: *haryataḥ* means beautiful; *hiraṇyayaḥ* means golden; *śrathitā* means one whose nature is to strike down enemies; *vajraḥ* is the thunderbolt; *parvate* means upon the mountain, that is, upon the high peak or Vṛtra; *yat* or *yad vā* means "when"; *na samaśīta* means he did not become exhausted or ceased from being impelled (*saṃsutaḥ*).
However, the meaning is that he slew [Vṛtra] while awake;
the sense is that from the very moment Indra’s impelled thunderbolt, being irresistible, slew Vṛtra, all sacrificers began to perform sacrifices to him.

"Like the earth" (kṣoṇīr iva): just as the earth (kṣoṇī), the world, desires its own multitudes of beings. *carāmasi*: The suffix *masi* takes the ending *-id*. Since the root *śap* is marked with *pi*, it is unaccented; thus, the accent of the verbal root remains. Due to its connection with *yad-vṛtta*, there is no *anighāta* (non-suppression of accent). *saghat*: From the root *pac* in the sense of "harming. Here, the meaning is "to consume," because roots have multiple meanings. In the *leṭ* mood, the augment *aṭ* is added. Because it stands at the beginning of a *pāda*, there is an absence of *nighāta* (suppression of accent). *kṣoṇīr iva*: The absence of elision (*sulopa*) of the case-ending *su* after *kṣoṇīḥ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

In the eleventh anuvāka there are seven hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "nū cit," is the seerly composition of Nodhas Gautama and is addressed to Agni.
The first five verses are in the *jagatī* meter;
the remaining four are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Thus it has been declared in the *Anukramaṇī*: "Now, Javana Nodhas Gautama [composed] the hymn to Agni beginning with 'hi cit' and containing four *cits*."
By the word "hi" [in the sūtra], it is indicated that the two subsequent hymns have Agni as their deity.
On the fifth day of the *abhiplava* six-day period, in the *āgnimāruta* śastra, this *jātavedas* hymn serves as the locus for the *nivid*.

This is prescribed in the section beginning with "tṛtīyasya" in the Sūtra: "‘pṛkṣasya vṛṣṇo’, ‘vṛṣṇe śardhāya’, and ‘nū cit sahojā’ constitute the *āgnimāruta* [śastra]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.7).
In the *prātaranuvāka* for the fire-oblation (*āgneya*) and when the *aśvin* recitation (*śastra*) is performed in the *jagatī* metre, the first five verses are used.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "‘O Agni, you are the first Aṅgiras...’—these five [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
Never indeed does the one born of strength, the immortal, tire; he has become the Hotṛ priest invoked by Vivasvat.

This Agni, undecaying and free from old age, "yuvamānaḥ"—mingling with his own flame "svam" his own "annam" food, such as grass, shrubs, and so forth—and thereafter "atṛpyan," consuming it. The word *aviṣyan* is read in the sense of "transgressing" (Nirukta 2.8.6).
Such is Agni: he quickly "ascends" (*ātiṣṭhati*) and mounts upon the "much *atasa* wood.
Here the word *atasa* denotes wood, as seen in the passage, "like dry *atasa*" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 4.4.4).
The back (*pṛṣṭha*)—the mass of flames situated above—of the fire that has been seized and set ablaze here and there, "shines like iron" (*ayaḥ*).
The sense is that just as a horse accustomed to constant movement shines while galloping here and there, so too the flame shines as it moves everywhere.
At that time, belonging to the *div* (the heavenly world), the lofty cloud-like ridge (*sānu*) "thundered"—that is, making a sound as if roaring—and produced a deep resonance for itself.
[This was] the one being measured.

In this case, there is no elision [of the suffix] because of the rule "bahulam chandasi.
Since the root is taught with a short *a* (adupadeśa), the suffixes of the *lasārvadhātuka* class are unaccented, and thus the accent of the *vikaraṇa* alone remains. Hence, *ajaraḥ*.

In the bahuvrīhi compound, by the rule "anajo jaramaramitramṛtānām," there is udātta accent on the initial syllable of the final member. *Acikradat*: [from] the roots *kadi*, *kradi*, and *krudi*, meaning "to call out" and "to weep."

From this root with the causative suffix *ṇic*, in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense and with the *caṅ* (reduplication), there is an absence of the augment *num* because the rule prescribing it is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Then follow reduplication, the *halādi-śeṣa* (retention of the first consonant), the *saṃvadbhāva* (treatment like the root *san*), and the substitution of *itva*.
[The verse continues: "Seated as the Hotṛ-priest, preceded by the Rudras and Vasus, the immortal one who bestows wealth."
Like a chariot that spreads among the people, O God, you, the noble one, extend yourself through the living beings.

Having acted with the Rudras and the Vasus, the appointed priest, seated as the Hotṛ, the immortal conqueror of wealth—like wealth itself striving among the people for the sake of men—the god distributes desirable boons in succession.

Performing the act of carrying the oblation (*krāṇā havirvahanaṃ kurvāṇaḥ*), accompanied by the *Rudras* and the *Vasus*, appointed as the presiding priest (*purohitaḥ*), the invoker of the gods (*hotā devānām*), seated at the place of sacrifice for the acceptance of the oblation (*niṣattaḥ*), a conqueror of wealth (*rayiṣāṭ*)—that is, the overcomer of the riches of enemies—and immortal (*amartyaḥ*), free from death.

Being thus, the radiant god Agni, like a chariot among the people— the folk of the world— moving among the living beings characterized as sacrificers, being praised (*ṛñjānaḥ*), distributes (*vi ṛṇvati*) the desirable (*vāryāṇi*) riches that are to be honored, in a continuous (*ānuṣak*) manner. Or alternatively,
he himself attains the desirable oblations (*havīṃṣi*).
*Krāṇā*: From the root *kṛ*, with the suffix *śānac*, there is the elision of the *vikaraṇa* by the rule "there is frequently [elision] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Because the *śānac* suffix is marked with *ṅit*, there is an absence of *guṇa*, and consequently, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.

The word *citaḥ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). The substitution of the long vowel for the case-ending *su* follows the rule *supāṃ suluk*, resulting in the same vowel quality as the preceding syllable. [The form is] *niṣattaḥ*.

The root *pad* is used in the senses of "falling," "going," and "sinking. From this root, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed. By the rule *na-sattaniṣatta-...* (Pāṇini 8.2.61), the absence of the substitution of *ṇ* for *t* in the suffix is prescribed as a nipātana (irregularity).
In the phrase "gatiranantaraḥ," the word *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). [The term] *rayiṣāṭ*:
[from the root] *sah* (in the sense of) "overpowering."
The suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *chandasi sahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.63).
The substitution of *ṣ* is applied by the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.56).
[Thus we have] *ṛñjānaḥ*.
The root *ṛñj* has the sense of praising (*stuti*).
Following the recurrence of the suffix *asānac*, the suffix *asānac* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule *ṛñjivadhimandisahibhyaḥ kit* (Uṇādisūtra 2.244).
By the rule *citaḥ*, it receives the udātta accent on the final syllable.
Regarding *āyuṣu*: *āyavaḥ* is a name for humans (*Nirukta* 2.3.17). From the root *iṇ* "to go," the suffix *uṇ* is applied according to the rule *chandasy uṇ* [Pāṇini 3.2.169].
The substitutions *vṛddhi* and *āya* [are applied]. *Vāryā*.
[From] the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "to choose" (*saṃbhaktau*).

By the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied. When the circumflex (*svarita*) accent would have been obtained, the rule *īḍvandvvaṃśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ* provides for the acute (*udātta*) accent on the first syllable.
By the rule *śeṣchandasi*, there is elision of the suffix *ś*.
It flows; from the root *ṛ* (in the sense of "going"),
there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The augment *num* is applied because the stem ends in a long vowel (*idittvāt*).
The suffix *śap* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
According to Pāṇini 8.4.40 (*cha-ḍa-gha-na-śa-sa-atyaḥ aśvaḥ*), the *ś* of *śap* becomes *ṣ*; thus, *ḍha-jātyaśvaḥ*.
2. Deep-sounding.
3. Continuous. Impelled by the wind, he dwells at will among the brushwood; with his tongues, the loudly roaring Sūrya [flames] leaps about.
When you, O Agni, the bull, thirst for the trees, then this black path of yours appears, O you of radiant waves, undecaying one.

Impelled by the wind, he stands among the brushwood at will; with his tongues he roars loudly like the sun. When you, O Agni, the bull, thirstily consume the trees, your path is black, O bright-waved and ageless one.

Driven by the wind (*vātajūtaḥ*): impelled by the wind. *Tuvisvaṇiḥ*: possessing a great roar; Agni being such as this. *Juhūbhiḥ*: with his own tongues. *Sūryā*: being endowed with a mass of splendor that is prone to movement. *Vṛthā*: a word meaning "without effort. Without effort (*vṛthā*), he stands out (*vi tiṣṭhate*)—that is, he stands preeminently—among the *atasa* trees, which are tall trees. O Agni, when (*yat*) you, like a bull (*vṛṣā*), act as a bull toward the forest-born trees—that is, you burn them—O *ruśadūrme* (one whose waves of flame are bright), O *ajara* (undecaying) Agni, your path (*ema*) becomes black (*kṛṣṇa*). Regarding *vātajūtaḥ*: the root *jū* belongs to the ninth class (*ju hotyādi*). *Vātena jūtaḥ* = *vātajūtaḥ*. By the rule "in the sense of action [the compound is] *kṛt*," there is the original accent of the first member. Regarding *vi tiṣṭhate*: by the rule "after *sam*, *ava*, *pra*, and *vi*, the root *sthā* takes the middle voice" (*ātmanepada*). Regarding *juhūbhiḥ*: from the root *hu* (to give or eat). That in which oblations are offered is *juhūḥ*. By the rule "from *hu*, *bhluvac*" (Uṇādisūtra 2.218), there is the suffix *kip*, and by the letter *ca*, there is lengthening. Because of the *bhluvac*-nature, there is reduplication and so forth. By the rule "of the root," there is the udātta accent on the final syllable. Regarding *sūryā*: from the root *sṛ* (to go). That which moves is *sṛṇiḥ*. By the rule "from *sṛ* and *vi*, the suffix *kin*" (Uṇādisūtra 4.489), there is the suffix *nip*. Regarding *ema*: one goes by means of this, thus *ema* is the path. From the root *iṇ* (to go), the suffix *manin* is added in the sense of instrument (by Uṇādi rules). Because of the *nic*-suffix, there is the udātta accent on the initial syllable.
With burning jaws, driven by the wind through the forest, he rushes like a bull among the herds;
as he advances, the dust of the earth rises, and the winged creatures fear both what stands still and the chariot.

With burning jaws, driven by the wind in the forest, he rushes like a powerful stallion among the herds; as he hastens toward the inexhaustible realm of the waters, even the winged creatures of the sky and the chariot of that which stands still tremble before him. 5.
*Tapurjambhaḥ*: He whose *jambhas*—meaning flames, weapons, or mouths—are *tapūṃṣi* (fiery); thus he is so described.
*Vātacoditaḥ*: impelled by the wind.

When Agni is thus situated amidst the herd—that is, within a mass of flames—he moves forward with his *pājas*, his splendor and power, toward the inexhaustible *rajas*—the moisture contained within the wet trees. Advancing directly into the forest wilderness, he overcomes all (*sāhān*) and pervades it completely.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a bull (*vaṃsagaḥ*).
Just as a bull, seeking desirable pasture, moves about overwhelming the entire herd of cows, so it is here.
Because this is so, everything—both that which is stationary (*sthāvara*) and that which moves (*caratha*), meaning the mobile—fears, being terrified, of the winged, flying Agni.
*sāhān*—this is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word ending in the *kasu* suffix, derived from the root *sah*.
In the *saṃhitā*, the *n* becomes *r* according to the rule: "After a long vowel, [there is] *ṛt* [before a following vowel] within the same foot."
By the rule "āto 'ṭi nityam," the vowel *ā* is nasalized; there is elision of the *yat* suffix and of the vowel *u*;
and the shortening of the vowel is Vedic.
[The suffix] *nu* [is applied] to the root *sthā*.
The suffix *nu*, prescribed by the rule "kaminajani" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.72) and others, also applies to the root *sthā* due to the word "bahulam" (in various ways).
Alternatively:
The moving fears that which stands immediately after it; the meaning is that the stationary first fears that which stands, and afterwards [fears] that which moves.
The moving.
The root *cara* has the meaning "to go.
From this [root], the [suffix] is derived according to the *uṇādi* rules.
Now...

1. *ḍha-sa-dagdhum*: eager to burn quickly. 2. *ḍha-sa-hūyantam*: being invoked. 3. *ḍha-ābhimukhyena gacchan*: going towards [the goal]. 4. *ḍha-vṛṣabhaḥ*: the bull. Ṛgveda 5.1: The suffix (*pratyaya*). [The root] *bhī* (to fear). From the root *bhi*, meaning "fear. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). The absence of the *ślu* suffix is according to the rule "in the Veda, [rules apply] diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). There is the substitution of *guṇa* and the replacement of the vowel (*avādeśa*). || 23 ||

The Bhr̥gus established among men Agni as the Hotr̥, the guest, the one most worthy of choice— like a friend, auspicious for the divine race— and as a treasure, fair and easy to invoke for all people.
The Bhr̥gus have established you among men like lovely wealth, easy to invoke for the people—the Hotr̥, O Agni, the most excellent guest, as dear as a friend to the divine race. 6.

O Agni, the Bhrigus—great seers by this name—among men have established you, the beautiful one, like excellent wealth for the sake of divine birth, that is, for the attainment of godhood; they consecrated you by means of mantras during the preparatory rites of installation.
Of what sort are you? You are easy to invoke for the people—that is, easy to call upon for the sake of the sacrificer—the invoker of the gods, and a guest to be honored like a guest.
Or rather:
[him who is] one who constantly goes to the places of sacrifice;
[who is] desirable, worthy of being chosen, like a friend, and auspicious.
The meaning is that it provides happiness just as a friend provides happiness.
They placed [them]. In the perfect tense (liṭ), with the suffix usi, there is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule “*āto lopa iṭi ca*” (Pāṇini 6.4.64).
By the rule “*yuṣmattattakṣuḥvantaḥpādam*” (Pāṇini 8.3.103), the *visarjanīya* is changed to *pa*.
*Suhavam*: from the root *hve*, the suffix *khal* is applied by the rule *īṣadduḥ-suṣu*;
the vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
The state of having another as a prior [syllable];
the substitution of a *guṇa* vowel;
and by the rule "liti," the acute accent (*udātta*) on the syllable preceding the suffix.
The original accent of the final member of a compound ending in a *kṛt* suffix [is retained].
The Hotṛ, the most excellent sacrificer whom the seven tongues and the priests choose at the sacrifices—
Agni, the steward of all treasures— I serve with an offering and approach him for jewels.

The Hotṛ, the sevenfold tongue, the most skilled in sacrifice—him whom the priests choose at the rituals, Agni, the steward of all treasures—to him I offer worship with nourishment; I entreat for wealth. 7.

The seven—meaning those numbering seven—the *juhū* priests, the invokers (*vāghataḥ*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), choose and honor that Agni who is the most excellent sacrificer (*yajiṣṭham*), the invoker of the gods (*hotāram*), and the carrier (*aratim*) who brings [the offerings] to all the *vasus*. That Agni I worship (*saparyāmi*) with sacrificial food (*prayasā*), characterized by oblations;
and I pray for (*yāmi*) delight (*śnam*) and the fruit of ritual action.
They choose (*vṛṇate*). The root *vṛṅ* means "to partake of" (*sambhaktau*);
it belongs to the *kryādi* class.
The accent is that of the suffix (pratyayasvara). [The root is] *ṛ*, in the sense of “going” and “reaching. *Aratim*. “*Ṛ* [is used] in the senses of going and reaching.”

This [word] is derived from the *auṇādika* [suffixes]. According to the rule *vahivasyatibhyaścit* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.500), the suffix *ati* is applied. Because it is marked with the *c*-diacritic (*cittvāt*), it has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
I worship. The root *saparyati* has the sense of attending upon; it is the root *sapar*, meaning "to worship," belonging to the *kaṇvādi* (Kryādigaṇa) class.
Therefore, only the accent of *yáka* remains;
there is no loss of accent (*nighāta*) because it belongs to the *pātrādi* group.
[The form is] *yāmi*.
The elision of the syllable "m" in the word "yācāmi" is a Vedic archaism.

1. O Agni, lord of the Vasus (riches), grant us today unassailable protection for our singers; O you who are great as Mitra, bestow shelter upon those who praise you here. O Son of Strength, protect this singer with your iron fortresses from harm.

O flawless one, O Son of Strength, grant us today protection like Mitra’s for those who praise you; O Agni, great in glory, deliver the singer from distress, O Son of Vigor, with your iron fortresses. 8.
O Son of Strength, Son of Force— for fire is indeed born when churned with force—
O Agni of friendly luster, grant and bestow upon us, your worshippers, today at this rite, flawless and indestructible protections and comforts.
Furthermore: O *ūrjo napāt*, son of food!
For the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) increases through the consumption of food, Agni is thus the "son of food.
O Agni of such a nature, [protect] us who praise you with songs, with iron-like [strength].
Or rather,
with protections as firm as iron, rescue and protect us from distress and sin.
"Uruṣyati means to protect," says Yāska (Nirukta 5.23).
"Acchidrā" [is formed] by the elision of the *śi* suffix according to the rule "śe chandasi.
O Son of Strength (*sūno sahasaḥ*).

In the phrase *paramapicchandasi*, since the subsequent word ending in the genitive case (*parasya*) undergoes the state of being a constituent part of the preceding mantra, the entire two-word compound possesses the status of being entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*) according to the eighth [chapter of Pāṇini].
[The form] *śarma* [is derived as follows]: by the rule *surāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending.
Ūrjonapāt:
he is called *napāt* because he does not cause [his progeny] to fall (*na pātayati*).
In the word *ūrjonapāt*, the negative particle *nañ* undergoes its original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule "nabhrāṇnapāt... etc.

In the expression *subā-mantrita*, because the word ending in the genitive case (*subāḥ*) undergoes the treatment of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅvad-bhāva*), the eighth-century rule [Pāṇini 8.1.28] does not apply due to its status as the beginning of a *pāda*; consequently, the sixth-century rule [Pāṇini 6.1.198] applies, resulting in the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the vocative.

Regarding *pūrbhiḥ*: from the root *pṛ* in the sense of "protecting" and "filling," the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad-ādi* formations.
The [stems] *uta* and *dīrgha* [are udātta];
the accentuation of the case-ending follows from the rule "sāvekācaḥ."
Be a shelter for the singer, O radiant one; be a protection for the generous patrons, O Maghavan.
O Agni, deliver the singer from distress. May he who is enriched by prayer come quickly in the morning.

Be a protector for the one who praises you, O radiant one; be a refuge for the generous patrons, O bounteous Lord. O Agni, deliver the singer from distress. May he who is rich in wisdom come quickly in the morning. 9.
O Vibhāvasu, you who possess distinguished radiance, become a *varūtha*—a dwelling place that wards off what is undesirable—for the sacrificer who praises you with song.
(Note: *Varūtha* is a name for a house. Be a home that protects against evil.

O Maghavan, O possessor of wealth, be such that you grant protection (*śarma*)—that is, happiness—to the sacrificers who are themselves wealthy, being endowed with the wealth characterized by oblations. O Agni, protect (*uruṣya*) the one who praises you—that is, the singer—from *aṃhas*, the evil-doing enemy. You are the one whose wealth is found through wisdom (*dhiyāvasu*).
Agni, who has obtained wealth through his ritual action or his intellect,
shall come quickly and swiftly even on the morrow, just as he does now this morning.
*Varūtham*:
from the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "covering" (*varaṇe*).
By the rule *jṛbhyāṃ pāūthan* (Uṇādisūtra 2.163), the suffix *ūthan* is applied.
The word *nitti* has the udātta accent on its first syllable. In *gṛṇate*,
the case ending has the udātta accent according to the rule "śaturanumaḥ."
Vibhātraḥ: *viśiṣṭā bhā* is *vibhā*. [The suffix] *vip* is applied according to the rule *āto manin*.
The suffix *matup* is applied in the sense of "he who has this" (*tad asyāsti*).
By the rule *mādupadhāyāḥ*, the letter *v* is substituted for the *m* of *matup*.
Then, by the rule *matuvaso ruḥ*, the *n* of [the base] becomes *r*.
In *maghavadbhyaḥ*,
the substitution of *tv-* for the word *maghavan* occurs by Pāṇini’s rule 6.4.128 (*maghavā bahulam*).
And that [substitution] is not considered to have multiple phonemes (*anekāltva*) on account of its *anubandha*.
1. After "ḍha-sa-luk," add: "'yaccha | dāṇ in the sense of giving; the substitution of yaccha occurs by [the rule] pāghnyādi'. 2. ḍha: averter of misfortune (ariṣṭa).

Because of the statement [in Paribhāṣā 6], "of the final [alophon]" (Pāṇini 1.1.52), it applies to the final [letter]. *makṣu*. By the rule "in the Ṛgveda, after *tu*, *nu*, *gha*, and *makṣu*," there is lengthening. *dhiyāvasuḥ*. In a Bahuvrīhi compound, there is the original accent of the prior member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratvam*). In the prior member, by the rule "the case-ending of that which has only one vowel (*ekāc*) is acute when followed by *su*," the case-ending is acute. The absence of elision (*luk*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*). *jagamyāt*. From the roots *gamu* and *sṛp* meaning "to go. In the *liṅ* mood, by the rule "diversely in the Chandas," there is the elision (*bhlu*) of the *śap* suffix. || 24 ||
The second hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “vayā it,” is the ṛṣi Nodhas’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Its deity is Agni, characterized by the Vaiśvānara quality.
Thus it has been enumerated: “vayā it—this belongs to Vaiśvānara.”
The application of the hymn is to be understood from its indicative power (*liṅga*).
These other trees here are inferior; in you alone all the immortals rejoice.
O Vaiśvānara, you are the navel of the settlements; like a pillar, you support the people.

O Agni, these others are indeed your branches; in you all the immortals rejoice. You are the head of heaven, the navel of the earth; thus have you become the messenger between the two worlds. As such, O Vaiśvānara, the gods generated you as a god, a light for the Ārya. The head of heaven, the navel of the earth—Agni has indeed become the messenger between the two worlds. You, that god, the gods generated, O Vaiśvānara, as a light for the Ārya.
This Agni is the "head" (mūrdhā)—meaning he is the preeminent one like the head—of the "sky" (divaḥ), the celestial world;
and he is the "navel" (nābhi)—meaning the binder or protector—of the "earth" (pṛthivyāḥ).
Furthermore, immediately thereafter, he became the "charioteer" (aratiḥ), that is, the sovereign lord, of the two worlds, heaven and earth (rodasyoḥ).

The gods—all the deities—generated and brought forth you, O Vaiśvānara, such a god endowed with qualities such as generosity, as light itself for the sake of the noble, wise Manu, or for the sacrificer.
Because "that which is formed is placed within this," the two vast worlds, heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyau*), became as it were great for their own son, Vaiśvānara.

Vaiśvānara’s sonship with respect to heaven and earth is clearly understood from another mantra: "Both parents, these two worlds, heaven and earth, rich in seed, recognized me" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.3.11).
The meaning is that heaven and earth were born expanded for the dwelling of the great Vaiśvānara.

Furthermore, this Hotṛ, the capable and skillful one, offered many various great hymns of praise to Agni Vaiśvānara; "he offered"—this is the ellipsis. To what kind of [Agni]? To him who is... [the remainder of the verse].
To him who possesses beautiful gait in every respect, whose vigor is truth, whose power is unfailing, who is ever-new, and who is the supreme eye for all—
therein lies the illustration:
he is not like a human being.
Just as an ordinary worldly bard praises a generous lord with manifold hymns of praise, so it is in this case.
*Manuṣyaḥ*. When the sense of "birth" (*jāti*) is understood, the suffix *yat* is applied after the word *manu*, and the augment *puK* is added by the rule "*manojātau anyatau puK ca*".
The circumflex accent (*svarita*) is applied according to the rule "*tisvaritam*".
The acute accent (*udātta*) does not occur in cases such as *yato’nāvaḥ*, for in that rule the term *añ* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). [This applies] to *svarvate*.
From the root *am* preceded by the prefix *su*, the suffix *vic* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
From that, the possessive suffix *matup* is added. By the rule "mādupadhāyāḥ," the letter *v* is substituted for *m*.
O Jātavedas Vaiśvānara, your greatness has surpassed even the two worlds and the vast expanse;
you are the king of the human tribes, and through battle you have created wide space for the gods.
Even from the great heaven, O Jātavedas Vaiśvānara, thy majesty has surpassed all; thou art the king of the human tribes, and by battle thou hast created wide space for the gods. 5.
O Jātavedas, knower of all that is born, O Vaiśvānara Agni, your greatness—the majesty of you, the vast and mighty—has surpassed even the great celestial realm (div) and has increased beyond it.
Furthermore, you are the king and sovereign lord of the human tribes (kṛṣṭīḥ), those beings born of mind.
Likewise, through battle, you have secured for the gods the wealth (varivas) seized by the Asuras, making it subject to the gods.
Vaiśvānara.
Because it begins with a *pāda*, there is no absence of the initial *amikā*-accent (*ādyamikani ghāta*). *Ririce*.
The root *ric* means "to purge" (*virecana*);
here, by the influence of the prefix, it functions in its opposite sense, namely "increase.
[This refers to] "of the people" (*kṛṣṭīnām*).

The name [of the word] has the acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule *nāmyatarasyām*. [The word] *mānuṣīṇām* [is derived from] the word *mānuṣa*, which ends in the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule *manojātāv añ*.
When the suffix *ṅīp* would have been required by the rule for feminine gender (*jātilakṣaṇe*), it is superseded by the rule ‘*śārṅgaravādyañaḥ*’ which prescribes *ṅīn*.
Because of the marker *n*, the word is udātta on its first syllable.
However, due to the word “*bahulam*” (variously) in the rule ‘*ḍyācchandasi bahulam*’ (Pāṇini 6.1.108), there is an absence of the udātta accent.

From the root *yudh* in the sense of "striking" (*saṃprahāre*), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad-ādi* formations. *Varivas* is a name for wealth.
The initial syllable [of the word] "jabbi" in the phrase "jabbi vapasyasya" and so forth is udātta (accented).
I shall now proclaim the greatness of the Bull, whom the ancients followed as the slayer of Vṛtra.
Agni Vaiśvānara, having struck down the Dasyu, shook the quarters and cast Śambara down.
Now I shall proclaim the greatness of the Bull, whom the ancients celebrate as the slayer of Vṛtra. Vaiśvānara Agni, having struck down the Dasyu, shook the barriers and cast Śambara down.
Here, by the word *vaiśvānara*, the lightning fire situated in the middle region is denoted.
*Pūrva* is a name for humans;
"the former humans worship that Vaiśvānara who is the slayer of Vṛtra—the destroyer of the cloud called Ovāraka"—those seeking rain.
1. For the purpose of establishing [the sound] *ḍha*.
2. The absence of the acute accent (*udāttatva*) for *ḍha*.
I shall quickly proclaim—I declare now—the greatness, the majesty, of that bull, the showerer of waters, Vaiśvānara.
To the question "What was that?", he says:
This Vaiśvānara Agni, having struck down—that is, slain—the *dasyu*, who is a consumer (*upakṣayitṛ*) of the *rasas* (essences) or of ritual actions, namely the Rākṣasa and others;
likewise, he shook—that is, caused to fall headlong—the *kāṣṭhās*, which are the waters of creation.
He struck down and pierced Śambara, who was intent on obstructing that [liberation].
I spoke (*vocaṃ*).

While the rule "luṅ-laṅ-liṭaḥ" (the aorist, imperfect, and perfect suffixes are used in the Veda) is in force, the substitution of *aṭ* for *ciṇ* occurs in the aorist according to the rule "asyativakti," etc. Then, by the rule "vaca um," the augment *um* is added.
The suffix *guṇa* [is applied].
By the rule "In the Vedic language (*chandasa*), [the augment *aṭ*] is frequently absent even when combined with *māṅ*," there is an absence of *aṭ*.
[Thus we have] *jaghanvān*.
The suffix *kasu* is substituted for the reduplicated perfect (*liṭ*) of the root *han*.
By the rule "and after a reduplication" (*abhyāsācca*), the letter *h* following the reduplication becomes *dh*.
Due to the optionality provided by the rule "optionally for *gam* and *han*" (*vibhāṣā gamahana*), there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*.
*bhet* | [This is derived from] the root *bhidir* in the sense of "tearing apart.
In the *laṅ* tense, by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (the suffix is frequently omitted in Vedic), there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
By the rule *halḍyābbhyaḥ*, there is the elision of the letter *t*.

As before, there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*. Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "I proclaim that greatness of the Bull, the showerer of waters, who is possessed of great fortune; whom the Purus—the humans who are to be fulfilled—serve, they being desirous of rain and seeking the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of clouds. [The word] *dasyu* [is derived from] the root *das*, in the sense of 'to destroy'; he destroys the works of the enemy. That Agni Vaiśvānara, never failing, split apart the waters, the goals, and the cloud Śambara" (*Nirukta* 7.23).
In this regard, the following must be considered:
who is this Vaiśvānara?
On this point, some say:
The wind situated in the intermediate space is Indra or Vaiśvānara;
for with it, praise is appropriate on account of its function of raining, but not with Agni, because his station is the earth.
Others, however, think as follows.
"The sun, Vaiśvānara, has heaven as his abode. And they state the reasoning:
the three pressings, beginning with the morning pressing, consist of the three worlds.
In that regard, when the sacrificer reaches the third libation (*savana*), he would be considered as having fallen from heaven;
to prevent such a fall, at the final *śastra* in the *Āgnimāruta* litany, the Hotṛ priest descends from heaven back to earth.
How this is done is now explained.
Having stated the commencement as a *stotriya* according to other treatises, he begins the *śastra* with the *vaiśvānara* hymn (*sūkta*) connected to the celestial realm.
Thereafter, he descends by reciting hymns addressed to those deities, directed toward Rudra and the Maruts associated with the intermediate realm;
therein, [he addresses] Agni, who resides on the earth.
If Vaiśvānara were not the sun here, then a descent would not be possible;
therefore, this objection regarding the material substance is also untenable.
This very fire is Vaiśvānara.
Why? Because it conforms to the etymological derivation of the word Vaiśvānara.
Vaiśvānara is so called because he is connected with all men (viśveṣāṃ narāṇām) as their leader toward other worlds.
And thus it is stated in the scripture: "O Vaiśvānara, son of the Pitṛs, O Jātavedas, carry [the offerings] to the world-makers where the worlds of the doers of good deeds are.
Or else, he is called Vaiśvānara because all (viśve) men (narāḥ) please this Agni at sacrifices and other rites; he is so named due to that connection.
Alternatively,
*viśvānarau* refers to the two deities of the middle and highest [sacrificial] fires, because they go toward (*uta*) all living beings (*viśvān*).
[The term is derived] from the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *ac* according to the rule for *pac-ādi* roots.
The absence of the letter *g* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
Because he is produced from those two, this Agni Vaiśvānara is the lightning-fire;
for the lightning-fire indeed arises from the intermediate [space].
At the very moment immediately following the fall of a thunderbolt, the terrestrial fire comes into being.
Furthermore, it is well known that even from the sun during the summer season, fire is produced in sun-crystals and other such gems.
Therefore, it is logical that this alone is the fire Vaiśvānara, in accordance with the etymological derivation of the name.

Praise for this [sacrificial fire] is also possible through its function as rain; for it is recorded in the Smṛti: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings" (Manu 3.76).
Nor should one perform the *pratyavaroha* (the ritual descent).
This is because the third *savana* has already attained its share of heaven.
All of this has been explained extensively by Yāska in passages such as "Vaiśvānara: from what? (*Nirukta* 7.21).
Whatever has not been stated here should be understood in that very same manner from those [other sources].

1. One who causes the destruction of wealth and grain;
2. "When [the fruit] has been obtained";
3. Because of having attained the state of heaven that is with-outflow (*savyākṛta*).
"Agni Vaiśvānara" is so called because, by his greatness, he belongs to all people (*viśvakṛṣṭi*). "People" (*kṛṣṭi*) refers to human beings;
he is thus described as one to whom all men belong.

In the sacrifices performed by the Bharadvājas—characterized by rites for prosperity and the like—or rather, among the sages bearing that name, Agni is the one to be worshipped (*yajataḥ*), the one worthy of sacrifice; he is *vibhāvā*, the special illuminator, and *sūnṛtāvān*, possessed of *sūnṛtā*—that is, speech which is both pleasant and true. Such is Agni in the lineage of Śātavaneya.

One who wins or partakes in a hundred sacrifices is called *śatavani*; his son is *śātavaneya*. In him—referring to the king named *Puruṇītha*, the leader of many—he is praised (*jarate*) with numerous (*śatinībhiḥ*) hymns of praise (*stutibhiḥ*).
In the *bhāradvāja* [sacrifices].
They are called *bharantaḥ* because they bear or nourish those who enjoy [the offerings]. Those sacrifices in which such *vājāḥ* (strengths/offerings) exist [are the *bhāradvājāḥ*].

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, although the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member would normally apply, the final syllable of the first member is acute (*antodātta*) because it belongs to the class beginning with *marud-vṛdha*.
[The word] *yajataḥ* [is formed] by the rule: "The suffix *atac* is added after the roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *dṛś*, *yaji*, *pad*, *ṛdh*, *pac*, *yam*, *tam*, *nam*, *miha*, and *hya*. (Uṇādisūtra 3.107).
The suffix *than* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). "Sadyo-artha" means one who goes immediately;
it is an indeclinable compound where the accent remains on the original form of the first member (*avyayapūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).

If, however, by the inclusion of the term "avyaya" [in the rule]—according to the statement "it should be stated that for indeclinables, nañ, and particles" (Pāṇini 6.2.2.3)—the triad [of particles, etc. were to be grasped, then the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* would apply:
*mātariśvā*. Because he is the cause of the creation of all things, the mother (*mātṛ*) is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
In this context, the root *śvas* has the sense of "going.
He goes (*śvasiti*) in the mother, that is, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), hence he is Mātariśvan.
The formation of the word is established through irregular derivation (*nipātana*), as seen in examples such as *śrukṣan*.
Alternatively,
he is called Mātariśvan because he moves swiftly (śu) in the mother (mātari), that is, in the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
The suffix *ḍun* is added to the root *as*, meaning "to go," "to shine," and so forth, according to the rules of the Uṇādi-sūtras.
And this has been stated by Yāska (Nirukta 7.26).
Peace attends him from both sides: those who bring oblations and those who are eager with their prayers.
Even before the dawns, he has sat down as the Hotṛ-priest, the one to be questioned, the lord of the people among the clans, the ordainer.
Both groups— both gods and humans—
or alternatively,
the praisers with their hymns and the sacrificers with their sacrifices, attend upon and serve this Agni, the ruler who commands.
The *uśijas*— the gods who desire [the sacrifice], being possessed of oblations and joined with the offering— and the mortal sacrificers who offer prayers;
or rather,
*uśijas* is a name for the wise.
The *uśijaḥ*—the wise ones who offer oblations, the chanters endowed with sacrificial offerings, and the sacrificers who present their prayers—[approach].

Furthermore, this *hotṛ*, Agni, the performer of the oblation, being present even before the sun (*divaś cit*) at the dawns, has been seated among the people, among the sacrificers, for the purpose of the *agnihotra* offering; he has been placed and established by the *adhvaryu* priest in his sacred seat.
Of what sort is this *hotṛ*?
*Vāpṛcchyaḥ* means one who is to be asked for leave or one who is worthy of being honored;
*viśapatiḥ* is the protector of the people (*viśām*), that is, of the subjects (*prajānām*); and *vedhāḥ* is the ordainer, the creator of desired results.
The root is *śās*, meaning "to instruct" (*anuśiṣṭau*).

By the rule "The suffixes *tṛn* and *cvi* are added after the roots *śaṃs*, *pidhā*, *kṣā*, etc., when a name [is to be formed], and [the roots] do not take the augment *it*" (Uṇādisūtra 2.250), the suffix *tṛn* is applied and there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*.
In the singular genitive case, there is the elision of the letter *t*, which is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Due to the suffix *nic*, the word is udātta-accented on the first syllable. [The form is] *uśijaḥ*.
By the rule *vaśaḥ kit* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.229), the suffix *iñ* is added to the root *vaś*;
there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule *grahijyādinā*.
[The form is] *matīḥ*.
The root *mṛ* is used in the sense of "giving up life. The suffix *tan* is applied according to the rule beginning with *asihasimṛṇvomi*.
Due to the presence of the *niṭ* augment, the word is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable).

*Āpṛcchyaḥ*: [derived from] *praccha* in the sense of "desire to know. From this root preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *kyap* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātita*) in rules such as *chandasi niṣṭaryaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.123).
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.16] *grahijyādinā*.
Since the suffix *kyap* is marked with *p*, it is anudātta; thus, the accent of the verbal root remains. [The result is] *viśapatiḥ*.

Although the original accent of the first member would have applied by the rule *patyāvaiśvarye*, the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member is established by the rule *parādiśchandasi bahulam*.
May our good fame reach him, the one who is cherished in the heart, the honey-tongued,
whom the human priests, the Āyus, have generated at the sacrificial gathering while offering oblations.

May our excellent praise reach him who is being kindled from the heart—him who is most human, honey-tongued, whom the human priests, the Āyus, have generated while providing milk within the sacrificial enclosure.
1. Before the suffix -ḍha.
2. By the rule beginning with "ḍha," etc. (Pāṇini 8.2.40). Ka. 52.
"May our new, most recent, and excellent praise—our hymn of praise—be born from this *ida*, arising from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) situated within the heart;
for fire is kindled from wind, and wind is indeed the vital breath, according to the scriptural teaching: 'That which is the vital breath is wind.'"
May he reach— that is, may he pervade from all sides— that Agni who has honeyed tongues and intoxicating flames;
that Agni whom the *āyavaḥ*, the men, generated and produced for the sake of sacrifice when the *vṛjana*, the battle, had arrived.
What kind of men [are they]?
They are the *ṛtvijas*—those who sacrifice at the proper time (*ṛtu*)—the descendants of Manu, full of zeal (*prayasvantaḥ*), and endowed with oblations characterized by sacrificial food (*havis*).
*navyasī*: in the word *navīyasī*, the elision of the vowel *ī* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). *hṛdaḥ*.

Here, by the word *hṛdaya*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) residing therein is indicated. By [the rule] beginning with *padn*, the substitution of *hṛd* for the word *hṛdaya* occurs. [The term is] *jāyamānaṃ*.
The root *jan* is used in the sense of manifestation.

In the form *iyani*, the substitution of *jā* for *jñā* and *jan* occurs according to the rule *jñājanorjā*. Since the root is taught with a short *a* (*adupadeśāt*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix is unaccented; however, because the suffix *iyani* has the augment *niC*, it is acutely accented on its first syllable.
*asmata*: by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case ending. *aśśyāḥ*.
The root *aś* means "to pervade.

In the potential mood (*liṅ*), the suffix is elided according to the rule "in the Vedic language, [suffixes] are frequently elided" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). By transposition (*vyatyaya*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is used here.
*jījananta* [is derived from] the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation.
From the causative form (*ṇyanta*), in the *luṅ* tense, there is the substitution of *caṅ* for *cli*.
Due to reduplication, the substitution of *l* for *s*, the *saṃvadbhāva* (treatment as if it were the same as the root), and the lengthening of the vowel, [the form is established].

Since the root is taught with a short *a* (*adupadeśāt*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix would be unaccented; however, when the accent of the *caṅ* itself is about to apply, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatvam*) of the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) is applied by way of exception (*vyatyayena*).
Desirable, purifying, and a benefactor among men, the excellent Hotṛ has been established among the clans;
as the domestic friend and lord of the house within the home, Agni has become the master of riches.

The beloved one, the purifier, the Vasu, most excellent among men—the Hotṛ has been established among the people. As the friend of the house, the master of the home within the dwelling, Agni has become the lord of riches among all treasures. 4.

The Hotṛ Agni—desirous as a seeker (*uśika*), purifying as a cleanser (*pāvaka*), a benefactor (*vasu*), a dweller (*vasu* as one who causes to dwell), excellent (*vareṇya*) as one who is worthy of being chosen—being thus constituted, is established among the *viśaḥ*, that is, among the human sacrificers who have entered the sacrificial hall.

And that Agni, being a *damūnāḥ* (one endowed with a mind capable of subduing the Rākṣasas) and a *gṛhapatiḥ* (protector of the household), becomes the lord of wealth (*rayipatiḥ*) within the *dama*, the sacrificial home; he is present everywhere (*ā bhuvat*). He says "of all riches" (*rayīṇām*) to indicate that he is not merely the lord of one kind of wealth, but of all.
Or alternatively, it means: the lord of that wealth which is the most excellent among riches.
It has been placed [in the text].

According to the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.6), while the suffixes *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* apply in the Vedic language, here there is the *luṅ* in the passive voice; for the *cli* suffix, there is the substitution of *ciṇ*, and by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33), the augment *yuk* is added.
He who subdues (*damayati*) the Rākṣasas through his prowess is called *damūnāḥ*.
The root *dam* means "to pacify.
The suffix *-ūnas-* is added according to the rule *damerūnasiḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.674).

Yāska says: "Damūnā is one whose mind is subdued (*damamanā*), or whose mind is giving (*dānamanā*), or whose mind is self-controlled (*dāntamanā*); or else, *dama* is a name for the house, and he may be one whose mind is fixed on that" (Nirukta 4.4).
*dama* [is the word]; *agniḥ*. According to the rule *āṅo 'nunāsikaś chandasi*, the vowel *ā-* becomes nasalized and undergoes *prakṛtibhāva* (absence of sandhi). Thus: *bhuvat*.
In *leṭi*, the augment *aṭ* is added;
then, by the rule "there is elision of [the final vowel] after *it*," the vowel *i* is elided,
resulting in *rayipatiḥ*.
The acute accent on the initial syllable of the second member [of the compound] is due to the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.2.199). Regarding *rayīṇām*,
the acute accent on *nāma* is due to the rule *nāmanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.177).
1. He is described as having the form of the *ḍa* and *sa* sounds, for it is heard in scripture that he is the wind (*vāyu*). 2. He is the one to be chosen (*varaṇīya*).
We, the Gotamas, praise you with our hymns as the lord of riches;
grooming you like a swift prize-winning steed, may he who fulfills our thoughts come quickly at dawn.
We, the Gotamas, praise you with our hymns, O Agni, as the lord of riches—polishing you like a swift steed that brings booty. May he who possesses wealth through prayer come quickly at dawn. 5.
We, the Gotamas— born of the lineage of Gotama— and we,
the Nodhasas (the plural is used for honor,
even though there is but one singer), O Agni, praise you preeminently with hymns worthy of reflection; we celebrate you, the lord and protector of riches.
What are they doing?
They are cleansing you, the bearer of *vāja*—that is, the bearer of the oblation characterized as *vāja*.
Regarding this, there is an illustration:
Like a horse, as men mounting a horse rub its back with their hands, so do we rub the place where Agni carries the oblation; this is the meaning.

And thus it is recorded by the Vājasaneyins in the section on the cleansing of the fire: "He silently cleanses [the fire] three times in the middle; just as one, having yoked [a horse], urges it forward so that it may go, even so he, having yoked the fire, urges it on, saying: 'Go forth, carry the oblation to the gods!'"
May he who has acquired wealth through his action or intellect—that Agni—come quickly and swiftly at the break of day, at the early morning of the auspicious day.
By means of the *vmatibhiḥ*. From the root *man* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāne*), the suffix *kin* is applied in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*).
Its acute accent (*udāttatva*) is established by the rule beginning with *mantre vṛṣeṣap*.

"Vājambharaḥ. This is a Vedic name for Agni. According to Pāṇini’s rule *saṃjñāyāṃ bhṛtṛvṛji* (3.2.46), the suffix *khac* is applied when the word *vāja* is used as the object (*karman*) in composition.
The augment *mum* is applied by the rule *varudviṣadajantasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67).
By the rule *citaḥ*, the word is oxytone (*antodātta*). [They are] purifying themselves (*marjayantaḥ*).

Because a rule conditioned by a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not invariably applicable, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution [in the case of *sṛj*] according to Pāṇini 7.2.114 (*vsṛjer vṛddhiḥ*).
Since the root is taught with an initial *a* (*adupadeśa*), the *anudātta* accent of the *l*-affixes belonging to the *sārvadhātuka* class applies; thus, only the accent of the *ṇic* suffix remains.
[The form is] *jamyāt*.
In the optative (liṅ), there is elision (ślu) of the suffix śap by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in the Vedic language, [elision] occurs diversely).
The fourth hymn, consisting of sixteen verses beginning with “asmā idu pra tavase,” is the seerly composition of Nodhas, addressed to Indra, and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
It is thus enumerated: “asmā idu poḷaśa.
Regarding this hymn, it is recorded in the Brāhmaṇa that Nodhas was its seer: “asmā idu pra tavase turāyeti nodhāsta ete prātaḥsavane” (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 6.18).

In the days such as the Caturviṃśa and Mahāvrata which possess *paḷahastotriyas* and *vāpas*, during the Mādhyandina-savana, following the *ārambhagīyā* verse "brahmaṇa te brahmayujā," this hymn known as the *ahīnasūkta* is to be recited by the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.

Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The other two [priests] recite the *ahīnasūkte* beginning with 'asmā idu pra tavase śāmdhi'. And there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "These, being the *paḷahastotriyas* at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), they recite as *ahīnasūktas* at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*)."
To him alone, the powerful and swift one, I offer this hymn like a pleasing meal— this great praise to the one who is worthy of song, to Indra, the subduer of enemies, with most abundant prayers.

To him, the powerful and swift one, I offer this hymn like a refreshing draught—this praise to the majestic Indra, who is worthy of song, the slayer of Ahi, and the recipient of our most excellent prayers. 1.
1. In the middle of *ḍha*. 2. Of that which has *ḍhastya*. The two particles *it* and *u* are for the purpose of completing the meter.
Furthermore, Yāska states that "kam" and "id" are used for the purpose of filling out the meter;
or else, they serve to indicate emphasis.
[The words are: "to the powerful," "to the increased," "to the swift," "to the hastening."
Or rather:
to the destroyer of enemies,
the invincible one who is great in his qualities, to the one equal to a hymn, who is worthy of praise.
The meaning is that it is equal to whatever praise is performed.
"Adhigave" means for one who has gone or for one whose going is unimpeded; the meaning is "for one whose movement is unobstructed."
And thus Yāska says: "Indra is also called āśrīgṛ, like one whose action consists of coming and going" (Nirukta 5.11).
"To such a one as this Indra, I offer a *stoma*, that is, a hymn of praise; I present it—I perform it, is the meaning.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
*Prayaḥ* and *anaprayaḥ* are names for food. For example, as when someone offers food to a man who is hungry.
What kind of hymn?
"Oham" means it is to be carried [on the head] or to be prayed for;
that is to say, it is exceedingly excellent.
Not only the hymn (*stoma*), but what then? The sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*), that is, sacrifices characterized by oblations (*havis*). Of what kind [are they]?
By what means is there conviction (*pratyaya*)?
Because it ends in a verbal suffix (*ejantatvāt*), the case-ending (*sup*) is elided due to its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
[The form] *manīṣā* [is derived thus]. By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the third case ending.

For *patye*: since the technical designation *pati* (as defined by Pāṇini 1.4.8, "the word *pati* [is so called] only in a compound"), the rule *verhiti* does not apply because it pertains specifically to compounds; thus, there is no substitution of *guṇa*, and instead the *yaṇ* replacement occurs.
To him indeed I bring this nourishing food, winning the light of heaven, with my mouth;
with the most liberal hymns of our thoughts and well-fashioned praises, I exalt the patron sage.
To him indeed—to that most generous one, the lord of heaven—I bring this highest praise with my mouth, with the eloquent and well-fashioned hymns of my thoughts, so that I may exalt the patron. 3.

"To this very Indra"— to him who is well-known, "that one," the "exemplar" (upama), meaning the cause of comparison, the "winner of light" (svarṣām), the giver of desirable wealth, the "wise patron" (sūri)— in order to "strengthen" (vavṛdhadhyai) Indra with "well-fashioned hymns" (suvṛktibhiḥ), that is, with skillful compositions; with the "connections of thoughts" (matīnām saṃdhibhiḥ), meaning with praises, and with "clear utterances" (acchoktibhiḥ), that is, with distinct words— I bring forth, by means of my mouth, the "most bountiful" (maṃhiṣṭham), most exalted praise (āṅguṣam)— the meaning is that I perform it.
*Upamā*.

It is called *upama* because it is that by which something is compared (*upamīyate*). The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), according to the rule "the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of the *ghañ* suffix."
The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca.
[The form] *svarṣām* [is derived from] the word *svara*, which is formed with the suffix *viñ* from the root *ṛ* preceded by the prefix *su*.
In the sense of "giving" (*dāna*), [the root *pan* becomes *paṇ*].
According to the rule *janasanakhanakramagamo viṭ*, the suffix *viṭ* is applied;
and by the rule *viḍnoranunāsikasyāt*, the substitution of *ā* occurs [for the nasal].
The substitution of *d* [for *t*] is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 8.3.108 (*sanoteranaḥ*).
[In the word] *bharāma*,
there is an absence of *nighāta* because it begins with a *pāda*.
By means of clear utterances (*acchoktibhiḥ*). Those whose utterances are clear (*acchā uktayaḥ*)—
in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
In *matīnām*,
the word *nāman* receives the acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule *nāmanyatarasyām*.
[The form] *vavṛdhadhyai*.

From the root *vṛdh* in the sense of "to increase" (*vṛdha vṛddhau*), with the causative meaning (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *kadhyaip* is applied according to the rule *tumarthe seṣen*.
Due to its *kit* status, there is an absence of *guṇa* strengthening;
the reduplication is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively, because the rule regarding the addition of augments is not universal, there is an absence of *rīk* and so forth when this suffix follows a stem with the *yaṅ*-lopa;

the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is according to the rule "it is also seen in other cases" (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*), which applies to Vedic sandhi (*sāṃhitika*), and the suffix has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
For him alone I fashion this hymn, as a carpenter fashions a chariot for its master; and I offer songs and well-wrought praises to Indra, the lord of songs, the wise one who pervades all things.

To him indeed I send forth this hymn, as a carpenter fashions a chariot for one who bends the bow; and with well-fashioned songs, I offer praise to Indra, the lover of song, the wise one, who stirs all things. 4.
For this very Indra, I offer—that is, I impel—the *stoma*, the hymn in the form of a *śastra*.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"for him who desires that."
*Sinam* is a name for food;
Yāska says, "It is called *sinam* because it binds (*sināti*) living beings" (Nirukta 5.7). He is thus described as one whose *sinama* is that chariot.
To that lord of the chariot, as a skilled carpenter (*takṣaka*) fashions a chariot as if he were not a carpenter at all—
*iva* here being used merely for metrical completion—
in the same way, [he offers] songs (*giraḥ*) connected with the scriptures to Indra, who is being praised with hymns (*girbhiḥ*).
I impel the pure *ṛc*s with beautiful (*suvṛkti*) and excellent invocation, so that it may come to pass;
likewise for the wise one.
(1. Ḍha: the state of being a *ṛk* and a *gāthā*).

"To Indra, the wise one, I offer the oblation that is all-encompassing (*viśvaminvam*), all-pervading (*viśvavyāpakam*), and most excellent among all things (*viśvairyāsam*); "—thus the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅgaḥ*) is supplied.
I offer (*hinomi*). [The root] *hi* means "to go" and "to increase."
The root *kṣu* is [included] because it begins with *svādi*.
Likewise:
*takṣū* and *tvakṣū*, meaning "to make thin."
The suffix *tan* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*).
Because of the prefix *ud*, there is optionally an absence of the augment *iṭ*. By the rule "the *k* and *s* of a conjunct consonant [are elided] at the end [of a word]," the letter *k* is dropped.
The word *nisvāda* has its initial syllable accented acute (*udātta*). In that [context], there is the word *sina*.
The word *sina* ends in the suffix *nak*, derived from the root *piñ* in the sense of "binding," according to the Unādi Sūtra 3.282: *iṇ-sṛj-dīṅ-bhyaś-cibhyo nak*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is maintained]. As in *girvāhasa*:
by the rule "after *vahi*, *hā*, *dhā*, and *bhyaḥ* in the Veda," the suffix *asun* is added to the root *vah* alone, marked with the *ṅit* indicator.

By the rule "There is also the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member even when [the suffix] *gi* follows a word denoting a destination or an agent," there is also the preservation of the original accent of the first member for that which has a word denoting an agent (*kāraka*) as its prior member. This is because the term "*gi*" is understood from the previous context.
There is then the vṛddhi strengthening of the penultimate vowel.

In the phrase *hali ca*, there is an absence of lengthening [of the vowel], while in *cha* there is lengthening. In forms such as *nasataniṣvatta* (Pāṇini 8.2.61), there is an absence of the nasalization (*natva*) of the *niṣṭhā* suffix due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). [The compound] means "he whose fame (*śravaḥ*) is celebrated (*gṛtam*). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent remains on the original form of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*). Regarding *darmāṇam*: from the root *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing," the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule *anyebhyo'pi dṛśyante*. There is a prohibition of the *it*-augment by the rule *nedṛśi kṛti*. By transposition (*vyatyaya*), the suffix has its initial syllable accented. Alternatively, the suffix *man* should be understood as an *uṇādi* formation. || 27 ||
For him indeed Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the thunderbolt, most skillful in its work, for the winning of booty;
it struck the very vitals of Vṛtra, for he, the lord, was able to strike down that which was so vast.

For him, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the thunderbolt, most skillfully wrought, resounding for the fray; with which, striking, he found even Vṛtra’s vital spot—the Lord, the all-pervading, striking with his blow. 6.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the creator of all things, fashioned—that is, made sharp—for this very Indra a thunderbolt, a striking weapon for the sake of battle.
What kind of thunderbolt?
Most skillful in its action (*svapastama*), exceedingly beautiful in its work, and itself well-impelled against enemies, or rather, worthy of praise.

Indra—impelling and destroying his enemies, possessing lordly power (*īśāna*), and endowed with great strength (*kīyedhāḥ*)—is distinguished by such qualities. With that very thunderbolt (*vajra*) which he impels and strikes at the *marman*, the vital organ of even Vṛtra, the concealing Asura, he "found" (attained) him; that is to say, he struck him down. He is one whose work (*apas*) is beautiful (*svapn-*)—one who performs excellent deeds.

*Atiśayena svāpaḥ* means "sleeping excessively"; *svapastamaḥ*. Because the suffix *tamaP* is *pit*, the word is unaccented (*anudātta*). By the rule "*somarnasī alomopasī*," there is udātta accent on the initial syllable of the second member of the compound.
*svaryam*:
This is explained in the verse "svayaṃ tatakṣa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.32.2). *vidat*.
In the expression *vida lābhe*:
because the root is marked with *ḷ* (indicating *ḷdit*), the substitute *aṭ* is applied to *cli*.
However, by the rule "in the Veda, [the augment] is frequently absent even when there is conjunction with *mā*" (*bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge’pi*), the absence of *aṭ* occurs.
Because of its connection with the *vṛtta* (metre), there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*). [The suffix] *tun*.
[The root] *tuja* in the sense of "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*).
When *śap* is expected, *śa* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Since the root is taught with an initial *a*, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, and thus the accent falls on the *vikaraṇa* suffix.
[Thus we have] *īśānaḥ*.
In the root *īś* in the sense of "lordship" (*aiśvarya*),
when the suffix *śānac* is applied, there is elision of *śap* because it belongs to the *adādi* class.
Since the root is *anudātta-it*, the *lasārvadhātuka* accent is *anudātta*, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
*tujatā* (impelling): the accentuation of the case ending is due to the rule *śataranumaḥ*. *kiyedhāḥ*.
Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "Kiyedhāḥ means 'possessing how much' or 'possessing a certain measure,' or it means 'one who bestows [the power] while moving forward'" (Nirukta 6.20).
This is its intended meaning:
*kiyat* means "of what measure? and that which bestows (*dadhāti*) or maintains (*dhārayati*) such strength for that force is called *kiyaddhāḥ*.
The meaning is that no one knows the extent of this power.
Alternatively,
he is "kramamāṇadhāḥ," meaning he who holds— that is, restrains— the advancing force of his enemies.
In both cases, the change of the first member [of the compound] to *kiya* occurs by virtue of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group;
[the suffix] *vic* is applied after the root *dhā*.
At his mother’s every libation, he immediately devoured the great food, having drunk it;
the more powerful Viṣṇu stole the two things that were cooked, and he cast the mountain aside with a single stroke.

Having drunk at once the great draught from his mother’s udder at all her pressings, Viṣṇu, the stronger one, stole away the lovely food; he split the cooked offering and, as an archer, shot the boar through the mountain.

The two particles *it* and *u* here serve as verse-fillers (*pādapūraṇa*), or alternatively, they have the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). [O Indra,] at the *savanas*—the constituent parts consisting of the morning libation and the other two—of this great (*mahaḥ*) sacrifice of the Creator (*mātuḥ*), who fashions the entire universe by means of rain; at these three *savanas*.
1. Ḍha: [The word] *āvaraka* belongs to the Asura as well. 2. Ḍha: What is its measure (*kiṃparimāṇa*)? 3. Ḍha: *nan* is a word-filler (*padapūraṇa*).
"Drinking" (pivant) "food" (pitum)—that is, the food characterized by Soma—"immediately" (sadyas):
the meaning is that as soon as it is offered into the fire, he has drunk it.

Likewise, he has "eaten" (the rest of the sentence being understood) "beautiful things" (cāruṇyā)—that is, beautiful, excellent foods such as parched grains (dhānā), ground meal (karambha), and so forth.

Furthermore, Viṣṇu, the pervader of the entire world, while stealing away— that is, seizing— the wealth of the gods that was being cooked [prepared], Indra, who is more powerful (sahīyān), the supreme overcomer of enemies, and the hurler of the stone (adrí)— that is, the thunderbolt— being thus situated, having "passed through" (tiras)— according to Yāska, "it means 'having reached'" (Nirukta 3.20)—
he pierced, that is, struck, the boar, namely the cloud.

Alternatively, Viṣṇu consists of the day of the Soma-pressing and so forth, according to the Vedic tradition: "The sacrifice, having assumed the form of Viṣṇu, hid itself away from the gods" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.4.2).
That Viṣṇu is that which is the *pacataṃ*—the one who moves around and bestows wealth. That is *mu*.
He surpassed them by his own splendor; that is the meaning.
Those two, heaven and earth, do not encompass his greatness—that is, they do not equal it—O Indra.
They have spoken.
The root *veñ* is used in the sense of "weaving" (*tantu-saṃtāna*).
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), by Pāṇini’s rule 2.4.41, *vejo vayiḥ*, the substitute *vayi* is applied for *veñ*.

Because the *liṭ* affixes are marked with the *kittva* indicator, when the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is to be performed due to the root belonging to the *yajādi* class, the substitution of the *yakāra* is prohibited by Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.38, *liṭi vayo yaḥ*. Consequently, the vocalization of the *vakāra* occurs, followed by the replacement of the preceding vowel (*parapūrvatva*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*), and so forth.
By the rule *vaśvāsthānyatarasyāṃ kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.39), the substitution of *v* for *y* occurs [in the case of the root *vah*].
*Jabhre*.
[The root] *hañ* means "to carry."
