In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], because it is marked with *j*, the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] is used when the action benefits the agent.
The form *bharaṃ* is derived according to the rule "ha-graha-bhaiḥ.
[The word is] *urvī*.

From the word *uru*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*. By the rule *vā chandasi*, the long vowel of the same class as the preceding [vowel] is substituted. Thus: *urū*. *staḥ*.
This is a form of the *leṭ* mood.
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] in *asyedeva* is a phonetic (*sāṃhitika*) application of the rule *upasargaprādurbhyām*.
His greatness indeed surpasses that of heaven, earth, and the intermediate space.
The lord of the sun, praised by all in his own home, the one who brings light and is worthy of praise, has grown strong for the sake of battle.
His greatness indeed surpasses that of heaven, earth, and the intermediate space.
The self-ruling Indra, praised by all, the noble lord and mighty one, has grown great within the house for the sake of battle. 9.
"Of this very one"— the particle *iti* is for filling out the meter. "The greatness," that is, the majesty, of this very Indra "surpasses," meaning it exceeds [all others].
The meaning is that it becomes more.
In this context, the prefix expresses the cessation of the root's original meaning,
as in *prasmaraṇam* (forgetting) or *prasthānam* (setting out).
From what source does it appear to overflow? He says:

"From heaven" (divaḥ), that is, from the world of the sky; "from earth" (pṛthivyāḥ), that is, from the world of the ground; and "from the intermediate space" (antarikṣāt), that is, from the world of the atmosphere situated between heaven and earth—the word *pari* here has the sense of "above. The meaning is that it overflows above, transcending these three worlds.

In the matter of what is to be subdued, he is "asvarāṭ," shining by his own splendor; he is "viśvagūrtaḥ," exalted or capable in every action. Alternatively, he is so called because all (viśvam) his weapons (āyudham) are "gūrtam," raised up;
he is "svariḥ," one who has excellent enemies.

When a formidable enemy is to be slain, it is understood that the slayer is most heroic, as in: "Indra, the divine ruler of unassailable power" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.47.5). For its meaning is indeed "one whose enemies are uncrushed."
"Amatra" means skilled in moving in battles and other such activities;
or it means devoid of "mātrā," that is, measure or limitation.
Yāska [states]: "Amatra is amātra, meaning great, or unassailable" (Nirukta 6.23).
Indra, being thus, "for the sake of battle" (raṇāya)—that is, for the purpose of combat—“has brought” (āvavakṣe), meaning he brings or causes the clouds to arrive;
the sense is that by means of the clouds, a mutual conflict is brought about, and thus he has caused rain.
Or alternatively:
He sends his own soldiers to battle.
In this case, the case ending (vibhakteḥ) is udātta according to the rule "aḍiḍam."
*ririce*.
The root *√ric* is used in the sense of "purging" (*virecana*).
The suffix *liṭ* is applied in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*) while the rule "*chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*" (Vedic usage permits the use of *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* for all tenses) is in effect.
Of the earth.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule "udāttayaṇaḥ.
[The word] *svarāṭ*.
From the root *dīp* (meaning "to shine") in the sense of "king" (*rājan*), the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *satsūdviṣa*.
Due to the presence of *aśva* etc., the change to *ṣ* occurs, followed by the change to the corresponding voiced stop (*jaśtva*). [The form is] *dame*.

From the root *dam* in the sense of "to pacify," with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*), there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *nodāttopadeśasya māntasthānācameḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.34).
Because the suffix *ghañ* has the marker *j*, the word is udātta-accented on its first syllable.
[The word is] *viśvagūrtaḥ*.
The root *gṛ* is used in the sense of "swallowing.

From this root, when the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix) follows, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *śryukaḥ kiti*. The substitution of *u* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "hali ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.111).
Alternatively,
[the root is] "gūrī udyame" (to exert oneself).
From this [root], the suffix *niṣṭhā* [is applied]. Due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) beginning with "na-sat-ta-ni-patta," there is an absence of the status of *niṣṭhā*.
In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, by virtue of belonging to the *marudvṛdha*-class, there is acute accent on the final syllable of the first member.

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, however, by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, when it is a name, *viśva* [is acute on the final syllable]," there is acute accent on the final syllable of the first member even when it is not a name.
*Amatraḥ*:
from the root *am* in the sense of "going" and so forth.
In the word *vavakṣe*, the suffix *at* is applied according to the Uṇādi rule beginning with "amimakṣiyajibandhi";
because the suffix is marked with *j*, the word is udātta on its first syllable. *Vavakṣe*.
In the *leṭ* [mood], *sip* is applied by the rule "in the *leṭ*, *sip* is frequent.
By the rule "in the Veda, it is frequent," there is the elision (*lup*) of the *śap* [suffix].
There is no substitution of *ṇal* for the root vowel.
‘Lopasta’: 1. A mutual battle between Ḍha and Na.

In the *ātmanepada* [forms], there is the elision of the suffix *ta*. [The form] *raṇāya* [is used] because the object is treated as a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) due to the rule “the mention of the action must be made” (*kriyāgrahaṇaṃ kartavyam*), hence the dative case; or else, it is the dative according to Pāṇini 2.3.12: “in the case of the object of a verb meaning ‘to go’... (*gatyarthakarmaṇi*).
With his very own impetus, Indra shattered Vṛtra, who was swelling with strength, with his thunderbolt;
like cows from their pens, he released the rivers, being mindful to bestow glory upon us.
With his very own impetuosity, Indra shattered the panting Vṛtra with his thunderbolt; he released the rivers like penned-up cattle, being well-disposed to bestow glory. 10.
By the power (*śavasā*) and strength (*balena*) of this very Indra, he cut apart (*vi vṛścat*), that is, split asunder, Vṛtra who was withering away (*aśuṣantam*).

Likewise, like cows stolen by thieves, he released (*amuñcat*)—that is, he caused to rain down—the rivers, the waters that were the cause of protection, which had been enclosed by the thunderbolt (*vajreṇa āvṛtāḥ*).

Similarly, being of one mind (*sacetāḥ*) with that sacrificer, the giver of the oblation (*dāvane havirdātre*), he bestows (*dadāti*) fame (*śravaḥ*), meaning the food that is the fruit of the ritual, directed toward him; this is the sense of the remainder of the verse.
Regarding *śuṣantam*: since the root *śuṣ* means "to dry," the suffix *ini* would have been expected; however, by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *śa* is used instead.
Because there is no specific instruction [to the contrary], when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are rendered unaccented, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* alone remains. Thus, *trāṇāḥ*.
[The root is] *vṛ* in the sense of "covering" (*varaṇe*).

In the sense of the object (karmaṇi), from the present suffix *laṭ*, the suffix *śānac* is applied; by the rule "optionally (*bahulam*) in the Veda (*chandasi*)," there is elision (*luk*) of the *yak*.
Because the *śānac* has the marker *ṭ*, there is an absence of *guṇa*, and the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs [for the vowel *u*]. Thus: *avanīḥ*.
The suffix *ani* is applied to the root *av* in the sense of an instrument by [Uṇādi-sūtra] 2.259, *atisṛṣṭadharmi*, etc.;
the accent falls on the initial syllable of the suffix.
[The form is] *dāvane*.
The suffix *vanip* is applied by the rule *āto manin-kvanib-vanipaḥ*.
The absence of elision (*alopa*) in the singular dative case is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

Truly, the rivers flowed around him, for he, the wielder of power, having acted as a lord for the one who offers oblations, restrained their rush with his thunderbolt; the victorious one made a ford for the seeker’s enjoyment.

At his roar, the rivers trembled when he, the wielder of power, acting as lord and bestowing gifts upon the donor, struck them all around with his thunderbolt; Turvaṇi provided a ford for Turvīti. 11.
"Of this very Indra, by his fierce and blazing power, the rivers— the oceans,
or else the seven rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā— rejoice, each in its own place."
Because this Indra, with his *vajra*, has encompassed—meaning he has completely restrained—these rivers;

and furthermore, acting as a lord (*īśānakṛt*) by making himself sovereign through the slaying of enemies such as Vṛtra, Indra, bestowing the fruit upon the donor—the sacrificer who has offered the oblation—being one who quickly grants (*turvaṇiḥ*), that is, one who swiftly distributes.
Regarding this, Yāska says: “*Turvaṇiḥ* means one who bestows quickly” (*Nirukta* 6.14).
Or rather: Turvittā is the destroyer of enemies.
Indra, being such, what did he do for Turvīti—the one known by that name, the seer submerged in water—for him he made a ford, a place suitable for standing, a shallow region?

*ranta* [is derived from] the root *rasu* in the sense of "play. In the Vedic language (*chāndasa*), due to the *laṅ* suffix in the plural, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* affix according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
The elision of the suffix other than the root is Vedic; [the form] *ayacchat* [is derived from] the root *yama* in the sense of "ceasing."
By the rule *‘iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ’*, the substitution of *cha* [for the root-final *m*] occurs.
[In the form] *kaḥ*: in the *luṅ* tense of the root *kṛ*, by the rule *‘mantre ghasahvaraṇaḥ’* (Pāṇini 2.4.80) and others, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *cli*.

The suffix *guṇa*. The elision of the *t* [of *at*] occurs by the rule *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "In the Veda, [the augment *aṭ* is] frequently absent even when there is conjunction with a word beginning with a vowel."
1. Ḍha.—They were plundered by thieves. 2. Ḍha.—To one bearing this name.
3. Ḍha.—To that king.
For him indeed, the lord, possessing manifold power, having struck out repeatedly, hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra;
he tore him asunder like the joints of a cow, crossing over the floods.

To him, indeed, bring forth the thunderbolt, O impetuous one! Thou who art the lord, possessing manifold power, cleave Vṛtra as if the joint of an ox, striking crosswise, so that the floods of the waters may flow. 12.
*tṛtujānaḥ* is a name for "swift"; *tṛtujānaḥ* means "resounding. Or else:
Slaying the enemies,
the sovereign lord (vīśānaḥ) of all, the bestower (dhātā) of whatever measure of strength (kiyedhāḥ)— that is, of power whose extent is not limited—
or rather:
*Kiyedhāḥ* means one who, while advancing, holds fast and brings the enemy force to a standstill.
O Indra, being such as you are, hurl the thunderbolt at this Vṛtra;
the meaning is that you strike down this Vṛtra with the thunderbolt.

And having struck down the clouds, you released the waters of rain; from that Vṛtra, you granted fearlessness for the flowing forth (*caraṇāya*)—that is, for the movement toward the regions of the earth—of those waters. With your thunderbolt positioned crosswise, cut apart (*vi vrada*) the joints (*parva*), the unions of the limbs of that Vṛtra who has the form of a cloud.
"Cut" is the meaning.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

"Strike quickly! Just as worldly men, having determined the various parts of meat, divide the limbs of the animal, so it is here. Regarding this, the Nirukta says: "O Lord, striking swiftly, hurl the thunderbolt at Vṛtra; how great is your power!"
"Whether it be 'how many [steps]' or 'the manner of stepping,' break apart its joints like those of a cow; [break] the masses of the cloud like waters for the sake of movement" (Nirukta 6.20).
The word *bhara* [is derived] from the root *bhṛ*; the form *hmobhaiḥ* is according to Pāṇini 6.1.215;
the long vowel in *adyo'tamindaḥ* is according to Pāṇini 6.1.72, which prescribes the *sāṃhitika* (euphonic) lengthening.

*tṛtujānaḥ*: [derived from] the root *tuja* in the sense of "to injure. With the suffix *kānac*, the lengthening of the reduplication occurs according to the rule: "there is lengthening of the reduplication for roots beginning with *tuja*."

Because of the rule "chandasyubhayathā" (Pāṇini 3.4.117), the suffix *kānac* is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*; consequently, by the rule "abhyastānāmādiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.189), the first syllable is udātta.
Thus, [the word] is *kiyedhāḥ*.
This is stated in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā (1.61.6): "tujatā kiyedhāḥ."
*rada*: from the root *rada* in the sense of "scratching" (*vilekhane*).
The *nighāta* (elision of the accent) is applied by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.
*Tiraścā* [is derived as follows]:
that which moves crosswise is *tiryaṅ*.
The suffix *kvin* is applied by the rule beginning with "ṛtvik" (Pāṇini 3.2.59).
In the form *aniditām*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*);
in the third case singular, when the designation *bha* applies, there is the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *acaḥ*;
and by the rule *śrutva*, the *s* becomes *ś*.
The accentuation of the case-ending is by means of the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*. [In the word] *iṣyan*:

from the root *iṣ* "to go," with the causative sense (*ṇic*) inherent within it, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied, and then the suffix *iyan* is added according to the rule "after roots beginning with *div*."
Because it is a nit suffix, it has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
Regarding *caradhyai*: by the rule "sesen for the sense of the infinitive suffix," the suffix *adhyai* is added to the root *car*.
Proclaim with hymns these ancient deeds of this swift hero, worthy of men;
when, eager for battle, he brandishes his weapons and, seeking to strike, lays low his enemies.

Proclaim his deeds, the ancient ones, of him the swift one—his manly acts performed with hymns of praise; how, when he brandishes his weapons for battle, he, roaring in his fury, utterly destroys his enemies. 13.

With hymns (*vukthaiḥ*) and words (*śabdaiḥ*), O singer, praise Indra who is worthy of praise. Proclaim, O singer, the ancient deeds (*pūrvyāṇi karmāṇi*), the acts of power performed by this very Indra when he roared for the sake of battle. When, for the purpose of fighting (*yudhe*), Indra—brandishing his weapons such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*) repeatedly, and increasing his strength against his enemies—goes forth to encounter them, then proclaim [these deeds]. This is the connection with what precedes.
"Pūryam" is a name for "purāṇa" (the ancient), because it is listed among the names for the ancient in the passage: "pūryam ahnāya" (Nirukta 3.7.5).
Of *tura*. [The root] *tura* means "to hasten. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*.

1. In manuscript Ḍha, "śatrūn" is not present. 2. In manuscript Ḍha, [it reads] "indraḥ śatrūn," acting like a destroyer (hiṃsaka). 3. In manuscript Ḍha, "sa" [means] he utterly destroys (nitarām upakṣapayati). 4. In manuscript Ḍha, it refers to those names.

*namyaḥ*: from the root *ṇu* in the sense of "praise" (*stuti*). By the rule *aco yat*, the suffix *yat* is applied; there is *guṇa* substitution. By the rule *dhātostannimittasyaiva*, the *av* substitution occurs. *iṣṇānaḥ*: from the root *iṣ* in the sense of "repetition" (*ābhīkṣṇya*). It belongs to the *kaiyādika* class. The *ātmanepada* ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). The *cittavat* accentuation applies because of the suffix *jñānac*. *ṛdhāyamāṇaḥ*: This has been explained in the passage "nahi tvā rodasi ubhe ṛdhāyamāṇam" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.10.8). *niraṇāti*: from the root *rī* in the senses of "motion" (*gati*) and "desiring" (*eṣaṇa*). By the rule *śrayādibhyaḥ śrā*, the suffix *śrā* is applied. There is shortening by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*. Since the *tip* suffix is marked as *pit*, it is unaccented, and thus the accent of the *vikaraṇa* remains. By the rule *tiṅi codāttavati*, the *gati* prefix is unaccented (*nighāta*). However, due to its connection with *yad-vṛtta*, the rule *tiṅaṅatiṅaḥ* does not apply, and thus there is no suppression of the accent (*nighātābhāva*).
Out of fear of him, even the firm mountains and heaven and earth tremble at his birth. Nodhas, praising the protection of the beloved one, has instantly become ready for heroic deeds.
Of this: "it" and "ū~".
"Bhūri" means "much";
"īśāna" means "lord" or "master. "Ekaḥ" means "alone," [in the sense that] he alone is capable of conquering enemies. He entreated Vajra for this hymn which belongs to these singers;
or alternatively—
The indeclinable [particle] *vibhakti*:
by these [means], that well-known hymn was "given over" (*anūdāyi*) to this Indra; the meaning is that it was performed.
This is the narrative concerning the second half-verse.
There was a certain king named Svaśva. Desiring a son, he worshipped the Sun;
and the Sun himself became his son.
A battle took place between him and the great seer named Etaśa; that very event is described here.

This Indra, while at the *Svaśvya* sacrifice (the sacrifice of Svaśva), protected—that is, rescued—the seer named Etaśa, who was pressing the Soma juices (*sunvin*), contending against *Sūra*, the son of Svaśva (*apasyadhānam*).
[The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule: "In the Veda (*chandasi*), the augment *aṭ* is absent even when used with *māṅ*."]
In *vajre*,
[the root] *avan* (meaning "to request") is used;
in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), there is an elision of the penultimate vowel by way of a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).
*pasyadhānam*:
from the root *spṛdh* in the sense of "rivalry" (*saṃgharṣe*),
the suffix *kānac* is applied after the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
In the case of double consonance, according to the rule *dvirvacane 'śapūrvāḥ khayaḥ*, the letter *p* remains.
By virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group, there is elision of the vowel *dh* and vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *r*.
The word is finally acute (*antodātta*) because it ends in a long vowel.
In the case of *mautraśvye*:

the word *svaśva* is a name for a country (*janapadaśabda*) used as a designation for a Kṣatriya. Since it possesses the designation "vṛddha" according to the rule "The designation *vṛddha* should be stated optionally for a proper name" (Pāṇini 1.1.73), the suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*) by the rule "After a *vṛddha* [stem] ending in *it*, and after *kosala* and *āja*, [comes] *ñyaṅ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.101).

By the rule *na svābhyāṃ padāntābhyām* (Pāṇini 7.3.3), there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and the introduction of the augment *aij*. Because it has the marker *j*, it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). Thus: *sunvim*.
In the word *suṣabhipave*,
the suffix *kin* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.171: *utsargaśchandasī*.
Or rather, the doubling [of the consonant] occurs due to the force of the grammatical indicator (liṅga);
there is the substitution of *yaṇ*,
and the absence of the substitution of *uvaṅ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Thus have the Gotamas fashioned these well-wrought hymns for you, O Indra, at the yoking of the bay steeds.
Bestow upon them a thought adorned with every beauty; may he who seeks the prize through prayer come swiftly in the morning.

Thus, O Indra, the Gṛtsamadas have fashioned these prayers for you with beautiful hymns, O Bearer of the Yoke. Bestow upon them a thought adorned with every beauty; may he who is rich in wisdom come quickly at dawn through our prayer. 16.
That chariot to which two bay horses (*harī*) are yoked is called *haryo-yojana*.
One who has a connection with that [chariot] by virtue of being its master is *hāriyojana*.

O *hāriyojana* Indra, the *gotamāsaḥ*—the seers born from the lineage of Gotama—have performed *suvṛkti*, well-fashioned prayers consisting of hymns of praise (*brahmāṇi*), which are skillful in turning you toward them; they have fashioned these for you alone.
"Among these praisers, bestow *dhi*—that which possesses manifold forms (*viśvapeśas*).
Because it is obtained through *dhi*, *dhi* is said to mean wealth;
or else, [it refers to the prayer itself].

The word *dhī* signifies action. "Bestow" (*ā dhāḥ*) means bestow or establish that wealth which takes many forms such as cattle and so forth, or that action which takes many forms such as the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and so forth. "Dhehi" means "place" or "establish."

"O Indra, just as you were Adhiyāvasu—one who has acquired wealth through intelligence or action—at dawn today, so may you come quickly and immediately at dawn tomorrow as well, for the sake of partaking of our offerings."
In the *saṃhitā* [text], there is a long vowel according to the rule "nipātasya ca" (Pāṇini 6.3.134). *suvṛkti*.

The *luk* (elision) of the *śas* [case-ending] occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. In *akran*, the *liṭ* [perfect tense] suffix is replaced by *luṅ* [aorist], and the elision of the root *ghas* occurs in the *mantra* by the rule *mantre ghasahra*.
The substitution of *ant* [for *atman*]:
because that [suffix] is marked with *ḍ*, there is an absence of *guṇa*, and the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs.
Then, by the rule "itaśca" (Pāṇini 3.4.97), the *ik* vowel is elided, and after the elision of the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*), the augment *aṭ* is added.

The root *dhā* takes the *luṅ* suffix in the sense of the *loṭ* (imperative) by the rule "In the Veda, *luṅ* and *liṭ* [are used for other tenses]"; by the rule "The elision of *sic* after roots meaning 'motion' or 'standing'," there is elision of *sic*;
and by the rule "In the Veda, the augment *aṭ* is frequently absent even when not joined with *māṅ*," there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness within the heart,
may the Great Lord of the Supreme Holy Place (Yatīrtha-maheśvara) bestow the four aims of human existence.

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first book of the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial authority of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
1. In manuscript ḍha, the phrase "tadetadihocyate" is absent.
2. In manuscript ḍha, it reads "evā te"; [in others] it reads "sa evā". 3.
In manuscripts va, śa, and sā, it reads "sāyaṇācāryeṇa viracite"; in manuscript sa, it reads "sāyaṇācāryaviracite".
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the fifth chapter begins.
In the first maṇḍala, four hymns have passed in the eleventh anuvāka.
This fifth hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "pra manmahe," now follows.
Regarding this, the sequence is stated: “*Pra sasāna*...;
the unexpressed number is twenty” (Anuvāka 12.4). Since it has been so stated, when *pra sasāna* is uttered, thirteen is thereby expressed.
By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "and the seer from another," Nodhas is the seer (*ṛṣi*).
By the technical rule regarding the lack of specific instruction, *triṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandaḥ*).
Indra is the deity (*devatā*).
The general application has been explained;
the specific application, however, is to be understood from indicative power (liṅga).

We meditate upon the impetuous might of the powerful one, who delights in songs like Aṅgiras; with well-fashioned hymns, let us praise him who is worthy of praise, the all-pervading hero, as we honor Marka.
We meditate upon the roar of the powerful one, the praise-song for the lover of hymns, in the manner of Aṅgiras; may he grant strength to the singer with well-fashioned prayers. (Note:
Due to the non-universality of grammatical rules conditioned by a preceding specific term, there is no lengthening of the vowel according to the rule *hali ca*.)
By the rule "There is also the original accent of the first member even when [the compound] denotes a direction (gati) or an agent (kāraka)," there is the original accent of the first member.
Thus: *aṅgirasvat*. The suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule "that which is equal to that."

In the word *namaḥ*, because the designation *bha* applies according to the rule *namo-'ṅgiromanuṣāṃ vatyupasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 1.4.18.3), there is no shortening [of the vowel]. It takes the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). [The word is] *suvṛkkibhiḥ*.
The root *vṛj* means "to avoid. The suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). By the rule *titutra*, there is a prohibition of the *it*-augment.

"Those whose attraction (*āvarjana*) is beautiful. [In this compound,] the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is accented acute (*udātta*) by the rule *nam-syām*. But surely, since the second member ends in a suffix marked with *ṅ*, the initial syllable of the second member should be acute according to the rule *ādyudāttaṃ yac chandasi*? [Response: No, because the rule *nam-syām* specifically prescribes the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member. Furthermore, the rule *ādyudāttaṃ yac chandasi* applies only when the word is not governed by another specific rule; since *nam-syām* is a more specific injunction, it prevails. Thus, the final syllable of the second member is indeed acute.
In that case, let it be a *tatpuruṣa* compound:
"those by which you are beautifully won over" (*suvṛktibhiḥ*) are the hymns of praise (*stotrāṇi*).
The suffix *kin* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).

Since the rule "tādau ca niti" would otherwise cause the *gati* [prefix] to retain its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*), the rule "manuktin" etc. prescribes that the final syllable of the following member (*uttarapada*)—which is a *kin* suffix—should be udātta when following a *kāraka*. This [rule] applies by way of exception (*vyatyaya*) even when the preceding word is not a *kāraka*.
Thus: *stuvate*. Here, the case ending receives the udātta accent according to the rule "śataranumaḥ."
This is *ṛcimayī*.

According to the rule "They desire the suffix *mayaṭ* invariably after a word ending in a single vowel" (Kāśikā 4.3.144), the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied to the word *ṛc* in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*).

Then, by the rule "In the presence of case endings other than those called *sarvanāmasthāna*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.17), the technical designation *pada* is assigned, resulting in the substitution of *kutva* and *jaśtva*.
The substitution of *i* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively,
the suffix *mak* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) to the root *arc* (meaning "to praise").
By virtue of the rule regarding frequent occurrence (*bahulavacanāt*), there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*) and the substitution of *jaś* (i.e., *g*).
That which is worthy of praise (*stuti*) is called *ṛgmayaḥ*;
here the suffix *ghac* is used in the sense of being worthy (*arha*).
The word "citaḥ" has its final syllable accented (antodātta).
[We] worship:
the root "arc" is used in the sense of "worship."
It belongs to the *bhū* class (*bhauvādika*).
Due to the *pit* designation of the suffix *śap*, it is *anudātta*.
By the rule regarding the accent of *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
*Arka*. It is called *arka* because it is worshipped (*arcyate*) by means of it.
The suffix *gha* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *gha* is generally used in the masculine when forming a proper name."
The substitution of *k* for *c* and *j* occurs by the rule "cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ.
In the form *nare*,
the *guṇa* [substitution] after the word *nṛ* in the dative singular is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
To the renowned one;
from the root *śru* in the sense of "hearing," the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used in the objective sense.
In the phrase "gatiranantaraḥ," the word *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

Bring forth great homage to the Great One; offer a song of praise to him who is exalted by his own power—that by which our ancient fathers, the Aṅgirases, knowers of the path, found the cows while singing their hymns.

Bring forth great homage for the Great One; offer a song of praise to the Mighty One, by which our ancient fathers, the Aṅgirases, who knew the path, found the cattle while offering their hymns. || 2 ||

O officiating priests (ṛtvijas), you [are for] the great one who acts with power (śavasāna)— that is, for the exceedingly powerful one. Since the word *yat* is heard in the subsequent sentence, the word *tam* is to be supplied [as the correlative].
To that Indra who has become thus, offer forth—that is, accomplish with excellence—a great, vast, and mature *namas*, a hymn of praise.
What is that hymn? He says:
it is the *āṅgūṣya* *sāman*, the *Sāman* suitable for loud chanting, such as the *Rathantara* and others.
The meaning is that it should be brought about by that [chanting].
In the *ṛks* beginning with "abhi tvā śūra" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 7.32.22), the name "Sāman" is applied to the singing (*gāna*).
Thus it has been stated: "The designation 'Sāman' applies to the melodic chants" (*Jaimini Sūtra* 2.1.36).

"By that Indra, our fathers—specific ancestors, the ancient Aṅgirases—who, being knowers of the tracks and thus knowers of the path, found and recovered the cows that had been seized by the Asura Paṇi, while they were indeed offering worship to him."
To you;
in the first noble [verse], the second [is]:
"those who know the words."
Regarding the word *padāni jānanti*: the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*;
then, the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*.
They found.
[The root] *vid* is used in the sense of "obtaining.
The augment *num* is applied by the rule *śe mucādīnām*.
1. The word "ḍha" is to be supplied from the context. 2. Regarding the sequence "ca-cha-ṇa-ta-na-pha," he says it is a hymn (stotra).
3. "Ḍha" means that which is to be accomplished by that [hymn].

At the sacrifice of Indra and the Aṅgirases, Saramā found nourishment for her offspring; Bṛhaspati split the mountain and found the cows; the men lowed together with the dawns. 3. At the sacrifice of Indra and the Aṅgirases, Saramā found nourishment for her offspring; Bṛhaspati split the mountain and found the cows; the men lowed together with the dawns. 3.
In this regard, there is this narrative:
There was a divine dog named Saramā.
When the cows had been carried off by the Paṇis, Indra dispatched Saramā in order to search for them.
Just as in the world a hunter releases a dog to search for deer within the forest, so it was;
and Saramā spoke thus:
"O Indra, if you provide food such as milk belonging to that place for our child, then I shall go."
He said, "So be it.
And thus says the Śāṭyāyanaka: "O Saramā, I shall provide food and progeny for you who have found our cows. Then, having gone there, he discovered the location of the cows;
and having discovered it, he reported it to him.
Likewise, it is explained in this [text] that after the cows had been reported [stolen], Indra killed that Asura and recovered those cows.
This is the meaning established herein.
When Indra and the Aṅgirases were sent forth on their quest, Saramā, the divine dog, found food for her own offspring;
"food" (*dhāsi*) is a name for nourishment, as it is listed among the names for food in the Nirukta (2.7.11): "Food is *irā*.
Likewise, when the cows had been announced, Bṛhaspati—Indra, the sovereign lord of the great gods (*bṛhatām devānām*)—smote the devouring mountain-demon (*adri*).
By him the "cows" were struck down; he "found," that is, obtained them.
Then the "leaders," the gods, [obtained them] together with the "ustriyās," that is, cows—"ustriyā" being a name for a cow.
"Saṃ vāvaśanta" means they lowed loudly with sounds of joy;
or rather, it means that by means of the cows as instruments, they desired his milk and so forth, or they came together.

In the word *iṣṭau*: from the root *iṣ* "to go," the suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), and by the rule *mantre vṛṣa-* etc., the acute accent (*udāttatva*) is assigned to the *ktin*.
[The form] *vidat*.

In the case of *vida lābhe* (the root *vid* meaning "to obtain"), the suffix *aṅ* is applied because it belongs to the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. The absence of the augment *aṭ* occurs due to the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), by virtue of its diversity (*bāhulyam*), [the augment is absent] even when there is conjunction with *ām*."
Only this vowel remains;
because it occurs at the beginning of a quarter-verse (*pādādi*), there is no elision by *nighāta*.
*Saramā*.
Yāska [states]: "Saramā is so called because of her running" (Nirukta 11.24).
The suffix *am* is an *auṇādika* [derivative] from the root *sṛ*.
[The word is] *dhāsim*.
The root *dheṭ* means "to drink. That which is held (*dhīyate*) or drunk (*pīyate*) is called *dhāsi*.
The suffix *si* is [added] according to the *uṇādi* rules.
Alternatively,
from the root *dadhāti* in the sense of "nourishing," the suffix *map* is applied; thus,
*bṛhaspatiḥ*.
By the rule "tadbṛhatoḥ karapatyoścoradevatyayoḥ suṭ talopaśca" (Pāṇini 6.1.157), there is the addition of the augment *suṭ* and the elision (*lopa*) of the *tal*.
The word *gṛha* has its accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). Regarding this, it has been stated that some authorities maintain that it has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
The word *pati* ends in the suffix *ati* and is accented on its first syllable.
Therefore, by the rule "in the case of *vanaspati* and similar compounds," both the preceding and following members simultaneously retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
[Thus it is] *ustriyābhiḥ*.

The word *gauḥ* (cow) is explained as "that which dwells in [the pasture] where milk and such are found. From the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling," the suffix *rak* is applied in the locative sense according to the rule *sphāyitañci*, etc.;
the semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs according to the rule *vacisvapi*, etc.
"In the word *uṣṭra*, the suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of the base itself according to the rule for the *pṛṣodarādi* group," so says the Nighaṇṭubhāṣya.
For *gha* is indeed the substitute [for *tra*];
it bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).

*vāvaśanta*: from the root *vāś* meaning "to sound," in the *yaṅ*-intensive form, with the *laṅ* suffix, the substitution of *jha* by *an*, and because it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, there is the elision of the *at* (the *yaṅ*) and the elision of the *y*.
The shortening of the verbal root occurs by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

Alternatively, from the root *vaś* in the sense of "desire" (*kāntau*), when the *yaṅ* suffix is applied, the rule *na vaśaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.20) prohibits the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); thus, the grammatical derivation proceeds as before.

1. *la-kṣīrādikamajamaka* means they did not obtain milk and so forth; *sa-kṣīrādikamalabhanta* means they obtained milk and so forth. 2. *ḍha-kṣīrāditi*. 3. *u-pratiṣiddhe laṅi*; when there is a prohibition, the *laṅ* [tense] is used.
[A. 1. 11. Sū. 62] First Chapter, 425:
He, the one worthy of praise, together with the *suṣṭubh* and *stobha* chants, seated with the sages, by his celestial voice, [shattered] the mountain for the sake of the Navagvas.
O Indra, O Śakra, with your thundering roar you shattered the enclosure of Vala, which was filled with cattle, by means of your swift-moving weapons.

He, with the *suṣṭubh* chant, he with the *stobha*, seated with the seers, by means of his resonant voice—O Indra, O Śakra, you who are worthy of praise, with the Navagvas and the Saraṇyus, you rent asunder the mountain Phaliga and Vala with a roar, using the ten cows.
The Aṅgirases are of two kinds. Those who performed the sacrificial session (*sattra*) and departed after completing it in nine months are the Navagvas.
Yāska explained [them] thus: "The Navagvas are those whose movement is like fresh butter" (*Nirukta* 11.19).
But those who completed [the sacrifice] in ten months were the Daśagvas.
With such twice-born men—both types—being wise (*medhāvin*) and *saraṇyu*, desiring a beautiful course (*saraṇam*), seven in number;
for here, seven Aṅgirases beginning with Medhātithi are seen.

By the Aṅgirases who have become thus, [he is] "svaryaḥ," meaning well-attainable through "suṣṭubhā," that is, by means of a beautiful hymn (stoma) joined with a "svara," a melodious tone such as the udātta and others;
or alternatively,
by means of a "stubh" or praise performed in tones such as the low (mandra) and middle (madhyama).
Alternatively, "śabdanīyaḥ" means "to be praised. O "Śakra," O powerful one, O "Indra," you who are such as this, [you struck] "adrim," meaning the mountain that was to be split with the thunderbolt.
‘Phaliga’ means a reflection or a reflected image.
Since that [reflection] exists in it, water that is clear is called *phali*.
It is called *phaliga* because it goes (*gacchati*) as a support (*ādhāratvena*);
or else,
it is the fruit (*phala*), such as rice and other grains.
That which exists when this is present is *phali*, meaning water that increases;
that which goes toward it is *phaliga*.
You caused such a cloud (*vala*) to tremble—that is, to fear—by means of your own roar (*raveṇa*).
The meaning is that the cloud is terrified merely by hearing your voice.
Alternatively,
"adri" refers to a mountain.
In this [cloud], layers and so forth are eaten (*adyate*).
*Phaliga* means a cloud,
because it is listed among its names in [the Nirukta] as "phaliga is a stone" (Nirukta 1.10.17).
Valoḍasura:
because [the word] is used with reference to an Asura in such passages as, "The gods indeed searched for the cows among Vala" (Ai.
Brā. 6.24). The meaning is that even these three were struck with fear merely by hearing your name.
*saḥ* is a single word used here to fill out the meter; *suṣṭubhā*;
the root *stobhati* means "to praise."
The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) characterized by perfection and so forth.
He is one whose *stobha* (chanting) is beautiful.
By the rule “*nambsumyām...*” (Pāṇini 6.2.172), there is udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *upasargātsunoti*.

In the word *stubhā*, although the hymn (*stotra*) functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is treated as the agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to its own operation; thus, from the root *stubh* meaning "to praise," the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kvip ca*.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. [The form] *sasa* [is derived from *sadbhiḥ*]; the elision (*luk*) of the *bhis* ending is by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
The word *svaryaḥ* [is derived as follows]: from the root *svṛ*, meaning "to sound" or "to afflict," the suffix *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *ṛhaloṇyat*.
The absence of *vṛddhi* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
There is the *svarita* accent according to the rule “*tisrvaritam*”.
[The word is] *navagvaiḥ*.

When the word *nava* is used as an upapada with the root *gam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). By the rule *gamaḥ kau* (Pāṇini 6.4.40), there is the elision of the nasal; then, by the statement *uca gamādīnām iti vaktavyam* (Pāṇini 6.4.40.2), the substitution of the vowel *u* for the final syllable occurs. Thus, *navagvāḥ* means "those whose going (*gūḥ*) is by means of nine.
The addition of the vowel *a* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively,
the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*);
the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed as before.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [prevails].
*Saraṇyubhiḥ*:
those who desire for themselves a course (*saraṇa*) are *saraṇyavaḥ*.
In the case of *kyac*, there is the elision of another [suffix], which is Vedic;
by the rule *kyācchandasī*, the suffix *u* is applied,
as in *phaligam*.
*Phaliga* means that which goes through water;
the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* according to the rule *ḍo ’nyatrāpi dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 3.2.48).
It means strength (*valam*).
It covers (*vṛṇoti*), thus it is *vala*.
[The suffix] *ac* is added according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).
The substitution of *l* for *v* occurs by virtue of its inclusion in the *kapilakādi* group (Pāṇini Mañjarī 8.2.18).

*darayaḥ* | [The root] *dṛ* is used in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*). Since it is listed among the *ghaṭādi* group in the rule *dṛ bhaye*, it possesses the marker *m*; consequently, by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*, there is shortening of the vowel.
1. Those beginning with ḍha are the roots of the adādi class.
2. Ḍha refers to [the group] beginning with sa and phala, and so forth. (Ka.

O wondrous Indra, with the Aṅgirases you disclosed the light through the dawn and the sun; with the rays of light you spread out the darkness upon the earth. You have propped up the ridge of heaven and established the intermediate region.

Seeking virtues, O wondrous one, with the Aṅgirases, you have spread out the darkness with the Dawns, with Sūrya, and with the rays of light; O Indra, you have extended the ridges of the earth and propped up the highest realm of heaven. 5.

O *dasma*, O wondrous one, O subduer of enemies, Indra, being praised (*guṇānaḥ*) by the Aṅgirases, the seers, together with the Dawn and the Sun, you pierced apart (*vi vaḥ*), that is, destroyed, the darkness with the rays of light.
Likewise, O Indra, you spread out (*vi aprathayaḥ*), that is, made extensive, the high ridge (*sānu*) of the earth;
you leveled this uneven ground.
Likewise, you have propped up the base—the root region—of the *rajas*, the world of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) from heaven;
that is to say, you have made it so that the foundation of the intermediate world becomes firm.
[The word] *guṇānaḥ* [is used].
In the sense of the object (karmaṇi), when the suffix śānac would have been expected after the present stem (laṭ) by virtue of the *yak* affix, there is instead the substitution of *bhā*.
By the rule “the short vowel [is substituted] for roots beginning with *pū*,” the vowel becomes short;
and by the property of being marked with *cit*, the word is oxytone (antodātta).
*Dasma*:
[derived from] the root *dasu* in the sense of "to destroy" (*upakṣaye*).
By the rule *ipiyudhīndhidasi°* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.142), the suffix *avina* is applied.
*vaḥ*:

from the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*), in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *sip*, the *clelṛ* substitute is applied by the rule "in mantras, [the substitution of] *ghas* etc. (*mantre ghasa°*).
There is elision of the *s* by the rule *guṇe ‘halūṅyābhyaḥ*. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge ‘pi*. [The word is] *andhaḥ*.
Yāska [states]: “Darkness (tamas) is also called blind; meditation does not exist therein” (Nirukta 5.1).
Regarding *rajas*: having stated that “worlds (lokas) are called *rājāṃsi*” (Nirukta 4.19), the word *rajas* denotes the worlds.
The elision of the genitive case ending is by the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39].
Regarding *astabhāyaḥ*: in the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *ā* is applied according to the rule *stambhustambhu* [Pāṇini 3.1.82] and others.

By the rule *chandasi śāyaj api* (Pāṇini 3.1.84), even in the case of the root *ah*, there is the substitution of *śāyac* for the suffix *śān* by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*). There is the elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *aniditām* [6.4.24],
and the augment *aṭ* is added.
In the *pravargya* recitation during the *abhiṣṭava*, this verse beginning with "That indeed is most manifest" (*tadu prayakṣatamam*) is used.

Regarding the verse beginning with "Then for the hero" (*atho naram*), it is stated in the Sūtra: "That indeed is most manifest; his deed follows; they milk the ghee and the milk" (*tadu prayakṣatamamasya karma manvajñabho duhāte ghṛtaṃ payaḥ*; Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.7).
That deed of the most manifest, wondrous one is most beautiful;
it is his marvelous power that he poured forth the rivers, flowing with honey-colored waters, at the close of day.

That indeed is his most manifest deed; it is the most beautiful marvel of this wondrous one: that he caused the four rivers, whose waters are honey-sweet, to pour forth their floods into the lower valley. 6.
That very deed of this Indra, the wondrous one worthy of being seen, is most manifest—that is, preeminently worthy of worship.
*Damsas* is a name for a deed;
that very deed is most beautiful—that is, preeminently splendid.

To the question "What was that?", he says: This Indra, at *upahre*—in the vicinity of the earth where [the waters] were to be brought (*upahartavye*)—caused the four principal rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, which possess sweet water (*madhvarṇasaḥ*) and whose dawns (*uparāḥ*) were established there, to overflow (*apinvat*), that is, he poured them out. This is the deed [performed]. (1.
ḍha-sa: Or, [Indra is] the destroyer of enemies.)
2. There is the excellence of the letters *ḍha* and *sa*.
Because it cannot be performed by anyone else, the meaning is that it is "worthy of worship" (*pūjya*).
[This is derived from] the root *yakṣ*, meaning "to worship."
One who will sacrifice is a *yakṣa*;
one who is most excellent among *yakṣas* is *yakṣatama*.
Furthermore, in this *prādi*-compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable preceding member (*avyayapūrvapada*) is applied.
*Daṃsaḥ*: [derived from] the root *das*, meaning "to see" or "to show. It belongs to the *curādi* class and is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

It is called *daṃsa* because it is seen (*dṛśyate*) as something to be performed; it is an action (*karman*). The suffix *asun* is applied in the sense of the object according to the *uṇādi* rules. [The word occurs] in the context of *upahre*.
The root *hū* means "crookedness" (*kauṭilya*).
Here, by a term denoting movement characterized by crookedness, mere movement is indicated.
A region of land is called *upahra* because rivers flow toward it; that is, they go (*gacchanti*) to it.
By the rule *puṃsi saṃjñāyāṃ ghaḥ prāyeṇa* (Pāṇini 3.3.118), the suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*). [The resulting form is] *guṇaḥ*.
There is the accentuation of the original form of the final member of the compound (*kruduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
Furthermore:
the root *piv* means "to sprinkle";
it belongs to the Bhūvādi class.

Four: *śas*. By the rule "In the feminine, *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* [are substituted] for *tri* and *catur*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.59), the substitution of *catasṛ* for the word *catur* is prescribed as having an udātta accent on its first syllable.

When the substitution of a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would otherwise apply, the substitution of *r* [for *ṛ*] is prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* (6.1.100).

Although the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) of the substitute *catvār-* for the word *catur-* is established through the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original), the fact that the accent is specifically prescribed as initial once again indicates that the substitution of *yaṇ* [for *i*] does not function as a *sthānivadbhāva* in a preceding operation; consequently, there is no occurrence of the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) that would otherwise apply by the rule *caturaḥ śasi*.

And there is no prohibition of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule "not at the end of a word" (*na padānta*), because of the restrictive rule (Pāṇini 1.1.58): "In the case of vowel [substitution], lengthening, and elision, only a substitute for an elided letter (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as the original; everything else is indeed treated as the original."
Twice he chose the two ancient, co-dwelling [worlds] with his unwearied hymns of praise;
like Bhaga with his consorts, the one of wondrous deeds sustained heaven and earth in the highest firmament.
Twofold he chose the two ancient, co-dwelling ones; Ayāsya, with his hymns of praise, like Bhaga with his two wives, has sustained the two worlds in the highest expanse, he of wondrous deeds.
*Vayāsyaḥ*:
*yāsaḥ* means effort;
that which is to be accomplished by that [effort] is *yāsya*.
"Na-yāsyaḥ" means "not to be abandoned";
the sense is that it cannot be accomplished by efforts consisting of battle. To the question "How then is it accomplished?", he says:
Being praised with hymns—
mantras in the form of praises— by men who have arisen and are performing the stotra, Indra becomes easily accomplished (susādhya).
Alternatively,
Ayāsya is the fivefold vital breath (prāṇa) that is the sun;
for it indeed moves away from, or issues forth from, the mouth (āsya).
Therefore, Aṅgiras, though he was his disciple, is called Ayāsya by way of figurative designation.
And thus it is handed down by the Chandogas: "Ayāsya meditated upon that Udgītha; they indeed consider him to be Ayāsya because he went forth from the mouth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.12).
Or alternatively:
He exists in the mouth (*āsya*), thus he is *Ayāsya*.
And so says the Vājasaneyaka: "They said, 'Where indeed was he who has thus spoken for us? [He was] within the mouth (*ayāsye antaḥ*)'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.8).
As before, the worshipper is also called *Ayāsya*.

Being praised by that sage through the hymns (*arkaiḥ*)—which function as the means of praise characterized by the expression of qualities established in the virtuous—one who is born eternally; *sanā* is a particle meaning "eternally";
the sense is: "born eternally," meaning existing at all times by nature.
By the term *janmin* (*born*), which denotes the first modification of being (*bhāvavikāra*), the second modification of being, namely *sattā* (existence), is indicated.
This is as in the statement: "The connection of a word with its meaning is innate" (*autpattika*).
For its commentary states: "'Autpattika' means eternal. (Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.5).
Those two whose dwelling place (*okaḥ*), that is, their abode, is the same dark-blue (*nīla*) in the dark-blue space (*vyanīle*);
the meaning is that they have come together.
Such were heaven and earth; he separated them (*vi vavre*) in two ways (*dvitā*), that is, he made them distinct and established them apart.

In the supreme, most excellent, and manifold-supporting sky (*vyoman*), Indra— like the Sun (*bhaga*) possessing beautiful deeds (*sudaṃsāḥ*)— upheld and nourished the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*). Or alternatively,
*menā* is a name for a woman.
And thus Yāska says: "Menā, jhā—these are names for women; they honor them as menā" (Nighaṇṭu 3.21).
The meaning is that Indra nourished the two worlds, which were in the form of women.
Dvitā.
Dvidhā. 1. ḍha-na-sa-śasi. 2. ḍha-su-sādhaḥ.
3. "Ḍha-aupattika" means:
4. "Ḍha-sa" has the sense of "he did not nourish."

In this form, the *takāra* is Vedic. [The suffix] *sanaj*: from the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*), the suffix *ḍa* is applied even to the simple root *jan*, because the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* in the rule *anyeṣvapi dṛśyate* is intended to override all restrictive conditions. Thus, *sanaja* means those two whose constant (*sanā*) birth (*ja*) is [such]. The shortening of the first member is Vedic. Because it belongs to the class beginning with *evam-ādi*, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable; that very accent remains by the accentual rule of the *bahuvrīhi*. The change of the case-ending to *ā* is according to *supāṃ suluk*. *Ayāsya*: from the root *yasu* in the sense of "exertion" (*prayatne*). *Yāsaḥ* means exertion. That which exists therein is *yāsya*. The suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "being there" (*bhave chandasi*). *Ayāsya* is one who is not *yāsya*. The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member is by the rule *parādiśchandasibahulām*. However, regarding the etymology stated in the *Śruti*, the desired form and accent are established through the *pṛṣodarādi* group. *Mene*: this is the substitution of *śeṣa* for the singular instrumental ending *bhyām*, according to *supāṃ suluk*. It is treated as a *pragṛhya* by the rule *śe* (Pāṇini 1.1.13). Alternatively, *menā* is derived from *man* (to think), with the suffix *pacādyac*. The elision of the vowel *a* after the roots *naś* and *man* should be stated as a grammatical rule (*vaktavyam*).
‘Performing beautiful deeds’— *svapaḥ* means beautiful action;
performing that, [he is] ‘the son of strength,’ that is, the son of *śavas*, which is power.
The meaning is "possessing exceeding strength.
"Sudaṃsāḥ" means endowed with excellent sacrificial acts and the like.
Indra, being such as this, "dādhāra"—that is, maintains and nourishes—the "sakhyam," the friendship, "sanemi," that is, ancient, of the sacrificers.
‘Sanemi’ is an ancient name [for ‘old’],
based on the reading ‘pravayāḥ sanemi’ (Nirukta 3.27.4).
Furthermore, even within the raw, moist, and unripened cows, you hold— indeed, you maintain— the ripened milk within their midst.
Likewise, from the black cows—those of black color—and from the ruddy cows—those of red color—you have produced, by contrast, white-colored milk that shines with brilliance.
Friendship (*sakhya*). Friendship is the state of being a friend (*sakhi*);
[the suffix] *ya* is applied by the rule "after *sakhi*, [the suffix] *ya*."
The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
[The root is] *dādhāra*. [The root is] *śṛñ* in the sense of "holding."
Due to its inclusion in the *tujādi* group, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
[The form] *pakkam* [is derived from the root *pac*].
According to Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.52, "paco vaḥ," [the substitution of *va* for *k* occurs].

For him who seeks the ancient [truth], Gotama has fashioned a new prayer for Indra, for the yoking of the two bay steeds. O powerful one, may Nodhas, our good leader, come quickly at dawn with his thought, bringing wealth as a kinsman. sanāyate | gautamaḥ | indra | navyam | atakṣat | brahma | hari-yojanāya | su-nīthāya | naḥ | śavasāna | nodhāḥ | prātar | makṣu | dhiyā-vasuḥ | jagmyāt || 13 ||

That Indra, being eternal, acts as if he were constant; he becomes the foremost of all. O *aśvasāna*, O powerful one, O Indra, for the *hariyojana*—one who yokes the two bay horses (*harī*) to the chariot.
"To Sunītha, the excellent leader— to you who are such, Gotama, the son of the seer Gotama, the seer Nodhas, has fashioned for our sake this new prayer,
this hymn in the form of a Sūkta. Therefore, being praised by us with this hymn, may Indra, the possessor of wealth, come quickly and at once at dawn, through our thought, wisdom, or ritual action."
Regarding *sanāyate*: *sanā* is a particle (*nipāta*) having the same meaning as the word *nitya* (eternal).
Therefore, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied in the sense of habitual practice (*ācāra*).
For *sunītha*: from the root *ṇīñ* in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*), the *thak* suffix is added according to the *uṇādi* rules;
the accent is that of the *thāthādi* group.
The sixth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "tvaṃ mahān," is the seerly work of Nodhas, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and addressed to Indra. It is cataloged as "tvaṃ nava.
This hymn is used in the Marutvatīya Śastra during the second Chandoma day of the Daśarātra sacrifice, which includes the Samūla-ha portion.
In the section beginning with "viśvajito 'gniṃ naraḥ," it is sūtra-ed: "tāṃ su te kīrtiṃ tvaṃ mahāṃ indra yo ha" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).

You, O Indra, are great, you who at your birth with your vital powers established heaven and earth in their places; when all the mountains, even the vast and difficult-to-overcome ones, trembled before you in fear like scattered rays of light. You, O Indra, are great, you who at your birth with your vital powers established heaven and earth in their places; when all the mountains, even the vast and difficult-to-overcome ones, trembled before you in fear like scattered rays of light.
O Indra, you are great and preeminent in all virtues.
You, indeed, who were born— having manifested at that very moment when there was fear caused by the Asuras— then, by means of your own powers (*śuṣma*) which wither the enemies,
you sustained heaven and earth.
The meaning is: "from such a one as you, who do not release [them].
Furthermore:
"O you, by whose very fear (*abhiyā*) all created beings (*viśvā bhūtajātāni*) are pervaded (*viśvā*), and even the mountains (*girayaḥ*), those accumulations of rock."
"O non-existent one! O great one! O my great one! Whatever other great things there may be."
All of them, though difficult to shake and firm, were made to tremble by the people.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like rays."
Just as the rays of the sun quiver here and there in the sky, so too [is this].
*jajñānaḥ* [is derived from] the root *janī* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*),
with the suffix *kānac* applied in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
By the rule "gamahana," etc., there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*).
Due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), reduplication and other operations follow.
By the rule "citaḥ," the word-final syllable is udātta-accented.
In the middle of this *samanapada* "dyāvāpṛthivī," the reading "jajñāna" is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). This is because,
according to the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the elision (*luk*) of the genitive case ending.
*Abhvāḥ*: they are called *abhvāḥ* because they "attain greatness" (*majjāvam prāpnuvanti*) on all sides (*ā samantāt*). They are the great ones.
The suffix *ḍun* is added to the root *bhū* preceded by the prefix *ā*, according to the *uṇādi* rules.
And there is the shortening of the prefix.
Alternatively,
from the root *bhū* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, in the sense of "desire," the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *naji bhuvo ḍit*.
For the great cannot be attained. The elision of *śi* is by the rule "śelopaḥ bahulam chandasi. [The word is] *kiraṇāḥ*.

They are scattered and dispersed, thus they are *kiraṇāḥ*. [The root] *kṛ* means "to scatter. The suffix *kyu* is applied according to *Uṇādisūtra* 2.239: *kṛpvṛjimandi-dhābhyaḥ kyuḥ*. With the substitution of *y* for *v*, the suffix is udātta by virtue of being the first member of the suffix. By the rule *ṛta iddhātoḥ*, the short vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *i*. *Pejana*: [The root] *ejṛ* means "to tremble. In the *laṅ* tense, there is the augment *āṭ*; this is udātta, and there is also *vṛddhi*.
When you, O Indra, bring your two bay horses to the opposing sides, your singer places the thunderbolt in your arms;
with it, O Lord of unyielding will, you, invoked by many, shatter the numerous fortresses of our enemies.

O Indra, when you drive forth your two bay steeds of different courses, your singer places the thunderbolt in your arms—by which, O Lord of unyielding will, you, invoked by many, hurl against your enemies many ancient fortresses.
O Indra, whenever you—whose two bay horses (*harī*) are of various activities (*vivratā*)—bring them to the chariot (*āveḥ*), meaning you yoke the chariot;
at that time, the singer (*jaritā*), your praiser, places (*ādhāt*) the thunderbolt (*vajram*) in your two arms (*bāhvoḥ*), that is, in your hands, by means of his hymn of praise.
The meaning is that through the act of praising, the thunderbolt appears in your hand without any further effort on your part.

O Indra, of unwearied resolve, you who perform the desired rites—with that thunderbolt (*vajra*) with which you strike down or approach your enemies and foes—O you who are invoked by many (*puruhūta*), you approach in order to shatter the numerous fortresses (*puraḥ*), the cities of the Asuras. This is the meaning.
*Vivratā*: "Vrata" is a name for ritual action (*karman*). Those two who possess various *vratas* are [called] *vivratā*.
By the rule *supām suluk*, there is the substitution of the long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent remains on the original form of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
[The word] *veḥ*.
The root *vī* is used in the senses of "motion," "procreation," "beauty," "eating," and "devouring.

Here, from the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) applied in the Vedic *laṅ* tense with the suffix *sip*, the *śap* affix is elided because it belongs to the *adādi* class. The absence of the augment *aṭ* occurs due to the rule: "In the Veda, [the augment] is often absent even when not joined with *māṅ*."
*Dhāt*: from the root *dadhāti*, in the Vedic *luṅ* tense, there is elision of *sic* according to Pāṇini 2.4.77 (*gātisthā...*);
as before, there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*.
O you whose will is not to be resisted!
Yāska [states] that "the root *haryati* has the sense of desiring to obtain" (Nirukta 7.17);
[it is also used in the senses of] "going" and "leaping."
*Kāntiḥ* means lamentation (*vilāpaḥ*). It refers to that which is not desired by one who is enjoying himself, whereas it is desired by one who is not enjoying himself; such is the meaning.
One whose ritual (*kratu*) or action (*karman*) is of such a kind is described as "tādṛśaḥ kratuḥ.

Regarding the word *amitrān*: in the *bahuvrīhi* compound *na santi mitrāṇy eṣām*, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the final syllable of the second member according to the rule *naño jaramaramitramṛtāḥ*.
*iṣṇāsi*.
[The root] *iṣ* [is used] in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*);
here, however, it has the meaning of motion (*gati*).
‘The suffix śnā is applied after roots such as √kri.

Since the ending *sip* is unaccented (*anudātta*) due to its being marked with *p*, its own accent remains; however, because it is connected with a word that has already occurred [in the preceding rule], it does not undergo the *anighāta* (non-suppression) of its accent.

You, O Indra, are the truthful and bold; you are R̥bhukṣan, the friend of men, and the six [rivers]. You slew Śuṣṇa in the battle for nourishment amidst the waters, together with the youthful Kutsa, the possessor of splendor.

You, O Indra, are the true one; you are the bold. You, as the Lord of the Rbhus, are the friend of men. You [have slain] six; you have slain Śuṣṇa in the battle for nourishment at the ocean, together with the youthful, radiant Kutsa. 3.

O Indra, you are *satyaḥ*, meaning truly existent among the existent ones, that is, preeminent among all. Having advanced against these enemies, you are *dhṛṣṇuḥ*, their overcomer and scorner. Furthermore, you are *ṛbhukṣāḥ*, the lord of the *ṛbhus*, or one who has made his dwelling among them; or else, this is a name for greatness—you are great and exalted. You are *naryaḥ*, beneficial to men. Likewise, you are *ṣāṭ*, the subduer of enemies, meaning their slayer. Moreover, *vṛjane* and the following three words are names of battles; here they serve as prior qualifiers. In *vṛjane*, which means characterized by exclusion (*varjana*); for in battle, heroic men are excluded—that is, they are slain. In *pṛkṣe*, which refers to what is to be attained by heroes for the sake of combat; in such a battle, [you are the victor].
1. In the manuscript ḍha, there is no reading “āgamayasi”; rather, it says “āgamanayasi. 2.
In the manuscript ḍha, it reads: “in the sense of desire, sitting, and eating. 3.
In the manuscripts ca, cha, ṇa, ma, and pha, it reads: “with vī.”

Having become a companion (*sacā*)—that is, a helper—to the youthful *Kutsa*, who is brilliant (*dyumat*) and radiant (*dītimat*), you slew (*ahan*) *Śuṣṇa*, the witherer, the son of *Sūrya* known by this name. Regarding *Ṛbhukṣāḥ*: *Ṛbhu* is a name for the wise. He shines (*bhāti*) widely (*uru*). Alternatively, he is called *Ṛbhu* because he shines (*bhāti*) or exists (*bhavati*) through *ṛta* (the sacrifice). When the words *uru* or *ṛta* are used as upapadas [with the roots] *bhā* or *bhū*, the suffix *ku* is applied according to the rule "and *amṛgavādayaḥ*" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.38); the substitution of *ṛ* for the first part of the word is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). The root *kṣai* signifies the act of ruling or sovereignty. He is the lord (*īṭe*) over them, thus *Ṛbhukṣāḥ*. Alternatively, from the root *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling" or "going," the suffix *ini* prescribed by the rule "after *pati* and *stha*" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.452) is applied here due to the force of the term "variously" (*bahulavacanāt*), even though it is not explicitly mentioned; there is also the elision of the *ṭi* portion. In the nominative singular (*sau*), the form becomes *Ṛbhukṣāḥ* according to the rule "for *pathin*, *madhu*, and *ṛbhukṣas*, [the final vowel is replaced by] *ā*" (Pāṇini 7.1.85). The accent is that of the suffix. The *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*). [The word] *saha* is used in the sense of "overpowering. According to the rule "in the Veda, after *saha*" (Pāṇini 3.2.63), the suffix *ṇic* is applied even to the simple root. The change to *ṣ* is Vedic. *Da...* [The rest of the commentary follows].
O Indra, you are indeed such a one that you are ever intent on not harming anyone— no matter how great or small their power— but rather you possess a nature that seeks to favor them,

for you are a deity who bestows grace. Nevertheless, when our enemies find no pleasure in us— that is, when they seek to cause us displeasure— then open wide for us from all sides the paths and directions so that we may reach our goal.
The meaning is: "Act in such a way that our horses may proceed in all directions without obstruction.

Furthermore: "O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), shatter the enemies there like a thunderbolt; slay them with the thunderbolt, which is as hard as a cloud or a mountain—meaning, strike them down fearlessly.
Or alternatively: [the text continues...]
Among mortals, among men, whenever there is displeasure toward anyone, you proceed desiring the non-harming—that is, the absence of injury or destruction—of that enemy’s punishment;
yet toward one such as Kutsa, toward whom there is pleasure, you perform the slaying of the enemy.
Therefore, for us who are dear to you, [grant] the horse, and so forth, as before.
In that case, by the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision (luk) of the genitive case ending.
[The form is] *ariṣyan*.

From the word *riṣ*, when the suffix *kyac* is applied, the substitution of *riṣ* for *riṣ* is prescribed by the rule *durastudrvinasyutrṛṣyati ripyati* (Pāṇini 7.4.36). In a compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member. [The form is] *asmata*.
As before, there is elision of the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-luk*).
In *arbate*,
the letter *n* is replaced by *t* according to the rule "the *n* of *aveṇa* and *khasva* is replaced by *t* when not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*."
The *van* and *niṣ* suffixes are unaccented (*anudātta*).
By elimination, the accent belongs to the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*). Thus: *ghaneva*.

By the rule *mūrtau ghanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.77), when solidity is implied, the root *han* is irregularly formed (*nipātita*) without the suffix *ap*. [The form] *bhathihi* is derived from the root *bha*, which has the sense of "to injure."
In the imperative (loṭ) after a root ending in *py*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap* by the rule "there is diversely [elision] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
O Indra, in that battle for waters, for light, and for the prize, men call upon you;
O self-dependent one, let this protection of yours be present at the gathering, so that it may win us strength in the contests for booty.
O Indra, in the struggle for waters, in the contest for light, and in the battle, men invoke you; O self-dependent one, let this aid of yours be effective for us in the fray for booty. 6.
O Indra, in that battle for the acquisition of waters— of those who go forth and of many men engaged in combat— in which there is *sāti*, the gain, and *svaḥ-mīḷha*;
*mīḷha* being a name for wealth,
it is a battle in which there is well-desirable wealth.
In such a battle, in that well-known conflict, men— those persons desiring to fight— invoke you alone for the sake of assistance;
or rather,
it means in that battle against Vṛtra and others in which there is the *sāti*, the acquisition of water from the flood (*arṇas*).
The sense is that the singers encourage the sound of their hymns for the sake of your battle against Vṛtra, the obstructor of the waters.
Since this is so, O *svadhāvan*—O possessor of food or power, O Indra—let this protection (*ūti*) belonging to you, this your defense, come toward us in the encounter, in the battle;
for in the contests, this protection is that which is to be attained by those who impel it.
That; [here] there is elision of the accusative case ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. In the word *arṇasātau*.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.
Due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacana*), the *uṇādi* suffix *nap* is applied.

From the root *paṇ* meaning "to give," the suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*); by the rule "of *jan*, *man*, and *khan*," there is the substitution of *ā* for the nasal (*anunāsika*).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [prevails]. [The word] *aṅgā*:
by the rule "in *udaka*, there is also *nuṭ*" (*u. sū.* 4. 636), the suffix *asun* is applied to the root *añj*, along with the augment *nuṭ*.
The elision of the *s* in *pīvopavasana* and other such forms is to be stated as occurring in the Vedic language (Pāṇini’s Mahābhāṣya on 6.1.109.6).
There is an acute accent (*udātta*) on the initial syllable due to the rule *nistvādādyudāttatvam*.
As before, the accentuation follows that of a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
In *svarmīḍhe*,
the word *svara* is a *svarita* accent according to the rule "anyaṅkuśvarī svaritau" (Phiṭ-sūtra 74). By the principle of the *bahuvrīhi* compound, that very accent remains.
*Ājā*: by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is replaced by the suffix *ḍā*. *Svadhāvaḥ*.
In the word *matavaso haḥ*, the suffix *matup* undergoes *ruva* (substitution with *u*). [The form] *atasāvyā* [is derived from] the root *ata*, meaning "to go."
The suffix *sādhya* is derived from the *auṇādika* [list];
it has the augment *āt*,
and since the augment is unaccented (*anudātta*), the initial syllable of the suffix is accented (*udātta*).

Regarding the word *bhūta*: by the rule "In the sense of praying (*prārthanā*), [the suffixes] *luṅ* and *luṭ* [are used]," the suffix *luṅ* is employed; and by the rule "In Vedic usage (*chandas*), [the augment *aṭ* is] optional even when not joined with *māṅ*," there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.
1. Crush the enemies, the foes.
2. O Indra, there is no "ha" (interjection/particle).
O wielder of the thunderbolt, you who fight, having shattered the fortresses, destroy that [enemy] while the Soma is pressed.
O King, O Lord of wealth, you who were the first to grant protection freely to Sudās, like sacrificial grass.

O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, you who fight with the pressed soma, you shattered those fortresses for Purukutsa; as you effortlessly tore up the sacrificial grass for Sudās, O King, you formerly provided wide space and prosperity.

O wielder of the thunderbolt, O possessor of the thunderbolt, O Indra, while you were fighting—that is, engaging in battle—with the enemies of Purukutsa, that seer named Saṃjaya, you indeed shattered those fortresses—meaning you destroyed his cities. Moreover, for King Sudās, that person named Saṃjaya, whatever wealth belonged to that demon, you stripped away—that is, you cut off—as easily as one cuts sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Immediately after that, O Indra, Lord of the Vrājas, for that Sudās who has filled you with the oblation, you have created wide space—that is, wealth.
That [word]. By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision (luk) of the case-ending.
[The form] *dardeḥ*.
The root *dṛ* is used in the sense of "tearing apart.

From this root, in its *yaṅ*-lopped (*yaṅluk*) form, when the suffix *sip* of the present tense (*laṭ*) follows, there is elision of the *śap* affix by virtue of the rule stating "it is like the roots beginning with *ad*" (*adādibacca*). Then, the elision of the *s* occurs by the rule "after a consonant, a long vowel, or *ā*, [the *s* of the second person ending is elided]" (*halṅyābbhyaḥ*).
The absence of the augment *aṭ* [in the form *sudāse*] is due to the rule "the augment *aṭ* is generally not applied when joined with a prefix beginning with *cha*.
*Sudāse*: one who gives beautifully (*sudāḥ*) is called *sudāḥ*.
Asun: Yāska [states] that "sudāḥ" means "one who gives auspiciously" (Nirukta 2.24).
Vark.
The root *vṛj* means "to avoid.

In the *laṅ* tense, with the suffix *sip*, there is elision of the *vikaraṇa* by the rule "there is frequent elision in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). Following this, the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the light penultimate vowel, and as before, there is elision of the *s*.
There is also the absence of the augment *aṭ*.
By the rule "the substitute *ku* [is applied] for *cu*," there is the substitution of *ku*; thus, *kaḥ*.
The root *ḍukṛñ* is used in the sense of "making. In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with the suffix *sip*, there is elision (*luk*) of *cli* by the rule "in mantras, [there is elision] of *ghas*" etc.
As before, there is elision of *s* and the absence of *āṭ*.
O Indra, O God, you have made that wondrous nourishment swell for us, like waters flowing in every direction;
so that, O Hero, you may grant it to us yourself, so that it may flow forth at all times like vital strength.

O Indra, O God, you have made that wondrous nourishment of ours swell like waters in its course; so that, O Hero, you may yourself bestow upon us strength at all times, so that it may flow forth for us forever. 8.
O shining god Indra, you have caused that wonderful and admirable food (*tyāṃ viṣam*) of ours to swell (*pīpayaḥ*) throughout the entire expanse of the earth (*parijman*).
The meaning is: act so that the whole earth becomes filled with food.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Or "vāpa" means "water.
Just as you cause the waters—the rainwaters—to flow forth upon the earth by raining them down, so it is here; or rather, it means "to spread."
The sense is: "Just as you cause us, who remain upon the earth, to drink water, so too cause us to drink various kinds of food.
O heroic Indra, just as you bestow (*vyaṃsi*) upon us our own self (*ātmanam*), that is, life (*jīvam*), through food (*iṣā*);
therein lies the illustration.
"From every side, from all directions, flow forth"—that is, flow like water, *ūrjaḥ* (strength/sustenance).
The sense is: "Just as you bestow abundant water upon us, so too do you bestow life in the form of the maintenance of vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
The word *āpaḥ*: when the case-ending *śas* was expected, *jas* is substituted by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*);
the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule beginning with “*asu-” etc.
*pīpayaḥ*.

[The roots] *sphāyī* and *opyāyī* mean "to grow. From the form ending in *pya*, in the Vedic *luṅ* (aorist), there is the substitution of *pī* for *pyā* according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.28 (*pyāyaḥ pī*), by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
1. From the roots ni, śri, dru, and sru, [the suffix *kta* takes the augment *iṭ*]. 2.
[In the case of these roots], there is both the elision of the *ḍha*-suffix and the absence of the elision of the *sel*.

Thus, *ch* is replaced by *caṅ*. [The rules for] the elision of *ṇi*, etc., apply. Alternatively, from the root *pīṅ* (to drink), in the *luṅ* tense with *caṅ*, it is as before. The absence of *aṭ* is due to the rule: “In the Veda, [the augment *aṭ* is] optional even when not joined with a verbal prefix. *Parijman*: The root *jam* means motion; *aj* means motion and throwing. From these two roots preceded by *pari*, the form is derived with the suffix *kanin* as prescribed in the rule beginning with *śvasukṣan*. The locative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *Yamsi*: From the root *yam* (to rest). The elision of *śap* is due to the rule: “In the Veda, [it is] optional. *Ramanam*: By the rule *āṅṅo 'nyatrāpi chandasi dṛśyate*, there is the elision of the *ā* of *ātman*. Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is no lengthening of the penultimate vowel. *Viśvadha*: From the word *viśva*, the suffix *tasil* has its *s* elided and its *t* changed to *dh* by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. *Kṣaradhyai*: From the root *kṣara* (to move). The suffix *adhyai* is added by the rule *tumarthe sesen*. It is acute-accented on the first syllable because it is marked with the *nit* designation.

For you, O Indra, the Gṛtsamadas have uttered prayers with reverence for the sake of the two bay horses. Bring us well-fashioned booty; may he who is enriched by prayer come quickly in the morning. 9. *arkāri te indra gortamebhirbrahmāṇyoktā narmasā haribhyām | supeśasaṃ vājamā bhara no prātarmakṣu dhiyāvasurjagamyāt || 9 ||* It has been chanted for you, O Indra, by the Gṛtsamadas; prayers have been spoken with homage for the two bay steeds. Bring to us booty that is beautifully adorned. May he, the possessor of wealth through our prayer, come swiftly in the morning. 9.
O Indra, this hymn has been performed for you by the Gāutama-s, that is, by the officiating priests (ṛtvij) of that name who are capable of approaching [you]; this is what is meant by "it was made.
He clarifies this very point:

the sacred prayers (*brahmāṇi*), which are collections of mantras, along with *namas*—characterized here as the oblation (*havis*)—have been addressed directly to you, who are joined with your two bay horses (*haribhyām*).
Alternatively,
the suffix *ākāra* denotes a limit (*maryādā*);
that is, they were employed in accordance with the scriptures.

"Bring—meaning, bestow upon us—the *sattvam* (strength) that is 'well-formed' (*supeśas*); for *peśas* is a name for form; that which is endowed with many kinds of forms, and the *vāja* (food)—bring it, that is to say, give it to us."
May Indra, the possessor of wealth, come at dawn—whether by means of wisdom, intellect, or action—for the sake of our protection during the early morning.
It has been stated: "In the Vedic language, the elision of *śi* occurs diversely" (*śe’cchandasi bahulam*); thus there is the elision of *śi*.
[The word is] *supeśasam*.
The root *kṣi* means "a part. The suffix *asun* is applied.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "in the Veda, the first syllable of the final member is udātta," there is the acute accent on the first syllable of the final member.
[The word] *bhava* [is derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *ap*]; by the rule “*hy-ah-amo-h*” [the *m* is elided];
and by the rule “*aco ’ti tiṅaḥ*” [the long vowel is applied] in the *saṃhitā*.
