The seventh hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with “vṛṣṇe śardhāya,” is addressed to the Maruts; it was revealed by Nodhas. The final verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The remaining fourteen verses are in the *jagatī* meter.
Thus it has been enumerated: “*vṛṣṇe panno...* [is] the *māruta* hymn ending in *triṣṭubh*.
On the twenty-fourth day, this *māruta* hymn is to be recited with the *nivid* during the *āgnimāruta* litany.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*pṛkṣasya vṛṣṇe vṛṣṇe śardhāya yajñena vardhateyāgnimārutam*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
On the fifth day of the *ābhiplavika* [six-day period] as well, this is the *mārutanividāna* in the *āgnimāruta* [śastra].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*pṛkṣasya vṛṣṇo vṛṣṇe śardhāya na cit sahotā ityāgnimārutam*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).

To the bull-like host, the well-sacrificing, wise Maruts, bring forth a pure hymn of praise. Like a skillful craftsman with a steady hand, I, the wise one, fashion these songs with my mind—songs that are present at the assemblies. To the bull-like host, the well-sacrificing, wise one; bring forth a pure hymn of praise to the Maruts. Like a skillful craftsman with a steady hand, I, the wise one, fashion these songs with my mind—songs that are present at the assemblies.
1. These have been stated; here, by the first half [of the verse], Nodhas is exhorted in praise:
"O Nodhas, for the showerer (vṛṣṇe) of desires, for the one of excellent sacrifice (sumakhāya), for the wise ordainer (vedhase) who is the creator of flowers, fruits, and so forth."
For when there is wind, flowers and fruits arise; [this is] for such winds. The case ending is indeclinable.
Offer forth—that is, utter—the hymn of praise (*suvṛkti*), which is well-disposed or well-composed, to the host (*śardha*) of the Maruts, those who cry out in measured fashion.
Being thus urged to praise, Nodhas says:
[I am] wise (*dhīraḥ*), intelligent, and possessed of beautiful hands (*suhastyaḥ*), endowed with lovely fingers.
The meaning is "with palms joined in reverence.
Being thus disposed, I "utter" (*samaje*)—that is, I clearly and perfectly pronounce—"with my mind" the "words" (*giraḥ*), which are speech characterized by praise.
These words are those that "prevail" (*ābhuvaḥ*) "in the sciences" (*vidyeṣu*) and "in the sacrifices" (*yajñeṣu*).
The term *ābhū* is used in the sense of a limit;
they are called *ābhūvaḥ* because they are employed according to the scriptures (*yathāśāstram*) and are capable of bringing [the deities] face-to-face.

With hymns and mantras suitable for sacrifice, they praise the ancient host of Maruts—the youthful Rudras, ageless, slayers of the stingy, who have grown mighty like mountains reaching toward the sky.

With their impetuous strength, they cause even all the firm earthly realms to tremble, and likewise those of heaven. The youthful Rudras, ageless, slayers of the stingy, have grown mighty; like mountains reaching toward the sky, they cause even all the firm earthly realms to tremble, and likewise those of heaven, with their impetuous strength.

"The youthful ones" means the young; "the Rudras" means the sons of Rudra; "the ageless" means those free from old age; "the devourers of non-eaters" means the slayers of those gods who do not gratify [them] with oblations; "those whose way is reached" means those whose movement is unimpeded by others; "firm as a mountain"—such are the Maruts, who "have carried [us]," meaning they desire to bring about the fulfillment of the wishes of their worshippers.

Moreover, "all" (viśvā) "beings" (bhuvanāni)—that is, those "born" or "attained"—whether "terrestrial" (pārthivā), meaning existing on earth, or "celestial" (divyā), meaning existing in heaven; even "firm" (dṛḷhā) things, they cause to "fall forward" or "shake" by means of "mujman," for *mujman* is a name for strength.
By means of purifying strength, they cause them to tremble.
It is the destroyer of enjoyment (*abhogghana*).
Those who cause one to enjoy are "the enjoyers" (*bhoja*); that which is not an enjoyer is "non-enjoyer" (*abhoja*).

They are the slayers of those [demons]. The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *han* by the rule "in the Vedic language, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). By the rule "the *h* of a *jhay* [consonant] may optionally become *dh*" (*jhayo ho 'nyatarasyām*, Pāṇini 8.4.62), the *h* is changed to *dh*.
Due to the restrictive rule (niyama) "inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau" (Pāṇini 6.4.12), there is an absence of the long vowel [in the nominative plural].
[The form] is *vavakṣuḥ*. [The root] *vah* [is used] in the sense of "carrying."
From this [root], by the rule "asmāt icchāsani," there is a prohibition of *it*.
There is reduplication (*dvirbhāva*). Then the substitution of *ḍha*, *ka*, and *ṣa* take place.
In the word *saṃyataḥ*, the absence of *it* (the augment *i*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

Due to the prohibition in Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.1.35 (*amantre*), which applies to the *liṭ* tense and the *us* suffix, there is no application of the *ām* affix; consequently, by the rule *ato lopaḥ*, the vowel *a* is elided. The accent is that of the affix (*pratyayasvara*).
There is no *nighāta* because it begins with the first syllable of a *pāda*.

With brilliant ointments they adorn themselves for beauty; upon their chests they have fastened golden ornaments for splendor. Upon their shoulders rest their spears; these heroes were born together by their own inherent power from heaven. With brilliant ointments, they adorn themselves for beauty; upon their chests they have fastened golden ornaments for splendor. With brilliant ointments, they adorn themselves for beauty; upon their chests they have fastened golden ornaments for splendor. Upon their shoulders rest their spears; these heroes were born together by their own inherent power from heaven. 4.
"Vapuḥ" is a name for form.

"For the sake of *vapuḥ*—that is, for the sake of form or beauty—the Maruts manifest their own bodies with various (*citraiḥ*) kinds of ornaments (*añjibhiḥ*) capable of revealing their appearance; they make them manifest.
The meaning is that they adorn themselves."
Upon their chests and between their arms, they placed—meaning they fastened—shining golden necklaces for the sake of beauty.
For what purpose?
For the sake of splendor (*śubhe*).
Moreover: "Upon the shoulders of these Maruts, spears—that is, weapons—were rubbed down; they remained there, polished.
Together with those weapons, the leaders, the Maruts, were born—that is, they manifested—from heaven, from the intermediate space, along with *svadhā*, their own inherent power."
*yatire*: from the root *yat* (meaning "to strive"),
in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is elision of the *e* augment and the reduplication by the rule *ata ekahalmadhye*.
In the case of *śubhe*: [the root] *śubh* means "to shine. The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad* and so forth.
The word *mimṛkṣuḥ* has an acute accent on the fourth syllable by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. [The root] *mṛj* means "to cleanse."
Because it is preceded by *san*, there is the absence of *iṭ*.
Due to the *kit* status of *san* according to the rule "halantācca," there is an absence of *guṇa*. [Then follow] reduplication and so forth.
In the word *saṃyataḥ*, the substitution of *it* (the long vowel *ī*) occurs.
In the case of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *us*, there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule *ato lopaḥ*. Thus, [we have] *jajñire*.
The root *jan* is used in the sense of "manifestation.
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), there is elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule beginning with *gamahana*.
1. The ḍa- and sa-vastus. 2. Likewise, the ḍha-vastus on the chests.
The sons of Īśāna, the destroyers of enemies, have created the winds and lightnings by means of their powers.
The steadfast ones milk the celestial waters from above; with their flowing streams, they cause the earth to swell with milk.

Created by Īśāna, the roaring ones, destroyers of enemies, have made themselves like winds and lightnings through their powers. They milk the heights; as sustainers, they draw down the celestial waters; moving all around, they nourish the earth with milk.
Making the worshiper their sovereign lord and the master of wealth, they are the *dhunayaḥ*— the shakers of clouds and the like— and the *riṣādasaḥ*— the devourers of those who cause harm;
or alternatively, the *riṣādasaḥ* are those who cast away (*asitāraḥ*) the injury (*riṣāt*) of those who do harm.

The Maruts, being thus constituted, by their own powers (*taviṣībhiḥ*)—that is, by their own strengths—produce the winds, such as the *purovāta* (fore-winds), and the lightnings, that is, the flashing flashes of lightning. And having done so, the Maruts—the wanderers (*parijrayaḥ*), the shakers (*dhṛtayaḥ*)—milk the celestial udders (*divyāni ūdhaḥ*), which exist in heaven and serve as the source of water; they empty them. The meaning is that they render them devoid of water.
Immediately thereafter, they nourish and sprinkle the earth with water that has come from the clouds.
*Ṛṣādamaḥ*: [derived from] the root *ṛś* in the sense of "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*). The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*).
They are called *riṣāḥ* because they injure or harm; those who devour them are *riṣādasaḥ*.
[The suffix] *asun* [is applied here].
The first member [of the compound] has the udātta accent;
the second member retains its original accent (prakṛtisvara).
Or else:

From the word *riśat*, which is formed with the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle), the suffix *kip* is applied after the root *asu* in the sense of "casting" (*kṣepaṇe*). By metathesis (*vyatyaya*), there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the first member, and the word is also oxytone (*antodāttatva*).
*akrata*. The *luṅ* (aorist) suffix is used for the present tense due to Vedic usage;
by the rule "in mantras [the root] *ghas* [is substituted]," there is the elision (*luk*) of *cli*.
*Ūdhaḥ*:
the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
In the *Maruttīya* treatise, the verse "pinvanty apaḥ" is a *dhāyyā*.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "The *dhāyyās* are 'agnir netā', 'tvaṃ soma kratubhiḥ', and 'pinvanty apaḥ'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.14).

The bounteous Maruts pour forth the waters; they increase the milk and the ghee, becoming as they are. Like a steed for the sake of rain, they lead forth the vigorous one; they milk the thundering, inexhaustible spring.

The Maruts, the bounteous givers, pour forth the waters; they have brought the butter-rich milk in three portions. Like a steed for the sake of rain, they lead forth the vigorous one; they milk the thundering, inexhaustible spring.

The Maruts, who are "givers of good gifts" (sudānavaḥ) meaning those whose giving is beautiful, cause the waters—which are like milk, full of essence—to swell and pour forth. They are the "active ones" (ābhuvah); they are called "active" (ābhuvah) because they come into being; they are the officiating priests (ṛtvijaḥ).
"In the sacrifices accompanied by offerings of clarified butter (*ghṛtavat*).
The sense is that just as one pours clarified butter, so too do the Maruts bring rain.
He states the reason for this:

Just as riders train a horse for the sake of battle, they thus lead forth the swift, impetuous cloud; they bring it under their control, O brother. And having trained it, [they lead] the thundering, roaring, inexhaustible fountain—*utsa* meaning a fountain, and *utsa-vanya-sad-āpaḥ* meaning the cloud whose waters dwell in the fountain.
They milk it; they empty it.
*Sudānavaḥ*: *suprayantaḥ* [is derived from] the word *dānu*, which is udātta on its first syllable.
In a bahuvrīhi compound, by the rule "that which is udātta on the first syllable in the Veda," there is udāttatva on the first syllable of the final member.
*Mihe*:
from the root *miha* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (*secane*),
the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpadādi*.
Regarding the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168), according to the Vaśikṣā, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is udātta.

In the word *stanayantam*, the root *stan* means "to sound"; it belongs to the curādi class and ends in *n*. Due to the status of the elision of the suffix *aṇ* as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no occurrence of vṛddhi.

O bulls, masters of magic, with wondrous luster, like mountains, possessing self-radiant power, swift-moving—you devour the forests like wild elephants when you have harnessed your might to the ruddy dawns. mahiṣāsaḥ | māyinaḥ | citrabhānavaḥ | girayaḥ | na | svarṇavasas | raghupradas | mṛgāiva | hastinaḥ | khādatha | vanā | yat | aruṇīṣu | tavīṣīḥ | ayugdhvam || 7 ||
"Mahipāsaḥ" is a name for "great.

O "mahipāsaḥ," you who are great; "māyinaḥ," wise; "citrabhānavaḥ," possessing beautiful luster; "girayo na," like mountains; "svatavasaḥ," endowed with your own strength; "raghuṣyadaḥ," swift-moving—O you who are distinguished by such qualities, O "hastinaḥ," possessors of hands, like "mṛgā iva," wild beasts, namely elephants, you "khādaya," devour, "vanā," the forests, that is, the multitudes of trees.
The meaning is as follows: "Because" (*yat*) you have "yoked" (*ayugdhvam*) "powers" (*taviṣīḥ*), that is, strengths, "to the ruddy ones" (*aruṇīṣu*), that is, to the ruddy-colored mares;
therefore, since your vehicle is likewise powerful, the sense is that you, being joined with it, enjoy everything.
*Raghuṣyadaḥ*: from the root *syand*, meaning "to flow" or "to move. They are called *raghuṣyadaḥ* because they move or go swiftly (*raghu*).
In the word *‘kiṃca’*, there is the suffix *kip*. By the rule *‘aniditām’* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), there is elision of the nasal (*n*).
By the rule *‘vālamūlaladhvalam’* (Pāṇini-mahābhāṣya 8.2.18), there is an optional substitution of *la* for *ra*.
The word retains the original accent of the final member of the compound (kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam).
*Khādatha*:
from the root *khād* in the sense of "eating."
*ayugdhvam*. [The root] *yujir* [is used] in the sense of "joining.
In the *luṅ* tense, *sic* is substituted for *cli*.
The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* is by the rule "ekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.39).
The elision of the letter *m* is by the rule "dhi ca" (Pāṇini 8.2.25).
The substitution of the guttural (*ku*) is by the rule "coḥ kuḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.30).
The augment *aṭ* is acute;
because it is connected with a word-break (*yadvṛtta*), it does not undergo elision (*anighāta*).

Like lions they roar, the wise ones; like well-adorned deer, the all-knowing ones. Enlivening the nights with spotted deer and spears, they press together in their onset, powerful and wrathful as serpents. 8. Like lions, they roar; the wise ones; like well-adorned deer, the all-knowing ones; enlivening the nights; with spotted deer and spears; together; pressing hard; by their might; serpent-wrathful. 8.
"Pracetasaḥ" means those of preeminent knowledge; "like lions" they "roar," making a loud sound.
The sense is that just as lions make a deep sound in mountain caves, so too when the Maruts have arrived, a deep sound arises.
Likewise, they are "well-formed" (supiśaḥ), meaning they possess beautiful limbs or beautiful ornaments.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a *piśāca*.
*Piśa* is a name for form (*rūpa*).
Just as they are adorned with white spots found upon their own bodies, so too are they:

*viśvavedasaḥ*, all-knowing; *kṣapaḥ*, destroyers of enemies; *jinvantaḥ*, gladdening or pleasing the worshippers; and by *śavasā*, through their power, they are *ahimanyavaḥ*—possessing a wrath characterized by striking. The meaning is that they are capable of slaying whatever object gives rise to their anger.
Or alternatively:
*manana* (thinking) is knowledge; thus, *manyu* means knowledge. They are those whose knowledge is not deficient.
The meaning is "those of superior intellect. Such [beings], with the *pṛṣatīs*— *pṛṣatī* being the name for the vehicle of the Maruts— [of the great one].
The *pṛṣatyaḥ* are spotted deer with white spots, according to the historians (*aitihāsikāḥ*);
they are multicolored garlands of clouds, according to the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*).
Accompanied by those *ṛṣṭayaḥ*, which are weapons, and being *sabādhaḥ*, oppressed by enemies—

1. There is an absence of the *vṛddhi* [strengthening] of the *ha*. 2. Indeed, they do not possess such qualities. The ellipsis is: "They come together at once to protect the sacrificers in exactly the same way."
It roars.
[The root] *mad* is used in the sense of "an indistinct sound";
from this, with the *yaṅ-luk* suffix, the present tense (*laṭ*) is formed.
*Piśācva*: [derived from] the root *piś* in the sense of "to divide" (*avayave*). The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*).
*supiśaḥ*: from the root *piś* meaning "to divide" (*avayave*), with the suffix *krip* according to the rule *krip ca*. *pṛpatībhiḥ*.

From the root *pṛṣu* in the sense of "to sprinkle" (*secane*), the suffix *śatṛ* is applied according to *Uṇādisūtra* 2.241: *vartamāne pṛṣadbṛhanmahajjagaccatṛmṛvakṣa*. Because of this treatment as a *śatṛ*-stem, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ugitaśca*.

Consequently, although the rule *śaturanumaḥ* would have required the acute accent (*udātta*) on the feminine noun ending in *nadi*, it does not occur here due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*): *bṛhanmahattor upasaṃkhyānam*.
Address Heaven and Earth, O you who are glorious in your hosts,
who seek men, heroes by your might, and full of pride in your power. Like a brilliant light upon a chariot-seat, the lightning has taken its place upon your chariots, O Maruts.

He has called upon Heaven and Earth—the hosts who bring glory, who follow men, heroes by their might, whose wrath is like that of serpents. Like a brilliant vision upon a chariot-seat, like lightning, O Maruts, your splendor stands upon your chariots.

O Maruts, you who possess the glory of hosts, being sought after in groups and abiding in the form of seven troops; you who are "man-eaters" (nṛṣācaḥ), serving the sacrificers (nṛn) to accept their oblations; you who are heroes by virtue of your valor—being thus endowed with power (śavasā) and possessing a wrathful nature inclined toward striking (ahimanyavaḥ)—you fill the two worlds, heaven and earth (rodasī), with your roar. The sense is: when you arrive, fill heaven and earth with your sound.
Furthermore, O Maruts, your brilliance stands upon your chariots— those vehicles equipped with *vandhurāḥ*, so called because the seat of the charioteer is the place for binding;
it is seen by all as it remains stationed there.
In this regard, two examples are stated:
"It is not non-intelligence.
"Non-intelligence" is a designation for form (*rūpa*).

Just as a stainless form is seen by all, yet lightning is not visible [when obscured], or just as beautiful lightning situated within the clouds is seen by all, so too the light of you who are seated upon the chariot is seen by all; this is the meaning.
Speak! [The lengthening of the vowel occurs] by the rule beginning with "ṛci tunugha," etc. [Thus we have] *nṛṣācaḥ*.
The initial syllable of words beginning with *pāda* is udātta by virtue of being a member of the *atri* group.
*Amatiḥ*:
from the root *am*, meaning "to go" and so forth.
The suffix *ati* in *amartiḥ* is an *auṇādika* suffix [according to Uṇādisūtra 4.499]. It has the udātta accent on the first syllable of the suffix.
[The word] *darśatā*.
The suffix *atac* is applied by the rule “*bhṛ-mṛ-dṛ-ś-*” etc.; because it is marked with the indicator *c*, it bears an udātta accent on its final syllable.

Possessors of all knowledge, equal in wealth, united with their powers, and overflowing with vigor, these heroes— archers who discharge the arrow from the belly of the quiver, possessing infinite strength and wearing lion-like armor— have taken their stand.

The all-knowing ones, dwelling together with riches, mingled with splendors, and overflowing with power—the heroes who are like bulls in their roar, possessing infinite strength—have fixed their arrows within the two quivers. 10.
O you who possess all wealth, the omniscient ones; those who dwell together with riches, having a common abode or being assembled together—meaning, the lords of wealth;
those who are mingled with powers and strengths.
"United" is the meaning.
"Virapśinaḥ" means those who are greatly intoxicated;
that is, the great ones.

The destroyers of enemies, the casters out [of foes], possessing infinite vigor and uninterrupted strength, the Vṛṣakhādas—the term *vṛṣan* here refers to Indra. 1. [This applies] to those whose cause for bondage is the letter *ḍha*.
2. [It applies] to those situated on chariots with *ḍha*, *da*, *dha*, and *sa*; and to those situated on chariots with *ca*, *cha*, *na*, and *pha*.

Those whose weapon is the *khādi* are so described. Alternatively, they are those for whom the bull-like Soma is the *khādi*—that is, to be chewed or drunk. They have the thunderbolt (*vajra*) as their leader; such are the Maruts. *Gabhasti* is a name for the arm. They hold the arrow in their two arms (*gabhastyoḥ*); they carry weapons such as bows and arrows for the purpose of destroying enemies. *Samokasah*: from the root *uc* meaning "to assemble," the suffix *asun* is applied, and by virtue of the rule allowing for various forms (*bahulavacanāt*), there is the substitution of *k* for *c*, as stated in the rule *oka ucaḥ ke* (Pāṇini 7.3.64). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent remains on the first member. *Mamiśvāsaḥ*: the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs according to the rule beginning with *kapilaka*. *Virapśānaḥ*: from the roots *rap* and *lap* meaning "articulate speech," the suffix *śa* is applied after the prefix *vi-* by virtue of the rule allowing for various forms (*bahulavacanāt*). Those who utter various sounds are *virapśāḥ*; those who possess such [voices] are *virapśānaḥ*. Alternatively, *virapśam* means "various shouting"; those who possess that are *virapśānaḥ*. For the Maruts indeed produce various sounds. The accent is that of the suffix *ini*. *Astāraḥ*: the suffix *tṛn* has the sense of agency (*tācchilika*); the absence of the augment *iṭ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The initial vowel is acute (*udātta*) due to the rule *nistvādi*. *Anantaśuṣmāḥ*: that which has no end is *anantaḥ*. By the rule *na subhyām*, the final syllable of the second member is acute. Those whose strength (*śuṣma*) or power is endless are *anantaśuṣmāḥ*. In a *bahuvrīhi*, the accent remains on the first member. Regarding *vṛṣā* and the others: from the root *khād* meaning "to eat," the suffix *ina* is added according to the *augādika* rules. The word *nṛpāḥ* ends in the suffix *kanin* and is acute on the first syllable. With their golden fellies, increasing the waters, they strike up against the mountains like kinsmen; the Maruts—unwearied, self-moving, casting down the firm, makers of the storm, with glittering spears—[rush forth]. With their golden fellies, increasing the waters, they strike up against the mountains like kinsmen; the Maruts—unwearied, self-moving, casting down the firm, makers of the storm, with glittering spears—[rush forth].

The Maruts, with their golden, sun-bright (*suvarṇamaya*)—or rather, delightful (*hitaramaṇīya*)—wheels (*pavi*), strike upwards (*urjighnante*) the mountains, the peaked ones, the clouds, or the heaps of rocks; that is to say, they cause them to rise up from their place, they displace them. Therein lies the illustration: *padhyaḥ na*—just as a chariot traveling on a road crushes and carries upward the grass, trees, and so forth standing in its path; or, just as yoked cows break down the trees and other obstacles situated on the way. What kind of Maruts are they? *Payovṛdhaḥ*: increasers of milk, that is, of the rain-water; or, growing by means of the milk of the spotted deer (*pṛśni*). For it is heard in scripture: "The Maruts were born from the milk of the spotted deer" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.2.11.4). *Makhāḥ*: *Makha* is a name for sacrifice; they possess that. *Ayāsaḥ*: those who go toward the place of sacrifice. *Svasṛtaḥ*: those who move or go by themselves against the enemies. *Dhruvacyutaḥ*: shakers even of the firm, immovable things such as mountains. *Dudhrakṛtaḥ*: making themselves the sustainers (*dhārayitṛ*) of the visible world (*dudhra*); or, making themselves difficult to be held by others (*durdhara*). *Bhrājadṛṣṭayaḥ*: possessing shining weapons. Regarding *urjighnante*: the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by transposition (*vyatyaya*) from the root *han*. By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the elision (*ślau*) of the suffix *śap*. By "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplication. By "gamahana... etc., there is the elision of the penultimate vowel. By "ho hanteḥ," there is the substitution of *gh* for *h*. The change to the final letter (*antādeśa*) is by transposition. *Padhyaḥ*: existing on the path (*pathi*). By the rule "bhave chandasi," the suffix *yat* is applied. By "nastaddhite," there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the *i* of *pathi*). The accent on the final syllable is by transposition. Or, by the rule "chandasyubhayathā," the suffix *īn* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). The circumflex (*svarita*) of the case-ending follows the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ. *Ayāsaḥ*: from the roots *aya* or *paya* meaning "to go. They go, thus they are *ayāḥ*. The suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of the present participle (*pacādyac*). The form *ājaserasuk* applies here. *Dudhrakṛtaḥ*: here, by the word *duḥ*, the wicked (*duṣṭa*) are indicated. From the root *dhṛṣ* meaning "to hold," that which holds the wicked is *dudhraḥ*. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule "mūlavibhujādi" (Pāṇini 3.2.5.2). Or, by the rule "īpsuḥsuṣu," when *duḥ* is the governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *khal* is used in the sense of the object. The absence of *guṇa* is Vedic. They make him [themselves] such, thus they are *dudhrakṛtaḥ*. The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *kṛ* by the rule "kvip ca"; the elision of the *r* is Vedic.

O Maruts, bestow upon our patrons a fame that is difficult for enemies to overcome in battles, a brilliant and invincible strength, and a preeminent, all-people-loving lineage. May we nourish our children and progeny for a hundred winters.

O Maruts, bestow upon our patrons that which is worthy of celebration, invincible in battles, radiant, and impetuous strength; grant them a bow that strikes the foe, a hymn of praise, and a son who is the light of all people. May we nourish our offspring and progeny for a hundred winters. 14.
O Maruts, "place"— that is, bestow— a son upon the "magnificent" (maghavatsu) sacrificers, those endowed with wealth characterized by oblations. What kind of son?
"He should be repeatedly placed at the forefront in all undertakings;
the meaning is that he is skilled in every task.
In battles among the sons [of kings], he is difficult to overcome—that is, he is hard to surpass."

The meaning is "unconquerable. "Ghumnantam" means radiant; "śuṣmam" means the dryer of enemies, the powerful one; "dhanaspṛtam" means the toucher of wealth, or one who is pleased by riches; "uktham"—*uktha* being a hymn of praise.
Then this [word]: it means "praiseworthy. "Viśvacarṣaṇim" means the one who specifically beholds all, the omniscient one.
May we, living for a hundred winters— whereby "winters" (himāḥ) refers here to the hundred years characterized by the Hemanta season— nourish and sustain such a son, grandson, and great-grandson.
In this context, the word *hima* denotes the Hemanta seasons associated with cold.
And thus it is recited in the Brāhmaṇa: "He says, 'A hundred winters,' whereby he indeed says, 'May I honor you for a hundred winters'" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.8.5).
It is *carkṛtyam*.

By the maxim "when a root is mentioned, that which ends in *yaṅ* as well is included" (Paribhāṣā 93), the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *kṛ* in its *yaṅ*-luṅ form by Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.120, "vibhāṣā kṛtpvoḥ. The augment *tuk* is then added.
Because the suffix *pratyaya* has the marker *pittva*, it is *anudātta* (unaccented), and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.

In the case of *putsu*, the word *pṛtanā* undergoes the substitution of *pṛd* according to the rule: "An addition to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.63 is that the words *māṃs*, *tṛs*, and *tṛn* [undergo specific changes] when preceded by *pad*. Thus, there is the replacement of *pṛtanā* with *pṛd*.
*Duṣtaram*:
[derived from] the root *tṛ*, meaning "to swim" or "to cross over.
By the rule *īpsu-suṣu*, the suffix *khal* is applied.
The substitution of *p* for *m* occurs because [the root] belongs to the *supām ādeśa* class of irregular forms.
By the rule regarding the accent of the suffix (*ltisvara*), the syllable preceding the suffix is udātta. *Dhattana*.
In the expression "tasana-sana-dhanāśca," there is the substitution of "tasa" for that [word].
For the offering of the omentum of the animal victim belonging to the Ekādaśina group dedicated to the Maruts, "nū ṣṭiraṃ" is the *yājyā* verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "śucī vo havyā marutaḥ śucīnāṃ nū ṣṭiraṃ masto vīravantam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).

O Maruts, bestow upon us enduring wealth, rich in heroes, which overcomes the onset of enemies—a thousandfold, a hundredfold, and ever-increasing. May he who is enriched by prayer come quickly in the morning.
Now, O Maruts, bestow upon us stable wealth, accompanied by heroes, overcoming enemies, thousandfold, hundredfold, and ever-increasing. May he who is rich in prayer come quickly in the morning. 15.
O Maruts, make [this] firm, well-established, and possessed of heroes— meaning endowed with heroic sons—
or rather,
endowed with valor.
"Bestow upon us—that is, establish within us—such wealth characterized by sons as one who overcomes enemies and withstands the onset of misfortune.
[Wealth] consisting of thousands and hundreds, and thus abundant and increasing;
moreover, may the host of Maruts, having obtained wealth through prayer, intellect, or ritual action, come to us at dawn for our protection."
*nū ṣṭhiram*:
[The lengthening occurs] by the rule *ṛci tunuca*;
[the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] by the rule *pūrvapadāt*.
*Ṛtīṣāham*:
[derived from] the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
‘vaha abhibhave’ | 1. not in the case of the duties of a son;
2. ḍha—bestow [this] upon us quickly!

In the mantra *gameluṃḍi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli* by the rule *ghasa*. There is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) by the rule *gamahana*, etc. The absence of the augment *aṭ* occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅ-yoge 'pi*. [The word] *yajatrāḥ*: the suffix *atran* is added by the rule *aminakṣi*, etc.; due to its being *niṣ* (a kṛt suffix), it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.
The gods have followed the ordinances of *ṛta*; as the sky encompasses the earth, so has he become the encompassing one.
These waters have increased the well-nourished infant in the womb, the well-born offspring in the seat of *ṛta*.

The gods have followed the ordinances of *Ṛta*. He has become an encompassing presence, like the sky over the earth. The waters increase him, the well-nourished one, with praise, in the womb of *Ṛta*, well-born in the embryo. 3-4.
The very meaning already stated is now made clear:

"The gods" went "after" (*anu*) the "vows"—that is, the activities consisting of going, staying, lying down, and so forth—of Agni who had "gone," that is, had fled. Following that, "searching on all sides" (*pariṣṭhiḥ*), a thorough investigation everywhere, "came to be."
"Even the earth became like heaven (dyaus), as if it were the celestial realm, by the gods who were searching for Agni.
The meaning is that all the gods, Indra and the others, reached the earthly world (bhūloka) in order to search for Agni.
"The waters"—that is, the deities of the waters—"increase him," meaning they cause this Agni, who has entered the water, to grow.
The meaning is that he protects him in such a way that even the gods do not see him.
Of what sort [is he]? "By means of praise" (*panvā stotreṇa*), he is "well-nourished" (*suśiśvim*), meaning well-prospered.
"In the womb of Ṛta"—
"womb" (yoni) is a name for water;
[it means] "in the water which is the cause of this Ṛta or sacrifice," "in the embryo," that is, in the middle of the place of the embryo, "well-born," meaning perfectly manifested.
Thus, the fish informed the gods about the fire that was dwelling within the waters;
the meaning is that immediately thereafter, the gods came to know it.
And so says the Taittirīyaka: "He hid himself; he entered the waters; the deities sought him out; the fish told them. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.6.1).
In the Vedic language (*śeṣacchandasi*), there is frequently an elision of the *ślu* suffix according to the rule "vratā | śeṣacchandasi bahulam";
thus [the form] *guḥ*.
The root *iṇ* means "to go.
By the rule *iṇo gā luṅi*, there is the substitution of *gā* [for *iṇ*] in the *luṅ* tense.
By the rule *gātisthā*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*.
From *ātas*, *s* becomes *jus*.
By the rule "usyapadāntāt," there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*). [Thus: *pariṣṭhiḥ*.

The root *iṣ* is used in the sense of "desire. The suffix *ktin* is applied; by the rule *titutra* (Pāṇini 7.2.9), there is a prohibition of the substitution of *it*. By the rule *śakandhvādiṣv āt pararūpam* (Pāṇini 6.1.94), the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is substituted for the vowel *ā*.
By the rule "tādau ca niti," the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) of the verbal root applies. *Bhūma*:
by the rule "supāṃ suluk," the substitution of *ḍā* for the genitive suffix *su*.
The vowel is short by Vedic license (*chandas*).
They cause to increase (*vardhanti*):

because the suffix *śap* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* in the Veda according to the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*), there is the elision of the *ṇi* by the rule "the *ṇi* is elided before an affix that does not take *iṭ*" (*ṇeraniṭi*).
The suffix *śap* is acute by virtue of being *pittva*.
Furthermore, by the accent rule for *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
*Panvā*.
But in the sense of praise, the suffix *u* is added by the *auṇādika* rules to denote the action (*bhāva*). Thus:
*suśiśvi*.
The root *duośri* is used in the senses of "going" and "increasing.
In the word *ādamañjanañjanaḥ*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *utsargācchandasi* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.171).
Subsequently, *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) occurs by the rule *vacisvapi* etc. (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.15).
Because it functions as a *liṅga* (indicative mark), by the rule "in the Veda, [the substitution of] a short vowel is frequent (*bahulam chandasi*)," there is a shortening of the vowel *u*.
There is also a Vedic substitution of *yaṇ*.
By the rule "the prefix *su-* [expresses] honor" (*suḥ pūjāyām*, Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.94), *su-* has the status of a *karmapravacanīya*.
The compound *svatī* is a *prādi-samāsa* according to Pāṇini 2.2.18.4 (*svatī prajāyām*).
It takes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) which constitutes the first member of the compound.
Like nourishment that sustains, like the earth, the broad ground; like a mountain, his arm; like the surging flood, he is the source of bliss.
Like a steed urged forward in its course, like the rushing current of a river—who could restrain him?

Like nourishment, he is not obstructed; like the earth, he is the dwelling place; like a mountain, he is the arm; like the rushing water, he is the source of bliss; like a steed urged forward in its course, like the flood of a river—Who can restrain him? 5–6.
1. They have attained [the goal].

2. And *ca-cha-ṇa-na* increase the fruit. Like nourishment (*puṣṭi*)—which is delightful (*raṇvā*) to the hearts of all and brings about the increase of desired fruits—the fire is delightful to everyone.
Because all worldly and otherworldly activity depends upon fire;
or else, *raṇvā* means nourishment itself, that which is to be approached, to be uttered, or to be praised.

The sense is that just as nourishment is obtained, so too is Agni obtained by means of oblations. Like the *pṛthvī*—the vast *kṣiti*, or earth—Agni is also extensive because he exists in all beings in the form of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*). Like a *giri*, or mountain, he is *bhujma*, the nourisher of all.
Just as everyone, having gathered fruits, roots, and so forth existing on a mountain, partakes of them, so too do all partake while cooking upon fire.
Or rather, having offered oblations into the fire, the sacrificers enjoy the fruit of heaven.

Alternatively, just as a mountain (*giri*) protects all living beings during a famine by sustaining them with its own fruits, roots, and so forth, so too does Agni liberate those who perform sinful deeds.
And thus it is recorded in the Veda: "May Agni release me from that sin" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.8.5.3).
Like water (*kṣodaḥ*), he is *śambhu*, the bringer of happiness.
The meaning is that just as water brings happiness, so too does fire bring happiness to all. *Ajman* is a name for battle.

In the battle at Añjana, like a noble steed—that is, like a well-bred horse characterized by constant movement—impelled forward by its release (*sarga*), Agni likewise, urged on by the singers, goes swiftly with his mind to slay the enemies; this is the sense. And he is like the ocean’s flood (*kṣodaḥ*).
Like water that has the nature of flowing, this [fire] too moves swiftly;
just as a current of water directed toward a low-lying place is difficult to turn back, so too is fire directed toward another fire—this is the meaning.
Therefore, since this is so, who (*kaḥ*) could restrain (*varate*) this fire? Who indeed could stop it?
The meaning is that no one at all is able to prevent it.
*Raṇvā*. The root *ravi* has the meaning "to go. That which is reached or attained is called *raṇva*.

Because of the word "bahulam" (variously) in the rule *kṛbhvastiyoge saṃpadyakartari cviḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.50), the suffix *ac* (as in *pac-ādi*) is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, *bhujma*.
[The root] *bhuja* [is used] in the senses of protecting and eating.
The suffix *mak*, which is prescribed by the rule "yudhrīndhi," also occurs here due to the word *bahula*.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *su*. Thus: *ajman*.
The root *aj* is used in the senses of "going" and "throwing.
The suffix *manin* is applied.

According to the rule, "In the case of roots beginning with *bal*, the substitution of *vī* for *ay* is optionally desired when an affix beginning with a consonant follows that is not a *dhātu*," there is an absence of the *vī* substitution.

The elision of the locative case ending is by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Regarding the word *sarga*: from the root *sṛj* (in the sense of "emission"), the word *sarga* is formed with the suffix *ghañ*, and it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable).
The root *tanj* means "to go.

From this root, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix *-ta*) is applied; by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
By the rule "aniditām," there is the elision of the nasal (*n*).
In *sargeṇa* [the suffix] *prataḥ* is used;
by the rule "the third case [is used] in the sense of the object," there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.
[The word] *varāte*.

The root *vṛñ* is used in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*). From this root, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the suffix *leṭ* is applied; by the rule *leṭoḍaḍāṭau*, the augment *āṭ* is added.
By means of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *śap* is employed.
The absence of the substitution of *ai* occurs because, according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.4.96 (*vaito 'nyatra*), this substitution is optional.
The kinsman of the rivers, like a brother of his sisters, he devours the forests like a king his subjects;
when, impelled by the wind, he has spread through the woods, he shears the hair of the earth as a razor does.

A kinsman of the rivers, like a brother to his sisters, Agni devours the forests as a king devours elephants; when, impelled by the wind, he has spread through the woods, Agni indeed shears the hair of the earth. 7–8.

This Agni is the *jāmi*—the kinsman or relative—of the *sindhūn*, the waters characterized by their flowing nature, because he is their progenitor; thus it is declared in the scripture: "From Agni, the waters" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 8.1). Or rather, the meaning is that having fled from the gods and remaining within the waters, he became their kinsman. Therein is an illustration: like a brother (*bhrātā*) toward his sisters (*svasṝṇām*), for just as he is exceedingly beneficial to them, so is Agni. Such an Agni *atti*—eats or consumes—the *vanāni*, the great forests; that is, he burns them. In this regard, there is a comparison: like a king (*rājā*) [consuming] the *ibhyān*.

1. By the giving of one’s own roots, fruits, and so forth, represented by *ṭa*, *ṇa*, *la*, and *śa*. 2. He wards off the fruits represented by *ca*, *la*, *ṇa*, *da*, *dha*, and *na*. 3. *Ṭha* and *ra* signify the sense of movement; he is praised (*rapyate*). 4. *Ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *pha*, *śa*, and *sa* are illustrative examples.
According to etymological derivation (*nairuktya*), enemies are called *havyāḥ* because they "go with fear" (*bhiyaṃ yanti*);
just as he destroys them along with their very roots, so it is here.
Or alternatively:
"havyā" means the wealthy;
the meaning is that just as a king harms those [wealthy ones] by seizing their wealth, so it is here.

Moreover, whenever he, impelled by the wind—that is, being driven by the wind—variously occupies (*vyasthāt*) forest after forest (*vanā vanāni*), meaning he proceeds to burn them in the manner described, then this very Agni cuts down (*dāti*) the "hairs" (*roma*) belonging to the earth—that is, the plants in the form of hair. The sense is that he burns everything that exists on the earth, whether it be herbs or the multitude of trees.
Svallām.
The absence of the augment *nuṭ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). [He] stood.
In the *luṅ* [aorist], there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic* according to the rule "agānisthā. [The form] *dāti* [is derived from] the root *dāp* in the sense of cutting (*lavana*).
Because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
He breathes in the waters like a swan, never failing; by his mental power he is the most wise among the people, awakening at dawn.
Like Soma, he is a creator born of Truth; he is the protector of cattle, the master of the house, and the possessor of many forms.

He breathes within the waters like a swan resting; most wise in his mental power, he awakens at the dawning of the people. Like Soma, he is the ordainer, born of the Eternal Law (*ṛta*); like a beast, he is auspicious, all-pervading, and difficult to deceive. 9–10.
This Agni, having fled from the gods, breathes—that is, lives—within the waters;
the meaning is that he remains hidden there.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like a swan that does not sink while sitting in the midst of water, such is the fire. What kind of fire is it?

By means of *kratvā kratunā*—that is, by his own light which is the cause of knowledge—he is the most conscious (*cetiṣṭhaḥ*), the one who most excellently makes known, the one who causes all creatures to perceive.
For at night, all people perceive everything enveloped in darkness only through the light of fire.
He is awakened at *uparbud*, that is, at the time of dawn, for the Agnihotra and other rites.
Like Soma, the creator; like Soma, the ordainer and the fashioner.
Just as Soma creates the entire range of edible things in the form of herbs—as in the Vedic revelation:
"Soma is indeed the king of herbs" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.9.1; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.9.17.1).

In the same way, it creates the entire class of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*), because fire itself manifests in the form of the enjoyer. Thus, the Taittirīyaka states: "Fire is the eater of food, the lord of food" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 2.5.7.3).

In the Vājasaneyaka as well, the identity of the enjoyer and the enjoyed with fire and Soma is declared: "This much indeed is this: the food and the eater of food; Soma is the food, and Agni is the eater of food."
Born from *ṛta*.
*Ṛta* is a name for water;
he has manifested from *ṛta*, that is, from water.
With his limbs like those of a beast;
fire dwelling within the midst of water;
he became like a recumbent animal, emaciated and with his limbs contracted.
Then, having become manifest, the All-pervading Lord (Vibhu) became fully developed.
Alternatively, the meaning is that the All-pervading Lord was born with sovereign power, like a cow accompanied by her calf—the infant (Śiśu) still residing within the womb.
[This is] the protection from distress.
"Whose light (*bhās*) extends even to a distant place—that is what is meant by that expression.
Such is the fire that breathes within these [mountains]; this is how it connects with the preceding statement."
It breathes. [The root] *śvas* [is used] in the sense of "breathing.
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *‘rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke’* (Pāṇini 7.2.76).
Since the suffix *tip* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
[The form is] *kratvā*.
Due to the rule "In the Vedic language, there is optionally [the absence of] the *nā* substitute in words such as *jasa*," the absence of *nā* does not occur;
thus, from *uṣas* and *budh*, we have *uṣarbudh*. The root *budh* means "to awaken" or "to perceive."
‘Kip ca’:
[the suffix] *kip*; by the rule ‘*ekāco baśaḥ*’, there is the substitution of a *bha*-sound.
By the rule *aharādīnāṃ patyādau saṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 8.2.70), the substitution of *r* for the *s* [occurs].
*Śirvā*:
from the root *śo* in the sense of "making thin."
The substitution of *ā* [for *e*] occurs by the rule *ādecaḥ*.
The suffix *u* is added by the rule *śaḥ kiṣ chandasi ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.20). Due to the status of being like *san*, there is reduplication.
For this very reason, there is the udātta accent on the first syllable due to the suffix *ni*.
Because it is treated as having the *kit* designation, the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca.
In the first alternative, the *s* [of the nominative] becomes *ā* by the rule "supāṃ suluk."
But in the second [case], as before, there is no absence of non-existence (*nābhāvābhāvaḥ*). [The form] *duremāḥ* [is derived thus]:
because of the rule “*turupe kṛti bahulam*,” even in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the elision (*luk*) does not occur due to the mention of the word “*bahulam*” (variously).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member is maintained.
1. Commencing with *śa* and *sa*.
2. The group of foods beginning with *cha*, *ta*, and *śa*.
The second hymn, consisting of ten verses, is composed of two pādas each; it begins from the middle of the fifth verse. It is the seer Parāśara’s *ṛṣi*-hymn dedicated to Agni.
And it is praised as ‘wealth’ (rayiḥ).
The application [of the mantra] is based on its indicative mark (liṅga):
“Like wealth, manifold; like the sun, beautiful to behold; like life, like breath, eternal; like a son.”
Like a restless bird, thought does not cling to him; like a cow to her calf, he is pure and radiant.

Like wealth, he is manifold; like the sun, he is all-seeing; like life, he is the breath; like a son, he is eternal. Like a swift bird, he haunts the forests; like a cow with milk, he is pure and radiant. 1. 2.

This Agni is like wealth (*vrayiḥ*), desirable and wonderful in form; he is like the sun (*sūraḥ*), the beholder (*saṃdṛk*) who reveals all things. He is like the vital breath (*vāyuḥ*), moving at the beginning of life as the breath that exhales, most dear like the wind.
Or rather:
just as the vital air (*prāṇavāyuḥ*) establishes life (*āyuḥ*).
And thus it is declared in the scripture: "As long as the vital breath dwells in this body, so long is there life" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.2).
In this way, Agni also, in the form of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), is the sustainer of life. He is *nityaḥ sūnuḥ*: like an eternal, constant son who acts for one's pleasure.
Just as a legitimate son acts only for the benefit of his father, so too is this [fire] the bringer of the beneficial heaven.
And thus it is declared in the Agni-veda: "O Jātavedas, the son is the maker of the world for the father" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.7.10).
Like a swift horse that has attained its goal, he is the wakeful sustainer.
The meaning is that Agni likewise supports, sustains, or nourishes the person mounted upon him, just as a horse bears its rider.
Like milk from a cow—that is, like milk which satisfies—he is pure, radiant, and possessed of distinguished splendor (*vibhāvā*).
Agni, characterized by such qualities, *siṣakti*—that is, he comes together with, or attends to—the woods, the forests, in order to burn them.
Citrā:
By the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), there is the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding [vowel] for the case-ending *su*. It is obligatory (*nitya*).

By the rule *nedhuve* (Pāṇini 4.2.104), the suffix *dhyap* is applied. Since this suffix is marked with *p*, it is *anudātta*; thus, only the accent of the prefix (*upasarga*) remains. [The form is] *takkā*.
‘*Takkā* means one who laughs.
Because it is listed among the roots denoting motion (*gatikarmasu*), it has the sense of going here:
*takka-ti* means he goes; thus, a *takka*.
The suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule “it is also seen after other [roots]” (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*),
as in *bhūrṇīḥ*.
In forms such as *ghṛṇiḥ* and *gṛbhiḥ*, the root *bharati* is established with the suffix *nip*.
He maintains security like a dwelling, like a ripened barley grain;
a conqueror of men, like a praised Ṛṣi among the clans, like a joyful steed, he bestows vital strength.

He has established security, like the ocean its dwelling; like ripened barley, he is the conqueror of men; like a seer praised among the people, like a well-pleased steed, he bestows vital strength. 3. 4.
This Agni supports—that is, maintains—the preservation of wealth already acquired;
the sense is that he is capable of protecting the wealth bestowed upon his worshippers.
Like a dwelling place, like a house, he is beautiful to behold.
Alternatively,
"to be gone to" (gantavya) means that it is reached by all, like a house.
"Like ripened barley"—the meaning is that just as ripened barley becomes fit for use, so too is this [self] fit for use by being the cause of effects such as digestion (*pāka*).
"The conqueror of people"—a subduer among the ranks of enemy folk; [he is] powerful (*vṛṣiṇam*).

1. Like one who has exhaled. 2. Like the wind that breathes out (*praśvasana-vāyu*); like the wind that breathes in (*na-pha-dhsana-vāyu*); like the wind that breathes forth (*śa-praśvasana-vāyu*). 3. Just so, he is eternal (*nitya*). 4. Likewise, this [sacrifice] is also [eternal]. 5. Fit for application (*upayoga-yogya*). 6. Fit for application. Ṛ.57: Like a seer (*ṛṣi*) who perceives mantras, the pillar is a praiser of the gods; it is praised and renowned among men characterized as sacrificers (*yajamāna*); like a swift horse (*vājī*), it is pleased and filled with joy.
Just as a horse filled with excitement goes toward the front of battle, so too this [Agni] becomes filled with excitement in carrying the oblation for the gods; such is the meaning.
Being thus, may Agni bestow—may he grant—*vayaḥ*, which means food;
the sense is "may he give it to us."
*Vayaḥ* is a name for food,
because it is listed among the names for that in the lexicon.
He has upheld [it]. By the rule *tujādīnām*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable.
[The word is] *kṣemam*.
*Kṣema* means that in which one dwells (*nivasati*) with a deficiency (*ūnena*).
The suffix *man* is applied according to the rule *asti-tu-su-ity-ādinā*.
Due to the presence of the suffix *ni*, there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable.
The word *rṇavaḥ* [is derived as follows]: *ravi*, *dhavi*, and *gayarthāḥ*.
From this, the suffix *kapratyaya* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Due to the *it*-characteristic, the augment *num* is inserted.
*Jetā* [is formed];
that which ends in the suffix *tṛn* is acutely accented on its first syllable.
[This is] of people (*janānām*).

Since [the rule] "from which there is selection" (*yataśca nirdhāraṇam*, Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.41) prescribes the genitive case in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), this is not a genitive case in the sense of an object (*karman*); therefore, the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā* does not apply. [The word] *stambhā*.

The root *stobhati* means "to praise. By that very [root], he bestows this created [world] as a hymn of praise: "The lightning-flash, terrible in appearance—Yama indeed was born, Yama was the progenitor; he is the lover of the young women and the lord of the mothers."

Like an army, he has been released; he bestows freedom upon us. Like a flash of lightning with a brilliant countenance, he is not to be resisted. Yama was indeed born; Yama is the progenitor of all that is born. He is the lover of the young women and the husband of the mothers. 7–8.
1 Like an army created and dispatched, 2 like a host of soldiers standing together with their lord—this fire (1) bestows (2) fear upon the enemies; it instills it.
That is the meaning: it produces it.
Or else:
Like an army that has been mobilized, it bestows strength;
the meaning is that just as it is powerful, so too is Agni powerful. Another illustration is now stated.
*Didyut* is a name for the thunderbolt (*vajra*).
By this, the arrow (*iṣu*) is indicated here.
*Tveṣapratīkā* means having a blazing face. *Astunam*—may the two [sides] be like arrows belonging to the *didyut*.
Just as she strikes fear, so too does Agni strike fear into the Rākṣasas and others; this is the meaning.
Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "Like an army let loose, she bestows either fear or strength; like a lightning flash, her appearance is dazzling" (Nirukta 10.21), and so forth.
Because he restrains—that is, he grants—desires to his worshippers, Agni is called Yama.

Alternatively, because Indra and Agni were born simultaneously, Agni possesses the status of being "foremost" (*agra*). On this point, Yāska has shown it in both the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa: "Yama, having been born, was united with Indra."
Regarding this, there is also a Vedic verse: "O Yama, come hither, O Mother" (Nirukta 10.21).

That which has been born—that is, the multitude of beings already produced—and that which is yet to be born—that is, the class of beings currently coming into existence—both of these are indeed Yama, who is Agni himself.
This is because all entities are dependent upon Agni by way of being offered as oblations.

The lover (*jāra*) is the one who causes [the girls] to age (*jarayitṛ*). For at the time of marriage, when the offering of parched grain (*lāja*) and other substances is made into the fire, their status as virgins (*kanyātva*) ceases;
therefore, he is called "the one who causes to age."
Likewise, he is the husband and supporter of those women who have been married;
thus it is told: "Soma obtained a woman while she was still in a state where the desire for human enjoyment had not yet arisen.
And that Soma gave her, when the desire for enjoyment had slightly arisen, to the Gandharva Viśvāvasu."
"And that Gandharva gave her at the time of marriage to Agni;
and Agni bestowed her, together with wealth and sons, upon her human husband.
A certain Ṛgvedic verse clearly expresses this meaning: "Soma gave her to the Gandharva, and the Gandharva to Agni."
And [it says], "He gave the chariot and the sons to him, and also this [earth]" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.85.41).
Yāska, however, says: "There is also a Vedic passage stating that the third fire is the husband" (Nirukta 10.21).
Or else:
For he is the protector of mothers, since he bestows the fruit [of their labor] through the sacrifices performed by them.

It is called *senā* because it exists together with these [soldiers]. This is its inherent nature, according to the rule: “The [final vowel] of a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is optionally [shortened].”
The accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The state of being born (*janitva*).
[The root] *janī* means "to appear."

In the expression *kṛtyārthe tavaikena*, the suffix *khan* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). There is the augment *iṭ*. Due to the presence of the *niṭ* marker, the word has the acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable.

*Jāraḥ*: [The word] *jāraḥ* means "one who causes to age. It is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.3.20.4: "In the sense of the agent, [the roots] *dṛ* and *jṛ* take the suffix *ṇi*, with its elision (*luk*)."

Regarding *kanīnām*: from the word *kanyā*, in the genitive singular, the semi-vowel is vocalized (*saṃprasāraṇa*) due to the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*;
this results in the substitution of the preceding vowel with the subsequent one (*parapūrvatvam*).
Of mothers (*jananī*). They are called *janayaḥ* because they give birth (*janyante*); that is, women. The suffix *in* is applied according to the rule “*insarvadhātubhyaḥ*” [Pāṇini 5.2.50].
The first syllable of "nicca" and so forth is udātta.
Like cows returning to their own stall, we have reached him who is kindled by the chariot of the Vasus;
like the flood of a river, the powerful rays of light have moved downward toward the one who beholds the sun.

To him, your moving [flames], we approach with desire for his favor; they reach the kindled one as cows reach their home. Like the flood of a river, he has driven them downward—the cattle rich in heroes—to behold the light of heaven. 9, 10.
1. It is like the combination of heroes (*vīrasaṃhati*) [formed by] *ca*, *cha*, *na*, and *pha*.
2. *Ḍha* and *atrepuḥ* are observed. *Vaḥ* is a plural form used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
O Agni, that "caratha" refers to you;
"caratha" means a moving creature, namely cattle. The oblation to be accomplished by means of the heart and other organs produced from those cattle is also called "caratha."
The word for the cause is used figuratively for the effect.
By means of the *carathā* offering— that is, by means of the oblation consisting of the products of cattle, such as the heart and other organs—
one reaches the abode of the Vasus.

That which dwells or inhabits is "sthāvara" (stationary), such as rice and other grains; this is designated as the *vasati* offering, as previously explained, representing the oblation to be accomplished by it.
Through the *vasati* offering and the cake (*puroḍāśa*) offering, we shall reach—that is, attain—this well-kindled fire.
There is a change of gender.
An example for this is:
"astaṃ na gāvaḥ" (the cows have gone home).
*Astam* is a name for the house.

Just as cows pervade the house, so it is here. Regarding this, Yāska says: "They [the rays] reach him with the offering of the *vaśrā* cow, with the offering of cattle, with the offering of dwelling, and with the offering of herbs; we shall attain him just as cows pervade the house" (Nirukta 10.21).
This Agni impels his flames downward, like a river—a body of water characterized by flowing—toward lower ground, rising up intensely here and there.
The sense is that just as a current of water moves swiftly toward a low-lying place, so do the flames of Agni move toward the object to be consumed.
Upon him, who dwells in the sky (*svaḥ*) and is beautiful to behold (*dṛśīke*), the rays (*gāvaḥ*)—those things whose nature is to go—converge.
Ninety is the karma of the destinies.
*Carathā*:
the suffix *athak* is derived from the root *car* according to the *Uṇādi* rules;
the lengthening of the vowel is Vedic.
The vowel *ā* is substituted for the case-ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. [The form] *vasatyā* [is derived as follows]:
the suffix *ati* is added by the rule *vahivasyatibhyaścit* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.500).
The acute accent of the case-ending is due to the rule "udāttayaṇaḥ. As for *astam*: it is called *asta* because everything (*sarvam*) is set (*astyate*) in it; thus, *asta* means the home.
The form *asihasi* and so forth is derived from that [root]. By the rule *titutra*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*.
Due to the presence of the *niṭ* suffix, the word is udātta-accented on its first syllable.
They reach; *nakṣatṛ* has the sense of reaching or attaining;
[it is derived from] the root *nakṣ* meaning "to go."
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
There is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) due to the rule “*cādilope vibhāṣā*” [Pāṇini 8.1.63].
[The word is] *nīcīḥ*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *nipūrvād añcateś copasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 4.1.6.2).
Following the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *acaḥ*, lengthening occurs by the rule *cau*.
By the rule *nyadhī ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.53), the prefix (*gati*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
The root *iṇ* means "to go.

From this root, with the causative sense (*ṇic*) inherent within it, the suffix *śnu* is applied by virtue of the rule "in the Veda, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [are used]," while the *laṅ* tense is present; there is an irregularity (*vyatyaya*) regarding the suffix.
The augment *āṭ* and *vṛddhi* [are applied]. In the word *dṛśīke*:
the root *dṛśir* means "to see."
In the word *anidaśiśyām*, the suffix *kīkan* is applied;
due to its being marked with *n*, it has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*).
The two-word phrase "vaneṣu" has been shown [in the Anukramaṇī]. From the perspective of recitation, this third hymn consists of five verses; it is addressed to Agni and has Parāśara as its seer.
"vaneṣu" is the introductory heading.
The application (viniyoga) is indicated by the internal marks of the text.

In forests where the trees have grown, Mitra chooses obedience like an unaging king; he is like security, like a virtuous rite, like a blessing—he has become the self-dependent invoker and the bearer of oblations.

In the forests, the conqueror among those who have attained their purpose; like a king, the friend chooses obedience that does not decay. Like a secure dwelling, he is excellent; like a holy thought, he becomes auspicious—the self-dependent invoker, the bearer of oblations. 1. 2.
Born in the forests, being born in the wilds, among those who have understanding, he is a friend and a companion; this Agni attains *śruṣṭi*— that is,
the sacrificer who swiftly accomplishes his tasks—
meaning he is one who quickly performs the rites.
And thus Yāska says: “*Śruṣṭi* is a name for ‘quickly’; *aṣṭi* means ‘swiftly’” (Nirukta 6.12).
He chooses—that is, he favors—such a sacrificer.
The sense is that, having accepted the oblation offered by him, he protects it.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a king, undecaying.
"Undecaying" means free from old age; the meaning is that his limbs remain unimpaired and he is capable in all undertakings.
Such a person is like the one whom a king chooses;
he is security, not merely a protector; he is the virtuous one here, the accomplisher, the sacrifice—not a sacrifice in name only, but the actual performer of rites.
Like him, he is auspicious, worthy of worship, and beneficial; he is the *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods, the carrier of oblations, known as the bearer of offerings to the gods.
1. This consists of eight verses and ten pādas, each verse having two feet.
Thus it is handed down in the tradition: "There are indeed three fires: Havyavāhana for the gods, Kavyavāhana for the ancestors, and Saharakṣas for the Asuras" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.8.6).
May such an Agni be *svāgnīḥ*—one whose ritual action is excellent, or whose meditation is excellent. May he be so.
*Jāyuḥ*. [Derived from] the root *ji* in the sense of "to conquer" (*jaye*), with the suffix *uṇ* according to the rule *kṛvāpājī*.
*Ajaryam*:
[derived from] *jṛ* in the sense of "loss of age";
the suffix *pyat* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
When the vṛddhi [vowel] has been applied, the letter *a* is replaced by the letter *u*.
In the bahuvrīhi compound *juryam*, meaning "that which does not age," the final syllable of the second member is acute-accented according to the rule *nañsubhyām*. [The form] *bhuvat*.
In the *leṭ* [subjunctive] of the root *bhū*, there is the augment *aṭ*. By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
By the rule “*bhūsuvostiṅi*,” there is the prohibition of *guṇa* [vowel strengthening].

Holding all manly powers in his hand, O Agni, you bestow the gods while dwelling in the secret place. Here, the men who establish the sacred thought find it, for they have recited the mantras fashioned by the heart. 3–4. *haste* (in the hand), *dadhānaḥ* (holding), *nṛmṇā* (manly powers), *viśvāni* (all), *ame* (O Agni), *devān* (the gods), *dhāt* (bestowing), *guhā* (in the secret place), *niṣīdan* (dwelling), *vidanti* (they find), *īm* (it), *atra* (here), *naraḥ* (the men), *dhiyadhāḥ* (those who establish the sacred thought), *hṛdā* (by the heart), *yat* (since), *taṣṭān* (fashioned), *mantrān* (the mantras), *aśaṃsana* (they have recited). 3–4.

Holding in his own hand—that is, in his arm—all *nṛmṇāni*, all riches characterized by oblations, Agni took his seat in a secret place, either within the waters or in the beginning, remaining hidden in a concealed spot. While in that state of fear (*ame*), he established the gods;
the meaning is that when Agni fled with the oblations, all the gods were terrified.
At this time, the leaders (*naraḥ*)—the gods who sustain ritual actions or insights (*dhiyaṃdhāḥ*)—find him, that is, they recognize this very Agni.

Whenever they recited—that is, praised or spoke—the mantras composed by the heart, meaning fashioned by the intellect (buddhi) residing in the heart, which were intent upon praising the Immortal (amṛta).
Sitting down;
it is a *pada* by the rule "sadir aprateḥ";
they know.
The root *vid* means "to know.
Due to its inclusion in the *adādi* (second) class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. The accent is that of the affix (*pratyayasvara*).
*Dhiyaṃdhāḥ*:
[The suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*.
Due to the word *bahulam* in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the second case ending even here.
*Takṣṭān*. [The root] *takṣu* (or *tvaṣṭṛ*) means "to fashion" or "to shape.
[The suffix] *niṣṭhā*.
By the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," there is a prohibition of the *it* designation;
by the rule "skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ," there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *k*.

The Unborn has supported the earth as if it were a foundation; he has propped up the heavens with true mantras. O Agni, you who possess all life, protect the dear places of the cattle; you have entered from secret place to secret place. The Unborn has supported the earth as if it were a foundation; he has propped up the heavens with true mantras. O Agni, you who possess all life, protect the dear places of the cattle; you have entered from secret place to secret place.

"Aja" means "unborn"; he is called *aja* because he does not take birth (*ajati*) or moves (*gacchati*), namely the Sun. Alternatively, he is *aja* because he is not born; the meaning is that he is devoid of birth. Like him [the Sun], this Agni supports the earth—*kṣā* being a name for the earth—he sustains the ground by means of his luminosity. Furthermore, *pṛthivī* is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); thus, he supports both the earth and the intermediate space. He supports the sky, the world of heaven (*dyām*), with true mantras—mantras whose meanings are not false.

1. One whose meditation is beautiful through *ca*, *cha*, *na*, *pha*, and *sa*. 2. [The letter] *ḍha* is for the sake of completion (*niṣṭhā*). 3. There is no *ḍha* for "earth" (*pṛthivī*). 4. *Ca*, *ta*, and *pha* signify "he holds" (*dhārayati*).
Thus, *tastambha* means "he supports" (*stabhnāti*).
The meaning is that he acts in such a way that it does not fall downward, but remains precisely above.

The support of heaven by means of mantras is recorded in the *Taittirīya*: "The gods, indeed, were afraid that the sun, from the world of heaven, would step beyond [their reach]. They held it back with the meters" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.2.4.2).
Or alternatively:
"Being praised with true mantras, [the seer] said, 'He has checked the fire.

O Agni, you whose life (āyus)—that is, food—is all-encompassing (viśva), protect (nipāhi) the dear places of every animal (paśvaḥ)—places endowed with excellent grass and water—meaning, do not burn them.
If one asks, 'In that case, where shall I dwell? he says:"
"O cave-dweller, go to a cave even deeper than this cave—a place unfit for the wandering of cows; go there, meaning, dwell right there.

[The form] *paśvaḥ* [is derived as follows]: by the rule "In the case of *jas* and other suffixes in Vedic literature, the substitution is optional," there is an absence of *guṇa* (by the rule *gher ṅiti*), and thus the *yaṇ* substitution [of *v* for *u*] occurs.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *udāttayaṇaḥ*. In *guhā*,
the substitution of *āj* for the ablative case-ending is by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
Because it is a *cit* word, it has the anudātta accent.
In *guhám*, there is shortening by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
*gāḥ*. This is the *luṅ* (aorist) tense used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
The substitution of *gā* for the root *iṇ* occurs by the rule: "In the *luṅ*, *gā* is substituted for *iṇ*."

He who has perceived him dwelling in the secret cave, he who has sat down at the stream of the Eternal Order—those who, honoring the Truth, tear it asunder for him, to him indeed have the treasures been proclaimed. 7. 8.

He who has perceived him dwelling in the secret cave, he who has approached the stream of the Eternal Order—those who, honoring the Eternal Order, discern its manifestations—for him indeed has he proclaimed riches. 7–8.
The man who perceives—that is, knows—this Agni as he exists in the cave, dwelling in the secret place;
and who has sat down near this Agni, the sustainer of the stream of *ṛta* (the cosmic order) or of sacrifice;
and those persons who, honoring the *ṛtas*—that is, the truths or sacrifices—approaching or touching them, "unravel" this Agni, meaning they compose and offer hymns directed toward him.
Immediately after being praised, he has proclaimed—that is, made manifest—the riches and treasures for all these people who offer praise; he has taken cognizance of them.
[The root] *cit* is used in the sense of "knowing."
In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect] tense with the *ṇal* suffix, the accent of the *liṭ* applies. *Cṛtanti*.
[The root] *cṛt* means "to injure" and "to bind."
It belongs to the *tud-ādi* class.
When the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the accent falls on the *vikaraṇa*. Thus: *śibhyate*.
He said: "In the case of the *liṭ* [perfect tense], *bruva* becomes *vaci*";

and by the rule "in the *liṭ*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplication for both [the root and the reduplicative syllable]" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.17), there is vocalization of the reduplication.

Because of the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* [Pāṇini 6.1.108], the substitution of the *yaṇ* vowel occurs due to the optional application of the *parapūrvatva* (the preceding form) rule by *vā chandasi* [Pāṇini 6.1.106]. He who, by his greatness, has spread through the plants, and who is the impeller within them; he whose wisdom dwells in the house of all living beings—like wise men, they have made him their companion. 9 || 10 ||

He who grows among the plants by his greatness, and within offspring and in the wombs; he who is the consciousness of the waters, the life of all, in the house—like wise men sitting together at a gathering, they have fashioned him. 9, 10.

The Agni who, by his greatness—that is, those powers of greatness which exist—causes the plants (vīrudh) and herbs (oṣadhīṣu) to grow; he pierces them, he causes them to sprout, and he specifically envelops them rather than withering them.
Moreover, he causes the offspring—characterized by flowers, fruits, and so forth, produced in abundance—to grow within the mothers, that is, within the herbs who stand in the place of mothers.
The second occurrence of the word *uta* is for the purpose of completing the meter.
Likewise, *citti* is the one who wills.

The one who makes himself known in the dwelling of the waters—that is, in the house situated in the midst of the waters—he who moves about, possessing all life and all limbs; this is the ellipsis. Toward him, the wise—the intelligent ones—having performed *saṃmāya*, that is, having offered honor and worship; the meaning is, having praised him with hymns, they perform their rites. Therein lies the illustration: *sadhaiva*. Just as people first thoroughly honor a dwelling or a house and afterwards perform their activities therein, so it is here. Regarding *vīrudhaḥ*: from the root *ruh* preceded by *vi*, the suffix *kip* is applied. Because it is listed in the *nyaṅkvādi* group (Pāṇini 7.3.53, Gaṇapāṭha), there is lengthening of the prefix and the substitution of *dh* for the final letter. And it has been said: "Plants (*vīrudhaḥ*) are the herbs (*oṣadhayaḥ*)" (Nirukta 6.3). Regarding *rodhat*: from the root *rudh* in the sense of "obstructing. In the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, there is the augment *aṭ*. By the rule "and the elision of *i*" (Pāṇini 3.4.97), the *i* is dropped. Regarding *saṃmāya*: from the root *māṅ* in the senses of "measuring" and "sound. In a compound not preceded by *an*, the suffix *kvā* is replaced by *lyap* (Pāṇini 7.1.37). By the rule "not before *lyap*" (Pāṇini 6.4.69), the prohibition of the change to *ī* applies. 11. Translation complete.

The fourth hymn, consisting of ten verses and two padas, begins with the word "śrīṇan. According to the traditional recitation (*adhyayana*), it consists of five verses. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as before. The application (*viniyoga*) is determined by the indicative marks of the text (*laiṅgika*).
He, the impetuous one, fills heaven and earth; he envelops the nights and all that stands and moves, since as the sole god among all the gods, he surpasses them by his greatness. 1. 2.

Mixing [the offerings], he stands upon the earth; the impetuous one reaches unto heaven. He has uncovered the nights from that which stands and that which moves, since he, the one god, by his greatness, has encompassed all these gods. 1. 2.

The active one, the bearer and sustainer of oblations, mixing [the offering] with those oblations—such as the *śrayaṇa* substances beginning with the path—as one mixes Soma, he stands near heaven; that is to say, he reaches it. He has unrolled, by his own splendor, both the stationary (*sthātṛ*) and the moving (*caratha*) world—that is, the universe consisting of both—and all the nights; the sense is that while performing the transport of the oblation, he illuminated the entire world with his own light.

Among all the gods—Indra and the others—who are endowed with qualities such as liberality, this Agni alone is the shining god; because he encompasses, surpasses, and pervades on all sides the greatness and majesties of these aforementioned beings, beginning with the stationary world—the verb *bhavati* preceded by *pari* here signifies "to encompass" or "to include.
Alternatively:

Among all these beings, beginning with the stationary, this divine Agni, when he encompasses—that is, when he pervades—the greatnesses of the gods, then [he] covers [them]; thus the connection is with what precedes. He envelops.
The root *ūrṇu* means "to cover.
According to Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.2.6, "vibhāṣorṇoḥ," there is an option regarding the vṛddhi [strengthening of the vowel].

When you were born as the living one from the dry [wood], all the gods rejoiced in your seasonal power. May they all partake in the name of divinity, moving toward the immortal through the path of Truth (*ṛta*). 3–4.
Then indeed all of them rejoiced in your rite, O God, when you were born living from the dry wood. All of them shared in your divinity, moving toward the immortal truth by their courses. 3. 4.
1. From the study of the *ḍha-ta* [section];
2. By means of the substance for boiling (*śrapaṇadravya*) containing *ḍha* and *sa*.

O radiant Agni, O shining one, while living and blazing, when you were born—that is, when you manifested—from the dry, sapless wood that has become fuel through friction, then immediately thereafter all the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) offer to you their ritual act (*kratu*), they serve it, and perform it.
Having performed [the rites] accordingly, all those [beings], each according to its name, attain—attain, that is, reach—their respective divine status (*devatvam*), which is *ṛta*, meaning unerring.
What are they doing?
They are honoring you alone with hymns of praise (*stotra*) that lead to immortality (*amṛta*), meaning non-death; the sense is that they are approaching you.
The three verbal forms beginning with *jubanti*—namely *juhvati*, *juṣante*, and *juṣante*—are used in the sense of the present tense according to the rule *chandasi luṅ-luṅ-liṭaḥ*.
[The word] *evaiḥ*: they go toward the hymns (*stotrī*), that is, they proceed facing the hymns; thus, they are the hymns (*evāni*).
The suffix *van* is applied after the roots *iṇ* and *śīṅ*. (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.150)

The impulse of *ṛta*, the thought of *ṛta*—all have performed all their works for the sake of the full-lived one. To whosoever gives to you, or whosoever strives to serve you, to him do you, O wise one, grant protection.

The promptings of *ṛta*; the thought of *ṛta*. Viśvāyu and all [the gods] have performed their works. To him who shall offer gifts to you, or who shall strive for you—to him, O wise one, bestow wealth. 5–6.
The *preṣas*—the hymns being intensely recited—are offered for Agni who has arrived at the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*) according to the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
The *dhītīya* [offering] is that in which the *dhīti*—the Soma—is placed and drunk;
that too is performed for Agni alone, who has reached the sacrificial ground of the cosmic order.
Therefore, that fire is "Viśvāyu. He is such that his entire life-span (*viśvam āyuḥ*)—meaning all food—is his.
Moreover, all (*viśve*) sacrificers have performed, and continue to perform, for him the ritual acts (*apāṃsi*), such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
O Agni, to him who offers oblations such as the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa* unto you,
or to any other sacrificer who desires, "May I be capable of performing your ritual work"—
