to both such types of sacrificers, being the wise one (*cikitvān*) who knows their performance, grant wealth; bestow riches upon them.
From the root *dāś*, meaning "to give. In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *āṭ*.
From the root *śak*,
meaning "to be able";
the suffix *san* is added in the sense of desire (*icchā*).
By the rule *sani mīmādhurabhalabhaśak* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.54), the vowel *a* is replaced by *i*.
Here, by the rule *lopo'bhyāsasya*, there is elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
By the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*, there is elision of the letter *s*.
As before, there is the augment *āṬ* in the *leṭ* mood. *cikitvān*: from the root *kit*, meaning "to know."
The *liṭ* [perfect tense] substitutes *kasu*. [Root] *day*: to pity, to give, to go, to protect, to harm, and to give.
The Hotṛ priest is seated among the offspring of Manu; he is the lord of riches, clothed in wondrous garments.
Desiring seed within one another’s bodies, they—unerring through their own mental powers—have come together in full knowledge.

The Hotṛ priest, seated down, the offspring of Manu—he, clothed in variegated splendor, the lord of riches—desiring seed for one another within their own bodies, the unerring ones have come together through their own mental powers. 7–8.
O Agni, you, being the *hotṛ*—the invoker of the gods—among the offspring of Manu, that is, among the progeny whose nature is that of the sacrificer, are seated;
for the Brāhmaṇa states: "The offspring are indeed of Manu" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.1.5.6).
You alone, as such, are the lord and master of these progeny and of riches, such as cattle and other forms of wealth.
Therefore, those subjects [are established] within their own bodies.
1. In the manuscript *pha*, the word "gatasya" (of that which has gone) is absent.
2. In the manuscripts *ca*, *cha*, *na*, and *pha*, the reading is "tathā dhītiḥ" (thus, the intellect).
3. In the form of the sacrificer (yajamāna) represented by the letter *ḍha*:
they desired—that is, they sought—the semen (*retaḥ*), which is vigor (*vīrya*), that had become mutually blended and unified within their own bodies and had been transformed into the form of a son;
the meaning is that through your grace, they obtained a son.

Having obtained sons, those offspring— being *amūrāḥ* (unconfused) and *amūḍhāḥ* (undeluded), that is, true— *saṃ jānate*, meaning they fully understand and live for a long time together with their own respective *dakṣaiḥ* (capable) sons.
Alternatively,
the word *dakṣa* signifies "vital breath" (*prāṇa*).

According to the Vedic scripture, "The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed skill (*dakṣa*), and the in-breath (*apāna*) is wisdom (*kratu*)," those who are undeluded, being united with their own skills— their respective vital breaths— know everything through you alone.
They desire; the middle voice (ātmanepada) is used because of the effort involved;
they know.
The elision [of the suffix] is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

For this [verb], there is the substitution of *ad* [for *as*], and by the rule "the *ā* of the root and of reduplicated stems (*abhyasta*) is elided," there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. Thus: *amūrāḥ*.
Regarding the word *amūra*, Yāska explained it thus: "We are deluded (*mūḍha*), you are undeluded (*amūḍha*)" (Nirukta 6.8).
Therefore, here too, by the word *amūra*, the state of being undeluded is expressed;
the letter *ṭha* has been substituted for the letter *ra* through a transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*).
Alternatively:
the root *murch* means "to faint" and "to increase.
From this, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad* and other such formations.
By the rule "rālopaḥ," there is the elision of the *ra* suffix;
*raḥ* here denotes the possessive sense (*matvarthīya*).
Those who are not foolish (*mūra*) are "the non-foolish" (*amūrāḥ*).
Alternatively:
[the root] *ama* is used in the sense of "motion" and so forth;
from this, the suffix *uran* is applied according to the rules for *aṇ* and other suffixes.
The sons of the father did not take pleasure in his will; others, the swift ones, heeded the command of this powerful one.
He, rich in food, threw open the doors of wealth; the sustainer of the earth adorned the firmament with stars.

The sons did not take pleasure in the will of their father; but those swift ones who listened to his command—abundant in food, he threw open the doors of wealth for them; the friend of the house has adorned the firmament with stars. 9–10.
O swift ones, those sacrificers who, being attentive, hear the command—the instruction—of this Agni, they all delight in and perform the ritual action (*kratu*) directed by him;
in this regard, there is an illustration:
like sons [following] their father.
Just as sons are many and provide abundant protection—protecting their father from hell by carrying out his commands—so too [is he].
Yāska says: "A son (*putra*) saves (*trāyate*) one from hell (*niraṇāt*), or he saves his father (*tataḥ*) from there; thus he is *putraka*. (Nirukta 2.11). He is *purukṣuḥ*.
*Kṣu* is a name for food.

That Agni has many times opened wide (*vi-aurnot*) the doors—the gates that serve as the entrances to the sacrifice—of these sacrificers; that is to say, he reveals their riches, or rather, he bestows them.
Moreover, he whose mind is fixed on *dama*—the sacrificial hall—is Agni.
Because there is no *akaṃ* (suffering) in him, it is called *nāka*, the heavenly world (*dyuloka*). Him [Agni].

*Stṛbhiḥ* is a name for the constellations (*nakṣatra*). With *stṛbhiḥ*, meaning with the constellations, he *pipeśa*, that is, he made it variegated; the sense is that he endowed it with the constellations.
*śropan*: from the root *śru* in the sense of "hearing"; in the *leṭ* [subjunctive] mood, there is the augment *aṭ*.
In the form *sibbahula leṭi*, the suffix *sip* is applied;
by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*);
and by the rule *inaśca lopaḥ*, there is elision of the vowel *i*.
There is elision of a final conjunct consonant. *pipeśa* (he has formed); [from the root] *piśa* meaning "to form a part."
The hymn beginning with "Śukraḥ" consists of ten verses, though it is traditionally studied as five; it is the fifth hymn of Parāśara, addressed to Agni.
It is introduced by the words "Śukraḥ.
Its application is determined by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

Radiant and shining like the lover of the Dawn, you have become manifest like the light of heaven from its two united halves; born forth by your will, you have become the father of the gods while yet being their son.

The bright one, shining intensely like the lover of the Dawn, has been born from the two united worlds like the light of heaven. By thy wisdom thou hast become preeminent; being the son, thou hast become the father of the gods. 1–2.
1. Ḍha-nāka:
there is no "na" (negation) in this [section].
2. Ḍha-daśarca: consisting of ten verses; composed in two-footed meters.

"This [Agni] is bright, of white color; moreover, he is the 'unaging' (ajāra) of the dawns—that is, the one who causes the dawns to age—and like the sun, he is 'blazing' (śuśukvān), the burner and illuminator of all.
Likewise, when heaven and earth are joined together (samīcī), he is like the light of the shining sun from heaven, filling them with his own splendor."

O Agni, you, being thus born—that is, having manifested—have encompassed and pervaded the entire world in every direction through your ritual action (*ṛtvan*), or rather, through the light that is the cause of knowledge, in the manner described.
The gods are so called because they shine;
as their son, acting as a deliverer from the hell named Put, you have become their father—that is, their protector.
Or rather:
being the son of the gods, Indra and the others, you have become like a messenger; as such, you, the father, are the protector through oblations. You are the radiant one.
The root *śuc* means "to shine.
[In the form *śukrāḥ*,] the suffix *kasu* is applied to the perfect tense (*liṭ*),
and the substitution of *k* for *c* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
*Paprā*:

from the root *pṛ* in the sense of “protecting” or “filling,” the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule *ādyagamahanajanakhanaghasām hiṃsāyām* (Pāṇini 3.2.171). Then, by the rule *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇāccheyāḍāḍyāyājālaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), the case-ending *su* is replaced by *ḍā*.
*Samīcī*:
from the root *añc* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kin* is applied according to the rule *ṛtvig-dadhṛg-...* (Pāṇini 3.2.59).
The substitution of *sam* for *saṃ* is applied according to the rule *samaḥ sami* (Pāṇini 6.3.93).
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "it should be stated that [the suffix is added] after the root *añc*.
Following the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "of *ac*," the lengthening occurs by the rule "in the case of *cau*.
By the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*, the *ṅīp* becomes accented.
The long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is applied by the rule *vā chandasi*.
However, if the word division is made as *sam-īñcī*, then the substitution of *ī* prescribed by *ud īn* (Pāṇini 6.4.139) should be understood to apply even to what follows *samaḥ*. [Thus:
*babhūtha*.
The absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) [prescribed] by Pāṇini’s rule 7.2.64: *babhūthā tatantha*.

The Ordainer, Agni, who discerns that [treasure], is the upholder of wealth in cattle and the sweetener of foods; like one dear to the people, he is called upon as he sits in the midst, delightful within the dwelling. 3–4. The Ordainer; from yonder; Agni; discerning; the upholder; not; of cattle; the sweetener; of foods; like one dear; to the people; he who is to be invoked; being; in the midst; seated; delightful; in the dwelling. 3–4.
The creator:
this is for the wise;
the wise one.
Or rather:
the Ordainer (*vidhātṛ*) is the creator of all;

he who is "free from pride" (*adarpa*), who "knowing" (*vijānan*) the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, is like "Agni," the fire, which is the "support" (*ūdhana*)—the locus of the milk associated with cows—and the "taster" (*svātra*)—the one who makes savory—the "foods" (*pitūnām*), that is, the nourishments.
Just as a bull makes all foods delicious by providing milk, so too does Agni make all foods savory through his perfect cooking; such is the meaning.

Furthermore, Agni of this nature is "kind among people" (*jana-śevaḥ*), bringing happiness to the world like a man; being one who is to be invoked (*āhūryaḥ*) in the midst of sacrifices, he is seated (*niṣattaḥ*) in the sacrificial hall (*duruṇe*), and he is delightful (*raṇvaḥ*), a source of pleasure or worthy of praise.
Regarding *gonām*: by the rule *goḥ pādānte* (Pāṇini 7.1.57), the augment *nuṭ* is applied even when not at the end of a foot [of a verse]. Thus: *svātram*.

The root *svad* means "to taste. From it, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well. Then, by the rule "of *sup* [case endings], *suluk* [occurs]," the case ending *su* is elided.
Regarding *pitṝṇām*:
by the rule *nāmanyatarasyām*, the name [the first member] is acute-accented. They say: [so forth].

From the root *hi* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *aco yat*. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, and lengthening according to the rule *halaḥ*.
The addition of the letter *r* is due to Vedic usage;
by the rule “*yato ’nāvaḥ*,” the initial syllable is udātta.

Like a son born, delightful in the dwelling; like a spirited steed, well-pleased, he has crossed over the people. When the people, dwelling together with the heroes, have come to him, may Agni, by his divine power, attain all things. 5–6. Like a son, born, delightful in the home; like a vigorous horse, well-satisfied, he has traversed across the clans. When the clans, sharing the same nest with the men, have approached him, may Agni, through his divinity, reach all things. 5–6.
1. He who brings happiness to the world of mortals—born like a son, yet not merely as a son—I have appeared in the dwelling, the house. Being delightful, he becomes a source of pleasure.
Like a spirited horse, being full of joy, he has especially crossed over, transcended, and overcome the people—the hostile subjects existing in the midst of battle.

Moreover, when I, together with men characterized as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), call upon the divine subjects (*viśaḥ*)—the celestial populations who share the same dwelling place (*sanīḷāḥ*)—then this Agni attains (*aśyāḥ* = *aśnute*) all the various divine natures (*viśvāni devatvā*).
The meaning is that he himself becomes the very form of each respective deity.
Thus, another mantra is recited: "O Agni, you are born as Varuṇa; you become Mitra when you are kindled" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 7.3.1), and so forth.
*aśyāḥ*:
[from the root] *aś* in the sense of pervading (*vyāptau*);
in the potential mood (*liṅ*), there is a substitution of the active voice (*parasmaipada*) with the second person dual.
The elision of the verbal suffix occurs frequently in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
Those mortals violate these vows when they fail to grant obedience to these men;
and that—

In the beautiful sky, all those rays of yours roar—that is, they go forth; *navanti* is a word meaning "to go. The sense is that they reach the gods. [The root] *vas* is used in the sense of "dwelling. By the rule *sphāyitañci* etc., the suffix *rak* is added. Because it belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). [The form] *cikenan* is derived from *kit*, meaning "to know," belonging to the *jauhotyādi* class. In the *leṭ* tense, the augment *aṭ* is added. According to the statement “it should be stated that [the rules apply] abundantly in the Veda” (Kātyāyana on Pāṇini 7.3.7.1), there is no prohibition of the elision (*luk*) or the guna-substitution of the penultimate vowel by the rule *nābhyastasyāci piti*. The acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable is due to the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ*. Regarding *ṛṇvan*: the roots *ivi*, *rivi*, *ravi*, and *dhavi* have the sense of "motion. Because it is marked with the *it*-sign, the nasal augment *num* is added. The *lak* suffix is a Vedic usage. There is a metathesis (*vyatyaya*) of the *repha* (the letter *r*) for the sake of vocalization. Alternatively, [it comes from] *ṛṇu*, meaning "to go," belonging to the *tanādi* class. ||13||
The hymn beginning with "vanema" consists of eleven verses; according to the recensional tradition, it is a collection of six verses and is the sixth hymn [of this section].
The seer and other details are as before. It is enumerated thus: "Vanema, eleven [verses]."
The application is based on indicative marks.

May we win many heroic powers through our inspired thoughts; may Agni, the beautifully radiant one, pervade all things—he who, being wise, observes the divine ordinances and the lineage of the human race.
May Agni, with his beautiful flame, attain all the many prayers of the noble one; may he, the wise one, observe the divine ordinances and the lineage of the human race. 1, 2.

"May we win and enjoy abundant offerings; may Agni grant us such knowledge"—this is the meaning. "By wisdom (*manīṣā*), the goal (*aryaḥ*) is to be reached or attained. Or rather: by wisdom, the Lord (*arthaḥ*). "Well-shining" (*suśokaḥ*) means possessing beautiful luster. Such an Agni "attains" (*aśyāḥ*)—that is, pervades—all actions (*viśvāni karmāṇi*). Doing what? Being "aware" (*cikitvān*), that is, knowing fully the divine ordinances (*daivyāni vratā*)—the duties or rites existing among the gods. Likewise, being aware of the birth—that is, the origin-form—of the human race (*mānuṣasya janasya*), knowing it directly, he understands all those actions related to Heaven and Earth. Having understood them, he pervades them—this is the sense. *Vanema*: from the root *vana* (in the sense of "to enjoy"). Although *śap* would be expected, there is a substitution with *śa*. Because it is taught as beginning with *a*, when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the accent of the *vikaraṇa* remains. *Pūrvīḥ*: from the word *puraḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added by the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*; the lengthening occurs by *hali ca*. *Manīṣā*: the form *īṣā* replaces *akṣa* etc. by the rule *īpā-akṣādi-vā-ha-kṛti-bhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.127.2). *Suśokaḥ*: from the root *śuc* (in the sense of "shining"); the suffix *ghañ* is used in the abstract sense. By the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, there is the change to *k*. "He whose shining is beautiful. The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member occurs by the rule *ādyudāttaṃ yac chandasi*. *Aśyāḥ*: as in the verse "O God, thou hast attained all things" (*devatvā viśvānyaśyāḥ*, Ṛgveda 1.69.6). *Cikitvān*: from the root *kit* (in the sense of "knowing"); the suffix *kasu* is used for the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
He who is the germ of the waters, the germ of the forests, the germ of all that stands,
and the germ of all that moves— him, the immortal one, well-disposed, even in the rock and within the dwelling, all people honor as their own.

The embryo; he who is the embryo of the waters, the embryo of the forests, and the embryo of both that which stands and that which moves—within the rock, even within his own dwelling, like the all-encompassing immortal among the people, he is well-intentioned. 3.4.3–4.
1. For roots ending in ṭha, na, sa, and śa, the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) endings are also used.
That Agni who is the *garbha* (womb/embryo) of the waters—meaning he dwells within the waters, known by the name Apāmpati;
and he who is the *garbha* of the forests (*vanānām*), meaning he exists in their midst in the form of a forest fire (*dāvāgni*).

And he who is the *garbha*—the inner dweller—of the *sthātām*, the stationary things such as wood and the like; and the *garbha* of the *caratām*, the moving, walking creatures, who abides within the body in the form of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*): to such an Agni, [we offer] oblation (*havis*)—the sense being that they present it—within the *duruṇe*, the difficult-to-traverse dwelling, and even within the *adrau*, the mountain.
May this one—immortal (amṛta), meaning possessing the nature of being deathless; svādhīḥ, meaning endowed with excellent deeds or excellent meditation—be for us; this is the ellipsis.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a king who is viśvaḥ, a leader who establishes [people] in comfort, [so be he] for the people (viśām).
Just as he is engaged in the beautiful activity of protecting his subjects, so too [is he].
"sthātām. [This is derived] from the root *sthā* with the suffix *kip*; the augment *tuk* is Vedic.
Alternatively:
The suffix *tu* is derived from the *uṇādi* [list].
The elision of the final vowel before the genitive plural ending *ām* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
[The form is] *carathām*.
The suffix *ath* prescribed by the rule *śīṅśapihṛgami* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.393) should also be understood to apply to the root *car*, due to the word "variously" (*bahulavacanāt*).
Because the teaching regarding the suffix *ām* is not universally obligatory (*anityatvāt*), there is no insertion of *nuṭ*, and thus the long vowel by class-similarity (*savarṇadīrghaḥ*) occurs:
*viśvaḥ*.
The root *viś* means "to enter.

From this root, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule *aśigrupi0* et cetera. By virtue of being marked with *n*, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.
For he, the lord of the night, is the master of riches for the one who serves him with hymns; O Agni, knowing the lineage of the gods and mortals, protect these various dwellings upon the earth.

For he, Agni, the lord of the night, is indeed the master of riches—he who serves him properly with well-spoken hymns. O wise one, protect these many beings; you who know, guard the generations of gods and mortals alike. 5–6.
For that Agni is the protector of the night; "kṣapā" is a name for night;
thus, he is the possessor of the night.
For there is the Vedic scripture: "The night indeed belongs to Agni" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.7).
Furthermore, the night's connection with Agni is established because it is offered as an oblation with the mantra: "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 4.10.5).
Or else:

Endowed with the power to consume— that is, to destroy— the Rākṣasas and other such beings, Agni, being thus characterized, bestows— that is, grants— *rayīṇām*, riches, to the sacrificer who offers praise.

This refers to that sacrificer who performs a sufficient— that is, an adequate and complete— hymn for this Agni by means of *sūktaiḥ*, well-spoken hymns consisting of mantras employed according to the Śāstras.
O *cikitvaḥ*— Yāska [states in Nirukta 2.11] that "the meaning of *cikitvān* is 'possessing consciousness'"—

O conscious one, you who are all-knowing, knowing the *janma* births of the gods, Indra and the others, and the *martān* mortals, humans, protect (*ni pāhi*) thoroughly these *bhūma*, the multitudes of beings characterized by the earth.
The meaning is: because you know all beings, including gods and humans, for that very reason you are addressed in this way.

Regarding the word *rayīṇām*: since the object of the action is treated as a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) according to the rule "the mention of the action must be made," the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.
*dāśat* [is derived from] the root *dāśva* meaning "to give. In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *aṭ*.
Aram. By the rule "vālamūla" etc., there is an optional substitution of *l* for *r*. [The word is] *sūktaiḥ*.
By the rule *sūpamānāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.145), there is udātta accent on the final syllable of the second member [of the compound].
In *cikitvaḥ*,
the *n* is replaced by *r* according to the rule *matuvaso ruḥ*.
*bhūma*: By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the second case ending following the word *bhūman*;
at the time of the *pada* recitation, the short vowel is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly.
The many nights have passed away, diverse in form; the chariot of the one established in truth has moved forth. The Hotṛ-priest has been perfected, sent forth by the sun, performing all true deeds.

Through many nights of diverse forms, he has prospered the one who stands still and the chariot impelled by the Eternal Order (*ṛta*). The Hotṛ-priest, seated within the sun, has been successful, performing all true deeds. 7–8.
1. Of the stationary beings such as plants and the like; 2. and of the moving beings; 3. he possesses beautiful meditation characterized by the letters *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *sa*.
The many *pūrvīḥ* (ancient) *uṣasaḥ* (dawns) and the *kṣapaḥ* (nights), which are *virūpāḥ* (of diverse forms) due to their white and black aspects, truly *vardhān* (increase) that Agni.

Likewise, they increase that Agni who is *ṛtapravītam*—enveloped by *ṛta*, whether as water, truth, or sacrifice—and who is both *sthāt* (the stationary, such as trees and the like) and *ratham* (the moving, such as humans and the like).
That Agni, being *niṣat* (seated) in his own *svaḥ* (excellent place of refuge, the sacrificial ground), has become the *hotā* (invoker) of the gods and has been *arādhi* (accomplished/perfected).
Or alternatively:
he was propitiated (*ārādhi*) by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); that is to say, he was worshipped.
What was he doing?

Performing all (viśvāni) deeds (apāṃsi)— that is, all those existing among the sacrificers (satyā), or rather, those whose fruits are real (satyaphalāni)— he causes them to increase (vardhān). [This is from the root] vṛdh, in the subjunctive (leṭ) with the augment āṭ.
In the case of the root *chand*, because the suffix *śap* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, there is the elision of the *ṇi*.
Following the rule "there is also elision of the *i*," the *i* is elided, resulting in the elision of the final consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*). Thus:
*ṛtapravītam*.
The root *vyeñ* means "to cover.
From this root, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed;
by the rule beginning with *vacisvapi*, the semivowel is replaced by its corresponding vowel (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

Because a primary derivative (*kṛdanta*) includes that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or an agentive noun (*kāraka*), the rule "the third case [retains its accent] when used as an object" applies, resulting in the original accent of the first member of the compound.
*Arādhi*: from the root *rādha* (or *sādha*), meaning "to succeed" or "to be accomplished."
In the *luṅ* tense, by substitution, *cli* becomes *ciṇ*.
You bestow glory upon the cattle and you place it in the forests; all the singers bring tribute to you.
Men, approaching you from many sides, have gladdened you like a father; they bring forth the song of praise. 9–10.

Among the cattle you have established your excellence; among the forests, all bring their tribute to you, O golden-hued one. Men from many places worship you; like those seeking nourishment, they quicken you and bring forth their riches. 9, 10.
O Agni, you bestow praise—meaning you establish renown—among the *vanas*, that is, among the desirable and worshipful cattle, our own livestock;
the sense is: "May our cattle, such as cows and others, become famous.
May all people bring to us a tribute (*bali*) consisting of wealth worthy of being well-sought after.
O Agni, men have honored you in many places—in numerous sites for the sacrifice to the gods—performing various acts of worship.
Having honored you, they carry away and take from you wealth, that is, riches; this is the meaning.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
*jinvitha*: from the *jīrṇa*, the aged; *pitur na pituḥ*—like from a father, as sons take wealth from an aged father, so [you have taken it]. *dhiṣe*.
The *liṭ* [perfect tense] is used in the sense of the present according to Vedic usage.
There is an absence of reduplication because of the rule: "In the section on reduplication, it should be stated that in the Veda it is optional" (Kāśikā 6.1.8.1). [Thus we have:
*bharanta*.
The root *hṛ* means "to take away.
Even when used alone, it should be understood as having the sense of a prefix (*sopasarga*). The *laṅ* [tense] ending is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
In the word *ahamahorātraḥ*, the substitution of *bha* occurs [by Pāṇini 1.4.18].
In *purutrā*, the suffix *trā* is applied in the sense of the locative case by the rule beginning with “*devamanuṣyapuruṣapuruṣamartyebhyaḥ*.”
*jinvivi*:
[derived from] *jyū* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohānau*). [The suffix] *kin* is applied after the roots *jṛṣ*, *jṛ*, and *jāg* (Uṇādisūtra 4.494).
In the word *ṛteddhātoḥ*, the substitution of *it* [for *i*] occurs.

Because it has been stated that "the *ugādi* group consists of underived nominal stems (*prātipadika*s)," there is no lengthening in cases such as *jinviviḥ* and *kiyoṃgiyaḥ*. Furthermore, due to the absence of lengthening by the rule *hali ca*, there is a transposition of the *repha* and *vakāra*.
And it has been said: "The [suffix] *varga* goes [to the end], and there is a reversal of the phonemes" (Kātantra 6.3.109).
Due to the *nit*-designation, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.
*Veda* is a name for wealth.
It is called *veda* because it is found (*vidyate*) or obtained (*labhyate*). [The root] *vid* is used in the sense of "obtaining";
the suffix *asun* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
It has been stated that among these [verses], whichever other two-footed verse remains redundant should be recited in that same manner.
Such a subsequent two-footed verse is as follows:
"The virtuous one, not the greedy; the hero here, not the timid; he indeed is formidable in battles. (11)
He is like a falcon; he is like a hero who has set out; he is like a terrifying warrior, impetuous in battles. 11.

1. *ḍha-raṃhamāṇam* (rushing forward). This [Agni] is like a seeker (*sādhaka*) who is successful (*sādhu*). Like a seeker who quickly grasps the fruit to be attained (*sādhya*), so too Agni takes possession of everything; this is the meaning.
Likewise, this Agni is like a hero with arrows;
just as an archer who hurls arrows impels his enemies, so too does Agni, by burning, impel the entire host of living beings.
Likewise, he is as terrible as a wanderer.
For one who goes forth, who causes others to go forth, who is injurious and terrible—
he becomes a source of fear for all.
In the same way, fire also produces fear in everyone at the mere sight of it.
Therefore, such an Agni is "veṣaḥ" (clothed/manifest) in "samatsu" (in battles);
the meaning is: being radiant, may he become our ally.
*gṛdhu*: from the root *gṛdhu* in the sense of "desire. [The suffix] *ku* is applied after the roots *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣap*.

*Śūra*: [derived from] the root *śu*, meaning "to go. From this root, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the suffix *knu* is applied according to the rule *gṛṣicimīnāṃ dīrghaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.183).
"Upa pra" is the seventh hymn, consisting of ten verses. It is enumerated here as "Upa pra daśa.
According to the metrical rule "Ṛṣiṣv anyasmāt," the seer (ṛṣi) is Parāśara, the son of Śakti.

By the *anādeśaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding the default [metre]), it is *triṣṭubh*. Because it is characterized by the rule "that which is supreme belongs to Agni, [following] that which belongs to Indra," its deity is Agni.
These three hymns beginning with this one belong to the *prātaranuvāka* in the Agni-sacrifice, in the *triṣṭubh* metre.
In the section beginning with "athaitasyāḥ," it is likewise stated in the Sūtra: "'upa pra jinvan'—these three [verses] and the hymn 'kā ta upetiḥ' [are used].
Even regarding the word *āśvina*, by virtue of the extension (*atideśa*) from the *prātaranuvāka*, these first three hymns are included.
It is stated accordingly: "'One should continue with this *gāyatra* hymn addressed to Agni, according to the rule of the *prātaranuvāka*. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.5).

The longing ones have stirred him who longs, as wives of one dwelling together stir their own husband; the sisters have delighted in the dark one and the ruddy one, as cows delight in the dappled Dawn as she shines forth. upa | pra | jinvan | uśatīḥ | uśantam | patim | na | nityam | janayaḥ | sa'nīḻāḥ | svasāraḥ | śyāvīm | aruṣīm | ajuṣan | citram | ucchantīm | uṣasam | na | gāvaḥ ||1||
Desiring; longing; yearning.
Being of one nest.
*Nīla* means a place of residence.
They have a common place of residence because they are situated on the same hand.
*Svasāraḥ* is a name for the fingers.
Fingers such as these, like wives (*jāyāḥ*), have constantly and uniquely gladdened the desiring Agni, even as they do their husband;

having approached him, they please him through the performance of rites such as the offering of oblations. And having pleased him, they have enjoyed—that is, served—that wonderful Agni, who is worthy of admiration and worship, by means of their stretching toward him.

In this regard, there is an illustration: just as the rays (gāvaḥ) attend upon the goddess Uṣas—she who is "śyāvīm," dark-colored due to her connection with night; then "ucchantīm," dispelling darkness through her connection with the rays of the sun; and for that very reason "aruṣīm," shining brightly, or alternatively, endowed with a radiant form—so too do the fingers (the rays) always remain connected to Agni through the performance of service in all sacrifices. This is the intended meaning.
*jinvan* [is derived from] *jivi*, which means "to please"; because it is marked with the *it*-suffix, the augment *num* is applied.
*leṭi aḍagamaḥ* (the augment *aṭ* occurs before the suffix *leṭ*). *uśatīḥ*.
By the rule *vā chandasi*, there is the lengthening of the preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*).
In the word *śatanūmnaḥ*, the vowel becomes udātta because of the suffix *na*.
Regarding *svasāraḥ*: from the root *asu* in the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepaṇe*), the suffix *knu* is applied by the rule *subyaserṛn* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.253).
By the rule *na padasvasādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.10), there is a prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.
Due to the *nit* designation, the word is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
[The form is] *aruṣīm*.
*Aruṣi* is a name for form (*rūpa*). [It is derived from] the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *uṣac* added according to Uṇādi Sūtra 4.513 (*ṛhinibhyāmuṣac*).
The long vowel *ī* has the sense of the suffix *matup* (possessive), according to the rule *chandasīvanipau*.
The initial accentuation [of the prefix] occurs by way of reversal.
*ajuṣan*: from the root *juṣ* in the sense of "pleasure" and "service."
It belongs to the *tud-ādi* class.

In the *laṅ* [tense], the *parasmaipada* ending occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). With the word "ruda" understood from the previous rule, the augment *ruṭ* is applied to the final syllable by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi."

1. "All" does not exist. 2. *la* includes all living beings; like an oblation cast forth, it impels the offering toward the gods. 3. By the mere sight of *ca*, *cha*, *dha*, *na*, *pha*. 4. *ḍha* is prescribed by rule (*sūtrita*). 5. *cha*, *ta*, *śa*: the sisters (*svasāraḥ*). The sisters:
"Even the firm [obstacles], our parents, with hymns—the Aṅgirases with their roar—have shattered them.
They have made a path for us through the great heaven; the bright ones have found the light of day as a signal. (*vīḷu cid... ukthaiḥ... cakruḥ... viduḥ*)

Even though our parents were firm and difficult to move, the Aṅgirases, by means of their hymns and with a roar, shattered the mountain; they made a path for us toward the great heaven, and they found the light of day and the sun as the banner of the dawns.
"Our fathers," the seers known as the Aṅgirases, having praised with hymns— the *ukthas*—

the "breaker of the rock," even though it was "firm" (*vīḷu*)— that is, strong; they shattered by means of "roar" (*raveṇa*), that is, by the mere sound of their praise, the Asura named Paṇi, who was a devourer of the rock and possessed great strength.
The meaning is that, being praised by them, he slew the Asura.
Furthermore, they "made" (cakruḥ)—that is, prepared—"the path" (gātuṃ), the way to "the great" (bṛhataḥ) "heaven" (divaḥ), "for us" (asme);
for the obstructing Asura had been slain by Agni.
Having made a path—that which is "suṣṭhu araṇīyam," meaning easily attainable due to the absence of Asuras—they "viduḥ," that is, they knew or obtained "ahnaḥ," the day.

Likewise, there is an ellipsis to be supplied: "the Ustrās [the cows] also found the 'ketum ahnām,' the banner of the days, the one who makes known, the Āditya, as well as the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis."
*vīḷu*: by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case ending. *duhvā*.
The word *dṛḍha* is established as a nipātana (irregularly formed word) by Pāṇini’s rule *dṛḍhaḥ sthūlabalayoḥ* (7.2.20).
The substitution of *ḍā* for the case-ending is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* (7.1.39).
[He is] breaking (*rujan*).
The root *ruj* means "to break.

It belongs to the *tud*-class (the sixth class). The absence of the augment *a* is according to the rule: "In the Vedic language, [the substitution of *ar* for *as*] occurs diversely even when not preceded by *mā*."
They understood (*vividuḥ*). [The roots] *vida* in the sense of "knowing" or *vidlū* in the sense of "obtaining":
this is the form in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *us*.
The Ādityas, the sustainers, have established the truth and the inspired thought of the one who possesses wealth;
they, the waters, flow unthirsting toward the gods, increasing their generation with sacrificial food.

Establishing the cosmic order (*ṛta*), bestowing wealth, and following his inspired thought—then indeed do the noble ones, bearing their offerings, go toward the gods without thirst; they approach them, strengthening the divine race with sacrificial food. || 3 ||

"The great seers, Agni, and the Bharatas, having reached the place of sacrifice (*ṛta*) which is the site for the gods, 'held'—that is, they maintained it in the form of the *gārhapatya* and other sacrificial fires.
And having held it, they 'furthered'—that is, they performed—the 'thought' (*dhīti*), meaning the ritual action characterized by the *agnihotra* and so forth, of this Agni.
The meaning is that they carried out the rites for the sake of the god Agni, just as men acquire wealth."

Immediately after the performance of the rites of the Aṅgirases from the beginning, "then" (atha) [the women] become "mistresses of wealth" (aryāḥ), that is, "didhiṣvaḥ"; by means of that wealth, they perform the "didhiṣva-maintenance of the fires. The meaning is that they have performed the formal establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna).

"Supporting those who have established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) by performing rituals such as the *agnihotra*, being "unthirsty"—that is, free from craving for other objects of sense—therefore "active," endowed with ritual action (*apas*), such progeny characterized as sacrificers, "increasing the gods" Indra and others, as well as "mankind born of birth," by means of "pleasure-food" (*prayas*) characterized as oblation-material, "go toward" this Agni—that is, they approach and attend upon him."
*dadhan* [is derived from] *dadha* in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*).
In the *laṅ* tense, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyayena*).
The elision of the *a* is according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasyamāyoge 'pi" (Pāṇini 6.4.75).
[Thus] *dhanayan*.
From the word *dhana*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule "tat karoti" (Pāṇini 3.1.25).

Due to the treatment as if it were the desired form (*iṣṭavadbhāva*) according to the rule "the base undergoes the same changes as when the desired suffix follows," there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
In the *laṅ* [tense], it is as before. This is the meaning.
The word *arthaḥ* is derived as an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term by Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.1.103: *arthaḥ svāmivaiśyayoḥ*.
There is a deviation in gender and number.
According to the Phiṭ-sūtra 17: *arthaḥ svāmyākhyā cet*, it has an udātta accent on the final syllable.
*Didhiṣvaḥ*:
derived from the roots *dhā* (in the sense of "holding" and "nourishing") and *pā* (in the sense of "consuming"), by the rule *anūdambhūjambakapherūkkancūdidhiṣvaḥ*. [The commentary notes:
*ḍha* means "he has struck."

2. By the rule "ca-cha-ta-na-pha-śa-tadadabh-daivatya" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.93), the suffix *kru* is prescribed as an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) ending; it bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
The *svarita* accent of the suffix *jas* [in *vibhūtayas*] is due to the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ. [The root] *han* means "to take away."
From this root preceded by *vi*, the *katra* suffix is applied according to the *auṇādika* rules; by the rule "the substitution of *bha* for *hra* and *maha*," there is the change to *bha*.
[The form is] *atṛpyantīḥ*.
In *jituṣā*, [the suffix] *pipāsāyām* [is applied].

In the case of *jasi*, because the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is optional by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*), the homogeneous long vowel is applied.
There is the accent of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*) for the indeclinable (*avyaya*) which is the first member of the compound.
*Apasaḥ*.

From the word *apasa*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the possessive suffix *vin*—which is derived from the root *usap-*—by virtue of the term "extensively" (*bahula*) in Pāṇini’s rule 5.2.122: *vin-mator bahulam chandasi*.
Since the form ending in *vin* possesses three genders, it lacks the designation *naḍi-vat*; consequently, by the accent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-svara*), it is oxytone.
*Janma*: "Those who are born" (*jāyante*) are *janmānaḥ*, meaning human beings;
the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen [to be used] after other [roots] as well."
The elision of the suffix *śas* is by the rule "supāṃ suluk."
When Mātariśvan churned him forth, he became the white, victorious one present in every house. From him—

When he, the wise one, had fashioned the sap for the Father Heaven, he moved downward from Pṛśni. The archer boldly released the two-edged bolt at him; the God bestowed his brilliance upon his own daughter. When he, the wise one, had fashioned the sap for the Father Heaven, he moved downward from Pṛśni. The archer boldly released the two-edged bolt at him; the God bestowed his brilliance upon his own daughter. (15)

O Vmhe, for the great, O protector, for the shining host of gods, when the sacrificer offers this oblation—the very essence of the earth—then the *pṛśanya*, the one skilled in touch, such as a Rākṣasa, knowing you, O Agni, as the bearer of the oblations, flees from his own power. Then Agni, the shooter (*vastṛ*), with his bold bow, hurls a flaming arrow (*vidyut*) at that fleeing Rākṣasa or similar being.
The divine Agni, sporting at the time of dawn, places his own radiance— his brilliance— into his own daughter, that is, into the Dawn which follows immediately after;
for at the time of dawn, the rays of the sun appear,
and with them, he unifies his own light.
And thus says the Taittirīyaka: "The fire indeed ascends after the rising sun; therefore, smoke alone is seen from the fire by day" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.10).
Hence, it is said that he places his radiance in the dawn.
The form *vkaḥ* is derived from the root *kṛ* in the *luṅ* tense, with the elision of the suffix by the rule "In mantras, [the suffixes of] *ghas*, etc. (*mantre ghasa*).
*tsarat*: [derived from] the root *sṛ*, meaning "to go" (*chadgatau*), in the *leṭ* mood; there is the augment *aṭ*.
In the word *pṛśanyaḥ*, there is the elision of the vowel *i* [from the root *spṛś*], as indicated by the phrase "and from this [root]"; [the root is] *spṛśa* in the sense of "touching."
The suffix *kyu*, which is prescribed by the rule *kṛpṛji* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.239), also occurs after this root [√spṛś] due to the word "bahulam" (in various cases).
*Sparśaḥ* means "the act of touching. The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *tatra sādhuḥ* ("good or fit for that").
The addition of *l* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). By the rule "the third syllable is circumflex" (*tisvaritam*), it bears the circumflex accent (*svarita*).
[The word is] *dvidyum*.
*Dvidyut* is a name for the thunderbolt (*vajra*); the elision of the other [syllable] is a Vedic archaism. *Dhāt*.
In Vedic usage, the *luṅ* (aorist) tense is employed for the present.

He who shines for you within his own house, or who offers homage to you according to the desire of the yearning one—O Agni, increase his vital strength; may he, possessing double vigor, attain wealth along with his chariot, whomsoever you impel. He who shines for you within his own house, or who offers homage to you according to the desire of the yearning one—O Agni, increase his vital strength; may he, possessing double vigor, attain wealth along with his chariot, whomsoever you impel. (16)
O Agni, that sacrificer who, in his own sacrificial hall (*sve dame*), illumines you according to the scriptures—
here the particle *vā* functions as a delimiter (*maryādā*)—
kindles you completely with fuel-sticks and other materials.

O Agni, let one who desires you day after day offer homage to you, or indeed present the oblation characterized by the sacrificial offering. O Agni, for that sacrificer whom you—being established and increased in both the middle and highest stations—augment with all vigor and food, you impel that man who desires to fight along with his chariot into battle; that man shall obtain and attain wealth through his vehicle.
"To you.
Because [the recipient] is the object (*karman*) due to the rule "the mention of the action must be made," it takes the fourth case (*caturthī*) as a recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
From the giver (*dāśāt*).
In the root *dāś* (meaning "to give"),
there is the augment *aṭ* in the *leṭ* mood;
[the form is] *uśataḥ*.
In the phrase *śataranumaḥ*, the case ending (*vibhakti*) is udātta.
The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the dative according to the rule *caturthyarthe bahulaṃ chandasi*.
[The word is] *anughūna*.
*Gurau* is the name for "day.

*Anu* functions as a *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Consequently, the second case ending is applied according to the rule: "When joined with a *karmapravacanīya*... (Pāṇini 2.3.8).

*vardho* | *vardha u* | From the root *vṛdh* in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, because the *śap* suffix is treated as *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule "in the Veda both [types of suffixes apply]," there is the elision of the *ṇi* by the rule "after *gṛ*, when the following suffix is not *it*."
Because the suffix *śap* is marked with the *pit* indicator, it is udātta; thus, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
When there is a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with *uj*, the form is *ujaḥ*.

May he generate—may he cause to be born—a son characterized by the qualities about to be mentioned: one who is *śardhaṃ* (mighty), *balavantam* (strong), *anavadyam* (blameless, free from blemish), *yuvānam* (young, meaning devoid of old age), and *svādhyaṃ* (one of excellent deeds or excellent wisdom). And may he *sūdayatha* (impel)—may he urge forth—the son thus born toward sacrifices and other rites. Alternatively: *retaḥ* is a name for water. The poured rain-water, sent down by the cloud, *ānad* (has pervaded) for the sake of *iṣe* (food), that is, for the production of crops and the like. For when there is contact between the earth and the fire through the rain-water, crops arise. Of what nature is that fire? It is *nṛpatim* (the protector of men) and *śuci* (pure, shining). Endowed with such fire, may Agni, the shining one, at the very moment of proximity (*abhīke*), generate a son distinguished by qualities such as might, and impel him toward sacrifice and the like. Regarding the words: * iṣe*: The vowel of the case-ending is acute according to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. * nṛpatim*: The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member is due to the rule *parādiśchandasibahulām*. * ānad*: From the root *aśū* (to pervade). In the *laṅ* tense, there is a substitution for the *parasmaipada* ending; the augment *āṭ* is added. It is always [accented] in *brahmādi* groups. * niṣiktam*: From the root *picir* (to flow). The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used in the passive sense. By the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the preceding prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). By the rule *upasargātsunoti*, the final vowel becomes acute. * abhīke*: Derived from *abhi* + *hanti* with the suffix *ac*; the form is established by being included in the *ṭupodarādi* group. Alternatively, from the root *iṇ* (to go) with the *kvan* suffix (Uṇādi); in both cases, the accent is on the first member because it belongs to the *dāsībhārādi* group. * svādhyaṃ*: The *yaṇ* substitution occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ*. The *svarita* accent arises by the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*. * janayat*: From the causative of the root *jan* in the *leṭ* mood, with the augment *aṭ*. * sūdayat*: From the root *pūda* (to flow/impel). As before, in the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *aṭ*.
The mind does not reach him who alone traverses the paths instantly; as the Sun, he rules over wealth by his thread.
O kings Mitra and Varuṇa, you of beautiful hands, you guard the beloved nectar among the cattle.

Mind: No; he who goes alone instantly along the paths, the Sun, rules over wealth by his thread. O Mitra and Varuṇa, the two kings with beautiful hands, you guard the beloved nectar among the cattle. 9.
The Sun, being alone—solitary and without companion—traverses the celestial paths swiftly; he reaches them instantly.
Regarding his state of being without companion, it is heard in scripture: "He said that the Sun moves alone;
indeed, yonder Āditya moves alone" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.9.5.4).
And his swift movement is recorded in tradition: "O you who traverse two thousand yojanas, two hundred yojanas, and two more yojanas in half a moment—homage be to you!
This is an illustration of his swift movement.
Like the mind— just as the mind moves swiftly,
so too does that hero (sūra) possess sovereign power (īśe) over wealth (vasvaḥ) entirely (satrā), that is, simultaneously and all at once.
For he who moves swiftly attains wealth situated in many places.
Likewise, the two kings, Mitra and Varuṇa, who shine forth, possessing beautiful arms, protect the beloved, life-giving nectar—the milk which has the flavor of immortality—within our cows.
O Agni, the sense is that you yourself exist in those various forms.
*Vasvaḥ*:
there is a change of gender.
Regarding the absence of *guṇa* by the rule *gher ṅiti*, the *yaṇ* substitution applies according to the Vedic option stated in *jasādiṣu chandasi vāvacanam*.
*Īśe*. [The root] *īś* [is used] in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). There is the elision of the *ta* [augment] by the rule "there is elision of *ta* in the *ātmanepada* [endings]."
*Mitrāvaruṇā*:

by the rule *devatādvandve ca*, the substitution of *ān* for the final vowel of the first member occurs; by the same rule *devatādvandve ca*, both members retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
1. With water showered by *ta*, *da*, *dha*, *śa*, and *sa*:
O Agni, being a wise seer, do not forget our ancestral friendship; let not old age diminish our form. Before that assault [of death] comes, provide for us.
O Agni, do not forget our ancestral friendships; you are a wise seer who knows all. Old age impairs the form of man like a garment; before that curse reaches us, pass us by. 10.
O Agni, do not neglect—that is, do not destroy—the friendships and bonds of companionship that have come down from our ancestors, beginning with Vasiṣṭha;
for here, by the influence of the prefix, the root *mṛṣ* functions in a different sense.
Since you, being a seer (*kavi*) of far-reaching vision, are one who knows all things directly and fully.
Homage! It is not form.
Just as the sunbeams, though possessing form, pervade the atmosphere, so too does it pervade.
Old age—decay—mines me; it destroys me, the seer of this well-spoken hymn.
"From that curse—that cause of injury—before that old age reaches me, instruct me; be aware of it.
Act in such a way that she does not reach me;
that is to say, grant me immortality."
[The commentary] by Sakhya.
470. Rigveda [Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 5, Varga 17].

"Viśvā viśvāni svāni amṛtāni"—this is a name for gold, according to the Śruti: "Gold is immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.28.1). [The meaning is: making all the golds together at once (*satrā*) for the sake of the singers; that is, bestowing them simultaneously. Who? [This refers to Indra. Regarding the verb *karoti*, the Vedic *luṅ* (aorist) is used. By the rule "ghas etc. in mantras," the suffix *cli* takes the *luṅ* (aorist) ending. By the rule "after *ha*, *tha*, and *abhyasta*," there is the elision of the letter *t*. Regarding *naryā*: from the word *nara*, the suffix *yat*—characterized as applied after words like *go* in the sense of "beneficial to"—should be seen (Pāṇini 5.1.2). Alternatively, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "good for that" (Pāṇini 4.4.98). Regarding *cakrāṇaḥ*: this is the present participle (*laṭ* with *śānac*) of the root *kṛ*. By the rule "variously in the Chandas," the *vikaraṇa* suffix is elided. Now, if this were so, would it not follow that the first syllable must be udātta by the rule "the beginning of reduplicated stems (*abhyasta*)"? If so, let it be the *kānac* suffix of the perfect (*liṭ*). Since that is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the udātta of the *abhyasta* does not apply, and thus the *citsvara* (accent of the suffix) alone remains.
Like those seeking their calf that has wandered away, all the immortal and unerring gods searched for him.
Exhausted by toil, seeking the track, and cherishing the prayer, they stood at the highest station, the lovely place of Agni.

They did not find the calf hidden among us; though all the wise immortals sought him, those wearying seekers of the track, the upholders of prayer, stood at the highest, most beautiful station of Agni in the beginning. 2.
"ᵥasme" means "to us," "vatsam" means "the beloved one who possesses calves" (or alternatively,
"vatsaḥ" means "a son").
Because he is born later.
In that same way, Agni is the son of Atri.
Thus it is recorded in the sacred tradition: "Being mine indeed, carry my oblations, O son; you are the maker of worlds for your father, O Jātavedas" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.7.10).

Seeking Agni who was thus—*pari-pantam*, existing everywhere, having emerged from the gods and being hidden within the *cathas* and *veṇus*—all the *amṛtas*, all the immortal gods, and the *amūrās*, the undeluded Maruts, *vindan*: they found him; they obtained that Agni.

And not finding him, those young ones, exhausted by the toil born of the absence of the carrier of oblations (Agni) and the lack of offerings, and terrified by that distress, went upon his tracks with their feet in order to search for that Fire. Being thus "bearers of the thought" (dhiyaṃdhāḥ)— that is, sustainers of the thoughts characterized as the actions of Fire, such as its place of rest, seat, and location— they reached the "beautiful" (cāru), the most excellent and supreme place of the Fire, where indeed Agni remained hidden.
In that place they *tasthuḥ*, meaning they stood; the sense is that through various kinds of effort they beheld the fire. *Paribantam*.
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *upasargāt prādurbhyām astiryacparaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.87).
[The word is] *śramayuvaḥ*.
[The root] *yu* [is used] in the sense of “mixing.”

They are called *śramayuvaḥ* because they are exhausted by toil (*śrama*). The suffixes *kvip* and *dhr̥k*, which are prescribed by the rule "kvibvacipraccha" (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.215), apply even to this verbal root.
Due to its inclusion in the *tantv-ādi* group, the substitution *uvaṅ* occurs.
*Padvyaḥ*:
in *dhīgaya* and other such compounds.
Those who move or go by means of their feet (*padena*) are called *padvyaḥ*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule “*kvip ca*”. Thus, *dhiyaṃdhāḥ*. The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule “*āto ’nupasarge kaḥ*”.

Because of the word "bahulam" (in various ways) in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the second case ending as well. [The form] *tasthuḥ* lacks the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because it begins with *pāda*.
Cāru:
[The elision of the locative case ending occurs] by the rule "supāṃ suluk.
When, O Agni, they have honored you with oblations and clarified butter for three autumns, they, being pure, have served you.
They bestowed upon him worshipful names; the well-born ones brought their bodies to perfection.
When, O Agni, for three autumns the pure ones had served you, the pure one, with clarified butter, they bestowed upon him worshipful names; the well-born ones brought their bodies to perfection. 3.

1. Because he was born later, [he is] the son of Ta, Dha, Śa, and Pu. O Maruts, you who are pure, purifiers, or consecrated ones—O Agni, having brought you, who are pure, purified, or radiant, and who have emerged from among the gods, up for three autumns, that is, for three years, with clarified butter as an oblation, and while they were performing worship, you then became manifest. Immediately thereafter, those Maruts, being favored by you, assumed even names worthy of sacrifice, names fit to be employed in the sacrifice.
And these names are recorded in the Taittirīyaka: "Īdṛṅ, Anyāruṅ, Etādṛṅ, Pratidṛṅ, Mitra, Samita, and Sabhara" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.6.5.5), and so forth.
At the construction of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), oblations to the Maruts are offered with cakes on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) accompanied by these [names].
Having borne these names, they abandoned their former form and, having attained auspicious immortality, "made their own bodies (*tanvaḥ*) successful," meaning they caused them to reach heaven.

In the case of *tisraḥ* [the plural nominative/accusative feminine of *tri-*], when the rule *tricaturor striyāṃ tisṛcatasṛ* would have required the substitution of the homogeneous long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*), the rule *aci ra ṛtaḥ* prescribes the substitution of the letter *r*.
The word *tri-* is oxytone (*antodātta*) by the rule *phiṣaḥ*.

Even for the substitute *tisṛ*, by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitute behaving like the original), there is an acute accent on the final syllable; consequently, by the rule "udāttasvaritayor halsvaritodāttam" [Pāṇini 6.1.174], the nominative plural suffix *śas* becomes acute. Thus: *śaradaḥ*.
[The root] *bhṛ* is used in the sense of "injury."
The word *śarad* ("autumn") refers to the year, derived from the sense "in this [time] plants wither" (*śīryante 'syām oṣadhayaḥ*).
The suffix *adipratyaya* is applied according to the rule *śrṛdhabhasodiḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.127).
In both cases, the accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5).
*Saparyān* [is derived from] *sapara* in the sense of "worship";
it belongs to the *kaṇva*-class (of roots).
The augment *āṬ* is added by the rule *leṭo ’ḍāṭau*. By the rule *inaśca lopaḥ*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*. [Thus we have] *yajñiyāni*.
The suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of "belonging to the sacrificer (*yajñin*) and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)."

Making themselves known to the two great worlds, the worshipful sons of Rudra have come forth. With his thoughts, the wise one found Agni standing at the highest station, established in the place of the sacrificial division. ā rodasī bṛhatī vevidānāḥ pra rudriyā jabhiri yajñiyāsaḥ | vidat marta nemadhitā cikitvān agnim pade parame tasthivāṃsam || 4 || They made themselves known to the two great worlds; the worshipful sons of Rudra have come forth. The wise mortal found Agni, who had taken his stand at the highest station, through the sacrificial division. || 4 ||
"The two vast and great *rodasī*, heaven and earth, being fully aware— meaning making themselves known intensely—
and speaking to one another as to where they are turning toward;
the meaning is that they exist between heaven and earth."
Or alternatively:

"In the midst of the two great ones, heaven and earth, *āvevidānāḥ*—meaning perceiving or obtaining [the wealth]—such are the *yajñiyāsaḥ*, the gods worthy of sacrifice. Regarding the *rudriyāḥ*: Rudra is Agni. When the gods were at war with the Asuras, they took away the wealth that had been established by those gods for Agni, who had departed; the gods then arrived and, by force, seized that wealth from the presence of Agni."
At that time he wept; therefore, he is called Rudra.

And thus says the Taittirīyaka: "He desired that, and he departed from that; having conquered it, he brought it back; his kinsmen followed after it. It was exhausted by his exertion; he wept. Because he wept (arodat), that is the essence of Rudra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.1.1).
The hymns worthy of that Rudra were brought forth by the progeny; "cakṣuḥ" (the eye) is the meaning.
Regarding "nemadhitā":
the word *nema* signifies "half."
And thus Yāska says: "The word *nema* means half" (*Nirukta* 3.20). Indra is called *nemadhita* because he is placed or supported by the half-share of all the gods.
All the gods constitute one half, while Indra alone constitutes the other half; such is the meaning.
And so says the Taittirīyaka: "Since Indra is the counterpart of all [the gods], therefore Indra is the recipient of the greatest share among the deities" (Tait. Saṃ. 5.4.8.3).

Knowing this, the wise man found—that is, obtained—Agni, who, together with that Indra and accompanied by the host of Maruts (martaḥ), was stationed on the highest, most excellent other place, such as the Aśvattha tree.
*vevidānāḥ*: From the root *vid*, meaning "to know" as well as "to obtain," the suffix *śānac* is applied to the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root ending in *yan*.
By the rule "in the Vedic language [there is] diversely," there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

In the Vedic language, according to the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the suffix *śānac* is treated as both [present and aorist]; because it is an archaic verbal form (*ārṣadhātu*), there is the elision of the *at* and the substitution of *ya* for *la*.
By the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ*, the first syllable is acute-accented (*ādyudātta*).
1. ḍa-pṛṣṭhataḥ (from behind).

*vidat*: from the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining" (*lābhe*). In the *luṅ* tense, because it is marked with *ludit*, the *cli* suffix is replaced by *aṅ*. *Nemadhita*: the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *dhā* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). By the rule *sudhita vasudhita nemadhita* (Pāṇini 7.4.45), the substitution of *dhi* for *ta* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). The original accent of the first member is maintained by the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*. The third case ending is changed to *ā* by the rule *supāṃ suluk* etc. *Tasthivāṃsam*: from the root *sthā* with the *liṭ* suffix *kasu*. The augment *iṭ* is added by the rule *vastrekājādghasām*.
In the *Dharmābhiṣṭava*, the verse beginning with “*asaṃjānānāḥ*” is used;
it is prescribed in the section titled “Now, the subsequent” (*athottaram*) in the *Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* (4.7): “*saṃjānānā upasīdannabhijñvā daśabhirvivasvataḥ*.”
Perceiving [him], they sat down nearby with insight; accompanied by their wives, they paid homage to him who was worthy of homage.
Desiring to release themselves, they made their own bodies beautiful, as friends guarding the blink of an eye for a friend.

Knowing well, they sat down on their knees; accompanied by their wives, they paid homage to the one worthy of homage. Desiring to release themselves, they made their own bodies [ready]; as friends, they guarded the friend even during the winking of an eye. 5.
O Agni, the gods, being in agreement with you—that is, knowing you correctly—approach you; having approached, they reach you.
And having performed this act of approaching, being accompanied by their wives (*patnīvantaḥ*), they worshiped you, who are worthy of homage, bowing down with knees bent toward you (*abhijñu*).

And having worshipped [you], while the glance of your friend, your companion, served as the occasion for their appearance, the friends—the gods—being protected by you, being guarded by you, desiring to empty their own bodies (*tanvaḥ*), that is, their own forms, making them empty through the observance of initiation (*dīkṣā*) such as fasting and so forth, drying them up, they performed sacrifices.
This is according to the Śruti: "The gods indeed performed the sacrifice" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.11).
*namasyan*: [This is derived from the root] *namas* with the suffix *kyac* added in the sense of worship, according to the rule "namo-varivas-citraṅaḥ";
it is in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense.
In the phrase "bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge 'pi," there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.
[The form] is *ririkṣāṃsaḥ*. [The root] *ric* means "to empty" (*virecana*).
The suffix *kasu* is substituted for *liṭ*. [Example:
*nimiṣi*, from the root *miṣ* in the sense of "rivalry."
Here, by the force of the prefix (*upasarga*), the sense is that of seeing;
the suffix *kvip* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule beginning with *saṃpadādi*.
[Thus, the form is] *rakṣamāṇāḥ* (protecting).
The suffix *śānac* is substituted for *laṭ* in the sense of the object;
although *yak* would have been expected, *śap* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

The three times seven secret places which have been established by those who know your footprints, O worshipful ones—with these, being of one accord, you guard the immortal; protect both the cattle and that which is stationary and that which moves.

Three times seven—those secret things which the worshipful ones have discovered within you, in your footsteps—with those they guard the immortal nectar in unison; protect both the cattle and all that stands and moves. 6.
The "three times seven" refers to twenty-one secret and hidden matters that are to be understood through the Veda.
By the etymological derivation that "those by which one goes to heaven are *pada*s," the word *pada* here denotes sacrifices;
and these are twenty-one in number.
The seven *pākayajñas* consist of the *aupāsanahoma*, *vaiśvadeva*, and so forth;
the seven *haviryajñas* consist of the *agnyādheya*, *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and so forth;
and the seven *somayajñas* consist of the *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, and so forth.
In this way, the twenty-one sacrificial terms are placed and established in you alone, O Agni,
because all of them have you as their primary focus;
for indeed, sacrifices cannot be performed without Agni.
"Worthy of sacrifice" (*yajñiyāsaḥ*) means those who are fit for sacrifice, being endowed with the causes of qualification such as having a need, possessing wealth, and so forth.
As it has been said: "One who is desirous, capable, learned, and not excluded by the scriptures is qualified for the ritual.
Such sacrificers, possessed of these characteristics, "found"—that is, they obtained—those stations.

And having obtained these words characterized by sacrifice, they protect—that is, they preserve and worship—you, who are immortal and whose nature is deathlessness. *Sajopāḥ*: sharing the same joy with those sacrificers. Protect and guard the cattle—such as cows, horses, and other livestock—as well as the stationary beings—grains and other immobile things—and that which moves, namely the various other classes of living beings distinct from domestic animals; guard all of that.
For when those [sacrificial fires] are protected, your sacrifices can be performed, and not otherwise; this is the meaning of why you are addressed in this way. That is to say:
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision of the case ending. *guhāyāni* means "those which exist in a cave" (*guhāyām bhavāni*).
The suffix *yat* [is applied] by the rule "bhave chandasi";
the acute accent on the first syllable is by the rule "yato 'nāvaḥ";
[the form] *tve*.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the substitution of *śe* for the locative case ending. [The form] *avidan* [is derived from] the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining."

In the case of *luṅ*, because it is prescribed as *lṛd*, the suffix is *aṅ*. In *paśūn* and *sthātṝn*, because of the rule "in both ways in the ṛc" (*ubhayatharcu*; Pāṇini 8.3.8), there is an optionality; thus, there is an absence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) for the nasal *n*.
O wise Agni, bestow upon us for our living the means of subsistence for the people, distributed in due order;
knowing the paths traveled by the gods, you have become the tireless messenger and the bearer of the oblation.

O wise Agni, bestow in due order the settlements of the peoples and the spoils of war for our living; as one who knows the paths leading to the gods, you have become the unwearied messenger, the bearer of the oblation. 7.
O Agni, you who possess all *vayunāni*—this refers to knowledge;
here, however, it concerns that which is to be known.

You, the wise one, knowing all things that are to be known, bestow *śurudhaḥ*—the obstructors of hunger, distress, and sorrow—upon the *kṣitīnām*, meaning upon the people characterized as sacrificers, so that they may live (*jīvase*). Arrange them, that is, perform them, in three ways (*tri dhāḥ*), so that they become continuous and uninterrupted (*anuṣak*).

Having thus brought the sacrificers to fulfillment, immediately thereafter you became the messenger of the gods, carrying the oblation that had been given to them from the *havirdhāna*. What kind of messenger are you? You are one who knows within, knowing between heaven and earth.
Knowing what?
The paths;
of what kind? Those traveled by the gods.
The meaning is that he knows those paths by which the gods go and travel;
furthermore, he is unwearied, being untiring even in the repeated carrying of the oblation.

*Vayunāni*. [The root] *aja* means "to go" and "to throw. By the rule *ajiyamiśīṅbhyaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.341), the suffix *unan* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, *vayuna* is derived.
The substitution of *vī* for *vi* occurs by the rule *ajervy-ajapauḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.56).
Regarding the word *kṣitīnām*: those who dwell or reside are called *kṣitayaḥ*, meaning human beings.
In the rule *kṣiyatkau ca saṃjñāyām*, the suffix *ki* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Following the word *kṣiti*, which is oxytone and ends in a short vowel, the subsequent *nāmaḥ* receives an acute accent by the rule *nāmanpyatarasyām*.
[The form is] *śurudhaḥ*.
They are called *śurudhaḥ* because they obstruct (*rudhanti*) grief (*śucam*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *kvip ca*;
the elision of the final letter of the first member of the compound occurs by virtue of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
The two self-sustaining ones have come from heaven; the mighty ones have opened wide the doors of wealth. Knowing the secret, they have adorned themselves.
Saramā found the firm enclosure, by which the human race now enjoys its nourishment.

He is worthy of worship. From heaven he has come; the mighty ones, knowing the cosmic order (*ṛta*), have opened wide the doors of wealth. Saramā found the firm enclosure of the cattle, by which the human race now enjoys its sustenance.
1. By means of [qualities] such as desire, capacity, and learning;
2. one is qualified for the ritual actions (karma);
3. the suffix -ana.
