"Svādhyah" means endowed with auspicious deeds; "yahvah" means mighty; "mahasyah" means great; "sasra gaṅgādhāḥ sasra nadyaḥ"—the rivers that hold the Gaṅgā have come from the sky (divaḥ), i.e., from the heavenly world, and flow abundantly—this is the ellipsis.
O Agni, such rivers as these were established by you.
For when there is an oblation in the fire, through that, the sun causes rain for men;
the traditional authority (smṛti) regarding this matter has been cited previously.
Therefore, it is said that he indeed causes the rivers to flow by means of rain.

Likewise, the Aṅgirases, "knowers of Ṛta," meaning those who knew the sacrifice that had been performed, "knew" (*ajānan*) the "doors"—the paths of access—to the "wealth" in the form of cattle that had been seized by the Asura Vala.
Indra, pleased by the sacrifice accomplished through them, dispatched a divine dog named Saramā to search for the cattle;
and Saramā, having discovered the location of the cattle, reported it to Indra.
And Indra caused those Aṅgirases to obtain the cows;
therefore, you alone have performed all this.
From the Aṅgirases [you received] "gavyam"—that which pertains to the cow—"halam," meaning thick or massive.
The meaning is "abundantly.
"In this manner, they established that beautiful wealth characterized by milk upon it; when the immortals fashioned the two eyes from the ocean."
Then they flow forth like well-released rivers; O Agni, the downward-flowing ruddy ones have appeared.

They have bestowed glory upon him; for the immortals made his two beautiful eyes like those of heaven. Then they flow forth like well-guided rivers; O Agni, they have recognized the downward-flowing, ruddy ones. 10.
In this fire, the sacrificers established and deposited beautiful and splendid prosperity (*śrī*), consisting of the perfection of the sacrifice such as the carrying around and the sprinkling;
and having so established it, whenever they made the two eyes of the sacrifice—the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*)—they did so, for the Śruti says:
"These two portions of clarified butter are indeed the two eyes of the sacrifice" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.2.1).
At that time, the immortal gods (*amṛtāḥ*), whose nature is deathlessness, perceiving that [Agni] was born at the time of the sacrifice,
should lead him forth with ease.
Just as the instruction of the learned is led forward for the resolution of various doubts regarding all matters to be practiced, so too is Agni led forward in all sacrifices.

And that Agni—who, lying upon a pleasant bed in the Gārhapatya hearth and other such places, is like a guest seated on a comfortable seat, who is gratified like a guest honored with water for the feet and other offerings, and who is to be satisfied with oblations—he, being well-disposed toward the sacrificer who performs his service, extends or bestows a dwelling. In this regard, there is an illustration: "like a Hotṛ priest."

Just as the *hotṛ*, the performer of oblations, and the *adhvaryu* increase the house of the sacrificer with the fruits of their respective rites, so too does one who possesses paternal wealth. [The root] *vid* is used in the sense of "obtaining."
The suffix *niṣṭhā* [is applied] after the root *viś*.
By the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," there is a prohibition of the *it*-augment.

Regarding the *ka*s affix by the rule "vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām," since this root is optionally included therein, it has been stated that specifically the *vid* belonging to the Tudādi class is understood (Kāśikā 7.2.68).
In the rule "vitto bhogapratyayayoḥ" (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.58), the absence of the *niṣṭhā* designation is prescribed as a nipāta.
[Thus we have] *vayodhāḥ*.
The root *ḍudhāñ* means "to support" and "to nourish.
By the rule *āto manin*, the suffix *vic* is applied [to form *dhī*]. Thus, *supraṇītiḥ*.
It is called *praṇīti* because it is led forth (*praṇīyate*).
The suffix *ktin* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
By the rule "and when [a suffix] beginning with *tā* follows," the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the root *nī* is preserved.

Furthermore, when a compound ending in a *kṛt* suffix is included [in the rule] by the term "sukhādi," there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member because the rule also applies to that which has a *gati* or a *kāraka* as its prior member. Thus, in *cikitvān*:
the suffix *kasu* is used for the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

In the singular genitive case, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "there is vocalization for *avas-*," and the substitution of *ṣ* according to the rule "and for *śās*, *vas*, and *ghas*. [The form is] *śāsuḥ*.
The root *śās* means "to instruct.
The suffix *u*, which is prescribed by the rule beginning with *bhṛ-svṛ-snihi* etc., should be understood to apply to this root as well due to the use of the term "variously" (*bahula*).
In that case, because the term *nit* is carried over [from the previous rule], the word is udātta-accented on its first syllable.
*Syoṇaśīḥ*. *Syoṇa* is a name for happiness.
One who lies (*śete*) in a *syona*—that is, in a place such as the *gārhapatya* fire-hearth that causes happiness—is called *syonaśīḥ*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "kvip ca. [Thus we have] *prīṇānaḥ*. [The root is] *prīñ* in the sense of "satisfying."
In the sense of the object (karmaṇi), the suffix śānac is used; by transposition (vyatyaya), *kṣā* is substituted [for *śā*]. [The root is] *vidh*, as in "to ordain" (*vidha vidhāne*).
The etymologists (nairuktāḥ) state that *vidhatiḥ* means "the act of attending upon.
The suffix *śa* is applied because it belongs to the *tud-ādi* class.
The acute accent (*udāttatvam*) on the case-ending is due to the rule *śataranumaḥ*.
He who, like the god Savitṛ, protects all strongholds with his true-mindedness and wisdom;
he who is highly praised, true like the light of heaven, has become one to be cherished like a dear self.
The god who, with true thought and wisdom, protects all strongholds sent forth by Savitṛ—he, highly praised, like a true radiance, has become dear as one's own self and worthy of being cherished. 2.

Like the sun, that Agni who is the impeller of all, shining like Savitṛ, and whose mind is truth—that is, whose knowledge is true and who perceives things as they are—protects with his own power (*kratvā*) all strongholds (*viśvā vṛjanāni*);
there is a shift in case endings;
he guards them most firmly against all conflicts.
*Vṛjanam* means battle, in which people are excluded or slain.
Furthermore, Agni—who is praised much (*purupraśastaḥ*), that is, lauded by many sacrificers—is "like *amatiḥ*";
this is a name for form (*rūpa*).
Like *rūpa*, he is "unreal" (*asatya*), meaning free from obstruction.
*Rūpya* refers to *rūpa*, which is one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Just as the essential nature of earth and other elements remains eternally uniform in itself despite the presence of particular modifications that arise and pass away, so too does Fire remain as one alone, pervading all various ritual acts without undergoing change.
That fire is "śeva," meaning it brings happiness;
there is an illustration for this:
"like one's own self."
Just as the Self, being the object of supreme love and consisting of unsurpassed bliss, brings happiness to all—
as is heard in the scriptures: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32) and "For he alone causes bliss" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.7)—
so too does fire bring happiness by being the cause of fruits such as heaven.
The fire that has become thus is "didhiṣāvyo," meaning it must be maintained by all sacrificers;
for in the event of its abandonment, there occurs the fault characterized as the slaying of a hero (*vīrahatyā*).
And so says the Taittirīyaka: "He who extinguishes the fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods" (TS 1.5.2.1).
Satyam-anmā:
"Manma" means the act of thinking;
[it is derived from] the root "man," meaning "to know."
The suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other [roots] as well.
He is one whose thought (*manman*) is true (*satya*) and not false; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, and thus it bears the accent of the first member.
*vṛjanāni*:
[derived from] the root *vṛj* in the sense of "avoiding" or "excluding.
The suffix *kyu* is applied according to the rule beginning with "kṛpvṛji," etc.
Regarding *purupraśastaḥ*:

although the rule "the third case [member] retains its original accent when used as an object" (*tṛtīyā karmaṇi*) would have required the initial member to retain its natural accent, the rule "and in the case of *pravaṇa* and others" (*pravṛddhādīnāṃ ca*, Pāṇini 6.2.147) instead prescribes that the final syllable of the second member bears the udātta accent.
It has been stated that this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). *Amatiḥ*: from the root *ama*, meaning "to go" and so forth.
*Amateriḥ*. *Didhipāyyaḥ*: from the root *dadhāti*, the form *didhipāyyaḥ* ending in the suffix *prasyan* is irregularly derived according to [Uṇādi Sūtra] 3.377.
Like a god who dwells upon the earth with all-sustaining power, like a king who is a well-disposed friend;
like heroes who sit in the front and sit for protection, he is blameless like a woman beloved by her husband.
The god who dwells upon the earth as the sustainer of all, like a king with well-disposed friends, like heroes seated in their stronghold, is blameless like a woman beloved by her husband. 3.
That Agni who is radiant like the shining sun, the sustainer of all (viśvadhāyāḥ)—
just as the sun supports the entire world by bestowing rain and other benefits, so too Agni is the supporter of the whole universe through the means of sacrifice and the like—
that Agni dwells upon the earth (upakṣeti), residing in sacrificial halls and other places as one dear to all.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"a king with beneficial friends.
Just as a king who possesses beneficial and favorable friends dwells in happiness, so it is in this case.
The meaning is that just as a king who is a friend to all people, so too is Agni a friend to all people;
for no one indeed hates Agni.
Of this Agni, the men sitting down (*puraḥsadaḥ*) in front sit like heroes dwelling in their father’s house—sons, as it were, dwelling in the shelter (*śarmasadaḥ*).
The sense is that Agni protects his attendants just as a father protects his sons.
Thus, this very Agni becomes exceedingly pure and fit for ritual action.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Blameless and irreproachable, like a woman who is beloved by her husband—like a wife who has been accepted and served by her own lord;
just as she, being pure through her devotion to her husband, becomes fit for all tasks, so too is Agni.
He is the sustainer of all.

By the rule "There is also the preservation of the original accent of the first member even when [the second member] is a verbal root denoting motion or an agent," the suffix *asun* is applied to the root *dhā* preceded by an agentive word, according to the rule "After the roots *vah*, *hā*, *dhā*, and *añ*, [the suffix *asun* is used] in the Veda.
Because the term "ṇit" is understood [from the previous rule], the augment *yuk* is added by the rule "The augment *yuk* is added after a stem ending in long *ā* before the suffixes *ciṇ* and *kṛt*.
Due to its inclusion in the *marudvṛdha*-group, there is udātta-accent on the final syllable of the first member.
He dwells (*upakṣeti*).
[The root] *kṣi* [is used] in the senses of dwelling and going.
By the rule "in the Vedic language [the suffix] is frequently elided," there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
"Anavadyā" (blameless):
in a bahuvrīhi compound, by the rule "nañ-subhyām," the final syllable of the second member bears the udātta accent.
[She is] as if cherished by her husband.
By the rule "the third [case ending] is used for the object," the first member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). As for *nārī*:

because it is listed among the *śārṅgarava*-type words by the rule "there is vṛddhi for *nu* and *nṛ*, and [the suffix] *ṅīn*" (Pāṇini 4.1.73, Gaṇasūtra), it ends in *ṅīn* and has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
O Agni, men in their eternal homes attend upon you, kindled within their firm dwellings;
they have bestowed abundant splendor upon you, who become the all-sustaining bearer of riches.

O Agni, men have attended upon you, who are ever-kindled in their homes, within their firm dwellings. They have bestowed abundant splendor upon you; become the sustainer of all life and the bearer of riches. 4.

O Agni, those men— the leaders of the sacrifice, the sacrificers— having kindled you, who are distinguished by the previously mentioned qualities, perpetually with fuel, making you burn without ceasing in their own sacrificial hall within firm dwellings— that is, in stable lands free from agitation, in villages— attend upon you with devotion.
Furthermore, in this fire, they have placed and established abundant *dyumnam*—food characterized by oblations—and manifold forms such as the *puroḍāśa* cake.
Thus distinguished by these qualities...

That Agni who is you, being all-encompassing (*viśvāyuḥ*)—that is, having become the knower of all in the manner described—you have become the supporter (*dharuṇaḥ*), the sustainer, of riches (*rayīṇām*), that is to say, of wealth; the meaning is: "sustain [these] riches so as to give them to us. Regarding *sacanta*: from the root *vac* in the sense of "coming together" (*samavāye*). The present tense suffix *laṭ* is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasaḥ*). The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "in the Veda, it is frequent even when there is no connection with *mā*" (*bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge’pi*). Regarding *bhava*: in the *saṃhitā*, there is a long vowel according to the rule "the final vowel of a word ending in a vowel becomes long [before a following vowel]" (*aco'ntyadīrghaḥ*). Regarding *dharuṇaḥ*: the suffix *un* is added according to the rule "after the root *dhṛ*, there is elision of the *ṇi* suffix" (*dhārerṇiluk ca*).
May the liberal patrons, O Agni, obtain nourishment; may the sun rise for all life.
May we win booty in the contests, O Adhvaryu, as we establish our portion among the gods for the sake of glory.

O Agni, may the liberal patrons obtain nourishment; may the sun burst forth; may we win full life-span and booty in the clash of battle, establishing our share among the gods for the sake of glory. 5.

O Agni, may the liberal patrons—the sacrificers endowed with wealth characterized by oblations—attain and pervade all nourishments; being favored by you, may they obtain every sacrificial rite. And those wise ones who praise you, O Surya...
May all those who offer and present oblations (*havīṃṣi*) to you attain a full lifespan—may they enjoy the entirety of their life.

And may we, through your grace, win (*sanema*) the food (*vāja*) belonging to the enemy (*aryaḥ*, *areḥ*, the foe) in the battles (*samithedhu*). Thereafter, with the gods headed by Indra and others, may we remain establishing that portion—the share of the oblation—for the sake of glory (*śravase*) and fame (*yaśase*). (The word "may we be" is understood as the remainder.)
*aśyuḥ* | [from the root] *aśnu* ‘to pervade’;
the active voice (*parasmaipada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is elision (luk) of the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa). [Thus we have] *dadataḥ*.
By the rule "nābhyastāc chatuḥ," there is a prohibition of the augment *num*.
The word *abhyastānāmādiḥ* [Pāṇini 6.1.183] prescribes that the initial syllable is udātta.
[In the form] *sanema*,
[the root is] *vana* or *ṣaṇa* in the sense of "acquisition" (*sambhaktau*).
The suffix *śas* occurs by way of transposition.

[The form] *aryaḥ* [is derived as follows]: from the word *ari*, in the genitive singular (*ṣaṣṭhyekavacane*), the substitution of *yaṇ* takes place due to the absence of *guṇa*—by the rule "gher ṅiti"—in accordance with the Vedic option stated in "jasādiṣu chandasi vāvacanam."

The word *ari* ends in the suffix *i*, according to the rule *aca haḥ*, and is oxytone (acute-accented on the final syllable). By the rule *udāttayaṇaḥ*, the case-ending is also acute. [The word is] *bhāgam*.
The word *karṣātvataḥ* has its final syllable accented (antodātta).
For the lowing cows of Truth, distributed by the radiant one, have swelled with milk along with their calves;
seeking favor from afar, the rivers have flowed forth through the midst of the mountain.

For the lowing cows of Truth, sharing the radiant light, have caused their udders to swell with nourishment; seeking favor from afar, the rivers have flowed forth through the midst of the mountain. 6.

For, like cows that have reached the place of sacrifice for the sake of *ṛta*, the milch-cows—those who yield the oblations of the *agnihotra* and other rites—swelled; they caused to flow forth the milk and other products that are the goal [of the rite].
What kind of cows? "Vāvaśānāḥ," desiring Agni again and again; "smad-bhvīḥ," [the ones] being with us.
The word *smat* has the same meaning as the word *nitya*.
It means they are "always joined with the head" (*nityamūrdhasā yuktāḥ*), that is to say, they are always bestowers of milk (*payasaḥ pradāvya*).

Devoted by night and united with light by day—meaning they are closely joined and radiant—and moreover, the rivers, whose nature is to flow, begging for and entreating the *sumati* (benevolent mind) of this Agni—that is, his splendor and his grace-bestowing intellect—[approach him].
(Note: 1. The reading "dadataḥ" does not exist in manuscript Ḍha.)
2. *ca-cha-ṇa-na-pha-śravaḥ* [the sounds] *ajaṃ* [are present].
Truly, they go forth—either from the mountain, from near the mountain, or from afar, from a distant land; they flow forth specifically away from the enemy.
The meaning is that they flow forth for the production of the oblations to be given to *abhriya*.

Regarding *ṛtasya*: because the rule "the mention of action must be made" applies, the object (*karman*) is treated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and thus the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.
*Vāvaśānāḥ*.
The root *vaś* means "to desire.
From the intensive (*yaṅ*) form of this root, the suffix *śānac* is applied.
By the rule *na vaśaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.20), the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is prohibited.
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
By the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, because the suffix *śānac* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, there is the elision of the *at* (the *a* of *āna*) and the elision of the *ya* (of *āna*).
For this very reason, since the *lasārvadhātuka* accent does not apply, only the *cit-svara* remains.
*smadvṛṣīḥ*: those whose udders are always full (*smat*). The compound-final substitute *anaṅ* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.131: *ūdhaso'naṅ*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *saṃkhyāyāderdīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.26). Since it does not denote a name (*asaṃjñāyām*), the elision of the final vowel is applied by the rule *alopo'naḥ*. Because the *ṅīp* suffix is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus only the accent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound remains.
*pīpayanta* [is derived from] *pā*, "to drink"; from this root, with the causative suffix *ṇic* added because of the presence of a motive (*hetumati*).
In *śācchāsāhā*, there is the *yuk* augment. From the root ending in *py*, in the *luṅ* tense, there is the substitution of *caṅ* for *cli*.
By the rule *caṅyanyatarasyām*, the preceding syllable of the *caṅ* substitute receives the udātta accent.
The phrase "hi ca" [triggers] the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent. From *parāvataḥ*, meaning from that which has gone away; for that which has gone away is indeed far.
Since this meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is understood, the suffix *vati* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.118: *upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe*.

O Agni, seeking your favor, the worshipful ones have established glory in heaven; they have made Night and Dawn of different forms, and they have joined together the dark color and the ruddy color. (7) O Agni, those worthy of sacrifice, seeking your benevolence, have established renown in heaven. They have created Night and Dawn, which are of diverse forms; they have combined the black color and the ruddy color. (7)

O Agni, seeking from you a beautiful mind—that is, a benevolent intellect—and seeking from you [protection], all the gods worthy of sacrifice, established in heaven—the shining realm—your glory, that is, the food characterized by oblations;
for according to the Vedic revelation, "Agni is the eater of the food of the gods" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.1.4.1).
Thereafter, for the performance endowed with such oblations, [they established] the two of diverse forms, namely Night and Dawn, as indicated by the time of dawn.
They made the night and the night-time; they created it.
This very point he clarifies: they established the black color—the dark, shadowy hue—in the night, and the ruddy, shining, white-colored light in the day; they firmly established them both.
In the word *tve*, the substitute *śe* is applied to the locative case according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
[The form is] *naktā*.
By that same [rule], there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the second case ending: *upasā*.
By that same [rule], there is the substitution of *ā* for the case ending: *upābhyām*.
*dhuḥ* | [The root] *dudhāñ* is used in the senses of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*) and "nourishing" (*poṣaṇa*).
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, by the rule *gātisthā*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*.
"Ātaḥ": here *kṣi* is replaced by *jus*. "Bahulaṃ chandasyamāyoge'pi": there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.

O Agni, may we and those wealthy patrons be among those mortals whom you lead to prosperity. Like a shadow, you accompany the entire world; having filled the two worlds and the mid-air, you pervade them. (8) yān | rāye | martan | suṣūdaḥ | agne | te | syāma | maghavānaḥ | vayam | ca | chāyā'iva | viśvam | bhuvanam | sisakṣi | āpapri'vān | rodasī iti | antarikṣam ||8||
1. For the performance of the sacrifice accompanied by the *ḍha*-oblation:

"O [Agni], you who make us—these mortals, these human beings—'delightful' (*suṣvadaḥ*) for the sake of 'wealth' (*rāye*), may we, being such as those, become 'generous' (*maghavānaḥ*), that is, possessors of wealth. Having filled the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), and the intermediate space (*antarikṣam*) with your own splendor or with the water of rain, and having pervaded them, you 'desire to serve' (*sisakṣi*) the entire world (*viśvam bhuvanam*); the meaning is that you protect everything by bestowing your grace."
In this regard, there is an illustration: "Like a shadow.
Just as the shadow of a tree or the like protects by warding off the affliction produced by heat and so forth, so it is here.
In *rāye*, the vowel of the case-ending is udātta according to the rule *'asidam'*. [The word is] *suṣvadaḥ*.
In the sense of "impelling" (*preraṇe*),
the *leṭ* suffix is applied according to Pāṇini 3.4.7 (*aḍagamaḥ*).
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73), there is the elision (*bhlu*) of the *śap* suffix.

The word *abhyastānām* has an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) according to the rule "the first of reduplicated [verb forms] is acute. There is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) by the rule "in the presence of a [verb] beginning with *yat*. [The form is] *sisakṣi*.
In the case of *paca-samavāye*,
by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the substitution of *ślu* for *śap*.
When the term "it" is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
Maṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Chapter 1, Section 13, Sūtra 74. First Chapter, Verse 821.

May they be dear to you. May we be able—may we have the power—to perform the restraint (*yama*) or regulation of the wealth (*śaya*) belonging to you, who are *sudhuraḥ*, meaning one who carries well (*su-nirvāhaka*), or alternatively, one who destroys poverty by bearing it away beautifully (*śobhanaṃ dhūrvati*). What are we doing? Holding above [the fire] the *śravaḥ*—the food characterized by oblations—which is worthy of being honored by the gods (*devabhakta*); that is to say, performing the oblation with offerings into the fire. Regarding *ucathāni*: from the root *vac* (to speak), the suffix *atha* and its *kittva* (causing *saṃprasāraṇa*) are applied here despite the rule "from *ru* and *vid*, *kit*" (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.395), because of the frequentative usage (*bahulavacanāt*). The *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs according to the rule for roots beginning with *vac*. Regarding *juṣṭāni*: the acute accent on the first syllable follows Pāṇini 6.1.209–210, which states that *juṣṭa* and *pita* are always [accented] in the Veda (*mantra*). Regarding *hade*: the word *hṛdaya* undergoes the substitution *hada* according to the rule beginning with *padana*. Regarding *śakema*: from the root *śak* (to be able), the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśiṣi*). Regarding *sudhuraḥ*: the root *dhurvī* means to injure. The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "and *kvip*. By the rule "elision of *r* and *l*," the *v* is elided. The prohibition of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) applies by the rule "not after a word denoting praise" (*na pūjanāt*). Regarding *devabhaktaṃ*: the original accent of the first member remains by the rule "the third case [member retains its accent] when expressing the object" (*tṛtīyā karmaṇi*). || 20 || || 12 ||

In the thirteenth anuvāka, there are eleven sūktas. Among them, the first sūkta, consisting of nine verses, begins with "upaprayantaḥ. Regarding this, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Upaprayantaḥ—nine verses; Gotama Rāhūgaṇa is the seer; it is in the Gāyatrī meter."
This is its meaning:
there was a certain seer named Rahūgaṇa;
his son Gotama is the seer of this hymn.
Because it is stated, "But the Gāyatra," both this [first] and the subsequent [second] hymn are in the Gāyatrī meter.
Because it is defined by the rule, "The supreme deity here is Agni, [not Indra]," Agni is the deity.
For the Prātaranuvāka, these two hymns beginning with this one are dedicated to Agni at the Kratu-rite, in the Gāyatrī meter.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The hymn *āpo revatīḥ kṣayathā hi vasvaḥ* and the hymn *upaprayantaḥ* [are used] at the *āghāra* [offering]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.13).
These two hymns are also used in the *ādhīna-śastra*, because of the extension [of the rule] by the principle of the *prātaranuvāka* (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.5).
On the first day of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, this very hymn serves as the *ājya-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Ājya [laud] on the first day is 'upaprayantaḥ'. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.10)
Approaching the sacrifice, let us address a hymn to Agni, who hears us even from afar. Approaching the sacrifice, let us address a hymn to Agni, who hears us even from afar. (1)

"Approaching" (*upaprayantaḥ*) means approaching—that is, proceeding toward—the *adhvara*, a sacrifice such as the *agniṣṭoma* that is free from the cause of injury, performing it properly without interruption; this is the meaning.

Being such as we are, we "would speak" (*vocaema*)—it is thus prayed—that we may become speakers of the "mantra," a hymn in the form of this *ṛc* which is a means of meditation, for the sake of "Agni," the deity endowed with qualities such as moving forward (*aṅgana*).
For what kind of Agni? For him who is possessed of such attributes.
"Āre," "asme," and "śṛṇvate.

The word *ca* (and) should be understood as having the sense of *api* (even/also), and is to be placed after the word *āre*. Thus, it means: "to those who hear our praises even from afar (*āre*), that is, though situated at a distance."
The sense is that, because he acts toward us everywhere with an excess of affection, he listens to our very own hymn of praise.
We shall say: "The root *brū* becomes *vac*"; "In the sense of a benediction, the suffix *āśīrliṅ* takes the augment *aṅ*."
In *vaca um*, there is the augment *um*.
In *śṛṇvate*,
by the rule *śaturanumaḥ*, the case ending receives the udātta accent.

He who, worthy of praise among the eager ones when the peoples have gathered together, protected the household for the donor. 2. He—among the eager ones; worthy of praise; when the peoples have come together; protected; for the donor; the household. 2.

The ancient Agni, who has long existed—who protected (*arakṣat*) and protects (*rakṣati*) the wealth (*gaya*) for the donor (*dāśuṣe*), the sacrificer who has offered oblations—when the hostile subjects (*kṛṣṭiṣu*), those who act as slayers (*vadhakāriṇīṣu*), have come together (*saṃjagmānāsu*) and assembled; for him we would speak the mantra—thus is the connection with the preceding verse.
In the word *snīhitīṣu*:
the root *ṇiha* means "to moisten" (*snehane*);
it belongs to the *curādi* group.
"He causes to love" (Nirukta 2.15.13), Ṛgveda 6.1.13.

Thus it is recited among the words for the act of killing (*vadhakarma*). They are called *snehilayaḥ* because by means of them the subjects (*prajāḥ*) are harmed (*hiṃsyante*). The suffix *kin* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). According to the rule, "It should be stated that [the augment *iṭ* applies] after roots ending in *ti*, *tu*, *tri*, *tra*, and those beginning with *grah*" (*pā. ma. 7. 2. 9. 1*), there is the addition of the augment *iṭ*, as in the forms *nigṛhītiḥ* and *nipaṭhitiḥ*. By transposition (*vyatyayena*), the vowel *e* is replaced by *ī*, and the suffix *kin* undergoes lengthening. Because it has the marker *n*, it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). In the form *saṃjamānāsu*: the *ātmanepada* is applied by the rule "after the prefix *sam* with the roots *gam*, *yuccha*, etc. (*samo gamyuccha0*). The suffix *kānac* is used for the perfect tense (*liṭ*). There is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopaḥ*) according to the rule "of *gam*, *han*, etc. (*gamahana0*). In the form *arakṣat*: the *laṅ* is used while the rule "in the Veda, the *luṅ* and *liṭ* [are used for all tenses]" (*chandasi luṅliṭaḥ*) is in force.
When the command "Recite for the one who has not yet been born" (*ajāta*) is given during the *abhimanyana* rite, the verse "uta bruvantu... is to be recited as the *anuvākyā*.

This is prescribed in the section beginning with "In the morning, at the Vaidvadeva [offering]" (*prātarvaidhadevyām*) in the Sūtra: "With the remainder, [recite] the next: 'Let the people speak in approval' (*uttarānumata bruvantu jantavaḥ*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.16).
Likewise, among the Sākamedha rites, this same verse is the first *ājyānuvākyā* for the offering of the cake to the Maruts, the *krīḍins*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Let living beings say further and further, 'To the Maruts, the playful ones'. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.18).
And let the people say, "The Vṛtra-slayers,
the winners of wealth, have arisen in battle after battle."
And let the people say: "Agni, the slayer of Vṛtra, has been born, the winner of wealth in every battle. (3)
Agni has been born from the two fire-sticks;
immediately thereafter, let all the living beings—the officiating priests—speak of him, that is, praise that Agni.
Of what nature is Agni?
The slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of obstructing enemies; the winner of wealth, the conqueror of the riches of foes in every battle.
Dhanañjaya:
[The suffix] *khac* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ bhṛtṛji0* (Pāṇini 3.2.46);
[the augment] *suṭ* is applied by the rule *arudviṣadajantasya0* (Pāṇini 6.3.67).
The final syllable is udātta by virtue of the *citsvara* rule.
[In the word] *raṇeraṇe*,
the root *raṇ* has the meaning "sound."
*Raṇa* means battle (*saṃgrāma*), derived from the sense "in which drums resound" (*ranti dundubhayo'smin*).
The suffix *ap* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.3.58 (*vaśiraṇyoṣasaṃvyānam*).
The reduplication occurs by the rule "for the sake of continuity and pervasion" (*nityavīpsayoḥ*).
The repeated word is unaccented.
In whose house you are the messenger, you who desire the oblations for their enjoyment; O wondrous one, you make the sacrifice successful.
In whose dwelling you are the messenger, you desire the oblations for the feast; O wondrous one, you make the sacrifice successful. 4.
O Agni, you are the messenger of the gods in the dwelling—characterized by the sacrificial ground—of that sacrificer;
and for whom you bring the oblations, such as the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa*, for the consumption of the gods;
and for whom you make the sacrifice (*adhvara*) wondrous (*dasmata*), visible to all.
The connection is with the following verse: "tamisumahavyam."
*verṣi*. [This is] from the root *vī*, meaning "to go" and so forth;
it is the present indicative (*laṭ*) with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized.
Due to the root beginning with *ad*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix;
due to the root beginning with *pāda*, there is an absence of *nighāta* (accentual suppression).
[The form is] *dasmata*.
The root *das* is used in the senses of “to bite” (*daṃśana*) and “to see” (*darśana*).
By the rule beginning with *iṣiyudhīndhi*, the suffix *mak* is applied.
In the form *dasmita*, the letter *t* replaces the letter *m* through a phonetic substitution (*varṇavyāpatti*).
You perform (*kṛṇoṣi*).
[The root] *kṛv* is used in the senses of "injuring" and "doing. By the rule *ghinṛṇvyora ca*, the suffix *up* is applied; through its connection, the letter *v* is replaced by *a*.

Therefore, when that [suffix] is elided, due to the status of being as if occupying the original position (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel; and because of the inclusion of the word "yasya," there is an absence of the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*).
O Aṅgiras, O son of strength, people call him the one who offers good oblations, the one who possesses excellent gods, and the one who provides a fine sacrificial grass.
Him, O Aṅgiras, the people call one to whom oblations are well offered, a good god, the son of strength, and one for whom the sacrificial grass is well prepared. 5.

O *aṅgiraḥ*, son of strength (*sahasaḥ yaho*), Agni endowed with qualities such as being the "limb" (*aṅga*) and so forth—whichever sacrificer was previously mentioned, him alone do all people call a "good offerer" (*suhavyam*), one possessing excellent oblations; a "good deity" (*sudevam*), one possessing excellent deities;
and a "one with good sacrificial grass" (*subarhiṣam*)—*barhis* being a name for sacrifice—one who possesses an excellent sacrifice. Thus do all men speak of him.
In *suhavyam* and similar forms, the final syllable of the compound is udātta by the rule *namsubhyām*.
In *sahaso yaho*,

because of the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) according to the rule *subāmantrite*, the entire group consisting of the genitive case ending and the vocative (*āmantrita*) bears the inherent anudātta of the vocative.

Bring those gods here for our praise, O resplendent one, so that they may partake of the oblations. 6. Bring them here, those gods, for our glorification, O you of beautiful radiance, so that they may enjoy the sacrificial offerings. 6.
O Agni, you who possess beautiful splendor (*suśandra*), bring those gods here to this rite toward us for the sake of praise, and indeed cause them to arrive;
and having brought them, convey the oblations—such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*—to those who have arrived, so that they may partake of them.
*vahāsi* [is derived from] the root *vaha* in the sense of "to carry" (*prāpaṇe*). The augment *āṭ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood.
For the sake of praise; from the root *śaṃs* meaning "to praise," with the suffix *ktin* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).

In the word *titutra*, there is a prohibition of the substitution of *it*. By the rule *aniditām*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*). And by the rule *tādau ca*, the verbal prefix (*gati*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
*Suśandra*: [The form *suśandra* is derived] with the augment *muṭ* by the rule "In a mantra, when *śvan* follows a short vowel, [the augment *muṭ* is added]."

No sound at all of the swift horse-drawn chariot is heard when you go ahead to the dwelling-place. 7. No sound, no sound of the swift horses is heard of the chariot at all, when you go ahead to the dwelling-place. 7.

O Agni, whenever you go—that is, whenever you attain the office of messenger for the gods—at that time, and indeed always, the sound of your chariot drawn by horses, worthy of being heard as it moves along, is not heard;
the meaning is that because of the chariot’s swift motion, its sound is not perceived by us.
The word *yoḥ* [is derived as follows]: from the root *yā* in the sense of "to reach" (*prāpaṇe*), the *ku*-suffix prescribed by the Uṇādi-sūtra 1.21, namely *yo dve ca*, is applied;
due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacanāt*), there is no doubling of the consonant.
"Upandis"—this is the designation for the sound *śra*.
Thus, the *Prātiśākhya* of the Taittirīyas states: "The sound *śra* is called *upandi*" (Tai. Prā. 23.9).
[He] hears.

In the root *śru* meaning "to hear," when the present tense (*laṭ*) is applied in the passive voice, by the rule *śruvaḥ śru ca*, the suffix *dhyap* is replaced by *śru* and the root vowel is changed to *śra*. Then, by the rule *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu*, there is the elision of the *ta* suffix.
The substitution of *yaṇ* [for the semivowel] occurs by the rule "hubhuvoḥ sārvadhātuke."

Aided by you, O Agni, the prize-winner, the steed, has stepped forth from the former [place] toward the latter; the donor has advanced. 8. Aided by you (tvotau), the prize-winner (vājī), the steed (ahyaḥ), toward (abhi) the former (pūrvasmāt), the latter (aparaḥ); the donor (dāśvān), O Agni (agne), has stepped forth (prāsthāt). 8.

O Agni, that man who has become inferior—that is, degraded—compared to his former position, he, being now a giver of oblations to you, protected by you (*tvotaḥ*), possessed of food (*vājī*), and free from shame (*ahyaḥ*), having thus attained sovereignty, stands forth; the meaning is that he becomes pre-eminent among all.
*Ahyaḥ*: [The root] *hī* means "shame. That which feels shame is *hyaḥ*.
*na hyaḥ*, *ahyaḥ*: [these forms] have the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable as their prior member (*avyayapūrvapada*). *dāśvān*.
In the sense of "giving," the word *dāśvān*— meaning "one who has given"— is an irregularly formed (nipātita) stem ending in the *kasu* suffix, as in the form *dāśvān sāhān*.

And indeed, O divine Agni, you bestow upon the donor great, resplendent, and heroic power for the sake of the gods. 9. And indeed, O divine Agni, you bestow upon the donor great, resplendent, and heroic power for the sake of the gods. 9.

Moreover, O radiant Agni, for that sacrificer who has offered oblations such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* cakes to the gods, you desire to win—that is, you intend to bring and bestow—vast and abundant wealth.
Of what kind? It is exceedingly brilliant (*ghumat*) and endowed with excellent heroic power (*suvīrya*).
"Suvīryam": [the compound] "vīravīryam" has its first syllable of the final member accented acute (ādyudātta). [The verb form is] "vivāsasi."
The root *vā* means "to go" and "to scent.
With the suffix *san*, there is reduplication, and by the rule "after any other [consonant]," the vowel becomes short (*itva*).
[The form is] *dāśuṣe*.

In the fourth case singular, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vā-śuṣi-vasi-ghasi-vaṭi-vaci-vyadhi-ruci-sahi-bhyaś-ca," and the substitution of *ṣ* by the rule "śāsivasighasānāṃ ca."
"Juṣasva" is the second hymn, consisting of five verses. It is enumerated thus: "Juṣasva, five.
The seer and other details are as before.

The application of this hymn is stated together with the preceding hymn for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra. Regarding the animal sacrifice, the first verse is employed for the recitation of the *stokas*.
This is set forth in the Sūtra: "Being impelled, he recites the *stokas* [with the verses] beginning with 'prepitaḥ', 'stokebhyaḥ', 'juṣasva', and 'saprathasam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.4).

Accept this most expansive word, most delightful to the gods, as you offer the oblations into your mouth. 1. Accept; most expansive; word; most delightful to the gods; oblations; offering; into the mouth. 1.
O Agni, graciously accept (*juṣasva*) our speech, characterized by hymns of praise, which is most extensive (*asaprathastamam*).
Of what nature is it? It is that which most delights the gods (*devapsarastamam*).
Doing what?

"In your mouth," *āsani*, "offering" (*juhvānaḥ*), that is, casting into [your mouth] the "oblations" (*havyā*), namely the oblations characterized by hymns of praise. The meaning is: "Let these oblations characterized by hymns not be in vain; accept all of them through your own mouth."
"Devapsarastama":
[the root] *sṛj* is used in the sense of "to delight. A *devapsaras* is so called because she refreshes—that is, delights—the gods.

By the rules "gatikārakayor api" and "pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvaṃ ca," the suffix *asun* applies, resulting in both the formation of the word and the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member. There is an exchange of position between the letters *s* and *p*. Thus, from *deva-psaras*, we derive *devapsarastamaḥ* (meaning "most excellent among celestial nymphs").

*Juhvānaḥ*: This is derived from the root *hu* (to sacrifice) with the suffix *śānac* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Its initial syllable is acute-accented (*ādyudātta*) according to the rule "the first [syllable] of reduplicated forms" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*).
In the word *āsani*, the substitution of *āsana* for the word *āsya* occurs by the rule beginning with "padn."

Now, O Agni, most Aṅgiras-like, most wise, we would speak a dear prayer to you as you grant your favor. 2. Now, O Agni, most Aṅgiras-like, most wise, we would speak a dear prayer to you as you grant your favor. 2.

"O *aṅgirastama*, most excellently endowed with the qualities of the Aṅgirases; or rather, the most eminent among the Aṅgirases. O *vedhastama*, most wise—*vedhas* being a name for the intelligent—one, O Agni! Then, after this, may we *vocema*, may we become speakers, of that *sānasi*, worthy of being honored, *priya*, delightful, *brahma*, hymn of praise, directed toward *te*, you. Regarding *vocema*: the suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśiṣi*), and the augment *um* is added to the root *vac*. Regarding *sānasi*: from the roots *van* and *paṇ*, meaning "to acquire" or "to honor," the form *sānasi* is derived through the irregular application of the suffix *asac*.

Who among men is your kinsman, O Agni? Who is the offerer of the sacrifice? Who indeed? Upon whom are you dependent? 3. Who is your kinsman among men, O Agni? Who is the donor of the sacrifice? Who indeed? Upon whom are you resting? 3.
O Agni, among these people, among human beings, who is your kinsman (*jāmi*)? Who is your relative (*bandhu*)?
You are superior in all virtues;
the sense is that there is no relative equal to you.

"Who am I to offer the sacrifice?"— that is, who is there capable even of sacrificing to you? It means that no one at all is capable of performing the sacrifice (*adhvara*) which is offered (*dāśvat*).
"Who are you? Of what nature are you?
You are known by all as being of such a form. This is the meaning. "In what place are you situated?"—that is, where do you abide?
Even his location is not known by anyone;
therefore, how can he be perceived by us who possess only the vision of flesh? Thus Agni is praised with the words "dāśvadhvaraḥ" (he to whom the sacrifice is offered).
[The root] *dāś* [is used] in the sense of giving.
By the rule "uṇādayo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.2.1), the suffix *uṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), due to the word "bahulam" [indicating diversity].
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.

The substitution of *yaṇ* [for *i*] results in the circumflex (*svarita*) accent according to the rule: "The *yaṇ* substitute for an acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel followed by an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel is itself circumflex.

But what approach has been most propitious for the mind as a choice for Agni? What prayer has been most auspicious? Or who has attained your skill through sacrifices? Or with what mind may we worship you?

What is your approach? What prayer shall be for the choice of the mind? O Agni, what thought shall be most auspicious? Or who has attained your skill through sacrifices? Or with what mind shall we worship you? 1.
O Agni, what approach (upaiti) could there be for the sake of your mind’s desire—for its restraint and for establishing it within us?
None at all. We are unable to perform an approach that is worthy of you.
This is the sense.
*Manīṣā* means praise; what kind of praise could be most blissful (*śaṃtamā*)—that is, exceedingly conducive to happiness—for you? The meaning is that there is not even a praise suitable for you.
Or what sacrificer (*yajamāna*) has fully attained (*pari āpa*) through sacrifices related to you—namely, through *yāgas*—*dakṣa*, which means prosperity or strength? [None.]
The meaning is that no one [exists].

The sense is that even the idea that results are obtained by performing sacrifices appropriate for you is indeed difficult to establish. Setting aside for a moment such things as approaching [the sacrificial fire], he asks "by whom? because even the mind—which is the very means for all of that—is difficult for us to obtain.
O Agni, with what mind (*manas*) and with what kind of intellect (*buddhi*) shall we offer (*dāśema*) oblations (*havīṃṣi*) unto you?
The meaning is that a mind corresponding to your approach does not arise within us.
The prefix *upa* [is acute]; and by the rule *tādau ca*, the *gati* [prefix] retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*).
[The word is] *varāya*.
The root *vṛñ* means "to choose.

From this root, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the suffix *ap* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.3.58: *grahavṛdaniścigamaśca*. Because that suffix is marked with *p*, it is *anudātta* (unaccented), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains. Consequently, the word is *dhātusvara* (accented on the first syllable).
*bhuvat*: the augment *aṭ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood;
by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
There is a prohibition of *guṇa* substitution by the rule *bhūsuvostiṅi*. [The form is] *dakṣam*.
[The root is] *dakṣa* in the sense of "growth" (*vṛddhau*).
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of either the action (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*);
the accent falls on the first syllable of the word for "mind" (*citta*).
Come here, O Hotṛ; let him sit down, the undeceived one, becoming our excellent leader. With the swift horses, may you, whom both heaven and earth encompass, worship the gods for our great goodwill.
Come, O Agni; sit down here as the Hotṛ-priest. Be undeceivable and our excellent leader. You, whom both heaven and earth—the all-encompassing—cherish, worship the gods for our great goodwill. 2.
O Agni, come hither;
come to this sacrifice and sit down as the Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods. Be our leader, going before us, and be most auspicious.
Since you are *adabdha*— unassailable by Rākṣasas and other such beings—

the two worlds, Heaven and Earth (*rodasī*), which pervade the entire universe (*viśvaminve*), shall protect you, O protector of horses. Having arrived and taken your seat, being thus guarded by Heaven and Earth, worship with oblations the gods, Indra and others endowed with qualities such as generosity, for the sake of great goodwill and mental well-being.
*ni-pīda*. The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule *sadiprateḥ*. [The form is] *saumanasāya*.

The state of being *sumanas* is *saumanasya*. By the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of a general relationship; however, in this context, it culminates in a specific type of relationship characterized by a state (*bhāva*).
Alternatively,

the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.1.130, *hāyanāntayuvādibhyo’ṇ*; its inclusion in the *yuvādi* group [of words] should be understood.

1. In the versions marked ṭa, ḍha, and taiḥ, [the word] "upaviśa" does not exist. 2. In the versions marked ta, da, dha, and sa, it is "upaviśa upaviśya"; in the version marked kṣa, it is "upaviśa upaviśya ca". 3. In the versions marked ṭa and ḍha, [the suffix] is "aṇ". 4. In the versions marked ṭa, ḍha, and sa, [the suffix] is "ca" in the sense of "characterized by conjunction" (*samavāyalakṣaṇe*).
O you who are bold against all devourers, be at the forefront of the sacrifices as the protector from curses!
Then, O giver of good gifts, bring the Lord of Soma with his two bay horses to this hospitality that we have prepared for him.

Burn down all the Rākṣasas, O Agni; become the protector of our sacrifices from curses. Then, with your two bay horses, bring hither the Lord of Soma; we have prepared hospitality for him, O Bounteous One.
O Agni, burn away completely all the *rākṣasas*;
having burned them, become the protector—that is, the guardian—against the curse, which is injury, of our sacrifices, the rites to be performed by us.
Then, immediately after that, bring hither, by means of his two bay horses, Indra, the lord of Soma and the protector of all Soma-juices, and cause him to reach our sacrifice.
For this Indra, the giver of beautiful fruit, who has arrived, we perform the *ātithya*—the hospitality due to a guest.
*Dhakṣi*. [This is derived from] *daha* in the sense of "to reduce to ashes.
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
The changes are to *ṭha*, the absence of *bh* (*abh*), and *pa*.
[In the word] *abhiśastipāvā*:
[the root] *śasu* [is used] in the sense of "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*).
From this root *pā* preceded by the prefix *abhi*, the suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
Thus, one who protects (*pāti*) from being accused (*abhiśasteḥ*) is an *abhiśastipāvā*.
The root *pā* means "to protect" (*rakṣaṇe*).
The suffix *vanip* is applied by the rule "āto manin.
[In the word] *somapatim*,
the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*) is maintained according to the rule "patyāvaiśvarye."
In *sudāne*, as before, the suffix *vanip* is added to the root *dā*; by the rule "alo 'naḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *a*.
I invoke you, the bearer [of oblations], with offspring and splendor, and with my mouth; sit down here together with the gods.
You perform the office of the Hotṛ and also that of the Potṛ, O worshipful one; be mindful as the bestower and progenitor of riches.

With offspring, with splendor, as the bearer, with your mouth, I call you hither; sit down here with the gods. Perform the office of the Hotṛ and the Potṛ, O worshipful one; be the leader and the progenitor of riches. 4.

I invoke this Agni, who—being praised with a hymn of praise consisting of speech endowed with the fruit of offspring and prosperity—is the bearer (*vahnih*) who carries the oblations to the gods by means of his tongue-like flame;
him I call hither. Being thus invoked, do thou sit down here in this ritual together with the other gods.
Having sat down, O worshipful (*yajatra*) Agni, desire and perform the *hotra*, the rite performed by the *hotṛ*, and also the *potrā*, the rite performed by the *potṛ*.

O Agni, the progenitor who brings forth all through the medium of oblations, you who are the "bestowers"—those who excellently control and place the "vasus," the riches, under our dominion—be watchful; awaken us!
Regarding *āsā*: by the rule "padan" and so forth, the word *āsya* undergoes the substitution *āsya-*;
by the rule "supāṃ suluk," the third case ending undergoes the substitution *ḍā*.
Due to the elision of the *ṭi* suffix, the vowel of the case-ending becomes acute by the rule regarding the restoration of the accent (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). In *huve*,
there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rules "after a root ending in *ij*" and "frequently in the Veda."

The elision of the *śap* suffix occurs according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73). There is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent according to the rule "cavāyoge prathamā" (Pāṇini 8.1.59).
[Thus,] *bodhi*.

From the root *budh* in the sense of "understanding," following this [root] with the suffix *pya*, because of the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*), the *hi* [imperative suffix] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; consequently, by the rule "after *gi*, there is elision of *niṭ*" (*geraniṭī*), there is elision of the *ṇi*.
Then, by the rule "for *hi* after short vowels, there is *dhi*" (*husvebhyo herdhiḥ*), *dhi* is substituted for *hi*.
The elision of the other [suffix] from the verbal root is Vedic;
because of the rule *herapit*, its own accent remains.
For the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni in the Ekādaśina rite, the verse beginning with "yathā viprasya" serves as the *yājyā* for the *paśupuroḍāśa*.
This is stated in the section on "Pradānāni" in the Sūtra: "'yathā viprasya manuṣo havirbhiḥ; pra kāravo mananā vakṣyamāṇāḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
Just as you, O sage among sages, gratified the gods with the oblations of Manu the Brahmin through the seers,
even so, O most truthful Hotṛ, Agni, do thou worship today with thy joyous ladle.

Just as you, O Agni, being a seer among seers, have sacrificed to the gods with oblations through the seers—just as you did for the wise Manu—so now, O most truthful invoker, perform the sacrifice today with your joyous ladle. 5.

O Agni, you who are a seer with far-reaching vision, together with the seers, the wise ones, and the Vasus—at the sacrifice of the inspired sage Manu, through oblations such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and others—just as we have gratified the gods, O most truthful Hotṛ, performer of the sacrifice, O most excellent one among the virtuous, so now today at this sacrifice, with a delightful tongue, that is, with the ladle (*juhū*) which is the instrument of offering, worship the gods with oblations.
*Manuṣaḥ*:
[derived from] the root *man*, meaning "to know.
The suffix *usiN* is applied to *man* by the rule "it occurs diversely elsewhere as well."

The fourth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "kathā," is the Ṛju-bhāṣya; it is the seer Gotama's composition and is addressed to Agni. It is enumerated thus: "kathā. The application of this hymn is stated together with the preceding hymn for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.

How may we offer praise, O Agni? What song, beloved by the gods, is recited for him, the radiant one, who among mortals is the immortal, the observer of *ṛta*, the invoker, and the most excellent sacrificer, who indeed brings the gods hither?

Let us speak; let us offer worship to Agni. What god-pleasing song is uttered for him, the radiant one? He who, being immortal among mortals, the observer of Truth (Ṛtāvā), the Hotṛ-priest, and the most excellent sacrificer, brings the gods here. 1.
How shall we offer praise to this Agni? How shall we present the oblations? The meaning is:

"We are unable to perform a sacrifice that is a wide expanse for Agni. Alternatively: "What kind of speech—what hymn of praise—is said to be pleasing to the gods for this radiant, brilliant Agni? (Such speech is not possible for us.)
The meaning is that [others] are not even capable of composing such a hymn of praise.

He who is *amṛtaḥ* (immortal), free from death; *ṛtavān* (truthful), possessing truth or sacrifice; the *hotṛ* (invoker) of the gods, or the performer of the oblation; and *vyajiṣṭhaḥ* (the most excellent sacrificer)—that very Agni, existing among us mortals whose nature is subject to death, makes the gods present through the offerings. "How may we give to such an Agni?"—this is the connection with the preceding verse.
*Kathā*:
the suffix *thā* is applied according to the rule "thā hetau ca chandasi" (Pāṇini 5.3.26). *Bhāmine*.
The root *bhā* means "to shine.
By the rule *artistusu*, etc., the suffix *man* is applied;
from that, the possessive suffix *ini* is added.
*Ṛtāvā*:
the suffix *vanip* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) according to the rule *chandasīvanipau*;
the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*.
1. Furthermore, ṭa-ṭha:

Him who is most auspicious at the sacrifices, the upholder of *ṛta*, the Hotṛ—him bring hither with salutations! For Agni, when the sages [invoke] the gods, shall perceive them and worship with his mind.

Him who is most auspicious at the sacrifices, the upholder of cosmic order (*ṛtá*), the Hotṛ-priest—him bring hither with salutations! When Agni seeks out the thoughts [of men] for the gods, may he perceive them and worship with his mind. 2.

The Agni who is most auspicious (*śaṃtamaḥ*), meaning exceedingly pleasant, truthful (*ṛtāvā*)—that is, one who perceives reality as it is—and who is the invoker (*hotā*) of the gods at the sacrifices (*adhvareṣu*); O priests and sacrificers, you must bring that very same Agni hither with salutations (*namobhiḥ*), that is, with hymns of praise (*stotraih*). Bring him face to face.
Whenever this Agni goes to the gods for the sake of the human sacrificer (manāya), then he awakens and recognizes all the gods worthy of worship;
and having recognized them, he worships them with oblations, honoring them with his mind and with reverence (namas).
Therefore, one should apply the phrase "bring that very Agni hither."
*veḥ*.
[The root] *vī* is used in the sense of "motion" and so forth.
The suffix *laṭ* is applied while the rule "*chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*" (Vedic forms may take the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, or *liṭ* suffixes) is in effect.

The rule "the substitutes for *niṭ* are those of the *tiṅ*-suffixes" means that the singular of the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*) is replaced by the singular of the second person (*madhyamapuruṣa*). Thus:
*bodhāti*. [The root] *budh* means "to understand."
The augment *āṬ* is added by virtue of the *leṭ* suffix.

Since the suffix *śap* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains. There is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent) by the rule "the first [verb] is not elided when joined with *ca* or *vā*."
By means of the mind; there is a transposition of the places of the letters *ma* and *na*.
For he is the will, he is the mortal, he is the righteous one; like Mitra, he has become the charioteer of the wondrous.
Him, the wondrous one, the Aryan clans seeking the gods address first at the sacrifices.

For he is the will, he is the mortal, he is the righteous one; like Mitra, he has become the charioteer of the wondrous. Him, the wonder-worker, the Aryan clans seeking the gods address first at the sacrifices.
For he is Agni, the "kratu," the performer of actions;

he alone is the "martya," the slayer and the withdrawer of all; he is the "sādhu," the accomplisher and the establisher; and he alone has become, and continues to be, the "rathīḥ," the one who leaves behind or brings forth the "adbhutasya," the wonderful wealth that was previously non-existent.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Like a friend who brings wealth,
so it is with Agni; such as he is, him the subjects— the people, desiring the gods— address first at the sacrifices.
Having approached with hymns of praise, they declare him to be the preeminent one.
Of what sort are these people (*viśaḥ*)? "The *ārīḥ*—meaning those who go toward or resort to—that Agni who is beautiful (*darśanīyam*) to behold."

*Martyaḥ*: [derived from] the root *mṛṅ* "to die" (*prāṇatyāge*). From this root, with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *chandasi niṣṭakye* and others; furthermore, by virtue of the word *bahulam* ("variously") in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, it should be understood as having an active (*kartari*) sense.
The word *anāvaḥ* has its initial syllable udātta (accented) according to the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ*. In *devayantīḥ*,
the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity of the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is optionally applied by the rule *vā chandasi*.
*Ārīḥ*:
[derived from] the root *ṛ* meaning "to go.
By the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) in the rule *janicasibhyāmin* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.569), the suffix *iṇ* is applied even to this root.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*. The substitution of the preceding vowel with a long homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) occurs by the rule *vā chandasi*.
The acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) is due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
1. He also honors *ṭa* and *ḍha*.
2. There is no "acute accent on the first syllable due to transposition" for *ṭa* and *ḍha*.
