May that Agni, the most heroic among men, accept our songs and our devotion with his protection;
and may those most powerful patrons, impelled by strength, further this prayer for our nourishment.

May he, Agni—the most heroic among men, the bestower of wealth—accept our songs with his protection; and may he accept the devotion of those most powerful patrons who, impelled by the prize of battle, continually promote this prayer. 4.
Among men who lead the sacrifice, he is the most manly, the supreme leader; a *ridādaḥ*, that is, a devourer or consumer of *ridas*, meaning enemies;
or alternatively, one who has measured out—that is, dispelled—*rita*, meaning violence.
May such Agni as he accept our songs—our praises joined with the food characterized by oblations—and our *dhīti*, that is, our ritual action; may he desire them.
Moreover, those sacrificers who [possess] *tanā*;
this is a name for wealth.

Being possessed of extensive wealth, like Maghavans (lords of riches), wealthy, and most powerful—being exceedingly strong—and being impelled by *vāja* (food characterized as the oblation) by those for whom it has been sent forth (*prasūta*), they have stirred the *manman* (devotional thought).

[The root] *mṛ* [is used here in the sense of] *luhi*, meaning "to adhere" and so forth. *Joṣam*: from the root *juṣ* in the sense of "pleasure" and "service"; the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the abstract sense (*bhāve*). Due to the presence of the *ji*-class marker, there is an absence of *guṇa*. || 25 ||
The fifth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "abhi tvā," belongs to Gotama Ārṣabhya and is in the Gāyatrī meter.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "abhi tvā; [it is] Gāyatra.
Its application is indicated by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

O Jātavedas, far-seeing one, we the Gotamas exalt you with our song; we celebrate you aloud with glorious hymns. 1. Abhi tvā gotamā girā jātavedo vicarṣaṇe | ghumnairabhi pra ṇonumaḥ || 1 || Toward you, O Jātavedas, far-seeing one, the Gotamas [exalt] with their song; with splendors we celebrate you aloud. 1.

O *ajātavedas*, knower of all that is born, O *vicarṣaṇe*, special beholder of everything— such as you, O Agni, the *Gotamas*— the seer Gotama, the author of this hymn (the plural being used for honor despite the singularity of the seer)— have praised you with *girā*, that is, with speech characterized by hymns, directed toward you (*abhi*). This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
We both praise you aloud and repeatedly with hymns that manifest your glorious qualities; we extol you directly and again and again.
*nonumaḥ*:
from the root *ṇu* in the sense of "praising," this form is derived from the present tense (*laṭ*) of its *yaṅ*-lopped (*yaṅluk*) derivative.
The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "upasargādasamāse'pi" (Pāṇini 8.4.14).

Gotama, desiring wealth, honors you with his song; we celebrate you aloud with our glorious hymns. 2. *taṃ u tvā gotamo girā rāyakāmo duvasyati | ghumnairabhi pra ṇonumaḥ ||2||* Him indeed, you, Gotama, longing for riches, worships with his song; with our glories we praise him aloud. 2.
Desiring kingship, desiring wealth, we—the Gotamas—serve with our song that very Agni whom you honor; him, that same one, we praise again and again with radiant hymns directed toward you.
*Rāyaskāmaḥ*:
one who desires wealth (*rāyaḥ*); that is, one who desires riches (*dhanāni*). [The suffix] *aṇ* is applied [to the noun *rāyaḥ*] by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*.

In the compound *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*, the suffix *aluk* (non-elision) occurs due to the word *bahulam*. By the rule *uḍidam* etc., the case-ending of the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is acute (*udātta*).
Due to its inclusion in the *dāsībhāra* group, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member is maintained.
Therefore, by the rule *kṛkamikaṃsakumbha* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), the *visarjanīya* is changed to *s*.
[The root] *duvasyati* [is used]; [the root] *duvas* [means] "to cause affliction" and "to attend upon."
Kaṇva and others.

We invoke you, the greatest winner of booty, like the Aṅgirases; we celebrate you aloud with glorious praises. 3. We invoke you, the greatest winner of booty, like the Aṅgirases; we celebrate you aloud with glorious praises. 3.
O Agni, we invoke you—just as the Aṅgirases did—with the prayer for the winning of spoils (*vāja-sāti*), as the one who most excellently wins and bestows those spoils. The rest is explained.
*vājasātamam* [is derived from] the root *vañju* in the sense of "giving" (*dāna*),
with the suffix *vid* applied according to the rule *janasanakhanakramagamo vid*.

By the rule *vidvor anunāsikāt*, the substitution of *ā* occurs. *Vājasātam* means "most excellent at winning booty" (*atiśayena vājasā*). Since the suffix *tamap* is *pit*, it is unaccented; consequently, the original accent of the final member of the compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) alone remains.
"Aṅgirasvat":
the suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule "tena tulyam" (Pāṇini 5.1.117).

By the rule "namo'ṅgiromanuṣāṃ vatyupasaṃkhyānam" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.4.18), there is an absence of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) because the word lacks *padatva* (the status of being a complete word) due to the presence of *vati*.

To you, the greatest slayer of Vṛtra, who you shake off the Dasyus with your glorious powers—to you we sing aloud our praise. 4. To you, indeed, O greatest slayer of Vṛtra, who you shake off the Dasyus with your glorious powers—to you we sing aloud our praise. 4.

O Agni, you who shake off, cause to fall, and displace from their station the *adasyu*s—those who seek to destroy, such as the *rākṣasa*s and others—you who are the supreme slayer of *vṛtra*s, that is, the supreme destroyer of evils (*vṛtra*s); to you, that very same one, [I offer praise] with glories (*ghumna*), and so forth, as before.
*Vṛtrahantamam*:
"The supreme slayer of *vṛtra*s" means one who is the most excellent among those who slay *vṛtra*.
In the technical term *pada*, when there is elision of *n* by the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7), the *t* is replaced by *n* according to *anādeśe* (Pāṇini 8.2.17). Thus, *dasyan*.
Then, by the rule *dīrghādaṭi samānapāde* (Pāṇini 8.3.9), the *n* is changed to *r*.

By the rule "atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā," the letter *ū* is nasalized (*sānunāsika*). We have spoken, O Rahūgaṇas, sweet splendor for Agni. With glories, we praise him aloud. (5) We have spoken; O Rahūgaṇas; for Agni; sweet; splendor; with glories; toward; forth; we praise. (5)
The seer concludes the hymn composed by another:

"We, the Rahūgaṇas—the sons of Rahūgaṇa—belonging to the Gotama lineage, have spoken sweet words, words inspired by sweetness, to Agni, the god endowed with qualities such as being the leader (aṅgana) and so forth.
With glories (*ghumnaiḥ*) consisting of those very words—that is, with shining hymns—we praise him repeatedly, we praise him with intensity and directedness."

The sixth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "hiraṇyakeśaḥ," has Gotama, the son of Rahūgaṇa, as its seer. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: "The two triplets of the twelve-verse hymn beginning with 'hiraṇyakeśaḥ' are in the Triṣṭubh meter; the first is for Agni, or the middle one."
In the previous instance, after saying "sing ye two," this hymn was also designated as *gāyatram*;
however, there is this distinction:
the first triplet (*tṛca*) here is in the *traiṣṭubha* meter.
The second, however, belongs to the *auṣṇiha* meter.
For the first *ṛc*-triad, the deity is Agni of the middle station, either as Vaidyuta (the lightning fire) or as Śuddhāgni (the pure fire).
The remaining nine verses have Agni alone as their deity.
The first triplet for the *prātaranuvāka* belongs to Agni, in the *kratu* [ritual], in the *triṣṭubh* metre, and in the *āśvina-śastra*.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "The three verses beginning with 'hiraṇyakeśa' and the hymn 'asya mahataḥ'... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
In the *kārīrī* sacrifice, the two verses beginning with 'hiraṇyakeśa' serve as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for Agni *dhāmacchat*.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘The golden-haired one in the expansion of the mid-air’ and ‘Two [verses]—“Thou art indeed,” “The unshakable abodes”—and “Upon thee rests the entire world”’" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.13).

The golden-haired one in the expansion of the mid-air, like a serpent in a windless place, is swift-moving; with pure luster, the dawns are knowers of men, glorious, and true like those who bring forth water. *Hiraṇyakeśaḥ*. *Rajasaḥ*. *Visāre*. *Ahiḥ*. *Dhuniḥ*. *Vātaḥ-iva*. *Dhrajīmān*. *Śucibhrājāḥ*. *Uṣasaḥ*. *Narvedāḥ*. *Yaśasvatīḥ*. *Ap-suvaḥ*. *Na*. *Satyāḥ*. 1. Golden-haired. Of the mid-air. In the expansion. A serpent. Shaking. Like the wind. Swift-moving. Of pure brilliance. The dawns. Knowers of men. Glorious. Bringing forth waters. As it were. True. 1.
1. Of those whose sins are marked by *ṭa* and *ṭha*;
2. By means of expressions corresponding to *ṭa* and *ṭha*;
3. The hymn (*sūkta*) consisting of *ṭa* and *ṭha* is the *gāyatra*.

*v*Hiraṇyakeśaḥ: he whose flames, standing in the place of hair, are exceedingly beautiful or shine like gold; *v*ahiḥ: having come as the slayer (*hantā*) of the clouds; *v*vṛniḥ: the shaker (*kampayitā*) of them; *v*vāta iva*: like the wind (*vāyu*); *v*bhrajīmān*: possessed of swift motion—such being the case, the lightning-fire (*vaidyuta agni*), being *v*śucibhrājāḥ* (of brilliant luster), knows how to cause the waters of the clouds to issue forth when *v*rajasah* (of water) *v*visāre* (in the spreading, i.e., the dissolution of the cloud-forms) occurs. *v*uṣasaḥ*: the deities of the dawn (*uṣas*); *v*navedāḥ*: they do not know (*na vidanti*), hence they are called *navedāḥ*.
The meaning is that the *abhiras* alone know how to draw water out from the cloud, whereas the *upasas* do not; this is the sense.
An illustration for their ignorance follows:

like subjects (*prajās*) who are "glorious" (*yaśasvatīḥ*), "united with him" (*anayuktāḥ*), "not to be surpassed" (*anavaryāḥ*), "desiring water"—that is, desiring their own work (*apasyuvaḥ*)—and "true" (*satyāḥ*), meaning those whose undertakings are unfailing, the *upasas* are not like such beings.

In this context, [the sun] is praised by means of these [rays] known as *upasama*, but they are not being censured; for according to the maxim, "censure is not intended to censure that which is censurable, but rather to praise that which is praiseworthy.
[The word] *bhrajīmān* [is derived from] the root *brāj* in the sense of "motion."

In the word *insarvadhātubhyaḥ*, the suffix *in* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). From that, the suffix *manup* is added. Because [the suffix] *manup* has the marker *p*, it is unaccented; and because the suffix *in* has the marker *n*, the first syllable of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is acutely accented.
*an-avetāḥ*. [The form] *an-avetāḥ* is derived from the root *vid* preceded by *na*, with the suffix *ac* (according to Pāṇini 3.1.134).
The original form of the negative particle *nañ* is retained according to the rule beginning with *nannānapāt*.
Regarding *apasyuvaḥ*: from the word *apa*, [the suffix] *kyac* is applied by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*; then, by the rule *kyācchandasi*, the suffix *up* is added.

‘The substitution of *uvaṅ* for the diphthongs of words such as *tanu* is frequently applied in the Veda’ (Pāṇini 6.4.77.1). Thus, *te* becomes *taṃ*. “Thy well-winged ones have sped along their courses; the black bull has bellowed when this [world] was here. He has come with auspicious, remembered [waters]; the mists fall and the clouds thunder. (2) *ā* | *te* | *suparṇāḥ* | *aminantaḥ* | *evaiḥ* | *kṛṣṇaḥ* | *naunāva* | *vṛṣabhaḥ* | *yadi* | *idam* | *śivābhiḥ* | *na* | *smaryamāṇābhiḥ* | *ā* | *agāt* | *patanti* | *mihaḥ* | *stanayanti* | *abhrā* ||2||
O Agni, your beautiful-winged rays—those with excellent flight—along with the Maruts, the movers, have struck down the cloud on all sides;
they strike it for the sake of rain.
And the black, dark-colored bull, the showerer, the cloud, has bellowed loudly.

‘When this such-like work occurs, then Parjanya comes hither with lightning flashes—white-colored like beloved women who are smiling and laughing, accompanied by auspicious and pleasant waters, or like moons joined with foam;
immediately thereafter, the waters of the rain fall, poured down from the sky;
and the clouds, filled with water and food, thunder, making sound here and there.’
*Amimanta*: [derived from] the root *mīñ*, meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*),
belonging to the *krayādi* group.
The substitution of the final vowel occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Due to its inclusion in the *īdādi* group, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).

Furthermore, the optional nasality (*anunāsikatva*) prescribed for the end of a word by Pāṇini’s rule *aṇo'pragṛhyasya* (8.4.57) should be understood here as applying even within a *saṃhitā* by way of transposition.
He caused them to cross by boat (*naunāva*).

Because of the prohibition [of the *ām* suffix] in the rule "except in mantras" (*amantre*, Pāṇini 3.1.35), there is no application of the *ām* suffix after a root ending in *yaṅ* in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*).
[The word is] *smayamānābhiḥ*.
In the word *smit*, the root *smi* means "to smile slightly.

Because the suffix *śap* is marked with *pittva*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*). By the rule regarding the accent of the *la-sārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains in place over the suffix *śānac*.
They thunder. The root *stan* means "to sound";
it belongs to the *curādigaṇa* and ends in the vowel *a*.
The two lightnings fall thundering; because they begin a *pāda* and also begin a sentence, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent).

When he, flowing with the milk of *ṛta*, has become manly—when Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Parijman tear open the skin with broadest, straightest paths in the womb of the lower one. yat | īm | ṛtasya | payasā | piyānaḥ | naryaḥ | abhūt | ṛtasya | pṛthubhiḥ | rajiṣṭhaiḥ | aryamā | mitraḥ | varuṇaḥ | parijmā | tvacam | pṛśnanti | uparasya | yonau || 3 ||

When Agni, moving along, nourishing the world with the "milk" of *ṛta*—that is, with the essence that is the very substance of water—and when he exists bringing that nourished world along the most direct paths (*rajāṃsi*) related to *ṛta*, namely the ways of bathing, drinking, and so forth, then Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and the Marut host who moves all around (*pariṣman*), at the womb of the lower cloud—the place of origin for the rainwater—they "besmear the skin," meaning they join their own weapons with the surface covered by the rainwater; that is to say, they open it.
*piyānaḥ*:
[derived from] the root *opyāyī* (variant of *pyāyī*) meaning "to increase";
the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap* occurs by the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the suffixes are] frequently [elided]."
The change to *pī* occurs by means of the transposition (*vyatyaya*) of the verbal root.
Because it is unaccented (*anudātta*), the *lasārvadhātuka* affixes are also unaccented; thus, the accent of the root remains. [The form is] *rajasaiḥ*.

From the word *ṛju*, by the rule *vibhāṣārcaśchandasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.162), the substitution of *ra* for the letter *ṛ* occurs. Then, by the rule *ṭeḥ*, there is elision of the final vowel (*ṭi*). Thus, [the form] *pṛñjanti* is derived.
The root *pṛc* means "to join together" (*saṃparke*);
it belongs to the Raudhādika class.
In the Prātaranuvāka, during the Agni-ṛtu, in the Auṣṇiha metre, and in the Āśvina-śastra, there are three verses beginning with "ame vājasya.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "Three verses beginning with 'ame vājasya' and 'puru tvā tvām agne'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
O Agni, lord of wealth consisting of cattle, young son of strength,
bestow upon us, O Jātavedas, great renown.
O Agni, lord of wealth consisting of cattle, O son of strength, bestow upon us great renown, O Jātavedas! 4.
O Agni, son of strength, you are the lord and master of food consisting of many cattle and of wealth joined with many cows;
therefore, O Jātavedas—knower of all that is born—bestow and establish upon us great and abundant fame, that is, food.
O you, O son of strength!

Because it is directed away (*parāṅvad-bhāva*), the entire group of unaccented words (*anantrita*) beginning with *omninatratasya* is pronounced with a low tone (*nihanyate*) according to the rule "omninatratasya ca.
[The word] *asme*.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," the case ending of the locative case is replaced by the substitute "śeṣa."
Blazing here, O Vasukra, worthy of praise with our song, shine forth wealth upon us, O you of many forms!
Kindled, the Vasu, the sage Agni, who is to be praised with song—O you of many faces, shine forth wealthily for us. 5.

That Agni, being kindled—that is, having the nature of shining—is the Vasu, the dweller of all; he is the Kavi, one who sees afar or is wise; and by means of *girā*, speech in the form of hymns, he becomes worthy of praise, to be lauded.
O Purvaṇīka!
(*Anīka* means face.)
Since you are endowed with many eastern flames that stand as if at the head of an army, shine for us—that is, blaze so that there may be "revat," food accompanied by wealth.
The root *indh* here means "to shine.
The suffix *cānaś* is not used in the sense of habitual action (*nācchīlika*).
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the elision of the *śap* suffix. [The form is] *īḍenyaḥ*. [The root] *īḍ* means "to praise."
The suffix *enyap* is derived from the *auṇādika* [list].
In the word *revat*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "vocalization occurs diversely before the suffix *mat*."
The substitution of *v* for *matup* occurs by the rule "chandasīraḥ.
The acute accent (*udāttatva*) of *matup* after the word *ra-* is prescribed by the rule "reśabdāt matupa udāttatvaṃ vaktavyam" (Kātyāyana-vārttika 6.1.176.1).
[Thus,] "dīdihi."
The root *dīdeti* belongs to the *chandas* (Vedic) language and has the sense of shining.
O King Agni, you have awakened by yourself at night and at the break of dawn;
O you with sharpened jaws, burn up the demons.
O King Agni, by yourself, burn up the Rākṣasas at night, at dawn, and during the day—O you of sharp fangs, consume them! 6.
O King Agni, you who possess the nature of a king, destroy the night-dwellers—
such as the Rākṣasas and others— by means of your own manly power. Moreover, not only by others but also by yourself, do you repel them.
If it is asked "When?", it is said: "On all days" (vastauḥ) and also "the dawns" (uṣasaḥ)—that is, the nights characterized by the time of dawn.
The accusative case is used here to denote continuous duration.
The meaning is: on all days and during all nights.
O *tigmajambha*, Agni with the sharp mouth, having utterly destroyed the *rakṣasa*s, the demons, you yourself, *pratidaha*—burn each one individually.
The acute accent (*udātta*) is used to express that nothing at all should remain.
*kṣapaḥ*:
[from] *kṣapa* in the sense of "patience" (*kṣānti*).
The *laṅ* suffix is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*) as a Vedic archaism.
In the Vedic language, according to the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the suffix *śap* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, by the rule *geraniṭi*, there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi*.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of *śap* is established by the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent that takes effect when the original accent is removed).
[The word is] *tmanā*.
In the case of mantras, by the rule "the [final vowel] of the word *ātman* following *āḍ* is elided," there is the elision of the vowel *ā*. Thus: *rakṣasaḥ*.

The root *rakṣ* means "to protect. A *rakṣas* is that from which one must be protected; the suffix *asi* is applied in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*) according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.4.74, because it belongs to the *bhīma*-class.
Alternatively, from the root *kṣar* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *asun* is applied; there is the elision of the *ṇic* suffix and a transposition of the phonemes.
And because this word *rakṣas* ends in the suffix *asun*, the accent of the suffix alone remains.

In the *prātaranuvāka* during the Agneya rite in the Gāyatrī metre, there are six verses beginning with "avā no agne. This is also stated in the Sūtra: "With the six [verses] beginning 'avā no agne,' he worships Agni Dṛta" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
And these [verses] are to be recited in the Āśvina-śastra, because of the extension of the rules from the Prātaranuvāka.
O Agni, worthy of praise in all our prayers, come hither with your aids at the offering of the Gāyatra hymn.
Come to us, O Agni, with your protections, at the bringing forth of the Gāyatra hymn, you who are to be praised in all our prayers. 7.

O Agni, worthy of praise and hymn in all thoughts and in all works, when there is the bringing forth—that is, the accomplishment—of the Gāyatra, i.e., of the hymn composed in the Gāyatrī meter, protect us with your aids, that is, with your protections.
Ava:
In the *saṃhitā* [text], there is lengthening according to the rule "aco 'tastiṅaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.135).
O Agni, bring to us wealth that is all-conquering, excellent, and invincible in all battles.
O Agni, bring to us wealth that is ever-conquering, most excellent, and invincible in all battles. 8.

O Agni, bring—that is, bestow—wealth (*rayi*) upon us; what kind of wealth? That which is *satrāsāham*, ever-conquering, capable of destroying poverty all at once; *vareṇyam*, desirable by all; and *duṣṭaram*, invincible by enemies in *viśvāsu pṛtsu*, in all battles.
Satrāsāham:
[the suffix] *ṇvi* is applied by the rule "sahaḥ chandasi" (Pāṇini 3.2.63).
Vareṇyam.

‘vṛja eṇyaḥ’. In the word *pṛtsu*, the substitution of *pṛt* for the word *pṛtanā* occurs according to the rule: “The addition of *māṃs*, *pṛt*, *stṛt*, and *mām* should be enumerated among the items beginning with *pada*.”
The acute accent on the case-ending is due to the rule "sāvekācaḥ."
In the *Āyuṣkāmeṣṭi* sacrifice, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the first *ājyabhāga* offering is “ā no agne.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “In the *Āyuṣkāmeṣṭi*, [the verses] ‘jīvātumantau’ and ‘ā no agne sucetanā’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.10).
This same verse is also the invitatory verse for the first *ājyabhāga* in the *Mahāpitṛyajña*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Possessing life-breath and having the left side as its seat" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).
The Rigveda [Book 1, Adhyāya 5, Varga 28]
O Agni, bestow upon us, through your excellent wisdom, wealth that nourishes all life and grant us compassion so that we may live. || 9 ||

O Agni, bestow upon us, for our living—that is, for our life—wealth (*rayi*) endowed with beautiful wisdom (*sucetana*). Of what kind? *Mārḍīkam*: *mārḍīka* means happiness; that which is the cause of it. *Viśvāyupoṣasam*: nourishing the body and so forth throughout the entire lifespan; the meaning is that it is sufficient for our enjoyment as long as we live. Regarding *sucetana*: from the root *citī* (in the sense of "perception"), the suffix *up* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules. The accent falls on the first syllable of the second member of the compound (*ṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*). Regarding *viśvāyupoṣasam*: that in which the whole lifespan (*viśvamāyu*) resides, such as the body, is called *viśvāyu*. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when used as a name, the final syllable of the first member is accented (*bahuvrīhau viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām*). That which nourishes (*puṣṇāti*) this [lifespan] is *viśvāyupoṣaḥ*. The suffix *asun* is applied here, and by the rule "the original accent of the first member remains even when preceded by a preverb or a kāraka," the accent is preserved.
This Agni—thousand-eyed, possessing innumerable flames, and *vicaraṇī*, meaning especially the beholder of all—drives away, that is, repels, the *rakṣases*.
The sacrificial fire causes them to depart.
And this Agni, being praised by us with powerful hymns (*ukthas*), becomes the *hotṛ* who summons the gods, and as such, he *gṛṇīte*: he lauds them.
*Sahasrākṣaḥ*:
The suffix *ṣaṣ* is applied by the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, [the suffix] *ṣaṣ* [is added] after *sakthi* and *akṣi*.
Because it is taught later (and thus has greater force), its accent alone remains.
It wards off; [the root] *ṣidhu* means "to go.
In this context, even though it is used alone, it should be understood as having the sense of a verb with a prefix.
He utters (*gṛṇīte*).
[The root] *gṛ* is used in the sense of "sound. The shortening of the vowel occurs according to the rule: "The roots beginning with *pvā* undergo shortening."
The seventh hymn, consisting of sixteen verses beginning with "itthā," is the seerly composition of Gautama; it is addressed to Indra and composed in the Paṅkti meter.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī: "itthā ṣoḍaśendraṃ paṅkti hi.
Because of the presence of the word "hi," according to the technical paribhāṣā rule regarding "tu" and so forth, this and the two following [verses] are in the Paṅkti meter.
On the fifth day of the *pṛṣṭha-ṣaḍaha*, this hymn is the *marutvatīya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *marutvatīya* [is] 'avitāsītthā hīndra', 'piba', and 'tuyam'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.12).
On the twenty-fourth day, the first [verse] of the Acchāvāka is an optional *anurūpa*.
In the section concerning the *hotṛ* priests (*hotrakāṇām*), it is sūtra-ed: "‘Itthā hi soma inmada ubhe yadindra rodasī’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
At the Mahāvrata, in the southern wing of the *niṣkevalya* [śastra], there is the single verse beginning with ‘itthā hi’.
Likewise, it is sūtra-ed in the fifth Āraṇyaka: "‘Itthā hi soma inmada’ is a *paṅkti* [verse]" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.2.2).
Thus indeed has the priest fashioned this Soma for exhilaration, an invigorating draught;
O most powerful wielder of the thunderbolt, by your might you have driven the serpent from the earth,
while celebrating your own sovereign dominion.

Thus indeed has the priest prepared this Soma for exhilaration as a means of strengthening; O most powerful wielder of the thunderbolt, by your might you have driven the serpent from the earth, chanting in accordance with your own sovereign dominion.

O most powerful (*śaviṣṭha*), O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), O Indra—indeed, in this very manner, according to the method prescribed by the scriptures, when the exhilarating Soma that causes joy has been drunk by you, the Brahmin, the singer, has performed a hymn of praise (*vardhana*) that increases your greatness; he has composed it with this *sūkta*. The particle *it* is used here for metrical completion.
Therefore, by your might (*ojasā*), from the earth, you have utterly destroyed (*niḥ śaśāḥ*) Vṛtra, the slayer who had come as a serpent (*ahi*).
The meaning is that, having issued the command "Do not harass [me]," he emerged from the presence of the Earth;
what was he doing?
He was honoring—meaning, manifesting his own sovereignty—his own kingdom, that is, his royal status, directed toward it (*anu*).

The root is *śās* (from *śāsu* in the sense of "instructing"). When the *laṅ* [suffix] would have required the elision [of the suffix], the *śap* [augment] is replaced by *blu* according to the rule "it is manifold in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
*Svarājyam*:
"The state or activity of a king is *rājyam*. The suffix *yak* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *yak* is added after words ending in *pati*, and after *purohita*, etc."
For in that context, the rule "rājāse" (Pāṇini 5.1.128 Ga. is recited.
*Svarājyam* means one's own kingdom (*svasya rājyam*).
By the rule "akarmadhāraye rājyam" (Pāṇini 6.2.130), there is acute accent on the first syllable of the second member of the compound.

That exhilarating, bull-like Soma, pressed and brought by the falcon, has gladdened you— that [Soma] by which, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you struck down Vṛtra with your might while singing in accordance with your own sovereignty.

That bull, the exhilarating Soma juice, pressed and brought by the falcon, has intoxicated you—that draught by which, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you drank up Vṛtra and slew him with your might, while singing in accordance with your own sovereignty.
1. *kṣa-hi* [is used as a filler].
2. *kṣa-ṭa-ha-na-sa* [are used] for filling out the verse-pāda.
O Indra, that Soma has exhilarated you—has brought you joy.

Of what nature is that Soma? It is a bull (*vṛṣan*), characterized by its power to pour; it is a gladdening drink (*mada*) that causes intoxication and rapture; it is brought from heaven by the Gāyatrī, which assumed the form of a falcon (*śyena*) and took the shape of a bird; and it is pressed (*suta*).

O *vajrin*, wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, by drinking which Soma you, through that strength (*ojas*) which produces power, struck down Vṛtra from the midst of the atmosphere—*aṅga* being an emphatic particle.
The rest is as before.
He gladdened (*amadat*).
[The root] *mad* is used in the sense of "joy" (*harṣe*).

From this, by adding the causative suffix *ṇic*, there is shortening (*hrasvatvam*) according to the rule "the short vowel for roots marked with *m*" (*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*), because it is listed among the *ghaṭādi* group in the rule "the root *mad* [is used] in the senses of joy and intoxication."

In the *laṅ* [tense], because of the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*), the *śap* [suffix] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, by the rule "the *ṇi* is elided before a suffix that does not take *iṭ*" (*ṇeraniṭi*), there is the elision of the *ṇi*.
[The form is] *aṅgaḥ*.
*Āpaḥ* is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
By the rule *apo bhi* (Pāṇini 7.4.48), the letter *pa* becomes *ta*. In *jaghantha*,
the augment *iṭ* which would have been required by the rule governing roots beginning with *kr* (kṛtī), is prohibited by the rule *upadeśe'tvataḥ*.
By the rule "abhyāsācca," the letter *h* becomes *gh*.
By the rule "liti," the syllable preceding the suffix is acute (*udātta*). Due to its connection with a word-break (*yadvṛtta*), it is not subject to suppression (*anighāta*). 2.
Threaten boldly, be courageous; your thunderbolt shall not be held back, for your strength is manly power, O Indra. Slay Vṛtra, win the waters, and sing praise to your own sovereign dominion!
Go forth! Advance! Be bold! Your thunderbolt shall not be held back. For your strength is manly power, O Indra; slay Vṛtra, win the waters, and sing in praise of your own sovereignty. 3.

O *indra*, go forth (*pra-ihi*), proceed with vigor; come toward (*abhīhi*) the enemies who are to be slain; having reached them, be bold (*dhṛṣṇuhi*)—overcome those enemies. Your *vajra* is not restrained (*ni-yaṃsate*) by the enemies; that is to say, its course is unimpeded. Likewise, since your own strength (*śavaḥ*) and manly power (*nṛmṇaṃ*)—which is the name for men and which overcomes them—are indeed such, therefore slay (*hanaḥ*) Vṛtra, whether he be an *asura* or a cloud. Immediately thereafter, conquer (*jayāḥ*) the waters (*apaḥ*) held back by him; the meaning is: having struck down Vṛtra, obtain the water obstructed by him. The rest is the same. Regarding *yaṃsate*: from the root *yam*, in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, the suffix *sip* is added according to the rule "sibbahulam"; the augment *aṭ* is added according to "leṭo'ḍāṭau. Regarding *hanaḥ*: in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*), the *laṅ* (imperfect) ending is used as a Vedic archaism; the *śap* suffix is elided according to "bahulaṃ chandasi. Since *śap* is marked with *pittva*, it is unaccented, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains. Because the preceding word does not belong to the same sentence, there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent). Regarding *jayāḥ*: from the root *ji*, in the *leṭ* mood, the augment *āṭ* is added; the accentuation is as before.
From the earth you struck down Vṛtra, O Indra-less one; from heaven [you struck him down].
Like the well-born Maruts, these life-sustaining waters have celebrated your self-sovereignty.
O Indra, you struck Vṛtra down from the earth; release the waters from heaven like the Maruts. Singing praises, follow these life-sustaining waters according to your own sovereign dominion.
O Indra, from above the earth, from the world of Bhūloka, you struck Vṛtra down, slaying him utterly;
likewise, you struck him down from heaven, from Dyuloka. Having slain him, release these waters—the waters of rain—downward and let them fall.

1. *kṣa*, *ḍha*, *hana*, *sa-indra*, *vajrin*, *vajravan*; 2. Due to the application of the rules for *kṣa* and *ḍha*, there is no occurrence of the particle (*nipāta*); 3. *kṣa*, *ḍha*, immediately after that (*tadanantaram*).
What kind of waters?
1. *Maruvatīḥ*: accompanied by the Maruts; *jīvadhanyāḥ*: those by which living beings (*jīva*)—that is, creatures—are blessed (*dhanya*), meaning satisfied. The rest is the same.

Indra, incensed, having advanced with his thunderbolt against the ridge of the surging Vṛtra, smites him down; driving the waters toward their flow, he celebrates his own sovereign rule. || 5 || Indra, enraged, having approached with his thunderbolt, strikes down the ridge of the surging Vṛtra; impelling the waters to flow, he rejoices in his own sovereignty. || 5 ||

Indra, provoked and enraged, having advanced and turned toward him with force, strikes down—that is, he smites—with his thunderbolt the lofty ridge, the region of the jaws, of Vṛtra who is violently trembling.
What is he doing?
Driving—that is, impelling—the waters, the rain-waters, for their flowing forth, that is, for their release; [he strikes] the trembling one.
The root *dhūñ* means "to shake.
From this root, in its form with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix (*yaṅluk*), the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is added; the elision of the final letter is Vedic.
By the rule "the first syllable of reduplicated forms is acute," the initial vowel receives the acute accent (*udātta*).
*hīlitaḥ* [is derived from] *heḍ* / *hoḍ* [in the sense of] "disrespect. This [root],
as in *heḷate* (Nirukta 2.12.2), is listed among the verbs signifying anger.
From this [root], in the sense of completion (niṣṭhā), the vowel *ī* is substituted due to the transgression of the [prescribed] phonetic class (*varṇa-adhyāpatti*). [Thus we have] *jighnate*.
In the case of the root *han*, in the present tense (*laṭ*), there is an irregular (*vyatyaya*) substitution for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the plural number.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the substitution of *bh* for *śap*.
With the word "it" being carried over [from the previous rule], by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," the vowel *i* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
By the rule beginning with "gamahana," there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).
*Samāya*:
[derived from] the root *sṛ*, meaning "to go.
The suffix *man* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule beginning with *arti-tusi-*.
1. By virtue of being a *niti*, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable.

He strikes down upon the ridge with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt; Indra, exhilarated by the soma-juice, seeks a path for his friends, praising his own sovereign rule. 6. Upon the ridge, he strikes down with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt; Indra, gladdened by the draught, desires a way for his companions, celebrating his own self-sovereignty. 6.
Indra strikes down with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt—that is, one endowed with a hundred streams—upon the ridge;
the prefix *adhi* here reiterates the sense of "together with.
He utterly destroys upon the elevated parts, such as Vṛtra’s cheeks and so forth.
And that Indra, being exhilarated—rejoicing while being praised—desires for his friends, those who are yoked together as singers of praise, a path, a way to the *andhas* (the food);
the rest is as before.
*Mandānaḥ*:
[derived from] the root *madi* in the sense of "praising";
the suffix *śānac* is applied in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*), followed by *yak*.
According to the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, because the suffix *śānac* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, there is elision of the vowel *a* and the suffix *ya*.
Since it follows a root ending in an *anudātta* vowel, the *lasārvadhātuka* suffix *śānac* is *anudātta*, and thus the accent falls on *yak* alone.

When *yak* is elided after the *anudātta* *śānac*, the *śānac* would then acquire an acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule regarding the accentuation of the substitute for an acute vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*).
In that case, since the suffix *śānac* is an *ārdhadhātuka*, the *lasārvadhātuka* accent does not apply; thus, only the *cit-svara* remains.
1. What kind of waters [are intended]? 2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-* [indicate] the state of being udātta.
But in that case, would not the state of being udātta apply even to an initial anudātta?
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, O lord of the stone, your heroic power is indeed unsurpassed;
for when you slew that illusory beast with your magic, you manifested your own sovereign rule.

O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, lord of the pressing-stones, to you alone was that heroic power granted, when you, by your own creative might, struck down that guileful beast; thus you celebrated your own sovereign dominion. 7.
"Adri" is a name for a cloud.

O *adrivaḥ* (O possessor of clouds), O *vajrin* (O wielder of the thunderbolt), Indra—you who possess the cloud as your vehicle—this dative case (*tubhyam*) is used in the sense of the genitive (*tava*). Your own heroism and power (*vīrya*) is *anuttam*, meaning unassailable by enemies.

Indeed, because you slew even that well-known Vṛtra— who was a deceiver, a master of illusion, who had taken the form of a deer, and whose meaning is one who causes affliction to the world— by means of your very own illusion.
*anuttam*: due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) of the word *anasatnipatta*, there is an absence of the cerebralization (*niṣṭhānatva*) [of the dental *t*].
*avadhīḥ*.
For the root *han*, there is the substitution of *vadh* by the rule "luṅi ca" (Pāṇini 2.4.43). This substitute ends in a short vowel (*adanta*).
When the *at* of that [substitute] is elided, the absence of *vṛddhi* before the suffix *sic* occurs due to the status of the elided element as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Your thunderbolts have been launched along the ninety navigable rivers;
O Indra, great is your heroic power, and strength has been placed within your two arms—let them sing in praise of your self-sovereignty.

Your thunderbolts have been firmly established along the ninety navigable rivers. Great is your heroic power, O Indra; strength has been placed within your arms. Singing praises, we acknowledge your sovereign dominion.
O Indra, those *vajras*—your weapons that have issued forth from you—have spread out in various ways along the ninety rivers, the navigable streams obstructed by Vṛtra.

The meaning is that although your *vajra* is singular, it acted as if it were manifold in order to strike down Vṛtra, who pervaded everywhere. Furthermore, O Indra, your heroic power (*vīrya*) is great and abundant.
The meaning is "I am invincible.
Likewise, strength has been placed—that is, deposited—in your two arms, your two hands;
the sense is that your two arms are exceedingly powerful.
The rest is as before.
[The form] *asthiran* is derived from the root *sthā* (to stand) in the *luṅ* tense; the *ātmanepada* ending is applied by the rule *samavapravibhyaḥ sthaḥ*.
In the mantra "ghasa," there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli*.
By the rule "sthādhvoricca" (Pāṇini 1.2.17), the substitution of *i* occurs.
By transposition (*vyatyaya*), the replacement of *jha* by *ran* takes place.

The word *nāvyāḥ* [is derived as follows]: the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *nau-vayo-gha-dharmam* (Pāṇini 4.4.91). Because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, the vowel receives the *svarita* accent according to the rule *tisr-ā-svaritam*.
In the case of *bāhvoḥ*, the accentuation of the case ending is governed by the rule "udāttayaṇaḥ. 1.
kṣa—The phrase "in the sense of the genitive, [the dative is used]" does not exist.

2. [To] him who causes one to abandon the syllables *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ḍha*, and *tya*—worship him together by the thousands! Let twenty chant the hymn of praise around him! A hundred have shouted after him; let them worship the prayer offered up for Indra, following his own sovereignty. *Sahasram* (thousand), *sākam* (together), *arcata* (worship), *pari* (around), *stobhata* (chant the hymn of praise), *viṃśatiḥ* (twenty), *śatā* (hundred), *enam* (him), *anu* (after), *anonavuḥ* (they have shouted), *indrāya* (for Indra), *brahma* (prayer), *uta* (and), *udyatam* (offered up), *arcana* (let them worship), *anu* (following), *svarājyam* (own sovereignty).
A thousand— that is, a number of people amounting to one thousand—
worshipped this Indra simultaneously;
likewise, twenty [did so].
The sixteen officiating priests, the sacrificer, the wife, the member of the assembly (*sadasya*), and the slaughterer—these constitute a number of twenty.
That number twenty "resounds around" (*paristobhati*), that is, it praises him from all sides.
And likewise, the seers numbering one hundred have repeatedly praised this Indra again and again.
For this very Indra, offer up the *brahman*—the food characterized by the oblation (*havis*)—and pour it out;
for it is for such an Indra as this that Vṛtra was slain.
The rest is as before.
*pari stobhata*: it has the sense of praising (*stuti-karman*). The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs according to the rule *upasargāt sunoti*.
They praised (*anonavuḥ*). [The root] *ṇu* means "to praise.
From this root, in the *yaṅ*-lopped form (*yaṅ-luganta*), the substitution of *us* for *jhi* occurs in the *luṅ* tense by the rule "*sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*."
*Udyatam*:
[The root] *yam* means "to cease.
From this root, preceded by the prefix *ut*, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The elision of the nasal [of *pra*] occurs by the rule beginning with “anudāttopadeśa. The original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the prefix (*gati*) is applied by the rule “gatiranantaraḥ.”

Indra struck down the power of Vṛtra with his overwhelming force. That was his great manly deed: having slain Vṛtra, he released the waters while praising his own sovereign rule. 10. Indra. Of Vṛtra. The power. Out. Struck. With might. Might. Great. That. His. Manly deed. Vṛtra. Having slain. He released. Praising. Along. His own sovereignty. 10.
Indra struck down the power and strength of Vṛtra, the Asura, by means of his own strength;
with *sahas*, that is, with overcoming force—the weapon that effects subjugation—he struck down *sahas*, the weapon of Vṛtra that effects subjugation.
That manly might (*pauṃsya*) of this Indra is great, exceedingly mature.
Because he, having struck—that is, having slain—Vṛtra, released the waters that were obstructed by him, therefore he caused Vṛtra to go to destruction (*vṛtrāñjiragamayat*).
The rest is as before.
*Pauṃsyam*. [The root] *puṃs* [is used] in the sense of “increasing” (*abhivardhana*).
It belongs to the *curādi* (cur-class) group.
The suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "aco yat";
its initial vowel is acute by the rule "yato 'nācaḥ";
[the form] is *jaghanvān*.

The suffix *kasu* is applied after the root *han* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Due to the rule "optionally [the augment] *iṭ* is added to *gam*, *han*, and *vid*," the presence of *iṭ* is optional. Furthermore, by the rule "also after a reduplicated syllable," the *ha* of *han* following the reduplication is changed to *gh*.
Even these two great worlds tremble with fear at your wrath, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, when you, accompanied by the Maruts, slew Vṛtra by your might, celebrating your own sovereignty. (11)
1. In the *kṣa* and *ṭa* recensions, "tathā" does not exist.
2. In the *kṣa* and *sa* recensions, "ca" does not exist.
O Indra, even these two, the great Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), tremble and shake out of fear of your wrath (*manyu*).

O *vajrin*, wielder of the thunderbolt, O *indra*, when you, being great and joined by the Maruts, slew Vṛtra with your *ojas*—that is, with your strength—then even heaven and earth trembled with fear; such is the meaning.
It trembles; [the root] *duviṣṭa* means "to shake.
Out of fear.
The word *jibhī* means "fearful"; the suffix *kas* is applied according to the rules of the *uṇādi* class.
Neither by his physical power nor by his thunder did Vṛtra terrify Indra;
rather, the iron thunderbolt with its thousand points fell upon him as he roared, while Indra, shining, established his own sovereignty.
Neither by his trembling nor by his thundering did Vṛtra terrify Indra; against him the iron thunderbolt with its thousand points was hurled, as he sang praise unto his own sovereign rule.
Vṛtra did not terrify Indra with his own trembling or shaking; he did not frighten him.
Nor did he terrify him with his own terrible thundering roar.
Furthermore, the iron (*āyasa*) vajra, released by Indra, possessing a thousand points (*sahasrabhṛṣṭi*) and many edges, came toward Vṛtra to slay him, approaching him face-to-face.
The rest is as before.
The root *tan* [is used here]. In the sense of "sound" (*stana*),
the suffix *yatuc* prescribed for the root *tan* by the rule beginning with “*ṛtanyañji*” etc., occurs after this root as well due to the mention of the word *bahula* ("in various ways").
For this very reason, there is also the elision of the *s*.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the third case ending is replaced by *ḍā*;
its acute accent (*udāttatva*) is established by the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent that arises when an original acute accent is removed).
*bībhayat* [is used];
[the root] *jibhī* means "to fear";
the suffix *ṇic* is applied because there is a causal agent (*hetumati*).

In this context, in the words *vepatanyatubhyām*, there is no lengthening of the vowel (*ātvābhāva*) because the fear is not caused by a cause such as *Vṛtra*; thus, according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.56, *bibheter-hetubhaye*, the substitution of *ā* does not occur.
From the causative form (*ṇyantāt*), in the *luṅ* tense, [the forms] *śleṣāt* and so forth arise;
[and] *āyata*.
The root *aya* (in the form *paya*) means "to go";
it belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa* and is conjugated in the Ātmanepada.
When you struck Vṛtra and Aśani with your thunderbolt,
O Indra, as you sought to slay the serpent, your power was bound in heaven while you proclaimed your own sovereignty.
When you, O Indra, struck Vṛtra and Aśani with your thunderbolt as you sought to slay the dragon, your power was bound in heaven; singing [your praise], we acknowledge your sovereign rule.

O Indra, when you struck Vṛtra with your thunderbolt and completely smote the arrow discharged by him for the purpose of slaying you—then, as you desired to kill Vṛtra, the slayer who had come against you, your power (*śavas*) was bound in heaven, woven through and pervading it.
The rest is as before.

In *jighāṃsataḥ*: after the root *han* with the desiderative suffix (*san*) in the sense of wishing to kill, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel according to Pāṇini 6.4.16, *añjanagamāṃ sani*. In *baddhe*: [the same rule applies].
The root *badh* means "to bind.
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) used here for the object, there is an irregularity (*vyatyaya*) whereby the substitution of the remaining initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*) does not take place.
At your shout, O wielder of the stone, both that which stands and that which moves trembles;
even Tvaṣṭṛ, at your wrathful impulse, O Indra, quakes with fear before your sovereign majesty.

At your thunderous roar, O wielder of the stone, both that which stands and that which moves tremble; even Tvaṣṭṛ himself quakes before your wrath, O Indra, out of fear, singing in accordance with your sovereign rule.

O wielder of the stone, O Indra, possessor of the thunderbolt, when your shout of triumph and your lion’s roar arise there, both that which is stationary and that which is moving—the entire world—trembles and quakes. Even Tvaṣṭṛ himself, the fashioner of the thunderbolt, I believe, trembles violently and shakes with fear at your wrath.
The rest is the same.
*sthāḥ*: from the root *sthā*, the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule “*kvip ca*” (*Pāṇini 3.2.76*). *vevijyate*.
The root *ovijī* is used in the sense of "fear" and "trembling.
From this root, the intensive suffix *yaṅ* is applied in the sense of frequent repetition of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāre*).
By the rule "for *saṃ* and *baḍ*, there is reduplication," the doubling of the syllable occurs.

Because it is taught as having an initial vowel (adupadeśāt), when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the accent of the *yaṅ* itself remains. Since it occurs at the beginning of a verse-quarter (*pāda*) belonging to Indra, and because of the rule “the preceding vocative is as if non-existent” (*āmantritaṃ pūrvamavidyamānavat*), it is treated as non-existent; consequently, because it stands at the beginning of a quarter, the prohibition by the rule “not at the beginning of a quarter” (*apādādau*) results in the absence of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent).
For truly, whatever we conceive— O Indra, what heroic powers before us?—
in him the gods have concentrated manly strength, wisdom, and vital forces, as well as his own sovereign rule.
Not indeed! Nay, who is beyond Indra in heroic deeds? Upon him the gods have bestowed manly strength, wisdom, and powers, as they sing praise to his own sovereignty. 15.
We do not indeed comprehend Indra— who exists pervading everywhere as he moves along—
because we are but small;
for the word *paraḥ*, ending in the letter *s*, is an indeclinable that denotes "Vaidūrya."
As it is said: “Beyond heaven, beyond this [world]” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.82.5).
“Beyond” means *parastāt*, that is, in a distant place unfathomable by humans; who among men would know Indra, who exists there by his *vīrya*—that is, by his heroic power and capacity?
The meaning is: no one at all.
If it is asked "Why?", he says here: "In him.

Because in that Indra, the gods deposited (*saṃ dadhuḥ*)—that is, established—manly strength (*nṛmṇam*), wealth (*dhanam*), as well as mental power (*kratum*), heroic deeds (*vīrya-karma*), and vital energies (*ojāṃsi*); such is the meaning.
From the root *yā*, meaning "to go" or "to reach," the suffix *śatṛ* is applied to the present tense (*laṭ*).
The elision of the second case ending occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. [Thus we have] *adhīmasi*.
[The root] *iṇ* means "to go."
The word *masiḥ* ends in *-id*.
[The form] *vīryā* is derived from the third case ending by applying the rule *supāṃ suluk*, which substitutes the vowel *ā* for it.
The prayer which Manu’s father Atharvan, the sage, meditated upon and offered—unto that Indra have ancient prayers and hymns gathered together; sing forth unto his own sovereignty!
Atharvan, Manu the father, and Dadhyañc stretched out the prayer; to him, as of old, Indra gathered the sacred formulations and hymns, while he sang praise according to his own sovereignty. 16.

The *ṛṣi* named Atharvan, who is the father of all progeny and has become their progenitor, and Manu—the son of Atharvan named Dudyat—whatever prayer (*dhi*) they conceived and whatever rites (*karman*) they performed, in those rites all the sacred formulas (*brahmāṇi*) characterized by oblations, as well as the hymns (*ukthā*) consisting of recitations and praises (*stotrāṇi*), came together (*sam agmata*) in that Indra.
Therein lies the illustration:

Just as in former times, in the sacrifices of these and other [sages] such as Vasiṣṭha, the oblations and hymns were united with Indra, so too is it here. That Indra, honoring— that is, praising— his own sovereignty (*svarājyam*),
[performed] the slaying of Vṛtra and so forth.
1. [Objection: To this, he says:

The meaning is that he manifested his own status as the lord of honey through his form and action. [Regarding the word *alata*]: from the root *tan* (in the sense of "to expand"), the suffix is elided by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*; the penultimate vowel is dropped by the rule *tanipatyobhchandasi*. [Regarding *pūrvathā*]: by the rule *pratnapūrvaviśvemātthālū chandasi*, the suffix *thāl* is added to the word *pūrva* in the sense of "like" (*iva*). By the accentual rule concerning *lit*, the syllable preceding the suffix is udātta. [Regarding *ukthā*]: the suffix *śe* is elided by the rule *śebhchandasi bahulam*. [Regarding *samam-mata*]: the Ātmanepada ending is used by the rule *samo gamyucchibhyām*. In the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *cli* is elided by the rule *mantre ghasa*; the penultimate vowel is dropped by the rule *gamahana* etc. || 131 ||

May Vidyātīrthamaheśvara, dispelling the darkness of the heart by illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, bestow the four goals of human existence. Thus ends the fifth chapter of the first book (*aṣṭaka*) in the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā-bhāṣya* titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the sustainer of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the supreme sovereign of kings, the highest lord, and the promoter of the Vedic path— under the patronage of Mādhava.
1. Kṣa, rending asunder!
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Oṃ. This fifth chapter of the Daśatayī has been previously explained by the wise Sāyaṇārya; now the sixth chapter is being described.
In the first maṇḍala, in the thirteenth anuvāka, seven hymns have been explained.
The eighth hymn consists of nine verses beginning with “indro madāya.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “indro nava” (Indra [is the deity] of the nine).

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the seer [is the same] as for the preceding [hymn]," the seer of this hymn is Gautama, the son of Rahūgaṇa, because he is the one who continues from the previous hymn.
Since it was stated in the preceding hymn that "it is indeed fivefold" (*pāṅktam hi*), by that same technical rule, both this and the subsequent hymn are fivefold (*pāṅkta*).
According to the technical rule regarding the lack of specific instruction, Indra is the deity.
This hymn is recited at the Niṣkevalya-śastra on the fifth day of the Pṛṣṭhya [Ṣaḍaha].
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*predaṃ brahmendro madāya satrā madasa* is the Niṣkevalya” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).
It is also used in the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s śastra at the Mādhyandina-savana on the *ārambhaṇīya* day of the Caturviṃśa [Ahargaṇa].

The augment *aṭ* is added. By the rule "itaśca lopaḥ," there is the elision of the *ikāra*. By the rule "sibbahulaṃ leṭi," the suffix *sip* is applied. Because it belongs to the *ārdhadhātuka* category, the augment *iṭ* is added by virtue of its being preceded by a consonant (*valādi*).
For you, O hero, are a warrior-like fire who bestows much;
you are the one who seizes even the meager, yet you grant abundance to the sacrificer who presses the soma for you—abundant is your wealth.

For you, O Hero, are the leader of armies; you are the one who bestows much. You are the eager seeker even of the meager; you grant wealth to the sacrificer who presses the soma. Abundant is your treasure.
O hero, O Indra skilled in hurling back the enemies, you are *sainya*; that is, you are the one who seizes the army (*senāhā*).
The meaning is that even though you are alone, you are like an entire army.
For this reason, you are the one who gives away (*parādātā*) the abundant wealth of the enemies; you are the one who takes it so that the enemies turn their backs and flee.
Even for one who is *dabhra*—
this is a name for "small"—
even for you, the small one, the singer (*smotuḥ*), you are the one who increases (*vṛdhá*) [them].

Likewise, you bestow—that is, you give—the wealth required to the person who is a sacrificer (*yajamāna*), performing the sacrifice, and who is a presser (*sunvate*), performing the pressing of the *soma*. The root *śikṣ* has the sense of giving. The meaning is: because your wealth (*vasu*) is abundant, manifold, and inexhaustible, therefore you give.
*parādadi*: [derived from] the root *dāp* in the sense of "giving. The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *ā-dṛ-gama-hana-janaḥ kvip*.
Because it is a nominal stem (*liṅga*), there is shortening in the dual;
by the rule "there is elision of *ā* before *iṭ* and [suffixes beginning with vowels]," the *ā* is elided: *gṛdhau*.
The root *gṛdh* contains an implied causative sense; hence, by the rule regarding roots ending in *i* or *u*, the suffix *ka* is applied.
For *sunvate*, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending is due to the rule "the [first syllable] of a word ending in *śatṛ* or *anunāsika* [is acute]."

When they utter their cries in battle, wealth is bestowed upon the bold one; yoking your two intoxication-dripping bay horses, whom will you slay, whom will you enrich, O Vasu? O Indra, enrich us with wealth!

When the battles arise, wealth is bestowed upon the bold one. Having yoked your two bay steeds that stir the exhilaration, whom will you slay, O Vasu, and whom will you enrich? O Indra, O Vasu, enrich us! 3.
On this point, there is this narrative:
Gautama, the son of Rahūgaṇa, was the domestic priest of the Kuruśravaṇas, who were kings.
When those kings were engaged in battle with their enemies, that seer, having praised Indra with this hymn, prayed for the victory of his own people.
And his role as that priest is recorded by the Vājasaneyins: "Gautama Rāhūgaṇa was indeed the domestic priest of both the Kuru and Śravaṇa clans.

When battles (*vājayaḥ*) arise—that is, when they break out or occur—then wealth (*dhanā*) is bestowed (*dhīyate*) upon the bold one (*dhṛṣṇave*), who is the one that dares (*dhṛṣṇuḥ*) and is the conqueror of enemies. The meaning is that wealth belongs to the victor.
O Indra, when such battles have commenced, yoke to your chariot your two bay horses (*harī*), which cause the intoxication—the pride—of enemies to fall away.
Having yoked them, you slay any king whatsoever who does not perform service for you;
and you establish in wealth—that is, in riches—anyone whatsoever who serves you.
Therefore, you alone shall be the one who ordains victory and defeat.
For that reason, O Indra, establish us—our kings—in wealth and riches. Let them rise up!
The root *īr* means "to move";
it belongs to the first class (*ādādika*); [the prefix] *anu*.
1. Regarding *kṣa-ṭa-ḍha*, here is this explanatory narrative.
2. Regarding *kṣa-vṛtteṣu*.
3. Regarding *kṣa- 'vasuni', it does not exist.

Because of the *dāttitva* (the acute accent on the suffix), when the *lasārvadhātuka* [suffixes] are unaccented (*anudātta*), the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) alone remains. Due to its connection with *yad-vṛtta*, there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent). *Dhanā*: the substitution of *ḍā* occurs according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *Yukṣva*: from the root *yujir* in the sense of "joining" (*yoge*). From the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) in the imperative (*loṭ*), there is the elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. The lengthening in the *saṃhitā* occurs by the rule *vaco 'tastiṅaḥ*. *Hanaḥ*: from the root *han* in the *leṭ* tense with the suffix *sip*; the augment *aṭ* is added. Because of the perception of the particle *ca* in the rule *hanaś ca dadhaś ca*, there is an optional prohibition of *nighāta* for the first case-ending (*prathamā*) which is a *tiṅ*-suffix, according to the rule *cādilope vibhāṣā*. *Vasau*: this is the *liṅ* suffix. *Dadhaḥ*: from the root *dadha* in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*). In the *leṭ* tense, the *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
By his power, the great and terrible one has turned according to his own will;
the lofty, fair-cheeked, and golden-hued one, possessing the thunderbolt of iron, has taken up the bolt in his hands for the sake of glory at the nearby place of sacrifice.

Great by his power, the terrible one has grown according to his own nature; for the sake of glory, the lofty one, the possessor of the golden jaws, the lord of bay horses, has taken up the iron thunderbolt in his hands at his nearby dwelling-place.
By his skill, his action, or his wisdom, he is great and preeminent among all;
Indra is the terrible one who strikes fear into his enemies;
[he acts] according to the sacred tradition.
*svadhā* is a name for food.
*Svadhāyām* is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*).
The meaning is that he partook of food characterized by Soma.
He increased his own strength (*śavaḥ*) directly (*ā*).
Immediately after that, he, the broad (*vṛṣvaḥ*), the beautiful to behold, and the fair-cheeked (*śiprī*).
*Śipre* means the jaws or the two nostrils;

joined with those, Indra—called *hari*, meaning "the tawny one" or "possessed of tawny horses"—places, for the sake of prosperity (*śriye*), the iron (*ayasa*) thunderbolt (*vajram*) in his two hands or arms, which are near to him (*upākayoḥ*). He deposits it there.
The essential meaning is that Indra, exhilarated by the drinking of soma, grasps the thunderbolt (*vajra*) in his hand for the slaying of his enemies.

Regarding the form *kratvā*: because the rule "in the Vedic language, there is optionally no substitution" (*jasādiṣu chandasi vāvacanam*) allows for the non-substitution of the vowel, the form *kratvā* (with the long vowel) occurs.
[The suffix] -ya [is applied] in the sense of "its modification" (tasya vikāraḥ).
He has filled the earthly region and has established the luminous realms in heaven.
O Indra, no one like you has ever been born, nor will anyone be born; you have carried all things beyond.
He has filled the earthly realm; he has established the luminous spheres in heaven. O Indra, no one like you has been born, nor will anyone be born; you have carried yourself beyond all.

Indra, by his own splendor, has filled the earthly realm—the multitude of objects connected to the earth—and the mid-air world (*vraja*). Likewise, in the heavenly world (*divi*), he has established the shining, radiant stars. Therefore, O Indra, there has never been anyone born who is even equal to you; indeed, there is no one at all like you.
And it will not be born;
even that which is about to arise does not exist.
You have desired to carry—indeed, you wish to carry with exceeding effort—the entire universe, the whole world, which is of such a nature.
The meaning is that he becomes the fulfiller of the entire world.
The root *pṛ* (in the form *paprau*) is used in the sense of "filling" (*prā pūraṇe*).
In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is the substitution of *au* by the rule "āta au ṇalaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.34).
[Thus we have] *pārthivam*. [The suffix] *añ* [is applied] after *pṛthivī* by the rule "pṛthivyā jāñau" (Pāṇini 4.1.85).
1. Because it occurs after *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ḍha*, or *yat*, there is a constant prohibition of the *nighāta* accent; furthermore, because of its connection with *sa-* and *yat*, the *nighāta* applies.
2. [The syllable] *dha* is not augmented (*na vāvṛdhe*). 3. In manuscript *kṣa*, the word "establishes" (*sthāpayati*) is absent.
4. The category of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ḍha*.

Thus ends the suffix *an*. Due to its being marked with *j*, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable. *Rajaḥ*: [the word] *rajaḥ* refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), because in this [space] Gandharvas and others "shine" (*rajanti*). From the root *rañj* "to color," with the suffix *asu*, there is the elision of *n* by the rule: "The addition of *rajan*, *rajaḥ*, and *sū* is prescribed for *rañj*" (Kātyāyana Vārttika 6.4.24.4). *Baddhadhe*: from the root *badh* "to bind. In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is an absence of the *halādiśeṣa* (retention of the first consonant) by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*). Because the root does not consist of a single consonant situated between vowels, there is also no occurrence of *etva* (change to *e*) or the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*). Because it begins a quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent). *Khāvān*: the suffix *vatup* is applied by the rule: "In the Vedic language, the addition of *vatup* is prescribed after *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when expressing similarity. There is the substitution of *ā* by the rule "ā of the pronoun. *Vavaktha*: from the root *vah* "to carry. After this, in the desiderative (*san*), the substitution of *i* by the rule "for *at* in *san*" does not occur, according to the principle: "All rules are optional in the Vedic language. Following the desiderative form, in the perfect tense, there is an absence of the *ām* suffix due to the prohibition "not in a mantra. || 1 ||

The noble one who bestows the food of mortals upon the donor—may Indra grant us his aid. Distribute your abundant wealth; may I partake of it. At every exhilaration of Soma-drinking, when you are filled with joy, that Indra of upright intent and straight actions is indeed the giver of herds of cattle to us. He is truly the bestower of flocks of kine.

O Indra, you who are such, grasp together with both hands—that is, take hold of—to give to us, those many, numerous, and vast hundreds of treasures; that is to say, immeasurable riches. Sharpen us; make us keen.
The meaning is: "Make them possessed of sharp intelligence.
O Vrāya, bring—take and bestow—the riches that are held in your hands.
*Dadiḥ*: [derived from] the root *dudāñ* in the sense of "giving. The suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule *ādyamahanajanaḥ*.
*yūthā*:
the elision of *śi* occurs by the rule "in the Veda, *śi* is frequently [elided]";
[this refers to] *gavām*.
The elision [of the *s*] prescribed by the rule "sāvekācaḥ" is prohibited by the rule "na gośvansāvavarṇa. [Thus:
*gṛbhāya*. [The root] *grah* [is used here in the sense of] "taking up."

O Indra, these beings—namely the people characterized as sacrificers—who are yours by nature (*te tava svabhūtāḥ*), nourish and cause to increase the entire (*viśvam*) offering (*haviḥ*), which is desirable (*vāḥ*) and to be honored by all. You, the master (*arthyaḥ*) and lord of all, surely see—that is, you know—the wealth (*vedaḥ*) existing within (*antaḥ*) those people who do not give offerings (*adāśuṣām*) and do not accept the oblations. (Note: The form *loṭi* refers to the imperative mood; *hau* is the dual ending; the rule *chandasi śāyajapi* [Pāṇini 3.1.84] permits the substitution of *śāyac* for the imperative suffixes in Vedic usage.)

"Bring to us, our wealth—the Veda—of those who do not sacrifice; that is to say, bring it and bestow it. Since the wealth existing with those who do not sacrifice would be utterly useless due to their lack of engagement in sacrifice, the intended meaning is:
"In order to make that wealth meaningful, seize their wealth and bestow it upon those who do sacrifice."
The root *ruy* [is used] in the sense of speaking clearly;
this [root] also has the meaning of seeing.
In the present tense, the *luṅ* suffix is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
By the rule *asyativaktītyādinā*, there is the substitution of *aṭ* for *cli*.
[Then] by the rule *ātolopa iṭi ca*, there is the elision of the long *ā*.

Since there is no difference in meaning because *luṅ* and the others are prescribed in one place, this root has been explained by us in this manner in the *Dhātuvṛtti*. Therefore, the form *arthayāse* is established by means of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The root *arth* is used in the sense of "begging for wealth";
it belongs to the *curādi* class and is conjugated in the *ātmanepada*.
In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *āṭ*.

*yojaya*. From the root *yuj* in the sense of "joining," with the suffix *ṇic*, in the imperative (*loṭ*), because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), the *śap* [augment] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, by the rule *ṇeraniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51), there is the elision of the *ṇic*.
"aco 'taṣṭaṅaḥ"—by this rule, there is lengthening in the *saṃhitā*.

They have eaten; they have rejoiced; indeed, the dear ones have shaken themselves free. The self-luminous sages have offered praise with a most recent hymn. Now, O Indra, yoke your two bay steeds! akṣan | amīmadanta | hi | ava | priyāḥ | adhūṣata | astoṣata | svabhānavaḥ | viprāḥ | naviṣṭhayā | matī | yojā | nu | indra | te | harī || 2 ||
O Indra, the sacrificers have eaten the foods given by you;
having eaten, they were indeed satisfied.
They have shaken their own dear food [as an offering].
Unable to speak due to the tasting of an extraordinary flavor, they made their bodies tremble.
Immediately thereafter, the wise ones—the *vipras* who possess self-dependent splendor—praised [him] with a most recent hymn of praise (*mati*). The rest is to be understood as before.
*akṣan*. In the *luṅ* tense, there is the substitution of *ghas* by the rule "luṅ-sanoḥ ghas" (Pāṇini 2.4.37).
Then, by the rule "mantre ghasa... and so forth, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli*.

By the rule "agama-hana" and so forth, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*). By the rule "śvari ca," there is the substitution of *c* for *ś*. By the rule "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca," there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *ś*.
The augment *aṭ* is acute (*udātta*). [Example:
*amīmadanta*. [Root:
*mada* in the sense of "satiety."
The root *cur* is conjugated in the *ātmanepada*.

In the *luṅ* (aorist), after the substitution of *caṅ* for *cli*, there occurs the elision of the *ṇi*-affix, the shortening of the penultimate vowel, reduplication, the *saṃvadbhāva* (treatment like the *san* suffix), the substitution of *it* for the radical vowel, and the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable. Thus: *adhūpata*.
The root *dhūṣ* means "to shake.

In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with the suffix *sic*, there is an absence of *guṇa* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Alternatively, according to the rule "in the Veda, both ways," the *sic* is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; because it is then *ṅit*, the prohibition [of *guṇa*] applies by the rule "and when followed by *kriḍati*."
Alternatively, [the root] *dhū* is used in the sense of "shaking";
it belongs to the *tudādigaṇa* and the *kuṭādigaṇa*.

In this case, because the suffix *luṅ* denotes the object (*karman*), the *sic* [augment] is *ṅit* by the rule "gāṅ-kuṭādibhyaḥ," and thus there is an absence of *guṇa*. [The form] *naviṣṭhayā* [is derived from] the root *ṇu* in the sense of "praising" (*stutau*).
Although *stuti* (praise) is an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is expressed by the suffix *tṛc* because it possesses agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to its own operation.
From that form ending in *tṛc*, the suffix *iṣ* is applied according to the rule *tucchandasi*. Then, by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*, there is the elision of the *tṛ* portion.
The form *matī* results from the substitution of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) with the long vowel of the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
The acute accent (*udātta*) on the suffix *ktin* is applied by the rule *mantre vṛṣeṣapacamana*.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, the verse "susaṃdṛśam" is employed for the worship of the Āhavanīya fire;
and it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Āhavanīya [is worshipped] with the Paṅkti verse beginning 'susaṃdṛśaṃ tvā'. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.10).

We would praise you, O Maghavan, who are so beautiful to behold. Now, indeed, being praised and with your chariot-seat filled, go according to your will; now, O Indra, yoke your two bay horses. susaṃdṛśam | tvā | vayam | maghavan | vandiṣīmahi | pra | nūnam | pūrṇavandhuraḥ | stutaḥ | yāhi | vaśān | anu | yoja | nu | indra | te | harī iti ||3||
"O Maghavan, O Indra, O Lord of great power, we shall praise you—us who behold all with a most gracious eye; may we become those who offer hymns of praise.
Thus it is hoped that we may become performers of praise.

"Praised by us, your worshippers, and being joined with a chariot filled with riches to be given to the singers, go forth indeed toward the other yearning sacrificers; surely, establish yourself among them."
"Yojayitvā" and so forth are as explained previously.
We shall worship.
[The root] *vadi* means "salutation" and "praise. This is the optative (*āśīr-liṅ*) mood.

By the rule *liṅ āśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.4.116), because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, it lacks the accent of a *lasārvadhātuka* suffix and instead possesses the acute accent on its first syllable as a suffix-initial.

As for the word *maghavan*, since it is treated as non-existent by the rule *āmantritaṃ pūrvam avidyamānavat*, there is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent) because it stands at the beginning of a *pāda*.
May he indeed mount that bull-like chariot, the winner of cattle, which, O Indra, one knows to be the full vessel for the yoking of the bay steeds; now, O Indra, yoke thy two bay horses!
He shall mount that bull-like chariot which finds cattle, he who, O Indra, keeps in mind the full vessel for the yoking of the bay steeds. Now, O Indra, yoke thy two bay horses! 4.

May that Indra indeed mount this chariot—this chariot which rains down desires (*vṛṣaṇam*), which finds cattle (*govidam*). May he be seated upon such a chariot; may he ascend it. O Indra, that chariot which makes known the vessel called *Hāriyojana*—filled with parched grain mixed [with Soma] and full of Soma—upon that chariot let him mount; thus the connection is with what precedes.
And having taken hold of your two horses, yoke them quickly.
In the word *ratham*, there is a long vowel according to the rule "ṛci tunugha. Ratha.

By the rule *adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.46), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) receives the technical designation of object (*karman*). [The form] *tiṣṭhāti* [is derived from] the root *sthā* in the *leṭ* mood with the augment *āṭ*.
He perceives. [The root] *kit* means "to know.
The augment *āṭ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood.
Because [the root *hu*] belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, the suffix *śap* is replaced by *il*.

Due to the statement "it should be stated that [this applies] abundantly in the Veda" (*Kāśikā* 7.3.87.1), the prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel—by the rule "there is no [guṇa] for a reduplicated stem before a vowel beginning with *p*" (*Pāṇini* 7.3.87)—does not take effect here.
May your right hand and your left be skillful, O Śatakratu;
with that, being exhilarated by the soma-juice, go toward your beloved wife. Now, O Indra, yoke your two bay steeds.
May your right arm be ready, O Śatakratu, and also your left. With that, being exhilarated by the soma-juice, go toward your beloved wife. Now, O Indra, yoke your two bay horses. ||5||

O Indra, Lord of a hundred powers, O performer of many deeds, let the horse on the right—the one stationed at the right side—be yoked to your chariot; and furthermore, let the left-hand horse also be yoked. Rejoicing and intoxicated by the drinking of *andhas*, the food characterized as Soma, come with that chariot unto your beloved wife, she who brings delight.
The meaning is: "Go to where she resides.
For that purpose, O Indra, yoke your two horses quickly to the chariot.
By this verse and the following one, Indra’s departure toward his own home after having drunk the Soma is set forth.
*Mandānaḥ*: [derived from] the root *madi* in the sense of "praising, delighting, intoxication, sleeping, beauty, and motion";
[formed with] the suffix *kānac* after the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
In the section on dual endings:
1. *kṣa-stavāma*; 2. *kṣa-na-sa-bahukarmendra*.
3. *kṣapra-sthāpamam*.
According to the rule "it should be stated that [the doubling] is optional in the Vedic language (*chandasi veti vaktavyam*)," there is an absence of reduplication. It is different from others.
The root *ad* means "to eat. According to the Uṇādi Sūtra 4.645, *ader-num dhaś-ca*, the suffix *asun* is applied, with the augment *num* added to the root and the final substitution of *dh* for *d*.
On other days, the verse beginning with "yunajma" is the *yājyā* for the *hāriyojana* offering.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two verses, 'We yoke for thee the two long-maned bay horses with a sacred prayer' and [the other], are the invitatory and offering verses on the other days" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.11).

We yoke for you, O long-maned one, the two bay horses with a sacred prayer; come hither, for you hold them in your hands. The impetuous pressed juices have gladdened you; accompanied by Pūṣan, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you have rejoiced together with your wife. We yoke for you, O long-maned one, the two bay horses with a sacred prayer; come hither, for you hold them in your hands. The impetuous pressed juices have gladdened you; accompanied by Pūṣan, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you have rejoiced together with your wife.
O Indra, O Keśin—one possessing long hair—your two horses are tawny-maned and crested.
O Indra, that mortal man who is well-protected (suprāvīḥ) by your aids (tavotibhiḥ), that mortal dwells in a home abounding in horses and goes foremost among those seeking cattle;
the meaning is that he becomes possessed of kine even before all other sacrificers.
You satisfy—that is, you make complete and full—that very person with most abundant, most extensive, or even hundreds of thousands of units of *vasu*, that is, wealth.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as waters, which are the cause of superior knowledge, fill the ocean from all sides—that is, in every direction—so too [do you satisfy him].
*aśvāvati*: the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *mantre somāśva* when the suffix *matup* is present. *suprāvīḥ*.

The suffix *ī* is applied to the root *av* according to the rule *avitṛstṛntantribhya īḥ* (Uṇādisūtra 3.438). Thus, from *ūti*, the feminine suffix *ktin* receives the udātta accent by the rule *ūtiyūti* etc. (Pāṇini 3.3.97).
*pṛṇakṣi* [is derived from] the root *pṛcī* in the sense of "contact"; it belongs to the *raudhādika* (rudhādi) class.
