From the word *bahu*, when the suffix *īyasun* is added, the substitution of *bhū* for the word *bahu* occurs and the long vowel *ī* of *īyasun* is elided by the rule "the [final] *u* of *bahu* is elided, and *bhū* replaces *bahu*" (*bahor lopo bhū ca bahoḥ*). However, in this case, due to the archaic nature of the Vedic language (*chāndasatvāt*), the elision of the long vowel *ī* is not performed, while the substitution of *bhū* is applied.

Alternatively, from the word *bhavitṛ*, the suffix *īyasun* is applied according to the rule "in the Veda [the suffix] *tṛc* [is replaced by *īyasun*]. Then, the elision of the *t* occurs according to the rule "there is elision of *t* before *nu*, *iṣ*, *im*, and *īyas*.
While the *hotṛ-camasa* of the Aṅgirases is being filled with the *apanonnīya* [water], these verses beginning with "O divine waters (*āpo na devīḥ*)" should be recited.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having completed [the recitation], [the Adhvaryu says]: 'The divine waters approach the Hotṛ's cup'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.1). And there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "'The divine waters approach the Hotṛ's cup,' [this] he says while the waters are being poured together into the Hotṛ's cup" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 2.20).
"The divine waters approach the Hotṛ's cup; they behold the wide expanse as if it were the intermediate space."

The divine waters—the shining goddesses—approach the *hotṛ*’s own *hotrīya* cup, just as water flows toward its source; likewise, the gods, positioned above, look down from below at this very cup.
Their gaze has become fixed upon it, thinking, "Our waters have been poured into the *hotṛ*’s cup for the pressing of the Soma.
In this regard, there is an illustration.

Just as the pervasive and extensive dust or light related to the sun falls down without interruption, so too they lead forward this cup— desiring the gods (*devayu*)— eastward, that is, toward the *uttaravedi* at the time of the oblation, by means of forward movements (*prāñcaiḥ*). Having been led forward for the sake of the oblation, it is dear to the *brahman*, meaning it is filled or pervaded by the *brahman* characterized by the Soma.
All the gods take pleasure in that cup and attend upon it, just as suitors attend upon a maiden.

Just as suitors attend upon a maiden, each thinking, "She shall be mine, she shall be mine," so too the gods remain by its side, each thinking, "This Soma is mine, this Soma is mine. This is the meaning.
Thus, it has been applied according to its application (*viniyoga*) in the *Aponaptrīya* ritual, because a mantra illuminates the meaning of that which is to be performed.
However, when its application occurs during the *rātriparyāya*, it should be explained as follows:
"O Indra, just as the divine waters go toward the low-lying land, even so do the gods, hearing your hymn of praise, go toward the *hotrīya*, the place of the *hotṛ* priest."

Having approached, they behold from below him spread out like light—this one who seeks the gods, who desires the gods for himself, the reciter. All the gods have come and lead him forward; from the immortal realm, they sustain him.
Like excellent maidens serving a suitor, they attend upon him as he recites—he who is dear to the *brahman*, dear to the hymn of praise.
The term *hotriya* is derived from the word *hotṛ* with the suffix *gha* in the sense of "belonging to that. *Avaḥ*.

to animals with dewlaps, such as goats, sheep, and others. 2. In the versions *ca*, *cha*, *ta*, *da*, *na*, *pha*, and *śa*, the word "garvati" does not exist. 3. In *kṣa*, it is for the sake of the oblation. 4. In *kṣa*, it is "taṃ devaṃ". 5. In *kṣa*, "vitataṃ vitatam". 6. In *kṣa*, *na*, and *sa*, "icchantam enam".
"The Aṅgirases first established this age, they who kindled the fires through their skillful work and the sacrificial post."
All the men obtained their share of the Paṇi’s food, consisting of cattle and horses, and all kinds of livestock.

The Aṅgiras first assumed their vital strength; with kindled fires, through their skillful work and the sacrificial pin, they gathered together all the wealth of Paṇi—the cattle and the horses—as their food, O heroes. ||4||

When the cattle were carried away by the Paṇis, then the Aṅgiras—the descendants of Aṅgiras—first of all prepared the sacrificial food, characterized as the *vayaḥ* (strength), for the sake of Indra. Immediately thereafter, those Aṅgirasas, being possessed of kindled fires and engaged in fervent practice, worshipped Indra with a beautiful rite (*śamyā*) endowed with excellent performance—that is, through a magnificent sacrifice; this is the sense of the remainder.
Those Aṅgirases, the leaders of the sacrifice, obtained—that is, they acquired—all the food and wealth belonging to the Asura named Paṇi.
Of what kind? It was "rich in horses," meaning joined with horses, and "rich in cows," meaning joined with cows.
The particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction;
they also obtained other species of cattle distinct from cows and horses.
Aṅgirāḥ: by the rule "supāṃ suluk," the suffix *jas* is replaced by *su*. Śamyā.
*Śamī* is a name for ritual action (*karman*). It is called *śamī* because by means of this performance, the collection of defects is pacified (*śāmyati*);
the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
There is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "nodāttopadeśasya māntasyānācameḥ" (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.34).
The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *gaurādi* group.
The initial udātta accent is due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
*Sukṛtyā*: that in which there is a beautiful performance or action; thus it is so called.
By the rule *nassubhyām*, the final syllable of the second member of the compound is udātta.
Atharvan first laid out the paths with sacrifices; from that, Sūrya was born as the guardian of the vow and the beloved one.
Uśanas Kāvya drove forth the cows together; we sacrifice to the most renowned immortality of Yama.

Through sacrifices, Atharvan first stretched out the paths; from there Sūrya was born as the guardian of the sacred law, the Seer. Uśanas Kāvya drove forth the cows along with him. We worship the immortal knowledge of Yama. 5.

When the cows had been carried off by the Paṇis, the seer Atharvan, with sacrifices—meaning sacrifices performed for the sake of Indra as the deity—first stretched out the paths belonging to the cows;
that is to say, he prepared them even before all other seers.
Thereafter, Vrata-pā, the protector of rites (vratāni), Vena, the beloved, Sūrya—Indra in the form of the Sun—was born; he appeared for the purpose of revealing the cows.
Then Atharvan drove those cows toward him;
for such an Indra, Uśanas Kāvya—the son of the sage Kavi—and Bhṛgu became companions in order to repel the Asuras.
We worship with oblations that Indra, who was born—that is, manifested—for the purpose of restraining the Asuras of Yama, and who is immortal, being free from death.

In the case of *pathas*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) by the rule "there is elision of the *ṭi* of a *bha*-stem before the suffix *śas*. The acute accent of the case-ending is due to the "accent of the removal of an acute" (*udāttanivṛtti-svara*).
In *tate*:
from the root *tanu* in the sense of "extension" (*vistāre*). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
The elision of the nasal [of the root *jan*] occurs by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa" (Pāṇini 6.4.37). *Ajani*.
[The root] *janī* means "to appear."

By the rule *'dīpanabudha' etc.* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.61), the suffix *ciṇ* is applied to the root *cal* in the *luṅ* tense when denoting the agent; thus, *ājat*. [The root] *aj* means "to move" or "to cast."

Whether the sacrificial grass is trimmed for the sake of noble offspring, or the hymn proclaims its fame in heaven, or where the pressing-stone speaks as the praiser recites his praise—Indra truly delights in those arrivals. barhir vā yat svapatyārya vṛjyate 'rko vā ślokam āghoṣate divi | grāvā yatra vadati kārur ukthyas tasyed indro abhipitveṣu raṇyati || 6 || Whether the sacrificial grass is trimmed for the sake of noble offspring, or the hymn proclaims its fame in heaven; wherever the pressing-stone speaks and the praiser recites his praise, Indra truly delights in those arrivals.

When the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is trimmed and cut by the *adhvaryu* for the sake of the sacrifice— which serves as the cause for obtaining beautiful offspring— or when the *vakra*, that is, the *hotṛ* who effects the hymn of praise, utters the *śloka*, the speech consisting of praise, during the shining sacrifice in heaven; and when the pressing-stone (*grāvan*),
set in motion for the purpose of extraction, sounds forth— therein lies the illustration.
"vkārurukthyaḥ": this is an elliptical simile (*luptopama*). Just as a poet (*kāru*) who recites hymns (*uktha*) produces the desired sound, so too [is he].
In the attainment— that is, the reaching— of all that was previously mentioned, Indra rejoices; or rather,
when there is the attainment of the aforementioned items such as the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and so forth, Indra rejoices and utters a cry of joy, thinking, "Our sacrifice shall take place."
It is excluded. [The root] *vṛjī* means "to avoid.
Because it is taught with a short *a* vowel (*adupadeśa*), when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the accent remains solely on the *yak* affix.

There is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule "with particles such as *yad*, *yadi*, *iha*, and *anta*. [The word] *āghoṣate* [is derived from] the root *ghuṣir* in the sense of "making a sound."
It belongs to the *bhū* class (*bhauvādika*).
Here too, due to the elision (*anupaṅga*) of the particle *yat*, there is no loss of accent (*nivātābhāva*).
[Thus] one delights (*raṇyati*).

The root *ras* is used in the sense of "playing. Here, the suffix *iyan* and the *parasmaipada* (active voice) occur by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*); other grammatical modifications are Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively, *raṇa* has the meaning of "sound";
[the form] *iyam* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The eleventh hymn, consisting of twenty verses, begins with "asāvi.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Asāvi... twenty [verses]; [the meters are] anuṣṭubhs, uṣṇiks, paṅktis, gāyatrīs, and aṣṭubhs; [there are] three triplets (tṛcas) and a pragātha.
Of these, the first six are anuṣṭubhs, and the next three, beginning with the seventh, are uṣṇiks.
The first three verses beginning with the tenth are *paṅkti*s;
the first three beginning with the thirteenth are *gāyatrī*s;

Gautama is the seer (ṛṣi) because of the continuity [of the hymn].
By the rule regarding unspecified cases, Indra is the deity.
The application of the hymns (*sūkta*) is to be understood from their indicative marks (*liṅga*). Furthermore, the first two *ṛc*s of the unimpeded *ṣoḍaśin* are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “Now, for the *ṣoḍaśin*, ‘saṃ soma indra ta’ are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.2).

At the third pressing during the Ukthya rites when the [Soma] has been pressed, these two verses are the optional *stotriya* and *anurūpa* for the Acchāvāka: "Asāvi soma indra te" and "Imamindra sutam piba. This is prescribed in the section beginning with "Ehū ṣu" in the *Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* (7.8).

And having arrived, may it fill (*v pṛṇaktu*) you with *indriya*—the capacity produced by the drinking of Soma.
The Vraja [is] the atmosphere; [it is] like the Sun with its rays (kiraṇaiḥ). 1. *kṣa-ṣoḍasyasāvi*:

just as the Sun fills [the world], so [does he]. *Śaviṣṭha*: from the root *śavas* (strength), with the suffix *iṣṭhan*; by the rule *vinmatorluk*, there is elision of the *matup* suffix; by the rule *ṭeḥ*, there is elision of the final *ṭi*; because it begins a quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent). *Gahi*: from the root *gam* in the imperative (*loṭ*); by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision of the *śap* suffix; by the rule *anudāttopadeśa* etc., there is elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*); because that [elision] is treated as "not yet accomplished" (*asiddhavadatrā bhāt*), there is no elision of the particle *hi*.

toward the praises of the seers and toward the sacrifice of human beings.
The two bay steeds carry Indra alone, whose power is unassailable, toward the praises of the seers and toward the sacrifice of men. 2.

[He] whose power is unassailable, meaning his strength is not overcome by anyone— that is, his strength is unhurt— Indra himself; [his] two bay horses (*hari*) bring the praises of the seers, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, as well as those of other humans, and the sacrifice, near to him, that is, they cause them to reach his presence.
The meaning is that wherever they praise and wherever they sacrifice, there in every such place they cause Indra and the two horses to arrive.
[The suffix] *añ* is applied after the word *mānuṣa*,
with the augment *puṅ*, according to the rule beginning with “*manojñādi*.”

O Vṛtrahan, O Indra, slayer of enemies, mount and ascend the chariot, because your two bay horses (harī) have been yoked to the chariot by us through the *brahman*—the mantra characterized by praise; therefore, mount the chariot.
And may the pressing-stone (*grāvan*), the stone set in motion for the purpose of pressing, with its resonant sound of pressing, turn your mind toward us and make it well-disposed.
It is joined [to the suffix]; the vowel *ā* is substituted by the rule "supāṃ suluk" (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
[The form is] *vadhunā*.

O *indra*, drink this pressed, poured-out *soma*. Of what kind?

The streams of this bright, radiant Soma— excellent (*jyeṣṭha*), exceedingly praiseworthy, intoxicating (*mada*), and immortal (*amartya*) [in the sense that the intoxication produced by drinking Soma does not kill like other forms of intoxication]— flowing in the dwelling (*sadana*) or house belonging to *ṛta* (the sacrifice), have flowed toward you; they move toward you, reaching you, coming of their own accord.
*Jyeṣṭham*:
from the word *praśasta* with the suffix *iṣṭhan*, there is the substitution of *jy* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.61 (*jya ca*). They flowed forth.

O officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), praise now—quickly—Indra; perform worship.
This very point is made clear:
recite the *ukthas*, the hymns of praise accomplished by means of non-chanted mantras.
Let the pressed-out *indus*, the Soma juices, exhilarate this Indra who has arrived; let them make him intoxicated.
Immediately thereafter, pay homage to that Indra, the most excellent, the most praiseworthy, the powerful one possessed of might (*sahasvin*);
speak [words of praise] to him.

[Thus, it means] "you should pay homage."

nor has anyone else, even one with beautiful horses (*svaśvaḥ*), attained you (*ānaśe*).

In the *ābhiplāvika* *ukthya* sacrifices, at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), the triplet (*tṛca*) "He who alone is kindled" (*ya eka iddhiyate*) is the optional *stotriya* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest.
This is prescribed in the section beginning with "Eba pu" in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (7.8): "O friends, we desire blessings; he who alone is kindled."
Even in the Mahānāmnya and Kevalya hymns, another triplet is prescribed for the Aṣṭādaśa-stoma;
likewise, it is stated in the Pañcama Āraṇyaka: "He who alone is the sole foundation—come hither with the stones to the pressed [juice]" (Ai. Ā. 5.2.5).
He alone bestows wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations;
Indra, indeed, is the sovereign lord, irresistible and unopposed.
He alone who is bestowed as wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations—Indra, indeed, is the sovereign and the unopposed. 7.

Indra—who alone, by himself, bestows (*vidayate*) wealth (*vasu*) upon the mortal man who offers oblations (*dāśuṣe martyāya*), that is, the sacrificer—verily (*aṅga*), meaning swiftly; he who is "unopposed" (*apratiṣkutaḥ*), meaning not answered back by others, i.e., free from any contrary sound; such an Indra quickly becomes the sovereign (*īśānaḥ*), the lord of the entire world. [Grammatical notes: The root *day* (in *vidayate*) means "giving, going, protecting, harming, or taking. Because the suffix *śap* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*). By the rule regarding the accent of *tiṅ* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root itself remains. Due to its connection with *yad-vṛtta* (the relative pronoun *yad*), there is no elision of the accent (*anighāta*). Regarding *apratiṣkutaḥ*: the root *ku* means "sound. That which is sounded (*kyate*) against (*prati*) is *pratiṣkuta*. Because the group beginning with *pāraskara* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the augment *muṭ* is applied. By the rule *supāmādi*, the case-ending is substituted by the following word. In a compound where the first member is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the original accent of the first member prevails.
When will he trample the devouring demon with his foot like a shrub?
When, indeed, will Indra hear our songs?
When will he trample with his foot the one who offers no gifts, like a mushroom? When will Indra, indeed, hear our songs? 8.

Indra will, at some point, trample with his foot—just as one crushes a *kṣumpa* (a mushroom)—that mortal man who is devoid of wealth, whose characteristic is the offering yet who possesses no gift; that is to say, one who does not bestow. When will he strike him down? He will strike him down.
Just as one might strike a snake lying in a circular coil with a blow that does not cause it to move, so too [the meaning is]: "When will Indra slay our enemies?
The root *sphur* signifies the act of killing, because it is listed among the verbs for killing in the Nirukta (2.19.15): "sphurati, sphulati."
It is being deliberated: "When—indeed, at what time—will Indra quickly hear our songs, the words characterized by praise of us who sacrifice?
Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "The *kṣumpa* is a large mushroom; it is so called because it trembles (*kṣubhyate*). [The question is:
'When will he, with his foot, kick him who seeks to propitiate him, as one would a mushroom with the foot'?"
"When will they hear our songs? O Indra!
Indeed, 'aṅga' is a word for 'quickly' (Nirukta 5.17). Thus [it is said] with respect to the word.
For the word *pāda*, the substitution of *pada* is applied by the rule "padn" etc.;
the acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule "uḍiḍm";
[the compound] is like *kṣumpam*.
The root *kṣubh* is used in the sense of "to move" (*saṃcalane*).
From this root, with the suffix *ghañ* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*), the augment *num* is added to the root due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacanāt*).
Furthermore, by the process of phonetic substitution (*varṇyāpattyā*), the letter *bh* is replaced by *p*.
*sphurat* [is derived from] the root *sphur*, meaning "to vibrate" or "to move. According to the rule *chandasi luṅliṭaḥ*, the *laṅ* (imperfect) is used in the sense of the *luṅ* (aorist).
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge 'pi.
[He] heard (*śuśravat*). [The root] *śru* means "to hear."
The root *lag* takes *aḍ* as its augment.
By the rule "in the Vedic language [the suffix] *śap* is frequently elided," there is the elision (*bhlu*) of *śap*.
1. Because it begins with *kṣa* and ends with *vṛtta*, there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
2. *kṣa-ṭha*: like Ahicchatra.

Whosoever, having pressed the Soma, seeks to win you over from among many—Indra indeed masters that fierce power; truly so! 9 Whosoever, having pressed the Soma, seeks to win you over from among many—Indra indeed masters that fierce power; truly so! 9
From among many men, whosoever indeed— that sacrificer who, being possessed of the pressed Soma, O Indra, attends upon you with service—
*vivāsati* being a verb meaning "to serve"—
for that sacrificer, Indra quickly (*aṅga*) bestows, casts down, or brings forth his fierce, surging power (*ugram śavaḥ*).
That [is the case]; by the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision (luk) of the dative case ending.
It is ruled over.
From the root *pat* in the sense of "going," the suffix *iyan* is applied by way of transposition (vyatyaya), with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), the triplet beginning with “*svādoritthā viṣuvataḥ*” is the optional *stotriya* for the Acchāvāka priest.
This is prescribed in the section titled “Of the Hotṛ-priests” (*hotrāṇām*) in the Sūtra: “*yaḥ sannāhā vicarṣaṇiḥ svādoritthā viṣuvataḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
Furthermore, on the fifth day of the *pṛṣṭha* period, this same triplet serves as the *anurūpa* for the *niṣkevalya* chant.
In the section beginning with “*stome vardhamāne*,” it is sūtra-ed: “*svādoritthā viṣuvata upa no haribhiḥ sutam*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).
From this very central place, the tawny cows drink of the sweet mead;
they who, together with the bull Indra, rejoice in the exhilarating draught, beautiful in their own sovereignty over wealth.
The Gaurī cows drink of this sweet, level-flowing honeyed draught; they who, moving together with the bull Indra, rejoice for the sake of splendor—rich ones, according to their own sovereignty. 10.
Of the sweet, of that which has become most sweet, endowed with flavor—thus, in this manner, of the *madhu* (sweet Soma) which is pervasively present in all sacrifices;
[here the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative because the Soma is the recipient of the action, according to the rule] "the mention of the object must be made.

Such Soma as this the *gaurīs* (the cows of golden hue) drink—those cows who, moving together (*sayāvarīḥ*) for the sake of beauty (*śobhase*), rejoice (*madanti*) in the company of *vṛṣṇā* (Indra), the showerer of desires.

The meaning is that they drink the remnant of the Soma drunk by Indra. Being "excellent" (vasvīḥ) because they provide milk, those cows remain directed toward the sovereignty (svarājyam)—that is, the kingship or state of ruling—of their own Indra; this is the sense.
Regarding *viṣuvataḥ*:
from the root *viṣ* in the sense of "pervasion," the suffix *ku* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
Then follows the suffix *matup*.
By the rule “*hrasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup*,” the *matup* is acute-accented (*udātta*).
By the rule “*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*,” there is a long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the *saṃhitā* [text].
By metrical transposition (vyatyaya), there is the substitution of *v* for *m* in the suffix *mat*. Thus, *madhvaḥ*.

Regarding the form *madhvaḥ*, since it is stated that "in the Veda, the rule may optionally apply to bases ending in *jasa* and so forth," the guna substitution prescribed by the rule *gher ḍiti* does not occur, and instead the *yaṇ* substitution takes place.
[Gau]ryaḥ: the suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *pidgaurādibhyaśca*.
In the nominative plural (*jasi*), when the *yaṇ*-substitution occurs, the following unaccented vowel becomes *svarita* by the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*.
*sayāvarīḥ* [is derived from] *yā* in the sense of "going" (*prāpaṇe*). [The suffix] *vanip* is applied according to the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*.
The suffixes *ṅīp* and *vibhakti* [are applied] by the rule "vano ra ca. They rejoice (*madanti*). [The root] *madī* means "to rejoice."
In this *prāsa* (verse), there is a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*) regarding the suffix *śap*. [The word] *vasvīḥ* [is derived from the root] *vasa nivāse* ("to dwell").
In the word *śvasvastihi*, the suffix *u* is applied to the root *vas* by the rule *śvasvastihi*;
because the phrase *dhānye nita* is understood [from the preceding sūtra], there is lengthening of the vowel.
1. This occurs in the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*).
2. The technical term *kṣa* [is used here]. According to Pāṇini 6.2.66, it has the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).

In the rule "after a word expressing a quality" (*voto guṇavacanāt*), because of the statement "after a word expressing a quality, [the suffix] *ṅīp* is added for the sake of the initial udātta accent" (*kā. 4.1.44.1*), the *ṅīp* suffix is applied after the word *ṅamu*, resulting in the *yaṇ* substitution.
In the case of the *jas* ending, there is the long vowel of the same class as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) according to the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*).
One's own kingdom is *svarājyam*.
By the rule "akarmadhāraye rājyam" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.130), there is acute accent on the first syllable of the final member [of the compound].
Longing for him, these dappled cows mix the Soma;
Indra’s dear milch-cows impel his thunderbolt, the missile, toward his excellent self-rule.
The dappled cows, longing for him, mix the Soma; the beloved milch-cows of Indra send forth his thunderbolt, the missile, according to their own excellent sovereignty. 11.
The dappled cows of various colors, longing for contact—that is, desiring to touch him—of that aforementioned Indra, who yearns for contact, mix the *soma* to be drunk by Indra with milk.
Indra, unassailable, struck down ninety-nine Vṛtras with the bones of Dadhyañc. (13) Indra; with the bones of Dadhyañc; the Vṛtras; unassailable; he struck down; ninety-nine. (13)
Regarding this, the followers of the Śāṭyāyana school relate a historical narrative: "By the sight of the living Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, the Asuras were utterly defeated.
Then, when he had departed for heaven, the earth became filled with Asuras.
Indra, being unable to wage war against those Asuras, heard that the seer had gone to heaven while searching for him."
Then he asked those present there, "Is there any remaining limb of his here?
They said to him, "This is his tenth head, with which he taught the Madhu-vidyā to the two Ādibhyas;
however, we do not know where it is."
Again Indra said,
"Search for that.
They searched for it.
Having investigated it at Śaryaṇāvat, they abandoned it;
for there is a lake named Śaryaṇāvat, the swift-flowing boundary of Kurukṣetra. With the bones from its head, Indra struck down the Asuras.

"Unopposed"— meaning unresounded by others and free from discordant sounds— "Indra," with "the bones" of the seer named Dadhīca, the son of Atharvan— specifically the bones belonging to the horse's head— "nine times ninety," that is, nine hundred and eighty-one. For instance,
in order to conquer the gods residing in the three worlds, the illusory power (*māyā*) of the Asuras first becomes threefold.
The threefold [division] occurs through the distinction of the past, future, and present times; furthermore, in order to conquer the gods existing at those times, each is again multiplied by three.
Thus, nine are obtained.
Again, when there is a threefold division in the form of the three powers of enthusiasm (*utsāha*) and so forth, twenty-seven are obtained.
Furthermore, when the three qualities (guṇas) are distinguished according to their threefold nature—sattva and so forth—the total number becomes eighty-one.

Thus, when the tripled māyā is situated in each of the ten directions by means of these four [factors], nine nineties (810) are produced. He "struck down" (jaghāna)—that is, killed—the "Vṛtras," meaning the obstructing classes of Asuras, which are of such a nature as this māyā.
Dadhīca: from *dadhi* (curd) and the root *añj* (to anoint), [the form] *dadhy-añc*. By the rule beginning with "ṛtvig" etc., the suffix *kvin* is applied after the root *akṣ*.
By the rule "aniditām," there is the elision of the *n*.
In the singular case-ending (*ekavacana*), after the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "acaḥ," lengthening occurs by the rule "cau.

When the rule for the accent of the disappearance of an acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*) would have resulted in the acute accent on *viśvasya*, that is set aside; and although the rule "cau" would have resulted in the final acute of the preceding member, that too is superseded by the further prescription of the acute accent on the case-ending (*vibhaktyudātta*) in the rule "agner chandasy asarvanāmasthānam" (Pāṇini 6.1.170).
By [the rule] *asthabhiḥ*;
according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 7.1.76, *chandasy api dṛśyate*, the substitution of *anaḍ* for the word *asthi* occurs even before vowels other than *a* and so forth, and that [substitute] is udātta.
Seeking the horse’s head which was hidden among the mountains, he found it at Śaryaṇāvat. 14. Seeking; the horse’s; which; head; among the mountains; hidden; that; he found; at Śaryaṇāvat. 14.
Indra, seeking the head of Dadhyañc—which belonged to a horse and was hidden, having gone away and remained concealed, among the mountains and hills—found it at the lake named Śaryaṇāvat.
Having found it, he brought it back and, with his bones, struck down the Vṛtras; such is the connection with the preceding ṛc.
Desiring; from the root *iṣ* in the sense of "desire.
Because it belongs to the *tudadi* class, the suffix *śa* is applied.
*vidat*: in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense of the root *vid*, there is the substitution of *aṭ* for *cli* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). *Śaryaṇāvati*.
The regions named Śaryaṇā have a lake situated not far from them called Śaryaṇāvat.
Because the word *śaryaṇa* is listed among the *madhu* group, the suffix *matup* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 4.2.86 (*madhvādibhyaśca*), yielding the fourfold derivative meaning.
In the word *saṃjñāyām*, the *m* of the suffix *matup* becomes *v*.
The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *matau bahvo'najirādīnām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.119).

1. That [sacrifice] is of three kinds: with *kṣa*, with *ṭa*, and with *ḍha*. 2. They are accomplished with *kṣa*. 3. They are not accomplished with *na-kṣa*. 4. They are accomplished with *kṣa*. 5. In that which is designated by this [term], when the final one-day rite is to be performed by one who is extremely emaciated, one month must first be sacrificed with two Maurya and Cāndramasī *iṣṭi*s. Among those, the Cāndramasī *iṣṭi* takes place during the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Regarding this, the verse “atrāha gauh” is the *anuvākyā* for the principal [offering].
This is prescribed in the section beginning with “atimūrtenā” in the Sūtra: “atrāha goramanvat navonavo bhavati jāyamānaḥ” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.8).
Here, indeed, is the secret name of Tvaṣṭṛ, Gauramanda;
thus [it is] in the house of the moon.
Here he spoke: "The name of Tvaṣṭṛ’s bull was hidden; thus it is in the dwelling of the moon. (15)

1. Here it is said: in this very house—the orb of the moon, which is the traveler of the sky—there is the secret (*apīcya*) light belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, the radiant Āditya, which is his own name that is hidden during the night. The rays of Āditya perceived (*amanvat*) it in this manner (*itthā*). The meaning is that the rays of the sun reflect in the clear, water-like lunar disc;
there, the rays, having been reflected, receive the same designation in the moon as they do in the sun.
This is what is meant:
during the new moon night, the solar light, having vanished, enters that lunar orb and, like fire, dispels the darkness and illuminates everything.
And the Sun, joined with such elemental light, is indeed Indra himself, because he is counted as one of the twelve [Adityas], and the Moon is likewise included therein.

Therefore, since Indra alone is perceived as the illuminator of day and night through this praise of Indra, it is established that Indra is the deity. Furthermore, because the moon is intended to be the primary locus for this manifested light, its application to the Cāndramasī sacrifice is also justified.
Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "Moreover, one of its rays shines toward the moon; by this it should be understood that its illumination comes from the sun."
“Supuṣṇa, Sūryaśmi, and Candramas are also Gandharvas,” so says a Vedic text (nigama).
He too is called *go*.

Regarding this, it is said: “The *go* followed after” (Nirukta 2.6), and “In this matter, the rays of the sun agreed upon the name of the *go*—the secret, the diminished, the departed, the covered, or the hidden” (Nirukta 4.25).
They understood; "manu" means "to perceive.
It is secret (apīcyam).
The suffix *yat* is applied to the root *ci* preceded by *apa*, according to the rule *adyādayaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.551), which prescribes it as a *nipāta*.
For this very reason, the desired form is established.
Alternatively:
From the root *añj* preceded by the prefix *apa*, the suffix *kin* is applied according to the rule “*ṛtvig-ādi*” (Pāṇini 3.2.59).
By the rule “*aniditām-āmaḥ-ṅiti*” (Pāṇini 6.4.24), there is elision of the nasal (*n*). That which exists in what has gone away or departed is called *apīcyam*.
The form "bhave" arises from the rule "chandasi" (in Vedic usage);
by the rule "acaḥ" (elision of a vowel), there is the elision of the letter *a*;
and by the rule "cau" (when *au* follows), there is lengthening.
The *svarita* accent.
Bhaṭṭabhāskaramiśra [explains] that *apīcyaḥ* means "not manifest. *Itthā*.
From the word *idam*. In the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*), the suffix *thā* is applied according to the rule *thā hetau ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.26).
If the word *idam* does not recur there [in that rule], then the suffix *thamu* is applied according to the rule *idamasthamuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.24).

In the word *candramasaḥ*, the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule *anyārāditarartedikchabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte* (2.3.29) is set aside, and the substitution of *-ḍā* (which becomes *-as*) is applied by the rule *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇāccheyāḍāḍyāyājālaḥ* (7.1.39).
[The term] *candramāḥ* means that which produces (*nirmāti* or *nirmimīte*) the delight (*āhlādanam*) of the moon (*candra-*). Thus, it is called *candramāḥ*.
The suffix *asi* is applied by the rule *‘candre māṅo ḍin’* (Uṇādisūtra 4.667).
Because the word is listed among the *dāsībhāra* group, it retains the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound.
Furthermore, the first member ends in the suffix *sva*, which, according to the rule *‘sphāyitañci’* etc., is udātta on its final syllable.
In the Sarvapṛṣṭhā sacrifice, for the body as the oblation, the two verses beginning with “Who today” (*ko adya*) are the invitatory and offering verses (*yājyānuvākye*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “The tenth [offering] is for Kāya; ‘Who today yokes the oxen to the pole of Order’—these two [verses]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.12).

1. *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ḍha*, *na*, *ta*, *da*—these are the rays of the Sun. 2. After *ta* and *śa*, when preceded by *api*. 3. After *ca* and *pha*, when *apa* has departed. 4. After *kṣa*, *ca*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *ḍha*, and *pha*, when they have emerged. 5. *kṣa* does not follow *na*. Who today yokes to the pole of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*) the vigorous, impetuous, and fiercely striking oxen?
Those who strike with their jaws, who are sources of bliss, and whose service one must heed to live.

Who today yokes to the pole the vigorous, impetuous, and difficult-to-restrain bulls of Order—those who reach the mouth, who flow within the heart, and who bring delight? Only he who fulfills their service shall live. (16)

Today, in this ritual, who indeed can yoke—that is, who is able to harness—the swift-moving horses at the pole (dhuri) of Indra’s chariot? The meaning is: no one at all. Of what sort are they? They are *śimīvataḥ*, desiring heroic deeds; *bhāminaḥ*, endowed with brilliance; and *durhaṇāyūn*, possessed of an anger difficult for others to withstand.
The root *haṇīyati* means "to be angry" (*kupyati*).
Regarding the verse: "When Indra, the bestower of favor upon those who sit near him, has arrived, who flees—fearing the enemy? Who goes forth?"—the meaning is: "No one at all."
"Who is tormented? Who is harmed?"—the meaning is that there is no one, even one vulnerable to enemies, who is harmed.
"Who, the sacrificer, is afraid?"—since Indra is his protector, fear does not arise; far removed from him is any injury caused by an enemy.
"Who is the man who knows—that is, who perceives—Indra, who is near, close at hand, and acting as our protector?
The meaning is: we alone know him, no one else. The word *ekaḥ* means 'one' (or 'only')."

When Indra arrived to provide assistance in battle, [the question arose]: "Which sacrificer would speak *adhibravat* for his offspring—that is, for his son? Such an *adhivacana*, or partisan speech, takes the form: 'O Indra, protect our son,' just as in the expression, 'one should speak *adhibrūyāt* to a Brāhmaṇa.'"
Who would offer such a designation?
The sense is that Indra himself protects it.
Who would speak out against "ibhāya," meaning for the elephant?
"Furthermore, who would offer protection for wealth being carried off by enemies?
That is to say, what sacrificer would even utter the words, 'Protect our wealth that is being stolen'?
The meaning is: no one at all."
Moreover, who would provide protection for one's own body, for one's people, or for one's retinue?
For the sake of protecting his own body and his retinue, Indra does not require an invocation.
The meaning is that Indra, being pleased by the hymn of praise, protects them himself.

But when there is an application to a ritual act related to Prajāpati—who is the referent of the word *ka*—then, through connection with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), Prajāpati himself is denoted by the word *indra*.

This is just as, according to the application "one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī [verse]," the Indra present in the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "kadā cana" is interpreted as referring to the Gārhapatya fire; so it is here.
[The root] *īṣ* [is used].
The root *īp* is used in the senses of moving, injuring, seeing, and desiring;
it belongs to the Bhūvādigaṇa and is conjugated in the Ātmanepada.
[Example: *tujyate*.
In the root *hiṃs* (meaning "to injure"), the suffix *yak* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Because the root is taught with a short *a* vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the *lasārvadhātuka* affixes are unaccented; thus, the accent remains solely on the *yak*.
Due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) expressed by "not *tiṅ*," there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent). In "maṃsate," the augment *aṭ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood.
In the expression *sibbahula leṭi*, there is the suffix *sip*; [in the form] *anti*, there is the elision of *k* according to the rule *kādilopo bahulam*.
*bravat*: from the root *brū*, in the *leṭ* mood with the augment *aṭ*.
For the sake of the body (*tanve*).

From the word *tanu* in the dative singular, by the rule "In the Vedic language, there is optionally [the substitution of] *ajaS* etc.," and by the absence of the *guṇa* substitution according to the rule "For a *ghi* stem before a suffix beginning with *ḍi*," the *yaṇ* substitution (*u*) occurs.
By the rule "The *yaṇ* following an udātta or svarita vowel becomes svarita," the case-ending receives the svarita accent.
Who shall worship Agni with an oblation of clarified butter, sacrificing with the ladle according to the fixed seasons?
To whom shall the gods bring the swift oblation? Who will consider himself a welcome host for the sacrifice?

Ka? [I am Ka. I praise Agni with oblation and ghee; with the ladle, let him sacrifice according to the fixed seasons. To whom shall the gods swiftly bring the offering? Who will consider himself the master of the sacrifice? ||18||
The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) "invokes" (*īṭṭe*) Agni for the sake of Indra, praising Agni after having prepared the oblation (*havis*). Yet,
even the preparation of the oblation for Indra cannot be accomplished,
because Indra is difficult to discern.

Or who indeed would sacrifice with the *sruva* and *juhū* ladles into the fire for the sake of Indra’s sacrifice, using clarified butter as the oblation during the fixed and eternal seasons, characterized by the times such as spring and so forth?
Or rather,
the seasons (*ṛtavaḥ*) are the deities of the *prayāja* offerings.
According to the Śruti text, "The *prayāja*s are indeed the seasons" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.6.11.5),

one should worship the deity Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt with clarified butter as the oblation along with those fixed, faultless seasons— which are to be performed in both the archetypal (*prakṛti*) and modified (*vikṛti*) rites.
The meaning is that there is no exception whatsoever.
"To what sacrificer (*yajamāna*) do the gods bring—*ā vahanti*, that is, they bestow—the praiseworthy wealth quickly and swiftly? To no one at all; this is the meaning.
Indra alone is the giver of wealth, not other gods; thus Indra is praised."

‘Vītihotra’ means one who has attained the sacrifice; ‘Sudeva’ means one who possesses auspicious deities. What kind of sacrificer ‘bhansate’—that is, knows Indra correctly? The meaning is: no one at all.
The intended sense is that Indra becomes manifest through manifold praise and long-term worship, and not by any other means.
‘īḍe’.
[The root] ‘īḍ’ [is used] in the sense of praising.
Due to its belonging to the adādi class, there is elision (luk) of the śap suffix.
In *sucā*,
the acute accent of the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. [The form] *yajātai* [is derived similarly].
In the *leṭ* [augment] after *yajati*, there is the augment *aṭ*. According to the rule "vaito'nyatra" (Pāṇini 3.4.96), [the substitution of *ai* for *e* occurs];
however, the phrase "and in the case of modification" (*vikṛtau ca*) does not appear in the manuscripts marked kṣa, ṭa, ḍha, na, and sa.
2. kṣa is to be offered as an oblation;
3. kṣa-ḍha-ḍha is indeed Indra himself.

The word *aikāraḥ* [is derived as follows]: from the root *vah* (to carry), in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, there is the augment *āṭ*; by the rule "itaśca lopaḥ," the *ikāra* is elided; and by the rule "saṃyogāntasya," the *takāra* is elided. *Homa*: From the root *hū* (to sacrifice), the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "āto manin" (Pāṇini 3.2.74). While the term *hraḥ* is being carried over, the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 6.1.34). Alternatively, the word *homa* ending in the suffix *manin* is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) according to the list beginning with "nāmansīman" (Uṇādisūtra 4.590). *Maṃste*: From the root *man* (to know/think), in the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *āṭ*; the suffix *sip* is added by the rule "sibbahulaṃ leṭi" (Pāṇini 3.1.34). *Vītihotraḥ*: From the root *vī* (in the sense of motion, etc.), the suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule "mantre vṛṣa... (Pāṇini 3.2.71); this suffix is acute-accented (*udātta*). *Hotram* means sacrifice (*homa*); the suffix *van* is applied by the rule "huyāmāśubhasibhyaśvan" (Uṇādisūtra 4.607). *Vītiḥ* means that by whom the sacrifice is attained. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member remains. *Sudevaḥ*: By the rule "nañsubhyām" (Pāṇini 6.2.172), the final syllable of the second member takes the acute accent.
O most powerful god, you indeed shall praise the mortal;
O Maghavan, there is no other besides you who is a comforter, O Indra—I speak these words to you.
O Lord, most powerful one, you indeed have praised the mortal;
O Maghavan, there is no other comforter besides you. Indra, I speak these words to you. 19.

*Aṅga*: an exclamation used for addressing. O *śaviṣṭha*, most powerful Indra, you who are radiant (*deva*), you have praised (*pra śaṃsipaḥ*) the mortal (*martya*)—the person who has offered praise to you. By this [praise], you have commended him, thinking, "He has praised me. O *maghavan*, possessor of wealth, Indra, there is no one other than you (*tvad anyaḥ*) who is a *marditā*, a comforter. For that reason, I speak (*bravīmi*) these words characterized by praise to you; I utter them. *Śaṃsipaḥ*: from the root *śaṃsu* (to praise). In the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood with the suffix *sip*, there is the augment *āṭ*. By the rule "the suffix *sip* is frequent in the *leṭ*," the *vikaraṇa* suffix *mip* is applied. Because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the augment *iṭ* is added. *Śaviṣṭha*: "Most powerful" (*śaviṣṭhaḥ*). From *śavas* with the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*. By the rule "elision of *vin* and *mat*," the suffix is elided. By the rule "elision of *ṭi*," the final vowel is dropped. *Marditā*: from the root *mṛḍ* (to comfort). The suffix *tṛc* is applied, and the augment *iṭ* is added.
O Vasu, let not your bounties nor your protections ever fail us;
O Manu’s son, bestow upon us all human riches from every side.
May your bounties and your aids, O Vasu, never fail us at any time. And, O Manava, bestow upon us all riches from among the human tribes.

O Vāsu, may those riches belonging to you, O Indra—those which are called *rādhas* because they are things that have come to us—never at any time (*kadā cana*) deceive us; that is, may they not destroy us.
Likewise, may your aids (*ūtayaḥ*), which go toward us, [protect us].
Or else:
In the word *dhṛtayaḥ*, there is an elision of a syllable (*varṇalopa*).
Let those *dhṛtayaḥ*—the shakers, your Maruts—not harm us.

O Indra, who art beneficial to men (*mānuṣa*), bestow upon us, the seers of the mantras (*carṣaṇibhyaḥ*), all (*viśvā*) riches (*vasūni*) from every side; having brought them together, place them near us.
The meaning is: "Grant us wealth that exists everywhere."

When [is it used]? From the word *kim*, the suffix *dā* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.15 (*sarvaikānyakiyattadaḥ kāle dā*), and the substitution of *ka-* for *kim-* occurs according to Pāṇini 7.2.103 (*kimaḥ kaḥ*). Thus, *kadā*.

The initial udātta accent occurs due to a grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*). 1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-ūtayaḥ*. *Dabhan*: from the root *dambhu* (to deceive). In the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*), the *laṭ* (present) ending is used by Vedic license; the suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is elided by the rule "variously in the Veda" (*bahulam chandasi*). The augment *aṭ* is absent due to the rule "not when there is connection with *māṅ*" (*na māṅyoge*). *Mimīhi*: from the root *māṅ* (to measure and to sound). The Parasmaipada ending occurs by transposition. Because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is reduplication (*ślu*). By the rule "of *bhṛj* etc.," the vowel of the reduplication is shortened. Due to the doubling of the *hi* suffix, the *ī* substitution occurs by the rule "of *ghu*, *mā*, and *sthā*" (*ghumāsthā*). || 8 || 13 ||
In the fourteenth anuvāka, there are nine hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "pra ye," is the ṛṣi-seer Gotama's;
its fifth and twelfth verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The remaining verses are in the Jagatī meter;
the Maruts are the deity. Thus it has been enumerated: "Pra ye [dvādaśa], the Māruta [sūkta]—the fifth ends in a Triṣṭubh."
Due to the use of the word "ha," these four hymns beginning with "vidam" have the Maruts as their deity.
On the fourth day of the Abhilava-ṣaḍaha, this hymn is to be recited in the Āgnimāruta-śastra as the Māruta-vinirvidvānīya.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "‘pra ye śubhante janasya gopāḥ’ is the Āgnimāruta [śastra]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.7).

They who shine forth like wives, like coursers on their way—the sons of Udra, doers of wondrous deeds—for the Maruts have indeed made heaven and earth grow; these bold heroes rejoice in the assemblies.

They who shine forth like wives, like coursers on their way—the sons of Rudra, doers of wondrous deeds—for the Maruts have indeed caused heaven and earth to increase; these heroes, impetuous in the assemblies, rejoice.

Those Maruts who, when the "yāman"—that is, the journey or movement serving as the occasion—takes place, "pra śubhante," meaning they adorn their own limbs with excellence, like "janayaḥ," that is, like wives; just as women adorn their own limbs, so do they. What kind of Maruts? "Saptayaḥ," those whose nature is to glide; "sūnavaḥ" (sons) of Rudra. Rudra is the Supreme Lord, so called because he makes all weep at the time of universal dissolution. They are his sons. "Sudaṃsasaḥ," those of beautiful deeds. He establishes this very point: for the Maruts "cakrire" (have made) "rodasī" (the two worlds, heaven and earth) "vṛdhe," for the sake of increase through providing growth and so forth. Therefore, they are of beautiful deeds. "Vīrāḥ," those whose nature is especially to cast down enemies; "ghṛṣvayaḥ," those whose nature is to crush; meaning they are breakers of trees, mountains, and the like. Being such, those Maruts "madanti" (rejoice) in the "vidatheṣu. Vidathas are sacrifices, so called because the gods are to be worshipped therein. In them, they rejoice by drinking Soma. *Śubhante*: from the root *śubha* (to shine), belonging to the *Bhvādi* class. *Janayaḥ*: from the root *jan* (to be born); "janayas" are wives, so called because offspring are born (*jāyante*) in them. The suffix *in* is added according to the rule *insarvadhātubhyaḥ*. *Yāman*: from the root *yā* (to go). By the rule *kṛñyalyuṭo bahulam*, due to the word "bahulam," the suffix *manin* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) according to *āto manin*. The locative case ending is elided by *supāṃ suluk*. *Sudaṃsasaḥ*: *daṃsaḥ* is a name for action. Those whose action (*daṃsaḥ*) is beautiful (*śobhanaṃ*). The acute accent on the final syllable of the compound follows the rule *sormanyau alopoyasī*. *Cakrire*: the prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent applies by the rule *hi ca*. *Vṛdhe*: from the root *vṛdh* (to grow). The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the *saṃpadādi* group. The acute accent of the case-ending follows *sāvekācaḥ*. *Madanti*: from the root *mad* (to rejoice). Where *ini* was expected, there is a substitution (*vyatyaya*) of *śap*. There is no *nighāta* because it begins a new quarter-verse (*pāda*). *Vidatheṣu*: from the root *vid* (to know). The suffix *athan* is applied according to *rivibhyāṃ kit*. *Ghṛṣvayaḥ*: from the root *ghṛṣu* (to rub/scratch). It is an irregular form (*nipātana*) ending in the suffix *vin* according to the rule *kṛvighṛṣvi*.
1. O Kṣas, you adorn yourselves.
2. O Kṣas and Ḍhas, you are skilled in hurling away enemies. Having grown strong, they have attained greatness; the Rudras have established their dwelling in heaven.
Worshipping the Sun and generating vital power, those whose mother is Pṛśni have assumed glorious splendor.

Having grown strong, they have attained greatness; the Rudras have established their seat in heaven. Singing their hymn and generating power, those whose mother is Pṛśni have clothed themselves in splendor.

Those Maruts, distinguished by the qualities previously mentioned, having been sprinkled (ukṣitāsaḥ) by the gods—that is, consecrated—attained (āśata), that is, reached, greatness (mahimānam), which is their majesty.
They are the Rudras, the sons of Rudra;
the word "progenitor" (janaka) is used figuratively for the offspring (janya).
Those Maruts, the sons of Rudra, established for themselves a seat—a dwelling place—in the sky that shone in the heavens, making it preeminent and most excellent.

Praising Arka, the one worthy of worship, namely Indra, they honored him while generating *indriya*—the characteristic mark or heroic power of Indra—producing it through such utterances as, "Strike, O Blessed One! Slay! Be valiant! (Ai. Brā. 3.20).

The Maruts, sons of Pṛśni—the earth whose form is variegated—have assumed their splendors; they have established their sovereign powers (aiśvaryāṇi) with preeminence. They are "ukṣitāsaḥ" [sprinkled/nourished], from the root *ukṣ* meaning "to sprinkle."
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
[In the case of the word *mahi*,] *asuk* is substituted for the *ājas* ending.
[Thus one forms the word] *mahimānam*.
From the word *mahat*, the suffix *iman* is applied according to the rule for *pṛthu* and others;
by the rule *ṭeḥ*, there is elision of the final syllable (*ṭi*); thus, *māhiman*.
It pervaded.
In the sense of pervading (*vyāpti*), the suffix *laṅ* is used; by the rule "there is frequent elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) in the Veda," the suffix is elided,
resulting in *indriyam*.
The word *indriya* is derived as a form ending in the suffix *ghañ*, being a nipātana (irregular formation) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.93: *indraliṅgam indradṛṣṭam*.
[The term] *pṛśnimātaraḥ* [refers to those whose mother is the earth], for the earth (*bhūmi*) is called *pṛśni* because she brings forth (*prāśrute*) all forms.
And it is heard [in scripture]: "This indeed is Pṛśni" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.4.1.5).
In such cases as *pṛśniḥ* and *pṛśniḥ*, the desired form is established through grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). Those whose mother is Pṛśni are thus described.
By the rule *kṛtaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.4.158), there is a prohibition of the compound-final suffix *kap*.
When the cow-mothers beautify themselves with ointments, they assume splendor and radiant luster upon their bodies;
they drive away every adversary, and along their paths, clarified butter flows.
The cow-mothers, who shine with their ornaments, have assumed splendor upon their bodies; they are radiant and drive away every adversary. Ghee flows along their paths.

The Maruts, whose mother is the Earth in the form of a cow (*gomātaraḥ*), when they adorn themselves—making their own limbs beautiful with *añjibhiḥ*, ornaments that manifest their forms—then those radiant Maruts wear upon their own bodies (*tanuṣu*) ornaments that shine forth intensely (*virukmataḥ*).
Furthermore, they drive away and destroy every hostile enemy (*viśvam abhimātinam*).
Following the paths (*vartmāni*) of these Maruts, the flowing water (*ghṛtam*) pours forth.
The meaning is that wherever the Maruts go, the rainwater also goes there, following after them.
They beautify themselves.
Because a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific designation (saṃjñā) is not invariably obligatory, there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate short vowel (*laghūpadha*).
[The word is] *añjibhiḥ*.
The root *añj* is used in the senses of manifestation (*vyakti*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), beauty (*kānti*), and movement (*gati*).
By the rule *khanika-pikasyasi-visadhi-vāni-stani-vani-sanni-granthi-caribhyaś-ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.579), the suffix *ip* is applied [to form *añji*]. Thus, they are auspicious (*śubhāḥ*).
In the sense of "shining beautifully," the suffix *rak* is applied by the rule beginning with *sphāyitañci*, etc.; hence,
*virukamataḥ*.
*Viśiṣṭā* (distinguished) *ruk* (light) is *viruk*. That which ends in this is *virukamant*.
In the formation of the possessive suffix *matup*, there is the substitution of *k* for *r* because the word is treated as a *pada* according to the rule beginning with *ayasmaya*.
You are one who has conquered his breath.
He flows. [The root] *rīṅ* means "to flow."
It belongs to the *daivātiga* class.
1. Attaining the sounds *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ḍha*.
2. The desired forms and vowels of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ḍha* are not established.
(Verse 67)
Those who, well-skilled in sacrifice, together with the seers, cause even the unshakable things to tremble by their might—
when you Maruts, the bulls and protectors, have harnessed the horses swift as thought to your chariots and yoked your backs.

When the Maruts, the performers of fair sacrifices, together with the seers, exert themselves with their power, shaking even the immovable things; when you, O bulls, have yoked to your chariots your mind-swift and rain-showering flanks.

"Sumakhāsaḥ" means those of beautiful sacrifices. Those Maruts who shine forth—that is, who especially blaze—with their weapons (the ṛṣis) [or, with their ṛṣi-like weapons], those Maruts, by their own power (*ojas*), cause even the immovable—that is, even firm things such as mountains which are impossible to shake—to be shaken; they are the pre-eminent shakers and impellers.
The second half-verse is addressed in the direct style (*pratyakṣakṛta*).

O Maruts, swift as thought, whose speed is as impetuous as the mind, you who are protectors of the bull and consist of hosts capable of pouring down rainwater— when you harnessed to your own chariots the *pṛṣtis*,
which are the spotted deer (the name *pṛṣtis* being a designation for the vehicles of the Maruts, as stated in Nirukta 1.15.6),
and when you joined them with white spots (*pṛṣat*), you directed them toward us.
The meaning is that at that time, the mountains and so forth fall away.

Regarding *sumakhāsaḥ*: since all rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), when the rule *nam-subhyām* does not apply, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Acyutāḥ; the elision of the *śi* case-ending occurs frequently in the Vedic language (*śeṣ chandasi bahulam*). Manojuvaḥ.
The root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "to go.
By the rule *kvaci* etc., the suffix *kvi* is applied and the vowel is lengthened.
[The result is] *ayugdhvam*.
The root *yuj* is used in the sense of "joining.
In the *luṅ* tense, there is the elision of the *s* by the rule *dhi ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.25).
When you have harnessed your flanks to the chariots, O Maruts, speeding the pressing-stone for the sake of booty, then the streams of the ruddy one burst forth;
with their waters they moisten the dry land like a hide.

When you have yoked the flanks to the chariot-poles, O Maruts, speeding the stone in the contest for booty; then the streams of the ruddy one burst forth, and they drench the broad earth with water as if with a hide.
O Maruts, when you have harnessed your flanks to the chariot-poles—
what were you doing?— when the prize of food (*vāja*) was the occasion, you were impelling the cloud (*adri*), driving it forth for the sake of rain.
And then, from the presence of the ruddy, shining sun, as if from lightning itself, the streams of rain-water come forth; they burst open and release themselves.

Once released, those streams, like a leather hide limited [in size], thoroughly moisten the entire earth with their waters—just as a leather hide is soaked without effort—and they cause it to become especially wet, speeding along.
*raha* means "to go";
*viṣyanti* [is derived from] *vi*; *pa* [is used] in the sense of an intermediate action (*antarkarman*).
It belongs to the *daivādika* class.
By the rule *otaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.71), there is the elision of the vowel *o*.
By the rule *upasargāt sunoti*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.
By [the rule] beginning with *padan*, there is the substitution of *ud* for the word *udaka*.
They moisten (*vyundanti*).
The root *undī* means "to moisten.
[In the word *bhūmyām*: by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the suffix *am* following the word *bhūmi* is replaced by *ḍā*.
The shortening [of the vowel] is a Vedic (chāndasa) phenomenon.
At the third pressing, "ā vo vahantu" is the standing *yājyā* of the *potr̥*.
And it is stated in the *Mūdhita*: "ā vo vahantu saptayo raghuṣyado 'meva naḥ suhavā ā hi gantana" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.5).
1. In the chariot of *kṣa*. 2. The streams of *kṣa-ṭa-ḍha-vṛṣapuka*. 3. The strength of *kṣa-pīrāmibala*. 4. *Kṣa-ṭa-ḍha-sa* makes them moist.
May your swift-gliding, rapid-horsed steeds carry you hither; come forward with your arms. Sit down upon the sacrificial grass;
a wide seat has been prepared for you. O Maruts, being quick, rejoice in the soma-juice.

May your steeds, swift-gliding and fleet-footed, carry you hither. Come forth with your arms; sit down upon the sacred grass. A wide seat has been prepared for you. O Maruts, exhilarate yourselves quickly with the soma-juice.
O Maruts, let your coursers—horses characterized by their habit of gliding—bring you hither; that is, let them convey you to our sacrifice.
Of what nature are these coursers? They are *raghuṣyadaḥ*, flowing swiftly and rapidly.
The meaning is "going with speed.
O you who fly swiftly and lightly among the *raghus*, having brought back the wealth to be given to us with your own arms—your hands—go forth pre-eminently!
O Maruts, your seat—the place characterized by the altar—has been made wide and spacious.
In that regard, when the sacrificial grass (barhis) has been spread, sit down upon that grass;
having sat down, drink quickly and exhilarate yourselves with the drinking of this swift food, namely the Soma characterized as such; be satisfied.
*raghuṣyadaḥ*. They flow swiftly (*raghu*)—thus they are *raghuṣyadaḥ*. [The root] *syanda* means "to flow" (*prastravaṇe*).

The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule “*kvip ca*”. There is elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule “*aniditām*”. The original accent of the final member of the compound (*kud-uttarapada-prakṛti-svaratvam*) applies.
*raghuṣvavānaḥ*: [The root] *patu* means "to go"; the suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well. [Thus:
*jigāta*.
The root *gā* is used in the sense of "praising" (*stuti*),
belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class.
However, because it is listed among the verbs meaning "motion" (*gati*) in [the list] beginning with *jigāti* (Nirukta 2.14.113), it has the sense of "going" (*gati*) here.
In the case of the plural form of the stem *lopman*, the substitution of *ta* for the suffix is prescribed by the rule “*tasan-asan-athanāś-ca*”.

Because that [suffix] is marked with *p* (indicating it is not *ṅit*), it lacks the status of being *ṅit*; consequently, there is no application of the rule “*ī halyaghoḥ*”, and thus the substitution of *ī* does not occur. The form is *sadaḥ*.
In the word *kukami*, the *visarjanīya* is changed to *s* according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.3.46 (*ataḥ kukami*).
[Thus: *mādayadhvam*. [The root] *mad* is used in the sense of "satiation."
The *cur*-class [of roots] takes the *ātmanepada* endings.
By them they grew strong in their own might; through their greatness they ascended to the firmament and made for themselves a wide dwelling.
When Viṣṇu had increased the exhilarating, intoxicating draught, they sat down upon the dear sacrificial grass like birds.

They grew strong by their own power and majesty; they ascended to the firmament and made for themselves a wide dwelling, when Viṣṇu protected the exhilarating, intoxicating strength. Like birds, they settled upon the dear sacrificial grass.
Those Maruts grew; they attained increase. Of what sort were they? They were *svatavas*, possessing strength inherent to themselves.
They do not depend on the strength of anyone else.
Having attained growth, they have taken their stand upon the firmament (nāka), that is, heaven, by means of their majesty, greatness, and vastness;
and they have made for themselves a wide, spacious dwelling-place (sadas), a seat characterized by the sky, as their own abode.

For the sake of which Maruts—for whom—Viṣṇu indeed protected the sacrifice, which was rain-bestowing (*vṛṣaṇam*), satisfying desires, and distilling exhilaration (*madacyutam*), that is, the shedder of joy; Viṣṇu himself having come, guards them. Those Maruts, like birds (*vayaḥ*) swiftly arriving, having arrived quickly, may they sit down—that is, may they settle—upon the sacred grass (*barhiṣi*) in our sacrifice, which is dear and delightful.
They grew.
By the rule *svarito vānudātte padādau* (Pāṇini 8.2.6), the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) has the *svarita* accent.
[The word is] *mahitvanā*.

After the suffix denoting abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*), the substitution of *nā* for the following *āṅ* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), as well as its acute accent (*udāttatva*). Alternatively, the form arises through the substitution of *ā* for the case-ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*, along with the insertion of the letter *n*.
They stood;
they ascended to heaven and made the assembly hall spacious—such is the understanding of the meaning.
According to the rule "cādilope vibhāṣā," there is an option regarding the non-placement (anudātta) of the first finite verb.

1. Having brought wealth with their *kṣa-sa* [hands], they pierce the mid-air with their arms. 2. Regarding *yat* of that which is characterized by *kṣa-soma*: the fourth case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *Āvat*: the *laṅ* is used for the present tense due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). *Vṛṣaṇam*: the absence of lengthening of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *vā papūrvasya nigame*. *Madacyutam*: it sheds (*cyu*) intoxication (*mada*); thus it is *madacyut*. The root *dyuti* is used in the sense of "pouring" (*āsecane*). The suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *kip ca*. *Sīdan*: in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*), there is the *leṭ* suffix; *aṭ* is not added.
Like heroes eager for battle, like those who roar in combat, like those seeking glory they have rushed forward in the fray.
All beings tremble before the Maruts; these men are like kings, terrible to behold.
Like heroes, like warriors, they roar; like those seeking glory, they have exerted themselves in battles. All beings are afraid of the Maruts; the men are like kings, terrible to behold. 8.
This is a collective description:

like heroes (*śūrāḥ*) in their valor, like men eager for battle (*yuyutsavaḥ*), and like swift-moving *jarmaryas*, the Maruts—like men desiring fame (*śravasyavaḥ*), that is, seeking food for themselves—exert themselves (*yetire*) in battles (*pṛtanāsu*), meaning they are occupied in fighting against Vṛtra and other foes. All beings (*viśvā bhuvanā*), all classes of living creatures, are afraid (*bibhyati*) of such Maruts.

The meaning is: to those Maruts who are the leaders of rain and so forth, who shine like kings, who are like sovereign lords, and whose appearance is brilliant—meaning they are impossible to behold due to their fierce form—to them [be this offering].

*Yuyudhiyaḥ*: [derived from] *yudh* in the sense of "striking together. In this case, the suffix *kin* is applied according to the statement “the general rule applies in the Veda” (*utsargaś chandasi*, Pāṇini 3.2.171, vārttika 2).
Because it has the nature of a *liṅ* suffix, there is reduplication and so forth; because it has the nature of a *kit*, there is an absence of *guṇa*;
and because it has the nature of a *nit*, there is acute accent on the first syllable.
The form *jarmayaḥ* is derived from that same root with the suffix *kin*; the elision of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule beginning with “*gamahana*” and so forth.
Due to the status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is reduplication and so forth.
*Śravasyavaḥ*:
he desires fame (*śravaḥ*)—he seeks fame, *śravasyati*.
In the phrase ‘kyācchandasī’, the suffix *up* is applied. [The root] *yat* is used; it means ‘exertion’.
The suffix *liṭ* applies while the rule “*luṅ-liṭ* in the Veda” (*chandasi luṅ-liṭ*) remains in force.
[They] are afraid.
From the root *bhī*, meaning “to fear.”
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the absence of the substitution of *ślu* for the suffix *śap*.
[The word is] *tveṣasaṃdṛśaḥ*;
[the root] *tviṣ* means "to shine."
The suffix *ac* is added according to the rule *pacādyac*.
The root *dṛś* means "to see.
From this root, preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *saṃpadādi-lakṣaṇe*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is maintained].
When Tvaṣṭṛ, the skillful artisan, whirled the well-fashioned golden thunderbolt with its thousand points, Indra took it up to perform manly deeds; he struck Vṛtra and cast down the ocean of waters.
When Tvaṣṭṛ, the skillful craftsman, fashioned the well-made golden thunderbolt with a thousand points, Indra took it up to perform manly deeds; he slew Vṛtra and released the flood of waters. 9.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the creator of all things, who performs beautiful deeds (*svapāḥ*), fashioned the thunderbolt; that is to say, he directed it toward Indra and gave it to him.
Of what nature was it? It was well-made (*sukṛtam*), perfectly fashioned, golden (*hiraṇyayam*), and possessed of a thousand points (*sahasrabhṛṣṭim*), meaning it was endowed with many edges.
Indra wields—that is, holds—that vajra. For what purpose? "In man" (nari).

In this context, by the word *nṛ* (man), which is connected with a human being, "battle" is denoted. In that battle, "deeds" (*apāṃsi*)—actions characterized by the slaying of enemies—"were to be performed" (*kartave*).
Having thus grasped the thunderbolt (*vajra*), he "slew" (*ahan*) "Vṛtra"—the obstructer of the rainwater—"the ocean," that is, the cloud filled with water (*arṇas*).
"By that [bow], he blocked the waters and he bent the 'vani' [river]; he caused it to fall down without remainder, with its mouth of iron; the meaning is that he made it rain."

On this point there is the following narrative: The seer Gotama, being afflicted by thirst, requested water from the Maruts.

This meaning is established by this [verse] and by the following one as well.
Those Maruts [are called] *avataḥ*. Because they exist "downward" (*avastāt*) from there, they are *avataḥ*, meaning a well (*kūpa*).

They pushed that [well] upward, as high as possible, with their own vigor—that is, by their own strength;

Having thus excavated the well, while leading it toward the hermitage of the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Maruts, in the middle of the path, completely shattered—even the mountain, the solid mass of rock that was grown large and obstructing their progress. They broke it apart specifically.

And having reached the desire—the longing—of the wise Brahmin Gotama, they gratified him, satisfying him with *dhāmabhiḥ*: that is, with weapons, sustainers, and waters.

O Maruts, you men of true power (*satyaśavasas*), whose strength is unfailing, are the leaders of the one who exerts himself (*śaśamānasya*)—that is, of the one who honors you with hymns of praise, whose limbs perspire from the exertion produced by the recitation of the mantra, and who longs (*venataḥ*). The root *ven* signifies longing; thus, it means "of the one desiring. The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction. To such a praiser, grant (*vida*) the fulfillment of his desire (*kāmasya kāmam*); that is, bestow his wish. Regarding *śaśamānasya*: the root *śaś* means "to leap" (in the sense of moving quickly). The suffix *cānaś* is added here in the sense of habituality (*tācchīlika*). Regarding *svedasya*: the root *ṣvid* means "to flow from the body. The suffix *ghañ* is applied here in the sense of the object (*karman*) because the causative sense is implied within the root. Due to the *ji*-class, the acute accent falls on the first syllable. Regarding *vida*: the root *vid* means "to obtain. This is the imperative (*loṭ*), second person plural; there is a substitution [of *dhi* for *ta*] by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*). By the rule "abundantly in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), the intermediate suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is elided. *Jha* is replaced by *ad*. By the rule "there is elision of *ta* in the *ātmanepada*," the *ta* is dropped. The acute accent belongs to the beginning of the suffix. There is no suppression (*nighāta*) because it occurs at the beginning of the quarter-verse (*pāda*). In the *saṃhitā*, there is lengthening by the rule "after *vacas*, before a *tiṅ* ending. Regarding *kāmasya*: due to its inclusion in the list beginning with *tṛc*, the acute accent falls on the first syllable. Because of the rule "the mention of the action must be made," the object takes the status of a recipient (*saṃpradāna*); hence, the genitive is used in the sense of the dative.

O you of true strength, manifest that [deed] with your greatness; pierce the demon with your lightning! 9. You. That. O you of true strength. Manifest. With greatness. Pierce. With lightning. The demon. 9.

O Maruts, you who possess true vigor, true strength, and power unassailable by others—reveal, manifest, and make known that greatness of yours which is well-known from the slaying of Vṛtra and other deeds.
With that great majesty, shining like lightning, pierce—that is, strike and destroy—the *rakṣas*, the demons and others who cause us affliction.

*Kartā*: From the root *kṛ* (to do), in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix by the rule "in the Veda, [the suffix] is frequently [elided]. Then, the substitution of *ta* for the ending is applied by the rule "the endings *ta*, *na*, *sa*, *tha*, *na*, and *nā* [are substituted]."
The grammatical quality (*guṇa*). By the rule "idu-dupadhasya cāpratyayasya" (Pāṇini 8.3.41), the *visarjanīya* in the word *āviḥ* becomes *pa*.
[Thus it is] *mahattvena*.
After a word ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), the substitution of *nā* for the following prefix *āṅ* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*),
as does its acute accent (*udāttatva*).
Alternatively:
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the substitution of *āj* for the third case ending and the insertion of the letter *n*.
[The verb form is] *vidhyata*;
[the root is] *vyadha*, meaning "to strike."

In the case of *śyani*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by [Pāṇini 6.1.15] *prahijyāvinā*. Since the suffix *ta* is marked as having the *ṅit* designation by [Pāṇini 1.2.4] *sārvadhātukamapit*, there is a long vowel in the *saṃhitā* stage by [Pāṇini 6.3.137] *ṛci tunudhamaśrutad*.

Taking hold of the house, may darkness depart entirely; may it drive away every devouring spirit. May he who creates light grant us that which we desire. 10. Taking hold. Of the house. Darkness. Away. May it go. Every. Devouring one. Light. Maker. That. Which. We desire. 10.
O you two, seize—that is, envelop—the "great darkness" (tamas) which is hidden, situated in the cave, and pervading everywhere;
cause it to become invisible so that it is not seen by the waters; the meaning is that you must destroy it.
"Drive away—expel from our presence—the 'viśvam' (entire) 'atriṇam' (devourer), such as the Rākṣasas and others.
Produce that 'jyotiḥ' (light), such as the sun and so forth, which 'uśmasi' (we desire).
Or else: [the verse may be interpreted otherwise].
Destroy the darkness—that is, the ignorance consisting of positive existence—which dwells in the secret place, namely the heart within the cavity of the body.
Drive out the devourer of man, such as desire, anger, and all other [afflictions].
O Maruts, whose forms are the five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, perform that light which we desire, the knowledge consisting of the direct realization of the supreme reality.
From the root *guh*, meaning "to conceal" (*saṃvaraṇe*).
When the suffix *śap* is applied, the penultimate vowel undergoes guṇa substitution; then, by the rule *udupadhāyā gohaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.89), the penultimate vowel *u* is replaced by *ū*.
*yāta* [is derived from] *yā* in the sense of "to reach" (*prāpaṇe*). From this root, the imperative (*loṭ*) is formed with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied.
Atriṇam:
the suffix *trin* is applied according to *Uṇādisūtra* 4.508, *aderdhini ca*.
Uśmasi.
The root *vaś* means "to desire.
The suffix *masi* ends in *i*.
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment.
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by means of *hijyā* and other rules.
"Those of broad chests" (*pr̥thuvakṣasaḥ*): this third hymn consists of six verses; it is the seer's work of Gautama, composed in the Jagatī meter, and addressed to the Maruts.

And thus it has been introduced in the Anukramaṇī: "The [hymn] beginning with *pratvakṣasaḥ* consists of six verses in the Jāgata metre. In the Āgnimāruta-śastra of the Agniṣṭoma, this hymn is the specific praise of the Maruts.
It is prescribed in the section beginning with "Now, as to this" (*atha yathemam*) in the Sūtra: "*pratvakṣasaḥ*, *pratavaso yajñā yajñā vo agnaye*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).
With broad chests, mighty, roaring, infinite, unshakable, and drinkers of the dregs;
most beloved and most manly, they have adorned themselves with ointments as some bright ones are adorned with their rays.
Broad-chested, powerful, roaring, infinite, unshakable, drinkers of the dregs, most beloved, most manly—they have anointed themselves with ointments, like certain bulls with their dewlaps. 1.

"Pratavakṣasaḥ" means those who crush their enemies exceedingly; that is to say, slayers of foes. Because they are "pratavasaḥ," endowed with preeminent strength, for that very reason they are "virapsinaḥ," possessed of various shouts of victory.
Or alternatively:
This is not a great matter for me;
for the great are praised by various epithets.
Therefore, "infinite" (anantāḥ) means being devoid of limitation (ānati-rahitāḥ), that is, being supreme in every respect.
"Unwavering" means not separated;
the meaning is that they have become united in the form of seven groups.
"Possessors of the *ṛjīṣa*."
Because the *ṛjīṣa* is consumed at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) and the Maruts are praised therein, they possess the quality of being *ṛjīṣins*.
Alternatively,
the *ṛjīṣins* are the impellers of the essences (*rasas*).

The Maruts—those most highly honored (*juṣṭatamāsaḥ*), being served by the sacrificers beyond measure; those most truly human (*nṛtamāsaḥ*), being carriers of men through their supreme wisdom—such as these, have adorned themselves in the sky with *stṛbhiḥ*, their own body-coverings, and with *añjibhiḥ*, ornaments that manifest their forms.
Therein lies the illustration:
like certain *uṣṭrāḥ* (rays), just as whatever rays of the sun shine in the sky, so do they appear.
*Pratavakṣasaḥ*:
they are called *pratavakṣasaḥ* because they "cut" (*tvakṣante*) or "hew" (*tankurvanti*) with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa*).
[The root] *takṣū*, *tvakṣū* [is used] in the sense of hewing (*tankaraṇe*).

By the rule "There is also the preservation of the original accent of the first member even for [the suffixes] gati and kāraka," the suffix *asun* applies and the original accent of the first member is preserved:
*pratavasaḥ*. *Tavaḥ* is a name for strength.
Those whose austerity (*tapas*) is preeminent;
in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accent remains on the original form of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*). [The term is] *virapsinaḥ*.
The root *rap* (or *lap*) is used in the sense of "distinct speech. *Virapsā* means "repeated speaking" (*virapaṇam*).
The suffix *śa* is added according to the rules of the *uṇādi* class.
In the same way, O Virapsin,
we are infinite;
we are bowed down, bent low, and prostrated.
They are not bent; they are infinite.
[The compound] has the accent of the original form of the first member because it is an indeclinable (avyaya).
They are unwavering.
The root *vyath* is used in the senses of "fear" and "trembling.
According to the rule "vyatheḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ dhaḥ kicca," [the suffix *kvan* is applied, with vocalization of the semivowel and the substitution of *dh* for *th*].
[Variant reading: *kṣa-gṛhat*.]
2. The [consonant] cluster ṭa-ḍha-sa-’ye does not exist.

(From *Uṇādisūtra* 1.39) the suffix *urac* is applied. However, here, by virtue of the rule of *bahulādhikāra* (diversity), the change to *dh* is not performed. The accents of the compound are as before. In *juṣṭamāsaḥ*: the word *juṣṭa* is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) according to the rule *nirya mantre*. Then, because the suffix *tamap* of the comparative degree is grave (*anudātta*) due to its being marked with *p*, that same accent remains.
