In *ānañje*: the root *añj* means "to manifest, to smear, to shine, or to go. The suffix *liṭ* is used in the sense of the present tense according to the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*. By the rule *ata ādeḥ*, the reduplication vowel becomes *ā*. By the rule *tasmācchun dvihalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.71), the augment *nuṭ* is added. There is a loss of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) by transposition (*vyatyaya*). [The *r* in *ānarje*] is by the rule *iryo re*. In *stṛbhiḥ*: the root *stṛñ* means "to cover. The suffix *krip* is applied; the absence of the augment *tuk* is due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rules regarding augments.

When you have settled in the recesses like birds, O Maruts, by whatever path; the water-vessels drip upon your chariots. Sprinkle the honey-colored ghee for the one who sings your praise. In the recesses—when you have settled.
Like birds: that which trembles with great force.
Or rather: [it refers to the Maruts].

When indeed the Maruts harness their own chariots with horses and conquer, then, during the journeys of these chariots over the mountain-like elevations that toss them up, the earth trembles with fear. Therein lies the illustration: "as if unsteady."

Just as a wife separated from her husband trembles when faced with royal oppression and other such calamities, being left without support, so too are those Maruts. They are playful (*krīḷayaḥ*), habituated to sport; they are *dhunayaḥ*, having a nature of movement; they have *bhrājad-ṛṣṭayaḥ*, blazing weapons. Being such, the Maruts—*dhūtayaḥ*, shaking mountains and the like—while manifesting their own greatness (*mahi-rava*) through their own power, "panayanta," which means they conduct themselves or display themselves.
[In] the un-born (*ajeṣu*).
The root *aja* is used in the senses of "going" (*gati*) and "throwing" (*kṣepaṇa*).
Although the suffix *man* is prescribed by the rule *atiṃstusu* etc., it should be understood as applying here as well due to the word *bahulavacanāt* ("by virtue of the frequentative statement").

According to the statement *balādāvardhadhātuke vikalpa iṣyate* (Kāśikā 2.4.56.2), there is an option regarding the substitution of *vī* for *aj*; thus, there is an absence of the *vī*-substitution [in this case].
The initial syllable is udātta.
[The root] *rev* [is used];
*rej* means "to tremble."
Yāska [states in Nirukta 3.21]: "He trembles and shakes" refers to fear and trembling.
[The word occurs] in the sense of "journeys" (*yāmeṣu*);
[the root] *yam* means "to cease" (*uparame*).
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an action (*bhāva*).
Although the rule "karṣātvataḥ" would have resulted in an udātta accent on the final syllable, its placement among the *vṛṣādi* group results in an udātta accent on the first syllable.
Alternatively:
The suffix *man* is applied after the root *prāp* (in the sense of "attaining") by the rule beginning with *atiṃstusu* and so forth. [The word] *śubhe*:
from the root *śubh* (in the sense of "shining").
The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *mand* and others in the sense of an object;
the acute accent of the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
[They] praise.
But in common usage [the form is derived as follows]:
by Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.28, *gupū-dhūpa-vichi*, the suffix *āya* is applied; from this root, the Vedic *laṅ* [aorist] is used.

There is a metrical inversion and shortening [of vowels]. For he is the one who moves with his sisters, whose horses are spotted, the youthful host; through this [power], the sovereign, surrounded by his mighty strengths—he is the true one, the payer of debts, the blameless, the protector of this prayer; and thus the host is the showerer [of blessings]. 4. He indeed; for; moving with his sisters; having spotted horses; the youth; the host; through this; the sovereign; with his powers; encompassed; you are; true; the pursuer of debt; blameless; the promoter; of this; prayer; and then; the showerer; the host. 4.
For indeed, that host of Maruts becomes the lord of this entire world, possessing the nature of a sovereign;
of what sort?
Moving by itself, flowing spontaneously.
Indeed, there is no other instigator of this host of Maruts.
He whose horses are *pṛṣadaśva*—that is, spotted deer marked with white spots serving as his steeds—is so described.

He is youthful, eternally fresh; he is encompassed by *tavipībhiḥ*, that is, by extraordinary powers not shared by others. He is the true one, worthy of his own deeds, the fulfiller of the hopes of his worshippers (*ṛṇayāvā*), meaning the giver of abundant wealth.
He who is without fuel, whose name is praised,

who is irreproachable by all, the bull, the showerer of waters— such is the host of Maruts; immediately after this, he becomes the protector, the one who guards with excellence, of this *dhi* (our thought) or this our ritual act.

In the form *ayā*, the fifth case ending is replaced by *yāj* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Then, by the rule *hali lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.113), the form *idam* is elided before a consonant.

Īśānaḥ. From the root *īś* in the sense of "lordship," the suffix *cānaś* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). Since that suffix lacks the designation *sārvadhātuka*, the final syllable is udātta by virtue of the *cit* accent.

In the phrase *ayā īśānaḥ*, there is the preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) due to its inclusion in the *īpāakṣa* group. [The form] *asi* [is used] with a change of person (*puruṣavyatyaya*).

*Ṛṇayāvā*: [This is derived] from the root *yā* in the sense of "reaching" (*prāpaṇe*), with the causative meaning (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied; the suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule *āto manin-kvanib-vanipaśca*. *Anedhaḥ*.
The root *jidi* is used in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*).

By the rule *ṛhalor ṇyat*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied. Because the instruction regarding augments (*āgama*) is not universally obligatory, there is an absence of the augment *num*; consequently, the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇaḥ*).
In a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) which constitutes the first member.
1. When [the suffixes] *kṣan* and *sas* are present in the sense of "going" (*gamana*).
2. Because *kṣa* and *ḍha* lack the status of being *lāsarvadhātuka*, the accent of a *lāsarvadhātuka* does not apply.
We speak by the ancient birth of our father; the tongue of Soma goes forth with his vision.
When the hymns reached Indra, they assumed their sacrificial names.

Through the birth of our ancient father, we speak. The tongue of Soma goes forth with its vision, when they, through their labor, reached Indra and the singers; then indeed they assumed names worthy of sacrifice. ||5||
We speak—that is, we declare—the birth [we received] from our ancient (*vpratnasya*) and long-standing (*ciraṃtanasya*) father (*pituḥ*), Rahūgaṇa;
that is to say, our father taught us this narrative which we are about to relate, and therefore we speak of it.
If one asks what that narrative is, it is said:
At the sacrifices of Soma, his tongue—the speech consisting of praise—proceeds forth toward the host of Maruts, accompanied by the light of the oblation of the Soma-substance which is being offered.
In the sacrifices, both the Soma-oblation and the praise are directed toward the host of Maruts;
therefore, he [Soma] approaches them.

*Śobhanakhādirbhakṣaṇaḥ*: those whose eating consists of beautiful *khadira* wood. The final syllable of the compound is accented (*antodātta*) by the rule *nañsubhyām*. *Iṣmin*: from the root *iṣ* (to go); the suffix *man* is added by the rule *iṣiyudhīndhi...* etc., and then the possessive suffix *ini* is added. *Vide*: from the root *vid* (to obtain). In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), there is an absence of reduplication according to the statement "in the Veda, it may optionally [not be reduplicated]" within the section on reduplication. By the rule *iryo re*, the *ir* is changed to *re*. || 13 ||
"Ā vidyunmadbhiḥ" is the fourth hymn, consisting of six verses.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Ā vidyunmadbhir ādhāmnthe; the [first] two are Prastārapaṅkti, the fifth is a Virāṭpādā.
As before, it has two deities.
The first and the sixth [of the ten types of *paṅkti*] are two *prastārapaṅktis*.
That [verse] whose first two quarters are *jāgatī* and the third and fourth are *gāyatrī* is a *prastārapaṅkti*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *prastārapaṅkti* has [the *jāgatī*] at the beginning" (*Piṅgala Sūtra* 3.40).
This is its meaning:
the phrase "two *jāgata* and two *gāyatra*" is understood from the preceding context.
If there are two *jāgata* feet at the beginning (purastāt) and the other two are *gāyatra*, that is the *prastārapaṅkti*.
The fifth [verse], "etaccayat," is the Virāj-footed [verse].
When the first three feet consist of eleven syllables each and the other consists of eight, it is called a Virāj-footed verse.
The application [of this verse] is based on its indicative mark (liṅga).
O Maruts, come hither with your lightning-bright chariots, well-sounding, equipped with spears and falcon-feathered shafts;
like birds, fly to us with your most abundant nourishment, O you of wondrous power!

O Maruts, come hither with your lightning-bright chariots, resonant with song, equipped with spears, and winged with horses; like birds, O masters of wondrous power, fly to us with most abundant nourishment. 1.
O Maruts! They are called *marutaḥ* because, having reached the measured (*mitam*) intermediate space (*antarikṣam*), they roar—that is, they produce sound;
or alternatively, because they produce sound excessively (*amitam*).

Alternatively, they are called *marutaḥ* because, having reached the cloud measured (*mitam*) by themselves, they shine with a pure soul; or because they run (*dravanti*) within the earth and the atmosphere. Those hosts of gods known to reside in the intermediate space are all designated as the *maruts*.
And so they have said: "Every woman is situated in the middle, the man is all-pervading, and all the hosts are the Maruts—such is the teaching of the elders.
The Paurāṇikas, however, declare: "Seventy-seven groups of Maruts, sons of Kaśyapa and Māricā, were born in the number of forty-nine."
O Maruts, being such as you are, come hither with your own chariots; that is, come to this sacrifice of ours.
With what kind of chariots? With those "possessing lightning."

*Vidyotana* means lightning. [The phrase] "by those endowed with distinguished brilliance" refers to their own rays (*svarka*), which are their own cognitions (*svajñāna*) and are characterized by an excellent course.
Or rather:
by those who possess worship—meaning praise—of beautiful deeds;
or else, by those endowed with beautiful luster.
"With spears (*ṛṣṭibhiḥ*):
spears are weapons in the form of javelins (*śakti*);
others say they are pillars (*sthuṇā*)."
By those [arrows] swift as horses; "aśvaparṇaiḥ" means by those that possess the flight or movement of horses.
Alternatively:
"Ratha" refers to clouds, which have the nature of rushing;
come through the atmosphere together with them for the purpose of raining.
By what kind? By those possessing lightning— by those with *ṛṣṭi*s (spears) that have lightning (*taḍit*) and possess beautiful movement (*svarka*).
*Arpaṇam* means going;
[it is performed] by those not bound to that nature, namely,
those whose wings are horses (*aśvaparṇaiḥ*).
"Those whose movement is like that of a horse, pervading and spreading out"—the meaning is:
those existing by pervading the intermediate space.
O you of excellent creative power!
"Māyā" is a designation for both actions and knowledge. The Maruts, possessing auspicious actions or auspicious wisdom, [attain this] by means of the most excellent [māyā].
"O Vaya, come toward us with food that is more abundant—that is, with food to be given to us.
Do not fly away like birds; rather, fly hither, meaning, come quickly."

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "Now, next are the groups of gods belonging to the middle station; among them, the Maruts come first. They are called *marutaḥ* because they are measured in their sound (*mita-rāviṇaḥ*), or measured in their light (*mita-rociṇaḥ*), or because they run greatly (*mahad-vantīti*). "O Maruts, come with your lightning-laden chariots, which are well-sounding, or well-known, or well-praised, or full of splendor; with spears, and with horses that have wings like birds and fall like arrows. O you of excellent wisdom, or of auspicious deeds, fly toward us like birds with our most abundant food. (Nirukta 11.13–14)
1. *kṣa-ṭa-ḍha-marutaḥ*—thus [it is said]. |||

[The word] *vidyunmadbhiḥ* [is formed as follows]: because the word *vidyut* is included within the *yavādi* group—which is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*)—the suffix *matup* does not undergo the substitution of *v* by rule *Pāṇini 8.2.10* (*jhayaḥ*), since the exclusion "not after *yava* and so forth" (*ayavādibhyaḥ*) is understood to carry over from rule *Pāṇini 8.2.9*. [Similarly,] *ṛṣṭidbhiḥ*.

The suffix *matup* is acute-accented by the rule "after a short vowel and after *nuṭ*, *matup* [is acute]. [The word] *aśmaparṇaiḥ* [is derived from] the root *aśū* in the sense of pervasion (*vyāptau*).
The suffix *kan* is applied by the rule *aśimuṣi* etc.;
in the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) prevails;
[the form is] *varṣiṣṭhyā*.
From the word *vṛddha*, when the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied, the substitution of *varṣa* occurs according to the rule "priyasthira... and so forth.
[The root] *paṭ* [is used]; "paṭṛ" means "to go."
Since the suffix *laṅ* is present, there is the substitution of *aṭ* for *cli*;
furthermore, by the rule *pataḥ pum* (Pāṇini 7.4.19), the augment *pum* is added.
With those beautiful, reddish-brown, and tawny horses that draw the chariot, they go toward what is auspicious;
like a brilliant golden ornament, they strike the earth with the tire of their chariot as if with an axe.

With their ruddy, excellent, and tawny steeds that draw the chariot, they come for the sake of glory; brilliant like a golden ornament, equipped with axes, they strike the earth with the tires of their chariot.

Those aforementioned Maruts come—arrive—with their horses, which are ruddy-colored, tawny-colored, or endowed with both colors, and which are the drivers of the chariot; they come toward the sacrificer who chooses the gods as his choicest portion, who calls out, and who praises them.
For what purpose? For beauty—to bring him splendor—or else for "śubhe," meaning for water.
The meaning is "for the sake of rain.
The host of those Maruts is *rukmo na*, shining like gold; *citrah*, exceedingly beautiful to behold; and *svadhitīvān*.
*Svadhitih* is a name for the thunderbolt (*vajra*).
Equipped with a weapon that shatters enemies,
those Maruts, appearing in such a multitude of forms, *jaṅghananta*— that is, they strike or crush excessively— the *bhūm*, the earth, with the *pavyā*, the rim or edge of their chariot wheel.
The meaning is that the earth became oppressed, unable to bear the weight of those great beings who had arrived for the sake of protecting the hymns of praise.
*Vara*. It is called *vara* because the gods are chosen (*vriyante*) by means of it;
the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to the rule *grahavṛdṛniśri*.
What [is meant by] *ka*?
From the roots *kai* and *gai*, meaning "to sound"; that which sounds is *ka*.
The suffix *ka* is applied due to the rule regarding frequentative forms (*bahulavacanāt*).
[Thus we have] *rathūtṛbhiḥ*. The root *tṝ* is used in the sense of "hastening" (*tvaraṇe*).
They are called *rathaturaḥ* because they cause the chariot to move swiftly;
[the suffix] *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvip ca*. In the *bhisi* case-ending, lengthening occurs by the rule *hali ca*.
The word *pavyā*.
Yāska states: "The *pavi* is the rim of a chariot wheel" (*Nirukta* 5.5).
[It is derived from] the root *pūṅ*, meaning "to purify."
From this [root], the suffix *ip* is applied by the rule "aca haḥ. The acute accent of the case-ending is due to the rule "udāttayaṇaḥ. [The form] is *jaṅghananta*.

From the root *han* with the suffix *yaṅ*, the *laṅ* (imperfect) is used in the sense of the present tense according to Vedic usage. By the rule "in the Veda, both ways," the *śap* suffix is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, there is the elision of the vowel *a* and the elision of the *y* of the suffix. [The result is] *bhūm*.

The word *bhūmi* is [the form] of *bhūmi* following the word *śabda*; the substitution of *ḍā* for the case-ending *am* is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*, and the shortening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
For glory, what [is it] for you? Upon your bodies are the axes; may they raise them up like trees through their inspired wisdom.
For you, O Maruts of noble birth and great splendor, they direct the pressing-stone to yield wealth.
For glory—what [is it] for you? Upon your bodies are axes; may they, like forests, fashion their wisdom uprightly.
For you, O Maruts of noble birth and great splendor, they urge the pressing-stone for the sake of wealth. 3.

O Maruts, your *vāśī*—the weapon that cries out against enemies—is for the sake of glory (*śriye*), that is, for the sake of sovereignty (*īśvaryārtha*), within your bodies (*tanuṣu*), meaning in the parts of your limbs where the body might be destroyed; this is the sense. The word *kam* is used here as a filler (*pādapūraṇa*). As it has been said: "Furthermore, there are fillers [of the verse]," and "such as *kam*, *īm*, and *it*."

Such Maruts cause the sacrificers to perform—like trees raised up in a forest—the "medhas," that is, the sacrifices, which are "ūrdhvān," meaning raised up in the form of Ekāhas, Ahīnas, and Satras. O well-born (sujātāḥ) Maruts, endowed with noble birth, for you—for your sake—the sacrificers, possessing abundant wealth (tuvidyumnāsaḥ), "dhanayante," that is, they make it their wealth; the meaning is that for your sacrifice, they press [the Soma] with stones (grāvabhiḥ), the pressing-stone (adrim) which brings about happiness (kam) for you when engaged in the extraction of Soma.
Vāśī: Vāśa is the making of a shouting sound by instilling fear in enemies;
from that, the suffix *ī* is added in the sense of possession according to the rule "chandasīvanipau."
The initial udātta accent occurs by way of transposition.
Regarding *medhā*, the substitution of *ḍā* for *śas* is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
*vanā*: the elision of the *śi* suffix occurs by the rule "in the Veda, [the substitution] is frequent" (*aśecchandasi bahulam*). *kṛṇvante*.

The root *kṛv* is used in the senses of "injuring" and "doing. In the present tense (*laṭ*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). The suffix *upratyaya* is applied according to the rule "dhinvikṛṇvyora ca."
Furthermore, there is a substitution of the final letter by transposition.
According to the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, because it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the substitute *jha* is not *it*; thus, after *guṇa*, there is the substitution of *ava*.
[The form is] *ūrdhvā*.
As before, there is the substitution of *ḍa*.
[The form] *dhanayante* is derived from the root *dhana* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, according to the rule "that which one does" (*tat karoti*).
Day after day the vultures have come around you; the Gṛtsamadas, performing prayer, have fashioned this divine hymn and song.
Making the sacred word, they have pushed up the well from below so that it may flow for them to drink.

The days have come; the vultures have gathered around. Performing this prayer and the divine rite with their chants, the Gōtamas, fashioning the sacred word (*brahman*), have pushed the water-source upward so that they may drink. 4.
The thirsty Gautamas praised the Maruts, and they brought a well-mouth from another region and gave it to them.
Seeing this, a certain seer said:
"O Gautamas, the days—days endowed with beautiful light—have come around (*pari-ā-aguḥ*) to you (*vaḥ*), who are full of longing for water."

And having obtained the ritual action (*vākrīyā*) to be accomplished by the waters—that is, the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites—the sages known as the Gotamas made the "divine" (*devī*) [waters] shine; performing the *brahman*—the food characterized by the oblation—for the Maruts with hymns (*arkaiḥ*) accomplished through mantras, they pushed the well (*utsadhi*) upward for their own drinking. A *utsadhi* is a well, so called because a flow of water (*utso*) is led into it; they pushed that well, which was situated in another place, upward from its opening.
The fact that the Maruts were praised by his hymns and emerged from the mouth of the well is figuratively attributed to these [Maruts] as being caused by his hymns.
*Gṛdhra*s: from the root *gṛdhu* in the sense of "desire. The suffix *kran* is applied according to the rule "after *su*, *sudhā*, and *gṛdhi*, [the suffix] *kran*."
By the rule "the case endings (sup) become case endings," the suffix *śas* becomes *jas*.
Due to its being marked with the *ni*-augment, it is udātta on the first syllable. [Thus] *aguḥ*.
In these cases, by the rule "in the *luṅ* [augment] after *iṇ*, there is *gā*," there is the substitution of *gā*.
By the rule "after *āt*," there is *jum* for *m*.
Optionally, it is as in the *krī* [root].
The root *ḍukuñ* means "to do.
By the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*, [the suffix] *ṇyat* is applied; thus, that which is to be done by means of waters is "vākrīyā" (water-work).
The final syllable of the compound is udātta according to the rule *tricakrādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.2.196). [They] pushed away (*nunudre*). [The root is] *ṇuda* in the sense of "impelling."
In the word *irayo re*, there is the substitution of *re* [for the final vowel].
In *utsadhim*,
the suffix *kvip* is applied to the verbal root in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), according to the rule "after a root, when the object or the locus is to be expressed."
*pibadhyai* | [The root] *pā* [is used] in the sense of "drinking. The suffix *śadhyai* is applied according to the rule *tum-arthe śeṣeṇa*.
By the rule beginning with "pāghrā," there is the substitution of *piba*.
1. *kṣa* is for filling the verse. 2. *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *na*, and *sa* are for filling the verses. 3. They gave water with the *sajala* [mantra]. 4. They made it shine with the *sadīptamāna* [mantra].
This which you did not perceive as a *yojana*—O Maruts, that which Gaurtama sang for you, seeing the golden-wheeled boars running about with tusks like oars.
This—that deed—was not perceived as a mere league’s distance, O Maruts, when Gṛtsamada, pressing the Soma for you, beheld the wild boars with golden wheels and sharp tusks as they rushed about. 5.
O Maruts!
That which is joined by this deity is the *yojana*—the hymn of praise accomplished by this *sūkta*.
It is known by all as something celebrated, like some other preeminent hymn of praise.
For your sake, the seer Gotama has indeed uttered with a resonant voice this hymn in the form of a *sūkta*;
while doing so,
[he addressed] those who are mounted upon golden wheels (*hiraṇyacakrān*), or who are engaged in deeds that are beneficial and delightful, or who have iron tusks (*ayodaṃṣṭrān*).
It bites, thus it is a *daṃṣṭrā*, meaning the edge of a wheel.
[The phrase] "furnished with edges of wheels made of iron" means this.
Alternatively, the seers (*ṛṣi*) who are the instruments of biting are the *daṃṣṭrās*.
The sages who possess iron [limbs];
those boars who are running about, moving here and there in various ways;
the slayers of the enemy, that is, the most excellent foe.
Alternatively, [the term refers to] those who bring the excellent rain-water;
or else, those who summon the exalted deities, or those who consume the choice oblation.
Seeing—that is, correctly knowing—the Maruts as being thus, Gotama composed this hymn. The meaning is that this, which is the most excellent of all things, is now obtained by us all.
Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "Furthermore, these Mādhyamaka hosts of gods are called Varāhas;
'beholding those with golden wheels'" (Nirukta 5.4). Thus it is said.
The root *cit* means "to perceive.
The form *sasvaḥ* is the aorist (*luṅ*) used in the sense of the present tense, according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). It is the third person plural middle voice.

In the sense of "one's own" (*sva*) and "afflicting" (*upatāpa*), with the *laṅ* suffix and the *tip* ending, there is the elision (*ślu*) of the *śap* by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. Following the application of *guṇa*, the elision of the *t* occurs by the rule "halḍyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal."
By the accent of the *dhātu*, there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable. Regarding *varāhūn*:

Skandasvāmin states that this word is derived from the root *hu*—preceded by the prefix *āṅ* and having *vara* as its upapada—from one of the following roots: *han*, *hṛ*, *hayati*, *juhoti*, or *ad*.
The formation of this word is established by its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
O Maruts, this voice of the singer here reverberates toward you like a responsive chant;
it has spontaneously resounded according to its own nature from the hands that hold the Soma-stalks.
O Maruts, may this song of praise be for you as a follower; let it resound like the voice of a priest. He has sung it freely according to their own nature from his hands. 6.
O Maruts, this our praise here resounds toward you—following after you, accompanying you, and resembling you; it praises each of you individually.
The root *stobh* means "to praise.
Likewise, it is like the voice of the singers (*vāghataḥ*).
The word *na* is used in the sense of "now.

As Yāska has stated: "The particle *na* is employed in the sense of comparison (*upamārtha*) and in the sense of 'now' (*saṃprati*)" (Nirukta 7.31). Now, even the speech associated with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) "vainly," that is, without effort, "praised" (*astauṣīt*) these [goddesses] by means of these *ṛc*s.
When it is asked, "What is meant by 'now'?", he says:
"In the two wombs," that is, in our two arms; "svadhā" is a name for food.
When the Maruts set forth various kinds of food— meaning,
with reference to that.
The suffix *tṛc* [is applied] after the root *hṛ*, meaning "to take away," to form the word *anubhartṛ*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ṛtvebhyaḥ";
the word *nadī* receives an acute accent (*udāttatva*) by the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt."
1. One should abandon the praise of those who are wicked, cruel, and deceitful. 2. One should be a summoner of the gods, *kṣa-na-sa*. (Ka.
‘Ā no bhadrāḥ’ is the fifth hymn, consisting of ten verses. It is the seer Gotama’s, addressed to the Viśvedevas.
Of these, the first five verses and the seventh are Jagatī; the sixth, ‘Svasti na indraḥ’, is a Virāṭ-sthāna verse.
This is because they possess the characteristics described in the statement: “The *navakti* consists of the *vairāja* and the *bārhata-triṣṭubh*” (Anuvāka 9.5).
The three hymns beginning with the eighth are *triṣṭubhs*.
Accordingly, it has been enumerated: “*Ā no* [10 verses] is addressed to the Viśvedevas; however, the first five and the seventh are *jagatīs*, while the sixth is in the *virāṭ-sthāna*.”
In the Vaiśvadeva-śastra of the Agniṣṭoma, this hymn, with the exception of the last [verse], is to be used as the *vaiśvadevi-nividdhānīya*.
That [last verse], however, serves as the *paridhānīyā* for the Vaiśvadeva-śastra both in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*).

Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: “*ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvato’dabdhāso...*”—this is the nine-verse Vaiśvadeva hymn—and also: “One should conclude (*paridadhyāt*) with *aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam* in every Vaiśvadeva [śastra]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.18).
And there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: “One should always conclude with the *pañcajanīyā*” (AiB 3.31).
This hymn is used in the *niṣkevalya* section of the Mahāvrata.
Accordingly, it is stated in the fifth Āraṇyaka: “The *ānobhadrīya* [hymn] is in its place” (AiĀ 5.3.2).

May auspicious thoughts come to us from every side—unfailing, unassailed, and breaking forth. May the gods be ever with us for our prosperity, our protectors day by day, never failing in their care. ā | naḥ | bhadrāḥ | kratavaḥ | yantu | viśvataḥ | adabdhāsaḥ | aparītāsaḥ | ud'bhidah | devāḥ | naḥ | yathā | sadam | it | vṛdhe | asan | apra'yuvaḥ | rakṣitāraḥ | dive'dive ||1||
May the *kratavaḥ*—the great sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others—come from every direction (*viśvataḥ*) to us (*naḥ*), even from every part of the sky.

Of what nature are these *kratavaḥ*? They are auspicious (*bhadrāḥ*), being either beneficial because they bring about favorable results or worthy of devotion; they are inviolable (*adabdhāsaḥ*), meaning they have not been harmed by the Asuras; they are unassailable (*aparītāsaḥ*), meaning they have not been surrounded or obstructed by enemies;
and they are breakers-through (*udbhidah*), that is, destroyers of our foes.
May such sacrifices come to us in this manner.

"Aprāyuvaḥ" means not departing, not abandoning what is to be protected by themselves; therefore, "divedive" means day after day, acting as protectors, performing protection—may all the gods, distinguished in such ways, come so that they may be present for our "sadamit vṛdhe," that is, always for our prosperity; such is the connection of the words.
*Adabdhāsaḥ*:
*dambhu* means "to injure.
The prohibition of the augment *iṭ* after the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied according to the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*.
In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) preceding member is maintained. For example: *aparītāsaḥ*.
[The root] *iṇ* means "to go."
As before, the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied to the verbal root.
In both cases, *asuk* is substituted for *ājaseras*.
[The form is] *vṛdhaḥ*.
The root *vṛdh* means "to increase.
The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule beginning with *saṃpādādi*.
The acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
*as* [is used] in the sense of existence (*bhuvi*). In the *leṭ* [mood], there is the elision of the augment (*aḍagamaḥ*).
The absence of the elision of the *śap* suffix occurs because of the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage, [elision] is optional).
Because that [suffix] ends in a vowel, the elision of the *a* in *kṣas* and *oras* does not occur by the rule "kṣasoralopaḥ. Thus, [the form is] *aprāyuvaḥ*.
The root *iṇ* means "to go.
From this [root], by the rule *chandasi niṣṭarky-āry-ūka-ṛtūkāḥ*, the suffix *u* is applied.
In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the original accent of the first member, being an indeclinable (*avyaya*), is retained.

In the case of *yasi*, *jasādiṣu*, and so forth, because the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*chandasi vāvacanam*) allows for the optional application of *guṇa*, there is *uvaṅ* substitution in the neuter state due to its belonging to the *tanvādi* group.

May the auspicious favor of the upright gods be ours; may the bounty of the gods turn toward us. We have entered into the friendship of the gods; may the gods extend our life-span that we may live. Of the gods: auspicious; the benevolent thought; of the upright ones. Of the gods: the gift; toward us; may it descend. Of the gods: the friendship; we have approached; we. May the gods: our; life-span; prolong; for living. 2.
1. *Kṣa* means "just so"; *na* means "not so.
The remainder [of the sense] is: "May there be for us the auspicious, bliss-bestowing, and worshipful benevolent mind (*sumati*) of the gods—their beautiful intention (*mati*) whose nature is grace.
Of what kind [of gods]?
May the straight path—characterized by rectitude and sincerity—be followed by the sacrificer who desires it for himself and performs it correctly.
Likewise, may the gift (*rāti*) of the gods turn fully toward us;
that is, the granting of the fruits resulting from that [sacrifice] shall also be ours.
And we have attained—have reached—the number, the friendship, or the deeds of a friend of those gods.
May such gods extend and increase our life-span so that we may live.
*Bhadrā*: [The root] *bhad* is used in the senses of "auspiciousness" and "happiness. It is established as a derivative ending in the suffix *ran* by the rule *ṛjendrāga-* (Uṇādisūtra 2.186), etc.
Let him desire straightness. He desires straightness for himself; he "straightens" (ṛjūyati).
[This is formed] by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*.
After that [suffix], the *laṭ* takes the suffix *śatṛ*.
By the rule "śataranumaḥ," the case-ending beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) receives the udātta accent. Thus: *rātiḥ*.

In *rā*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] because of the rule *dāne*. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. [The form] *astidham* [is derived from the root] *sidhu* in the sense of drying up; the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad* and so forth. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final syllable of the second member is acute by the rule *nambubhyām*. In *mayaskarat*: the suffix *leṭ* is applied to the root *kṛ*, with the augment *aṭ*; by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix; and by the rule *ataḥ kṛkami*, the visarga is changed to *s*.
May that wind blow upon us as a source of well-being, a healing balm; may Mother Earth grant it, and Father Heaven grant it.
May the pressing-stones that extract Soma grant that which brings well-being; O Ashvins, you who are worthy of praise, hear this!

May that wind blow upon us as a bringer of joy; may it blow healing medicine. May Mother Earth grant it, and Father Heaven grant it; may the pressing-stones that extract Soma, the bringers of joy, grant it. O Aśvins, you who are worthy of our prayers, hear this! 4.
May the wind, the air—that medicine—reach us;
may it bring that healing remedy. May the mother, the earth, the ground—the nourisher of happiness—also bring that medicine to us.
"May the Father, the sky—the heavenly world which protects all by bestowing rain—bring us that medicine.

May the pressing-stones—the stones that are the means of extraction, which have pressed the Soma, which have overcome the Soma, and which bring about the bliss (*maya*) consisting of the happiness derived from sacrifice—bring us that medicine. O you who are worthy of praise (*dhiṣṇyāḥ*)!"
*Dhiṣaṇā* means intellect.

On that day, O Aśvins, "you two" *śṛṇutam*—that is, listen to—that *bheṣajam*, the medicine which is sought by us in sacrifices and in the assemblies; the meaning is: "O physicians of the gods, you two should understand it in such a way as to be favorable toward us."
Mayobhu.
The shortening [of the final vowel] occurs by the rule *hasvo napuṃsake prātipadikasya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.47).
Vātu.

The root *vā* has the sense of "going" (*gati*) and "smelling" (*gandha*). Here, it is used in the sense of "praying" (*prārthanā*) with the *leṭ* suffix, which implies a causative meaning (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*).
[He is] a Soma-presser (*somasya sut*).
In the word *dhiṣṇyā*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the past tense (*bhūte*) according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.90. From the word *dhiṣaṇā*,
the suffix *ya* is applied in the same sense by the rule “*chandasi ca*” [Pāṇini 4.1.45].
The elision of the vowel is Vedic;
the form [with the long vowel] is due to the rule "supāṃ suluk" (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
We invoke that Īśāna, the Lord of all that moves and stands, the stimulator of the intellect,
for our protection— just as Pūṣan, the undeceivable guardian and protector, is present for the preservation of our wealth and for our well-being.

Him, the Lord of all that moves and stands, the inspirer of the intellect, we invoke for protection. May Pūṣan be the increaser of our wealth, our guardian and infallible protector for our well-being. 5.
In the first half-verse Indra is praised; in the second half-verse Pūṣan [is praised].

"We invoke for protection—that is, for our preservation—that very Indra, who is the Lord (īśāna), the possessor of sovereignty (aiśvaryavanta); therefore, the Lord (pati) of all that moves (jaṅgama), the class of living beings, and all that is stationary (tasthuḥ), the immobile; who gratifies the intellect (dhiyaṃjinva), being one who is to be pleased by thoughts and ritual acts. Such is he whom we call upon.

May Pūṣan be our protector for the increase of our wealth; in whatever manner he may be so, in that very manner may the undeceivable Pūṣan, unharmed by anyone, be our guardian for our well-being and our protector for our non-destruction.
*tasthuṣaḥ*:
[this is] the *kasu* suffix in the third person singular of the present indicative (*leṭ*) derived from the root *sthā*,
used in the genitive case.
1. When the *visarjanīya* following *kṣam* is elided, there is a collective (*sāṃghātika*) *satva*.

2. From *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *sa*, [the form] *bhavati* becomes *bhavet*. By that very same process, may he who is the protector (*rakṣitā*), the guardian (*pālayitā*), the protector (*pāyuḥ*), the savior (*pātā*) of that which has entered [into him], the undeceived (*adabdhaḥ*)—not harmed by anyone—he himself, as Pūṣan, be for our well-being (*svastaye*) and for our non-destruction.

In the word *vasoḥ*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule “*vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*”. There is the substitution of *ṣ* according to the rule “*śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*”. There is the substitution of *s* for the *visarjanīya* according to the rule “*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ patiputra...*”. [The word] *dhiyaṃjinvan*: the root *jiv* means "to please. The suffix *khac* is applied by virtue of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) in the rule “*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*”. The augment *am* is added according to the rule “*ica ekāco'm pratyayavat ca*” (Pāṇini 6.3.68). [The word] *asan*: from the root *as* meaning "to be," in the *leṭ* mood, with the augment *aṭ*. The elision of the suffix *śap* occurs by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*”. [The word] *pāyuḥ*: from the root *pā* meaning "to protect," the suffix *uṇ* is applied according to the rule “*kṛvāpājī...*”. Regarding *svastaye*: it is derived from the prefix *su-* and the root *as* in the sense of abstract state (*bhāve*), with the suffix *ktin*. It is stated in the commentary that because the suffix is treated as both [sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka] in Vedic, the substitution of *bhū* for *as* (Pāṇini 2.4.52) does not take place. || 15 ||
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with uninjured wheels grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.

May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all things, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbroken, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. 6.

Vṛddhaśravāḥ: He whose fame (*śravaḥ*), hearing, praise, or food characterized by oblations (*havis*) is great (*vṛddham*, *prabhūtam*). That Indra—may he grant us (*naḥ*) *svasti*; "Svasti" is a name for non-destruction (*avināśa*); may he bestow, may he ordain, may he effect our well-being. Viśvavedāḥ: One who knows all things is Viśvavedāḥ; or rather, one whose possessions (*vedāṃsi*)—that is, all knowledges or riches—are universal. May such a Pūṣan, the nourishing deity, grant us *svasti*. Ariṣṭanemiḥ: "Nemi" is a name for a weapon. One whose weapon is unharmed (*ariṣṭa*) or uninjured is Ariṣṭanemi. Or, "nemi" refers to the rim of a chariot wheel; one whose chariot's rim is not damaged is Ariṣṭanemi. May Tārkṣya, the son of Takṣan, namely Garuḍa, being such as this, grant us *svasti*, that is, non-destruction. Likewise, Bṛhaspati—the protector (*pati*) of the great gods (*bṛhatām devānām*)—may he grant us *svasti*, non-destruction. Regarding the accentuation: in *vṛddhaśravāḥ*, the first member of the *bahuvrīhi* compound retains its original accent. In *viśvavedāḥ*, from the roots *vida* (to know) and *vidl* (to obtain), the word *veda* is formed with the suffix *un*. In the *bahuvrīhi* "Viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām," the final syllable of the first member is udātta. *Tārkṣyaḥ*: the descendant of Takṣan; by *Pāṇini* 4.1.105 (*gargādibhyo yañ*), the suffix *yañ* is applied. Because it has the marker *ji*, the first syllable is udātta. *Ariṣṭanemiḥ*: "Not harmed" is *ariṣṭā*. This is an *avyaya-pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara* (the first member, being an indeclinable, retains its original accent). One whose rim is *ariṣṭa* is so called. *Bṛhaspatiḥ*: by the rule *tadbṛhatoḥ karapatyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.157, Gaṇapāṭha), there is elision of the suffix *sut*. By the rule *ubhe vanaspatyādiṣu*, both the preceding and following members simultaneously retain their original accents.
The Maruts, whose horses are spotted, whose mother is Pṛśni, who move in splendor and frequent the assemblies;
the wise ones who have Agni for their tongue and the sun for their eyes—may all the gods come here with their protection.

The Maruts, with spotted horses, sons of Pṛśni, who move in splendor, who go to the assemblies, whose tongue is Agni, who are wise, and who have the sun as their eye—may all those gods come here to us with their protection. 7.

*vṛṣadaśvāḥ*: those whose horses are *pṛśni*, meaning marked with white spots; thus they are so called. *vṛśnimātaraḥ*: those whose mother is a *pṛśni* cow—that is, a cow of variegated color. *śubhaṃyāvānaḥ*: those who go toward or attain what is auspicious (*śubham*); that is, those of beautiful movement. (Note: 1. The root *kṣa* is *sa-pā pāne*; 2.
In the *ḍha* recension, there is an absence of the substitution of *bhū* for *as*).
In the sacrifices being performed, let those who have the sacrifice as their vehicle, the fire-tongued ones—meaning those who abide upon the tongue of Agni—come;
for all the gods abide upon the tongue of Agni for the purpose of accepting the oblation.
Such is the designation [of the gods] based on that [fact].

The Manavas, the thinkers of all, possessing beautiful vision—those Maruts known as the Maruts, whose vision shines like the light of the sun—may all those gods come here at this time to us with protection.
*Śubhaṃyāvānaḥ*: [The root] *yā* means "to reach" (*prāpaṇe*). The suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule *ātāṃ manin*.
In the compound *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*, because of the word *bahulam* (variously), there is no elision (*aluk*) even of the second case ending. [Thus we have] *gaman*.
From the root *gam*, in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*), the suffix *leṭ* is applied with the augment *aṭ*.
The elision of the letter *i* occurs by the rule "itaśca lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.97),
and the elision of the suffix *śap* occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73).

At the third pressing, there is an oblation of cooked rice (caru) for Agni-Soma. Having offered that caru to the deity, one should pour a great deal of clarified butter into the remains of the offering. Within that [butter], one’s own shadow should be seen as the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call.
If it is not seen, then at that time the single verse beginning with “bhadram” should be recited.
In the section beginning with “*tvaṃ soma*,” it is likewise enjoined: “*rājñā somena tadvayamasmāsu dhārayāmasi bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ śṛṇuyāma devā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.19).
This [verse] is also to be muttered (*japya*) upon touching the ground at the conclusion of the Mahānāmnī hymns.
And it is prescribed in the section beginning with “*etadvidam*”: “*bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ śṛṇuyāma devāḥ śaṃ na indrāgnī bhavatāmavobhiḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.14).
O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.
With steady limbs and bodies, may we, offering praise, attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.

O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. With firm limbs and bodies, having offered praise, may we attain the full span of life ordained by the Gods. 8.

O Gods—those endowed with qualities such as generosity—may all the gods hear auspicious, worshipful, and beneficial speech with our ears; through your grace, may we be capable of hearing, and may deafness never befall us. O Sacrificial Ones—O gods who are to be worshipped in sacrifices with offerings of *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and so forth—may we see what is auspicious and beautiful with our eyes, our physical organs of sight; may we be capable of seeing.
May there be no obstruction to our vision.

Endowed with firm and strong limbs—such as hands, feet, and other members—as well as with healthy bodies, may we, while offering praise and extolling you, attain that lifespan of one hundred and sixteen or one hundred and twenty years which is ordained by the Divine, established by Prajāpati.
In *karṇebhiḥ*, the substitution of *ais* for the case-ending *bhis* occurs by the rule *bahulam chandasi*;
in *akṣabhiḥ*,
the substitution of *anaṅ* occurs by the rule *chandasy api dṛśyate*, and that [substitute] is acute-accented (*udātta*).
“Worshipful ones” (*yajatrāḥ*): the suffix *atrap* is applied to the root *yaj* by [Pāṇini 3.2.134], *aminakṣa*, etc.; [the participle] “having praised” (*tuṣṭuvāṃsaḥ*).
The root *duṣ* is used in the sense of "praising poorly.
After the *liṭ* suffix, the *kasu* affix is applied;
by the rule *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ*, the letter *n* remains [as the substitute for the final consonant].
Aśeṣa:
from the root *aś* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāptau*),
with the suffix *liṅ* in the sense of a benediction (*āśiṣi*) and the augment *aṅ*.
If, however, the enumeration there is for the purpose of excluding others, then the *śap* affix occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) in place of the *liṅ*. [The word] *devahitam*:
by the rule “the third case retains its original accent when used as the object,” the first member of the compound retains its natural accent.
1. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, and ḍha, the word "devāḥ" is absent.
2. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, and ḍha, it is as follows (ityeṣā). 3. It is not formulated as a sūtra in the manuscript na.
4. *Kṣa*-bhūmi-contact.
5. In *kṣa-ṭa-ḍha*, the phrase "all the gods" (*sarve devāḥ*) is absent.

6. In *kṣa-ṭa-ḍha-sa*, immediately after the word "beings" (*bhūt*), [it is stated]: "The hearing of auspicious and inauspicious objects by the ear and the seeing by the eye are restricted [to their respective domains]."
Therefore, it is prayed that there may always be hearing and seeing of auspicious objects; this is the prayer (*sa-prārthyam*).
[The verse continues: "O Gods, a hundred autumns are near us, within which you have ordained the aging of our bodies; therein sons become fathers. Do not harm our life-span in its middle course."
A hundred autumns are indeed before us, O gods, within which you have ordained the aging of our bodies—that time when sons become fathers. Do not harm our life-span in its midst as it passes away. 9.
O Gods, those autumns—the years—ordained by you as the lifespan for human beings, are indeed but a hundred.
Since at the time of creation it was ordained by you that the lifespan of humans is a hundred years, therefore, before the departure of our full lifespan, do not harm us in the midst of it.
Of what sort [are we]?
"Make for us, for our bodies, old age—that state in which [you have made it]—and in which our sons become our protectors, like fathers.
Such is the meaning of what has been attained.

[The form] *anti* [is derived from] the word *antika*; the elision of the *ka* suffix is established by the rule stating that "the elision of *ka* and other suffixes occurs diversely (*bahulam*). [This applies] where...

In the *saṃhitā*, there is lengthening [of the vowel] according to the rule “*ṛci tunughamakṣutaṅkutra*”. [The form] *cakre* [is derived from the root *kṛ*]; because the middle voice plural ending of the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is *kit*, there is an absence of *guṇa*, and consequently, the *yaṇ* substitution [of *ṛ* for *ar*] occurs.
In the *saṃhitā* [text], there is lengthening according to the rule "brāhmaṇo'stiṅaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.154).
Regarding *jarasam*: the substitution of *jaras-* occurs by the rule "jarāyā jaras anyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 7.2.101).
*madhyā*: the substitution of *ḍā* for the locative case ending is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *ririṣat*.

From the root *rūp* (in the sense of "injury"), with the suffix *pya*, in the *luṅ* tense, in the second person plural, after the substitution of *caṅ* for *cli*, there occurs the elision of *ṇi*, the substitution of *svat* for the penultimate vowel, reduplication, the remaining of the initial consonant (*halādiśeṣa*), the treatment as *saṇvat*, the substitution of *it*, and the lengthening of the vowel.
The shortening [of the vowel] is Vedic and occurs at the time of the *pada* recitation.
[The form is] *gantauḥ*.
The suffix *tosun* is applied to the root *gam* by the rule *bhāvalakṣaṇe stheṇ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.16).
‘Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space’—this verse is the invitatory formula (*yājyā*) for the oblation in an animal sacrifice dedicated to the deity Aditi.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space... neither one being born nor one already born [surpasses thee], O Viṣṇu’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).
Aditi is the sky, Aditi is the mid-air; Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son;
all the gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi; Aditi is what has been born, Aditi is what is to be born.

Aditi is the sky; Aditi is the mid-air; Aditi is the mother; she is the father; she is the son; all the gods are Aditi; the five peoples are Aditi; Aditi is what has been born; Aditi is what is to be born. 10.
*Aditi*—whether as the undepressed or indivisible Earth, or as the Mother of the Gods—is herself *dyauḥ*, the luminous firmament;
she is herself *antarikṣam*, the sky visible between heaven and earth;
and she is herself *mātā*, the fashioner and mother of the world.
She alone is the father, the progenitor;
and therefore she is also the son, for even the son born of mother and father is she alone.
All the gods, every deity whatsoever, are Aditi herself.
The "five peoples" (pañca janāḥ) are the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth;
or alternatively, they are the Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Devas, Asuras, and Rakṣases. In that state where sons—meaning fathers of their own sons—are [present], [the verse continues].
2. Between the word *sa-* and *bhavanti*, there is an addition: “Or rather:
in which state (*yatra yasyām avasthāyām*) our sons (*putrāsaḥ*), being fathers of their own sons, become [the grandsons] of us;

that is, when they become our grandsons (*pautrāḥ*). 3. [The following operations apply: elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*), substitution of *a* for the penultimate vowel (*upadhāsvatva*), substitution of *ar* (*arvatva*), reduplication (*dvirvacana*), application of the rule for the *sa*-class (*halādiśeṣa*), the *sa*-class treatment (*sanvadbhāva*), substitution of *it* (*itva*), and lengthening (*dīrgha*).
4. And [the fifth] is the *kṣatriya* (*kṣana-satāt*).

This was stated by Yāska: "Some say that the Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Devas, Asuras, and Rakṣases [are the five]; Aupamanyava says there are four castes (*varṇas*) and the Niṣādas as the fifth" (*Nirukta* 3.8).

In the Brāhmaṇa, however, it is handed down thus: "This is indeed the generative hymn (*uktha*) for all—of gods, humans, Gandharvas, Apsarases, serpents (*sarpas*), and Pitṛs" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 3.31).

In that context, the Gandharvas and Apsarases constitute the "five people" (*pañca-janatva*) because they form a single unity. Furthermore, the fivefold "five people" are indeed Aditi; likewise, birth—the production of progeny—is also Aditi;
and the locus of birth is also Aditi alone.
Thus Aditi is praised as the self of the entire world. And it has been stated by Yāska: "In this way, he describes the all-pervading nature of Aditi" (Nirukta 4.23).
*Aditi*:
[derived from] the root *dā* in the sense of "cutting" (*avakhaṇḍane*).
From this, with the suffix *ktin* in the passive sense, the substitution of *i* for *ā* occurs by Pāṇini’s rule 7.4.40: *ghatisyatimāsthām*.
According to Yāska’s view, however, from the root *dīṅ* "to perish" with the suffix *ktin*, there is shortening by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
In the compound *nabhasāse*, the original accent of the indeclinable preceding member (*avyayapūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratva*) applies. He is the father.

All measures of proof bring about the identity between that which is being indicated and that which is being further specified; they assume its gender alternately, and thus the gender of the subject is masculine.
[The word *janitva* is derived as follows: from the root *jan*, with the suffix *tvan* according to the *uṇādi* list. 2.
The sixth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "ṛjunītī," is the seerly work of Gautama.
It is enumerated there as: "ṛjunītī [has] nine; Gāyatrī, with one [verse] in Triṣṭubh.
Since it was previously stated that [the preceding hymn] was addressed to the Viśvedevas, by the technical rule regarding the *tuṣṭādi* group, this hymn as well has multiple deities.
The application of the *sūkta* is based on its indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
On the twenty-fourth day, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), this verse, "ṛjunītī naḥ," is the *ārambhaṇīyā* for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest.
This is prescribed in the section titled "Caturviṃśe" in the Sūtra: "ṛjunītī no varuṇa indra vo viśvataspari" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.2).
In the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), the *ārambhaṇīyā* [offering] should be recited even on the second and subsequent days.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The *ārambhaṇīyās*, the *paryāsa*s, and the *dhāyyā*s are to be recited by the Hotṛ-priests on the second and subsequent days alone" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.1).

May Varuṇa and Mitra, the wise one, lead us with upright guidance; may Aryaman, in harmony with the gods, do the same. (1) May Varuṇa and Mitra, the wise one, lead us with upright guidance; may Aryaman, in harmony with the gods, do the same. (1)

May the god Mitra, who presides over the day, and Varuṇa, who presides over sovereignty—Mitra and Varuṇa, the "knowing" ones who know the supreme station to which we are to be led—lead us by a straight path (*ṛjunītī*), that is, by a straightforward course free from crookedness, and cause us to attain our desired goal. Likewise, may Aryaman, the maker of the division of day and night, and Sūrya, acting in harmony (*sajoṣaḥ*) with the other gods such as Indra, lead us to the desired place by following after us.
In the word *ṛjunītī*,
the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) undergoes a long vowel substitution with the preceding vowel according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).

For they, as masters of wealth, are the possessors of riches; they, being unassailable through their greatness, protect the sacred laws at all times. 2. They—for they are the possessors of wealth; they, being unassailable, by means of their greatness, protect the sacred laws every day. 2.
For those aforementioned ones, Mitra and the others, are "vasavaḥ"—that is, possessors of wealth (*vasu*), providers, or coverers; the meaning is that they cover the entire world with it.

Therefore, those Mitra and the others, being "apramūrāḥ"—that is, not perishing, undeluded, and wise—[shine] "viśvāhā" (all days) with their own "maho-bhiḥ," that is, with their splendors. The accusative case is used here to denote continuous duration.
All of them, through their respective vows—which consist of the maintenance of the world—protect and preserve their own duties.
Of the *Āgama-anuśāsana* (the instruction on traditional grammar).

1. *Kṣa*: The section on birth (*janmādhikaraṇam*). Or rather, that which has been born, produced, or is about to be produced—whatever exists as "birth-ness" (*janitvam*). 2. *Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa*: The elision of *it* (the *it*-marker). 3. *Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: The phrase "for us, [lead] by a straight path" (*ṛjunītāṃ naḥ*) is not present here. 4. *Kṣa-ṭe-ṭha*: The augment *āy*. 5. *Na-sa*: The divider of day and night (*ahorātrasya vibhāgakartā*).

Because of its being *anitya* (non-eternal), there is no addition of the suffix *num*. In the case of the forms beginning with *ajasra*, because of the rule "optionally in the Veda for *ghi*-stems before endings beginning with *ḍit*" (*gher ḍiti*), the *guṇa* substitution is optional; when it is absent, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs. Thus: *vasavānāḥ*. [The root] *vas* means "to cover. From this, with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the present participle suffix *śānac* is applied. By the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulam chandasi*), there is no elision of the *śap* suffix. Through the substitution of one letter for another (*varṇavyāpatti*), the *m* is changed to *v*. *Apramūrāḥ*: [The root] *murch* means "to faint" or "to rise up. From this, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad* and others. By the rule "elision after *ra* and *l*" (*rāllopaḥ*), the *ch* is dropped. *Prabhūḥ* is "excellent rising. From that, the possessive suffix *ura* is added. By the rule "the *r* is elided before *r*" (*ro ri*), the first *r* is dropped. Those who do not faint are *apramūrāḥ*. The accent is that of the original form of the indeclinable as the prior member of the compound. *Rakṣante*: [The root] *rakṣ* means "to protect. The *taṅ* (middle voice) ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
May they, the immortals, grant protection to us mortals,
driving away our enemies.
May they, the immortals, grant protection to us mortals, driving away our enemies. 3.

May all those gods, who are immortal and possess the nature of the immortals, grant—bestow—upon us mortals, that is, upon us practitioners who are subject to death, *śarma*, meaning happiness characterized by immortality.
What are they doing?
Driving away—that is, bringing to destruction—our enemies, which are of the nature of sin.
*Yamsan*: from the root *yam*, meaning "to cease" (*uparame*). In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *ad*.
Regarding the form *sipbahula leṭi*: the suffix is *sip*. *Amṛtāḥ*:
those for whom death (*mṛtaṃ*), meaning dying, does not exist are *amṛtāḥ* (immortals).
In the word *ajara-mara-mitra-mṛtaḥ*, the final syllable of the compound is udātta according to the rule "naño jaramaramitramṛtāḥ."
May Indra, the Maruts, Pūṣan, and Bhaga— those worthy of praise— clear our paths for us toward a prosperous journey.
May Indra, the Maruts, Pūṣan, and Bhaga—the ones worthy of praise—prepare our paths for a prosperous journey. 4.
May the gods, Indra and the others—who are to be revered by all, worthy of praise, worthy of hymns, and worthy of salutation—discern our paths; that is, may they separate us from unseemly paths.
For what purpose? For *suvitāya*: for the attainment of excellent results, such as heaven and the like.

In the case of the [suffix] *śas*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* by the rule "the *ṭi* of a *bha*-stem is elided. The acute accent (*udātta*) of the *śas* is due to the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*.
For "suvitāya": the suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) to the root *iṇ* meaning "to go.
The substitution *uvaṅ* occurs according to the rule: "In the Vedic language, there is an extensive extension (*bahulam upasaṃkhyānam*) of the application [of *uvaṅ*] to stems beginning with *tanu*."

In the phrase "gatiranantaraḥ," although the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member would have applied, the rule "sūpamānāt kaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.145) results in the final syllable of the subsequent member being accented. *Ciyan tu*: from the root *ciñ* in the sense of "accumulating."

By the rule "bahulam chandasi," there is elision (luk) of the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa). The substitution *iyaṅ* occurs. Because it begins a quarter-verse (*pāda*), there is no suppression of accent (*nighāta*).
They are to be revered (*vandyāsaḥ*). [The root] *vadi* [is used] in the sense of salutation and praise. [The suffix] *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*.
The initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is due to the rule *īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ pyataḥ*;
[the substitution] *asuk* occurs by the rule *ājaserasuk*.
In the *Asūyām* there are four *atiriktoktha* [additional hymns].
Among them, in the fourth *atiriktoktha* belonging to the *acchāvāka*, the verse "uta no dhiyaḥ" is the optional third verse of the *anurūpa-trca*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Or, 'uta no dhiyo goagrāḥ' is the last [verse] of the *anurūpa*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 9.11).
And may you, O Pūṣan, make our prayers—headed by the desire for cattle—successful for Viṣṇu, O swift one;
make us possessed of well-being.
And also, O Pūṣan, O Viṣṇu, who move with rapid strides, make our prayers rich in cattle and grant us prosperity. 5.
O Pūṣan, the nourishing god; O Viṣṇu, the all-pervading god;
O Evayāvas—the host of Maruts so called because they go (*yāti*) with swift-moving horses (*evaiḥ*).
O host of Maruts, may you all [further] our thoughts (*dhiyaḥ*), characterized by non-confusion. (Ṛgveda 7.39.5)
O performers of rites, make for us from our side five kinds of animals, headed by the cow and the bull, accompanied by eight other animals.

For it is traditionally taught that these serve as the cause for grasping the sacrificial animals: "He by whom the animals might fall away prematurely should sacrifice with this [rite]" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.7.14.2).
And furthermore, make us possessed of well-being, that is, free from destruction.
*Evayāvaḥ*: [derived from] the root *iṇ* ‘to go’; the suffix *van* is applied according to the rule *iṇdhīṅbhyāṃ van*.
In this word *jup* [of *jupamāna*], the suffix *vanip* is applied after the root *yā* in the sense of "attaining," according to the rule *āto maninkvanibvanipaśca*.
In the vocative case, the *n* becomes *r* by the rule *vana upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 8.2.1).
The recipient, such as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), should gaze upon the *madhuparka* that has been brought for his sake while reciting the three verses beginning with "madhu vātāḥ.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Having gazed [upon it] with the three verses beginning 'madhu vātā ṛtāyate'" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.24.14).

*madhu vātā ṛtāyate madhu kṣaranti sindhavaḥ | mādhvīrnaḥ santvoṣadhīḥ ||6||* Honey for the one who acts according to the Truth; honey the winds blow; honey the rivers flow. May the plants be sweet for us. ||6|| *madhu* | *vātāḥ* | *ṛtāyate* | *madhu* | *kṣaranti* | *sindhavaḥ* | *mādhvīḥ* | *naḥ* | *santu* | *oṣadhīḥ* ||6||

For the sacrificer who seeks the sacrifice—the truth—for himself, the winds (āvātāḥ), meaning the breezes, "flow" (kṣaranti)—that is, they rain down or bestow—honey (madhu), meaning the fruit of action endowed with sweetness.
Likewise, the rivers (sindhavaḥ)—those characterized by flowing—or the oceans, flow their own essence endowed with sweetness.
In this way, may the plants (oṣadhīḥ)—the herbs that end with the ripening of their fruit—be sweet (mādhvīḥ) for us (naḥ); may they be endowed with sweetness.
*madhu*.

By the rule "the suffix expressing the possessive sense (*matvarthīya*) following this [word] is elided, and *kāra*, *īkāra*, and *repha* are to be stated as substitutes" (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.4.128.2), there is elision (*luk*).
Thus: *ṛtāyate*.

One desires the *ṛta* for oneself. [This is derived] by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*. The prohibition of the substitution of *ī* and lengthening [of the vowel] is applied by the rule *na chandasyaputrasya*.
For others as well, there is lengthening in *saṃhitā*. From a consonant, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied to the present tense (*laṭ*).
By the rule "the case-ending following *śatṛ* when it ends in *an* is udātta," the case-ending is accented.
*Mādhvīḥ*:
The suffix *ap* is added in the sense of possession according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 4.4.129 (*madhoraśca*).
In forms such as *ṛtvyāvasya*, the substitution of *yaṇ* is prescribed by nipātana (irregular derivation) when the suffix *añ* follows.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) is applied [to form] *oṣadhīḥ*. [The word] *oṣadhayaḥ* [is derived as follows]: that which contains ripening (*pāka*) within itself is called an *oṣadhi*.
The suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca*;
the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *kṛdikārād aktinaḥ*;
and in the nominative plural (*jasi*), there is the long vowel resulting from the homogeneity with the preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*), as before.

Because it is read in the *dāsībhārādi* group, the first member of the compound retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Furthermore, that [first member] ending in the suffix *-gha* is acute on the first syllable. May the night be honey-sweet; may the dawns be honey-sweet; may the earthly realm be full of honey. May the sky, our father, be honey-sweet for us. (7) madhu | naktam | uta | uṣasaḥ | madhumat | pārthivam | rajaḥ | madhu | dyauḥ | astu | naḥ | pitā ||7||
"May the night be honeyed for us"—that is, may it grant fruits endowed with sweetness.
"And also," may the dawns—the days characterized by the time of dawn—be honeyed.
May the earthly realm—the world connected to the earth—be honeyed for us, that is, possessed of fruits distinguished by sweetness.
"May the Father, the heavenly world (*dyauḥ*), which protects all by bestowing rain, also become *madhu*—that is, full of sweetness.
[The word] *pārthivaṃ* [is derived from *pṛthivī*]; according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 4.1.85.2, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of *prāgdīvyatīya*."
*Rajas*. The word *rajas* denotes the worlds; Yāska [states] that "the worlds are called *rajāṃsi*" (Nirukta 4.19).

*Rajas* is so called because people are colored (*rañjanti*) therein. Regarding the suffix *asun*, there is the elision of the root *rañj* according to the rule *rañjakarajanarajaḥsūpasaṃkhyānam* (Kāśikā 6.4.24.4). 1. [The scribes] have made a mistake; it should be *kuruta*.
2. Kṣa—[the scribes] indeed do not provide [this]. 3. Kṣa—"thus" does not exist [in this version].

4. Kṣa—the lengthening is euphonic (sāṃhitika) according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well"; Sa—the lengthening in the *saṃhitā* is according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well."

5. Endowed with the sweetness of kṣa, ṭa, ḍha, and ma: "May the lord of the forest be full of honey for us; may the sun be full of honey; may our cows be sweet for us. (8) madhumān | naḥ | vanaspatiḥ | madhumān | astu | sūryaḥ | mādhvīḥ | gāvaḥ | bhavantu | naḥ ||8|| May the lord of the forest be full of honey for us; may the sun be full of honey; may our cows be sweet for us. (8)
May the *vanaspati*—the protector of the forests, the deity presiding over the sacrificial post—be full of sweetness (*madhumat*) for us;
that is to say, may he grant us such sweet fruit.
May Sūrya, the impeller of all, and Savitṛ also be full of sweetness.
May the cows—the milch-cows intended for the Agnihotra and other rites—be ours, endowed with sweetness through their honeyed milk. Vanaspati:
the Lord of the Forests (vanaspati) is the master of the woods (vana).
The augment *suṭ* is applied because [the compound] belongs to the *pāraskara*-class.
The word *vanaspati* has its acute accent on the first syllable.

According to the rule "In the case of *vanaspati* and similar compounds, both [members] simultaneously," both the preceding and following members take their original (prākṛta) accent at the same time.
May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious, and may Aryaman be auspicious to us;
may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us, and may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us.
Peace! Rigveda [Book 1, Chapter 6, Section 19]:
O Soma, you are distinguished by wisdom; you lead us along the most direct path.
Under your guidance, O Indu, our wise fathers obtained their share of treasure among the gods.
You, O Soma, are discerning through your wisdom; you lead us along the straightest path. Under your guidance, O Indu, our wise fathers obtained their share of treasure among the gods. 1.
O Soma, you have been thoroughly recognized by our *manīṣā*—that is, by our intellect; the meaning is that we have come to know you through hymns of praise.
Therefore, you lead us along the straightest path—the most direct, unswerving way that serves as the cause for attaining the fruits of action.

Furthermore, O *indu*, you who are by nature moistening, O Soma who drenches the entire world with nectar: by your *praṇīti*—by your excellent guidance, that is, by the leading brought about by you—the *dhīrāḥ*, the wise ones, the performers of ritual acts or the possessors of insight, our *pitaraḥ*, our ancestors, *abhajanta*, partook of, or attained, *ratnam*, delightful wealth, among the *devāḥ*, such as Indra and the other gods.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Grant us also such wealth.
Thus he has made it known (*pracakitaḥ*).
‘Kita jñāne. From this root, the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The dual number is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively,
since the *niṣṭhā* suffix follows a form ending in *yalluk*,

there is an absence of *guṇa* in the reduplication according to the rule "guggo yallukoḥ," because a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not invariably obligatory.
Alternatively,

by the rule "chandasyubhayathā," the *niṣṭhā* [suffix] is designated as a *sārvadhātuka*; consequently, the *śap* [augment] is applied, and because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu*.
"Blau" is a dual form. By the rule "gatiranantaraḥ," the preceding member retains its original accent (prakṛtisvara).
[The word is] *manīṣā*.
The substitution of *ḍā* for the third case ending is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
[The form] *rajiṣṭham*: from the word *ṛju*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added, the substitution of *r* occurs by the rule *vibhāṣārchaṇdasi* (Pāṇini 6.4.162).
By the rule "ṭeḥ," there is elision of the final *ṭi*.
[The form] *neṣi* [is derived from] the root *nī* in the *leṭ* mood; by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.

Regarding *panthām*: by the rule *pathimadhyukṣāmān* (Pāṇini 7.1.85), the vowel *ā* occurs here by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Furthermore, by the rule *pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne*, it bears an udātta accent on the initial syllable.

In *praṇītī*, by the rule *tādau ca*, the verbal root *gam* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the third case ending undergoes lengthening to the preceding vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*).
In the Agniṣṭoma, at the Marutvatīya [śastra], the verse "O Soma, you with your powers... is the dhāyyā. And it is stated:
"The dhāyyās are 'Agni as leader,' 'O Soma, with your powers,' and 'Swelling [the waters]'... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.14).
"O Soma, through your powers you have become one of excellent power; through your skills you have become one of excellent skill, the knower of all."
You are the bull by means of your bull-like powers, great through your greatness; you have become resplendent with splendors, O beholder of men. 2.

You, O Soma, by your mental powers have become possessed of good wisdom; you, by your skills, have become highly skilled, the knower of all. You are the bull by means of your bull-like powers, great through your greatness; you have become resplendent with splendors, O beholder of men. 2.

O Soma, through your *kratavaḥ*—that is, through the rites such as the *iṣṭoma* associated with you, or through your own sacrifices—you become one of *sukratu*, possessing excellent deeds or excellent wisdom.
Likewise, as the possessor of all wealth (*viśvavedāḥ*), you become one of *sudakṣa*, possessing excellent strength, through your own *dakṣas*, or powers.

Similarly, through your *vṛṣatvas*, that is, through your qualities of raining down desires, and through your greatness (*mahitvā*) or majesty, you become a *vṛṣan*, a showerer of desires and a great being.
Likewise, you are *nṛcakṣas*, the beholder of men—that is, the one who reveals the intended fruit of the sacrifice for the sacrificers who lead the rite.
[The accent on] *kṣa-* is udātta according to Pāṇini 6.1.197. Of you.
By the rule "yuṣmadasmador ṅe," there is the udātta accent on the initial syllable.

O you who are truly auspicious through your wide-stepping strides, your teeth, and your glances, you have become auspicious; you become abundant for us, O one of excellent wisdom (*sukratu*). In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule “*ṛtvādyaśca*,” there is acute accent on the first syllable of the final member. *Sudakṣaḥ*: from the root *dakṣ* meaning "to increase" or "to be skillful. That by which one increases is *dakṣaḥ*, meaning strength; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). By the rule “*jiravādādyudāttatvam*,” there is acute accent on the first syllable. In the *bahuvrīhi* with the word *su-*, by the rule “*ādyudāttaṃ vyacchandasi*,” there is acute accent on the first syllable of the final member. *Viśvavedāḥ*: he whose wealth (*vedāṃsi*) is all-encompassing (*viśvāni*). In the *bahuvrīhi* “*viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām*,” there is acute accent on the final syllable of the first member. *Vṛṣabhebhiḥ*: the state of being a bull (*vṛṣan*) is *vṛṣabha*. By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” the *ais* ending of the instrumental plural becomes *ais*. *Mahitvā*: from the root *mahi* (related to *mahat*), the suffix *vin* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules. From the noun ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyayāntāt*), the case-ending becomes *ā* by the rule “*supāṃ suluk*.”
O Soma, King Varuṇa, your laws are indeed great;

with all those powers of yours that are in heaven, on earth, in the mountains, in the plants, and in the waters— with them all, being well-disposed and free from malice, O King Soma, accept our offerings.

Those abodes of yours which are in heaven, those on earth, those in the mountains, in the plants, and in the waters—with all of them, O King Soma, being well-disposed and free from malice, accept our offerings. 4.
O Soma, those various abodes or splendors of yours which exist in the sky, the celestial realm;
likewise those which exist on the earth;
and likewise those which exist in the mountains, upon the high peaks of the rocky masses—[all these are yours].

Likewise, O King Soma, you who shine like Soma— endowed with all those splendors that reside in the rice and other plants as well as in the waters, being well-disposed (sumanāḥ) and free from malice (ahailan), that is, not angry— accept, that is, receive, the oblations (havyā), the offerings presented by us.
The elision of the *śi* suffix occurs by the rule "in the remaining Vedic meters, [the suffix] is frequently [elided]"; thus,
[it becomes] *pṛthivyām*.

The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule "udāttayaṇaḥ. In *oṣadhīṣu*, the lengthening is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.132: "oṣadheśca vibhaktāvaprathamāyām" (and there is lengthening of *oṣadhi* before a case-ending that is not the first [nominative]).
In the word *apsu*, the case-ending is acute according to the rule beginning with "uḍidam.
[The word] *sumanāḥ*.

In the word *somānasyā alomapṛṣā*, there is the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member of the compound. [The form] *gṛbhāya* [is derived from] the root *graha* in the sense of "taking" (*upādāne*).
In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), by the rule "śāyaj api," there is the substitution of *śāyac* for the suffix *hvā*.
In the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice, "O thou, O Soma" (*tvaṃ soma*) is the invitatory verse (*anuṣākyā*) for the butter-portion (*ājyabhāga*) dedicated to Soma.
As it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Agniṃ trāṇi jajñāna’ is the invitatory verse for the first butter-portion; ‘tvaṃ somāsi satpatiḥ’ is for the latter" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.5).
Thus, wherever the two butter-portions are "slayers of Vṛtra" (*vātraghnau*), this verse is to be employed in all such instances.
In the morning *upasad*, this very [verse] is the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*) for the principal *saumya* offering;
in the afternoon *upasad*, that same [verse] is the offering formula (*yājyā*).

This is stated in the Sūtra: "O Soma, you are the lord of the virtuous, the increaser of the household, the slayer of enemies," and "The wise ones [are the masters] of the invitatory and offering formulas" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.8).
You are the boundary, the lord of the good; you are the king and the slayer of Vṛtra;
you are the auspicious power of will.
O Soma, you are the lord of the good; you are the king and the slayer of Vṛtra; you are auspicious power. ||5||

O Soma, you are the lord of the virtuous; you are the sovereign of the Brāhmaṇas who abide in their sacred duties, according to the Vedic revelation: "Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas have Soma as their king" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.7.4.2).
Or alternatively:
You are such a Soma as has for its lords and protectors the peaceful Svānas;
thus it is recited in the scripture: "The Svānas, indeed, protected the Soma in that world when the sacrifice was being performed" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.10.5).
Furthermore, you are a king, shining resplendently, and a slayer of Vṛtra—the demon or the enemy.
The auspicious and beautiful sacrifice— this very rite such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others— is you yourself who take that form, because sacrifices are to be accomplished through you.
*Satpatiḥ*: In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
However, in the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is the original accent of the first member according to the rule "patyāvaiśvarye" (Pāṇini 6.2.18).
Following the *sāmidhenī* verses and the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the animal offering to Agni and Soma, eight oblations for the *devasū* deities are offered.
Among these, for the oblation of Vanaspati belonging to Soma, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is "And you, O Soma...

This is prescribed in the section beginning with "Now, by means of the [offering] to Agni and Soma" in the *Sūtra*: "And you, O Soma, who are our will, the Brahman of the gods, the path-maker of the seers" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.11).
1. [The syllables] kṣa-ṭa-ḍha belong to Vṛtra, the obstructing Asura.
2. Even the sacrifice such as the Agniṣṭoma consists of kṣa-ṭa-ḍha.

And you, O Soma, being subject to our will, we shall not die; for you are the beloved Vanaspati praised in the hymn. 6. You, and you, O Soma, being subject to our will, we shall not die; for you are the beloved Vanaspati praised in the hymn. 6.

O Soma, if you and you alone—should so desire (*vaśaḥ*)—then we, your worshippers, shall not die; we shall not perish. What kind of one are you? You are "one whose praises are dear" (*priyastotraḥ*), meaning one for whom hymns of praise are beloved; that is to say, you are one who is to be praised by many.
