You are the "Lord of the Forest" (*vanaspatiḥ*), the protector of the forests consisting of herbs and trees, according to the Vedic revelation: "Soma is indeed the king of herbs" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 6.1.9.1). Regarding *vaśaḥ*: from the root *vaś* "to desire. This is in the *leṭ* mood with the suffix *sip*; the augment *ad* is added. Since the augment is unaccented, the accent of the verbal root remains. The word *tvaṃ ca* contains the particle *ca*, which here functions as the particle *caṇ* in the sense of *ced* ("if"). Consequently, by the rule "when used with particles such as *yat*, *yadi*, *hanta*, etc.," there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of the accent). Regarding *jīvātūm*: from the root *jīv* "to sustain life. By the *Uṇādi* sūtra *jīverātaḥ* (1.79), the suffix *ātu* is applied. Regarding *marāmahe*: from the root *mṛ* "to die. The suffix *śap* is applied by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
In the *Āyuṣkāmeṣṭi*, the verse “*tvaṃ soma mahe bhagam*” is the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*) for the second portion of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*).
This is stated in the section beginning with “Now, the optional rites” (*atha kāmyāḥ*) in the Sūtra: “*ā no agne sucetunā, tvaṃ soma mahe bhagam*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.10).

O Soma, you bestow great fortune; you bestow skill upon the youth who follows the cosmic order, so that he may live. 7. You, O Soma... great... fortune... you... the youth... to the one who follows the cosmic order... skill... you bestow... for living. 7.

O Soma, for the great, the mighty, the ancient one who observes the *ṛta*, who desires the *ṛta*—that is, the sacrifice—for himself, you bestow, provide, and grant *dakṣa*, meaning wealth capable of enjoyment, so that he may live. Likewise, you provide wealth for the youth, the young man who observes the *ṛta*, so that he may live. *Mahe*: "for the great. The elision of the case-ending (*acchada-lopa*) is Vedic. The acute accent on the case-ending is according to the rule "an addition to *brahman* and *mahat*. *Yūna*: "for the youth. The vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule "the substitution of *u* for *yu*, *va*, and *magha* when no *taddhita* suffix follows. *Ṛtāyate*: "who desires the *ṛta*. He desires it for himself (*ṛtam ātmana icchati*). The suffix *kyac* is added after a noun ending in a case-suffix to express self-interest (*supa ātmanaḥ kyac*). The prohibition of the *ī*-vowel and the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule "not in the Veda for words other than *putra*" applies here. The lengthening in the *saṃhitā* text is according to the rule "it is seen in others as well. From the stem ending in *kyac*, the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is added. The acute accent on the case-ending is according to the rule "the case-ending following a word ending in *śatṛ* or *anu* is acute, provided it does not begin with a vowel. *Jīvase*: "in order to live. The root *jīv* means "to sustain life. The suffix *ase* is added in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*) by the rule "the suffix *ase* is used in the sense of *tumun*."
The verse beginning with "tvaṃ naḥ soma" is the invitatory formula (*anu-vākyā*) for the second *ājyabhāga* offering, which is the *svastyayanī*.
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "The *svastyayanī*, 'rakṣitavanta', 'avame rakṣā ṇo ahasaḥ', and 'tvaṃ naḥ soma viśvataḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.10).

O Soma, O King, protect us from every side against the one who intends evil; may the friend who relies upon you never come to harm. 8. You. Us. O Soma. From all sides. Protect. O King. From the malevolent. May not. Perish. The friend. Of you. 8.
O King Soma, you who possess the nature of a king, [ward off] evil from him who intends evil— evil meaning sin—
and who desires to cause us suffering on account of that.
Protect and preserve us from every person, from everyone whatsoever.
A man who has attained friendship with one such as you—your equal—is not to suffer harm; he shall not perish. What need is there to say that your friend shall not perish?

*aghāyataḥ*: 1. *kṣa* has the sense of "if. One who desires evil (*agha*), that is, sin, against others is *aghāyan*. [The suffix] *kyac* is applied according to the rule “in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the suffix *kyac* is added] even for the desire of another. [The substitution of] *ā* [for the final vowel] occurs according to the rule “*aghāghasyāt*. *riyet*: from the roots *rup* and *rip*, meaning “to injure. *svāvataḥ*: the suffix *vatup* is applied according to the rule “in the section on *vatup*, there is an addition for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the Vedic language when expressing similarity. [The substitution of] *tvā* [for the portion ending in *m*] occurs according to the rule “*pratyayottarapadayośca*. [The substitution of] *ā* [for the final vowel] occurs according to the rule “*ā sarvanāmnaḥ*.”

In the *somapravahaṇa* [rite], the triplet beginning with "O Soma, those [streams] of yours which... (*soma yāste*) should be recited. This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The three verses beginning with 'O Soma, those [streams] of yours which bring delight' (*soma yāste mayobhuvaḥ*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.4).
In the *āgrayaṇa* [offering], this same verse, "O Soma, those [streams] of yours," serves as the invitatory formula (*anuṣākyā*) for the offering to Soma.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “O Soma, those [powers] of yours which bring delight, those which are your abodes in heaven and those on earth” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.9).
This same verse is also used as the invitatory mantra for the second *ājyabhāga* offering in the *pauṣṇa-iṣṭi* during the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘Thou, O Agni, art far-extending; O Soma, those [powers] of yours which bring delight’—these two [mantras] are to be recited together” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 10.6).
O Soma, those bliss-bestowing aids of yours that exist for the donor—
with those, be our protector.
O Soma, with those bliss-bestowing aids of yours that exist for the donor, with those become our protector. 9.

O Soma, those protections (*ūtayaḥ*) of yours which exist—those which bring forth joy (*mayobhuvaḥ*), meaning they are the producers of happiness for the sacrificer who has given the *caru*, the *puroḍāśa*, and other offerings—by means of those protections, be our protector (*avitā*), that is, our guardian. Regarding the form *mayobhuvaḥ*: since it functions here as a feminine adjective qualifying *ūti* (protection), the suffix *ṅīṣ* would apply by the rule *bhuvaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.47).

Because of the rule "after a word denoting a quality" (*voto guṇavacanāt*), and because the specification *utaḥ* (the vowel *u* with a long *ṛ*) is carried over from that [rule], [the substitution] does not occur.
O Soma, enjoying this sacrifice and this speech, come hither;
may you be for our prosperity.
Enjoying this sacrifice and this speech, come hither; O Soma, be for our prosperity. 10.

O Soma, having graciously accepted (*jujuṣāṇaḥ*) this sacrifice being performed by us and this speech—the words characterized as praise being uttered now—come hither (*upāgahi*), reach the house characterized by the *prācīnavaṃśa* beam;
and having reached it, be for our increase (*vṛdhe*), that is, for the prosperity of the sacrifice.
[The word] *jujuṣāṇaḥ*.
The root *juṣ* means "to delight in" and "to serve.
In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) is used;
for the *liṭ*, the suffix *kānac* is applied.
The word *citaḥ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). [In the phrase] *upāgahi*,
there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* applied to the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *gam*.
The elision of the letter *m* occurs by the rule beginning with “anudāttopadeśa...”.
Because of the status of this [rule] as "not established" (*asiddha*) by the principle “asiddhavadatrā bhāt”, there is no elision (*luk*) of the imperative suffix *hi*.
By the rule “gatirgatau” (Pāṇini 8.1.70), the preceding verb is unaccented (*nighāta*).
In the Darśa sacrifice, for the *saumya* portion of the clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is "O Soma, with our songs...
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "Agni with a forward-moving mind, or we with songs, O Soma" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.5).

Elsewhere also, wherever the two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word *vṛdhanvat*, this verse serves as the second *anuvākyā* for the *ājyabhāga*: "O Soma, we who know the sacred word magnify you with our songs; enter into us, being most gracious."
O Soma, we increase you with our songs, we who know the sacred word; as one most gracious, enter into us. 11.
1. *kṣa*—of him.

O *soma*, we—the performers of the rite who are *vacovidaḥ*, knowers of the words characterized by praise—strengthen (*vardhayāmaḥ*) you with *gīrbhiḥ*, with words characterized by praise; we cause you to grow.
And you, being such, as one who bestows excellent happiness (*sumṛḍīkaḥ*), enter (*ā viśa*) us; come to us.
*Sumṛḷīkaḥ*:
[derived from] the root *mṛḍ* in the sense of "to gladden" (*sukhane*).
According to the *Uṇādisūtra* 4.464, *mṛḍeḥ kīkankanau*, the suffix *kīkan* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
In the bahuvrīhi compound *śobhanaṃ mṛḍīkaṃ yasya*, the final syllable of the second member is udātta according to the rule *nañsubhyām*.
There are three [hymns] dedicated to Pavamāna.
Among them, for the third sacrifice, this verse beginning with "gayasphānaḥ" is the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the second *ājyabhāga* offering.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] containing the word *puṣṭi*, [beginning with] 'agninā rayimakṣavat' and 'gayasphāno amīvahā'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.1).
This very [verse] is the *yājyā* for the Soma sacrifice during the morning *upasat*, while it serves as the *anuvākyā* for the evening *upasat*.

And it is stated in the section beginning with "Now, the *upasat*" (*athopasat*) in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (4.8): "O Soma, you are the lord of the world, the increaser of wealth, the dispeller of disease."
Increasing our cattle-pastures, driving away disease, finding wealth, and increasing prosperity— O Soma, be a kind friend to us.
Increasing our cattle, driving away disease, finding wealth, augmenting prosperity, a good friend—O Soma, be such to us. 12.
*Gayasphānaḥ*: *Gaya* is a name for wealth;

thus, he is the increaser of wealth. *Amīvahā*: the destroyer of *amīva*s, that is, of diseases. *Vasuvit*: the finder of wealth, the one who causes the singers to obtain and reach it. *Puṣṭivardhanaḥ*: the increaser of nourishment and prosperity. *Sumitraḥ*: the good friend.
He who possesses beautiful friends and companions is thus described.
O Soma, may you, distinguished by such qualities, be ours—belong to us.
*Gayasphānaḥ*.
[The root] *sphāyī* means "to increase. Since the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) is inherent, the suffix *hyuṭ* (ana) is applied, and by the rule *dhyalope*, there is the elision of *y*.
In these four words beginning with *idam*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member of the compound when preceded by *ku*.
In *sumitraḥ*, the final syllable of the second member is udātta according to the rule *nañsubhyām*.
O Soma, take delight in our heart, as cattle do in pastures,
like a young man in his own home.
O Soma, take delight in our heart, as cattle in pastures, or as a young man in his own home.
O Soma, do you take delight—that is, rejoice—in our heart;
regarding this, two illustrations are given:
"like cows."

Just as cows delight in the direction of *yavasa*, excellent grass; or just as a mortal, a human subject to death, delights in his own *okya*, his own home with his sons and others— so too, being a benefactor (*nṛmaṇas*) through the oblation offered by us, remain established among us alone.
"Do not go elsewhere"—this is the intended meaning of the two illustrations.
*Rarandhi*:
from the root *ram*, meaning "to sport" or "to delight."
The *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
By the rule "in the Veda [the suffixes] are manifold" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), there is the elision (*ślu*) of the *śap* augment.

Because the *hi* imperative suffix is treated as having both forms (*ubhayathā*) in the Veda, it lacks the *ṅit* quality; consequently, by the rule "also after a root ending in *ad*" (*aditaśca*), the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* does not occur.

For this very reason, because it is not an affix (*adit*), there is no elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*). Since the substitute *hi* (in *serhyapicca*) is not marked with *p*, its own accent remains. The lengthening of the vowel in the reduplication is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Because of the rule "an initial vocative is treated as non-existent," the preceding vocative is considered non-existent; consequently, since it does not follow from a word (*padāt*), there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accentuation).
[In the word] *maryeva*, the word *marya* is a derivative formed with the suffix *-yat*, being irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*) in rules such as "in the Veda, *niṣṭakya*... and so forth.
The word *anāvaḥ* has its initial syllable udātta (accented) according to the rule beginning with "yato ’nāvaḥ. Regarding *okye*:
[it is derived from] the root *uc*, meaning "to gather" (*samavāye*).
It is called *okya* because it is inhabited (*samaveyate*) or reached (*prāpyate*); thus, *okya* means "home. [The suffix] *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*.
The substitution of *k* for the consonants *c* and *j* occurs according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*.
The *titsvarita* accent.
1. The three [syllables] following *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ḍha*, and *pavamāna* are unaccented (*anudātta*).
2. [A word] beginning with *sa* is unaccented when followed by *pāda*. 3. A word beginning with *sa* is unaccented when followed by *na*.

O Soma, the wise and skillful one attends to him who delights in your friendship, as mortals do with those they love. 14. O Soma! He who delights in your friendship, as mortals [delight]—him the skillful sage attends. 14.

O shining Soma, when your friendship—that is, your state of being a friend—is the cause, that mortal sacrificer who is subject to death rejoices greatly; he praises you with this hymn of praise. You, the seer (kavi) of far-reaching vision and the skillful (dakṣa) one capable of all deeds, attend to that sacrificer;
you favor him—this is the meaning.
"He rejoices greatly" (rāraṇheva).
The meaning of the word is "battle" (*raṇa*).
In the *leṭ* [subjunctive] mood, there is the augment *aṭ*.
By the rule "in the Veda, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), there is the elision (*ślu*) of the suffix *śap*.

By the rule "itaśca lopaḥ," there is the elision of the letter *i*. Because of the rule "chandasyubhayathā," [the suffix] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, since the accentuation of the initial syllable of the reduplicated stem (*abhyastādyudāttatva*)—which is prescribed for a following *lac-sārvadhātuka* vowel that does not take *it*—is absent, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
Thus: *sacate*.
"In the case of the five-fold conjunction," there is a transposition of persons (purusavyatyaya).
Protect us from the curse; O Soma, guard us from distress. Be a most gracious friend to us. 15. Protect us; from the curse; O Soma; guard; from distress; as a friend; be very kind; to us. 15.
O Soma, protect us from censure—that is, from the act of reviling in the form of a curse—and guard us;
for Yāska states that "uruṣyati" means "to protect" (Nirukta 5.23).
Likewise, protect us thoroughly from distress—that is, from the sin committed by ourselves.
Thus, having warded off our sin, being "suśevaḥ"—endowed with excellent happiness that is to be granted to us—be "sakhā," a benefactor who acts for our welfare.
From *abhi-śasti*,
[derived from] *śaṃsu* in the sense of "praise" (*stuti*),
the suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*).
By the rule "tādau ca," the verbal root *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratvam*). *edhi*:
from the root *as* meaning "to be."
By the rule *loṭi sehiḥ*, [the suffix] *si* is replaced by *hi*.
Because that [suffix] is marked with the *ḍi*-indicator, there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule *kṣasorallopaḥ*.
Then, by the rule *ghasoraidvābhyāsalopaśca*, the *s* of *si* is changed to *e*.

Because of the rule "asiddhavadatrā bhāt" (in this [section], that which follows is to be treated as not yet established), the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* by the rule "hujhalyo hedhiḥ" does not apply.
The triplet beginning with "ā pyāyasva sametu te" is prescribed for the Grāvastotṛ priest;
this is stated in the Sūtra: "ā pyāyasva sametu te—these three [verses]; 'sṛjanti tvā daśa kṣipaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.12).
Among the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, "ā pyāyasva" alone is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) for the offering to Soma.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "May you swell; may [the waters] come together unto you; may your milks come together; may the strengths come together" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.10).
This [verse] is also employed for the filling of the *camasa* cups;

and it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the verses, 'Swell up,' 'May they come to thee,' 'May thy milks come together,' and 'May the strengths come together,' one should fill the *camasa*s" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 5.6).

Swell up; let virile power come to you from every side, O Soma; be present in the gathering of strength. 16. Swell up; let [it] come together for you from all sides, O Soma; let there be [strength] in the assembly of booty. 16.
"O Soma, swell! Increase!
Let your virile power—your manliness, your heroic strength and capacity—come together from all sides; let it be united with you.
Being thus, become present at the gathering, at the meeting, of food."
The meaning is: "Be the provider of food for us."
*vṛṣṇyam*.
[Derived from] the root *vṛṣ* "to sprinkle" (or "to rain"),
with the suffix *kanin* according to the rule beginning with *kaniyuvṛṣi*.

In the commentary on *vṛṣiṇa* 1. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa, after the phrase "the meaning is 'you favor'," there is the additional remark: "'sakhye | sakhyuryaḥ'—the suffix *ya* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*)."
2. There is no *sa* or *rāraṇha*.
3. There is no *ṭa*, *ṭha*, or the word *tvam*.

*bhavaṃ vṛṣṇyam*. The suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *bhave chandasi*. The elision of the vowel *a* is by the rule *alopo’naḥ*. The preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāvaḥ*) by the rule *ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ* does not apply here due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*). The acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatvam*) is by the rule *yato’nāvaḥ*. [The form] *bhava*: the lengthening in the *saṃhitā* is by the rule *aco’ntyādi ṭiḥ*. [The word] *saṃgathe*: the suffix *thak*, which is prescribed by the rule beginning with *pātṛdivāci*, also applies to the root *gam* due to the term *bahulavacanāt*. The acute accent on the final syllable of the second member is by the rule beginning with *tāthādinā*.
Swell up, O most intoxicating Soma, with all your rays;
be for us a most glorious friend for our increase.
Swell up, O Soma, most intoxicating, with all your stalks; become for us a most glorious friend for our prosperity. 17.
O Soma, most intoxicating, swell yourself with all your stalks—that is, with all the parts of the plant.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the dative because [the Soma] is the recipient of the ritual action.
[You are] the one who strikes down the adversaries.
‘This [is] *abhibhave*. The suffix *ṇvi* is applied by the rule *chandasi sahaḥ*. Due to its inclusion in the *mupāmādi* group, there is the substitution of *p* for *s*.
For immortality. According to the rule “*nañ* [is compounded] with *jara*, *mara*, *mitra*, and *amṛta*,” the first syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*) is udātta.
The highest ones.

From the root *ucchand* (to excel), which denotes an action accompanied by its means, the suffix *tamap* is added in the sense of excellence (*ātiśāyanika*). The word is oxytone because it is listed among the *ucchādi* group in Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.160, which states: "The words *uttama* and *śaśvat* are always [oxytone] when occurring in the *ucchādi* group. [Then follows:
*dhiṣva*.
By the rule *sudhita vasudhita nemadhita dhiṣva dhiṣīya ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.45), the substitution of *dhi* is prescribed as a nipātana.
In the *Sobhapravahaṇa* sacrifice, the verse "yā te dhāmāni" is used.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "At the conclusion of the [offering] deposited [on the altar], one should recite 'yā te dhāmāni haviṣā yajanti... imāṃ dhiyaṃ śikṣamāṇasya deva' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.4).
This very verse serves as the *yājyā* for the oblation of the eleven-fold animal sacrifice dedicated to Soma.
In the section titled "Pradānānām," it is sūtra-ed: "Invincible in battles and in combats, those stations of yours which they worship with oblation" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
Those abodes of yours which they worship with oblation—may you encompass all those for the sake of the sacrifice.
Increasing our wealth, furthering us, possessing good heroes and not slaying our men, O Soma, enter the dwellings.

Those abodes of yours which they worship with oblation—may all those be encompassing for you. Increasing the household, furthering us, rich in heroic sons, not slaying our heroes—O Soma, enter the dwellings. 19.

O Soma, those various abodes (*dhāmāni*) of yours—those splendors established in the *śubhra* and other vessels—which the sacrificers worship and honor with oblations such as cooked rice (*caru*), parched grain (*parodāśa*), and so forth; may all those abodes of yours encompass (*paribhūḥ*) our sacrifice, our ritual (*adhvara*), becoming fully present and pervasive.
Or alternatively:
may our sacrificer be the one who encompasses, accepts, and appropriates through the sacrifice all those various abodes of yours.
The verb *bhū* preceded by *pari* has the sense of avoiding (*parihṛ*).
[He approaches] all such dwellings (*durya*)—characterized by the eastern hall (*prācīnavaṃśa*) and so forth—which belong to us;
for the Śruti states: "Dwellings (*gṛha*) are indeed *duryas*" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.9.1).
Proceed forth, go with excellence! Of what kind [are you]?

A multiplier of the *gaya*—that is, of the house or of wealth; a furtherer, one who excellently delivers from misfortune; possessed of excellent heroes (*suvīra*), and not a slayer of heroes (*avīrahā*).
Sons are called *vīra*s because they are born from valor; he is their slayer.
*Paribhūḥ*. [The root] *bhū* means "to reach. From this, by the rule *kvip ca*, the suffix *kvip* is applied.
By the rule "vyatyayo bahulam" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.85), there is a reversal of gender and number.
Let it be so;
by way of this reversal, the singular number is employed.
Gayasphānaḥ. "Gaya" is a name for both a house and wealth;
[he is] the one who causes them to swell, the increaser of them.

In the word *avīrahā*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*; the elision of the *y* is Vedic. Thus, *vīrahā* means "the slayer of heroes" (*vīrāṇāṃ hantā*).
One who does not kill a hero is an "avīrahā" (one who does not slay a hero).

In the Mahāpitṛyajña, during the sacrifice to Soma Pitṛmat, the verse “Somo dhenum” is the second invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*). In that context, two invitatory verses are prescribed for each oblation (*havis*) by way of combination.
Accordingly, it is stated in the section on the *Dakṣiṇāgni* in the Sūtra: “‘Somo dhenum,’ ‘Somo arvantamāśum,’ and ‘Tvaṃ soma pitṛbhiḥ saṃvidānaḥ’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).
1. Endowed with brave men who are destroyers of enemies.

In the word *nigame* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.113), by virtue of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is an absence of the substitution of *o* for *ava* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.112 (*sahivahoradavarṇasya*). By the rule *saheḥ sāḍaḥ saḥ*, the retroflex *ṣ* is applied. *Paprim*: from the root *pṛ* (meaning "to protect" and "to fill"). The suffix *kin* is applied by the rule *ādgamahanajanaḥ*. *Svarṣām*: [He who] wins (*sanoti*) heaven (*svaḥ*); thus, *svarṣāḥ*. From the root *paṇ* (meaning "to give"). The suffix *viṭ* is applied by the rule *janasanakhana*. By the rule *viḍnoranunāsikasyāt*, the vowel *ā* is substituted. *Apsām*: From the root *san* with the word *ap* as an upapada, the suffix *viṭ* is applied as before. Alternatively: from the root *psā* (meaning "to eat"). He eats (*psāti*) or consumes; thus, *psāḥ*. The suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *kip ca*. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one for whom eating (*psā*) does not exist," the final syllable of the second member is udātta by the rule *nabnubhyām*. *Arepasām*: from the root *jan* (meaning "to appear"). As before, the suffix *viṭ* and the substitution of *ā* are applied. *Madam*: from the root *mad* (meaning "joy"). The suffix *śap* is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

"O Soma, you generated all these herbs; you generated the waters and the cows; you have stretched out the wide mid-air. [In the word *vyātantha*, the augment *iṭ* is added according to Pāṇini 7.2.77. [The root] *kit* [in *cikitsa*] means "to know. [The suffix] *san* [is added] after roots ending in *gu*, *si*, and *vid* (Pāṇini 3.1.5). [In the compound] *gaviṣṭau*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those in which there are desires (*icchya*) or pursuits (*eṣaṇāni*) for the cows (*gavām*) or arrows (*bāṇānām*)," and thus the accent of the first member remains as its original form (*prakṛtisvara*). || 23 ||
The eighth hymn, consisting of eighteen verses beginning with "etā u tyāḥ," is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Gautama.
Of these, the first four are Jagatī meters;
the five beginning with the thirteenth are Uṣṇih meters.
The remaining eight verses are *triṣṭubh*s; their deity is *Upā*. The other triplet beginning with “*aśvinā vartiḥ*” has the *Aśvins* as its deity.

And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "These [verses] beginning with 'etā u tyāḥ' belong to Uṣas; they consist of four Jagatīs and end with five Uṣṇiks; the last triplet is addressed to the Aśvins.
The application of this hymn is worldly (secular).
However, in the Prātaranuvāka, during the Uṣas-rite, in the Jagatī metre, and in the Aśvin-śastra, the four verses beginning with 'etā u tyāḥ' are employed.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘etā u tyā’—these four [verses] are in the Jāgata metre" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.14).

These very Dawns have made their signal; in the eastern half of the mid-air they deck themselves with light. Like bold men preparing their weapons, the ruddy cows, the mothers, come forth toward us. These, indeed, those Dawns, have made their banner; in the eastern quarter of the region they anoint themselves with radiance. Like valiant warriors fashioning their arms, the ruddy cows, the mothers, advance toward us.
The particle *u* here serves as a metrical filler (*pādapūraṇa*). *Tyāḥ* means "those"; *etāḥ uṣasaḥ* refers to the deities presiding over the time of dawn.
They *akrata*, that is, they made or produced, *ketum*—the light that makes known the entire world enveloped in darkness.

Since this is so, therefore the Dawns, in the eastern half—the eastern quarter—of the *rajas*, the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*), manifest their light. Like bold warriors who prepare their weapons such as swords and the like, they, making manifest by their own splendor, perfecting the world, the "cows" (rays) whose nature is to move, the "ruddy ones" ascending upward, the "mothers"—the fashioners of the sun's light or the mothers of the universe—the Dawns go forth day after day.
The meaning is: "May such Dawns as these protect us.

Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "These very Dawns have fashioned their banner, [that is] their means of perception; the plural number is used for the sake of honoring that which is singular. They adorn themselves with light in the eastern half of the intermediate world (*antarikṣa-loka*), like bold warriors preparing their weapons.
In the *Nirukta*, this is substituted for the word *samidhye* (in the phrase *uṣāḥ samidhye*)."
"Emi deṣām niṣkṛtam jāriṇīvā" (I go to their appointed place like a mistress)—thus also there is a Vedic verse.
"The cows go toward [them] because of their movement; they are ruddy, the mothers from the shining, the makers of light" (Nirukta 12.7).
*akrata*: from the root *kṛ*, in the *luṅ* tense, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli* according to the rule “*mantre ghasa*”. *niṣkṛṇvānāḥ*.

The root *kṛv* belongs to the meaning of "injuring" and "doing. From this root, the suffix *cānaś* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlaka*). Then, by the rule “*dhinvikṛṇvyora ca*,” the suffix *u* is added.
By the rule "idudupadhasya cāpratyayasya," the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *p*;
it has the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member of a *kṛt*-derived compound.

The ruddy rays have risen; the well-yoked ones have effortlessly harnessed their red cows. The dawns have performed their works as of old; the ruddy ones have clothed themselves in radiant light. The ruddy rays have risen; the well-yoked ones have effortlessly harnessed their red cows. The dawns have performed their works as of old; the ruddy ones have clothed themselves in radiant light. || 2 ||

1. *kṣa-ṭa-na-sa* is for filling the meter; *ṭa* is used as a filler. The *varuṇāḥ*, meaning the shining ones; the *bhānavaḥ*, the splendors of the dawn; *vṛthā*, without effort, rose up spontaneously.

Immediately thereafter, the *uṣasaḥ* (dawns), whose yokes are easy (*svāyujaḥ*), capable of being easily harnessed to the chariot, and who possess beautiful-colored (*varūtrīḥ*) cows—such [cows] that were previously risen rays, or perhaps long-tailed draft animals serving as their own vehicles—they yoked them to their own chariot.
And it is said: “The rays of the Dawn are the cows” (Nirukta 1.15.7).

Thus, having mounted the chariot yoked with cows, the Dawns have made manifest the *vayunāni*—the knowledges of all living beings—just as they did in former days (*pūrvathā*). For when the time of dawn has arrived, all living beings become endowed with knowledge.
Immediately after that, *varūpī*: "Those dawns, shining brightly, have approached the one who cuts down.
Regarding this, Yāska states in the *Nirukta* (2.20): "'Varuṣat' is a name for color, from the root *ruc*, which means 'to shine' or 'to blaze'.
They have resorted to, or served, the *bhānu*, the sun, which is of beautiful color.
The meaning is that they become one with him.
(Having cast aside) Dawn *peśāṃsi*— the dark colors of the world resting upon it— *adhivapate*, she cuts them away.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a *nūtu*.
A *nūtu* is one who, by means of his hair (*keśa*), overcomes (*tūrvati*) men—that is, he renders them empty. Thus, it is called *nūtārpita*.
Just as one cuts hair with the remainder [of a blade], so too does *upā* destroy darkness along with its very root; this is the meaning. Or rather, like a dancing woman, she destroys the *peśas*.
She puts on forms that are visible to all; she wears them upon herself, holding them in excess within her own being.
Thus, having first dispelled the darkness with her rays, she uncovers her own breast—that region of her chest which had been concealed by gloom.
The meaning is that she manifests herself of her own accord.
Just as a cow (*uṣṭrā*) reveals the source of milk—that is, the udder—at the time of milking, so does she.
What is she doing?
Just as cows quickly enter their own stall on their own accord, even so, having reached the eastern direction by herself, she makes light for the entire world, illuminating all existence.
In this manner, Uṣas has dispelled the darkness, making it open and separated.
Like one who has danced.
The root *nṛ* means "to injure.
The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "kvip ca."
By the rule “*rālopaḥ*,” there is the elision of *v*;
by the rule “*voḥ samprasāraṇe*,” there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel.
Alternatively:
The root *nṛt* means "to bend the limbs. The suffix *kū* is applied according to *Uṇādi Sūtra* 1.91, *nṛtthabhyo: kū:*; thus, [the word] *varjaham* [is derived].
The root *vṛṅ* means "to share" (*saṃbhakti*). One shares in or enjoys the cow; thus, it is *vaḥ*, meaning milk.
The suffix is *vic*.
*Tajjahāti* means "he abandons," from the root *ohāk* in the sense of "abandoning" (*tyāge*).

According to the rule *khaśprakaraṇe vātaśunītilagarbhedhvajadhetṛdajahātibhya upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 3.2.28.1), the suffix *khaś* is applied even when the word *agara* is used as an upapada, by virtue of the term *bahulam* in the rule *kṛtyuṭo bahulam*. Thus, [the form] *varjahaḥ* is derived.

Because it is *sārvadhātuka*, the suffix *śap* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); since it belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is *ślulopa*. This results in reduplication and so forth.
Because there is a distinction between *ba* and *va*, the form is *bavati*.
In *divodāsa* and similar forms, the initial syllable of the first member is acute by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.119].
*Āvaḥ*:
from the root *vṛñ*, meaning "to choose."
In the Vedic passage, by the rule "ghas in the sense of 'to eat' in mantras," *ghas* is substituted for *ad*; then, by the rule "elision after a consonant and *ī*, *ū*, or *ṣ*," there is elision;
and by the rule "it is also seen in the Veda" (Pāṇini 6.4.73), the augment *āṭ* is added.
In the *upasthāna* of the *prātaranuvāka*, there are eight invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) beginning with "pratyarcis," as well as in the *āśvina-śastra*.
Thus it is stated in the *Sūtra*: "The eight [verses] beginning with 'pratyarcis' and 'vyupā vo divijāḥ' are recited; they are in the *triṣṭubh* meter" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.14).

Her radiant beam has been seen; she spreads abroad and drives away the black darkness. Like a well-fashioned ornament at the assemblies, the Daughter of Heaven has assumed her wondrous luster. The radiant beam of hers has been seen; it spreads abroad and drives away the black, monstrous darkness. Like a well-fashioned ornament at the assemblies, the Daughter of Heaven has assumed her wondrous luster.
The bright, shining luster of this Dawn has been seen facing [us] by all; it is first perceived in the eastern quarter.
It stands forth, meaning it establishes itself or pervades, in all directions.
And having pervaded all the quarters, it [reveals] the vastness.
This is a great name.
She dispels—that is, drives away—the exceedingly vast *kṛṣṇa*, the black-colored darkness.

At the *vidathas*, the sacrifices, she anoints her own form (*peśas*), just as the Adhvaryu priests anoint with clarified butter the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) which is joined with a splinter named *svaru*; in that same way, Dawn anoints—makes closely united—her own form.
Immediately after that, the Daughter of Heaven (Uṣas), born from the world of heaven, has extended—that is, she has manifested—the wonderful and praiseworthy light of the sun.
He stands apart.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule *sam-ava-pra-vi-bhyaḥ*.
He has leaned against.
The root *śri* is used in the sense of "service.
In the *laṅ* tense, the suffix *śap* is elided by the rule "there is frequently [elision] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

1. The region of the lips, which is a part of *kṣa* and *khā*. 2. *Kṣa-sa* is like a camel (*uṣṭra*); just as a cow (*gauḥ*) [is not] a camel. 3. *Kṣa-uṣṭrā* is like a cow that does not exist; *sa-yathā* (as for example). 4. *Kṣa* they attain. 5. *Kṣa-na* elision of *til*. 6. *Kṣa* it is seen; therefore. 7. From *sam*, *ava*, and *pra* [the prefix], the root *sthā*:
Ṛgveda 7.81.1— "We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; the Dawn, shining forth, makes the paths clear.
Like a song of praise (*chandas*) arrayed for glory, she shines with a beautiful countenance; she has awakened us for well-being."

We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness. Dawn, shining forth, makes the ways discernible. Like a lover smiling for the sake of beauty, she beams with radiant countenance; she has awakened us for well-being. 6.

We have crossed over, we have reached the further shore—the place of completion—of this nocturnal darkness. Immediately thereafter, Dawn, dispelling the night's gloom, creates, that is, brings forth, *vayunāni*—the insights of all living beings.
For the sake of prosperity, she smiles like a song.

Just as a man skilled in subduing others, having approached a woman, smiles and laughs for the sake of winning her over, so too does the Dawn (*uṣas*), shining—that is, producing a distinguished light—appear as if laughing with her own stainless radiance.

Thus, being *supratīkā*, one with beautiful limbs due to her form of distinguished light, she has awakened (*ajīgaḥ*) all for the sake of *saumanasāya*, that is, for the mental well-being of all, having devoured the darkness.
We have crossed over (*atāriṣma*).
[The root] *tṛ* is used in the sense of "floating" and "crossing.
In the *luṅ* tense, with the suffix *sic*, there is *vṛddhi*.
From *tamasas*: by the rule “*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ patiputrau*,” the *visarjanīya* becomes *s* in *saṃhitā*. It is smiled at (*smayate*).
The root *smiṅ* is used in the sense of "slight laughter";
it belongs to the *bhvādi* class.
[Its form is] *ajīgaḥ*.
The root *gṛ* is used in the sense of "swallowing.
In the *laṅ* tense, by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” the suffix *śap* is replaced by *śru*.
By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
The vowel is lengthened because it belongs to the *tujādi* group.
Radiant leader of true blessings, daughter of heaven, you are praised by the Gāutama-s;
do thou grant us strengths that consist of offspring, heroes, and horses, with cattle at their head, in succession.
Radiant leader of pleasant truths, daughter of heaven, you are praised by the Gōtamas. Bestow upon us strengths consisting of offspring, heroes, and horses, with cattle at their head. (7)
*Bhāsvatī* means radiant or luminous.
*Sūnṛtā* is a name for speech;
she is the *netrī*, that is, the leader, the guide, and the cause of *sūnṛtās*—those things whose nature consists of pleasant truth.
For when Dawn has arisen, living beings, headed by humans, make sounds here and there for their respective activities.
Thus, this Daughter of Heaven, born from the celestial realm, is praised by us, the seers of the Gotama clan.
O Dawn, being praised by us, do thou bestow upon us nourishments and foods.
What kind of *vāja*s?

Those possessed of progeny (*prajāvataḥ*), meaning endowed with offspring such as sons, grandsons, and so forth; those possessed of men (*nṛvataḥ*), meaning accompanied by men characterized as servants; and those in which horses are to be recognized (*aśvabudhyān*), that is, those *vāja*s in which horses are to be understood as being present.
Alternatively, [the term] *aśvabudhān* [is used];
due to the transposition of letters (*varṇavyatyaya*), the letter *ya* [is substituted for *ba*], thus meaning *aśvamūlān*.
For kings obtain wealth and various possessions by means of horses;
therefore, for the ignorant, that [possession of horses] is the root. "Go-agrān" (those who have cows as the foremost).
Those for whom cows are foremost, i.e., at the head.
*Bhāsvatī*: [derived from] the root *bhā* in the sense of "shining," with the suffix *asun*.
Then there is the suffix *matup*. By the rule *mādupadhāyāḥ*, the *t* of *matup* becomes *v*.
By the rule *ugitaśca*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied] by the rule *ṛnnebhyo ṅīp*.
By the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*, the *ṅīp* receives the udātta accent.
In the word *stave*, [it is derived from] the root *stu* with the sense of "praise" (*stutau*).

In the present tense (*laṭ*) used for the object (*karmaṇi*), by virtue of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is also the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *yak*.

1. [The letters] ca, cha, ṇa, ta, tha, na, pha, la, śa, sa, and śa are beautiful; 2. [She] is the leader of the sounds kṣa, ṭa, and ḍha; 3. [She is] the awakening of kṣa, ta, sa, and aśva; 4. In place of the letter la and the letter na, there is the letter ya; 5. In the case of kṣa, ṭa, and ḍha, there is the substitution of v for m.

In *paṃdeṣ*, there is the elision of the *t* [of the suffix *tas*]. Because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the *e*-vowel is treated as belonging to an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; consequently, due to the absence of the doubling [of the consonant], the *guṇa* and *avādeśa* substitutions take place. In *nṛtavataḥ*, the substitution of *vat* for *mat* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). The acute accent of the suffix *matup* is according to the rule *hasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup*. In *māsi*, [the root] is *mā* in the sense of "measuring"; it belongs to the *āśādika* group.

O Dawn, may I obtain wealth that is glorious, rich in heroes, with a multitude of servants, and characterized by horses— wealth that you, O auspicious one, who shine forth with wondrous fame and are impelled by strength, bestow as great abundance.

O Dawn, may I attain that glorious wealth, rich in heroic sons, free from the incursions of Dāsas, and characterized by horses—wealth which you, O auspicious one, illumine with wondrous fame, impelled by strength, and vast. 8.

May I obtain, may I attain, that wealth (*rayi*) which has risen up—what kind? *Yaśasam*, endowed with glory (*yaśas*), that is, with fame; the meaning is that it is praised by all. *Suvīram*, endowed with excellent heroes (*vīra*), such as sons and others. *Dāsapravargam*: a *pravarga* is an eminent group or assembly; [it refers to] an assembly of slaves (*dāsa*).

The Dawn (uṣas), awakening [beings] from sleep so as to set them in motion toward their activities, has found—that is, obtained—the speech of the entire world, of every living being endowed with mind and capable of verbal expression; for this very reason, the name "possessing pleasant truth" (sūnṛtāvatī) is appropriate for the Dawn.
Having made manifest (*abhicakṣya*). [The root] *cakṣiṅ* [is used] in the sense of "distinct speech"; this [root] also has the meaning of "making manifest."
In the compound *anañpūrve* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.30), there is the substitution of *lyap* for the suffix *ktvā*.
[The form] *pratīcī* is derived from the root *añj-* preceded by *prati*, with the suffix *kin* according to the rule beginning with *ṛtvik*.
By the rule *aniditām*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*).
By the supplementary rule *añjateścopasaṃkhyānam*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added.
Then, by the rule *acaḥ*, the vowel *a* is elided, and by the rule *cau*, lengthening occurs.

The feminine suffix *ṅīp* receives the acute accent by the rule regarding the accent of the cessation of the acute (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). In the form *urvīyā*, because it is derived from *urvī*, the substitution of *ḍiyā* for the following *s* occurs according to Pāṇini 7.1.39.1: "There is an addition of the rule for *iyāṭ*, *iyāc*, and *īkāra*. Thus, the substitute *ḍiyā* is applied.
By the force of the grammatical injunction (*ādeśa*), its elision (*lopa*) does not take place.

*manāyoḥ* | *vyurṇvatī* | *divaḥ* | *antān* | *abodhi* | *apa* | *svasāram* | *sanutaḥ* | *yuyoti* | *praminatī* | *manuṣyā* | *yugāni* | *yoṣā* | *jārasya* | *cakṣasā* | *vi* | *bhāti* || 11 || Unveiling the ends of heaven, she has awakened; she drives her sister far away. Diminishing the human generations, the maiden shines forth with the light of her lover. || 11 ||

The Dawn has awakened— unveiling the ends, that is, the horizons of heaven, making them free from darkness— and she has become known by her own living beings. Immediately thereafter, at the manifestation of the Dawn, the Night herself departs to a distance,
for "sanutaḥ" is a term meaning "hidden away."
In the hidden region, she drives away— that is,

she causes to depart and separates— the *yugas*, the ages belonging to men, such as the Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth, destroying them by her coming and going; she, the wife of the lover, the wife of the Sun who wears down the night, shines forth especially with her own light, unveiling [the world].
The root *ūrṇu* means "to cover.
From this root preceded by the prefix *vi-*, the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is applied;
then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added according to the rule *ugitaśca*.
The word *śatru* is acute on the first syllable by the rule "śatruranumaḥ.
The word *sanutaḥ* is listed as an initial-acute (svarādi) nipātana ending in an acute accent on the final syllable.
Therefore, when the designation *avyaya* (indeclinable) applies, there is elision of the locative case ending by the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*. [The form] *yuyoti* [is derived from] the root *yu*,
meaning "to mix" or "to not mix."
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is *ślū* (elision) of the *śap* suffix.
[The form] *manuṣyāḥ*: by the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the substitution of *ḍā* for the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*).

*Yugāni*. [The word] *yuja-* takes the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the object (*karman*). By the rule "cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ," there is the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *g*).

Because the word *yuga* is listed among the *ucchādi* group and in the section on specific time-periods (*kālaviśeṣa*), there is an absence of the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.160, Gaṇapāṭha).
Furthermore, by the rule "and [the acute accent] of *ucchādi* words," the word has an acute accent on its final syllable.
[The form is] *jārasya*.
The word *praśūnā* is derived as a *ghañ*-formed noun by the rule *dārajārau kartari ṇiluk ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.20.4).

She has burst forth, brilliant, auspicious, spreading wide; like the Sindhu river with its flood, she has expanded far and wide. Breaking through the divine ordinances, she shines, visible through the rays of the sun. *praśūnā na citrā subhagā prathānā sindhur na kṣoda urviyā vyathait | abhinatī daivyāni vratāni sūryasya ceti raśmibhir dṛśānā || 12 ||*

The auspicious one (subhagā), possessing beautiful wealth (śobhanadhanā), the variegated (citrá) and worthy of praise—Uṣas, who spreads forth her splendors (tejas) like a cowherd spreading his cattle in the forest, expanding (prathānā) widely (urviyā)—she, being thus vast (urvī), pervades this entire world.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
she is like the flood (kṣodaḥ) of a river (sindhuḥ).
Just as water, by its very nature of flowing, quickly pervades low-lying ground, so it was with her.
That same Uṣas, becoming visible along with the rays—meaning the beams—of the Sun, became known; that is, she became recognized.
What was she doing?
She does not harm the divine ordinances—those rites related to the gods, such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
that is to say, she impels the sacrificers toward their performance.
For it is only after the appearance of the dawn that all rituals, such as the Agnihotra, are performed, and not during the night.
"O gods, do not find this evening disagreeable," according to the Śruti (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.77.2). *Prathānā*: [from] the root *prath*, meaning "to become manifest."
1. kṣa, ṭa, ḍha, sa, eṣa, uṣa.

From this root *as* (to throw), with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *cānaś* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” there is the elision (*luk*) of the present tense marker (*śap*). [Thus we have] *sindhuḥ*. [The root] *syandū* means “to flow. By the rule “*syandeḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ dhaśca*” (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.11), the suffix *upratyaya* is added, and because of the continued application of the term “*nit*,” the word is acutely accented on its first syllable. Now, [the word] *athait*. [The root] *duośvi* means “to move” or “to increase. In the aorist (*luṅ*), since the *aṅ* augment is optional (Pāṇini 3.1.58; 49), the suffix *sic* is used for the *cli* substitute. Because the instruction regarding augments is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*), there is an absence of the *iṭ* augment. By the rule “*sici vṛddhiḥ*” (Pāṇini 7.2.1), there is *vṛddhi* substitution. Since the root is not one that ends in *ha*, *ya*, *kṣa*, or *ṇa*, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule “*hayantakṣaṇa*” does not apply. By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” (Pāṇini 7.3.97), there is an absence of the *īṭ* augment. By the rule “*skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ*,” there is the elision of the *s*. [The word] *cet*. [The root] *citī* means “to perceive. In the aorist (*luṅ*) in the passive sense, there is an absence of the augment *aṭ* by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi māṅyoge 'pi*. [The word] *haśānā*. From the root *dṛś*, the suffix *śānac* is used in the present tense (*laṭ*) in the passive sense. By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” there is the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
The triplet beginning with "upastaccitram" is prescribed for the *prātaranuvāka* in the *ṛtavān* section, within the *uṣṇih* metre, and also for the *āśvina-śastra*.
This is stated in the section beginning with "athosthaḥ" in the Sūtra: "The three verses beginning with 'upastaccitram ā bhara' are in the *uṣṇih* metre" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.14).
O possessor of many steeds, bring hither for us that wonderful wealth by which we may support both our children and our progeny.
O Dawn, rich in booty, bring to us that wondrous gift by which we may obtain offspring and descendants. 13.
"O thou rich in sacrificial food (vājinīvatī)! 'Sacrificial food' (vāja) refers to the oblation characterized as food; the ritual action associated with that is 'rich in sacrificial food' (vājinī)."
O Goddess Uṣas, endowed with that action, bring to us—that is, bestow upon us—that wonderful (*citra*) wealth worthy of admiration (*cāyanīya*).
With that wealth, may we support (*dhāmahe*), maintain, and provide for our children (*toka*), our sons (*putra*), and their sons (*tanaya*).
Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "Uṣas says to us: 'Bring that wonderful, admirable wealth, which is full of food, by means of which we may obtain sons and grandsons'" (*Nirukta* 12.6).
*Dhāmahe*:
from the root *dhā*, in the present tense (*laṭ*), there is elision of the suffix *śap* according to the rule "there is frequent elision in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
By transposition (*vyatyaya*), the initial syllable bears the udātta accent.
Alternatively,
in the case of the imperative (loṭ), there is the augment āṬ by the rule "āḍuttamasya picca"; because the suffix is marked with P, this augment is mandatory.
Therefore, because the suffix *pratyaya* is marked with *pittva*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.

In this view, the absence of the substitution of *ai* for *e* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 3.4.93) should be understood as an irregularity (*vyatyaya*). Furthermore, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*) due to its connection with a word that begins a new clause (*yadvṛtta*).
O Uṣas, rich in cattle and horses, resplendent one, shine forth here today for us,
O you who are full of truth and bringers of wealth.
O Uṣas, today here, O radiant one rich in cattle and horses, shine forth upon us with wealth and with true blessings. 14.
O Gomatī, endowed with cows that are to be given to us; O Aśvavatī, endowed with horses; O Vibhāvarī, possessed of distinguished light;
O Sūnṛtāvani—*sūnṛtā* being speech consisting of what is dear—O Dawn, O Goddess Uṣas, who art thus endowed with such speech, [be present] today.
1. Because of the rule "kṣayadvṛttān nityam," there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent.

Now, at this time of dawn, "here" (iha) in this place, "for us" (asme), that is, for our sake, "O wealthy one" (revat), so that our action may be endowed with wealth, "shine forth" (vyuccha); dispel the darkness.
*aśvāvati*:
According to the rule *mantre somāśvendriya*, there is lengthening of the vowel in the feminine suffix *matup*.
Because it begins with a *pāda*, the eighth-case (anudātta) suppression of the vocative does not apply.
Revata:
there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.37.6 (*aryametau bahulam*); and the substitution of *v* for *m* in the suffix *matup* occurs by the rule *chandasi iraḥ*.
The acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the suffix *matup* is prescribed by the rule: "And after a word ending in *re*, the acute accent of *matup* must be stated" (Pāṇini 6.1.176.1).
[The root] *ucch* [is used];
it means "to shine" (*vivāsa*).
In the case of a funeral rite, there is avoidance.
For you, O Uṣas, possessor of many steeds, have yoked the ruddy horses;
therefore, bring us all auspicious fortunes.
Yoke, O possessor of rich spoils, your ruddy horses; then, O Dawn, bring to us all auspicious fortunes. 15.

O Uṣas, goddess rich in steeds (*vājinīvati*), possessed of sacrificial food (*havirlakṣaṇannavatī*), yoke at this very moment the ruddy-colored (*aruṇa*) horses—that is, those specific cattle that stand in the place of horses.
Indeed, "hi" is used for emphasis.
Then, immediately after, having mounted the chariot, bring to us all blessings (*viśvā saubhagāni*). Bring them hither!
Regarding *aśvān*: by the rule "after a long vowel, [there is] *ru* before *aṭ* when the *pāda* is the same," the *n* becomes *ru* in the *saṃhitā*;
and by the rule "an *ā* is always substituted for an *āt* before *aṭ*," the *ā* is nasalized.

Regarding *saubhagāni*: because the word *subhaga* is listed among the words beginning with *udātta* in the rule "subhagān mantre" (*Pāṇini* 4.1.127), the suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or object (*karman*) by the rule "prāṇabhṛjjātī-vayovacana-nodgātrādibhyo 'ṅ" (*Pāṇini* 5.1.129).

When the rule "haṅgasandhvante pūrvapadasya ca" (*Pāṇini* 7.3.18) would have required the strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of both parts of the compound, it is stated that because all grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), the strengthening of the second member does not occur here (*Kāśikā* 7.3.19).
In the *prātaranuvāka* for the *āśvina* [śastra], this triplet beginning with "aśvinā vartiḥ" is used in the *chandah* addressed to the Aśvins and Viṣṇu, as well as in the *ādhina* *śastra*.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two triplets beginning with 'aśvinā vartirasmad' and 'āśvināveha gacchatam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.15).
O Aśvins, with your great power, come to our dwelling which is rich in cattle and gold; with one mind, direct your chariot toward us.
O Aśvins, you two wonder-workers, direct your chariot toward us with one mind—toward our dwelling that abounds in cattle and gold. 16.
Due to their association with Uṣas, the two Aśvins present in the mind are praised by means of this triplet of verses beginning with "idam.
O Aśvins—possessors of horses, or gods whose nature is to pervade; O Dastras—destroyers of enemies—[come] from all sides to our *vartiḥ*, the home which is the cause of our turning [toward you].
(Note: *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* indicates the variant reading *upasā sāhacaryāt*.)

O you two of one mind, being of like intent, bring down your chariot toward us—toward our house—so that it may be provided with cattle, joined with many cows, and likewise endowed with gold and desirable wealth; turn it hitherward.
O Aśvins! [The form] *aśvinā* [is derived from *aśvin*] with the substitution of the vowel *ā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
[The word] *vartiḥ* [is used].
"Varti" means a house, because it is "that in which one dwells" (*vartate 'smin*). The suffix *is* is applied according to the *Uṇādi* rules, and the suffix *asmat* is added.
By the rule "supām suluk," there is elision of the genitive case ending.
*Samanasā* means those two whose mind (*manas*) is the same (*samāna*).
The substitution of *sabhāva* (the long vowel *ā*) occurs [for the final *i*] of the word *samāna* in the Vedic language (*chandas*), according to the rule "of *samāna* in the Veda."
As far as this world and up to the light in heaven, you two have created a light for the people;
O Aśvins, bring nourishment to us.
You two who have thus brought forth the hymn from heaven as light for mankind—O Aśvins, bring nourishment hither to us. 17.
O Aśvins, you two who from the sky (*divaḥ*) have thus (*itthā*) created—that is, produced in this manner experienced by us—the *śloka*, the praiseworthy light (*jyotiḥ*), the splendor;
according to the opinion of some, the Sun and Moon are called the Aśvins.
As it has been said by Yāska: "Regarding those two Aśvins, some say they are Heaven and Earth, others say they are Day and Night" (Nirukta 12.1).
And thus, their nature as illuminators is established.
"You two"—meaning you both—"bring" (ā vahataṃ), that is, bring hither and bestow upon us "ūrjam," food that provides strength.
The word *śloka*: "the root *ślok* means 'to collect' (*saṃghāta*);
it also has the meaning of 'praise' (*stuti*)."
The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Due to the presence of the marker *ṣit*, the word is accented on the first syllable.
May these two gods, the bounteous ones who travel on golden paths, being awakened, bring us here for the drinking of Soma.
Hither, O gods who bring delight, you two divine ones with golden paths, waking at dawn, may you come to drink the Soma. 18.
May the two Aśvins—the destroyers of enemies—who have awakened at dawn, bring hither for this sacrifice the drinking of Soma;
what are they like?
They are divine, delighting in play or endowed with qualities such as generosity, and they are the bringers of well-being, that is, of happiness which bestows health.
According to the Śruti, "The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods" (Ai. Brā. 1.18).
[They are called] *hiraṇyavartanī* based on the etymological derivation: that by which they move (*vartate*).
By the word *varti*, a chariot is meant;
those two [chariots] which have golden *vartis*.

In the three words beginning with *deva*, the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the case-ending] according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. [The word] *somapītaye* [is derived from] the root *pā* meaning "to drink."
In the sense of an abstract action (bhāva), the suffix *ktin* is applied; by the rule "ghu-ā-sthā," the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final *ā*]. Thus, *somasya pītiḥ* becomes *somapītiḥ*.
Due to its inclusion in the *dāsībhāra* group, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is retained.

The ninth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "agnīṣomau," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Gotama. The first three verses are *anuṣṭubh*s; the last three, beginning with the ninth, are *gāyatrī*s; the eighth is a *jagatī* and a *triṣṭubh*; and the remaining five are *triṣṭubh*s. The deities are Agni and Soma. Thus it has been enumerated [in the Anukramaṇī]: 1. [The hymn is] directed toward us (*asmadābhimukham*); 2. [the two deities] are the Ashvins, the bringers of being (*bhāvayitārau*).
3. [The word] *kṣaṇasa* does not exist in the sense of "in three.
Regarding the Agniṣomīya [offering]: "Agniṣomau; the first three [verses] of the twelve Agniṣomīya [hymns] are Anuṣṭubhs, the next three are Gāyatrīs, and the eighth is a Jagatī.
Of the omentum, the cake, and the oblation of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the first three verses are respectively the invitatory verses (*anuvākyās*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two triplets beginning with 'Agnīṣomau' and 'Imaṃ me' and 'Yuvam etāni divi rocanāni' [are used] at the third pressing" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
O Agni and Soma, you two bulls, hear this my invocation well; graciously accept these hymns and be present for the sake of the donor, O heroes.
O Agni and Soma, you two bulls, hear this my call well; graciously accept these well-spoken hymns and be a source of strength for the donor. 1.
O you two bulls, the showerers of desires, Agni and Soma, listen well now to this my invocation being offered; understand it thoroughly.
Accept with delight each of the beautiful hymns, the words composed by us characterized by praise.
Thereafter, become givers of joy (*marya*)—bestowers of happiness—to the sacrificer who has presented the sacrificial porridge, the cake, and other offerings.

Agnīṣomau: Agni and Soma. In the case of a dvandva compound, the rule *īdagneḥ somavaruṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.27) prescribes the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of *agni* before *soma* and *varuṇa*.
By the rule *agneḥ stotrasomāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.82), the status of being a word (*padatva*) is established.

Although the rule *devatādvandve ca* would have resulted in the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) for both members of the compound, the rule *āmantritasya ca* assigns the acute accent (*udātta*) to the beginning [of the vocative].
[The form is] *vṛṣaṇā*.
The vowel *ā* [in *havam*] is substituted by the rule *supām suluk*.
The lengthening of the vowel before the suffix occurs optionally by the rule *vā papūrvasya*, due to the absence of a penultimate vowel (*anupadhā*). [Thus, the form is] *havam*.
In the sense of "state" (*bhāva*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the root *hyat* (from which *sūkta* is derived) due to the rule "anupasargasya," and there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*).
The term *sūktāni* consists of the prefix *su-* followed by the root *vac*, with the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The word *sūpānāt* has its final syllable accented because of the rule *'sūpānāt ktaḥ'*. [The word] *haryatam*:
[from the root] *harya* in the sense of "motion" and "desire."
It belongs to the *bhū* class.
When Agni and Soma are the deities of the Upāṃśuyāja on the full moon day, then "O Agni and Soma, he who today... is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).

And it is stated in the section beginning with "The deities have been mentioned" in the Sūtra: "O Agni and Soma, he who today brought you from another place, Mātariśvan from heaven" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.6).
O Agni and Soma, whoever honors you today with this splendor—
for him grant heroic strength, the nourishment of cattle, and sovereign power.
O Agni and Soma, he who today honors you with this splendor—for him grant heroic vigor, the increase of cattle, and excellent lordship over horses. 2.

O Agni and Soma, that sacrificer who today, in this ritual, honors (*saparyati*)—that is, makes worthy of worship—this speech (*vacaḥ*), namely this hymn (*stuti-lakṣaṇa*) intended for you two, to that sacrificer grant (*dhattam*) the nourishment (*poṣam*) and increase of cattle and livestock. Of what kind of nourishment?
One endowed with excellent vigor (*suvīrya*)—that is, possessed of noble power—and excellent sovereignty (*svaśvarya*).
In the word *gavām*, there is a prohibition— by the rule *na gośvannāvavarṇa*— of the acute accent on the case-ending which would otherwise have been required by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
The triplet ending in *kṣa* consists of *gāyatrī* verses, with the eighth being [a *triṣṭubh*]. (Ka.
O Agni and Soma, he who offers an oblation to you, or whoever presents you with a gift,
shall through his offspring and heroic vigor enjoy a full span of life.
O Agni and Soma! He who offers an oblation to you both, he who presents the prepared sacrificial gift—may he, through his offspring, attain heroic vigor and a full span of life. 3.
O Agni and Soma, that sacrificer who shall offer an oblation— whether an offering of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) to you two,
or an oblation prepared with sacrificial food (haviskṛti) such as cooked rice (caru), cake (puroḍāśa), and so forth— that sacrificer,
endowed with offspring such as sons and grandsons, and possessed of excellent vigor (suvīrya), shall attain a full lifespan (viśvam āyuḥ), pervading it like Vyaśva.
*Āhuti*:
By the rule "tādau ca" [Pāṇini 6.2.50], the *gati* [prefix] retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) after the root *hu-* when followed by the suffix *ktin*.
*Dāśāt*.
In the root *dāś* meaning "to give," there is the augment *āṭ* in the *leṭ* tense;
because it is not joined with a preceding word (*yadavṛtta*), it does not undergo the loss of accent (*anighāta*).
*Haviṣkṛtim*:
that in which there is the making (*kṛti*) or preparation (*karaṇa*) of the oblation (*havir*).
In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member is retained.

In the compound *nityaṃ samāse'nuttarapadasthasya*, the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *va*. [The form] *aśvat* is derived from the root *aś* (to reach), with the *parasmaipada* ending applied by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
In the case of the *leṭ* suffix, the augment *āṬ* is added.
O Agni and Soma, such is your heroic power that you stole away the Pani’s cattle for the sake of help;
you caused the remnant of Bṛsaya to cross over, and you found the one light for many.
O Agni and Soma, that was your heroic power by which you stole away the cow of Paṇi; you caused his wealth to fall and bypassed the offspring of Bṛsaya; you found the single light for many. 4.
O Agni and Soma, that heroic power and capability of yours which is about to be described has become known to us—
that power by which you recovered the cattle, that is, food in the form of cows, from Paṇi (the genitive case is changed to the accusative).
From this asura named [so-and-so], you two stole— that is, you carried it away—
and likewise from Vṛsaya.
The root *vṛs* means "to envelop."
He who envelops everything is *vṛsaya*, an Asura; [the word] belongs to that Asura. *Śeṣa* is his offspring.
Yāska states: "The word *śeṣa* is a name for offspring, for he remains (*śiṣyate*) through effort" (Nirukta 3.2).
"You two overcame—that is, you slew—Vṛtra, who was born from Tvaṣṭṛ.
The root *avati* here has the sense of killing.
Because of the disturbance of the two of you, who are of the nature of prāṇa and apāna, he met his death due to the displacement of his vital breaths."
And thus it is handed down in the tradition: "From him, as he was being known, Agni and Soma departed; indeed, Prāṇa and Apāna then left him" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.2.4).
Therefore, after the slaying of Vṛtra, you two found the light—the shining Sun—moving alone in the sky for the sake of many people, [you who were] yourselves of little standing.
The meaning is: "We have come to know that heroic power by which all this is accomplished."
And [the root] *cit*: in the sense of "perception" (*saṃjñāna*).
In the *luṅ* tense, by the rule *ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.66), there is the substitution of *ciṇ* for *cli*.
By the rule *ciṇo luk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ta*.
[The form is] *amuṣṇītam*.
[The root is] *muṣ* in the sense of stealing.
*Kaiyādikaḥ* [is derived from *kai*] with the suffix *ādi*.
*Avasam* [is derived from the root] *ava* with the suffix *asac*, which belongs to the *uṇādi* group.
The remainder [is as follows]:
by the rule "supāṃ suluk," the second case ending is replaced by *su*. One.
The root *iṇ* means "to go.

The suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule *iṇ-bhī-kā-pā-śalya-timarcibhyaḥ kan* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.123). Because it is marked with the *niṭ* indicatory letter (*n*), the word is accented on its first syllable.
1. That which is to be done by means of *kṣa*. 2. The seat (*vṛsi*) made of *kṣa*. 3.
He causes [it] to be covered with *kṣa* grass (*sa-bṛsayati*).
For the omentum, the cake, and the oblation of the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, the first three verses beginning with "yuvametāni" are respectively the *yājyās*.
The Sūtra has already been cited previously (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
In the Full Moon sacrifice, this verse "yuvametāni" is the *yājyā* for the cake dedicated to Agni and Soma.
In the section titled "The Deities Have Been Stated," it is aphoristically formulated: "O Indra and Agni, come with your protection to these luminous realms in heaven" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.6).
O Soma and Agni, you two of one mind have placed these luminous realms in heaven;
O Agni and Soma, you released the rivers from reproach and from blame when they were seized.

You two, O Agni and Soma, acting with one will, have placed these luminous realms in heaven; you two, O Agni and Soma, have released the rivers from reproach and from disgrace when they were seized. 5.

O Soma, you two, being unmixed yet possessing equal power (*sakratū*) and performing the same action, placed these shining, radiant lights—these stars and great luminaries visible by us at night—in the sky, in the celestial world. This is the narrative concerning Uttara-Āṣāḍhā:

Indra, having slain Vṛtra and being terrified of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter (*brahmahatyā*), cast that slaughter upon the earth, the trees, women, and the waters; the purification of those waters was brought about through Agni and Soma.

O Agni and Soma, you two liberated the Sindhus—specific rivers seized, taken, and overwhelmed by the portion of the sin of Brahman-slaughter—from that reproach, from the blame manifested all around as they were being censured; that is, from that evil.
Or alternatively:
Vṛtra, having been slain by Indra, fell into the rivers.

Then, because of the dead body of Vṛtra, all the rivers became defiled. Thus says the Taittirīyaka: "Indra slew Vṛtra; he was seized by the waters. Whatever in them was pure, fit for sacrifice, and divine, that departed from them" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.5.1).
Afflicted by that defect, Agni and Soma released the rivers from that impurity.
*rocanāni*. [Derived from] the root *ruc* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*).
The suffix *yuc* is applied according to the rule *anudāttettaśca halādeḥ*.
In *sindhūn*,
the letter *n* undergoes the substitution of *r* by the rule "after a long vowel, before a vowel (*aṭ*), within the same metrical foot.
Then, by the rule "here [the preceding vowel] may be nasalized," it becomes nasalized.
*gṛbhītān*:
the status of *bha* is established by the rule *hy-ama-hor-bhaḥ*.
For the *upāṃśuyāja* dedicated to Agni and Soma, "ānyaṃ divaḥ" is the *yājyā*.
Regarding "agnīṣomā yo adya vām," the *sūtra* has already been cited.
Mātariśvan brought one from heaven; the falcon brought the other from the mountain.
O Agni and Soma, having grown strong through our prayer, you have made wide space for the sacrifice.

Mātariśvan brought one from heaven; the falcon deposited the other from the mountain. O Agni and Soma, growing strong through the sacred word (*brahman*), you have made wide space for the sacrifice. 6.
O Agni and Soma, Mātariśvan—Vāyu—brought one of you two, Agni, from the sky, the heavenly world, for Bhṛgu, the sacrificer;
as another mantra states: "Mātariśvan brought to Bhṛgu the twice-born one, like celebrated wealth, bringing delight" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.60.1).
And the Falcon—the Gāyatrī, which has the form of a bird and possesses a praiseworthy course—forcibly seized the other, Soma, from the mountain, Meru, situated in heaven.

Thus, you two of such great power— having been magnified (*vavṛdhānā*), that is, increasing, by the Creator Brahmā through the *Ṛgveda* in the form of mantras or through the hymn characterized by oblations— you have made (*cakrathuḥ*), that is, created, a vast world or station (*loka*) for the sacrifice, namely for the worship of the other gods.
The particle *u* is used here for the purpose of completing the meter.
The two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) are offered to the deities Agni and Soma in the northern and southern halves [of the fire];
in the middle of those, all other oblations (*havīṃṣi*) intended for other deities are offered.
That middle position is established by Agni and Soma.

Thus says the Taittirīyaka: "These two, indeed, are the kings among the deities; that Agni and Soma are worshipped between [the other deities] is for the support of the deities" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.2.1–2).
*vavṛdhānā*:
from the root *vṛdh* (to grow), the suffix *kānac* is applied in the perfect tense (*liṭ*);
the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is Vedic.
The vowel *ā* [in *sugandhā*] is substituted [for the case ending] by the rule "supām suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
O Agni and Soma, enjoy this presented oblation; O bulls, desire it and take pleasure in it!
Since you have become providers of good protection and a bright dwelling, bestow health and well-being upon the sacrificer.
O Agni and Soma,
[partake] of the oblation! Forward!
He serves Agni and Soma with clarified butter as an oblation;
protect the vow— the ritual duty— of that sacrificer,
and guard that sacrificer from distress and evil.
O Agni and Soma, grant great, abundant, and ample protection and happiness to that person, the sacrificer, who enters into the various sacrifices. [In the term *agnīṣomā*,
the accent on both members of the compound is retained according to the rule *devatādvandve ca*.]
*Saparyāta*:
[The root] *sapar* is used in the sense of worship;
it belongs to the *kaṇvādi* class.
The augment *āṬ* is applied before the suffix *leṭ*. *Devadīcā*:
[it is derived from] *devagaḍ*, which means "one who goes beyond the gods."
The suffix *kin* is applied by the rule “*ṛtvig*” etc.;
there is elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule “*aniditām*” [Pāṇini 6.4.24];
and the final vowel (*ṭi*) of the word *deva* is replaced by *ad* by the rule “*viśvadevayośca ṭerañjatātrapratyaye*” (Pāṇini 6.3.92).
In the third case singular, by the rule *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138), there is elision of the vowel *a*; then, by the rule *cau* (Pāṇini 6.3.138), lengthening occurs.

When the original accent of the final member of the compound (*kruduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) would have applied, the substitution *adyādeśaḥ* is treated as having an udātta accent on its final syllable, according to the statement: “The substitution of *adi* for *adr̥s* and *savya* is prescribed with an udātta on the final syllable in order to prevent [the application of] the accent of the kṛt-affix” (Pāṇini 6.3.95.1).
[The word is] *viśe*.
The acute accent on the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
In the Parṇamāsa sacrifice, "O Agni and Soma" (*agnīṣomā*) is the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the Agnīṣomīya offering.

This is stated in the section beginning with "Having mentioned the deities" (*uktā devatāḥ*) in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra: "O Agni and Soma, you two who possess common wealth, [place] these luminous realms in heaven" (*agnīṣomā savedasā yuvametāni divi rocanāni*).
O Agni and Soma, you who possess all wealth, being invoked together, accept our songs; you have both become present among the divine beings. 9.
O Agni and Soma, you who possess common wealth and are invoked together, accept our songs; you have both become present among the gods.

O Agni and Soma, you two who possess common wealth (*savedasā*)—that is, being endowed with the same single wealth characterized by the oblation—and who are invoked together (*sahūtī*), accept (*vanataṃ*) our songs, that is, our praises.
Among all the gods (*devatrā*), you two have become united (*saṃ babhūvathuḥ*), being esteemed and celebrated.
For the Śruti states: "These two deities, Agni and Soma, are indeed kings."
*savedasā*: those whose *veda* (knowledge) is the same. The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by the rule "samānasya chandasi" [Pāṇini 6.3.84].
*vanatam*:
[from] *vana-paṇa*, meaning "to enjoy" or "to serve.
*Devatrā*.
In the phrase “*devamanuṣyapuruṣapurumartyaḥ*,” the suffix *trā* is used in the sense of the locative case. O Agni and Soma, to him who honors you both with clarified butter, grant great wealth. 10.
O Agni and Soma! To him who honors you both with this [oblation] and with clarified butter, grant great wealth. 10.

O Agni and Soma, to that sacrificer who belongs to you two and who offers to you both an oblation prepared with this clarified butter—refined through heating and other processes—grant him abundant wealth; that is to say, bestow it upon him. [The word] *dārśati* [is derived from] the root *dāś*, meaning "to give."
Since the suffix *śasi* is marked with *pittva*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains.
Because it is not joined with a word beginning with *yad* (i.e., it is not part of a *yadvṛtti* compound), there is no elision of the accent (*anighāta*).
[The form is] *dīyatām*.
The root *dī* signifies the act of giving.
O Agni and Soma, may you both graciously accept these our oblations; come hither together with us. 11.
O Agni and Soma, may you both enjoy these our oblations; come together unto us. 11.
1. The [phonemes] ending in ca, cha, ta, na, pha, śa, and sa are designated as having the udātta accent on their final syllable.
2. The phonemes ṭa and ṭha have the same name as sa. 3. Kṣa is the root dīdheti.
O Agni and Soma, may you two enjoy these our oblations;
for that purpose, come together with us and approach us. May you two enjoy them.
The root *juṣ* means "to delight in" and "to serve.
In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, there is an irregular substitution for the *śap* suffix;
the reduplication is Vedic.
Alternatively,
the *vikaraṇa* suffix is elided by the rule "there is frequent elision (*bahulam*) in the Vedic language" (*chandasi*);
thereafter, the *śap* suffix is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

By virtue of the statement "it should be stated that [the rule] applies frequently in the Vedic language," there is an absence of the prohibition against the *guṇa* substitution for the penultimate light vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) which is prescribed by the rule "not [after a reduplicated stem] before a vowel-initial suffix beginning with *p*."
O Agni and Soma, fulfill our desires; let the cows that yield the oblation swell with milk.
Bestow strength upon us and upon our patrons, and make our sacrifice successful and full of prompt obedience.
O Agni and Soma, satisfy our horses; let the cows swell with milk that provide the oblations.
Bestow strength upon us and upon our liberal patrons; make our sacrifice rich in swift success. 12.

O Agni and Soma, protect our horses; let our cows, which produce the oblations of milk and other offerings, swell with nourishment and thrive. Bestow strength upon us, who are possessed of wealth in the form of sacrificial offerings; likewise, make our sacrifice full of success and rich in riches. *Pipṛtam*: from the root *pṛ*, meaning "to protect" or "to fill. Some authorities read it as *pṛ*. Because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu*-elision of the suffix *śap*. By the rule "of *arti* and *piparti*," there is *hvam* (guṇa) in the reduplicative syllable. *Havyasūdaḥ*: those who cause the oblation (*havya*) to flow or drip (*sūdante*). From the root *pūda*, meaning "to flow. The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "and *kvip*. *Asme*: the locative case ending is replaced by *śe* according to the rule "for case-endings, *suluk*. *Śruṣṭimantam*: *śruṣṭi* is a name for wealth. It is derived from *śu* (quickly) + *aśyate* (is pervaded), thus *śruṣṭi*. It belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. The suffix *matup* is acute-accented according to the rule "after a short vowel and *nuḍ*, *matup*. 29 || 14 ||
In the fifteenth section, there are twelve hymns. Among them, the first hymn, consisting of sixteen verses beginning with "imaṃ stomam," is the seerage of Kutsa, a descendant of Aṅgiras.
The fifteenth and sixteenth verses are *triṣṭubh*s; the remaining ones are *jagatī*s.
Agni is the deity.
In the verse "May the chariot of the one who presses [the soma] be foremost, O gods," three quarters have the gods as their deity.
