The half-verse beginning with "tanno mitro varuṇaḥ" has six deities—Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others—as indicated by their respective marks (liṅga).
Alternatively, Agni alone is its deity, while Mitra, Varuṇa, and the rest are subordinate as mere incidental mentions (nipāta).

All of this has been enumerated [in the Anukramaṇī]: "These sixteen [verses] are by Kutsa; they are addressed to Agni, except for those ending in the Tristubh meter; the first three feet are addressed to the gods; the [next] three are addressed to the gods; the half-verse beginning with 'mitraḥ' has deities indicated by their marks; or rather, the entire hymn [is so]."
This hymn is used in the Prātaranuvāka during the Āgneya kratu in the Jāgata metre, as well as in the Āśvina Śastra;
thus it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "imaṃ stomamarhate saṃ jāgavadbhiḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
Furthermore, on the sixth day of the Abhiplava period, this hymn is also used in the Ābhimāruta Śastra as the Nivid-vessel for the Jātavedas section.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the verse beginning 'prayajya imam stomam,' [one performs] the Ābhimāruta [offering]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).

At the third pressing, this verse "imaṃ stomam" is the *prasthitayājyā* for Agni and Viṣṇu. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the verse 'imaṃ stomamarhate jātavedase,' [one performs] the offerings belonging to the third pressing" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5).
1. [The rule regarding the substitution of *ām* for the case endings *kṣe*, *ṭā*, *ṭha*, and *si*: Gaṇapāṭha 1, Adhyāya 15, Sūtra 94. 583.
Let us fashion this hymn with our intellect, as one fashions a chariot, for Jātavedas who is worthy of it.
For auspicious is his providence in the assembly; may we, in your friendship, never suffer harm.

For this worthy Jātavedas, let us fashion this hymn with our inspired thought, as one fashions a chariot. For his providence toward us is auspicious in the assembly; O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm. 1.

To the Arhat, the worshipful Jātavedas—the knower of all that is born, produced, or arisen; to Agni, who possesses innate wisdom or innate wealth—with sharpened *manīṣā*, that is, with keen intellect, we shall thoroughly fashion (*saṃmahema*) this hymn (*stoma*), this song of praise, just as a carpenter constructs a chariot.
In the assembly (*saṃsad*) of this Agni, during our partaking [of his favor], may our *pramati*—our preeminent, auspicious, and capable intelligence—be indeed favorable.
Therefore, by means of that intelligence, we offer praise; such is the meaning.
O Agni, may we be able to accomplish this in your friendship; may we perfect our prayers through you. In you the gods eat the offered oblation.
Bring hither the Ādityas for the sake of this sacrifice; may we, in your companionship, suffer no harm.
May we be able to kindle thee; fulfill our prayers. In thee the gods eat the offered oblation.
Bring hither the Ādityas, for we long for them. O Agni, in thy friendship may we never suffer harm. 3.
O Agni, may we be able—that is, may we have the power—to properly prepare you as the fuel.
And you, indeed, accomplish—that is, bring to completion—our ritual acts such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
for by you all sacrifices are perfected.

Since this oblation has been offered to you by the priests, O Agni, the protector of the people, the creatures of the clans move about—both bipeds and quadrupeds—through the nights. Wondrous, a great light of the dawn art thou; O Agni, in thy friendship may we never suffer harm.

The guardian of the people, his creatures move about—both those that are two-footed and those that are four-footed—by his rays. O Agni, you are the wonderful, great herald of the dawn; in your friendship, may we never suffer harm. 5.

The creatures born from this Agni—his rays—are the guardians, the protectors, and the defenders of all people, of all living beings; they move, that is, they rise up. Thereafter, both that which is two-footed, such as humans and the like, and also that which is four-footed, such as cattle and the like—both of these [are protected] by the nights.
In that state, you are the accomplisher of the sacrifice;
you are the *potṛ*, the purifier and cleanser of the sacrifice.
Or rather, presiding over the officiant named *potṛ* as before, you are the accomplisher of the sacrifice.
Likewise, by birth— that is, by your very nature— you are the *purohita*, one who acts favorably for the benefit of [the sacrificer] in the future, such as in heaven; or rather,
you are established in the eastern direction at the *āhavanīya* fire for all ritual actions.
Alternatively, the *purohita* is Brahmā because he acts as the representative of Bṛhaspati, the priest of the gods.
Accordingly, another mantra states: "Bṛhaspati is the priest (*brahmán*) of the gods; I am the priest of men" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.6.3).

Therefore, O wise and intelligent Agni, while remaining in that state as Brahmā as before, being one who knows all the sacrificial duties (*ārviñjyā*)—that is, the rituals of the *adhvaryu* and other priests—you make them perfect, free from deficiency or excess.
The rest is the same.
By birth;
from the root *jan*, the suffix *usi*; the domestic priest (*purohita*).
The word is formed from the root *dadhāti* with the suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) in the sense of the object;
it ends in the suffix *asip* according to the rule "pūrvāndhra" etc.,
and the word *pūra* is oxytone (accented on the final syllable).

By the rule "and that which ends in a taddhita suffix is an indeclinable provided it does not end in a case-suffix," the term receives the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Consequently, by the rule "puro'dhvaryu," [the word *adhvaryu*] functions as a *gati* (preverb), and by the rule "a preceding *gati* retains its original accent," the first member of the compound retains its natural accent.
[The form] *ārviñyā* [is derived] with the suffix *vyañ* because [the base *ṛtvij*] belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class.
The first syllable of *jiṣṇu* and other such words is udātta.
You who are beautiful of countenance on every side and very firm, you shine even from afar, though you are close at hand.
O God, you see even beyond the night; in this friendship of yours, may we never suffer harm.

You who are fair of countenance on every side, you are very firm; even though you are far away, you shine forth as if from close at hand. Even beyond the night, O God, you look out. O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm. 7.
O Agni, you who are *supratīka*— possessing beautiful limbs— and who, being complete, are *sahṛḍḍha*, that is, equal to all without deficiency; you, though remaining *dūre cit*, even at a distance,
shine forth (*ati rocase*) exceedingly, like one standing *tuliva*— this is a name for "near"— as if you were present nearby.

This has been stated by Yāska: "Even though you are far away, you appear as if you were near" (Nirukta 3.11). O radiant Agni, even through the night—indeed, even the dense darkness (*andhas*) of the night—you see beyond it; you shine forth exceedingly.
The rest is as before.
Supratīkaḥ:
one whose limbs (pratīka) or body parts (aṅga) are beautiful (śobhana).
By the rule "ṛvādyaśca," the first syllable of the second member of the compound is udātta.

*sahṛd* [is formed] from the root *dṛś* with the prefix *samāna* as its upapada, according to the rule "it should be stated that [the suffix *kvip* applies] after *samāna* and *anya*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.60.1).
[The suffix is] *kvip*.
By the rule *dṛśavatuṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.89), there is the substitution of *sa* for *samāna*.
By the rule *hrasvatvaḥ svatavasāṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.83), the augment *num* is added.
Then, the final consonant of the conjunct cluster is elided (*saṃyogāntalopaḥ*).
The substitution of *k* for the suffix *kin* occurs by the rule "kuḥ.
There is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of the compound.
[This applies to] *rātryāḥ*.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 4.1.31: *rātreḥ śrajjasau*.
O Gods, let the chariot of the one who presses the soma be foremost; may our hymn of praise overcome the enemy.
Then recognize this word and cause it to prosper; O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm.

[The Seer: O Gods, let it be so! May the chariot of the one who presses the soma be foremost; may our hymn overcome the malicious enemy. Take note of this and cause these words to flourish. O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm. 8.

O gods—meaning all the gods who constitute the limbs of Agni—may the chariot of the sacrificer, who performs the pressing of Soma, be foremost; that is, may it be preeminent compared to the chariots of other sacrificers. Furthermore, may our praise overcome—that is, surpass—the evil intention (dudhiyaḥ) of those who are ill-disposed toward us and intent on hostile conduct; may it afflict them.
O gods, recognize this one called Madra; come to know him directly.
Furthermore, nourish and honor our word by acting in accordance with its meaning.
O Agni, who embodies all the gods!
“*Sakhye*,” etc., is as before. Regarding *sunvataḥ*:
by the rule “*śatru-ajumaḥ*,” the case ending receives the udātta accent.
Śaṃsa: [It is so called] because it is praised (*śaṃsyate*) or scattered (*kīryate*); thus, *śaṃsa* means a curse. The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The word *jisu* has the udātta accent on its first syllable. *Dukhyaḥ*:
those who meditate poorly are called *dudhiyaḥ*.
From the root *dhyai* in the sense of “thinking” (*cintā*), the suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule *kvip ca*.
Because the mention of the root *dṛś* is carried over [from a previous rule], and because that [mention] is intended to include other rules as well, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
Furthermore, because the reading “*dhyai ca*” occurs in the *pṛṣodarādi* group, the vowel *u* replaces the *r* of *dur*, and the initial letter of the following member becomes *du*.
Strike down with your weapons those who speak evil and the malicious; slay all devourers, whether they be far away or near.
Then, for the sake of the sacrifice, make the path easy for the one who praises you; O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm.

Strike down the evil-speakers; strike the malevolent ones. Whether they be far away or near, whoever are devourers, crush them. Prepare a good path for the sacrifice and for the one who praises you. O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm. 9.
O Agni, with your weapons—the instruments of slaughter—drive away and strike down those of evil speech, who are difficult to mention, the wicked, and the evil-minded.
Whosoever there may be, whether they dwell in a distant land or in the vicinity nearby, those devourers such as Rākṣasas and others who exist—drive away those evil-minded ones; this is the meaning.
Then, immediately thereafter, for the sake of the sacrifice, for the lord of the sacrifice, and for the one who praises you, create and provide a beautiful path for the sacrificer.

The rest is as before. Regarding *vadhaiḥ*: by the rule "hanaśca vadhaḥ," the suffix *ap* is applied to the root *han*, and *vadha* is the substitute [for *han*] in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
And that [suffix] is unaccented and has its final syllable acute (antodātta).
When the *at* of that [suffix] is elided, the suffix becomes acute by the rule regarding the accentuation of the disappearance of an acute vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). Thus: *duḥśasān*.
By the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu* [Pāṇini 3.3.126], the suffix *khal* is applied in the sense of the object;
by the rule *liti* [Pāṇini 6.1.193], the syllable preceding the suffix is acute-accented. [The form is] *jahi*.
In the imperative (*loṭ*): by the rule "the substitute *ja* [is applied] for *han*", there is the substitution of *ja*.
Because that [substitution] is "treated as not having taken effect" (*asiddhavat*) with respect to what precedes within the same verbal complex (*ābhāt*), there is no elision of the *hi*.
*anti*: the *ka* of *antika* is elided by the rule "the elision of *ka* etc. occurs frequently" (*kādilopo bahulam*). [The form is] *atriṇaḥ*.
In the word *adestrini*, there are three suffixes (*pratyaya*):
the vowel *i* is for the purpose of protecting the letter *n*;
[the form is] *gṛṇate*.
In the word *śatruranumaḥ*, the case ending is udātta.
This is easily understood. [The suffix] *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* by the rule *suduroradhikaraṇe* (Pāṇini 3.2.48.3).
"Make [it]!"— the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs by the rule "In the Veda, after the roots *śru*, *śṛ*, *ṇu*, and *kṛ*";
the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) occurs by the rule "Frequently in the Veda."
When you have yoked the two ruddy, red steeds to your chariot, driven by the wind, your roar is like that of a bull.
You consume the forests with your smoke-bannered flame; O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm.

When you have yoked the ruddy, red steeds to your chariot, impelled by the wind—your roar is like that of a bull; then you stir the forests with your smoke-bannered flame. O Agni, in your friendship, may we never suffer harm. 10.
1. *kṣa* is praised;
2. *sa* [is used] in the sense of "nearby" (*antike*); 3.
*kṣa* is [the substitute for] the imperative (*loṭ*).
"O Agni, the two ruddy ones, shining, the two red-colored ones.
For *rohita* is a name for Agni, as seen in the statement, "Rohita is a name of Agni" (Nirukta 1.15.2), and also from the wording of the mantra:
"May Rohita cause you to go to the deity" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.4.3).
For it is explained there [in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.4.3]: "These indeed are the divine horses.
"Impelled by the wind" (*vātajūtā*):
those two whose speed (*java*) or velocity (*vega*) is like that of Vāta, the wind.
When you yoked or have harnessed such two horses to the chariot, then the sound of your *ratha* (chariot) as it burns the forests becomes deep like the bellowing of a bull or a great ox.
Immediately thereafter, with your flame whose banner is smoke—that is, with that light which has smoke as its indicator—you pervade the *vaninaḥ*, the trees associated with the forest.
The rest is as before.
*Ayukthāḥ*:
[derived from] the root *yujir* in the sense of "joining" (*yoge*).
[In the form] *luṅi*, there is the elision of the *s* by the rule *jhalo jhali*.
May this singer of praise for Agni be for the sustenance—that is, for the support and maintenance—of Mitra, the deity presiding over the day, and of Varuṇa, the deity presiding over sovereignty.
The meaning is: "May Mitra and Varuṇa sustain this singer of praise for Agni.

The wrath of the Maruts—the gods so named who dwell in the intermediate space below the heavenly world—is truly great and formidable. May they descend from above, moving downward through the atmosphere.
*Adbhuta* is a name for the Great One (*mahat*).
Therefore, [the meaning is: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect this singer of Agni from that wrath"—this is the ellipsis. Furthermore, O Agni, *su mṛḷa*: graciously show mercy; bring us happiness.
May the mind of these great ones become clear once again;
the rest is the same.
For the sake of nourishing (*dhāyase*). The suffix *asun* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*) by the rule "after *vahi*, *hā*, and *dhā* in the Veda" (*vahihādhābhyaśchandasi*).

Because the term "*nit*" is understood from the previous rule, the augment *yuk* is added by the rule "the augment *yuk* is added after a root ending in long *ā* before the suffixes *ciṇ* and *kṛt*" (*āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*).
*avayātām*. [The root] *yā* [is used] in the sense of "reaching.
From this [root], preceded by the prefix *ava*, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied to the present tense (*laṭ*).
In the phrase “śatruranumaḥ,” the case ending is udātta (accented). [The word] mṛḷa [is used]; [the root] mṛḍ means “to gladden” or “to be gracious.”
Because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the suffix *śap* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, by the rule *ṇeraniṭi*, there is the elision of the *ṇi*.
By the rule *aco 'ntyādi ṭi*, the *ṭi*-portion is elided. Then, by the rule *aco 'ti tiṅaḥ*, there is lengthening in the *saṃhitā* [reading].
Thus: *bhūtu*.
The elision of the *śap* suffix occurs frequently in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
You are the god of gods, a wondrous Mitra; you are the Vasu of Vasus, beautiful in your power. May we abide in your most expansive shelter; O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm.

You are the god of the gods, a wondrous friend; you are the Vasu of the Vasus, beloved in the lower realm. May we abide in your most extensive protection; O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm. 13.
O Agni, you, the radiant god, are the wondrous and great friend (*mitra*) of all the gods; you are the mature protector.
Likewise, you are beautiful and auspicious; in the sacrifice (*adhvara*), you are the treasure (*vasu*) of all treasures (*vasūnām*), that is, the one who provides them.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Grant us riches."
Furthermore, may we abide—remaining—in your own protection, which is most extensive, meaning most wide-reaching and exceedingly vast; that is, in the sacrificial hall.
The rest is as before.
In *śarman*, the locative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
That indeed is auspicious for you, that being kindled in your own abode, invoked with Soma, you roar as the most compassionate one.
You bestow jewels and wealth upon the donor; O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm.

That is your blessing: that, kindled in your own home and offered oblations of Soma, you sing forth as the most merciful one. You bestow jewels and wealth upon the donor. O Agni, in your friendship may we never suffer harm. 14.
O Agni, that which belongs to you (*te*) is indeed *bhadram*—that is, worthy of being enjoyed;
the meaning is that it is praiseworthy.
But what, then, is that?
In his own home, that is, in his dwelling place characterized by the *uttaravedi* altar—as the Śruti states: "His very own world is the navel of the *uttaravedi*" (*Ai.

Brā.* 1.28)—there he is kindled, thoroughly ignited, and blazing; and having been satiated with the offered oblation of meat-juice (*somāhuta*), he is praised for the sake of longevity by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). That which exists [in this state] is auspicious—this is the meaning.
Thus you are praised as the most compassionate;
[in the versions] kṣa, ṭa, ḍha, and sa, you are "immeasurable" (ame);
and in kṣa and sa, it is "again, being [a state] not separated from anger."

Having become our preeminent bringer of happiness, you bestow—upon the *dāśuṣe*, the sacrificer who has offered oblations—the *ratnam*, the delightful fruit of action, and the *draviṇam*, wealth. The rest is the same. Regarding *sāṃmiddhaḥ*: the root *mih* (in the form *jihvandhī*) means "to shine. It is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*). By the rule *śrīdito niṣṭhāyām*, there is a prohibition against the substitution of *i*. By the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the preceding prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). Regarding *somāhutaḥ*: [meaning] "one to whom Soma has been offered" (*somenāhutaḥ*). By the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*, the first member of the compound retains its original accent. Regarding *jarase*: the root *jṛ* signifies "to praise. By a transposition (*vyatyaya*), the agent suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) is used in the sense of the object. Because of its connection with *yad-vṛtta*, it does not lose its accent (*anighāta*). Regarding *dadhāsi*: by the rule *anudātte ca*, the reduplicated stem (*abhyasta*) has the acute accent on its first syllable.
To whomsoever you, O possessor of excellent wealth, grant sinlessness and wholeness through Aditi—
to him whom you impel with auspicious power, may we be those who possess your wealth accompanied by progeny.
To whomsoever you, O possessor of good wealth, grant sinlessness, O Aditi, in every respect—him [you protect].

The deities: and all these [deities] have increased the life-span of the one who is great—this is the syntactical connection with what precedes. Regarding *saubhagavasya*: *saubhagam* is the state (*bhāva*) of being fortunate (*subhaga*). Because *subhaga* is listed among the *udgātrādi* group, the suffix *añ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Furthermore, the production of this abstract suffix is Vedic (*chāndasī*). Regarding *mamahantām*: the root *maha* means "to honor" (*pūjāyām*); it belongs to the *bhauvādika* class. In the imperative (*loṭ*), by the rule "variously in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), the *śap* is replaced by *śnu*. Due to its inclusion in the *tujādi* group, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). || 32 ||
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human existence.

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the first book in the *Rgveda-saṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial authority of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
1. Destroying the moment (kṣa-vināśayan). 2. Together with the minister named Kṣasa (kṣa-sa-sāyaṇāmātyena).
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas.
The first hymn in the fifteenth section of the first maṇḍala has been explained.
The second hymn consists of eleven verses beginning with “dve virūpe.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: “dve ekādaśau sāyavāmaye.”
By the paribhāṣā rule "from another seer," because of the recurrence of Kutsa, the seer is Kutsa Āṅgirasa.
By the paribhāṣā rule regarding the lack of specific instruction, the metre is Triṣṭubh.
The deity is Agni, who partakes of the oblation at dawn (upasi).
Alternatively,

since it was previously stated that "that belongs to Agni," according to the technical rule (paribhāṣā) regarding *tu* and so forth, these five hymns beginning with this one have Agni alone as their deity.
Therefore, the meaning of the word *vā* ("or") is that the deity of this hymn is either Agni characterized by the quality of being associated with the *aupasadha* rite, or pure Agni.

These two hymns beginning with "idam" belong to the *prātaranuvāka* in the *kratu* dedicated to Agni and in the *triṣṭubh* metre. Thus it is stated in the section beginning with "atha etasyāḥ": "The two hymns 'dve virūpe' [are used]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.13). Furthermore, these two are also employed in the *āśvina-śastra*, because they are extended [to that context] by the rule: "According to the procedure of the *prātaranuvāka*, of that very same *samāmnāya*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.5).
Two of different forms move about for their own purpose; one after the other, they suckle the calf.
With the one, he becomes golden-hued, self-sustaining; with the other, he is seen bright and full of splendor.

Two, of different forms, move toward their own purpose; one after another, they cause the calf to suckle. The tawny one, possessing self-power, exists in the one; the bright one, of beautiful luster, is seen in the other. ||1||
‘Sva’ means one’s own; ‘artha’ means sounding, or beautiful coming and going.
Alternatively, ‘artha’ means purpose.
In that which is endowed with a beautiful purpose, yet is not uniform—being of diverse forms through its white and black aspects—the two, day and night, move about and revolve again and again.
These two, day and night, are the mothers of Agni and Sūrya;
therein, Sūrya is the son of Night.
For he, having been hidden during the night of the womb, is born from its final portion.
Day is the son Agni;
for although he exists there, being as if non-existent due to the absence of light, he becomes manifest and attains his own self once he is released from that day.
The status of these two as the offspring of those two is recorded by the Taittirīyas: "Of those two, these are the two calves:
Agni and Āditya.
The calf of the night is [Agni]."
"The sun is white; by day it is fire; it is coppery and ruddy" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.10).
And during day and night, they both cause their own respective calves—their own sons—to suckle by means of mutual exchange; that is, they cause them to drink their own milk.
What must be done by the Night for her son, the Sun, namely the causing of him to drink his milk, that she performs during the Day.
And what must be done by the Day for her son, Agni, namely the causing of him to drink his milk, that the Night performs.
And this refers to the offerings made in the evening and in the morning.
For it is heard in scripture: “Therefore, an offering is made to Agni in the evening and to Sūrya in the morning” (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.6).

Because of this, in another mother—other than his own [natural] mother, namely in the mother who consists of the day—the Sun, who is "hari" (one whose nature is to move swiftly), "svadhāvān" (possessing the oblation as his characteristic), comes to be.

1. By the two [letters] śa-ṭa-ṭha; 2. ṭa-ṭha [denote] day and night; 3. a-ṭa-ḍha arise in the final portion; 4. śa-ṭa-ṭha [occur] at that time; 5. jha [denotes] one's own son; 6. kṣa [denotes] the drinking of juice; 7. kṣa-na-sa [indicate] that there is no juice.

Śukra, possessing stainless brilliance like fire, was seen—being endowed with beautiful luster (suvarcas)—on another night, on the night of the mother of the Sun (Sūrya). [The suffix] -sva is used in its own sense.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.
According to the rule *uṣikupigātibhyasthan*, the suffix *than* is applied in the sense of either the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
Due to its *nit*-designation, it bears the acute accent on the first syllable.
Those two [words] have the sense of "excellent. According to the rule *āyudāttaṃ chandasi*, there is acute accent on the first syllable of the second member of the compound.
*Anyānyā*.

According to the rule "it should be stated that when there is a reciprocal action (*karmavyatihāra*), two forms of the pronoun occur, and [the compound] is frequently treated as a *samāsa*" (Pāṇini Mañjarī 8.1.12.11), there is reduplication.

Because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*), even in the absence of the status of a *samāsa*, the subsequent form receives the designation *ānneḍita* by the rule "that which follows it is called *ānneḍita*," and by the rule "and it is unaccented" (*anudāttaṃ ca*), the *ānneḍita* is unaccented.
Thus: *dhāpayete*.
[The root] *pā* [is used] in the sense of drinking. By the rule "ādeca upadeśe'śiti," there is the substitution of *ā*.
Then, the suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of causing to do (*hetumati*).
By the rule *atihrī* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.36), the augment *puK* is added to the root.

For in that context, it has been indicated that the paribhāṣā concerning "that which is taught by a specific rule versus that which is taught by its general definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) does not apply, as evidenced by the mention of forms such as *kṛtāstha* in the rule *śācchāsāhlāvyā*.
That [mention] is indeed for the purpose of indicating that [the paribhāṣā] is restricted.
If the *puk* augment were not applicable there by virtue of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning "that which is taught by its specific form," then that [rule] would be purposeless.
Therefore, just as in *adhyāpayati* and similar forms, the *puk* augment is established here in *dhāpayete* as well.

Furthermore, although the Parasmaipada ending would have been required by the rule *nigaraṇacalanārthebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.87), the Ātmanepada is used instead because of the prohibition stated in the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) *pādiṣu dheṭa upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 1.3.89.1).
Hari: [derived from] the root *hṛñ* in the sense of "taking away," with the suffix *in* according to the *uṇādi* rules.
In the case of *anityādi-nityam* and so forth, there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable.
By the rule *ekānyābhyāṃ samarthābhyām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.65), there is a prohibition of the suppression (*nivāta*) of the first-case (*prathamā*) nominative ending.
He was seen.
Regarding the root *dṛś* (to see): the suffix *liṭ* is used here because the rule "in Vedic usage, *luṅ* and *liṭ* [may be used for all tenses]" is in effect.
He was radiant.
One whose splendor (*varcas*) and brilliance (*tejas*) are beautiful;
the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the compound is due to the rule *sormanasī alomopasī*.
Ten tireless young women have brought forth this embryo of Tvaṣṭṛ, who is to be borne by many;
him of sharp aspect, self-glorious among the people, shining brightly, they lead around on all sides.
Ten [fingers], unwearied and youthful maidens, have generated this embryo of Tvaṣṭṛ, which is wide-spreading, sharp-pointed, self-glorious among men, and shining brightly; they lead him around. 2.

"Atandrāsaḥ" means untiring; that is, they are not indolent but vigilant in nourishing the world through their own work. "Yuvatayaḥ" means eternally youthful; that is, they are free from old age and death.

In this manner, the ten directions— the ten numbered ones beginning with the east— generate the Vaidyuta fire, which exists as an embryo within the clouds, from Tvaṣṭṛ, that is, from the radiant intermediate wind (*madhyama-vāyu*). Alternatively, the ten fingers generate the embryo of Agni— which exists as an embryo within the wind, its own cause,
since "wind is the cause of fire" according to the Śruti (*vāyor agniḥ*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.1)— from Tvaṣṭṛ, who is the wind perceived by sight.
They generate—that is, they produce—this fire from the proximity of the Arani wood.
Of what sort are the fingers?
They are "atandrasaḥ," meaning free from lassitude in the repeated performance of their task.
The young women exist without being separated;
the meaning is that they abide united within a single vital breath (*prāṇa*). "Pervasive" (*vibhṛtram*) means extended throughout all beings.
The meaning is that it exists by dividing itself in the form of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara-agni*).
It has a sharp array, a sharp mouth, and sharp brilliance;
for this very reason, the sight is obstructed when one looks at the fire in a forge.
"Self-glorious" means one whose glory is under his own control;
that is to say, exceedingly illustrious. "Shining forth among people" means shining preeminently throughout the countryside, in all lands.
The meaning is: "beneficial to many.
All people lead this Agni, who is of such a nature, around—that is, on all sides—for their own respective benefit, bringing him to their own respective regions.
*Tvaṣṭṛ*: [derived] from the root *ṣvi-p* in the sense of "to shine.
It is listed among the *uṇādi* suffixes as ending in *tṛn* by the rule *na-ṣṭṛ-tvaṣṭṛ* (*Uṇādisūtra* 2.252).
Therefore, it has the udātta accent on the first syllable by virtue of being a *nic* [term].
*Vibhṛtram*:
from the root *hṛñ*, meaning "to take away."
The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used in this sense [of the object].

1. *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *śānt*, *sāhā*. 2. *kṣa*, *sa*: by means of having attained. 3. *kṣa*, *ṭha*, *nam*: of this verbal suffix (*tiṅ-vibhakti*). 4. *kṣa*, *ṭha*, *ṭhan*, *sa*: "the fire was not known" does not exist [in these versions]. 5. *kṣa*, *na*, *sa*: in those very regions. 6. *kṣa*, *sa*: ending in a present active participle (*tṛn*). Ka. 75.

The addition of one *repha* is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). By the rule “*gatiranantaraḥ*,” the preceding verbal prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). By the rule “*hmrahorbheḥ*,” there is the substitution of *bh* for *m*. Alternatively, the suffix *ku* is derived from the *uṇādi* list. *Tigmānīkam*: [from] *tija* in the sense of sharpening. By the *Uṇādi-sūtra* 1.143, “*yujisarcatijāṃ kutvaṃ ca*,” the suffix *mak* is added, and there is a change to *k* (*kutva*). [From] *ana* in the sense of breathing. By the rule “*anidṛśibhyāṃ ca*,” the suffix *kīkan* is added. Thus, it means that whose face (*anīka*) is sharp (*tigma*, i.e., keen). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first member retains its original accent. *Pari pīmam*: by the rule “*pūrvapadāt*,” there is the substitution of *ph* for *m*.
Three births encompass him: one in the ocean, one in heaven, and one in the waters.
Governing the seasons in two ways according to his will, he has entered the stronghold of the earthly realms in every direction.

Three [abodes] they adorn: one in the ocean, one in heaven, and one in the waters. Governing the seasons according to the eastern direction of the earthly realms, he has distributed them in succession. 3.
The three—meaning the threefold—births or origins of this Agni adorn him, embellishing him on all sides from every direction;
or rather, "pari" (around) may stand in place of "sam" (together). Thus, three births of this Agni come into being.
One birth in the ocean, in the form of the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*);
one in heaven, in the world of the sky, as the soul of the sun;
[and one] in the waters.
"Water" is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
In the intermediate space, it exists as one [form] in the form of lightning.
Thus, the meaning is that fire itself, having divided its own self, abides in three locations.

There, Agni, existing in the form of the sun, governing— that is, clearly indicating by means of their distinct divisions— the six seasons beginning with spring, duly (*anuṣṭhu*)— this is an indeclinable meaning "properly" or "well"— distributed (*vy adadhau*) the eastern direction (*prācīm pra diśam*), the preeminent quarter, among all terrestrial beings related to the earth. He established it in due order.

The distinction between directions such as "east" and so forth, as well as the distinction between seasons such as "spring" and so forth, arises through the motion of the sun within space and time—which are themselves devoid of internal differentiation and partless.
Therefore, the meaning is that the sun alone is the creator of these two.
The root *jan* [is used] in the sense of manifestation (*prādurbhāva*).
[The suffix] *ghañ*.

Since the rule *karṣātvataḥ* would otherwise require the final syllable to be udātta, the word takes an initial udātta because it belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* headed by *vṛṣan*. The elision of the suffix *śe* occurs by the rule *śecchandasi bahulam*.
[The form] is *bhūpanti*.
The root *bhūṣ* [is used] in the sense of ‘adornment’ (*alaṃkāra*). It belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*.
Alternatively:

In the case of the root *bhū* in the *leṭ* mood, the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule "sibbahulaṃ leṭi. Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rules governing augments, there is no insertion of *iṭ*; and due to the non-universality of rules conditioned by a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is no *guṇa* substitution. [The form is] *divi*.
In "apsu," in both instances, the case ending is acute according to the rule "ud-īd-bahuvrīher am-nady-aj-aś. [The word] "pārthivānām" [is explained as follows].
In the word *pṛthivyāḥ*, the suffix *an* is applied according to the rule for derivatives meaning "belonging to" (*prāgdīvyatīya*).
[The root] *praśāsat* [is derived from] *śās* in the sense of "governing" (*anuśiṣṭau*).
From this [root], the suffix *śatṛ* is applied by the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛ*.
Since the six roots beginning with *jakṣ* receive the designation *abhyasta* (repeated) by the rule *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ*, there is a prohibition of the augment *num* by the rule *nābhyastāc chatuḥ*.
The accentuation follows the rule for the natural accent of the final member of a compound ending in a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
[The meter is] Anuṣṭubh.
The suffix *ku*, which is prescribed by the rule “*apaduḥsupu sthaḥ*” (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.25), is also applied to the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *anu* due to the word *bahulam* (“variously”).
Who among you has perceived this secret? The calf has brought forth his mothers by his own inherent powers;
the great seer, the offspring of many, the possessor of self-power, emerges from the lap of the active ones.

Who among you has perceived this secret? The calf, by its own inherent powers, has brought forth its mothers; the embryo of many, from the lap of the active ones, the great sage, goes forth, possessed of his own power. 4.
1. *kṣa-ṭha-so'bhiḥ* does not exist; 2. *kṣa-niṣpadyate*; 3. *kṣa-na-rā-bhāve ghañ*; 4. *kṣa-bhavatereva*.
O officiating priests (*ṛtvijyamānāḥ*), *niṇyam* means "determined" (*nirṇītam*);
this is a term for that which is hidden (*antarhita*).
Within the waters and so forth, he is hidden in the form of an embryo.
Thus says another mantra: "He who is the embryo of the waters, the embryo of the forests, the embryo of the stationary, and the embryo of the moving" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.70.2).
Who among you knows—*ā ciketa*—this Agni who is such as this?
The meaning is that there is no one else.

This Agni, being the "calf"—that is, the son in the form of lightning to the waters residing in the clouds—produces his "mothers," the rain-waters which stand in the place of mothers, by means of "svadhās," that is, by means of food characterized as oblations.
And thus it is recorded in the Smṛti: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun."

"From the sun rain is born; from rain, food; and from that, creatures" (Manu Smṛti 3.76). Furthermore, he is the "embryo" (*garbha*) of the many waters situated in the clouds; as Agni, existing in the form of lightning, he occupies the place of the embryo. He "emerges from the lap of the waters," that is, from the ocean, appearing in the form of the sun. Of what nature is he? He is "great," mature in his splendor; a "seer" (*kavi*), one who perceives all things; and "possessing self-sustenance" (*svadhāvan*), meaning he possesses the sacrificial oblation as his food.

The meaning is that fire, though one alone, exists by being divided into the terrestrial form characterized as the accomplisher of oblations, the nature of lightning, the nature of the sacrificial fire (aupasada), and the nature of the sun.
He perceived (*ciketa*). [The root] *kit* means "to know"; the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix is used according to Vedic usage.
"Janayata.
Because of the rule "janījphakasurao'mantāśca," [the root] is designated as *mit*, and by the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ," shortening occurs.
As before, the *laṅ* [tense] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Regarding the word *bahvīnām*: by the rule *nityaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 4.1.46), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied after the word *bahu*; by the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1) and *ṅayābhyo dīrghāt syamoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the nominative case ending is replaced by *ām*.
Furthermore, by the rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1) and *ṅayāpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1) combined with *chandasy ubhayathā* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), the name [of the stem] is acute (*udātta*).
[The word] *apasām*. [From the root] *āp* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāptau*).

According to the *Uṇādi-sūtra* 4.647, which states: “In the sense of the agent (*kartari*), there is the suffix *as*, and optionally a short vowel and the augment *nuṭ*,” the suffix *as* is applied to the root *āp* even in the sense of the agent (*kartrī*), and the vowel is shortened due to the use of the word "optionally" (*bahulavacanāt*) in that rule.

It is called *upastha* because the waters stand near (*upatiṣṭhanti*) there. The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*), based on the rule *ātaścopasarge* and the frequentative statement (*bahulavacanāt*) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.
In the case of *marud-gṛdhra* and similar compounds, the final syllable of the first member is udātta.
When the two worlds have been entered by him, the lovely one increases; rising upward in his lap, he is resplendent with the glory of his voice.
Both worlds were afraid of Tvaṣṭṛ as he was being born; turning toward him, they find delight in the lion.

Manifesting himself, he grows strong; beautiful among these [waters], he rises up, glorious in his voice. Both worlds tremble at Tvaṣṭṛ’s son as he is being born; turning toward him, they both delight in the lion. ||5||

Agni, existing in the form of lightning within these waters situated in the clouds, being "cāru" (beautiful) with splendid luster, "increases" (*vardhate*)—that is, having become manifest and shining, he attains growth.
What does he do?

Being "self-glorious" (*svayaśāḥ*), Agni, whose fame is under his own control, stands "upright" (*ūrdhvaḥ*) with upward-flaming fire in the "lap" (*upasthe*) or bosom of those waters, which are "tongues" (*jihvānām*)—meaning crooked and situated obliquely within the clouds.
The meaning is that, although the waters—which constitute its own cause—remain horizontal, it itself blazes upward.
This has been stated by the Vaiśeṣikas: "The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of wind, and the initial motion of atoms and the mind—these are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
Furthermore, both Heaven and Earth were struck with fear, having attained dread, of that Agni as he was being kindled and born from the glowing heat of Tvaṣṭṛ.

Immediately after that, the two [fires] moving westward—going toward—that fire which is in the generative organ (*upastha*), which is "lion-like" (*siṃha*) in its nature of greatness and its nature of overcoming, find pleasure in it; that is, they serve it with direct orientation.

Yāska says: "From the time of his manifestation, he grows; he is beautiful, and he moves beautifully; he stretches out his tongue; he rises up and becomes exalted; he is self-glorious, glorious by his own nature. Both [worlds] tremble at him as he is being born; the two, heaven and earth, or day and night, or the two protectors, turn toward the lion and wait upon him with delight; indeed, these two, facing him, serve the powerful one."

1. Of one's own [nature], characterized by deceit and passion; 2. from the proximity of water, that is, from the vicinity of water; 3. the suffix *asun* [is applied] after *śa* and *ṭha*; 4. the horizontal movement of Vāyu.

(Nighaṇṭu 8.15), thus [it is said]. *Āviṣṭyaḥ*: from the word *āvis*, by the rule "in the Veda" (Pāṇini 4.2.104.1), the suffix *śaiṣika* *yañ* is applied. By the rule "after a short vowel, when a taddhita suffix beginning with *t* follows" (Pāṇini 8.3.101), there is the substitution of *pluta*. *Āsu*: in the case of *idam* used as an anuvāda, the substitute *aś* is anudātta; and since the case-ending is also anudātta because it begins with *s*, the entire word is anudātta. Nor should one suspect that the case-ending becomes udātta by the rule "after *aḍ* and *idam*" (Pāṇini 6.1.171), for that rule applies to the word *idam* which is oxytone (*antodātta*). *Pratīcī*: from the root *añj* preceded by *prati*, the suffix *kin* is applied by the rule "ṛtvig... etc. (Pāṇini 3.2.59). There is elision of *n* by the rule "of those not having *it*" (Pāṇini 6.4.24). The suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule "there is an addition for the root *añj*" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 4.1.5). After the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "of the vowel" (Pāṇini 6.4.148), there is lengthening by the rule "in the case of *ca*" (Pāṇini 6.3.138). The *ṅīp* becomes udātta by the "anudātta-nivṛtti-svara" (the accent of the replacement of an anudātta). The long vowel resulting from the homogeneous combination of the preceding vowel is optionally applied by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (Pāṇini 6.1.106). *Jopayete*: from the root *jup* in the sense of "pleasure" or "service," the causative suffix *ṇic* is added in its own sense. || 1 ||
Both auspicious ones take delight, like two women;

just as Savitṛ, the impeller of all, raises his arms—the rays that stand in place of arms—so too does this Agni of the Dawn raise up his own splendors, making them intensely uplifted and directed toward the darkness. Thereafter, the formidable Agni, the source of fear for all, striving to perfect both "seats"—both heaven and earth—by adorning them with his own brilliance, exerts himself toward the fulfillment of his own meditation.
Immediately thereafter, from all this multitude of messengers, he draws upward by means of his rays the bright, pure, and essential sap.
Moreover, from the "mothers"—that is, from the waters of rain which stand in the place of a mother—he casts forth, or raises up, ever-new garments that clothe the entire world.
He moves toward them.
The root *yam* means "to cease.
From this root, after the elision of the six affixes (*ṣaḍluk*), the augment *nuṭ* is added to the reduplicated syllable according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.85: *nugato’nunāsikāntasya*.
This [mention of *nuṭ*] is intended as an illustration for the *anusvāra*.
*Sicau* [is derived from] the root *ṣic*, meaning "to sprinkle.
Since they sprinkle— that is, they endow— with fruit, the two *sicau* are heaven and earth.
The suffix *kip* is applied after the root *yat*, as in *yatate*. The root *yat* means "to exert effort."
Askam: derived from the root *as*, meaning "to go continuously. The suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule *iṇ-bhī-kā-pā-śalya-timaci-bhyaḥ kan* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.323).
The word *sima* has the udātta accent on its first syllable due to the rule *nistvādādyudāttatvam*.
[In the form] *simasmān*,
the word *sima* is a synonym for the word *sarva* (all).
"New garments.
In both cases, there is the elision of the *śi* case-ending by the rule "In the Veda, the elision of *śi* is frequent. [He] abandons.
The root *ohāk* means "to abandon";
it belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class.
"Produce that higher form which, touching the dwellings enriched by cattle, becomes manifest."
The seer polishes the tawny one with his prayer; he has become the assembly at the gathering of the gods.

He assumes a brilliant form, most excellent, when the Seer, touching the dwellings with the unerring rays of light, polishes the tawny one with his prayer; he has become the assembly at the gathering of the gods. 8.

In his abode, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), he comes into contact with the rays (*gobhiḥ*) that move there and with the waters situated in the clouds; joined with the form of lightning, when he manifests his brilliant, blazing, and most excellent (*uttara*) form—the lightning-light which is impossible for all to behold—then that Agni, the seer (*kavi*) of beautiful vision, the supporter (*dhīḥ*) of all, thoroughly polishes (*pari marmṛjyate*) the brown (*bubhram*) atmosphere, the source of all water, covering it entirely with his own splendor.
In his presence, that divine state was extended and expanded by the god of divine nature, Agni; when praised by us, his radiance became a *samiti*—a gathering or collection of splendors.
[He is] "touching" (*saṃpṛśvānaḥ*);
[the root] *pṛcī* means "to join together."
It belongs to the *raudhādika* class.
From this [root], the suffix *śānac* is applied in place of *laṭ*;
by the rule “*kṣoralopaḥ*,” there is the elision of the vowel *a*.
The atmosphere (*antarikṣa*) is called *sadanam* because Gandharvas and others sit (*sidanti*) therein;
the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
It is thoroughly cleansed (*marmṛjyate*).
The root *mṛj* means "to cleanse.

From this root, if [the form] *marmṛjyate* occurs, the augment *rya* is applied to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) by the rule *marmṛjyate marmṛjyamānāsa upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 7.4.91, vārttika).
[Thus we have] *devatātā*.
"By the god, in the state of divinity. This is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *tan* (to extend) used in the sense of the object.
The nasal is elided by the rule beginning with "anudāttaupadeśa... [Pāṇini 6.4.37].
The substitution of *ā* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
By the rule “the third case [is used] in the sense of the object,” the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound is maintained.
1. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha: it proceeds; 2. kṣa-sa: the suffix *kan*; 3. kṣa-na-sa: the phrase “simasmāt” does not exist; 4. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha: prosperity residing in the clouds; 5. kṣa-sa: joined together.
The three [worlds] go around your broad foundation, the shining abode of the Great One.
Kindled with all your own glories, you are rich in protection through your undeceivable guardians.
Wide around the base of your threefold station goes the radiance of the Great Bull’s abode. O Agni, kindled with all your own glorious and infallible protections, guard us! 9.

O Agni, those three [fires] of yours, belonging to the great Mahiṣa—[the fire] that overcomes the enemies of the Rākṣasas, which is brilliantly shining (*virocamāna*), especially radiant, vast (*uru*), and wide-spreading (*vistīrṇa*)—surrounds and pervades the *dhāman*, the light, which is the foundation (*budhna*) of the waters, namely the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Being kindled (*iddha*) by us, O Agni, protect (*pāhi*) us with all your own glories (*svayaśobhiḥ*), that is, with your own inherent splendors.
Of what sort are they?
By means of the *pāyubhiḥ*—those capable of protection—who are *adabdhebhiḥ*, meaning unharmed by Rākṣasas and other such beings; [there are] three [stages].
The root *ji* with the prefix *tri-* signifies overcoming (*abhibhave*).
"asun | adabdhebhiḥ |" [The root] "dambhu" [is used] in the sense of "deception."
In the case of the suffix *niṣṭhā*, there is a prohibition of *it* by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā";
there is the elision of *n* by the rule "aniditām";
and there is the substitution of *dh* for *t* and *th* following a *jhap* sound by the rule "jhapastathordhaḥ."

In a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the original accent of the initial member, which is an indeclinable (*avyaya-pūrvapada-prakṛti-svaratvam*), applies; furthermore, by the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandasi*) [the substitution] is diverse (*bahulam*)," the absence of *aim* (i.e., the replacement of *nañ* with *a-*) occurs.
The archer makes for himself a path and a wave; with his bright rays he reaches the earth.
He places all ancient things within his bellies; he moves within the ships, among the mothers.

He makes a path for himself through the desert; he creates a wave with his bright waves and reaches the earth. He places all ancient things within his bellies; he moves swiftly within the ships as a progenitor. 10.
In the sky, this Agni creates a stream—a flowing current consisting of masses of water—possessing the nature of movement; he makes it endowed with the form of a torrent.
With those bright, pure waves—that is, with those masses of water—he reaches, that is, pervades, the earth.
The meaning is that by producing masses of water in the atmosphere through his own splendors, he overspreads the entire earth with them.
Afterwards, he places— that is, establishes— all, that is, every, *sanāni*—
this is a name for food—
all foods within the bellies.
For that purpose, he moves within—that is, exists in the midst of—those plants which have arisen after the rain in the "ships" (clouds) and which bring forth all kinds of food;
by means of the terrestrial fire situated within them, all the plants are ripened.
In the word *dhanvan*, [the root] *dhav* belongs to the class of roots meaning "to go," such as *riv*, *ravi*, and *dhavi*.
Because it is marked with the *it* (indicatory letter *i*), the augment *num* is applied.
The suffix *kanin* is applied by the rule *kaninyuvṛṣi* and so forth;
the locative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
Yāska [states]: "The desert (*dhanvan*) is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), for from it the waters flow. (Nirukta 5.5).
Because it is a *niti* [ending in *i*], there is the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatvam*).
Regarding *gātum*: [the root] *gāṅ* means "to go."
The suffix *tu* is applied by the rule "krami-manijani," etc.;
[the form] *ūrmim* [is derived] with the suffix *mi* by the rule "ater eva ca."
It approaches; [from] the root *nakṣ* in the sense of "going."
1. [The substitution of *k* occurs] for the *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *sa*, and *rākṣasa* [suffixes].
2. [The substitution of *ca* occurs] for the *dhanvan* [suffix], when it is *dhanvan*. 3. There is elision (*luk*) of the seventh case singular ending after *ṭa* and *ṭha*.
Thus, increasing at the beginning for us by means of our kindled fuel, O Purifier, shine forth with wealth for the sake of glory!
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this.
Thus, increasing by our kindled fuel at the beginning, O purifier, shine forth with wealth for the sake of glory! May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us that. 11.

O purifying fire, Agni, growing (vṛdhānaḥ) in this manner by means of the fuel (samidhā)— that is, by the materials such as fuel-sticks offered by us— shine forth (vi bhāhi) specifically for our glory (śravase), that is, for food (annāya) associated with wealth (revat),
meaning "bestow such food upon us. May Mitra and the other gods honor (mamahantām)— meaning protect— that food of ours.
The word *uta* signifies conjunction;
the meaning is "both the earth and the sky."
Thus; by the rule "nipātasya ca," there is a long vowel in the *saṃhitā* [of *eva*].
[The form] is *vṛdhānaḥ*.

In *vṛdhe*, the suffix *cānaś* is applied after the root *vṛdh* with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇic*) in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). By the rule "the *śap* is frequently elided in the Veda," there is elision of *śap*.

Because the suffix *cānaś* is treated as *sārvadhātuka*, it is *ṅit*; consequently, by virtue of being *ṅit*, the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*) does not occur.
Since it lacks the status of being a member of the *lamārvadhātuka* class, it does not possess the anudātta accent; thus, the *citsvara* alone remains.
*Revat*: from the word *rayi*, the suffix *matup* is added.
There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule *rayer mato bahulam*;
the substitution of *vat* for *matup* by the rule *chandasy iraḥ*;
and the acute accent (*udātta*) on *matup* after the word *re-* by the rule *reśabdācca*.
The elision of the dative case ending is by the rule *supāṃ suluk* etc.
The third hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “sa pratnathā,” is the seerly composition of Kasyapa and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.

Its deity is Agni as distinguished by the quality of being Draviṇodas, or alternatively, the pure fires (Śuddhāgnis). Thus it has been cataloged: “ma pratnathā—nine [verses]; [the deity is] Draviṇodas.”
The application of this hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been stated together with the preceding hymn for the *Prātaranuvāka* and the *Āśvina-śastra*.
On the sixth day of the ten-night *vyūḍha* sacrifice, this hymn serves as the insertion (*nivid-vāna*) for the *Jātavedasīya* section of the *Āgnimāruta* recitation.
It is prescribed in the section beginning with “*vyūḍhaśveta*” by the Sūtra: “*sa pratnathāgnimārutam*” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.8).
The Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with “*sa pratnathā sahasā jāyamāna* [‘He, being born in the ancient way through power... (AiB 5.15) concerns the *jātavedasya* [verse].
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, this verse “*sa pratnathā*” serves as the *yājyā* for Kavyavāhana, who occupies the position of the Sviṣṭakṛt.
This is prescribed in the section on the Dakṣiṇāgni: “*sa pratnathā sahasā jāyamāna ityagniḥ sviṣṭakṛtkavyavāhanaḥ*” (ĀśvŚS 2.19).
Born with power as of old, he has instantly assumed all poetic wisdom.
Both the waters and the Dhiṣaṇā have made him their friend; the gods have maintained Agni, the giver of wealth.
He, being born by ancient power and by force, has truly assumed all poetic wisdom instantly. Both the waters and the Dhiṣaṇā furthered him as a friend; the gods maintained Agni, the giver of wealth.

Born suddenly by force, being produced through friction, that Agni, immediately upon arising, at that very moment, like the ancient one—just as of old—truly (baṭ) sustained all (viśvā) the poetic works (kāvyāni), the deeds of the seer (kaveḥ), the bold one. The meaning is that, as if already existing previously, he performed all his functions, such as carrying the oblation, simultaneously with his manifestation.
And the waters (āpaḥ) dwelling in the clouds, along with the intellects (dhiṣaṇā), [sustained] this Agni existing in the form of Vaiśvānara.

1. Because the *la* suffix lacks the status of being a *sārvadhātuka*, the rule "the *tās* [suffix] is unaccented" does not apply; thus, there is an absence of the unaccented nature of the *lasārvadhātuka*.
2. That which arises through friction (*nirmathana*).
And that speech which is intermediate (*mādhyamikī*) is both "friendly" (*mitra*), meaning it has become a friend, and "accomplishing" (*sādhana*), meaning it effects what is to be accomplished.

The gods— the officiating priests— maintain this Agni as the "giver of wealth" (*draviṇodā*), that is, the giver of *draviṇa*, or riches, by sustaining him in the form of the *gārhapatya* and other sacred fires.
Alternatively, the gods themselves, such as Indra and others, having made this Agni the giver of wealth characterized by the oblation (*havis*), maintain him in his role as messenger (*dūtya*).
*Pranathā*:
the suffix *thāla* is applied in the sense of "calling" (*hvārtha*) according to the rule *pra-napūrva-viśvebhyo māthāl chandasi*.
*Kādhyāni*.
The work of a poet (*kavi*) is *kāvyam*.
The suffix *vyañ* is applied according to the rule "from words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*), from *brāhmaṇa*, and so forth. Because it has the marker *j*, it is udātta on its first syllable.
*Sādhan*: [derived from] the root *ṣidhu* in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃrāddhi*). By the rule *ṇau sidhyater apalaukike* (Pāṇini 6.1.49), the augment *aṭ* is applied.

Furthermore, by the rule "itaśca lopaḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *i*. By the rule "chandasyubhayathā," because the suffix *śap* is treated as an ārdhadhātuka, there is the elision of the *ṇi* by the rule "ṇeraniṭi. Thus: *draviṇodām*.
He is called *draviṇodāḥ* because he gives wealth (*draviṇa*). [The root] *du* means "to go. [The suffix] *inan* is applied after the roots *du* and *dakṣ*.
In Vedic usage, there is the substitution of *su* for the first member [of the compound]. From the root *dā*, the suffix *vic* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well.
However, the form ending in *s* is produced when the suffix *asun* is applied.
Through his ancient invocation and his wisdom, he brought these progeny of men into being;
together with Vivasvat as their eye, the gods established Agni, the giver of wealth, in heaven.

He, by means of the ancient invocation and through the wisdom of Āyu, brought forth these progeny of men. Together with Vivasvat as his eye, he produced the heavens and the waters. O gods, you have sustained Agni, the bestower of wealth.

That Agni, being praised by the *nivid* beginning with "He [Agni] knows through the first [verse]"—which consists of praise characterized by the description of qualities residing in the qualified—and by the *uktha* belonging to Āyu Manu, that Agni brought forth these progeny belonging to the Manus;
that is to say, being praised by Manu, he generated all the offspring of Manu.

Likewise, with his "avivasvatā"—meaning by that which possesses the power of dispersing, or specifically by that which covers—his own "acakṣasā" [eye], namely his brilliance, he pervades both "dyām" (the heavenly world) and "apaḥ" (the waters), that is, the intermediate space; this is the sense.
The rest is the same. [The term is] "kavyatā."
The root *ku* means "to sound.
By the rule *aco yat*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of an action (*bhāve*).
Thus, *kavyam* means "the act of composing poetry" (*kavanam*) or "praise" (*stutim*); he performs this.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.1.26 (*tat karoti*). From that form ending in *ṇic*, the suffix *kip* is added.
By the rule "the suffix *ṇic* is frequently elided elsewhere as well, in the case of technical names and Vedic meters," there is the elision of *ṇic*.
*Tatan-t*: by the rule *bhrātṛvya-reṇa*, there is an acute accent on the final syllable. *Āyoḥ*.

The root *iṇ* means "to go. The suffix *uṇ* is applied according to the rule "in the Veda, after *iṇ*. Praise him first, the accomplisher of sacrifice, who is brought hither by the people and who is being adorned.
The gods maintained Agni, the giver of wealth, to bestow Bharata, the son of Ūrja, as a liberal donor.

Praise him, the first accomplisher of sacrifice; the Āryan clans praised him, the invoked one who advances—the son of Ūrja, Bharata, the liberal donor; the gods maintained Agni, the giver of wealth. 3.
O all you *viśaḥ*, all human subjects, approaching Agni as your lord, do you praise that Agni!

Of what sort? The foremost, the chief among all the gods; the accomplisher of sacrifice, the one who brings to completion sacrifices such as the New and Full Moon rites; the one invoked with oblations, satiated by offerings; the one being propitiated by hymns of praise; the son of *ūrj* (strength/nourishment), that is, of food.
1. From the increase of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) by means of consumed food;
2. [The functions] of the poet (*kavi*) beginning with *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *ka*;
3. [The functions] of *kṣa*, *sa*, and *ṇic*.
3. Likewise, there is no *kṣa*, *ṭa*, or *ṭha*; and likewise, there is *sa*.

Agni’s status as the nourisher of food and progeny: "The sustainer (*bharata*) of the oblation. Or rather, the sustainer of all creatures by means of the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). And it is heard in scripture: "Having become this very breath within one's own body, he supports the creatures; therefore, he is the sustainer (*bharata*). "Possessing gifts" (*sapradānum*): meaning one who bestows wealth continuously, endowed with the nature of flowing (*sarpaṇaśīla*) and giving (*dāna*). The word "gods" (*devāḥ*) and so forth has been explained previously. *Īḷata*: from the root *īḍ* "to praise. In the imperative (*loṭ*), there is a substitution for the parasmaipada ending. By the rule "in the Veda [there is] much [irregularity]," there is no elision of the *śap* suffix. *Yajñasāt*: "One who accomplishes the sacrifice. From the root *sādh* with the suffix *kvip*. By the rule "the *ṇi* is elided before a non-*iṭ* suffix," the *ṇi* is dropped. *Ārīḥ*: from the root *ṛ* "to go. By the rule beginning with "sūci-sūtri... (Pāṇini 3.1.22), the *yaṅ* suffix is applied. Because of the word *ca* in the rule "yaṅe'ci ca," the inclusion of the term "much [irregularity]" (*bahulagrahaṇa*) is carried over, resulting in an irregular elision. By the principle of "characterization by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), there is reduplication, followed by the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* and the elision of the remaining consonants. By the rule "ruk after *k* and *l* when *luk* follows," the augment *ruk* is added. This is derived from the *yaṅ*-elided form (*yaṅluganta*) using an *uṇādi* suffix.

"Naktoṣāsā" refers to Night and Dawn. "Avarṇam" means their own respective forms. "Āmemyāne" means those two who are repeatedly calling out to one another. "Samīcī" means joined together or closely united. Being such, these two—Night and Dawn—"ahastriyāmā" (the three-night period of the day)—"dhāpayete" cause the "ekam śiśum" (the single infant), Agni the son of Day, to drink the oblations. "Rukmaḥ," meaning shining, that Agni "vi bhāti" shines forth especially "antar dyāvākṣāmā," between Heaven and Earth.
The rest is as before.
Naktopāsā. *Naktā* is a name for night; *naktā* and *uṣas* together are *naktopāsā*.
The vowel *ā* [in *indrāgnī*] is the substitution for the case-ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
The lengthening of the penultimate vowel is due to the rule *anyeṣām api*, which accounts for the *sāṃhitika* [euphonic] combination.
By the rule *devatādvandve ca*, both the preceding and following members of the compound simultaneously retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
In the word *āmemyāne*: from the root *mīṅ* in the sense of "to injure," the suffix *śānac* is applied by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*) to this [root] when it is in the *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive) form.
By the rule "adādi," there is elision (luk) of the suffix śap;
by "eranekācaḥ," there is the substitution of yaṇ;
and by "abhyastānāmādiḥ," there is the udātta accent on the first syllable.
The rule regarding the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of a compound applies here.
*Dhāpayate*. [The root] *dhā* is used in the sense of "drinking."

From this causative form (*ṇyantāt*), the rule *nigaraṇa-calana-* (Pāṇini 1.3.87) would normally require the use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice). However, by the statement *pādiṣu gheṭa upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 1.3.89), there is a prohibition against it according to *na pādyāḍyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.89). Since the root is taught with a short *a* as its penultimate vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented; thus, the accent of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) alone remains.
Because it begins with *pā*, there is no suppression (*nighāta*) of the preceding word's accent.

*Samīcī*: From the root *añc* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kvin* is applied according to the rule "ṛtvig... etc.; the elision of the nasal *n* occurs according to the rule "aniditām... etc.
By the rule "samaḥ sami" (Pāṇini 6.3.93), the substitute *sami* is applied.
By the supplementary rule "añcateścopasaṃkhyānam," the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
Following the rule "acaḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and by the rule "cau," lengthening occurs.
The feminine suffix *aṅīp* receives the acute accent (*udāttatva*) by virtue of the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*. This is the personal opinion of the author of the *Padapāṭha*:
that the substitution of *ī* prescribed by the rule *uda īt* (Pāṇini 6.4.139) occurs even for what follows *sam*, by way of transference (*vyatyaya*).
In the word *dyāvākṣāmā*, there is the lengthening of the vowel to its homogeneous counterpart (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatva*) by the rule *vā chandasi*. Furthermore,
the substitution of *dyāvā* for *divaḥ* occurs by the rule *divo dyāvā*.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," the fifth case ending is replaced by the suffix *ḍā*;
by the rule "devatādvandve ca," both the preceding and following members of the compound simultaneously retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
The source of wealth, the gatherer of treasures, the banner of sacrifice, the accomplisher of man’s purpose,
the bird— protecting their immortality, the gods have maintained this Agni, the giver of riches.

The king, the nourisher, the gatherer of riches, the banner of sacrifice, the accomplisher for mankind—the gods, guarding him as their own immortal nature, have maintained this Agni, the giver of wealth. 6.
That Agni who is the "source" (ūṣman) of "wealth" (rāyaḥ)— that is, the root cause of riches—
because he is the cause of all forms of wealth by means of the oblation.

The gods—those who protect their own immortality (*amṛtatvam rakṣamāṇāsaḥ*)—sustain this Agni, the giver of wealth. He is the "conductor" (*saṃgamanaḥ*), the one who brings together or causes the attainment of "riches" (*vasūnām*) which are the causes of dwelling; he is the "banner" (*ketuḥ*), the one who makes known or informs the "sacrifice" (*yajñasya*, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*); he is the "accomplisher by mind" (*manasādhanaḥ*) for the person who approaches him, accomplishing that which is to be meditated upon and desired; and thus the gods sustain him.
[In the word] *rāyaḥ*, the accentuation of the case-ending is according to the rule "uḍidam."
*Saṃgamanaḥ*: [the suffix] *lyu* (an) is applied according to the rule beginning with *nandi* (Pāṇini 3.1.18). [The word] *veḥ*.
The root *vī* is used in the sense of "going" and so forth.
From this root, the suffix *imap* is added according to the *auṇādika* rules,
and there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
1. The form *kṣa-sa*.
2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa* in *naktoṣāsā*. 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sāṃhina* in *sāṃhinaka*, with lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhādīrghaḥ*).
4. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, the phrase "by the *udāttanivṛtti*-accent, the *ṅīp* [suffix] becomes accented" is absent.
5. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, ṭha, and sa, the phrase "of the causes of dwelling" (*nivāsahetūnām*) is absent.

6. In the manuscript kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, the reading is "one's own nature of mortality" (*svakīyamaraṇadharmatvam*); in the manuscript na and sa, the reading "one's own mortality" (*svakīyamaraṇatvam*) is absent.

Now and of old, he is the seat of riches, the dwelling place of what is born and what is being born. O gods, you have maintained Agni, the giver of wealth, who is the protector of the pressed juice and of abundant prosperity. nu | ca | purā | ca | sadanam | rayīṇām | jñātasya | ca | jāyamānasya | ca | kṣām | sutaḥ | ca | gopām | bhavataḥ | ca | bhūreḥ | devāḥ | agnim | dhārayan | draviṇaḥ'dām ||7||
The compound particle *nū ca* has the meaning of "now" (*adya*).
Yāska states: "The particle *nū cid* [is used] in the sense of 'formerly' and 'now' (*nū ca*)" (Nirukta 4.17).

The gods maintain—that is, they sustain as the carrier of oblations—Agni, who is thus distinguished by these qualities: he who is the abode and dwelling place of all riches (wealth) both now at this time and in the past; the one who dwells within the multitude of things born, those already produced and those currently being produced; the one who is the inhabitant of the existent, that which has a manifest nature and is eternal such as space, and of that which has come into being; the protector and guardian of the vast and innumerable other classes of beings; and the giver of wealth. The gods maintain him as the bearer of the sacrificial offering.
And now: by the rule "ṛci tunugha," there is a long vowel [in *rayīṇām*]. Of riches.
By the rule *nāmanyatarasyām*, the word *nāman* optionally receives the acute accent (*udātta*). *Kṣām*: [from] the root *kṣi* in the sense of "dwelling" and "going."
The suffix *ṇic* is added after this [root].
The *vṛddhi* and *yā* substitutions occur.
From the form ending in *ṇic*, the suffix *kvip* is applied.
The elision of *ṇi* occurs by the rule "ṇer aniṭi.

First, the elision of *y* occurs by the rule "lopo vyor vali," according to the principle that "the elision of *v* and an uncombined vowel (*apṛkta*) is stronger than the elision of a non-hal [consonant].

Nor does the elision of *ṇi* possess the status of a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), because of the prohibition: "not in the case of a word-final position, a reduplication, or the elision of *vara* and *ya*."
Alternatively:
from the root *kṣai* (or *jai*, or *pai*) in the sense of "perishing," the suffix *kvip* is applied.
The substitution of *ā* (ātvam) occurs because of the rule "ādeśaḥ.
[In the form] *sataḥ*,
there is elision of the suffix *śap* due to the root *as* belonging to the *adādi* class when followed by the suffix *śatṛ*.

There is elision of the letter *a* according to the rule "śmorallopaḥ. There is acute accent on the case-ending according to the rule "śaturanumaḥ. May Draviṇodas bestow [wealth] upon the seeker of wealth, he who is the giver of riches to one accompanied by men.
May the Giver of Wealth grant us food accompanied by heroes; may the Giver of Wealth bestow upon us long life.

May the giver of wealth grant us the wealth of the swift one; may the giver of wealth bestow the wealth of the noble man. May the giver of wealth extend our life; may the giver of wealth grant us food accompanied by heroes and long-lasting vitality. 8.

May Agni, the giver of *draviṇas*—whether that be wealth, riches, or strength—bestow upon us a portion of the *draviṇas*, which is swift, resonant, moving, and animate. Likewise, as the giver of *draviṇas*, may he grant us a portion of the *draviṇas* that is desirable, worthy of acquisition, and stable in nature. Furthermore, as the giver of *draviṇas*, may he grant us nourishment (*iṣ*) accompanied by heroes (*vīravatīṃ*), that is, endowed with sons and other such progeny.
Likewise, may "Draviṇodas" grant—that is, bestow—"long life" upon us.
Of the swift one; "tura" means "to hasten."
The suffix *ka* is applied by virtue of the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (igupadha).
[This applies] to the root *vana*, as in *sanara-vana*, meaning "to enjoy" (*saṃbhakti*).
The suffix *aran* is applied according to the rule *kṛdādayaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 5.719).
[Thus] *yaṃsat*.
[The root is] *yama* in the sense of "ceasing" (*uparame*).
The augment *aṭ* is added;
by the rule "the suffix *sip* is frequently used in the *leṭ*," the suffix *sip* is applied:
*rāsate*.
The root *rā* means "to give.
As before, the suffix *sip* occurs in the *leṭ* mood;
there is an irregular substitution for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
1. *Kṣa-sa-purā*: in the past; 2.
*Kṣa-na-sa*: always; 3.
*Kṣa-yuktām iṣam*: joined with the syllable *kṣa*.
Thus, O Agni, increasing by our fuel, O Purifier, bestow upon us wealth for glory;
may Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this.
Thus, O Agni, increasing through our fuel, O Purifier, grant us wealth for glory; for may Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant this to us. 10.
This has been explained in the preceding hymn (*pūrvasūkta*).
As for the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*):
O Agni, O practitioner, increasing—that is, growing—by means of the fuel and other substances thus offered by us, shine forth especially for our sake, for the sake of food accompanied by wealth.
May Mitra and the others honor—that is, revere and protect—that food of ours;
likewise, may Sindhu, the deity of the waters, and Heaven and Earth also honor it.
The fourth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "apa naḥ," is the ṛṣi-seer Kutsa's composition; it is in the Gāyatrī meter.
Its deity is Agni characterized by the quality of purity, or simply Śuddha-Agni (the Pure Fire). Thus it has been cataloged: "apa naḥ—eight [verses], for Śuci, in Gāyatrī."
The application is ritual.
Herein is this narrative:
a Rākṣasī named Dīrghajihvī harassed all sacrifices.
Being unable to kill her himself, Indra spoke to Kutsa, who was a friend to all, saying, "She must be killed by you. He replied,
and a voice addressed him, saying, "This is improper conduct on your part, that being a friend to all, you have committed such a cruel act."
In that situation, the seer Śoka fell into grief.

That seer, having praised Agni with this hymn (*sūkta*), drove away his sorrow. And so says the *Tāṇḍaka*: "Dīrghajihvī, this Rakṣas, the destroyer of sacrifice and the plunderer of sacrifice, was wandering about. Indra did not intend to slay her by any means whatsoever. Then Sumitra Kutsa was there, being auspicious; Indra spoke to him," and so forth (*Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa* 13.6.9).
Therefore, this hymn (*sūkta*) is to be employed for the removal of impurity (*śuk*).

For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras, Bhāradvāja, employs this hymn—which is recited in the Yajurveda—for the peace-rite (*śāntikarman*) to be performed on the tenth day, stating: "And nine beautiful oblations; may it burn away our sin."
May it burn away our evil; may it purify wealth for us; may it burn away our evil.
Drive away from us, O Agni, the burning evil; shine forth wealth upon us; drive away from us the burning evil. 1.
O Agni, may you burn away our evil and sin; having gone forth from us, may it consume our enemy.
Or rather:
may our sin be scorched, overwhelmed by grief, and utterly destroyed.
Moreover, O charioteer, purify and illuminate our wealth from all sides.
Although the meaning has already been stated, the words are repeated here to manifest an excess of reverence, [expressing the thought]:
"May our sin certainly perish!"
*śoṣucat*. From the root *śuc* in the sense of "to grieve," in the *yaṅ-luk* (intensive) form, with the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, there is the augment *ad*.

By the rule "and like *adādi*," there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. By the rule "the first [syllable] of reduplicated forms," there is acute accent on the initial syllable. Because the sense of "and" (*ca*) is understood from the words "may you burn away evil (*agham śoṣucad*)" and "purify wealth (*rayim śuśudhi)," there is an optional prohibition of the grave accent (*nighāta*) by the rule "optionally when *ca* and others are elided."
*Śuśudhi*. [The root] *śuc* means "to shine. In the *loṭ* [imperative] mood, by the rule "there is much [irregularity] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), there is the substitution of *plu* for *śap*.
‘Huślambo herdhiḥ. By the rule ‘coḥ kuḥ,’ there is the substitution of *k* for *c*.

1. In manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, the word *avṛdhānaḥ* is absent. 2. In manuscripts ṭa and ṭha, it reads "Agni endowed with the quality of purity" or "the deities who are pure"; in manuscript na, it reads "the deity Agni characterized by the quality of purity"; in manuscript kṣa, it reads "Agni endowed with the quality of purity" or "the deities who are pure. 3. In manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, [the text continues]: "Then he offered four oblations."

4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha- ‘Distressed by grief. With a desire for good fields, with a desire for a good path, and with a desire for wealth, we sacrifice. May our sin be burned away. (2) With a desire for good fields, with a desire for a good path, with a desire for wealth, and indeed—we sacrifice. Away—from us—may it burn away—the evil. (2)

"By means of *sukṣetriyā*—the desire for a good field; by *sugātuyā*—the desire for a good path; and by *avasuyā*—the desire for wealth, acting as the instrumental cause—we worship Agni with oblations, that is, we honor him.
Or rather, by means of the oblation connected to a beautiful place characterized as a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), we worship 'Agni.
May our 'sin' (*agha*) be 'purified away' (*apa śoṃśucat*), that is, may it perish."
Sukṣetriyā:
a beautiful field is a *sukṣetra*;
the desire for such a field is *sukṣetriyā*.
By the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*,
and by the prohibition of the substitution of *īś* and lengthening (*dīrgha*) according to *na cchandasyaputrasya*,
there is a substitution of *it* [for the final vowel] by way of anomaly (*vyatyaya*).
From a word ending in *kyac*, the suffix *a* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule "after a suffix [ending in] *a*.
From that, the suffix *ṭāp* is added. Then, by the rule "for case-endings, there is *su*, *luk*, etc.," there is elision (*luk*) of the third-case ending.
The same applies to the subsequent cases as well.
Alternatively,
it is a "good field" (*sukṣetra*) because it possesses an excellent field.
By the rule *‘iyāḍiyājīkāraṇāāpasaṃkhyānam’* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.39.1), the substitute *ḍiyāc* is applied to the third case ending.

When their praise resounds forth, and when our wise patrons resound forth, may he burn away our sin. 3. When their praise resounds forth, and when our wise patrons resound forth, may he burn away our sin. 3.
"Just as among these singers this Kutsa is most excellent in praise, so too may our patrons, our singers, be most excellent in praise.
The rest is the same.
And *bhandi*.
The root *bhandati* has the sense of praising (*stuti*). However, the verbal root is *bhadi*, meaning "in auspiciousness" and "in what is good."
From this [root] *tuj*, by the rule *tubh chandasi*, the suffix *iṇ* is applied; then, by the rule *turiṣṭhemayaḥsu*, there is the elision of *tu*. Thus, [we have] *asmākāsaḥ*.
