“Belonging to us” means “our own.
The substitution of *asmākā-* occurs according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 4.3.2: *tasmiñ chaṇa ca yuṣmākāsmākau*.
There is the elision of the suffix *aṇ* due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution].

[The suffix] *asuk* is substituted for the nominative plural ending *ājas*. Furthermore, even though the substitute (*ādeśa*) is like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the vowel *ā* following the *m* remains acute (*udātta*).
Alternatively,
since the word *asmākam* is observed to have its middle syllable accented when used in the genitive plural, that very accentuation is what is being indicated by the Teacher.
When your sun is born, O Agni, may we be born through you; may we be born through you. May your brilliance burn away our sin. 4.

O Agni, since your worshippers are born as Sūrya and become manifold in the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth, may we also, being your worshippers, be procreated through sons, grandsons, and the like.
"May we be born.
The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of a benediction (*prārthanā*).
In this instance, the substitution *jā* for the roots *jñā* and *jan* (according to the rule *jñājanorjā*) has been applied.
Because it is not explicitly taught [as such], the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented; however, due to the *nittva* designation of the suffix *iyaN*, the first syllable is acutely accented.

1. In kṣa, sa, and ‘ca’, [the word] does not exist. 2. In kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, [the word] ‘haviṣā’ does not exist. 3. ga-ā. 4. In a, ṭa, ṭha, and ma, ‘agham’ means sin. 5. In kṣa, ṭa, ṭha, and ma, ‘apa’ does not exist. 6. In a, ṭa, and ṭha, there is the substitution of ‘ḍiya’. 7. In kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, [it is said] “they become” (bhavanti). 8. In kṣa and sa, ‘tu’ does not exist. 9. In kṣa, ṭa, ṭha, and sa, there is the elision (luk) of the Vedic suffix ‘aṇ’. For this very reason, there is an absence of vṛddhi; it is not that the Vedic suffix ‘aṇ’ is simply dropped. The absence of vṛddhi is due to the non-universality (anityatva) of the rules governing augments. 10. In kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, [the word] ‘prāyaṇa’.

When the rays of the powerful Agni go forth from every side, may he burn away our sin. (5) When the rays—the flames—of the powerful Agni, who overcomes his enemies, go forth from every direction—that is, from all places—excellently upward; since this is so, therefore by that brilliance of his, may our sin perish. [The word] *yanti* [is formed] with the substitution of *yaṇ* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.81.

For you indeed, O you whose face is on every side, are the one who encompasses everything from all sides. Drive away our sin with your glowing light. 6 O Agni, for you indeed—you, who have faces on every side—your flames, which stand in place of mouths, meet no obstruction anywhere. Therefore, O Agni whose face is on every side, you are the one who encompasses us from all sides; that is, you are the one who protects us from every kind of calamity. The rest is the same as before.

O you whose face is turned in every direction, carry us across our enemies as if with a boat; cast away from us the burning sin. dviṣaḥ | naḥ | viśvatomukha | ati | nāva-iva | pāraya | apa | naḥ | śośucat | agham || 7 || O Viśvatomukha—O Agni whose face is everywhere—carry us across our enemies (dviṣaḥ) as if with a boat (nāva-iva), like crossing a river; lead us beyond them to a place free of foes. Regarding *nāva-iva*: the acute accent on the case-ending is by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. Regarding *pāraya*: the root is *pāra* or *tīra*, meaning "to cross over" or "to complete."

May he carry us across, as one crosses a river with a boat, for our well-being; may he burn away our evil. (8) He—O Agni, may you carry us across, as one crosses a river with a boat, for our well-being (*svastaye*), that is, for the sake of safety. Carry us beyond the enemies and protect us; the meaning is: lead us to a place free from enemies. By your grace, may our evil (*agha*) and sin be burnt away; let it depart from us and let our enemy become filled with grief. Regarding *nāvā*: the substitution of the vowel *a* for the third case ending is prescribed by the rule *āṅyājayārāṃ copasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). The acute accent (*udātta*) on the vowel *a* is due to the rule *upottamaṃ riti* (Pāṇini 6.1.217). The very same meaning as previously stated is here requested once more for the sake of reinforcement.

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-asmākam*. 2. Regarding *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha- ‘he ame tvaṃ hi……anyattasmān’*, in place of this, [it means]: O Viśvatomukha (O you whose faces are on all sides), O you whose flames pervade everywhere (*sarvato vyāptajvālāme*), you are indeed beneficial (*hitam eva*) from all sides; that is, you are the one who encompasses us (*paribhūr asi*) from every kind of calamity (*sarvasmād upadravajātāt*). You are our protector (*parigrahītāsi*); the meaning is "be our guardian" (*rakṣakī bhava*). The rest is the same.
3. Having passed beyond *kṣa*. 4. Having passed beyond *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*.
5. The region of *kṣa* and *sa*.

6. *Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-pāpam apa śośucat*: May the evil (*pāpa*) consisting of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha* burn away from us and pass beyond; may it be joined with sorrow elsewhere (in one other than us who is joined with sorrow). *Parṇa*. [The root] *pṛ* is used in the senses of "protecting" and "filling. In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* ("there is much irregularity in the Veda"), there is the absence of *śap* (the verbal suffix), resulting in *ślau* (doubling). By the rule *sibbahulaṃ leṭi* ("*sip* is frequently added in the *leṭ* [subjunctive]"), *sip* is added due to the word *bahulam*. There is *guṇa* (vowel strengthening). By the rule *aco 'taḥ sthāne jhali* ("lengthening occurs in place of *at* before a *jhal* [consonant]"), there is lengthening. || 5 ||
The fifth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with "vaiśvānarasya," is the ṛṣi-seer Kutsa's composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Its deity is Agni characterized by the qualities of Vaiśvānara, or simply the pure gods.
Thus it has been cataloged: "The triad beginning with 'vaiśvānarasya' belongs to Vaiśvānara."
On the fourth day of the *vyūḍha* [shadaha], this hymn addressed to Vaiśvānara serves as the insertion (*nivid*) for the *ābhimāruta* [śastra];

it is prescribed in the section beginning with "If there is a *vyūha*" (*vyūhaś cet*) in the Sūtra: "In the benevolence of Vaiśvānara... who has manifested him? (*vaiśvānarasya sumatau ka īṃ vyaktāḥ*; Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.8).
May we abide in the good graces of Vaiśvānara; for he is the king, the glory over all beings.
Born from here, he beholds this entire universe; Vaiśvānara strives in unison with the Sun.
May we abide in the good-will of Vaiśvānara; for he is indeed the king, the glory of all beings. Born from here, he beholds this entire universe; Vaiśvānara strives in unison with the Sun.
"May we abide in the benevolent favor—that is, in the gracious, favoring intellect—of Vaiśvānara, the fire who is connected to men as their leader to other worlds or as their lord.
For "hi kam" has the sense of the particle "hi" (for/indeed).
For that Vaiśvānara, being "abhiśrīḥ"—meaning worthy of being resorted to or to be served with devotion—is the king, the sovereign, of all "bhuvanānām," that is, of all classes of beings.

That Vaiśvānara Agni, as soon as he is born from these two fires, beholds—sees distinctly—this entire world; he exerts himself with the early-rising sun and unites with him. As the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa states: "Verily, the fire ascends after the rising sun" (Tait.
Br. 2.1.2.10). Or alternatively:
The splendors of the terrestrial fire rise upward, and the rays of the sun spread downward;
seeing their meeting, [the seer] said, "Vaiśvānara strives with the sun.
Thus Yāska says: "From there, the rays of that [sun] appear; from here, those of this [fire]. Having seen the union of these two lights, he would have spoken thus" (Nirukta 7.23).
The connection is: "May we be in the good favor of such a one of great majesty, Vaiśvānara."
Of Vaiśvānara:
belonging to the "excellent" (viśeṣa) among men (nara).
The lengthening of the first member of the compound is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.129: *nare saṃjñāyām*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied [to form a possessive compound] in the sense of "this belongs to him. Regarding *sumati*:
a beautiful mind (*mati*) is *sumati*.

When the rule "tādau ca" (Pāṇini 6.2.50) would have applied the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) to the verbal root (*gati*), the rule "mantrin" etc. (Pāṇini 6.2.151) instead prescribes that the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) is udātta.
Now, one might object: since the term "from a *kāraka*" (*kārakāt*) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*) there, the suffix *kin* cannot apply to what follows.
If this is the case, then *mati* is simply "thinking" (*manana*).
In the sense of "state" (bhāva), the suffix *kin* is applied.
That intellect (*buddhi*) in which there is beautiful reflection (*manana*) is *sumati*.
By the rule "after *nan* and *su*," the final syllable of the compound is udātta.
It is said:
"The root *cakṣiṅ* is used in the sense of distinct speech," and it is also used in the sense of seeing.
Due to the root beginning with *ad*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*;
by the rule "the first of a conjunct [consonants] is elided after *s* or *k*," there is the elision of *k*.
Thus: *yatate*.
The root *yat* is used in the sense of effort.
The Anvārambhaṇīyā [iṣṭi] for the Cāturmāsyas consists of offerings to Vaiśvānara and Parjanya.

For that [iṣṭi], the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*) is "pṛṣṭho divi," and the offering verse (*yājyā*) for the oblation to Vaiśvānara is "pṛṣṭho divi. This is prescribed in the section on the Cāturmāsyas in the Sūtra: "pṛṣṭho divi pṛṣṭho agniḥ pṛthivyāṃ parjanyāya pragāyata" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.15).

1. Agni is distinguished by the qualities of the syllables *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*. 2. Or, because he is the leader of the worlds (*loka*) denoted by *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*. 3. He is to be served (*sevanīya*) by those represented by *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*. 4. From the syllables *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha* comes the name Vaiśvānara.
"Seeked in heaven, sought on earth, sought among all plants, Agni Vaiśvānara has entered them all.
Sought with power, may that Agni protect us from harm by day and by night."
Sought in heaven, sought on earth, Agni has entered all the plants; Vaiśvānara, sought with power, may that Agni protect us by day and from the enemy by night. ||2||
This Vaiśvānara Agni is indeed "touched" (pṛṣṭa)—that is, in contact with or established within—the sky (*div*) in the form of the sun; or alternatively, he exists as "placed" (*nipikta*, *nihita*).
There, on the earth (*pṛthivī*), he is "touched," in contact with, or placed in the form of the Gārhapatya and other sacrificial fires.
Likewise, that Agni has "entered" (*ā viveśa*) all (*viśvāḥ*) plants (*oṣadhīḥ*), having entered within them for the purpose of digestion.
All herbs are ripened by the fire within the earth;
may Vaiśvānara, touched— that is, brought into contact— with our food by means of his sudden and extraordinary power, protect us from the injurious enemy by day,
and likewise may that Vaiśvānara protect us at night from the one who seeks to harm us.
He was asked:
"The root *spṛś* means 'to touch';
the elision of the letter *s* is Vedic."
Alternatively,
[the root] *pṛp* means "to sprinkle";
in the word *niśā*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*.
In "divi," the case ending is udātta according to the rule "uḍiḍam. In "pṛthivyām," [the same applies].
In the phrase "udāttayaṇaḥ," the case-ending is acute (udātta). Regarding "ripaḥ":
[the root] "rip" is used in the sense of "injury."
The suffix *kip* is applied by the rule "kip ca";
the acute accent (*udātta*) on the fifth case ending is applied by the rule "sāvekācaḥ."
O Vaiśvānara, that truth of yours has been established; may the liberal patrons grant us protection.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this.
O Vaiśvānara, let that be true for you: may the liberal lords grant us riches. May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us that. ||3||
O Vaiśvānara, may this work of ours being performed for you be true—that is, may it have unfailing results.
Thereafter, may the *maghavan*s—those possessing wealth—our beloved sons who are like riches, attend upon us.

Thus, may that which we have prayed for be ours: may Mitra, the deity presiding over the day; Varuṇa, the deity presiding over sovereignty; Aditi, the undecaying Mother of the Gods; and Sindhu, the deity presiding over the flowing waters, [grant it].
The word *uta* signifies conjunction.
All these [deities], beginning with Mitra, "may they honor"—that is to say, "may they worship" or "may they protect"—me.
The sixth hymn, consisting of a single verse beginning with "jātavedasam," is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter.

Its deity is either Agni Jātavedas or the pure fire (śuddhāgni). Thus it has been cataloged: "This [hymn] beginning with 'jātavedasam' is dedicated to Jātavedas; this collection of many thousand hymns consists of single-verse hymns, and this indeed is the seerly composition of Kaśyapa."
In the multi-day sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*), on the second and subsequent days, this [hymn] is to be recited before the *Jātavedasya* *Nivid* in the *Āgnimāruta* Śastra.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The verses beginning with 'jātavedasaṃ sunavāma somam' are the *Jātavedasya* verses in the *Āgnimāruta* [Śastra]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.1).

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-hi* is [the fire] belonging to the earthly one (*pārthiva*). 2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa* is indeed *vaiśvānara*. 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-na-sa*—the term "*maghavantaḥ*" (the bounteous ones) is not present. 4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*—[he is] the foremost among the givers of wealth (*dhanada*). 5. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*—Agni is distinguished by the qualities of *jātavedas*. He is *indra*, the bull (*vṛṣā*), the showerer of desires; he is *samokāḥ*, perfectly united and gathered together with *vṛṣṇibhiḥ*, the virile powers; he is the lord (*īśvara*) from the great *divaḥ*, the heavenly world, and from the *pṛthivyāḥ*, the spread-out earth; he is *satīn-satvā*, the true being.
"Satīn" is a name for water;

he who causes the flow of water to settle or move, who is to be invoked in battles by all the singers, who is thus accompanied by the Maruts—may that Indra be our protection for our aid and preservation.
Regarding *vṛṣyebhiḥ*: from the word *vṛṣan*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *bhave chandasi*;
then, by the rule *alopo'naḥ*, there is the elision of the letter *a*.

In the rule "ye cābhāvakarmaṇoḥ," the state of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) does not occur due to a transposition [of the terms]. [The word] *mahaḥ* [is derived from] the root *maha* in the sense of worship (*pūjā*).
Or rather:
in the word *maha*, there is the elision of the suffix *ac*.
The acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
In *sannād*,
the substitution of the letter *m* for the *m* of *sama-* occurs before a *kṛt*-suffix ending in *kviṣ* when *rājati* is the following word, according to the rule *mo rāji samaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.25).
The explicit mention of the letter *ma* is for the purpose of precluding the *anusvāra*.
[The root] *sat* means "to exist";
[the root] *paṭ* is used in the senses of "falling apart," "going," and "depression."
It is called *satīna* because it settles (*nipīdati*) in the clouds;
the suffix *īna* is derived according to the *uṇādi* rules, along with the substitution of the letter *t* for the final syllable.
Alternatively:
The word *satī* refers to the speech of the Madhyamikas.
That which has her as its mistress (*inā*) is *satīn*.
There is an absence of the masculine form due to a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).

*tatsatvā*³: from the root *sad* with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) included within it, the suffix *vanip* is applied according to the Uṇādi Sūtra 4.556, *pra īrasayostad ca*, along with the augment *tuṭ*.
Like *marudvṛdha* and other such forms, there is udātta accent on the final syllable of the first member of the compound.
*Marutvān*: the *m* of the suffix *matup* becomes *v* according to the rule *jhayaḥ*. *Ūtī*.
By the rule *uniyūti* etc., the *kin* suffix is acute;
by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the dative case ending undergoes a long vowel of the same class as the preceding vowel.
He whose course is like that of the sun, who possesses the strength of a Vṛtra-slayer in every battle,
the most virile one with his own friends and his own ways— may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection.

He whose course is like that of the sun, who in every battle is the slayer of Vṛtra and possesses impetuous strength, he who is most virile with his own friends and through his own movements—may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection. 2.
The stride of Indra is wide-reaching; his movement is like that of the sun, unattainable by others.
Just as even the course of the sun cannot be reached, so it is with him.

May that Indra—who, together with his own, moving, and friendly companions, the Maruts; who is the most excellent showerer of desires (*vṛṣantama*); who is the slayer of Vṛtra (*vṛtrahā*), the destroyer of enemies in every battle (*bhare-bhare*); and who is the witherer of all Asuras (*śuṣma*)—that Indra, accompanied by the Maruts (*marutvān*), be for our protection.
[The suffix *man* is applied here in the sense of the abstract state, according to Pāṇini 3.3.94 and 6.4.157.]
The word *śuṣma* has its initial syllable accented because it is derived from a verbal root. [It is formed from] the root *śuṣ*, meaning "to dry."
The suffix *ma* is applied by the rule "after the roots *avi*, *si*, and *suṣi*, [the suffix *ma* is added] with the *kit* designation" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.141).
Due to its *nittva* status, it bears the udātta accent on the first syllable. Thus, the form is *asti*.
There is no elision (*anighāta*) due to the suffix *vṛtti*.

In the word *vṛṣantamaḥ*, the augment *nuṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 8.2.17: "The augment *nuṭ* is added after the word *vṛṣan* before the suffix *tamap*, provided it does not begin with a vowel."
The root *iṇ* means "to go.
[The suffix] *van* is applied after the roots *iṇ* and *śī*.
Whose paths, like the streams of heaven’s seed being milked, go forth unassailable by might;
he who overcomes hatreds with manly deeds and aids—may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection.

He from whose seed the milch-cows flow like those of heaven—whose paths go forth by his might, irresistible—may Indra, the overcomer of hatreds through his manly powers, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protector with his aid. 3.
1. In the calls of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *bha*.
2. The name of those who possess *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *sa*.
3. The being (*satva*) of that which possesses *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *ta*.

The paths of that Indra are his rays; possessing excellent seed, drawing forth the waters of rain, milking them out, and pouring them down, they weave—that is, they issue forth and spread from here and there from the world of heaven.
In this regard, there is an illustration: like the woods of heaven.
Just as the rays of the shining sun, bringing rain, travel through the expanse of the sky;
of what kind are those rays?
They are accompanied by *vaśavasā*, that is, by strength (*bala*), and are *aparītāḥ*, meaning not overcome by others.
The meaning is "one whose protection is unerring.
This very Indra, *vataradveṣaḥ*—meaning one who crosses over (*taran*) hostilities (*dveṣāṃsi*), that is, one who has conquered his enemies;

*vapauṣyebhiḥ*, with these powers; *vasasahiḥ*, the subduer of enemies—one who is thus characterized, this mighty (*vamahasvān*) Indra, the *vanaḥ* (the one who desires), may he be for our protection.
Of semen. "Semen" (retas) is a name for water;
it is called semen because it flows (rīyate) or moves.
The root *sṛ* is used in the sense of "going" (*gati*) and "seeking" (*eṣaṇa*).
According to the Unādi Sūtra 4.641, *surībhyāṃ tud ca*, the suffix *asun* is applied along with the augment *tuṭ*.
For the nominative plural *śas*, there is a substitution by *ḍas* through metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
*duhānāḥ*:
[from] *duha* "to fill," present participle (*laṭ*) in the active voice (*kartari*).

Accompanied by the Maruts— the sons of Rudra who are like grandsons or sons— he, Indra, having grown great, thus endowed, overcame his enemies, the adversaries, in a battle that must be endured by men; moreover,
together with the Maruts who share the same dwelling place,
he attained glories— "śrava" being a name for food.
May Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, who causes the waters that serve as the cause of those [showers] to fall from the cloud, be our protector.

The term *nṛpāha* [is derived as follows]: from the root *mṛṣ* in the sense of "endurance" (*marṣaṇe*), with the suffix *yat* applied in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.99: *śaki sahośca*.
In the word *sasadvān*, the vowel of the verbal root is lengthened according to the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* regarding *saṃhitā*.
Since the initial syllable is acute by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*, it retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) as a *kṛt*-derived compound with a final member.
*Sasadvān*.
‘This [occurs] in the sense of overcoming.
The suffix is *liṭ* with the *kasu* affix;
the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is Vedic.
*Amitrān*:
"Those among whom friends (*mitra*) do not exist are *amitra*s.
According to the rule *naño jaramaramitramṛtāḥ*, the first syllable of the final member of the compound is udātta.
"Sanīḷebhiḥ": those whose *nīḷa* (abode) is the same are *sanīḷāḥ*. [The substitution of] *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs by the rule "samānasya chandasi."
He who quells the fury, the creator of the battle, may he win the sun for us; may Indra, the lord of the truth, invoked by many, accompanied by the Maruts, be with us for our protection on this day.

He, the subduer of wrath, the maker of harmony, may he win the sun for us with these men; on this day, may Indra—the lord of the settlement, invoked by many, accompanied by the Maruts—be ours for our protection. 6.
When their cattle had been carried off by enemies, Atri and the others went forth for the sake of battle against them and praised Indra with this hymn.
That Indra is *manyumīḥ*, the subduer of *manyuḥ* (wrath), that is, the creator of anger;
or alternatively:

He who strikes down the enemy who considers himself superior; moreover, he who is the creator of the battle of the *vṛṣan* (the showerer/strengthener), the lord of the good (*satpati*), the protector of the virtuous, and the much-invoked (*puruhūta*) by many sacrificers— endowed with such qualities, may he on this day cause us, our men, and our people to obtain the light of the sun (*sūrya*),
and let him join the enemies with darkness that obstructs their vision.
And may that Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be for our protection.
*Manyumīḥ*: one who diminishes *manyu* (wrath); that is, he diminishes wrath. [The root] *mīñ* is used in the sense of "injuring."
Kip [is the suffix]. *Samadana*: that in which they rejoice together is *samadana*, namely, battle (*saṃgrāma*).
The root *mad* means "to rejoice.
The suffix *hyuc* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
By the rule *sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.78), the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

In the word *asmākebhiḥ*, the substitution of *asmāka-* for the word *asmad-* occurs by the rule *tasminniti ca yuṣmākāsmākau* when the suffix *aṇ* follows. Due to the fact that a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not invariably obligatory, there is no occurrence of *vṛddhi*.
The substitution of *ais* for the case-ending *bhis* is according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
As for the accent, it is as stated in the verse *prāsākāsaśca sūrayaḥ* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.97.3). [He] won.
The root *vana* is used in the sense of "to gather.
In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *ad*.
[This forms] *ahan*.
The elision of the locative case ending occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
[Thus we have] *satpatiḥ*. By the rule *paryāyaiśvarye*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member.
Him the allies seek for joy in the contest for booty; him the people make their protector in times of peace.
He alone is the lord of every deed that is done. May Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be with us for our aid.

Him [men call] for aid; he delights in the prize-winning contest; him the people make their protector in times of peace. He alone is the lord of every deed that is done. May Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be with us for our protection. 7.
1. They go forth together. 2. [The variants] *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha* do not contain the word *āsmākaiḥ*.
"To that Indra, at the *śūrasātī*—the battle to be honored by heroes, by brave men—the *ūtayaḥ* (protective aids), the goers, bring delight by causing great joy."
Or rather, they utter such words as "Strike, O Blessed One! Slay! Be heroic! directed toward Indra.
Moreover, the "peoples"—that is, human beings—make that Indra the "trāṃ," the protector and guardian, of all wealth that is "kṣamasya," worthy of being preserved.
If it is asked, "What is his excellence over other deities?", it is said:
"He, Indra, alone (ekaḥ), without any companion, rules (īśe) over all (viśvasya) compassionate action (karuṇasya)—that is, action consisting in the accomplishment of desired results.
The rest is as before.
Regarding *utayaḥ*:

from the root *ava* in the sense of "going," the suffix *ktin* is applied in the active sense (*kartari*) according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. The prohibition of the *it* augment is applied by the rule *titutra-tathasisusarakaseṣu ca*.

By the rule "jvaratvara0" and so forth, there is the substitution of *uṭ* for the letter *v* and for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). By the rule "ūtiyuti0" and so forth, the *kin* suffix is acute-accented (*udātta*).
Alternatively:

The suffix *ktic* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). [The form] *raṇayan* is derived from the root *ram*, with the causative suffix *ṇic*, in the present tense; it is a Vedic usage of the imperfect (*laṅ*).
The other grammatical modification is Vedic;
or alternatively,
the root *raṇ* has the meaning "to sound."
From this causative form (*ṇijanta*), the *laṅ* suffix is applied as before; [the result is] *atrāṃ*. The root *traiṅ* means "to protect."

That which protects (*trāyate*) is *trā*. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule *'kip ca'*, the root *dṛś* is also included; thus, the suffix *kip* is applied even after roots ending in *ṣ* or *jhirūpa*. [This refers to] compassion (*karuṇasya*).
The root *ḍukuñ* is used in the sense of "making.

By the rule *kṛvṛdadāribhya unan* (Uṇādi-sūtra 3.333), the suffix *unan* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Due to metathesis (*vyatyaya*), the accent falls on the first syllable of the suffix.
*Īśe*.
[The root] *īśa* is used in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
The elision of the *ta* suffix occurs by the rule "lopasta ātmanepadeṣu" (Pāṇini 7.1.41).
Men praise him at the festivals of Śarva, that hero for the sake of man, for speed, and for wealth.
May Indra, who finds light even in the blind darkness of thought, become our protector through his great power and aid.

Men have sought him at the festivals of Śarva; they seek the Hero for protection, and him for wealth. He, accompanied by the Maruts, has found light even in the darkness; may Indra be with us for our aid. 8.

The *naras*, meaning leaders or praisers, in connection with the festivals of *śarvas*, that is, of strength, or in battles, reach— that is, they obtain— *Indra*, the leader of victory, for the sake of *avas*,
meaning for the purpose of protection.
Thus, for the sake of wealth and for the purpose of obtaining riches, they reach that Indra;
because that Indra, even in the darkness—that which obstructs vision—and even in the blind, thoughtless battle that causes mental delusion, finds and provides the light characterized by victory.
Therefore, the meaning is that they reach him alone.
The rest is the same.
*Āpsanta*.
[The root] *āp* means "to pervade. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) in the *laṅ* tense.
The suffix *kṣa* occurs by way of transposition;
the shortening of the verbal root also occurs by way of transposition.
[Thus one forms] *vidat*.
Regarding the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining":
while the rule *chandasi luṅliṭau* (Pāṇini 3.4.6) is in force, this is a Vedic form in the *luṅ* tense.
Because it is of the nature of *luṭ*, the substitute *aṭ* is applied to the *kṛt* suffix *kleḥ*.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the augment is] frequently absent even when there is connection with *mā*."
With his bow he restrains the minds of the swelling [foes]; on the right hand his deeds are firmly grasped.
Even with a humble singer he wins riches; may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection.
He restrains even the powerful with his right hand; he gathers the spoils of victory; even through the humble singer, he wins riches. May Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection. 9.
1. Of that which is delightful through the letters *va*, *cha*, *ta*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *pha*, and *śa*.
2. For the sake of knowing and protecting [that which is denoted by] *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*.

*Vsah*: Indra; with *vsavyena*, i.e., the left hand (*vāmahastena*), by means of a single hand, he indeed *vvrādhataḥ*—even those who are harmful (*hiṃsataḥ*) and great (*mahataḥ*)—*śatrūn* (enemies), he *vyamati*, i.e., restrains (*niyamayati*).
Likewise, that Indra, with his single right hand situated on his right side, gathers together the oblations offered by the sacrificers;
moreover, that Indra, being praised by those who proclaim [his deeds] and by hymns of praise, becomes a winner of wealth— that is, one whose nature is to bestow—
granting riches even to the singers as he does to the offerers of oblations.
The remainder is clear.
Regarding *yamati*: the root *yama* means "to cease" (*uparame*).
Because [the root] ends in *m* when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), it is designated as *mit*; consequently, by the rule "there is shortening for *am* roots," the vowel is shortened.
Since the rule "in the Veda, both ways" applies, the *śap* [suffix] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; thus, by the rule "there is elision of *ṇi* before an *aniṭ* [suffix]," the *ṇi* is elided.
[The form is] *vrādhataḥ*.
The root *vṛdh* means "to grow. From this [root], the suffix *ati* is applied according to the *auṇādika* rules, along with the augment *ām*.
Due to its inclusion in the *vṛṣādi* group, it has the acute accent on the first syllable.
*Saṃgṛbhītā*. [The root] *grah* means "to seize.
In the *liṭ* [perfect tense], there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) according to the rule "there is diversely [elision] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
‘There is elision of the suffix *sal* in the optative (*liṅ*).’

When he comes together—that is, when he joins—with the Maruts for the sake of battle, Indra becomes the one who leads those two kinds of waters and men toward the victory of their offspring (*toka*), their sons (*tanaya*), and their grandsons (*tūtuji*). What need is there to say that victory belongs to us, his worshippers? The rest is the same. Regarding *samajāti*: from the root *aja* in the sense of "motion" or "throwing," used in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood with the augment *āṭ*. Regarding *jeṣe*: from the root *ji* in the sense of "victory"; the suffix *sap* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules. The locative case is used in the sense of the dative. Alternatively, from the root *jeṣ*, *ṇeṣ*, or *preṣ* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *kip* by the rule *kip ca*; the acute accent of the case-ending follows the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
May Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra, the terrible, the fierce, the one of a thousand insights, the one with a hundred hymns, the impetuous,
who is like Camīṣa in might and is beloved by all peoples— may he, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection.

He, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the slayer of the Dasyus, the terrible, the fierce, the one of a thousand insights, the one of a hundred ways, the impetuous, the drinker of the Soma—may Indra, who is all-pervading through his might like a universal lord, accompanied by the Maruts, come to our aid. 12.

That Indra is the wielder of the thunderbolt (vajrabhṛt), the bearer of the vajra which cannot be sustained by others; the slayer of the Dasyus, the destroyer of the Dasyus—the Asuras who cause oppression; the terrible one (bhīmaḥ), the cause of fear for all; the fierce one (ugraḥ), whose energy is aroused; the one of a thousand insights (sahasracetāḥ), meaning he possesses manifold knowledge—that is, he is omniscient;

the one with a hundred songs (śatanīthaḥ), meaning he has many praises or many ways of attaining [his grace]; the swift one (ṛvvā), shining widely or great; like the Soma (camīṣo na), situated in the vessel (camū) or the cup (camasa) in the form of its essence; and by his power (śavasā) or strength, he belongs to the five peoples (pāśvajanyaḥ): the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Devas, Asuras, and Rakṣasas.
Or, the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth;
he exists as their protector.
May such Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be for our protection.
*Dasyuhā*:
[the suffix] *kip* is applied to the root *han* by the rule "in the Veda, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). *Bhīmaḥ*.

‘Born from fear’ (*jibhī bhaye*). By the rule *bhīmādayo’pādāne* (Pāṇini 3.4.74), [the suffix] *kha* is applied in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*); by the rule *bhiyaḥ puvvā* (Uṇādi-sūtra 1.145), the augment *mak* is added.
Thus, *śatam-bhīyaḥ*.
The root *ṇīñ* means "to lead" (*prāpaṇe*).
The suffix *kthan* is applied according to the rule *hanikuṣinīramikāśibhyaḥ kthan* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.159). Thus, [the word] *camīṣaḥ* [is derived].
The root *i* means "to go. That which moves toward the *camū* (the sacrificial ladle) is called *camīṣa*.
The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* (*igupadhalaṅkṣaṇa*).
The letter *ra* and the long vowel [are derived] through the corruption of the phonemes;
or alternatively, from the root *cam*, the suffix *īṣan* is applied according to the *Uṇādi* rules,
and as before, the letter *ra* is added.
*Pārśvajaṇyaḥ*:

the suffix *jya* is applied in the sense of "being there" (*bhavārtha*) according to the rule "it should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *bahiṣ*, *deva*, and *pañcajanya*" (Kāśikā 4.3.58.1).
Because it contains the indicatory letter *j*, it has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
His thunderbolt roars with a resonant sound, like the brilliant, impetuous chariot of heaven;
it follows him, winning booty and wealth—may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection.

His thunderbolt roars along with him; like the brilliant chariot of heaven, it is impetuous and full of power. Gains follow it, and riches follow it. May Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protector with his aid. 13.
The thunderbolt (*vajra*), the sharp weapon of that Indra, resounds loudly; it causes the enemies to cry out—that is, it makes them weep.

That Indra is the winner of light (*svarṣāḥ*), the giver of beautiful water; like the sun belonging to heaven (*divaḥ*), he is brilliant. His chariot is dazzling, the maker of sound characterized by roaring, and he is full of power (*śimīvān*).
*Śimī* is a name for action.
1. Endowed with action that benefits the world;
1. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha—by those going; 2. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha—at that time, of these; sa—at that time, of them; 3. kṣa—what is it called?; 4. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha—Indra accompanied by the Maruts; 616.

The Rigveda: the oldest of the four Vedas, consisting primarily of metrical hymns (ṛcas) addressed to various deities, which were composed over several centuries between approximately 1500 and 900 BCE. It is traditionally divided into ten maṇḍalas and is the foundational scripture for the Ṛgvedic school of Vedic religion.

The gifts of wealth follow and attend upon that Indra; likewise, riches themselves attend him. May that glorious Indra be for our protection. He roars. [In the root] *kadi*, *kradi*, and *kdi*, the meaning is "to rejoice" and "to weep. According to the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), because the suffix *śap* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, the *ṇi*-affix is elided by the rule *geraniṭī* (Pāṇini 6.4.51). *Svarṣāḥ*: From the prefix *su-* and the root *ṛ* (to go), the suffix *vic* is applied. That which goes well toward the waters is *svar* (the water). One who acquires (*tsanoti*) this is *svarṣāḥ*. [The root] *paṇ* means "to give. By the rule *janasanakhanakramagamo viṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.67), the suffix *viṭ* is applied. By the rule *viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.41), the vowel is replaced by *ā*. By the rule *sanoteranaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.108), the *s* is changed to *ṣ*. *Tvepaḥ*: [The root] *tviṣ* means "to shine. The suffix *pacādyac* is applied. *Ravataḥ*: [The root] *ru* means "to sound. By the rule *śīṅśapiragamaviñjīviprāṇibhyo'thaḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.393), the suffix *atha* is applied. There is the substitution of *guṇa* and the replacement by *av*. *Sanayaḥ*: From the root *san*, the suffix *ip* is added in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāva*).
May that Indra, whose straight praise and hymn encompass heaven and earth on every side,
being exhilarated by those who prepare him, come to us with the Maruts for our protection.

May that Indra, who completely encompasses with his might the straight praise-song and the measure [of the sacrifice], who surrounds both heaven and earth on every side—he, adorned by the seasons and exhilarated, accompanied by the Maruts, may he be our protector with his aid. 14.

That Indra, whose hymn of praise is extolled, by whom—through his might (*aśavasā*)—the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), which are the measure of all and the standard for the strength of all, are encompassed on every side and protected from all quarters; may that Indra, being exhilarated and rejoicing through the *ṛtus* (seasons) and the sacrifices performed by us, deliver us across from distress.
*Uktham*:
[derived from] the root *vac*, meaning "to speak.
By the rule "pātṛtudivaci... and so forth, the suffix *thak* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule *vacisvapi-* etc. [Pāṇini 6.1.15].
*Paribhuñjat*. [The root] *bhuja* [means] "to protect" and "to eat."
The augment *aṭ* is added to *leṭ*;
by transposition, *śa* [is substituted];
thus, *pāriṣpat*.
The root *pāra* is used in the sense of "completion of an action" (*karmasamāptau*).
In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *aṭ*.
By the rule "there is frequent insertion of *sip* in the *leṭ*," the suffix *sip* is applied.
Because it belongs to the *ārdhadhātuka* category, [the suffix] *it* is applied.
By transposition, there is the elision of *ṇi*. Thus: *mandasānaḥ*.
The word *mada* is used in the senses of praise (*stuti*), joy (*moda*), intoxication (*mada*), and natural luster (*prakānti*).
The suffix *asānac* is applied according to the rule: "From the roots *ṛji*, *vadhi*, and *mandi*, the suffix *kin* [is added]" (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.244).
Of whom neither the gods among the divine nor mortals have reached the limit of his power—
may that Indra, the bull who roams over the earth and heaven, accompanied by the Maruts, be our protection.

No; for whomsoever the gods are the deities, neither mortals nor even the waters have reached the limit of his power. May that Indra, the protector of the earth and the heavens, accompanied by the Maruts, be our aid. 15.

The gods—the hosts of deities such as Vasu and others—did not reach, nor did they attain, the limit or the end of the power (*śavas*) of that Indra who is endowed with qualities such as generosity; likewise, mortals—human beings—and even the waters (*āpaḥ*) did not reach it.

Such an Indra is the "shatterer" (*takṣā*), the one who makes the bodies of his enemies small; by his own strength, he is the preeminent "remover" (*parikāḥ*, i.e., the one who casts out) of both the earth and the heaven.
The meaning is that his strength exceeds even those two worlds.
Accompanied by the Maruts, that Indra goes to the letters kṣa, ṭa, ṭha, and ṛ.

"May he be for us (naḥ), for our (asmākam) aid (ūtī), that is, for our protection (rakṣaṇāya). [Grammatical Analysis: *Devatā*: A god (*deva*) is indeed *devatā*. By the rule "devāt-tal," the suffix *tal* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision (*luk*) of the genitive case ending. *Martāḥ*: From the root *mṛṅ* (in the sense of "leaving life"). The suffix *tan* is applied by the rule beginning with "asihasi. Due to its being a *niṣ* [root], it has the acute accent on the first syllable. *Prikā*: From the root *ricir* (in the sense of "separating"). The suffix *kanip* is applied by the rule "anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante. The change to *pra-* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). *Tvakṣā*: From the root *takṣū* (in the sense of "shaping" or "making thin"). The suffix *asun* is applied. Due to its being a *niṣ* [root], it has the acute accent on the first syllable. *Imaḥ*: *Kṣamā* is a name for the earth. In the rule "āto dhātoḥ," the separation of the word "ātaḥ" allows for the formation of this form. Because of this designation, when the term *bha* applies to the genitive (*ḍasi*), there is elision of the vowel *ā*. Alternatively, from the root *kṣamāyī* (in the sense of "shaking"), the suffix *kip* is applied by the rule "kip ca. Due to the elision of the *v* of *verapṛkta*, the preceding *vali* elision occurs. The rest is the same. The acute accent of the case-ending is due to the "accent of the disappearance of the acute" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*). || 10 ||
The daughter of Rohita, the delighter of the fair region, the milch-cow of R̥jūśva,
bearing a chariot with powerful stallions at its yoke-poles, has been noticed— she, the joyous one, among the non-hostile clans.

The ruddy one, the dark-hued, the one with beautiful reins, the bright-marked, the milch-cow—bearing for wealth the stallion-drawn chariot at the yoke-poles of R̥jvaśva, the joyous one has shone forth among the non-hostile clans. 16.
"Rohit" means red-colored; "aśyāvā" means dark-colored.
The meaning is that she possesses both types of color on both sides.
"Sumadaṃśuḥ" means naturally tall; as Yāska has stated: "'Sumat' means 'naturally'" (Nirukta 6.22).

The row of horses—possessing very long limbs, adorned with forehead-marks (*lalāmīḥ*), marked with *puṇḍra* designs, or equipped with horse-ornaments; having milked [the earth] and made their dwelling in heaven, the celestial realm—the chariot-yoked team of *Ṛjvaśva*, the royal seer (rājarṣi) of this name, for the sake of wealth (*rāye*), bearing and drawing at the poles (*dhūrṣu*)—that is, in the parts of the yoke connected to the vehicle—is joined with the "bull" (*vṛṣan*), Indra the showerer; it is delightful (*mandrā*), bringing joy to all.
This row of horses belonging to the *Nāhuṣīs*—for *nahuṣas* are humans—is known among the *vikṣu*, that is, among the subjects characterized as armies. It is thus recognized.
The meaning is that Indra manifests as a helper in battles, joined with such a row of horses.

*Lalāmīḥ*: From the word *lalāma*, the suffix *ī* is added in the sense of possession according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.109.2 (*chandasīvanipau*), which states that the suffixes *van* and *ī* are used in Vedic literature. Because the stem ends in a vowel (*a*), there is no elision of the case-ending *su*.
*Dhukṣā*: from the root *akṣi* in the sense of "dwelling" or "going," with the suffix *ḍa* added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
From that, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* [is applied].
Regarding *ṛjvāśva*:
the root *ṛj* [is used] in the senses of "going," "standing," "earning," and "acquiring."
By the rule beginning with "ṛjindra," [the word] ending in the suffix *khac* is derived as a nipāta (irregular formation). It means "one whose horses possess a straight course.
In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the accentuation is that of the original form of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*).
*vṛṣaṇavantam* | By the rule *ano nuṭ* (Pāṇini 8.2.16), the augment *nuṭ* is added to the suffix *matup*.
*ciketa*.
"In what knowledge?"— the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is used for the object in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), according to the rule "In the Veda, the *luṅ*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ* [tenses are used]";
the suffix *tip* is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
O Indra, Bull, this is your hymn of praise; the Vārṣāgiras celebrate this gift:
Ṛjvāśva with his side-horses, Ambarīṣa, Sahadeva, Bhayamāna, and Surādhās.
This, that—O Indra, for you the bull—these Vārṣāgiras sing forth as a hymn of praise for your bounty: Ṛjrāśva with his side-horses, Ambarīṣa, Sahadeva, Bhayamāna, and Surādhas. 17.

1. From the statement "kṣa-ṭha". 2. Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha is red in color. 3. Kṣa-sa-khata is indeed [that]. 4. Together with rays (sa-aṃśuḥ). 5. Of that which is designated by kṣa-sa. 6. Producing intoxication (sa-madakārī). Ka. 78.

O Indra, for you, the showerer of desires (*vṛṣṇe kāmānām*), this hymn (*uktham*)—this song of praise (*stotram*) which brings about success (*rādhaḥ saṃrādhakam*)—is being recited. The descendants of Vṛpāgir, namely Ṛtrāśva and others, the sons of King Vṛpāgir, address you directly (*abhi gṛṇanti*). He explains the term *Vāpāgirāḥ*: the royal sage named Ṛtrāśva praised Indra together with other ṛṣis standing at his side. Who were those standing at his side? The four royal sages beginning with Ambarīṣa. *Vāpāgirāḥ*: The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.92 (*tasyāpatyam*), forming the patronymic. *Gṛṇanti*: From the root *gṛ* (to sound). The shortening occurs by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*. *Rādhaḥ*: From the roots *rādha* and *sādha* (in the sense of accomplishment). That by which one attains or becomes prosperous is *rādhaḥ*; the suffix *asun* is used in the instrumental sense. *Ṛtrāśvaḥ*: One whose horses (*aśvāḥ*) are swift-moving (*ṛtrāḥ*); thus he is so called. *Ambarīṣaḥ*: From the root *abi* (to sound); the suffix *iṣan* is added according to the Uṇādi-sūtra 4.469. *Sahadevaḥ*: One who exists together with the gods (*devaiḥ saha vartate*); the absence of the *samā* (long vowel) is optional according to the rule *vopasarjanasya*. *Bhayamānaḥ*: From the root *abhi* (in the sense of fear). Here, the causative sense is internalized; the suffix *śānac* is used by transposition (*vyatyayena*). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is no substitution of *ślu* for *śap*. Since the root begins with a vowel (*adupadeśāt*), the suffix is unaccented, and thus the accent of the root itself remains. *Suvajraḥ*: *Rādhaḥ* is a name for wealth. O priests, sing forth—that is, utter with excellence—the speech characterized by praise, which consists of oblations in the form of food accompanied by sacrificial offerings, for Indra, who is gladdened and who possesses the hymns of the singer. That Indra, being joined in friendship with the king named Ṛjiśvan, struck down the wives of the one whose womb was impregnated by the Asura named Kṛṣṇa; that is, he slew those women whose embryos had been infused by him.
The meaning is that after slaying the Asura Kṛṣṇa, he even killed her pregnant wives so that no offspring of his sons might remain.

Desiring protection (*avasyavaḥ*), we—those who wish for safety—invoke Indra, the showerer of desires (*vṛṣaṇam*), who is endowed with a thunderbolt in his right hand (*vajradakṣiṇam*), accompanied by the Maruts (*marutvantam*), for the sake of friendship (*sakhyāya*) and for the deeds of a friend.
