*Sudhuma*:
[This is derived from] the root *yuj* in the sense of "consecration" (*abhiṣava*).

Regarding the augment *iṭ* which would otherwise be required by the rule *kādinīyama* in the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, its absence follows from the statement: "The teaching concerning augments is not absolute" (*anityam āgama-śāsanam*).
Rejoice with the tawny steeds which are yours, O Indra; unclose your jaws and let loose the milch-cows.
Let the bay horses with beautiful jaws bring you hither; graciously accept our offerings.

Rejoice with the tawny ones! O Indra, those which are yours—uncover your jaws and open wide your lips. O fair-jawed one, let the tawny steeds bring you hither; desiring our offerings, graciously accept them. 10.
O Indra, rejoice together with your bay horses; be satisfied.
Open wide your jaws, your own [lips], for the sake of drinking the Soma;
spread them apart. Likewise, release your two tongues, the means of drinking, for the sake of consuming the Soma.
O you of beautiful jaws— *śipre* meaning either the jaws or the nostrils—
O Indra, let your bay horses (*harayaḥ*) bring you hither; let them carry you to our sacrifice.
And you, being desirous of us, O Uśan, accept each of our oblations; partake of them one by one; do not remain indifferent.
"vi vyasva," [from the root] *ap* in the sense of "internal action"; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The suffix *śyan* is applied by the rule *divādibhyaḥ śyan*.
There is the elision of the vowel *o* according to *otaḥ śyani* (Pāṇini 7.3.71). The substitution of *parasmaipada* endings occurs by the rule *upasargāt sunoti*.
Marutta praised [him]: "O guardians of this stronghold, may we, through Indra, win booty.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us that."
O guardians of the stronghold, may we, through Indra, win booty. May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this. 11.

Maruttastotra refers to one whose hymn of praise is accompanied by the Maruts; he belongs to that Indra who is the destroyer (kṣetṛ) of the host (vṛjana) of enemies. We, who are his protectors (gopāḥ)—that is, those worthy of being protected and guarded—may we, through that Indra, win (sanuyāma) and obtain (labhemahi) booty (vāja), that is, food.
May Mitra and the others, as well as Heaven and Earth, honor—that is, make worthy of praise—that which we have thus requested for ourselves.
Regarding *vṛjana*:
from the root *vṛj* in the sense of "excluding" (*varjane*),
the suffix *kyu* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *kyu* is added after the roots *kṛ*, *pṛ*, *vṛj*, *mand*, and *indh*."
"imāṃ te" is the ninth hymn, consisting of eleven verses; it is the seer Kutsa's composition addressed to Indra.
Of these, the first is a Triṣṭubh, while the remaining ten are Jagatīs.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "imāṃ te; the other [first verse] is a Triṣṭubh."
The application is inferential.

1. The *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*, and *la* [syllables] characterize the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*); the *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *sa* [syllables] characterize the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes; the *dha* [syllable] characterizes the animal sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
I offer forth this great prayer to you, the Great One; for in his praise, the inspired thought (*dhiṣaṇā*) has been cleansed for you.
Him, the victorious one, the gods together with Indra have strengthened with power at the festival and at the impulse [of sacrifice].

I offer this prayer to you, the great one; for in the praise of this [singer], your vast inspiration has been manifested. At his exultation and at his impulse, the gods rejoiced in Indra’s victorious power.

O Indra, I offer forth—that is, I accomplish with excellence—this great, vast, and most excellent *dhi* (hymn of praise) for you, who are mighty. For your own intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*) has become anointed—that is, closely united—with this hymn of praise from me, the singer;
therefore, I compose this hymn which is dear to you. This is the meaning.
The second half-verse is composed in the indirect (parokṣakṛta) style:

"The gods"—the officiating priests engaged in the ritual acts—"rejoiced after" that aforementioned Indra, the "conqueror of enemies," by means of "strength"—that is, the power celebrated through their hymns—bestowing joy upon him in due order.
For what purpose?
"And at a festival" means for the sake of a festival or for the sake of increase; and "at the production" means for the sake of the arising of wealth or of rainwater.
*Ānaje*. [The root] *añj*, meaning "to manifest," "to eat," or "to go.
From this, the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is used in the passive voice (*karman*).
The dual suffix and the *halādi-śeṣa* [apply].
By the rule "ata ādeḥ," there is the substitution of *ā* for the reduplication.
By the rule "tasmāddu dīrghāt ahalah" (Pāṇini 7.4.71), the augment *nuṭ* is added.
There is a transposition [of sounds] and the elision of the vowel *u* in the suffix;
[the root is] *utsav-*.
[The root] *yu* [is used] in the sense of "impelling."
The suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) by the rule *ṛdorap*.
The locative case is used according to the rule *nimittāt karmasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.36).
The final syllable of the compound is accented acute by the rule *thāthādisvareṇa* (Pāṇini 6.2.144).
*Sāsahima*.
[The root] *paha* means "to overcome.
In the case of *āhagamanahana*, the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule "utsarga-chandasi" (the general rule applies in the Vedic language).
The dual number is used because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
According to the rule "it is also seen in other cases," there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) in *saṃhitā*. [Thus: *amadan*.
The root *mad* means "to rejoice.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of causation (*hetumati*).
Because *mard* is listed among the *ghaṭādi* roots in the rule "mardā harṣalapanayoḥ," the shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ."
By the rule "chandasyubhayathā," the root is treated as if it were ārdhadhātuka; consequently, by the rule "ṇeraniṭi," there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi*.

The seven rivers bear his fame; heaven and earth and the broad world bear his beautiful form. For us, O Indra, the sun and the moon move in their alternating course, so that we may behold them and have faith.

The seven rivers bear his fame; heaven and earth and the wide world bear his most beautiful form. To us, sun and moon move in their alternating course so that we may behold them and have faith, O Indra. ||2||
The seven rivers—the Ganges and the others, primarily set forth in this verse beginning with "asya indrasya... imaṃ me gaṅge"—bear and sustain his fame, glory, and renown.
The meaning is that these rivers, filled with heated elemental waters, manifest Indra’s capacity as the giver of rain through his slaying of Vṛtra.
Moreover, there are "dyāvākṣāmā," heaven and earth.

‘Pṛthivī’ is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). And this intermediate space is the ‘darśataṃ vapuḥ’—the visible form, that is, the beautiful appearance—of this Indra as he exists in the nature of the sun. This is his very form.
They maintain a form consisting of light.
Furthermore, O Indra, for the sake of our direct perception—that is, for the manifestation toward us of objects worthy of being seen—and for the sake of faith (*śraddhā*);
for it is only when an object is seen with the eye that faith arises in the thought, "This is true."
This [particle] *kam* is for the purpose of filling the meter.

For the sake of both meanings, the sun and the moon perform an "over-crossing" (*avitarturam*), which is a crossing by way of mutual exchange, occurring as a repeated going back and forth. (Note 1: The word *tava* does not exist in the *kṣa* and *sa* manuscripts.)
2. *kṣaṇa* is for the purpose of filling the meter.
(Kārikā 79)

"Thus moving": it exists; the meaning is that you yourself exist in that very form. Regarding the word *asya*: the acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending is by the rule "ūḍidam. *Cāvākṣāmā*: "gauśca kṣāmā ca" (the earth and the sky). The substitution of *dyāvā* for *divaḥ* occurs by the rule "divo dyāvā. The substitution of *ḍā* for the case-ending is by the rule "supāṃ suluk. The original accent of both members of the compound is maintained by the rule "devatādvandve ca. This has been demonstrated. [The suffix] *ac* is added by the rule "mṛdṛśi," etc. *Sūryācandramasā*: "sūryaśca candramāśca" (the sun and the moon). The substitution of *ānaṅ* for the first member occurs by the rule "devatādvandve ca. The vowel *ā* replaces the case-ending by the rule "supāṃ suluk. The word *candramas-* has its middle syllable acute by the original accent of the first member, according to the class beginning with *dāsībhāra*. Therefore, there is a prohibition of the application of the original accent of both members—which would have applied by the rule "devatādvandve ca"—by the rule "nottarapadenudāttādāvapṛthivī. *Abhicakṣe*: from the root *cakṣ*, in the sense of "manifesting," the suffix *kvip* is added in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāva*) by the rule "saṃpadādi. The dative case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). *Śraddhe*: because of the inclusion of the root *dṛś*, the suffix *vic* is added to the root *dhā* in the sense of an abstract noun. In the singular dative, the long *ā* is elided by the rule "āto dhātoḥ. The acute accent of the case-ending is by the rule "udāttanivṛttisvara. *Vitanuram*: from the root *tṝ* in the *laṅ* tense, the suffix *kurac* is added by the *uṇādi* rules. The change to *u* occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi."
O Maghavan, drive that victorious chariot toward us for our gain, which we shall cheer on in the encounter;
O Indra, praised by many, come with your mind to this sacrifice, and O Maghavan, grant us protection through your two bay steeds.

O Maghavan, drive that victorious chariot hither for our gain, which we shall hail with joy in the encounter of battle. O Indra, praised by many, grant us protection with your mind, O Maghavan, to us who are devoted to you. 3.

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, for our gain of wealth, impel—that very chariot—drive it forward! O Puruṣṭuta, praised by many, with our mind and intellect, we shall celebrate in succession that victorious chariot belonging to you, O Indra, which we praise in the encounter, when there is a meeting with enemies in the fray of battle. Moreover, O Maghavan, grant and bestow upon us, who desire you, protection and happiness.
Ava:
Since it is stated that "ava" [expresses] protection, motion, and beauty, here it has the sense of motion; [it occurs] in the context of union.
In "ājā," the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) by the rule "grahavṛdhniśrigamaśca";
the acute accent on the final syllable of the second member is established by the rule "thāthādinā. Thus, [the word] is *ājā*.
In the expression *tvāyaddhayaḥ*, the suffix *ḍā* is substituted for the locative case ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. [The form *tvāyat* is derived from] *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*.
By the rule *pratyayottarapadayoś ca*, the substitution of *tvā* occurs for everything up to the final *m*.
By transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is the substitution of *ā* for the letter *d*.
From a root ending in a semivowel (*vyañjan*), the suffix *śatṛ* is applied to the present tense marker (*laṭ*).

Because it is taught as having a short vowel (*adupadeśāt*), when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) formed with the *gati* prefix and the *kyac* affix is accented by the rule "a single substitute [for an unaccented element] with an accented one is accented. Thus, it possesses the acute accent (*udāttatvam*).
May we, with you as our ally, conquer the enemy; bring to us our share in every battle.
O Indra, grant us wide space and easy passage; O Maghavan, shatter the virile strength of our foes.

May we conquer with you as our ally; strike down the enemy arrayed against us. In every battle, lift up our portion. O Indra, grant us wide space and easy passage; O Maghavan, shatter the manly strength of our enemies.

1. The words *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *ḍa* have their original accent on both members of the compound (*ubhayapada-prakṛtisvaratvam*). 2. The suffix *kura* is added after *kṣa*. 3. *Kṣa*, *ṭha*, *ṭha*, and *sa*—cause [them] to proceed. 4. *Kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *sa*—in the battle (*ājau*).
O Indra, with you as our ally (*yujā*), joined with us as our helper, may we, the singers, conquer—that is, overcome—the enemy who attacks us.
Furthermore, in every battle (*bhare-bhare*), lift up (*udava*) our share—that is, our portion—by means of removing the affliction caused by the enemy; that is, protect it preeminently.
Likewise, O Indra, grant us wealth (*varivas*) that is easy to attain, easy to access, and easy to acquire;
so do it, O Maghavan! Break down, utterly shatter, and drive away the hostilities (*vṛṇyā*)—that is, the heroic assaults—of our enemies who cause us distress.
*Vṛtam*.
The root *vṛñ* means "to choose.
By the rule *kip ca*, the suffix *kip* is applied; there is the addition of the augment *tuk*.
It is easy to understand.
In the rule "suduror adhikaraṇe," the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam*. [The form] *krudhi* [is derived similarly].
By the rule *śruśrupakṛvṛbhyaḥ*, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs. *Ruja*: the root *ruj* means "to break."
The *taudādika* [section]:

For these various people, seeking to win over wealth with their aid, call upon you, O Sustainer of riches, O seekers of distinction. Mount our chariot for the sake of gain; for victorious, O Indra, is your well-composed mind. For these various people, calling upon you, O Sustainer of riches, with their aid, are seekers of distinction. Mount our chariot for the sake of gain; for victorious, O Indra, is your well-composed mind.
O Indra, sustainer of riches— of substances such as cattle, gold, and so forth— these people,
the singers of praise (for *vipanyavaḥ* is a name for those who laud),
calling upon you with their protection (*avasā*) as the motive, invoke you; for they are indeed diverse and distinct.
In their midst, for our very own gain—that is, for the giving of wealth—mount, that is, ascend, our chariot.
O Indra, your mind is indeed composed and undisturbed, and it is victorious;
that is to say, it is capable of conquering enemies and bestowing wealth upon us.

The root *paṇ* means "to give"; the suffix *kni* is applied after the roots *jan*, *san*, and *khan* when followed by the suffix *saṃbhal*, according to Pāṇini 3.2.171. Thus, [the form] *āśvam* is derived.

The winner of cattle, whose arms are his [weapons], he of immeasurable will, the preeminent one, who at every deed provides a hundredfold aid, the stirrer of the battle-drum, the peerless Indra—by his might he is the standard of comparison; for people seeking to win his favor are divided among themselves. 6. Winner of cattle, O you whose arms are [your weapons], you of immeasurable will, the preeminent one, at every deed, you who provide a hundredfold aid, the stirrer of the battle-drum, the peerless Indra—by his might he is the standard of comparison; indeed, people desiring to win [his favor] are divided [among themselves]. 6.

O Indra, your two arms and hands are winners of cattle, having been made victorious through the winning of cows. And you, O one of immeasurable power (*amitakratu*), are the most excellent (*sima*), whose knowledge is unbounded.
Thus says the Śāṅkhāyana: "They indeed call the most excellent *sima*."
Or rather:
*simaḥ* means the binder of enemies;
at every action—indeed, even when the actions of the worshippers are practiced—he possesses a hundred forms, is endowed with manifold protections, and is the agitator of the foe (*khajaṅkaraḥ*).
"Khaja" is battle, so called because it "scatters" (khajati) or "crushes" (makṣāti) men;
its agent is the one who performs it.
"Akalpa" means devoid of conceptualization by another.
The meaning is "independent.
Being measured as a standard—that is, being determined as a match—by the *ojas*, the vigor and strength that exists in all living beings, through all of that;
because Indra is distinguished by divine qualities, for this reason, people who desire to win wealth (*sipāsavaḥ*), wishing to obtain riches, call upon him in various ways (*vi hyante*).
*Gojitā*:
"Conquerors of cows" (*gā jayataḥ*) are the *gojin* (cow-conquerors). The vowel *ā* [at the end] is due to the rule *supāṃ suluk* [Pāṇini 7.1.39], which substitutes *ā* for the case-ending.
The root *si* means "to bind";
from this, the suffix *mak* is added according to the *auṇādika* rules.
*Khajaṃkaraḥ*:
[The suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the root *khaj*,
meaning "to churn," according to the rule for *pacādyac*.

And because of the word *ca* in the rule *kṣamapriyamadeṇa ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.44), which serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned, [the suffix *kvip*] applies even when the word *khaja* is the upapada:
1. *kṣasa-analābhāya*; 2. *kṣa-labdhyāmacchavaḥ*; 3. *kṣasa-gojitā*. [The suffix] *kvip*.

From the root *kṛ*, the suffix *khac* is applied. By the rule *arudvipadajantasya mum*, the augment *mum* is added. The accentuation follows the rule for the natural accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of a compound whose final member is a *kṛt*-derived word. Thus, *akalpaḥ*. By the rule *namsumyām*, the final syllable of the second member of the compound receives the udātta accent. Regarding *siṣāsavaḥ*: the roots *vana* and *ṣaṇa* mean "to share" or "to bestow. With the desiderative suffix *san*, the absence of the augment *iṭ* occurs due to the optionality provided by the rule *sanīvantardha*. By the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ*, the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the radical *a*]. Then reduplication and other operations take place. Finally, the suffix *u* is applied by the rule *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.168). Because it is the last enjoined element (*sati śiṣṭatvāt*), its accent alone remains.

O Madhavan, your fame has risen above a hundred and even more than a thousand among the peoples; you have surpassed all measure. Your wisdom has reached its full extent, for you, O Purandara, strike down the great Vritras.

O Maghavan, your fame has surpassed a hundred, and even more than that; it has exceeded a thousand among the peoples. You, the immeasurable one, have been sustained by the *dhiṣaṇā* (the sacred vessel/inspiration). O slayer of Vṛtra, breaker of forts, you strike down the great obstacles with your power.
O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, among the peoples, among the human worshippers, that fame which exists as food bestowed by yourself—that exceeds, it is more abundant than, a hundredfold wealth;
indeed, it exceeds even more than a greater number, more than a hundredfold wealth.
What more need be said?
It has surpassed even the thousand—that is, it exceeds the number one thousand;
the meaning is that the food offered by you is inexhaustible.
Moreover, our great and venerable speech, characterized by praise, illuminates you—who are immeasurable (amātra), being devoid of limit and beyond all calculation—with all your [powers].
It reveals your qualities, O Purandara—O Indra, destroyer of the cities of your enemies; for after this praise, you slay, strike down, and destroy the Vṛtras, the obstructing foes.
*ririce* | *ricir* [is used] in the sense of "purging" (*virecana*).
[This form is derived from the root] in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*) with the perfect tense suffix (*liṭ*).
*titiviṣe* (you have shone); from the root *tviṣ* meaning "to shine.
*jighnase* (you strike).
In *hantīr liṭi*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

The augment *aṭ* is added according to the rule "the augments *aṭ* and *āṭ* [are added] to the *leṭ*. By the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), there is the elision (*bhlu*) of the suffix *śap*.
By the rule "gamahana," etc., there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*).
Due to the status of being as if the original were present (*sthānivadbhāva*), reduplication and so forth occur.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," the *it* (vocalization) of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) takes place.
*Puraṃdara*:
[The suffix] *khac* is applied by the rule "pṛṣodarādisahoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.41);
[by the rule] "khaci hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.94), there is shortening of the vowel.
The form *am* [is used] due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.3.69: "And [the word] *apuraṃdara* [is formed with the suffix *am*]."
O King Indra, you have surpassed the three worlds in vigor; you have extended beyond the three earths and the three luminous realms.
You have grown beyond this entire universe; O Indra, by your very birth, you have been the enemyless one from of old.

O Lord of men, you have surpassed the three worlds, the measure of vigor, the three earths, and the three luminous realms; indeed, you have grown beyond this entire universe. O Indra, from birth you have been without a rival since of old. 8.
O King, O Indra, protector of men, you are the counterpart and representative of the vigor of all living beings; what kind of counterpart? That which belongs to the third heaven.
The word *dhātu* refers to a portion of a rope, as in the expression, "he makes a cord of three or five *dhātus*.
Just as a rope that is tripled or doubled is more secure, so too is Indra more firmly established; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, you [have pervaded] the three earths, the three worlds, the three luminous realms, and the three splendors: that which is called the Sun in heaven, the form of lightning in the intermediate space, and Agni on earth.
1. kṣa-sa-asmāt sāna | 2. kṣa-tvā svām |
3. It becomes more firmly established. O Agni, you who exist on earth in the form of the Āhavanīya fire and others, you thus desire to carry across the three worlds and the three splendors;
moreover, you desire to carry across this entire universe and all created beings.
The meaning is that by protecting the entire world, you alone are the sustainer of all.
For, O Indra, since you have been so from of old—beginning from birth (*sanāt*), from the very moment of your birth—you have been *atruḥ*, free from enemies.

*Triviṣṭadhātu*: it is established (*vidhīyate*) or made by means of a threefold (*tridhā*) entry (*viṣṭi*) or penetration; thus it is *triviṣṭadhātu*, meaning a cord tripled. The suffix *ktin* is used here in the sense of a specific state (*viśeṣabhāva*).
The suffix *tun* is applied in sequence according to [Uṇādi Sūtra] 1.69, *dhājaḥ sitani-gamimasi*.
The accentuation is that of the original form of the final member (*kuduttarapada-prakṛtisvaratvam*).

Here, the word denoting "firmness" (*dṛḍharajju*) indicates "firmness" (*dārḍhyam*) by secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*), and thus functions to denote the object of comparison (*pratimāna*) which possesses that quality.
Just as the word "fire" is applied to a young brahmin boy;
[in the case of] *tisraḥ*, by the rule *tricaturor striyām* [Pāṇini 7.2.99], there is the substitution of *tistri-* which is oxytone (having the udātta accent on the final syllable).
O Indra, you have conquered the enemies; you conquer them.
Likewise, you have not withheld the wealth—that is, the wealth taken from the enemies—but bestow it upon those who praise you. This is the meaning.

O Indra, possessor of wealth, in small and insignificant battles, as well as in great and mature conflicts, we sharpen you—the fierce, the exalted, the exceedingly powerful one—with our hymns for the sake of our protection. Then, O Indra, having come to our invocations—that is, to the calls made for battle—impel us; that is to say, urge us forward in the contests and cause us to attain victory.

*jigetha*. The root *ji* means "to conquer. In the case of the *liṭ* suffix *thāl*, there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*—which would otherwise be required by the rule for roots beginning with *krā-*—by the rule *acastāsvathyalyaniṭo nityam* (Pāṇini 7.2.61).
By the rule *san-liṭor jeḥ*, there is the substitution of *ku* (the guttural *g*) for the letter *j* following the reduplication.
This light, which is to be grasped, exists upon the earth, in the ground.
The other, the one called the sun, is in the sky, in the heavenly world. This twofold light of Indra becomes united—that is, it joins with one another;
at night, the sun becomes joined with fire.
According to the Śruti: "The sun indeed enters into fire at night; therefore, fire is seen glowing at night.
But during the day, fire unites with the sun;
according to the Śruti: "Fire indeed ascends after the setting sun; therefore, only smoke is seen from fire during the day" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.9–10).
There is an illustration for the mutual union of these two:
"like a banner in battle. The word *samana* denotes a battle.
Just as when two combatants are fighting in a close battle, their banners and standards come into contact with one another, so it is in this case.

*Indriya*. It is the mark (*liṅga*) or the power (*bala*) of *indra*; it is derived as a word ending in the suffix *yat*, being irregularly formed according to the rule: "The word *indriya* is [derived from] *indra-liṅga*."
*Parācaiḥ*:
this is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), like *uccais* or *nīcais*.
Yāska, however, says: "Parācaiḥ means with those turned away" (*Nirukta* 11.25).
*Kṣamā*: By the rule *supāṃ suluk* etc., there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending; the elision of the *m* in *īmaḥ* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) sandhi phenomenon.
It is indeed the same.
[The root] *pam* means "to be complete" (*avaikalya*). The suffix *yuc* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.3.130: "It is also seen after other [roots]."
The vowel *ā* is substituted for the locative case-ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk°*.

The compound is formed according to the rule *ivena vibhaktyalopaḥ pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvaṃ ca*, whereby the case-ending is not elided and the original accentuation of the preceding member is maintained.
He supported the earth and spread it out; having struck with his thunderbolt, he released the waters.
Maghavan slew the serpent of Druhyu and struck down Ahi-vyaṃsa with his mighty powers.
He sustained the earth and spread it out; having struck with his thunderbolt, he released the waters. He slew the serpent, he split Rauhiṇa asunder, and Maghavan shattered Viḍaṃsa with his powers.

That Indra supported—that is, he sustained—the earth oppressed by the Asuras; the meaning is that he caused it to remain free from affliction. Thereafter, he spread it out—he made that earth extensive.
Moreover, having slain Vṛtra and others who were to be struck down with the weapon *vajra*, he released the waters—the seasonal rains—causing them to flow forth from the clouds.
This very point is made clear:
he slew the serpent-like cloud abiding in the atmosphere, striking it with the *vajra* for the sake of bringing rain.
Rauhiṇa: a certain asura named Rauhiṇa;
and him he split apart, tore asunder.
Moreover, Maghavan, the wealthy Indra, by means of his own powers—his deeds of war—slew Vṛtra, the Asura who was deprived of his arms.
He spreads out;
he makes broad, he causes to expand.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "he treats as such" (*taskaroti*).

By the rule "The operation [pertaining to] a nominal stem does not apply as if it were *ṇit*" (Pāṇini 6.4.155), the substitution of *ra* for the *ṛ*-vowel occurs according to "The *ṛ* of a light vowel preceded by a consonant is replaced by *ra*" (Pāṇini 6.4.161).

There is elision of the final *ṭi* by the rule "of the *ṭi*" (Pāṇini 6.4.143). Due to the status of that [elision] as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is an absence of *vṛddhi*.
In the *luṅ* [aorist] of the root *prath*, after the *caṅ* [augment], there is the elision of the *ṇi*.
Upon reduplication, the preceding syllable receives the udātta accent by the rule *caṅyanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.218).

The elision of the *ṇi* does not possess the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*), because its prohibition applies with respect to rules concerning accent by the rule *na padānta...* and so forth.
Because the preceding word does not reside within the same sentence, there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
Born for the sake of the Law, he split apart the Dāsa fortresses with his faith and vigor;
knowing well the weapon of the impetuous Indra, O Indra, increase the Aryan power and glory.

He, the one whose nature is born of truth, who maintains what has been heard, moved about shattering the fortresses with his might, dispersing the Dāsa hosts. O wielder of the thunderbolt, you who know, hurl your weapon at the Dasyu; increase our Aryan power and our glorious splendor, O Indra!

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-na-sa* and another [letter]. 2. *kṣa* between both armies. 3. *kṣa-sa* for "firm. 4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa*, or else in the *luṅ* (aorist) of the root *prath*. 5. *kṣa-na-sa* for the dual number. 6. *kṣa-na* and [the following]. *Vjātabharmā*. *Jātu* is said to mean "visible" (*dṛśya*) or "lightning" (*śani*).
"Bharma-āyudha" means one whose weapon is like a thunderbolt; or alternatively, it refers to the sustainer (*bhartṛ*) of living beings (*jānānām prajānām*).

Indra—believing with great reverence (*śraddhānaḥ*) that the task was accomplished through seed (*vājaḥ*), vigor (*ojasā*), and strength (*balena*), and desiring it with excessive zeal (*kāmayamānaḥ*)—being such as this, he went forth in various ways (*vivicaran*), shattering and destroying the ancient fortresses (*purāḥ*) belonging to the Dasyus (*dāsīḥ*).

O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), O Indra, you who are wise (*vidvān*) and recognize our hymns of praise, release your weapon (*hetiḥ*) against the enemy (*damyave*) who seeks to destroy the singer; this is the implied sense.
Furthermore, O Indra, [grant] desirable power (*vārya sahaḥ*).
O noble ones, you who are wise and are his praisers,
increase his strength— make it exceedingly great—
and likewise increase his bold renown.
*Jātabharma*. [The root] *janī* [is used] in the sense of "manifestation.

Because of the inclusion of the word "seen" (*dṛś*) in the rule "it is seen in other cases as well," and because that inclusion is intended to signify the deviation [of the suffix] from all restrictive conditions (*upādhi*), the suffix *ḍa* is applied even to the simple root.

Behold this abundant nourishment of his; place your faith in the heroic power of Indra! He found the cattle; he found the horses; he found the plants; he found the waters; he found the forests. 5. Behold this! His! This! Look! Abundant! Nourishment! Faith! Of Indra! Place! Heroic power! He! Cattle! Found! He! Found! Horses! He! Plants! He! Waters! He! Forests! 5.
O people characterized as priests and sacrificers, behold this very heroic power of this Indra—nourished and fully grown;
for that reason, see it as vast and extensive!
And for the sake of that heroism, bestow upon it *śraddhā* (faith and high esteem).
If it is asked what that heroism (*vīrya*) is, it is said: by means of that heroism, Indra recovered—that is, obtained—the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis;
likewise, by means of that [heroism], Indra recovered the horses that had been carried off by them.
Moreover, that Indra, by means of which heroic power he obtained the plants— by which all the earth is indicated— and likewise the waters,
the waters of rain obstructed by Vṛtra;
and likewise the forests, the desirable and worshipful riches— that Indra obtained them by means of which heroic power.
*dhattana* [is derived from] *dadhāna*, and *tasanāsanāthāśca* [is derived from] *tad-*, with the substitution of *tan-* for that;
[thus he] found.
The root *vit* is used in the sense of acquisition (*lābha*).
By the rule *śe sucādīnām*, the augment *num* is applied.

For Indra—the one endowed with manifold deeds consisting of the slaying of enemies and the like; the bull (*vṛṣabha*) among all the gods; the showerer (*vṛṣan*) capable of bestowing [rain]; he of true vigor (*satya-śuṣma*) whose strength is unfailing—we shall press the *soma* for his sake, we shall prepare the essence-form for the purpose of oblation. He who is Indra, possessed of heroism (*śūra*), having seized the wealth of the non-sacrificer (*ayajvan*)—that is, having shown regard for the matter of riches—and distributing it, that is, taking away the wealth from that non-sacrificer and dividing it, he comes.
He goes to give that wealth to the sacrificers.
Herein is an illustration:
like a highwayman, just as a robber who obstructs the road goes along forcibly seizing the wealth of virtuous men passing by, so too does he.
Having struck [the drum].
The root *hṛ* is used in the sense of respect (*ādara*).
In a compound where it is not preceded by *an-*, the suffix *ktvā* is replaced by *lyap* (Pāṇini 7.1.37).
Since the status of being a *kṛt*-suffix applies to it by virtue of its being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the augment *tuk* is added according to the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti*.
Thus, it becomes *paripanthīva*.

In the Vedic language, the form ending in the suffix *ini* is irregularly derived as *paripanthin* and *pariparin* in the sense of "one who stands in the way" (*paryavasthātṛ*), according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.2.89.

Truly, O Indra, you performed that heroic deed when you awakened the sleeping serpent with your thunderbolt; after you, the joyful one, the wives, the flocks, and all the gods rejoiced in your wake. Truly, O Indra, you performed that heroic deed when you awakened the sleeping serpent with your thunderbolt; after you, the joyful one, the wives, the flocks, and all the gods rejoiced in your wake.
1. Of the persons [beginning with] kṣa, ṭa, ṭha, and sa.
2. He goes out from kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha. (Ka. 80)
O Indra, you have proclaimed—that is, made known—that heroic deed, that act of a hero, which you performed with joy. What indeed was that heroic deed?
It was that by means of which—by that heroism—you awakened Ahi Vṛtra, who was sleeping, slumbering, and intoxicated with pride, using the vajra, the thunderbolt.
"May he, being awakened, engage in battle with me"—thinking thus, the wives of the gods rejoiced after the slaughter of such a Vṛtra, attaining joy.
Moreover, the birds, which are wont to fly even from great heights, and all the other Viśvedevas likewise rejoiced after you.
With the suffix *s* present:
*yama-sva-me*.
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
*patnīḥ*: the long vowel *ī* is substituted by the preceding homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) according to the rule *vā chandasi*. *Amadan*.
‘madī’ means ‘joy’; may we cause [the gods] to rejoice. May we attain the sacred word (śap).
When you, O Indra, slew Śuṣṇa, Pipru, Kuyava, and Vṛtra, and shattered the fortresses of Śambara—
may Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us that as a great gift.
Śuṣṇa, the roaring one, with his ship—
*arvan* is a name for horse.

Just as a horse, neighing—that is, making the sound of "hepā"—quickly returns to its own place; having done what? Having unloosed the *vayaḥ*, the reins for binding the horse, releasing them from the chariot; and likewise, having unharnessed (*avasāya*) the horses, the steeds yoked to the chariot, and released them.
Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "The root *as* with the prefix *ava* signifies 'to release' (*vimocane*)," as found in Nirukta 1.17.
What kind of horses?
Those [horses] when the time for sacrifice (*prapitve*) has arrived.
"‘In the onset,’ when it has arrived, ‘in the encounter,’ in the manifest [battle]—so says Yāska (Nirukta 3.20).
‘At night’ (doṣā) and ‘by day’ (vastoḥ), [we invoke] those who carry with exceeding zeal (vahiyaḥ)."
Niṣade:
from the root *sad*, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad* and so forth;
[thus] *svānaḥ*.
The root *śvan* (in the sense of sound) is *syamu* with the suffix *ghañ*;
due to the rule of frequent occurrence (*bahulavacanāt*), the agentive suffix is applied.
In the form *karpotavataḥ*, there is udātta accent on the final syllable.
*Vayaḥ*.
Because they move together with the chariot, the word *vi-* refers to the rays;
[the root] *vī* is used in the sense of motion and so forth.
The suffix *i* is added according to the *auṇādika* rules,
and there is the elision of the *ṭi* portion.
The nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Having determined [the root]: "The root *pū* is used in the sense of an intermediate action (*antarkarman*). Then, by the rule "ādecaḥ," the substitution of *ā* occurs.
In the compound *samāse 'nañpūrve*, the suffix *lyap* is substituted for *ktvā*. [The form] *vahīyasaḥ* [is derived from] the root *vaha* in the sense of "carrying" (*prāpaṇe*).
From the word *voḍhṛ*, which ends in the suffix *tṛc*, the suffix *īyasun* is applied according to the rule *tṛc chandasi*.

When the elision of *ṭ* (in *ṭer*) is to be performed by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*, since the rules for the substitution of *ḍha* for *dha*, the substitution of *ṭu* for *da*, and the elision of *ḍha* are considered asiddha (not yet applied), the short *o* (*osvatva*) dependent upon them also does not occur; thus, only the elision of *ṭ* is carried out.
May those men, through their devotion to Indra, traverse the paths of the enemy with their thoughts;
may the gods, hearing our cry against the fury of the Dāsa, bring our people to prosperity.
"O! These heroes have gone to Indra for his aid; may he never come upon those paths of destruction. O gods, having heard the fury of the Dāsa, may they lead our people toward prosperity. 2.
Those men who are the leaders of the sacrifice, the sacrificers, come to Indra for protection;
*u* is a particle used here as a conjunction, and the combination of the two particles (*ā u*) has the sense of *ā* (towards).
They come.
And may that Indra, having come, swiftly cause them—those very ones—to go along the paths of the journey at that very moment; let him lead them there.

O all you gods, consume—the meaning is, destroy—the wrath of the Dāsa, the Asura who oppresses. Moreover, may those gods bring hither, for our well-being and for the sacrifice to be successfully attained, Indra, the dispeller of what is undesirable.
*jagamyāta*: from the root *gam* with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, in the *liṅ* mood, the *śap* suffix is elided by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi.
*śrumana*.
The root *cam* means "to eat.
The substitution of *kṣā* for *leṭ* is due to a transposition;
the addition of the letter *śa* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively,
the root *śru* should be regarded as a different verbal base meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsā*),
[as in the form] *vakṣan*.
The root *vah* means "to carry.
In the *leṭ* mood, the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule *sibbahulaṃ leṭi*. Then, the changes to *ḍha*, *tva*, and *ka* occur, followed by the substitution of *ṣ*.

For the sake of well-being (*suvitāya*). This is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *pūr* with the prefix *su-*. Because it belongs to the *tan*-class, the substitution *uvaṅ* applies.
In the word *sūmānāt*, the final syllable of the compound is udātta according to the rule *kaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.173].
[The root] *vṛñ* means "to choose" (*varaṇe*).

From this root, with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *na* is applied according to Uṇādi Sūtra 3.290: “The suffix *na* is added after the roots *kṛ*, *vṛ*, *sṛ*, *dru*, *pan*, *pi*, *ani*, and *svapi*, and it is marked as *nic*.
Due to its being *nic*, the word is accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
He himself brings forth the one who knows the signal; he himself brings forth the foam from the water.
Bathed in milk, the two wives of Kuryava—may they both be slain in the steep descent of the Śiphā river.

He himself brings forth the one who knows the signal; he himself brings forth the foam from the water. Bathed in milk are the two wives of Kuryava; may they both be slain in the cleft of the Śiphā river.
1. The roots *kṣi*, *sa*, and *ṣaṭ* are used in the senses of perishing, going, and causing dejection.

*Keta* means "known"; *veda* refers to the wealth of others which [the demon] knows. Such a demon named Kuyava himself (*ātmanā*) indeed (*eva*) brings down (*ava bharate*), that is, he carries away, the known wealth of others. Moreover, that demon, while remaining within the water (*udani udake*), himself indeed brings down—that is, he carries away—the foam (*phena*), the water accompanied by foam.

With that water which has the nature of flowing (*kṣaraṇaśīla*) like milk (*kṣīra*), having been struck down by him, the two wives (*yoṣe*) of the Asura Kuyava perform their ablutions (*snātau*). Such two women [bathe] at the Śiphā;
Śiphā is the name of a river.
In its steep descent, in the bottomless depth that is impossible to enter, they two were slain—that is, they perished.
O Indra, having stripped the wealth from your enemies, you slew Kuyava along with his family in the midst of the waters, a place difficult for others to traverse.

In the words *yamanā* and *bharate*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* according to the rule: “In mantras, the *ā* of the first member [of a compound] is elided before *aḍ* and so forth. Thus, *bharate*.
‘Haj haraṇe’;
‘hmrahorbheḥ’—thus [is] Bhava;
Ketavedas.
‘Jñāne’ [is derived from] the root *jñā* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
In the word *udak*, by the rule beginning with *udan pad* (Pāṇini 6.1.124), the substitution of *uda-* occurs;
and by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), there is the elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending.
The navel of the dwelling has been well-nourished; the hero advances with many [allies] and rules as sovereign.
Añjasī, Kuliśī, and Vīrapatnī, swelling with milk, bring forth water with their floods.
He has protected the navel of Upastya Āyu. The hero prevails with many ancient [deeds]; he rules. Añjasī, Kuliśī, and Vīrapatnī, being urged on, bring forth the milk with their waters. 4.
The navel—the bound dwelling place—of the Asura Kuyava, who was situated within the waters of the upper region, moving here and there for the purpose of afflicting others, was hidden away (*yuyopa*).
The meaning is that the Asura acted in such a way that he remained concealed from others.
Furthermore, by means of ancient, filling, or self-subduing words, that Asura continued to advance and grow.
And that hero, endowed with valor, rules and shines;
the meaning is that he becomes renowned in the world by his own prowess.

Him, this Asura, the three rivers—*Añjasī* (possessing directness), *Kuliśī* (shattering the lineage), and *Vīrapatnī* (the protector of the hero)—all-knowing as they are, gladden him with their milk—that is, with the essence consisting of water associated with it—and they sustain him with their own waters.
He has obstructed. The root *yup* means "to delude.
The navel.
The word *indraya* is derived from the root *rāj* with the suffix *na*, according to Uṇādi Sūtra 4.565 (*nahobhaśra*). The root *rājṛ* means "to shine."
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*;
by the rule beginning with *vrādhāt* (Pāṇini 8.2.36), the substitution of *p* occurs, followed by the insertion of the *dhuṭ* augment. Thus:
*payaḥ*.
By the rule "supām suluk," there is elision of the third case ending. *Hinvānāḥ*:
the root *hivi* means "to please."
The augment *num* is applied because the stem ends in a long vowel (*idittvāt*).
From this [root], the suffix *ānaś* is added in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*).
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rules governing augments, the augment *suk* does not occur.
Because the suffix *cānaś* lacks the status of a *l-sārvadhātuka*, when its accent is applied, only the *cit-svara* remains.
When the dwelling of the Dasyu was revealed to you as you advanced, he went toward his lair like one who knows the way.
O Maghavan, remember us; do not cast us away like a gambler who has lost his stake at the game.
When the path of the Dasyu was seen, she who knows her home went toward his dwelling as if to her own. O Maghavan, remember us; do not cast us away like a careless gambler throws down his stakes. 5.

1. *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *sa*, and *te* are like that. 2. *ta*, *da*, *dha*, and *sa* are in the midst of water. 3. *na*, *ta*, *pha*, and *śa* are of the sun; *da* and *dha* are of what has arisen. 4. *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *sa* are the state of existence. 5. *kṣa* is the bank.
When that path (*nīthā*), which serves as the cause for leading, was seen by us—that path went toward, reached, the dwelling, the house of the *dasyu*, the destroyer who establishes himself in evil.
Therein is an illustration.

The cow knows her own calf and recognizes it; just as she reaches her own stall, her dwelling place, directly, so too has the path reached the house of the Asura. O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, immediately thereafter (adha sma), protect us from that repeated affliction caused by the Asura; this is the remainder of the sense.
The word *it* is used for emphasis.
"Protect us indeed" (*asmān rakṣaiva*); "do not abandon us" (*mā parā dāḥ*), meaning do not forsake us.
The intended meaning is: "Having gone by the path known to us, slay the Asura who causes us affliction."
In this regard, an example by way of contrast (*vyatireka*) is stated:
"Like Maghavan, like Niṣpapī.

Just as one whose wealth has departed, or one who has lost his remainder, or a master of slave-girls who wanders at will, or like Maghavan who casts away riches in an improper place—so too, do not abandon us; such is the meaning.
Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "Niṣpapī means one who desires women, being devoid of *sapaḥ* (water/oblation). *Sapaḥ* [is derived] from the root *sapati*, meaning clear action.
'Do not give her away like a wealthy man, O Niṣpapī!'"
"Just as he distributes his wealth, do not you abandon us in that same way" (Nirukta 5.16).
*Nīthā*:
from the root *nīñ* in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*).
According to the rule "the suffix *kthan* is added after the roots *hani*, *kup*, *nī*, *ram*, and *kāśi*," the suffix *kthan* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
[The form] *gāt* [is derived as follows]: in the *luṅ* tense, by the rule "iṇo gā luṅi," there is the substitution of *gā*;
and by the rule "gātisthā," there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge'pi.
[The form] *carkutāt* is derived from the root *kṛ* with the *yaṅ*-luṅ suffix, followed by the *kap* suffix according to the rule for *niṣṭhā*.
Like Maghā;
the elision of *śe* occurs by the rule "śec chandasi.
Niṣpapī.

Regarding the term *papa-samavāye*: it is called *sapa* because it *sapati*, that is, it comes together with or unites with the womb (*yoni*). It is a remainder (*śeṣa*). The suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).
He from whom sin has departed and who is eternally arisen is "niṣpāpaḥ" (sinless); he whose sin is exhausted is "kṣīṇavyasanī.
The vowel *ī* results from a transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*).
[The term] is *dāḥ*.
The root *ḍudāñ* means "to give. In the *luṅ* tense, by the rule *gātisthā*, there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*.
By the rule *na māṅyoge*, there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*.
As such, O Indra, grant us our share in the sun, in the Apsarases, and in the Nāgas, for the sake of living praise.
Do not harm our inner enjoyment; we have placed our trust in your great power.
O Indra, as such, grant us a share in the sun, in the waters, and in sinlessness; grant us a share in the praise of life. Do not harm our inner enjoyment. We have faith in your great Indra-power. 6.

O Indra, as such, grant us our share in Sūrya, the impeller of all, the Āditya; cause us to be fully partakers, making us recipients of his grace. Likewise, O you, grant us our share in the waters, the divine powers;
and furthermore, grant us our share in blamelessness—being free from sin and worthy of praise by living beings, desired by all creatures.

Moreover, do not harm (*riripaḥ*)—that is, do not injure (*mā hiṃsīḥ*)—our offspring (*prajām*), who are within us as embryos (*antarām garbhatvena antarvartamānām*) and who are our protectors (*bhujaṃ pālayitrīm*).
We have placed our faith (*śraddhitam*) in your great and abundant power (*mahate prabhūtaye indriyāya balāya*);
the meaning is that we praise your strength with great reverence.
Therefore, being endowed with such power, do not cause harm; this is how it connects with the preceding statement.
Regarding "anāgāstva": one for whom *āgas*—that is, sin or fault—does not exist is *anāgas*; the state of being such is *anāgāstva*.
The lengthening of the vowel in the penultimate position is a Vedic (chāndasa) phenomenon. [The word] *jīvaśaṃse* [is derived from the root] *śaṃsu*,
meaning "to praise."
The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
By the rule beginning with *thā-tha-*, the final syllable of the compound receives the udātta accent. [Thus:
*bhujam*.
One who enjoys (bhunakti) or protects (pālayati) is *bhuk*; the suffix *kip* is applied;
[the result is] *ririkṣaḥ*.
The root *ṛṣ* is used in the sense of "to injure.

From this root, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) added in its own sense (*svārthe*), in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* reduplication, there is the elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*), followed by the shortening of the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*upadhā-svaratva*) and other operations.
The shortening of the reduplicated syllable is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) feature occurring at the time of the word-division (*padakāla*).
It is *śraddhitam*.

Since the word *śrat* is a *gati* by virtue of being listed among the words beginning with *ūrdhva* (Pāṇini 1.4.61), it takes the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*) according to the rule "a *gati* that is immediately preceding [the verb] retains its own accent" (Pāṇini 6.2.49).

1. *Kṣa* [denotes] one who is fully born (*abhijānan*). 2. *Kṣa* [denotes] one from whom austerity has departed (*nirgatapasas*) and from whom impurity has departed (*nirgata-malaḥ*). 3. *Śa-ṭa-la* [denote] one from whom austerity has departed; "austerity" (*pasaḥ*) is derived from the root *sap* (to serve/attain). 4. *Ca-pha* [denotes] that which destroys (*vināśayati*). 5. *Kṣa-ṭa* [denotes] frequency (*ābhīkṣṇye*). 6. *Kṣa* [denotes] that which has become the womb (*garbha-bhūtām*). 7. *Kṣa* [denotes] that which is to be protected (*pālanīyām*).

I believe half [of the work] has been performed for him; O Bull, incite us toward great wealth. O Indra, invoked by many, do not leave us in an empty dwelling; give food to those who hunger for it. I believe, O Indra, that faith has been established in you. As a bull, impel us toward great wealth. O much-invoked one, do not leave us in a desolate place; give nourishment to us who are hungry.
O Indra, "then" (adha) "after that" (atha), "I consider you"—that is, I know you with my mind.
"For this strength of yours," "faith" (śrat)—meaning confidence—has been established by us;
the sense is that a hymn of praise has been composed with an exceeding degree of reverence toward your power.
"O showerer of desires, you who are the rain-giver— urge us on, impel us toward great and mature wealth!
O Indra, invoked by many, [lead us] to the unmade, unfashioned, and wealthless womb—
a term for the home."
"Do not place us in the house"—the sense of "niṣedhe" (in the prohibition) is: "Dwell us in a house filled with wealth and grain.
Moreover, O Indra, "give" (*dāḥ*) "food" (*vayaḥ*) and "drinks" (*āsutiṃ*), such as milk and so forth, even to other worshippers who are "hungry" (*kṣudhyadbhyaḥ*).
*adhāyi*: from the root *dhā*, in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*) with the *luṅ* suffix, the *ciṇ* substitute is applied for *cli*;
by the rule *āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ*, the augment *yuk* is added.
"To those who are hungry. [The root] *kṣudh* [is used] in the sense of "hunger" (*bubhukṣā*).
Because it belongs to the *divādi* class, the suffix *śyan* is applied.
The acute accent belongs to the initial syllable.
Do not slay us, O Indra; do not abandon us; do not steal away our dear provisions. Do not shatter our eggs, O Maghavan, O Śakra; do not break our vessels that are born together with us. 8.
O Indra, do not strike us; do not harm us. This means that you should always protect us. Furthermore, do not abandon us; do not cast us aside.

The meaning is: "the relinquishing of others [to us]"—that is, "always accept the worship performed by us. Furthermore, "do not steal away"—do not take away—"our dear things," that is, the desired foods and wealth to be enjoyed.
The meaning is: "Act in such a way that our riches remain with us.

Likewise, O Maghavan, O Śakra, O Indra who is capable of all deeds, "do not" (mā) "fear" (bhīt)—that is, do not destroy—"our" (naḥ) "eggs," meaning the offspring related to the eggs that have been infused in the form of embryos.
The sense is that you should protect our sons who reside in the form of embryos.
"And let not our vessels fall"— those offspring which are vessels, meaning those capable of moving,
let them not be broken; let there be no shattering.
"Sahajānuṣāṇi" means those which move along the ground by means of their knees; and these are the "jānuṣāṇi."
Do not let them perish along with those [others].
"Vadhīḥ" [is used]; by the rule "luṅi ca" under the heading of "māṅi," there is the substitution of "vadh" for the root "han."
And not [when] ending in *ad*. [The suffix] *sic* [is added]; by the rule "elision of *a*" (*ato lopaḥ*), there is elision of the vowel *a*.
Due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element), there is no *vṛddhi* by the rule *ato halādeḥ*.
By the rule *iṭa īṭi*, there is the elision of the *sic* suffix. Thus: *moṣīḥ*.
In the case of the root *muṣ* meaning "to steal," when the suffix *luṅ* follows,
the substitution of *ta*, *tha*, *pha*, *śa*, *ma*, and *na* for the *sic* augment is prohibited.
2. O you who possess the *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *sa*, and *da* [sounds], grant [it].
3. O you who possess the *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ma*, and *pa*, do not mock [it].
4. O you who possess the *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *sa*, and *ha*, in place of the word “destroyer” (*vināśanaḥ*), [there is] “Moreover, vessels for vessels, debts, capable ones, and those with innate defects.”
*Januḥ* means birth.
The meaning is that those who are connected with that—namely, the co-born (*sahaja*), the followers (*anuṣa*), and those of the same birth (*samānajanman*)—are to be understood as such.
The offspring born together with them, and they themselves, *mā bhet*, "may not be broken" (may they not perish).
The meaning is that he protects even those sons who have arisen as his own.

Here, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* is by the rule "neṭi. [Regarding] *bhet*: the root *bhidir* is used in the sense of "tearing apart. In the *laṅ* tense with the suffix *sip*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. There is the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel. The elision of the *sip* suffix occurs by the rule "halḍyābbhyaḥ."
"At the midday pressing, 'Come hither'—this is the *prasthitayājyā* of the *potr̥*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: 'Come hither, O lover of Soma; this Soma is pressed for you to praise; come hither' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5)."
Come hither; they say you are one who desires Soma—drink of this pressed juice for exhilaration.
O wide-extending one, pour it into your belly; being invoked, hear us like a father.

Come hither! They call you one who desires Soma. This [juice] has been pressed; drink of it for exhilaration. O wide-extending one, pour it into your belly. Listen to us like a father when you are being invoked. 9.
O Indra, come hither toward us;
why? Because those who know the past say that you desire Soma—that is, they declare you to have a longing for Soma—and this Soma of ours has been pressed, pressed by the officiating priests.
Therefore, the meaning is "come hither.
And having come, "for the sake of exhilaration," that is, for the sake of joy, "drink" this Soma of ours which has been pressed.
This very point is now made explicit.

"O you of wide extent (*uruvyacas*), having become one whose reach (*vyacas*) is vast and expansive—that is, possessing great limbs—pour the *soma* into your own belly; that is to say, fill it completely. Being thus addressed, and being invoked by our hymns of praise, just as a father hears the words of his sons, so too hear our words."
*Somakāmam*:
one whose desire (*kāmaḥ*), that is, longing, has *soma* as its object. In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is retained.
They say:
by the rule *bruvaḥ pañcānāmādita āho bruvaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.4.84), there is the substitution of *us* for the suffix *jhi*, and the substitution of *āha* for the root; [this refers to] that [form].

Because the action [of giving] is included [in the definition of the recipient], the object (karman) takes the status of a recipient (saṃpradāna); thus, the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.
*madāya* [is used here]. [The root] *madī* [means] "to rejoice."
In the word *uruvyacas*, the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *made'nupasarge*.
The root *vyac* means "to extend" or "to encompass."
The suffix *as* is derived according to the *uṇādi* rules.

Due to the statement "the root *vyac* is treated as belonging to the *kuṭādi* class when not followed by *manas*" (Kāśikā 1.2.1.1), there is an absence of *ṅit*-status, and consequently, no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs.
By the rule "in Vedic [usage], the beginning of the subsequent member is frequently [accented]," the acute accent falls on the first syllable of the second member.
Alternatively,
he is called *uruvyacāḥ* because he moves widely or pervades extensively;
[this is an example of] the accentuation of the original form of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
"Be sprinkled. [The root] *vṛṣ* means "to sprinkle.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) and the suffix *śap* occur by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Listen:
by the rule "utaśca pratyayācchandasi vāvacanam," there is an optional absence of the *l* elision.
The twelfth hymn, "candramāḥ," consists of nineteen verses.
It is the seer-poem (*ārṣa*) of Trita, the son of the Waters, who had fallen into a well;
thus it is known from both [verses] concerning the well: "Trita was cast down into the well" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.105.17) and "The seer was pulled out from the pit" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.106.6).

The Taittirīyas explicitly declare Trita’s status as the son of the waters: "From him [Aja Ekapād] one was born; he struck down a second [from himself]; from that Dvita was born; he struck down a third; from that Trita was born. Because they were born from the waters (adbhyaḥ), that is the etymological derivation of the name 'Āpyas'" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.8.10–11).
We study this very Ṛṣi-tradition by adding the letter *t* to the word, as in the verse: "Trita, that one who knows the way" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.105.9).

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-*: [the word] *somaviṣayābhilāṣavantam* (possessing a desire for the realm of Soma). 2. *kṣa-ṭa-d-*: [the word] *spaṣṭīkaroti* (makes clear). 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ma-*: [the word] *yathā śṛṇoti* (as he hears). 4. *ṭa-ṭha-sa-*: [the word] *stutivākyāni* (words of praise). 5. *kṣa-some*: [the word] *some* (in Soma). 6. *kṣa-sa-ṅittvābhāve*: [the word] *ṅittvābhāve* (in the absence of the *ṅit*-designation). 7. *kṣasa-*: [the word] *vyatyayenātmanepadaṃ śapratyayaḥ* (by way of transposition, the middle voice and the suffix *śa*). 8. *kṣa-sa-*: [the word] *iti* does not exist. The final [verse] is a *triṣṭubh*. The verse beginning with *saṃ mā tapanti* is a *yavamadhyā mahābṛhatī*.

The first two feet consist of eight syllables each, the third consists of twelve syllables, and then there are two more of eight syllables; this is the *yavamadhyā* *mahābṛhatī*, because it possesses the characteristics described in the statement, “A *mahābṛhatī* consists of four [feet] of eight [syllables] and one of twelve” (Anu. 9.9), followed by the rule, “If [the twelve-syllable foot] is in the middle, it is *yavamadhyā*” (Anu. 9.10).
The remaining verses are *paṅktis*.

The Viśvedevas are the deity. Thus it has been enumerated: “The moon is the deity of the [first] hymn; the second is addressed to Agni; the third is Vaiśvadeva; the fourth is Pāṅkta; the fifth is Triṣṭubh; the eighth is Mahābṛhatī and Yavamadhyā.
Because of the use of the word “hi” (indeed), these first three hymns are Vaiśvadeva.
The application (viniyoga) is as follows:
4. Regarding this, the followers of the Śāṭyāyana school relate an ancient legend: "In former times, there were three sages named Ekata, Dvita, and Trita.
Once, while they were wandering in a desert region, their limbs were tormented by thirst, and they discovered a single well."
There, one named Trita entered a well for the purpose of drinking water. Having drunk himself, he drew up water from the well and gave it to the other two.
After they had drunk that water, they cast Trita into the well, seized all of his wealth, and having blocked the well with a chariot wheel, departed.
Then Trita, having fallen into the well and being unable to climb out, remembered in his mind, "May all the gods lift me up.
Thereupon, he beheld this hymn (*sūkta*) in praise of them.
Therein, seeing the rays of the moon within the well during the night, he lamented.
The moon moves within the waters; the bird flies in the sky.
Your tracks, O lightnings with golden rims, are not found; O Heaven and Earth, acknowledge this of mine.
The moon moves within the waters; the fair-winged bird rushes through the sky. O you whose rims are golden, the lightnings find not your track. Mark this for me, O Heaven and Earth!
In the intermediate regions (antarikṣa), within the water-like orb, existing in the midst— that is, in the center— is the *suparṇa*, one of beautiful flight; or rather,
*suparṇa* is a name for the sun.
Joined with the solar ray called *suṣumnā*, the moon runs toward the sky, that is, the celestial world.
[The author] says: [the word] "toward" (*ā*) indicates a limit;
it runs in one way alone—that is, it moves swiftly.
Belonging to such a moon, they are *hiraṇyanemayaḥ*, having golden-like edges;
or alternatively,
having pleasant and beautiful peripheries.

The flashes of lightning are your rays (verse 19). Your food, which stands in place of your feet (verse 20), my senses do not find (verse 21); because it is covered by a well, they do not obtain it (verse 22).
Therefore, this is improper;
the meaning is that you should lift it out from that well (verse 25).
Moreover, O Heaven and Earth (rodasī), know— understand— this hymn of mine;
or rather,
understand this suffering of mine consisting of my falling into the well.
The meaning is: "Having heard my hymn of praise, or having understood my suffering, please lift me up from this well."
Candramas.
He is called Candramas because he produces delight for the entire world;
[the suffix] *asun* is applied by the rule “*candre māṅo ḍit*” (Uṇādi-sūtra 4.667).
In compounds such as *dāsībhāra*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member due to their inclusion in the [Gaṇapāṭha] list.
[The root] *dhāvati* [is derived from] *sṛ*, meaning "to go."
By the rule beginning with "pāghrā," there is the substitution of *dhāv* for the sense of speed;
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by transposition;
[the result is] *vittam*.
The root *vid* is used in the sense of "knowing.

In the imperative (*loṭ*), there is elision of the suffix *śap* because it belongs to the *adādi* class. Due to its position at the beginning of the sentence, there is no suppression of accent according to the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.
Regarding this [word *asmai*]:
because the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is treated as the object (*karman*) by the rule "The mention of 'action' (kriyā) must be made," the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative;
thus, the case-ending is acute according to the rule "aḍiḍadam."

1. In the versions *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*, the phrase “having said” (*ityuktvā*) is absent. 2. Because of the statement “*kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*” [the reading is established]. 3. In *kṣa*, it ends with the *triṣṭubh* meter. 4. In *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *sa*, the application (*viniyoga*) is that of the written text (*laikhika*). 5. According to the opinion of *ta* and *śa*. 6. From *kṣa*, from Trita. 7. In *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *sa*, it is “that Trita”; in *ṭha*, it is “there, him. 8. In *kṣa* and *sa*, regarding the verses on the intermediate space (*āntarikṣāsu*). 9. In *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *sa*, after the word “in the middle” (*madhye*), there is the addition: “Or rather, ‘waters’ (*āpaḥ*) is a name for the intermediate space; therein, in the middle. 10. In *kṣa* and *sa*, [the commentary says] “*āha* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*); he runs in only one manner”; this phrase is absent. 11. In *kṣa*, “our own senses” (*asmadīyānīndriyāṇi*). 12. In *kṣa*, “from which” (*yataḥ*). 13. In *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *ḍi*. 14. In *kṣa* and *sa*, “in a swift motion” (*vegitāyāṃ gatau*).
Desiring wealth, indeed, the seekers come; the wife unites with her husband.
They stir up virile vigor; having bestowed the milk, she milks out the essence. O Heaven and Earth, take note of this for me!

Truly for the sake of wealth, indeed, O *ū*, the seeker of wealth brings his wife to her husband; she brings forth manly vigor. Having bestowed the milk, she milks out the essence. Mark this for me, O Heaven and Earth! 2.
Men who are seekers, looking for wealth, surely obtain the very object they desire— that is, the wealth they seek. "I do not obtain it"—
the particle *u* here is for the purpose of filling out the meter.

Moreover, the wife belonging to another approaches her own husband; however, my own wife was distressed due to separation from me. Furthermore, those two, the wife and husband, being united, impel—that is, they urge forth—the *vṛṣṇyam*, which is the fluid in the form of semen, for the sake of procreation through their mutual friction.

Immediately thereafter, having bestowed the essence of the man’s *rasa*, his vital energy (*vīrya*), the womb takes it up, holds it in the form of an embryo, and milks it forth—it brings it to birth in the form of a son.
Yet for me, even a son is not produced.
Therefore, O Heaven and Earth, know this sorrow of mine!

3 | By the opinion of Śākalya, according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.1.17 (*uñaḥ*), the vowel *u* is a *pragṛhya*; therefore, by the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
Thus: *yuvate*.

The root *yu* is used in the sense of "mixing. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*). Although the suffix *śap* would normally be applied, *śa* is used instead by way of irregularity.

*tujāte*: [This is derived from] the root *tuji* (and *piji*) in the sense of "injuring," "bestowing strength," and "destruction. Because it is marked with the *iṭ* augment, the *num* augment is applied.
By transposition, there is *śam*;
the elision of *āñj* occurs; [the root] *duh*.
The root *duh* means "to fill.
The elision of the *t* occurs by the rule "lopasta ātmanepadeṣu" (Pāṇini 7.1.41).
O gods, let not that light of heaven fall away from the sky; let there never be a lack of the auspicious Soma for us. O Heaven and Earth, take note of this from me!

O gods, that light over there has indeed fallen down from heaven; it has reached the earth. O Heaven and Earth, never at any time have you been empty of the Soma that brings prosperity; take note of this for me.

O gods, let not that lineage of ours—consisting of my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—which exists in the heavenly light (*svar*) in the celestial realm, and which dwells even above the heavens (*divaḥ pari*), fall here; let it not perish, be ruined, or be cast down due to my lack of a son.
For the Vedic scripture declares: "By means of a son one conquers the worlds; there is no world for one who has no son" (Ai. Brā. 7.13).

Therefore, may we never—at any time whatsoever—be in the absence of our son, who belongs to the class of Soma-drinking Pitṛs known as the *Somyas*, who is *śambhuvaḥ* (the bringer of well-being), and who is the source of happiness. By your grace, may sons be born to me;
thus, the meaning is: "Lift me up from this distress."
O Heaven and Earth, you two also know my petition.
*Mo* is a compound of the two particles *mā* and *u*, used in the sense of *mā eva*.
*Su* is used for emphasis.
In the word *sṛjaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*]. [The root] *pad* means "to go."

In the form *'ṣiṇ te padaḥ'* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.60), there is the substitution of *ciṇ* for the suffix *liṭ* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) in the *luṅ* tense. [The word] *divaḥ*: by the rule *'aḍidam'* etc., the case-ending is acute (*udātta*).
In the word *somyasya*, the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s* according to the rule *pañcamyāḥ parāvadhyarthe* (Pāṇini 8.3.51).
[The suffix] *yat* is applied [to *soma*] in the sense of "one who deserves *soma*" according to Pāṇini 4.4.137.

1. Immediately after "na-tujāte," there is the addition: "he attains [it] by way of facing toward it; he, by way of facing toward it. 2. In the versions śa and ṭa: "by means of procreation through mutual union"; in the version sa: "by means of sexual enjoyment through mutual union. 3. In the versions kṣa and na: "in the cases of harming, taking what is not given, and [engaging in] improper conduct."
4. ṭa—this belongs to us;
5. kṣa-ṭa—*divaspari* (from heaven); *pāraḥ* restates the sense of the ablative case.
"From heaven," that is, from the celestial realm; "sa-divaspari" means existing above heaven (*divaścopari*).
The particle *pari* here restates the sense of the ablative case.
The group of particles *kṣa-sa-mā u* is a collective compound of indeclinables.

Ka. 81: Thus, the suffix *ya* is applied. *Śambhavaḥ*: from the root *bhū*, with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇic*) elided, followed by the suffix *kvip*. [The form] *śūna*: from the root *śvi* (with the prefix *pra*) meaning "to go" or "to increase. The suffix *niṣṭhā* (past participle) is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*). By the rule "the augment *iṭ* is prohibited after roots ending in long *ī* or *ū* before the *niṣṭhā* suffix," there is no *iṭ*. By the rule "for *vac*, *svap*, etc.," there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization). By the rule "also for roots ending in *od*" (Pāṇini 8.2.45), the suffix takes the *kta* designation. The acute accent on the first syllable is due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*), or it should be understood as belonging to the *vṛṣādi* group.
I ask about the sacrifice, the most recent one; when it is offered, may he declare it to you. Who has gone to the ancient *ṛta*? Who maintains it today? Learn this from me, O Heaven and Earth!
I ask about the sacrifice, the most recent one; may he, the messenger, proclaim it. Who has gone to the ancient *ṛta*? Who maintains that new one? Know this for me, O Heaven and Earth! 4.
The sacrifice to be performed is the "lowest" (*avama*), meaning the first among all the gods, according to the Vedic revelation:
"Agni is the mouth, the first of the deities" (*Ai. Brā.
1.4*), and from the *Brāhmaṇa*: "Agni indeed is the lowest of the gods" (*Ai. Brā. 1.1*).
I ask that Agni:
may he, the messenger of the gods, whom I have questioned, speak it forth—that is, let him declare it clearly.
If it is asked, "What is it that is being asked? it is said in reply:

O Agni, where has that ancient, auspicious *ṛta*—the well-being you bestowed upon your worshippers in former times—gone? Where does it abide now? What other person, more recent than you, sustains and maintains that auspiciousness?
Had it not resided in you, even my present condition would not have come to be.
Therefore, tell me: where has that gone?
He calls out.
[The root] *vac* is used in the sense of "addressing" (*paribhāṣaṇe*).
In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *aṭ*.
In the word *vaca-um*, the augment *um* is added to the root by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
What [is the suffix]? By the rule *kimo't* (Pāṇini 5.3.12), the suffix *at* is applied in the sense of the locative case.
By the rule *krāti* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.105), there is the substitution of *kā* for *kimaḥ*. By the rule *tisrvaritam*, it receives the *svarita* accent.
The *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) occurs in the case of "kṛtyaka" when it is followed by another word.
O you gods who abide in the three luminous realms of heaven—what is truth, what is untruth? Who among you knows the ancient invocation? Tell me this, O Heaven and Earth!

"O you who are these gods, dwelling in the three luminous realms of heaven—what is your truth? What is untruth? What is the ancient oblation for you? Take note of this of mine, O Heaven and Earth! (5)
"O gods," those of you who "are" (sthana)— that is, exist— “in the three places,” namely on earth and the other two locations;
those places which "are in the luminous realm" (ā rocane) of the shining sun—
that is to say, in the regions illuminated by the sun.
Where is that *ṛta*—the truth concerning you, directed toward the worshippers?
Where has that *anṛta*—the untruth concerning the haters and the incapacity [to worship]—gone?
Moreover, where was that ancient *āhuti*—the sacrifice previously performed by me, belonging to you?
I infer that the collection of sacrifices previously performed by me has reached you through this experience of such suffering;
the rest is as before.
*sthāna*: By the rule "tasanasanathanāśca," the substitute *than* is applied for the word-element *ta*. *kat*.
The word *ka* becomes *katra* through the substitution of the phoneme *t*.
1. In these moments, in these places—when shall we behold the upholder of *ṛta*, when the manifestation of the bountiful one?
When shall we traverse the great path of the noble one without stumbling? O Heaven and Earth, bear witness to this for me!

What is the support of your *ṛta*? What is the gaze of Varuṇa? What is the wide stride of the great Aryaman? How may we pass over those who are difficult to overcome? O Heaven and Earth, take note of this for me!

O gods, where has that which belongs to you—the support (*dharṇasi*) of *ṛta*, the truth that brings about desired fruits—gone? Where has the glance (*cakṣaṇa*) of Varuṇa, the god who wards off the undesirable, gone—that is, his vision of favor? Where has the beautiful path belonging to Aryaman, the great one of mighty power and the restrainer of enemies, gone—that path by which the attainment of the desired place occurs? Where has it gone?
All this exists only within yourselves;
it has not gone anywhere else.
Therefore, may we transcend, may we surpass, those who are wicked, evil-minded, and of sinful intellect—our enemies intent upon performing what is harmful to us.
May we be delivered from this suffering characterized by falling into a pit or the underworld, out of respect for what has been done by them;
O Heaven and Earth, recognize this act of mine.
*Dharṇasi*. [Derived from] the root *dhṛñ* in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*).
It is an irregular form (*nipātita*) ending in the suffix *asic*, according to the rule beginning with "sānasi-dharṇasi-parṇasi... (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.547).
In the case of *aryamṇaḥ*, there is elision of the vowel *a* by the rule "allopo 'naḥ" in the singular sixth case;
the acute accent of the case-ending is due to the "acute accent of the elided [final vowel]" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*) rule.
*mahaḥ*: [This is] from *mahataḥ*; the elision of the case-ending (*acchandalopa*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Or else:
In the word *mahāpūjāyām*, [the suffix] *kviP* is applied.
In both cases, the case-ending receives the udātta accent by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
*Duṣṭyaḥ*:
[This is] from the *pṛṣodarādi* group;
for it is recited therein [in the rule] "dhye ca," whereby there is the substitution of *u* for the *r* of *duraḥ*, and the substitution of *dh* for the initial letter of the following member.
The circumflex (svarita) accent applies here by the rule "udātta-svaritayoryaṇaḥ...".
I am he who formerly spoke many things to my mother;
do not let anxieties seize me, as a wolf seizes a thirsty deer—know this of me, O Heaven and Earth!

I am he who, in former times, spoke some words at the pressing. Those who possess evil designs do not overcome me, any more than a wolf overcomes a thirsty deer. Mark this of me, O Heaven and Earth! 7.
O gods, in former times, when the Soma had been pressed for your sacrifice, I spoke certain hymns—whatever few I have uttered; I am that very same person, and not anyone else.
Therefore, for what reason do you abandon me?
Such afflictions—the agonies born from the failure to obtain desired sons and other blessings—devour me.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a wolf does not devour a deer born of craving—one who has developed thirst and is going toward water—while it is still in the forest on the way, so it is here;
the rest is as before.
*vyanti*. The root *vī* is used in the sense of "going" and so forth.
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
The substitution of *yaṇ* [for the semivowel] occurs due to the word "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule: "An addition should be made for *tanu* and others frequently in the Veda. Thus, *ādhiḥ*.
It is called *ādhi* because it is placed within the mind (*manasi ādhīyate*).
By the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.92), the suffix *ki* is applied.

By the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca*, the vowel *a* is elided. Since the rule *jasādiṣu cchandasi vāvacanam* allows for the optionality of the rule *jasi ca*, the *guṇa* substitution is optional; in its absence, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs.
*tṛṣṇaja* [is derived from] *tṛṣ* in the sense of "thirst" (*pipāsā*). [The suffix *nijak* is applied] by the rule *svapitṛpornijak* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.102).
1. Related to *kṣan* and *sa*. 2. Ending in the suffix *asi* after *kṣata*. Thus ends the section on *nañ-iṅ*.

The author of the *Padapāṭha*, however, thinks as follows: because the inclusion of the word "also seen" (*dṛś*) in the rule "it is also seen in other cases" (*anyeṣv api dṛśyate*) indicates that it applies even when all conditions are absent, the suffix *ḍa* is added even to the root *jan* alone. Thus, [the form] *tṛṣṇaja* means "one in whom thirst has arisen.
The shortening of the vowel occurs by the rule: "In names and Vedic meters, the vowels *ū* and *ā* are frequently shortened."
My ribs pain me on all sides like rival wives;
they gnaw at me like rats upon their tails. O Śatakratu, the mid-region devours your praiser; O Heaven and Earth, protect me from this!

My ribs pain me on all sides like rival wives; my thoughts gnaw at me like rats devouring their own tails. O Śatakratu, you who possess a hundred powers, [protect] your praiser! O Heaven and Earth, take note of this for me! 8.
O Indra, the *aindrīpā*— that is, the ribs (*parśavaḥ*), which by implication here stand for the ribs themselves—
