Moreover, these two, Night and Dawn, have a common kinsman; they are joined with a single common kinsman, a friend named Sūrya.
Or rather:
[the two] are connected with the sun.
Just as the night is connected with the sun even while it is rising, so too is the night connected with the sun even while it is setting.

7. In the immortal, which is free from death because it is eternal by virtue of being the nature of time; *anūcī* means following one another. They proceed in this order: first Night, and afterwards Dawn.

Moving in accordance with the course of the sun;
being thus, they cause the color—that is, the form—of all living beings to fade away, that is, they cause it to decay.

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "The word *ruśat* [is derived from] *ruh*, meaning 'to grow' or 'to shine'; it is a name for color, as it belongs to the verbal root *ruc*, whose function is to shine or blaze.

Then he praises them: "Having a common bond, having a common support, immortal, possessing the nature of the immortals, following one after the other, mutually facing each other, O Heaven and Earth, you two move through your own color—or rather, 'dyāvā' [means] from shining (*dyotana*), or perhaps it means 'you two move together with her'—alternating, blending, making their inner selves [one with the other]" (Nirukta 2.20).

*Anūcī*: from the root *añc* preceded by the prefix *anu*, the suffix *kin* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.59 (*ṛtvig-ādinā kin*). By the rule *aniditām* (6.4.24), there is elision of the nasal *n*.

Common is the path of the two sisters, endless; taught by the gods, they move one after the other. They do not clash, nor do they stand still; well-established, Night and Dawn are of one mind though different in form.

Common is the path of the two sisters; it is endless. Taught by the gods, they move one after the other. They do not clash; they have not stood still. Well-established, Night and Dawn, like-minded yet diverse in form. || 3 ||
The path—the way that serves as the means of movement—for the two sisters, Night and Dawn, is identical, being one and the same.
By that very path through the sky by which Dawn goes forth, Night likewise goes;
and that path is infinite, devoid of end.
On that path, instructed and taught by the radiant Sun (deva), the two—Night and Dawn—move in succession, each following the other.

Moreover, though they are "well-measured" (sumeke), meaning possessing excellent offspring because they give birth to all things, and though Night and Dawn are "of different forms" (virūpe), being endowed with opposing natures characterized by darkness and light, they are "of one mind" (samanasā), having attained unanimity;
thus they do not contend with or harm one another, nor do they ever stand still.
The meaning is that he goes at all times for the sake of favoring the world.

Radiant, the leader of pleasant truths, she comes; wonderful, she has thrown open the doors for us. For our attainment, she has revealed the world and our riches; Dawn has awakened all living beings. 4. Radiant, the leader, of pleasant truths, she approaches; wonderful, she has opened wide the doors for us. For our acquisition, she has disclosed the world and our wealth; Dawn has awakened all creatures. 4.

Radiant (*bhāsvatī*), endowed with distinguished light; *sūnṛtā* is a name for speech—she is the leader (*netrī*) and the producer of pleasant and true words. For immediately after the manifestation of the Dawn, all animals, birds, and so forth, utter sounds. Such is the Dawn who approaches (*acaíti*); she has been perceived by us. Wondrous (*citrā*) and worthy of being known, she has opened wide (*vy āvaḥ*) our doors (*duraḥ*), which were hidden by darkness. The meaning is that she dispels the darkness and illuminates them so that they may be seen by us. (2) Moreover, having reached the entire world (*jagat*) and brought it to light, she has made our riches (*rāyaḥ*) manifest, endowing them with distinguished illumination. The particle *u* is used here merely to fill out the meter. This very Dawn awakens (*ajīgaḥ*) all beings (*viśvā bhuvanāni*), making them emerge from her own mouth as if they had been non-existent due to being hidden by darkness. The meaning is that, having expelled the darkness by her own light, she makes them appear as if newly born. Grammatical notes: * *netrī*: From the root *ṇīñ* (to lead). The suffix *tṛc*. By the rule *ṛtvebhyo ḍīp*, and by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied, resulting in the acute accent. * *acaíti*: From the root *cit* (to perceive). * *duraḥ*: From the word *dvāra*. By the rule *rayermatau bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.1.37), the semi-vowel is substituted (samprasāraṇa) because of the word *bahulam*. * *āvaḥ*: From the root *vṛñ* (to cover). In the *luṅ* tense, by the rule *mantre ghasa*, there is elision of the suffix *cli*. There is *guṇa* substitution. By the rule *halṅayābhyaḥ*, there is elision of the *ti*. By the rule *chandasyapi dṛśyate*, the augment *āṭ* is added. * *prāpya*: From the root *ṛ* (to go). By the rule *ṇī-atir-hī-ityādinā puk*, the suffix *puk* is added. In a compound not preceded by *nañ*, the suffix *ksva* becomes *lyap*. * *akhyat*: From the root *khyā* (to speak). In the *luṅ* tense, by the rule *asyativakti-ityādinā*, the suffix *cli* is replaced by *aṭ*. * *ajīgaḥ*: From the root *gṛ* (to swallow). In the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *tip* is used. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, the *vikaraṇa* suffix *śnu* is applied. There is reduplication, and by the rules of reduplication (*urad-*, *halādiśeṣaḥ*), the vowel of the reduplicated syllable becomes *i* by the rule *artipipatyośca bahulaṃ chandasi*. The long *ī* is a Vedic usage. Alternatively, from this root with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the *luṅ* tense with *caṅ*, there is reduplication, and the rules for *man-*, *aj-*, *bhāva-*, *itva-*, and *dīrgha-* apply. The elision of *caṅ* is a Vedic usage.

She is a young woman (*yuvati*), one who brings forth fruits, or one who causes them to be obtained by men, or one endowed with eternal youth. She is clad in white garments (*śukravāsas*), meaning she wears white clothes or possesses stainless radiance.

[derived from] the root *īś*, meaning "to rule" (*aiśvarye*).

1. The path belonging to the dawns that have departed, that are going away, and that have passed; 2. *pāthaḥ* is the place characterized as the region of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

3. The present dawn follows after, that is, goes along with it.
The meaning is that just as the past dawns have shone forth, even so does she shine forth now.
Likewise, among the many *śaśvatīḥ*—that is, the numerous *āyatīnām*, the approaching—dawns, she is the first, the very beginning.
The meaning is that just as this dawn proceeds, even so will the future dawns proceed.

"Such as she is, the Dawn (uṣas), shining forth, casting away darkness, rousing the living soul (jīva) of creatures—that is, the individual self (jīvātman)—by impelling it upward from its bed; awakening any person whatsoever who was like one dead during the time of sleep due to the dissolution of the senses; and setting him in motion by making him conscious again through the re-entry of the senses—so she proceeds. This is the remainder of the sense.

O Uṣas, that you have kindled—meaning you have made to blaze—the fire in its form as the Gārhapatya and other hearths;

Yearning for the former ones, she follows them lowing; shining brightly, she goes gladly with others.

How much is it? It is as far as the dawn extends—those that have shone before and those that shall surely shine now. Longing for them, she yearns after the former ones; shining forth, she approaches gladly with the others.
The word *samayā* signifies proximity.
When it is said that "the dawn is *samayā* [near]," the intention is to ask: "At what time has this occurred, or when will it be completed?
This is what is being expressed.
By what time is the Dawn joined? How long is that time? What is its measure? By this, the infinity of the Dawn is stated. He clarifies that very point:
Those dawns which shone forth in the past have now become manifest;
indeed, those dawns which shall shine forth hereafter,

and those that are currently shining forth— among them, the former dawns that have already passed and the present dawn, longing [for the future], the current dawn takes pity upon them and provides for them, becoming capable [of fulfilling their purpose].

The meaning is that, just as the past dawns made light appear, so too does this dawn now make light appear. Likewise, shining intensely (*pradīdhyānā*), Dawn goes together with, or meets, other future dawns; the meaning is that the future dawns also imitate her light.

As long as she, the guardian of Truth, born of Truth, the bringer of joy, the sender of pleasant truths, auspicious, and bearing the favor of the gods— O Uṣas, most excellent one, shine forth here today!

O Dawn, who drives away hatreds, who protects the cosmic order, who is born from the cosmic order, who is most gracious, who brings true speech, who sends forth [all things], who is most auspicious, and who bears the feast for the gods—shine forth here today as the most excellent one! 12.

"Yāvadyadveṣāḥ": she is so called because she drives away (*yāvayanti*) from us those hostile forces (*dveṣāṃsi*), such as Rākṣasas and others, who are characterized by hatred (*dveṣṭṛṇi*). For indeed, once you are born, the Rākṣasas and other such beings do not remain, since they are night-stalkers (*niśācarāḥ*).

Guardian of *ṛta*—that is, the protector of truth or of sacrifice; born of *ṛta*, she has manifested for the sake of sacrifice. Since sacrifices are performed during the true dawn or during the day, she is called "born for the sake of sacrifice.
She is the bestower of bliss (*sumnāvarī*).
*Sumna* is a name for happiness; that which possesses it is *sūnṛtā*. This is a term for speech.
She causes the voices of beasts, birds, deer, and so forth to issue forth—that is, she impels or produces them.
She is *sumaṅgalī*, endowed with auspiciousness;
the meaning is that she is never separated from her husband at any time.

O Uṣas, bearing and sustaining the feast for the gods—a sacrifice desired by the gods—you, the most excellent and most highly praised in the highest manner, shine forth today in this place of the divine folk at this time of sacrifice.
Up to "yadveṣāḥ. [The root] *yu* is used in the sense of "mixing" and "not mixing. From this [root], with the suffix *pyañ*, and from the present tense (*laṭ*), the suffix *śatṛ* is applied.
Because of the rule "chandasyubhayathā," it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; therefore, [the following apply]:
1. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-mṛtāḥ;
2. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha—[the word] "ahani" is not present.
3. Regarding *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: "She is said to have been born for the sake of sacrifice"—this does not exist.

Because the *sārvadhātuka* suffix lacks the *anudātta* accent, the accent of the suffix itself remains. In the subsequent *bahuvrīhi* compound, that same accent persists. The short vowel is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) form occurring at the stage of the word (*padakāla*). *Ṛtapāḥ*: "He who protects the *ṛta*. From the root *pā* in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣaṇe*), with the suffix *vic*. *Ṛtejāḥ*: "Born from the *ṛta* as its cause. From the root *jan* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*), with the suffix *viṭ* according to the rule *janasanakhanakramagamaviṭ*. The substitution of *ā* for the nasalized vowel occurs by the rule *viṣṇoranunāsikasyāt*. The non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending occurs by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*. *Sumnāvarī*: The possessive suffix *vanip* is added by the rule *chandasi vanipau*. By the rule *vano ra ca*, the feminine suffix *ḍīp* is applied and the *n* is replaced by *r*. The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*. The initial *udātta* accent of the suffix is due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*). *Sumnalīḥ*: The suffix *ḍīṣ* is applied because the word is listed in the *gaurādi* group by the rule *sumnallān saṃjñāyām*. Since all rules are optional in the Veda (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*), the elision of the nominative case ending prescribed by *halḍyābbhyaḥ* is optional; in its absence, the short vowel and the visarga appear. *Devavītim*: From the root *vī* in the senses of "going, procreation, beauty, eating, and devouring. A sacrifice is called *devavīti* because it is desired (*kāmyate*) for the sake of the gods' enjoyment. The suffix *ktin* is used in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*). The original accent of the first member of the compound is maintained because it belongs to the *dāsībhāra* class.

Eternally the goddess Dawn has shone forth from of old; now this wealthy one has revealed these riches. And she shall shine forth through future days as well; ageless and immortal, she moves by her own powers. śaśvat | purā | uṣāḥ | vi | uvāsa | devī | atho iti | agha | idam | vi | āvaḥ | maghonī | atho iti | vi | ucchāt | uttarān | anu | dyūn | ajarā | amṛtā | carati | svadhābhiḥ ||13||

The goddess Uṣas, who is by nature radiant, shone forth—meaning she dawned—constantly and perpetually in former times. Then, immediately thereafter, at this present time, the wealthy Uṣas has caused this entire world, which was concealed by darkness, to shine forth—that is, she has made it free from darkness through her illumination.
Furthermore, looking toward the future days that lie ahead, she will continue to shine and cause [the world] to shine even on the days to come.

Therefore, she who pervades the three periods of time, who possesses steps, who is ageless—being devoid of old age—and who is always uniform and immortal—being free from death—moves and exists together with her own *svadhās*, that is, her own splendors.
He dwelt (*uvāsa*). [This is derived from] the root *vas* ‘to dwell. According to the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayepām*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the reduplicated syllable.
He protected (*āvaḥ*).

From that very root, by the rule "the *liṭ* [suffix] occurs frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), there is elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). Then, by the rule "after a consonant, *ṅī*, or a long vowel," there is elision of the *ti*.
The augment *āṭ* occurs even in the Veda, according to the rule "it is seen even in the Veda.
Thus: *ucchāt*. In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *āṭ*.
Regarding *uttarān*: by the rule "after a long vowel, [there is ru] before a vowel (*aṭ*) in the same metrical foot," the *n* becomes *r*.
By the rule "the vowel *ā* is always nasalized before *aṭ*," the vowel *ā* is nasalized.
*Anu*: By the rule *anu-lakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.4.84), *anu* has the status of a *karmapravacanīya*. *Ajarāḥ amṛtāḥ*: "unaging and immortal."
In that case, regarding the bahuvrīhi compound, the rule "anajo jaramaramitramṛtāḥ" prescribes that the first syllable of the final member (uttarapada) is udātta.

1. [The suffix] occurs when *kṣa*, *ṭa*, or *ṭha* follow as the cause (*nimitta*). 2. There is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*) after *ta*, *da*, or *śa*. 3. [The suffix] occurs only after *ṭha*. 4. For *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*, the rule "the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the following member (*uttarapada*)" does not apply. (Page 88) [This refers to] the quarters (*diś*) belonging to *nabhas* (the sky), which is connected with *div*. This is a designation for the directions.

When the quarters have expanded far and wide, Dawn has shone forth, illuminating with her fires—her radiant, manifesting splendors. This goddess, whose nature is divine, [has cast off] her dark garment;
"nirṇij" is a name for form.
She has driven away, that is, she has uncovered, the black form created by night;
she has obscured it with her light.
Moreover, Uṣas approaches, coming with a well-yoked chariot drawn by her own reddish-brown, red-colored horses—rays or steeds—that are characterized by their power of pervasion.
Doing what?
Awakening sleeping beings, making them wakeful.
Then [the root] *dyut*, meaning "to shine," [is used];
[the suffix] *luṅ* [is applied].

The *parasmaipada* ending is applied by the rule *‘dyutyo luṅi’* (Pāṇini 1.3.91). By means of transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli*. Although *guṇa* would have been expected, the *vṛddhi* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively,
[the root] *dyu* means "to go towards";
it belongs to the *ad-ādi* (second) class.
The vowel strengthening (vṛddhi) occurs by the rule "uto vṛddhir luki hali" (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.89).
In the oblations to the goddesses, the verse beginning with “āvahantī” serves as the *upasayājyā*.
This is stated in the Sūtra: “‘Ā dyāṃ tanoṣi raśmibhirāvahantī poṣvā vāryāṇi na tā arvā rejukakāṭo aśnute’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.14).

Bringing desirable nourishments, she, being observed, makes her wondrous banner. She has shone forth as the first of the eternal dawns that have passed away, the foremost of those shining ones. 15. *ā vahantī* (bringing), *poṣvā* (nourishments), *vāryāṇi* (desirable things), *citram* (wondrous), *ketum* (banner), *kṛṇute* (she makes), *cerkitānā* (being observed), *īyuṣīṇām* (of those that have gone by), *upamā* (the likeness), *śaśvatīnām* (of the eternal ones), *vibhātīnām* (of those shining forth), *prathamā* (the first), *uṣāḥ* (Dawn), *vi adhait* (has shone forth). 15.

Having nourished us, bringing to us desirable and choice riches that are capable of sustaining us for as long as life lasts, Uṣas—she who is observant, making all people aware, and making her own signal—the wonderful, variegated, marvelous, and worthy-of-admiration banner, the light capable of illuminating the entire world, produces from her own radiance.

This very Dawn, who is the model for the many eternal dawns that have gone before—those that have departed, moved on, been previously perfected, and passed away—shines forth as if fashioned as a likeness near them; she is the first and foremost of the dawns yet to come, shining with special brilliance, and thus has she become augmented by her splendor.
*Poṣvā*. [The root] *puṣ* [is used] in the sense of nourishing (*puṣṭau*). Nourishing is *poṣaḥ*.

The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*). [The word *bhāvya* means] "those which exist therein. The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule "in the Vedic language, when meaning 'existing in' (*bhave*)."
The word *anāvaḥ* has its initial syllable accented because of the rule “*yato ’nāvaḥ*”.
The elision of the suffix *śas* occurs by the rule “*śeṣacchandasi bahulam*”.
[The form is] *vāryāṇi*.
The root *vṛñ* is used in the sense of “to gather” (*saṃbhakti*).
By the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied.
Furthermore, by the rule *īḍvandvavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ pyataḥ*, the initial syllable receives the udātta accent.
*Cekitānā*:
[derived] from the root *kit* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāne*), with the suffix *yaṅ*, followed by the present participle suffix *śānac*.

Because of the rule "chandasyubhayathā," [the suffix] is treated as both [sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka]; since it is here an ārdhadhātuka, there is the elision of the *at* (the *a* of the root) and the elision of the *yal*.
By the rule "abhyastānāmādiḥ," the first syllable has the udātta accent.
[The form is] *īyuṣīṇām*.
The root *iṇ* means "to go.
[In the perfect tense (*liṭ*),] the suffix *kasu* is applied;
[this triggers] reduplication and so forth.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ugitaśca";
there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam";
and the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs by the rule "iṇe yaṇ".
The lengthening of the reduplicated syllable is according to the rule *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti*; the substitution of *ṣ* is according to the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*;
and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the nominative suffix *sup* are acute (*udātta*) because they are marked with *p*.
Of those that are shining. [The root] *bhā* means "to shine.
From this [root], with the suffix *śatṛ*, as before, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
The name [of this suffix] is *udātta* by the rule “*ṅyāp chandasi bahulam*” (Pāṇini 6.1.171). Now, [the root] *dhauk* means “to go” and “to increase.”
In the *laṅ* [tense], by the rule "there is diversely elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix in Vedic," there is elision of the suffix;
then, once the *guṇa* has been applied, the substitution of *ai* occurs by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).
1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-jagata* (the world of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*).
2. *kṣa-ṭa-gatavatīnām* (of those who have gone to *kṣa* and *ṭa*).
3. Near *ṭha*, the metaphors (*upamā*) that are constructed are the standards of comparison (*upamāna*).
Arise! Life has come to this man; death has departed from him. He goes toward the light.
The path has been cleared for the Sun to travel; we have arrived where they prolong life.
Arise! The breath of life has come to us; darkness has departed and light approaches. It has cleared a path for the Sun to travel; we have arrived where they prolong their span of life. 16.

"O men, arise! Abandoning your bed, come forth! Our *asu*—the impeller of the body, the *jīva*, the individual soul—has arrived. Darkness has departed. When light appears, there is the engagement in all activities of life. Therefore, that *jīva*, being of the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), comes toward that very *jyotis* (light). He has cleared the path for the sun, making it distinct for its journey. To that place we have gone, where life exists. *Āyuḥ* is a name for food; they increase it. The prefix *pra-* in *pratirante* signifies growth; they cause it to increase through generous giving. Grammatical notes: * *īrdhvam*: From the root *īr* "to go," belonging to the *adādi* class, which is *anudātta*. * *āraik*: From the root *ric* "to leave/empty. In the *laṅ* tense, the suffix is elided by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*; the *guṇa* vowel is replaced by *ī* by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*). * *panthām*: Even in the accusative case, the form *panthām* is used by irregular substitution (*vyatyaya*) according to the rule *pathimathyubhukṣāmāt*. * *aganma*: From the root *gam* in the *laṅ* tense, the suffix is elided by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*; the *m* is changed to *n* by the rule *mvośca* (Pāṇini 8.2.65).
The priest, being praised, raises his voice with a thread-like continuity like a singer at the dawning of the radiant Uṣas.
Shine forth today, O Maghavan, for the one who praises you; bestow upon us a life rich in progeny.

The singer, the bearer of the sacrifice, being praised, raises up the threads of speech as he lauds the shining dawns. O bounteous one, shine forth that light today for the one who sings your praise; bestow upon us a life rich in progeny.
'Vahni' means the bearer of hymns;
'rebha' is a name for a hymn.

The praiser, praising the Dawns who shine forth by dispelling the darkness—those secondary deities—raises up, that is, utters and pronounces, the "threads," meaning the continuous and interconnected hymns (*ukthas*) belonging to the Veda. Therefore, O bountiful Dawn, at this very moment, shine upon that person who praises you;
dispel and drive away the night-time darkness well known for obstructing vision.
"And for us (asme), may life (āyuḥ) endowed with progeny (prajāvat)—meaning possessed of children, grandchildren, and so forth—and food (anna) come hither.

The thickest darkness (tamaḥ), that is, ignorance, has departed; even the darkness (tamaḥ) produced by night has departed, having gone away completely. Since the light (jyotiḥ) of the dawn (auṣasa) arrives, moreover, Uṣas has cleared (āraik), that is, prepared (recitavatī), the path (panthānam) for Sūrya to travel."
Therefore, O friends, we have come;
let us go to that place where there is life, which is called immortality.
The prefix *pra-* in the verb *tirante* signifies "to increase" (*prapūrvaḥ tiratir vardhanārthaḥ*).
The noble ones cause [the world] to flourish through their giving (*udārā dānena pravardhayanti*). When the dawn (*uṣas*) has appeared, there occurs the engagement in all activities of living beings.

Therefore, by virtue of being of the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātmarūpatayā*), that individual soul (*jīva*) approaches that very light (*tadeva jyotiḥ upeti*); he comes to the light (*jyotir ā eti āgacchati*) in that place where we go, in that place where she has cleared a path (*panthām āraik*) for the Sun to travel as his protector (*rakṣakāya*).
Life; that which ends in a consonant is food; they extend their life through food.
The prefix *pra-* in *prati* has the sense of "increasing.
They cause [the hymns] to increase through their generosity.
3. [The variants] kṣa-ṭa-ṭha- read "of praises. 4. [The variants] kṣa-ṭa-ṭha- read: "He raises up the *ukthas*, which have been consecrated by the *sāmans* along the thread [of the ritual]."
5. Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-dhanavati.

*dīdihi*—shine forth intensely; *dīdi* is a Vedic root meaning "to shine," and its sense here is "bestow. *syūsanā*: from the root *siv* (tantusantāne, "to weave"), the suffix *manin* is applied in the sense of the object according to the rule *anyebhyo'pi dṛśyante*, which is intended to override all restrictive conditions. By the rule *chūḥ śū*, there is the substitution of *ūṭ*. According to the supplementary rule *āḍyājayārāṃ copasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 7.1.39.1), the case-ending takes the substitute *āṭ*. Alternatively, *mak* is an Uṇādi suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāve*), and *naḥ* is added as a possessive suffix according to the *pāmādi* group. Thus, the meaning is "provided with bonds. The elision of the *śel* suffix is by the rule *śe śchandasi bahulam*; the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatvam*) occurs by transposition (*vyatyaya*). *vācaḥ*: the acute accent on the *ṅam* ending is by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. *iyarti*: from the root *ṛ* (gatau, "to go"), belonging to the *juhotyādi* class; the shortening of the reduplicated syllable is by the rule *atipiparyośca*. *stavānaḥ*: from the root *ṣṭuñ* (stutau, "to praise"); in the present participle (*śānac*), there is elision of *śap* because it belongs to the *adādi* class. Since this [suffix] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, it lacks the *ṅit* quality, and thus the *guṇa* and *avādeśa* substitutions apply. The initial acute accent is by transposition. *vibhātīḥ*: the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is acute by the rule *śatarunnamo nathajādī*. *gṛṇate*: from the root *gṛ* (śabde, "to sound"), belonging to the *krayādi* class; the shortening is by the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*. The acute accent of the case-ending is by the preceding rule. *aste*: the fourth case (*caturthī*) takes the substitute *śe* by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

Those Dawns which shine forth, rich in cattle, with all heroes, for the mortal who offers oblations—like the outburst of Vāyu’s pleasant truths, may they, as givers of horses, grant horses to the Soma-presser. 18. Those Dawns, rich in cattle, with all heroes, which shine forth for the mortal who offers oblations—like the outburst of Vāyu’s pleasant truths, may they, as givers of horses, grant horses to the Soma-presser. 18.

To the mortal, the human sacrificer who has offered oblations (*havīṃṣi*), may those Dawns come—rich in cattle, joined with many cows, and accompanied by all heroic warriors capable of swift movement—who shine forth, dispelling the darkness. At the conclusion of the *sūnṛtā* (joyful and truthful) words, which proceed as swiftly as the wind, may the sacrificer who presses the Soma—the giver of horses—attain those Dawns that bestow horses.
To the one who offers!
Regarding the root *dāś* in the sense of "giving":
the form *dāśvān* (and likewise *sāhvān*) is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) ending in the suffix *kamu*.
In the singular dative case, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam."
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca.
It became *abhavat*.
[The root] *aś* is used in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The *parasmaipada* ending occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *aṭ*. By the rule "and after [a verbal root] ending in *i*, there is elision," the *ikāra* is elided.
*Somasutvā*:
[derived from] the root *puj* (in the sense of) "pressing," with the suffix *kanip* according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well."
The augment *nuk* is applied by the rule "hrasvasya piti."

Mother of the gods, face of Aditi, banner of the sacrifice, great one, shine forth! Bringing us praise, dawn for our sacred prayer; O possessor of all boons, awaken us and bring forth offspring for us. 19. Mother. Of the gods. Of Aditi. The face. Of the sacrifice. The banner. Great. Shine forth. Maker of praise. For our sacred prayer. Dawn upon us. Bring forth for us. O you who possess all desirable things. 19.
You are the lap of the gods, the mother, the progenitress;
upon you all the gods are awakened by praise, and therefore she is called "possessing that progeny.
For this very reason, she is the face, the counterpart, of Aditi, the mother of the gods.
The meaning is that you are a rival.
1. *sa-* [is used] with the root *hu* (to sacrifice) etc., where there is *ślu*-elision.
2. In the variants *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*, the phrase "the vowels *vi-bhātīḥ*... are acute" is absent.
3. In *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-śatarun namaḥ*, there is the acute accent (*udātta*) on the case ending (*vibhakti*).
4. [The suffixes] *cha*, *dha*, *ya*, *la*, and *śa* are used for the sense of "capable of providing refuge" (*śaraṇasamartha*).
5. For indeed, in *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*, it is in the locative (*upasi*).
Alternatively,
"devas" are the rays because they shine;
she is their creator.
The face of the earth that is to be praised by Aditi is her army;
just as the face is illuminating because it is the abode of Indra, so too Uṣas is the illuminator of the earth—this is the meaning.
Being great (*bṛhatī*), shine forth as the banner (*ketu*) of the sacrifice, that is, as its indicator and informer. Shine forth!

Moreover, O Uṣas, you who bestow praise, acknowledging our hymn with the words "it is well-praised," shine forth for our *brahman*—that is, for our mantra-form prayer or song of praise. Immediately thereafter, O Viśvavāre, you who are worthy of being praised by all, bring us forth among the people—that is, manifest yourself before us in the inhabited land and establish us there.
[The meter is] Bṛhatī.
By the rule “*brahmamahatopasaṃkhyānam*,” the suffix *ṅīp* is applied and becomes udātta. [The word] *praśastikṛt* [is derived from] the root *śaṃs* in the sense of praising (*stuti*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the action (*bhāva*). By the rule *titutra*, there is a prohibition of the *iṭ* augment. By the rule *aniditām*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*).

With that word as an upapada, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *kṛ* by the rule "kvip ca. Thus, [the form] *janaya* is derived from the root *jan* in the sense of "manifestation" (*prādurbhāve*).
There is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel due to the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Because [the roots] *jan*, *jṛ*, *ksu*, *raj*, and those ending in *am* are designated as having the *mit* marker, there is shortening of the vowel by the rule "there is shortening for those with the *mit* marker.
That wonderful, auspicious [light], which the Dawns bring to the one who has performed the ritual service and is striving for his goal—
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us that.
(20) That wonderful, auspicious wealth which the Dawns bring for the one who has sacrificed and labored—the gods Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven shall grant that to us. (20)

Whether it be *vicitram*, that which is wonderful and worthy of admiration; *vāpnaḥ*, wealth to be obtained; *vāsabhyam*, that which belongs to the assembly; or *yaddhanam*, whatever riches; *vopasaḥ*, which the Dawns bring or cause to be brought for the man who has sacrificed with oblations (*ījānāya*), who has offered worship (*iṣṭavate*), who has exerted himself with praises (*śaśamānāya*), and who honors [the gods]—that becomes *bhadram*, auspicious and worthy of being enjoyed; this is the remainder of the sense.
Whatever has been prayed for by us through this hymn, may the six deities, beginning with Mitra, *vāmamahantām*, honor and fulfill it.
*Apraḥ*.
The root *āp* means "to pervade.

According to the rule “*āpaḥ karmalyāyāṃ hrasvo nud ca vā*,” the suffix *asun* is applied even when there is no object (*akarmalyāyām*), due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam*; furthermore, the root vowel is shortened and the augment *nuṭ* is added.
[Thus we have] *ījānāya*.
In the Vedic language, the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix is used after the root *yaj*.
By the rule “*liṭaḥ kānaj vā*,” the *kānac* suffix may optionally replace *liṭ*. Then, by the rule beginning with “*vacisvapi*,” there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
Examples of double consonants and so forth:
*śaśamānāya*. [The root] *śaś* [is used in the sense of] "leaping" (*plutagati*).
The suffix *śānac* denotes habitual action (*tācchīlika*).

Since it lacks the status of being a *lasārvadhātuka*, and because there is no accentuation of a *lasārvadhātuka* due to its being taught with an initial *a* (*adupadeśa*), the *cita*-accent alone remains.
The eleventh hymn, "imā rudrāya," is the ninth [hymn] of the entire [maṇḍala].
The tenth and eleventh verses are triṣṭubhs;
the remaining nine are jagatīs.
Rudra is the deity.

Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: “These eleven [verses] belong to Rudra; the last two have two and three [feet] respectively. In rituals such as the Śūlagava where Rudra is the deity, the quarters should be worshipped with this hymn.

And so it is well-stated in the *Suśruta*: “‘To what Rudra? To this Rudra, O Father! To this Rudra with the firm bow—these songs!’—with these [verses], one performs the worship of the quarters for all the Rudras” (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 4.9.21).

“We offer these prayers to Rudra, the powerful one, the one with matted hair, the lord of heroes, so that there may be peace for bipeds and quadrupeds, and so that everything in this village may be prosperous and free from disease.”

1 | These prayers we bring forth to the powerful Rudra, the one with matted hair, the lord of heroes, so that there may be well-being for our bipeds and quadrupeds; so that everything in this village may be prosperous and free from disease. ||1||

To Rudra. He is called Rudra because he causes everything to weep at the time of the end (*antakāla*). Alternatively, *rut* refers to the suffering known as *saṃsāra*; he is Rudra because he causes that to flow away, to depart, or to perish. Or again, *rutaḥ* refers to the Upaniṣads in the form of sound; he is Rudra because he is dwelt in, reached, or expounded by them. Or again—

*Rudra* is so called because he bestows (*rāti*) or gives (*dadāti*) to his worshippers either *rut*— speech consisting of sound— or the *ātmavidyā* (knowledge of the Self) which is expressed by it. Alternatively:
*Rut* means that which obstructs or covers, such as darkness and so forth;
*rudra* is one who destroys (*haṇāti*) or tears apart (*vidārayati*) that.
Alternatively:
Once, during a battle between the gods and the asuras, Rudra, assuming another form, stole the wealth deposited by the Ṛbhus and departed.
Having defeated the asuras, the gods searched for him; finding him while he was carrying off the wealth, they then wept.
Therefore, he is called "Rudra.
Accordingly, the Taittirīyaka states: "He wept; because he wept, that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.1.1).
To that Rudra, we bring forward—that is, we produce with excellence—these "matis," these hymns worthy of contemplation.
To what kind [of one]?

To the "mighty" (*tavase*), the "increased" (*pravṛddhāya*), the "one with matted hair" (*kapardine*), the "one with braided locks" (*jaṭilāya*), and the "one in whom heroes perish" (*kṣayadvīrāya*)—that is, to him in whom heroes (*vīrāḥ*) perish or are destroyed.
Or alternatively:
The root *kṣayi* has the sense of exercising sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
To him whose sons are the hosts of Maruts—heroes who exercise sovereignty through their spears—to him [be this prayer].

"In what manner" (*yathā*) and "by what means" (*yena*), may there be "peace" (*śam*), the pacification of diseases that are to be pacified, "for our two-footed human being" and "for our four-footed [beings]" such as cows, horses, and so forth. May it come to pass.
The meaning is that we offer praises in that manner.

Therefore, "in this our foremost village," may "the entire universe"—the whole multitude of living beings—"be free from affliction"; being devoid of those who are afflicted, that is, those who are diseased, may it be "thriving" and "prosperous."
To Rudra;
the suffix *rak* is applied by the rule "roderṇil k ca" (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.179). To Tavas.
The root *tavi* has the sense of "increase. It is a verbal root found in the Sūtras; the suffix *as* is an *auṇādika* (derivative) suffix.
To Kṣayadvīra;
from the root *kṣi* in the sense of "perishing," with the suffix *śatṛ* applied to the present tense (*laṭ*).

According to the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the suffix *śatṛ* is treated as if it were part of the verbal root (*ārṣadhātuka*). Consequently, because it is taught with a short vowel (*adupadeśa*), the *lasārvadhātuka* accent does not apply; thus, its own accent remains.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the accent of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. [The word] is *asat*.
In *asa bhuvi*,
the substitution of *aḍ* occurs by the rule *leṭo ’ḍāṭau*. Then, by the rule *itaśca lopaḥ*, there is the elision of the vowel *i*.
Regarding *dvipada*: it means "one who has two feet. By the rule *saṃkhyāsupūrvasya*, there is elision of the final syllable of the word *pāda* as a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*).

In the dative singular, when the technical designation *bha* applies, the substitution of *pat* for *pāda-* occurs by the rule *pādaḥ pat*. Since that which has undergone a partial modification is not considered different from the original (*paribhāṣā* 37), the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pādanmūrdhasu bahuvrīhau* prescribes the acute accent on the first syllable of the final member [of the compound]. Thus: *catuṣpade*.
With the exception of the accent, it is as before.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member;
and in this case, the first member is acute-accented (*udātta*) by the rule "after *tri*, [the accent falls on] a numeral" (*phiṭ-sūtra* 28).

For Rudradeva’s animal sacrifice, there are two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*) and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), beginning with "Be gracious to us, O Rudra" (*mṛḷā no rudra*).
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Be gracious to us, O Rudra,’ and ‘And grant us happiness’—these two; and ‘May the favor of the Maruts come to thee, O Father’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
Be gracious to us, O Rudra, and grant us well-being; we shall worship you with homage, you who rule over heroes.
Whatever health and prosperity our father Manu won through sacrifice, may we attain that under your guidance, O Rudra.

Be gracious to us, O Rudra, and grant us joy. We shall worship you with homage, you who rule over heroes. Whatever health and well-being our father Manu won by sacrifice, may we attain that under your guidance, O Rudra. 2.
O Rudra, be gracious to us; for our sake, become our bringer of happiness.
Moreover, immediately thereafter, grant us joy—that is, happiness.
And may we [attain] one who possesses the power to subdue all heroes, or who is endowed with noble heroism and sovereign authority.
"May we serve you with reverence—either with oblations characterized by *havis* or with prostration;
for the root *vidh* signifies the act of service.

Furthermore, O Rudra, that which the progenitor Manu obtained from the gods and bestowed upon his own offspring—the twofold gift of *śam*, the pacification of diseases, and *yoḥ*, the warding off of fears—may we attain that very thing through your excellent guidances (*praṇītisu*), your sublime leadings."
*mṛḷa*. *Amṛḍa* means "to give happiness";
it belongs to the Taudādi class.
In the *saṃhitā* text, there is a long vowel according to the rule "dvayaco'tastiṅaḥ.
[The form] *kṛdhi* is derived from the root *kṛ* in the imperative (*loṭ*), with the elision of the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi."
By the rule "śṛṇupukṛvṛbhyaśchandasi," the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs.
By the rule "ataḥ kṛkami," the *visarjanīya* of *mayaḥ* becomes *s*. [Thus:
*kṣayadvīrāya*.

The word *kriyā* (action) must be supplied [in the rule], because the object (*karman*) becomes the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), hence the dative case. *Vidhema*: from the root *vidh* in the sense of "to arrange" or "to perform," belonging to the *tudādigaṇa*. *Āyeje*: from the root *yaj* in the sense of "worshiping the gods," "forming an alliance," or "giving. In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, because a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific technical designation is not necessarily permanent, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution), and thus *etva* (the change of *i* to *e*) and the elision of the reduplication occur. *Aśyāma*: from the root *aś* in the sense of "pervasion. The *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending occurs by transposition (*vyatyaya*); the elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix occurs according to the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
May we obtain your benevolence through devotion to the gods, O bounteous Rudra, ruler of heroes;
coming with goodwill, approach our people, and may we, with our heroes unharmed, offer the oblation to you.

May we obtain your favor through devotion to the gods, O Rudra, bounteous one, ruler of heroes. Seeking your goodwill, come to our people; with our heroes unharmed, may we offer the oblation to you. 3.

O *mīḍhvān*, the showerer, O rain-giver of desires, O eternal deliverer, or O Rudra, [approach] with your auspicious, benevolent, and gracious intellect—the intellect belonging to you, who possess a dwelling of heroes (*kṣayadvīra*), who have destroyed adversaries, and who are endowed with great supernatural power (*maharddhi*). May we, through our devotion to the gods (*devayujyā*)—that is, by means of the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice dedicated to our own deity—attain that [intellect].
And you, looking toward our people (*viśaḥ*), our progeny, come hither.
What are you doing?
"sumnāyan" means "desiring happiness. "Sumna" is a name for happiness.
The meaning is: "May you be one who desires the happiness of those creatures, that is, may you be a bestower of happiness."
Therefore, we—possessing unharmed heroes—are such that our heroes (*vīra*) are born from valor (*vīrya*);

being those whose heroes are unharmed (*ariṣṭa*) and uninjured, we offer (*juhavāma*) the oblation (*havis*), consisting of cooked rice, sacrificial cakes, and so forth, to you; that is, we cast it into the consecrated receptacle as directed.
Sumati: *mati* means reflection. That intellect in which there is excellent reflection is *sumati*.
In the form *nambubhyām*, the final syllable of the second member of the compound is udātta.
In *devayujyayā*,
the suffix *yap* is applied to the root *yaj* and its feminine gender is prescribed by rules such as *chandasi niṣṭarkye*.
*mīḍhvaḥ*: from the root *miha* in the sense of "to sprinkle. It is an irregularly formed word (nipātita) ending in the suffix *vasu*, according to the rule "dādhvānsāhvānmīḍhvān."

In the word *saṃbuddhau*, by the rule *matuvaso ruḥ*, there is the substitution of *ru* [for the suffix *matup*]; thus, *sumnāyan*. [The term] *sumna* means one who desires the welfare (*sumna*) of others.
The suffix *kyac* is applied by the rule “*chandasi parecchāyām api*” [Pāṇini 3.1.8].
The prohibition of the substitution of *ī* and the lengthening [of the vowel] is stated by the rule “*na cchandasyaputrasya*” [Pāṇini 7.4.35].
Furthermore, the substitution of *ā* prescribed by the rule “*devasudyayoryujapi kāṭhake*” [Pāṇini 7.4.38] should be understood as applying here as well by way of transference (*vyatyaya*).
We invoke for our protection the impetuous Rudra, the fulfiller of sacrifice, the swift, the wise;
may he cast his wrath far away from us, and we choose his benevolent favor.
We bring down for our protection the impetuous Rudra, the fulfiller of sacrifice, the bountiful one, and the wise. May he cast far away from us his wrath; we choose only his goodwill. ||4||
For protection—that is, for the sake of guarding us—we invoke Rudra, Mahādeva, calling him forth intensely.
Of what nature is he?
He is the radiant, blazing one, the accomplisher of sacrifice, the one who brings the sacrifice to fulfillment.
For he indeed makes the sacrifice his own.

And thus it is recorded in the Taittirīyaka, beginning with: "The gods, indeed, went away from the sacrifice," followed by: "This [sacrifice] of ours will surely be well-performed (sviṣṭha) if we shall gratify him; that is the reason for the Sviṣṭakṛt’s name 'Sviṣṭakṛt'" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.8.3).
[He is] the one who goes crookedly (vaḍuṃku), the poet (kavi) who possesses far-reaching vision (krāntadarśin).
1. She who has reached the letters *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*.
2. She who has measured out *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*.
3. She who goes crookedly through *kṣa* and *ṭa*.

And may that Rudra cast away (*asyatu*)—that is, propel far from us, to a distant place—the non-divine (*adaivyam*), i.e., the wrath (*helaḥ*) belonging to the shining one (*devasya*). We choose for ourselves, with devotion, the excellent favor (*sumatim*) of this Mahādeva—that is, we seek his benevolent, gracious mind. [Grammatical notes: *Yajñasādham*: "One who accomplishes the sacrifice" (*yajñaṃ sādhayati*). From the root *ṣidh* in the sense of "accomplishment," there is the substitution of *ā* according to the rule "for *sidhyati* when not referring to worldly matters. Alternatively, from the roots *rādh* or *sādh* in the sense of "success," there is the suffix *kvip* after the causative form (*ṇyanta*). *Vaṅkukam*: From the root *vaki* in the sense of "crookedness," with the *uṇādi* suffix *u*. *Ni hayāmahe*: From the prefix *ni* with the root *hve*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule "after *ni*, *sam*, *upa*, and *vi*, [the root] *hve* [takes the middle voice]. *Daivyam*: The suffix *yañ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to a deity" (*prāgdīvyatīya*) by the rule "after *deva*, [the suffixes] *yañ* and *yañ*. *Asyatu*: From the root *asu* in the sense of "throwing," belonging to the *divādi* class. *Vṛṇīmahe*: From the root *vṛṅ* in the sense of "choosing" or "seeking," belonging to the *kryādi* class.

With reverence, we offer this speech characterized by praise to Rudra, the Lord and progenitor of the Maruts—those fifty-nine specific deities—with the words: "We invoke with homage the wild boar of heaven, the ruddy one, the one with matted hair, the brilliant form. Of what nature is it? It is said and uttered as an address to Rudra, the Father and Creator of the Maruts, who number forty-nine, and who are a particular class of gods. What is its character? It is addressed to the Lord. What is it like? It is the invocation of the divine form.
6. *Svādoḥ*: more delicious than even flavorful things such as honey and ghee;
the meaning is that it produces an exceeding degree of joy.
7. *Vardhanam*: that which causes the increase of that which is worthy of praise.
For when a deity is pleased by a hymn of praise, it increases in power.
And thus is the fatherhood of Rudra toward the Maruts recounted.
Once in ancient times, Indra conquered the Asuras.

At that time, Diti, the mother of the Asuras, desiring a son capable of slaying Indra, obtained a conception from her husband through the power of ascetic penance. Becoming aware of this event, Indra, holding his thunderbolt in hand, assumed a subtle form, entered her womb, and divided that embryo into seven parts;
he then further divided each of those into seven fragments.
All of them, having emerged from the womb through the region of the birth canal, cried out.
At that moment, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, who were walking about for the sake of sport, saw them.
Pārvatī spoke thus to Maheśa:
"May these pieces of flesh each become sons; you must act toward me in this way if you have affection for me.
Then Maheśvara, having made those sons identical in form, identical in age, and identical in ornaments, gave them to Gaurī, saying, "Let these be your sons.
Therefore, in all the *māruta* hymns (*sūkta*), the Maruts are praised as the sons of Rudra.
And among the fierce ones, the father of the Maruts is Rudra.

Furthermore: O immortal (amṛta), deathless Rudra, grant (rāsva)—that is, bestow—upon us (naḥ) the food (martabhojanam) that is the means of enjoyment for mortals (martānām), namely human beings. Likewise, [grant it] to me (mane), that is, to myself (ātmane).
The dative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
"Māṃ" (me); "tokāya" means for the son; "tanayāya" means for the grandson and his son; "mṛḷa" means be gracious, i.e., grant happiness;
[and] for the father.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *udāttayaṇaḥ*. [The form] *rāsva* [is derived from the root] *rā*, meaning "to give."
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition.

Regarding the form *mane*: in the rule "In mantras, [the substitution] of *āt* for *ātman-* [occurs] after *āṅ*" (Pāṇini 7.1.35), there is the elision of the vowel *ā* of *ātman-* because of the statement "Elsewhere than after *āṅ*, [this substitution] is also seen in the Veda" (Kātyāyana-vārttika 6.4.141.1).
Do not harm our great ones, nor our small ones; do not harm our growing ones, nor those already grown. Do not slay our father, nor our mother; O Rudra, do not injure our dear bodies.
Not our great one, nor our small one; not our growing one, nor our grown one; do not slay our father, nor yet our mother; O Rudra, do not harm our dear bodies. 7.
O Rudra, do not slay—that is, do not harm—the great or the aged among us;
nor indeed harm our child or infant;
likewise, do not slay the bull, the one who sprinkles, the middle-aged youth among us.
12 And furthermore, 13 do not slay our 13 *ukṣita*—the offspring conceived as an embryo and infused into the womb. Likewise, 15 do not slay our 15 father, the progenitor; 16 do not slay him.
17 And furthermore, 17 do not slay our 18 mother, the one who gave us birth; 18 do not slay her.
Likewise, O Rudra, do not harm (mā rīriṣaḥ) our dear ones—the objects of our affection—our bodies, or the offspring born of our bodies.
*vadhīḥ*. In the *luṅ* tense, the root *han* undergoes the substitution *vadh* by the rule "luṅi ca"; and that [substitute] ends in a short vowel (*adanta*).
And here [in *sica*], due to the status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the elision (*lopa*), there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. [The form] *riṣaḥ*.
The root *ṛṣ* is used in the sense of "to injure.

From the causative form (*pyantāt*), in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix, there occurs the elision of the causative marker (*ṇilopa*), the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhāsvatva*), and so forth.
The shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsahasva*) is Vedic (*chāndasaḥ*) and occurs at the time of the word-segmentation (*padakālīna*).
1. Of the specific deities Kṣa, Ṭa, and Ṭha;
2. [The syllable] Kṣa, Ṭa, and Sa proceed;
3. It is recited [in the tradition]; it is not recited in this manner.
4. Of the husband of kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-pa;
5. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa wept bitterly;
6. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha in this interval.
7. If *na*, *sa*, and *ma* are present, it is not Maheśvara.
8. If *ba*, *cha*, *ṇa*, and *pha* are present, there is affection for you (*tvatprīti*); if *da* and *tha* are present, there is also affection for you.
9. If *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha* are present, it is Maheśa; if *na* is present, it is Parameśvara.

10. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-martabhojanaṃ*: food for mortals; food sufficient for humans to eat (*'ṭha-martānāṃ bhojanaṃ' is not [present]*). 11. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-ātmane annam*: food for oneself. 12. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-hiṃsīḥ*: do not harm.
13. [The substitution] is as if the original (sthānin) were present because of the rule *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sthānivattvāt*.

"O Rudra, do not harm us in our children, nor in our descendants, nor in our life, nor in our cattle, nor in our horses. Do not slay our heroes in your wrath; bearing oblations, we ever invoke you. (RV 2.33.14) *mā* | *naḥ* | *toke* | *tanaye* | *mā* | *naḥ* | *āyau* | *mā* | *naḥ* | *goṣu* | *mā* | *naḥ* | *aśveṣu* | *rīriṣaḥ* | *vīrān* | *mā* | *naḥ* | *rudra* | *bhāmitaḥ* | *vadhīḥ* | *haviṣmantaḥ* | *sadam* | *it* | *tvā* | *havāmahe* || 8 ||
O Rudra, do not harm us; do not injure our offspring (*toka*) and descendants (*tanaya*). The word *toka* denotes sons, and *tanaya* denotes their sons.

The word *āyuḥ* is accented on the final syllable; it is a name for a human being. O [Agni], do not harm—that is, do not cause injury—to any other human being belonging to us, whether among our cattle, livestock, or horses.
Thus, O Rudra, being provoked to anger, do not slay nor harm our heroic, valiant, and courageous men;
and we, being possessed of oblations, shall always, at all times, invoke you.
Āyuḥ. [Derived from] the root iṇ meaning "to go," with the suffix uṇ added according to the rule "chandasyuṇaḥ."
*Bhāmitaḥ* [is derived from] *bhāma* [in the sense of] "anger. The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (kartari) according to the rule *kaḥ adhikaraṇe ca*.
We invoke.
In the root *hve*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vocalization occurs frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
In the *devasuvām havīṃṣi* offerings during the sacrifice to Rudra Paśupati, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses begin with "upa te stomān.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'upa te stomān paśupā ivākaram'—these two [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.11).

Like a herdsman, I have brought these hymns of praise near to you; O Father of the Maruts, grant us your favor. For your benevolence is auspicious and most compassionate; therefore, we choose only your protection. upa | te | stomān | paśupaḥ | iva | ā | akaram | rasva | pitaḥ | marutām | sumnam | asme | iti || bhadrā | hi | te | sumatiḥ | mṛḻayattamā | atha | vayam | avaḥ | it | te | vṛṇīmahe || 9 ||
O Rudra, I have brought these hymns—mantras consisting of praise—to you; I offer them, I present them to you.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"just as a herdsman [offers his flock]."

Just as a cowherd (*gopa*), the protector of cattle, returns at evening time to his owners the animals entrusted to him in the morning, so too do I return to you these mantras in the form of hymns—which have been obtained from you—as the very means for your praise; this is the meaning.

O Father of the Maruts, O Rudra, the progenitor of the gods known as the Maruts, grant us (*naḥ*) *sumnam*, that is, happiness. Furthermore, may your benevolent intellect (*sumatiḥ*), your auspicious thought, be most merciful (*mṛḷayattamā*), that is, exceedingly inclined toward bringing us joy.
Therefore she is indeed auspicious and worthy of worship;
because it is so, we therefore choose—that is, we accept—your protection (*avaḥ*) immediately thereafter.
I performed [the action].

The suffix *luṅ* is used here because the rule "in the Veda, *luṅ* and *liṭ* [are used for all tenses]" is in force; furthermore, the substitution of *aṭ* for *śli* occurs by the rule "after the roots *kṛ*, *mṛ*, and *dṛh*... etc.
"Also after *ṛt*, there is guṇa before the suffix *aṅ*.
[Thus, *pitaramarutām* is formed.

Since, by the rule "In the Vedic language, even that which follows may [be treated as preceding]," the subsequent genitive case ending is incorporated into the preceding vocative, both words become unaccented according to the rule "And [the first syllable] of a vocative."
*asme*: [this form arises] by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*). 2. O [Maruts], do not cause harm to that human being who belongs to us (*naḥ*); moreover, do not cause harm to our cows and horses. 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: our people. 4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: those known as the Maruts. 5. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: O progenitor. 6. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: auspicious ones; this is the substitute for the nominative plural of the *śeṣa* (remaining) forms. *Mṛḍayadhvam*.
The root *mṛḍ* means "to delight.
From this causative form (*ṇyantāt*), the suffix *śatṛ* is applied in the sense of the present tense (*laṭ*).
Since, by the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, this suffix is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, the *lasārvadhātuka* accent does not apply; thus, the accent of the suffix itself remains.

Far from us be your cow-slaying bolt and your man-slaying bolt, O Lord of heroes; let your favor be with us. Be gracious to us and speak for us, O God; and then, O you of double strength, grant us protection. āre te go-ghnam uta pūruṣa-ghnam kṣayad-vīra sumnam asme te astu | mṛḷa ca naḥ adhi ca brūhi deva atha ca naḥ śarma yaccha dvi-barhāḥ || 10 || Far from us be that which slays cattle and that which slays men, O Lord of heroes! Let your benevolence be with us. Be gracious to us and speak for us, O God; and then, O you of double might, bestow upon us shelter.

O Rudra, hero who brings about destruction, you who have destroyed all enemy folk—let that which is yours, namely the cow-slaying blow or the weapon that is the means for slaying cows, and likewise the man-slaying blow or the weapon that is the means for slaying men—let both of these be far away from us, in a distant place. Let your favor, your happiness, be with us; and furthermore, be gracious toward us for the sake of our well-being.
O radiant Rudra, speak for us;
that is, speak with partiality toward us, as in the scriptural injunction: "One should speak for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.11.9).
And furthermore, immediately thereafter, you are *dvibarhāḥ*, meaning you are preeminent in two places: on earth and in the intermediate space.
Or alternatively:
you are the sovereign lord (*parivṛḍha*) over the two paths—the southern and the northern—or over knowledge and action.
As such, grant (*yaccha*), that is, bestow (*dehi*), *śarma*, which is happiness, upon us.

*goghna* [cow-killer]. From the root *han* (in the sense of "to injure" or "to go"), the suffix *ka* is applied— either in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*)— according to the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam*.

In the word *gamahana*, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālāpa*). By the rule *ho hanteḥ*, there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *ha* becomes *gha*). Thus, [the form] is *dvibarhāḥ*.
The root *bṛh* (in the sense of *vṛddhau*, "to increase") is used here. Because he increases or grows in two places, he is called *dvibarhāḥ*.
[The suffix] *asun* is applied.
The original accentuation of the final member of the compound is retained.

We have spoken our salutation to him, seeking his favor; may Rudra, accompanied by the Maruts, hear our invocation. May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us that. We have spoken: salutation; to him; seeking favor; may he hear; our; invocation; Rudra; accompanied by the Maruts; that; for us; Mitra; Varuṇa; may they grant; Aditi; Sindhu; Earth; and; Heaven. 11.

Desiring protection (*avasyavaḥ*), we have spoken this hymn in the form of a praise; we have uttered it. Let there be reverence (*namaḥ*) to this Rudra. May Rudra, accompanied by the Maruts—his own sons—hear and accept our invocation (*havam*). May Mitra and the other six deities honor everything that has been spoken by us. The word *uta* is used in the sense of "also. Regarding *avocāma*: from the root *brū* (to speak clearly), in the *luṅ* tense, by the rule *bhuvo vaciḥ*, and by the rule *asyativakti* etc., there is the substitution of *aṭ* for *cli*; then by the rule *vaca um*, the augment *um* is added. Regarding *avasyavaḥ*: from the root *ava* (in the sense of protecting), the suffix *asun* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). Then, by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*, the suffix *kyac* is added; subsequently, by the rule *kyāc chandasi*, the suffix *u* is added. Regarding *havam*: [this is derived] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) when the prefix is absent.

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-avasyavaḥ*: "Desiring protection" (*avana* means protection). 2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-yad asmābhir uktam tan mitrādayo mama hantām* (with *ṭha*, *mahyantām*): "May Mitra and the others fulfill that which has been requested by us.
Thus, there is the substitution of *ap* and vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).

*Marutvān*: By the rule *jhayaḥ*, the *m* of the possessive suffix *matup* is replaced by *v*. By the rule *tasau matvarthe*, since there is an absence of *padatva* (word-status) due to the presence of *bhava*, there is an absence of *j* [i.e., no substitution of *j* for *t*].

The tenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “citraṃ,” is the seer Kutsa’s composition; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and has Sūrya as its deity. Thus it is enumerated: “‘citraṃ,’ [the first] verse is addressed to Soma. At the *āśvina* litany, the hymns dedicated to Sūrya are to be recited after sunrise.
In this regard, this hymn is to be recited;
and it has been formulated in the Sūtra: "‘Citraṃ devānām’, ‘namo mitrasya’" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.5).
The first three verses are, in order, the invitatory verses (*anuvākyās*) for the omentum, the sacrificial cake, and the oblation of the Surya animal sacrifice.
Following those, two are the offering verses (*yājyās*) for the omentum and the sacrificial cake.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘The brilliant countenance of the gods has risen’—these five [verses], and ‘Be gracious to us with your eye, be gracious to us by day’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

At the one-day sacrifice named Atimūrtti, at the Śunāsīrya, and at the seasonal festival (parvan), for the oblation to Sūrya: "The wondrous [beauty] of the gods," thus [it is said]. Sūrya approaches the radiant goddess Uṣas from behind, as a youth approaches a maiden. Wherein the god-seeking men extend the ages (yugas) toward auspiciousness for the sake of the auspicious. Sūrya approaches the radiant goddess Uṣas from behind, as a youth approaches a maiden. Wherein the god-seeking men extend the ages toward auspiciousness for the sake of the auspicious.

The Sun approaches the Goddess Uṣas from behind—her who is endowed with virtues such as generosity and who shines resplendently; that is, immediately after the appearance of the Dawn, he moves toward her.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a young man [approaching] his maiden."
It is just as when a certain man constantly follows a young woman with beautiful limbs as she walks.
When that dawn has arisen, the *naras*—the leaders of the sacrifice, the sacrificers who, desiring the gods, seek the shining Sun—[attain] the *yugas*.
The word *yuga* here denotes time.
And by that, the rites to be performed therein are indicated, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa;
[the word *tantra*] extends—that is, it elaborates—the rites such as the Agnihotra and others.
Or alternatively:

The sacrificial patrons (*yajamāna-puruṣāḥ*), desiring the gods—that is, seeking wealth for the purpose of sacrificing to the gods—stretch out the *yugas*, which are parts of the plow, for the sake of plowing.

The meaning is that [the Sun] follows after such [a path]. We praise the auspicious (*bhadram*) and beneficial (*kalyāṇam*) Sūrya; the ellipsis is "for the sake of auspicious fruit of action" (*bhadrāya karmaphalāya*).
Or rather:

desiring the gods (*devayantaḥ*), the sacrificers, becoming [renewed] age after age (*yugāni yugāni bhūtvā*) and accompanied by their wives, perform for the sake of prosperity (*bhadrāya*)—that is, for the sake of its fruit—the auspicious (*bhadram*) rite such as the *agnihotra* and so forth; they extend (*vitanvate*) it individually whenever that dawn (*uṣas-*) has set in.
*Maryaḥ*:
derived from the root *mṛṅ* (meaning "to die" or "to abandon life"),
this word is formed by the addition of the suffix *yat* according to rules such as *chandasi niṣṭyā* and others.
The initial udātta accent [of the word *anāvaḥ*] is due to the rule beginning with *yato 'nāvaḥ*.
[The word] *yugāni* [is derived from] the root *yuj-* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The word *yuga* [is derived] with the absence of the *guṇa* vowel and with an udātta accent on the final syllable, due to its inclusion among the *uṇhādi* suffixes in the rule *yugaśabdaḥ kālaviśeṣe rathādyupakaraṇe ca* (Uṇādisūtra 6.1.160).
[The root] *tan* [in the verb] *vitanvate* means "to expand" (*vistāre*).
By the rule *tanādikṛbhya uḥ*,
and by the separation of the *yoga* [of the sūtra] as *saha*, when there is a compound with a verbal prefix (*tiṅ-upasarga*), the final syllable of the compound is udātta by the rule *samāsasya*.

The auspicious, bay horses of the Sun—brilliant, dappled, and worthy of our praise—standing in homage, have mounted the back of heaven; in an instant, they traverse heaven and earth. Auspicious, bay horses of the Sun—brilliant, dappled, and worthy of our praise—standing in homage, have mounted the back of heaven; in an instant, they traverse heaven and earth. (3)
"Bhadrāḥ" means auspicious;
"aśvāḥ" and "etagvāḥ"—both of these are names for horses (*aśvanāman*).
Among them, one [term] should be applied as referring to the action (*kriyā*).

The horses of the Sun—swift, fleet-footed, or of a restless nature; greenish-yellow, meaning they are "seizers" (haritah); variegated, with diverse limbs; and "to be praised in succession," meaning they are to be gladdened by hymns one after another—such are the *etagvas*, the horses of Sūrya.
Alternatively, they are the horses that go along *etam*, the path to be traversed.
These horses, attaining this variegated color,
bowing down while being bowed to by us, have ascended— indeed, they reach— the back, the upper region characterized as the eastern part, of heaven, the intermediate space.
Or alternatively:

The green rays are of a nature to carry away the essence (rasa). 1. For the sake of the fruit of *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*. 2. In the manuscripts *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*, the word "devayantaḥ" is absent. 3. In the manuscripts *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*, the word "kalyāṇam" is absent. 4. In the manuscript *kṣa-ṭa*, there is the prefix *vi-* [before the root]. 5. In the manuscripts *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*, both [readings] occur. 6. In the manuscript *śa*, it is "etaṃ etavyam". 7. In the manuscript *kṣa-ṭa* it is "vā"; in *ṭha*, the word "mārgam" is absent. 8. In the manuscripts *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*, the word "prāpnuvanti" is absent; in *sa*, it is "āpnuvanti". 9. In the manuscripts *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-na-sa*, [the term is] "haraṇaśīlāḥ".

Distinguished by auspicious characteristics and other marks, they stand upon the back of heaven, the expanse of the sky. Having taken their stand, they traverse—that is, they go around and pervade—the two worlds, heaven and earth, immediately, at that very moment, in a single day. *Ashvāḥ*: from the root *aś* (to pervade), with the suffix *kan* according to the rule "aśi-muṣi... etc. *Etargvāḥ*: from the root *iṇ* (to go), with the suffix *tan* in the sense of the object according to the rule "asi-has-i... etc.; the suffix *ḍu* is added in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*) according to the *uṇādi* rules. They are so called because their movement (*gva*) is directed toward what is to be gone to (*etavya*). In this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member is retained. *Anumāthāsaḥ*: from the root *mad* (to praise) with the causative suffix (*ṣyan*), followed by the suffix *yat* according to the rule "aco yat"; it has the acute accent on the first syllable according to the rule "yato ’nāvaḥ" etc. *Namasyantaḥ*: the suffix *kyac* is added in the sense of worship according to the rule "namo-varivas-... etc.; by transposition, the suffix denoting the agent is used in the sense of the object. *Asthuḥ*: from the root *sthā*, the *luṅ* tense is used for the present in Vedic usage; the *sic* suffix is elided by the rule "gati-sthā-..."; the *jus* substitution for the *ṅe* ending occurs by the rule "ātaḥ".
Such is the divinity of the Sun, such his greatness: from the center of his work he has spread himself out;
when he has unyoked his bay steeds from their station, Night spreads her garment over him entirely.

That is the godhead of Sūrya; that is his greatness. At midday, he has gathered together what was spread out by the maker. As soon as he has unyoked his bay horses from their station, then Night spreads her garment over all.
That divinity— that is, lordship, meaning independence— of Sūrya, the Sun who impels all;
and that very greatness, magnitude, and majesty as well.
Because of the hearing of the word *tat*, the word *yat* is to be supplied; "that which" refers to the agent. This is a name for the object (*karman*).

While a work characterized by skill and so forth has been commenced but not yet completed, even in the midst of that unfinished task, the setting sun gathers together his own wide-spreading net of rays; as he goes to his setting, he withdraws them into himself from this world.
And the laborer likewise abandons the work he has begun but not yet finished upon seeing the sun going to its setting. Who other than the Sun possesses such independence and majesty?
It belongs to no one else;
only the Sun penetrates such independence and majesty.
Moreover, the word *it* is used here for emphasis.

When, at that very time, having taken up his green rays— which have the nature of carrying away moisture— from this earthly world, their common dwelling place (*sadhasthāt*), he unyokes them, making them joined elsewhere;
or rather, the root *yuj* itself, even when not preceded by the prefix *vi*, should be understood as having that sense.

As soon as he [the Sun] released his own rays from the *sadhastha*— whereby *sadhastha* means that which stands together (*saha tiṣṭhat*), namely the chariot— from that [chariot] he unyoked them. Immediately thereafter, Night, the darkness for the purpose of covering, came upon him.
The word *sima* is a synonym for *sarva* (all). The dative case is used here in the sense of the locative.
He "spreads" or extends [his light] throughout the entire world.
Or rather:
"vāsas" means the day, the bright period;
having removed that from this entire world, Night spreads out darkness.

Regarding this, it has been stated: "That is the divinity of the Sun, that is his greatness, that among the deeds being performed he is spread out and then withdrawn; when he has yoked his coursers, the green ones, he brings them back; then Night spreads her garment for him alone, and the young Dawn takes away the day from everyone" (Nirukta 4.11).
The word *mahitva* [is derived from] the root *maha*, meaning "to worship. The suffix *in* is added according to the *auṇādika* rules.
The rule "tasya bhāvas tvatalau" (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.119) applies here.
[The form] *madhyā* is derived from the word *madhya*; the substitution of *ḍā* for the seventh case singular ending is according to the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.39).
*Kartauḥ*:
[The form] *karotu* [is derived from the root *kṛ*] with the *uṇādi* suffix *sun*.
*Vitatam*: spread out.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*) to the root *as* preceded by the prefix *vi*.

Because the augment *iṭ* is optional after roots ending in *u* or *ī* when the suffix *ktvā* follows, there is a prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "yasya vibhāṣā. By the rule "the prefix [is unaccented] when not separated [by another word]," the prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
He bore [it].
The status of being a *bha*-stem is established by the rule "haprahorbhaḥ".
1. Distinguished by specific qualifiers such as *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *bhadra*; distinguished by the qualifier *sa-bhadra* and so forth. 2.
Of the impeller (*preraka*) of everything—*kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *na*, and *sa*.
3. Of that which has begun but is not yet completed—*ṭha*; of that which has been commenced but is not yet completed—*sa*.

4. [The suffix *ya*] follows *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *sa*, when preceded by *vi*. 5. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-amuñcata*: [This is derived from] *ayukta*. In the *laṅ* [present tense], there is the elision of *m* [of the root *yuj*] according to the rule “*jhalo jhali*”. *Sadhasthāt*: the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the rule “*ghañarthe kavidhānam*”. There is the substitution of *sadh-* [for *saha-*] according to the rule “*sadha mādasthayośchandasi*”. Because it belongs to the *dāsībhārādi* group, the original accent of the first member is maintained. *Rātrī*: the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule “*rātrerbhājasau*”.
In the lap of heaven, the Sun assumes the form of Varuṇa, his close friend, for all to behold.
One part of his radiant power is infinite and brilliant; the other is dark, which his bay steeds gather together.
In the lap of heaven, Sūrya assumes his form for the beholding of Mitra and Varuṇa; one part is infinite and bright, while his other radiant power is dark—the bay steeds bring them both together. 5.

Then, at the time of rising, for the purpose of manifesting toward all the world—characterized by both Mitra and Varuṇa—the Sun, the impeller of all, Savitṛ, creates his form: the light that defines and illuminates everything, in the lap, that is, in the midst of the sky.

Moreover, the sun's rays—golden-hued, or like horses whose nature is to carry away moisture—bring together [at daybreak] another light, distinct from darkness, which is infinite (without end), pervasive throughout the entire world, shining and white in color; for "pājaḥ" is a name for strength. This light is capable of overcoming even the exceedingly powerful nocturnal darkness; they bring it together by their arrival during the day.
Likewise, it makes the night black—that is, dark-colored—by its own departure;
since even its rays act in this way, what need is there to speak of its majesty? Thus is the praise of the Sun.
*Abhicakṣe*:
the suffix *kip* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) following roots such as *sam-pada*;
it retains the original accent of the final member of the compound (*kṛd-uttarapada-prakṛti-svaratvam*).
*dyauḥ* (heaven): by the rule *isisosra* (Pāṇini 6.1.110), there is the formation of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpatā*). *upasthe* (in the lap).
The suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule “*ghañarthe kavidhānam*” (Pāṇini 3.3.58).
Due to its inclusion in the *marudvṛdhādi* group, there is udātta accent on the final syllable of the first member of the compound.
[The form is] *pājaḥ*.

*Pājaḥ* means strength (*bala*), because it protects (*pāti rakṣati*). [This is derived] from the root *pāti* with the suffix *asun* and the augment *juṭ*, according to the rule *pāter bale juṭ ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.642). The elision of the possessive suffix *vin* is a Vedic anomaly.
O gods, at the rising of the sun today, deliver us from distress and from blame.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this.
Today, O gods, as the sun has risen, deliver us from distress and from reproach. May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this. 6.

O radiant gods, possessing the rays of the sun, at this very time, when the sun—the Āditya—has risen, you who spread yourselves here and there, deliver us from distress; having drawn us out from sin, protect us.
Whatever has been spoken by us, O Mitra and the other six deities, may you honor and approve that which belongs to us;
that is to say, may you guard it.
Mitra is the leader who protects from death; he is the god presiding over the day.
Varuṇa is the warder-off of what is undesirable; he is the presiding deity of the night.
Aditi is the inviolable or the undepressed mother of the gods.
The deity of Sindhu is the one who identifies with the flowing water;
the earth is [represented by] the letters kṣa, ṭa, ṭha, and the color green.
2. Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-ya: May the six deities, beginning with Mitra, protect (or, according to the Ṭa manuscript, worship) that which has been prayed for by us.

Dyaus is the presiding deity of the earth (bhūloka), [and] of the sky (dyuloka). The word *uta* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*). Regarding *agra*: the lengthening occurs in the *saṃhitā* by the rule *nipātasya ca*. Regarding *uditā*: from the root *i* with the prefix *ud*, the suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). The substitution of *ḍā* occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. By the rule *tādau ca*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the prefix *ut* is maintained. Regarding *pipṛt*: the root *pṛ* means "to protect" and "to fill"; according to some, it is simply *pṛ*. In the imperative (*loṭ*), there is elision of the suffix *śap* because the root belongs to the *juhotyādi* class. There follow reduplication (*dvirvacana*), the substitution of *u* for *ra*, and the elision of the remaining non-initial vowels (*ahalādiśeṣa*).
