In the seventeenth anuvāka, there are five hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of twenty-five verses, begins with "To the Nāsatyas.
By the greatness of Uśanas Kāvya, Kakṣīvat—the son of Dṛṣadvat and grandson of Dīrghatamas—is the seer (ṛṣi) of this hymn.
The meter is Triṣṭubh;
the deities are the Aśvins.
Thus it has been enumerated: "Nāsatyābhyām pañcādhikā: Kakṣīvān, the son of Devatamasa, impelled by Uśij, [composed] five [hymns] dedicated to the Aśvins."
According to the technical definition beginning with *tuhmādi*, these five hymns beginning with this one have the Aśvins as their deities.
In the *Prātaranuvāka* of the *Āśvina* ritual, within the *Triṣṭubh* metre, there are these three hymns beginning with this one.
This is prescribed in the section titled "Now the Āśvina" [in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra*]: "The three beginning with *prāvāṇeva nāsatyābhyām*" (Āśva. Śr. S. 4.15).
And these [verses] are to be recited during the Āśvina-śastra, because it is extended [to that context] by the rule: "according to the procedure of the Prātaranuvāka" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.5).
Like one who spreads the sacrificial grass, I offer these hymns to the two Nāsatyas; I send them forth like the wind driving grain.
You two, with your swift chariot, carried home the wife for Vimada, the son of Meṣa, as Senajit urged you on.

Like sacrificial grass, he chooses out the hymns for the two Nāsatyas; I send them forth like the wind driven by fire—those two who, with a chariot swift as an army, carried away the wife for the young Viḍmada.

Just as a certain sacrificer, for the sake of the sacrifice, *pra-vṛṅkte*— that is, he selects, cuts, and prepares the *barhis* (sacrificial grass), making it neither deficient nor excessive, but sufficient for the rite— so do I send forth, that is, I prepare and offer, hymns of praise (*stomān*) to the two *Nāsatyas*, the Aśvins. This very point is now clarified.
Just as the wind,
the air, repeatedly impels the waters contained within the clouds by means of the fires for the sake of rain, even so do I repeatedly impel hymns of praise toward the Aśvins.

What kind of Aśvins were they? For the sake of the young Arbhaga—known by the name Vimada, a royal seer who had obtained his wife through a *svayaṃvara*—when he arrived at the central region for the *svayaṃvara*, he was unable to fight with the other kings who had not obtained her. For him, the Aśvins—who, by means of their chariot that impelled the enemy army (*senājuvā*) and was difficult for enemies to assail (*duṣṭāpena*)—recovered his wife who had been seized by others; that is to say, they caused her to reach the house of him whose tongue was the enemy. It is for those two [Aśvins] that [the hymn is intended].
From the two Nāsatyas.
Those who exist among the good are "truthful" (satyau); those who are not truthful are "untruthful" (asatyau).

From this, *arbhakaḥ* [is derived].

‘The suffix *kan* is applied after [the word] *saṃjñā*’ (Pāṇini 5.3.87). 1. This is also formulated in the *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* manuscripts. 2. In the *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* manuscripts, it reads *āśvinaśastre*. 3. The letter *ga*. Another says: he sings (*gāyati*) or sounds forth (*śabdayati*) the child, thus he is *arbha-gaḥ*. [This is derived from] the roots *kai* and *gai* in the sense of "sound. With well-fashioned plates, with ornaments of gold, or with swift steeds, the two gods, the Nāsatyas, displaying their prowess,
won a thousand cattle from Yama in the contest for the prize.
With swift-winged steeds, or with those of golden hue, or with the coursers of the gods, the two Nāsatyas, exulting as they were, won a thousand at the contest of Yama in the prize-fight. 2.
Toward the firm-winged [birds]:
*vī* is a name for strength;
[the birds] with powerful, swift, and golden wings.
Swift-moving ones!
The word *vā* is used for conjunction.

O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, by means of such impetuses (*jūtibhiḥ*)—that is, the promptings (*preraṇaiḥ*)—of the gods, Indra and the others, you two, who are *śāśadānā*, that is, being exceedingly urged forward, possess a *vṛṣabha* (bull) as your vehicle, which was given by Prajāpati. In the *pradhana*, a battle where wealth is scattered, that bull won a thousand of the enemies of Vya-masya, the son of Vivasvat, in the contest (*āja*). He conquered them.
For Vaivasvata is pleased by battle, which is the cause of death for many.
Or rather,
the donkey, endowed with swift movement, conquered and won through victory that *ṛksahasra* (thousand verses) which had been established as something to be won by Prajāpati.
Having already won the race before the other gods, you two caused victory to be attained.
In this regard, the *Brāhmaṇa* passage beginning with "Prajāpati indeed gave his daughter to King Soma" (*Ai. Brā.* 4.7) should be consulted.
[The phrase] "with firm-footed [horses]" (*vīḷupattabhiḥ*).
Those that fly with firm strength are *vīḷupatmānaḥ*. Those that move swiftly are *āśuhemānaḥ*, for they go (*hinvanti*) quickly (*āśu*), that is, rapidly (*śīghram*).
*tai* (the root *tai*) means "to go" and "to increase. The suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule: "It is seen [applied] after other roots as well."

The word *jūtībhiḥ* has the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of its final member due to being a *kuduttarapada* compound. The acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the suffix *ktin* is established by the rule beginning with “*utiyūtijūti*” and so forth.
*Śāśadānā*:
[derived from] *śad*, meaning "to cut" (*śātane*).
Here, it has the sense of "to go," because verbal roots have multiple meanings.

From this [root] ending in *yat*, the suffix *śānac* is applied in place of *laṭ*. Because of the rule "in the Veda, both ways," it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; consequently, there is no substitution of *śap*. Then, the elision of the *at* and the elision of the *ya* take place.
In the word *abhymānādi*, there is the acute accent on the first syllable according to the rule *ādyudātta*.
In the form *ājā*, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has been replaced by a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
By that same rule, there is the substitution of *ḍ* [for *j*]:
*jigāya*.
[The root] *ji* means "to conquer."

O Aśvins, Tugra indeed brought Bhujyu out from the cloud, as no one else had carried him away like a swift horse.
You carried him across with self-propelled ships that glide through the atmosphere and are free from water.

Tugra, O Aśvins, [called] upon you for Bhujyu in the midst of the cloud; like a charioteer, no one could restrain that swift steed. You carried him away with ships endowed with life, gliding through the atmosphere, with waters flowing from within. 3.

1. *ṭha-sa-anabhitam*. 2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-ṛcāṃ sahasram*. 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-anyebhyo'pi*. 4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-balavat patanti utpatantīti*. 5. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa- ‘taiḥ’ nāsti*. 6. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-pata gatau; hi gatau*. [Note: *ī. 90* refers to a specific section]. Herein is this narrative: There was a certain royal seer named Tumburu, who was dear to the Aśvins.
Being utterly harassed by enemies dwelling on other continents, he dispatched his son Bhujyu along with an army by ship to conquer them.
That ship, having gone very far out into the middle of the ocean, was shattered by the force of the wind.
At that time, Bhujyu quickly offered praise to the Aśvins.

Having praised those two, they placed them along with their army upon their own ships and reached the presence of that father Tama in three days and nights; this matter is set forth by the first *ṛc* [of the hymn]. The word *ha* indicates well-known tradition.
Formerly, indeed, Tumra, being oppressed by enemies, for the sake of conquering them, [resorted to] Udamegha;
"Udamegha" means that which is sprinkled or moistened with waters, namely the ocean. In that [ocean], he caused his beloved son named Bhujyu to go by boat;
he sent him forth to travel across it.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

just as a certain man, being wealthy and greedy for riches, does not relinquish his *rayi*—that is, his wealth—so it was with him. O Aśvins, you two brought *Bhujyu*, who was submerged in the middle of the ocean, by means of ships to the presence of his father.
By what kind [of words]?
By those "possessing a self," meaning belonging to oneself—that is, belonging to the two of you.
Or alternatively:
The meaning is: “with those that sustain themselves” (dhṛtibhiḥ), that is, with those that hold [the water];

“filling the intermediate space” (antarikṣapṛdbhiḥ), because of their extreme transparency, they move only above the water in the atmosphere; “waterless” (apodakābhiḥ), because of their perfect cohesion, they are devoid of water—that is, water has not entered them.

*Udamegha*: [The root] *miha* means "to sprinkle. The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). By Pāṇini 7.3.53, *nyaṅkādīnāṃ ca*, there is *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *m*). By Pāṇini 6.3.50, *udakasyodaḥ saṃjñāyām*, *udaka* is replaced by *uda*. The final syllable of the second member is acute by the rule *thāthādinā* (Pāṇini 6.2.144). *Maghavān*: [The root] *mṛ* means "to abandon life. The suffix *kasu* is applied after the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Although the augment *iṭ* would normally apply due to the rule *kādi-niyamāt*, it is absent here because of the restrictive rule *vasvekājādghasām*. *Ahāḥ*: [The root] *ohāk* means "to abandon. In the aorist (*luṅ*), with the suffix *tip*, the substitute *sic* is applied. Because the rules regarding augments are not always mandatory (*anityatva*), the augment *maṅ* is not added. The absence of *iṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. The elision of *ti* occurs by the rule *hrasvādyaḥ*. Then the accent and *visarga* are applied. Alternatively, in a mantra, the *clerluk* is applied by the rule *mantre ghasa*. Since *clerluk* is present, *iṇ* is not added. *Naubhiḥ*: The case ending is acute by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. *Ātmanvatībhiḥ*: The suffix *matup* is added to *ātman*. The substitution of *v* occurs by the rule *mādupadhāyāḥ*. The *nud* is applied by the rule *ano nud* (Pāṇini 8.2.16). There is elision of *n*. The suffix *matup* is acute by the rule *hrasvanḍbhyāṃ matup*. *Antarikṣapṛbhiḥ*: [The root] *mṛ* means "to go. The suffix *kip* is applied by the rule *kip ca*.
Having traversed three nights and three days, O Nāsatyas,
you twice rescued Bhujyu with winged steeds across the dry expanse of the ocean, on its far shore, by means of three hundred-footed, spotted chariots.

Three nights, three days—by those who traverse them, O Nāsatyas, you carried Bhujyu with winged steeds across the dry and the wet expanse of the ocean, by means of three chariots having a hundred feet and six horses. 4.

O Nāsatyas, you two carried Bhujyu—who was submerged in the waters—along with his army, by means of three chariots that possess wings and travel through the air; having traversed three nights (three in number) and three days (occurring three times), passing over such a duration of time, you two carried him.

If this is said, it is because [you did so] in the midst of the ocean’s mass of water, in a desert-like place devoid of water (dhanvan), and on the shore of the ocean where it has become moistened by water (ārdrasya).
Of what kind were the chariots?
They were equipped with wheels having a hundred spokes as their characteristic feature, and they were yoked to six horses and six wheels.
*Tisraḥ*: by the rule *tricaturor striyām*, the word *tri* undergoes the substitution *tisṛ*;
and that [substitute] is accented on the final syllable.
In *acira ṛtaḥ*, because of the substitution of the letter *r* [for *ṛ*], the case ending receives the acute accent (*udāttatva*) by the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*.
In *kṣapaḥ*, the shortening of the final vowel of the case ending is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly.

Indeed, together with that; 2. from greed for wealth [beginning] with *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*; 3. above *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*; 4. by those [waters] devoid of water [beginning] with *kṣa* and *ṭa*; 5. throughout the time [beginning] with *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*; 6. likewise, of the moist [element] [beginning] with *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *nsa*.

Alternatively: in *śasi*, by the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "ātaḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *ā* even after [the suffix] *āt*. In *ahā*, there is the elision of the case-ending *śe* according to "śe chandasi bahulam. In *patatraiḥ*: from the root *pattṛ* in the sense of "going"; by the *uṇādi-sūtra* "paterañcu" (1.116). In *dhanvan*: from the root *dhavi*; [the suffix] *ara* is added; because it has the marker *it*, the augment *num* is applied; [the suffix] *kanin* is added by the rule beginning with "kaninyuvṛṣi" etc.; by "supāṃ suluk," there is the elision of the locative case ending. In *śatapadbhiḥ*: those whose feet are a hundred; by the rule "saṃkhyāsupūrvasya," there is the elision of the final member of the word *pāda* as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*). Since this [word *dhanvan*] is a *bha*-stem due to its initial status, there is the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* according to "pādaḥ pat. Alternatively, the word *paccha* should be regarded as a different base having the same meaning as *pāda*.
O Aśvins, you displayed your heroism in the supportless, shoreless, and bottomless ocean when you carried Bhujyu away,
who had boarded a ship equipped with a hundred oars.

When there was no foothold, when there was no support, no place to stand, and no means of grasping, in the midst of the ocean, O Aśvins, you carried Bhujyu home, who had boarded a ship with a hundred oars. ||5||

O Aśvins, you two performed that heroic deed in the ocean which was without support—devoid of anything to hold onto. He clarifies this very lack of support: "in the placeless" (*anāsthāne*). That which is stood upon is a "place" (*āsthāna*), namely a region of land; the meaning is "in that which is devoid of such, in water where it is impossible to stand. "Without a hold" (*agrabhaṇe*) means without anything to grasp; the meaning is "in that where even branches or the like to be grasped by the hand do not exist. What, then, was that deed? Having caused Bhujyu—who had boarded a ship with a hundred oars, a ship with many oars (whereby the ship moves swiftly when much water is displaced by the sides through those wooden oars)—to reach "Asta," this being a name for home, you two brought him to his father’s house when he was satisfied. The meaning is that you two performed that which is difficult to accomplish in the midst of the ocean. Regarding *anārambhaṇe*: "that which is begun" is *ārambhaṇa*. By the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). By the rule *nañsubhyām*, the final syllable of the compound is udātta. Regarding *abīrayethām*: the root *śūra/vīra* means "to be valiant"; it belongs to the *curādi* class and is *ātmanepadin*. The suffix *lyuṭ* and the accentuation for *anāsthāna* and *agrabhaṇa* are as before; however, there is a difference in the meaning. [The word] *hmahomaiḥ* is from the root *bhū*. Regarding *asta*: "in which everything is cast" (*asyate*) is *asta*, the home. The suffix *tan* is applied by the rule *asihasi*, etc. Regarding *śatāritrām*: the root *ṛ* means "to go. By the rule *artilūtrasū* (Pāṇini 3.2.184), the suffix *inan* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member remains. || 8 ||
O Aśvins, you two gave a white horse to Aghāśva from here for all time. That gift of yours was great and worthy of praise; it became a prize-winning steed, ever to be invoked by the pious man.

That white horse which you two, O Aśvins, gave to Aghaśva, from that time forth has been a constant blessing; that gift of yours is great and worthy of praise. The steed of Pedu has ever been to be invoked by the noble man. 6.

In this regard, the following story is told: There was a certain man named Pedu who praised the Aśvins. Being pleased with him, they gave him a white horse, and that horse brought about his great victory. This is what is set forth here: O Aśvins, you two [gave] to Aghaśāsa...

Having explained [the preceding], regarding the king Pedunānna, those two who gave him this white-colored horse—may that horse always (*śaśvat*) and eternally (*nityam*) bring him well-being (*svasti*), the auspicious mark of victory (*jayalakṣaṇa*).
O you two, that gift of yours—great, vast, and profound, and for that very reason praiseworthy (*kīrtenya*), to be celebrated by all, and excellent—has come to be.
Therefore, the horse (*vājī*)—belonging to Pedu (*paidaḥ*), meaning either related to Pedu or swift-moving; the one who impels the enemies or is to be impelled in battles;
the one possessing vigor (*vejanavān*)—is always (*sadam*) to be invoked (*havya*) by us as well.

O Heroes, for the praising Kakṣīvat, son of Pajra, you two brought forth abundant wisdom;
from the hoof of the stallion Kārotara, you poured out a hundred jars of surā-liquor.
O Heroes, for Kakṣīvat Pajra who praises you, you dug out abundant wealth; from the hoof of a stallion marked with a horn-like protuberance, you poured forth a hundred jars of wine. 7.
Regarding this, there is the following narrative: In ancient times, the seer Kakṣīvat, his knowledge being obscured by darkness, praised the Aśvins for the sake of wisdom;
the Aśvins then bestowed upon him inspired intelligence.
Thus it says: "O men," that is, O leaders, the Aśvins; "you two" refers to you both [for] Pajra.
"Pajra" is a name for the Aṅgirases, because of the traditional scriptural statement: "The Aṅgirases are indeed Pajras."
For Kakṣīvat, who was born in their lineage—
*kakṣī* meaning a rope, and he being one who possesses it—

for him, for that person so named, for you two who offer praise, performing a hymn of praise, you two have carved out (*aradat*), that is, you two have inscribed, the great *purandhī*, the intellect or thought that has been brought forth.
The meaning is that he has acted in such a way that [his speech] becomes the range for all purposes.
Furthermore, it is from *kārotara*.
A *kārotara* is a specific kind of vessel made of split bamboo and covered with a cloth, in which the distillation of liquor (*surā*) is performed.
This is an elliptical comparison (*luptopama*).

Just as those who prepare liquor extract it from the *kārottara* [fermenting vessel], even so did you two pour out a hundred jars—that is, countless pots—of liquor from the hoof, that is, the hoof of your own vigorous horse, capable of sprinkling [semen].
Or alternatively:
The root *siñcati* means "to fill.
From the horse's hoof, which serves as a strainer (*kārotara*), the liquor flows; with that, you two poured—that is, filled—an innumerable number of jars.
The meaning is: for those people who request liquor from you in rituals such as the *sautrāmaṇī*.
"Stuvate": from the root *stu*, the present indicative (*laṭ*) takes the suffix *śatṛ*; due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
In the phrase ‘śataranumaḥ’, the case ending is udātta. Regarding *pajrāya*:
the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the word *pajra* by the rule governing residual formations (*śeṣika*).
For Kakṣīvat:
by the rule "āsandi-dadhivat-cakrīvat-kakṣīvat," there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the word *kakṣin* and the substitution of *v* for *n*.
He dug.
*Puraṃdhim*: [the word] *puraṃdhi* is used in the sense of "scratching" (*vilekhana*). Yāska states: "*Puraṃdhi* is one who possesses abundant wisdom" (Nirukta 6.13).
The form *puraṃdhri* arises from its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular formations].
Alternatively,
*puraṃdhri* refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), because in it (*asyām*) all objects of the senses (*sarvaviṣayajātam*), which are to be filled (*pūraṇīyam*), are placed (*dhīyate*) or established.
The suffix *ki* is applied to the root *dhā* by the rule *karmaṇy adhikaraṇe ca*;
the absence of elision (*aluk*) is due to the word *bahulam* (‘frequently’) in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam*.
However, this is merely an etymological derivation; in reality, the word belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
"You two sprinkled.
The root *ṣic* (in the form *siñc*) means "to flow" or "to sprinkle";
it belongs to the *taudādi* class.
The augment *num* is applied by the rule *śe mucādīnām*.

1. ṭa-ṭha-ahatāśyāya | 2. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha—there is no ‘vā’. 3. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha—in. 4. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha—ayam. 5. kṣa-ṭa—nirodhitajñānaḥ. 6. kṣa-ṭha-ṭha—kuleṣu. 7. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha—the accomplisher accomplishes that: "With snow you two warded off the burning fire; you bestowed upon him nourishing vigor. O Aśvins, you rescued Atri from the cleft of the earth; you brought back Muni with his entire troop in safety."
With snow, you two warded off the burning heat; you bestowed upon him nourishing strength. O Aśvins, you raised up Atri, who had been cast into the pit, together with all his followers, in safety. 8.
In this regard, there is this narrative:
The Asuras imprisoned the seer Atri in a torture-chamber with a hundred doors and afflicted him with fire.
Then these two Aśvins, being praised by that seer, extinguished the fire with water and led him out from that chamber of suffering, his faculties entirely unimpaired.
This is now explained:

O Aśvins, you two warded off—that is, you extinguished and cooled—the glowing embers of chaff-fire (*tuṣāgni*) cast by the Asuras for the purpose of harming Atri with *himena*, meaning with snow-cold water. Furthermore, for this Agni, who had become emaciated due to the oppression of the Asuras, [you brought] his father...

In this regard, here is a minor narrative: Once, while the sage Gautama was wandering in a desert region, the Aśvins dug up a well located in another land and brought it to him. Having brought that well, they placed it with its opening above and its base below, for the sake of providing ease in bathing, drinking, and so forth. This is what is said: O *anāsatyā*, you two whose nature is truth, leaders of truth, or born from the nose—O Aśvins known by this name—you two *avatam* [protected]. This is a name for a well. You pushed that well downward and then *parānudethām*, you sent it toward the vicinity of the sage Gautama. Immediately after that, you *cakrathuḥ*, you fashioned that well as being characterized by such qualities: *ujjābujham*, that whose base (*jubha*) is held up (*ujja*) on both sides; *jihvabāram*, that whose opening (*bāra*) is curved (*jihva*) because it is held down at the bottom. From that well, *āpaḥ*—and also *naḥ* (waters)—flowed out in a stream for the *pāyanāya*, the purpose of drinking, of *tṛpyate*, the thirsty Gautama. For what kind of man? For *rāye*, the one who has given oblations, for *sahasāya*, the enduring one; or rather, for wealth (*rāye*) numbering in the thousands, and for the sake of obtaining such wealth, they flowed out. *Anudethām*: from the root *ṇud* in the sense of "impelling," belonging to the Taudādika class. *jihvabāram*: the substitution of *bāra* for the word *dvāra* occurs because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. *kṣaran*: from the root *kṣar* in the sense of "moving. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "in the Veda, there is frequently no *aṭ* even when preceded by *mā*" (*bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge'pi*). The *śap* suffix is unaccented because it is marked with *p*; thus, by the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*, the accent of the root remains. *pāyanāya*: the causative suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of "causing to drink" (*hetumati*). The suffix *yuk* is applied according to the rule "after *jñā*, *śās*, *dhā*, etc. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). *rāye*: from the root *rā* in the sense of "giving. One who gives (*rāti*) is *rāḥ*. The suffix *uṇ* is applied according to the Unādi Sūtra 2.224. The case-ending is accented because of the rule "for *uṇ*, *iṭ*, and *am*. *tṛpyate*: from the root *tṛp* in the sense of "thirst. The suffix *śyan* is added, then the present participle suffix *śatṛ*. The suffix *śyan* is accented because it is marked with *ni*. The dative case is used in the sense of "purpose" according to the Vārttika: "The fourth case should be stated in the sense of *padārtha* (purpose). O Nāsatyas, you released Vṛtra from the curse like a garment from Cyavāna;
you prolonged the life of the abandoned man from the Daśa, and you restored the eyesight of the blind.
O Nāsatyas, you released Vṛtra from the wrathful man like a garment; you prolonged the life of Cyavāna when he was abandoned. O Dastras, you then made him the husband of the Kuntīs.
In this regard, there is this [account]:

when the sage was overcome by wrinkles, grey hair, and other signs of age, his limbs decayed and his ears and mouth failing, he was abandoned by his sons and others; he then praised the Aśvins, saying, "O sons of Aśvin, remove old age from this sage and grant him youth once again."
This is what [the text] says:

O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, from Cyavāna—the seer named Cyavana—who was *ajuruṣaḥ* (worn out/aged), you two *prāmuñcatam*, that is, you released with excellence the *vṛtim*, the decrepitude that remained enveloping his entire body.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
"Like a cloak"— *drāpi* is a name for armor.
Just as someone, having put on armor that covers the entire body, subsequently separates it from the body, so too [is this].
Moreover, O Aśvins, you who are called Adastras—meaning "the two handsome ones"—extended the life-span, that is, the longevity, of the seer who had been abandoned by his sons and others;
the root *tṛ* preceded by *pra* has the sense of increasing.
Immediately thereafter (*āt*), you made him young again, the husband and lord of maidens (*kanīnām*).
*Juruṣaḥ*:
[derived from] *jṛṣ* in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohānau*);
[the suffix] *kasuḥ* [is applied] in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The substitution of *u* occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Vedic usage is diverse). There is reduplication.
In the singular ablative case, the semivowel is vocalized (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam."
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca.
*Vatrim*.
[The root is] *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*).
The suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule "āhagamahana. [This refers to] that which has been abandoned (*jahitasya*).
[The root] *ohāk* means "to abandon."

The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied to the object (*karman*). Because it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* by the rule "in the Veda, both ways," the suffix *yak* is added. Of that [suffix], [the elision occurs] "frequently in the Veda."

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-jñātuḥ* (of the knower). 2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-prāpyatām* (let it be attained). 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-kuṭilam* (crookedness). 4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-bārabhāvaḥ* (the state of being a burden). 5. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa-pāyanāya* (for the sake of drinking); [from] the root *pā* in the sense of "drinking" (*pāne*), thus *bhluḥ*;
by the rule *jahāteśca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.116), there is shortening [of the vowel].
Regarding *kanīnām*: by virtue of the rule "the [final vowel] of *rayi* and *matu* is frequently [lengthened]" (*rayimaṃtau bahulam*), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the word *kanyā* here.
Then, O Nāsatyas, men praise that praiseworthy, successful, and desirable protection of yours, when you two,
having seen it like a hidden treasure, brought it to light for Vandana.

Therefore, O Heroes, Nāsatyas, that protection of yours which is worthy of praise, worthy of attainment, and full of favor—since you two, being wise, brought it forth like a hidden treasure for Vandana from its concealment, do you now reveal it. 11.
In this regard, there is this narrative: There was a certain person named Vandana;
he was cast into a well by the asuras.
The Aśvins praised him as he was sinking like a horse in a pit;
then the Aśvins drew him out from the well.
Regarding that, it is said:

"O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, you two who are the leaders of men toward health—your deed, which is connected with seeking aid (*abhiṣṭimat*), attainable through the pressing of Soma (*ābhisutyena*), as well as the protection (*avarūtham*) that is desirable and longed for—that deed is to be praised by us, it is to be extolled, and it is to be accomplished.
But what, then, is that deed?

"O wise ones, you two who know—like a treasure (*nidhi*) or wealth (*dhana*) deposited and hidden (*apagūḷham*) in a deserted place, namely in the middle of a well, concealed by the Asuras—you raised up (*ut ūpathuḥ*) for Vanda the seer (*vandana ṛṣim*), having been shown [the way] out of that well which was unseen by thirsty travelers.
Such is the meaning: that this very act of raising him from the well."
*Śaṃsyam*. From the root *śaṃs* in the sense of "to praise," with the suffix *ṇi* added, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *aco yat*.

The word *anāvaḥ* has its initial syllable udātta according to the rule "yato ’nāvaḥ. [The word] *abhiṣṭimat* is derived from the root *iṣ* (meaning "to go") preceded by the prefix *abhi*, with the suffix *ktin* added in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
Why is there not an acute accent (*udāttatva*) on the word *vṛṣan* in the compound *mantravṛṣan*?
It is because that very accent remains by virtue of the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*).
Furthermore, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs by virtue of its inclusion in the *śakandhvādi* group.

Because of the rule "tādau ca," the accent of a *gati* [particle] does not apply here, since all rules [of accentuation] are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Following that, there is the suffix *matup*.
Since the word ending in it is oxytone, the vowel following it receives the acute accent by the rule "hasvajaḍabhyām."
A protection;
[formed] by the rule "ūthan after the roots jṛ and vṛ"; the two who know.
The vowel *ā* is the substitution for the case-ending according to the rule "supām suluk... [Pāṇini 7.1.39]. *Apagūḍham*: from the root *guhū*, meaning "to conceal."
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied after the verbal root *kṛ*.

By the rule "yasya vibhāṣā," there is a prohibition of the augment *iṭ*. Then follow the substitution of *hatva*, the substitution of *dharatva*, the substitution of *vaṣṭva*, the elision (*lopa*) of the *da*, and the lengthening (*dīrgha*).

In the expression "gatiranantaraḥ," the word *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) because it has been shown [to be a *gati*] by the rule beginning with "bhṛmṛdṛśi" and so forth, which prescribes the suffix *ac*.
*ūpathuḥ*.
[The root] *ḍuvap* [is used in the sense of] "the continuous spreading of seeds or threads.
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), with the suffix *athus*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the *yajādi* group.
The dual and other case endings [are used].
In the word *vandanāya*, the fourth case ending is applied because the object (*karman*) functions as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), according to the rule: "The mention of the action must be made."

Then men shall perceive my fierce deed; I make it manifest like thunder making rain manifest, since the Atharvan milked the honey from you both with the head of a horse, when he proclaimed this to you.

Therefore, O heroes, I make manifest for you that ancient, powerful deed, as thunder makes rain manifest—since the Atharvan milked from the head of the horse that honey which he proclaimed to you. 12.
On this point there is the following narrative:
Indra, having instructed Dadhyañc in the Pravargya-vidyā and the Madhu-vidyā, said, "If you shall teach this to another, I will cut off your head.
Thereupon, the Aśvins, having cut off the horse's head and severed Dadhyañc's own head, set it aside elsewhere.
1. Struck down by *kṣa* and *ṭha*. 2. That which is concealed by *kṣa* and *ṭha*.
3. In the continuum of the seed-syllable *ṭha*.
Thereupon, the two Aśvins fitted that head back onto him.
And with that head, Dadhyañc taught the Aśvins the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the Yajus-formulas pertaining to the Pravargya rite, as well as the Brāhmaṇa text expounding the Madhu-vidyā.
Indra, having learned of this, struck off that head with his thunderbolt.
Now, it is explained at length in the *Śāṭyāyana* and *Vājasaneyi* [Brāhmaṇas] that the two Aśvins restored his own human head;
this very point is set forth here:
O *nara*, O two heroes, O Aśvins, your union was fierce, a deed difficult to perform for those who pride themselves on their woolly [strength].
This is the name of the action:
that action performed by you two in the past for the sake of winning (*sanaye*), that is, for the purpose of acquiring wealth (*dhanalābhārtha*), I make manifest (*āviṣkṛṇomi*), I reveal.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Just as the sound residing in a cloud, by means of raining down, makes manifest everywhere the rain—the water existing within the cloud—so it is here.
What is that action?
When indeed the seer named Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, by means of the horse's head—a head provided through your power—to you two [Aśvins] this very Madhu-vidyā... [he revealed].

In the rule *āto maninkvanipvanipaśca*, the suffix *manin* is applied. By the rule *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇāccheyāḍāḍyāyājālaḥ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending. [The form] *śrutam* [is derived from the root] *śru*; in the *laṅ* tense, by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge’pi*, there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*. [The forms] *śāsuḥ* and *śāstuḥ* [are derived from] the root *śās* in the sense of "instruction" (*anuśiṣṭau*). By the rule *śaṃśiśaśisāśi* (Uṇādisūtra 2.250), the suffix *tṛn* is applied in the sense of a name (*saṃjñāyām*). There is an absence of the augment *iṭ*. The elision of *tal* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
From the jaws of the wolf, O heroes, O Nāsatyas, you released the quail in the encounter;
and you, O lords of many enjoyments, made the lamenting seer see clearly once more.
From the mouth of the wolf, O heroes, Nāsatyas, you released the quail in the encounter; and indeed, O lords of many enjoyments, you made the lamenting seer see clearly.
The *vartikā* is the female of a bird resembling a sparrow.
It is said that in ancient times, when she was seized by a dog in the forest, the two Aśvins liberated her;
this very fact is stated [in the following verse].

O leaders, you two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins—you both—released Vartikā, who is like a sparrow, from the mouth of Vṛka, the wolf, in the battle that had arrived against Vṛka and Vikartaka. Yāska said: "Vartikā is the Dawn (uṣas), for she turns again and again, returning every day."
"May the Aśvins release her from the mouth of that Sun, who is like a wolf—a concealer and an obstructor—who has seized her while illuminating the entire world.
Furthermore, O you two of many enjoyments, great arms, or many hands, you indeed made the blind seer named Kavi—him who was praising you out of compassion—capable of seeing clearly once more.
*Āsnaḥ*: By the rule beginning with *‘apahna’*, *āsya* is replaced by *āsna*.

When the vowel *a* is elided by the rule *‘allopo’naḥ’*, the case ending becomes acute according to the rule *‘ūḍidam’*, which prescribes the acute accent (*udāttatva*) for a case ending following a word ending in *ūṭh* or *idam*.

He released him. From the root *muc*, with the sense of the causative (*ṇic*) included within it, the suffix is elided in the *laṅ* tense according to the rule "there is frequent elision of the verbal suffix in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
[The word is] *kṛpamāṇam*.
The root *kṛp* (meaning "to praise") is to be found among the *tud*-class roots.
When the accent of the *vikaraṇa* suffix would otherwise apply, the rule “*vṛṣādīnāṃ ca*” (Pāṇini 6.1.203) prescribes that the initial syllable is udātta. [Thus:
*vicakṣe*.
The suffix *sen* is applied by the rule "tumarthe śeṣena"; the letter *s* is elided by the rule "skoḥ saṃyogādyoḥ."
For you two cut through the full course of the enemy in the contest for the prize;
instantly, with your wealth, you provided a noble shank for Viśpalā to run forth.

Indeed, like the flight of a bird, your conduct was unbroken; in the full assembly, while the game was being played, you instantly restored the noble thigh to Viśpalā so that she might run swiftly for the sake of her wealth. 15.
There was a king named Khela, who had Agastya as his domestic priest.
A woman related to him, named Viśpalā, had her foot severed by enemies in battle.
Praised by the priest Agastya, the Aśvins arrived at night and restored her with an iron foot.

This he says: "In the battle of Ājī, [the hymn] of Viśpalā, who was related to Khela whose domestic priest was Agastya; her *caritra* (deed/footing) was like that of a *veḥ*—that is, of a bird (specifically, according to some, a sparrow).

[Notes: 1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: of the one named *caṭaka* (sparrow). 2. *sa*: of the *vikarṣaka*. 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: the *caṭakalī*. 4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: having covered the entire world with light. 5. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa*: of the word *āsya*. 6. *ca-ṇa-pha*: a royal seer (*rājarṣi*). 7. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa*: she, in the battle. 8. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*: "they two placed together" (*samadhattām iti*).
Like the wing or feather of a bird, it was indeed cut; for in former times it had been severed. O Aśvins, being praised by Agastya, you two were present at the *paritakmyā*.
The night is *paritakmyā*. Yāska [states] (*Nirukta* 11.25): “It stretches around her (*parita enāṃ takati*).
Its meaning is that the sun moves on both sides of her.

Having arrived at night, they immediately—while the wealth was still being placed among the enemies as a prize to be won and while the territory remained to be conquered—they fitted an iron leg (an iron limb characterized by a shank) for Viśpalā so that she might go to the soma-pressing;
that is to say, they performed the joining, the unification [of her foot]. This is the narrative.
In the word *ārtīladhūs-khana-sahacara*, the suffix *itra* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
[The form] *ājā* results from the substitution of the case ending with *dā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
[The word] *āyasī* [is formed as follows]: from the word *ayas*, by adding the suffix *añ* in the sense of a secondary derivative (*adhikāra*), according to Pāṇini 4.3.145 (*aprāṇirajatādibhyo 'ñ*).
Then, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.15 (*ṭiḍḍhāñ*).
To him who had cut up a hundred rams for the she-wolf, R̥jāśva—who was blind—his father made whole.
To him, O Nāsatyas, you two Dastras, the physicians, bestowed eyes that see clearly, according to his desire.

He who was carving out a hundred rams for the she-wolf—him, R̥jāśva, his father made blind. To him, O Nāsatyas, you two, the wonder-workers and physicians, bestowed eyes that see clearly, O Dastras. 16.
The son of Vṛṣāgir was a royal sage named Ṛjāśva.
Near him, a donkey that served as the vehicle for the Aśvins stood transformed into a female wolf.
For her food, he slaughtered and gave to her one hundred and one sheep belonging to the citizens who were his own subjects.
This is because it is seen in another mantra: “Ṛjāśva [gave] one hundred and one rams” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.117.18).
Thus, when the son engaged in what was harmful to the Pauras, his father deprived him of his eyesight by means of a curse.
Thereupon, the Aśvins, who were aware that his blindness had arisen from their seizing him, bestowed two eyes upon him.
This is what [the author] says:
here, because of the hearing of the word *tat* (that), the word *yat* (which) is to be supplied.
He who, having cut into pieces a hundred—that is, a number of one hundred—rams, gave them to Vṛkī, the female wolf whom he himself had nourished, him, the devourer (*cakṣadāna*), [he slew].
The root *kṣad* means "to eat," but here it has the sense of "cutting into pieces.
Having cut [the horse] into pieces and given them [to him], his father made Ṛjāśva blind, devoid of sight, by means of a curse.
O Nāsatyas—those whose nature is truth, who are not other than Truth, the two physicians who serve as the healers of the gods!
According to the Vedic revelation, "The Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods" (AiB 1.18; TS 2.3.11).

O Aśvins—known as the Dastras, meaning "the beautiful ones"—O you who are free from injury (*anarvan*), bestow (*ādhattam*) upon that Ṛjāśva two eyes (*akṣī*) capable of seeing clearly (*vicakṣe*) toward what is to be seen, which were previously deprived of sight due to a father’s curse.
[Bestow them] for Vṛkī.
A *vṛka* is a wild dog;
its female is a *vṛkī*. The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 4.1.63: "The suffix *ṅīṣ* is added after a genus name (*jāti*) that does not denote a feminine."

By the rule *jasādiṣu cchandasi vāvacanam*, there is an option regarding the fourth case singular; when the augment *āṬ* is absent, the *yaṇ* substitution applies, and by the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*, the following unaccented vowel becomes circumflex (*svarita*).
[The form is] *cakṣadānam*.
[This is derived from] the root *kṣad-* with the suffix *kānac* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The word *akṣī* has a long vowel;
for, by the rule "īṃ ca dvivacane" (Pāṇini 7.1.77), the substitution of the vowel *ī* for the final syllable of the word *akṣan* takes precedence [over other rules].
And that [suffix] is udātta.

Once that has been applied, by the paribhāṣā "when two operations apply simultaneously, the one which is prohibited [by a subsequent rule takes effect]" (Paribhāṣā 40), the *num* augment does not occur again. Thus:
*vicakṣe*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *cakṣ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad-ādi* formations.
*Anarvan*:
[from] the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go."
Because the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* in the rule *asmād anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante* serves to subsume other suffixes, the suffix *vanip* occurs here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).

In the compound *arvāg-vanī*, since these two [suffixes] do not exist with respect to the object of going (*gamana*), it is a *bahuvrīhi*; by the rule *nañ-subhyām*, the final syllable of the latter member is udātta.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the dual ending.

The absence of the elision of *n* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). 1. The suffix *itrac* is added after *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*. 2. [The form] *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-asya*. 3. [The form] *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-aśvinau*. 4. There is the substitution of *sa* for *yaṇ*. 5. Regarding *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha*, the phrase "because of the word *akṣa*" does not exist. 6. [The form] *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-anayoḥ*.
"The daughter of Sūrya mounted upon your chariot, as if upon a wooden pole, winning with her swift movement."
All the gods approved with their hearts; you two, O Nāsatyas, are united with glory.
The daughter of Sūrya mounted your chariot like a branch upon a tree, winning it with her horse. All the gods approved in their hearts; O Nāsatyas, you are united with glory. 17.
Savitṛ desired to give his daughter Sūryā to King Soma. All the gods sought her hand in marriage;
they said to one another:
"Taking the sun as our limit, let us run a race;
whoever among us wins shall possess this [victory].
Thereupon, the Aśvins won.
And she, Sūryā, ascended the chariot of those two who had won.
In this regard, the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with “Prajāpati gave his daughter to King Soma” (AiB 4.7) should be consulted.
Furthermore, this narrative is [connected] with the hymn *Satyenottabhitā bhūmiḥ* (ṚV 10.85.1), which praises the marriage of Sūryā.

The first member of the compound [bharadvāja] has the acute accent on its initial syllable. Regarding *bharadvājāya*: from the root *bhṛñ* in the sense of "bearing" (*bharaṇe*), the suffix *śatṛ* is added in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) with the indeclinable particle *avyaya*. Because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the root is treated as archaic (*ārṣa*), and since the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes do not lose their accent, the suffix itself takes the acute accent on its initial syllable. In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) prevails. Regarding *hayantā*: from the root *hej* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), the suffix *śatṛ* is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. After the addition of the suffix *śap*, there is the substitution of *ay* for *e* as a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Regarding *revat*: from the word *rayi*, the suffix *matup* is added. There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *rayermatau bahulam*. By the rule *chandasīraḥ*, the *m* of *matup* becomes *v*. According to the rule *rayiśabdācca* (Kāśikā 6.1.176.1), the suffix *matup* retains its acute accent. Regarding *sacanaḥ*: from the root *paca* in the sense of "serving" (*sevane*), the suffix *yuc* is added according to the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ*. Regarding *yuktā*: the case ending is replaced by *ā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
O Nāsatyas, bringing wealth, a good kingdom, offspring, long life, and heroic vigor,
you have caused the Jāhvavī to flow;
she was a barren cow (starīḥ) due to the lack of power for procreation.
The suffix *ī* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.4.38 (*avitṛstanitanmaya iḥ*).

Since the rule *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.106) allows for the optionality of the single-substitute *pūrva-rūpa* (the preceding vowel) before the case-ending *am*, its absence results in the *yaṇ*-substitution (*avītī*).
By the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.4), the following unaccented vowel becomes circumflex (*svarita*).
*pipyathuḥ*. [The root] *pyāyī* [is used] in the sense of “to grow.
In the *liṭ* [perfect tense], the *parasmaipada* ending is applied by virtue of the [Vedic] substitution *bhyas*.
The substitution of *pī* occurs by the rule *liṅya-hodhra* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.29).

To the one seeking aid, to the one who praises, to the noble Kṛṣṇīya, and to the one moving straight forward—with your powers, O Nāsatyas—you gave Viṣṇāpū back to Viśvaka, like a lost animal, so that he might see him again. 23. To the one seeking aid; to the one who praises; to the noble Kṛṣṇīya; to the one moving straight forward; O Nāsatyas; with your powers; like a lost animal; as if for the sake of seeing; Viṣṇāpū; you gave; to Viśvaka. 23.
To one who desires protection— that is, one who wishes for his own preservation—
to one who praises— that is, to one who performs praise— [the root] *kṛ* [is applied].

The Adhvaryu priest raises—that is, he lifts upwards—the [oblation] situated within the vessel by means of the *sruva* spoon; it is just like that. *Avanaddham*: from the root √*ṇaha* "to bind. The suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). By *Pāṇini Sūtra* 8.2.34, *naho dhaḥ*, the *n* of *naha* becomes *dh*. By *Pāṇini Sūtra* 8.2.40, *jhapastathordhaḥ*, the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix becomes *dh*. By *Pāṇini Sūtra* 6.2.49, *gatiranantaraḥ*, the prefix (*gati*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). *Kathitam*: from the root √*katha* "to injure" (or "to strike"). The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied. *Vimuktam*: from the root √*muc* "to release. The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied. In *avanaddha*, the accents of the suffixes are as previously stated. There is an option for the substitution of *l* by virtue of the class beginning with *kapilaka*. *Udani*: by the rule beginning with *udakasyodaḥ peṣam-vāsa-paṇyeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.1.52), the word *udaka* undergoes the substitution of *udan*. 3.
I have proclaimed your wondrous deeds, O Aśvins; may I be the master of this [wealth], possessing easy-going strength and noble sons.
And seeing the long life of Śvavandī, may I reach my full measure of years before I am worn out by old age.

I have proclaimed your wondrous deeds, O Aśvins. May I be the lord of this [wealth], possessing good fortune and noble sons; and beholding long life, may I reach old age here, possessed of horses. 25.
Having thus praised the greatness of the Aśvins with this hymn, the seer of the mantra now prays for his own desired object:
"O Aśvins, I have proclaimed aloud (*pra vocam*) your deeds (*daṃsāṃsi*) performed in the past;
having spoken thus, may I become the lord (*pati*), the sovereign ruler (*adhipati*), of that kingdom, being possessed of excellent cattle (*su-gavaḥ*) and excellent heroes (*su-vīraḥ*)."
Furthermore, "seeing with the eyes" means seeing;
this is an elliptical expression [for] seeing with all the sense faculties capable of perceiving their respective objects.

May the wind, assuming the form of a long hundred years, extend my life; and as a master enters his own home free from thorns, so may I reach old age—that is, may I attain a state of aging devoid of thorns—and being thus aged, may I dwell for a long time. This is the meaning.
May I be. The suffix *liṅ* is used for the optative (*prārthanā*) of the root *as* (to be). [The augment] *yāsuṭ* [is added].
By the rule "śasoralopaḥ," there is the elision of the letter *a*. Thus, *aśvavat*.
[The root] *aś* is used in the sense of pervading (*vyāptau*).
The suffix *śat* is used in the reverse order [to form a present participle]. [The word] *jarimāṇam* [is derived from the root] *jṛṣ*, meaning "the loss of vitality" (*vayohānau*).
From this [root], the suffix *iman* is applied according to the *auṇādika* rules.
In the form *jagamyām*,

the suffix *śru* is substituted for the verbal augment (*vikaraṇa*) of the root *gam* in the optative (*liṅ*) expressing a prayerful wish, by virtue of the rule "in the Veda, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
"Madhvaḥ" is the second hymn, consisting of twenty-five verses.
It is the seerly composition of Kakṣīvān Auśija, in the Triṣṭubh meter, addressed to the Aśvins.
This is indicated by the introductory heading "Madhvaḥ."
The application of the Prātaranuvāka and the Aśvina-śastra has been stated together with the preceding hymn.

O Aśvins, for the exhilaration of the sweet Soma, the ancient Hotṛ priest seeks you; the sacrificial grass is spread, the offering is prepared, and the song is sung—come hither with strength, O Nāsatyas!

Of the honeyed Soma, O Aśvins, for your exhilaration—the ancient Hotar-priest invites you both. The sacrificial grass is spread, the offering is prepared, and the song is intoned; come hither with nourishment and with strengths, O Nāsatyas! 1.
O Aśvins, the ancient Hotṛ—the sacrificer who performs the oblation—desires to serve you both with the honeyed Soma, that is, with the Soma endowed with sweetness, for the sake of your exhilaration.
The root *vivāsati* signifies the act of attending upon or serving. Āṅ... [end of fragment].

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is situated (*avasthitam*). 2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is bound (*avanaddham*); these are the accents of the primary suffixes (*niṣṭhā-svarau*), just as in the case of *sa-avanaddha*, where they are the accents of the secondary suffixes (*pratyaya-svarau*). 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is the substitute *udana*. 4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is clearly manifest (*pra spaṣṭam*). 5. *ṭha* [is] by means of those capable of grasping their respective objects (*svasvaviṣayagrahaṇasamarthaiḥ*). 6. *vañcha-ṇapha* is established (*sthāpitam*). 7. *va-cha-ṇa* is a householder (*gṛhasthaḥ*). 8. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is a mark (*liṅ*); in the sense of a limit (*maryādāyām*); he attends according to the scriptures (*yathāśāstraṃ paricarati*).

Moreover, the oblation (*havis*) is to be given; it is "provided with *barhis*," meaning it is prepared upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that has been spread out for your sake. Likewise, the "song" (*gīḥ*), characterized as praise, is "extended," being gathered among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
The meaning is that praise is also offered by them.
Therefore, O Nāsatyas, Aśvins, come hither to us together with *hṛṣā* (joy), with food (*nāka*), and with strengths (*vāja*) and powers (*bala*). Arrive at our presence.
*Maghavaḥ*:
By the rule "subāṃ supo bhavanti," the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
By the rule "jasādiṣu chandasi vāvacanam," there is an option regarding the application of the *gher ṅiti* rule; thus, in the absence of the *guṇa* substitution, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs.
For the sake of intoxication (*mada*).
[The root] *mad* [is used] in the sense of joy (*harṣa*). [The suffix] *ap* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *ap* occurs after *mad* when no prefix is present."
*rātiḥ* [is derived from] the root *rā* in the sense of "giving" (*dāne*). The suffix *ktin* is applied in the passive/objective sense (*karmaṇi*).
Its accentuation as udātta is established by the rule *mantre vṛṣeṇa* and so forth. [The word] *viśritā* [is derived from] the root *śriñ* in the sense of "service" (*sevā*).
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied after the verbal root.
By the rule "the preceding element [is unaccented] when followed by a *gati*," the *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

O Aśvins, that chariot of yours which is swifter than thought, drawn by noble horses and traversing all things— by that very chariot with which you go to the dwelling of the righteous-doer, come, O heroes, for our protection.

O Aśvins, that chariot of yours which is swifter than thought, drawn by noble horses and reaching every place—by which you go to the dwelling of the righteous performer of good deeds—come to us with that, O Heroes, as our protection. 2.

O Aśvins, that chariot of yours which belongs to you, which is swifter than thought—possessing a speed exceeding even that of the mind—and which has beautiful horses (*svaśva*), such a chariot approaches all creatures (*viśvaḥ prajāḥ*).
With that chariot by which you two go to the *duroṇa*—the house characterized as the place of sacrifice—for the well-performing sacrificer who performs a beautiful sacrifice;
O leaders, O Aśvins, with that chariot come (*yātam*) to our *varti*—our home, the locus of our path.
*Javīyān*:
one who possesses speed is *javavān*;
the suffix *matup* is applied according to the rule "that which belongs to this."

Then, the suffix *īyasun* is applied in the sense of comparison (*ātiśāyanika*). By the rule *vinmator luk*, there is elision of the suffix *mat*. By the rule *ṭeḥ*, there is elision of the final phoneme *ṭi*.
*jigāti* [is derived from] the root *gā* in the sense of "praising";
it belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class.
Because it is listed among the roots meaning motion (*gatikarma*), it has the sense of "going" here;
the shortening of the reduplicated syllable is according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
O heroes, you released this seer of the five tribes from his distress by means of your skill;
O bulls, driving on in succession, you destroyed the magic arts of the malevolent Dasyu.

The seer, the two men, Ahiṃsa, and Pañcajanya—from the pit you released Atri by means of your power, subduing the magical arts of the malevolent Dasyu, O showerers of blessings, as you urged them on one after another.

The meaning expressed in the verse "himenāgnim" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.8) is the very same here; however, it is set forth again by this [verse] in a different manner. Everything stated in that mantra should be understood to apply here as well.
As for the literal meaning: O leaders (*narau*), O showerers of desires (*vṛṣaṇā*), O Aśvins, [protect] the *pāñcajanya*.
The five peoples (*pañcajana*) consist of the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth.
That which exists among them [is "tatra-bhava"].
Atri is called "tatra-bhava" because he acted for the welfare of all while liberating this Sun, who had been seized by Svarbhānu.

Such a seer (*ṛṣi*), having been cast into a hundred-gated prison-house (*ṛbīsa*)—a place of suffering (*aṃhas*) consisting of sin—by the Asuras for the sake of tormenting Atri, [was released] from the presence of Tuṣāgni by means of his quality (*guṇa*), that is, by the aggregate of his senses (*indriya-varga*).
1. And by kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa-ya;
2. ṭha-sa illuminating;
3. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa-Agni.
Together with your host of sons, grandsons, and so forth, you two released the one who was well-disposed. What were you doing?

Destroying—that is, harming—the enemies; and repelling, by means of that fire, the illusions employed by the *dasyu*—the oppressor, the inauspicious one who causes suffering—the *asura*, impelling them away in due order, one after another.
Pāñjanya:
the suffix *ṇya* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-artha*) according to the rule, "It should be stated that [the suffix applies] after *deva* and *pañjana*" (Kāśikā 4.3.58.1).
Minantā.
The root *mīñ* is used in the sense of "injuring";
it belongs to the *kryādi* class;
[the suffix] *śatṛ* is applied to the present tense (*laṭ*).
By the rule "mīnāter nigame," there is shortening of the vowel.
O Aśvins, heroes, bulls, like a horse hidden by the evil-minded, you rescued Rebha in the waters, O sages;
you restored him who was shattered by your wondrous deeds. Your ancient exploits do not grow old.

O Aśvins, O heroes, O bulls, you rescued with your wondrous deeds the seer Rebha, who was hidden by evil-doers in the waters; you brought him out when he was scattered. Your ancient exploits do not grow old. 4.

O leaders, O bulls who shower down desires, O Aśvins: from the waters—the waters hidden in the well—ye rescued Rebha, the seer who was concealed and buried; him, like a diseased horse, ye restored with your wondrous deeds, that is, with your acts in the form of medicines.
Ye endowed him once more with all his limbs; this is the meaning.
The ancient deeds performed by you two do not decay; they do not become worn out.
[In the word *jūryanti*, the vowel is shortened according to the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*. They decay (*jūryanti*).
The root *jṛṣ* is used in the sense of “loss of vitality.
Because it belongs to the *devādi* group, the suffix *śyan* is applied.
By the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* takes place.

By the rule "hali ca," [the vowel] is long. O Aśvins, you raised up Vandana for glory— him who was lying low like one who has slept soundly, like the sun in the lap of destruction, or like a beautiful golden ornament buried in darkness.
Like one who has slept in the lap of Nirṛti, like the sun dwelling in darkness, O Dastras, you two Aśvins raised up for Vanda the most beautiful one, like a golden ornament buried for splendor.
“Nikṛti” is a name for the earth.

In the lap—that is, the bosom—of Nikṛti, the earth, he saw one who had fallen asleep like a man lying in the middle of a well; [he saw] the Sun, as it were, dwelling in the darkness within the well, meaning that he was radiant like the Sun.

Like gold fashioned for the sake of beauty upon a fair object—shining like a golden ornament, beautiful and truly worthy of being seen—such was the [well] distinguished by these qualities which the Asuras had cast into the pit; O Dastras, O Ashvins worthy of being seen, you two raised it up for Vanda, even though it was like a [buried] well.
[He who was] sleeping:
from the root *ṣivvap*, "to lie down."
The suffix *kasu* replaces *liṭ*. By the rule beginning with *vacisvapi*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*),
followed by reduplication and so forth.
In the vicinity; he stands near: the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the rule "the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of *ghañ*";
[this refers to] the great void.

1. By the group beginning with *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *pu*, *tra*, etc. 2. In the sequence and order of *ca*, *cha*, *ṇa*, *da*, *dha*, *la*. 3. *Kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*—there is no "hi. 4. *Kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*—because it belongs to the *divādi* (fourth) class. 5. *Kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*—in the darkness situated within a well. 6. *Kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*—the meaning is that he stands radiant like the sun. 7. *Kṣa*, *sa*—for the sake of beauty. ka. 12: From the root *dis*, there is the udātta accent on the final syllable of the preceding word;
for the purpose of salutation (*vandanāya*).
Because the word "action" (*kriyā*) must be supplied [in the rule], the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used for the object (*karman*) due to its status as a recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
O Nāsatyas, that deed of yours was worthy of praise by Pajriya Kukṣīvat, O heroes, as you traveled around;
from the hoof of a swift horse, you poured out for the people a hundred jars of honey.
Therefore, O Heroes, Nāsatyas, you bestowed upon the man Pajriya Kukṣīvat a hundred jars of honey as a gift to be praised, which you brought around from the hoof of a swift horse. 6.

When the two leaders, the Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, were present at the *parijman*—the circumambulation that serves as the means for attaining what is desired—I, Kukṣīvat, born in the lineage of the Pajras, the Aṅgirases, [performed] that deed of yours, which is worthy of praise and most highly extolable. Upon hearing the word "that" (*tat*), the word "which" (*yat*) is to be supplied: when, for the sake of a person who was looking on, you poured out from the hoof of my swift horse a hundred jars of honey with the drops of honey; you made them flow.
In that context, "siñcati" (he sprinkles) has the sense of "pūrṇa" (filled).
The meaning is that what is filled with honey is to be praised.
O Heroes, you gave all things to Viśvaka, the son of Kṛṣṇi, who praised you;
O Aśvins, you bestowed a husband upon Ghoṣā, who was growing old in her father’s house.

O Heroes, you two gave all things to Viśvāpī, the daughter of Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of her husband; O Aśvins, you bestowed a husband upon Ghoṣā even though she was wasting away in her father’s house as she grew old. 7.
O leaders, O Aśvins, you two gave Viśvaka—the son of Kṛṣṇī—to Viśvaka, who was offering praise and performing a hymn of laudation;
that is, you restored his son named Viśvāp, who had perished.
Ghoṣā by name was the daughter of Kakṣīvat and a speaker of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinī*).
Being a daughter of Kṛṣṇa, she remained in her father’s house unmarried and grew old;
through the grace of the Aśvins, having been freed from leprosy, she obtained a husband.
This is what he says.

O Aśvins, in the dwelling of her father—that is, in the house of her own father—Ghoṣā, by name, a teacher of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinī), having not obtained a husband due to leprosy and being seated near her father as she grew old and reached decrepitude, you two granted her a husband by alleviating her disease.
The word *pitṛṣada* is derived from the root *sad*, meaning "to sit" or "to perish," with the suffix *kvi* added according to the rule "kvi ca."
For *jūryantyai*:
[the root] *jṛ* in the sense of "decay of age";
[this is formed from] the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the present tense (*laṭ*).

The form *divādivāt* occurs here; the substitution of *u* for *i* is applied by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in the Vedic language, [substitutions] occur diversely), and the lengthening is applied by the rule "hali ca" (and when followed by a consonant).
Because it is taught as having an *a* vowel, when the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the word ending in *-iyat* is accented on its first syllable due to the *nit* designation.

1. From the root *kṣa* (to destroy), *ṭa* (to stretch), *ṭha* (to obstruct), *sa* (to flow), and *śapha* (hoof); 2. *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha* are praised; 3. In the reading *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-na-sa*, the phrase "you two gave away all things" (*viṣvāpṃ dadathuḥ*) is absent; 4. *sa-dadathuḥ* means "the two of you have given"; 5. *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *sa* [are used] in the senses of destruction, motion, and non-destruction.

O Aśvins, you two gave the bright [cow] to the dark Kaṇva, the descendant of Mahat Kṣoṇa. O mighty ones, that deed of yours is to be proclaimed: that you bestowed glory upon the son of Nṛṣad. 8. You two gave the bright one to the dark Kaṇva, the descendant of Mahat Kṣoṇa, O Aśvins. That deed of yours, O mighty ones, is to be proclaimed: that you bestowed glory upon the son of Nṛṣad. 8.

O Aśvins, you two bestowed radiant splendor upon the sage Īyāyu, who was dark-complexioned due to leprosy (kuṣṭha). Moreover, for Kaṇva—the one who dwells in a single place because he is "wasted" (kṣoṇa), being unable to move due to the absence of sight—you two gave great luster, that is, the faculty of vision. O showerers of desires (vṛṣaṇā), that deed of yours is to be proclaimed, to be spoken of with excellence, and to be celebrated.
"O you two who bestow men, what glory—that is, the faculty of hearing—did you bestow (*adhyadhattam*), meaning you gave, to the son of Nārṣada, the deaf seer? This is the meaning.
Another [commentator] says:
for the purpose of testing the Brāhmaṇa, the Asuras placed the seer Kaṇva in hidden darkness.
Remaining right here, understand the dawn when it has broken, "if you are indeed a Brāhmaṇa. Then the Aśvins approached him and said:
"We two shall come playing the lute upon the roof of your palace."
Having heard that sound, say to Uṣas, "Dawn has arrived.
This very point is being set forth:
O Vṛṣaṇau, you two Ashvins who shower down desires, your deed is to be proclaimed—that which is worthy of praise performed for Kaṇva, the son of Nṛpada, [the giver] of the dwelling.
*Kṣoṇa* is a particular kind of sounding lute. *Mahaḥ* means "of the great *kṣoṇa*. You two bestowed *śravaḥ*, meaning sound, [upon it] for the sake of the dawn's recognition; you made it superior.
*Mahaḥ*:
[derived] from the root *maha* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjā*), with the *as* suffix added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
In the alternative interpretation, however, from the word *mahat* in the genitive singular, there is a Vedic elision of the vowel;
the acute accent of the case-ending is due to the rule "the addition of *brahmahatyā* [is prescribed].
Or else:
*Krivantāt* is the genitive singular. *Kṣoṇasya*:
from the root *kṣi*, meaning "to dwell" or "to go."
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*;
the change to *kṣoṇa* occurs because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* class.
This has been stated by Yāska: "Of that which is diminished (*kṣoṇa*) and which causes diminution (*kṣayaṇa*)" (Nirukta 6.6).
In the alternative view, however, the suffix *na* is added via the *uṇādi* rules to the root *dukh* (meaning "to sound"),
resulting in *nārṣada*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "ṛṣy-andhaka-".

Assuming many forms, O Aśvins, you brought down for Pedu a swift horse that won a thousandfold, a vigorous steed, irresistible, slaying the serpent, renowned, and a deliverer. 9. *Puru varpāṃsy aśvinā dadhānā ni pedave ūhathur āśum aśvaṃ sahasrasāṃ vājinaṃ apratītam ahihanam śrutyaṃ tarutram.* 9.

O Aśvins, you two, assuming many— meaning numerous— forms (for *varpāṃsi* is a name for forms), that is, maintaining the forms created by your own deeds, brought forth— that is, you fully conveyed or gave— the swift-moving horse to Pedu, the one named Pedu who praises you. This is the meaning.

"O you who bestow a thousand—that is, a giver of wealth numbering in the thousands; O powerful one (*vājin*), therefore unassailable by enemies; O slayer of serpents (*ahi-han*), who come to destroy those [who oppose]; [to him] whose glory is praiseworthy... [Notes on variants: 1. *ca-da-dha-pha* read *śriyam*. 2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-na-sa* do not have "yaḥ". 3. *na* reads "unable to go. 4. *na* reads "dwelling. 5. *sa* reads "to that dwelling one. 6. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-na* do not have "praiseworthy. 7. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa* read "speak thus. 8. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* read "of his greatness. 9. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* note the elision of the word *accha*.

The slayer of enemies or one who possesses enemies; worthy of fame (*śravasyam*); *śravaḥ* means that which is to be heard, namely a hymn of praise; "belonging to that" means having praise as its object; a deliverer (*tarutram*), one who crosses over. *Vapāṃsi*: from the root *vṛṣ* (to choose). By the rule *vṛṣībhyāṃ rūpasvāñjayoḥ puvañca* (Uṇādisūtra 4.640), the suffix *asun* is applied with the augment *pu*. *Dadhānā*: the present participle (*laṭ*) of the root *dhā* in the *śānac* form. The first syllable is acute by the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ*. *Sahasrasām*: from the root *paṇu* (to give). The suffix *viṭ* is applied by the rule *janasanakhana* (Uṇādisūtra 4.105). The vowel *ā* is substituted for the nasal by the rule *viḍnoranunāsikasyāt*. *Śravasyam*: from the word *śravaḥ*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "being" (*bhave chandasi*). It has a circumflex accent (*svarita*). *Tarutram*: from the roots *tṛ* (to leap/cross). The suffix *utran* is applied by the rule *aśvitrādibhya inottrau* (Uṇādisūtra 4.612). The acute accent falls on the first syllable by transposition (*nyatyayena*). Alternatively, in forms such as *asitarambhita*, by the force of a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*), the suffix *tun* is added to the stem *taru*; since the rule based on a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not always obligatory, there is no *guṇa* substitution, and the *yaṇ* sandhi occurs. The acute accent on the first syllable follows the general accent rule (*nisvara*).

These glorious deeds of yours, O bounteous givers, are worthy of praise; they are the dwelling place of prayer for the two worlds. When the progeny offers oblations to you, O Aśvins, come with nourishment and grant strength to the wise man.

These [are for you], O bounteous ones, seeking renown; this prayer is pleasing to you, the dwelling place of heaven and earth. Since the progeny call upon you, O Aśvins, come with nourishment and bring strength to the wise man. 10.
O Sudānus, O Aśvins of beautiful bounty, these heroic deeds belonging to you two, which have just been described, are worthy of renown (*śravasyā*), to be heard of, and known by all.
For that purpose, [they belong] to you two who exist in the form of Rodasī, Heaven and Earth.
And it has been said by Yāska: “Some say those two Aśvins are Heaven and Earth” (Nirukta 12.1).
And so says the Taittirīyaka: “These two Aśvins, the Saṃvatsara, and Agni Vaidhānara” (Tait. Saṃ. 5.6.4.1).

The remainder of the sense is: for you two, a seat—a dwelling place near the praiser, or that which causes gratification, or something worthy of being proclaimed—has been produced as a *brahma*, that is, a hymn in the form of a mantra.

Whenever the descendants of Aṅgiras, born of the Gotra lineage, being sacrificers, invoke you two, O Aśvins, with hymns for the sake of self-protection—at that time, come hither with *iṣ*, the food to be given; and bestow upon me, who am wise and know the praise intended for you, *vāja*, which is food or strength—this is the remainder of the sense.
"Go!"— there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent because of the rule "the first word [is unaccented] when joined with *ca* or *vā*".
To the wise one.

The root *vid* means "to know. [In the formation of the present participle], the suffix *śatṛ* is applied to *vid*, and by the rule "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *vasu*," the vocalization takes place.
The substitution of the sibilant *ṣ* occurs by the rule "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca."
O Aśvins, praised by our hymns, you who are swift and bestow strength upon the sage,
having grown mighty through the prayer of Agastya, O Nāsatyas, you brought Viśpalā back to us.
Listen: O Aśvins, you who are praised as the swift ones, bestowing strength upon the sage; having grown great through the sacred prayer for Agastya, O Nāsatyas, you two set Viśpalā free.

O active ones, the two supporters and nourishers, O Nāsatyas whose very nature is truth, O Aśvins, being praised by the hymn—the measure of praise—of Agastya, the son of Khela and family priest, who was born from a jar and is worthy of laudation, you were extolled for the sake of the sage.
(Note: The variants *ca-cha-ṇa-pha-ya-la* do not contain the letter ‘ā’.)

The suffix *vibhāṣā* indicates an optional prohibition [of the augment]. By the rule *janasanakhanāṃ sañjhaloḥ*, the substitution of *ākār* (*ā*) occurs. By the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the preceding prefix (*gati*) retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). In the word *ahan*, by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *s*. By the rule *na ḍisaṃbuddhayoḥ*, the elision of the final *n* is prohibited.
O Aśvins, by your powers you restored Cyavāna, who was wasting away with age, and made him young again;
O Nāsatyas, the Daughter of the Sun chose your chariot together with glory.
O Aśvins, by your powers you restored Cyavāna, who was wasting away with age, to youth again; O Nāsatyas, the Daughter of the Sun chose your chariot together with its splendor.

O Aśvins, you two, by means of your own powers—namely, your deeds characterized by healing medicines—made Cyavāna, who was growing old, that is, decaying, this very sage named Cyavāna, the one who causes hymns to flow forth, young again, endowed with youth. Moreover, O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, the daughter of Sūrya, known as Sūryā, chose your chariot together with Śrī—that is, with the splendor consisting of a thousand *ṛc*s, or with beauty—meaning she approached and ascended it.
The narrative written here regarding the verse "ā vāṃ rathaṃ duhitā" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.17) should also be understood in this context. [Regarding the word] *jarantam*:
[the root] *jap* [is used] in the sense of "loss of vitality."
There is an irregular substitution for *śas*.
Regarding *yuvoḥ*:

from the word *yuṣmad* in the dual sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhīdvivacana*), when the substitution of *ya* (by the rule *yo'ci*) does not occur due to an irregularity, there is the elision of the letter *d* by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ*.
Therefore, by the rule "ato guṇe," there is the substitution of the single substitute (ekādeśa) [for a and i];
by the rule "an ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ," it is acute-accented. Thus: *avṛṇīta*.
The root *vṛṅ* means "to choose" or "to select";
it belongs to the *krayādi* class.
"O you two, through ancient aids, you have become young again for Tugra, O you who possess renewed thought."
You two carried Bhujyu out from the ocean by means of the waters, with swift and straight-moving horses.
You two, as youthful ones, again became mindful for Tugra with your ancient steeds; you two carried Bhujyu out from the ocean by means of the waters, with swift and straight-moving horses.
O Aśvins, you two young ones, the dispellers of sorrows— by means of ancient,

time-honored hymns that go forth toward the one worthy of praise, you became [the objects of worship] for Tugra, through the mediations of Bhujyu, the son of Janaka; just as you were to be praised by Bhujyu before his departure across the ocean, so too have you become worthy of praise once again now.

When you two, by means of flying ships (*vibhiḥ*) and swift-moving horses (*ṛjebhir aśvaiḥ*), rescued Bhujyu, the son of Tugra, who was submerged with his army in the midst of the ocean—drawing him out from the watery expanse of the surging sea and bringing him back to his father’s side—at that time, you became even more worthy of praise. This is the meaning.
The narrative told in the verse "tumro ha bhujyum" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.3) should also be considered here. Regarding the word *evaiḥ*: [it is derived from] the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going."
From the roots *iṇ* and *śī*, the suffix *van* is applied. Again, regarding *man*:
from the root *man* in the sense of "knowing."
In this context, it has the sense of praise. "Manā" means praise, derived from the root *man* in the sense of "to praise"; the suffix *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).
In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the suffix *ya* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule "and in the Veda" (*chandasi ca*).
[Thus we have] *yuvānā*.
[The root] *yu* means "to mix" and "not to mix."
The suffix *kanin* is applied by the rule beginning with "kaninyuṣi," etc.
1. [This is] designated as such by the variants kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha.
2. By the variant kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, it is [formed] with *surūpayā*.
The vowel *ā* [in *arṇasā*] is the replacement for the case-ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Regarding *arṇasaḥ*:
there is elision of the suffix *matup* (which expresses possession) following the word *arṇas*, due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (‘optionally’) in the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*.
*vibhīḥ*:
Because of the rule “all rules are optional in the Veda” (*sarve vidhayaś chandasi vikalpyante*), the acute accent on the case-ending is optional; thus, its absence [occurs].
*ṛjebhiḥ*.
The word *ṛju* is used in the senses of "straight," "gait," "position," "acquisition," and "earning.

In forms such as *ṛjendra*, it is established as a nipāta (irregular formation) ending in the suffix *ran*. The substitution of *ais* for *bhis* follows from the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* ("diversely in Vedic usage").

The son of Tugra called upon you, O Aśvins, having been cast into the ocean, unshaken even while sinking. You two, O Bulls, brought him out in safety with your well-yoked chariot that is swift as thought. 15. He called upon: O Aśvins; the son of Tugra; you two; having been cast into; the ocean; unshaken; while sinking; you two brought him out; with a well-yoked chariot; swift as thought; O Bulls; in safety. 15.

O Aśvins, you two— the son of Tugra, Bhujyu, who was brought by his father to the ocean like one blind, and who, though submerged in the water, called out with hymns of praise while remaining untroubled and free from pain—
you, O Aśvins, the showerers of desires, swift as thought and possessing well-yoked chariots, carried him out safely to well-being;
you brought him out from the water and delivered him to his father's house.

*jagnvān*: from the root *gam*, the suffix *krasun* is applied in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Due to the optionality expressed in the rule “*vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām*,” the substitution of *ha* for *ga* occurs.
In the phrase "svośca," the letter *m* becomes *n*. This is the established rule (*niṣṭam*).
Furthermore, according to the rule "yuṣmattattatkṣuḥpvantaḥpādam," the dental *t* is replaced by the retroflex *ṭ*.
*Manojavasā*:
those two whose speed is like the speed of the mind (*manas*) are so described.
The vowel *ā* is substituted for the case-ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

Because it begins with a word-form that is not a vocative, there is an absence of the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the suppression of accent for vocatives), and consequently, there is optionally the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*).

The quail called out to you, O Aśvins, from her seat when you rescued her from the wolf. With your swift horses you traversed the ridges of the mountains; you struck down the offspring of Viṣvāc, the devouring serpent, with poison. 16. The quail called out to you, O Aśvins, from her seat when you rescued her from the wolf. With your swift horses you traversed the ridges of the mountains; you struck down the offspring of Viṣvāc, the devouring serpent, with poison. 16.

The meaning of the verse *‘āsano vṛkasya’* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.14), which was previously stated, is here established by the first half-verse: When the female of a bird resembling a sparrow (*vartikā*) had been seized by a wolf (*vṛka*), a wild dog, O Aśvins, she then called out to you both (*vām ajohavīt*). At that very moment (*yatsīm*), you two released her from the mouth (*āstas*) of the wolf.
