Moreover, with your victorious chariot, you two traversed the high ridge of the mountain—the peak of the rock—where the singer named Jāhuṣa was surrounded by enemies; that is to say, you went to the mountain summit which could not be reached by others along with Agni, the consumer of the host of foes.
This is stated in the verse: “Jāhuṣa, who was besieged” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.20).
Likewise, you two slew with poison the offspring born of the Asura named Viṣvāc, who was endowed with various movements (viṣvācaḥ), having struck him down with a lethal weapon (kṣava).
Or alternatively: [the text continues with variants regarding the slaying of Bhujyu].
She who exists and turns back day by day is the Dawn (*uṣas*), called *vartikā*.
The wolf (*vṛka*) is said to be the Sun, whose light is fully expanded.
Being seized by him, she, O Aśvins, called out to you both—she invoked you.

Indeed, when you two released Vṛka from the seat, from his place of sitting, from the solar orb—meaning that having separated Uṣas who had become one with the Sun, you established her prior to sunrise, in the latter part of the night;
and thus Yāska says: "The Sun is also called Vṛka because he envelops."
It is said: "When the earth was seized by the Aśvins and the Āditya, the Aśvins released her"—this is the narrative (Nirukta 5.21).

Furthermore, with a victorious chariot (*jayuṣā*), characterized by the quality of victory, you two went specifically to the ridge (*sānu*)—the elevated region—of Adrimedha, desiring to scatter rain. And by means of the excellent water belonging to Viśvāc—the cloud possessed of various movements—you caused all living beings (*sarvaṃ bhūtajātam*) that had arisen to reach [their goal]; the meaning is that you brought about rain.
*Ajohavīt*:
from the root *hve* (to call) in its *yaṅ*-luṅ form, with the suffix *tip* in the *laṅ* tense, the augment *īṭ* is applied according to the rule "yaṅo vā.
By the rule "abhyastasya ca," the *saṃprasāraṇa* of *hve* occurs even before reduplication.
Regarding *āsana*: by the rule beginning with "padan," the word *āsya* undergoes the substitution *āsana*; then, by the rule "ahno'panaḥ," there is the elision of the vowel *a*.
Jayuṣā:
from the root *ji* in the sense of "victory," with the *us* suffix added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
*Viśvācaḥ*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which moves (*añcati*) in various directions (*viṣu*), that is, toward [all things] (*ābhimukhyena*).
The suffix *kvin* is applied according to the rule beginning with "ṛtvik" (Pāṇini 3.2.59).

By the rule *acaḥ*, there is elision of the vowel *a*; by the rule *cau*, there is lengthening. When the acute accent of the case-ending would have been obtained by the *udāttanivṛtti-svara* (the accent that takes effect when an acute vowel is elided), the rule *cau* instead prescribes an acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*).
*ahatm* | [The root] *han*, meaning "to kill" or "to go," [is used here]. In the *laṅ* tense, due to its belonging to the *adādi* (second) class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
The elision of the nasal [consonant] occurs by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa."
A hundred rams were offered by my father, who was led into darkness by ill fortune;
O Aśvins, you restored sight to Ṛjrāśva and provided light for him as he cried out.
A hundred rams did you bestow upon the she-wolf. Led into darkness by his father, O Aśvins, you restored his two eyes to Ṛjraśva. You gave light to the blind so that he might see clearly. 17.

Regarding the narrative we have previously related concerning the verse, "He who gave a hundred rams to the she-wolf" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.116.16), that same account should be kept in mind here as well.

[The meaning is: "May the Aśvins make Ṛjāśva, who was brought to blindness—meaning he was rendered sightless—by his own father, an ill-disposed one who caused him unhappiness, because he had honored and offered a hundred—that is, a number amounting to a hundred—rams to the donkey, which stood in the form of a she-wolf and served as the vehicle for the Aśvins, for the purpose of food; [may they] restore his sight. This is the sense to be supplied.
This very point is clarified:
O Aśvins, you restored the two eyes—the sight that had been lost due to the curse of his father—to the royal sage named Ṛjāśva; that is to say, you made them capable of seeing once again.
This is the meaning.
"For the blind one who was deprived of sight, you two have created light—the eye—for the purpose of seeing the manifold world."
*mamahānam*:
[derived from] the root *maha* in the sense of "worship" (*pūjāyām*),
with the suffix *kānac* applied after the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

In the *saṃhitā*, there is lengthening of the vowel due to Vedic usage. *Praṇītam* is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) derived from the root *ji* preceded by the prefix *pra*, used in the sense of the object.
In the word *gatiranantaraḥ*, the *prakṛtisvara* (original accent) of *gati* applies. In *pitrā*, the case ending receives the acute accent (*udātta*) by the rule *udāttayaṇaḥ*.
Regarding the word *akṣī*: from the word *akṣi*, when the dual number is applied, the augment *num* would be required, as well as the substitution of the vowel *ī* by the rule "and *ī* in the dual.
However, the substitution of *ī* takes precedence due to its higher status [in the order of rules].
Once that [substitution] has been performed, the elision (*lu*) does not occur again by virtue of the "once-occurred" maxim (*sakṛdgataparibhāṣā*).
Because the term "udātta" (acute) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), the vowel *ī* becomes acute.
1. Having placed *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha* before [the suffixes].
2. The enlargement (*vṛddhi*) of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*.
3. That which is produced by *jha*, *ṭa*, *ṭhana*, and *sa* does not exist.
"Bring wealth for our prosperity, O Aśvins, you bulls among men! Thus spoke Sāvitrī.
Like a lover toward his beloved wife, R̥jāśva cut off one hundred and one rams for me.

A load was brought for the blind man, bringing good fortune; she [became] a she-wolf. O Aśvins, bulls, heroes—thus [she cried]. Like a lover, like a weakling, R̥jraśva, carving up a hundred and one rams. 18.

*Śunam* is a name for happiness. *Bharam* refers to the happiness produced by the faculty of sight, which serves as the cause of nourishment. Desiring this for that blind man, *Ṛjāśva*, she—she being the *vṛkī* (the she-wolf)—O Aśvins, you who are yoked with horses (*aśvayu*), O *vṛṣaṇā*, you who pervade the prostrate world and shower down desires—having thus addressed them, O leaders (*narā*), she called out to the two Aśvins.
If one asks what was the intention of her who was calling out, it is stated as follows:

Just as a youthful paramour, having attained his prime, being a lover who commits adultery, gives all his wealth to another's wife; even so, Ṛjāśva, having seized one hundred and one—namely, a total of one hundred and one—rams belonging to the citizens, gave them away while "cutting them up" (cakṣadānaḥ), that is, making them into pieces. By that act, he has fallen into such a miserable state.
*Kanīnaḥ*:
From the word *yuva*, with the suffix *iṣn*, the substitution of *kan* for *yuva* occurs by the rule "yuvālpayoḥ kanyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 5.3.64).
By transposition (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *iṣn* is replaced by *kh*.
Alternatively:
the root *kan* is used in the senses of shining, beauty, and motion;
from this, the suffix *īna* is added according to the rules of the *auṇādika* [appendix].
O Aśvins, your aid is great and brings delight; O you who are worthy of our thought, you heal the wounded man.
Then, when Puraṃdhi was burning, you two came to her with your aids, O powerful ones.

O Aśvins, your aid is great; it brings us joy. O you who are worthy of our devotion, you heal even the cripple. Therefore, Purandhi called upon you alone; you two, O bulls, came to her with your protections.
O Aśvins, yours— your two— is a great, vast protection (*ūti*), a source of joy (*mayobhūḥ*), that which brings about happiness (*mayaḥ*).
Moreover, O *dhiṣṇyā*—
*dhiṣaṇā* being speech characterized by praise.
By that [praise], you two restore the exhausted, diseased man whose limbs are impaired, making his members whole once again;
moreover, Purandhi—the one of many thoughts, or Ghoṣā, the all-pervading—has invoked you two alone for the sake of healing the disease.
O Ashvins, showerers of desires, come hither with your protections and deliver her who is thus afflicted.
Mahī means "great.
There is an elision of a phoneme according to Vedic usage (chāndasa).
Or alternatively:
The suffix *in* is applied after words such as *maheraṇa*;
the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to the rule "after a word ending in the kṛt-suffix *ik*, except for *ktin*.
Thus: *mayobhūḥ*.
The form *riṇīthaḥ* is derived from the root *rī*, meaning "to go" or "to flow," with the suffix *kvi* added after the sense of "to cause to flow" (*rantābhāvitavyartha*) has been applied.
Thus: *riṇīthaḥ*. The root is *rī* in the sense of "motion" (*gati*) and "flowing" (*eṣaṇa*).
It belongs to the *kry-ādi* class;
by the rule "the short vowel for roots beginning with *pū*," there is shortening of the vowel.
1. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-aśvavantau | ka.
93 O Aśvins, you who possess horses, you bestowed upon Śayu the barren cow that was hanging, the milkless one, as a gift.
By your powers, you two carried away the wife of Vimada, the daughter of Purumitra.
O Aśvins, you restored the barren cow that had been abandoned and cast away for Śayu; by your powers, O Aśvins, you brought back the wife for Vimada—the maiden of Purumitra.

O Aśvins, you who are *dastrā*, meaning "wondrous" or "beautiful to behold," you two filled with milk for the sake of the seer named Śayu a cow that was *viṣaktām*— meaning specifically one whose limbs were stuck together, that is, emaciated in her members— and therefore *staryam*, one whose productive capacity had ceased, and consequently *adhenum*, one that no longer gave milk. Furthermore, [you restored] the [cow] of Purumitra.
There was a certain king named Purumitra.

By means of his own ritual acts (*śacībhiḥ*), he carried away the maiden Yoṣā from him; and you two brought her to the house of the seer Vimada—so called because he was unable to fight with his enemies—having thus delivered her to him.
The word is *staryam*. [It is derived from] the root *stṛñ* in the sense of "covering.
The suffix *ī* is applied according to the rule "after the roots *avi*, *stṛ*, and *tan*, the suffix *ī* [is added]."

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), because the rule "or in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*) allows for an option regarding the substitution of the preceding vowel in the case of the accusative singular ending *am*, there is an absence [of that substitution], and thus the *yaṇ* replacement occurs.
By the rule "of a *yaṇ* following an acute or circumflex vowel" (*udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*), the following grave (*anudātta*) vowel becomes circumflex (*svarita*). Thus: *viṣaktām*.
In the word *pañca-saṅge*,
the suffix is the *niṣṭhā* [kta].
By the rule *aniditām*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the nasal *n*.

In the phrase "gatiranantaraḥ," the word *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). [The root] *piv* is from the root *piv* meaning "to drink. *Apinavatam*. [The root] *piv* means "to sprinkle" (*secane*).
The augment *num* is applied because it is specifically prescribed [in this rule].
It belongs to the *bhū* class (*bhauvādika*).
[This refers to the root] of *purumitra*.
"Of whom there are many friends (*puruṇi mitrāṇi yasya*).

In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final syllable of the second member is accented acute by the rule "In a technical name (*saṃjñā*), [the final syllable of] *mitra* and *ajina* [is acute]" (Pāṇini 6.2.165).
O Aśvins, destroyers of foes, you sowed barley with the wolf, milking out vigor for mankind;
with the *barkura* [weapon], you scorched the Dasyu and created broad light for the Ārya.
With the wolf, O Aśvins, you two sowers, milking nourishment for Manu, O wonder-workers, with the barkura-bird according to the law, have brought wide light to the Ārya against the Dasyu. 21.
To the noble one, to the wise one.
The word *manuṣa* is a synonym for the word *manu*.

O *dastrā*, O visible Aśvins, for the sake of Manu—for the human being—while sowing barley and all species of grain, such as barley and the rest, in the ploughed ground by means of a plough and by cultivators, [sow] likewise joy (*irṣam*).
This is another name for it.
Just as rainwater, having been produced from the clouds, milks [the earth] and consumes [it], so too does he [consume] the *dasyu*—the destructive Asura, Piśāca, and others—with the *barkura*.
*Barkura* refers to the shining thunderbolt (*vajra*).

By blowing [upon it] with that—*dhamati* meaning the act of killing; thus, performing these three kinds of actions while striking [the fire], you two have made (*cakrathuḥ*), that is, performed and displayed, *uru*—broad, extensive—*jyotiḥ*, your own light, your majesty and greatness. This is the meaning.
Or rather:
by means of the performance of the threefold ritual action, you two fashioned—that is, created—for the wise Manu, who had come [to you], the vast light known as the sun;
for it is through living that one beholds the sun.
The sense is that three actions, which have become the causes of that [result], were performed by you two.
Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "Bakura means one who causes light, one who causes fear, or one who moves while shining.
One should also consider such passages as: "O Aśvins, sowing like barley with a wolf; the wolf is the plough, because of its cutting" (*Nirukta* 6.25–26).
For *manuṣa*,
the suffix *upan* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
1. In a ploughed field:
"O Aśvins, you restored the horse's head to Dadhyañc, the descendant of Atharvan. He proclaimed the honey to you—the Tvaṣṭṛ-made [drink] which was hidden within his jaw."

To Atharvan, to the Aśvins, [you] restored the horse-head for Dadhyañc. He, following the Truth (Ṛta), proclaimed to you both the honeyed secret of Tvaṣṭṛ which was hidden within you, O wonder-workers (Dastrau). 22.

The narrative mentioned here in the verse, "tadvāṃ narā sanaye" (Rigveda Saṃhitā 1.116.12), should also be kept in mind in this context. O Aśvins, you two restored the horse's head (*aśvyam śiraḥ*) to Dadhyañc, the great seer named Dadhyañc, who was the son of Atharvan (*ātharvaṇāya*).
The meaning is that, having cut off his own human head and set it aside elsewhere, you joined that seer with the horse's head.

He, desiring to act truthfully (*ṛtāyan*)—that is, seeking to make his own promise true—proclaimed the *madhu* (the honey-knowledge) which had been received from Tvaṣṭṛ; that is, he declared the *madhuvidyā*.

He also proclaimed to you two, O *dastrau* (O handsome Aśvins), that secret called the *pravargya-vidyā*, which pertains to you both and consists of the rejoining of the severed head of the sacrifice by means of its side-regions (*apikakṣya*). This is the meaning: he told it to you two.
In *dadhīcaḥ* and *aśnataḥ*, the suffix *kin* is applied by the rule "ṛtvig-... etc.; the elision of the nasal (*n*) occurs by the rule "aniditām-... etc.
In the singular dative case, following the elision of the vowel *a* by the rule *acaḥ*, lengthening occurs by the rule *cau*.

When the acute accent of the case-ending would have been obtained by the *udāttanivṛtti-svara*, the rule *cau*—as an exception to that—would have caused the acute accent of the syllable preceding the case-ending; this present rule is an exception even to that.
By the rule *añceśchandasīsarvanāmasthānam*, the case-ending receives the acute accent.
O Sages, I have always sought your favor; O Aśvins, further all my prayers.
O Nāsatyas, grant us a great chariot, one that is never-failing and worthy of renown for our journey.
O poets, I have always yearned for your good-will; O Aśvins, further all my prayers. O Nāsatyas, grant us great wealth that is abundant, worthy of praise, and fit for the chariot. 23.

O Aśvins, you two who are seers (*kavī*), of lovely aspect and possessed of wisdom—I always (*sadā*) solicit (*ā cake*) your auspicious, benevolent favor (*sumatim*). Protect (*prāvataṃ*) all my thoughts (*viśvā dhiyaḥ*), that is, all my ritual actions. Furthermore, O Nāsatyas, Aśvins, bestow upon us (*asme*) a great (*bṛhantam*), abundant (*apyasācam*), praiseworthy (*śrutyam*), and excellent wealth (*rathim*) consisting of chariots along with offspring, such as sons and others.
The word *kai* means "to sound. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here by way of grammatical substitution.
This is the form in the first person singular of the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*).
[In the word] *asme*, the substitution of *śe* for the dative plural occurs according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
*Apysāca*: he who dwells together with or associates with his offspring (*apatyaiḥ*) is *apysāca*. The suffix *ṇvi* is used here according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Śrutyam. Śruti means praise; that which exists therein is śrutyam.
The suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *bhave chandasi*;
its initial syllable is acute by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ*.
[The form is] *rathāthām*.

The root *rā* means "to give. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs here by way of transposition; furthermore, the substitution of *plu* for *śap* occurs according to the rule "there is much variation in the Vedic language" (*bahulam chandasi*).
1. Having placed *kṣa*, *ṭha*, *na*, and *sa* together.
2. *kṣa*, *ṭha*, *yat*; *sa*, *yat*—this is the secret.
3. In *kṣa*, *ṭha*, there is no acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

O Aśvins, bestowing gifts, O heroes, you gave a son with golden hands to the deaf Matī. O Aśvins, you of noble bounty, you raised up Śyāva, who was bitten three times by a wolf, so that he might live. hiraṇyahastam | aśvinā | rarāṇā | putram | narā | vadhira'matyāḥ | adattam || tridhā | ha | śyāvam | aśvinā | vi'rkestam | ut | jīvasai | airayatam | sudānū iti su'dānū ||24||

O Aśvins, you who are generous, delightful, givers, men, and leaders—you gave and bestowed upon the daughter of Ati, the wife of one named Hiraṇyahasta, a son called Vadhiḥ, to her who was a speaker of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinī). Moreover, O Aśvins of beautiful bounty, you raised up for life the seer named Śyāvāśva, who had been cut into three parts and shattered; that is to say, having reunited his body which had been divided into three pieces by the Asuras, you caused him to rise up again.
*rarāṇā*: from the root *ram*, with the suffix *śānac*; by the rule "in the Veda [the substitution] is frequent," the *śap* is replaced by *śnu*;
and by the rule *myayyeṇa*, the *m* is replaced by *ā*.
Or, [the form] *rāti* is derived from the root *rā* with the suffix *śānac* by transposition;
as before, there is the substitution of *śru*; [this is] the speech of Vadhīramatī.
O Aśvins, may your chariot, flying like a falcon, most gracious and self-reliant, come hither—
your chariot that is swifter than the mind of a mortal, three-seated, O Bulls, with the speed of the wind.

O Aśvins, may your chariot, flying like a falcon, most gracious, well-provided, and swift as the thought of a mortal, come hither—your three-seated, bull-like vehicle that possesses the speed of the wind. 1.

O Aśvins, may that chariot which belongs to you two come hither toward us. What kind of chariot? One that flies like a hawk—*śyenapatavā*; "hawk" (*śyena*) is a name for a horse; thus, it means moving by flying with horses whose gait is worthy of praise. Or rather, *śyena* is a bird; it means flying swiftly like one. *Sumuḷīkaḥ*: endowed with excellent happiness. *Svavān*: possessed of wealth. O *vṛṣaṇā*, you two showerers of desires, O Aśvins, that chariot of yours which is swifter than the mind of a mortal, a human—meaning that by such speed it pervades the entire world, and even more so, it traverses the whole world in a mere moment. *Trivandhuraḥ*: *vandhura* is the enclosed seat of the charioteer; it is equipped with a threefold *vandhura*. *Vātaraṃhaḥ*: its speed is like the speed (*raṃhas*) of the wind (*vāta*); by this, its unimpeded motion is expressed. That chariot [is the subject]—this connects with the preceding. Regarding *śyenapatavā*: from the root *patu* (to go). By the rule *anyeṣv api dṛśyante*, the suffix *vanip* is applied. It belongs to the *dāsībhāra*-class. Alternatively, since the mention of *dṛśi* (in the rule *anyeṣv api dṛśyante*) is intended to include other rules, *vanip* is applied in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*). Then, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the original accent of the first member. Regarding *javīyān*: "having speed" is *javavān*; "swifter" is *atiśayena javavān*. The comparative suffix *īyasun* is added. There is elision of the *vin* and *matup* suffixes. By the rule *ṭeḥ*, there is the elision of the final *ṭi*.
Come hither in your well-rolling chariot, which has three seats, is triple-formed, and possesses three wheels;
swell our cows, quicken our steeds, and, O Aśvins, increase the hero among us.
Come hither on your chariot with its triple seat, triple-formed, three-wheeled, and easy-rolling; bestow abundance upon our cattle, quicken our horses, and, O Aśvins, increase the hero among us.

Come hither, toward us, with the chariot that has three seats—the seat being the place where the charioteer stands—equipped with three kinds of seats, moving in three ways, possessing three wheels, well-rolling, and proceeding beautifully. Come! Come!
And having come, O Aśvins, cause our cows to swell—that is, fill them with milk;
gladden—that is, delight—our coursers, the horses;
and furthermore, O Aśvins, increase—that is, cause to grow—the hero, such as a son, for us.
By means of the *tricakrā* [chariot].
That which has three wheels (*trīṇi cakrāṇi*) is thus described.
The acute accent on the final syllable of the second member of the compound follows from the rule: *tricakrādīnāṃ chandasyupasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.199.1).
1. *kṣa-ṭa-sa* is "to be known.
2. *ca-cha-ṇa-pha-javavān* means "possessing speed" or "swifter"; *ta-javavān* likewise means "swifter. 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* refers to "sons, grandsons," and so forth.
Being praised as you travel on your well-rolling chariot, O Dastras, hear this hymn of Adri.
Why indeed do the ancient sages say that you, O Aśvins, are the ones most ready to come to our aid?

On your easy-rolling chariot descending the slope, O Dāstṛs, hear this cry from the pressing-stone. Why indeed do the ancient sages say that you, O Aśvins, are the ones most ready to come to our distress?

O Aśvins, you two who are worthy of being seen, having arrived on a well-rolling chariot that moves with excellent speed and swift motion, listen to this word—this speech characterized by praise—which is the *śloka* (praise) of the singer, Dru, who shows respect. O Aśvins, the ancient, long-standing sages (*vipras*) say that you two are the most ready to go (*gamiṣṭhā*), moving toward the state of the singers to remove their poverty.
The word *kiṃ* functions here as an interrogative particle expressing inquiry regarding the result of the demonstration. "Do they not speak?"—
indeed, they all speak.
That being so, it must be understood as follows.

The word *pravadyamānā* [is derived as follows]: from the prefix *pra*, which denotes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) when it is itself employed, the suffix *vati* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.118:
*upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe*.
The root *yā* is used in the sense of "attaining.
By the rule *āto manin-kvanib-vanipaś ca*, the suffix *manin* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) due to the word *bahulam* (variously).
Subsequently, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is retained.
Regarding *adreḥ*: [the root] *dṛ* means "to respect. From this root, preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *kvi* (forming a noun) is added according to the *īṇādi* group.
"Also [the substitution of] a short vowel for the prefix *ā-*.
[The form] *gamiṣṭha-* [is derived as follows]: from the word *gantṛ-* (goer), the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied according to the rule *tuchandasi*."
In the rule "turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu," there is elision of the suffix *tu*.
In the rule "supāṃ suluk," the case ending is replaced by the vowel *ā*. They say: [this].
The accent is that of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*). Because it begins the quarter-verse (*pādādi*), there is no suppression of accent (*nighāta*).
O Aśvins, let the falcons carry you both on the chariot— those swift-flying birds yoked together,
which, like divine eagles crossing the waters, bring you toward the offerings, O Nāsatyas.
O Aśvins, let the falcons carry you hither—those swift-flying birds yoked to your chariot, which, like divine vultures crossing the waters, bring you toward the sacrificial food, O Nāsatyas.

O Aśvins, let those horses—yoked to your chariot by the charioteer at the place of departure, neighing, capable of flight, and possessing praiseworthy speed—bring you both to us. Those horses, swift as waters, like celestial vultures moving through the mid-air, carry you, O Nāsatyas, toward the *prayaḥ*—the food characterized by oblations—and bring it to you.
Such are they.
Thus, the connection is with what precedes.
*Asura*: [derived from] the root *tura* in the sense of "to sound" (*svaraṇe*). From this root, with the prefix *apa-* as an upapada, the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule *kip ca*.
1. When the question concerns the result indicated by *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*; when the question concerns the result of going indicated by *va*, *cha*, *ṇa*, and *pha*.
2. Regarding *va*, *cha*, *pha*, and *abhi*:
"The young daughter of Sūrya has mounted your chariot here, O Heroes, out of love."
May your beautiful, winged steeds, the ruddy birds, carry you both forward in the encounter.
O Heroes, let the youthful daughter of Sūrya ascend your chariot here with delight; let your beautiful, winged, ruddy horses carry you on their flight at the encounter. 5.
The two Aśvins, the leaders of men, [were met by] the youthful daughter of Sūrya; being pleased, she joyfully ascended this chariot of yours here.
Together with her, may your horses carry you both around that chariot in the vicinity of the house—that is, bring it to its destination.
Of what sort are the horses?
*Vapuṣaḥ* is the name for *vapuḥ*, meaning either form or body; it is within that [body]. The suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) has been elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
The *pataṅgas* are those capable of flying up;
the *vayas* are those moving through the air;
and the *aruṣas* are those shining brightly or, alternatively, those free from harm.

In this regard, because of the inclusion of the term *dṛśi* in the rule *itarābhyo ’pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 5.3.14), [the suffix *kvip*] occurs even in connection with *bhavat* and other such words. Thus:

"O Aśvins, you two—having approached Atri who was situated within a hundred-gated house of torment for the sake of protection—you warded off with cold water the fire of chaff that had been cast in there for the purpose of torture."
Moreover, you two bestowed—meaning, you granted—to this Atri a protection (*omānam*) that brings happiness, as well as strengthening food (*ūrjam*) rich in essence.

Likewise, enjoying (*jujupāṇā*) his beautiful hymn of praise (*suṣṭutim*), you two provided sight (*cakṣuḥ*)—the sound of the lute which reveals the dawning dawn—to the seer Kaṇva, who had been ushered into a dark house by the Asuras with the intent of testing him, saying, "Recognize the dawn as it breaks.
Or alternatively:
To such a Kaṇva—who was emaciated, smeared with filth, and whose vision was covered over—you two restored, that is, re-established, the faculty of sight.

*Omānam*: The suffix *mani* is added to the root *ava* according to the rule for roots beginning with *ava*. By the rule "jvaratvara" etc., the letter *v* and the penultimate vowel are replaced by *ū*.
The suffix *guṇa* [is applied]. The word *api* has this meaning. [The root] *lip* [means] "to smear."
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied after this verbal root.
There is an optional lightening of the vowel due to its inclusion in the *kapilakādi* group.
By the rule "a preceding prefix [is unaccented]," the prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
A slayer, one who loudly calls out, a preeminent challenger in battles; the subduer of the enemy, the foe; fierce, meaning exalted and full of heroic power;
a winner of thousands, a distributor or giver of wealth numbering in the thousands; a showerer, meaning youthful;
loathsome [in appearance], yet firm-limbed.
*Indrajūtam*. The root *ju* is a Vedic (sautra) root meaning "to go.
From this root, with the sense of the gerundive (*tavya*) inherent within it, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is formed in the objective sense.
In the third case, by the rule *karmaṇi*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. *Johatram*:
from the root *hve* (to call) with the elision of the suffix (*luka*), the *auṇādika* suffix *trap* is added.
Because the suffix *pratyaya* has the marker *pittva*, it is udātta on the final syllable; however, the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) remains in effect.
This is the meaning.

From the word *ari*, in the sixth case singular, because of the rule "in the Veda there is optionally [the substitution] of *jas* etc.," the substitution of *guṇa* by *veriti* is optional; thus, in its absence, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs.
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *udāttayaṇaḥ*. Regarding *abhibhūtim*:
it is called *abhibhūti* because one is overcome (*abhibhūyate*) by it.
The suffix *kin* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). By the rule *tādau ca*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratvam*) of the verbal root *gam* (to go) is preserved.
[Thus we have] *sahasrasām*.
The suffix *vid* is applied after the roots *sanoti* or *manati* by the rule *janasanakhanām sañjhaloḥ*;
the substitution of *ā* for the nasal vowel occurs by the rule *vidvoranunāsikasyāt*.

O heroes, well-born Aśvins, we invoke you for excellent protection, we who are in need. Come now with your wealth-bearing chariot, enjoying our songs, for the sake of our welfare. 10. Those two, O heroes, for good protection, we, the well-born ones, invoke, we Aśvins, being in need. Come now hither with your chariot full of riches, enjoying our songs, for the sake of our prosperity. 10.

O Aśvins, leaders, well-born ones of auspicious birth—those two of you, we your praisers, imploring for wealth, call upon you beautifully for protection. Accepting our songs of praise, come hither to us on a chariot laden with riches. For what purpose? For the sake of *suvitá*, that which is to be well-attained—wealth or happiness. *Sujātā*: those whose birth (*jāta*) or origin (*janman*) is beautiful (*śobhana*). The vowel *ā* is substituted for the case-ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). The final syllable of the compound is accented by the rule *nam-subhyām...* (Pāṇini 6.2.172). *Nādhamānāḥ*: from the root *nāth*, meaning "to beg" or "to implore. *Juṣāṇā*: from the root *juṣ*, meaning "to delight in" or "to serve. The suffix *cānaś* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). The suffix *śa* is applied because the root belongs to the *tudādi* class. As before, the vowel *ā* is substituted for the case-ending. *Suvitāya*: derived from the prefix *su-* and the root *i* (from *eti*), in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). The substitution *uvaṅ* occurs because it belongs to the *tanvādi* group. The final syllable of the compound is accented by the rule *sūpamānāt ktaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.145).

Come to us with the fresh swiftness of a hawk, O Nāsatyas, well-disposed toward us; for we, offering oblations, call upon you both, O Aśvins, at the dawning of the most frequent night. 11. Come to us with the fresh swiftness of a hawk, O Nāsatyas, well-disposed toward us; for we, offering oblations, call upon you both, O Aśvins, at the dawning of the most frequent night. 11.

O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, being of one mind (*sajoṣas*), endowed with equal delight, you two go toward that which is worthy of praise from the hawk; accompanied by the horse’s newest, most recent impulse and speed, come (*ā yātam*) to us (*asme*).

O Aśvins, being joined with the oblation (*havis*) to be given to you both, I call upon you two at the breaking forth of the dawn (*vyuṣṭi*), which is eternal in its nature as time—indeed, for all time. For this is the reason.
Since it is so, therefore [the meaning is] "it has come."
*asme*:
by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), there is the substitution of *śe* for the case-ending *śas*.
*sajoṣāḥ*.

By that same [rule], the *su* suffix of the dual is replaced [by *au*]. In *have* and *hemo*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) in the first person singular of the present indicative (*laṭ*) according to the rule "vocalization occurs abundantly in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). There is the substitution of *guṇa* and *avādeśa*. In *śaśvanmāyāḥ*, the final syllable is udātta because it is listed among the *unchādi* group by the rule "the first and last persons are [udātta] everywhere" (*uttamaśca bhaktamau sarvatra*, Pāṇini 6.1.160, Gaṇapāṭha). ||19||
The fourth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "ā vāṃ ratham," is the ṛṣi-seer Dīrghatamas Kakṣīvat’s; it is composed in the Jagatī meter and addressed to the Aśvins.
Thus it is described [in the Anukramaṇī]: "ā vāṃ ratham, ten verses, Jagatī.
This hymn is employed in the Prātaranuvāka of the Aśvina-śastra during the Jāgata-chandas portion, as well as in the recitation for the Aśvins.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "O you two, let your chariot come hither; he who avoids you three times... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15).

I invoke for the sake of life your chariot, which is many-formed, swift as thought, drawn by vigorous horses, and worthy of sacrifice; it has a thousand banners, is victorious, bestows hundreds, is full of strength, and brings us toward the desired food.

I call hither for the sake of life your wondrous chariot, swift as thought with fleet horses, worthy of sacrifice—possessing a thousand banners, victorious, performing a hundred deeds, bringing forth abundance, and bestowing wide space—to the pleasant feast.

O Aśvins, for the sake of life, I invoke your chariot toward the *prayaḥ*—food characterized by oblations. Of what sort is it? It is *purumāyam*, possessing many wonders or many diverse deeds; *manojuvam*, moving as swiftly as thought; *jīraśvam*, endowed with swift horses; *yajñiyam*, worthy of invocation in sacrifices; *sahasraketum*, having many banners or being the indicator (*ketayitṛ*) of a thousandfold wealth; *vaninam*, possessing water (*vana* being a name for water); *śatadaṃsam*, joined with hundreds of riches; *śṛṣṭīvānam*, quickly enjoying or, alternatively, possessing happiness (*śṛṣṭī* being a name for speed or happiness); and *varivodhām*, the giver of *varivas*—wealth. Regarding *purumāyam*: in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final syllable is udātta according to the rule for *tricakra* and others; or else, the suffix *ac* is added after that [word] ending in *purū-*, following the *arśa-ādi* group. Regarding *jīraśvam*: *ju* is a Vedic root meaning "to go"; by the rule *jorī ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.181), the suffix *rak* is applied and the vowel *ī* is substituted for the final *u*. In the *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent of the first member is maintained. Regarding *yajñiyam*: by the rule *yajñirvabhyāṃ ghañjñau*, the suffix *gha* is used in the sense of "worthy of" (*ahārtha*). Regarding *huve*: from the root *hve* in the present tense, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*; and while *luk* is understood [from the previous rule], the elision of the *śap* suffix occurs frequently in the Veda. Regarding *uvaha*: [this refers to the verb *vah*]. Regarding *śatadaṃsam*: [it means] "possessing a hundred riches" (*śatavasum*); the addition of the letter *t* is a Vedic phenomenon (*chāndasa*).
The prayer has been raised up; it has been established for his journey amidst the hymn. All the quarters have turned their minds toward him.
I prepare the hot milk-offering (gharma); the aids come back to us. O Aśvins, may the nourishment ascend your chariot.

The prayer has been raised up; it is directed toward him. It has been placed upon the sacred grass. The quarters of space come together. I prepare the Gharma offering; the aids approach. O Aśvins, the nourishing food has mounted your chariot. 2.

When this chariot proceeds—that is, when it moves forward—at the praising and chanting of the Aśvins, our intellect is directed upward and remains fixed upon them. Immediately thereafter, the directions and the hymns to be recited [are also established]. (Note: Regarding the variants *kṣa-ṭa-prātaranuvāka āśvine* and *na-sa-prātaranuvākasya āśvine*, the meaning is that these occur in the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) during the *āśvina* ceremony.)
2. [The mantra] ending with *kṣaṭ* and situated within the Great Hero (*mahāvīra*).
They come together, they meet, they assemble. The vowel *ā* is used for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

And I, the praiser, offer—that is, I make savory—the most excellent oblation consisting of clarified butter and other substances which are by nature perishable, as it rests within the Great Hero. The protectors (*ūtayaḥ*), that is, the assisting priests (*ṛtvij*), go toward it;
they proceed toward the armor for the sake of consecration.
Moreover, O Aśvins, Ūrjānī, the daughter of Sūrya, has ascended your chariot.
It moves forward (*prayāti*). [The root] *yā* is used in the sense of "reaching" (*prāpaṇe*).
By the rule *āto manin-kvanib-vanipaś ca*, and by the word *bahulam* (variously) in the rule *kṛtya-lyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *manin* is applied here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
The original accent of the first member [of the compound] applies because it belongs to the class beginning with *dāsībhāra*.
[The root] *śas* [is used]; [it is derived from] *śaṃsu*, meaning "to praise."

The suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule *agner api dṛśyante*. Because the inclusion of the root *dṛś* (to see) is intended to encompass all [roots] ending in *-ś*, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
The locative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
*Ayante*: [The root] *aya*, meaning "to go," belongs to the Bhūvādigaṇa and is anudātta.
Regarding *ūtayaḥ*: the suffix *ktic* is applied to the root *av* in the sense of the agent by the rule *kiccakau ca saṃjñāyām*;
furthermore, by the rule *jvaratvara* etc., the vowel *u* is substituted for both the penultimate *v* and the final *a*.
He ascended; by the rule "kṛmṛharuhabhyaś ca," the *aṅ* substitute is applied to the suffix *cli*.
When they met together, vying with one another, the vigorous and immeasurable heroes contended for glory in the fray.
Your chariot, O Aśvins, is indeed renowned on the slope when you carry the patron to his desired bridegroom.

When they, contending with one another, have come together for glory—those unrestrained, eager victors in battle—then your chariot is made manifest on the slope, O Aśvins, when you carry the patron to his chosen bride.

When the *makhas*—the possessors of *makha*, endowed with sacrifice—the immeasurable (*amitāḥ*), limitless, and victorious (*jāyavaḥ*) men, striving for the sake of beautiful wealth (*śubhe dhanāya*) in battle (*raṇe*), contend (*paspṛdhānāsaḥ*) with one another and come together (*sam agmata*), then, O Aśvins, your very chariot (*yuvoraha rathaḥ*) is perceived (*cekitē*) upon the surface of the earth (*pravaṇe*), which is preeminently worthy of worship; that is to say, among the gods, you two alone come swiftly on your chariot for the sake of protection.
The meaning is: that chariot by which you two, O patrons (*sūri*), bring to the worshipper (*stotṛ*) the most excellent wealth (*varam śreṣṭham dhanam*); that is the chariot.
*Paspṛdhānāsaḥ*:
from the root *spṛdh*, meaning "to contend" or "to vie."
The *liṭ* [perfect tense] is Vedic;
for that *liṭ*, there is the substitution of *kānac*. The vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *repha* and the elision of the vowel *a* are Vedic.
"Agamata. The form "agamaḥ" is [derived from] the root *gam* with the *laṅ* suffix;
the *ātmanepada* ending is according to the rule "samo gamyucchi... and so forth.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is elision of the suffix *śap*;
*jha* is replaced by *at*;
and by the rule "gamahana," there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*).
*makhāḥ*. *Makha* means sacrifice (*yajña*). The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule beginning with *arśa-* (Pāṇini 5.2.127).
*Jāyavaḥ*: [derived from] the root *ji* in the sense of "to conquer"; the suffix *uṇ* is applied according to the rule "kṛvāpāj... and so forth.
He observes (*cekite*).
[The root] *kit* means "to know.
From this root, with the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*), the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) is used in the sense of the present tense according to Vedic usage.
The elision of the case-ending occurs because of the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), whereby the third-case ending is dropped.
You two, with your self-yoked birds, went to Bhujyu as he was sinking in the waters, carrying him back to his ancestors.
O showerers of blessings, you went to the dwelling of Vṛtidhṛṣaṇa; for Divodāsa, your great protection became manifest.

You two came with your self-yoked birds to Bhujyu as he was being carried away. O Bulls, you brought him back from the waters for his kinsmen; your aid was celebrated greatly for Dāsa Vṛjinīvat from heaven. 4.
1. *Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* refers to clarified butter (*ājya*) and so forth, which have the nature of flowing (*kṣaraṇa*).
2. *Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is for the sake of beauty (*śobhana*). 3. *Kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is for that which is worthy of being honored (*saṃbhajana*).

O Ashvins, you two showerers of desires, O bulls, you carried Bhujyu—the son of Tugra—who was being carried away by the birds (Vibhis), having gone down and sunk into the ocean; you brought him up with your own yoked horses, that is, with special vessels (ships) harnessed by yourselves, as far as the fathers—meaning, as far as the place where the fathers, such as Tugra and others, reside. (The prefix *ā* here denotes a limit.)
They say "vijenyam" means situated at a distance;

you two went toward the dwelling of Tumas, which was located far away. Moreover, we know that the great (*mahi*), profound (*gambhīram*) protection (*avaḥ*) provided by you two for King Divodāsa—consisting of the slaying of Śambara—is indeed known to us.
*bharamāṇam* (bearing):
from the root *ḍubhṛñ*, meaning "to support" or "to nourish";
the suffix *śānac* is applied to the present participle (*laṭ*) in the passive sense (*karman*).
The substitution of *ś* occurs by way of transposition;
the substitution of *u* [for *i*] occurs frequently in the Vedic language (*bahulam chandasi*). [Thus:
*pitṛbhya ā*.

The word *āṅ* has the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* when it denotes a limit (*maryādā*) [Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.89]. Consequently, the ablative case is used according to [Pāṇini Sūtra] 2.3.10: "The ablative is used with *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*.
Thus, [the form] *yāsiṣṭa* [is derived].
O Aśvins, you two protected the seer Rebha from *uruvyathaḥ*—from a surrounding affliction, whether from being driven away or from falling into a well;
for Yāska states that "the word *uruvyati* denotes the act of protecting" (Nirukta 5.23).

Likewise, for the seer Agni, you two warded off with cold water—that is, with frost—the *gharma*, which was heated on all sides and cast by the Asuras for the sake of causing pain, and which was blazing like fire.
Or rather:
with the oblation, I consecrate the *gharma*—a constant heat [produced] by the rays of the sun for Agni, the consumer;
this is a name for the day.
With the cool rainwater, you two warded off the heat so that such an oblation might be prepared for the sake of rising up.
Moreover, in the cow of the seer named Śayu—a cow whose milk had ceased—you two caused the protective milk to swell;
thus, the aged seer Vandana was extended with a long life, being made to flourish by you both.
The term *apūrva* has the sense of crossing over and increasing.

O Aśvins, you two came to Bhujyu— who was distressed and oppressed by the abandonment of his own father Tugra in the midst of the ocean, far away in a distant land— as he was praising you with compassion;
you went there for the sake of protecting him.

Therefore, O Aśvins, your aids (*ūtīḥ*)—which are *svarvatīḥ* (possessing splendor), *itáḥ* (proceeding from this source of happiness), *citráḥ* (wonderful and worthy of admiration)—have indeed become, and continue to be, *abhīke* (in close proximity) *abhiṣṭayaḥ* (objects of invocation by all living beings).
[The word] *kṛpamāṇam* [is used];
the root *kṛp-* signifies the act of praising.
And *bhaya* should be understood as belonging to the *tud-ādi* class.
[The word] *svarvatīḥ* [is derived from] *suparvan* with the suffix *viṣ* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*) after the root *bhṛ*.
Then follows the suffix *matup*.
By the rule “*chandasīraḥ*,” there is the substitution of *v* for the *m* of *matup*.
[Thus we have] *abhiṣṭayaḥ*.
The root *iṣ* is used in the sense of "desiring.
The suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
The substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatva*) occurs according to the rule governing *śakandhu* and similar words.
Or indeed, the honey-bee of the *uśij* clan calls out to you both for the intoxication of the Soma;
you two entered into the mind of Dadhyañc, and then the horse's head spoke to you.
Or perhaps a honey-bee has buzzed for you both, sweet with the Soma; the son of Uśij calls you hither. You have entered the mind of Dadhyac, and then the horse's head spoke to you. 9.
Moreover, O Aśvins, the honey-loving *saradhā* (bee) praised you two who possess sweetness (*madhumantau*).
Likewise, Kakṣīvān, the son of Uśij, invokes you both with the drinking of Soma when exhilaration (*mada*) has become the cause.
And you two, desiring the knowledge of honey in order to give honey to that bee, attended upon the mind—the thought—of the seer Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa with serviceful obedience.

Then, immediately after he had become pleased, that horse’s head—which was sent by you two as a gift related to the horse—he spoke the science of honey (*madhuvidyā*) back to you both; the meaning is that the seer taught it with that horse's head.
It is full of sweetness (*madhumat*).
The elision of the case-ending is by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. [The root] *rap* [is used]; [the roots] *rap* and *lap* mean "articulate speech."
The root *mad* [is used] in the sense of joy (*harṣe*).
According to the rule *maḍo 'nupasarge*, the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).
*huvantyati* | [The root] *heñ* is used in the sense of rivalry (*spardhā*) and sound (*śabda*).
By the rule *lyuṭ ca*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule "it is frequent in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). He desires invocation for himself;
[this is expressed by] *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*.
The elision of another [letter] is Vedic;
the substitution of *u* for the vowel is due to the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*).
Having bent down.
Having approached for the sake of existence,

[the suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule "in the Veda, when meaning 'existence'. O Aśvins, you two bestowed upon Pedu the white horse, the granter of many boons, the conqueror, and the savior.

With arrows, you two protected for Pedu the white steed, the winner of much wealth, the conqueror, the one who shines with glory, invincible in battles, difficult to overcome, and active like Indra, the subduer of peoples.

You two [protected] for Pedu the one of many boons, O Aśvins, the prize-winner, the white, the overcomer, you who dwell in the dwelling; with arrows, the shining one, invincible in battles, difficult to overcome, active like Indra, the subduer of peoples. 10.

O Aśvins, you two gave to King Pedu—named Pedu—the horse Śveta, which was white in color, possessed many desirable qualities, was a conqueror of enemies contending in battle, and was a savior; you two bestowed it upon him. Furthermore, of what nature was it? By means of arrows... [the rest of the verse].
"Śaryas" means warriors, so called because they "perish" (śīryante).

By them, [the chariot] is "unassailable" (dustaram), meaning impossible to overcome in battles (*pṛtanāsu*) or conflicts; it is "radiant" (*abhidyum*), possessing arrived splendor; it is "to be employed" (*cakṛtyam*), to be used again and again in all tasks; and it is "like Indra, the subduer of peoples" (*indram iva carṣaṇīsaham*).
The meaning is that, just as Indra overcomes his enemies, so too is it the conqueror of the enemy hosts.
*spudhām* | [The root *spṛdh*] means "in rivalry" or "in competition.
[It is formed] by the rule *kip ca*.

*Kip*: Because the word *vaś* draws along with it the inclusion of *hi*, and because that [inclusion] serves to incorporate other rules, there is the elision of the vowel *a* and the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *r*. The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*. *Taratāram*: From the root *tṛ* in the sense of "floating" or "crossing over," the suffix *tṛṣi* is applied; the formation of the form is established through the specific grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*) found in the list beginning with *prasita-skabhita-stabhita*. *Kartṛyam*: From the root *kṛ* with the suffix *yaṅ* elided (*yaṅluk*), the suffix *kyap* is applied by the rule *vibhāṣā druvapoḥ*; from that, the suffix *tuk* is added. 21.

The fifth hymn, consisting of twelve verses, begins with “kā rādhat. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: “‘Kā rādhat’: twelve verses; [the seer is] Anyā Duḥsvapnanāśanī; the meter is Gāyatrī except for the second, which is Kakubh, the third and fourth are Kāvirāṭ and Naṣṭarūpī respectively, the fifth is Tanuśirā, the sixth is Padyakṣara, the seventh is Uṣṇih, the eighth is Vihārabṛhatī, the ninth is Kṛti, the tenth has twenty syllables, and the last three are Gāyatrīs.”
This is its meaning:
Kakṣīvān is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [hymn] by way of lineage from Auśija Dīrghatamas; the first [verse] is a Gāyatrī.
The verse beginning with “vidvāṃsau” is a Kakubh, because the middle foot consists of twelve syllables.

The ignorant man should ask the two wise ones at the doors; for another who is thus unwise is indeed not at all a knower among mortals. The ignorant man should ask the two wise ones at the doors; for another who is thus unwise is indeed not at all a knower among mortals.

In this manner—as previously described—the ignorant, unlearned praiser (*avit*) should ask about the paths (*vit*), that is, the means consisting of praise and service, which lead to the two all-knowing Aśvins (*vidvāṃsau vit*). He ought to inquire about the doors (*dvāraḥ*), the gateways to these approaches. Furthermore, he is one who must be enlightened by others; he is devoid of consciousness (*acetāḥ*), lacking the wisdom of the mind (*cetasā*).
Therefore, the meaning is that one should ask the Aśvins alone.

And those two, the Aśvins, who are free from being assailed by enemies, bestow *sani* (gain) upon the mortal—the human worshipper—very quickly (*vcit*) by virtue of their disposition to grant the shares of their devotees; such is the completion of the sentence.
*Itthā*:
the suffix *thā* is applied according to the rule "In the Vedic language, *thā* is used for the sense of cause (*hetau*)";
[the base] *idam* becomes *iṣ*.

"O Dāstṛs, I ask these two [questions] with simple-mindedness, not as one skilled in the ways of the gods: from where does the Vaṣaṭ-call come for the oblation that has been offered? [Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 17, Sūkta 120, Verse 1] *The First Aṣṭaka: 753*
And protect us, O you two, from the violent ones and from those who are most formidable.

I ask the gods with simple sincerity; O Dastṛs, drink of the oblation consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call and of that which is unmarked. And do you two protect us from the violent and from the impetuous. 4.

O Aśvins, I ask you both; I desire to question you specifically. I do not ask other gods who are "pākyā"—those of immature understanding whose intellects have not yet reached full maturity. Rather, the meaning is that I ask only you two, the omniscient ones. O "dastrā," you two who are worthy of being seen, drink your own portion, characterized as a single part, of this "adbhutasya" (wondrous), "mahataḥ" (great), "sahasaḥ" (exceedingly powerful and strength-bestowing) Soma offered with the "vaṣaṭ" call. And make us "rabhyasaḥ"—exceedingly impetuous and possessed of mature effort. Regarding the word *pākyā*: from the root *pac* (to cook/mature), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied by the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*. By the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for *c*. It has the accent on the first syllable (*tisvara*). The case-ending is replaced by *darśa* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Regarding *vaṣaṭkṛtasya*: since the word *vaṣaṭ* belongs to the class beginning with *ūryādi*, it functions as a *gati*; thus, by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the preceding *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvaratvam*). Regarding *pātam*: from the root *pā* (to drink). The elision of the suffix *śap* occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. Regarding *sahasaḥ*: that by which one overcomes or prevails is *sahaḥ*, i.e., strength. The suffix *asun* is added. That which possesses this is *sahasvī*. The possessive suffix *vini* is added in the sense of possession. From that, the comparative suffix *īyasun* is added. By the rule *vinmatoluk*, the suffixes *vin* and *matup* are elided. The elision of the vowel *ī* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Regarding *rabhyasaḥ*: from the root *rabh* (in the sense of *rābhasya*). *Rabhasyam* is the commencement of an action. The grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) is to be understood as before.
The speech which shines forth like [the song] of Ghoṣa Bhr̥gavāṇa, with which the Pajnya priest worships you both—
like a wise messenger.
The speech which shines forth like [a singer] at Ghosha or Bhr̥gavāṇa—that speech with which the one worthy of sacrifice worships you both, like a wise man seeking arrows. 5.

He [is] the two Aśvins; she becomes pre-eminent, she becomes capable—that speech which consists of praise for you—shines in Ghoṣa, the son of Ghoṣā and Alavī, in the seer named Suhastya, and in Bhṛgavaṇa, that is, in Bhṛgu.
And just as by means of this speech characterized as praise, the Aṅgirases attained immortality.
Kakṣīvān, born of their lineage, worships—that is, honors and praises—*vām*, you two;
the meaning is that he also shines thereby.
Like one desiring food for himself, Kakṣīvān, who is wise and skilled in praise, may also "prevail"—that is, by your grace, may his desires be fulfilled.
Ghoṣe:
There was a certain female exponent of the Veda named Ghoṣā, the daughter of Kakṣīvān.
Here, by way of metonymy (*upacāra*), the nominal stem denoting her is used to refer to her son.
In *bhṛgavāṇe*:
he acts like the ancient Bhṛgu.
The suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule "after all nominal stems (*sarvaprātipadika*)... [Pāṇini 3.2.76].
In the term *dhātusaṃjñā*, the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is replaced by the suffix *śānac* through metathesis; then the *śap* augment and so forth are applied.
Because the rule for the addition of *suk* is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), the form *sugābhavaḥ* is possible.
The root *vṛṣ* and others;
in the sense of "shining": *śubh* means "to shine."
The elision of the suffix *tal* occurs by the rule "lopasta ātmanepadeṣu. [Thus] *iṣayuḥ*.
[The root is] *iṣa* in the sense of "going."
It is called *iṣ* (food) because it is desired (*iṣyati*) or it goes (*gacchati*). The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*.
Alternatively:
The root *iṣ* means "to desire.
That which is desired by all living beings is *iṣ*, meaning food (*anna*).
Here, the agentive suffix is used for the object by way of grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

As stated previously regarding the *saṃhitā*, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.1.89.4: "In the case of *pra* followed by *ūha*, *ūḍha*, *ūḍhi*, *eṣa*, and *edha*, lengthening should be prescribed.

1. Those whose intellects are unripened by *kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *na*. 2. Drink the *pāta* of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*; and drink the *sapāta*. 3. To be known as *ca*, *ta*, *da*, *pha*, and *śa*. 4. By means of the form of praise consisting of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*. 5. *Kṣa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and his son. Ka. 15: I have heard the Māyatra hymn; I am possessed of reasoning regarding this. O Aśvins, you two have indeed delighted my mind.
O Lords of Splendor, bestow [favor] upon our eyes.
It has been heard: it is the Gāyatra. He possesses reasoning. I—indeed, I have sung forth to you both, O Aśvins. O Lords of Splendor, open wide my eyes. 6.

O Aśvins, that Gāyatra song—fit for chanting, joined with the Gāyatrī meter, and to be accomplished through the Gāyatra-sāman hymn—of him who is swift, of another who is self-giving and a performer of rites, has been heard or not heard. Even I, like you, have indeed praised you; for he has sung your praise.
What was he doing?
O you two lords of beauty (*śubhaspati*), protectors of auspicious action or masters of the waters, you have bestowed eyes upon me;
taking them as it were from him, grant them to me also as my desired fruit—this is the intended meaning.
*Śrutam*. [The root] *śru* means "to hear.
In the *laṭ* [present tense], there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) according to the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the suffixes] are frequently [elided]."
Regarding *takavāna*:
the root *taka* means "to go.
Here, by means of that which denotes the general act of going, its specific location indicates slow movement.
The suffix *u* is derived according to the *auṇādika* rules;
the formation should be understood as being like *bhṛgavāṇa*.
[He] has sung repeatedly (*rirēbha*).
The root *rebh* means "to sound. [In the word] *akṣī*:
by the rule "and *ī* in the dual," the substitution of the vowel *ī* occurs for the word *akṣi*.
And that [first word] is udātta.

In "śubhaspatī," because of the rule "subāmantritaṃ parāṅgavatsvare" (Pāṇini 2.1.2), the genitive ending is treated as if it were part of the subsequent member; consequently, the entire two-word compound undergoes the anudātta accentuation of the vocative prescribed in the eighth chapter.

The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used after the root *dā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, according to Pāṇini’s rule 1.3.20: "The middle voice is used for *ā-dā* [meaning] taking, except when it refers to opening the mouth.
The suffix *śatṛ* is used here by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The suffix *bhluṅ* is applied because [the root] belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class.
The absence of reduplication occurs due to the rule stating, "In the section on reduplication, it should be stated that in the Veda it is optional.
Because of the mention of "in both ways" (*ubhayathā*) in the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, the *śatṛ* suffix is treated as *sārvadhātuka*, and thus possesses the *ṅit* property.
Because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* [affix], there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64).

For you two are indeed the masters of great wealth, or you are those who bestow it when it is exhausted; as such, O Vasus, be our good protectors and guard us from the wolf, from the one who intends evil.
For you two indeed are the great delighters at home, or you two are those from whom one departs; as such, O Vasus, be our good protectors and guard us from the wolf who seeks to do us harm. 7.
The Aśvins are the bestowers, the givers of great and mighty wealth. You two have caused even the most distant person to reach their home; you have brought forth riches from the depths.

The meaning is that you two alone are the protectors who ward off those who would destroy. O Vasūs, O Aśvins, you who provide dwelling—may you two be our excellent guardians, our perfect protectors and defenders.
Moreover, protect us from the one who seeks to harm us—the wolf-like thief who desires evil fruit for us. Save us!
*mahaḥ* [is the nominative singular of] *mahataḥ*; the elision of the suffix *-ac* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
"Ran" is to be understood as a derivative of "dakṣiti"; the singular number is used by way of grammatical substitution (vyatyaya).

*nirataṃtasat*: [This is derived] from the root *taṃs* with the suffix *alaṃkāre* (Pāṇini 3.2.15). From this *pant*-ending root, by the rule *ṇiśridrusrubhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.48), there is *caṅ* in place of *cli* in the *luṅ* tense, as well as reduplication (*dvivacana*) and so forth.
Because it is obstructed by the designation *gus* (genitive) and the designation *kayu* (nominative), there is an absence of the *sañc* state.
[In the form] *sugopā*, the case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
*aghāyoḥ*:
one who desires evil for others. The suffix *kyac* is applied according to the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the suffix is used] to express the desire of another."
The form *āstham* is derived from the root *ās* with the suffix *u*, according to the rule *kyācchandasī*.
The suffix *u* is applied here because it belongs to the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
1. When *jha*, *ṭa*, or *ṭha* [follow], the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is obtained. 2. *jha*: *āstaṃ hi abhavatam*; *ṭha*: *āstamabhavatam*.
May they not go to anyone who is unfriendly toward us; may they not go from our houses anywhere, O cows.
He has breasts for arms and is devoid of the beauty of a child.

Do not [give us up] to anyone; do not [give us up] to the enemy. Let not our milch-cows go away from our homes anywhere—those who provide nourishment with their udders, yet are themselves without young. 8.

O Aśvins, do not place us face-to-face with any enemy—*amitriṇe* means one who lacks friends (*amitra*), that is, an adversary; [do not place] us [in such a state] for anyone. Furthermore, let not our milch-cows (*dhenavaḥ*)—which nourish calves and men with their milk (*stanābhujaḥ*)—go anywhere out of our houses, separated from their young (*aśiśrīḥ*), or failing to find rest in our homes. Let them not go to any place inaccessible to us. Regarding *ghātam*: from the root *dhā*, in the *luṅ* tense with the prohibitive particle *māṅ*, there is the elision of *sic* by *gāti-sthā-*; the absence of *aṭ* is due to *na māṅ-yoge*. Regarding *akutra*: the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member is due to *parādiś chandasi bahulam*. Regarding *guḥ*: from the root *iṇ* "to go," there is the substitution of *gā* in the *luṅ* tense; the *sic* is elided by *gāti-sthā-*, and *jhi* becomes *jus* by *ātaḥ*. Regarding *stanābhujaḥ*: from the root *bhuja* "to protect" or "to eat. They protect with their milk, thus *stanābhujaḥ*; the suffix *kvip* is applied, and the lengthening is Vedic (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*). Regarding *aśiśrīḥ*: this should be seen as a Vedic irregular formation even outside the rules of Pāṇini 4.1.62 (*sasya śiśrī-*) as noted in the Bhāṣya. Alternatively, *śiśrī* means "one who has a young one" (*śiśu*); the suffix *ī* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) according to *chandasy-īvan-pau*. In the negative compound, the original accent of the first member remains (*avyaya-pūrva-prakṛti-svara*). Or, alternatively, from the root *śīṅ* "to lie down," the suffix *kvip* is applied in the Veda (*utsargaś chandasi*), followed by reduplication and shortening. By *en-e-kācaḥ*, *yaṇ* is substituted, and the *v* is a Vedic anomaly. The accents of the compounds are as previously stated.
May you both milk [the cow] for the sake of our friendship; measure out for us wealth consisting of booty, and measure out for us nourishment consisting of milch-cows.

May they milk for us [their] friendship; may you two measure out for us wealth, and may you two measure out for us food accompanied by strength, and may you two measure out for us food accompanied by cattle. 9.

O Aśvins, those who desire you—praisers who either separate [evil] or unite [the good] with hymns—milk for themselves, that is, they obtain, bounties from you for the sake of *mitradhiti*, the maintenance of their kinsmen and friends.
Therefore, measure out for us also wealth consisting of *vāja* (strength/food) and for riches joined with *vāja*;
likewise, measure out for us food consisting of cows and for nourishment.
The meaning is: "Bestow upon your praisers wealth that is peerless and accompanied by tribute, as well as food provided with cattle."
*duhīyan*. *Duha* [is used] in the sense of filling.
*Duhiḥ* becomes *dehaḥ*.
The suffix *i* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) by the rule *igupadhātkin* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.559). Thus, from *duh*, one forms *duhīyati*, meaning "he desires to milk for himself.
This is derived by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*.
In the *leṭ* [subjunctive] of the root *duhīyati*, there is the augment *aṭ*. By the rule "and after *it*" (*itaśca lopaḥ*), there is the elision of the vowel *i*.

This form arises because, by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*), the substitution of *ran* [for *m*] prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.4.105 (*duher liṅi masya ran*) does not occur;
furthermore, the elision of the other [suffixes] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
