When the substitution of *r* for *ra* is made according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), the *repha* becomes *va*. For this very reason, because the etymological derivation cannot be determined, they do not perform an avagraha. [Example: *yuvāku*.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *-jas*. [The form] *mimītam* [is derived from] the root *māṅ* in the sense of measuring.
1. [The roots] preceded by *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha* are as before; [the root] *svap* takes the vowels [as its augment]. 2.

For the [root] *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa-balyukāya*, and in the word *śabda*, [it belongs to] the *juhotyādi* class. The *parasmaipada* [ending] occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). By the rule "of *bhṛj* etc.," there is shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). By the rule "when connected with *ca* or *vā*, the first [verb is not unaccented]," there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (non-accentuation).

The chariot of the Aśvins, which wins the prize, is without horses, yet it possesses powerful steeds; with that, I have great delight. 10. Of the Aśvins: the prize-winning chariot, horseless, yet possessing powerful steeds; with that, I have great delight. 10.

I, the singer, have obtained as my share the chariot of the two Aśvins, who possess *vāja*—that is, food or strength—and who are endowed with such activity; a chariot that is *anaśva*, meaning not drawn by horses, yet which moves even without horses through its own extraordinary power. By means of that chariot, I desire (*cākana*) abundant (*bhūri*) welfare. Regarding *asanum*: from the roots *vana* and *ṣaṇa* in the sense of "to obtain" or "to share," this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) form. Regarding *cākana*: from the root *kana* in the senses of "shining," "beauty," or "motion," this is the Vedic *liṭ* (perfect). It may also be considered equivalent to *jalus*.

Because it is impermanent (*anitya*), the suffix *tum* is absent. [The word] *revataḥ*: from the word *rayi*, the suffix *matup* is added. By the rule “*rayermatau bahulam*,” there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). By the rule “*chandasīraḥ*,” the *m* of *matup* becomes *v*. By the rule “*reśabdācca matupa udāttatvam*,” that [suffix] is acute-accented (*udātta*). In both instances [of *ubhau*], the vowel *ā* is substituted by the rule “*supāṃ suluk*. || 23 || || 17 ||

In the eighteenth section (anuvāka), there are seven hymns (sūktas). Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fifteen verses, begins with "katthā. It is enumerated thus: "katthā; [it has] five [verses]; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas, or [to Indra]. The seer (ṛṣi) is Kakṣīvān, who continues from the previous context. By the rule governing the absence of a specific instruction, the meter is Triṣṭubh. The deity is either the Viśvedevas or Indra. The application (viniyoga) is according to the ritual manual (laidika).
Where is our vessel among those seeking the gods—the one that brings fame, surpassing the Aṅgirases?
When he, the worshipful one, having driven away the hostile powers, strides boldly forward at the sacrifice toward the wide dwelling.

When will he hear our vessel, as he hastens toward the songs of the Aṅgirases who seek the gods? When the worshipful one has come forth from the dwelling to the clans, he strides widely at the sacrifice.

Indra—the protector (*pātā*) of men (*nṛṇām*), the one whose nature is to guard (*netṛṇām*) those who offer praise—driving forth the wealth in the form of cattle (*turuṇyan*), when will he hear our hymns (*giraḥ*) being thus employed by us, the Aṅgirases, who desire the radiant Indra (*devayatām*) who is endowed with qualities such as generosity? When will he hear them at what time? When that Indra reaches (*pra ānaṭ*) the people (*viśaḥ*) characterized by the priests, belonging to the sacrificer indicated by the word *harmya* (the sacrificial hall), then, being worthy of worship (*yajatraḥ*) in our sacrifice (*adhvare*), he strides (*kraṃsate*) widely; that is, he exerts himself of his own accord. *Kat*: "When? The elision of the vowel is Vedic. *Naḥ*: "Of us. *Pātram*: "Protector. By the rule *nṛpye* (Pāṇini 8.3.10), the *n* becomes *s* in the *saṃhitā*; here, by the rule *atrānunāsikaḥ pūrvasya tu vā*, the *ṛ* is nasalized. *Pātram*: From the root *pā* "to protect," with the suffix *tṛn* denoting habit; there is an irregular substitution of *am* for the case-ending *su*. Because a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific technical name is not necessarily permanent, there is no *guṇa* strengthening, and thus the *yaṇ* sandhi occurs. *Devayatām*: From the suffix *kyac* added to the *sup* ending *ātmanaḥ* (by *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*), then the suffix *chaṭ* (which is *śatṛ*), and finally the acute accent on the case-ending by the rule *śaturanumaḥ*. *Śravat*: From the root *śru* "to hear," in the *leṭ* mood; the augment *aṭ* is added, and the *vikaraṇa* suffix is elided by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. *Turuṇyan*: From the root *turu* "to hasten," belonging to the *kaṇvādi* class. *Ānaṭ*: From the root *abhi-an* (or *an* with prefix *abhi*); in the *liṭ* tense, there is an irregular substitution of the *parasmaipada* ending. Where *śap* was expected, there is an irregular *śnu* suffix; the change of *n* to *ṇ* occurs by the rule *naśchavyapraśān*; the augment *āṭ* is added. *Harmyasya*: From the word *harmya*, the suffix *ac* is added because it belongs to the *arśādi* group. *Kraṃsate*: From the root *kramu* "to step"; the *ātmanepada* is used by the rule *vṛttisargatāyaneṣu kramaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.38). In the *leṭ* mood, the augment *aṭ* is added, and the suffix *sip* is added by the rule *sibbahulaṃ leṭi*. *Yajatraḥ*: The suffix *atrap* is added to the root *yaj* by the rule *aminakṣi* etc. (Pāṇini 3.2.72).
He, the supporter, propped up the sky; he, the bull, bestowed wealth upon the hero for the sake of the cow.
The mighty one looked toward his own kin; they beheld the mother of the world’s purpose, the cow.

He has propped up the sky; he has made the earth a firm foundation. For the sake of the prize, the hero has bestowed the wealth of the cow. The buffalo has looked upon his own kin; you two have beheld the mate of the purpose, the mother of the cow.
1. The fruit of *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is protection (*rakṣaṇa*).
2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha* is wealth; *na-sa* is wealth in the form of cattle.
That *saḥ*, namely Indra, indeed supports (*stambhīta*) the *yām*, the heavenly world.

Likewise, "anaraḥ" means the leader (*netā*) of the cows that were stolen by the Paṇis; he is Indra. Being "Ṛbhu," shining as the expansive (*uru*) and vast (*vistīrṇa*) sun, he "puṣāyat"—that is, he nourishes, accomplishes, or causes to rain down—the "draviṇam," which is water (a name for water), the support (*dharaṇa*) to be sought after (*abhidravaṇīya*) by all living beings, the sustainer of everything, namely the rainwater—for the sake of food (*vājāya*) or for the sake of strength (*balārtha*). Thus, the meaning is that he succeeds or pours forth rain.
Moreover, "Mahiṣaḥ":
this is a name for the Great One.
Indra, in the form of the Sun, [seizes] the "Vām," which is his own, produced from his own light.
It is called *rātri* because it envelops everything with darkness, or it covers it;
alternatively,
it is called *uṣas* because it envelops [the world] with light.
They looked upon it;
*caṣṭiḥ* is a word for the act of seeing. It sees after, that is, it shines forth.
The meaning is: "Though he himself possesses full radiance, he rises after the night and the dawn brought about by his own movement.
Furthermore, there is this other point of reference: that which is called "the mare" (*aśvasya menām*)—this is a name for a female.
He made the female horse— the mother, the progenitress of the cow—
into its opposite;
he reversed it.
Once, Indra sportingly produced a cow from a mare;
this is established here and is clearly understood from another mantra in the form of Indra’s own words.
[This is] the support.
The suffix *un* is applied by the rule "dhārerṇiluk ca. [Thus] *puṣāyat*.
[The root] *puṣ* [is used] in the sense of "moistening, sprinkling, and filling," as well as "nourishing" (*pluṣa*).
It belongs to the *kry-ādi* class.
In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *aṭ*.
According to the rule "in the Veda, *śāyaj* also [is substituted]," even for the root *ah*, the substitute *śāyaj* is applied in place of the suffix *śap*.
*Naraḥ*:
[derived from] the root *nṛ* in the sense of "leading" (*naye*).
By virtue of the rule stating "in many cases" (*bahulavacanāt*), the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule *ṛdorap*.
They spoke. The root *cakṣiṅ* means "in distinct speech";
this is the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

"According to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is no elision of the suffix *śap*. He has approached the call; the ruddy ones [the dawns], the ancient king, the swift one, following the tribes of the Aṅgirases, the shaker. He fashioned the thunderbolt, the harnessed team; he propped up the sky for the four-footed, for manly man, and for the two-footed. He has approached the call; the ruddy ones; the ancient; the king; the swift one; of the tribes; of the Aṅgirases; following; the shaker; he fashioned; the thunderbolt; the harnessed team; he propped up; the sky; for the four-footed; for manly man; for the two-footed."

May the Dawn-goddesses—ruddy in color or radiant—[and] Indra, the Sun-soul, shining forth, reach (*nakṣat*) and hear this ancient invocation (*havam*), offered by former seers and now being performed by us.
Of what nature is he?
Day after day, he is the impeller of wealth for the clans of men, the Aṅgirases, and the praising seers.
Moreover, that Indra "fashioned" (takṣat) his own weapon, the thunderbolt, "yoked" (niyutam)— meaning thoroughly joined—
with the one to be slain; likewise, he "stabilized" (tastambhat) the sky,
meaning he acted so that it would not fall downward.
For what purpose? "For the benefit of men" means for the welfare of human beings; "for the four-footed" refers to cattle and so forth; and "for the two-footed" refers to humans.
The meaning is that it is for the sake of both these groups.
*nakṣat* [is derived from] *nakṣa gatau* (to go);
the augment *aṭ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood.
The suffix *ya* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 4.4.133, "pūrvyam | pūrvaiḥ kṛtam ity au ca," [yielding] *pūrvyam*. [The word] *rāṭ*.
The root *rāj* means "to shine.
From this root, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it, the suffix *kvip* is applied,
resulting in *turaḥ*.
The root *tur* is used in the sense of "hastening. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*. Thus: *takṣat*.

The root *takṣ* (in the sense of "to fashion" or "to thin") is used here; the absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "the augment *aṭ* is frequently omitted in the Veda even when not preceded by *mā*. Thus: *tastambhat*.

The root *skabh* (in the form *stabhi*) means "to obstruct movement. This form is derived from that root with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the aorist marker (*luṅ*), followed by the augment (*caṅ*).
The acute accent on the penultimate syllable is due to the rule "caṅyanyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 6.1.218).
Because the preceding word does not reside in the same sentence (*asamānavākyasthatvāt*), there is an absence of *nighāta* (the low-pitched accent).
[The term] *catuṣpade* means "he who has four feet" (*satvāraḥ pādā asya*).
‘saṃkhyāsupūrvasya’ [Pāṇini 5.4.140].
1. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha reads ‘anūdita’.
2. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha reads ‘tadrūpām’.
3. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, "jananīm" (mother) is not present.
4. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, it reads "pari parītya" (having gone around).
5. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṭa, and ṭha, it reads "sūryātmanā" (as the nature of the sun).
6. *sa-* [is used] in the sense of "may he hear"; *na-* [is used] in the sense of "may he not hear"; *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-* [is used] in the sense of "may he pervade" (*vyāpnotu*).
Thus, there is the elision of the indeclinable form of the word *pāda* as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*).
In the singular dative case, when it bears the designation *mas*, by the rule *pādaḥ pat*, the substitution of *pat* occurs.
In the case of two feet,
the procedure is as before;
however, this is the distinction.
Because [the word] begins with *ayas* (iron) and so forth, it is a nominal stem (*pada*); thus, in the absence of the designation *mas*, there is an absence of the [substitution of] *pañcamī*.
[The accentuation] follows from the rule: “In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, when *pāda*, *hana*, or *mūrdhan* follow *dvi* or *tri*, the final syllable of the subsequent member is udātta.”
In his exhilaration, he bestowed the resonant voice upon the one who upholds the cosmic order; he opened the obstructed herd of cows.
When he, the three-peaked one, turned back your streams, he drove away the malice of man from your dwelling.

At his exhilaration, you gave the heavenly host for the sake of Truth—the face of the kine which Trikakup brought back when he set out. You have thrown open the doors of the darkness for the human race. 4. At his exhilaration, you gave the heavenly host for the sake of Truth—the face of the kine which Trikakup brought back when he set out. You have thrown open the doors of the darkness for the human race.

O Indra, when you were exhilarated by the drinking of this soma, for the sake of the *ṛta*—that is, for the purpose of sacrifice—you gave the host of cows (*ustriyāṇāṃ gavām*), which was hidden in secret caves by the Paṇis and praised as worthy of hymns; Agni gave them to the Aṅgirases.
The second half-verse is composed in the indirect (past) tense.

Or rather, when indeed Indra, exalted throughout the three worlds (*trikakup*) during the onset of battle, turns back—that is, he prevails completely—then that Indra opens wide (*apa vaḥ*) the doors (*duraḥ*), which had been closed to prevent the cows from escaping, belonging to the *paṇi* Asura who is the "milker" (*duhaḥ*) or "oppressor" (*drodhuḥ*) of the human mind.
*svaryam*.
[The root] *svṛ* [is used] in the sense of "sound" and "affliction. [The suffix] *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*.
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of grammatical rules based on technical designations (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution].
*Apivṛtam*: this is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the object (*karman*) derived from the root *vṛ* preceded by the prefix *api*.
By the rule *nipātasya ca*, there is lengthening of the first member;
by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) of the prefix is maintained. Thus: *prasarge*.

*Prasarga* means that in this [state] arrows (*iṣavaḥ*) are intensely emitted (*prakarṣeṇa sṛjyante*) or released (*vimucyante*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). The accentuation follows the rule for the original form of the final member of a compound beginning with a *ku*-word (*kud-uttarapada-prakṛti-svaratvam*).
The absence of the accentuation beginning with *thā* and *thāt* is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
[The root] *nivartat* [is used];
[the root] *vṛt* means "to turn."
The augment *aṭ* is added before the optative suffix (*leṭ*).
By transposition, the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is used.
[The ending] is *vaḥ*.
The root *vṛñ* is used in the sense of "choosing.
In the Vedic *luṅ* tense, by the rule "ghas etc. in mantras," *cli* is replaced by *luk*.
After the substitution of *guṇa*, there is the elision of the *hal* and *ṅī* suffixes according to the rule beginning with *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt*.
For you was that milk which your parents brought, a gift of fertile seed, O swift and active one;
that pure wealth which they, seeking to awaken you, extracted from the cow.
For you [is] the milk, which the two parents brought as a gift, well-seeded, hurrying, and active; that pure wealth of yours which they, seeking awakening, have offered from the cow. 5.

O Indra, when the two parents, Heaven and Earth—who are active, who nourish the entire world, and who bring it forth—brought the milk, characterized as the *sānnāyya* oblation, into the cows (that is, they poured it out), for you, O swift-acting one;
what kind of milk?
It was *rādhas*, that which bestows prosperity, and *suretas*, possessing excellent seed—that is, capable of producing the entire world.
For the world arises from the sacrificial oblation:
"The oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings" (Manu 3.76).
Whenever and wherever that pure [substance] has been brought into heaven, earth, and the cows, it exists; here,
the elision of the *ti* suffix occurs according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*.
3. From the essence of *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*; that is, from the cause (*sa-kāraṇāt*).

The sacrificers offered to you this auspicious oblation—belonging to the cow Unnī, who yields the milk of the Sabandhū; a path [of milk], a *rekaṇas* (a name for wealth, meaning "possessing wealth" or "abundant and increased")—they presented it to you face-to-face. At that time, he opens the doors of the human world; thus is the connection with the preceding verse. Regarding the words: *Anītām*: from the root *ṇīñ* "to lead," in the *laṅ* tense, the *śap* suffix is elided by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. *Suretaḥ*: the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member follows the rule "somārnasī alomoṣī. *Turaṇe*: from the root *turaṇa* "to hasten," belonging to the *kaṇva*-class; the suffix *kip* is added by the rule "kip ca," followed by the elision of the vowel and the *y*. *Bhuraṇyū*: from the root *bhuraṇa* "to support and nourish"; this also belongs to the *kaṇva*-class, with the *uṇādi* suffix *u*. 24. Translation complete.
Then he has been born, the one who carries us across, eating with his radiant mouth like the Sun at dawn—
the Indu by whom he has reached the dwelling places, dripping with sweat for those who offer oblations, pouring with the ladle toward the songs of praise.

He was born as the one who crosses over; may he exhilarate us. He has shone forth like the sun from this dawn. Indu, with those [drops] which, sweet for the oblation, have reached the dwelling-place while pouring with the ladle at the time of the aging [of the sacrifice]. 6.

Now, at this moment, this Indra, being pleased by our hymns, has "been born" (pra-jajñe)—that is, he has appeared preeminently. May he, the "crosser" (taraṇiḥ), the one who overcomes enemies, "gladden" (mamattu) us. And may he "shine forth" (pra-roci), shining brilliantly. Therein is an illustration: like the "sun" (sūraḥ), the sun, which is present near "this" (asyāḥ) Dawn as we behold her. The "Indu," the Soma, who is "to be praised" (jaraṇā)—meaning worthy of praise—while being poured with the ladle toward his "station" (dhāma), characterized by the Āhavanīya fire, and while being sprinkled, may he gladden those by whom he was "fed" (āṣṭa)—that is, those among us who have partaken of the offering. This is the meaning: may he gladden us. *Jajñe*: from the root *jan* (to appear/become manifest). In the Perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule *gamahana*. *Mamattu*: from the root *mad* (to rejoice). By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, the suffix *śnu* is replaced by *ślu*. *Roci*: from the root *ruc* (to shine). This is an Aorist (*luṅ*) used in the sense of the Present; by transposition (*vyatyaya*), the *cli* suffix is replaced by *ciṇ*. *Āṣṭa*: from the root *aś* (to eat/consume). In the Passive (*karman*) Aorist, by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision of the suffix. It is included in the *vaśādi* group, hence the augment *āṭ*. The prohibition of the *nighāta* accent applies because of the rule *yadvṛttānnityam*. *Sveduhavyaiḥ*: [The derivation is: *id* (supremacy) + the *uṇādi* suffix *up*; the absence of the nasal augment (*num*) follows the rule *aniyamāgamaśāsanam*. Or: *indh* (to shine) + *up*. Or again: *sva-bhūta-havyāni* (offerings belonging to themselves) are those of whom [the singers] are possessed. Or else: *sva-bhūtam idaṃ puro-varti havyam* (this very offering standing before them) belongs to whom; they are thus called. The desired form is established through the *pṛṣodarādi* class. *Siñcan*: from the root *sic* (to pour). By transposition, the agent suffix is used in the sense of the object. The nasal augment (*num*) is added by the rule *śe mujādīnām*. *Jaraṇā*: the root *jar* means "to praise. From this, the suffix *vyuṭ* is added in the sense of the object. The vowel *ā* replaces the case-ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. By transposition, there is an absence of the *liṭ-svara* accent.

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-sa* means "to you" (*tubhyam*). 2. *sa-āhavanīyasthānam* means "the location of the Āhavanīya fire. 3. *kṣa-ṭa-sa-aśitaḥ pītaḥ*; *ṭha-āśitaḥ pītaḥ*. 4. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-havyāni* means "oblations" (*iduhavyāni*). 5. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-iduhavyāni*. 6. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-adhavā...tathoktāḥ*; [this is] not found. 7. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-abhimatarūpasvarasiddhiḥ* means "the accomplishment of the desired form and accent."

When the well-kindled wood, performing service, has shone forth at the rite of the impetuous one, surrounding the enclosures of the cow; when you indeed shine forth, O roaring one, following after the ritual acts for the sake of the swift one who seeks cattle for the people. 7. When the well-kindled wood, performing service, has shone forth at the rite of the impetuous one, surrounding the enclosures of the cow; when you indeed shine forth, O roaring one, following after the ritual acts for the sake of the swift one who seeks cattle for the people.

If indeed the well-kindled *svidhamā*—the wooden implement (*vanadhiti*) intended for the wood, that is, the collection of trees to be cut—should desire to perform its own work consisting of the piercing and the sitting upon the waters, then the impeller (*sūra*), the Adhvaryu priest, becomes capable (*pari bhavati*) at the sacrifice (*adhvara*) for the confinement (*rodhanā*) of the cow, that is, for binding it to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Or alternatively:
*svidhamā* [is so called] because it is well-kindled by the rays of the sun; and *vanadhiti* is the vessel-tray (*mecamālā*), for water (*vana*) is placed within it.

When she (the lightning) performs her work characterized by the raining down of waters, then Sūra—the impeller, Indra—abiding in the *adhvara*, that is, in the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*) which is the occasion for the sacrifice and is itself inviolable (*ahiṃsya*), completely wards off the obstructions, that is, the barriers that confine the rain-water of the cow. The latter half-verse is addressed directly:
"O Indra, existing in the form of the Sun, do thou perform thy deeds" (*kṛtyān* is a name for ritual actions).

When you indeed shine forth—that is, when you blaze intensely—aiming at the days of the full moon for the sake of performing sacred rites, then success shall be achieved for one entering the forest with a cart (*anas*) to fetch fuel;
or rather, for a person unable to reach his destination, and for a swift, shouting cowherd driving his cattle, his desired goal shall be accomplished. This is the completion of the sentence.
*Svidhamā*:
she whose mouth (*āsya*) is a beautiful flame (*śobhana-idhma*), that is, one whose face is like a long-tongued fire; thus she is so described.
By the rule *nam-subhyām*, there is udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound.
*apasyāt*: from the word *apaḥ*, [the suffix] *kyac* is added according to the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac*;
then, in the *leṭ* tense, the augment *āṭ* is applied.
*Rodhanā*:
from the root *rudh*, meaning "to obstruct";
by the rule *hy-ud-a-c* [Pāṇini 3.3.56], the suffix *hy-ud-a* is applied in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
The elision of *śi* occurs frequently in the Vedic language (*chandas*) according to the rule *śechandasi bahulam*.
[The term] *anaviś* means that which enters or reaches by means of a cart (*ana-*). Thus, it is called *anavid*.
The suffix *kip* is applied after the root *viśati*.

According to the *Pāṇinīya-mahābhāṣya* (8.2.70.1), there is an addition [to the rule] stating that for words such as *ahar*, the substitution of *r* occurs for the *s* in the context of *pathin* and so forth.
Alternatively:
The suffix *viṣ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) after the root *at*.
That which enters or reaches toward what is to be gone to (*gantavya*) is called *arvid*. *Anavid* means "not *avid*."

The initial member of the compound retains its original accent because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). For this very reason, there is no *davagraha* (separation mark) due to a lack of attention to the etymological derivation.
[In the word] *paṣidhe*.
The root *iṣ* means "to go. From this root, with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *kvip ca*.

O Indra, from the great, vast heaven, drink the exhilarating Soma; let your two bay horses, *harī*, who are accustomed to this place, drink here at this rite the Soma remaining from what has been drunk.
Likewise, [grant] *ghumsāham*, [the power] over our wealth (*ghumna*).
[Notes: 1. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-tatra madhye | 2. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-bhāvārakāṇi | 3. sa-godhanapālāya | 4. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-svidhamā | 5. kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-asmin yajñe | 16]
O you who are by nature a warrior, overcome the enemy who seeks to overpower you and who tries to drain the spring [of our strength].
Whenever, for your own increase, [you take] the golden-hued, mind-captivating, exhilarating, and cattle-impelling [Soma]—
here the word "go" (gavi) refers to milk.
"Payas" means strength;
likewise, "vega-vantam" means possessing vigor, which is to say, possessing heroism (*vīrya*).
"Vātāpyam" means that which is to be reached by the wind.
The meaning is that it must be drunk by you, who act swiftly like the wind.
In this manner, the priests milk—that is, they press—the Soma with the pressing-stones (*adri*) and the wooden vessels (*prāvan*).
At that time, the word *aṣṭau* is to be connected with what precedes.
Aṣṭā: from the root *aś* "to eat," with the suffix *tṛc*.
Because the traditional grammatical instruction is not universally fixed, the substitution of *it* occurs;
thus we have *dhukṣan*. The change to *bhaṣ* at the end of the word is Vedic.
You turned back the iron [fortress] of the bull, having reached up to the archway of heaven;
where, O Much-invoked One, favoring Kutsa, you encompassed Śuṣṇa with your boundless, increasing powers.
You turned back the iron [missile] of the bull; O much-invoked one, when you, favoring Kutsa, won over Śuṣṇa with endless strengthening aids as the stone brought from heaven was hurled. 9.
O Indra, you turned toward and hurled the iron thunderbolt for the sake of slaying Śuṣṇa, the Asura.
Of what kind was that thunderbolt?
It was brought from heaven by the radiant Tvaṣṭṛ, fashioned from stone, swift, and pervasive against the enemy.

O Puruhūta, invoked by many, when you, O Indra, were destroying Śuṣṇa—the withering Asura—for the sake of Kutsa, this seer, by means of endless, limitless weapons that are instruments of slaughter, striking him down and moving all around him—then, for the purpose of his destruction, you turned back the thunderbolt; such is the meaning.
*Aśmānam*:
[derived from] the root *aś* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāptau*);
the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after roots ending in *m* as well."

Or rather: because the substitution of *nā* is optional by the rule "In the Vedic language, there is an option regarding the suffixes beginning with *jas*," the *yaṇ* substitution [of *i* for *ī*] occurs,
resulting in *vanvan*.

In the root *van* with the sense of "begging," it has here the meaning of "killing. Thus Yāska says: "The root *vanuṣyati* is used in the sense of killing, having undergone a change of form" (Nirukta 5.2).

Regarding *vadhaiḥ*: by the rule "hanaśca vadhaḥ," the suffix *ap* is added to the root *han* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), and by virtue of that same rule, the substitution of *vadh* for *han* occurs. This [noun] ends in *a*, and its final syllable is udātta.
Therefore, when that [suffix] is elided, the suffix becomes accented by the *udāttanivṛtti* accent.

1. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-* means "possessing agitation" (*payodvegavantam*). 2. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-* means "that which is to be obtained" (*prāptavyam*). 3. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-* means "they press out" (*abhiṣunvanti*). 4. *adaḥ*. From the root *ad* (to eat), with the suffix *tap* added to the end, the *laṅ* (imperfect) is used. By the rule *adaḥ sarveṣām*, the augment *aṭ* is applied. *yodhanaḥ*: from the root *yudh* (to fight), the suffix *śānaś* is added in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*). *sadivaḥ*: [it refers to] playing within limits (*maryādā*). By the rule *diveḥ kṛt*, the suffix *ḍivi* is applied. *ādaḥ*: from the root *ad* (to eat), with the suffix *tap* added to the end, the *luk* elision occurs before the ending *sip*; by the rule *adaḥ sarveṣām*, the augment *aṭ* is applied. *śumnāsāham*: one who overcomes or surpasses wealth (*śumna*) is *śumnāsāṭ*. By the rule *chandasi sahaḥ*, the suffix *ṇvi* is applied. *yodhanaḥ*: from the root *yudh* (to fight), the suffix *śānaś* is added in the sense of habitual action. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). 5. *sadhuksan*: from the root *duh* (to milk/fill), there is Vedic (*chāndasa*) elision. By the rule *ata igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*, the suffix *ksa* is applied. The changes to *ṭha*, *ka*, and *va* occur. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasy akayoge 'pi*, there is absence of the augment *aṭ*. The change to *bhaṣ* at the time of the word-division (*padakāla*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). 6. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-* means "to him who has this name. 7. *kṣa-ṭa-ṭha-* means "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*).

O wielder of the stone, long ago you struck down the bolt of Sūra, which had been hidden within the darkness; O Lord of the Stone, you seized that power of Śuṣṇa, which was well-fastened and enveloped from the sky.

Long ago, when the sun was still enveloped in darkness, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you hurled that bolt at him—the rocky one. You brought down even that strength of Śuṣṇa which was spread abroad and firmly bound from heaven; you seized it. 10.

Formerly, when the Sun, Sūrya, was released from the darkness—the devouring form of the Asura Śuṣṇa—from that battle; this is the sense of the remaining words. At that time, O wielder of the stone (adrivah)—the *adrivajra* is so called because it strikes (*āhaṇāti*) with it.
O Indra, you have driven out that *vṛtra*,
which is a cloud— this being a name for a cloud— as it was enveloping [the world]; you have cast down the Asura Śuṣṇa, the slayer of *hiti*.
Or rather:

you shattered the *phaliga*—the weapon used for slaying, characterized as a cloud—of this *śuṣṇa*, the Asura; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Likewise, the *ojaḥ* (obscuring power) of that *śuṣṇa*, the drying-up Asura—which was placed above the shining sun (*divas pari*), covered, and well-fastened—you loosened that power from the sun; the meaning is that you made it distinct from the sun.
O wielder of the thunderbolt (*adrivas*): the substitution of *v* for the suffix *matup* is according to the rule *chandasīraḥ*;
the substitution of *r* for the letter *n* is according to the rule *matuvaso ruḥ*.

Regarding *hetim*: by virtue of the rule “*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*” (Pāṇini 3.3.113), which states that the suffixes *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* are used diversely, the suffix *ktin* is applied to the root *han* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

The formation of the word-form and its being oxytone (*antodāttatva*) are established through the specific grammatical substitution (*nipātana*) taught in the rule beginning with “*utiyuti*” (Pāṇini 6.1.135).
Of this [root]: ‘asu kṣepaṇe’ (to throw). The suffix *sip* of the present indicative (*laṭ*).
In its place, there is the substitution of *hva*;
by the rule "ato heḥ," there is the elision (*luk*) of *hi*.
[The word is] *divaspari*.
In the word *adaḥ*, the visarga is replaced by *s* according to the rule *pañcamyāḥ parāvadhyarthe*.
[The root] *dṛ* means "to split."

In the case of *laḍ* and *sip*, there is elision of the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi"; then, following the *guṇa* substitution, there is elision of *si* by the rule "halḍyābbhyaḥ."
The two great, bright, and unclouded worlds, Heaven and Earth, rejoiced in your deed, O Indra;
you, with your mighty thunderbolt, struck down Vṛtra as he lay upon the rivers, like a wild boar.

The two great, bright, and unwearied worlds, Heaven and Earth, rejoiced after you, O Indra, in your deed; you sent the great Vṛtra, the boar who lay upon the rivers, to his sleep with your thunderbolt. 11.

He, Indra, the great one, the mighty, the powerful, the two of great vigor and strength, having pervaded everywhere, strode across heaven and earth (*dyāvā-kṣāmā*). While you were engaged in the deed characterized by the slaying of Vṛtra, they both rejoiced in you—that is, they became glad or gave their consent.
Thus says the Taittirīyaka: "Impelled by these two, Indra slew Vṛtra" (TS 2.5.2.6).
Immediately thereafter, you, pervading from all sides the vast Vṛtra—the demon who lies within the waters—slew him, that great boar, with your mighty thunderbolt;
that is to say, having struck him with the thunderbolt, you caused him to fall.
*mahī*: by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is a long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) for the case ending. *pājasī*.
The word *pāja* denotes strength.

By metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the word here refers to that which possesses those characteristics. The substitution of *ī* for the case-ending follows the rule: “The addition of *ī* is prescribed for words ending in *iy* and so forth. *Dyāvākṣāmā*: *nauśca kṣāmā ca* (the sky and the earth). The substitution of *dyāvā* for *div* follows the rule: “*dyāvā* is the substitute for *div* [in a Dvandva compound]. The preservation of the original stem accent for both members follows the rule: “In a Dvandva of deities. The elision of the case-ending follows the rule: “*su*, *luk*, etc., for case-endings. *Mahatām*: [from] *mahī haye*. The *śap* suffix is applied by transposition (*vyatyaya*). The absence of *aṭ* augment follows the rule: “In the Veda, [the augment] is optional even when not preceded by *māṅ*. *Mahaḥ*: [from] *mahataḥ*. When the instrument (*karaṇa*) is intended to be expressed as the residual factor (*śeṣatva*), the genitive is used. The elision of the vowel *a* is Vedic. *Sipivapaḥ*: [from the root] *ṛṣvap* (to lie down). From this, with the suffix *pyan* and its subsequent elision, and in the *caṅ* reduplication, the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.18—“[the *u* of] *svāpi* is vocalized before *caṅ*”—is not performed, because a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not necessarily obligatory.
O Indra, you who are manly, mount those aids of yours that protect men— the well-yoked, most-swift steeds of Vāta—
whom Kaṇva Uśanas fashioned for you as a gladdening, foe-slaying, and victorious thunderbolt.

O Indra, you who protect men—be the protector of those heroes! Mount the well-yoked, most swift steeds of Vāta. For you, Kaṇva Uśanas fashioned the exhilarating, Vṛtra-slaying thunderbolt, the weapon of Pārthya. 12.

O Indra, you who are beneficial to men (*naryaḥ*), you protect and guard those men whom you favor as their leaders; mount (*ātiṣṭha*)—that is, ascend—the swift horses of Vāta, which go rapidly toward that goal, well-yoked to the chariot, most excellent, and pre-eminent carriers.

O Sage, from Kābhya [the son of Kaśyapa], Uśanas gave you that exhilarating, intoxicating thunderbolt; having given it, you fashioned that Vṛtra-slaying bolt—the slayer of the Asura Vṛtra—and capable of overcoming (pārthya) enemies in their transgression.
*avaḥ*:
from the root *av* in the *leṭ* mood, with the augment *aṭ*.
The elision of the vowel *i* occurs by the rule "itaśca lopaḥ.
[The form] *vahiṣṭhān* is derived from the word *voḍhṛ* with the suffix *iṣṭhan* according to the rule "turiṣṭhemeyassu chandasi."
In the rule “*turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*,” there is the elision of *tu*. [The word] *pārthya* [is derived from] *pāra*, according to the rule “*pāra tīra karmasamāptau*.”
From this root ending in *py*, [the suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule *aco yat*.
Thus: *tatakṣa*. [The root] *takṣū* (or *tvaṣṭṛ*) means "to fashion" or "to make thin."
There is a change of gender.
You, O Hero, calmed the two bay steeds for the men; Etaśa brought the wheel here, O Indra.
You carried him across to the further shore of the navigable waters, and you turned back those who sought to harm the noble ones.

You, O Indra, the hero, made the two bay steeds delight the men; Etaśa brought the wheel. Having cast it forth, O Indra, you sent it across the navigable waters to the further shore; you overturned those who were hostile to sacrifice.

O Indra, you who exist as the Sun through the nature of Sūrya, you have caused the bay-colored ones—the men who lead, or rather, the rays whose nature is to carry away moisture—to rest, that is, to cease their course. Like Etaśa; "Etaśa" is the name of the Sun’s horse.
And thus it is heard in scripture: "May Sūrya, the deity, cause you to go by means of Etaśa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.6.4.6).
The particle *na* has the sense of *ca* (and).
And Etaśa bore the wheel of the chariot while he was carrying [him].
Moreover, having crossed over ninety-nine rivers that are navigable by boat, you [reached] the further shore—
the region on the bank (the accusative used in the sense of the locative).
On that bank, [you found] those who do not sacrifice, those who do not perform worship, those who are devoid of sacrifice.

1. You have made them thin with *va*, *cha*, *pha*, and *ta*; you have weakened them (*da-kṣata-vān asi*). 2. With *śa*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, and *sa*—you made them subject to *rāma*. Having cast away (*prāsya*) the Asuras and others, you caused them to revolve there; having also performed what was to be done (*kartavyam*), you brought them back to those two who were being oppressed. [Regarding *rabhyaḥ*: the absence of *ad* occurs by the rule *kaḍi bahuḷaṃ chandasy amāṅyoge 'pi*; the long vowel is by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate*, which is a Vedic phonetic combination (*sāṃhitika*). Regarding *prāsya*: from the root *asu* (to throw), this form is derived with the suffix *lyap*. Regarding *nābhyānām*: the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *naur dharmye*; it is circumflex (*svarita*) according to the rule *tisvaritaḥ*].
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, protect us from this malevolence in the encounter;
grant us wealth consisting of chariots and horses for our sustenance, for the sake of glory and true prosperity.

O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, protect us from this ill-disposed woman; shield us from misfortune in the encounter. Bestow upon us wealth that brings chariots and horses, for our nourishment, for our renown, and for the sake of true prosperity. 14.
He goes.

"O [Indra], may we, being your most generous (*maṃhiṣṭhāḥ*)—that is, those who exceedingly magnify you with hymns—be your *sadhamādaḥ*: may we rejoice together with our sons, grandsons, and others. *asmata*: By the rule "supāṃ suluk... there is elision of the locative case ending. *dasat*: From the root *dasu* meaning "to perish. With the prohibitive particle *māḍi* and the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the suffix *aṅ* is applied because it belongs to the *puṣādi* class. *vājapramahaḥ*: One whose great splendor (*pramahaḥ*) is preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*) through riches (*vājaiḥ*). Because it begins with a *pāda*, there is no initial *anudātta* accent. There is optionally the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative. *varanta*: From the root *vṛñ* meaning "to choose. The *śap* suffix is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). *goṣu*: The prohibition of the acute accent on the case-ending, which would otherwise apply by the rule "sāvekācaḥ...", occurs here by the rule "na gośvansāvavarṇa...". *arthaḥ*: This is a *nipātana* (irregular formation) for the meanings "master" or "vaiśya. It has an acute accent on the final syllable by the rule "ayeḥ svāmyākhyā cet" (Phiṭ-sūtra 17). *maṃhiṣṭhāḥ*: From the root *mahi* meaning "to increase. Because it is marked with *idit*, the *num* augment is added. From this, the suffix *tṛc* is added in the sense of "agent. The *iṇ* substitution occurs by the rule "tucchandasi. The *tu* suffix is elided by the rule "turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu. *sadhamādaḥ*: From the root *mad* meaning "in connection with satisfaction," belonging to the *curādika* class. Houses where people rejoice together (*saha mādyante*) are called *sadhamādaḥ*. The suffix *kip* is added by the rule "kip ca. Then the nominative plural *jas* is added. By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara dispel the darkness of ignorance and bestow the four aims of human life out of compassion.

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the Commentary on the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, entitled the *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial authority of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
Thus ends the first Aṣṭaka.
1. In the absence of elision (*nighāta*) for the eighth [letter] following *kṣa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭha*.
2. *Kṣa* and *ṭa* [are explained] by the teacher Sāyaṇa.
Om.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by whom Vāgīśa and the other wise ones, upon undertaking all their tasks, become successful after having paid homage;
he whose breath is the Vedas, and from whose Vedas the entire universe has arisen.
I bow to that Vidya-tirtha-maheshvara, by whom he was created.
The systematic exposition (*prakriyā*) has been described in its entirety in the first section (*kāṇḍa*);
from this point onward, it is to be understood as implicit, though it is occasionally recalled here and there.
Now begins the first chapter of the second Aṣṭaka.
In the first Maṇḍala of the Śatacina, there are twenty-four Anuvākas.
Among them, in the eighteenth Anuvāka beginning with "kaditthā," there are six Sūktas.
Therein, "pra vaḥ pāntam" is the second hymn.

Since the term "pañconā" (five less) carries over, it consists of fifteen verses. According to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "the seer and the metre are [determined] by the seer's tradition," Kakṣīvān is the seer.
By the paribhāṣā regarding the absence of specific instruction, [the metre] is Triṣṭubh;
the Viśvedevas are the deity.
This is according to the Anukramaṇikā: "Pra vo vaiśvadevam."
The specific application of this [hymn] is indicated by its characteristic marks (*laiṅgika*).
"Bring forward for the wrathful Rudra the Soma-juice, the food, at the sacrifice;
you who are well-disposed, praise the Maruts with the heroes of the sun-like Asura, as if for the purification of heaven and earth."

O you of impetuous wrath, bring forth the soma-juice for your protection; offer the oblation to Rudra, the bountiful one. With the heroes of the Asura of heaven, I have praised the Maruts as if with a prayer for the two worlds.

O you who are swift in spirit, quick to anger yet free from malice—O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), offer for Rudra, the one who drives away (*drāvayitre*) suffering (*rut*) or the misfortune that causes it, for the bountiful giver (*mīḍhuṣe*) who showers forth rewards, the sacrificial substance (*andhas*)—the food consisting of clarified butter, *soma*, and so forth—which is your means of sacrifice, which is worthy of protection or itself protects you; prepare this with excellence for his sake.

And I, through my very archery— just as one repels enemies with arrows— with heroes who cause various terrors to the foes, or with his followers such as the Maruts who are endowed with valor, [I shall drive him] from heaven, that is, from the celestial world;
this is an elliptical expression meaning even from the three worlds, [driving him] away from the Asura, the one who must expel the Asuras who are to be expelled.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object.

I praise—that is, I laud—that very god who is the one who casts out, who dwells between the two worlds, Rodasī—the heaven and earth which are subject to confinement—and who is great. [I praise him] as the protector.
In the word *pāntam*, [the suffix] is either the *śatṛ* of the root *pā-* (to drink) or the *jha* of the root *pib-* according to the *uṇādi* rules. Regarding *mīḷahuṣe*:
it is a nipāta ending in the *kasu* suffix, according to the rule *dādhānsāhvān*.
In the dative singular, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*.
Then, by the rule *śāsivasi* etc., the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. Thus:
*divaḥ*.

By the passage beginning with *uḍidam*, etc.: 1. In the case of *kṣa-na-ṭa*, it is to be inferred that [the suffix] *-uttari* follows; thus it is remembered. 2. Because of the recurrence (*anuvartana*) of *kṣa-na-ṭa*. 3. In *kṣa-na-ṭa*, the word “*asya*” is absent. 4. In *kṣa-na-ṭa*, after the word “*akrodhanaḥ*,” there is the addition: “*yadvā manyatiracākarmo | śīghrastutayaḥ*. 5. By the prohibition through *iṣudhyā* in *kṣa-na-ṭa*. 6. With *māyā* joined to *kha-ca-ja-ṇa-pha-va*. (Ka. 97)

The case ending is udātta. *astoṣi*: this is the aorist (*luṅ*) of the root *stu* used in the Vedic language (*chāndasa*). *iṣudhyeva*: [the word] *iṣudhiḥ* means "that in which arrows (*iṣavaḥ*) are placed (*dhīyante*). The suffix *ki* is applied to the root by the rule "after a root, when the object or the locus [is to be expressed]" (*karmaṇyadhikaraṇe ca*). It is oxytone (*antodātta*) due to the accent of the prefix *kru*. The case ending is udātta by the rule "after a vowel that is udātta and preceded by a consonant" (*udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*).
Like two wives eager for the first invocation, Night and Dawn have grown strong, manifesting in many ways;
wearing apart their dark garments, they are beautiful to behold with the golden splendor of the Sun.

Like a wife, to be magnified, she who was first invoked—Night and Dawn, appearing in many forms—clad in wide-spreading light as if in a garment, beautiful to behold with the splendor of the sun and with golden hues. 2.

Just as a wife, like a wife, hastens to her husband's morning invocation to increase his prosperity, so too may Dawn and Night—the two deities of day and night—being recognized in many ways through various hymns, hasten to our morning invocation to increase it; that is, let them come quickly to augment our early praise.
Or alternatively:

The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "May you two grow for our sake; knowing [us] in many ways, that is, in manifold manners, and being cognizant of the means of growth, may you become [our benefactors]."
*Upāsānaktā*. According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.3.31, *upāsoṣasaḥ*, the substitution of *upāsā* for the first member [of the compound] occurs.
By the rule *devatādvandve ca*, both members retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
Now the *upā* alone is described:

she who is like the sun—himself a destroyer (*starīḥ*) of enemies, enveloped in splendor—is clothed in, that is, wearing and sustaining, the *arka*, which is spread out, extended, and specifically connected, or whose form is continuous; she is beautiful to behold, possessing the lovely appearance of the sun’s radiance.
Indeed, as the precursor of the sun, she illuminates the world with her rays.
The meaning is that such a Dawn should protect us from the assault of our enemies;
or alternatively, she should come together with gold— that is, with delightful splendors or specific forms of wealth.
*nyūtam*. In the case of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) of *nīj*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule beginning with "vacisvapi... [Pāṇini 6.1.15]. *starīḥ*.
In the word ‘avitṛstṛ’, the suffix *ī* is applied.
May Parjanya, the possessor of wealth, be gracious to us; may Vāta, the bull of the waters, be gracious.
O Indra and Parvata, sharpen our weapons for us! May all the gods grant us wide space.
May the earth protect us; may the wind, the showerer of waters, protect us. O Indra and Parvata, do you two sharpen our [minds]. May all the gods grant us wide space. 3.
"Naḥ" means us; "vasahā" means one who provides clothing in the form of the Gārhapatya fire and others.
Alternatively, it refers to Agni, the destroyer of trees and other things that serve as coverings or garments.
Alternatively:
*vasahā* means "one who causes the day to pass" (*vāsāhau vāsarasya gamayitā*);
*pariṃjamā* means "the one who goes around" (*parito gantā*), namely the Sun; may he *mamartu*, that is, "may he exhilarate."
Likewise, may the wind (*vāta*), possessing rain (*vṛṣaṇvān*)—that is, possessing showers (*varṣaṇavān*) and being the producer of rain (*vṛṣṭyutpādaka*)—blow toward us.
And, O Indra and Parvata!
Indra is well known.
*Parvata*: "Possessing joints" (*parvavān*), meaning Parjanya, who possesses the filling [of the world] with rain and so forth.
*Tau yuvaṃ naḥ*: "You two, for us"—that is, sharpen us, meaning purify us, whether in the vocative or not.
*Tat*: "Therefore," because I [invoke] all the gods.
1. Covered by the splendor of *kṣa*, *a*, *ṭa*, and *te*.
2. The beautiful form of *ca*, *ja*, *pha*, *ba*, and *ṣa*.
3. With *kṣa*, *kha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pha*, *va*, and others preceding them.
4. *kṣa-ṭa-uṣā* also [is added].

5. After *kṣa-ja-ṭa-*, following the word "asmān" (us), the phrase "pariṃjamā parito gantā vyāptaḥ" (the one who moves around, the pervader) is additionally inserted. Therefore, I praise; may all (*viśve*) the gods (*devāḥ*) desire to grant us (*naḥ*) abundant food (*varivasyantu*).
The meaning is: "May they gladden [the gods] by the offering of much wealth. *Mamattu*: the root *mad* means "to rejoice."

From the root *śo* with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, in the imperative (*loṭ*), there is the elision (*ślu*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) by Vedic usage; then reduplication occurs, resulting in *śiśītam*.
In the word *ī*, there is the substitution of *ī* by the rule *ī halyaghoḥ*; in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), there is the substitution of *i* by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*;
and in the phrase *indrāparvatā*, there is the substitution of the initial vowel of the first member (*pūrvapada*) with *ān* by the rule *devatādvandve ca*.
And indeed, those two glorious ones who hasten toward the white radiance, the protectors, shall the descendant of Uśij call upon for me.
Bring forward the Son of Waters for you; bring forward the two Parents of the roaring Āyu.

And also those two glorious ones, for my sake, who enjoy and drink [the offerings]—them, the son of Uśij, shall call upon for the sake of white splendor. Bring forward for yourselves the Son of the Waters; bring forward the two parents of the roaring Āyu.
Kakṣīvān, the son of Auśija, [says]: "I" refers to myself;
the dative case is used here in the sense of purpose (tādarthye), meaning "for my sake" or "for the sake of glory."

"Yaśas" means food, strength, or fame. "Tyantau" means those two who consume—eating the sacrificial porridge, cakes, and so forth—and "pāntā" means those two who drink—the clarified butter, soma, and so forth.
The word *tya* has the same meaning as the word *tat*.
The two who are renowned as being worthy of praise are the Aśvins.

Although no specific distinction is heard here, nevertheless, because this hymn (*sūkta*) is addressed to the Viśvedevas, because of its connection with the Dawn (*uṣas*), and because of the dual number [of the pronoun], it is understood that they are the Aśvins—such are the Aśvins.
In the word *śvetanāyai*, the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
The entire world [belongs] to the dawning Uṣas;
[the meaning is: "I shall strive for the arrival of the day connected with her," at the time belonging to that [Uṣas].
O priests, you—[this is the sense].

The second [case ending] is used in the sense of the object (*pramārthe*). [The phrase] "napātam apām" means the grandson of the waters—that is, the one who causes them to flow away—or Agni, who is their leader.
Since plants and trees are [born from] the fires, and Agni is born from them, Agni possesses the status of being the grandson of the waters (*apāṃ naptṛtva*).
"Exalt that god.
Here, the verb *karoti* (he makes), which expresses action in general, culminates in the specific action of praise;
the meaning is "exalt him thoroughly."
Furthermore, regarding *rāspinasya*:

from the verbal roots *rap* or *ras*, meaning "to sound" and so forth, the form *rāspa* arises through the addition of the suffix *ghañ* and the insertion of the letters *s* and *p*. That which possesses this is *rāspi*, namely, a hymn of praise (*stotra*).
The singer is one who possesses that [quality], a *rāspin*.
For such a man, for me—an *āyu*—you two deities, Day and Night, who act like mothers (*mātṛvat*), make manifest my two mothers;
or rather, [make them manifest] for the *rāspin*.
There is one possessive suffix (*mattvartha-pratyaya*) used in the Vedic style (*chāndasa*).
Fashion two filters (*nirmāṇyau*) for the rainwater—which is characterized by the sound of raining and is of a nature to flow—which [the gods] consume and drink; [fashion them] for day and night.
In both cases, the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the case-ending] according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
O you who are worthy of praise, Auśija shall invoke you for the sake of winning; like a shout, he shall proclaim the hymn of the people to obtain [your favor].
I shall indeed speak forth to Pūṣan for the sake of giving, toward the bestowal of wealth, so that I may attain the highest excellence.

May Auśija call upon your roaring [chariot] for the sake of attaining the praise of Arjuna, like a shout at the winning of the prize. For the sake of Pūṣan’s giving, may I proclaim the abundance of wealth belonging to Agni.
O gods, I, Kakṣīvān, the son of Uśij, call upon your praise—the hymn that is to be invoked, celebrated, and proclaimed—for the sake of summoning you; I speak toward you, I address you face-to-face.
Or rather, it may also be understood here as follows:
1. After the rule *kṣa-ja-ṭa- ‘dvivacanam’*, there is the additional text: *‘tinhī(mīhī)tyādinā piti pratyayāt pūrvasyodāttatvam’*. 2. In the versions *kṣa-ja-ṭa-na-pha*, the word *‘iti’* is absent.
3. In *kṣa-ja-ṭa*, the reading is *yateya*; in *na-ma*, it is *yajeyam*.

4. In the manuscripts Kṣa, Ja, and Ṭa, "of me" (mama) is not present; in Ja and Va, it is "to me" (me). 5. In the manuscripts Kṣa, Ja, and Ṭa, [the term] is "the deities of day and night" (ahorātradevatā). 6. In the manuscript Kṣa, [the term] is "having the nature of crying out" (ravaṇaśīla).
It is said, "aśnāveva. In that interpretation, the plural number is used for the sake of honor.
O Aśvins, *vaḥ* means "you"; *ghoṣeva* means like a woman named Ghoṣā, or like a woman who speaks of Brahman.

The meaning is: "Just as [the Aśvins] performed a praise for the sake of the destruction—that is, for the eradication—of the white disease located upon Arjuna’s own body, which was white in color, so too have I done.
O gods, to this god named Pūṣan, who belongs to you and who bestows fruit directly (*ā-dāvane*) as a nourisher (*pūṣṇe*), [I offer praise].
Regarding the prefix *ā*, its original form is maintained by the rule "āṅo 'nunāsikaś chandasi" (Pāṇini 6.1.126).
I shall speak—that is, I shall praise—with *accha*, meaning by approaching face-to-face.
The root *vac* is used in the sense of speaking.
By the rule *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ*, the suffix *āśīrliṅ* takes the augment *aṅ*. Then, by the rule *vaca um*, the substitution *um* is applied.
Furthermore, I shall speak of Agni’s *vasutāti*—his wealth as well—and I praise that very Agni.
Hear my invocation, O Mitra and Varuṇa; hear it from every side as you sit upon your throne.
May the giver of our hearing hear us—the one who hears well, the possessor of fair fields, the river, the destroyer of foes.

Hear my invocations, O Mitra and Varuṇa; hear them from every side with your constant presence. May the one who hears our call, the one who bestows gifts, the one who hears well, the one with fair fields, and the flowing river hear us. 6.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two gods who preside over day and night and bear these names, hear—listen to—these our invocations;
not only our invocation, but also hear this hymn being performed everywhere by the Udgātṛ and others within this sacrificial hall.

Furthermore, the *sukṣetrā* (good fields) [are those] which the *sindhu*, the god presiding over the waters—the one who is a good listener (*suśrotr*) hearing wealth everywhere or bestowing such gifts—hears our invocation; [he does so] with *addhiḥ*, that is, with waters of satisfaction, [as understood from the context]. Or rather, making our fields "good fields" (*sukṣetrā*) through *addhiḥ*, meaning making them abundant with crops and the like, may he hear our call.
The meaning is: "May he listen for the sake of gain, because [he] is a good field."

These are the vowels. In both cases, the vowel *ā* is substituted for the case-ending. Regarding the form *śrutamati*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) by virtue of the rule "frequently in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
I praise that gift of yours, O Varuṇa and Mitra; it is yours, a hundredfold, among the five peoples.
Those who place their trust in the famous chariot, the beloved chariot, have come hither, securing for themselves abundant prosperity.
I praise that gift of yours, O Varuṇa and Mitra: hundreds of cattle bestowed upon the Puṣkayāmas, Pañja, Śrutaratha, and Priyaratha. Having secured prosperity together, they have arrived. 7.
O Mitra, O Varuṇa, O gods, I praise you both.
[The word *vyayayena* is middle. That well-known gift belonging to you two—a gift consisting of hundreds, that is, of countless cattle—is for me, Kakṣīvat Pañji, among these [offerings].
The word *pukṣ* also exists ending in the vowel *a*.
The ellipsis is: "May it be for those hymns or sacrifices which serve as the occasion for the restraint of ignorant *pukṣas*.

Furthermore, may the gods, beginning with Mitra—[who are] *śrutaratha*, possessed of a chariot renowned everywhere; *priyaratha*, endowed with a beloved chariot; and always fond of the chariot—place [their favor] in me alone, who am *pañja*.

1. *Kṣa-a-ṭa*: Of the white disease (leprosy) affecting one's own body. 2. *Kṣa-a-ṭa*: *Devayāpi*. The letter *ā* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*). 3. *Ca-pha*: *Me havā*. 4. *Ca-ya*: *Śrotu*, meaning "may he hear. 5. *Ca-pha*: For the sake of gain, because it is a fertile field (*sukṣetratvāt*). 6. *Kṣa-a-ṭa*: [The word] *pukṣya* ends in *e* when followed by the suffix *ghan*.

"Maintaining joy" (*prītiṃ dhārayantaḥ*), immediately upon their arrival (*sadyaḥ āgamanānantaram eva*), "conferring nourishment" (*puṣṭiṃ nirundhānāsaḥ*)—that is, providing nourishment such as cattle and so forth—and "establishing it in us alone" (*asmāsv eva sthāpayantaḥ*).
Or else:

Bestowing nourishment upon me, performing [their duties], and securing it—making the nourishment already prepared firm within me—let them come with their speech. *Rātiḥ*: from the root *rā*, "to give."
In the sense of "being," [the suffix] *kin* is applied; by the rule "in the sense of a mantra, after *vṛṣan* etc.," *kin* receives the udātta accent.
[The form is] *śatā*.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the substitution of the preceding long vowel (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) for the ablative case ending.
[The form] *dadhānāḥ* [is derived from *dhā*:
because it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class, there is *ślu* (elision) of the *śap* suffix].
The initial vowel [of *abhyastānām*] is udātta according to the rule "the first of reduplicated forms" (*abhyastānāmādiḥ*).
[In *agman*:
from the root *gam*, in the Vedic *luṅ* tense, there is elision of the suffix by the rule "in mantras, [there is elision] of *ghas* etc. (*mantre ghasa*...).
In the word *gamahana*, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*).
I praise the bounty of this one of great wealth; may we, together with the *nahuṣas*, obtain it along with brave sons.
He is a person rich in sacrificial offerings, a possessor of horses, a lord of chariots, and a great patron.
8 | Of this,
let me praise.
O Mahādeva, there is indeed fear and inexhaustible malice.
That foolish person of two kinds himself places— that is, establishes— the sacrifice within his own heart, in his own mind.
The meaning is that he becomes distressed upon seeing the enjoyments of those who perform [the rites].
The word "yat" is a change of gender (from neuter to masculine).
The man who possesses the characteristics already described— being *ṛtāvā*, i.e., possessing sacrifice, having undertaken the sacrifice—
with the *hotrās* (an epithet for the arms)—
that is, with praises— he reaches (*āpa*), that is, pervades, this Soma juice.
"Praising the Soma, he presses it"—this extends up to that point;
its connection is with what will be said later: "that hero goes forth into the battles."
*Abhidhuk*: from the root *duh*, the suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule "asatsadviṣa";
the change to *m* in the *saṃhitā* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
In the word *ṛtāvā*, the suffix *vanip* is used in the sense of the possessive suffix *matup* according to the rule "in Vedic literature (*chandasi*), *vanip* [is used] after roots ending in *i*.
The lengthening of the vowel in the *saṃhitā* is due to the rule "it is also seen in other cases as well."

He, impelled by wondrous deeds, the most powerful subduer of the Nahuṣas, he whose fame is praised among men—having rushed forward with speed, the hero goes forth at all times to encounter the enemy in every battle. He, the subduer of the Nahuṣas, impelled by wondrous deeds, the most powerful, whose glory is celebrated among men—he goes forth with unrestrained bounty, rushing with force, ever the hero in all battles.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two— [to] that person who has come for refuge with the characteristics previously mentioned, who is your worshiper, and who is *daṃsujūtaḥ*, well-impelled by tamed horses, and therefore the greatest overcomer (*śardhastaraḥ*) among men (*narām*),
or rather, exceedingly powerful; [who is] *gurtaśravāḥ* among his own peers, possessing exalted splendor or renowned luster, and *visṛśarātiḥ*, one to whom wealth is bestowed for the sake of goals.
Thus, being of such great majesty and a hero, he overcomes those who cause harm— *vādhataḥ* being a name for the great— in all battles, in all encounters with hostile forces,
even those as great as *Nahuṣa*.
This belongs to men;
having rushed swiftly against human enemies, he always—indeed, at all times—goes forth, moving with complete fearlessness toward the virtuous.
*daṃsujūtaḥ*:
[the suffix] *vic* is added to the root *dam*.
By the rule "the third case [is compounded] with the object," the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member is retained.
*Gurtaśravāḥ*: [The root] *gurī* means "to lift up. Due to its inclusion in the list beginning with *nasat-tanipat*, there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
*visṛjrarātiḥ*. This is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the objective sense derived from the root *sṛj* preceded by the prefix *vi*.
According to the rule "the preceding [prefix] is the original accent" (*gatiranantaraḥ*), the prefix retains its natural accent.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that [accent] alone remains by virtue of the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*). Regarding *pṛtsu*: by the rule "the addition of *pṛt* etc. to *pada* and so forth," there is the substitution of *pṛt* for the word *pṛtanā*.

The acute accent on the case-ending is due to the rule "sāvekācaḥ. [The word] *bāḍhasṛtvā* [is derived from the root] *sati* with the suffix *kanip*, according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well."

Then let them come at the call of the liberal Nahusha; let the kings, the joyous ones of immortality, hear us. They who speed through the clouds with their aids, grant wealth for the sake of praise to the one possessed of the chariot by his greatness. 11. Then let them come at the call of the liberal Nahusha; let the kings, the joyous ones of immortality, hear us. They who speed through the clouds with their aids, grant wealth for the sake of praise to the one possessed of the chariot by his greatness. 11.

1. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-drohaḥ*. 2. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-*—the phrase "iti yāvat" is absent. 3. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-*—the phrase "saṃhitāyāṃ mbhāvābhchāndasaḥ" is absent. 4. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-sa*—he is characterized by the aforementioned definition. 5. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-satvā*—one who moves without hesitation. 6. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-damervic*. O kings, O resplendent ones, or lords of all; O exhilarating ones, you who cause delight: hear my invocation, my call, I who am Nahuṣa, a mortal man, directed toward the immortal, divine one who impels [us] through hymns and the like.
[The absence of the suffix *śap* is due to the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the substitution is] frequent."

In the word *amṛtasya*, within this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the initial vowel of the final member is acute according to the rule: *anajo jaramaramitramṛtāḥ*. *Adha* means "then," that is, immediately after hearing [this]. "Come hither" (*gamanta*) is derived from the root *gam*; the elision [of the suffix] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
In place of the middle plural ending, *jha* is substituted by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
By the rule *gamahana*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*).
For what purpose have you come? It is said:

O sky-goers, because you pervade the sky, [you have come] for the sake of that one who is "nirava"—meaning one from whom the rākṣasa has departed, and who is devoid of any other protection apart from yourselves.
Alternatively:
[it belongs] to the sacrificer who possesses a chariot (*rathavate*), that from whose mouth (*mukhāt*) has gone forth—that is, been uttered—a sound (*ravaḥ*) in the form of a hymn of praise;
here the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
"By greatness"—that is, by majesty or magnanimity;
the elision of the letter *m* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) usage.

By that [greatness], you desire to praise—that is, to extol—the *rādhas*, which is the means of prosperity consisting of the oblation or the propitiating hymn (*saṃrādhaka-stotra*), for the sake of glory.
Therefore, listen to the summons: "Come! or "Enter!"
This is the host whose abode the gods have proclaimed as the domain of the ten-fingered one;
may they, in whom the abundance of wealth delights, all together win the prize in these offered gifts.

"This host, this abode of the Lord," so they have said, "in the portions of the tenfold [sacrifice], in those among whom you, the possessors of wealth, have taken delight. May all win the prize in the offerings presented. 12.

The gods said: "We have been summoned to the portion of this patron (*yajamāna*), the lord of the gods who impels the oblation and the like, who possesses ten parts by virtue of nourishing the ten sense organs; for that patron, we shall now bestow—make manifest—this *śardhaḥ*, which exists as something to be given, namely food that overcomes enemies or the strength that is the cause for consuming it.
[Regarding the word *dhāma*: it is derived from the root *dhā* (to place) in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, with the elision of *sic* according to Pāṇini’s rule *gāti-sthā-gā-pā-ghrā-dhmo-liṭoḥ*].
The vowel *u* is substituted for the *a* of the root *vac*. By the rule "asyativakti... and so forth, *ah* is substituted for *ch*.
In those gods among whom you—those shining ones—the abundance (*tāti*) of wealth (*vasu*), that is, the expansion of riches, or indeed the riches themselves, greatly delight (*rāran*).
*Tātiḥ*: [This is derived] from the root *tan* with the suffix *ktin*; the substitution of *ā* for *i* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
The acute accent on the final syllable of the first member is due to its belonging to the class beginning with *maradvṛdha*.
Alternatively:
*svādhikastānila* is a form of the root *ram*, in its yaṅ-luk (intensive) stem, in the imperfect (*laṅ*) tense.
May all those gods together bestow, grant, and give *vāja*—that is, food—at the *prabhṛta* sacrifices, which provide excellent sustenance.
[The root] *ṣaṇ* [is used] in the sense of giving.
Or alternatively:
To that Lord, who is our own self and consists of ten parts—the Soma situated in the ten cups for whose consumption we have been summoned—they said, "Bestow this strength upon him.
Therefore, may all the gods (Viśve Devāḥ) partake of such sacrificial food (vāja), characterized by Soma, in these abundant sacrifices.
[The form] *sanvantu* is derived from the root *vana* (or *paṇa*) meaning "to partake," with the suffix *upratyaya* applied by way of grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).
In what kind of sacrifices?
Those in which the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the extenders of *vasutāti*—that is, of riches characterized by oblations or of wealth;
there is an irregularity in the grammatical number.
O shining ones, you take pleasure in the oblations;
[the root] *rā* means "to give. In the *leṭ* mood, there is the *blu*-elision of the *śap* suffix according to Vedic usage.

By the rule "chandasyubhayathā" (Pāṇini 3.4.117), [the suffix] is treated as both [sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka]; therefore, because it is an ārdhadhātuka, there is elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "āto lopa iṭi ca" (Pāṇini 6.4.64).
For this very reason, there is also an absence of the acute accent on the first syllable by the rule "abhyastānāmādiḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.189).

1. According to Kṣīrasvāmī, Jayāditya, and Ṭīkāsarvasva, all [the gods] (sarve devāḥ). 2. According to Kṣīrasvāmī, Jayāditya, and Ṭīkāsarvasva, there is no "vā" after "na". 3. According to Caṇḍeśvara and Phullarāja, the Viśvedevas. 4. According to Caṇḍeśvara and Phullarāja, there is elision (luk). 5. According to Kṣīrasvāmī, Jayāditya, and Ṭīkāsarvasva, wealth which is the means for achieving prosperity (samṛddhisādhanaṃ dhanam). 6. According to Kṣīrasvāmī, Jayāditya, and Ṭīkāsarvasva, the power that serves as the cause for attaining that [wealth]. 7. According to Kṣīrasvāmī, Jayāditya, and Ṭīkāsarvasva, and in those [verses] where... 8. According to Kṣīrasvāmī, Jayāditya, and Ṭīkāsarvasva, and that expansion (vistāraḥ).

9. According to Kṣīrasvāmī, Jayāditya, and Ṭīkāsarvasva, there is no "vā". 10. According to Kṣīrasvāmī, Jayāditya, and Ṭīkāsarvasva, there is no "ca". We rejoice in the gift of the one who is beautiful to behold, who bestows strength, and who brings forth the light of the sun.
Those who possess desired horses and desired reins, the masters, they urge on their men as they strive to overcome.

We rejoice at the offering of the one worthy to be seen, when they go twice, bearing food from behind. What is it that these masters of swift horses and swift reins—these powerful conquerors—urge on against men? 13.
"We rejoice; we praise the gods. [The root] √mad means "to praise";
[the suffix] -itvān [is added], and [the augment] -num [is applied].
For what purpose?
Because of the "visible food"—that is, because food consisting of ten parts is the means for satisfying the sense of sight—and since there are "twice five," that is, fifteen kinds of food;
the food is of ten kinds because it is taken up in ten cups (*camasa*).
Bearing such food, the ten *camasādhvaryu* priests [are present];

four are the young sons of Maśarāra, and three are those of King Āryavasa, the victorious. Your chariot, O Mitra and Varuṇa, with its long-reaching jaws and well-joined reins, has shone like the Sun. 15. Four; me; of Maśarāra; the young ones; three; of the king; Āryavasa; the victorious; the chariot; of you two; O Mitra and Varuṇa; with long-reaching jaws; with well-joined reins; like the Sun; has shone. 15.

"Do not, do not [harm] me, Kakṣīvant! Having turned me into a mosquito, Maśarāra—so called because he 'shatters' (śroṇati) or 'scatters' (śārayati), that is, strikes [his enemies]—[has four sons]. The four sons of this king, who are like children, unawakened like infants, are oppressing me"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In the word *śiśu*, there is an absence of *guṇa* [substitution] due to the rule: "In the Vedic language, there is optionally the non-application [of *guṇa*] before suffixes beginning with *jas*."
Likewise, the three sons of King Āryavasa—born of a Prāptā mother, known by this name, victorious, and ever-conquering—they too oppress [the people]; this is the ellipsis.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, gods bearing these names, your chariot is *dīrghapsas*;
*apsas* is a name for form.
Possessing an exceedingly vast form and a web-like radiance—
*syūma* being a name for happiness—
he, having a light that produces happiness, shone like *sūra*, the sun.
The meaning is: "May he appear before those mentioned who oppose us, causing them to tremble with fear."
In the case of *yuti*, the *luṅ* suffix is applied by the rule "In the Veda, *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [are used for all tenses].
The *parasmaipada* ending is applied by the rule "After roots ending in *yut*, [the *parasmaipada* is used] in the *luṅ*" (Pāṇini 1.3.91).
The *vṛddhi* substitution is applied by the rule "There is *vṛddhi* in place of the penultimate vowel before the *sic* augment when *parasmaipada* endings follow" (Pāṇini 7.2.1).

By the rule "bahulam chandasi," there is the absence of the augment *iṭ*, followed by the elision of the *hal* and the final consonant according to the rules beginning with "halḍyādibhyaḥ" and "saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ.
Alternatively,
[the root is] *yu* in the sense of "approaching with desire."
It belongs to the *ad-ādi* class.

In the Vedic *laṅ*, there is a vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.3.89: "There is *vṛddhi* for [the root-final] *u* when *luk* follows and a consonant (*hal*) begins [the suffix]."
In this eighteenth section (*anuvāka*) titled ‘kaditthā’, there are six hymns (*sūktas*).
Among them, the third hymn, beginning with ‘pṛthurathaḥ’, consists of thirteen verses (*ṛcas*).
Regarding this, the index (*anukramaṇikā*) states: “Pṛthu [composed] the Sasonopasya.”
The seer is Kakṣīvān, the son of Dīrghatamas, because of the technical rule (paribhāṣā) stating “a seer [is named] from another [source]” (*ṛṣiś cānyasmād yeḥ*).
By the rule regarding the lack of specific instruction (*anādeśa-paribhāṣā*), the metre is Triṣṭubh.
Due to the employment of the word *tu*, the deity in this hymn beginning with the word *idam* is Upā.
The application of this [hymn] and the following one is in the *prātaranuvāka* during the *upasthāna* (ritual attendance).

It is prescribed in the section beginning with "Now, the approach" (*athogamya*) in the Sūtra: "In the hymn beginning with 'pṛthūratha', [one recites] the eight verses beginning with 'pratyarciḥ'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.14).
Likewise, the application of these first two hymns is in the *āśvina-śastra*, as indicated by the extended rule: "According to the procedure of the *prātaranuvāka*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.5).

Broad was the chariot of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); he fought in Ayodhyā. The immortal gods stood by him. From the darkness arose the noble one, the far-reaching one, healing for the dwelling of mankind. *pṛthuḥ* | *rathaḥ* | *dakṣiṇāyāḥ* | *ayodhi* | *ā* | *enam* | *devāsaḥ* | *amṛtāsaḥ* | *asthuḥ* | *kṛṣṇāt* | *ut* | *asthāt* | *aryā* | *vihāyāḥ* | *cikitsantī* | *mānuṣāya* | *kṣayāya* || 1 ||
The broad and expansive chariot of Upā, the goddess who is ever-increasing and skilled in her own functions, was harnessed with horses and made ready for battle.

Although a specific deity is not explicitly mentioned here, she is understood to be Upas based on her proximity [to Dawn]. (Note: 1. *śṛṇāti*; 2. *māṃ bādhante*; 3. *sphurat*; 4. *vadamejeti vṛddhiḥ*; 5. two hymns; ṚV 98).

The immortal gods—those whose nature is immortality, who possess the character of deities, and who partake of the oblation—mounted this equipped chariot; that is to say, they ascended it in order to proceed to the place of divine sacrifice.
Immediately thereafter, that Dawn rose up from the darkness, from that base-colored [state] of night.
Regarding this, Yāska says: "Kṛṣṇa is a color derived from the root *kṛṣ*. (Nirukta 2.20).
What is she like?
She is noble (*āryā*), worthy of being sought after (*araṇīyā*), and worthy of worship (*pūjanīyā*). She is *vihāyāḥ*, meaning endowed with various modes of movement or great in extent.
For *vihāyāḥ* is a name for the "great," as it is listed among those names in the passage: “*vihāyāḥ*, *yahaḥ*” (Nirukta 3.3.12).
For the sake of the human dwelling—that is, for the habitation of men—she heals, meaning she performs a healing that takes the form of dispelling darkness; the sense is that she wards off the gloom.
The East has awakened from the entire world, winning great booty, vast and bestowing gifts.
The youthful maiden, born again, has cried out on high; Dawn has come first at the morning invocation.

From the east, she has awakened from the entire world—she who is victorious, winning the prize, the lofty one, the bestower. The youthful maiden, born again, has roared aloud on high; Uṣas has arrived as the first at the morning invocation.
Being the first (*pūrvā*) among all created beings from every world (*viśvasmād bhuvanāt*), this Dawn (*uṣāḥ*) has awakened (*abodhi*).
For it is by perceiving the time of dawn that all living beings subsequently wake up.
Of what nature is she?
Having brought forth *vāja*— meaning light that is characterized by movement— and conquering darkness, that is, causing its defeat; or alternatively,
since the word *vāja* is listed among the names for food, it is a name for food.
And because of the Vedic revelation: "Food, indeed, is *vāja*" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 9.3.4.1; *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.3.6.2).
She brings about food for the sake of the sacrificer.
She is *bṛhatī*, the great; she is *sanutrī*, either one who shares out the entire world or one who bestows light.
Furthermore, that Dawn, being *uccā*—highly elevated—*vyaraut*, meaning she looks upon the entire world; such is the sense.
Of what nature is she?
She is *yuvatiḥ*, one who is inclined toward mixing or who possesses eternal youth; she is *punarbhūḥ*, one whose nature is to be born again and again, because she exists every day.
That Dawn, being true at the first invocation, comes as the foremost, the principal, the preeminent one, having arrived at the region of the gods;
for Yāska says, "Prathama is a name for the chief; he is the foremost" (Nirukta 2.22).
The meaning is that, being invoked before the other gods, she arrives most swiftly.
O goddess Uṣas, well-born one, if you distribute a portion among men for the sake of mortals here,
may the god Savitṛ, the friend of the home, declare us sinless before Sūrya.
When today, O Goddess Uṣas, well-born, you distribute the portion among men for the sake of mortals, may the divine Savitṛ, the friend of the house, declare us sinless here before Sūrya. 3.
