O *sujāte* (well-born), O *devi* (shining goddess) *uṣas*, you who are the presiding deity of the dawn-time, O protectress of mortals (*martyatrā*), at this time, for the sake of men (*nṛbhyaḥ*), that portion (*yat*)—namely, your own form of light which is worthy of being enjoyed (*bhāgam*)—[you bestow]. (Note: Regarding the commentary fragments provided: "What is she doing?
and "The meaning is 'warding off'"; following this, the additional text "the roots *gup*, *tij*, and *jñap* take the suffix *san* in the sense of pervasion and counteraction" is supplied.)
3. [The syllable] *kṣa* signifies "making manifest" (*prakāśayantīti*). 4. [The syllable] *kṣa* means "he sees" (*paśyatīti*).
The word division (*cheda*) is "in the mantras" (*mantreṣv iti*).
5. Because [the suffix] *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa* are applied again in the present tense. 6. O Goddess who presides over the time of dawn (*uṣaḥkāla*), you divide; that is, having divided, you give.
Or rather:
among mortals, that is, in the midst of mortals, you distribute and bestow the portion of the gods upon us, the sacrificers;
for since the oblation is offered when the dawn has begun to proceed, the dawn is figuratively designated as the giver.
5. Here, in this context of the portion [of the sacrifice], *damanāḥ* means "one whose mind is intent on bestowing desired fruits upon the sacrificers.
The statement from the *Nighaṇṭu* is: "Damanā, damanā, or dānamanā, or dāntamanā" (Niha. 4.4).
Such a *Savitṛ*, the impelling god, shall declare us to be *anāgasaḥ*—sinless and fit for sacrifice; that is to say, he shall graciously favor us. 6.
For what purpose?
For the sake of the sun’s arrival toward our region, that is, for the purpose of the sun coming toward us.
Striking down house after house, she goes forth clearly day by day, assuming her names.
Flashing and shining, she has come again and again; she takes possession of the very best of treasures.
From house to house she goes; day after day she comes hither, assuming her name. Seeking to be seen, shining, she has come repeatedly. She partakes of the very best of treasures. 4.
"Vahanā"—
this is a name for Uṣas,
because it is listed among her names in the Nirukta (1.8.11) with the gloss: "vahanā means shining."

That goddess goes toward every house— that is, each sacrificial hall— day by day, for the word *divedive* is listed among the names for "day" in the Nirukta (1.9.11) as meaning "day after day. She approaches each one with direct intent.
Of what sort?
Holding—that is, maintaining—*vadhī*, meaning excessive *vanāma*, which is bowing, humility, or the exertion of receiving [the guest] in the form of manifesting [hospitality].
Or else:

Supporting— that is, holding fast to— the superior [light], and moreover desiring to share it (*sisāsantī*), she who is luminous, shining upon the entire world, comes (*āgāt*) every day (*śaśvat*). Since it was previously stated that she "goes forth," the statement that she "has come" again is intended to highlight her essential necessity.

And having arrived, he partakes of—that is, enjoys, serves, and takes as his own—the very best portion, the foremost of the foremost, of the *vasus*, which are riches characterized by sacrificial offerings (*havis*).
O Sūnṛtā, sister of Bhaga and kinswoman of Varuṇa, be the first to be awakened!
May he who provides for us be mindful of our cattle; may we conquer him with the chariot of the sacrificial fee.

The sister of Bhaga, the kinswoman of Varuṇa, O Urvaśī, first among the joyful ones, do thou awaken! May he who is the supporter of the lowly be mindful of us; may we conquer him with the sacrificial fee as our chariot. 5.
O *Sūnṛtā*, you who lead men well, O goddess *Uṣas*, you are the sister of *Bhaga*, the Āditya who is to be shared by all;
that is to say, because you are born together with him, you possess his very nature.
Likewise, you are the kinswoman (*jāmi*)—that is, you occupy the position of a sister—of the god Savitṛ, the *Varuṇa* who wards off darkness.
Because they arise in one and the same place;
and they arise in great numbers.
1. *ca-pha-vibhajāsi* means "you divide, you divide."
2. From *jha*, *nu*, and *netṛ*; 3. from *kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *natṛ*. 4.
After *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa* in the word *dadāsi*, there is the additional rule: "By [the rule] beginning with *devamanuṣya*, the suffix *tran* is added.
5. In *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [the reading is] *abhimataphaladānamanāḥ*, or alternatively, *dāntamanāḥ*.
6. This means *kṣa-ja-ṭa*.
It has the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable as the first member of the compound.
7. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: Of what nature is it? 8. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: Unimpeded (*apratihata*).

9. [The syllables] *kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and those respective excellent [syllables] constitute the portion. 10. *Ta-jāmiḥ*: you are the *jāmi* (uterine sister) of him whose beginning is *ma*; you are his sister, occupying the position of a sister.
In this context, *jāmi* means "one's own offspring," O Mother (*ambe*). Or else:
"Jamati" means she goes from her place of origin to another.

With reference to the two upward-moving [rays], Yāska said: "Regarding *jāmi*, [it refers to] a sister; others produce offspring in her, thus it is *jāmapatya*. Or it may derive from the root *jam* (to go), as it is mostly used in the sense of departure" (*Nirukta* 3.6). Being such, O thou who art *prathamā*—either prior to or superior to the other gods—be *jarasva*, that is, be praised.
The root *jarati* means "to praise";
Yāska states: "The word *jarā* is praise, for the root *jar* has the sense of praising" (Nirukta 10.8).

After [the act of] seeing (*paśvā*), that is, immediately after your gratification—whatever person (*yaḥ*) is the sustainer (*avasya*) or the upholder (*dhātā*) of that evil (*ava*) which produces it, let him (*saḥ*) go (*daṃdhyāḥ*).
There is a transposition of words.
This is because [the root] is listed among the meanings of the *gatyarthas* (verbs meaning "to go") in the statement: "v dadhyati, v dadhnoti" (Nirukta 2.14.61).

Whether he be a sinner or powerful, may we conquer him—either by means of the *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) which has increased, or by you acting as an ally, or by the chariot, or by our own chariots and other implements.
Let the pleasant truths rise up, let the inspired songs arise; the foremost, brightly shining ones have stood forth.
Desirable, rich in treasures, moving swiftly, the Dawns, shining forth, reveal the hidden wealth.
Let the true words rise up; let the prayers rise up. The flames, brightly shining, have ascended. The desirable riches, hidden by darkness, the Dawns, shining forth, make manifest. 6.
Let the *sūnṛtāḥ*—words whose essence is dear and true—arise; let them go forth.
O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), proceed with the hymn of praise in an excellent manner.
Likewise, let the *puraṃdhrīs*—
those in whom the city (*puraṃ*, the body) is established, or by whom it is supported— namely, the insights (*prajñās*) pertaining to practical application—
also open their eyes.
The meaning is: "Let actions proceed as characterized by wisdom (*prajñā*).

Although the body is sustained by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), nevertheless, because of the scriptural statement, "That which is indeed *prāṇa* is wisdom; that which is wisdom is *prāṇa*" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3), there is an identity between *prāṇa* and wisdom; thus, the sustaining of the body by wisdom is not contradictory.
Likewise, let the sacrificial fires—such as the Āhavanīya and others—being *śuśucānāsaḥ*, i.e., intensely blazing, *udvasthuḥ*, i.e., rise up and flare forth. This is the meaning.
To explain why it is so, it is said:

because the Dawns (*uṣasaḥ*), the deities of the dawn, shining forth in various ways (*vibhātīḥ*), make manifest (*āviḥ kṛṇvanti*)—that is, they reveal according to their true nature—the desirable (*spārhā*) objects worthy of being clothed (*vasni*), such as the oblations and other materials for sacrifice that were completely hidden (*apagūḷahāni*) by darkness (*tamasā*). Therefore, the meaning is that they should perform the hymns of praise and other rites.
One departs and the other arrives; the two days of diverse forms proceed together.
One of them, dwelling around, makes for the darkness, while Dawn appears with her brilliantly shining chariot.

One goes away; another comes toward it. The two days of different forms move together, dwelling all around. One has made darkness hidden in the cave; the other, Dawn, shines forth with her glowing chariot.
Now, Dawn is praised by way of a hymn to day and night:
"In two forms of diverse appearance"—that is, in the manner to be described, in two forms of various kinds—"the two days" (meaning both day and night) "move together.
The prefix *sam* denotes unification.
They proceed together without any interval. Regarding this, [the commentary] says:

due to their association—1. words in the form of praise; 2. "kṣa-ja-ṭa" means "cause to increase"; the root *īr* (to go) belongs to the *adādi* class; 3. "kṣa-ma-ṭa" means "let them become manifest"; 4. "ca-pha" means "let them blaze forth"; 5. "ca-pha" means "hidden things" (*apagūḍhāni*); 6. "kṣa-ma-ṭa" means "they make manifest."
And because it is the counter-correlative of that [day], the night is also called "day.

This same meaning is made explicit in another mantra later on: "The black day and the white day revolve, [alternating] with the two regions through the knowable ones" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.9.1). Between those two, one—the day in the form of night—*apaiti*, i.e., goes away or moves in the reverse direction.
"‘Apetya’ means the reverse of this," says Yāska (Nirukta 1.3).
Furthermore, it "goes toward" (*abhyeti*), that is, it moves in the direction of the day called *div*.
"'Abhi' signifies directionality," says Yāska (Nirukta 1.3).
When the night has returned, it means that the day is approaching.
What was stated as "they move together in diverse forms" is now clarified:
they dwell around [the world] by way of succession, or they encompass it by their passing.

As the days of living beings pass away, the exhaustion of their lifespan through its depletion is well known. Between those two, one night—darkness itself in the form of gloom, a cave that conceals all objects—acts as the agent of concealment. The other, which is the counterpart of the day, is Dawn; she has arrived upon a chariot that is intensely blazing with great splendor.
It shines, is luminous, or illuminates everything. Night, because of its nature as darkness, veils the entire world.
Dawn, however, illuminates all things; such is the praise of Dawn.
Like mares with their riders, like mares with their riders, they follow the long path of Varuṇa’s ordinance;
blameless, they traverse thirty yojanas in an instant, encompassing his will in a single moment.

They are well-formed; indeed, they are well-formed. Tomorrow, truly, they shall follow the long path of Varuṇa’s ordinance. Blameless, one by one, they reach the further shore—their goal—over thirty leagues in a single day. 8.
Now, on this day,
they are indeed similar to one another;
likewise, on the following day, they are indeed similar to one another.
The word *api* has the sense of "also" (*uśat*).
The word *eva* has the sense of "only" (*evārtha*).
That which is of today (*adyatana*) is similar to those of yesterday (*bharatanī*), and that which is of tomorrow (*dhastanya*) is also similar to those of today.
Thus is the similarity [of the days] with respect to the interval.
How there is similarity is now explained:
when the stars are no longer visible and the sun has not yet risen, it is the time of dawn (upaḥkāla).
And that [day] is measured by twenty-one *ghaṭikās* and twenty-six *parās*.
For the sun revolves around Mount Meru clockwise every day for five thousand and forty-nine *yojanas*.
This being so, wherever the sun goes over a terrestrial region such as Laṅkā and the like, the dawn also travels thirty *yojanas* ahead of it.
In whatever region the sun goes, it is seen as risen by those situated thirty *yojanas* ahead of it;
this is likewise the case for all regions.
Similarly, wherever the moon (*upāḥ*) goes, it is seen as risen by those residing on the ground thirty *yojanas* ahead of it.
In this manner, the rising of the dawn should be understood for all locations, such as Laṅkā and others.
This being so, for as long a time as the dawn illuminates one region of the earth, it likewise illuminates another region for that same duration.
Thus, according to the method described, the dawns are perceived similarly by those situated in all locations on a single day.
The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of dawns (*uṣas*) in view of the vastness of their regions.
Thus, these dawns are of one form, blameless, and pure;
[this is said] because of their rising.

1. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-spaṣṭam* (clear). 2. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-iti yāskaḥ* (thus says Yāska). The first case ending (*prathamā*) of the verbal suffix (*tiṅvibhakti*) "ekābhyām" is not elided (*nihanyate*). 3. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-rātrām*. 4. *jha-guhā guhāṃ gṛhaṇam*; *kṣa-ja-ṭa-guhā*. *guhā* is the grasping (*gṛhaṇam*) of things to be hidden (*gopanīyanām*). 5. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: Following the word "karoti," there is the additional passage: "In the cave (*guhāyām*), he makes the entire world dark, having the form of darkness. In the word 'akaḥ,' because the word 'vibhāṣā' is understood from the rule 'ekānyābhyām,' there is the absence of the long vowel. 6. *ja-pha-va-ṣa-tamobhūtvā*. 7. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-u*. 8. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-sadaśāḥ*. 9. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-sadaśā u*. 10. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-evakārārthaḥ* (the meaning of the particle *eva*). 11. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-dhastanābhiḥ*. 12. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-adyatanābhiḥ*. 13. *jha-sa uṣaḥkālaḥ*; *kṣa-ja-ṭa-sa upasaḥ kālaḥ*. 14. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-tataḥ*. 15. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-tathaiva prakāśayati*. 16. *ka-kṣa-ma-ṭa-ṇa-ta-ba-ūrnnītyā*. 17. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-tāsāmudayāta*.

All things will become faultless; what need is there to mention the faultlessness of those [women]? 1) "Long" means upward and extremely extended; 2) "Of Varuṇa," that is, of the sun who dispels darkness; 3) "Dhāma" means the place, the Meru-circumference; 4) "They frequent" means they resort to it every day. To what distance? That is stated:
Thirty-three *yojanas* [is the distance] thirty *yojanas* ahead.

The meaning is that wherever the sun rises, it rises thirty *yojanas* further ahead from there. Furthermore, among these, each individual dawn [brings about] the *kratu*—meaning the activity consisting of going and coming, or the wisdom directed toward that object—for those situated in each respective portion of the earth in Laṅkā.
And thus it is stated in the Nirukta: "They have established *kratu*, which means either action or wisdom" (Nirukta 2.28).
*Sadyas* means at that very time, namely at the moment of their own rising; *paryanti* means they go around, that is to say, they carry out [their functions].
The rising of the sun at various specific locations is demonstrated in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*): "That which is sunrise in Laṅkā is sunset for the sun in Siddhapura;
it is midday in Yavakoṭi and midnight in the region of Romaka" (Āryabhaṭīya 4.13).
The wise one is the name of the first; the bright, white-rayed one was born from the black.
The maiden of Cosmic Order does not violate her laws, coming day after day to the appointed place.
Knowing the name of the first day, the bright one has been born from the dark, white-robed. The maiden of Cosmic Order does not violate her station, coming daily to the appointed place.
Uṣas: Knowing—understanding—the name, that is, the arrival, of the first, meaning either the primary or the foremost day; she makes known [the time] to living beings.

That Uṣas, bright and shining by her own nature, and therefore moving toward whiteness—that is, attaining light—is born, i.e., becomes manifest, from the black, inferior darkness. Although she is produced from darkness, she is nevertheless figuratively said to be produced from it because she arises immediately after it.
She has arisen from the *ṛta*, the true Aditya; she does not diminish—that is, she does not injure or cause the loss of—his resplendent abode (*dhāma*).
Rather, day after day, on all days, she performs her appointed task (*niṣkṛtam*), adorning herself with beauty.
Or alternatively:

The Dawn does not violate—that is, she does not harm—the abode of *ṛta*, the sacrifice that has become reality, namely the place of the gods' worship (*devayajana*), for she is of a mingling nature (*yoṣā*).

Rather, the connection with the preceding verse is as follows: "Every day, on all days of sacrifice, performing the *niṣkṛti*—the adornment consisting of the manifestation of the oblations and other elements—such a Dawn has been born. (16–17)
1. *kṣa-ca-ja-jha-ja-ṭa-pha-va* — [the group] to be pronounced with the upward breath (*ūrdhvanīya*).

2. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-uṣasaḥ pari*. 3. After *kṣa-ja-ṭa - 'nirvahantītyarthaḥ'*, there is an additional passage: "In the case of the repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhivahāra*), it should be stated that two forms of the pronoun occur; thus, there is reduplication (*dvirbhāva*)."

4. Regarding *kṣa-ja-ṭa*—after the word ‘prāpnuvatī’, [the commentary] adds: “By the rule *vṛṣādibhyaḥ*, [the suffix] *ka* [is applied]; by the rule *ṛtvig-ādinā kvin*, when *nakāra* and *akāra* are elided, there is lengthening of the preceding vowel by the rule *cau*. The acute accent of the *śap* [suffix] is due to the accent of the final syllable (*udāttaniṣṭṛtti-svara*)”—this is additional. 15. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-satī*.

6. *Jha*—The *dhāman* (abode) of the *ṛta-bhūtayajña* (the sacrifice to beings), which is the place of the *devayajana* (the sacrifice to the gods), is the woman (*yoṣā*), who is by nature prone to mixing.
7. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*—After the word "hinasti" (he injures), there is an addition: "In the sense of injuring (*mīṅ hiṃsāyām*), there is shortening [of the vowel] according to the rule *mīnāter nigame*."
8. Regarding *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: after the phrase "the connection is with what precedes," there is the additional [text]:
"The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
And by the rule *praṣṭhaprabhṛtīnāṃ ca*, the first syllable of the final member [of the compound] is acute."

Like a maiden, shining with her body, you go forth, O Goddess, toward the God who desires to sacrifice. Smiling, a young woman, you reveal your breasts as you shine brightly in the east. Like a maiden, with her body, shining, you go, O Goddess, toward the God who desires to sacrifice. Smiling, a young woman, from the front, you reveal your breasts, shining brightly.
With her body (*tanvā*), shining (*śaśadānā*)—that is, shining brightly or becoming manifest;
as Yāska states: "‘Śaśadānaḥ’ and ‘śaśādhamānaḥ’ [mean shining]" (Nirukta 6.16).
Like a maiden, she is lovely like a maiden.
"‘A maiden is desirable; who is she that is to be led? (Nirukta 4.15)—so says Yāska.
Just as she moves about unveiled in the presence of people, so, O Upas (Dawn), you, being a maiden, lovely and modest, are seen with your body (*tanvā*) becoming manifest (*śaśadānā*).

Afterwards, having become bold, O Goddess (*devi*), you who are radiant by nature (*devanaśīle*), you go toward the beloved Sun, who is of the nature of light (*deva*), desiring to sacrifice (*iyakṣamāṇam*) or desiring to grant what is desired."

Thereafter, the young woman, endowed with youth, standing before her husband— the Sun— smiling slightly, laughing, and manifesting her radiance, reveals her breasts, that is, the parts of the body characterized by the chest. Or rather,
"the young woman" (*yuvati*) is used here as a metaphorical elision (*luptopamā*).

The meaning is: just as a bold woman in this world, smiling before her beloved—smiling slightly to reveal her teeth—discloses her breasts, that is, those secret parts characterized by the chest, such as the armpits, nipples, and so forth; so too do you.
Or alternatively:
in the eastern direction (*purastāt*), a young woman smiling—that is, emitting a light resembling a smile—who is of a nature to mingle with all states of being, [reveals] her breasts.
"Vakṣa" is a name for form;
you manifest forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, which correspond to teeth.

Radiant like a woman adorned by her mother, you reveal your body for all to see. O auspicious Dawn, shine forth even more brightly; no other Dawns can attain that splendor of yours. Radiant like a woman adorned by her mother, you reveal your body for all to see. O auspicious Dawn, shine forth even more brightly; no other Dawns can attain that splendor of yours.

O Upodevī, you who have been cleansed by your mothers—their progenitors—and purified by them, like a woman of beautiful appearance shining exceedingly brightly, you manifest (*āviḥ kṛṇuṣe*) your own body for all to see. The meaning is: just as in the world a woman, well-adorned by her mother and others and being exceedingly beautiful, reveals her entire body endowed with loveliness for the sake of being seen, so too do you.
Here, the word *kam* is a filler (*pādapūraṇa*), because there is no specific [meaning] intended, as in the expression “the cool [water] for life, *kam*.”
And thus says the teacher Yāska: “In the *Mitākṣara* [Nighaṇṭu], *kam*, *īm*, and *it* are meaningless [particles]” (*Nighaṇṭu* 1.9). Alternatively, *kam* is a word for happiness.
The meaning is: "You manifest [yourself] in such a way that there is happiness.
O Uṣas, since you act thus, therefore—[the word *saṃgacchantam* (or *vā*) may be supplied].
1. The suffix *san* is added to the root *yaj*, and the *y* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) as a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasam*).
2. O Kṣamaṭa, you who effect the perfect attainment (*samyagāpatti*) of laughter (*hasana*). 3. O Kṣamaṭa, you manifest [it].
4. Immediately after *kṣamaṭa-darśanāya*, there is the additional rule: “*dṛśe vikhya ca* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātyate*). 5. *Kṣamaṭa-śobhamānā*. 7. *Kṣamaṭa-śarīraṃ sarveṣām*.

8. *kṣama-ṭa-*: Because there is no specific object [to be removed], [the word] *bhadra* (auspicious) means one of virtuous character who is worthy of praise. *Vitarām* means "more excellently. *Vyuccha* means "dispel. [The phrase] "the darkness of the disciple" means: dispel it so that it becomes distant. Although no specific [object] is heard here, nevertheless, because it is something to be countered by light and because it is something to be avoided, it is understood that what must be dispelled is indeed darkness (*tamas*).

Furthermore, O you, those past dawns that have passed by and those future ones that are yet to come do not reach—that is, they do not pervade—this *vratam* (your sacred vow/ordinance) of yours; such is the sense.

The verb *naś* has the meaning "to reach" (*āpti*), because it is listed among the roots with the sense of "reaching" (*nāsikarma*) in the *Nyāsa*. Thus, [the dawn] shines forth. The forms *invati* and *nanakṣa* are cited in the list of roots meaning "to reach."
Rich in horses, rich in cattle, possessing all desirable things, striving with the rays of the sun,
the Dawns go forth and come back again, bearing auspicious names.
Rich in horses, rich in cattle, possessing all desirable things, striving together with the rays of the sun, the Dawns go forth and come back again, bearing auspicious names. 12.

"Vaśvāvatīḥ" means possessing horses; "aśvavatyaḥ" means [possessing horses] with many horses that bring delight. Likewise, "gomatīḥ" means possessing cows; "tadvatyaḥ" means [possessing them] with many cows.
"Viśvavārāḥ" means those whose desirable times (*vārāḥ*), which are to be chosen (*varaṇīyāḥ*), are universal (*viśve*). Such are they called.
The meaning is "belonging to all times. Alternatively, they are called *viśvavārāḥ* because in them all (*viśve*) choose (*varitāraḥ*).
The meaning is "to be chosen by all.
"Spreading with the rays of the sun" means making an effort together with the sun's rays for the purpose of dispelling darkness.
Although the rays of the sun alone are capable of illuminating the world, nevertheless, because the removal of darkness is required even before sunrise, their exertion is not contradictory.

The meaning is that the deities of the rays are also illuminators. Furthermore, the *uṣas* (dawn-deities), who carry—that is, possess—the name *bhadra*, meaning auspiciousness, praise, or the favorability toward all people, go forth and depart.
Likewise, they go forth again and they come back again;
the word "and" (ca) is used in both cases in reference to their mutual relationship.
Those very same [beings] who departed in past days come again and again on subsequent days as well.
The meaning is that they perform the coming and going to the heavenly world every day.
Following the rein of Truth, bestow upon us every blessing;
O Uṣas, easy to invoke, dawn upon us today, and may riches be with us and with our patrons.
Following the rein of Cosmic Order, bestow upon us what is ever more auspicious; O Dawn, easy to invoke, shine forth for us today! May there be riches for us and for our patrons. 13.

O Uṣas, you who are pursuing the rays—the beams—of the Sun, who is the truth of that which was encompassed [by darkness], proceeding with favor, bestow (dhehi)—that is, establish—the auspicious (bhadrā) intention (kratum), whether it be a praiseworthy worldly or Vedic action, or the wisdom concerning it.
O Uṣas, for our sake (naḥ), being well-invoked (suhavā), dawn forth; dispel the darkness, meaning "make light.
For what purpose?
1. "O you whose voice is light, dispel our darkness most excellently by means of the letters *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*"; this is the meaning. 2. [The root] *invati* means "he reaches" or "he attains.

3. [This is] the meaning of *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*. Following the word "this is the meaning," there is an additional passage: "'In the sense of a name, when there is a compound with many members, the final syllable of the preceding member is udātta.'"
4. Those who perform the effort of *ca* and *pha* without conflict;
5. *Kṣa*, *Ja*, *Ṭa*, *Ra*, *Śmi*, and *Deva*;
6. Those who are intent upon *Ca*.
7. Due to the connection with the words *kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *ca*, there is no elision (of the accent). 8. [The suffixes] *kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *yāt*. 9. [The suffix] *āhya* is to be added.

10. Immediately after the statement "the meaning is 'do you endure' (*kṣama-ta*)," there is the following: because of the rule *hūyateḥ bahulaṃ chandasi*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs even before the suffix has arisen; consequently, since the suffix *yu* characterized by a final long *ā* does not apply, the accent of the *lit* suffix prevails by virtue of the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratva*.
Alternatively, [one may add] that according to the rule *bhāve 'nupasarge 'pa*, the suffix *ap* is applied and there is also *saṃprasāraṇa*. Thus, [the text] is redundant.
This is what is said:
"Among the bounteous ones. "Bounty" (magha) is a name for wealth.

The word "ca" (and) serves to connect this with the previously mentioned *ṛtu*, meaning: "May there also be riches (*rāyaḥ*) for us, the sacrificers who possess wealth characterized by sacrificial offerings; may various kinds of riches come into being."
The fourth hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "uṣā ucchantī," is the seer's work of Kakṣīvān Dīrghatamas; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Uṣas.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry "uṣā ucchantī.
As for its ritual application (viniyoga), it has already been stated in the preceding hymn.
As the dawn shines forth while the fire is kindled, and as the sun rises, it has spread its light far and wide.
May the god Savitṛ impel our purpose here, for the sake of the two-footed and the four-footed creatures.

As the Dawn shines forth, while the fire is kindled, and as the Sun rises, he has spread his light far and wide. May the divine Savitṛ here now impel our purpose, so that bipeds and quadrupeds may go forth.
This Dawn [shines] while the fire is being kindled;
the singular number is used because of the commonality of the term "fire," referring to the fires as they are being kindled.
*Daivyāni vratāni* refers to the divine ordinances—the rituals related to the gods, such as the *agnihotra* and others.
"Vrata" is a name for ritual action, as it is listed among the names for action in the Nirukta (2.1.7): "vrataṃ karvaram.
She honors—that is, she does not harm—those rituals, making them favorable by bestowing light upon them.

Likewise, "human beings [measure] the ages of humans"— that is, they measure, meaning they excessively harm or destroy, the temporal divisions such as *nimeṣas* and so forth, which are characterized by the *yugas*; or alternatively, they measure, meaning they harm or destroy,
the "ages" (*yugāni*) as pairs— that is, they effect separation by destroying their mutual union.
It is well known that at the time of dawn, everyone goes about their respective duties.
Furthermore, she is the likeness (*upamā*) of the *śaśvatīḥ* (eternal) *niśānām* (nights)—that is, of the past dawns that have gone by;
the meaning is that she is similar to them.
And regarding "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), it is stated: "The suffix *aca* [is applied] after the root *sadṛś*, as in *sadṛśīḥ* [meaning] 'like'" (*Kṛṣṇa Saṃhitā* 1.123.8).
Likewise, being the first among the future dawns (*āyatīnām uṣasām*), she shines forth preeminently (*vyadhaut*).
Or else:
Of those who have gone, that is, of those whose nature is to depart, this Dawn— *upa* being a single particle consisting of a combination of two particles—
is seen in close proximity by all.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"śumbhyuvau na vakṣaḥ. Here, the letter *n* serves the purpose of expressing a comparison (*upamārthīya*).
Because it is broadened at the top;
however, where a negation is intended, the negative particle *na* is employed before [the word]. And thus Yāska says: "Its usage is prior, in that which it negates" (Nirukta 1.4).
Its example is: "They did not perceive Indra as a god" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.86.1), according to the rule: "That which is placed above is that with which one compares" (Nirukta 1.4).
Its example is: "Like those intoxicated by wine" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.2.12). Śumbhyuḥ is Āditya.
Because it purifies all things.
"His chest" refers to the mass of rays situated in the region of the chest;
the meaning is that it is just as it appears when shining forth.
Alternatively,
*śumbhyu* refers to a white-colored aquatic bird;
the meaning is that it is like that [bird] being seen as it reveals its own breast.
Furthermore, "like Nodhas, he has revealed dear things. Nodhas is so called because he holds (dhārayati) a new hymn (navanaṃ stotraṃ).
A great seer (maharṣi) of this name, under the pretext of praising the deities, revealed his own cherished desires through various kinds of mantras.
In the same way, this [goddess] also manifests her own splendors, which are beloved by all the worlds;
moreover, she "devoured" (agrasat).
Here too, the letter *na* has the sense of a simile (*upamā*).
That which is eaten is "agra," meaning food;

she sits in the house for its cooking, thus she is the "agrasat-pācikā," the woman who cooks the food. She awakens those who sleep, just as a mother awakens her sleeping sons and others for their meal.
Alternatively,
*agra* is a name for the house, as it is listed among its synonyms in the passage beginning “*varutham agra*. She sat there, thus she is *agrasat*, the mother.

Just as she awakens her sleeping sons and others at the time of dawn, so too, seated in the house called the world, she awakens the living beings therein; thus she is *uṣas*. Among the women who are accustomed to coming (*eyuṣīṇām*), she is the most constant (*śaśvattamā*), returning again and again.
The intended meaning is that among the courtesans who regularly arrive in the morning, she alone comes as one who is invariably present.

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "The term *śumbhyu* belongs to the Ādityas; it arises from the sense of 'purifying. This very [word] refers to the chest (*vakṣas*) as something placed upon the light (*bhās*). Another [meaning] is that which is placed upon the body (*adhyūham*), for this reason it is called *adhyūha*. A bird (*śakuni*) is also called *śumbhyu*, because it moves about purifying itself in water.
Water itself is also called *śumbhyu*, precisely because of its purifying nature."
"The seer does not become new; he bestows what is ever-new. Just as one manifests desires through praise, so does Uṣas manifest forms.
She is called *agrasat* because she devours, or because she has been devoured, or because she is desirous of devouring.
Awaking those who sleep, she has come most constantly among those who return; awakening those who sleep, she has come most perpetually among those who come again" (Nirukta 4.16).
In the eastern half of this space, the mother of the cows has raised her banner;
she spreads herself out further and wider, purifying both the laps of her parents.
In the eastern half of this region, the Mother has established her banner among the cattle. She spreads herself out further and wider, filling the laps of both parents.
Of this pervasive and extensive *rajas*— the intermediate region (*antarikṣaloka*),
for Yāska has stated that "the worlds are called *rajaḥ*s" (Nirukta 4.19)—
having been born in its eastern half, in the eastern part, she, as the progenitor, has brought forth, or performs preeminently, the *kenū*, the discernment, of the *gāvaḥ*, the quarters or the rays.
Alternatively, it is the day of *rajas*, that is, of the washerman (*rajaka*).
For the word *rajas* refers to days, as Yāska has stated: "The two *rajas* are called *asu* and *gahani*" (Nirukta 4.19).
In its eastern half—that is, in its eastern part—at the time of dawn, she is the progenitor, the generator, the producer of the speech of cows.
It is well known that at the time of dawn, the speech of all living beings vibrates forth.
Or else:
For this living being established in its actions, the "banner" (ketu) consists of action in the form of coming and going;
for "banner" is a name for action, as it is listed among those names in the passage: "ketaḥ ketuḥ. It is natural.
He acts with excellence. Furthermore, standing within the lap— the interior space— of the two parents, Heaven and Earth, who are protectors, he fills both Heaven and Earth with his own splendor.
Alternatively, the connection is "of both parents.

It spreads out—that is, it becomes especially renowned and shines forth—more widely, more excellently, and more extensively than before, in such a way that it becomes particularly celebrated; this is the meaning.

The particle *u* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) or serves as a verse-filler (*pādapūraṇa*); for it has been stated by Yāska that particles such as *kam*, *īm*, and *id* are meaningless (*anarthaka*).
Truly, this most abundant one is for all to see; she avoids neither the stranger nor the kinsman.
Boasting with her stainless body, she does not merely blaze from the navel [of the earth], but shines forth mightily.
Thus indeed, she, most abundant for all to behold, spares neither the stranger nor the kin. Exulting in her stainless body, she does not shrink from anyone; she shines forth mightily. 6.
This Dawn indeed— indeed (*eva*) being the very word used for emphasis—

just so (*evam eva*), in this very manner as she now appears, being most abundant (*purutamā*), that is, most extensive and exceedingly vast, does not avoid (*na pari vṛṇakti*), that is, does not exclude from all sides, the *ajāmi*, meaning the dissimilar class such as humans and the like.
Likewise, it does not exclude or avoid its own kind (*sajātīya*), that is, the class of gods;
rather, it reveals in its entirety both worlds characterized by humans and so forth, as well as those characterized by gods and so forth—this is the meaning.
For what purpose? That is now stated:

Visible to all for them to behold; or rather, so that there may be happiness, she reveals herself to everyone. Furthermore, with a stainless, sinless, and pure body, she shines forth, manifesting herself.
"Śāśadānaḥ śāśayamānaḥ" (Nirukta 6.16), says Yāska;
the meaning is "becoming manifest.
She, shining forth (*vibhāti*) by illuminating specifically, "does not flee" (*na īrṣate*), that is, she does not move away from even the slightest [creature], such as a gnat.
It illuminates even that;
likewise, it illuminates even that which does not move—that is, does not go—from the great [mountain] Meru and others.
Previously, it was stated that two worlds shine forth.
The meaning is that it now illuminates everything in this world, from the smallest atom up to the mountains.
Like a woman coming toward her lover, like one who climbs a chariot-seat for the winning of riches, like a longing wife beautifully robed for her husband, Dawn bares her bosom like a hand.
Like a protector comes toward a man; like one climbing from a pit for the winning of riches; like a longing wife for her husband, well-attired, Dawn bares her bosom with her hands. 7.
Here, as if she were without a brother, she goes toward men—her father and others—with her face turned back from her own place.
Just as in the world a woman without a brother goes to her paternal kinsmen to obtain the clothing, ornaments, and other things that reside in her heart;
for when a brother exists, he alone properly satisfies her by providing what is appropriate and so forth.
Due to the absence of that [intermediate state], one reaches the father himself;
or else, when [the father is present]...

1. By the rule *kṣa-ja-ṭa-pitroḥ*. 2. By the distinction of *kṣa-ja-ṭa*. 3. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-śāśayamānā*. 4. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-śāśayamānaḥ*. 5. The meaning is "he illuminates" (*prakāśayati*). 6. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-asminneva loke* (in this very world). 7. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-svocita-vāso’laṃkārāya* (for the sake of clothing and ornaments suitable for himself). He performs that duty of lineage, such as the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to his father, for his own brother. In the absence of [such a brother], he himself, acting as the performer of that rite, goes to [the realm of] his ancestors and so forth.
Likewise, Uṣas also approaches the Sun—who is her father—in order to obtain the light and other benefits appropriate for herself, or to bestow her own radiance;
this is one illustration.
Similarly, "as one ascending a chariot-seat for the acquisition of wealth" is another illustration.

*Garta* is a name for a house, as it is listed among its synonyms in the *Nighaṇṭu* (3.4.3), where it says, "Rudra is the *garta*. Here, by virtue of propriety, it refers to a place presided over by royal officials and judges; one who ascends such a place is called a *gartārū*.
Just as in the world, a certain woman whose husband has passed away goes to a gambling den (*garta*) for the sake of winning back her own depleted wealth.
If the members of the assembly, after deliberating, determine that she shall receive this inheritance, they strike her with dice and distribute her wealth [among themselves].
Likewise, for the sake of gaining—that is, obtaining—wealth, means of gratification, and splendors, he ascends the pit, the sky, the abode of the sun.
This illustration is given in consideration of the customs of a particular region.
Furthermore: "Behold her, longing and desiring, well-attired like a bride"—this is another simile.

Just as in the world a woman well-dressed—adorned with beautiful garments such as fine linen (*dukūla*) and well-ornamented—who previously, during her menstrual period, was clad in soiled clothes, now, after bathing, shines resplendent in beautiful raiment and jewelry, and especially desiring enjoyment with her husband, sports with him; even so this Dawn (*uṣas*), though she was like one in soiled clothing because she was enveloped by the intense darkness of night, becomes as if well-dressed at dawn because she is covered by her own radiance, and sporting together with the Sun who stands in the place of a husband, she truly laughs, as it were, with her *apsas*—the forms of blue, yellow, and other colors standing in the place of teeth.
Alternatively:
the various categories of objects being examined;
*nirīṇate* means it flows out, that is, it causes them to flow forth or brings them to light.

The meaning is that just as a certain beautiful woman in the world reveals her teeth under the pretext of a smile, so too does she manifest all forms. This mantra is clearly explained in the *Nirukta*: "Like a woman without a brother-in-law who goes toward her father's [kin] for the sake of the act of procreation and the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), she does not go to her husband; like a courtesan from the Deccan who mounts a chariot-seat (*garta*) for the sake of gaining wealth.
A 'chariot-seat' (*garta*) is the pillar of an assembly hall; he is one whose promise is true, for he is derived from the root *gaṇ* (to count)."

Regarding her, it is said: "Whichever woman there, being childless or husbandless, mounts [the chariot], they strike her there with dice, saying, 'May she not obtain the inheritance,'" and also: "Like a wife desiring her husband, well-dressed at the time of her season, Uṣas reveals her teeth like one smiling" (Nirukta 3.5).
The sister has yielded her womb to the elder sister, having merely looked upon her who was to be her offspring;
shining forth with the rays of the sun, she follows her like a woman following her husband.

Sister! To the sister! To the elder sister! The womb! O friend! Enter! As if to be beheld by her, shining forth with the rays of the sun, she has entered her own body like waters flowing down from the mountains. 8.
Because they have both arisen from the same intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), they possess their respective natures in relation to one another.
Nevertheless, because it comes first and because it is of the nature of light (*tejas*), the day is superior.
Or, because it moves by itself, it is called *svasā* (sister).
To the elder sister, Night (7), by way of the *ukthā* (11), he has bestowed, filled, or extended the womb—the place of origin—whose form is the latter part of the night (7) unto the eldest (7).
And thus it is declared previously: "Night [approaches]..."

1. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, the phrase “the function of continuity” (*saṃtānakṛtyam*) is absent. 2. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [it is] "become a self-luminous father" (*svaprakāśapitṛbhūtam*). 3. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, there is another illustration: "like one ascending a pit" (*gartārohiṇīva*); [another reading is] *gartāruhiriva*. 4. In the manuscripts *ca* and *pha*, [it is] *āsthitam*. 5. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [it refers to] "of light and so forth" (*prakāśādīnām*). 6. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [it says] "this too is another. 7. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [it says] "this Dawn too" (*iyamapyuṣāḥ*). 8. In manuscript *jha*, [it says] "also by the nocturnal" (*api naiśena*). 9. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [it says] "as if with this" (*samaneneva*). [The suffix] *rak* is applied according to the rule beginning with *sphāyitaśca*. 10. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, after the phrase "the meaning is 'he illuminates'" (*prakāśayatītyarthaḥ*), there is an addition: "The root *rī* is used in the sense of motion and seeking; it belongs to the *kyādigaṇa*. By transposition, the *ātmanepada* ending is used. By the rule 'pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ', there is shortening. This [root] has the sense of 'to cause' (*antarbhāvitavyartho'yam*) internalized within it. 11. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [it says] "by the manner of rising" (*ujjanītyā*). 12. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [it says] "she opened" (*āraik*).
"O slayer of the good" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.113.1).
And having given [the gift], as if intending to look back at the dawning dawn that has arisen,
he himself likewise departs.

The sense is that when the elder [dawn] has arrived, she (the younger dawn) gives her own place to her and, realizing it is improper for her to remain in her presence, departs. Thus, by means of the rays of the sun, this Dawn shines forth, driving away the darkness, like fire— that is, the revealing light— or rather, [it is like] fire.
Agni makes the world manifest;
he adorns it—that is, he illuminates it.
Like what?
Likewise, "samanagāḥ":
waters are called *samanāḥ* because they are the cause of moving correctly (*samyaggamana*). Those [waters] go forth, thus they are "samanagāḥ," namely, the lightnings.
The *vbrāḥ* are protectors,
like a multitude of lightning flashes;
or else:
They are called *samanaga* because they go toward perfect movement; these are the rays of the sun.
Or, like them, they are protectors who have become unified.
The meaning is that they illuminate the world at the end, just as those [rays] do.
In the word *trātaḥ*, the elision of the letter *t* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) phenomenon. Regarding these [words], Yāska states: "The *paṇi* is a merchant" (Nirukta 2.17).

Like greedy hunters who are "unawakened"—meaning those who do not perform sacrifices and the like, who are uncharitable, and who are evil enemies—let them "sleep," that is, let them slumber in a long sleep; let them perish. Thus says another mantra: "Let those enemies sleep, O Hero, let the givers be awake" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.29.4).

Furthermore, O Uṣas, rich in our oblations (*maghoni*), shine forth for the sake of the sacrificers—you who possess wealth in the form of oblations and horses—as *revat*, which means wealthy and prosperous.

Furthermore, O Ṛsunṛte—O Goddess who leads men well—O Jarayantī, you who cause all living beings to age and pass away, you rise for the sake of the Ṣtotre, the one who offers praise and performs sacrifice; for his sake, you rise toward wealth (revat) and prosperity. This is the sense.
Now he stirs this immovable [world]: before him, yoked, is the vanguard of the ruddy cows.
Truly, his signal now rises up; Agni takes his station in every house.
She has shone forth from the east, this young woman; she has yoked the team of ruddy cows. Now indeed let her shine abroad; let the herald appear. Agni stands near every single house. 11.
"This Dawn is a young woman," meaning she stands in the place of a woman endowed with youth;
or alternatively,
she is one who mingles [all things] among all existing beings.
"ᐃ" means "in front," that is, in the eastern direction; "ᐄ" means "arising"; and "ᐆatha" means "then it comes" or "it increases.
Here, the word "ava" is used in the sense of restriction, as Yāska stated: "'anya' and 'ava' are used in the sense of restriction" (Nirukta 1.3).
To explain how this is understood, he says: [the following].
She yokes to the chariot the *anīkam*, the multitude, of these *aruṇānām*—of the well-known *aruṇa*-colored cows or horses bearing that name.
As it is said: "The *aruṇa* [cows] belong to the *uṣas*; the dark-brown ones (*iyāvāḥ*) belong to Savitṛ" (Nirukta 1.15.7–8).
Just as in the world, seeing the yoking of vehicles and armor one infers an impending departure, so too here, from the sight of the red rays of light, it is determined that the Dawn is arriving.
Or rather, she yokes the multitude of the red rays.
Likewise, "certainly" (*nūnam*) means with certainty: she will surely dispel the darkness.
Because she yokes the cows, for that very reason, just as in the world one infers the rising of the sun upon seeing the horses being harnessed, so it is here; this is the meaning.

Such a one, even when the dawn has not yet arrived, shines forth pre-eminently and diversely in the formless intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), or in the unlovely darkness, acting as a "banner" (*ketu*)—that is, like a banner, a signifier. This is the sense.
Due to the force of the prefix (*upasarga*), a suitable verb must be supplied.

Alternatively, the connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "In the absence of darkness consisting of *tamas*, being a *praketa*—that is, a preeminent illuminator—she will surely shine forth."

At that time, Agni—in the form of the Āhavanīya and other sacrificial fires—stands near every house, that is, the house of every sacrificer, for the purpose of the Agnihotra; "stands near" means he shines forth.

1. After the word "samṛddhimat" in the manuscripts kṣa, ja, and ṭa, there is the additional passage: "By the rule *rayematī bahulam*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*); and by the rule *reśabdācca*, the suffix *matup* is acute. 2. After the word "śeṣaḥ" in the manuscripts kṣa, ja, and ṭa, there is the additional passage: "Because [the roots] *jan*, *dṛś*, *kṛ*, *su*, *raj*, and those ending in *am* are marked with the indicator *m* (by the rule *janīdṛṣkṛsurajo'mantāśca*), there is shortening of the vowel by the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*."

3. After "kṣa-ja-ṭa- 'vā'," there is the additional [text]: "'śrayateśchāndase luṅi sici vṛddhau iḍabhāve rūpam'" (it is a form [derived] from the root *śri* in the Vedic *luṅ* tense with *sic*, after the *vṛddhi* [strengthening], in the absence of *iṭ*).
4. kṣa-ja-ṭa: for the purpose of restraint (*vinigrahārthaḥ*). 5. kṣa-ja-ṭa: that which is this (*yat iyam*).
6. After "yojayati" in the manuscripts kṣa, ja, and ṭa, there is the additional passage: "The cows are ruddy because they are restricted to the dawns;
and so it is stated in the Nirukta.
7. In the manuscripts ca, jha, pha, and ṣa, the reading is "nidhitameṣā."
8. Having seen the armor in that world, victory is inferred. 9. After the word "upatiṣṭhate" in the Kṣa-ja-ṭa [recension], there is "saṃgacchate"; the augment *āṭ* is applied.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here because of the rule: "The [roots] *upa-ā-dā*, *pūj*, *saṃ-gat-kṛ*, and others take the middle voice.

Thy birds have flown forth from the dwelling, and the men who partake of the ancestral portion at the breaking of dawn. O Goddess Uṣas, thou bringest much wealth to the mortal who offers oblations when the Soma is pressed. *uta* (also), *te* (thy), *vayaḥ* (birds), *cit* (even), *vasteḥ* (from the dwelling), *apaptan* (have flown away), *naraḥ* (men), *ca* (and), *ye* (who), *pitṛbhājaḥ* (partakers of the ancestral portion), *vyuṣṭau* (at the breaking of dawn). *Amā* (at home), *sute* (when the Soma is pressed), *vahasi* (thou bringest), *bhūri* (much), *vāmam* (wealth), *uṣaḥ* (O Uṣas), *devi* (O Goddess), *dāśuṣe* (to the giver), *martyāya* (to the mortal).
O Vāyu, when your dawn has truly broken, even the birds—those that possess wings and are capable of flight—even they [citi] shall fly forth;
for the word *cit* here carries the sense of "even" (*api*), since particles have multiple meanings, as Yāska stated: "Particles fall upon various meanings" (Nirukta 1.4).

From their dwelling places, such as their homes and so forth, they descend; that is, after ascending, they do not fall [back down]. Since the preceding sentence stated, "The fire attends every house," the word *api* (also/even) is used in reference to that. Furthermore, men—human beings who partake of the ancestral offerings (*pitṛbhājaḥ*), possess horses, and seek food, namely those engaged in agriculture, trade, and other such activities—descend and go forth, intent upon their respective occupations.
Likewise, another mantra says: "He who gives the path causes the birds to fly up" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.48.5).

Thus, O Goddess, you who are playful (*devanśīlā*), for the sake of the sacrificer who dwells (*sate*) in his own home—the sacrificial ground—O *upodak* (you who are near the water), [I call upon you].
*Amā* is a name for "home," as it is listed among the names in the Nirukta (3.4.11): "In the home (*amā*), in the house (*dame*)."
Or rather:
it dwells together (*amā*) with the fire that is being sacrificed (*hūyamāna*), for the sacrificer;
since in expressions such as *amā vasetām* ("let them dwell together"), the word is used in the sense of "together."
To the immortal one, to the mortal man who has offered the oblation—the sacrificer—you bring, you cause to arrive, abundant and beautiful wealth.

We have praised you, O worthy of praise; through my prayer, O longing Dawns, you have increased my wealth. O goddesses, by your protection may we win booty consisting of hundreds and thousands. (13) We have praised you, O worthy of praise; through my prayer, O longing Dawns, you have increased [my wealth]. O goddesses, by your protection may we win booty consisting of hundreds and thousands. (13)

Having praised her in many ways according to the manner described in these two hymns, and having offered this praise, he prays for his own desired object: "O you who are worthy of praise! *Stoma* means a hymn of praise."
Because they deserve that, they are "worthy of praise" (*stomyāḥ*).
The *uṣas* (dawns) are worthy of hymns of praise;
since you are such, therefore, with this *brahman*—that is, with the hymn consisting of the mantras found in these two *sūkta*s—let us truly praise you; may you be praised.
Furthermore, O *uṣasaḥ* (Dawns), you who are *vuśatīḥ*, desiring us—the singers—or our prosperity, do you *vavīvṛdhadhvam*, cause us to increase.
Moreover, O *devīḥ*, goddesses whose nature is to shine, through *vasā*, your protection, may we *sanema*, obtain *sahasriṇam*, wealth desired in the number of thousands;
likewise, may we obtain *śatinam*, strength (*vāja*) in the number of hundreds, that is, immeasurable wealth.

The meaning is: "By means of the protection of wealth and other assets amounting to hundreds of thousands provided by you, may we also become bestowers of wealth amounting to hundreds of thousands upon those who seek it."

1. After the entry for *kṣa-ja-ṭa- ‘apaśabdaḥ’, there is the additional text: “After *luṭ* [the suffix] of *patati* in Vedic usage, because it is marked with *l*, the augment *pum* is added, resulting in *pataḥ pum*. 2. kṣa-ja-ṭa-tathā ca 3. kṣa-ja-ṭa-bhūri

I give you this abundant, lovely, and desirable form consisting of wealth, gold, and so forth—according to the principle stated in the two hymns *kṣa-ja-ṭa* (4), and according to the principle stated in the two hymns *ja-jha-ta-pha-ṣa* (5).

[Note: 5. In the version *kṣa-ja-ṭa*, after the word *bhavataḥ*, there is the additional remark: "In the *luṅ* tense for the object, by the rule *ḍuṇaḥ pīcca*, there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *dh*."]
The fifth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "prātā ratnam," is the Kākṣīvata hymn.

Because the act of giving is being praised, it has the deity of giving as its presiding deity, according to the rule stated in the Anukramaṇī: "That by which [the praise] is uttered is the deity" (Anu. 2.5).
It is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The two verses beginning with "upetya" are *jagatī*s;
as stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*: "The [hymns] beginning with 'prātā ratnam' and 'sapta svanasya dānastṛtiḥ' are *upajagatī*s."
The early-coming one bestows treasure at dawn; the wise man, having recognized him, receives and deposits it.
By means of that, increasing his progeny and his life, he, possessed of brave sons, dwells in the abundance of wealth.

At dawn, having come, he bestows a treasure; perceiving him, one receives it and deposits it. By means of that, increasing his progeny, he is accompanied by long life and the abundance of wealth, being rich in heroic sons. 1.
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend:

The seer Kakṣīvān, the son of Dīrghatamas, while practicing celibacy, dwelt for a long time in the teacher’s household for the purpose of studying the Vedas. Having thoroughly mastered the Vedas and performed his vows, he was permitted by his teacher to return to his own home. While traveling on the road, he rested there one night.
At dawn, a king named Svanaya, the son of Bhāvayavya, who was sporting with his attendants, happened to come into the presence of Kakṣīvān.
He woke up with a start and rose suddenly.

The king, taking his hand and seating him upon his own throne, perceived his beauty and, intent on bestowing his daughter upon him, asked: "Venerable sir, whose son are you, and what is your name? Being thus questioned, he related everything concerning his mother, his father, and his own life story.

Realizing that the king was worthy of honor, he returned home with a joyful heart; having prepared the *madhuparka* offering for him and honored him with garments, garlands, and other gifts, he gave him ten maidens with their chariots, a hundred *niṣkas*, a thousand bulls, a thousand cows, one hundred and sixty more, and eleven additional items.
Having accepted everything in due order, he went into the presence of Dīrghatamas and presented it all to him.
Now, what indeed is a "kakṣīvān"? It is a rope for tethering horses;
and the possession of such a horse-tether is fitting only for a king.

Therefore, because he is a member of the royal caste (*rājanya*), the acceptance of gifts is not appropriate for him; for it has been stated: "Sacrificing for others, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts—these are the pure means of livelihood for the Brāhmaṇa" (Manu 10.76). Consequently, the qualification belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone, and not to the Kṣatriya.
This is not a fault.

Even though he was the son of that King of Kaliṅga, nevertheless, because the King himself was old and lacked the capacity to procreate, he requested the sage Dīrghatamas to produce offspring for him. When the King’s wife was sent to the village of Uśī to bear children, she felt ashamed to sport with the extremely aged great seer; she therefore adorned her own attendant, the woman Uśīgrāmikā, with her own ornaments and sent her as her representative. The sage, perceiving her to be a maidservant, consecrated her with water purified by mantras, made her his "daughter," and took pleasure with her.
The seer Kakṣīvat was born from that [union].
All of this has been explained in detail by us previously in the hymn beginning with "To the two Nāsatyas" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116).
Therefore, because of his connection to a Kṣatriya, the name Kakṣīvat is appropriate.
Since he was born from the great seer Dīrghatamas and is therefore a Brāhmaṇa, his acceptance of gifts is entirely appropriate.
This first pair of hymns (sūktas) sets forth the narrative praising the generosity of King Svanaya.

Now, it may be objected that according to the Anukramaṇī—stating both "the praise of Svanaya’s gift" and "pleased by the gift, Bhāvayavya praised [him]"—it appears that in both cases the object of praise is understood to be distinct. To this it is replied: [text continues]

In the first verse of the subsequent hymn (*uttarasūkta*), because the giver Bhāvayavya is heard of in the words “of Bhāvayavya who dwells on high,” that [verse] is treated separately by relying on its initial position.

However, in reality, since a son may be designated by the name of his father, and because such usage is seen frequently—as in “O Rudras” and so forth—and furthermore, because Svanaya himself is mentioned in that very same hymn in the words “given by Svanaya,” it is well known that the narrative in both cases consists of a praise of the gift, wherein the giver and the recipient are essentially one and the same.

And that Kakṣīvat brought all the wealth that his father had acquired through weariness; [this was] because of his kingship (variant: by the King of Kaliṅga). Having made the seer into a mountain (variant: having made the son also...), [the gift] was accomplished. With one hundred verses, [the poet] praises the manner of giving in its absence.

A king named Svanabha, having arrived in the very early morning from his own presence, places—that is, bestows—a beautiful jewel, such as a *niṣka* coin and so forth, in the early morning, at the time of dawn, in our vicinity; he establishes it there. Being discerning and conscious, he perceives that which was previously unseen; having accepted and taken possession of that established treasure, he deposits it near his father.

Immediately thereafter, by means of the gold coins and other wealth given by him, increasing and nourishing his progeny—consisting of sons, servants, and so forth—and extending his lifespan and life, being endowed with excellent heroes such as sons, servants, and others, he prospers through the increase of wealth (*rāyaspoṣa*) by the repeated augmentation of riches.
"May this king attain [prosperity]"—thus does the giver pray for your blessing.
To him who, at the break of dawn, releases you— who are rich in heroes, rich in gold, and rich in horses— like one untying a tethered foot, Indra bestows great vital strength.
Rich in cattle, rich in gold, rich in horses—Indra bestows great vital strength upon him who, O Lord of the Dawn, seizes you as you approach with wealth, like one catching a bird in a snare. ||2||
Here, Kakṣīvat’s father, satisfied with the wealth brought [to him], offers many blessings to the king:
"May this King Svanaya be *suguḥ*—
that is, may he be possessed of many excellent cows."
Likewise, 3. *suhiraṇya*: may he be possessed of excellent, beneficial, and delightful wealth;

likewise, 4. *svaśva*: being possessed of beautiful horses, 5. *asmai*—to this king who is the giver—6. *bṛhat*—abundant—7. *vayaḥ*—food—8. *indraḥ*—the Supreme Lord, the deity of Dharma—9. *dadhāti*—may He bestow, may He grant.
Since this king has given him numerous cows, gold, horses, and chariots, it is entirely appropriate to pray for their increase.
To whom is such a blessing addressed? That is explained: [to] 10 *vayaḥ*—the king; 11 *prātaritvaḥ*—one who will arrive in the morning, a guest;

12 *putra*—a son; 13 *āyantam*—one returning from the teacher’s house; 14 *padim*—a traveler, one who goes by chance; 15 *tvā*—you; 16 *vasunā*—with wealth consisting of means of sustenance such as cattle and so forth; 17 *utsināti*—he binds you away from going, meaning he holds you back from departing.
An example regarding obstruction is stated:
"Like a *mukṣījā*.
A *mukṣījā* is a rope used for binding deer, cattle, and so forth; it is so called because, while being released [from its coil], it produces a bond.

Just as a snare catches and binds a deer, a beast, or the like that comes to its path, so too, by obstructing your departure even though you were not permitted to go, the king who gratifies me with gifts of cattle and the like—may he be thus [rewarded]. Regarding the word *padim*, Yāska, while explaining it as "path" (*pada*), has explained this mantra with the example: "It becomes easy to traverse because of that" (Nirukta 5.19).

O noble Aśvin, you who bestow wealth upon the doer of good deeds, at the break of dawn, cause the son of Aṃśu to drink of the exhilarating Soma with your treasure-laden chariot; increase him, the lord of heroes, with your truthful songs of praise.

Noble one, desiring well-performed deeds in the morning, cause the son of the sacrifice to drink the pressed juice of the exhilarating Aṃśu with your wealth-laden chariot; increase him, the ruler of heroes, with pleasant truths. 3.
1. After *kṣa-na-ṭa-‘asan*, there is the additional [rule]: *“anyeṣv api dṛśyante iti kanip tuk”*.
2. *jha-asat*; *kṣa-na-ṭa-asat*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first member is udātta.

3. After *putra* [in the rule] *kṣa-na-ṭa*, there is the additional [text]: “the addition of *vata* (*na*)” [and] “in the vocative, the substitution of *ru* for the letter *n*. 4. *kṣa-na-ṭa*: *āgacchantam*. 5. *kṣa-na-ṭa*: *badhnāti*.
The root *piṣ* means "to bind";
it belongs to the *kaiyādika* (curādi) class.
6. By means of [bestowing] whatever is desired, such as food, clothing, and so forth.

7. This mantra [is cited] by way of illustration for *ka*, *ja*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ṭa*, *va*, *ta*, and *da*; the mantra [is cited] by way of illustration for *pha* and *ta*. 8. In the case of *ka*, *kṣa*, *ja*, *jha*, *ṭa*, *ṇa*, *va*, *ṣa*, and so forth, the passage from the *Nirukta* beginning with "it becomes heavy... because of its extension" (*sugur-bhavati... tatanācca*) is quoted in full. "In the morning, on the previous day, at the time of dawn, he gave this wealth. At that very time, "desiring you—the doer of beautiful deeds (*sukṛtaṃ śobhanasya kartāram*)—wishing to obtain you, longing [and thinking], 'When shall I see you?', I have now, on this very day, fallen into fear."

In this context, although only "in the morning" (*prātar*) is explicitly heard and not "on the previous day" (*pūrveṣuḥ*), nevertheless, because it is stated [elsewhere] that "then he comes," it is understood by implication that "he comes in the morning on the previous day. Of what kind?
"A son who is a protector in many ways" (*putraṃ puru trātāram*) of the sacrifice (*iṣṭeḥ*)—that is, of the sacrifice which is the means for accomplishing what is desired.
"‘The son protects in many places’ (Nirukta 2.11), so says Yāska;
the meaning is ‘the agent. By what means? That is now stated."
"With an earth-bearing chariot," that is, with a chariot (ratha) as a means of transport that is richly endowed with wealth;
or alternatively,
the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*), meaning "accompanied by that."

Furthermore, with great and abundant wealth, [we offer] to the *matsara*—the exhilarating Soma, which is the "portion" (*aṃśu*) of the "possessor of portions" (*aṃśumat*), having the form of fire (*vahni*), and being the means for intoxication (*mādana*).
As it is said in the Nirukta: "The Soma is *matsara* because it causes exhilaration; it is a word denoting the act of praising. (Nirukta 5.4)
He who gives stands supported upon the ridge of heaven; he indeed goes among the gods.
For him the rivers flow with ghee and water; for him this sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) ever overflows.

He who bestows gifts stands supported upon the back of heaven; he indeed goes among the gods. For him the waters and the rivers flow with clarified butter; for him this sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) ever overflows. 5.
In the context of praising the Soma sacrifice, [the author] praises giving in general through these three [verses] beginning with this one.
Alternatively,

since the Soma itself has been praised and because the word *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) is well-established as referring specifically to the sacrifice, the Soma sacrifice alone is introduced here until the conclusion of the hymn.
Whosoever is a mortal who satisfies—that is, pleases—the gods and others by means of offerings and other gifts—he [attains] the summit of Nāka.
*Kam* is a name for happiness;
that which is contrary to it is *akam*.

There is no *aka*—that is, no suffering (*duḥkha*) or the evil (*pāpa*) that causes it; thus, *nāka* refers to the heavenly world (*dyuloka*). As it is heard in scripture: "Indeed, for one who has gone to that world, there is nothing that is not *nāka*" (Nirukta 2.14; Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā 21.2).
Being supported upon its *pṛṣṭha*—the elevated upper region—it stands *adhi*, meaning preeminently, until the end of the kalpa.
Alternatively:
he presides over it;
having presided over it, he stands facing forward.
It is not merely that he goes to heaven; rather, the meaning is that he "goes among" or "dwells within" the gods himself.
The word "ha" indicates well-known fact.

For that person who gratifies [the gods], the "rivers"—meaning the waters characterized by flowing—flow as "clarified butter," which is the essence possessing brilliance; the meaning is that they become full of vital sap.
Furthermore, this earth also—being "dakṣiṇā," meaning skillful in producing fruits such as grain—"pinvate," that is, she sprinkles or satisfies at all times;
the meaning is that the beautiful and abundant waters that sustain the life of the giver come to be.

For those who give sacrificial fees, these wondrous things belong; for those who give sacrificial fees, there are suns in heaven. Those who give sacrificial fees partake of immortality; those who give sacrificial fees prolong their life.

Truly, these brilliant things belong to those who give sacrificial gifts; in heaven, the suns belong to those who give sacrificial gifts. Those who give sacrificial gifts partake of immortality; those who give sacrificial gifts prolong their life.

"For those who give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇāvatām*), that is, for those who bestow various kinds of sacrificial gifts such as cattle, gold, and so forth—the word *iti* has the sense of *eva* (only). For their sake alone, these variegated and praiseworthy objects seen on the earth—consisting of garlands, sandalwood, jewels, pearls, and the like—are abundant; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*)."

Furthermore, "only those who give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇāvat) possess in the heavenly world (divi) solar regions (sūryāṃsaḥ)— that is, worlds related to the sun, or the abundant enjoyments sustained by them. Moreover, "only those who give sacrificial fees partake of— meaning they enjoy— the immortal (amṛtam) state, which is free from old age and death."
Or rather:
having had their evil removed by giving, they know the Self and attain—reach—immortality, which is imperishable liberation;
for so says the Vedic scripture: "By sacrifice and by giving" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Furthermore, "only those who possess the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇāvantas) prolong their life"—that is, they increase and obtain an exceedingly long lifespan.
The root *tṛ* preceded by *pra* has the sense of increasing.
The particle *iti* is to be connected everywhere [in this context].
1. Because [the letters] *kṣa*, *kha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*, *pha*, and *va* have been introduced.

2. There is *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) according to the rule *kṣa-ja-ṭa-na-trāṇa-pāt*. 3. Having resorted to the gods in the upper region (*uparideśe*) among the deities, and being served by them alone.

4. *Kabha-kiṃca-tasmai* (Ka-bha-kiṃca for him). 5. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-jīvanasādhanāntyudakādīni* (Kṣa-ja-ṭa: the means of livelihood, water at the end, and so forth). 6. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-atīva dīrgham āyuṣyaṃ vardhayante labhante* (Kṣa-ja-ṭa: they greatly increase and obtain a long life).
May those who give not fall into misfortune and sin; may the wise ones who observe good vows never decay.
Let there be some other boundary for them; let sorrows gather upon the one who gives nothing.

May those who offer gifts not fall into misfortune or sin; may the wise ones, firm in their vows, never suffer decay. Let there be some other protector for them; let all sorrows fall upon the one who neglects his duty.

He speaks in order to praise giving through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "May those who satisfy (*pṛṇantaḥ*)—meaning those who please the gods and others with oblations and the like—not encounter (*mā āran*) misfortune (*duritam*), that is, suffering as it occurs, nor sin (*enaḥ*), which is the means to that [suffering]. Not only the givers, but also the wise ones (*sūrayaḥ*), the learned singers of praise for the gods, may they not grow old (*mā jāriṣuḥ*), meaning may they not become worn out by aging."
Likewise, let even those of good vows (*suvratāsaḥ*), who possess the excellent observances of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth, not grow old [in vain].
If that is so, who then is this other person among them? That is stated:
let any man whatsoever other than those givers or singers be the "encircler" (*paridhiḥ*)—the one who holds [the burden] of sin on all sides.
Alternatively,

let some other wicked deity act as their *paridhi* (enclosing-stick), serving as a barrier; just as the *paridhi* of the fire, though itself afflicted by demons and the like, protects the fire hidden within it, so too [should this deity protect them].
Alternatively, let another specific quality be their *paridhi*—that is, their surrounding enclosure; let it serve as their armor.
If so, what would they obtain? It is said:

May sorrows—meaning mental afflictions—and the evils that cause them, come together toward one who does not praise the gods and others, who does not bow down, and who is ungenerous; [may they come] so that we may become happy. This is the meaning.
The hymn beginning with “amandān” consists of five verses; because of the recurrence of the word “sas,” it constitutes a *sasarca*.

For the first five verses, Kakṣīvān is the seer (*ṛṣi*). For the sixth verse, Bhāvayavya is the seer; for the seventh, the seer is the woman named Romaśā, a teacher of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinī*).
For the first five verses, the deity is Bhāvayavya himself, because he is remembered as such, according to the principle: “The deity of that which is spoken by him is he [himself]” (Anuvāka 2.5).
Regarding these two verses, the sixth and the seventh, there is a discussion concerning Bhāvayavya and Romaśā.
Of the sixth verse, the subject is Bhāvayavya; of the seventh, it is Romaśā.

Although, because it is heard in the *Ṛgveda* (1.126.3) that she was "given by Svanaya," the praise ought to belong to her alone, nevertheless—due to the distinction between father and son, as in the case of [the hymn] beginning with "ā rudrāsaḥ" (8.20.17)—it is possible to refer to him by his father's name; furthermore, since it is said in the first *ṛc*, "of these two" (*ābhyasya*), the statement that "he praised Bhāvayavya" is not contradictory, as was rightly argued in the preceding hymn.
The first five verses are *triṣṭubh*s;
the last two are *anuṣṭubh*s.

Thus it has been recorded in the Anukramaṇī: “‘Amandān’—Kakṣīvān, having seen [the seer] Daṣṭuṣṭa, praised Bhāvayavya with five verses; the last two are *anuṣṭubh*s; this is a dialogue between Bhāvayavya and Romaśa.”
The application has been stated.
With inspired thought, I bring forth abundant Soma-offerings for Bhāvya, who dwells on high by the river;
he, the King, desiring glory, has measured out for me a thousand pressed drops as a gift.

With my inspired thought, I offer forth abundant hymns of praise for Bhāvya, who dwells upon the Sindhu and who, being pressed and unconquered, desiring glory, measured out a thousand [gifts] for me as king.

1. After the word *prāpnuvan* in the manuscripts kṣa, ja, and ṭa, there is the additional passage: "In the case of this difficult-to-understand compound, the suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*); by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the prefix (*gati*) is maintained.
2. In the manuscripts kṣa, ja, and ṭa, the word *hīyante* occurs.
3. [The suffix] ena is applied after *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa* when expressing "vessel" (*bhājana*).
4. [The suffix] *kam* is applied after *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*.
5. Or, [the suffix *kam* is applied] after *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa* when expressing "evil" (*pāpman*).

6. After the phrase *‘abhavemeti arthaḥ’*, the following is added in the manuscripts marked ka, kṣa, ja, ṭa, and ṇa: “In this context, although it is stated in general terms that ‘merely giving [is intended], nevertheless, because this hymn (*sūkta*) consists of a praise of the gift of self-guidance (*svanaya-dāna*)—[variant: a praise of giving]—the meaning is that they should endure suffering accordingly.

7. In the manuscripts marked kṣa, ja, ṭa, and tatra, the reading is: “In the first verse (*ṛc*) there. 8. In the manuscripts marked ca, jña, ta, pha, and bhāva, the reading is: “of the state of being (*bhāva-vyañjasya*)”.

I offer forth with my intellect (*manīṣā*), through the excellence of my thought regarding his supreme affection, the abundant gifts and the hymns of praise—those recitations of various kinds of offerings and so forth—of *Bhāvya* (also called *Bhāvayavya*), who dwells or resides in *Sindhu*, that is, in the land of Sindhu, or perhaps by metonymy on the banks of the Sindhu river, on the shore of the ocean; [the hymns] of his son, *Svanaya*. I bring these together with great distinction.
Regarding the question, "What is his distinction?", he says in that regard: "A bull (*vr̥ṣan*) who has not been harmed by anyone—[I shall give] a thousand (*sahasram*) of such bulls for my sake.
*Savān* refers to the Soma sacrifices, so called because Soma juices (*somāḥ*) are pressed (*sūyante*) in them.
He fashioned them by means of a gift of complete wealth;
desiring what?
Desiring—that is, longing for—fame for himself that is heard by all.

Since he bestowed much wealth for the sake of glory alone, even without the pretext of officiating at sacrifices and the like, therefore I shall praise him—this is the meaning. A hundred gold coins from the king who was not in need, a hundred well-given horses, and a hundred cows from the Asura Kukṣīvān; thus he has spread his undecaying fame throughout the heavens.

A hundred [pieces of gold], not half of what was requested, from the king; a hundred gold coins; a hundred horses presented by Sudās—I have received them. Kukkṣīvan has obtained a hundred cows from the Asura; he has spread his undecaying fame throughout the heavens. 2.

"I have accepted the gold coins—specific ornaments or gold distinguished by a particular measure—or even hundreds of them; for 'hundred' and 'thousand' are words signifying the unlimited. I, Kakṣīvān, have immediately, right after my request, taken and accepted them from the king who was imploring me, who was accustomed to giving, who bestows wealth upon those who ask, who shines with his own splendor, and who belongs to himself.
(Note: *śata* and *sahasra* are used here as expressions for the immeasurable.
I, Kakṣīvān, have accepted them instantly, immediately following my prayer. This is the meaning.
Likewise, he took— having seized— horses that were well-trained, pure, endowed with auspicious marks, swift, and capable of galloping;
likewise, bulls— that is, oxen or draft cattle—
since females are mentioned in the subsequent mantra.
I have taken a hundred of them.

Thus, as a donor, the king has spread out—extended—undecaying and eternal fame (*śravaḥ*, *kīrti*) in heaven, in the celestial world. The meaning is: "As a receiver of cows and other gifts, I have established my fame in the heavenly realm."
The dark steeds given by Svanaya, ten chariots with their brides, have come to me;
sixty thousand of the cattle-herd followed after, as Kakṣīvat won them at the turning of the days.
The dark bay horses, given by Svanaya, ten chariots with their brides, have arrived; six thousand head of cattle followed after. Kakṣīvat won them at the turning of the days. 3.

The *śyāva* horses were given by Vṣvanaya; they are called *śyāva* because they are joined with that color. They possess brides who have mounted them; there are ten of them, so many in number. The *rathāsaḥ* are chariots; they have arrived (*upāvasthuḥ*), meaning they have drawn near. The word *gavya* denotes a herd of cows; [there are] sixty.

1. In the manuscripts *ca*, *ña*, *ta*, and *pha*, the word ‘*abhāṇasya*’ does not exist. 2. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *bhāvyasya*, there is an elision of the phoneme (*varṇalopa*). 3. In the manuscripts *jña*, *kṣa*, and *ta*, [the reading is] specifically ‘*viśeṣeṇa*’. 4. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [the reading is] ‘*dhanapradānena*’. 5. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [the reading is] ‘*yācamānasya*’. [The root] *nādh* is used in the sense of “begging” (*śabde*); it is *anudātta* (unaccented). 6. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, after the phrase ‘*asvīkṛtavānasmītyarthaḥ*’, there is an additional passage: “After the root *dadāti* preceded by *āṅ*, the absence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*)—according to the rule *āṅo do’nāsyaviharaṇe*—is Vedic (*chāndasa*). There is the addition of the augment (*lekhyādāgamaḥ*). There is the elision of the suffix *śap* due to being Vedic (*chāndasaḥ śapo luk*).
