There is the elision of the vowel *i* according to the rule *itaścalopaḥ*. 7. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ca*, and *pha*, [the reading is] ‘*śyāmavarṇaścaḥ*’. 8. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [the reading is] ‘*upasthitāḥ*’. [The elision of *s* in the aorist marker *sic* occurs] according to the rule *gātistheti sico luk*. 9. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, [the word] here denotes a collection of cows. [The suffix] *ya* is applied to denote a collection according to the rule *khalagorathāditi* (Pāṇini 4.2.50). Due to transposition (*vyatyayāt*), there is the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatvam*).
A thousand, a herd of cows numbering one thousand and sixty, has come; it has arrived.
Then he speaks of himself in the third person:
having accepted all that, this Kakṣīvān won it on a day among the days, on a day that was close at hand.
He offers the chariot, the horses, and so forth, which he has accepted, to his own father, or he accepts them himself.
The word *abhi* signifies proximity, just like the word *prapi*.
And since it is stated by Yāska in Nirukta 1.20, "‘Prapi’ [means] near (*abhīka*) for the son of Ajasa," it denotes proximity.
Even when there is a difference in prefixes, there is no difference in meaning.
Forty horses, worn out, lead the procession in front of a thousand; the sons, full of vigor, have drawn forth the spirited, jewel-adorned, and well-flanked steeds.

Forty [horses] of Daśaratha, worn out, lead the line at the head of a thousand. Those possessing golden ornaments have groomed the steeds that shed their ichor; the sons of Kukṣīvant have adorned them. 4.

In front of Daśaratha—who possesses ten chariots—or of Kakṣīvat, who is accompanied by a thousand followers, or before a thousand herds of cattle, there are forty horses of a reddish-brown color (*śoṇa*). Since each chariot has four horses, there are forty horses in total when the ten chariots are combined.
These horses lead the chariots by following a row (*śreṇi*) or a line, bringing them to the desired destination.
Or alternatively:
They lead the chariots yoked with horses into a row; that is to say, they cause each individual chariot to be drawn by four [horses] in the form of a line. Now, those [horses] are *kakṣīvantaḥ*.
*Kakṣyā* refers to the girth-rope belonging to a horse, as Yāska has stated: "The *kakṣyā* is the rope of a horse" (*Nirukta* 2.2). He is characterized by having those [robes] as his end.
Or rather, all the sons of Aṅgiras are Kakṣīvantas;
or else, by the logic of the umbrella-bearer, all the followers of Kakṣīvat are also Kakṣīvantas.

The sons, possessing fodder and other food, exuding exhilaration— meaning they cause the flow of intoxication, or rather, they cause the pride of their enemies to fall away— and adorned with *kṛśanas*, that is, golden ornaments (for *kṛśana* is a name for gold, as it is listed among those names in Nirukta 1.2.7: "gold is *kṛśana*"), they have washed the steeds— those who are constantly moving— to cleanse them thoroughly of the sweat produced by the fatigue of the journey.
Following the former impulse, I have seized eight oxen that were yoked and ready to carry the burden;
those who are well-allied, like subjects on their way, have sent forth their fame as sons within the dwellings.

I have accepted from you the former offering: three yoked horses and eight oxen that carry the burden. Those who are well-disposed, like subjects, or like those possessing wealth, these sons have sent forth their fame. 5.
Now, announcing the wealth brought back to his kinsmen, he says:
"O good kinsmen, following my previous effort—that is, my former gift—I have taken for you (vaḥ) these things to be mentioned, such as chariots and so forth.
Or alternatively:

1. He has partaken of the former offering (*prayati*). 2. Like the word *prapiva*. 3. In each of the four [groups]. 4. The two horse-tethers (*aśvabandhana*). 5. Illumination (*kāśana*). 6. Those born together are true kinsmen (*sahaja-subandhu*). I have accepted—that is, I have received—the gift to be given, such as chariots and so forth, according to the very order of giving.
"What are they?
[The answer is: "Three and eight," meaning "yoked in groups of four each"—the word "chariots" is to be supplied.
Here, the separate mention of the numbers is not intended to be significant.
Likewise, I accepted from Vadhryaśva numerous, highly valuable, and countless *vṛ* (oxen) that were to be borne by his enemies as burdens.
It is appropriate here to understand these as being greater than those previously received;

for since it was impossible to announce again to his kinsmen what had already been announced to his father, and because ten chariots were mentioned in the verse, "Ten chariots with brides stood there" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.126.3), while eleven—including three and eight—are to be mentioned here, and because it is improper to give away those distinguished by their brides to others, it is logical to conclude they were different ones.
In the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those very things already mentioned, the distinction is that there are ten chariots with their brides and one chariot filled with wealth.
The re-mention of the chariots and so forth, which have already been stated, is for the purpose of indicating excellence;
the distinction is like saying, "All the Brāhmaṇas have arrived" and then "Vasiṣṭha has also arrived."
Now he speaks by way of indirect description (*parokṣa*):
those whose excellent kinsmen—meaning those connected to them through learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*)—are such as they are described;
or alternatively:
"Endowed with excellent kinsmen" means being free from mutual ill-will;
"viśaḥ" refers to the subjects.
In that context, "bhavāḥ" refers to the Viśyas;
they are called "dhāḥ" because they go forth (viyanti);
they are the brothers.
The elision of the letter *t* is a Vedic archaism (chāndasa). 3.
The meaning is that these [priests] are likewise mutually affectionate, just as brothers among the common people (*viś*) are.

Those who are *pannāḥ*—ignorant ones—and those *Aṅgirases* who are born from the lineage, all of them being *subandhavaḥ* (good kinsmen), possessing *vanasvantah* (forests) and *śakaṭavantah* (carts)—that is, being possessed of the Soma-sacrifice characterized by the sacrificial carts—they *vaiṣanta* (desire) *śravaḥ*, the fame heard everywhere; or let them desire it.
"I take [this]" is the ellipsis to be supplied for that purpose.

She who is bolted and barred, who like a girdle clings to the thigh—she, the far-reaching one, gives me hundreds of things to enjoy from the swift steeds. 6. She who is bolted, she who is barred; she who, like a girdle, clings to the thigh; she, the far-reaching one, gives me hundreds of things to enjoy from the swift steeds.
Desiring sexual enjoyment, he meditated upon his own wife as being covered in hair; then, mocking her with his intellect, he said:

"She has been made fit for enjoyment (*vaiśā*), she has been embraced (*āgadhitā*)—that is, accepted and taken hold of on all sides—and likewise she has been encircled (*parighitā*)—taken hold of all around."
The repetition is for the sake of emphasizing the excellence [of the meaning].
Yāska says: "That which is to be grasped is *gādham*" (Nirukta 5.15).
Or else:
"Āgadhitā" means mingling from all sides;
that is to say, internally by way of procreation and externally by means of the arms and so forth.
Yāska [states]: "The word *gadhyati* signifies the state of being mixed" (Nirukta 5.15).
The distinction is that in the former case the man is predominant, whereas in the latter it is the woman.
Of what sort is she?
She who "Vjaṅghahe"—that is, she who grasps excessively and never lets go.
The example for non-abandonment is:
"like the *kakṣīkā*. The *kakṣīkā* is a female mongoose that has given birth to a colt.
Just as she plays for a long time with her companion and never lets go of her, so too is this case.
Furthermore, this *bhojyā* is called *vyādurī*;
*yādu* is a name for water.
She who gives abundant water characterized by much semen is called *yādurī*.
[This is according to the interpretation that takes *bahu-retas* as a compound ending in the suffix *ṭa* (i.e., *bahuretasaḥ*).]

2. In the manuscripts Kṣa, Na, and Ṭa, after the words "in the sense of ‘thus’," there is an additional passage: "In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule *ādyudāttaṃ chandasi*, the initial syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*) is acute.

3. In the manuscripts Kṣa, Na, and Ṭa, after the words "the elision of the letter *t* is Vedic," there is an additional passage: "Alternatively, they are called *bhrātṛ*s because they go apart (*vi-yanti*). The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the suffix *ghañ* according to the rule *ka-vidhānam*."

4. After the word "sarve" in Kṣa, Na, and Ṭa, there is the additional passage: "they are called 'pannāḥ', for according to the Śruti, they are the Aṅgirases. 5. After the word "śeṣaḥ" in Kṣa, Na, and Ṭa, there is the additional passage: "in the root iṣ, there is an absence of the substitution of *ch* due to the Vedic (chāndasa) aorist (luṅ), and the middle voice (ātmanepada)."
6. Immediately after "kṣaṇaṭa-amīśrayantī," the text in Kṣa, Na, and Ṭa adds: "likewise, being encircled (parighitā), she mixes [them] all around.
7. Kṣa, Na, and Ṭa: "What is she like?
Having seized [him] excessively by the shanks (jaṅghahe), she does not let go."

In the case of the root *pra-hṛ*, which has the sense of "seizing," when there is elision (*luk*), there is the addition of the augment *num* to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), according to Vedic usage.
8. *kṣa-na-ṭa-vaśā*: the meaning is "joined."
Such being the case, "yāśūnām" refers to enjoyments.
"Yaśas" is a name for procreation;
the actions associated with that are the "yāśu-bhogas" (enjoyments of progeny).
He gives me hundreds upon hundreds of them, beyond counting.
The daughter of Bṛhaspati, named Romaśā, who was a teacher of the Veda, replied to her husband as he was mocking her.
"Come closer, come closer; do not touch me from afar, nor think that I am naked.
I am entirely covered in hair, like a ewe from among the Gandhāris."
"Upa-upa! Do not touch me! Do not think that my thighs are smooth; I am covered all over with hair, like a ewe from Gandhāra. (7)

O husband, touch me—here the fourth case is used in the sense of the accusative. "Upoṣa": the second syllable *upa* is for the purpose of completing the meter. Having approached (*upetya*), touch (*parāmṛśa*) me thoroughly; that is, perceive me as fit for enjoyment. Or rather: touch (*parāmṛśa*) my limb which is to be protected (*me gopanīyam aṅgam*); touch it most deeply within. He wards off the suspicion that this is merely a physical touch: do not think (*mā manyathāḥ*) my limbs (*me mad-aṅgāni*) are small (*dabhra*). Do not consider them insignificant. Regarding the word *dabhra*, Yāska says in Nirukta 3.20: "The word *dabhra* [is derived] from the root *dabhnoti* (to deceive/to diminish), meaning 'small'. He clarifies its non-smallness: I am *romaśā*, possessed of much hair; I am so. Therefore, I am *sarvā*, complete in all my limbs. An illustration for this hairy-ness is given: like a ewe (*avikā*) of the Gandhāris. The Gandhāras are regions; like the breed of sheep belonging to those regions—that is, just as the sheep of those lands are hairy, so am I. Or rather: like the ewe (*avikā*) of the Gandhārīs—that is, of women who bear children—which excessively satisfies; for according to the scriptures, the cutting away of hair and such from their [genitals] until delivery is forbidden, and thus their vulva is hairy. Therefore she is used as a comparison. Since I am such, do not perceive me as unadorned (*abhauḍhām*). [End of Section 11, Verse 18]
In the nineteenth Anuvāka, there are seven Sūktas.
Among them, the first Sūkta, “Agniṃ hotāram,” consists of eleven verses; it belongs to Parucchepa, the son of Divodāsa, and is dedicated to Agni Āptya.
The verse beginning with “sa hi śardhaḥ” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.127.6) is an Atidhṛti, containing seventy-six syllables.

In the case of *utkṛti*, *abhikṛti*, *saṃkṛti*, *vikṛti*, *ākṛti*, *prakṛti*, *dhṛti*, *vidhṛti*, *vyaṣṭi*, *aṣṭi*, and *atyaṣṭi*, beginning from the one hundred and four syllables, each meter arises by adding four syllables in succession.
This being so, these two [meters] would be included as supplementary additions to the *atyaṣṭi*.
All of this has been established in the *Chandograntha* by such sūtras as "The *utkṛti* consists of four hundred [syllables]" (*Piṅgala 4.1*).
And thus it has been enumerated: "Parucchepa Devadāsi [composed] eleven [verses] for Agni; however, the entire Parucchepa [collection] is dedicated to Agni, among which the sixth is an Atidhṛti.
The specific application of this hymn is based on its indicative marks (*liṅga*).

On the sixth day of the *daśarātra* sacrifice, during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), one should perform the sacrifice by placing other verses before the *prasthitayājyā* formulas and combining them with the original ones.
Among those, this is the first for the Aprī verses.

It is prescribed in the section titled "The Morning Pressing of the Sixth [Day]" in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (8.1): "I consider Agni the Hotṛ, the bountiful; Dadhyañc, the ancient Aṅgiras, [knew] my birth."

1. After the entry *kṣa-ja-ṭa-‘bahuretāyuphetyarthaḥ’, there is the additional text: *‘āto’nupasarge kaḥ | chāndasa īkārastrīpratyayaḥ | pṛṣodarādiḥ’. 2. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-bhogāḥ*. [Derived from] *pṛṣodarādi*. 3. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-pūraṇaḥ*. 4. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-prasamupoṣa* is a double compound (*dvisukti*). 5. *ka-kha-ca-ja-jñā-ṇa-va-* is a *nighaṇṭu* (lexicon). 6. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-romanakhādikartanasya*. 7. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-caturṇāṃ caturṇāṃ paryāyeṇa*; *va-pha-caturṇāṃ paryāyeṇa*. 8. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-prakṛtābhiḥ*. [Ṛgveda 10.1]

I meditate upon Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, the bountiful, the Vasu, the Son of Strength, Jātavedas— the wise one, like a sage, Jātavedas— who, as a god with his god-ward form, performs the upright sacrifice; he desires the radiant splendor of the clarified butter, following the flame of the offered fat.

I honor Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, the bountiful, the Vasu, the Son of Strength, Jātavedas—the wise one, like a sage, Jātavedas—who, with his well-performed sacrifice, the god, with his god-ward form, desires the radiant glow of the clarified butter with his flame as it is poured as dripping fat. 1.
Agni, the leader of all the divine armies, who is led forward in sacrifices as the Hotṛ— the invoker of the gods toward our sacrifice—
or, alternatively,
one who is devoted to the oblation (homa).
O wise and radiant Śukra, we who are sacrificers—sacrificers with blazing flames—invoke you, the most excellent sacrificer (*yajiṣṭha*), the one who sacrifices preeminently.
The intention is that we invoke you because we are the sacrificers and you are the most excellent sacrificer.
Of what nature are you?
The eldest among the Aṅgirases, those born of the Aṅgiras lineage;
or alternatively,
the eldest among the embers, because he is endowed with flames.

"Aṅgiras is the embers," says Yāska (Nirukta 3.17). This is based on the Śruti: "Those who were the embers became the Aṅgirases" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 3.24). By what means [did this occur]? That is now explained.

With *manmabhiḥ*, meaning with the means of thought; with *vipraiḥ*, meaning with those who especially please [the gods]; that is, with *manmabhiḥ*, the mantras. Alternatively, the connection is: "We, together with the *vipras*—the wise ones—and with the *manmabhiḥ*, the mantras."
Immediately after you have been kindled, [we praise] you who move all around like the sun, the invoker of the gods— for whose sake? For the sake of the people (carṣaṇīnām).
This is for human beings;
that is, for the sake of human beings who are sacrificers.
Or alternatively:
[He is] the invoker of the *carṣaṇīs*—those who were originally human beings and later attained the state of gods through the performance of sacrifices and other means.

Likewise, [he is] the one with flaming hair (*śociṣkeśa*), possessing hair-like rays, the showerer (*vṛṣan*) of rain; may these *viśaḥ*—these subjects in the form of sacrificers—approach you, who are of such a nature, for their own impulsion (*jūtaye*), that is, for the attainment of desired fruits such as heaven, and may they favor you, that is, please you exceedingly.
"May we invoke you, such as you are"—this is the connection.
For he indeed shines forth with his many-fold, resplendent vigor; he is a destroyer of the malicious, like an axe—a destroyer of the malicious.
At whose onset even the firmest thing yields like reeds;
when he strikes down, he holds it fast, yet he does not let it go; as one who conquers on the field, he does not let it go.

For he, shining with abundant, radiant power, becomes the dispeller of deceit; like an axe, he is the dispeller of deceit. At whose onset even that which is firm resounds like forests; subduing all, he holds his ground and does not waver, like one who endures the bowstring, he does not waver. 3.

For he is that very Agni who was praised before; with his shining, specifically radiant, and powerful energy in the form of flames, blazing exceedingly intensely, he becomes the subduer of those who seek to harm—meaning he becomes the destroyer of enemies who plot malice against us. In this regard, there is an illustration:
"druhaṃtaḥ" means like an axe (*paraśu*) employed for the cutting down of those who wish to do harm.
Just as that [missile] strikes infallibly, so too does this one.
Furthermore, when there is the meeting, the coming together, or the union with this fire, even that which is *vīḷu*—even something very firm such as stone and the like—goes asunder; it would shatter.
Likewise, whatever is stable and whatever is immovable, such as mountains and the like, that too goes asunder.
*Vīḷu* is a name for "firm," as it is listed among those names in *Nirukta* 2.9.14: *vīḷu cyautnam*.
Therein is an illustration:
*vaneva*, like water in a forest.
The meaning is that it dries up water just as it does upon contact.
The intention is: if it destroys even that which is exceedingly firm and stable, then what need is there to mention that it destroys an enemy who is our source of malice?
Furthermore, this—

1. *Kṣa-ṅa-ña-ṭa*: The eldest (*jyeṣṭham*), the most excellent (*jyāyāṃsam*). Alternatively: [the fire] of the *Aṅgirases*, that is, of the embers (*aṅgārāṇām*). 2. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*: And by means of the mantras (*mantraiḥ*). 3. *Kṣa-ṅa-jha-ja-ṭa*: The showerer (*varṣitāram*) of desires (*kāmānām*). 4. *Jha*: The deliverer (*nistārayitā*). 5. *Kṣa-ṅa-jha-ṭa*: After the phrase "so too this one" (*tathāyam api*), there is the following addition: "From the root *druh* [is derived the word *drogdhṛ*], with the suffix *ka* prescribed for roots ending in a short vowel (*igupadhalakṣaṇaḥ kaḥ*). In that word, because it is a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*), the suffix *khac* is applied according to *Pāṇini* 3.2.5 (*man-tṛ-vṛji*). By *Pāṇini* 6.3.67 (*arha-dviṣad-duhāṃ hy-ac-para-sya*), the augment *mum* is added"). 6. *Kṣa-ṅa-jha-ṭa*: After the word "would be shattered" (*śīryeta*), there is the following addition: "'*Śru* and '*Śrū*' mean 'to go' (*gatau*). It belongs to the *Bhvādigaṇa*. The augment *leṭ* is applied. Because a rule conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not universally obligatory (*anityatvāt*), there is no *guṇa* substitution. 7. *Kṣa-a-ṭa*: "Firmly" (*vīḷu*). 8. *Kṣa-ṅa-a-ṭha*: "Like a forest" (*banaiva*). The change of *s* to *ā* occurs due to the *sū* suffix.
Not being overcome by his enemies, but conquering them completely, he restrains himself—he desists from further hostility—and sports among the enemies, destroying them.
Acting thus, he does not go away; he does not flee from the presence of the enemy.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

Not [the same as] *dhanvasaha*. One who overcomes enemies with a bow (*dhanus*) is a *dhanvasaha*, that is, an archer (*dhānuṣka*). The suffix *saha* takes the *itarac* suffix; the elision of the final syllable is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The meaning is that he is like one who pierces toward the enemy and does not flee;
or alternatively,
"dhanvasaha" means capable of bearing a firm bow.
In this view, the suffix *ac* is applied after the root *pac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134).
The form [dṛḍhadhanvā] contains the vowel *ā* by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
Being one whose bow is firm (*dṛḍhadhanvā*), he does not waver; he does not move.

Even firm things yield to him as he finds his way through the doors; with most brilliant kindling-sticks, he has been kindled for the sake of the Dāśarājña, for the sake of Agni, for the sake of the Dāśarājña.
He who plunges into many forests, fashions them as if with wood, and even solid foods he destroys with his might—yes, even solid things he destroys with his might.
We place his nourishing strength within the nearby [waters], he who is more visible by night than by day, more visible by day than for one whose life is spent;
from him comes long life, as a father utters a firm blessing for his son.
Consuming both what is eaten and what is not eaten, they are ageless and foremost; consuming both, they are ageless.

We meditate upon that nourishment of his which dwells in the near-by [plants]. He who is more beautiful to behold by night than by day, more so for one whose life is not yet spent than by day. Then his life-force resounds aloud; like firm protection to a son, they enjoy what has been consumed and what has not been consumed. Seeking help, the ageless flames move forward; seeking it, the ageless ones move forward. 5.
To him we offer this food characterized by the oblation (*havis*) in the *uparā*—those in which the oblations cease; the *uparā* are the regions in close proximity.
In them we place and maintain it.
Having said "to him," he asks: "To whom? [The answer follows: "To him."
Agni is renowned as the one to be praised; he is indeed the one who resounds far and wide.
*Tuvi* is a name for "much," because it is listed among those names in the statement *uru tuvi* (Nirukta 3.1.2). *Bahusvaniḥ* means that which is joined with abundant sound;
the meaning is that when fire is intensely blazing, a sound like *bhug-bhug* arises due to contact with the wind as it burns.

An illustration regarding the act of resounding (*dhvanana*) is stated: "like the power associated with the winds. The meaning is that it resounds just as a multitude of winds (*marutām saṃūhaḥ*) resounds.
Where does this occur? It is said:
in the *vamasyatī* verses, after they have been dug and sprinkled with water.
*Ama* is a name for ritual action (*karman*), because it is listed among the names for such actions in the *Nighaṇṭu* (2.1.2): "ama, daṃsaḥ."
On the most excellent sacrificial grounds, which are vast and provided with wide enclosures—
of what nature is this?
He is *viṣṭan*, meaning he is to be sacrificed to.
The suffix *ani* is [added] according to the *auṇādika* rules, and there is also the augment *tuṭ*.
Furthermore, regarding the *ārtanās*:
one causes distress, thus "he distresses" (*ārtayati*).
Those which distress are *ārtanās*.
The fallings: among them.
The suffix *yu* is applied after the root *tṛṣ* [by Pāṇini 3.3.107]. Because it belongs to the *vṛṣādi* group, it has the udātta accent on its first syllable.
For their conquest, one who is seen must be sought or sacrificed to;
moreover, while they are thus shouting, he eats the oblations, such as clarified butter and sacrificial cakes.
The *luṅ* [aorist] suffix is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

Alternatively, from the root *dā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, there is an absence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), according to Pāṇini’s rule 1.3.28: *āṅo yamahanaḥ*.
In the word *agātisthāḥ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *sic*.

The short vowel is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, by the rule "it is also seen in the Veda," the augment *āṭ* is applied even after a root that does not begin with a vowel (*anajādi*).
Therefore, being without obstruction, that alone remains.

He is the one who speaks, whose nature is to take up the oblation everywhere; likewise, he is the banner of the sacrifice, its proclaimer, or standing in the place of the banner; he is the one to be honored with *varhaṇā*.
The substitution of *ā* for *su* is according to the rule *supām suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). The acute accent on the first syllable of the suffix is a Vedic peculiarity (*chāndasa*).
Furthermore, it refers to one who is intensely filled with joy (*harṣataḥ*) due to the consumption of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) and other such causes.
Alternatively:

All men (*viśve manuṣyāḥ*) have delighted in, or cultivated, the path (*panthām*) of Agni—who, being *harṣivat* (joyful), gladdens the sacrificers by granting their desired fruits, and who is filled with joy through the acceptance of the clarified butter (*ājya*). For what purpose?
For the auspicious, for the sake of what is auspicious and beautiful, for the attainment of happiness;

the path that must be traversed by all for the sake of results in this world and the next is indeed the path of fire. All follow after fire alone; having gratified fire alone, they achieve their goals.
The illustration regarding taking recourse to the path is as follows:
just as in the world, people (*nara*) take a path that is auspicious for attaining beautiful happiness—a path to be traveled by all, free from fear, and well-established.
When the hymns, seeking heaven, have cried out to him for the second time, the Bhr̥gus have invoked him with reverence; the Bhr̥gus, performing the sacrifice, have kindled him.
Agni is the lord of treasures, he who is pure and their sustainer.
May the wise one open the dear secret chamber; may the wise one cause us to obtain it.

Twofold is he whom the Kīstas, seeking heaven and paying homage, have addressed; whom the Bhr̥gus have praised while kindling him—the Bhr̥gus offering their gifts. Agni is the lord of treasures, he who is pure and resolute among them. May the wise one win the beloved coverings; may the wise one win them. 7.
"Vyatyaṃ" means having become twofold; that is, having attained a dual form through the distinction between *śrauta* (Vedic) and *smārta* (traditional) rites.
Alternatively, this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
It is manifold in the form of the Āhavanīya fire and others;
or rather,
it is twofold (dvitā), for both kinds of results— those pertaining to this world and those pertaining to the next.
In the case of the word *vibhaktaḥ*: there is a substitute beginning with *ā*.
The singers (*stotāraḥ*), praising—that is, performing the glorification (*kīrtanam*)—of this Agni.
The substitution of *s* for *ś* occurs by virtue of the suffix *ac* added after roots beginning with *pac*, which is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasam*).
The *Vabhidyavas*, shining on all sides; the *Bhṛgus*, belonging to the Bhṛgu lineage, paying homage—performing a service characterized by salutation—rejoiced in or resorted to [the path].
(1) *kṣa-ña-juṣanta* means they enjoyed or served it. (2) *kṣa-ña-mārgaśrayaṇe* means resorting to the path.
3. *kṣatha* [is] in both ways.
By means of their breath, the great seers (*maharṣayaḥ*) awaken; having approached, they release it.
What are they doing?

The *dāśas*, by means of giving—which serves as the instrumental cause—perform the friction in the fire-drill (*araṇi*) for the purpose of offering oblations; likewise, the *Bhṛgus* are "without arrows," that is, free from the evil of their offerings.
Furthermore, this Agni, who is pure (*śuci*), radiant, and skillful in sustaining (*ghṛṇi*), is the lord (*īśe*)—that is, he is capable—of these *vasus* characterized as oblations being offered.
The elision of the *t* occurs by the rule "lopasta ātmanepadeṣu" (Pāṇini 7.1.41).
Or rather:
he is the lord (īśe), that is, capable of bestowing these visible riches such as jewels, pearls, and so forth—the word "of the giver" being understood.
Furthermore, this Agni is wise (medhiraḥ).
*Medha* is sacrifice.

Being possessed of that—being himself the primary object as one to be sacrificed—he should *vaniṣīṣṭa*, meaning he should partake of or enjoy the *priyān apidhīn*, the dear coverings such as clarified butter and other offerings, until they are fully exhausted.
Or, it may mean "let him partake."
Likewise, may that wise and intelligent one partake;
even in sacrifices dedicated to other deities, he himself enjoys the oblation in the form of the *ājyabhāga*, *prayāja*, and so forth.
We invoke you, the lord of all people, the common husband of all tribes, for our enjoyment; we invoke him who is borne by true hymns, for our enjoyment.

He is the guest of men, through whose mouth [all things] are as through a father’s. And may all these immortals come to us for the sake of life, and may there be offerings among the gods for the sake of life.

We invoke you, the lord of all people, the common husband of all for our enjoyment—the one who carries true songs for our enjoyment. He is the guest of mortals, by whose presence, as by that of a father, all these immortals likewise attain vital strength, and our oblations among the gods attain vital strength. 8.
We invoke him, the lord of all people—that is, of all subjects and sacrificers—as their protector by granting their desired fruits.
Not only for the sacrificers, but for all subjects alike; he is common (equal) to all because the assistance provided through cooking, heating, and so forth is the same for everyone.
Likewise, we invoke the lord of the household, the protector of the home in the form of the *gārhapatya* fire and others.
*Dama* is a name for the house, because it is listed among the names of the house in the Nirukta (3.4.12): "In the house is the skin."
The elision of the vowel *a* is due to Vedic license.
For what purpose? "We invoke for enjoyment"—that is, we call upon him.
Furthermore, he himself is further specified.

"Carrying true speech" (*satyagirvāhasam*): one who conveys hymns that are consistent with reality and yield non-contradictory results. Alternatively, *girvāhasaḥ* refers to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), so called because they convey the *giraḥ*, which are the mantras.
We invoke him whose [hymns] are true, whose fruits are non-contradictory, and who is borne by songs; such is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The suffix *asun* is applied by the rule ‘vahidhādhābhyaḥ 0’.
Because the term ‘ṇit’ is understood from the previous context, there is vocalic strengthening (*upadhāvṛddhi*) of the penultimate vowel.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?
He is the guest (*atithi*) of humans (*mānuṣāṇām*), worthy of worship like a guest, or one who arrives in expectation of the new-moon day (*darśa*).
Moreover, by the presence (*āsayā*)—that is, in the vicinity—of that Agni.
It is called *āsayantika* because it is listed among its names in the Nirukta (2.16.2) with the statement, "The hopes are mothers.
All these *amṛtāsas*, the immortals—namely, all the gods renowned as partakers of the oblation—also come into its presence.
Due to the influence of a prefix, an appropriate verb must be supplied.
For what purpose?
Because the oblation, characterized by the *vayas*, is given specifically toward [the deity] alone, as opposed to others.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as sons and others serve their father in his presence for the sake of food and other needs,
so too do the *vayaḥ*, the leaders— the officiating priests— among the other gods who are being worshipped, present the *havyā*, the oblations, to Agni.
The suffix *ḍi* is applied after verbal roots ending in *v*, *tṛ*, *ī*, *ṇā*, and so forth;
or, when the suffix *vic* follows, there is optionally *guṇa*.

1. From the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) [arise] *kṣa*, *ja*, and *jha*. 2. Of those having the forms of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), [there are] *kṣa*, *ja*, and *yajamāna*. 3. By means of the form of the *gārhapatya* fire, [there are] *kṣa*, *ha*, and *jha*. 4. *Kṣa* and *ja* are the seekers (*vetāraḥ*).
O Agni, you are born with overwhelming power, the most victorious and the most impetuous, for the sake of the assembly of gods; [you are born] for the sake of the assembly of gods to bestow wealth.
For in your exhilaration you are most impetuous, and your mental power (*kratu*) is most resonant.
And so, O undecaying one, they attend upon you, like obedient servants, O ageless one.

O Agni, you are born through power as the most victorious, the most impetuous, for the service of the gods—like wealth for the service of the gods. For your exhilaration is most impetuous, and your mental power is most resonant. Therefore, O ageless one, they move around you in obedience, like obedient servants, O ageless one. 9.

O Agni, you are born as the most powerful (*sahantamaḥ*) through force (*sahasā*), the supreme conqueror of enemies, and likewise as the most radiant (*śuṣmintamaḥ*). [The suffix] *kan* is added to the root *sah* according to the *Uṇādi* rules; [the *ṇatva* is applied] by the rule "of *nāda*. For what purpose? "For the sake of the gods" (*devatātaye*), that is, for the sacrifice which involves the expansion of the gods; this is a name for sacrifice. Or rather: endowed with the aforementioned qualities, you are born; you arise from the two kindling woods (*araṇyoḥ*). There is an illustration regarding your purpose being the sacrifice: "wealth for the sake of the gods" (*rayiṃ devatātaye*). Just as wealth is produced for the sake of sacrifice—as it has been said, "substance is produced for the sake of sacrifice"—so too is this. Furthermore, your "intoxication" (*madaḥ*)—the joy produced by the acceptance of the clarified butter—is "most powerful" (*śuṣmintamaḥ*), exceedingly strong. The word *hi* indicates well-known fact; it is well known that Agni becomes intoxicated by the clarified butter. Moreover, your "will" (*kratuḥ*), your specific ritual action, is also "most powerful," or rather, it is indeed endowed with glory (*yaśas*). Yāska says: "Glory (*śuṣma*) is derived from the root *śvit* [meaning to shine], or it is fame, or speech" (Nirukta 5.5). Therefore, O "ageless" (*ajara*) Agni—one who is free from decay—the sacrificers "attend upon" (*pari caranti*) you. Therein is an illustration: "like obedient messengers" (*śruṣṭīvānaḥ na dūtāḥ*). Just as they serve a king by providing specific news, so do they [serve you]. [The suffix] *vanip* is used here according to the rule "in Vedic meters, *vanip* [is added]" (*chandasi vanipau*); the acute accent on the first syllable is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasam*). Or, "O ageless one" (*ajara*) means "one who causes the devotees to age [with vigor]. [The suffix] *ac* is added after the root *pac* with the sense of causation implied within. Or again: "O ageless one" (*ajara*) means "O you whose praise is ageless. He is not the praiser of anyone, but is himself praised by all; such as you, they attend upon—this is the meaning.
Let a hymn of praise be offered for you to the great Agni, who by his might overcomes all that is powerful, who awakens at dawn, the protector of cattle, the one worthy of renown.
When he, rich in oblations, has breathed forth among the dwellings, he roars like a singer;
O Agni, like a bard, you awaken the flames of the kindling-sticks—you, the swift invoker of the kindling-sticks.

Let your hymn of praise go forth to the great Agni, who is mighty by his power, who awakens at dawn, the seeker of cattle, the one worthy of renown—to Agni, so that the offerer of oblations may sing him aloud in all dwellings; like a singer, O Agni, he chants for the sake of the kindled flames, the Hotṛ-priest for the sake of the kindled flames. 10.
May this hymn (*stoma*), which is yours— belonging to you— the chanters (*stotṛ*) such as the *udgātṛ* and others, be capable of pleasing (*prīṇayitum*) Agni.
[The form] *prababhūtu* is derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *śap* (which is replaced by *ślau* due to Vedic usage),
and there is the substitution of *a* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

In the phrase "bhūsuvostiṣṭhi," there is an absence of *guṇa* [substitution]. To what kind of Agni? To the "great" (*mahe*), that is, the vast and worshipful one; to the one who "slays by force" (*sahasā taddhate*), meaning through the power of overcoming; and to the "awakening at dawn" (*uṣarbudhe*), that is, at the time of daybreak.
To the powerful one, who possesses the capacity for the destruction of obstacles,
and who is awakening.

The substitution of *s* occurs [for the final *r*] of words such as *ahar* when followed by words such as *pati*, according to the rule "there is the addition of *pati* etc. to *ahar* etc. (*aharādīnāṃ patyādipūpasaṃkhyānam*).
"To Paśupati, the bestower of the fruit of cattle.
Here, the word *na* has the sense of the prefix *adhi*.
Alternatively:
Just as praise is offered to Paśupati, the giver of cattle, and to the Lord (Prabhu), so it is here.
For what purpose? That is stated:

"Facing this very Agni, the sacrificer, 'endowed with oblations'—that is, possessed of offerings such as clarified butter and the like—'praises' (*joguve*) him and approaches to worship him upon 'all' (*viśvāsu*), that is, all the sacrificial grounds which serve as his dwelling places."

The *liṭ* [perfect] suffix occurs after the root *guvati* when it takes the *yaṅluk* (intensive without *yaṅ*) affix, according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Because of the exclusion [of the *ām* augment] by the rule "not in a mantra" (*amantre*), there is an absence of the *ām* augment.
*Kṣiti* is the name for the earth, as it is listed among its names in *Nirukta* 1.1.5 (*kṣā kṣāmā*).
Among the *ṛṣūṇām*, the visiting gods, Agni is the most excellent; the *jūrṇiḥ*, one skilled in praise, the *hotṛ*, praises him first, prior to the other gods.
Therein lies the illustration.
Like a singer before wealthy and great seers, he has cried out like a panegyrist.
‘Be disciplined’— this is the remainder [of the sentence].
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Fierce as one by his might; just as some cruel person becomes a crusher through his might, that is to say, through his strength.
"This one is born" (*ayaṃ jāyate*) is the second hymn, consisting of eight verses. The *Anukramaṇikā* states: "This one is born, etc. Parucchepa is the seer (*ṛṣi*).

Because it is stated that "all [verses] consist of eight noble [syllables]," the meter is *atyaṣṭi*. Because the word "but" (*tu*) is used in the phrase "but [it belongs] to Agni," this too belongs to Agni.
This hymn is prescribed as the *ājya* recitation for the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭha* sacrifice.
And it is stated in the *Sūtra* in the section on "the sixth": "This [offering] is born for the human, the sustainer of the earth, the clarified butter" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.1).
This one has been born among men as the sustainer, the most excellent invoker according to the vow of the *uśij*—
he who hears all, like wealth for the one seeking friendship, for the one seeking renown.
The undeceived invoker has sat down in the place of *iḷā*, encircled in the place of *iḷā*.

He has been born for the support of man, the most excellent sacrificer among the *uśij*, according to his law; Agni, according to his own law, the creator of all, like wealth to one who seeks friendship, like glory to one who strives for renown—the undeceivable Hotṛ has sat down in the place of *iḷā*, encircled in the place of *iḷā*. 1.
We [are] Agni; he was born from the presence of the human Adhvaryu priest, produced by the friction of the kindling woods. Of what nature is he?
He is the Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods, and the most excellent sacrificer.
For what purpose has he arisen?
He has arisen for the sake of the *vratam*—the vow consisting of the Soma sacrifice and so forth—of the *vuśijaḥ*, that is, the sacrificers who desire the fruit; having made this his objective.
It is not merely for the sake of others, but rather this very purpose is his own.
With regard to his own vow— his own action consisting of the acceptance of the oblation and so forth—
he is further qualified as the creator of the universe, one who possesses actions directed toward the entire world.
For whom? For the one who desires friendship— that is, who seeks friendship for himself—
and likewise for the one who desires renown— that is, who seeks great fame for himself— for such a sacrificer, [the sacrifice] becomes like *vrayi*, that is, like a source of wealth.
Just as wealth accomplishes both truth and the prosperity of the limbs, so too this fire accomplishes that same twofold purpose for him—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, this fire is in *viḷaspade*, that is, in the place of *iḍā*, the abundance.
The elision of the final [syllable] is a Vedic anomaly.
In the place that is the essence, namely the *vadhari* jewel, which is of the nature of the altar (*vedi*);
for according to the Śruti: "They call the altar the furthest limit of the earth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.4.18.2), and also:
"The earth is indeed as large as the altar" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.4.1).
That very [place] is further specified:
*viḷaspade*, that is, at the footprint (*pada*) of the goddess *iḍā*—the auspicious cow in the form of a cow belonging to Manu, who is described in the mantra for the offering of the *iḍā*.

For there is the Śruti: “*Viḍā, the daughter of Manu, was the one who revealed the sacrifices*” (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.4.4), and also: “*To the footprint of Viḍā, which is full of ghee, Svāhā!*" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.5.1).
He settles down; he sits down.

Of what nature is this Agni? He is *avadabdha*, unharmed by anyone; he is the *hotṛ*, the performer of the oblation; he is *parivīta*, surrounded on all sides by the officiating priests or by the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Having become thus, he sat down.
1. One who possesses the activity that is the refuge of all, characterized by *kṣa*, *ña*, and *ṭa*.
2. Or, one who attains extreme renown for the self, characterized by *kha*, *ca*, *pha*, and *bha*.
3. That pair, characterized by *kṣa*, *ña*, and *ṭa*.
Send forth that performer of sacrifice by the path of Truth, with reverence and an oblation, at the assembly of the gods, with an oblation.
May he bring us strength; through his grace, he does not grow old.
He whom Mātariśvan brought for Manu from afar—the god, the light—from afar.

Him, the accomplisher of sacrifice, we cause to blow hither by the path of Truth, with reverence accompanied by oblations, at the divine service accompanied by oblations. May he bring strength to us through this nourishment; by this form of his, he does not grow old—he whom Mātariśvan brought from afar as a god for Manu, bringing light from afar. 2.

"Yajñasādham" means the accomplisher of sacrifice. [The suffix] *krip* is added to the root *añj*, and there is the accentuation of the original form (*prakṛtisvara*) for the subsequent member ending in *kru*. "We cause that Agni, the ordainer (*vedhām*), who has been established, to be known (*avivātayāmasi*). The particle *api* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). We serve him until he is fully satisfied. The root *vāta* is used in the senses of movement and pleasant service; it belongs to the *curādika* (denominative) class. The suffix *masi* ends in *i*. By what means? That is stated: "By the path of *ṛta*," that is, by the way of sacrifice, through the performance of sacrifice. "By sacrifice, for the gods..."

This Agni, by means of his *evena*— whether by his movement or as the instrument of movement— has encompassed on all sides (*pari*) the earthly (*pārthiva*) place connected to the earth, namely the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), which is situated close to our vehicle; or else, *pari* is meaningless or has the sense of "towards."
He goes;
what kind of Agni?
One whose song is well-sung, being constantly celebrated.
By the word *retaḥ*, that body which is of the nature of an oblation (*havis*) is denoted; it possesses that [body].
The suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) is elided.
The bull, the showerer of desires, goes around bellowing.
He is further specified:
"holding the seed"—that is, assuming excessive power by accepting the clarified butter and other offerings—he goes around bellowing; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Furthermore, he is further qualified:
this Agni is the god who, in the woods—that is, in the gatherings or hymns serving as the occasion—acts with his flames, which stand in the place of dice.

When by his will his power is manifested in his strengths—like the bounty of the Maruts through Agni’s roar, like nourishment for the impetuous one, like nourishment for the vigorous one—he indeed bestows gifts by his greatness over all treasures. May he protect us from distress when invoked, from the curse and from evil when invoked. kratvā | yat | asya | tarviṣīṣu | pṛśrate | agneḥ | avena | marutām | na | bhojyā | iṣirāya | na | bhojyā || saḥ | hi | sma | dānum | invati | vasūnām | ca | majmanā | saḥ | naḥ | trāsate | duritāt | abhihutaḥ | śaṃsāt | aghāt | abhihutaḥ || 5 ||

Because all the sacrificers, by means of the *kratu*—the ritual act consisting of the offering of oblations and so forth—mix the foods to be eaten, such as the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and other edibles, for the sake of satisfaction (*avena*), into the *tarviṣīḥ*, the powerful flames of this Agni.
*Tarviṣī* is a name for strength, as it is listed among the names [of strength] in the Nirukta (2.9.10): “*tarviṣī* is splendor.
An illustration of this follows.
The meaning is: "Like the food of the Maruts," that is, like the grains such as rice which are the sustenance related to the winds.
Just as when the winds pierce the clouds and produce rain, the grains such as rice—which serve as food—flourish by means of the crops, so it is here;
this is the illustration for the act of giving.
"Like food for the seeker":
just as edible things, such as foods and drinks, are given to one who is endowed with desire, who is begging, and who is a petitioner; so it is here.
The word *iṣi* has been etymologically explained by Yāska thus: "In the sense of seeking (*īpaṇa*) or in the sense of wandering about (*vaipaṇa*)" (Nirukta 4.7).
For this reason, that sacrificer indeed promotes the gift; he extends the offering of the oblation to him.
Or rather, he promotes the gift that is personally desired.
The root *inv* has the sense of pervading, as it is listed among those roots with that meaning in the statement: "He pervades, he has reached" (*invati nanakṣa*, Nirukta 2.18.1).
By what capacity? By the very power (*majmanā*) of the *vasus*—that is, by the strength of the riches worthy of being dwelt in, which have been obtained through Agni.
Or alternatively:
that Agni, by his majesty—the power of his riches consisting of flames which are worthy of being the abode for the oblation of the Vasus—promotes the act of giving; this is the ellipsis.
Furthermore, that Agni, when invoked with oblations, protects—that is, rescues—us from misfortune, from evil, as we are being led forward by our prayers.

Likewise, from that which is to be praised because of its extreme abundance—or alternatively, from the harmful—He protects; He rescues those who are being drawn away on all sides from suffering, or from the sin that is its cause.

The all-pervading, far-reaching, benevolent steward has taken up [the sacrificial ladle] in his right hand; he does not let the swift one loose, nor does he let him loose for the sake of glory. To every seeker indeed, you have conveyed the oblation among the gods. To every doer of good, Agni opens the door; he opens wide the doors of the treasure. viśvaḥ | vi'hāyāḥ | aratiḥ | vasuḥ | dadhe | haste | dakṣiṇe | taraṇinam | na | śiśrathat | śravasyayā | na | śiśrathat || viśvasmai | it | iṣudhyate | deva'trā | havyam | ā | ūhiṣe | viśvasmai | it | su'kṛte | vāram | ṛṇvati | agniḥ | dvārā | vi | ṛṇvati || 6 ||

1. *kṣa-ṇa-ṭa-bhojyāni*. 2. After *kṣa-ṇa-ṭa* and *‘tadvat’*, there is an addition: *“Or rather, the meaning is that they become food (*bhojyā*), things to be enjoyed (*bhogyāni*), for *iṣirāya*—that is, for the one who desires (*eṣaṇāya*)—in such a way as to serve as its synonyms.”*

3. For he indeed is *kṣa-ṇa-ṭa-sa*. 4. By the power of *kṣa-ṇa-ṭa*, this Agni, with his right hand intent upon bestowing [the gift], holds—that is, maintains—the wealth to be given to the sacrificer in his non-left (right) hand, being endowed with the energy to grant what is desired.
What is he like?
He is *viśvaḥ*, to be traversed by all, or else he is the universal self (*viśvātmaka*); he is *vihāyāḥ*, that is, great.
For *vihāyāḥ* is a name for the great, as it is listed among the names for the great in the Nirukta (3.3.12): "The vast one (*vihāyāḥ*), the great one (*yahaḥ*)."
*Aratiḥ* means a lord (*īśvaraḥ*) or one who does not take pleasure (*aramamāṇaḥ*), or it means lack of affection (*aprītiḥ*).
Here, the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule "after the roots *vahi*, *vasi*, and *ati*, [the suffix] *ap* [is added]," which is marked with the *cit* designation.
Because of the presence of *cit*, the word is oxytone (accented on the final syllable).
And having grasped [it], he loosens it;
he relaxes—that is, gives away—the hand that was held for the sake of the sacrificer.
This is a form derived from the root *bhlath* in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a "crosser," that is, like the sun which enables one to cross; just as he [the sun] holds in his hand and bestows upon his worshipper whatever is desired, so too does he.
Or rather:
*taraṇiḥ* means the deliverer of all;
he does not loosen, that is, he does not slacken or release the sacrificer.
Furthermore, "by means of fame" (śravastayā) he does not loosen [us]; as if desiring the oblation-form, he does not loosen [us], he does not release [us].
He protects us solely through his favor; the sense is that the acceptance of the oblation is merely a formal designation.
Now, [the poet] addresses him directly.

O Agni, among the gods (*devatrā*), you carry forth in every direction (*ohiṣe*) the oblation (*havya*)—such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so on—intended for Indra and the other deities who, desiring the offering for themselves, seek it out (*iṣudhyate*).
The root *iṣudhyati* belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class.
You convey that very oblation, dedicated to each respective deity, everywhere.
In *vahelanti*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) because it belongs to the class beginning with *yaj*.

Furthermore, this Agni *ṛṇavati*—that is, he goes toward or provides—for *viśvasmai sukṛte*, for the sacrificer who performs an auspicious sacrifice, *vāram*, food and so forth that is desirable by all or that wards off hunger and other such needs.
Moreover, this Agni *vyuṇavati*, he opens up, *dvārāḥ*, the doors leading to heaven as desired.
The meaning is that it accomplishes one's desired goals by means of removing obstructive sins.
The root *ṛ* signifies the act of going.
Alternatively:
The meaning is "flowing.
Due to the presence of the *it*-marker, the augment *num* is applied.
The vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *r* is a Vedic archaism.
He has been established as the most auspicious one among the human community; Agni is like a noble lord of the people at the sacrifices, the dear lord of the people at the sacrifices.
He rules over the oblations of men that are prepared with sacred food.
He trembles before the guile of Varuṇa, before the guile of the great god.

He has been established as the most beneficent one among the human community; Agni is the noble lord of the people at the sacrifices, like a beloved lord of the people at the sacrifices. He rules over the oblations of men prepared with *iḷā*; may he protect us from the malice of Varuṇa, from the malice of the great god.

That Agni, when the "vṛjana"—the avoidable evil—belonging to the "mānuṣa," the human sacrificer, becomes the cause [of distress], is "śantamaḥ," most exceedingly blissful, because he wards off misfortune; for this very reason, he is "hitaḥ," beneficial, because he accomplishes the desired goal of heaven.
Furthermore, in sacrifices, he is the "viśpatiḥ," the supreme protector of the subjects consisting of the officiating priests and kings.

Although the rule "patyāvaiśvarye" would have required the original accent of the first member of the compound, the rule "parādiś chandasi bahulam" applies, resulting in the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member.
For this very reason, he becomes beloved.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a victorious lord of men, a king who is habituated to conquest.
Just as he becomes dear to his subjects by warding off calamities from enemy armies and by providing them with proper protection,
so too is this Agni dear to *mānuṣāṇām*, that is, to human beings.

1. In the right hand [is] *śra-ḍa-jha-ja-ṭa*. 2. Having abandoned *kṣa-a-ṭa*; the meaning is that he is to be approached by all as the Great One (*mahān*). 3. *kṣa-ḍa-jha-ja-ṭa* means "not delighting. 4. *ḍa* means "lack of affection toward those who do not sacrifice. 5. *jha-jha* means "having held" (*dhṛtvā*). 6. *kṣa-a-ṭa* means "merely a designation. 7. *ḍa-jha* means "for everyone" (*viśvasmai sarvasmai*). 8. *kṣa-a-ṭa* means "doors for attaining what is desired in heaven. 9. *kṣa-a-ṭa* means "in those things which have become the causes."

Agni beholds—that is, he comes toward and descends upon—the oblations (*havyā havīṃṣi*) belonging to the sacrificers, which have been prepared (*iḷā-kṛtāni*), that is, accomplished upon the *iḷā*, the sacrificial altar (*vedī*). Furthermore, that Agni protects (*trāyate*) us, the sacrificers, from the fear of Varuṇa’s *dhūrti*—that is, from the harm of the obstructer.
Or alternatively: [the same].
The word "dhūrtaiḥ" is in the ablative case (pañcamī).
[He] protects [us] from the injury caused by the "dhūrtas" (deceivers) of Varuṇa, the god of sin;
furthermore, he protects us from the injury caused by the "bhūtas" (beings) of the great god.
It is well known that fire destroys even iron;
or rather,
it is a single sentence.
From the beings of the great and powerful god Varuṇa, and from the beings of the malevolent deity Pāpadevatā, may that Agni protect and deliver us from their violence.

They praise Agni, the Hotṛ, the bestower of wealth; they have established him as the beloved, the most wise messenger; they have established him as the bearer of oblations. The gods, seeking wealth, have established with their songs the all-encompassing, all-knowing Hotṛ, the worshipful sage—the delightful one for protection, the delightful one, seeking wealth. Agni, the Hotṛ, they praise; the bestower of wealth, the beloved, the most wise, they have set down as the messenger; the bearer of oblations, they have set down. All-living, all-knowing, the Hotṛ, the worshipful sage—the delightful one for aid, the gods, seeking wealth, [have established] with their songs the delightful one, seeking wealth.
The officiating priests praise—that is, they extol—this Agni as the Hotṛ, the invoker, or the one who accomplishes the oblation;

likewise, as the sustainer of wealth (vasudhiti), the giver, and therefore beloved, the most beloved of all, and the most perceptive (cetiṣṭha)—that is, the one who most excellently brings the sacrificers to awareness, or the one possessed of preeminent consciousness.
From the word *citta*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied by the rule “*tucchaṃdasi*” (Pāṇini 5.3.59). Then, by the rule “*turiṣṭhemayaḥsu*” (Pāṇini 6.4.154), there is the elision of the syllable *-t*.
They reached—that is, they attained completely—the Lord Arati, such a god;
the prefix *pra-* is specifically emphasized here.
They reached—that is, they attained entirely—the Havyavāha.
They have attained a state such that they are fully capable of carrying the oblation to the other gods.
Furthermore, of what nature is he?

He is the one whose life-force (*āyu*) is universal, the sustainer of all living beings; the possessor of all knowledge (*viśvavedas*); the invoker (*hotṛ*) of the gods; the worshipful one worthy of sacrifice; and the seer (*kavi*), the omniscient.
This is a form in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) derived from either of the two roots *īr*, namely *īr* in the sense of "impelling" or *īr* in the sense of "motion."

Furthermore, O gods—meaning the officiating priests who delight in divine play—the seekers of wealth (*vasuyavaḥ*), desiring riches, have brought forth for protection (*avase*) the one who is *raṇva*, shouting with excessive intensity; and again, being seekers of wealth, they have directed toward him who is *raṇva*—either shouting or delightful—by means of songs of praise (*gīrbhiḥ*). Being seekers of wealth, they have placed him before themselves, desiring to bestow upon him the wealth consisting of oblations (*vasu*).
The meaning is that they have attained [the gods] through oblations and the like, just as one who is pleased bestows wealth.

The third hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “*yaṃ tvaṃ ratham*,” is composed in the *aty-aṣṭi* meter, as it is stated that “the entire [hymn] of Parucchepa consists of *aṣṭi* [verses] except for the eighth. Because it is addressed to Indra, it belongs to Indra.
The first two verses, beginning with "prapā vo asme," are *atiśakvarīs* because they are endowed with five syllables [per line].
The next, "pāhi naḥ," is an *aṣṭi* because it is endowed with four and five syllables [per line].
The sixth verse, "pra taddoceyam," has Indra as its deity.
And likewise, the Anukramaṇikā states: "The hymn beginning with 'yaṃ tvamekādaśa' belongs to Pañca Indavī Prapāvata, who was exceedingly powerful.

This hymn is prescribed in the section titled 'padyasya' within the Mahāvatīya Śastra on the sixth day of the Daśarātra sacrifice, in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (8.1): "yaṃ tvaṃ rathamindra sa yo mṛṣā."

O Indra, that chariot which you lead forward from afar for the winning of the prize, O blameless one—you lead it forth; you instantly make it swift of mind for our desire, and you bring the powerful steed under your control. Truly, O blameless one, you hasten toward the speech of the wise, as if toward the hymn of the wise.

O Indra, you who are swift and blameless, you lead the chariot forward for the winning of the sacrifice, even though it was far away; you lead it forth. At once, for our protection, you have made that steed subject to your will. O blameless one, being impetuous, [drive] this speech of ours, like the speech of the wise, toward us.

O Indra, O impetuous one, you who are accustomed to accepting sacrifice, you lead forth—that is, you bring to—the chariot for the sake of winning the prize of the sacrifice, or for its acquisition, toward whichever sacrificer it may be.
This [verb] takes two objects.
What kind of sacrificer?
"One who is unripe, yet possesses authority through non-insignificant wisdom.
Yāska [states]: "'Pāka' refers to one who is ripe" (Nirukta 3.12).
Therefore, [we praise] the wise one who is truly peaceful.
Furthermore, O *ana*, O Indra— you who are distinguished by the qualities about to be described— hear our invocation or our hymn of praise.
The state of being a herder.
You, who indeed were joined by men—by humans alone—and subsequently even by such Maruts;
those very ones are further specified.
"By men" means by those whose nature is to lead in battle.
Indra's assistance to the Maruts is well known from such passages as "Indra with the Maruts" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.5.1) and "The Maruts did not abandon him" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 3.20).

Being accompanied by them, [he acts] "in certain battles"—that is, in all mature and great conflicts—for the sake of Bharahatye, meaning for the purpose of striking down the enemy with distinguished maintenance and gifts, or for the sake of supreme destruction.
Or alternatively:

for the sake of supporting—that is, for the purpose of encouraging the brave with such words as "be a hero, strike!"—and for the sake of the destruction of those who are to be struck down, and for the superior slaying of the brave;
you are *dakṣāyyaḥ*, meaning you are of a nature that promotes growth.
Or rather:

being entreated by men—the leaders and sacrificers—for the sake of *pratartya*, that is, for the superior destruction of enemies or of evils, you are *dakṣāyyaḥ*, meaning you are capable. Furthermore, you who, accompanied by the Maruts endowed with heroism or by other wise ones, are yourself (*svaḥ*) the winner (*sanitā*) of battle or of whatever else is desired, are the distributor of it.

The meaning is that even when they provide assistance, you are a crosser [of obstacles] through your own independence alone. The form *tarutā* is derived from the root *tṛ*, being irregularly formed (nipātita) in such lists as "prasita-skabhita.
Furthermore, you, being praised by the wise Maruts, are *vāja-tarutā*—a giver of strength to them who are ignorant.
The connection is: "together with the wise Maruts.

The masters—meaning the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are capable of properly entreating him—delight, propitiate, and serve that such *vājin* (the swift one), who possesses *pṛkṣa* (food characterized by oblations) and is *inadra* (mighty).
Therein lies the illustration.

"Vājinam" means the one possessing vigor, the one possessing movement; "pṛkṣam" means the one possessing fodder and food. It is like a nobleman's horse—as people are able to nourish that [horse] by providing sweet fodder and so forth, in that same way [one nourishes this]. "Arya" is a name for wealth, because it is listed among the names for wealth in the *Nighaṇṭu* (1.14.1) as "aryaḥ hayaḥ" (the nobleman’s horse).

For you, O Dashma, are indeed the drinker of the bull; you rend the skin of every one who is hostile, O Hero. You spare no mortal, O Hero, you spare no mortal. And this, O Indra, I shall proclaim to Heaven, this to Rudra of glorious fame, this to Mitra and Varuna—far-reaching praise, far-reaching praise to the one who is well-disposed.

For you, O wondrous one, have indeed drunk from the bull’s skin; you have bypassed every wounded mortal, O hero—you avoid the mortal. Indra, I declare this far-reaching praise to you, to Dyaus, to Rudra of glorious fame, to Mitra, and to Varuṇa—this far-reaching praise to the most gracious one. 2.
O Indra, you are indeed a wonder-worker (*dasma*), the destroyer of enemies.

For this very reason, you drink—that is, having burst open—you sprinkle some cloud that is *vṛṣaṇam*, naturally raining, *tvacam*, possessing a covering, like a sealed vessel or encircled by water, and a bearer of waters.
Furthermore, O heroic and valiant one, you mix with some cloud that is *martyam*, like a mortal, *arum*, ruddy-colored, and *yāvin*, having the nature of movement.
In the word *yauteḥ*, the absence of the augment *aṭ* is Vedic, occurring in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense which is itself Vedic.
The meaning is: "By means of non-rain, you seize by force and cause [the enemy] who is advancing to rain.
The sense is that it is just as when a certain hero seizes and subdues a powerful enemy who is advancing.

Likewise, O Indra, you completely avoid—that is, you keep at a distance from all sides—a certain mortal cloud, which is subject to death, of a decaying nature, and devoid of water; this is the meaning of "you show indifference toward. O Indra, I shall proclaim to you that such deed, characterized by raining, as it may be *saprathaḥ*—that is, wide and extensive on every side.
Thus Indra himself is further specified.
To him who possesses his own glory (*svaryaśase*), that is, to one endowed with his own fame;
likewise, even to the deity of the heavenly world (*dive*), which serves as its support.

[Notes: 1. *ḍa*: of enemies. 2. *kṣa-cha-ṭa*: situated in victory in battle; *ca*: of battle. 3. *kṣa-cha-ṭa*: they propitiate; *ḍa*: they cause to prosper. 4. *ḍa-ca-pha*: the agent of destruction. 5. *kṣa-cha-ṭa*: you avoid/ward off. Page 103.
"I shall speak—that is, I shall declare—such an action.
The word *uta* has the sense of the particle *api*.
Since it is favorable to the pure deity of the act of raining, her mention as well is appropriate.
Likewise, I speak this to Rudra, the one who causes the burning of suffering for the worlds, or to Agni, who is characterized by weeping.
For his nature as Rudra is established by the Vedic scripture: "Rudra is indeed cruel because he is a slayer" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.3.2).
His nature of weeping is well known from the scripture: "He wept; because he wept (arodīt), that is the origin of Rudra's name (rudratvam)" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.1.1).
And since that [fire] is conducive to rain by way of the oblation (*āhuti*), its mention is also appropriate.
The word *svayaśase* is connected either with *rudrāya* or with *agnaye*, due to proximity and suitability;
the meaning is "to Agni who is endowed with his own glory."
Thus, I have spoken that to Mitra, the deity presiding over the day;
I have spoken that to Varuṇa, the deity presiding over the night.
For it is said: "Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 25.10.10), and "Verily, through day and night, Parjanya rains" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.7.3).
Likewise, from such scriptural passages as "The day is indeed Mitra, and the night is Varuṇa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.7.3), Mitra and Varuṇa are established as the presiding deities of day and night.
For this very reason, because of the authority of scripture, it is appropriate that they be mentioned first.
[I bow] to the one who is *sumṛḷīka*, the bestower of excellent happiness upon all creatures.
This [term] is connected with everything [that follows].
From the aforementioned gods, I proclaim that act of raining so as to be *saprathaḥ*—extensive on all sides, exceedingly vast.
For our sake, we desire Indra for assistance—the friend who sustains all life, the conqueror, the ally; the conqueror, the ally, in the contests for booty.
May you come swiftly to our aid in every battle;
no enemy can strike you down, for you strike down every enemy—yes, you strike him down.

We desire Indra for our aid—the friend who possesses all life, the conqueror, the ally; the conqueror, the ally in battles. May our prayer come hither for our protection in every fray; for no enemy can strike you down, but you strike him down—every enemy you strike down. 4.

O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), for our sake—that is, for your sake and for ours—for the purpose of sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) or for the seeking of what is desired, we desire Indra; that is, we long for what is desired. [The root] *vaś* means "to desire"; it belongs to the *ad-ādi* class.

The word *idvantaḥ* [is derived from *it*] with *masiḥ* [as the suffix]; there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule beginning with "prahijyā," or else the connection is "our friend" (*asmākaṃ sakhāyam*).
What kind of Indra?

A friend—one who acts for one's ultimate benefit like a friend, or one whose movement is equal; a Viśvāyu—one who goes to all sacrifices; a Prasaha—one who thoroughly overcomes enemies. [The suffix] *kvip* is applied to the root *sah*.
The vowel lengthening of the prefix occurs by the rule "nahivṛti" and so forth. "Yujam" means always joined, that is to say, acting as a companion.
That very [term] is further qualified.

In battles (*vājeṣu*), in the seizing of spoils (*havīrāpakṣeṣu*), or when sacrifices (*yajñeṣu*) are the occasion for giving—that is, when those who obstruct the sacrifice are being overcome—[protect] the companion who overcomes [them], who is joined with the Maruts, and who bestows desired fruits.

Furthermore, O Indra, for our protection (*ūtaye*), preserve (*ava rakṣa*) our *brahma*, that is, our exalted ritual action (*parivṛḍhaṃ karma*). To what specific purpose? He says this: [to grant] that [protection].
"Against whomever"— in battles,
for "pṛtsu samatsu" is listed among the names for battle in the *Nighaṇṭu* (2.17.21);
in those [battles], no one overcomes you, nor harms you, nor practices hostility toward you— whomsoever you strike down.
The meaning is: you strike down every enemy and ward them off so that no enemy at all can cause harm;
because of your greatness, all are terrified and become submissive, and since you have no enemies (ajātaśatru), no one ever adopts an attitude of enmity toward you.

1. The explanation of *kṣa*, *ña*, *ja*, and *ṭa*. 2. *Ṭha*: Just as it is for us, so it is for you—[our] friend (*sakhāyam*). 3. *Jha*: Having the nature of excellent rubbing (*prakṛṣṭa-mṛṣaṇa-śīla*); [the form] *prāsare* is derived with the suffix *kvip*. 4. *Ḍa*: Joined with desired horses (*abhimatāśvaiḥ*) or accompanied by great ones at the sacrifice (*yajñe*); *kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa*: joined with desired fruits (*abhimatāphalaiḥ*) or accompanied by great ones at the sacrifice. 5. *Kṣa*, *ña*, *ja*, *ṭa*: *kastana*. 6. *Śa*, *pha*: You are the enemy (*tvām śatruḥ*). 7. *Kṣa*, *ña*: States (*bhāvāḥ*). Drive away the arrogance and the overweening pride of anyone whatsoever with your most powerful waves, with your protections, and with your gladdening aids.
Be not envious of us as of old, O Hero, for you are considered blameless;
as a bearer, carry us across all difficulties with your mouth; as a bearer, bring us hither.

O you of exceeding wisdom, [bring] us [wealth] for every task with your most brilliant aids, as with surging waves—O fierce one, with your fierce aids! Do not neglect us as of old, O hero, for you are considered sinless. Drive away all [hostilities] from Puru; as a bearer, bring us [to our goal] with your mouth, like a bearer. 5.

O Indra, for every single devotee of yours who performs sacrifice, utterly subdue—that is, thoroughly and completely bend down—the enemy who has overstepped the mind, whose thoughts are hostile; make him bow down before us.
This [root] has the causative sense (ṇyartha) inherent within it.

He is "Ugra," one who is joined with "ugraṇabala" (mighty power), whether through "ūtibhiḥ" (protective aids) or "prītibhiḥ" (affections); and he is "man" (wise/mindful), possessing "tejiṣṭhābhiḥ arṇobhiḥ" (most brilliant waves)—that is, like paths that are exceedingly radiant and characterized by the desire for battle.
From *tejasvaccha-cchada*, the suffix *-ātiśāyanika* (denoting "exceedingly") is applied here.
By the rule *vinamata-oluk*, the *luk*-elision of the feminine suffix (*ṅīp*) occurs;
then, by the rule *ṭeḥ*, there is the elision of the final phoneme (*ṭi*).
The meaning is that just as he bent Atimati, Vṛtra, and others, so too [he bent] our adversary;
or rather,
it connects with what follows later.

Just as you have joined us with the most brilliant [paths]—like waves, endowed with splendor, serving as the means of motion, and being the paths of travel—in that same way, lead us (*naḥ*) with fierce, illuminating aids (*ūtibhiḥ*), which consist of the fruits of sacrifice; the meaning is that you lead us to attain the desired results such as heaven.
The elision of the *śap* suffix after the root *nayati* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) phenomenon.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Just as in former times you led our fathers and others with your aids (*ūtibhiḥ*), so do lead us"—this is the meaning.

O *śūra* (hero), one who is courageous, you are considered *anenaḥ* (sinless); that is to say, you are perceived by all as being free from sin because you are the means for attaining desired goals such as heaven. This is the intended sense.
Or rather:
you, being sinless, consider us also to be sinless.
Furthermore, O Indra, being the "carrier" (*vahni*)—that is, the sustainer of the worlds through the bestowing of trees and other gifts—for the sake of *puruḥ*, the human sacrificer.
*Puru* is a name for humans, as attested by the list of names in the Nirukta: "The *puru*s are the moving ones" (Ni.
2.3.20). For him, you carry across—having removed—all (*viśvāni*) these (*enāṃsi*) sins; that is, you protect him.
The elision of the *śap* suffix after the root *guṇāti* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Therefore, "O Agni, having come toward us—toward our place of sacrifice—being the bearer (*vahnih*) who carries what is desired, and having removed what is undesired, you fulfill (*parṣi*) the desired fruit."

This must be proclaimed for the sake of the praiseworthy Soma-drop, he who, like one to be invoked, stirs the mind with his purifying power; the demon-slayer stirs the prayer. May he himself drive away from us the reviler and the evil-minded one for our prosperity. May the scorner fall low; may he sink down like a tiny insect.

I shall proclaim this to the future Soma-drop, who, like one worthy of invocation, is full of joy and causes the prayer to tremble; he, the slayer of demons, causes the prayer to tremble. May he himself drive away ill-will from us with his strengthening powers; may the evil-plotters fall low, and may the wicked vanish like a tiny mote. 6.

1. O Indra among the *jha*-letters; 2. O you who cause the *kṣa*, *ṅa*, and *a* to bend; 3. O you who are bowed down by the *kṣa*, *ja*, and *da*; 4. O you who [proceed] by means of the paths beginning with battle (*ḍa*); 5. O you who possess a splendor that surpasses the *kṣa*, *ṅa*, and *ja*; 6. You have impelled the *ca* and *pha*; 7. O you who [protect] even us (*kṣa* and *na*); 8. Having dispelled [the obstacles] through the *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *jha*, *jha*, *na*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pha*.

May I be able to speak forth—that is, to speak pre-eminently—the deed or the hymn of praise for that purpose, which is about to be mentioned, for the sake of *indu* (the Moon), who is worthy of being honored (*bhabhya*), whose nature is to dwell in the celestial realm (*bhavanaśīla*), who increases day by day through the growth of his digits (*kalābhivṛddhyā vardhanaśīla*), and who is the cause of everything by means of nectar (*amṛta*).
The sense is that this is because the praise is exceedingly great.
[The grammatical form is derived from] the root *vac* with the suffix *aṅ* in the optative used as a benediction (*liṅyāśiṣyaṅ*).
"Vaca um. To whom does that belong?
It belongs to him who, being *indu* (the flowing one), full of impetus (*iṣaṇavat*), moves toward—goes forth for—the sake of *manma*, which is a hymn worthy of thought (*mananīya*) or a ritual act.
The root *rej* has the sense of "going," as it is listed among its synonyms in the passage, "He trembles, he moves" (*Ni.
2.14.60*). "Coming" is the illustrative example.
Like Indra, he is not merely one to whom offerings are made (*hotavya*), but one from whom they are to be received (*āhātavya*), thus being *havya*.
Generally, by [the mantra] "O Indra, come," and so forth, Indra alone is invoked;
he is the one being qualified, just as he is [in that context].

The slayer of *rakṣases*—the destroyer of those *rakṣases* who obstruct the sacrifice—their very deed, consisting of slaughter and so forth, *rejati*: it goes, it is shaken, that is to say, it is destroyed.
That very *indu* (Soma) himself is the reviler (*nidaḥ*).
[The root] *ṇidi* is used in the sense of "censure."
The meaning is that one should summon [the deity] with invocations such as "O you whose fruit is pride" (*mānaphala*) and "O Lord of the bay horses (*harivan*), come to the ram of Medhātithi.
Furthermore, those same [invocations] are specified:
"with invocations to you" (*yuṣmahūtibhiḥ*), meaning by means of calls characterized by oblations; the words "we shall seize" (*ā gṛbhīmahi*) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
"O you of shining fame, [speak] speech," says Yāska (Nirukta 5.5).

May Indra come forth to us with his own glories for our aid, in the driving away of the ill-minded, the shattering of the ill-minded! May that [host] which comes against us with devouring [weapons] destroy itself;
let it perish, let it carry off those who dwell in decay, let it carry off the withered.

Forth, forth [goes] Indra for you and for us with his self-glorious aids, in the avoidance of those of evil intent, in the rending of those of evil intent. Let that [hostile power] which seeks us through sorcerers perish by itself; let it be struck down, let it not carry us away; let the wasting fire consume it, let it not carry us away. 8.

O ṛtvij priests, for your sake (*vaḥ*) and for our sake (*asme*), this Indra, through his own glories (*svayaśobhiḥ*)—that is, through those joined with his own fame—and through his aids (*ūtī*), meaning protections, becomes ever more preeminent (*prapra*)—meaning he becomes fully capable—when there is the "complete exclusion" (*parivarge*) of the ill-minded (*durmatīnām*), that is, when there is the total avoidance of those possessed of evil intent.
The doubling [of *pra*] is for the purpose of completing the meter.
Or else:

O Ṛtviks, being pleased by these hymns of praise—which are for your sake, which belong to us, and which are capable of praising through their own inherent glory (svayaśas) independently of any other—he becomes exceedingly intent upon *ūtī*, that is, upon protection.
Upon hearing a prefix (upasarga), the appropriate verb must be supplied by ellipsis.
By what is that expressed? In the assembly (*parivarga*) of the wicked and evil-minded, or in a battle (*saṃgrāma*) or sacrifice (*yāga*) characterized by total avoidance (*parito varjana*).
Furthermore, that very [assembly] is further specified:
"Of those of evil mind, possessed of wicked pride, and intent on slaughter—[O Indra], the 'darīman', the one who excessively tears asunder;
while Indra thus protects correctly, by the 'atrāḥ', the devourers, our adversaries, that 'jūrṇiḥ', the army possessing [broken] joints.
Regarding 'jūrṇiḥ', Yāska says: 'It is derived from the root *ju* (to hasten), or *dru* (to run), or *du* (to burn)' (Nirukta 6.4)."
"Against us"—that is, toward us—"ariṣayadhyai," meaning to injure.
The suffix *śadhyai* is added after the root *ṛṣi* in the sense of "capable of" (*tum-artha*).
'Upeṣye' means to approach us, that is, to reach us.
The root *iṅ* means "to go. The suffix *kṣa* is applied in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*).
That army, though driven forward, was itself struck down—that is, it was indeed destroyed.
It will not carry us—that is, it does not reach us;
likewise, it will not carry our assailants—the enemies—either; that is, it does not bring them [to us].
In the leṭ suffix, there is the augment *aḍ*; the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule "sibbahulam."
The meaning is that, by the power of Indra, it was destroyed right there.

Come to us, O Indra, with abundant wealth by a path free from danger; go before us, drive away the demons. Come to us from afar, come to us from our home; protect us from far and near with your aids—protect us always with your aids.

O Indra, come to us with abundant wealth; come by a path free from danger. Go before us, providing protection; protect us in the distance, and protect us in our home. Guard us from afar and from near at hand with your aids; guard us always with your aids. 9.
1. By means of the oblations consisting of the syllables *kṣa*, *a*, *ja*, *ṭa*, *ya*, and *śo*.

2. The appropriate verbs are to be supplied according to the prefixes (*upasarga*): *kṣa*, *a*, and *ṭa* [take one verb], while *u* [takes] two [verbs]. 3. Of those whose battles have been destroyed by *ka*.
4. To the one who protects;
5. therefore not from *ha*. O Indra, you, proceed along our path—that is, come by the way belonging to us.
