There is elision of the suffix *ṭi*. By the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*, the third case ending becomes acute (*udātta*).
By what kind of path?
By one that is *arakṣas*, meaning devoid of demons (*rakṣas*), and *anehas*, meaning free from evil.
Because the path for going to the sacrifice is impelled by praise, it is called *anehas*.
Or alternatively: "Go toward us," that is, for our sake;
being of what nature? [Thus the question.]

O Indra, being endowed with abundant wealth (*parīṇas*)—that is, with various kinds of riches to be given to us from all sides through your pervasive power (*naḍda*)—come to us (*naḥ*) from *parāka*, that is, from the exceedingly distant region characterized as heaven; be united with us (*ā sacasva*). *Parāka* is a name for "distance," as it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (3.26.2): "from afar (*parāke*), from far away (*parācaiḥ*)."
Likewise, O Agni, dwell in this most proximate place of sacrifice; enjoy our oblation, or rather, come together with it.
Furthermore, protect us from afar—from distant places such as heaven—and protect us from nearby—from this world.
Or rather:
from afar, having dwelt in heaven itself at times when there is no sacrifice, protect us—that is, preserve us;
from near, when the time of sacrifice is present, protect us in the place of the sacrificial ground.
By what means? That is stated: by *abhiṣṭibhiḥ*, that is, by sacrifices performed face-to-face (*abhimukhya*), or by those vehicles;
[it refers to] their coming toward [us].
What need is there for more?

At all times, throughout every moment—whether at the time of sacrifice or not at the time of sacrifice, whether far or near—protect us perfectly with your constant guardianship through your desired aids.
O Indra, may your swift and fierce greatness come to our aid for our great protection, like a friend for our help.
O most powerful one, immortal one, protect our chariot;
ward off anyone who seeks to harm us, O Lord, even him who intends to strike us down.

O Indra, may your own greatness, powerful and radiant with wealth, come to our aid for great protection, even as Mitra comes for protection. O strongest savior, O immortal, protect our chariot; ward off anyone who would harm us, O wielder of the stone, even one who seeks to strike us down, O wielder of the stone. 10.

O Indra, may you—by means of *taruṣā*, that which is skilled in crossing over, and by means of *rāyā*, wealth or riches, capable of delivering us—be our deliverer from calamities; this is the sense of the remainder.

O Indra, even though you are *ugram*, possessed of full power, it is *mahi*, greatness—that excellence produced by our hymns of praise—a certain pre-eminence, that *sakṣat*, serves or honors you; the meaning is that it exalts you.
For what purpose?
For your favor and for our lack of displeasure.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
for great protection (*avase*), consisting of light, health, and so forth, [we approach you] like the sun, the friend of all people (*mitram*).
The meaning is that they cause him to sacrifice in accordance with his greatness;
or alternatively, like a friend (*mitra*)— that is, like a companion whose nature is to be dear and beneficial.
Just as they honor him for his greatness and for the sake of joy, so [should we].

Furthermore, O most powerful (*ojiṣṭha*), O most vigorous one, O protector (*trātṛ*), having protected us, O immortal (*amartya*) Indra whose nature is deathlessness, O you who satisfy us with wealth (*avitaḥ*), bring some swift chariot to us; let it come quickly to our journey—this is the sense of the ellipsis.
Likewise, O wielder of the stone (*adrivaḥ*), O Indra who utterly consumes the enemies, [drive away] even one who desires to harm us, whether he be insignificant or great.
"Enemy" is the word to be supplied. "Ririṣeḥ" means "destroy.
Likewise, O "adrivaḥ"—O wielder of the thunderbolt, or O consumer of the enemies' wealth.
"‘May he run even against the mountain, or even against the wind,’ so says the Nirukta (4.4).
Even toward a foe who desires to destroy (*ririkṣantam*), one who is exceedingly contemptible and harmful, you must *riiriṣeḥ*—that is, repel or strike him down."
The root *riph* is used in the sense of "injuring. Here, the suffix *śap* is replaced by *bhlu* according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*),
and then the *ś* is substituted for it by means of metathesis (*vyatyaya*).
[To you] who desire to protect;

from this very [root] *san*, because it is enjoined by the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) as "from a root ending in *h* or *n*" (Pāṇini 6.4.24); from afar (*parāvataḥ*); protect us completely (*paripālaya*); through the pacification of repeated practice (*abhyāsaśamanaiḥ*); in the arrival (*abhyāgamane*); at all times (*sārvakālam*); whether the sacrifice is performed far away or in close proximity (*yāgakāle dūre saṃnihite*); for the sake of your own pleasure or for the sake of [our] welfare (*tumaye*).

[Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 19, Sūkta 130] Second Aṣṭaka: 823. *Manah* [is used here]; however, there is an absence of the [usual] quality [of the suffix]. *Cit* is used in the sense of contempt, because Yāska stated: "‘Bring some *kulmāṣa* grains’—this is used in the sense of contempt" (Nirukta 1.4). Alternatively, it has the sense of conjunction; it is conjoined with the word *kaṃcit*.
Protect this excellent hymn of ours, O Indra; you are the eternal deliverer from distress for those of evil intent, the god who subdues even the well-intentioned.
You are the slayer of the wicked *rakṣas* and the protector of the inspired singer from every side.
For thus did the progenitor beget you, O Vasu; he begot you as the slayer of *rakṣases*, O Vasu.

Protect us, O Indra, from our adversaries through your excellent praise; you are the eternal deliverer from the evil-minded, being a god against the evil-minded. You are the slayer of the wicked *rakṣas*, the protector of the inspired singer like me; for indeed, the progenitor begot you, O Vasu, he begot you as the slayer of *rakṣases*, O Vasu.
O Indra, O well-praised one, protect us—that is, guard us—from *sridhaḥ*, meaning from sufferings or from the sins that produce them;
for you are the protector of those who possess evil minds, such as the Rākṣasas and others.
(The word *nāma* takes the acute accent according to the rule *nāmy-atarasyām*.)
"Always, indeed, you are the *avayātṛ*—the one who causes to descend, the one who brings [us] down;
therefore, protect us. For this very reason, O Indra, being a god gladdened by our praise, you are the *avayātṛ* of the *durmatīnām*—those of evil thoughts, the obstructors of the sacrifice."
Likewise, "of the Rakṣas" means of that which is the cause for protection;
Yāska [states] in the *Nirukta* (4.18): "Rakṣas is that from which one must be protected.
You are the "slayer," the destroyer, of "sin"—that is, of the evil which takes the form of an obstacle to the fruit [of action].
Or rather:
you are the slayer of the wicked, the sinful Rākṣasa and other such demons;
likewise, you are the protector and guardian of the wise sacrificer who is like me.

Now, for this reason: O Indra, O *avaso*, you who are the abode of all, the Creator—the Supreme Lord, the progenitor and original cause—*jīrjanat*, has generated; that is, He brought you into existence.
Likewise, O *avaso*, you who provide shelter, He generated you as *rakṣohaṇam*, for the purpose of slaying the demons (*rakṣas*).
This is the form [of the verb] *janayati* in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix.
For Indra’s incarnation was indeed for the purpose of destroying the obstructors of sacrifice, such as the Rākṣasas;
the word "hi" (indeed) is used to indicate well-known scriptural authority, such as the passage: "Indra, along with the gods, wiped him clean" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1.4).
The fourth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "O Indra, come to us" (*endra yāhyupa naḥ*), is addressed to Indra and composed by Parucchepa.
The final verse, "With these new [songs] for us" (*sa no navyebhiḥ*), is a *triṣṭubh*; the remaining verses are *atyaṣṭis*.

In this case, the general rule regarding the *triṣṭubh* as the concluding verse is not applied, because it was specifically stipulated that "the entire middle section" [of the *maṇḍala*] consists of *atyaṣṭis*.
"O Indra, come! Ten others [follow]; the *triṣṭubh* [is next]," so says the *Anukramaṇikā*.
This is stated as the *niṣkevalya* [śastra] on the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*.
It is prescribed in the section titled "Of the Sixth" in the sūtra: "'O Indra, come toward us; forward indeed [the song] of this... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.1)."
In the *Mahāvrata* sacrifice, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*), this verse, "O Indra, come hither" (*endra yāhi*), serves as the *anurūpa* for the *Brāhmaṇacchaṃsin*.

This is prescribed by Śaunaka in the section on "The twenty-five [verses] of the *Mahāvrata*" as follows: "O Indra, come to us from afar; for the broad heaven has adorned itself for Indra" (*endra yāhyupa naḥ parāvata indrāya hi dyauramuro anajyata*; AiĀ 5.1.1). 1. [Variant readings:
In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, the word *cit* is glossed as "in the sense of contempt."
2. From the suffering that withers *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*; from the sorrow (*śoka*) of *cha*.

3. O *kṣa*, O *a*, O *ṭa*, you who cause [us] to pass away. Come to us from afar, O Indra, as one comes to the sacrificial assemblies (*vidatha*), like a lord of the virtuous (*satpati*), like a king to his home, a lord of the virtuous.
We, possessing milk, call upon you at the pressed juice,
as sons call upon their father for the winning of booty— upon you, the most bountiful, for the winning of booty.

O Indra, come hither to us from afar, even as a lord of the virtuous comes to the assemblies, as a king, a lord of the virtuous, comes to his home. We call upon you with milk-mixtures while the soma is pressed, like sons calling their father for the winning of booty—upon you, the most bounteous, for the winning of booty. 1.
O Indra, come to us from afar—from the distant regions characterized as heaven—and return to our presence.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"this [is] not."
The fire present before one, or Soma, is indicated here because it has been introduced;
he is like that.

Although the negative particle *na* is everywhere used in the sense of prohibition due to its conventional usage at the beginning of a statement, nevertheless, in this context, it is understood in the sense of comparison according to propriety.
Or alternatively: "from afar" means as if from a distant place;
even though he is always present at the sacrifice, nevertheless...
Ma. 1. A. 19. Mṛ. 130] Second Aṣṭaka: 825.
O Indra, you whose movement is desirable (vaṃsaga), drink the Soma!
The vowel lengthening occurs according to the rule "byo'tastiṅaḥ."
Of what sort is he?
He who is being pressed (*suvāna*), that is, being extracted, by means of the stones (*adri*) which are the instruments of pressing, and by the cows (*go*).
In the case of the object, there is an agentive suffix.
"Sprinkled with a vessel" means purified by the *daśāpavitra*, which serves as a vessel;
or rather,
it is to be construed together with the word "in the pit" (*avatame*).
"With a vessel" means with a characteristic; "sprinkled" means filled with its own sprinkled water. It is like a pit—that is, a depression characterized by a hollow.
Just as a *vaṃsaga*—one who moves toward what is desirable, a thirsty bull moving swiftly—drinks from it, so too does he. His drinking is not like that of a *vaṃsaga*.
Just as a thirsty bull, seeking desirable pasture, or a swift-moving man, having come to a watering place and the like, drinks—so it is here.
To the question "For what purpose does he drink?", he says:
"For your exhilaration (*madāya*)."
Just as he had conquered the demon Tama and, having burst open the door, obtained Vraja, so too, desiring to win—that is, wishing to share in—the Soma.
Because of the option [provided] by the rule "sarvādīni sarvanāmāni," there is the absence of the substitution of *haḍ*; thus, by the rule "janasana," there is the substitution of *ātman*.
They found [him];
this matter is well known from such Vedic passages as "Like cows by Paṇi" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.32.11).

Likewise, this Indra "opened"—that is, he made open or unbarred—the "doors," meaning the gateways, of the "waters," which are the waters that serve as the cause of food, even though they were "enclosed," meaning surrounded on all sides by clouds.
Having done so, he "spread out" (*parīvṛtāḥ*)—that is, he distributed upon the earth—the "desirable foods" (*iṣaḥ*), such as rice and other grains.
The meaning is that, having split the cloud with his thunderbolt and brought about the abundance of crops through the downpour of water, he spread rice and the like over the earth.
Since he has acted in this manner, the acceptance of the Soma is appropriate.
Firmly grasping the thunderbolt in his two hands, Indra—like a whistling arrow, with sharp-pointed fury—rushed forward; he rushed forward for the slaying of the serpent.
Gathering himself together with might and powers, O Indra, well-pleased, you strike down the tree like a woodcutter, you strike it down as with an axe.

Grasping the thunderbolt in his two hands, Indra—like a whistling arrow, sharp for hurling—has brandished it; he has brandished it for the slaying of Ahi. Enveloping him with might and powers, O Indra, being well-disposed, you thus strike down the tree with its branches; you strike it down like an axe.

This Indra, "dādṛhāṇaḥ" (firmly grasping)—from the root *dṛh* (to grow strong), with the suffix *kānac* in the perfect tense—held the thunderbolt firmly in his two hands (*agabhastyoḥ*, i.e., in his arms).
The forms *haha* and *rahi* denote growth.
The suffix *kānac* is used here.
*Gabhastī* is a name for the arms, as it is listed among their names in the Nirukta (2.4.6): "The two *gabhastī* are the two arms.
For what purpose?
"For the sake of striking (*asanāya*)—that is, for the destruction of the enemy—he thoroughly sharpens (*sam iyat*) the thunderbolt (*vajram*), which is *tigma*, meaning exceedingly sharp."
The root *śo* means "to thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*). The elision of the vowel *o* occurs according to the rule *otaḥ ini*.
The change to *ad* is Vedic (*chāndasaḥ*).
Alternatively,
in the leṭ mood, there is the elision of the letter *h* by the rule "itaśca lopaḥ."
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Like *kṣava*, like water.
Just as water is made sharp through consecration and other rites for the purpose of repelling enemies, so it is here.
*Kṣava* is a name for water, because it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (1.12.3): *kṣabha nāmaḥ*. That very point is further clarified:
"For the slaying of the serpent"—that is, for the slaying of the serpent Vṛtra, or the cloud.
From the root *han*, by the rule "hanasta ca," there is the suffix *kyap* and the substitution of *t* for the final letter.
"Saṃ iyat.
Even though [the enemy] was already fierce, he makes that being fierce again for the sake of slaughter.

O Indra, being fully endowed with *bhojas*—that is, with strength consisting of the capacity for defeat—and with *śavas*, that is, forces characterized as armies, and with *manjas*, that is, bodily strength; thus being perfectly equipped.
The form *vinvāna* is derived from the root with the suffix *kānac* of the perfect tense (*liṭ*);
the vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs according to the rule "pra-hi-jyā-vayaḥ."

"Likewise, 'like a tree. Just as someone who is a skilled woodcutter cuts down trees belonging to the forest—'avanīn' meaning those connected to the forest—he fells them completely for his own use and makes them thin by carving; in that same way, you too, acting crookedly toward us, cut down this enemy.
Furthermore, you cut him down 'as with an axe.'"
Just as someone cuts down a tree with an axe, so too do you utterly destroy our enemy with various kinds of forces.

1. By means of *kṣa-ja-ṭa*, he recovered [it] again; by means of *u*, having lifted it up, he recovered [it] again. 2. By means of *ca-pha*, he caused them to be opened. 3. By means of the power of the defeat of *kṣa-ja-ṭa*.
O Indra, you have released the waters to flow in vain toward the ocean, like two chariots seeking booty, like two chariots.
From here they have harnessed their aids for a common, inexhaustible purpose—
like milch-cows yielding all-desired milk for Manu, yielding all-desired milk for mankind.

O Indra, you have in vain urged the waters toward the ocean to flow, like chariots seeking booty, like chariots seeking booty. From here they have harnessed their aids for a common, inexhaustible purpose—like milch-cows yielding all desires for mankind, yielding all desires for the people. 5.
O Indra, you released the rivers toward the ocean so that they might flow forth effortlessly, without exertion; you brought them forth by bursting open the cloud.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like chariots.

Just as you have released the chariots toward our speech so that they may rush forward to reach it, so too [are these beings]. Furthermore, like those seeking booty—kings and others desiring battle or food—they release their chariots as if toward a conflict;
just as they release chariots to overcome the enemy in battle or to surpass plants and the like, even so [is this].
Because it ends in a kya-affix, the case-ending receives the udātta accent according to the rule "śaturanumaḥ."
Furthermore, from here, to the place in our vicinity.
The suffix *tasil* is used in the sense of the second case.
Toward us, you have sent forth—like rivers—aid that is "going" (protective) or "preserving"; for a common purpose, with a single aim, they have "yoked" the inexhaustible water.
The sense is: "By your grace."
The word *artha*, being a qualifier of water, is neuter in gender.
*Akṣitam* is a name for food, as it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (1.12.77): "The imperishable is outside.
Therein is the illustration:
"For Manu—for the sake of human desire—they became like milch-cows, yielding all things (*viśvadauhasaḥ*), that is, capable of being milked for every purpose."
Or, for whatever person whatsoever, for that purpose they are "all-yielding" (*viśvadauhasaḥ*), meaning they become providers of all milk;

or rather, for the sake of people— that is, for the benefit of all people— with reference to fish and other creatures, the rivers are "all-yielding," meaning they possess full capacity for yielding, flowing everywhere.
In this context, the rivers are figuratively described as "yielding milk" (*prīṇāt*);
thus, this is a praise of Indra alone, as he is the one who bestows rain that benefits the world in such a manner.

For you, these mortal men have fashioned this speech seeking wealth, as a skillful craftsman fashions a chariot; I have fashioned it for your favor. O Sage, adorning you like a noble steed for battles, like a courser for strength, they have fashioned you to win all riches—to win all treasures.

This speech have you, seeking wealth, fashioned for yourselves, O Āyus, as a skillful craftsman fashions a chariot; we have fashioned you for favor. Adorning you like a noble steed among the prize-winning horses, O Sage, like a courser for strength and the winning of riches—[we have fashioned you] for the winning of all riches. 6.
1. Ṅa-jña-accha: to intend to die facing toward that. 2. Ṅa-sartum: to go. 3.
Ṅa-jha-kṣa: "aprāpta" (unobtained) does not exist.
4. Ṅa: to flow forth; 5. Kṣa, Ḍa, Jha, Ña: they emit, they release;
6. Kṣa, Ja, Ṭa: those who milk all objects of purpose.

7. *Kṣa-va-ṭa*: [He is] for any mortal whatsoever; *Ṅa*: for any capable person whatsoever; *Jha*: for one capable of performing sacrifice. 8. *Ṅa*: Because of milking (*dohana*), they are metaphorically called "milk" (*doha*).
9. *Kṣa-va-ṭa*: Bestower of rain that benefits the world in such a manner; *Ṅa*: Bestower of rain that does not benefit the world in such a manner.

O Indra, for your sake—desiring *vasyas*, that is, desiring wealth for themselves—the *āyavas*, namely the officiating priests who possess the horses that are to be given as sacrificial offerings, have fashioned (*atakṣipuḥ*), that is, accomplished, this speech consisting of the praise being performed.
"Āyava" is a name for humans, as it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (2.3.17): "Āyavaḥ, Anavaḥ. They have produced this speech in the form of a hymn.
"Svapāḥ" means one who possesses beautiful deeds, that is, one who is skillful.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "somanasī," the first syllable of the final member is acute-accented (*udātta*). "Dhīraḥ" means wise. "Rathe na" means like a chariot.

Just as one performs it well with effort, so too, having done this, they have "fashioned you" (*atakṣipuḥ*) for "sumnāya," that is, for happiness; they produce you as favorable. *Sumna* is a name for happiness, as it is listed among those names in [Nirukta] 3.6.16: "subhraṃ subhyam."

Furthermore, O wise Indra, while beautifying you—making you bestow [bounties] through your virtues—they have fashioned you as one possessing speed (*vājin*) in battles (*vājeṣu*); that is, they please you with hymns of praise.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"just as [they fashion] the noble one (*jenyam*)."
Accomplishing [his purpose] for King Divodāsa.

In the root *day* (meaning giving, protecting, movement, injury, and giving), because it is marked with *p* (indicating it is *anudātta*), the *śānac* suffix is *anudātta*; thus, by the accentual rule for *l-sārvadhātuka* suffixes, the accent of the verbal root remains.
Not only was wealth sufficient for them, but he, bestowing all riches—including jewels, pearls, and so forth—by his own power (*ojasā*), that is, by his own strength, brought them down.
Indra protected the Aryan sacrificer among the tribes during the battles, he who possesses a hundredfold prosperity in the contests for the light;
for Manu, he subdued the black one whose vows were like those of a predatory beast.
As if burning, it consumes the entire world; it consumes that vital breath, it consumes the one who acts with malice.

Indra, in the battles, protected the Aryan sacrificer; he, the one with a hundred aids, [protected him] in all contests, in the contests for the winning of light. For Manu, he crushed the untruths; he subdued the black skin. As if burning, he consumes everything that has breath; he utterly consumes the leper. 8.

This Indra protects—that is, guards—the sacrificer, the worshipper, who is noble (*ārya*), worthy of being sought after (*araṇīya*), and one to whom all should go, during the *samats*, that is, in battles;
for *samatsu* is a name for battle, as it is read among its names in the Nirukta (2.17.22): "in *samatsu*, in encounters.
Furthermore, Indra, possessing a hundred powers (*śatabhūtiḥ*)—one whose protection for his devotees is immeasurable—is present among all.
There is a change of gender.
In all *ājis*—that is, in battles characterized by competition—he protected the sacrificer.
Likewise, in the *ājis* where the regions of heaven (*svarmāḻha*) pour forth light, or in great battles, he protected him by granting him heaven.
Regarding those heroes slain facing the enemy in battle, heaven is recorded by Parāśara: "These two persons in the world pierce the solar orb..."
"And the wandering mendicant engaged in yoga who is slain facing the enemy" (Parāśara 3.25). Regarding this, they relate a traditional account: there is a river named Aṃśumatī.
On its bank lived an asura named Kṛṣṇa, who was black in complexion and accompanied by ten thousand followers;
he remained there, afflicting the inhabitants of that region. Then Indra, urged by Bṛhaspati and joined by the Maruts, spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa and slew him along with his followers.
This is the meaning: "The drop settled upon the Aṃśumatī" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.96.13), etc., will be stated further on;
that is what is being said here. This Indra [acted] for Manu, for mankind.
An indeclinable is that which does not undergo case-inflection.
For the sake of human beings. "Ava-tān" means "unbend. "Vrata" is a name for ritual action.
He indeed instructed and harmed those who were devoid of that [faith] and were hostile toward the sacrifice.
The augment *aṭ* is applied after the verbal root *śās*.
Likewise, having mentioned the "black" skin—that is, the skin of black color—he "subdued," meaning he struck it down.
The root *radh* is used in the sense of "to injure. The augment *num* is applied by the rule *radhijabhor aci*.
As to the manner in which this occurs, it is said:
"Burning, he reduces it to ashes."
The augment *leṭaḍāgamaḥ* [is applied];
the suffix *sip* [is used] according to the rule *sibbahuḷam*.
Likewise, "the universe" consumes its vital breath;
for everything that is injurious burns after following it.
He says, "whatever remains, not even that."
For he completely consumes—that is, he burns without remainder—all that remains of the destructive Arśasāna after it has been struck down.
1. Not in battles. 2. Living beings who abide in the sight of *kṣa*, *jña*, *ṅa*, *ṭa*, and *taṃ*. 3. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-tadendraḥ*. 4. *Kṣa-aṭa-dhakṣata*. He seems to reduce [them] to ashes.
And the Sun, having been born with power, spreads his wheel; at the onset [of dawn], the ruddy one steals away the voice; the subduer steals it away.
When Uśanas came from afar, O Sage, he became manifest through his power.
May he grant all blessings like Manu, overcoming all as if with days.

The hero, born with might, has cast his wheel far away; at the time of departure, the ruddy one steals away our speech—he, the lord, steals it away. When you, O Sage, came from afar for our protection, you brought all blessings like a conqueror among men, winning all days as a conqueror.
Regarding this, they also relate an ancient history:
certain Asuras, having previously obtained a boon from Brahmā so that they might not be slain by Indra’s thunderbolt, became arrogant and did not submit to Indra.
Indra, in order to kill them, seized the wheel of the sun and struck them down.
This is what is said:
"This Indra is the sun of the sun."
The nominative case is used for the meaning of the word itself.
Having taken the wheel—the chariot’s wheel—with his own vital energy and physical strength, he, being born and fully endowed with power, has cast it forth.
The root *bṛh* is used in the sense of "lifting up";
it belongs to the *tudādi* class.

Furthermore, being ruddy—that is, red-colored and endowed with extreme brilliance—or alternatively, being of a wandering nature (*gamanaśīla*), having approached *prapitve*—that is, in their vicinity or having come near them—he steals away the voice, meaning the vital breath (*prāṇa*) characterized by speech; he has thoroughly stolen it or thoroughly exhausted it.
*Prapitve* is a name for what is near.
Or else:
He steals away their speech, which is the sound of their shouting;
when they are struck down, the sound itself becomes stilled—meaning he has slain them.
Or alternatively:
Indra himself, while abiding in heaven, dies by means of the Āditya-self.

Sūra, the Sun, having been born and risen, endowed with his own *ojas* (vital power) and splendor, "pushes forth the wheel"—that is, he vigorously raises the chariot characterized by its wheels, either for the purpose of dispelling darkness or for victory.

Prior to that, Aruṇa, the driver of that chariot, at the *prapitve*—meaning in the vicinity of the *prapitva* (the onset) of the Mandra-Asuras—steals away, or robs them of, their sound such as "Slay! or "Pierce! and so forth.
In the phrase "muṣettarasya bho'hāv api," the substitution of *śay* for *j* occurs according to the rule "chandasi śayaj api."

Immediately thereafter, the Sun, being capable of dispelling all darknesses or the Asuras, shines forth from every side with his rays. Now follows the section addressed directly [to the deity]: O Seer (kave), you of far-reaching vision, since you, for the sake of protection (ūtaye) of Uśanas—the great seer of that name—came (ajagan) from afar (parāvataḥ), that is, from the distant abode of heaven.
In the form *gameḥ*, there is the elision (*ślu*) of the suffix *śap* by Vedic rule (*chāndasa*) before the suffix *sip*;
then, following the elision of the initial vowel and the preceding consonant according to *halyādilopa*, the substitution of *na* for *m* occurs by the rule *amo no dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.64).
Or alternatively:
being joined with Uśanā (Uśanas), come hither (ajagan);

and having come, O Turvaṇi—meaning one who bestows quickly or one who distributes rapidly—become the distributor of all (viśvā) means of happiness (sumnāni), that is, riches, for us; this is the sense of the ellipsis.
‘Turvaṇiḥ tūrṇavaniḥ’—this is the Nirukta [6.14]. Therein is the illustration: *manuṣeva*, that is, like a human being.
Just as wealth desired from another region is brought for a lord by his own servant, so it is; or rather, like that of men— for men—
having taken all the riches (*sumnāni*) of the other three classes (*atrivijām*), you become victorious (*turvaṇiḥ*).
The same applies to us as well.
Not only on a single day of sacrifice, but on all days—indeed, throughout every single day—be victorious;
or rather: [the same applies to us].
The meaning is: "O Turvaṇi, just as you grant all days—every single day—as well as super-sensory vitality and longevity, so too grant us blessings; give us both."

1. Struck by *kṣa-na-ṭa*; struck by *ḍa*. 2. *Kṣa-ḍa-ja-ṭa* robs [it]. 3. *Kṣa-ḍa-ya-ṭa* is shattered. 4. *Kṣa-ma-ṭa* has burned up. 5. *Kṣa-ḍa-ja-ṭa* [is] on all sides. 6. By the thief *kha*. 7. *A-ha-ja-ṭa* comes to be.

O Indra, shatterer of forts, protect us with your powerful protections through our new hymns of praise, O bull of mighty deeds! May you, being praised by us like Divodāsa, increase for us as the sky increases by days.

O Indra, performer of manly deeds, destroyer of forts, protect us with your powerful and effective guardians through our new hymns. O Indra, being praised by us like the Dāsa of heaven, may you increase us as the sky grows with the passing days.
O Indra, you of virile deeds, who rains down desired boons, who possesses abundant wealth, and who shatters the cities—O destroyer of the cities of the Asuras!

Regarding the reading "sudhā-mantritaiḥ," because the entire group of six words beginning with the vocative [“sudhā”] starts the quarter-verse (pāda), it possesses the udātta accent on its first syllable according to the rule for vocatives at the beginning of a pāda.

O you of such great majesty, being pleased now by our new hymns (*uktha*)— that is, by the modes of praise presented at this time— protect us with your guardianship (*pāyu*) and with beneficial (*śagma*) comforts pertaining to both this world and the next. Furthermore, O Indra, [be gracious] to those born of the lineage of Divodāsa (*divodāsa*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied because [the word] does not begin with the letter *ś*.
2. By us, the Parucchepas;
or rather, the plural number is used for the sake of honor.
Praising and being praised.
An agentive suffix occurs when the object is expressed.
May you grow; become fully grown.
In the case of the root *vṛdh*, there is the substitution of *bh* for *śap* in the *liṅ* [optative] mood; this is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Like what? Like the sky by means of the days.
Just as the radiant sun becomes fully increased by the well-known days, so too may he become exceedingly increased by our praise; this is the meaning.
The fifth hymn consists of seven verses beginning with “indrāya hi. According to the Anukramaṇikā, it begins with “indrāya sapta. Parucchepa is the seer (ṛṣi).
Now follows the *aṣṭicchandas* hymn.
Indra is the deity.

On the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭha* rite, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*), the *hotraka* priests, having formed this hymn into three recitations (*ṛc-traya*) within their respective *śastra*s, should introduce it after the *ārambhaṇīyā* verses.
In this regard, the division is as follows:
the first portion of the meat belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa;
the three portions beginning with the third belong to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
The last three [verses], beginning with the fifth, belong to the Acchāvāka.
This is formulated in the section on "the fourth day" as follows: "On the sixth day, for Indra indeed, the Asura Dyaus bent down; in this very same way... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).
On that very day, at that same pressing, the verses beginning with the sixth are to be recited one by one before the *praśna* (questioning) of the Praśāstṛ and others.
In the section titled "Of the Sixth," it is sūtra-ed: "'For Indra, indeed, the Asura Dyaus bowed down' is the *pada* [Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.1].
In the *Niṣkevalya* of the Mahāvrata, for the triplet beginning with "For Indra, indeed," the second verse is used as the *anurūpa* in case of deficiency.
In the section titled "Of the Mahāvrata," it is sūtra-ed: "'O Indra, come hither from afar; for Indra, indeed, the Asura Dyaus bowed down' [Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.1.1]."
For Indra indeed the heaven bent low its vastness; for Indra the great earth with its wide expanses, with the expanses of the joined ones.
All the gods, of one accord, have placed Indra at their head.
For Indra let all human libations be offered; let all human offerings be given to him.

For Indra indeed the Asura Dyaus bowed down; for Indra the great Earth with her expanses [bowed], in the winning of glory, with her expanses. All the gods, of one accord, have placed Indra at their head. For Indra let all human oblations be presented; let all human gifts be given to him. 1.
1. By means of the *uktha* verses containing the syllables kṣa, ṅa, jña, jha, a, ṭa, and hyai; 2. by means of those containing ca, pāhacchepaiḥ;
3. for those beginning with kṣa, ṅa, ña, ṭa, pra, ā, sthita, thā, and yā.

The heaven (*dyauḥ*)—meaning the luminous world of heaven (*dyuloka*) and the host of gods (*devasaṃgha*) residing therein—is *asuraḥ*, one who has the nature of expelling (*nirasanaśīlaḥ*) enemies; and that [host] indeed bows down (*anannata*), becoming spontaneously submissive, for *indrāya* alone, for Indra himself. The form *nameta* is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) used in the sense of the agent as object (*karmakartṛ*) in the *laṅ* tense according to Vedic usage. The absence of the *ya*-affix is due to the rule *na duhastunamām* (Pāṇini 3.1.89).
The *śap* [affix] is elided (*ślu*) by Vedic usage;
there is an absence of the *halādiśeṣa* [substitution];
and there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*).
The word *hi* has the sense of "well-known" (*prasiddha*).
Likewise, for Indra—that is, for the sake of Indra—the great earth, the ground, or all the people residing there, bowed down.
In both cases, by means of a word denoting the locus (*āśraya*), the occupant (*āśrayin*) is indicated, just as in the expression "the village has arrived."
By what means? That is now stated:
"With *varīmabhiḥ*—that is, with choice hymns or oblations (*havirbhiḥ*).
Furthermore, when there is the occasion for the attainment of *yunaḥ*—whether it be life-force or glory—the sacrificers, joined with these choice oblations (*varīmabhiḥ*), become *brahmāṇaḥ*."
The word *ki* is derived from the root *san*; it takes the suffix *in*, and is classified as belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
The root *pi* takes the *auṇādika* suffix *san*.
Of what sort are we?

We are *vāyavaḥ*, that is, humans who are sacrificers (*yajamānāḥ*). By means of sacrifices (*yajñaiḥ*) as instruments, we "make you conscious" (*citayantaḥ*), just as one makes Indra conscious; the meaning is that we contemplate you with the thought that you are the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). We meditate upon you with the realization that you are the Supreme Lord.
Alternatively, the word *na* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
"Knowing you alone as Indra"—
thus, with hymns (*stomebhiḥ*), that is, with praises, we, the *vāyus*, going toward Indra, meditate upon you, Indra alone.
The *śap* suffix is elided after the root *dadhāti* according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Desiring aid, the pairs of combatants have stretched themselves out against you; at the winning of the cattle-pen, O Indra, they have come forth seeking you, they have come forth.
When you bring together the two contending parties who are striving for heaven, you gather them up.
Making manifest the bull that is his constant companion, the thunderbolt that is his constant companion—O Indra, the pairs of men, seeking aid, have stretched themselves out for you;

at the winning of the stall of cattle, they release [the waters], O Indra, they release them together. When you bring together two contending peoples who seek the light of heaven, you make manifest the bull that is your constant companion, the thunderbolt, O Indra, your constant companion.
O Indra, for you, the sacrificers— accompanied by their wives as couples— stretch out the sacrifice;
or rather,
they cause themselves to be consumed in the sacrifice through the offering of milk and other such substances.
Regarding "tasu upakṣaye":
in the Vedic *liṭ* (perfect tense), there is the substitution of *rebh* for *ir* according to the rule "iryo re. For what purpose?

It should not be argued that, because the person alone is the subject of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) in all cases— whether in the obligatory injunctions such as the *agnihotra*, in the occasional injunctions such as the *kārīrī* and *citrayajña*, or in the conditional injunctions such as "for whom [the sun] rises" or "whose house [it enters]"— therefore only he has the qualification (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, it should not be claimed that although a woman possesses ownership (*svāmitva*), she lacks qualification because she lacks learning (*vidvattā*) due to the absence of Vedic study, and consequently lacks the requisite capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Although a woman has no independent entitlement (*adhikāra*), nevertheless, according to the third and fourth sections of the sixth chapter on entitlement in the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā*, this very entitlement belongs to the woman; and because she is not separate from her husband—as seen in the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires, "The wife and husband shall establish the fires together"—and because in the *Smṛtis* it is stated, "For women there is no separate knowledge, nor is there a vow" (Manu 5.155), which prohibits any independent entitlement, the woman’s entitlement is indeed that which is shared with her husband.

Even in the absence of formal study, because of the author of the Sūtras’ statement, "Having given the Veda to his wife, he should have her recite it" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.11), and because of the injunctions such as "the wife sits nearby" (*patny anvāste*) which prescribe the use of mantras like "May we [attain] good offspring through you" (*suprajasaḥ tvā vayam*) from the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (1.1.10.1), wherever there is such an injunction, she has the right to that very mantra. For according to the maxim, "What can one do with an injunction? There is no burden too heavy for an injunction," this is established. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that "the couple performed the sacrifice. Of what kind were they?
Desiring satisfaction for themselves or for Indra, they strove; they poured out the oblation entirely, consuming it. They were capable.
The meaning of *sakṣati* is "together with. [The phrase] *vītvā sambhajamānāḥ* means "dividing among themselves.
Those very same [beings] are further qualified.
"Vnisṛjaḥ" means those who cause the evil that obstructs the attainment of the fruit to depart.
What is the distinction therein? That is stated:
"Because," for which reason, "gavyantāḥ" means desiring the cow for themselves.
1. jha—“Like Indra.
2. kṣa-ja-ṭa-sa—“As if with a companion.
3. kṣa-ṅa-jha-ja-ṭa-ka—“One would not act according to the word”; ca—“What, then, would one do by means of the word?”
Ka. 105: Desiring.

From the word *go*, by the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* [Pāṇini 3.1.8], and by the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* [Pāṇini 6.1.79], there is the substitution of *av*. "O you who lead the two people—the husband and wife—who desire to go to heaven (*svaryantau*), you bring together the two persons in union; indeed, you cause them to attain their desired goal, such as heaven.
Or else:
Even though you have determined that they have performed [the rite] correctly, the meaning is that they perform it together with their wives (*pānīsahitā*).

Furthermore, O Indra, you manifest—that is, you exist—revealing the rain-bestowing (*vṛṣaṇam*), desire-granting thunderbolt (*vajram*) which is *sacābhuvam*, existing together with you, never being separate from you; likewise, by its capacity for activities such as the slaying of enemies, it is *sacābhuvam*, existing together with you. (The word "you exist" is to be supplied.)
Many fortresses were shattered by this heroism of yours, O Indra, when you, the subduer, overcame the autumnal waters.
O Indra, Lord of Might, punish the mortal who does not sacrifice; rejoicing, you won the vast earth and these waters—you won these waters.

The wise ones say: "O Indra, you are the one before whom these Purus stand, because you, O Indra, are the victorious one who overcomes the autumnal host; you are the one who overcomes them. O Indra, Lord of Might, punish that mortal who offers no sacrifice. Rejoicing, you have won for yourself this great earth and these waters—these very waters. 4.
O Indra, this [is] of your heroic power; it belongs to you, to this heroic power.
The sixth case ending is used in the sense of the object.
The wise know this vigor which is about to be described.
Those ancient men who, as sacrificers, knowing your greatness, worship you alone—they are the ones who know.
Or alternatively: [they know] that...
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "the greatness of this heroism."
In the word *viduṣṭe*, the *s* is substituted for the *visarjanīya* by the rule *yuṣmattattatthyu*.
Vigor alone is being distinguished here.

O Indra, because you have destroyed—the word *avārtaḥ* meaning "you caused to perish"—the autumnal cities of the enemies, those cities belonging to the year, fortified for the duration of a year with ramparts, moats, and the like.
The root *tṛ* preceded by the prefix *ava* has the meaning of destruction.
Doing what? Overpowering those residing there—overcoming them by seizing their wealth and so forth, and afflicting them.
The suffixes *tācchīlika* (denoting habitual action) and *cānaś* occur after a root ending in *yaṅ-luk*.

Furthermore: O Indra, you have subdued—that is, you have restrained—that mortal subject to death, the non-sacrificer, the obstructer of sacrifice, such as a Rākṣasa or similar being. O Lord of Might (*śavasas-pati*), O Indra, protector of strength, you forcibly seized the great earth and these waters—the waters that flow toward the ocean.
The meaning is that you have shattered their cities and carried away the waters associated with them—the earth and the waters that had been seized by the Asuras, those haters of sacrifice.
Why [should this be] a cause for sorrow?
He says: "No."
Smiling—that is, rejoicing—you indeed seized these waters and these foods, such as rice and other grains.
1. By the power of your own activity, [you possess] *kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*, *śa*, *va*, and so forth.
2. [You are] to be manifested by *kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa*.

3. You have indeed harmed *ḍa*, *rākṣasa*, and so forth; you have made *jha*, *rākṣasa*, and so forth thin; you have chastised (*śāsa*) *kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*, *rākṣasa*, and so forth—that is, you have restrained them or made them thin.
4. You have brought back the *kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa*.
5. Even while being satisfied:
"The sons of Aditi shall celebrate this heroism in their exhilarations, O Bull, when you protected; when you protected those who sought your friendship."
You have made them subject to the Kārakas so that they may prevail in battles; seeking glory and desiring to win, they shall surely win one victory after another.

Truly, O Bull, those who yearn for you shall celebrate this heroism of yours in their exhilarations, since you protected those fleeing in battle; since you protected them, you have performed a great deed for them so that they might prevail in the conflicts. Now, seeking glory and desiring to win, they shall surely gain one victory after another. 5.
O Indra, for this very reason—for the sake of that heroic power belonging to you, in order to increase it—they have repeatedly praised you; they scatter the Soma again and again.
From the root *kṛ* with the *yaṅ*-luṅ suffix, the affix *śa* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

Sacrificers bestow [offerings] during all the pressings (*savanas*). To the question "From where [do they do so]?", it is said: "In the exhilarations (*madeṣu*)"—that is, while the exhilarations produced by Soma exist—"O Showerer (*vṛṣan*), you who rain down desires, because (*yat*) you protect (*āvitha*) the 'eager ones' (*uśijaḥ*), the sacrificers who long for you."
Furthermore, since you have protected (*āvitha*)—that is, satisfied and gladdened with what is desired—us who desire friendship with you as your friends, they therefore celebrate you.
Moreover, O Indra, for these sacrificers you have made, and continue to make, a sound (*kāram*), characterized by the lion’s roar.
The suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *kṛ* in the sense of the object (*karman*);
by the rule "karṇāvataḥ," there is udātta accent on the final syllable.
Where is that? It is said:
"In *pṛtanāsu*, meaning in battles. For what purpose?"
"To advance" means to go forth pre-eminently, that is, to engage in battle;
for it is the brave who engage in combat.
The suffix *tasi* is applied in the sense of "going to" (*vanam atastum arthe*).
By the rule "tādau ca," the accent of the base (*prakṛtisvaratvam*) applies to the root *gam*.
Furthermore: "O you, the mistress of battle, those [enemies] of yours—'anyāmanyām' meaning one after another, and 'anyamanyaṃ prati' meaning toward one another."
In the case of reciprocal action, the dual number is used for a pronoun.
"And there is neither distress nor prosperity."
The root *ṛdhu* means "to increase" (*samṛddhau*).
Here, the substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvasvaratva*) is set aside by the Vedic (*chāndasa*) application of the *yaṇ* substitute.
Those who are about to attain [it] enjoy it together.
In *saner laṭi*, by the rule "sicaḥ kluḥ," there is *sip*.
By transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is again the suffix *ā*.
The substitution of *ad* [for the final letter] occurs because of the rule "ātmanepadadhvanataḥ"; the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule "śāmyamatoyorātaḥ";
and the absence of the change of *ṭi* to *e* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Likewise, "desiring," that is, longing for food not yet obtained, they "seek to win," that is, they strive to enjoy it.
And may he be pleased with us at this dawn; indeed, take notice of our hymn and our oblation through our invocations, in the winning of the light through our invocations.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, when you, the bull, intend to slay the adversaries, listen to this prayer of mine, of this most recent worshipper, listen to the prayer of this most recent one.

And so, may he indeed take pleasure in this dawning of ours; be mindful of the hymn and the oblation through our invocations, at the winning of the light through our invocations. O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, when you, the bull, intend to slay the adversaries, listen to the prayer of me, this most recent worshipper—listen to the prayer of this most recent one. 6.
This Indra [is the one] for us, our own, during these approaching dawns.
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
The sages have called this time of dawn "the thief of connections";
may Indra indeed take pleasure in it, may he even attend to our sacrifice at the very hour of dawn—
[in the intoxications produced by the drinking of Soma].
2. "Ṅa" signifies prosperity (samṛddhi).
"Dhā" signifies the act of holding or maintaining. "Hi" is for the purpose of filling out the meter.
And having gone, [there is] "of the oblation of Akṛśya.
As before, the sixth case ending follows the sequence.
The oblation is the means of worship; it is the oblation offered by means of "havīmabhiḥ," which are specific modes of offering.
"Utta said: 'May you indeed know [this].
Furthermore, at the sacrifice—which is the place for the enjoyment of heaven or some other specific happiness—may you be summoned by the *havis* offerings, that is, by the invocations;
the sense is: being summoned by us, may you accept the oblation of Upastheva Āgāra.'"
Why is this said?
Because, O Vajrin—O wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra—you, being a showerer (*vṛṣā*) of desires, perceive (*cike*) them in order to slay (*hantave*) the enemies (*mṛdhaḥ*), those who cause harm;
the root *kit* means "to know."
It belongs to the *juhotyādi* class. The suffix *leyya* is an augment.

According to the rule "not before a vowel following a reduplicated stem (*nābhyastasyāci pitī*)"—specifically due to the statement "frequently in the Veda (*chandasi bahulam*)"—there is no prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel.
Because it is the first word of a repeated passage, it has the udātta accent on its initial syllable.
Therefore, we say:
O Indra, "ā śrudhi"—listen from all sides to "me," my "manma," the hymn worthy of being meditated upon.
Of what kind am I? "Of a *vedhas*, that is, of one who is wise;
of a *navīyas*, that is, of one who is ever-new."

Because they have been refined by the consecratory rites (*dīkṣita-saṃskāra*), they possess a state of being "newer. They are further qualified as "newer" (*navīyāṃsaḥ*), meaning exceedingly fresh and possessing unique praise.
In this context, by means of these epithets of the sacrificer, the hymn performed by him is itself distinguished:

"O Indra, growing strong and well-disposed toward us, O many-born one, [protect] the mortal who seeks friendship; O hero, with your thunderbolt, slay the mortal who intends evil against us. Listen, you who are most renowned!"
Let not ill-will come upon us on our journey; let all ill-will depart from us.

O Indra, growing strong and well-disposed toward us, you who are born with great power, O hero, slay with your thunderbolt the mortal who acts as an enemy, the mortal who seeks to harm us. Listen, O most renowned of hearers! Let not ill-will come upon us on our journey; let all ill-will depart from us. 7. You... him... O Indra... increasing... well-disposed toward us... acting as an enemy... O one of many births... mortal... with the thunderbolt... O hero... mortal... slay... he who... seeks to harm us... listen... O most renowned of hearers... let not ill-will come upon us on our journey... let all ill-will depart from us. 7.

O Indra, you who are born after us, having attained great abundance through our praise, O hero, O valiant one, increasing exceedingly and desiring us—those devoted to you—you must strike down with your thunderbolt that mortal who acts as an enemy toward us, that mortal whose nature is subject to death.
[Note: Regarding the form *jahi*: there is a substitution of *han* for *hantejaḥ*;
because this is considered *asiddha* (unestablished) in this context by the rule "asiddvadatrā bhāt," the elision of the *hi* does not occur.]
Regarding that which was said as "him," he asks "whom? He says: "The mortal who 'aghāyati'—that is, desires evil or suffering for 'naḥ,' us—slay him.
The substitution of *ā* [for *i*] occurs according to the rule "aghāghasyāt."
Furthermore: "O you who are most excellent in hearing (*suśravastamaḥ*), listen to our words and cause them to be heard!
What is that [which we ask]? It is said: O Indra, by your grace, let *durmatiḥ*—the evil intention directed toward our destruction—*apa bhūnu*, that is, depart."
The *śap* suffix is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). There is a prohibition of *guṇa* substitution by the rule *bhūsuvostiṅi*.
Not only [the waters] in the form of snow, but indeed all (*viśvā*) forms such as anger and slander—[O Agni], "drive away" (*abhunūḥ*) them.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"On every path, on every journey, may there be no harm.

Just as one who is afflicted by the fatigue of the road—stricken and exhausted—is oppressed by a wicked thought directed toward food and drink, so too may that wicked thought which oppresses us depart.
Or alternatively:
just as you ward off obstacles on the path of the Yamas—such as the destruction of sacrifices and the like, or hindrances consisting of the injury caused by demons and so forth—in that same manner.
The sixth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "tvayā 'vayam," is addressed to Indra, composed by Parucchepa, and dedicated to the Āptyas.
The verse beginning with "yuvaṃ tam" is addressed to Indra and Pūṣan.
The Anukramaṇī states: "'tvayā 'vayam' [is] six [verses]; 'yuvaṃ nam' [is] addressed to Indra and Pūṣan."
The application is indicated by the context.

1. *kṣa-na-ṭa*—and your name is "Asan" (?). 2. It is said (*ucyate*). 3. *kṣa-ma-ṭa*—*asmaji*—possessed by the desire to strike. 4. *kṣa-na-ṭa*—*adhadhramaṇa*. 5. *kṣa-na-ṭa*—in such a way that you ward off obstacles (*vighna*).
O Maghavan, protected by you, O Indra, may we overcome those who attack us with ancient wealth; may we conquer those who seek to conquer us.
On this most proximate day, speak now in favor of the one who presses the Soma;
at this sacrifice, may we distribute the prepared portion, seeking booty—may we distribute the prepared portion.

Through you, O Maghavan, may we, aided by Indra, overcome those who advance with ancient riches; may we conquer those who seek to conquer us. On this most near day, speak now in favor of the one who presses the soma; at this sacrifice, may we, seeking strength, distribute the winnings; may we, seeking strength, distribute the winnings. 1.
O Maghavan! *Magha* means happiness;
you are endowed with that [happiness] as your means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
We—
precisely for this reason, being protected by you, Indra, who possess exceeding power; the substitution of *tvā* [for *tvayā*] occurs according to the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca*.
The first is the Vedic.
May we withstand—that is, overcome—the powerful armies of the enemies who extend their reach and desire to prevail over us.
Likewise, may we strike down those enemies who come against us with weapons; even before their arrival, may we be prepared to meet them.
Furthermore, speak on behalf of the sacrificer who presses the soma today—on this most proximate day, on this very present day—at this sacrifice for the sake of ancient wealth.
Speak now further and more extensively concerning that sacrificer who bestows the oblation, or concerning the sacrifice itself.
In the imperative (loṭ), by transposition, *ahaṭ* is substituted;
[and] *vac* becomes *um*.

Furthermore, O Indra, we, the sacrificers, seeking booty for the sake of victory in battle against those who have acted [against us], and offering oblations characterized by sacrificial food (*havis*) toward you— the achiever of victory— may we gather [for ourselves] hymns of praise and the like,
or the sacrificial offerings and the like.
The suffix *śap* is applied to the root *cinoti* by means of transposition.
Furthermore, what kind of you?
One who has acted—that is, a doer—at the *bhara* of the gods, meaning either in the victory over the Asuras in battle or in the perfect sustenance (*saṃbharaṇa*) of the gods.
*Bhara* is a name for battle; Yāska says, "It is derived from the root *bhṛ* (to bear) or *hṛ* (to carry)" (Nirukta 4.24).
In the pressing of the pure one, they have raised up the burden in his own praise, in his own wisdom;
in his own wisdom, Indra has slain [the foe] as is known, for every head he acts as a priest.
May those gifts of yours be gathered together—those auspicious gifts of the auspicious one.

In the winning of light, in the bringing of wealth, in the speech of the worshipper; at the dawning of the dawn, in his own wisdom; in the action of the active one, in his own wisdom. Indra slew [Vṛtra] as is known; he is to be praised head by head. O you who protect the waters, may your gifts be gathered together; auspicious are the gifts of the auspicious one. 2.
1. O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, [protect] the *ḍa*, *ca*, *pha*, and wealth. 2. In the eastern battle for wealth preceded by *jha*, they were protected by you, the exceedingly powerful Indra.
3. May we overcome *kṣa*, *jha*, and *ṭa*.
The form *sahorlīḍhi* is Vedic, involving the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*;
it is the end of a *yaṅ*-lopped (*yaṅ-luk*) formation.
Likewise.

4. In this sacrifice, there is no wealth preceded by *kṣa*, *ja*, *jha*, or *ṭa*. 5. For the one who presses [the Soma] (*sunvate*) and provides protection (*abhipadham kurva-te*), [there is wealth] preceded by *kṣa*, *ja*, or *ṭa*. 6. And for the sake of victory over the skin (*tvajayārtham*), [there is wealth] preceded by *ca* or *pa*.
7. Those who approach with patience and bestow [gifts]; those who conduct themselves with care and move about [righteously].
8. The one who maintains the victory of *ca* and *pha*.
This Indra, in the battle for the winning of light—that is, in the conflict for the attainment of heaven—[is the victor].
For one slain facing the enemy in battle, heaven is attained; this is well-known in such Smṛtis as: "These two persons in the world pierce the solar orb" (Parāśara 3.25).
[The word] *vāpra* means one who is prone to falling (*āpanna-śīla*). [It refers to] Vyāsa, who was intent on the destruction of his enemies. The suffix *ra* is derived according to the Uṇādi rules.
In his own horse, which is the path accessible to a hero, manifest, free from deceit and the like;
he is further qualified by the word "in his own":
in his own, primary, and direct [horse] during the battle.
Or alternatively:
when the enemy has come of his own accord, unmasked, upon one's own chariot (*añjasi*), he strikes—that is, he slays—the enemies.
In whose battle? That is now stated.

He strikes—that is, he destroys—the enemies of this sacrificer (amya), who is *āpra* (one whose nature is to obtain), who is *āpanaśīla* (of a habit to obtain), who acts as the one who pleases Indra on all sides (*ā samantāt*), who is *uparbudhaḥ* (awakening at dawn) for the sake of performing the rite at the time of dawn, and who is *pravadhyamānaḥ kāṇvasya* (being celebrated as belonging to the Kaṇva lineage) while performing the sacrifice;
[this is so] because of the elision of the *śap* suffix in the present participle (*śatṛ*) of the root *kṛ*, which is a Vedic usage.
He strikes the enemies of this sacrificer.
For this reason,
you have reached this state;
the meaning is that you are the bestower of rain.
Alternatively:
You are the one who leads the sacrificer to the *kṣaya*—the dwelling place, known as the heavenly world—of *ṛta*, the Āditya.
Therefore, proclaim, speak forth, that very deed which is about to be described.
Therefore, for this reason, they behold [the rain] within the intermediate space (antarikṣa) between the two—Heaven and Earth—by means of the rays, that is, the rays of the Sun.
Having pierced through the cloud, all people perceive directly the form of the pouring down of rain through the medium of the rays.
The meaning is that it is seen by everyone that you, having caused our offered oblation (havis) to reach the Sun, produce rain through those rays.
Now he praises [Indra] by way of indirect description:
"He, indeed, is that Indra, the seeker of cattle (*gaveṣaṇaḥ*), whose nature is to search for water;

likewise, he who has attained the state of a kinsman (*bandhuḥ*) through the offering of oblations and other acts, and who is the seeker of cattle (*gaveṣaṇaḥ*)—that is, the one who procures well-known cattle—for the sacrificers."
The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by virtue of the rule *bahulaka*;
or else,
[it is derived from] the root *gavep* in the sense of "searching."
For the suffix *hyuṭ* is applied as before.

The meaning is "one who seeks the fruit for the sacrificer. Furthermore, by following the aforementioned sequence, being the agent, he "finds" (vindet)—that is, he knows the manner of attaining water.
It is not to be proclaimed thus, nor as it was of old, how you opened the cow-pen for the Aṅgirasas, O Indra—opening the cow-pen while bestowing your favor.
To them, and to us, you have given in the same direction; you shall speak for us and you shall fight for us.
Yield up whosoever to those who press the Soma—the one who seeks to violate the sacred law, even him who violates the law.

Now, indeed, this is to be proclaimed for you as it was of old: that you, O Indra, opening the pen for the sake of the Aṅgiras, gave them their release—opening the pen while bestowing your aid. To them, in the same manner, you have granted your favor; for us, you shall win and fight. Subdue every lawless one, even the defiant lawless one, for those who press the Soma.

O Indra, this deed of yours—of the kind described or of the form about to be mentioned—is to be proclaimed quickly by all as being "just so," like that of former times; even now, it remains worthy of praise.
In the word *na itthā*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) because of the rule "haṃṣākṣaditvāt."
What was that? It is explained as follows:

You opened (*apāvṛṇoḥ*)—that is, you tore open—the *vraja*, the cloud moving in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), for the sake of the Aṅgirasas, those great seers (*maharṣi*) of successive generations; having torn the cloud apart, you brought forth rain.
*Vraja* is a name for a cloud, as it is listed among the names for clouds in the Nirukta: “*vrajaḥ*, *varāhaḥ*” (Nirukta 1.10.11).
Furthermore, O Indra, having struck down the Paṇis, you protected the herd of cows by bestowing them upon those very Aṅgirases.
Or rather,
you opened the cave in order to seize the herd of cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis and was situated within it.
You have opened the door. Moreover, O Indra, just as you give to these seers (ṛṣis) from this direction by a common way—that is, by an equal manner—so too do you grant us wealth or victory in battle;
for that purpose, strive and fight!
In accordance with Vedic usage, there is the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*);
by transposition, the *parasmaipada* ending is employed.

Furthermore, for us who press the soma for our own sake—those performing the extraction (*sunvadbhyaḥ*)—subject (*randhaya*) every single person who violates the vow (*vrata*), even one who does not sacrifice (*ayajvānam*) or acts in opposition to the sacrifice; that is to say, oppress and bring them under my control.
Not only those who do not sacrifice, but even one who seeks to harm (*ghnāyantam*) while violating the vow.
In that which is censured by consciousness.

Subdue him who bears malice toward us— himself the one who fails to sacrifice, or even he who is full of wrath; or rather, subdue him who seeks to strike us, even while he himself incurs our anger, making that lawless one, devoid of ritual action, incapable of striking back again.
‘Haṇīṅ’ means ‘to be angry.
It belongs to the *kaṇvādi* class; the vowel *ā* [in the root] occurs by way of metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

1. That which was stated in *kṣa-ja-ṭa* will be explained [here]. 2. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*: "In the midst" means in the intermediate space (*antarikṣe*). 3. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*: "To those who have attained. 4. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*: "It is said. 5. *Jha*: "Having produced. 6. *Ka-jha-kha-ca-jña-ṭa-ṇa-ta-pha-va*: "[The one] who made the door of the forest retreat open. 7. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*: "The middle. 8. *Kha-ca-ja-jha-ṇa-pha-va*: "[The one] possessing wrath. 9. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*: "Making. O Hero, you who inspire us with sacrifices and rites, when the goal is set, those seeking glory strive to overcome; those seeking glory press forward in worship. *saṃ yajñanān kratubhiḥ śūra īkṣayann aṃhite taruṣanta śravasyavaḥ | pra yakṣanta śravasyavaḥ ||*
For him, they sing with power for life accompanied by progeny;
Indra’s inspired thoughts desire a dwelling-place, as our inspired thoughts yearn toward the gods.

When the Hero causes men to perceive with their mental powers, they overcome [the enemy] when the prize is set; seeking glory, they press forward; seeking glory, they offer worship. To him, Indra, who possesses life and progeny, they sing with power in times of distress. The prayers desire to establish Indra as their home; the prayers go forth toward the gods. 5.
Indra, who is the heroic and valorous one, causes all people—that is, all living beings—to see correctly through his *kratus*, meaning through his powers of wisdom;
that is to say, abiding as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) within the intellects of all, he delineates their respective objects.
Or alternatively:
He joins [beings] with various fruits corresponding to their good and evil deeds through sacrifices and rituals that serve as the causes for those results.
While he thus impels them, the sacrificers—desiring food (*vśravasyavaḥ*)—find wealth in the form of cattle and other desirable things.
Or alternatively:
When the desired wealth that is beneficial is present,
they overcome— that is, they slay— their enemies;
for the root *tṛ* has the sense of killing.
In the Vedic *luṅ* tense, by transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is the *aṅ* suffix for *cli*;
or, in the *laṅ* tense, from the root *tṛ*, there is the vowel *u* [as *atarīt*]. Thus, there are three verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇas*) that are free from fault.
The meaning is "they cross over.
For this reason, being *śravasyavaḥ*—that is, desiring food characterized by the oblation for Indra or for themselves—they have *pravyakṣanta*, meaning they sacrifice with excellence.
In the Vedic *luṅ* tense, there is a substitution of *vas* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Furthermore, to him—to that well-known Indra alone—Vāyu offers food characterized by the oblation, accompanied by progeny, meaning together with sons and so forth;
that is, he is honored along with them. Moreover, when there is an occasion for the warding off of enemies (*bādhe*), let the sacrificers, endowed with their own strength, drive them away.

The suffix *ken* is applied [to the root *stu*] in the sense of "for the purpose of purchase," according to the rule: "After the roots *krī*, *drū*, and *stu*, the suffix *ken* is used when expressing the object of purchase."
They shine forth and worship;
or rather,
for that very sacrificer (yajamāna), when there is need or force as the cause.
*Bādha* is a name for strength, as it is listed among its synonyms in the Nirukta (2.9.8): *bādhas tadhipī*.
Endowed with *ojas*, that is, strength, they worship—that is, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) praise—Indra in order to obtain life accompanied by progeny, such as sons, and food.
Furthermore, the *dhītayas*, meaning the sacrificers who possess ritual action, [are] near Indra.
Just as in the expression "the hamlet on the Ganges," proximity is indicated;
the meaning is "in the world of Indra.
There, *vokya* means a dwelling place or abode.
The suffix *yat* is used in the sense of the word itself (*svārtha*).
*vdidhiṣanta* means "they hold" (dhārayanti).
[The root] *dhipa* is used in the sense of sound (*śabda*);
here, however, it has the meaning of holding (*dhāraṇa*).
It belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class;
the substitution of the final vowel occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
These same [beings] are further specified:

being *vidhātṛ*s—possessors of the rites that accomplish heaven—they desire (*didhiṣanti*) a dwelling place (*okya*) as if it were already attained in the presence of the gods (*devān*), just like the gods themselves; such is the syntactical connection.

On this day, after the mental cup-offering (*mānasa-graha*) has been consumed, when the constellations (*nakṣatra*) have become visible, all the priests, headed by the Adhvaryu, should mutter the verse, "O Indra and Parvata, you two...

This is prescribed in the section beginning with "They offer in the Gārhapatya fire" in the *Sūtra*: "Muttering, 'O Indra and Parvata, you two who fight at the front... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.13).
1. They offer along with the letter *jha* and evil; 2. they maintain and fashion with the letter *ha*;
3. they possess the karma that accomplishes the emission (*sarga*) by means of the letter *ṅa*.

O Indra and Parvata, you who fight in the van, strike down with your thunderbolt every one who attacks us, strike him down, indeed, strike him down! Even if he seeks to harm us from afar, let him perish like a fragile vessel. O Hero, may the destroyer rend our enemies on every side, rend them completely on every side!

O Indra and Parvata, you two who fight from the front—strike down each one who would attack us; strike him down with the thunderbolt, strike him down each and every one. May he flee far away, seeking a hiding place to escape; O Hero, may the Destroyer crush our enemies on every side, crush them from all directions.
Now, "O Indra and Parvata": Indra is well-known; Parvata is the cloud, so called because it possesses joints (parvan).
The deity presiding over that [sacrifice] is the god.

You two—meaning "you both"—acting as "puroyudhā," warriors fighting at the front in battle, [subdue] "naḥ" our "yaḥ śatruḥ" whatever enemy "pṛtnyāt" desires to strike us down in the fray; "taṃ tam it" every single such enemy, I burn up entirely within both heaven and earth by means of Truth (*ṛtena*), consuming those great ones who are devoid of Indra.
Where the enemies were struck down after being overwhelmed, they lay scattered all around Vailasthāna.

Both, by name, the two worlds, I burn with the *ṛta*—the oppressors. I consume the great ones who are without Indra, having overwhelmed them where the enemies, struck down and scattered, lay around the place of destruction. 1.

O Indra, by means of *ṛta*—that is, by the sacrifice directed toward you, by your power—I purify both *rodasī*, heaven and earth; indeed, I cleanse the two worlds by the removal of those who cause harm or by the departure of the unrighteous.

Furthermore, in this world, I utterly consume at once those great and vast regions that serve as the refuge for the *anindras*—those devoid of Indra—and which are themselves the abodes of the malicious (*duhas*) and thus inherently malicious; I burn them all together in a single stroke. Moreover, these very regions are further specified.
In whichever lands or regions enemies—that is, foes—having been surrounded, having gone around, and having been struck down on all sides, were either captured or slain by us.
The verbal root *vṛt* has the sense of "going" (*gati*), and it is a Vedic (archaic) root.
All of them were indeed completely consumed and destroyed.
The root *tṛh* has the meaning "to injure. Because it is marked with the letter *u*, the augment *iṭ* is prohibited by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*.
Having been struck down, they lay down, having reached their place of rest.
The *parasmaipada* ending is used for the root *śī* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). By Pāṇini’s rule 7.1.6, *ruṭ* is inserted after *śīṅ*.
Furthermore, there is *guṇa* substitution for *śīṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.
The term *bilasthāna*. The word *bila* has the same meaning as *garta* (a pit). And that pit refers to a cremation ground (*imaśāna*).
Therefore, this word also denotes a cemetery;
or else, it refers to the world of the Nāgas, a place connected to a cave,
where they resided.
Alternatively,
there is the verbal root *vil* in the sense of "to scatter" (*kṣepe*).
The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of "vajra."
The suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*).
Since corpses (*śava*) are cast there, it is called *vailasthāna*, meaning a cemetery (*imaśāna*).
There, having turned the ground into a cemetery by me, they all lie;
the meaning is that I burn them.
O Lord of the Maruts, even with your thunderbolt, sever the heads of the sorceresses;
trample them underfoot, trample the vaṭūrīs underfoot, trample the great vaṭūrīs underfoot.
Having praised thee, O wielder of the stone, sever the heads of the sorceresses; trample them with thy foot, O great one, trample them with thy foot.

O wielder of the thunderbolt (*adrivas*), O consumer of enemies (*vairiṇā bhakṣaka*), or rather, O Indra, you who consume the cloud (*adreḥ meghasya ādyataḥ*): [cut down] the armies of those possessed of *yātu*, that is, of those possessing harmful forces; or else, those possessing weapons which are the means of striking (*yātana-sādhanāni āyudhāni yātūni*); or again, those possessing *yātus*, that is, demons (*rakṣāṃsi*). [The genitive case here denotes the object. The armies of the enemies—having reached their very heads from all sides (*śīrṣā śīrṣāṇi abhivṛgya cit abhitaḥ prāpyaiva*), cut them down and crush them!

1. Or by the power of the six (cha-bala). 2. All [the letters] *ka*, *sa*, *ja*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *va*. 3. There is no [reading] "attained by *kṣa*, *ḍa*, *ña*, *ṭa*. 4. There is no [reading] "*kṣa*, *jha*, *jha*, *aṭa*-beyond. 5. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-hisantaḥ*: They lay around (*pari*) the cremation ground (*vailasthāna*), which is a cemetery (*smaśāna*). Alternatively, there is a verbal root *vila* meaning "to cast away" (*kṣepe*). The suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the *ghañ* suffix; the suffix *aṇ* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*). Since corpses (*śava*) are cast away (*kṣipyante*) there, it is the "place for casting" (*vailasthāna*), i.e., the cremation ground (*smaśāna*). The active voice (*parasmaipada*) is used by transposition (*vyatyaya*) from the root *śī*; the augment *ruṭ* is applied; and there is *guṇa* substitution for *śīṅ* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. The word *bila* has the same meaning as *garta* (pit/hole). That pit refers to the cremation ground; therefore, this [word *vailasthāna*] also denotes a cremation ground. Or else, it is a place connected to a hole, namely hell (*naraka*). It means they lay there. In that case, the earth struck by you... the meaning is: "I burn them. 6. *Kṣa-ña-ja-ṭa-he adrivaḥ* ("O wielder of the thunderbolt!"). 7. *Kṣa-ca-ña-ṭa-instruments of torment* (*yātanā-sādhanāni*). 8. *Kṣa-cha-aṭa-many* (*bahūni*). 9. *Jha*: Even by merely reaching (*abhivṛgyā cit*) the armies of the enemies from all sides (*abhitaḥ*), cut them down and crush them.
Alternatively, [it refers to] the chariots and other emblems belonging to them. By what means? That is now stated.
"With a foot that is encircling" (*vaṭṭariṇā padā*) means with one's own foot characterized by the habit of encircling— that is, with a very wide foot.
Alternatively,
"with a foot that is encircling" means with the foot belonging to an elephant— that is, with the foot of Airāvata.
He says that it is not with just any foot at all:
"With a great encircling foot"—that is, with a foot possessing a great coil, belonging to a female elephant or to Airāvata—stamp, that is, crush [it].
The root *vaṭ* means "to surround.
The suffix *ura* is applied according to the rule *kharjipiñjyādibhya urolacau* (Uṇādisūtra 4.530). Then, the suffix *ini* is applied according to the rule *ata iniṭanau*.

O Maghavan, strike down the host of these sorceresses here; at Vailasthānaka, at Arbhaka, at Mahāvailastha, at Arbhaka. 3. arvā | āsām | maghavan | jahi | śardhaḥ | yātumatīnām | vailasthānake | arbhake | mahāvailasthe | arbhake || 3 ||

O Indra, Maghavan, possessor of wealth, strike down and crush the force—the strength—of these sorceresses (*yātumatī*); that is, the armies of those possessing sorcery (*yātu*) or those possessing sorcerers (*yātudhāna*), which have weapons as their means of inflicting torment. Having done so, destroy them in the contemptible, wretched, and despicable *araṇīya* cremation ground (*vailasthānaka*) characterized by the previously mentioned features; this is the sense of the ellipsis.
Alternatively:
"In the place of the *bila*," that is, in a contemptible place connected to a cave, shrouded in darkness—the remainder of the sentence being "place [him] in the subterranean world (*adholoka*).
One might ask: "Not just anywhere, but in some lowly spot? To this he replies:
In the great cremation ground of Mahāvailasta, which must be traversed by all, or in the world of the Nāgas;
furthermore, of what nature?
It is desolate, loathsome, and uninhabitable by those whose life-force has departed.

Of those [waters], whose fifty-three [streams] you have poured down with your outpourings—that indeed pleases you; that indeed pleases you. 4. Of those; three; fifty; with outpourings; down; you poured; that; well; for you; it is pleasing; that; well; for you; it is pleasing. 4.
O Indra, with those armies characterized by the features mentioned in the preceding mantra—three times fifty, that is, a number of one hundred and fifty—with their advances and approaches.
It has been stated that the activity of going is obstructed.
Having approached, you have destroyed the enemy's stores.

O Indra, such an act—consisting of the army, wealth, and so forth—is *sumanāyati*, meaning it is highly esteemed. Furthermore, O Indra, even that great force of yours, consisting of hundreds upon hundreds of enemy armies, is *sumanāyati*; that is, it is well-regarded as being "sufficient" (*alam*) for the purpose.

O Indra, crush the tawny-tusked, voracious Piśāci; strike down every demon. piśaṅgī-bhṛṣṭim ambhuṇam piśācim indra saṃ mṛṇa | sarvaṃ rakṣo ni barhaya || 5 || O Indra, utterly destroy the Piśāci with her tawny teeth and insatiable hunger; strike down every demon.
1. It means by the foot belonging to the elephant *kṣajaṭahastin*. 2. The instruments of torment (*yātanā*) are *kṣajaṭa*.
3. One hundred and fifty is *kṣakaaṭa*.
4. [The syllable] *kṣa-ja-ṭa* is mounted upon the army of enemies.
5. *kṣa-a-ṭa* means "not come to mind.
The meaning is that the entire world, having severed its attachment, honors (*manāyati*) [it], that is, highly esteems or praises it.
O Indra, [he saw] a horse of reddish-brown appearance, slightly reddened in color, extremely terrifying, and neighing—
[the root] *aṇ* meaning "to sound";
from the yaṅ-luk form, with the suffix *ac*, there is the Vedic elision of the *m*.
Alternatively, "mahantam" means "extremely increased.
"Aśrum" is a name for "great," because it is listed there [in the Nighaṇṭu] as: "ambhraṇaḥ māhinaḥ" (Nighaṇṭu 3.3.16).
Some say that *piśāci* refers to a specific type of *piśāca*, namely *jarā*. Crush them thoroughly—that is, destroy them completely.
Not only him alone, but uproot and utterly annihilate every *rakṣas*, including the Rākṣasas and others who serve as the cause for protection.
The root *bṛh* is used in the sense of "injuring";
it belongs to the cur-ādi class.
[The form] is *nāmaya*.
This is a slayer, because it is stated therein [in Nirukta 2.19.30]: "It causes one to perish, it destroys.

On the sixth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), in the *prauga-śastra*, the first and second [verses] of the triplet dedicated to Indra begin with "O great Indra, protect us" (*ava no maha indra*).

In the section titled "Of the Sixth," it is sūtra-ed: "‘Avarmaha indra vṛṣannindra’" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.1). "Avarmaha indra dādṛhi śrudhī naḥ | śuśoca hi dyauḥ kṣā na bhīṣāṃ adrivo ghṛṇāt bhīṣāṃ adrivaḥ | śuṣmintamo hi śuṣmibhirvṛdhairebhirīyase ||" "O Indra, bestow great wealth upon us; hear our prayer!
