For the sky has blazed up as if from fear, O wielder of the thunderbolt, as if from the heat of the earth, O wielder of the thunderbolt! For you, the most powerful one, advance with these powerful strengtheners."
O Indra, slayer of men, unopposed hero with heroic warriors, O hero with heroic warriors!

Tear asunder the great [obstacle], O Indra; hear us! For heaven has glowed with fear, like the earth, O wielder of the stone, from the heat, as if from the heat, O wielder of the stone! For you, most powerful, go forth with your powerful, increasing, and fierce [companions]—O hero, slayer of men, unopposed, with your heroic warriors, three hundred heroes, O hero with heroic warriors! 6. Avaḥ | mahaḥ | indra | dādṛhi | śrudhi | naḥ | śuśoca | hi | dyauḥ | kṣāḥ | na | bhīṣā | adrivaḥ | ghṛṇāt | na | bhīṣā | adrivaḥ | śuṣmintamaḥ | hi | śuṣmibhiḥ | vṛdhaiḥ | ugraiḥ | īyase | apūruṣaghnaḥ | apratītaḥ | śūra | satvabhiḥ | triḥsataiḥ | śūra | satvabhiḥ || 6 ||
O Indra, [drive] the great one—
the sixth case here denotes the object—
[that is,] the great water-bearing cloud, or the great Vṛtra, downward, with its face turned downwards.
By the rule *pūrvādharā* etc., the suffix *asip* is applied and *ava* is substituted for *av*.
By the rule *annaradharavityubhayathā chandasi* (Pāṇini 8.2.70), the letter *r* is inserted.
*Dādṛhi* means "tear asunder."
Moreover, listen— pay heed— to our words,
O wielder of the thunderbolt (adrivah);
"adrivah" refers to the cloud that possesses the thunderbolt.
Therefore, O Indra, for this reason the sky—the celestial world that serves as the refuge of the gods—is grieving;
the implication is that it grieves because, in the state of being Vṛtra, there is a lack of oblations and other offerings.
In this regard, there is an illustrative example:
*Kṣāḥ* is not [the earth].
*Kṣi* is a name for the earth;
it is called *kṣāḥ* because beings dwell (*kṣāyanti*) or reside within it.
The root *kṣai* (to perish) takes the suffix *kvip* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), forming *kṣāḥ*. She is not like the earth, which is the support for the dwelling of all beings;
rather, she grieves just as that [earth] does out of fear—specifically, from the state of being *vṛtra* (an obstructor), or from the dread of the withering of crops and so forth.
The meaning is that both worlds grieve because of the nature of Vṛtra;
that is, Heaven and Earth grieve, being unable to sustain the two worlds as they expand while enveloping the side of the Asuras.
Therefore, the connection with the preceding clause is "shatter him."
The example is given out of fear. O *adrivaḥ*, devourer of enemies;
or alternatively:
Like one with a mountain-thunderbolt, by that [means].
O Indra, out of dread—that is, from fear—of the glowing fire within the head, as if out of self-fright;
just as previously heaven and earth were scorched by the fear of self, so too [is it now].
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend:
formerly, when the world was enveloped in great darkness, the gods, having reflected, prayed to Agni. And he arose from the presence of Heaven and Earth in his own form, dispelling the darkness.

Having seen that, both heaven and earth were terrified by the great darkness—[this is the connection]. 1. *dyāvākṣaṇata* (variant: *dyāvākṣanaṭa*): [the syllable] *vala* is elided before the suffix *upadha* (variant: *uvarṇa* is elided before *upadha*). 2. *ḍa*: as previously stated (*uktavidham*). 3. *ubarha* in the sense of "to destroy" (*hiṃsāyām*); it belongs to the *caurādika* (cur-class) group; [therefore] "destroy" (*nāśaya*); *kṣa-na-ṭa*: "bend" (*barha*)... "make straight" (*nāmaya*). 4. *u*: "he destroys" (*vināśayati*). 5. *kṣa-u-jña-na-ṭa*: "and furthermore" (*kiṃca*). 6. *ka-kṣa-kha-cha-ca-ja-jña-jha-ja-ṭa-te-va*: on the side of the Asuras (*asurapakṣe*). 7. *kṣa-na-ṭa*: the connection is with what precedes (*pūrveṇānvayaḥ*). 8. *kṣa-na-ṭa*: by means of a great darkness (*mahatāndhakāreṇa*). Thus, both heaven and earth were afraid.
And he is to be understood from such Vedic texts as, "Both Tvaṣṭṛ were afraid" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.95.5),
or alternatively,
*ghṛṇaḥ* refers to Agni alone.
Therefore, just as [the world] is terrified, that fear is to be understood from such Vedic texts as, "The two worlds, heaven and earth, trembled" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.31.3).
The meaning is: "Remove such fear by the bestowing of rain."
O Indra, you are indeed the most powerful of all through your mighty forces;
for this reason, accompanied by your fierce, surging weapons and their means of application, you advance against the enemies or the clouds.
The root *dhū* means "to move";
the suffix *śyan* is applied because it belongs to the *devādi* (div) class.

Or alternatively, the connection is with the words "with powerful weapons. O *śūra*, O valiant one; O *apratīta*, O you who are unassailable by enemies such as the *rakṣas* and others due to your companions, that is, because you have not been overcome in battle.

Or rather: with your friends, the living beings, you are the unadorned singer (arkah), one who has not encountered those who slay men (apuruṣaghnaḥ)— that is, you are the non-slayer of those endowed with manly vigor who are capable of performing sacrifice.
The grammatical construction is: being accompanied by "three times seven" (twenty-one) "heroic companions," that is, followers, you go.
At the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), before the *yājyā* of the *prasthita* offering for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the verse beginning with “*vanoti hi*” is to be inserted.
Regarding this very section, it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*vanoti hi sunvankṣayaṃ parīṇaso mo ṣu vo asmadabhi tāni pauṃsyā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).
For the one who presses the juice wins an abode of abundance; for the one who presses the juice indeed worships away his enemies—the enemies of the gods, away his enemies.
Pressing the juice, he indeed desires thousands of swift steeds;
to the one who presses the juice, Indra gives enduring wealth, he gives enduring wealth.

For the one who presses [the Soma] wins a dwelling of abundance; for the one who presses performs sacrifice and drives away enemies—drives away the enemies of the gods. The one who presses desires to win thousands of swift horses; Indra gives to the one who presses enduring wealth—he gives enduring wealth. 7.
O Indra, the sacrificer who presses the Soma juice for you attains *kṣaya*—the home that is to be inhabited by all or that which is to be reached—indeed, through your grace, he enjoys it.
The particle *hi* is used here for the sake of emphasis.

Furthermore, while indeed performing the Soma sacrifice, the one who presses the juice destroys—that is, causes the destruction of—the *dvipaḥ*, the haters, who are *parīṇasaḥ*, meaning those who are encompassing or closely connected [to him].
Not only does he sacrifice for those who hate the gods, but even for those who hate the gods, he sacrifices down.

Moreover, O Indra, while performing the sacrifice characterized by the pressing of the Soma, the sacrificer—being a *vājī* (possessing vigor), *vājavat* (rich in food), and *avrataḥ* (unassailable by others)—desires to win or to acquire for himself thousands upon thousands of cattle and other riches through your grace.

Because of the option [provided by Pāṇini] "saneḥ sani manīvantthaṃ," when the suffix *ḍaḍ* is absent, there is the substitution of *ā* [for the penultimate vowel] according to the rule "janayanta-manas."
Regarding the question "How is this obtained?", he says here:

To the one who presses [the Soma], that is, to the sacrificer performing the Soma sacrifice directed toward Indra, this Indra gives—bestows—*rayim*, wealth consisting of cattle and other riches, which is *ābhuvam*, characterized by being all-pervasive, and likewise *ābhuvam*, characterized by being repeatedly manifesting, that is, exceedingly abundant.
Therefore, the meaning is that the one who presses [the Soma] desires to obtain it.

1. And by means of those [methods] (ṅa); 2. not arrived (ṅa); 3. undesired (kṣa, ṅa, ja, ṭa); 4. non-egoity (jha); 5. the word "with friends" (sakhibhiḥ) is absent in kṣa, jha, ba, and ṭa; 6. indeed (kṣa, na, ṭa); 7. having the nature of arising again and again (ṅa). In this section (anuvāka), there are six hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, beginning with the verse "Come to you, O swift ones" (ā tvā juvaḥ), is the first of the Pārucchepa hymns.
The other ṛc, "ā tvā vāyo," consists of four padas and forty-four syllables.
Because it is stated that "[it] belongs to Vāyu" (vāyavyaṃ tu), both this one and the following one have Vāyu as their deity.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: "Ā tvā [has six verses]; [the next] is vāyavyaṃ tu, along with the others."
The application is according to the traditional interpretation:
"May the swift, eager steeds carry thee here toward the offerings, O Vāyu, for the first drinking, for the first drinking of the Soma!
May thy upright, joy-bestowing grace stand firm for the mortal man."
Come on your chariot drawn by teams of horses, O Vāyu, to the giving, to the giving of the sacrifice!

May the swift, eager steeds bring you here toward the offerings, O Vāyu, for the first draught of Soma, for the first draught! Let the upward-reaching, joyous spirit stand ready, knowing [the way]. Come on your chariot drawn by teams of horses, O Vāyu, to the giving, to the giving of the sacrifice! 1.
O Vāyu, let your swift, gliding, rapid-moving, and powerful horses— known as *niyut*— come to you;
[the root] *rah* means "to go," and the suffix *kānac* is used here for the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The elision of the nasal is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
"In this sacrifice" (*iha asmin yajñe*), let them "bring" (*vahantu*)—that is, cause to arrive—the "food" (*aprayaḥ*), characterized by oblations such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*.
For what purpose?
"For the first drinking" means for drinking as before.
Again, for what purpose? "For the first drinking" means for drinking prior to the other gods.
The acute accent on the final syllable of the first member [of the compound] is due to its belonging to the *marudvṛdhādi* group.

Furthermore, O Vāyu, may our speech in the form of praise—consisting of *sūnṛtā*, that is, pleasant truth—abide in accordance with your mind; that is to say, may it remain forever resting upon you and gladden you.
*Sūnṛtā* is a name for speech, as it is stated among the names of Brahman: "Brahman is *sūnṛtā*."

"Rising up," that is, elevated; likewise, "not knowing," meaning not specifically understanding your qualities. O Vāyu, for the sake of drinking Soma and for the sake of praise, [I call you] "to the giving," that is, for the sake of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) to be given at the sacrifice (*amakhasya yajñasya*), in order to accept it.
Furthermore, for what purpose?
‘*dāvane*’ means for the giving of gifts to us.
In both instances, the suffix *vani* is added to the root *dā* (to give) respectively in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the abstract action (*bhāva*), according to the *uṇādi* rules;
the elision of the penultimate vowel is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) irregularity.
Come hither with your chariot drawn by a team of horses, come with the chariot yoked with the *niyuts*.
May the exhilarating drops of Soma, well-prepared, well-made, and directed toward heaven, gladden you—prepared with milk and directed toward heaven.
Or rather, when they are prepared for the sake of glory, may the aids attend upon our skill.
The prayers, directed toward the granting of the teams of horses, speak to him; the prayers speak to him.

May the exhilarating drops, O Vāyu, delight you—drops prepared by us, well-fashioned, reaching toward heaven, prepared with milk, reaching toward heaven. When the aids, being prepared for success, attend upon his skill, the prayers, directed toward the granting of the teams of horses, speak to him; the prayers speak to him. 2.

1. *kha-ca-pha*: "For the first drinking of Soma—O Vāyu, may these Soma juices, which belong to us and which are exhilarating (*mādayitāraḥ*), gladden (*mandantu*) you. The use of the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is due to a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).

Of what nature are these Soma juices? They are *mandinaḥ*, exhilarating; *krāṇāsaḥ*, performing their own work such as causing joy and so forth; *sukṛtāḥ*, well-prepared through the processes of pressing, purification by the *daśapavitra* filter, and being drawn; *abhidhavaḥ*, shining forth on all sides; *gobhiḥ*, [prepared] with "cows" in the form of speech consisting of mantras; and *krāṇāḥ*, being made or offered. Or alternatively:

"By the rays" (gobhiḥ) means by those that go toward the Āhavanīya fire, i.e., by those that bring [the oblation]; "being made" (krāṇāḥ) means being offered. This is the present middle participle (śānac) of the root *kṛ*; the elision of the suffix *śap* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Likewise, *abhidhava* means "one who approaches. O Vāyu, for the reason that— here the word *ha* is used in the sense of what is well-known.

O you who are skillful (*dakṣa*), capable, and eager to go toward our place of sacrifice—O you, the *niyut* horses known by that name, your steeds, for the sake of giving (*dāvane*) the oblation, with a view toward the ritual acts (*dhīḥ*) intended for the acceptance of the offering, attend upon you or gather at the place of sacrifice.
For what purpose?
To bring [the gods] (*iradhyai*) or to serve them.
The root *īr* means "to go. The suffix *kyap* is added in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*).
The short vowel is a Vedic archaism.

*Irādhyati*: it means "one who performs the act of service," because its name is derived from the honorific sense in the passage, "We would worship [him] with service" (*iradhyati vidhema*, Nirukta 3.5.1).
What are they like? *Vkrāṇāḥ*: performing their own functions, such as drawing the chariot and so forth.
Yāska states: "*Krāṇāḥ* means 'performing'. (Nirukta 4.19)
*vūtayaḥ*: possessing protection (*rakṣaṇavatyaḥ*) or endowed with affection (*prītiyuktāḥ*); likewise *saprīcīnāḥ*: moving together with you (*añjanyo gacchantyaḥ*).
Regarding [the form] *sahasyam abhiḥ*:
by the rule *vibhāṣāñjeḥ*, the suffix *kha* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
[The word *vāyo*] has its accent on the final syllable due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

Furthermore, the wise ones—either the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who possess ritual action or the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) who possess intelligence—approach and speak (*upabruvate*), that is, they come forward and speak, or they make known their own intended purpose.
"Vāyu yokes the two ruddy steeds; Vāyu [yokes] the two tawny ones; Vāyu [yokes] the two swift ones to the chariot at the pole to draw it, the most excellent at the pole to draw it."
Awaken Puraṃdhi as a lover awakens his seventh [wife];
make the two worlds visible, clothe the dawns for glory, clothe the dawns.

Vāyu yokes his two ruddy steeds; Vāyu yokes his two crimson steeds. Vāyu yokes to the chariot his two swift ones to draw at the pole, the most capable to draw at the pole. Awaken Purandhi like a lover awakening his seventh wife. Make the two worlds visible; clothe the dawns; clothe the dawns for the sake of glory. 3.

Then Vāyu yokes two red horses, red in color, to the pole—the front part of the chariot, or rather, the place for bearing the load; that is, he joins them there at times. Likewise, he yokes two ruddy horses, ruddy in color, to the pole at times.
Similarly, he yokes two swift horses, characterized by rapid movement and possessing specific colors, at times.
Alternatively,
this [word] connects with both [contexts].
To explain for what purpose he yokes [the horse], he says:
*Volahave*: to bear the yoke (*dhuraṃ*), that is, for the carrying of the burden. Furthermore, *vahiṣṭhā*: the two most excellent carriers (*atiśayena voḍhārau*), namely the two horses.
From the word *voḍhṛ*, by the rule *turiṣṭhemayaḥsu* [Pāṇini 6.4.154], there is the elision of the suffix *-tu*.

Because it is *asiddha*, the substitution beginning with *ḍha* does not take effect. The vowel *ā* replaces the dual ending. When there is a great burden to be carried, [it is said: "on the yoke (*dhuri*)," "for the oxen (*voḷhave*)," that is, when a heavy load is to be borne.
The repeated mention of "wind" (*vāyu*) and the statement regarding its "course" (*ayojana*) are for the purpose of making it known that [the wind] arrives with extreme speed.
Now, he speaks by means of direct perception:
"O Wind (*vāyo*),"—by implication, "the wise one" (*puraṃdhi*), which is understood to mean the sacrificer.
‘The wise woman is a *purandhi*’ (Nirukta 6.13), says Yāska.
Awaken her!
Having come quickly by chariot, cause her to perceive the oblation—that is, to recognize it as having the form of the Sun; such is the intended meaning.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a paramour, a man who has illicit relations with another's wife, approaches a virtuous woman while she is slightly asleep through the meditation on approaching her for sexual union.

1. O Vāyu, you who possess the letters *kṣa*, *jha*, *na*, *ṭa*, and *va*. 2. *Kṣa-jha-na-ṭa-va*. 3. Of what kind are the horses? *Ya-ta-pha*: of what kind are they? 4. They possess protection (*rakṣaṇavant*). 5. In the manuscripts *ṅa* and *ca*, after the phrase "they make known" (*vijñāpayanti*), there is an additional passage: "The particle *īm* is meaningless; it was previously stated that it is for the purpose of filling the meter. 6. In manuscript *ṅa*, it says: "In that regard, he says. 7. By meditating on the arrival of her husband, she [became] like a woman possessing an excellent body.
Just as he awakens her by means of his own conventional signal, so too you, while occupied with your ritual duties, should awaken the sacrificer who has arrived with his desires.
Furthermore, for that purpose, "make the two worlds, heaven and earth (rodasī), visible"—that is, cause them to be clearly perceived and manifested.
And "make the dawns appear"—that is, properly establish the times of dawn, meaning make it morning.
That very thing is requested once more: "For hearing.
"Hearing" (śrava) is a name for food.
O Dawn, cause [them] to dwell so that they may accept your oblation-form weapons.
For you, the bright and auspicious dawns spread out their radiant garments in the distance; they display wondrous colors within their rays, within their ever-new rays.
For you the cow is milked full, yielding all treasures;
from the wombs of the Maruts she pours forth, from the wombs of heaven she pours forth.

For you, the bright Dawns spread out their auspicious garments in the distance, displaying wondrous power in their rays—brightly shining in their new rays. For you, the cow who milks at will pours forth all treasures; the Maruts, the sons of strength, have brought them forth from their bellies—from the bellies of heaven.

O Vāyu, for you, for your sake, the *uṣasaḥ* (dawns)—illuminated by you in the manner previously described—are *śucayaḥ*, meaning pure or radiant; they are in *parāvati*, in the extremely distant region of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), within *daṃsu*, that is, among those possessing deeds (*daṃsāṃsi*).
Or else, it is a name for houses.
The elision of the final syllable is a Vedic anomaly.
As if covering a house with their own rays, they spread out— meaning they extend— the "bhadra" garments, that is, auspicious and beautiful cloths suitable for wearing. Or alternatively:

The Dawns have appeared in the sacrificial halls, at the places of divine worship, and in the rays; may there be well-being for you who have come for the oblation. Auspicious garments are spread out for you—meaning that the flames of the fire itself spread out as garments;
because the fires are kindled at the time of dawn, those very flames are figuratively called "garments."
Is it not so that they wear only ordinary garments? No; he says: "in new ones," meaning in fresh garments being praised.
The root *ṇu* is used in the sense of praise.
In this regard,
the substitution of *ava* [for *avau*] occurs by the rule "vānto yi pratyaye," and the acute accent on the first syllable occurs by the rule "yato 'nāvaḥ."
"They spread wonders, endowed with various colors, within the rays"—
the sense is that at the time of dawn, the rays possess various colors.
In the alternative interpretation involving fire, the state of being a wonder arises because the flames possess various colors in forms such as Kālī and Karālī.
Furthermore, O Vāyu, for you—indeed for your sake and for the purpose of your arrival—there is a "milch-cow" (*adhenu*), a cow that brings forth [milk] such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*);
the singular number is used for the class.
She is "one who yields much milk" (*sraddughā*).
The name of nectar is "sabirita";
she is its milker.
By the rule "duhaḥ kapthaśca," the suffix *kap* is applied.
She milks out—that is, she herself yields or brings forth—all treasures, meaning all riches in the form of clarified butter and other such substances. 10. The meaning is that she leads them forward.
In the case of the agentive-reflexive construction (*karmakartṛ*), there is an absence of *yaK* according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.1.89, *na duhastunamām*.
The absence of the elision (*luk*) of *śap* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
If it is asked, "What is the distinction there? it is said:

O Vāyu, from the *diva*, the radiant atmosphere, you have generated—indeed, you generate and produce—the Maruts, those deities so named who disperse the clouds and are born as portions of yourself, acting as the producers of rain.
For what purpose? That is now stated.
"From the *vakṣaṇās*, meaning those characterized by flowing; from the *adris*, meaning those characterized by rain.
Likewise, 'from the *vakṣaṇās*';
this is a name for rivers, because it is listed among their names in [Nighaṇṭu] 1.13.9: 'the *vakṣaṇās* are the flowing ones'."
For their sake.
For you, the bright, pure, and swift Soma-drops have flowed toward exhilaration; they have flowed for the sake of the active one.
To you, the hunter who gazes upon the deer, I pray for splendor as a swift pursuer.
You protect the entire world by your law; you protect it from the power of the Asuras by your law.

For you, the bright, the pure, the swift, the fierce ones have surged in their exhilarations; they have surged in the stirring of the waters. The lurking thief, seeking to see, prays for splendor against the robber; you protect [him] from every world by your law, you protect him from the power of Asura by your law. 5.
O Vāyu, for you, for your sake, these "śukrāsaḥ" (bright ones) are "śucayaḥ" (radiant), that is, pure.
The drinkers of Soma become exceedingly pure;
what more need be said regarding their purity?

The "turaṇyavaḥ" (speeding ones), meaning those endowed with haste, desiring to reach you—the "ugrāḥ" (fierce) Soma juices of exalted luster—when your "madeṣu" (intoxications) have become the cause, they "iṣaṇta," that is, they go toward or desire to go toward the "bhurvaṇi" (nourishing) sacrifice for the purpose of being offered.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition;
there are two verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*).
Furthermore, "in the womb of the waters" means in the cloud; they "desire," that is, they seek to produce water.
This is because the two fires, through the medium of the oblation offered into them, are the producers of rain.
Or alternatively:
The sacrificers, offering oblations directed toward you, desire the rain of waters.

Furthermore, O Vāyu, the sacrificer—terrified, fleeing, and exhausted by the obstructors of the sacrifice or by the observances such as the milk-vow—praises you, the adorable one, with the word *takvīye*, meaning "for the departure elsewhere of the *takvan*s," those who cause the destruction of the sacrifice.
The root *īḍ* means "to praise.
Due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.

For this reason: "Thou protectest [pāsi] from all the world (viśvasmād bhuvanāt)—that is, from all the universe, or from the multitude of beings, or from the fear connected with the three worlds—by means of dharmaṇā, that is, by the sustaining of our oblations. Furthermore, thou especially protectest from the asuryāt, the fear associated with the Asuras, being endowed with dharmaṇā, meaning either by our sustenance or by nourishment. Since thou doest so, therefore I praise thee; such is the sense."
O Vāyu, you who are without predecessor, you deserve the first draught of our Soma juices; you deserve the draught of the pressed juices.
And they have turned toward the people of the Viśvāmitras, who possess many hymns.
All the milch-cows yield for you; they yield the milk-mixture and the clarified butter—the milk-mixture.

O Vāyu, you alone, without predecessor, deserve the first draught of these Soma juices; you deserve the draught of the pressed juices. And indeed, the people of the various clans who offer oblations have turned toward you; all your milch-cows yield the milk-mixture, they yield ghee, they yield the milk-mixture. 6.

1. *ha* is the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). *iṣa* means "to go. *śvan* is the suffix. 2. *ha* [is used] for that which is being invoked (*hūyamānāyāḥ*). 3. *i*: "sustaining us" (*asmān dhāyayan*). Ṛgveda 10.7:
"O you who are to be invoked (*avāyāṃ*), you are unprecedented (*apūrvyaḥ*).
That drinking from which nothing prior exists is "unprecedented" (*apūrva*).
O you who are without a second,
being such as you are, and therefore "the first," having existed prior to the other gods, you "deserve"— that is, you obtain— the "drinking" of the Soma juices;
you "deserve" the "drinking" of the pressed Soma juices.
The meaning is that wherever there is a pressing of Soma, you drink there invariably.

This separate mention—whereas previously it was stated with the intention of referring to the first [instance]—is now intended to make known that his drinking occurs at every sacrifice containing Soma.
It is not merely the drinking of Soma; "uto" (and also) refers to those [sacrifices] characterized by special oblations (*vihumatīnām*), or those involving invocations.
From the root *hu* (to sacrifice), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule beginning with *saṃpadādi*;

from that, the suffixes *matup* and *dīp* are added. [The compound means] "of those who avoid undesirable calamities. *Vavarjuṣīṇām* is the feminine form of the past passive participle of the root *vṛj* (to avoid). *Anabhimatāpāpām* is a genitive Tatpuruṣa compound meaning "of those whose misfortunes are not desired. *Varjayantīnām* is the present active participle of the root *vṛj* in the feminine.
From the root *varjayati* (to avoid), the forms *kasu*, *ṅī*, and *saṃprasāraṇa* [are applied].
The ellipsis is: "You accept the oblation belonging to the *viśas*—that is, the subjects in the form of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificers (*yajamāna*).
Or alternatively:
For those sacrificers, all the cows—the "people" (viśaḥ) who are like milch-cows—milk themselves for your sake the *āśira*, the milk used as the mixing substance.
In the reflexive passive construction (*karmakartari*), the suffix *ya* is absent according to the rule *na duhastunamām*;
furthermore, the *t* is elided by the rule *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu*.

The augment *ruṭ* is applied by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. Likewise, they milk the *āśiram*—the substance that serves as the instrument, being fit for the purpose of spreading the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) beneath and sprinkling it upon, and so forth—for the sake of mixing.

The hymn consisting of nine verses beginning with "stīrṇaṃ barhiḥ" is composed by Parucchepa and addressed to Agni; however, because of the word "tu" (but/however) in the preceding [section], its deity is Vāyu.
The five verses beginning with "ā vāṃ rathaḥ" are dedicated to Indra.
The seventh and eighth [verses] constitute eight [in total].
The table of contents (anukramaṇikā) for this is: "Stīrṇam; nine [verses]; those beginning with the fourth; five [verses] for Indra; and eight at the penultimate [verse].
The specific application of the hymn is based on its internal characteristics (laiṅgika).
On the sixth day of the ten-night rite (daśarātra), the first two triplets (ṛcas) in the Prauga-śastra are applied in place of the original Vāyu and Indravāyu verses.
In the section beginning with "At the morning pressing of the sixth [day]," it is sūtra-ed: "The two triplets beginning with *stīrṇaṃ barhiḥ*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).

*Stīrṇaṃ barhir upa no yāhi vītaye sahasreṇa niyutāṃ niyutvate śatinībhir niyutvate | tubhyaṃ hi pūrvapītaye devā devāya yemire ||* "Come to our sacrifice upon the strewn grass for our enjoyment, O Lord of the teams, with a thousand teams; O Lord of the teams, with hundreds of teams! For the gods have directed themselves toward you, the god, for the first draught."
Your sweet pressed juices have been set forth; they have been set forth for exhilaration, for the sake of the sacred rite (*ṛta*).

The sacred grass (*barhis*) has been strewn. Come to us for the feast, with a thousand teams, O Lord of teams (*niyutvān*), with hundreds of teams, O Lord of teams! For the gods have offered [the first portion] to you, the god, for your first draught. Your sweet pressed juices have been set forth; they have been set forth for exhilaration, for the sake of the sacred rite.

O Vāyu, come near to us, directed toward the sacrificial grass (barhis) spread out for our sake. For what purpose? For the "vīti," that is, for the consumption of the oblations. By what means? It is said: by the "niyuts" numbering a thousand; the singular is used for the genus.
1. u-tadapūrvam; kṣa-na-ṭa-tasmādapūrvaḥ | 2. kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa-pūrvamāhutaḥ |
3. Of these [soma vessels], namely the *kha*, *ca*, and *pha*. 4. You obtain (*prāpnoṣi*) [the portion]; you have become worthy to drink immediately after the *iḍā* portion.
In the vessel for Indra and Vāyu (*aindrāvāyava*), [the word] "vessel" (*gṛha*) is not present [in some versions] (in *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, "vessel" does not exist).
The sense is that even when the cup is for two deities, it is first drawn once for your sake and is not being shared [with another].
5. Furthermore (kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa), you deserve—that is, you obtain—the drinking of the *sutās*, the pressed juices.
6. (kha-pha), our connection with us, the progeny (*prajānām*).
7. kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa—worthy of being resorted to;
8. kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa—a substance that flows;
9. ḍa-ca-jha—the second hymn; 10. kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa—in the place of the Vāyavya and Aindravāyava cups.
Homage!
*Niyuta* is a name for Vāyu’s horses, as stated in the Nirukta: "The *niyuts* belong to Vāyu" (Nirukta 1.15.10).
Thus, the sense is: "Come with the *niyuts*, which are characterized by the number one hundred" (*śatinībhiḥ*).
Alternatively:
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "An oblation is offered to the god who possesses *niyuts*—that is, to him who has a thousand, a hundred thousand, and hundreds of *niyuts*.
Alternatively, it is connected with the word "to you" (*tubhyam*).
With the yoked horses (niyut) of the aforementioned number, [I offer] to you, that shining god.
The initial syllable has the udātta accent by virtue of the rule *ḍyāvo 't* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.212).
"For the first drinking"— for the sake of drinking before the other gods— "the gods" have restrained themselves;
or rather, the singers, the officiating priests, have restrained themselves for you, O God.
They have offered the Soma toward the Āhavanīya fire.
The word "hi" is used to indicate the well-known fact established by other mantras, such as "Drink first of the sweet juices, O Vāyu, the pressed [Soma]" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.46.1).
Furthermore, these "pressed" (*sutāsaḥ*) Soma juices, "sweetened" (*madhumantaḥ*) with honeyed flavor, "for thee"—that is, for your exhilaration—*asthiran*, meaning they remain present for your joy.
Furthermore, for the sake of the sacrifice—that is, for its accomplishment—they have stood firm;
they remain supported by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Therefore, the ellipsis is "you [should] drink."
"Let it remain [as *tiṣṭhet*]: in the Vedic *luṅ* (aorist), by transposition (*vyatyaya*), *jha* becomes *ran*.
By the rule *'sthādhvoricca'* there is the *kittva* of the *sic* suffix and the substitution of *it* for the root vowel.
Then, by the rule *'hasvādaṅgāt'* there is the elision of the *sic*."
For you this Soma, purified by the stones, flows toward the vat, clothing itself in desirable garments; clothing itself in bright raiment, it flows.
With you as his portion, Soma is offered among the gods.
O Vāyu, bring your teams; come, being well-disposed toward us; come, being well-disposed toward us.

For you, this Soma, purified by the stones, flows around the vat, clothing himself in desirable garments; clothing himself in bright [robes], he flows. This portion, O Āyudhva, is offered to you among the gods—this Soma. Bring your teams, O Vāyu; come, being well-disposed toward us; coming with pleasure, come, being well-disposed toward us. 2.
O Vāyu, for you, for you, for your sake.
The elision [of the case-ending] is by the rule "supāṃ suluk," which prescribes the elision (luk) of the dative case.
"This Soma, being offered, flows—that is, goes and reaches—the *kośa*, which stands in the place of a vessel or cup.
Of what nature is this Soma?
It is purified by the stones (*adribhiḥ*), having been cleansed through the removal of impurities by means of the pressing-stones used for extraction."
Or rather:
purified by the stones through cleansing with the *daśāpavitra* filter, or cleansed during the pressing;
likewise, clothing himself (*avasānaḥ*) in desirable (*aspārhā*), that is, longed-for splendors (*tejāṃsi*).
Furthermore, "wearing" (vasānaḥ) pure, stainless, or radiant splendors, Soma "approaches" (arpati), that is, reaches you.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.
The suffix *śap* is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
O Vāyu, that "portion" (*bhāgaḥ*)—the Soma worthy of being enjoyed—which exists among men as one to be sacrificed to, is "offered" (*hūyate*) for your sake (*tava*) among the gods.
The meaning is that although other gods exist, because Soma is your portion, it is offered to you first. Furthermore, O Vāyu, being "asmayuḥ"—that is, possessing us—we [offer] that Soma to you.
The one who belongs to the earth.
Thus: "O *niyut*, bring the horses known as *niyuts* for the purpose of transport;
thereafter, go toward heaven.
Acting in this manner, being "associated with us" (*asmayuḥ*)—that is, joined with us, favoring us, or desiring us.
In the case of *kyac* in Vedic usage, when there is the elision of another [suffix], the vowel *u* is substituted by the rule *akyācchandasi*.
"Being pleased," that is, being delighted, "go," that is, proceed.

1. Because it is stated in the *Nirukta* that [the sounds] *ka*, *ja*, *jha*, *ṇa*, and *va* [are used here]. 2. *Ḍa*: the Soma juices have been pressed. 3. *Ḍa*: accompanied by honey. 4. *Ḍa*: increased. 5. *Ḍa*, *jha*, *ña*: he goes toward the lord (*arpati*). 6. *Kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa*:
O Vāyu, come with your teams of horses—by the hundreds, by the thousands—to our sacrifice for the feast, to enjoy the offerings for the feast!
This is your seasonal portion, which is joined with the rays of the sun.
Being brought by the Adhvaryu priests, they have been offered; O Vāyu, the bright drops have been offered.

Come with your teams of horses, by the hundreds and by the thousands, to our sacrifice, to enjoy the feast—O Vāyu, to enjoy the offerings! This is your seasonal portion, accompanied by the rays of the sun; brought by the Adhvaryu priests, they have been offered—O Vāyu, the bright libations have been offered. 3.

O Vāyu, come to our sacrifice with your teams of horses— those that are incomparable, those numbering in the hundreds, and those numbering in the thousands— and approach us with your chariots for the sake of the feast (*vītaye*) and for the fulfillment of your desired desires.

And having arrived for the sake of enjoying the oblations—that is, for consuming the sacrificial offerings such as Soma—having observed the sacrifice and the oblations, come with hundreds of thousands of chariots with extreme speed for their consumption; this is the meaning. Furthermore, our portion for you—the Soma worthy of being enjoyed—is timely (*vṛtviya*), having reached the proper time for its offering.
The word *ṛta* indicates the time for giving.

Because of the technical designation *pada*—by the rules "ghas in the Veda" (Pāṇini 5.1.106) and "also when followed by *si*" (Pāṇini 1.4.16)—the designation *bha* is sublated; consequently, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *o*, and thus the *yaṇ* [sandhi] occurs.
Furthermore, [there is the word] *soma*.
When the sun has risen, it becomes *saraśmi*— that is, it becomes possessed of rays, having equal radiance—
or rather,
it becomes accompanied by them.

The meaning is that since the rays appear when the sun has risen, the time has arrived. Furthermore, "Somas" refers to the *camasādhvaryu* priests; the plural number is used because there are ten of them.
Being borne and carried by them, they became restrained;
moreover, O Vāyu, those Soma juices of yours—bright, exceedingly radiant, and uplifted—have become restrained. Therefore, the meaning is: "Come for their consumption."
May your chariot with its team of horses come for our protection, toward the well-prepared offerings for the feast, O Vāyu, toward the oblations for the feast.
Drink of the sweet juice, for the first draught has been set apart for you both;
O Vāyu, come with brilliant bounty, and Indra, come with bounty!

May your chariot, drawn by teams of horses, bring you both for our protection toward the well-prepared offerings for the feast; O Vāyu, toward the oblations for the feast! Drink of the sweet juice, for the first draught has been set apart for you both, O Vāyu. Come with brilliant bounty, and Indra, come with bounty! 4.

Having praised Vāyu alone, [the poet] now praises Indra and Vāyu together due to their close association. O Vāyu, may your chariot (*vām rathaḥ*), which belongs to you both and is drawn by the teams of horses (*niyutvān*), bring you both toward the place of sacrifice for the gods.
1. kṣa-ha-na-ṭa-sa: And Soma. 2. u: Thousand-rayed. 3. ṭha-jha: Saraśmi. 4. kṣa-na-ṭa: The time having arrived. 5. kṣa-ja-na-ṭa: For protection.
In *vaher leṭi*, there is the augment *aṭ*;
the suffix *sip* is applied by the rule *sibbahulam*.
Although ten million [horses] are indeed appropriate for Vāyu’s chariot alone, nevertheless, because they are shared with other deities, they carry it together even for Indra’s sake.
For what purpose? "For *avasa*"—that is, for going or for protection.

And again, for what purpose? "For the eating" (*vītaye*) of "the offerings" (*prayāṃsi*), namely the *soma* characterized as food, which are "well-placed" (*sudhitāni*), meaning well-received; likewise, "for the eating" (*vītaye*) of "the oblations" (*havyāni*), namely other sacrificial items such as the *puroḍāśa* cakes offered at the pressings.
The suffix *kin* is applied after the root *veti*;
its udātta accentuation is established by the rule “*mantre vṛṣa*” and so forth.
Furthermore, "of the *madhvaḥ*" means of the sweet-tasting "food" (*andhasaḥ*) in the form of Soma.
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
Drink the sweet Soma,
for the first draught is ordained for you two before the other gods.
From the root *pāt*, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "acco yat";
the sound *ī* is substituted by the rule "īyati."
This is the intended meaning; therefore, the sense is "drink first.

Although Vāyu’s drinking before even Indra is well-known everywhere from such passages as "For you are the first drinker" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.46.1) and "O God, you have established the first drinking" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.92.1), nevertheless, Indra’s drinking before the other gods together with Vāyu is set forth in the explanatory passage on the *Indraturīya* in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa: "The gods, indeed, could not agree upon the first drinking of King Soma" (AiB 2.25).

Furthermore, at the time of arrival, O Vāyu and you, Indra, come hither together with *candrena*—that is, with gold that gladdens us—and with this *rādhasā*, consisting of cattle and other such wealth;
come hither together with *rādhasā*, that is, with jewels and riches.
*Gameloṭi* is a Vedic form where there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix;
the nasal is elided by the rule “*anudāttaupadeśa*” [Pāṇini 6.4.37];
and in the *luṅ* tense, there is the elision of *cali* by the rule “*mantre ghasa*” [Pāṇini 2.4.80].
May our prayers and sacrifices draw you both hither; they have cleansed this vigorous Soma-drop, like a swift steed eager for the prize.
O you who drink the pressed juice, come here to us with joy;
O Indra and Vāyu, you two, givers of strength, [come] for the exhilaration of the juices pressed by the stones.

May our prayers bring you both to the sacrifices; they have cleansed this Soma-drop, the prize-winner, like a swift, vigorous steed. Drink of these juices, O you who are well-disposed toward us; come here to us with your aid. O Indra and Vāyu, givers of booty, you two are the ones to drink of the pressed juices from the stones for your exhilaration. 5.

O Indra and Vāyu, you two cause our *dhī*s—our ritual acts characterized by hymns of praise and the like—to turn toward and proceed toward our *adhvara*s, that is, our sacrifices, with great intensity. Furthermore, for your sake, the Adhvaryu priests cleanse this Soma, the *indu* standing before them, which is rich in nourishment (*vājina*), destined for the drawing [of the cup], and moving toward the great wooden vat (*droṇakalaśa*) or the vessel of meat; they purify it with the ten-strand filter (*daśāpavitra*).
As for the illustration regarding this purification:
"Like a swift steed—one that goes very rapidly, a constant traveler, a vigorous horse—just as they cleanse such a horse by removing sweat and other impurities, so [do you];
moreover, O Indra and Vāyu, drink those purified Soma juices belonging to these Adhvaryu priests; perform the act of drinking."
For that purpose, come now with your protection (*ūtyā*) to our sacrifice here;
moreover, O Indra and Vāyu, desiring us (*asmayū*), you two [come] to the pressed juices extracted by the stones.
As before, the genitive case is used for the object of the action.
The ellipsis is "drink them. For what purpose? "For intoxication, for satisfaction, or for exhilaration."
The syntactical connection is as follows: "Since you two are the givers of *vāja*, that is, of food (*anna*), therefore drink."

1. *ṅa-vahanam* (the carriage of the letter *ṅa*). 2. *kṣa-bha-ṭa-indraturīyārthavādabrāhmaṇe* (in the *Indraturīya-arthavāda-brāhmaṇa*, [the letters] *kṣa*, *bha*, and *ṭa*). 3. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-yuvayoḥ* (of the two, *yuvām*, [the letters] *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*). 4. *kṣa-i-ca-saṃmārjayanti* (they cleanse; the *ātmanepada* ending is used by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*) after the root *mṛj* with the suffix *yaṅ-luk*).

These Soma juices, pressed here in the waters by the Adhvaryu priests, have been offered to you both; O Vāyu, the bright ones have been offered. These swift ones have been poured out for you both across the filter; the Soma drops, seeking you, have passed through the sheep’s wool, across the fleece. These Soma juices, pressed here in the waters by the Adhvaryu priests, have been offered to you both; O Vāyu, the bright ones have been offered. These swift ones have been poured out for you both across the filter; the Soma drops, seeking you, have passed through the sheep’s wool, across the fleece. 6.
O Vāyu and Indra, these Soma juices belonging to you both—yours and his—are [prepared] in the waters during our ritual acts.
By the rule beginning with "ūdidam0," the case ending (vibhakti) is udātta.
Here, in this place of pressing, the [Soma juices] have been pressed; they are being brought by the Adhvaryu priests, being held by them, or having been taken up and carried by the Hotṛ.
The agentive suffix occurs in the sense of the object.
The peaceful ones have come and are being led to you two;
moreover, those very Soma juices, bright, beautiful, and radiant, are being restrained;
furthermore, these swift and pervasive Soma juices [are here] in order to please you two—this is the sense.

*Ti-raḥ-pavitram* means that which is placed crosswise, concealing the edge of the *soma*, namely the woolen *pavitra*; *abhyasṛkṣata* means they were emitted toward it, they were created, and thus they come into being.

In the case of the root *sṛj* in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*) with the suffix *luṅ*, there is an absence of *guṇa* and an absence of the augment *am*, because the *liṅ* and *sic* suffixes are *kit* when used in the *ātmanepada*.

Furthermore: "O you two young ones," [the Soma juices] desiring you both; "Somas" refers to the Soma juices; "through the sheep's wool" means through the woolly fibers belonging to the filter (*pavitra*), which are not coarse;
or alternatively, "avyayā" means those that are not absent (i.e., present).
The letter *ma* is elided.
Such hairs [are those] which, having passed beyond, go out from the vessel—this is the ellipsis.
Furthermore, they are qualified again:
*ati* means "exceedingly"; *avyayāḥ* means "undecaying," i.e., free from decay; *somāsaḥ* means "the Soma juices"—[they] have flowed forth, this is the ellipsis.

Pass by all those who sleep, O Vāyu; go to where the pressing-stone speaks. Go both of you to that house; Indra too, go there. The pleasant truth has been revealed; the clarified butter flows. With a full team of horses, come to the sacrifice; Indra too, come to the sacrifice. O Vāyu, pass by all those who sleep; go to where the pressing-stone speaks. Go both of you to that house; Indra too, go there. The pleasant truth has been revealed; the clarified butter flows. With a full team of horses, come to the sacrifice; Indra too, come to the sacrifice. 7.

O Vāyu, you who have come from all sides, having passed by—that is, having neglected—the many constant sacrificers who, due to laziness and other such causes, fall into sleep; [passing them by], [come to] our sacrifice.
*Note:* "Śaśvat" is a name for "many," as it is listed among those names in *Nirukta* 3.1.5: "śaśvat, viśvam.
"Ati" means "having transcended" or "having neglected."

1. In this house; 2. the sons of *kṣa*, *u*, *ña*, and *ṭa* have been pressed out; 3. "being held by them" does not exist in *kṣa*, *ña*, *ṭa*; 4. being held in *kṣa*, *ña*, *ṭa*; 5. the drinkers in *kṣa*, *ña*, *ṭa*; 6. while they are sitting or sleeping in *kṣa*, *ña*, *ṭa*.
¹ Go! Proceed! ² And Indra shall do likewise.
He tells him which region it is:
"Go to that place where the pressing-stone speaks"—that is, go toward that region where the sound of the stone for the purpose of pressing is heard;
"go to the house," that is, the sacrificial hall.
Furthermore, the very location is further specified:
where *sūnṛtā*—speech that is pleasant and truthful, in the form of praise—is *vidadṛśe*, meaning it is specifically seen or heard;
go there.
And where the ghee— extremely blazing clarified butter taken for the purpose of the oblation— flows, that is, moves, being led toward the *āhavanīya* fire;
[the root] *rīṅ* means "to flow," and the suffix *śyan* is applied because it belongs to the sixth class (*divādi*).
Go there!
The manner of going is specified as follows:
[go] with a full, complete, and well-nourished body, accompanied by a *niyuta* [of followers].
The singular number is used for the genus.
O Niyuts and Atis, come toward our sacrifice; come, that is, proceed toward it.
Furthermore, O Vāyu and you, Indra—both of you, come toward our sacrifice; come together.
Likewise, the meaning is: "Let us also go together. Regarding this, he says:
"In that place, offer an oblation of honey; the swift ones who wait upon the *aśvattha* tree—may they be swift for us!
Together the cows flow, the barley ripens; for you, O Vāyu, the milch-cows do not fail, the milch-cows do not fail."

8 | Here, I say: you two carry away the offering of honey, that *aśvattha* tree upon which the victorious ones wait; may those victorious ones be with us! Together the cows flow and the barley ripens; for you, O Vāyu, those milch-cows do not fail; they do not fail. 8 |||
O Indra and Vāyu, here indeed— at this very sacrifice—
bear and maintain that oblation, the substance to be offered, which is sweet or like honey.
That Soma which the victorious sacrificers approach and stand near for the purpose of purchase, [situated] in a place such as the vicinity of the Aśvattha tree and the mountains.

Furthermore, may those who are our own—victorious (*jāyavaḥ*), conquerors through the performance of ritual acts—be our officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*); that is, may they be capable and perform the sacrifice.
Or rather:
may those well-known, skillful performers, the victorious conquerors, be our priests and not those of anyone else.
Regarding this, it was said, "you two are carried here.
To explain what the distinction here is, he says:
O Indra and Vāyu, in this sacrifice the lowing cows bring forth [their milk] together, simultaneously; that is to say, they yield their milk specifically for your sake.
Or rather:
the cows bring forth their offspring together, simultaneously, for the sake of their own milking;
[the verb *sū*] belongs to the first class (*ādādika*).

Because it has the marker *ṅit*, by the rule "the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are anudātta when following a root ending in *tās* or an *anudātta* vowel," the accent of the verbal root remains. Furthermore, [the word] *yavaḥ* is in the singular number used for the genus (*jātāvekavacanam*).
This is an elliptical expression;

the meaning is that sacrificial cakes and the like are cooked with barley and other grains. Furthermore, O Vāyu and Indra, since the cows yield [milk] in this manner, therefore those milch-cows for your sake do not fail—that is, they do not become exhausted, nor do they become emaciated by disease and so forth.
Not only have they not been exhausted; rather, the cows that provide you with pleasure do not perish—that is, they are not lost or destroyed by the depredations of thieves and the like.
1. kṣa-ṅa-ja-ṭa: where you two are. 2. kṣa-ṅa-ṭa: for the purpose of pressing [the Soma].
3. In the manuscripts kṣa, ja, and ṭa, the phrase "go to the house, the sacrificial hall" (gṛhaṃ yajñagṛhaṃ gacchatam) is absent.

4. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṅa, and ṭa: "having approached the sacrifice" (yajñamāsādya), meaning you have reached it face-to-face; in manuscript ha: "having approached the sacrifice" (yajñamāsādya), meaning having reached it face-to-face, you go, that is, you reach it.
5. In manuscript ṅa: "to that sacrifice, just as you have come" (yāgaṃ tasmai yathā āyāthaḥ).

6. In a place for practice such as a mountain beginning with *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *ṭa*, etc.; 7. For the purpose of milking by means of the region of *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *la*; 8. It is cooked together with *ṅa*.
9. O Kṣa, Ṅa, Ja, Ṭa, and Yuṣman, I shall gladden you.
10. O Kṣa, Ṅa, Ja, and Ṭa, they have become free from the plundering of thieves and the like.
These, O Vāyu, are those bulls of yours with the strength of arms; they fly within the rivers, the bulls increasing in their great vigor.
Even those who are slow on the desert plain are swift, and though they dwell in the mountains, they are agile;
like the rays of the sun, they are difficult to restrain, difficult to control by the hands.

These, O Vāyu, are yours, you who possess the strength of arms; they fly within the river, those bulls, increasing greatly, those bulls. Even in the desert, they who are not swift, yet are quick, dwellers in the home of the Aṅgirases; like the rays of the sun, they are difficult to restrain, difficult to restrain in the hands. 9.

O Vāyu, bestower of auspicious fruits, these horses belonging to you which are seen here before us, they cause you to fly— that is, they carry you— between the two, namely between heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*) while they roar;
or rather, those horses related to you fly, that is, they go to the place of sacrifice.
Bring forth the most excellent, great, and worthy oblation with prayer for the two attentive ones who are gracious—the sweetest offering for the two who are gracious.
Those two sovereign kings, nourished by clarified butter, are praised at every sacrifice.
Thus, their dominion can never be assailed; their divinity can never be challenged.

Bring forth the most excellent, great homage, an oblation, and a prayer for the two who look upon us with favor; bring the sweetest offering for the two who show mercy. They are the two sovereign kings, nourished by clarified butter, praised at every sacrifice. Thus, their dominion cannot be assailed from any quarter, nor can their divinity ever be challenged. 1.

O priests, having praised Mitra and Varuṇa, bring forth—that is, accomplish—the *jyeṣṭham* (eldest/greatest), the *bṛhat* (vast), the *mahat* (great), and *atipravṛddham* (exceedingly increased) *namaḥ*: a hymn characterized by salutation, or the food characterized by such a hymn, namely the oblation.
For *namaḥ* is a name for food, as it is listed among the names for food in the Nirukta (2.7.22): "Food is life.
Furthermore, bring forth the *havyām matim*—the thought directed toward the offering.
Alternatively, they bring the mind as the object of worship and the oblation as the sacrificial offering.
The distinction is this: in the former case, it was the food to be eaten, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake; now, however, it is the drinkable oblation consisting of Soma, clarified butter, and so forth.
Of what kind were those two?
"Nicirābhyām" means by those that are exceedingly long-lasting, that is, eternal;
the sense is that they exist in a continuous flow.

Furthermore, "mṛḷayadbhyām" means by those who, having themselves been gratified through the acceptance of the praise and the oblation, also cause the sacrificer to be well-pleased; likewise, "sumayadbhyām" means by those who consume the oblation most sweetly and most pleasantly.
Regarding the distinction between the two [words], he says there:
*tā* refers to those two, Mitra and Varuṇa, who are *samrājau*, i.e., ruling perfectly.
[The suffix] *kvip* is applied to the root *rāj*.
According to the rule *‘mo rāji samaḥ kṣau’*, the *m* of *samaḥ* becomes *m*.
[Thus we have] *ghṛtāsutī*. Those two by whom clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is poured out—that is, taken up—are such [as those].
Alternatively, [the term *ghṛtaprasūtā*] refers to those two by whom clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and water (*udaka*)—characterized by rain—are produced and permitted everywhere.

Since these two are the deities presiding over day and night (*ahorātra*), they produce rain through the medium of day and night. This is well known from the Vedic scripture: "Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night; through day and night, Parjanya rains" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.7.3), as it establishes their role as the granters of permission for rain.
Furthermore, these two are praised at every sacrifice—in all sacrifices—being extolled by all the officiating priests.
[In this compound,] the accent of the preceding member (gati) is retained according to the rule "the immediately preceding gati retains its original accent.
Now, moreover, of these two—of them.

Because a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) preceded by a specific designation (*saṃjñā*) is not mandatory, there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution according to Pāṇini 7.3.104 (*osi ca*). Consequently, by Pāṇini 6.1.97 (*ato guṇe*), the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule applies. The word *kṣatram* means strength (*balam*). It cannot be overcome (*ādhṛṣe*)—that is, it is impossible to assail—from any source whatsoever, whether from an enemy such as a *rākṣasa*, or from any kind of misfortune (*ūna*).
The suffix *-ken* is used here in the sense of a *kṛtya* (gerundive) according to Pāṇini 3.4.14 (*kṛtyārthe tavaiken*).
Furthermore, their divinity—their very state of being gods—is such that it cannot be assailed; it is beyond the reach of assault. Or rather, as it was before, so it remains even now.
Because Yāska stated, “*nū cid* is a particle [used] for both the old and the new” (*Nirukta* 4.17), [the meaning is as follows]:
he is not to be overcome by anyone;
the sense is that even their strength is not to be assailed, let alone their divinity.
1. In manuscripts ca, pha, and ‘tadupalakṣitam’ is absent.
2. In manuscript kṣa-a-ṭa, it reads *niratiśayahaviḥ*; in manuscript ṅa, it reads *niratiśayaṃ haviḥ*. 3. In manuscripts ca, jña, ta, and pha, it reads *ādharṣituṃ nāma*.

The path has been seen, a wider way for the wide expanse; the course of *ṛta* has been set in motion with its rays, the eye of *bhargas* with its rays. The heavenly seat of Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa—therein they establish the great, praiseworthy, desirable, and highly laudable glory. It was seen: the path, for the wide expanse, the wider way; the course of *ṛta* has been set in motion with its rays; the eye of *bhargas* with its rays. The heavenly seat of Mitra, of Aryaman, and of Varuṇa; therein they establish the great, praiseworthy, desirable, and highly laudable glory. 2.
The wide-striding, most expansive Dawn has been seen by all for the sake of the vast sacrifice—that is, for the activity of movement and so forth.
Likewise, the path of the sun, characterized by the sky, which moves with a rolling motion, has become united with the rays, that is, with the lights.
And the eye of Bharga—the god worthy of universal worship, known by this name—has become united with the rays, the eyes of all living beings.
The meaning is that all became capable of seeing their respective objects.
This very point is clarified:

because he acts as a light for Mitra, the house or dwelling of him who is the friend of all people—the atmosphere—became *dyukṣam*, a place of residence for the luminous ones, and was joined together with his rays.
Likewise, for *varyaṃṇaḥ*, the name of a deity,
the case-ending is acute by virtue of the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti*.
They have adorned the celestial dwelling with rays.
Furthermore, the dwelling of the god named Varuṇa, the dispeller of darkness, has become such.

Although the sun is one, it is praised separately because of its distinctions due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); likewise, although the atmosphere is one and illuminated by all three [deities], it is praised in a threefold manner because of the distinction between the illuminators.
The meaning is that immediately after its rising, there was light for the performance of ritual acts (3).

And for this reason—precisely because it has risen—it holds, that is, sustains, *ukthya* (praiseworthy), *bṛhat* (vast) *vayas* (food) characterized by oblations. Furthermore, it is *upastutya*, meaning it is to be approached and praised.
The suffix *kyap* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *eti-stu-śāsa-* (3.1.109).
They bestow the great hymn (*vṛhat*), such as the *stoma*, and *vayas*, which is food characterized by the oblation.

They two, the watchful ones, day by day, day by day, come together—the radiant Aditi, the supporter of the earth, the possessor of heaven. They have attained radiant dominion, the two Ādityas, lords of liberal gifts. Of those two, Mitra and Varuṇa are the one who goes among the people, and Aryaman is the one who goes among the people. Radiant; Aditi; the supporter; the earth; possessed of heaven; they come together; day by day; the two who are ever-watchful; day by day. Radiant; dominion; they have attained; the two Ādityas; lords of liberal gifts. Mitra; of those two; Varuṇa; he who goes among the people; Aryaman; he who goes among the people. 3.

This sacrificer maintains—that is, he himself has fashioned—the *vāditim*, which is luminous (*jyotiṣmatīm*), endowed with the splendor of the Āhavanīya fire, free from deficiency, and possessing all auspicious characteristics; and he maintains the *kṣiti*, the ground characterized as the *uttaravedi* (northern altar), which is fit for Agni to dwell upon.
(Note: The phrase "etāvati" appears in the variants *ca-pa-pha-uttarā*.)
2. Or, it means for the purpose of going to the sacrificial altar (*cha*) or for activity (*vyāpāra*). 3. It has the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*).
This is according to the Vedic scripture (*śruti*): "The earth is as large as the sacrificial altar" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.6.4.1).
Likewise, O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two become united with her who is "svarvatī"—possessing heaven by way of the accomplishment of the sacrifice—on this very day;
but not only on this day, however, but "day after day" (divedive) throughout all the days. Of what nature are they?

Day by day, being ever-watchful— that is, never indolent in their movement— and having come to the sacrificial altar, they have attained *kṣatra*, meaning strength, which is exceedingly endowed with splendor through the acceptance of clarified butter and other offerings. Thus they have become possessed of light.
In the case of *abhūt*, because it is in the Vedic *liṭ* (perfect) tense, there is an absence of the augment *nuṭ* according to the rule "the prescription of augments is not mandatory.
Alternatively, in the *liṭ* tense, the *śap* suffix is elided (*ślau*) as a Vedic anomaly.

As to what kind they are, he says this: "The two Ādityas," the sons of Aditi, "lords of giving" (dānupati), that is, masters of the gift of clarified butter and other offerings, or rather, protectors of the desired gift.
In the *saṃhitā*, there is the substitution of *s* in "paṣṭyāḥ patiputra" according to the rule [Pāṇini 8.3.53].
Both those gods, Mitra and Varuṇa, as well as the god Aryaman— of those two, Mitra and Varuṇa, he is the one who brings people together for sacrifice.
Because of this connection between those two, the person who goes [between them] stands in the midst of both;
he is one who enjoins all people to their respective duties.
Mitra and Varuṇa are the deities of day and night.

The meaning is that *arthamā*, by virtue of its power over those two [the sun and the moon], impels all living beings. Furthermore, it is *yātayajjana*: he whose people, as servants, cause the world to move; such is he.
Alternatively:
He is such that by him people—living beings who are being tormented and cast down into hell—are made to suffer because they have not performed sacrifices.
The meaning is that, by virtue of being the witness of karma, he causes living beings to experience the results of their own respective actions according to their merit.
Such a person, dependent upon Mitra and Varuṇa, exists for the sake of wealth; this is the completion of the sense.
This Soma is most auspicious for Mitra and Varuṇa; let it be a share among the drinking-vessels, a god as a share among the gods.
May all the gods today enjoy it with one accord. O Kings, fulfill that which we implore you, you who are upholders of the Eternal Order (Ṛta), even that which we implore.

May this Soma be most auspicious for Mitra and Varuṇa; may it have a share in the drinking-vessels, a divine god having a share among the gods. May all the gods, being of one accord, enjoy it today. O Kings, you who uphold the cosmic order (*ṛtá*), grant us that which we implore, even that which we implore. 4.
May this Soma, being invoked by us and being drunk, be most auspicious and most pleasant for Mitra and Varuṇa.
The elision of the *śap* suffix is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
There is an absence of *guṇa* substitution by the rule "bhūsuvostiṅi."
In the drinking-vessels—that is, in the objects of enjoyment where the cups are turned downwards—the two of them are *bhaga*, that which is to be shared or enjoyed on all sides.
Furthermore, they are *deva*, shining among the gods; that is, among the other gods who follow Mitra and Varuṇa, they are *ābhaga*, to be shared by them.
Or alternatively:

Among the gods who are the praisers and the sacrificers, he is the shining god; likewise, he is *ābhaga*, to be honored by them from all sides. Furthermore, may all the gods (*viśve devāsaḥ*) enjoy (*juṣerata*) that Soma on this very day (*adya*).
In Vedic usage, there is an absence of the substitution of *ra* for *jha*;
furthermore, the augment *ruṭ* is applied according to the rule "in Vedic usage [it occurs] diversely."
Of what sort are they? "Sajoṣasaḥ," meaning endowed with equal affection;
likewise, "Rājānā," meaning the two shining ones, Mitra and Varuṇa—you two "karathaḥ," that is, you perform, meaning you enjoy [it].
The suffix *śap* is applied by way of transposition.
For whatever reason we seek that which we obtain, for that we entreat the gods.
The root *īṅ* means "to go. It belongs to the *divādi* class; the elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffix is Vedic.
Therefore, may they take pleasure [in our offerings].
Likewise, we implore the two Ṛtāvānā—the possessors of Ṛta (truth), or the possessors of sacrifice—Mitra and Varuṇa; we beg for their desired fruit or for their drink.
1. kṣa, ṅa, ṭa, ṭa—in one; 2. i, kiṃca, kīdṛśī;
3. kṣa, cha, ja, ṭa, kau.
Whosoever, O Mitra and Varuṇa, offers oblations to you both, him—unassailable—you protect from distress, that mortal who bestows gifts, from distress.
He protects this vow, following the vow of Ujjayanta;
he who encompasses their vow with hymns (uktha) masters the vow, and he who encompasses it with chants (stoma) masters the vow.

Whosoever is the person who has worshipped Mitra and Varuṇa, him you two protect from distress—the one who is free from enemies, the mortal who remains steadfast in his devotion, you save him from distress. Aryaman protects him who acts uprightly according to the sacred law; he who encompasses their law with hymns, he who fulfills their law with songs of praise. 5.
The person who is the sacrificer [offers] to Mitra and to Varuṇa.
The dative case is used because [the recipient] is the recipient (saṃpradāna) of the action.
He has honored Mitra and Varuṇa;
he serves that person who is your attendant—
one who is invincible and free from malice.
According to the Vedic revelation, "The noble ones are indeed brothers" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.8.4), [the text says]:
"O you who are *anarvāṇaḥ*—those who do not serve others—protect us on all sides; protect us completely.
By this, it is meant: "O Kaṇvas! [or, O you who are like Kaṇva].
[Protect us] from *aṃhas*, the evils produced by deficiency or excess—
not only from ordinary people, but also from the *dādhvāṃsam*, the one who has offered oblations, [protect him] from *aṃhas*, from every evil, even from that which leads to death.

Not only you two, but also the god *ayenā*, the controller of all, protects and guards on all sides the sacrificer who acts uprightly among the gods and follows his own vow according to his ritual duty.
He states what the distinction of this person is:
he who is the sacrificer;
by means of the *ukthas*, that is, the recited hymns (*śastras*); of these two, namely Mitra and Varuṇa.

The ritual act (*vrata*) adorns and encompasses [the sacrifice]; likewise, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) adorns and encompasses your ritual act with *stomas*—that is, with hymns consisting of the *yājyā* mantras and the chapters of the *anuvākas*.
He "adorns" (*ābhūpati*), meaning he decorates it on all sides;
from the root *bhūṣ*, "to decorate."
It belongs to the *bhū* class.
The grammatical connection is that he protects him.
Homage to the lofty heaven, to the two worlds, to Mitra, and to Varuṇa the bounteous, the one who hears well and is bounteous.
Praise Indra directly; praise Aryaman and Bhaga.
Living long, may we be united with progeny; may we be united with the protection of Soma.

Homage! To the great heaven, to the two worlds, to Mitra, I shall speak, and to Varuṇa the bounteous, the one who grants happiness, the bounteous one. Praise Indra and Agni; praise Aryaman and Bhaga, who are ever-yoked. May we live long and be united with progeny; may we be united by the protection of Soma. 6.

Salutation to Sūrya, who shines day by day. I shall speak—I utter, that is, I praise—a hymn characterized by salutation. To what kind of one? To him who is *bṛhat*, the great. [In the rule] "The case-ending of *bṛhat* and *mahat* is udātta," the case-ending is accented. [I speak] to the one who is praised. Likewise, I shall speak salutation to the two *rodasī*, namely Heaven and Earth, the deities presiding over them. I shall speak. (Note: Variants 1–4 regarding the presence or absence of *janaḥ* or *vājanamasya*; variants 3–4 regarding *rakṣatam* or *rakṣataḥ*; and variant 4 regarding *tathā yakṣa* or *yakṣa* are noted as textual differences.)
Likewise, I utter salutations to Mitra, for the welfare of all people, the deity presiding over the day;
likewise to Varuṇa, the enveloper, the deity presiding over sovereignty;
and likewise to Mīḍhuṣ, the showerer of desired fruits, Rudra.
To what kind of person?
To the *sumlīka*, the one who bestows beautiful happiness.
Furthermore, he is qualified by this very attribute.
The two words *mīḷhuṣe* and *sumlīkāya* function as individual qualifiers.
Now, the sacrificer speaks either to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or to himself:
"O Hotṛ, or O Self, having approached—that is, having reached through the intellect—Indra, Agni, Dyukṣa (the radiant one), Aryaman, and Bhaga, praise them; perform their hymn of praise."

Through your favor, living for a long time and endowed with life, may we be united with progeny—sons, servants, and so forth—and remain together. Furthermore, through the protection (*ūtī*) of Soma, the Chandas, may we be united; that is to say, by praising him as well, may we be accompanied by the preservation brought about by him.
"With the protection of the gods, may we, possessing Indra, be mindful of glorious fame along with the Maruts."
May Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa grant us protection; may we and the patrons attain it.

(7) Through the favor of the gods, may we, accompanied by Indra, be mindful [of our goals], possessing self-splendor along with the Maruts. May Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa grant us protection; may we and the patrons attain that. (7)

Accompanied by Indra— possessing him through the favor of the pleased Indra— we, the gods among gods (the genitive case here denotes the object), may we honor (maṃsīmahi) with our aid (ūtī)— that is, with satisfaction through oblations and the like. We shall so consider ourselves.
What kind of people are we? We are those who possess celestial glory, whose fame is under their own control, and who are favored by the Maruts—the joyful gods of the wind—worthy of their praise.
Or rather:
By protecting the gods, may we be protected; by our capacity, may we become their knowers of their very greatness.
Furthermore, may the gods Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa grant us *śarma*—may they bestow upon us various forms of happiness.
Being *maghavan* (possessors of wealth) ourselves through what is given by them, may we attain and pervade that happiness.
In the case of the *liṅ* [optative] ending in *aśīta*, there is the elision of *s* because it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix by the rule "in the Veda, both ways.
Illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, he dispels the darkness of ignorance.
"May the Great Lord of Sacrificial Places (Yātīrthamaheśvara) grant the goals of human existence to the body.

Thus ends the first chapter of the second book (*aṣṭaka*) in the *Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa*, a commentary on the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā* composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabuka—the supreme sovereign of kings and supreme lord who established the path of the Vedic way. 1. [Variant readings:
kṣa-ṅa-jha-ṭa-tadabhimānidevatābhyām]
2. We think; we worship.
3. By Kṣa-ṅa-jha-ṭa-Sāyaṇācārya.
|| Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. ||
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now begins the second chapter of the second octad.
The fourth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with "supumā yātam," is composed by Parucchepa; it is in the Atiśakvara meter because it possesses fifty syllables.
However, due to the use of the word "tu" in the preceding [hymn], it belongs to Mitra and Varuna.
In this case, the rule regarding the eight syllables (*aṣṭiparibhāṣā*) is not applied, because it is specifically qualified as *atiśākara*.
On this point, the table of contents (*anukramaṇikā*) states: "The *supuma* triplet is *atiśākara*."
On the sixth day of the *daśarātra* sacrifice, during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), this hymn dedicated to the deities Mitra and Varuṇa consists of three verses for the *prauga-śastra*.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘stīrṇaṃ barhiḥ’—these two triplets [and] ‘supumā yātama dribhiḥ’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).
Likewise, it is to be inserted before the *prasthitayājyā* of the Maitrāvaruṇa priest at this very point.
In the section titled "The Morning Pressing of the Sixth [Day]," it is stated in the Sūtra: "supumā yātamdribhiḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).
The Supreme Soul has come with his powers; these Soma juices, which bestow the glory of cattle, are exhilarating;
these Soma juices are exhilarating, being mixed with mantras characterized by praise.
For this very reason, it is said, "The consecrations have become bright," according to the Vedic text:
"He pours in the milk-mixture for the sake of its being accompanied by the bright [Soma]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.6.5).
Hither come these drops, these pressed Soma juices mixed with curds;
yea, O Dawn, they have awakened together with the rays of the Sun.
Pressed for Mitra and Varuṇa to drink, well-prepared for them to drink.

These drops, these Soma juices mixed with curds, have been pressed—mixed with curds. And for you two, awakening at dawn together with the rays of the sun, the juice has been pressed: a lovely draught for Mitra and Varuṇa to drink, a draught for the sake of Truth. 2.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, come hither!

Since these *indavas*—the Soma juices capable of moistening—which are mixed with curds (*dadhyāśiraḥ*), that is, endowed with the support of skill (*dakṣa*), and which have been taken up in the vessels before you, are present here, therefore come hither!
Furthermore, these Somas, mixed with curds, being poured out, pressed by the stones with mantras, and thus perfected, are ready.
Therefore, the words "come hither" (ā yātam) are understood as the ellipsis.

Because there is the pouring of curds into the Āditya-graha vessel, it is said "mixed with curds" (dadhyāśira) in reference to that. Furthermore, for the sake of your pleasure and protection, when there is awakening—that is, at the time of waking related to the dawn (upasaḥ budhi)—[we pray].
The suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) characterized by attainment and so forth;
the acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
This occurs when illumination has arisen.

It is not only at the approach [of dawn], but also at the awakening [of day]: when the light has arisen together with the rays of the sun—that is, along with the solar beams—for the purpose of offering the oblation, the Soma has been pressed and purified. Now it is spoken of separately:

for Mitra, the one who benefits all (and by this name refers to the deity presiding over the day), and likewise for Varuṇa, the enveloper (referring to the deity presiding over the night); for their sake, the Soma has been pressed—this is the ellipsis.
Furthermore: "For Ṛta," that is, for sacrifice and for that which accomplishes it; "for its sake," that is, for the purpose of drinking.
For the drinking of Soma by the gods is indeed for the sake of the success of the sacrifice.
Or else:

The suffix *ktic* is used in the active sense (*kartari*). For the sake of drinking (*pītaye*), for the vessel (*pātre*), for the sake of the priest and others (*ṛtvigādyaye*), and for the sacrifice (*ṛtāya*)— that is,
for the performance of the sacrifice— the beautiful (*cāruḥ*), that is, worthy of being practiced or consumed, Soma has been pressed (*sutaḥ*) and purified (*abhipūtaḥ*).
Like a milch-cow yielding her milk at dawn, they milk that stalk for you with the stones;
come hither toward us to drink our Soma.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, this Soma has been pressed by the men for your drinking; it has been pressed.

Like two milch-cows at dawn, they milk that stalk with the pressing-stones; they milk the Soma with the pressing-stones. Come hither toward us, both of you, for the drinking of the Soma. O Mitra and Varuna, this Soma has been pressed by the men for you; it is pressed for your drinking. 3.

1. Mixed with milk (payas). 2. According to the *cha* and *jha₁* versions, they are those that are soft (*mārdava*) for four months, or capable of moistening (*kledana*). 3. According to *kṣa*, *jha*, *jha₁*, *a*, and *ṭa*, they possess curd as their base (*dadhyāśrayaṇavat*). 4. According to *kṣa*, *jha₁*, *ja*, and *ṭa*, they exist; the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) is "to them, having come from the sun itself" (*svārkatam āyātam*). 5. According to *kṣa*, *a*, and *ṭa*, it is called *dadhyāśira*; the plural number is used in view of its constituent parts (*avayavāpekṣayā*). 6. According to *kṣa*, *cha*, *jha*, *jha₁*, *a*, and *ṭa*, it is "for drinking" (*pītaye*), meaning for the sake of consumption (*pānāya*). 7. According to *kṣa*, *cha*, *jha₁*, *a*, and *ṭa*, [the particle] *ca*. 8. According to *jha₁*, it is "for the sake of warding off" (*vārakāya*). 9. In the *ṅa*, *jha*, and *jha₁* versions, the phrase "for the sake of accomplishing that" (*tannirvāhakāya*) does not appear. 10. According to *kṣa*, *ma*, and *ṭa*, [the suffix] *phin*.
The Adhvaryu priests milk—that is, they produce—the *aṃśu* Soma, which is related to you two and takes the form of a creeper (*valī*).
What is it like? It is like that well-known *agrihotrāyathā*, meaning a *vāsarī* cow whose udders are covered by all her limbs and who possesses abundant milk.
Or rather,
[it means] that which covers with milk and so forth;
from the root *vas* in the sense of "covering."
The suffix *ara* is derived from the *auṇādika* [list];
the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule “*kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*.
Alternatively:
The suffix *ara* is purely derived from the *uṇādi* list; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*).
[He compares her] to a cow that does not please, as if she were a flame.
He then states by what means [this occurs]:

With the stones—the means of pressing—with those very stones, they milk for our sake the Soma that exists in the form of the *vala* mountain; having drenched it with water, they milk the essence for you alone.
Furthermore, being directed toward us (*arvāñcā*), for the drinking of Soma (*somapātaye*), may you two, our protectors (*asmatrā*), come near (*upa gantam*) to our sacrifice (*yajñam*).

Furthermore, this Soma has been pressed—that is, extracted—by men who are leaders, or by men who are knowers and executors, for your sake (*vām yuṣmadartham*). Moreover, it has been pressed for complete drinking (*ā pītaye*); therefore, the meaning is that you two should come.
The fifth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with "pra pra pūṣṇaḥ," is composed by Parucchepa, belongs to the middle [Maṇḍala], and has Pūṣan as its deity.
It is introduced in the Anukramaṇī as: "The group of four beginning with 'pra pra' is dedicated to Pūṣan.
Its application is determined by its indicative marks (liṅga).
