Onward, onward is the greatness of Pūṣan, who is born of himself, proclaimed; the praise of this powerful one does not falter, the hymn of him does not falter. I sing the prayer for favor, the protection that brings bliss, to him who has drawn to himself the mind of every man, the vigorous god who has drawn it to himself.

1. On and on is celebrated the greatness of Pūṣan, he who is born with many powers; the praise of this mighty one does not falter, his hymn of praise does not falter. Seeking favor, I sing of him who is within our call, the source of bliss; he who has drawn to himself the mind of every man—the liberal god has drawn it to himself. 1. On and on is celebrated the greatness of Pūṣan, he who is born with many powers; the praise of this mighty one does not falter, his hymn of praise does not falter. Seeking favor, I sing of him who is within our call, the source of bliss; he who has drawn to himself the mind of every man—the liberal god has drawn it to himself. 1.

The greatness of this powerful deity named Pūṣan—the nourisher who has arisen for the sake of many sacrificers—is proclaimed and celebrated by all as his majesty and the vastness of his strength. The repetition [of the particle] is for the purpose of completing the meter. No one tires him; no one harms him.
Furthermore, the hymn (*stotra*) of this Pūṣan does not falter; it does not harm him, nor does it cease.
The meaning is that every person praises him.
The sense is that this is because he nourishes the entire world.
For this reason, I too, as a sacrificer (*yajamāna*), desiring happiness (*sumnayan*), praise (*ardhāmi*) him. Of what kind is he?
One who provides protection (*anyyūti*) on all sides.
The elision of the letter *ka* occurs according to the rule "elision of *kādi* [letters] is frequent" (*kādilopo bahulam*).
The meaning is that immediately after being praised, [the deity] bestows boons.
*Mayobhuvam* means that which produces happiness or that which brings it about.

He who is Pūṣan, the vigorous one, possessed of sacrifice— the word *makh* being elided in its sense of "sacrifice"— stirs the mind of every praiser and every officiating priest, blending it thoroughly from all sides.
The sense is: "because of the swift granting of boons.
Furthermore, this *deva* (the shining one) has joined this *makha*—that is, the sacrifice—to the *makha*, meaning he unites it until its completion;
or alternatively:
If it is asked, "What has come of this regarding the sacrificer when there is a mixing of the mind of the universe?"—it is said:
This god Pūṣan, the executor of the sacrifice (*makha*), has thoroughly mixed (*āyuyuve*) the mind of the sacrificer;
by implication, it is understood that this refers to the mind of the sacrificer.

The *liṭ* [perfect tense] ending is used here according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). 1. [Variants]: kṣa, ṅa, jha, ña, ṭa—*ājñāvyākhyādhyāya*. 2. [Variant]: kha, pha—*somapānāya vām*. 3. [Variant]: jha—*upalakṣya āgacchatam*. 4. [Variants]: kṣa, ṅa, jha, ña, ṭa—*tuvijātasya asya yaṣṭavyasya tuvijātasya*. 5. [Variants]: kṣa, ṅa, jha, ña, ṭa—*pra* is used as a filler (*pādapūraṇe*). 6. [Variant]: ṅa, jha—*karṣvadāpa*. 7. [Variants]: kṣa, ṅa, jha, ña, ṭa—*ā* means "from all sides" (*samantāt*). 8. [Variants]: kṣa, ña, ṭa—[It is] "swiftly" because of the granting of the boon (*varapradānāt*). 9. [Variants]: ca, jha, kṣa, ta—*dīpyamānaḥ* (shining) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
For we urge you on, O Pūṣan, like a swift steed on its course with our hymns, so that you may overcome our adversaries; like a camel, carry us across our enemies.
We have called upon you, the bliss-bringing god, for friendship with mortals.
Make our songs of praise glorious; in the contests for booty, make them glorious.

For I urge you forward, O Pūṣan, like a swift steed on its path with songs of praise, so that you may drive away our adversaries; as a camel carries its load, carry us across our adversaries. When I, a mortal, call upon you, the god who dispels fear, for friendship, grant us glorious strength through our praises; in the battles for booty, grant us glorious strength. 2.
O Pūṣan, when the journey has become the occasion for my going toward the swift sacrificial ground, I exalt you with hymns; I make you preeminent there,
just as one exalts a swift-moving horse during a rapid journey.
It is just as it is being introduced;
furthermore, just as you would go toward battles (*mṛdhaḥ*) with joy (*ṛṇvaḥ*), so do I bring them forth.
Or rather:
Just as a creditor might go against one who does not recognize the debt.
The root *ṛ* means "to go. It belongs to the *tādi* group. In the *leṭ* mood, there is the addition of the augment *aṭ*.
Thus do I make you;
moreover, you carry across to the further shore the assailants—the hostile warriors—in battle.
This is the form [of the root] *pārayati* in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
it is not like a camel.
Just as a camel, being a bearer of burdens, carries them across, so too do you carry us across—from *mṛdhaḥ*, meaning from battle—you lead us to the further shore (*pāra*).
For this reason, I—a mortal subject to death—invoke you, Pūṣan, the god who delights in divine play, the bringer of bliss;
for what purpose? For friendship, that is, for a bond of equal companionship, and for dear union.
Thus being invoked, make our praises, our resonant songs, and our hymns—Yāska says, "Āḍguṣa means praise; āghoṣa means resonance"—resplendent; that is, make them full of light.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "Make the hymns glorious or rich in food; being pleased by our praise, you yourself shall do so. Furthermore, "in battles, make [our enemies] illustrious and rich in food"—the meaning is that I shall take their tongues and place them within me.
"O Pūṣan, those who, being wise in their own minds, have enjoyed the benefit of your friendship through your power"—yes, they have enjoyed it through your power.
Following that, we seek from you a newer team for the sake of wealth.
O benevolent one, wide-famed, be swift; in every contest, be swift.

O Pūṣan, those who, desiring to celebrate in your friendship, have enjoyed your protection through their wisdom—even while being [mere] mortals—have indeed enjoyed it through your wisdom. Following that most recent [path] of yours, we implore you for a chariot-load of wealth. Being free from anger, O you of wide renown, come hither; in every contest for booty, come hither. 3.
1. With the *jha-jha-1* hymns; 2. *jha-nayasi* means "you lead" or "you cause to tremble"; 3. *jha-jha-uṣṭra iva* (like a camel). As it says on page 109:

"O Pūṣan, O God, when there is friendship—that is, the performance of benefit—between you, who are renowned as a protector, and the crop (*sasye*), by means of *ṛtunā*, that is, by the very ritual act (*karma*) currently performed."
The absence of the name [of the suffix] occurs because of the rule: "In the Veda, there is optionally the non-application [of the feminine suffix] in words such as *jas*."
The "santas" (the good) are those who please you; the "vipanyavaḥ" are those especially characterized by the habit of praising—
or alternatively,
this is a term for the wise.
The wise sacrificers, being protected by their own performed protection (*avasā svakṛtena rakṣaṇena*), have enjoyed and do enjoy worldly pleasures;
in this very same way, all [beings] have always enjoyed and do enjoy through their ritual action (*ṛtā karmaṇā*), for they are all sustained.
In the case of the root *bhuj* with the *liṭ* suffix, the augment *ruṭ* is applied by the rule "there is much [irregularity] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

Following after that such most recent, newer praise or protection, immediately after that protection, we beg for—that is, we request—that much wealth, a number of riches equal to that. Furthermore, O you of wide renown, praised in many ways, being free from anger and well-disposed toward us, come hither; you must be one who is approached by us.
The suffix *ini* is derived from the *uṇādi* [rules];
it has an acute accent on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
Furthermore, in every battle, in every contest, be *sarī*—that is, be one who moves, meaning be a leader who goes at the front.
O you whose horses are goats, come quickly to us for our gain; do not be angry, O liberal giver, O you whose horses are goats, come to those who desire glory, O you whose horses are goats!
O Pūṣan, we have turned you hither with these excellent hymns of praise; for I do not neglect you in the press-house, nor do I deny your friendship.

Of this [hymn]: *Ūm*! Be well-disposed toward us for our gain, O ungrudging one, you who are a giver, O Lord of goats and horses, for those seeking glory, O Lord of goats and horses! *Oṃ*! We have truly turned you hither with effective hymns, O Wondrous One; for I do not disregard you, O Pūṣan, nor do I reject your friendship, O Guardian. 4.
"Pūṣan, whose horses are goats" (*ajāśva*); "He calls Pūṣan 'ajāśva'" (Nirukta 4.25), says Yāska.
[May he come] to our mouth (*asya*) of this [speech].
The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.
For the sake of gain and profit, being free from resentment, not becoming angry, and showing no disrespect—being both wealthy and a giver—be well-established in our presence.
The suffix *kasu* is used for the Vedic *liṭ* (perfect tense) of the root *rā*.
Although there is no [standard] word division (*padasaṃkhyā*) here, a Vedic pause (*avagraha*) is observed in examples such as *papivāṃsam* and *tasthivāṃsam*.
The particle *ū* serves to fill out the meter.
Furthermore, O Ajāśva— He for whom goats indeed stand in the place of horses— you, named Pūṣan, being a generous giver, have come near us who desire food and seek renown.

Regarding the phrase "ajāḥ pūṇāḥ" (Nirukta 1.15.5), Yāska states that "o" is a single particle consisting of a combination of two particles. O *dasma*, destroyer of enemies, O *pūṣan*, we would hold you—*o pu*—from all sides indeed; we would cause you to turn [toward us] most completely.

In the case of the root *vṛ*, because it has an internal causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*), the substitution of *śru* for *śap* occurs in the *liṭ* [perfect] by the rule "variously in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
The meaning is that we turn you away from proceeding to another sacrifice. By what means? That is stated:
"by means of *sādhubhiḥ stomabhiḥ*—that is, by hymns capable of pleasing you."
Furthermore, O Pūṣan, you who pour down rain from all sides—
or rather,
you who bring and accept the oblations— I do not show you any disregard or contempt in the churning.

Not only do I not transgress [this], but furthermore, I do not deny—that is, I do not take away or abandon—your friendship, your state of being a friend, and your role as a benefactor; rather, I establish it in every respect. This is the meaning.
1. By the original [reading] (jha). 2. By the well-known protection of *kha*, *ca*, and *pha*.
3. In the manuscript *ṅa*, the word "iti" after *jña* and *jha* is absent.
4. *kṣa-ca-ma-ṭa-tvā* refers to "you" (*tvām*).
5.3. *jha-1-saṃbhajamānāhānārtham* means for the purpose of not abandoning those who are devoted.
6. In the manuscripts *kṣa-jha-1-ṭa*, after the phrase "I do not at all disregard him," there is an additional passage: "or rather, no person whatsoever is excessively disparaged."
7. To perform what is beneficial for living beings;
8. I do not at all conceal [my faults];
9. I cause [them] to set forth.

The hymn beginning with “astu śrauṣaṭ” consists of eleven verses. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “*Astu śrauṣaṭ*: eleven verses; addressed to the Viśvedevas; the first three are addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa; [the next] two are addressed to Indra; [the next] one is addressed to the Maruts; [the next] one is addressed to Indra and Agni; [the next] one is addressed to Bṛhaspati; and the last is addressed to the Viśvedevas. The final [verse] is in Triṣṭubh meter, and the fifth is in Bṛhatī meter. This applies to the Viśvedeva hymns; likewise, when other hymns are employed, they belong to the Viśvedevas. When different hymns are employed, whichever deity is indicated by the characteristic mark (liṅga) is the presiding deity. The seer (ṛṣi) is Parucchepa.
Another [verse] is a Triṣṭubh, the fifth is a Bṛhatī,
and the others are Atyaṣṭis due to the absence of any specific distinction.
The entire hymn is dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
In that regard, the Viśvedevas are the deity of the first [verse];
Mitra and Varuṇa are the deities of the second;
and then there are three verses having the Aśvins as their deities.
The sixth [verse] belongs to Indra;
the seventh belongs to Indra;
the eighth belongs to the Maruts.
The ninth [offering] belongs to Indra and Agni;
the tenth belongs to Bṛhaspati;
the eleventh belongs to the Viśvedevas.
The application of the hymn is based on its indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
On the sixth day of the ten-day period (*daśarātra*), the first verse is used for the *vaiśvadeva* portion of the *prauga* recitation.
This is prescribed in the section titled "Of the Sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhasya*) in the Sūtra: "May there be the *śrauṣaṭ*; O Agni, [be] the guest" (*ādha. śrī. 8. 1*).
Let there be *śrauṣaṭ*; I place Agni at the forefront with my prayer. Now we choose that divine host; we choose Indra and Vāyu.
Or rather, when the newest [hymn] has been offered at the central point for Vivasvat;
then may our inspired thoughts go forth toward the gods, even as our inspired thoughts.

So be it! Let it be heard! I place Agni before me with my thought. Now we choose that divine host; we choose Indra and Vāyu. Since this newest [hymn] has been offered at the central point when the rite is performed for Vivasvat—therefore may our prayers go forth well toward us; let our prayers go toward the gods as they do now. 1.

I have established Agni, known as the Āhavanīya, in front—that is, upon the northern altar—by means of *dhiyā*, through the ritual acts such as the leading forward [of the fire]. We now quickly (*nu*) choose for ourselves that *tác chardhaḥ*—that powerful Agni, or rather, that *tác chardhaḥ*, the very form and strength of the Maruts—which is divine (*divyam*), existing in heaven; we encounter it face-to-face. Furthermore, we choose Indra and Vāyu.
Because, at the time of Vivasvat, the radiant one, in the *nābhi*— that is, in the navel, the place of sacrifice upon the earth which serves as the altar;
or alternatively, in the *nābhi*, the sacrifice that is connected with all fruits.
According to the Vedic scripture, "They call the sacrifice the navel of the world" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.4.18.2),
the newer, more recent speech in the form of praise, performing its own purpose of illumination, is joined together.
In Vedic usage, the *luṅ* suffix is employed in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The meaning is: "it is employed by us.
Since praise is being performed, therefore let there be *śrauṣaṭ*—let there be the hearing of this praise;
or rather, let there be a listener, whether through the roar of the Maruts or through the fires.
In the case of Indra and Vāyu, the singular number is used with reference to each individually.
Immediately thereafter (*adha*), may our *dhītayaḥ*—our ritual acts consisting of hymns of praise and the like—*pra su upa yantu*, that is, go forth excellently toward you.
Furthermore, may our *dhītayaḥ* go toward the gods; as if reaching the gods such as Agni and others face-to-face, may our ritual acts reach their presence.
1. *Ṅa-jha*-force or one possessing force;
become a Saṃgha. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*-force or one possessing force; [we approach] the Saṃgha. 2. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa*-we choose or we pray for.
3. According to Kṣa, Ja, Ṭa, and Yadva, [the word *krāṇā*] means "in the form of the sacrificial altar" (*vedirūpe*).
4. According to Kṣa, Ja, Ṭa, and Krāṇā, having been joined with action in the form of blazing, it signifies the manifestation of its own meaning.
5. According to Kṣa, Jha₁, Ba, and Ṭa, [the verb *kṛṇvanti*] means "may they cause to reach."
When indeed, O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two establish untruth from truth by your own will, by your own will of the skillful one.
We beheld your golden chariot as it stood upon the summit; we saw it through our prayers, through our mind, and with our own eyes—through our own eyes, as it were, of Soma.

That which you two, O Mitra and Varuṇa, have established from the Truth—yes, that very untruth you have established through your own wrath, through the wrath of Dakṣa, through your own wrath. Thus, in the places where you are seated, we beheld your golden chariot with our prayers, even with our mind, with our own eyes, with the eyes of Soma—with our own eyes. 2.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, from Ṛta, from Āditya, you two have established—that water—beyond it; for which reason, you have placed it abundantly on all sides.
Of what nature is that water? It is untruthful, perishable, and of a drying nature.
By what means?
By his own "manyu," that is, by his own splendor (*tejas*).
Indeed, the two gods Mitra and Varuṇa, who preside over day and night, release the rain.
The scriptural passage beginning with "or day and night" has already been cited.
[The word] *manyu* is qualified [as follows]: "of Dakṣa," meaning of the capable one; "by his own *manyu*," that is, by his inherent capacity which is to be contemplated as his very self.
Furthermore: "O Mitra and Varuna, yours..."
The elision of another [vowel] is a Vedic archaism.
The connection between you two is a golden, that is, made of gold, form.
In the rule *ṛvyavāstavyavāstavya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.175), the elision of the letter *m* from the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).
"In this manner"—that is, in the way about to be described—"we have seen" (or "may we see") "among those who sit at the sacrifice.
By what means? That is stated:

"by means of *dhī*s"—that is, by ritual acts such as the sacrifice directed toward you—and "even by the mind," that is, by a consciousness intent upon you, and "by our own eyes"—that is, by our own mental faculties such as sight and the rest.
Furthermore: "Of Soma, [protect] the Soma with your own eyes"—that is, with our own sense organs.
The plural number is used in view of the nose and so forth.
On the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], the triplet for the Aśvins in the *prauga-śastra* is "yuvāṃ stomebhiḥ.
This is prescribed in the section titled "of the sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhasya*) in the Sūtra: "yuvāṃ stomebhir devayanto aśvināśravamaha indra" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).
O Aśvins, those two who seek the gods with hymns of praise, like two Āyus, have caused the sound of their fame to be heard; you two have come to the oblations of the one who invokes you.
Upon your chariot, O possessors of all wealth, rest splendors and nourishments; they flow forth for you both upon your golden chariot, O wonder-workers, upon your golden chariot.

O Aśvins, those seeking the gods, with hymns of praise, like those making their voices heard, the living men call upon you both; the living men call upon you for the oblations. O possessors of all wealth, all glories and nourishments rest upon you both; your coursers foam at the mouth on your golden chariot, O doers of marvels, on your golden chariot. 3.
1. By the wrath (*manyu*) of Dakṣa—that is, by his own inherent splendor (*tejas*) which is capable of overcoming;
or alternatively, by the wrath of Dakṣa who is capable of praising you two, [meaning] by that which is endowed with the power of thought (*manana*) inherent to himself (*svabhūta*).
Furthermore:
2. by means of one's own sense faculties (indriya);

3. in relation to the mind (manas) and so forth—such as *ka*, *ja*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *va*, and *jña*; or in relation to the mind and so forth—such as *kṣa*, *na*, *kṣa*, *la*, *ṭa*, and *mana*.

O Aśvins, O divine Aśvins, those seeking the gods— the *bhāyavas*, a term for humans— namely the sacrificers, desiring you for themselves, praise you with hymns and chants, as if making your fame, in the form of praise directed toward you, heard everywhere by causing it to reach the range of all ears.
"Śloka" is a name for speech, because it is listed among its names in the Nirukta (1.11.1) as "ślokaḥ dhārā. Of what nature are they?
You two are the ones who go toward (*abhyāyavaḥ*), that is, those who approach face-to-face with the oblations (*havyā*) consisting of clarified butter and other offerings.
The word "to please" (*prīṇayitum*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Or, [the meaning is] "bringing the oblations (*havīṣi*) toward you.

Furthermore, O possessors of all wealth (*viśvavedasā*), all glories (*viśvāḥ śriyaḥ*)—all desirable fortunes consisting of wealth, fame, and so forth—belonging to you two, "dwell exceedingly" (*adhi... bhajante*); this is the ellipsis.
Moreover, by your grace, they obtain even more nourishment (*pṛkṣa*).
Furthermore, O *dastrau*—you two who destroy the enemies—the fellies (*pavayaḥ*) of your golden, honey-filled chariot are *tanmemayante*: they flow, they drip, they pour out.
In the Vedic usage of the present tense (*laṅ*), the absence of the augment is according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (the augment is often omitted in the Vedas).
The acute accent on the first syllable is Vedic (*cāndasa*).
Of what sort are they?
Like one on a good path—that is, by way of a fair road—they are going toward, or proceeding to, the *rajas*, which consists of passion (*rajjanātmaka*), namely heaven, in the supportless sky.
Because it has been stated that "the worlds are called 'dusts' (rajas)," they are those who,
while instructing, bring under their command those who are not compliant with their instruction.

In the case of the root *śās* with the suffix *śatṛ*, because it is classified as "abhyasta" according to the rule *jakṣityādayaḥ*, the first syllable receives the udātta accent by the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ*.
Furthermore, they are those who, by means of their command, forcibly bring under their control the "rajas" (water) characterized by rain, which is the primary subject at hand.
O Lords of Power, with your powers, grant us your favor by day and by night! May your delight never fail us, nor may there ever be a lack of your bounty.
O you two who possess power, with your powers, grant us your favor by day and by night! May your delight never fail us; may your delight never turn away from us at any time. 5.
O possessors of *śacī*!
*Śacī* is a name for ritual action (*karman*).

You two, whose wealth consists of the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other rites performed by us, through those *śacīs*—that is, our own actions such as sacrifices which serve as the cause—grant what is desired both by day and by night, during the day and at night.
This is a Vedic form of the root *dāś* meaning "to give";
or alternatively,
the root *daśasyati* has the sense of giving.
It should be understood as belonging to the *kaṇḍv-ādi* group.
O you two, may your delight—that is, your gift—never at any time, whether during the sacrifice or even outside the time of sacrifice, ever fail or diminish.
In the sense of "destruction" (*upakṣaya*),
[the root] *das* takes the suffix *aṅ* for the *luṅ* tense by the rule "after roots beginning with *pu* and *dyut*, [the suffix] *aṅ* replaces *cli*."

Not only yours, but ours as well—our delight, our giving, whether it be the offering of oblations and the like or the gift of all objects to those in need—may this never fail (*upa-dastvat*), may it never be exhausted; let it continue at all times.
The meaning is: "I too shall always give for your sake, and you two also shall always give what is desired by me."
On the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], in the *aindra* triplet of the *prauga-śastra*, this third verse is used:
“O Indra, you who are a bull, the Soma drops are bulls; come well with the pressing-stones” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).
In that very *savana*, having inserted other verses before the *prasthitayājyās*, one should sacrifice with both sets of verses.
Among these, this [verse] is to be inserted by the Hotṛ before the *prasthitayājyā*.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: “At the morning *savana* of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], they sacrifice without pausing, using both [sets of verses] inserted before the *prasthitayājyās*” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.1).
1. When *kṣa*, *ma*, *a*, *ṭa*, and *śaṇ* follow, there is elision (*luk*). In that case, *tipnaḥ*. 2.
When *kṣa*, *jha*, *a*, *ṭa*, and *kīdṛśau* follow: "What are you two like? (*yuvām*).

"By a path that is indeed a good path" means by a road; O [you two], what kind [of people] are you? [It means] by a road that is indeed a good path. 3. [The reading] "even in the sky" is found in the manuscripts kṣa, a, and ṭa.
4. *ca-pa-pha*: "The youth who possesses the wealth of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma is our [refuge]"; *jha-jyotiṣṭomādikarmadhano naḥ*.

5. *kṣa-jha1-a-ṭa*: "Bestowing. 6. *kṣa-ba-ṭa-ṅa-kṣa1*: After the word "draṣṭavyaḥ" (is to be seen), there is the additional passage: "He always consumes the oblation intended for us" (*asmatpratyarthaṃ haviḥ sarvadā makṣayate* [or *bhakṣayate*]).
7. *Jha* means "even in all states.
8. *Kṣa-a-ṭa* means "given"; such is the meaning.

O Bull-like Indra, these pressed juices are for you to drink, like drops of soma; these stones-pressed drops are overflowing, these pressed drops are overflowing for you. May they exhilarate you for the sake of giving, for great and wondrous bounty. O you who are borne by songs, being praised with hymns, come hither; as one who is gracious, come to us. O Bull-like Indra, these are the drinks for the bull-like one; like drops of soma, these are the pressed juices, these stones-pressed drops are overflowing, these pressed drops are overflowing for you. May they exhilarate you for the sake of giving, for great and wondrous bounty. O you who are borne by songs, being praised with hymns, come hither; as one who is gracious, come to us. 6.

O Indra, O bull, showerer of desires, these *indavas*—these Soma juices seen here before you—are pressed and purified for your sake. Of what nature are they? They are *vṛṣapānāsas*: to be drunk by the one who rains down desired boons.

"Pressed by the stones"—pressed by the firm stones which are the means of extraction; "up-pressers of rain," they are further specified as "up-pressers of strength," or "those who emerge from mountains and such places. Such Soma juices are "pressed for you," meaning they have been extracted specifically for your sake.

Furthermore, "those such Soma juices" (te tādṛśāḥ somāḥ) "may exhilarate you" (tvā mandantu)—that is, satisfy you. Where? That is stated: "at the giving," that is, at the sacrifice characterized by the act of giving.
Or [to him] who bestows what is desired;
likewise, for the sake of great (*maha*), wonderful (*citra*), or increasing (*cāyamāna*) wealth (*arādhas*) of various kinds (*vicitra*);
furthermore, O bearer of songs (*gīrvāhas*), you who carry our hymns of praise (*gir*).
The suffix *asun* is applied [to the root] according to the rule "vahi-hā-vā-bhyaḥ."
Being praised with our words—that is, with our hymns of praise—come hither;
being one who is most gracious, that is, a true benefactor, come hither to us.

On the sixth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), prior to the *sthitayājyā* of the Neṣṭṛ at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), there is an offering with both [verses] using the insertion verse (*āvapanīyā*) "O come to us, O Agni" (*o pū ṇo agne*). This is prescribed in the section on the "Sixth Day" in the Sūtra: "'O come to us, O Agni, hear us; thou art praised... Agni, the Hotṛ' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1)."
In that very *savana*, the second [verse] occurs in the *prauga-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘astu śrauṣaṭ’, ‘pū ṇo agne’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).

O Agni, hear us; being praised, do thou speak to the worshipful gods, to the worshipful kings. Since you, O gods, gave that cow to the Aṅgirases, Aryaman milks her apart for the one who performs the rite; he knows her well along with me. O Agni, hear us; being praised, do thou speak to the worshipful gods, to the worshipful kings. Since you, O gods, gave that cow to the Aṅgirases, Aryaman milks her apart for the one who performs the rite; he knows her well along with me.

1. [The reading] *harṣasya* is found in manuscripts kṣa, ṅa, jha₁, ja, and ṭa; 2. [the reading] *phalasya* is found in manuscripts kṣa, ṅa, jha₁, tra, and ṭa; 3. being the bearer (*voḍhaḥ*), while praising—meaning while being praised by us—come hither (*ā gahi*).

4. [The variants] kṣa-jha1-ja-ṭa read: "You ought to come. 5. [The variants] kṣa-ja-ṭa read: "Having unified with the *prākṛti*, the sacrifice is performed by both. O Agni, you—being praised (*vīlitaḥ*) by us, that is, having been lauded by us—hear (*śṛṇuhi*) our invocation (*āvāhana*) or our hymn of praise (*stuti*).
The word *o* is a single particle consisting of the combination of two particles;
[it means] "listen very well, facing me directly."
The phrase "utaśca pratyayāt" and "chandasi vāvacanam" contain a reason within them.
And having heard it from the gods—those who are divine by nature, worthy of sacrifice, entitled to the sacrificial oblation, and, in other words, recipients of hymns of praise.
The suffix *gha* is applied [to form *yājñika*] by the rule “*yajñarvibhyām*.”
To those worthy of sacrifice, those deserving of the rite, and to the sacrificers—proclaim their connected ritual action; speak it forth.
In the leṭ (subjunctive) mood, there is the augment *aṭ* after the root *brū*.
From what kind?
From the *vrājas*, that is, from those that are shining.
Now, the gods are being praised directly.
Regarding this, they relate an ancient history: Formerly, the great sages named Aṅgirasas, having gratified the gods with hymns for the sake of a sacrifice, requested cows from them.
Being pleased, the gods said, "We grant you the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadughā).
Having obtained that cow, [they took] its milk...

Whatever there is—of various kinds, central, new, worthy of praise, immortal (possessing the nature of immortality), or difficult for mortals to obtain; whatever exists among the *ghoṣas* (the word *ghoṣāt* is used with a shift of case, meaning the fifth)—whether they be cattle and the like endowed with sound, or villages, cities, and so forth characterized by sound—all that, in age after age (the word *yuga* indicating the respective time), let it belong to us alone; this is the ellipsis—let it not belong to anyone else.
Furthermore, O Maruts, bestow upon us that wealth which is difficult to attain—that which is hard to acquire—and maintain it for us.
Moreover, establish all that which is difficult to overcome—everything harmed by enemies—especially within us.
This verse, "Dadhyaṅ ha me," is to be recited before the *prasthitayājyā* of the *acchāvāka* on the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭha* rite.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Dadhyaṅ ha me januṣaṃ pūrvo aṅgirāḥ*—thus [the verse] is [recited] at the midday [libation]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).

“Dadhyaṅ, the ancient Aṅgiras, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, and Manu—they knew my birth; those ancients, Manu and the rest, knew them. Their lineage extends among the gods, and our navel [of kinship] is with them.”
To their station I bow down with my voice; to Indra and Agni I bow down with my song. 9.

Dadhyañc, Aṅgiras, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, and Manu know my birth through the ancients; those ancients and Manu know me. Their lineage extends among the gods, and our kinships are rooted in them. To their station I bow down with my voice; to Indra and Agni I bow down with my song. 9.

V Dadhyañc is the name of a great seer born of the Atharvan lineage; he is "V pūrvaḥ," meaning the filler of all or the ancient one. He is "V aṅgirāḥ," which means "aṅgāraḥ" (a glowing coal), signifying that he is radiant with splendor.
Alternatively, it is because "the glowing coals themselves became the Aṅgirases" (Ai. Brā. 3.34), according to the Śruti.
The *Nirukta* states: “Aṅgiras, aṅgārāḥ, aṅkanāḥ, aṅkanāḥ” (Nirukta 3.17).
There was also a great ṛṣi of this name, Priyamedha, meaning "one whose wisdom is dear.
Yāska says: “Priyamedha: his wisdoms (*medhāḥ*) are dear” (Nirukta 3.17).
And that Kaṇva is wise; and that Atri is free from bad dreams—the Nirukta states: “Atri means ‘the three’” (Nirukta 3.17).
And Manu is the great seer of that name, possessed of the power of reflection.

All these great-souled great seers (maharṣis) know—indeed, they fully understand—the birth and origin of Parucchepa, the son of Divodāsa. [This is from the root] *vid* with the substitution of *us* for the suffix *śn* according to the rule "vido laṭo vā. Furthermore, those aforementioned ones are "the former," meaning those belonging to a previous time who knew me in this state.

The word *manavaḥ* means those who possess wisdom (*jñānavantaḥ*). Since those ancient *manus* were such, they knew; this is the intended meaning. The elision of the case-ending (*jas*) is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
He states the logical justification for their knowledge as follows:
Among those [such as Dadhyañc and others], there is a long-standing connection (āyatiḥ) with the other gods—that is, with the great sages whose nature is divine;
therefore, the meaning is that they know [this]. And what follows from that? He says:
In our lives, there are three vital breaths (*prāṇas*) that are bound together;
or rather, sacrifices connected with their fruits proceed precisely through them.
Since it must be stated by them that "this person of distinguished birth is therefore fit for sacrifice," [the self] is dependent upon them.

Because of their status as great seers (*maharṣi*), the cause being their very station, all people bow down with speech in the form of praise—bowing greatly, that is, excessively—to Dadhyañc and the others. Furthermore, through their grace, being worthy of sacrifice and joined with speech in the form of praise, I bow down toward Indra and Agni; that is, I praise them, I bow down to them. (The middle voice ending *name* occurs by a grammatical substitution.)
Alternatively, in the case of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*), there is a prohibition of the *yak* suffix according to the rule "na duhastunamām"; thus,
it means "I bow down by myself."

1. After the word *dhārayata*, [the manuscripts] kṣa, jha, ṭa add: *dhārayatha | dhṛñ dhāraṇe | bahulaṃ chandasīti śapaḥ pluḥ | uhibhya (kṣa, na, ṭa: ididbhyaḥ? ityanuvṛttau bahulaṃ chandasīti abhyāsasyettvam* (‘you maintain; the root *dhṛñ* means to hold; by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the substitution of *plu* for *śap*; while the rule *uhibhyaḥ* [or *ididbhyaḥ*] is being followed, by *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the change of the reduplication vowel to *i*’). 2. In the manuscripts ca, pha, ya, ca, the reading is *dustaram*. 3. In the manuscript kṣa, jha, ṭa, the reading is *bandhanavantaḥ*. 4. In the manuscript jha, 1, the word *mahat* is added. 5. In the manuscripts cha, jha, 1, the reading is *ānato’smi*. [Verse] ka. 110.

Let the Hotṛ worship; let the seekers of wood win what is desirable. Bṛhaspati, the seer, performs the sacrifice with bulls—bulls rich in boons. He has yawned forth the far-reaching hymn from the rock by his own power. The one of noble will has maintained the treasures; the one of noble will has established them in many places. Let the Hotṛ worship; let the seekers of wood win what is desirable. Bṛhaspati, the seer, performs the sacrifice with bulls—bulls rich in boons. He has yawned forth the far-reaching hymn from the rock by his own power. The one of noble will has maintained the treasures; the one of noble will has established them in many places.
"This one—whether the divine *hotṛ* Agni or the human *hotṛ* who is the invoker of the gods—should sacrifice (*yakṣat*), that is, recite the *yajyā*.
In the form *yakṣat*, the augment *aṭ* is applied in the *liṭ* [sic: *leṭ*] tense;
the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *sip* is used diversely" (*sidbahuḷam*).
"May the Vaninas—the gods who possess power, or those who desire the oblation—enjoy (vanta) the desirable (vārya) Soma.
The *ātmanepada* ending is used by way of substitution for the *parasmaipada* due to the Vedic meter;
furthermore, the *śap* suffix is elided according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (the suffix is frequently omitted in the Veda).
The elision of the final vowel is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

For that purpose, Bṛhaspati—the Adhvaryu priest who is the protector of the great mantra or the oblation, or the divine Bṛhaspati himself—performs the sacrifice; that is, he carries out the ritual. Of what nature is he?
Vena, desiring [rain], asks:

"By what means? This is now explained: "by means of *ukṣan*—that is, by Soma juices that are sprinkling agents (*secaka*), possessing many desirable qualities (*puruvāra*); likewise, by *ukṣan*—that is, by waters at the time of sprinkling, and by the oblations (*havya*) offered as a cause for those [waters], which, through the medium of the Āditya, serve as the preparation for rain."
We, the sacrificers, [invoke him] whose command extends to a distant region—*dūra-ādiśam*, meaning that which has its *ādeśa* (command/instruction) in a far-off place.
The elision of the locative case ending (*al-luk*) is according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.3.9, *hal-adantāt saptamyāḥ*.
The word *adreḥ* (of the mountain) is used in the singular to denote a class (*jāti-ekavacanam*).
We grasp with our two ears the *śloka*—that is, speech and sound—of the *prāṣṇa*, which is the means for pressing [the soma];
the plural number is used for honor.
Now follows that which is performed indirectly (*parokṣakṛta*).

"This sacrificer, of good intent and beautiful deeds, after the completion of the sacrifice (*adha*), by himself (*ātmanā*) sustains (*adhārayat*) the waters characterized by rain; for *arindāni* is a name for water, as it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (1.12.26): 'The *arindāni* were poured down.'"
*Raridātā*:
There is no other *rari* (gift) that gives such a quenching of thirst as this; thus it is *arindāni*.
Or else:
*Arari* means going here and there.
The suffix *ari* is derived from the *uṇādi* [list], and [the form] is established by Pāṇini’s rule "āto ’nupasarge kaḥ" (P.
3.2.3); the correct formation of the word's internal accent is achieved through its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
Therefore, "arindāni" means "bestowing water," that is, bestowing movement;
for there is the Vedic scripture: "Breath consists of water" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4).
Alternatively:
*arari* means "giving. That kind of giving does not exist among other beings; therefore, it is *arari*.
The meaning is that they bestow gifts that cannot be given by others, namely the enjoyment of benefiting the world. The sense is that he produced such waters through sacrifice.

Furthermore: "He of good intent" (sukratuḥ), meaning one of auspicious action, "has maintained" (adhārayat) "many" (purupurūṇi) "seats" (sannāni)—that is, dwellings suitable for a pleasant residence, houses.
Or alternatively:

Bṛhaspati, being of good intent, [and] the Adhvaryu priest has maintained the "water-vessels" (arindāni)—the waters which are the means for pressing [the Soma] and characterized by their fruitfulness.
He has maintained [them].
Likewise, Sukratu, possessing excellent wisdom, has established many well-arranged *sadanāni*, that is, places for depositing the oblations (*havir*).
This verse, "ye devāḥ," is the second [verse] belonging to the Vaiśvadeva hymn in the *prauga-śastra* on the sixth day of the *daśarātra* sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The gods who abide in heaven, eleven in number, have bestowed this inviolable [sacrifice]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).
1. *kṣa-jha1-na-ṭa* read;
2. *kṣa-ha-a-ṭa* [read] *ādiśam ādeśaṃ yat*.
3. We have seized (jagṛmbha) the voice—the sound of the *hotṛ* and others, or the sound of the *stotra* and *śastra* chants.
[In the form] *tatantha jagṛmbha*, the absence of the augment *iṭ* is prescribed by rule; it is a case of elision (*haproharmaḥ*).
4. After "aripratyayaḥ," the following is added in ṅa-jha1: "They give by means of their own benefit, thus [they are] arindāni waters.

5. In kṣa-ṅa-ja-ṭa: "the attainment of the desired form and sound. 6. In kṣa-ja-ṭa: "the enjoyment of benefiting the world of living beings"; in jha1: "the enjoyment of benefiting the world of living beings."

7. O you who possess the sounds kṣa, ha, jha, bha, ṭa, and the auspicious seasons! You gods who are eleven in heaven, you who are eleven upon the earth, and you who are eleven in the waters by your greatness—O gods, may you graciously accept this sacrifice.
O gods who are eleven in heaven, who are eleven upon the earth, and who are eleven in greatness within the waters—you gods, may you graciously accept this sacrifice. 11.

O gods, you who are radiant, you who are eleven in number—both one and ten—in the sky, the world of heaven; and likewise, you who are eleven in number above and below upon the earth; furthermore, you are "apmukṣitaḥ," so called because of being the cause thereof:
you dwell and reside in the waters, that is, in the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *śī*.
There is no elision (*aluk*) due to the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, before a *kṛt*-suffix.
O gods dwelling in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), you are "eleven"—be of that number.
Alternatively, this is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), because it is listed among the names of the intermediate space in [Nirukta] 1.3.8: "The waters are the earth."

Although it has been stated that "there are only three deities" (Nirukta 7.5), and thus the deities are indeed those presiding over food and so forth, nevertheless, by virtue of their greatness—that is, through their respective manifestations—they become thirty-three in number.
This is because it is stated that there are other manifestations belonging to those respective stations.
The phrase "the gods by their greatness" is to be connected with all [the subsequent verses].

"O you gods, you who are the aforementioned number of deities, having assembled, do you take pleasure in this sacrifice of ours; enjoy it, and by partaking of the sacrificial oblation related to it, be gratified. Eleven is one and ten."
The long vowel [in *ekādaśan*] is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra 5.3.49: *prāgekādaśabhyaḥ*.
The accentuation of the first member remains as its original form (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvaratva*) because it is a numeral (*saṅkhyā*).
In the twenty-first anuvāka, there are seventeen sūktas.
Among them, the first sūkta, beginning with "vedipade," consists of thirteen ṛcs.
The *āpeya* hymn belongs to Dīrghatamas, the son of Ucathya; it is dedicated to Agni. The other two verses are *triṣṭubh*s.
The remaining verses are *jagatī*s, according to the rule regarding those ending in *triṣṭubh*.
The tenth [verse] is a *triṣṭubh* or a *jagatī*.
The general rule regarding the [preceding] meters has ceased to apply here.
Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: "At the words *vedi-pade*, Dīrghatamas Aucathya [composed] an *āgneya* hymn; it ends with two *triṣṭubhs*, but the tenth [verse] is a *triṣṭubh*."
In the *prātaranuvāka* of the *Āgneya* sacrifice, within the *Jagatī* metre, these six hymns, excluding the third, are prescribed for use.
Likewise, there is a prescription for six hymns, excluding the third, in the *Aśvina-śastra*.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "From the six [verses] beginning with *vediṣadaḥ*, one should omit the third" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.13).
To Agni, who sits upon the altar, whose abode is dear, and who shines with brilliant light, bring forth a dwelling-place like a nourishing draught;
clothe the pure one with a garment through my prayer—him whose vehicle is light, whose color is bright, and who destroys the darkness.

To the one who sits upon the altar, whose abode is dear, the brilliantly shining one—bring forth nourishment for Agni as if into his own womb. Clothe the pure one with a garment through my prayer; he whose chariot is light, whose color is bright, the slayer of darkness. 1.

O Adhvaryu, seat him upon the altar, which is the womb— the place— like a garment for Agni, who sits upon the site of the altar, whose abode is dear, who possesses a dear dwelling, who has a beloved station characterized by the high-altar (uttaravedi), who is beautifully radiant with excellent luster, and who is distinguished by qualities such as being led forth;
clothe him with this mental intention.
Pure;
having a chariot of light; of bright color.
The destroyer of darkness.
cha-jha1—O you who have been sprinkled with water!
2. *jha₁*-devāsaḥ means "the gods.
3. *ka-cha-jha₁-ja-ṭa*-bhavatha;
the plural number is used with reference to the multiplicity of locations.
4. The last two [vowels] of the *ka*, *cha*, *ba*, and *ṭa* [groups].
5. Of those [consonants] excluding the third [vowel] of the *jha*, *ja*, and *ṭa* [groups].
6. To the *ta*, *pha*, and *dha* [groups], [the vowel] *ā*.

7. To the one who loves the place characterized by the *uttaravedi* (high altar) with the letters *ka, ṇa, ṭa, jha*; and to the one who loves the place characterized by the *uttaravedi* with the letters *ca, pha*. 8.

To the one distinguished by qualities beginning with *agni* through the letters *ka, ja, jha, jha, ṇa, na, ba*; and to the one distinguished by qualities beginning with *agni* through the letters *ka, kha, cha, ca, jha, ṭa, pha*.
"Bring forth" (*vpra vbhara*) means "offer" or "prepare excellently," like food in the form of an oblation (*havīrūpa*).

And just as one spreads that very cloth over that place for the sake of softness, so too, with a mind (*manmanas*)—that is, with a mental preparation (*saṃbhāra*) worthy of contemplation—or with sacrificial grass (*barhis*), clothe and cover the site of the altar.
Of what nature is that place? It is described as follows:

it is *śuci*, pure, because impurities such as the Asuras have been removed through sprinkling and other rites; it is *jyotiratham*, a chariot of light, because it serves as the support for the gods, who are like a chariot, being the substratum for the clarified butter (*ājya*) and other offerings; it is *śukravarṇam*, white-colored, because it is endowed with fire and thus possesses a brilliant luster; and it is *tamohanam*, the destroyer of darkness—that is, the dispeller of physical gloom or ignorance.
The sense is that [this is so] because it consists of the investigation of knowledge by means of sacrifices and other rites to be accomplished.
Alternatively:
just as they conceal a thing that ought to be hidden with a cloth in that womb or place, so likewise establish this equal [state] for its dwelling.

Cover it, or rather, clothe it, with a horse that is "mind-like"—that is, worthy of being meditated upon—and like a garment, such as clay, wood, and so forth. Of what sort? One equipped with a chariot of light, meaning one possessed of a radiant vehicle.
The remainder is as before.
The twice-born one, threefold, is directed hither; what was consumed grows strong again within the year.
With one [tongue] he wins by his tongue, the noble bull; with the other, the elephant-like one wipes away the two enemies.

The twice-born one, threefold, hastens toward the food; in a year’s time, what was eaten grows again. With the mouth and tongue of one he is born anew as a noble bull; with the other, the wild beast wipes away the wood-shavings.
"Dvijanmā" means one who is born from two araṇis (fire-drills);
or alternatively,
he is called "twice-born" because he is produced through both churning and the consecration of the fire-implantation (*ādhāna*).
The suffix *manin* is also seen after other [roots] as well.

This Agni, as threefold food—consisting of the forms of clarified butter, the sacrificial cake, and Soma—is surrounded by, that is, reaches, and leads toward and consumes the three kinds of food from all sides.
"In the sense of going straight, standing, or acquiring people," [the suffix] *ini* is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Or rather:
it is roasted.
‘Ṛjo pāke.’
Or he makes it ripe.
And what is this?
In this instance, the form *īm* is a Vedic archaism (*upacchāndasa*) for the root *ī*.

That which was eaten and consumed grows again after a full year; it causes [the sacrificer] to increase. The meaning is that because the aged [sacrificial substance] returns to a dual state, it enables the sacrificer to perform the sacrifice every year through the growth of the oblation.
Or alternatively:
The oblation (*havis*) consumed once increases while remaining in the stomach, or it causes the eater to grow, when a full year has passed.
Furthermore, this Agni, being a bull (*vṛṣā*), a showerer [of benefits], becomes abundant (*jenyaḥ*) through the mouth—that is, by means of the tongue—of the wild oblation; such is the sense.
Or else:

Having rained down with one form, he becomes *jenya*, that is, increased, by means of the tongue of another—such as the *hotṛ* priest—at a sacrifice, [the tongue] being indicated by the sacrificial ladle (*sruca*).
Likewise, in the form of a forest fire (*dāvāgni*), being a *vāraṇa* or restrainer of all, he *vni mṛṣṭa*, meaning he rubs away or burns the *vni* trees belonging to the forest (*vana*).
The substitution of *la* for the root *mṛj* follows the Vedic usage, and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
1. Because it removes ignorance (kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-ajñānanivārakatvāt).
2. They conceal (kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-gopayanti). 3. Of what kind is that? (kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-kīdṛśaṃ tam).
4. Endowed with *kṣa*, *jha*, *1*, *a*, *ṭa*, *dī*, and *maratha*.
5. This fire, born twice (*dvijanmā*), [is characterized by] *kṣa*, *jha*, *1*, *a*, *ṭa*, and *aya*. 6. With these [syllables], he approaches for the sake of favor; he approaches and consumes.

7. Or else, it is derived from the root *ṛj* (in the sense of ripening) with the suffix *-ya*. It means "it causes [something] to ripen" (*pakvaṃ karoti*). Alternatively, it means "it makes [something] cooked" (*pakvaṃ karoti*).
8. In the year [marked by] *kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa*, when the year is complete, [the sacrifice] increases (*bavṛdhe*; in *kṣa-na-ṭa* it is *punarvavṛdhe*).
This [sacrifice] causes increase.

The meaning is that, for one who has diminished, it again brings about the capacity for sacrifice every year through the doubling of the sacrificial offering (*yajamāne havirvṛddhyā*) due to the presence of both [offerings].

9. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-bhakṣayitāram*: the devourer. 10. *kṣa-jha-ṭa-āsā*: by means of the tongue that tastes and appropriates; *jha-jha-1-āsā*: by means of the tongue that tastes and appropriates (*jha-1-svīkurvatyā*). 11. *kṣa-jha-jha-1-na-ṭa-stutyā*: by means of praise.
The two moving in the black waters tremble;
both, dwelling together, hasten toward the infant.

With forward-tongued, scattering, brightly shining, most excellent, companionable, stirring, and increasing the father. Moving in the black waters, they tremble; these two, co-dwellers, both hasten toward the infant. With forward-tongued, scattering, brightly shining, most excellent, companionable, stirring, and increasing the father.
The two mothers of this Agni—standing in the place of mothers, the two who produce him, known as the two kindling woods (araṇī)—both of them move to and fro.
The root *ovij* is used in the sense of "fear" and "trembling.
From this root, in its *yaṅluk* (intensive without suffix) form, the third person singular middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by way of grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).
The elision of the *ta* suffix occurs according to the rule: "There is elision of *ta* in the *ātmanepada* endings."
There is no elision of the *n* because of the rule "optionally when *ca* and others are elided."

In the process of churning, when the two black streaks—becoming black in color or causing the earth to become so due to the sparks of fire—have come together (*sakṣitau*) toward the same task of producing fire, these two mothers thus approach (*abhitarete*) the infant; they reach him face-to-face. At the time of his birth, he is like an infant, submerged in what is extremely small.
What kind of infant?

With a tongue extended forward, possessing a flame situated at the place of the tongue extending a span's length; destroying darkness, that is, dispelling it; "dropping from the chaff," quickly emerging from the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) without difficulty; being swiftly produced from the source (*yoni*); slightly to be bent together—that is, to be brought into alignment—with soft wood powder and the like; to be protected; the nourisher, the increaser, the cause of growth for the father—the protector, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
By these aforementioned modes common to worldly infants, he approaches the mother as a child; this is the meaning.

Desiring to release [the waters] for the mortal man who acts like a man, the swift-running, black-tracked, speeding steeds—unequalled, goat-like, lightly gliding, wind-impelled—are yoked for the race. mumukṣvaḥ | marnave | mānavasyate | raghūdruvaḥ | kṛṣṇasītāsaḥ | ū | jurvaḥ | asamanāḥ | ajikāsaḥ | raghūsyadaḥ | vātajūtāḥ | upa | yujyante | āśavaḥ || 4 ||

For the mortal man who possesses a mind, for the one desiring mental power—that is, for the sacrificer who desires the performance of ritual acts from the human priests—the flames of Agni are harnessed at the sacrifices by the Adhvaryu and others for his sake.
Because this hymn belongs to Agni, it is understood that these are "flames" by virtue of propriety.
Of what nature are they?
The *mumukṣavas*—desiring liberation—are those who, by means of the oblations, desire to liberate the sacrificer and lead him to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
The absence of *guṇa* [substitution] is due to the rule: "In the case of *jas* and so forth, there is an option in the Veda.

That the flames are the means for attaining the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) by way of the oblations is heard in the passage beginning with "Kālī, Karālī," and continuing: "He who moves among these blazing ones, and at the proper time the oblations are indeed offered—these rays of the sun lead him to where the sole lord of the gods has his abode" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.4–5).
"Raghudruvaḥ" means moving swiftly; "kṛṣṇasītāsaḥ" means having black paths.

The letter *u* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "Jurvaḥ" means being swift by nature, performing their tasks quickly; "asamanāḥ" means having unequalled minds in their respective activities.
Some were going facing east, and some facing west; thus they were of various dispositions of mind.
In the case of a reversal, the singular number is used.
Alternatively:
*asamanāḥ* means those of diverse colors (*bhinnavarṇāḥ*).
And their state of having diverse colors is heard of in that very same [text]: "Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, Sulohitā, and she who is of a beautiful smoky color."
"The goddesses are Sphuliṅginī, Viśvabhujī, and Lelāyamānā—these are the seven tongues.

1. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-dhvasayantam*: "Destroying darkness by his own splendor"; *ḍa-jha1-dhvasayantam*: "Destroying darkness by his own splendor. 2. *Kṣa-ḍa-jha1-ja-ṭa-tayoḥ*: "Of those two. 3. *Kṣa-jha1-ja-ṭa-uparītanyam (?)*: "[The state of being] transcended. 4. *Kṣa-ka-jha-jha1-ja-ṭa-laukikaśiśusādhāraṇadhamaiḥ*: "By means of qualities common to worldly children. 5. *Jha-anyāḥ*: "Others. *Ajirasaḥ*: "Moving," *raghusyadaḥ*: "flowing swiftly," *vātajūtāḥ*: "impelled by the wind."
By the rule "the third [case-ending] in the sense of the object," the first member of the compound retains its original accent.
*Āśavaḥ* means those whose nature is to pervade.
As they rush forth, scattering the darkness, they increase; performing great deeds, they create a vast and black expanse.
When he, not being terrified, roared aloud as he grasped that great earth, saying, "Let us stretch it out."

Then, his [flames], scattering [the darkness], surge forth at will; he creates a vast, black, and mighty mass of rain. When he has thoroughly grasped the great earth, he moves along, scattering [the gloom], thundering, and roaring.

Immediately thereafter, those well-known sparks of this Agni who is being praised move forth—that is, they go everywhere—in vain; for what purpose? They are "destroying the darkness," that is, dispelling it; likewise, "making great their own form and light"—overpowering the vast black-colored path of non-existence, they intensely produce their own manifestation.
At what time? That is stated:
when he repeatedly stroked—that is, touched—the great earth, the vast ground, on all sides.

[The word *marmṛśat*] is derived from the root *mṛś* with the suffix *yaṅ* dropped, followed by the present participle suffix *śatṛ*; its initial vowel is acute according to the rule "the first syllable of reduplicated stems is acute."
Roaring, being honored from all sides, thundering—making a sound—and bellowing—uttering a sound intensely;
the suffix and accent are as before.
He goes forth, proceeding with intensity on all sides.
The meaning is that when he blazes, licking here and there with his tongue and making a *bhugubhugu* sound, at that very moment sparks arise.
He who, as a bull, roars loudly, goes toward his wives, being naked among those who are tawny and adorned.
Exerting his strength, he adorns his body; like a terrifying beast with horns, he rushes about, difficult to seize.

He who, as an ornament, mounts upon the tawny ones; like a bull he goes toward his wives, bellowing loudly. Displaying his might, he adorns his own bodies; like a terrible beast with its horns, he is difficult to seize.

That Agni who, among the *babhru*— the brown-colored or those skilled in supporting (*bharaṇa*) the worlds— is preeminent (*adhi*), bends down (*namati*) toward the fuel-wood (*nagnate*). [This is from the root] *nam* in the present tense (*laṭ*), with the augment *adāgama*, and the substitution [of *na* for *ta*] by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively,
in the present tense (*laṭ*), there is the *bhlū* substitution for the *śap* suffix according to Vedic usage;
by transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is an absence of the *halādi-śeṣa* rule.
Adorning the very beings as if adorning them with his own splendor;

furthermore, entering like a bull—a sprinkler—toward his wives, he roars toward those very plants that protect and sustain him. [The form] *roravat* is derived from the root *ru* with the *yaṅ*-luṅ suffix, followed by the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), which is accented on the first syllable according to the rule: "the initial of reduplicated stems is acute."
Calling out for this purpose, he approaches; that is, he goes toward them.
Having first entered the plants, he subsequently burns them once he has awakened—this is the meaning. Furthermore, having acted in this manner, he becomes manifest with vigor (*ojāyamāna*).
*Ojas* is a name for strength.
Acting as if he were strength itself,
[the suffix] *kyaṅ* is applied according to the rule “*kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*” (Pāṇini 3.1.11), whereby both the *kyac* suffix and the *sal* affix are elided.
Without smoke and the like, being solely of the nature of light, he shines; that is to say, he illuminates and nourishes even the flames that constitute his own body.
Furthermore, with his flames fully increased, he is difficult to seize.

1. kṣa-jha-1-tava is in vain; 2. kṣa-ja-ṭa-black, having a black color; 3. kṣa-ḍa-ja-ṭa-the path of darkness; 4. kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-adhering to grass and such, clinging; 5. ka-kṣa-kha-jha-1-a-ṭa-na-va-at that very time; 6. kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-reflexive (ātmanepada); 7. kṣa-ḍa-sa-1-a-ṭa-what doing? adorning those very things; 8. kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-having entered. [Maṅgalā 1. a. 21 sū. 140] 879

Being impossible for anyone to seize, he is not terrifying like a wild beast; just as that [beast], though difficult to grasp, shakes its horn, so too he rends his heart. Like a horn, the flames are straight and fierce; they split him apart and shake him.
The form [dhunoti] is derived from the root *dhū* with the *yaṅ* and *luṅ* suffixes elided (*yaṅ-luk*), followed by the *liṭ* suffix;
its inclusion should be understood as occurring within the group beginning with *dādhry-*.
He, the disposer, spreads out the foundations; he gathers them together like two wise women who know the way.
He who lies within them grows again and again; they go toward the divine state, and with their own powers, they act together with their parents.

He, well-spread out, wide-spread out—He gathers them up, knowing them indeed as those who know. Eternal, He lies within them; again they grow, and they go toward their divine nature. Together with their parents, they assume another form. 7.
That Agni is covered by a layer of straw.
Because of its fullness, the suffix *ka* is applied to the root *stuṇāti* according to the rule for the *mūlavibhujādi* group (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.2.5.2).

The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member is due to the rule: "In the Veda, the initial of the following word is often [accented] as if it were the beginning of the compound" (*parādiś chandasi bahulam*).
Likewise, having once spread out—that is, having become extensive—he gathers together, he takes hold of, the plants.

Furthermore, understanding that "this [Agni] must grow for the sake of the sacrificer; therefore, he must be joined with flames," and thus perceiving the flames as "knowing"—that is, realizing that they must grow for the sake of the sacrificer—he, being constant and uninterrupted, lies down; the meaning is that he takes his rest.
The elision of the suffix *ta* occurs by the rule "lopasta ātmanepadeṣu."
The flames of such a nature, having previously increased, increase further so as to become fit for sacrifice;
they go to—that is, reach—the fire which is worthy of the ritual activities of sacrifice and the like, or which is worthy of praise.

Although there is identity between the fire and its flames, nevertheless, the relationship between the destination and that which is to be reached is figurative, as in the expression "the head of Rāhu."

Furthermore, these flames, having grown great along with the plants, together with Agni, produce—that is, they create—a form consisting of light, which was previously non-existent, belonging to the two parents, Heaven and Earth; the meaning is that they pervade both worlds.
The long-haired, dark ones have indeed stood up together with the singers; the seers have risen again for the sake of the living man.
From among them, they release old age while roaring, producing a further life that is invincible.

To him [the bull], the long-maned ones have indeed gathered together; upright they stood, the patient ones, for the sake of the living man. Releasing their old age, he goes forth bellowing, engendering the supreme life-force, the invincible living breath.
The maidens stood in front of that fire;
or rather,
this is a name for the fingers.
Like fingers, they are not crooked;
possessed of "hair-like" (keśinī) upward-reaching flames that stand in place of hair, they indeed cry out together—they embrace, they truly clasp one another.
Moreover, while doing so, they are "seers" (mṛṣī)—that is, though dead and having attained the state of charcoal—[they still act thus].
The form [triyatī] is derived from the root *tri* with the suffix *kasu*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

To Agni, who was coming for their sake, they—unaware of the calamity that had befallen them—stretched themselves upward; that is to say, with faces turned upwards and bodies raised, they rose up even though they were nearly dead.
While they were acting in this manner, that husband, Agni, [beheld] them...
(kṣa-jha-jha1-ja-ṭa-ṛjā śṭjāṇi).
2. In the manuscripts kṣa, jha₁, ja, ṭa, *prāṇaḥ* is to be read.

3. In the manuscripts kṣa, ḍa, jha₁, ja, ṭa, it is said that [it] is sometimes covered. 4. In the manuscripts kṣa, ḍa, jha₁, ja, ṭa, they are endowed with the specific quality of verticality resembling hair.

Releasing—that is, thoroughly liberating—the *jarā* (decay) of those flames, which is the loss of vitality; as if gathering together for the sake of avoiding decay, sounding [the word] "nāpadan" (do not perish); not only is there the removal of decay, but furthermore, generating—that is, producing—the *param* (supreme) *asu* (life-breath), the *astṛtam* (uninjured) *jīvam* (living power), which is the capacity to sustain life even when fuel such as wood and water is added;
he *eti*, meaning he goes—he reaches the vicinity of those flames.

Just as in the world, certain lovely women, having sported intensely with their lover, later endure the separation when he has gone abroad; yet, when he returns, they do not acknowledge their own weakness but strive for an embrace with joy—the idea here to be understood is that the husband, having removed old age through the utterance of mantras and sustaining them by providing what is fitting, thus "protects" them. *adhīvāsaṃ pari̭ mātu riha॒ha tuvi॒grebhiḥ satvabhi̭ryāti vi jrya̭ḥ |* (The hero) goes about his mother’s dwelling, licking her all over with his powerful, swift companions, displaying his prowess.
Bestowing vigor upon the one who follows his path, licking the gift, the dappled mare attends his tracks day by day.
Licking the upper garment of his mother, he goes forth with his many-fanged jaws, wearing his armor. Licking his feet, he ever follows the path of the two tawny ones. ||9||

The forest fire is being praised: this fire, too, licking—that is, consuming—on all sides the "upper garment" (adhīvāsa), which stands in the place of a covering, namely the grass, shrubs, and creepers belonging to the "mother," the earth that is the creator of beings;
"aha" is used as a particle of well-known fact.
Or rather:
licking (*rihan*) all around (*pari*) the fire (*vahni*) that is being maintained above the dwelling-place of the mother-earth (*mātṛbhūmi*),

accompanied by *satvabhiḥ*— beings or creatures that are *tuvigrebhiḥ*, meaning those that roar loudly or move extensively— he, the swift one (*jryaḥ*), goes forth in various ways (*vi yāti*) with his speed (*jryasā*).

Furthermore, O *paddhate* (O you who possess paths), bestowing—that is, giving—food appropriate to each for both bipeds and quadrupeds; [this is said] while [the fire] is burning in the forest (*vivane*).
It is well known that tigers and other predators devour living beings as they flee in fear from a forest fire (*dāvānala*).
What is he doing?

"Always," that is, at all times, "licking up" (re-rihat) grass and other things— that is, burning them— furthermore, the "path" (vartani), which is "hawk-colored" (śyenī), meaning dark-hued, "follows" (anu sacate) "him who goes forth" (viyantam) in due succession;
wherever Agni goes, there the path also becomes black.
Truly, it is well known:
among our liberal patrons, he has shone like a bull that bellows while subduing his foes.
He has caused the mothers of the young ones to shine; like a bird, he has moved about, leaping in the battles.
O Agni, shine among our liberal patrons; as a bull, you roar aloud, the subduer. You have shone down upon the mothers of the young [flames], moving to and fro like a ram in battles. 10.
O Agni, shine—be radiant—for us among our *maghavan*s, that is, among those possessing food at our sacrifices or in our homes.

Then, immediately thereafter, being *śasivān*—possessing sacrificial portions, possessed of flames, or possessed of our vital breaths—you, the *vṛṣabha*, the showerer of desired things, the *damūnā*—whose mind is inclined toward giving, or whose mind is self-controlled—be present everywhere; this is the sense.
You, characterized by such qualities, protect those who possess children.
By the word *śiśu* (child), that state [of the flame] is indicated.
Having abandoned the flames characterized by childhood (*śaiśavavatī*), you have blazed intensely (*adīdeḥ*).
[Note: 1. According to manuscripts kha, ca, pha: "he protects the vital breaths"; according to manuscripts kṣa, ma1, jha, ṭa: "pleasing them"].

2. Those fleeing from the fear of forest fires among the *jha*-openings; those dissolving from the fear of the long-enduring forest fire among the *kṣa*, *ma*, *ṭa*, and *ci* [consonants]; those dissolving by the long-enduring forest fire among the *ṅa*, *jha₁*, and *ci* [consonants].
3. *Kṣa-ma-jha₁ ma-ṭa-re*: licking excessively—that is, licking and burning. 4. *Kṣa-jha-jha-jha-ma-ṭa*: dark-colored.

5. O you who possess the qualities mentioned, be patient (kṣama). 6. O Agastya, born from the earth (kṣaja), shine forth without distinction! What kind of person are you? You are one who, in battles (vyuṣṭu), repeatedly wards off (paribhūrāṇaḥ) those who hate us, like a coat of mail (varma). Or rather: in battles, be one who completely encompasses (paribhūrāṇaḥ) [the enemy] like armor. [The form] *paribhūrāṇaḥ* is derived from the root *hṛ* with the suffix *yaṅluk*, and the present participle suffix (*śānac*) is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). The acute accent on the first syllable follows the rule "the beginning of reduplicated forms" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*). Possessing the aforementioned qualities, be present among the generous patrons (*maghavatsu*) and shine forth in the sacrifices. || 6 ||

O Agni, may this well-composed [prayer] be dearer to you than that which is ill-composed, even more so than your own beloved thought. With that pure, bright radiance of your body which shines forth, with that you yourself win wealth for us. O Agni! This well-composed [prayer], compared to that which is ill-composed, let it be dearer to you than even your own beloved thought. That bright, pure light of your body which shines—by means of that, you yourself win wealth for us.
He [knows] this our oblation consisting of Soma and other substances.
Of what nature is it?
It is *sudhita*—well-placed, well-situated, or properly offered—upon (*adhi*) wood and other materials that have been prepared (*duḥdhita*), established, or made firm.
From my mind— that which is to be meditated upon— from that which is dear, and even from your own heart;
the word *u* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*),
and the word *vi* has the sense of the word *api* (even).

"O Agni, that which is most dear (*vpreyaḥ*)—the object most beloved to you—is what? He says: O Agni, from your own body (*tanvaḥ*), from the flame made radiant by clarified butter (*ghṛtena*), your pure (*śuci*), stainless (*nirmala*), bright (*śukra*), and blazing (*dīpta*) splendor (*tejaḥ*) shines forth. Together with that, bestowing upon us delightful treasures (*ratnam*) such as jewels and pearls, favor us (*vanase*)—that is, accept us."
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *vanati* is used by way of transposition.

O Agni, grant us a ship for our chariot, and also a boat with constant oars and a path through the waters, which shall carry across our heroes, our wealthy patrons, and our people, and which shall provide us protection. 12 For the chariot, a ship; and also for us, one for the secret cavern—grant it, O Agni, with constant oars and a path through the fray. [Grant] those who shall carry across our heroes, and also our wealthy patrons and our people, and that which shall provide us protection. 12

To him who is hidden in the secret place, for the sake of protection and for the sake of dwelling in the cave—the abode of all—[we offer] a boat: a boat that carries us across the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of the Soma sacrifice.
For in such Vedic texts as, "The sacrifice is indeed a boat that carries one well across" (*Ai. Brā. 1.13*), it is praised as having the form of a boat.
Of what kind is that boat? It is a boat equipped with fixed, steady oars and a wooden rudder-pole (*paddhati*).

The word *matup* is accented according to the rule *hasvanuḍbhyām*. Bestow— that is, provide and bring about— such a boat whose form consists of the sacrifice, which is equipped with feet in the form of substances, deities, mantras, and so forth.
*Rati* is the name for the act of giving, as it is listed among its names in the passage: *adāsanati rati* (Nirukta 3.20.4).
That very [act] is further specified:
moreover (*uta*), through its pervasiveness (*vyānoḥ*), it makes our heroes—our own sons and so forth—possessors of wealth (*maghonaḥ*), that is, endowed with oblations characterized by horses.
And may he carry us across—both the people and the sacrificers—may he ferry us over, may he deliver us;
[this is from the root] *pṛ* (to cross) in the *leṭ* mood with the augment *āṭ*.
[He delivers us] from that which consists of the many sufferings of birth, death, and the divine [world].
1. Because it has been praised as *kṣa-kṣa-a-ṭa*, grasp that for the sake of welfare;
in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), according to the rule "for the root *hu* there is the substitution of *śāyac*," there is the replacement by *śāyac*.
Accomplish our purpose!
It would lead [the soul] to the other shore, the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), which is the abode of unsurpassed bliss;

for it is heard in scripture that this world of Brahman is attained by those who perform sacrifices and other rites, as stated in *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.2.6: "This is your holy, well-performed world of Brahman."

And that discipline which, having thus led [the seeker] forward, brings about the attainment of *brahman*—the unsurpassed bliss and peace—is so because it has been stated: "At the end of the supreme [state], those who have perfected their selves enter the highest station" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.2.6).
Furthermore, it does so by means of producing purity of mind, according to the Vedic scripture: "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice, through charity... (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.22).
O Agni, may our hymn be pleasing to you; may Heaven and Earth and the self-moving Rivers favor it.
Seeking cattle and long-lasting vigor, may the ruddy ones choose for us the most excellent boon.

O Agni, do you graciously accept our hymn; may Heaven and Earth and the Rivers, self-praised, grant us what we seek—cattle, wealth, and long-lasting nourishment; may the ruddy dawns choose for us the boon we desire. 13.
O Agni, may you graciously accept our hymn; praise us directly and acknowledge it as well-recited.
In the root *gṛ* meaning "to sound," when the *liṭ* suffix is applied, the *śru* augment replaces the verbal suffix by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (variously in the Veda). Furthermore,
the substitution of *u* for *ṝ* occurs by the same rule "bahulaṃ chandasi."
Likewise, may Heaven and Earth (dyāvākṣāmā) also gladden us by providing the means for the performance of sacrifice.
Likewise, may the rivers (sindhavaḥ)— the flowing streams that move by their own impulse (svagūrtāḥ)—
provide what pertains to the cow (gavyam), such as milk and other products, through the production of grass and other fodder for the cattle.
This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
[It refers to] those things such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) produced from barley, rice, and so forth; "bringing" means conveying them;
"may they cause to swell."
Likewise, the Aruṇyas are those endowed with a reddish-brown color.
The possessive suffix is elided.
The *upas* are the means for accomplishing the *āruṇya*; they bear that name because they are its cause. They are "long" (*dīrghāḥ*), meaning throughout all days and at all times.

May they cause us to obtain *iṣ*, that is, food consisting of flowing streams and the like; may they cause us to obtain the *vara*, the desirable and most excellent, as well as other means for the sacrifice.
[The root] *vṛ* means "to bestow" (*saṃbhakti*).
This is the *laṅ* (imperfect) in the Vedic style, from the causative form (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) of the root.
The suffix śap is applied by way of transposition.
"May they accomplish all this through the grace of Agni"— since this is indeed a hymn of praise, there is no contradiction in its being addressed to Agni (āgneyatva).
The second hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "balisthā," is composed by Dīrghatamas; it is in the Jagatī meter, with the exception of two Triṣṭubh verses. Its deity is Agni.
The application [of these verses] in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra has already been stated.
The most powerful and beautiful splendor of the god was established for his body, from which he was born through force;
when he seizes it, the inspired thoughts of the one who acts with wisdom bring forth well-fashioned songs of praise.

Truly, thus has that most beautiful splendor of the god been established for the sake of his wondrous form, since he was born from strength. When the prayer approaches him, it succeeds; they have led forth the well-flowing streams of the Truth.
The *bharga*—the celebrated splendor or brilliance—of the God, the radiant Āditya, which is *darśata*, visible to all;
thus (*itthā*), in this manner, by every means of invocation, it is established (*dhāyi*) for the sake of the body (*vapuṣe*), that is, for the bodily functions and for skillful action, by everyone.
Indeed, both *baṭ* and *itthā* are names for "truth" (*satya*), as they are listed among the names of truth in the Nirukta (3.10.1.5): "Baṭ, śrat, satrā, itthā."

1. Because it is being consumed by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*). 2. By means of producing partial purification (*ardhaśuddhi*). 3. To those who are inciting [the senses] that have not yet been disciplined (*aguṇita*). 4. At all times (*sārvakāla*). 5. Because it has been praised. The second *aṣṭaka*. 883.
It is well known that the maintenance of the body occurs through the digestion of what has been eaten;
he states the reason for this: "because he is born of strength."
The meaning is that because he was produced by force at the time of churning, he is therefore held for the sake of strength (*bala*).
As for this well-known, world-benefiting splendor of Agni, my own intellect (*mati*) approaches it; having approached, it abides [therein].
‘Hū’ is used in the sense of crookedness.
And by that very splendor, he accomplishes his own purposes;
moreover, by the splendor of *ṛta*—the fire that effects the sacrifice—the *dhenāḥ*, the voices of all living beings, proceed together, moving in unison.
The suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *svat* when it functions as an agent.
They lead, they guide, and they carry out the worldly affairs of the universe.
The middle voice (ātmanepada) occurs by way of transposition.
Or rather:

the "milk-streams" (*dhenāḥ*) of *ṛta*—that is, the words in the form of mantras related to the sacrifice—having issued forth, proceeding together through the mouths of the *hotṛ* and other priests, lead [the rite];
they carry out the hymn of praise for Agni.
Or they carry out the sacrifice by means of the brilliance of fire, according to the Vedic scripture:
"Speech consists of brilliance" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4).
For this reason, the meaning is that the intellect is offered up.
*Dhenā* is a name for speech, because it is listed among the names of speech in the statement: *dhenā grāḥ* (Nirukta 1.11.39).

Nourishing, wondrous, and full of food, he lies here eternally; his second [form] is among the seven auspicious mothers. For the milking of this bull, let the young women bring forth his third [form], whose wisdom is manifest. pṛkṣaḥ | vapuḥ | pitumān | nityaḥ | ā | śaye | dvitīyam | ā | saptaśivāsu | mātṛṣu | tṛtīyam | asya | vṛṣabhasya | dohase | darśapramatim | janayantu | yoṣaṇaḥ || 2 ||
