This Agni is *pṛkṣaḥ*, the accomplisher of food through cooking and other means; *vapuḥ*, possessed of a body, being the cause of the growth of the physical frame; *pitumān*, endowed with food characterized by oblations; and *nityaḥ*, eternal.

Being such, he first lies down (*ā śaye*) in his station upon the earth. The meaning is that, performing worldly tasks such as burning and cooking as well as sacrificial rites, he remains firm (*dhruvaḥ*) on the ground.
Likewise, he dwells in a second way within the seven auspicious mothers—the rains that bring welfare to the seven worlds, who stand in the place of mothers and act for our benefit;
he exists there in the form of lightning, occupying the intermediate space.

For the sake of the milking—that is, for the purpose of causing the rain of water from the sun—he is connected as a companion to this very bull, the showerer, the fire of lightning, to the solar ray that causes the raining down of water.
The suffix *asun* is applied after the root *duh* in the sense of the agent.
For its manifestation, it lies in the third;
it exists in the celestial realm.
Or else:
For the sake of that activity, [the text speaks] of the "milking" ray belonging to this celebrated showerer, the Sun.

It is well known that during the summer season, the rays of the Sun draw up the water situated on the earth, reach the Sun, remain there for a long time, and then, reaching the atmosphere and staying within the clouds, rain down during the rainy season.
Therefore, the ray possesses a twofold nature.
Women, who are by nature prone to mixing, produce—that is, they generate—this highly fortunate one who exists in three places;
the meaning is that he has spread throughout all directions.
Of what sort is he?
"Darśapramatim":
one who possesses eminent mindfulness in the ten directions, for the sake of being worthy of worship;
or alternatively:
The meaning is that at the time of churning, it was produced by the ten fingers and pervaded the three worlds and the ten directions.

When they, the masters, by their power brought forth from the greatness of the bull that which was hidden, as the sun; when Mātariśvan churned him who was dwelling in secret for the sake of the distillation of the honeyed juice throughout the days of old—3. When they, the masters, by their power brought forth from the greatness of the bull that which was hidden, as the sun; when Mātariśvan churned him who was dwelling in secret for the sake of the distillation of the honeyed juice throughout the days of old—3.
1. The letters ka, ja, jha, sa, ṇa, and na occur [in the name of the month].

2. The letters kha, ja, jha, ṇa, na, pa, pha, and va occur during the rainy season (varṣākāla). For this reason (yat), from which cause (yasmāt kāraṇāt), we [worship] this fire (enam agnim) of the buffalo (mahiṣasya).
This is a great sacrifice (*mahad-yajña*), because it is listed among its names in the *Nirukta* (3.3.8): "The buffalo, the sheep, and *Ṛbhukṣan*.
It belongs to the great sacrifice from its root—that is, from its foundation, beginning with the *ādhāna*—as something performed skillfully;
for this is a name for form (*rūpa*).

For the accomplishment of the form (*rūpa*) consisting of the beginning and the conclusion, the *īśānāsaḥ*— those capable of their own activity, the *sūrāyaḥ*, the wise officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)— by means of *śavasā*, that is, by power in the form of mantras or by bodily strength, *niḥ kranta*, they bring forth, accomplish, and produce [the fire] from the wood. Or alternatively,
they bring forth this Agni from the beginning— that is, starting from the friction— for the accomplishment of the *mahiṣasya vapasaḥ*, the great form capable of accepting the oblation.
In the Vedic *luṅ* tense after the root *kṛ*, there is the elision of the suffix *cli* by the rule "in mantras, [the suffix is elided] after *ghas* etc.";
furthermore, by transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is the substitution of the final letter (*antādeśa*). Moreover, if [they have praised] this very Agni from of old (*pradivaḥ*).
The meaning is that this has been so from time immemorial, not only now.

As before, when there is now the churning—*ādhava*—that is, the act of stirring or throwing [the wood] for the sake of honey, which is like honey (*madhu*), *mātariśvan*, the wind moving in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), gradually churns—that is, sets in motion—the one who was in the cave, being hidden within the cave, namely within the fire-drills (*veyā*) or the pieces of wood.
The meaning is that he pierces [it] upward.
Alternatively:

*mātariśvan* is he who breathes—that is, exerts himself—within the mother, namely the sacrifice. He [the sacrificer] churns, that is, produces, for the sake of manifestation, him who is dwelling in secret, hidden within the two fire-sticks (*araṇi*).
Since he is of such a nature, therefore he is to be praised; this is the meaning.

When he is led forth from the highest place of his father, he spreads over the nourishing plants and rises up wondrously. When both [worlds] celebrate his birth, he has become most brilliant and pure through his heat.
Because (yat) of that (tat)— the "father" (pituh), which refers to food characterized as cattle;
here the nominative is used in place of the genitive—
on account of its being supreme (paratvāt).
The meaning is "for the sake of excellence.
For that purpose, it is *pra*-*pari*-*nīyate*, which means it is led forth and led around; that is, it is carried around the fire (*paryagnikriyate*).
Alternatively:

From the father-like, supreme, and most excellent fire characterized as the *gārhapatya*, the *āhavanīya* fire is led forth—that is, it is led with distinction—toward the *āhavanīya*. The prefix *pari-* is here without specific meaning.
Furthermore, [the fires] are placed within the midst of the burning during the animal sacrifices, the *puroḍāśa* offerings, and so forth.
Alternatively,
there is the vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa) of the prefix *pra*;
[the root] *kṣudh* is used in the sense of hunger (*bubhukṣā*).
*Kip*: "Prakṣodhyāḥ" means those who are intensely hungry, desiring to eat.
"Vīrudhaḥ" [means] creepers; "ā rohati" means they ascend, that is to say, they enter among the teeth (*datsu*).
Because both—both those who consume [the oblation] or the two kindling woods (*araṇī*)—stir up (*invataḥ*), that is, they embrace (*vyāpṛtaḥ*), the birth, the origin, the production of this Agni;
[this is the meaning]. [The root] *ivi* means "to pervade.
Due to the *it*-suffix, there is the augment *num*.
For this very reason, this fire is pure (*śuci*) and stainless; it is *ghṛṇā*, meaning compassionate toward the sacrificers through its favor.
Alternatively, *ghṛṇā* means *ghṛṇin*, that is, radiant.
The meaning is lost.
Or rather, through meditation (*dīdhī*), he became most excellent (*yaviṣṭhaḥ*), that is, the youngest;
the sense is that he became capable of accepting [the offering].

Having entered the two mothers from the beginning, the pure one, even while being struck, has spread himself far and wide; when he has mounted the ancient swift ones, he rushes toward the new ones among the excellent steeds.
1. For the reason that, or because this very Agni [is] of the buffalo;
2. for which [reason], him;
3. the creator.

This Agni, being pure and blazing, immediately after having become the youngest (*yaviṣṭha*) as stated in the preceding mantra, entered the *mātṛs*—the ten directions that stand in the place of mothers—from all sides. Since it was said previously, "The young women generated him of tenfold wisdom" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.141.2), the directions are considered mothers;
the meaning is that he pervades the directions with his light.
The *māsara* offerings are distinguished [as follows]:
in those mothers (*mātṛ*), while being unharmed and unperturbed even by others, he grew extensively—that is, he became variously increased and vast—and entered them.

The sense is that it is just as when someone in the world, having been well nourished by his mother through the drinking of breast milk and protection from the harm of others, becomes manifest in the world and, upon returning, embraces his mother; such is the meaning.
Regarding the question "at what time?", he says this:
*yat*—when the *sanājuvaḥ*, meaning those [bricks] separated for a long duration, were indeed cast in at the very time of installation; therefore...

When he has spread out, impelled by the wind like doors opening wide, unobstructed and consuming; on the path of him who burns with blackened tracks, who is born of purity, the dust rises up along his course. 7. When he has spread out, impelled by the wind like doors opening wide, unobstructed and consuming; on the path of him who burns with blackened tracks, who is born of purity, the dust rises up along his course. 7.
Whenever this Agni, impelled by the wind— that is, driven by the wind—
the first member of the compound retaining its original accent according to the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi*—
stands forth as one to be worshipped (*yajataḥ*), meaning worthy of being sacrificed to by all, he stands apart; that is, he becomes diffused, pervading everywhere.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

*anākṛtaḥ* means one whose movement is unobstructed and unimpeded; *vaktrā* means "having many mouths. [The suffix] *-van* [is applied] to the root *vac* according to the rule: "it is seen after other roots as well."
The substitution of *ku* occurs due to the inclusion of the term *raśmi*. [The word] *dvāraḥ* is not like something crooked (*kuṭila*), as in the case of *viddhaṣaṇaka* and so forth;
it is derived from the root *dūr* with the suffix *ap* (pacādyac) added to the limit (*paryanta*).

Just as he (the fire) exists performing various praises—that is, spreading them out—so too does this [wind] remain established with its course unobstructed and its movement unrestrained. Then, at the falling, that is, upon the path of descent of that fire, the *rajas*—the world consisting of passion—*āsthāt*, meaning it stands or takes refuge on all sides; the sense is that it offers sacrifice in many ways within the fire.
Of what kind is that [fire]?
*Dhakṣuṣaḥ* means "of the burning one";
[this is derived from] the root *dah* with the suffix *kasu* after the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
*Kṛṣṇajaṃhasaḥ* means "of the one whose path is black."
It is called *jaṃhā* because it is gone to again and again (*punaḥpunar gamyate*).
[The word is derived] from the root *han* with the suffix *asun* in the sense of the object (*karman*) after the *yaṅ-luk* (elision of the *yaṅ* reduplication).
The absence of *kutva* (the substitution of *gh* for *h*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Because his birth is pure, he possesses a form accompanied by mantra; he is of many paths, with manifold flames, and of unfixed course. Like a chariot that has not yet departed, he is fashioned with ribs; he moves along with the ruddy, ignorant [steeds]. Then, O Sūrya, those black ones of yours burn; like the fierce [flight] of a hero, his vital power rushes forth. Like a chariot, he who has been fashioned with ribs moves along with the ruddy, ignorant [steeds]. Then, O Sūrya, those black ones of yours burn; like the fierce [flight] of a hero, his vital power rushes forth.
This Agni has been fashioned and bound with cords like a chariot;

just as that [chariot] moves by means of its own wheels and other parts, so too, having been established and set in motion, he moves—being gladdened by the clarified butter—toward the *ghā* (the atmosphere) by means of his reddish, moving limbs consisting of flames and the like.
(*Īṅ* means "to go.")
Immediately after being kindled, those paths of this fire—the tracks of the sun—become black, that is, of a black color.
Because they become thus, for that reason it burns the wood;
there is an ellipsis of the word *puruṣa* (person).
The *śap* suffix is elided by Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

Furthermore, from the brilliance (*tveṣāt*)—that is, from the radiant energy (*tejas*)—of the blazing fire, the winged creatures (*vayaḥ*), such as birds and the like, which possess the power of movement (*gamanavantaḥ*), fly away (*īṣate*).
The elision of the *śap* suffix occurs here as well, according to the rule "in the Veda [the suffix] is frequently elided" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
They flee;
in this regard, there is an illustration:
like birds at the glare of a hero.
As if fleeing out of fear from someone who is heroic and possesses blazing splendor, [the fire] touches the sky and burns on all sides; thus, it is always praised by way of its form as a forest fire.

1. Being worthy of sacrifice (kṣa-jha1-ja-ṭa-yaṣṭavyaḥ san). 2. [The reading] *vidvaṣaṇakādirva* is found in manuscripts ka-ṅa-jha-ma1. 3. He stands firm in praises (kṣa-ṅa-ga-ṭa-stutīrvyasthāt); he is established (viniṣṭhate). 4. He is well-established (kṣa-ja-ṭa-vyavasthāt). 5. Like the brilliance of a hero (jha-śūrasyeva tveṣāt); like the vigor (vaya) of someone. 6. Fleeing and swift-moving (kṣa-ha-jha1-jha-ṭa-palāyamānā śīghragāminaḥ). 7. The word "always" (*sarvadā*) is not present in manuscripts kṣa-jha-jha-jha1-jha-ṭa.
For by you, O Varuṇa, Mitra of steadfast vows, and the bountiful Aryaman have been praised.
O All-pervading One, according to the boundary and in accordance with the cosmic order, you were born as the sovereign who encompasses all, like the rim of a wheel.

For by you, O Agni, Varuṇa whose vows are firm, Mitra, and the bounteous Aryaman have been made to resound; since you, the all-pervading one, were born encompassing them in every way according to the cosmic order (ṛta), as the felly encompasses the spokes. 9.
O Agni, by you indeed Varuṇa—the deity presiding over sovereignty—becomes one whose vows are firm, having undertaken his duties such as the protection of the social orders (varṇas) and so forth.
Likewise, Mitra—the deity presiding over the day—dispels the darkness.
The root *śadlū* means "to cut off. The *liṭ* suffix is used according to Vedic usage; the *sṛ* augment is applied by the rule "there is much diversity in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Due to its inclusion in the *tujādi* group, there is lengthening of the vowel in the reduplication.
Likewise, Aryaman, the deity situated between the two, is "sudānavaḥ," one who possesses beautiful gifts.
The plural number is used by way of transposition.
Alternatively:
these [gods], Varuṇa and the others, who are "sudānavaḥ" (of beautiful gifts), meaning those who give auspiciously and perform their respective duties, are indeed sharpened by you;
the word "hi" (indeed) serves to indicate what is well-known from other mantras.
For there is another mantra: "O Agni, you are born as Varuṇa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.3.1).

The *liṭ* suffix is used for the root *śad* in the sense of an object according to Vedic usage; there is the substitution of *rebh* by the rule "iryo re," and the absence of the *nighāta* accent by the rule "hi ca."
He states the logical justification for Varuṇa’s becoming *enasya* (the one who removes sin) through the truth (*tattva*).

"Since," O Agni, "from that cause you were born—'asīm' meaning from all sides; 'ṛtunā' meaning by means of ritual action; 'viśvathā' meaning like the universe, as if possessing the nature of the universe; 'vibhuḥ' meaning all-pervading in the form of Mitra and Aryaman; and 'paribhūḥ' meaning having encompassed everything on all sides by your own splendor—you have been born, you are born, you manifest yourself in due order.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Like the spokes, the axle-pin, and the rim of a chariot—
just as the rim stands encompassing them all, so too does this [Self] stand encompassing Varuṇa and the others.
O Agni, youngest one, you bestow wealth upon the one who exerts himself and presses the soma for the gods;
as such, we now establish you, the new one, O youth of power, like Bhaga in our song of praise, you who possess great wealth.

O Agni, most youthful god, you bestow upon the one who exerts himself and presses the soma juice that treasure which is most dear to the gods. As such, O young son of strength, we now establish you, the new one, like Bhaga in our song of praise, as our great treasure. 10.
"O Agni, O youngest, O most youthful one! You [grant wealth] to the one who exerts himself (*śaśamānāya*) and to the one who praises you.
Yāska says: 'The one who exerts himself (*śaśamānaḥ*) is the one who recites (*śaṃsamānaḥ*).

To the sacrificer who presses the Soma and performs worship for his own sake, you likewise send forth (*invasi*), that is, pervade, the 'jewel' (*ratnam*)—the delightful oblation (*havis*)—which is being extended among the gods (*devatātām*)."
The meaning is: "You cause the oblation offered by us to reach the gods.
The root *inv* signifies pervasion (*vyāpti*), as it is listed among the names for that [pervading power] in the Nirukta (2.18.1): "He pervades (*invati*), he attains (*nanakṣa*).
O "youthful one of strength" (*sahasoyuvan*).
By the word *yuva*, production (*utpatti*) is indicated;
[this refers to] having mixed the power produced by force at the time of churning.
Alternatively:

O Son of Strength, O Youthful One, O Ever-Youthful One, O Great Jewel, O You who possess wealth most worthy of being given by us—such as you, the consumer of oblations, who are ever-new, more recent, and praiseworthy, we, the sacrificers, quickly establish you in the sound characterized by hymns;
that is to say, at the time of offering the oblation, we praise you immediately.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Bhagam" is like the sun;
or alternatively,
it is like a great king.
It is just as they praise it.
1. kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa-tvayā hi;
2. kṣa-a-ṭa-śātayati means it dispels darkness, that is, it goes [away];
3. kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-being expanded.
Grant us wealth that is self-sustaining, like Bhaga who is rooted in the mind; grant us enduring skill, like Dakṣa.
He who, like reins, controls both worlds of birth—the gods’ praise and his own—possesses excellent wisdom.

To us, grant wealth that is well-directed, like a dwelling, and fortune that is enduring like skill; he who, like reins, controls both worlds of birth, and being of noble will, brings the praise of the gods into accord with the Eternal Law. 11.
O Agni, grant us that which is well-aimed, most desirable, free from delusion, subduing, and easy to attain.
The suffix *ūnasi* is applied according to [Uṇādi Sūtra] 4.674: *damerūnasiḥ*.

Just as you bestow wealth—that is, riches—as one who fills them, so too do you bestow *bhaga*, that which is to be enjoyed by all, and *dakṣa*, like one who is energetic or awakened, and a son who is a *dharṇasi*, skilled in upholding knowledge and the like; the meaning is that you grant both.
The root *pṛc* means "to join" or "to mix.
In the *leṭ* mood, there is the augment *āṭ*.
According to the rule "in the Veda [there is] diversely," the suffix *śnu* is substituted for the verbal suffix.
Now he speaks by way of indirect description:

*yaḥ* (he who)— that *agniḥ* (Agni), just as one restrains (*yamati*), controls, and extends his own *raśmīn* (rays), so too does he restrain and govern *ubhe janmanī* (both births), that is, both worlds— the worlds of this life and the next— which serve as the foundations for birth.

Likewise, this one of "good intention" (sukratuḥ), meaning one of beautiful deeds, "restrains" (ā yamati)— that is, he constantly bestows— both the "praise" (śaṃsam) and the "deities" (devānām), that is, the praise pertaining to the gods, within our sacrifice (ṛte). Alternatively, in the first half-verse, the word *papṛcāsi* may also be construed in the first person to express a state of being beyond direct perception.
Moreover, may the radiant Hotṛ, with swift horses, the joyous one with the shining chariot, hear us.
May he, Agni, who is free from weariness and never fails, lead us toward the waterless desert, toward prosperity, and toward greater wealth.

And may he, the brightly shining one with swift horses, the delightful invoker with the radiant chariot, hear us. May that unerring Agni lead us with the best leaders toward what is desirable, prosperity, and greater wealth. 12.
The word *uta* has the sense of "also" (*artha*), and it is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
May that Agni "also hear" (*śṛṇavat*) our invocation (*uta*).
May he indeed hear it;
or rather, may he cause us to hear it— that is, may he restore it among the gods.
In the leṭ mood of the root *śru*, there is the augment *āṭ*.
Of what nature is this?
It is *sudyotmā*, meaning "shining brightly."
The root *dyu* means "to shine.
The suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule: "It is seen after other roots as well."

He whose horses are swift, whose mind is rapid, who is the invoker of the gods, who is delightful, and who possesses a golden chariot; moreover, he who is undeluded in strength, who is worthy of being dwelt in—that well-known Agni—may he lead us with his excellent guides, whether through rites or hymns;
indeed, may he lead us even further, bringing us to the completion of the sacrifice.
In the *leṭ* [mood], there is the augment *āṭ*;
[the ending] *sip* is substituted by *tacchilpabahulam*.
For what purpose?
To bring toward us—that is, directly before us—the *vāma*, which means desirable; the *suvita*, which means well-attainable and sought after by all; namely, heaven (*svarga*). May he lead it forth.
1. [The variants] kṣa, ṅa, jha, jha, 1, ja, ṭa suggest that it should be disregarded.
2. [The variant] jha, 1: A Hymn.
Agni has been praised with powerful hymns, exerting himself for sovereign power.
May both those Madhavas and we ourselves break through [the darkness], as the sun breaks through the mist.

Agni has been praised with powerful hymns, as he advances toward sovereign dominion. May both those who are wealthy and we ourselves spread forth beyond the mist, as the sun disperses the clouds. || 13 ||

This Agni has been praised and extolled by us, the sacrificers, with hymns (*arkaiḥ*)—that is, with mantras that are the means of worship—which are accompanied by *śimīvat* acts, such as the offering of oblations (*haviṣ-pradāna*).
*Śimī* is a name for action, as it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (2.1.24): "Śimī is power. Of what nature is he?

"Samrājyāya" [in the phrase] "samrājyasya" is a dative case used in place of the genitive in the sense of an object; it means "possessing the state of being a universal monarch (samrājatva) in a manner that is more excellent and more preeminent."
And by the rule "asu ca chandasi," the suffix *asu* is applied.

Furthermore, let this Agni who stands before us, as well as the officiating priests, the sons and others, and we ourselves—who were previously renowned for our hymns—also resound exceedingly, that is, let us all cry out together.
The root *stan* preceded by the prefix *ni* has "sound" as its object.
The meaning is that from now on, our sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as we ourselves, shall praise Agni.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like the sun [dispelling] mist."
Just as the sun, the maker of light, calls forth the cloud that has the nature of raining, so too [does he call] me.
In the optative (*liṅ*), there is the Vedic substitution of *bh* for the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "The *s* of *stan* following *abhi-nis* is changed to *ṣ* when it is a technical grammatical term" (Pāṇini 8.3.46).
The third hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "samiddhaḥ," belongs to both [Agni and Soma].
In the first verse, the deity is Agni as the fuel-kindler (samidhmaka); in the second, Agni as the kindled one (samiddha).

For the second verse onwards, the deities are, respectively: Tanūnapāt, Narāśaṃsa, Barhis, the two divine Doors, Dawn and Night (Upāsānaktā), the two divine Hotṛ-priests Pracetas, the three goddesses Sarasvatī, Ilā, and Bhāratī, Vanaspati, and Svāhākṛti.
Indra is the deity of [the hymn] beginning with "tisro devīḥ. Its detailed explanation is "Sarasvatī, Iḷā, and Bhāratī.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "The *āprī* verses beginning with 'samiddha' are in the *ānuṣṭubh* meter; the others have Indra as their deity."
In this context, the sacrifice itself is expressed by terms such as *idhma* (fuel) and *tanūnapāt*, which denote constituent parts of the sacrifice;
therefore, it is the opinion of Kāthakya that the deity is none other than that [sacrifice].
According to [the view of] Agni alone, it is [the deity] that is expressed by *samidh* and the others.
Therefore, Śākapūṇi’s view is that he alone is the deity.

In the *Nirukta*, after presenting various alternative positions—such as "What is the deity of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s?"—"The deities of the meters" (*chandodevatā*), and so forth—and having cited the *Brāhmaṇa* and other texts for their meaning, the final conclusion is established: "The other positions are merely explanatory statements (*arthavāda*); they belong to Agni alone," as stated in the passage beginning with "Now, what is the deity of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s? (*Nirukta* 8.21).
This Āprī-sūkta belongs to those born of the Aṅgiras gotra in the animal sacrifice.
It is prescribed in the section beginning with "There are eleven Prayājas" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.2): "The verse *samiddho agne* [is used] for all, or according to the respective Ṛṣi.
Here, because of the inclusion of the phrase "according to the respective Ṛṣi," [the specific application is determined].
The Āprī-sūktas are of three kinds.

Among them, the four beginning with the Vāsiṣṭha-Āgneya and ending with the Aśvagātsameda possess the Narāśaṃsa. Those having Mitra-Atithi as their deity, as well as the Mānasa and Praiṣika, possess both the Narāśaṃsa and the Tanūnapāt.
The others protect the body;
therein this hymn is both [a protection and a remedy] because it belongs to Dīrghatamas.

Kindled, O Agni, bring hither today the gods for the one who extends the ladle. Spin out the ancient thread for the donor who has pressed the Soma. samiddho agne ā vaha devān adya yatasruce | tantuṃ tanuṣva pūrvyaṃ sutasomāya dāśuṣe || 1 ||

1. *kṣa-na-ṭa-sāmrājyam* | 2. *kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa-tanotiḥ* | 3. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-samiddho'gnirvā* | 4. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-chandodevatā ṛtudevatāḥ*; *cha-jha-jha-chandodevatā ṛtudevatā vā* | 5. *kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa-brāhmaṇāni* | 6. *kṣa-ū-jha-na-ṭa-praiṣikāṇi ca*. Ṛgveda 1.12: O Agni, being well-kindled (*samiddhaḥ*)—that is, perfectly ignited—you who bear this name, bring today, on this day of sacrifice, the gods—the eaters of the oblations, such as Agni and others—to our sacrifice; cause them to arrive here.
Since you have prepared yourself for the sacrifice, [I call you] for the sake of that sacrificer;
and for the sake of Sutasoma—the one who has pressed the soma—for the purpose of the sacrifice, and for the donor (dāśuṣe) who has offered the oblation.
Although the gods are being invoked only now, nevertheless, with reference to previous performance or with reference to what is yet to come, he is called "the donor" (dāśuṣe).
Either for the giver of the oblation or for the sacrificer, extend—that is, expand—the ancient thread, the sacrifice, which is beneficial for the former gods or which belongs to the primordial time.

O Tanūnapāt, you measure out for me the sacrifice rich in ghee and full of sweetness—belonging to a sage like me, who is diligent and offers oblations. 2. Rich in ghee. Up. You measure out. Full of sweetness. O Tanūnapāt. The sacrifice. Of the sage. Like me. Diligent. Offering oblations. 2.
He is Tanūnapāt.
According to the Kāṭhaka school’s view, "Tanūnapāt is the clarified butter (ājya)"; for the "bodies" (tanvaḥ) are the cows, because [pleasures] are born from them.
From those [cows] milk is produced, and from milk comes clarified butter; thus, clarified butter is the grandson (naptṛ).
The sacrifice possesses that [water].
In the case of Agni, the waters are called his bodies;
from them come the plants and trees.
From them [comes] Agni; this refers to his status as a grandson (*naptṛ*).
The meaning is "from the two kindling woods" (*araṇī*).

O Agni, you who bear this name, for the wise (*vipra*), the striving (*śaśamāna*), the praising (*śaṃsamāna*) one—meaning the one who extols you—the donor (*dāśuṣ*) who has offered the oblation, for a sacrificer such as I am (*māvataḥ*).
The suffix *vatup* is applied by the rule “*yuṣmadasmad-bhyāṃ chandasi sādṛśye*” [Pāṇini 5.2.39],
and the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the pronoun occurs by the rule “*ā sarvanāmnaḥ*” [Pāṇini 6.3.91].

Having approached the sacrifice—which is provided with clarified butter (*ghṛtavat*), endowed with flowing ghee (*kṣaradājyopeta*), possessed of sweetness (*madhumat*) through sweet substances such as *soma*, and so forth—you, O Mā, have measured yourself out (*sinirmimīṣe*), that is, you become measured;
the meaning is that you remain until the completion [of the rite].
‘Mā māne’: this belongs to the *ad-ādi* class.

Pure, purifying, and wonderful, he sprinkles the sacrifice with honey. Narāśaṃsa, the god worthy of worship among the gods, comes thrice from heaven. 3 Pure, purifying, and wonderful, he sprinkles the sacrifice with honey. Narāśaṃsa, the god worthy of worship among the gods, comes thrice from heaven. 3.

Among the gods, he is pure, clean, radiant, or purifying—the wonderful one who shall become, as if unprecedented, the cleanser of the food that has fallen [into the fire]. The meaning is that he becomes the support. He is a god, shining by nature, worthy of sacrifice, fit for the performance of the *yajña*. Such is Agni, to be praised by men—the priests who lead the ritual—having come from heaven (*divaḥ*), he thrice sprinkles our sacrifice with honey, with sweet essence; that is to say, he moistens it three times on all sides, making it palatable.
Alternatively, the meaning is that he mixes it three times with sweet fruit, or joins it.

According to the view of Kāthakya, "Narāśaṃsa is the sacrifice"; thus, the deity who presides over the sacrifice, shining brightly, having come from the heavenly world, mixes the sacrifice being performed three times.
This god Narāśaṃsa is threefold.
Due to the influence of the prefix, there is an ellipsis of the verbal action associated with the yoga.
He comes three times,
or he brings fruit three times;
the remainder is to be understood as before.
1. Because it is being measured (*tāyamānatvāt*). 2. Endowed with honey (*madhunopetam*).

3. It will come into existence at this very moment (*adyakṣaṇe bhavitā*); because of its manifestation through that which is joined with fear (*bhāyuktena*), [or] because of its manifestation through that which is joined with clarified butter (*ājyāyuktena*).

4. *kṣa-cha-jha-ma-ṭa-bhā* from all sides. O Agni, being praised, bring hither Indra, the wonderful, the beloved. For this prayer of mine, O fair-tongued one, shall be uttered toward you. 4. Being praised, O Agni, bring hither Indra, the wonderful, the beloved. For this prayer of mine, O fair-tongued one, shall be uttered toward you.

O Agni, invoked by all and worthy of praise, bring here—into this sacrifice—Indra, who is named *iṭ*, the wonderful (*citram*), the venerable (*cāyanīyam*), the beloved (*priyam*), and the one who delights us or is intent on accepting our oblation; call him hither. O fair-tongued one, with beautiful flames from drinking the clarified butter, this my thought—the speech consisting of praise that is the means of meditation—is directed toward you; it is my very thought that is being expressed.
The particle *hi* serves to fill out the meter (*pūraṇārtha*).

Because the rule "also after *vac* and *ekī*" prescribes the substitution of the single preceding vowel (*pūrvarūpa*), and because that substitution is optional in the Vedic language (*vā chandasi*), the *yaṇ* replacement occurs when the former does not take place.
In this context, the word *puroḍāśādī* is treated as an irregular formation (*nipātita*).
Of what nature are they?

Increasing the cosmic order (*ṛtavṛdhaḥ*), they are the augmenters of the sacrifice, worthy of worship, great (*mahīḥ*), purifying (*pāvakāsaḥ*), desired by many (*puruspṛhaḥ*), and unrestrained (*asanrataḥ*)— that is to say,
not held back from one another. 10.
May Night and Dawn, the two neighboring goddesses, well-adorned and being praised, sit upon the sacrificial grass with their gracious favor, according to the measure of Eternal Order.

Ā | bhandamāne iti | upāke iti | naktoṣāsā | supeśasā | yahvī iti | ṛtasya | mātrā | sīdatām | barhiḥ | ā | sumat || 7 || May Night and Dawn, the two well-adorned, mighty daughters of Cosmic Order, sitting together upon the sacrificial grass with their favor, come hither.
7) While being praised by all, 7) in close proximity to one another, 7) well-adorned (supeśasā), meaning having beautiful forms—
*peśas* is a name for form; 7) they are great (*yahī*), either in their own nature or as offspring, because they are born day after day.
Their name is *yahurīśyapattrī*, because they are listed among the names [of the Maruts] in the Nirukta (2.2.11) as "the sons of *yahuḥ*.
They are the two mothers of *ṛta*, the fashioners of the sacrifice;
because the sacrifice comes from them, they are figuratively designated as the complete mothers of the sacrifice.
Alternatively,
since the Atirātra and other such rites have day and night as their presiding deities (adhidevatā),
[the phrase] "Night and Dawn" refers to the deities of day and night characterized by the aforementioned qualities; [they are] themselves well-disposed.
The meaning is: "requested by us.
Alternatively:
"Let them sit down—that is, let them take their seats—upon the well-prepared sacrificial grass (barhis) spread out on all sides."
Alternatively,
in the phrase "of the rta," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object; thus,
[the meaning is] "may they sit upon the sacrifice."

And having reached the strewn sacrificial grass, let them sit down of their own accord—the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the seers with gentle tongues who sing praises; may they perform for us this successful sacrifice that touches the heavens. 8.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the sages with lovely tongues who have ever been praised—may they perform for us this successful sacrifice that reaches unto heaven. 8.
Possessing lovely tongues, they are the two who delight the gods with their flames; they are the bestowers of wealth upon those who praise and extol them intensely.
The formation of the word *gṛṇantau* is established by Vedic license through the elision of the suffix *yaṅ* from the root *gṛ*, followed by the addition of the suffix *kip*.

With that as the governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *ini* is applied to the root *van* according to the rule: "In the Veda, the suffixes *ini*, *san*, *ana*, and *rakṣit* are added after [roots ending in] *math*."

The two sages (*kavī*), wise and far-sighted; the two divine *hotṛ*s, belonging to the gods—referring to both this one and the one situated in the intermediate region (*madhyama-sthāna*). *Sidhram*: that which is effective as a means of attaining the fruit.

[The suffix] *-rak* is added to the root *sidh* according to the rule "sphāyitañci... etc. *Divispṛśam*: touching the gods who dwell in the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), because the oblation is accepted by them; such is the sense.
"May they [the two] perform, carry out, or honor this such sacrifice of ours—that is to say, may they bring it to perfect completion.

1. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: "increasers of cosmic order" (*ṛtāvṛdhaḥ*). 2. *jha*: "fulfillment is the state of being a creator"; *kṣa-jha 1-a-ṭa*: "fulfillment is the state of being a fashioner" (*saṃpūrtirnimā[tṛ]tvam*).

Pure Hotrā is entrusted among the gods; Bhāratī among the Maruts; may Iḷā, Sarasvatī, and Mahī—the worshipful ones—sit upon the sacrificial grass. 9. Pure. Among the gods. Entrusted. Hotrā. Among the Maruts. Bhāratī. Iḷā. Sarasvatī. Mahī. Upon the sacrificial grass. May they sit. Worshipful ones. 9.

The pure, purified *bhāratī*—the speech residing in heaven, belonging to *Bharata* (the Sun)—is fixed and ordained among the *maruts*, who are immortal gods characterized by radiance and delight in praise; or [fixed] among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Likewise, there is *iḷā*, the earthly [speech] consisting of ritual commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth, and the great *sarasvatī*.
"Sara" is a name for water.

Likewise, the thundering voice and so forth, and the speech of the Mādhyamikas—these three deities presiding over speech in its three locations, who are worthy of sacrifice, true, and for whom the sacrificial grass is strewn—should sit down and take their seats.

May Tvaṣṭṛ, who is well-disposed toward us, release for our nourishment and for wealth that wonderful seed—fourfold, abundant, and sufficient by its own nature—at our very center. That, for us, the seed; wonderful; manifold; indeed; sufficient; manifold; by itself; Tvaṣṭṛ; for prosperity; may he release; for wealth; at our navel; being well-disposed toward us. 10.
For our sake, let that such [seed]— fertile, swiftly pervasive, wonderful, and suddenly manifesting like something non-existent becoming existent—
or rather, let this be great— [be ours].
Great in essence;
for the sake of many beings, it is *puru-vāram*, meaning sufficient, adequate, or capable.
Or alternatively:
"Puru" means many; "vāram" means abundant.
The word "vā" has the sense of "ca" (and).
"Aram" means sufficient or enough.
"By himself" (*ātmanā*) means by his own self;
this is an adverbial modifier for "many.
Such water [was created] by Tvaṣṭṛ, the agent of rain and other such phenomena.

The word *tvaṣṭṛ* has been explained by Yāska as follows: "The etymologists say *tvaṣṭṛ* means 'the swift one' or 'the wonderful one'; it may also be from *tviṣ*, a root meaning 'to increase,' or from *takṣ*, a root meaning 'to fashion'" (*Nirukta* 8.13).

That fire of lightning, named after him, being *asmayu*—desiring us—O God, for our nourishment (*poṣāya*) and for wealth (*rāye*) and prosperity, let him release (*vyatu*), that is, cause to flow forth in various ways, the water characterized by its upward motion which is situated at the *nābhi*—the navel, the central binding point of the cloud—at the very center of the rain-cloud.
[The root] *ṣo* is used in the sense of the act of ending.
In "otaḥ iyani," there is the elision of the vowel *o*;
in "upasargātsunoti," there is the substitution of the sibilant *ṣ*.
Or alternatively:
"In our navel"—that is, in the navel of the sacrifice related to us, namely on the *uttaravedi* (high altar)—"for wealth.
The dative case is used here in the sense of the genitive.
For the nourishment—that is, for the increase—of wealth consisting of cattle and other riches.
It may be that, being afflicted by them, there is the purpose of liberation.
May he release rain characterized by the signs of Utkala.

1. In the manuscripts kṣa, ja, and ṭa, there is the addition: "The deities presiding over speech occupy three places. 2. In the manuscript kṣa, following the phrase "let them sit down" (upaviśantu), there is the additional passage: "In the word *tisraḥ*, because of the rule *tisṛbhyo jasaḥ*, the *jas* ending is acute. 3. In the manuscripts ṅa and jha, the reading is *tūrṇavyāpi*. 4. In the manuscript kṣa, the word "eva" is absent.
5. [The letters] kṣa, ja, ṭa, and me belong to Megha;
6. [The letters] kṣa, ja, ṭa, and vā signify "stayed" (sthitam);
7. [The letters] kṣa, ṅa, jha, ña, ja, ṭa, and na signify "us" (asmān).
Releasing [the offerings] by yourself, O Vanaspati, worship the gods;
for Agni, the wise god among the gods, prepares the oblations well.
Releasing [the offerings], do thou thyself worship the gods, O Vanaspati; may Agni, the wise god among the gods, prepare the oblations well. 11.

O Vanaspati, protector of the forests, O Agni presiding over the sacrificial post, releasing [the animals] and setting them at liberty, and employing the officiating priests in their respective duties, do thou yourself worship the gods who consume the oblations, having approached them.
The elision of the *śap* suffix occurs frequently in the Vedic language (*chandas*).
The shining god, the wise Agni, the Āhavanīya fire, "among the gods"—that is, in the midst of both [classes]—"well-cooks," that is, impels or accepts the "oblations," the sacrificial offerings.
The root *pū* is used in the sense of "flowing" (*kṣaraṇe*).
According to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the substitution of *ślu* for *śap*. By the rule *kṣayo 'ḍāṭau*, the augment *aṭ* is added.
Alternatively,
it is the sacrificial post-fire itself that is being spoken of indirectly;
that fire thoroughly accepts the oblations.
To Pūṣan, to the one accompanied by the Maruts, to the Viśvedevas, and to Vāyu—svāhā! To Indra, who is moved by the Gāyatrī, prepare the oblation.
To Pūṣan, to him who is accompanied by the Maruts, to Viśvedevas, to Vāyu—svāhā! For Indra, who is moved by the Gāyatrī, prepare the oblation. 12.
"To Pūṣan belongs that which is struck by Pūṣan."
In *anu-nud*, the suffix *nud* [is applied]. In *anu-mat*, the suffix *matup* [is applied], which is udātta according to the rule *hasvanṅabhyāṃ matup*.

"To the one accompanied by the Maruts, to him who is honored by the Maruts; to the one belonging to all the gods (*viśvadeva*), that is, connected with all the gods; and to Vāyu, the god of wind whose nature is movement—likewise, to Indra, whose form is the *gāyatra* (the *gāyatra* word being indicative of the other *sāmans* as well), to him whose form is the *gāyatra*-chant—O priests, perform the *svāhā* call in order to offer the oblation (*havyam*) and the sacrificial food (*haviḥ*)."
In the imperative (loṭ) of the root *kṛ*, the substitute *tana* is applied [to the suffix] by the rule "tasanasanathanāśca."
O Indra, come for the enjoyment of these secret oblations consecrated with Svāhā; hear our call, for they invoke you at the sacrifice.
The offerings consecrated with "svāhā"—come, Indra, partake of the oblations for your enjoyment; come, Indra, hear our call; they invoke you at the sacrifice. 13.
"O Indra, [convey] the *svāhākṛtāni*.
An action (*kṛti*) preceded by the word "svāhā" is a performance (*karaṇa*), that is, an utterance directed toward the deities about to be worshipped; these are the *svāhākṛtayas*.
He offers those sacrificial portions (*havyāni*) as oblations (*havīṃṣi*).

In this context, regarding the *prayāja* offerings, the meaning is that the oblation (*havis*) is consecrated by the utterance of *svāhā* because it is presented with the *vaṣaṭ* call. 1. [Variant readings: *susūdati*; 2. [Variant readings: *svīkaroti vā*; 3. [Variant readings: *itarāsāmupalakṣakaḥ*; 4. [Variant readings: *svāhāntam*; *jha-jha*: *svāhutam*. Therefore: "Having approached, come (*gahi*) for the sake of enjoyment (*vītaye*), that is, for consumption (*bhakṣaṇāya*)."
The *gameḥ* is a Vedic form [of the root *gam*] with the elision of the *śap* suffix.
By the rule beginning with *anudāttopadeśa vaḥ*, there is the elision of the nasal.
Likewise: O Indra, come hither (*vā v gahi*) toward the hymns of praise (*stotrāṇi*).
Having come, hear—listen to—our invocation;
for from here the officiating priests call upon you at the sacrifice whose nature is non-violence, therefore hear us.
[In the word *iyate*, the vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs according to the rule: "The substitution is frequent in the Vedic language" (*bahulam chandasi*).]
The fourth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with *pra tavyasīm*, belongs to Dīrghatamas.
Thus it is enumerated: *pra tavyasīm aṣṭāv āgneyaṃ nu tat triṣṭub-antam ca*.
Because of the introductory phrase "Now that," Agni is the deity of this group of eight hymns beginning with "idam.
This [first verse] is in the *triṣṭubh* meter; by the rule regarding those ending in *triṣṭubh*, the remaining verses are in the *jagatī* meter.
Its application is appropriate for the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*.

In the *āgnimāruta* śastra of the *agniṣṭoma*, this hymn is to be used as the *jātavedasya-nivid-vānīya*. It is prescribed in the section beginning with "atha yathemam v" in the Sūtra: "‘pra tavyasīm navyasīm’, ‘āpo hi v’—these three verses" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.20).
It serves as the *jātavedasya-nivid-vānīya* on the first day of the ten-day rite (*daśarātra*), and as the *nivid-vānīya* on the middle day of the *aśvamedha*.

And thus there is the extension of the rule by the Teacher: "One should place the Nivids in those [Śastras] of the one-day sacrifice that have a concluding part; likewise in the Agnimāruta [Śastra]. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 10.10)

I bring forward a more powerful, newer prayer to Agni; I offer a song and a hymn to the Son of Strength. He who is the Son of the Waters, the beloved Hotṛ-priest, together with the Vasus, has sat down upon the earth according to the seasons. pra tavyasīm navyasīm dhītim agnaye vāce matim sahasaḥ sūnave bhare | apāṃ napād yo vasubhiḥ saha priyo hotā pṛthivyāṃ nyasīdad ṛtviyaḥ || 1 || I bring forward a more powerful, newer prayer to Agni; I offer a song and a hymn to the Son of Strength. He who is the Son of the Waters, the beloved Hotṛ-priest, together with the Vasus, has sat down upon the earth according to the seasons.
Or rather, [the word] *vājinīm* means "more powerful" (*vāyasīm*), that is, increasing [him] to the highest degree. The verbal root *vṛdh* (to increase) is a Vedic root;
from this, by adding the suffix *tṛc*, and subsequently the comparative suffix *īyasun* according to the rule *turiṣṭhemeyassu chandasi vā*, [the form *vājinī* is derived].
In the word *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*, there is the elision of the suffix *tu*. The elision of the vowel *ī* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
I offer forth—that is, I perform with excellence—the newer, more recent, and even the ancient *dhīti*, which is characterized by sacrifice or possesses superior qualities.
Thus, I shall offer to Agni—whose characteristics have been described—the work of speech, namely praise, as an act of devotion.
To what kind of Agni?
To the son (*sūnu*) of strength (*sahasa*).
Furthermore, Agni is the *napāt* (grandson) of the waters, meaning their descendant;
for it is said, "From fire come plants, and from plants comes fire," thus establishing his status as the grandson of fire.
Alternatively, the sense is that he is not a destroyer (*na pātayitā*) of the waters, because he manifests himself in the form of lightning.

Likewise, Agni—the beloved one, the most dear gratifier of the sacrificer, or his Hotṛ who accomplishes the oblation—being timely (*ṛtviya*), having reached the proper moment for the offering, sits down firmly (*nyasīdat*) upon the earth characterized as the altar, together with the *vasus*, the wealth such as cattle and other assets suitable for dwelling.

Being born in the highest heaven, Agni became manifest to Mātariśvan. By the power of his will and by the greatness of him who was kindled, he caused Heaven and Earth to shine forth with his brilliance. 2. He, being born in the highest firmament, became manifest as Agni to Mātariśvan. By his wisdom and by the might of him who was fully kindled, he caused both Heaven and Earth to glow with light. 2.

1. *kṣa-jña-1-ba-ṭa-upa* means having approached (*upetya*). 2. *kṣa-na-ṭa-śapi* means there is a vowel-protraction (*saṃprasāraṇa*). 3. *ca-prathame'yahani* means on the first day. 4. *ca-jña-pha-yāgalakṣaṇam* refers to the characteristic of sacrifice (*yajña*).

The aforementioned fire (*agni*), being produced—arising from the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) or appearing within pieces of wood—immediately became manifest (*pratyakṣa*) as the first (*prathamam*) [oblation] for Mātariśvan, the wind that moves through the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), who is in the highest (*parama*) and most excellent (*utkṛṣṭa*) sky (*vyoman*) which possesses various protections (*rakṣaṇa*), that is, upon the sacrificial altar (*vedi*).
This is because it is well-known from other Vedic texts such as, “O Agni, appear first for Mātariśvan” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.31.3).
The meaning is that [Agni] has been kindled through conjunction with the wind (*vāyu*).

Alternatively, *mātariśvā* refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), who is so called because he moves (*iṣṭe*) within the mother (*mātari*), that is, within the sacrificial post (*yaṣṭi*) which is the producer (*nirmātṛ*) of the fruit.
For that purpose.
Furthermore, by the *majman*— this is a name for strength— of the fire that is being properly increased (*samidhānasya*) by fuel-sticks (*samidhābhiḥ*).
Having performed his work with powerful heat—namely, the activity of blazing and so forth—he caused both heaven and earth to shine forth; he illuminated them intensely.
The word *śociḥ* (heat) in the middle [of the compound] is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Or, it may be construed as "having kindled [them] by means of his majesty" (*majmanā samidhānasya*).
The meaning is: "of him who is being kindled by a powerful operation such as the placing of fuel.
His flames are ageless; his rays are beautiful to behold, from him whose countenance is fair and whose luster is excellent.
Those whose power is light, like rivers that have overflowed their banks, tremble before him—unfailing, ageless, and never ceasing.

His flames are brilliant; his rays are ageless. The beams of this one, who is fair to behold, of beautiful countenance, and of splendid luster, possess radiant power. Like rivers overpassing a narrow pass, they tremble before Agni—unwavering and ageless. ||3||
Of that Agni who is being praised, the *vṛtvyāḥ*—the flickering—*dīptayaḥ*—flames—are *vajrāḥ*, meaning free from decay (*jarā-rahitāḥ*), not worn out, that is to say, uninterrupted.
[The accentuation of the final syllable of the compound is due to the rule] “*naño jaramara-” etc., which prescribes the udātta accent on the final member of the compound.
Likewise, the *bhānavaḥ*—the rays—of that Agni, who is *supratīkaḥ*, having a beautiful face.
Or, because they are sparks, they should be understood as such;
and they are "well-seeing" (vsusaṃdṛśaḥ), meaning they are excellent, perfect observers,
in the sense that they are all-pervading.
*Vsudyutaḥ*: shining well and brilliantly on all sides.
Likewise, *asya vagnaiḥ bhātvakṣasaḥ*.
*Tvakṣas* is a name for strength, because it is listed among the names for strength in *Nighaṇṭu* 2.9.6: "*tvakṣaḥ śardhaḥ*" (strength, vigor).
*bhāsamānabalāḥ* (those possessing manifest strength).
*Vakkuḥ* is a name for night, because that name is mentioned in [Nirukta] 1.7.4: *akkuḥ umbā*.
The nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative.

The sun, having transcended the nocturnal darkness that obstructs the world, shines forth; like rivers flowing everywhere and pervading all, it remains constant in its own functions, never ceasing and therefore undecaying—it neither wavers nor trembles.
In burning, cooking, and other such acts, it does not falter, nor is it moved by fire.
Or rather:

The word *na* expresses a comparison (*dṛṣṭānta*). Of this fire, whose strength (*tvakṣas*) is light (*bhās*) itself—that is, for whom light is the very power—his rays are like the rivers (*sindhavaḥ*). Just as they flow, pervasive, and having overcome the darkness (*akku*), they shine forth (*rejante*) without ceasing; in the same way, the sparks (*akṣaṇa*) or flames of this fire also shake, tremble, and pervade everywhere. This is the meaning.
The Bhṛgus have established Agni, the all-knowing, at the navel of the earth by the power of the world. Praise him with songs in his own home—he who alone rules over wealth like Varuṇa.

Him whom the Bhṛgus brought hither—the all-knowing one—at the navel of the earth, by the greatness of the world; that Agni, do thou urge on with songs in his own home, he who alone rules over wealth like Varuṇa. 4.

1. *ta*: of that sacrificer. 2. *kha-ja-jha-pha-asya agne:* [variant readings for] "of this Agni. 3. *kṣa-ṅa-jha-ja-ṭa-ta-jvālācālanādidhyāpāreṇa*: by means of the activity of moving the flames and so forth. 4. *kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-a-ṭa-śoci:* the heat produced; *teja:* brilliance. 5. *jha-akṣīṇā:* undecaying. 6. *kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-na-ṭa-dāhapākādiṣpi*: even in burning, cooking, and so forth. 7. *kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa-akkuriti*: [variant reading] "the sprout" (*akku*). 8. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-atikramya ajarā:* having transcended, they are ageless.
*viśvedesam sarvadhanam*: "All this" refers to all wealth. *Veda* is a name for wealth, because it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (2.10.4): "*vedaḥ varivaḥ*" ("wealth is *veda*").
Such an Agni as this, the Bhṛgus—those born of the Bhṛgu lineage and the burners of evil—are the creators (*vedhas*) of the earth;
the word "entire" (*kṛtsna*) is used for a single part.
Or alternatively:

"Indeed, so great is the earth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.4.3)—from such scriptural passages, the earth possesses the nature of a *vedi* (altar). At its navel, upon the *uttaravedi*, they have, by means of the power (*majmanā*) of the world—that is, the multitude of beings—as the instrumental cause, impelled and established [the fire] in a forward direction (*ābhimukhyena*).
That Agni, in his own home (*sve dame*), namely the *uttaravedi*, do thou further (*ā hinuhi*) and promote with songs of praise (*gīrbhiḥ*).
The root √hi means "to go" and "to grow";
the causal form [hepayati] is derived by the rule "utaśca pratyayāc chandasi vāvacanam" (Pāṇini 6.4.106), which allows for the optional elision of the *i* of the suffix in Vedic usage.

O Agni, being the one and foremost, or indeed being alone, you shine as the sovereign (*rājati*)—that is, you become the lord (*īśvara*)—of wealth (*vasu*), such as cattle and other possessions. The word "bestower" (*pradātṛ*) is to be supplied [as the object].
*Rājati* is a verb signifying sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), because it is listed among the names [of Agni] in the passage: “He dwells (*kṣiyati*), he shines (*rājati*)” (Nirukta 2.21.4).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Like Varuṇa, the restrainer," meaning like the Sun;
just as he rules over all, so does he.

Like the roar of the Maruts when they set out for battle, like a celestial thunderbolt hurled by an army, Agni devours with his sharpened jaws; he consumes the forests as a warrior strikes down his enemies.
No; like the roar of the Maruts, like an army set in motion, like a divine thunderbolt, Agni with his sharp jaws eats and chews; like a warrior against his enemies, he attacks the forests. 5.
O Agni, you are not incapable of choosing, selecting, or restraining;
in this regard, three examples are stated:
like the roar of the Maruts.
Just as that [army] was ungraspable, so too is it;
likewise, it is like a powerful army dispatched for the purpose of destroying the enemy's ranks, which cannot be obstructed by others. Just as that [army] is such, so too is it.

Likewise, just as a divine thunderbolt (*aśani*) that falls from the sky cannot be turned back, so too does he possess such power; this is what he demonstrates. This fire, with its sharpened—that is, whetted and made keen—flames...
The form *abhyavikāra* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
With *jambhaiḥ*—meaning with teeth, or rather with flames that stand in the place of teeth—he *atti*, i.e., he devours those who oppose us;
likewise, he *bharvati*, i.e., he destroys them.
The root *bhṛ* is used in the sense of harming.

Yāska, however, says: "The root *bharv* has the sense of 'eating' (*nirukta* 9.23). Although the roots *ad* and *bharv* both have 'eating' as their meaning, nevertheless, their internal distinction must be understood."
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a warrior who is not a gatherer [of spoils] but a hero;
just as he devours—that is, consumes—the enemies, so it is in that case.
Furthermore, that Agni thoroughly prepares—that is, he completely consumes—the *vanas*, which are collections of trees and the like;
for Yāska states: "The root *ṛñj* has the sense of preparing."
Will he not surely fulfill the desire of the one who seeks his favor? Will he not surely grant our wish with his riches?
Will he not surely impel our prayers toward the attainment of wealth? Him, whose face is radiant, I praise with this prayer.

Will not Agni be a hero for our purpose? Will he, the possessor of wealth, surely fulfill our desire with riches? Will he, the impeller, truly quicken our prayers for gain? Him of the radiant countenance, I praise with this prayer.

1. *kṣa-ja-ṭa* have established [this]. The root *īr* means "to go. 2. *jha1*: Of all the *vamuna*. 3. *ḍa-jha1-na*: It is not possible; it does not exist. *ca-pha-na*: It becomes capable. *jha-ta*: It does not become capable. 4. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: Unseizable; *jha*: Unseizable by all. 5. *kṣa-ja-jha-jha1-ja-ṭa*: For the purpose of conquering enemies. 6. *kṣa-u-jha-jha1-ja-ṭa*: He devours; he destroys. Ṛgveda 1.113:
This Agni shall be our (*naḥ*)—that is, ours—desirer (*vīḥ*, from *vī* meaning "to desire") of every hymn (*ukthasya ukthasya*), that is, of every praise-song (*stotra*), many times over.
[The form] *asat* is the third person singular of the root *as* in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood; the augment *aṭ* has been added.
Alternatively, the connection is with "naḥ" (us), [referring to] those originating from the lineage of the great seer named Uktha.

Likewise, may the Vasu— the dweller, or one who is like a treasure for all, or one accompanied by the Vasus who are dwellers— graciously bestow (*āvarāt*) upon us an exceedingly abundant (*kvit*) and highly desired boon.
The meaning is that desire should be turned away by granting what is desired.
[This form] is derived from the root *vṛ* (to choose) in the *leṭ* mood;
the augment *aṭ* is added, and there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), which is a Vedic usage.

This Agni, being the impeller (*codaḥ*) among our ritual acts, shall indeed greatly hasten—meaning he shall speed on or impel—our thoughts, that is, our actions, for the sake of attainment (*sātaye*).
The root *tuji* means "to impel.
The *śap* suffix is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasaḥ*).
I utter—that is, I praise with this prayer in the form of a hymn—the Agni whose face is pure, whose limbs are beautiful, and whose flames are radiant; I place him upon his attribute.
O you whose face is ghee, who sit at the pole of the Cosmic Order (ṛta), protect us like a friend!
Guard us! Preserve us!

Furthermore, O beloved one, worthy of being desired by all, being born—that is, shining forth—by us, you are [accompanied] by those who are undeceived (adabdha), unharmed (adapita), and unsubdued by anyone.
‘Hapa’ and ‘hampha’ mean affliction (utkleśa);
they belong to the *taudādi* group.
With unblinking—that is, devoid of winking—desirable characteristics whose nature is like fire, protect us, guard us on all sides.
Or alternatively:
they are called *jā* because they are born (*jāyante*) one after another.
Protect—that is, guard on all sides—our progeny (*prajā*), consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth;
protect not only us, but also our sons, grandsons, and the rest.
The fifth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “eti pra hotā,” belongs to Daidhiti Tamas and is composed in the Jagatī meter.
Since it was stated previously that “that [hymn] belongs to Agni,” this one also belongs to Agni.
Thus says the Anukramaṇikā: “eti pra—seven verses; Jagatī.”
The application of the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra has been stated.
The Hotṛ comes forward by his wondrous power, upholding the sacred law and the hymn of pure form;
he moves toward the ladles turned to the right, which were first established for his station.

The Hotṛ comes forward by his wondrous power to fulfill his office; raising aloft the pure-hued prayer, he moves toward the ladles, turning to the right, for that which is his first station has been established. ||1||

Then the Hotṛ—the Adhvaryu who performs the oblation—being endowed with *māyā*, that is, the specific wisdom required for the task, proceeds forward to perform the *vrata* of this Agni, namely the ritual action consisting of the offering of oblations and so forth.
*Māyā* is a name for wisdom (*prajñā*), as it is listed among its synonyms in the Nirukta (3.9.9): "māyā, vayuna. Of what nature is he?
Bearing a prayer—that is, wisdom—that is directed upward, ascended above, and possessed of pure beauty;
"peśas" is a name for form.
Bearing such wisdom.

Because it has been stated, "They look toward this [result] from the fourth ritual act onwards, thinking, 'He will do this,'" and having arrived, they proceed by turning to the right— that is, moving clockwise— and take up the *sruks*, such as the *juhū* and others. Of what kind are these *sruks*?
She who first, at the time of setting out the sacrificial vessels, entered the abode, the place of this Agni.
The verbal root *niṣ* means "to kiss."
"Kiss" (cumbanti) means they embrace;
that is, first one approaches the rite to be performed with the intellect, and afterwards one proceeds with the sacrificial ladles—this is the meaning.
The particle "ha" denotes well-known fact.
Alternatively:
this Agni, the invoker of the gods, being endowed with a specific wisdom regarding the *vrata*—the ritual act such as the Jyotiṣṭoma—of this sacrificer, proceeds;
that is, he goes toward the place of sacrifice.

Of what nature is he? He is one who, possessing an upward-tending intellect (*dhī*) that is pure and beautiful in form— meaning endowed with an excellent appearance— and who maintains an activity consisting of the movement of flames and so forth,
having arrived, proceeds toward and ascends the sacrificial ladles (*srucaḥ*), such as the *juhū* and *upabhṛt*, which are filled with clarified butter and turned to the right (*dakṣiṇāvṛtaḥ*).
The meaning is that the flames spread forth in order to take up the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Those ladles (*srucaḥ*) which first, at the time of placing the oblation (*havir-āsādana*), kiss—that is, reach—the abode (*dhāma*), namely the altar (*vedi*), of this fire;
the particle *ha* indicates well-known fact.

In the root *ṇiś* (meaning "to kiss"), there is elision of the suffix *śap* because it belongs to the *adādi* class; and due to its being marked with the indicatory letter *it*, the augment *num* is added.
1. By means of protection through *kṣa*, *jha*, *na*, *ṭa*, and *rakṣaṇa*;
2. Having looked toward us from the fourth action—*kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *na*, *ṭa*—and having said, "I shall do this, I shall do that";
3. *Kha*, *ca*, *ṇi*, *si*; 4. Endowed with a beautiful form: *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *ja*, *ṭa*.
5. Having the form of mountains of flame, kṣa, ṅa, jha, ṇa, ṭa, and jva;

they have lowed toward him in the womb of Order, encompassed in the seat of the god. When he dwelt in the lap of the waters, being distributed, then he sucked the nourishing powers (*svadhā*) by which he moves. 2. Toward him the milkings of Order have lowed, encompassed in the womb, in the seat of the god. When he dwelt in the lap of the waters, being distributed, then he sucked the nourishing powers (*svadhā*) by which he moves.
The streams of the encompassed water, having been turned back in the womb— the place of origin, namely the station of the radiant god Āditya— become surrounded;
being thus completely pervaded by those [streams], they become new (*abhyanūpata*), that is,
they come into being or are praised.
Kadeyata said: "When—meaning at that time—this Agni, having been specially supported by those [waters] in the lap of the waters (*udakānām upasthe*), dwelt and remained there;
then, indeed, now, all the world drinks the *svadhās*, the waters which are like nectar."
These are further specified:
this Agni goes forth together with the lightning bolts, or he unites with the earth;
he consumed them, and in the form of lightning, he causes the waters and the world to drink—this is the praise of Agni.

Desiring to win with equal vigor, they two, striving together for that same common goal, mutually advance. Then, like Bhaga, he is to be invoked by you in the assembly; like a charioteer, he has firmly guided the reins. Desiring to win with equal vigor—that very form—striving together for that same common goal, mutually. Then, like Bhaga, he is to be invoked by you in the assembly; like a charioteer, he has firmly guided the reins.
*Samānavayasā*: "of equal age.

By the word *vayas*, capability (*sāmarthya*) is indicated; thus, they are "possessing equal capability. At that very time, when [the fire] has grown great, then indeed, with a common purpose—that is, a common objective—the two, the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu, "crossing over intensely," each individually crossing over, "desire to unite"—that is, they wish to intermingle through their respective functions—the "body" (*vapus*), the physical form of Agni.

The division of duties is as follows: after the *praiṣa* (direction), the recitation of the *yājyā* and other verses belongs to the Hotṛ and Adhvaryu; after the *vaṣaṭkāra*, the offering (*homa*) belongs to the Adhvaryu.
Here, this should be kept in mind:
two of equal age (*savayasau*), being of the same age, each desiring to cross over specifically toward the attainment of happiness which is their common purpose.
The form *dādharti* is derived from the reduplicated (*yaṅluganta*) root *tṛ*, with the suffix *śatṛ*, as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) under Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.65;
the doubling [of the root] results in the vowel *ā*.
In the same way, the husband and wife desire to join their bodies together— that is, they wish to mingle them—
embracing one another. Likewise, the *hotṛ* and *adhvaryu* priests desire to join the fire together.
The proponent is to be addressed immediately thereafter: the *āhavanīya* fire is the charioteer; "charioteer" means one who is prone to moving, like a driver.
[Regarding the variants: 1. In the versions marked kṣa, ṅa, jha, jha₁, ga, ṭa, they appear or are praised with direct orientation (*ābhimukhyena*).
2. In the versions marked kṣa, jha, jha₂, jha₃, 1, ga, ṭa, he comes together or goes.
3. Kṣa, Ja, and Ṭa read *pālayate*.
4. Kṣa, Ja, and Ṭa read *samānaprayojanaṃ yajñaniṣpattim*; Ṅa, Jha, and 1 read *samānaprayojanayajñaniṣpattim*; Jha reads *samānaprayojananiṣpattim*.
5. Kṣa, Ja, and Ṭa read *vitarantau*.
6. [The letters] kṣa, ja, ṭa have the same meaning and the same purpose. 7. kṣa and ḷ have each other’s body.
8. kṣa, kha, ṅa, ja, jha, jha, ḷ, ga, and ṭa are together with their respective mates.
Or, being the driver of the chariot, he properly gathers—that is, he fully accepts—the reins, which are connected to us, and the streams of clarified butter extending from the possessor of the reins;
on this point, two similes are stated:
like Bhaga, the Sun who is to be served by all, who receives worship from every side, so does he.
The charioteer [says]: "Just as a driver of a chariot takes up the reins—the traces of the draft animal—so too has this Agni consumed the oblations."
The two, of like age, worship Yamī; they are a pair, dwelling together in a common womb and a common home.
Like day and night, the gray-haired one was born as a youth; moving through many human ages, he remains undecaying.

Him whom the two of equal age worship, the pair joined in common womb and sharing the same dwelling; he, the gray-haired youth, was born by night as by day—ageless, wandering far through many human generations.

These two, of equal age or equal power, dwelling together in the same womb—the place of origin for the fruit, namely the sacrifice—like a married couple joined in a single task, sharing the same abode and situated at the site of the divine sacrifice, honor this Agni; they worship him and gratify him with praise and the offering of oblations.
When? It is said: "By day," as it were, and also "by night."
This is the meaning of "all.

Thus, Agni, though previously "gray-haired" (palita)—meaning worn out in the state of embers—is born (ajani) as "young" (yuvā), fresh after being kindled, or as the "mixture" (miśrayitā) of all things through his brilliance.

Having been thus born, he exists "ageless" (ajara)—that is, undecayed and free from old age—while moving extensively for the sake of the "human ages" (mānuṣā yugā), namely the pairs consisting of husband and wife, or the pairs consisting of the Hotṛ and Adhvaryu priests, consuming the clarified butter and other offerings.
The ten thoughts impel him; we mortals call upon the god in three ways for protection.
From the distance he speeds along the slope; the hero, with his wisdom, has prepared the paths for our journey.
Him the prayers impel; ten times thirty mortals invoke the god for aid. From the hollow of the cloud he hastens down the slope; with those who come toward him, he has established new ways. 5.
The ten *dhītayaḥ*—the ten fingers—three by three, distinct from one another, impel and delight this Agni, the shining god, at the time of the libation.
Likewise, we mortals, the sacrificers, invoke him for protection.
What is his special quality? It is said:
This Agni is like arrows that go forth with great force from the bow of Dhana;
"like" (iva) is used here in the sense of a comparison, as they are released upon the enemy.
In the same way, that fire sends forth—that is, causes to go—its rays from its own body-protecting locus, which stands in the place of a bow, as they proceed with great velocity.
The meaning is "to carry across.
Here, this [root] has the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied. Because it is a *haviṣ* (a sacrificial oblation), there is the suffix *tum*.
The vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *repha* is Vedic;
the prefix *adhi-* is redundant, merely restating the meaning of the verbal root itself.
Furthermore, when the fire has thus grown large, it should be known that [the fuel] is being approached from all sides by those moving about for the sake of performing the ritual service.

1. Like the *bhaga* (the generative organ), which like the vulva (*upastha*) is not to be served by all [but only by the husband], so too [this Agni] receives the seed and so forth; or else, like the *bhaga*, the sun (*āditya*). 2. Furthermore, he is the charioteer (*sārathi*). 3. He pleases, or honors, the couple—the wife and husband. 4. Even though he is worn out (*śīrṇa*). 5. Him, this very Agni. 6. He impels (*mubhati*). 7. Belonging to Agni (*āgneya*).

May they approach you for that purpose; he has sustained (*adhita*) ever-new (*navā navāni*), fresh (*nūtanāni*) insights (*vayunāni*) concerning their performance—this is the meaning of "making known" (*jñāpanīya*).
Or alternatively:

approaching (*abhigacchat*) you directly, he sustains the ever-new insights, namely the hymns and other rites characterized by superior wisdom (*prajñā-viśiṣṭāni stotrādīni*), which are being performed through chanting and so forth.
In the Vedic *luṅ* [aorist] of the root *dhā*, there is shortening according to the rule "sthādhvoricca"; there is *kittva* for the following *sic*;
and the elision of *s* occurs according to the rule "hasvādaṅgāt."
For you, O Agni, rule over the celestial realm; you rule over the earthly realm by your own power like a guardian of cattle.
These two great, dappled ones, golden-hued and bleating, have approached the sacrificial grass.

For you, O Agni, rule over the celestial; you, by your own power, are the guardian of the terrestrial, like a herdsman. These two great, golden, dappled ewes of yours have taken their place upon the sacrificial grass. 6.

You rule over the divine—that which exists in heaven, such as the gods—either in the form of lightning or through rain and so forth; this is a name for sovereignty. Likewise, you reign over the earthly—that which pertains to the earth, such as humans—and thus you are the Lord.
He says "no" to the idea that it is dependent on anything else;
rather, it is by itself, by its own very nature, through its own power.
In this regard, there is an illustration: like a herdsman.
Just as a cowherd is capable, by his own power alone, of performing activities such as confining or releasing cattle, so it is here;
by this illustration, absolute sovereignty is expressed.

Furthermore, because it is thus, therefore your *barhis* (sacrificial grass) and your sacrifice—those two well-known, fair-colored, bright ones, namely Heaven and Earth—*vāśāte*, that is, they pervade all.
By the rule *varṇādanudāttāt* (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.1.39), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied, and the *n* of the suffix is replaced by *n*.

Of what sort are they? They are *bṛhatī*, meaning great and very extensive; *abhidhriyā*, meaning having attained sovereignty or worthy of being served on all sides; *hiraṇyayī*, meaning beneficial and delightful; and *karī*, meaning extremely skillful in the two treatises (*śāstra*).
From the root *vac*, [the form] is derived by adding the suffixes *ṅīp* and *repha* (ṛ) according to the rule “*vano ra ca*” (*Pāṇini* 4.1.7).
The substitution of *k* for *c* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively, from the root *vaki* meaning “crookedness,” the absence of the augment *num* is Vedic.
Such are Heaven and Earth; they have spread out the sacrificial grass.
O Agni, enjoy this speech and welcome it, O delightful one, self-sustained, born of Truth, of noble power;
for you are visible from every side, like a pleasant ocean, like a dwelling-place full of nourishment.

O Agni, take pleasure in it; accept this word with delight, O joyous one, self-sustained, born of the *ṛta*, O you of noble wisdom! For you are visible from every side, radiant as the sun, like a dwelling-place filled with nourishment. ||7||
O Vāg, graciously accept and enjoy the oblation;
be pleased by the hymn of praise.
Furthermore, yearn once more for that speech—such pleasing speech—in the form of a hymn.

O you who are gentle, O you whose nature is to gladden, O you worthy of praise; or, O you who possess *svadhā*—that is, food characterized by oblations; O you who are born of the *ṛta*, arisen for the sake of sacrifice; O you of good deeds (*sukrata*), or rather, of excellent wisdom!
You, being such as this, are *pratyaṅ*—facing toward, desired by, and favorable to—the entire world of moving and unmoving beings, meaning you are not turned away from them.
Likewise, you are *darśataḥ*—beautiful to behold by all.
Furthermore, you possess the two-fold vision (*saṃdṛśau*) of right insight (*samyagdarśana*); you are one who delights (*ramaṇaśīla*), or rather, the one who causes all beings to rejoice.
(Note: 1. *kṣa-kṣa1-la-ṭa-na* read as *navā navāni*;
2. *kṣa-6-kṣa1-a-ṭa* read as *āśāte*).

3. *Kṣacha-kṣa-a-ṭa*: [It is] dear to you; or rather, when you are gathered together, every person becomes a *kṣaya*, one who has a dwelling place. Therein is an illustration: *pitumān-iva*. Just as one who possesses abundant food and is a master must be inhabited by all and approached by all, so it is here. || 13 ||
"Ask him"—this is the fifth hymn, consisting of five verses.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "‘Ask him’; [it consists of] five [verses]; the metre is Triṣṭubh.
Dīrghatamas is the seer (ṛṣi).
Since it was stated previously that "that belongs to Agni," this too belongs to Agni.
The *abhaya* [verse] is a *triṣṭubh*;
the remaining verses, according to the rule of the *Śiṣṭa-vaśiṣṭa*, are *jagatīs*.
Its application has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Aśvina-śastra.
Ask him; he moves as one who goes; he knows, and as the wise one he proceeds, and thus he is impelled.
In him are the instructions, in him are the desires; he is the lord of strength, of power, and of the mighty.
Ask him! He has gone; he knows; he, the wise one, moves; he indeed moves. In him are the commands; in him are the sacrifices. He is the lord of strength, of powerful vigor. 1.
O sacrificers, ask that Agni whatever is to be asked regarding the heavenly world and other such matters. He speaks of the excellence of his being the very one to be questioned:
He has gone; he goes everywhere.
For this very reason, he knows; he knows what is to be asked.
He says that it is not by means of anything common to others.
He alone is *cikitvān*, meaning he is possessed of consciousness;
that is to say, he is the knower of distinctions.
He alone is *īyate*, meaning he goes toward the light of what is to be known.
Furthermore, the very course [of Agni] is specified:
*saḥ*—that very Agni—*nu* indeed *īyate*, meaning he goes swiftly;
the sense is that he goes very quickly to know whatever object is to be known by the sacrificer.
Or rather:
it is resorted to (*īyate*) for the sake of knowledge;
likewise, it is followed swiftly (*śīghram anusevyate*).
The meaning is: since he is endowed with the proper form, therefore ask him alone.
Regarding that, he says that there are "desires" (kāmāḥ) which are required;
in that fire, there are "praśipah," that is, commands or powers of restraint.
The meaning is that he is capable of accomplishing even that which is impossible to accomplish, despite its being restricted.
Furthermore, in that very fire there are *iṣṭayaḥ*—desirable enjoyments or sacrifices that bring about all fruits.
Moreover, that Agni is the lord, protector, and giver of *vāja* (food) and *śavas* (strength).
Furthermore, he is the lord and master even of the powerful, such as kings and others.
Since he possesses such great majesty, one should therefore accomplish one's human purpose after having first consulted him alone.
They question him, yet he does not question them; the wise one, being unafraid, acts according to his own mind.
He does not disregard the first word nor the subsequent one; impelled by his purpose, he follows through with his resolve.

They ask him; he does not inquire of others. Like a wise man with his own mind, when he has become fearless, he does not forget the first word nor the later one. He follows through with his resolve, being undeluded.
In the preceding mantra, it was said, "Ask Agni";
here, however, he says that he (Agni) is to be questioned by means of the *ṛju-naya* (straightforward method).
They ask about *tam-it*, that very same Agni, and he, even at the time of questioning, does not question anyone else.

Everyone indeed asks him; they do not ask anything contrary [to the truth]. (1. To be praised; 2. Furthermore, he; 3. He goes very swiftly to understand the matter desired to be known by the sacrificer—this is the meaning; 4. He is sought after by those desiring knowledge; 5. Indeed, swiftly; 6. Desired by us.
Even when questioned, this wise and intelligent one [knows] as if with his own mind.
The word *iha* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed).
Whatever task one undertakes with one's own intellect, thinking "I shall speak" and so forth, that alone is what is reflected upon (*pratibhūte*), and not that which conforms to another's power.
Thus, it is said that [the Lord] is independent (*svatantra*).

Alternatively, the meaning is this: the intelligent questioner, having reflected with his own mind upon what is to be expressed, asks only that which he has accepted as a statement to be spoken; he does not speak much.
Thus, he states his inability to withstand the words of others.
This Agni does not tolerate—that is, does not endure—the first speech, the word that precedes the *svadhā* offering;
nor does he tolerate the subsequent speech, the reply that follows immediately after his own utterance.
Since he is of such a nature, he is "unstruck" (*aprahita*), meaning unassailed.

Or rather, the entire world, having been instructed by him, follows along with this fire of great power through its *ṛtu*—that is, through its protective and other functions—and thus associates with it; the meaning is that it lives.
Him the ladles behold, him the swift mares; may he alone hear all my words.
