He who has many commands, the impetuous one, the accomplisher of the sacrifice—whenever the *adhvaryu*, having approached (*upasthāya*), performs his service (*carati*), that is, having approached again and again, he carries out the ritual activity conducive to the sacrifice.
When did this happen? He says:
when they came together—that is, when [the fire] appeared through churning.
In the expression “samo gamyṛccha,” the *ātmanepada* ending is used for the root √ar.

Having been born—that is, having arisen—at that very moment, he wandered about as one who was "hidden in the forest" (araṇyagūḍha), being endowed with "yoke-worthy" (yujyebhiḥ) fruits or splendors capable of being joined or connected.
Or alternatively:
as soon as he was born, he moved everywhere with those yoke-worthy [powers].
‘Isara-cchadma-gatau’:
this is the form [of the root] in the periphrastic perfect (liṭ) with the suffix -gā (gal).

Thus grown great, he touches—that is, he performs a stroking—for the sake of the joy and satisfaction of the sacrificer who has become weary or exhausted, whenever there is some other delightful rite serving as the occasion;
that is to say, by the bestowing of the fruit [of the sacrifice].
It is just as in the world when a teacher or similar elder touches a disciple or similar person who is fatigued.
If it is asked "When?", it is said: when the longing streams of clarified butter—or the hymns of praise—reach and pervade this Agni, then he touches [them].
Like a wild beast dwelling in the waters, he has been placed upon the surface of the earth;
the wise one, knowing the truth and perceiving the eternal law, has proclaimed the insights to mortals.
He, the aquatic beast, the seeker, has been placed upon the surface of the highest skin; Agni, the wise one who knows the sacred order and is true, has proclaimed the ways for mortals. || 5 ||
He—indeed that very Agni—is placed down, established for future enjoyment, upon the "highest" skin—that is, upon the sacrificial altar covered with plants and other materials.
Of what nature is he?
He is the "beast"—one who cleanses or one who is by nature a seeker.
‘*Mṛga* [is derived] from the root *mṛj*, meaning "to go,"' says Yāska (Nirukta 1.20).
*Apyaḥ* means "belonging to water" (*āpyaḥ*), that which is to be gone toward; or it means one who is effective therein, with *apaḥ* as the object.
*Vanarguḥ*: one who goes to the forest.
This form [is derived] either from the root *ṛcchati* meaning "to go," or else from the root *gam* itself.
The augment *ruṭ* is applied to the word *upapada* according to Vedic usage.

Agni, being thus, has specifically proclaimed—indeed, teaches—the *vayunāni*, that is, the insights or knowledges regarding what is to be performed, to the mortals, those subject to death, such as the sacrificers and others.
For *vayuna* is a name for wisdom, as it is listed among the names for wisdom in the Nirukta (3.9.10) with the phrase "wisdom is form.
Thus, he demonstrates that such power exists [in Agni].
This Agni is wise, all-knowing, and cognizant of *ṛta*— that is, the knower of sacrifice or of water— and he is true;
for *sat* refers to the action being performed,
and he is excellent therein.
Or, it means "existing among the good" (*sat-su bhavaḥ*).
Or, it means "one who deserves that fruit" (*san phalam tad arhati*); the sense is "one who bestows the perfect fruit."
Since this [person] is endowed with the capacity thus described, therefore the instruction in wisdom is appropriate;
the word "hi" (for/since) indicates well-known fact.

The hymn beginning with “trimūrdhānam” consists of five verses; it is attributed to Dīrghatamas and is dedicated to Agni. Previously, [the author] stated, “But that is dedicated to Agni. This is confirmed by the Anukramaṇikā, which says, “trimūrdhānam. The application of these first three hymns in both Vedic meters occurs during the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.
In the section beginning with "Now, of this," it is stated in the sūtra: "'Trimūrdhānam'—three [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).

1. When [the letters] kṣa, ṅa, na, ṭa, ya, and da [occur]. 2. [The letters] kṣa, ja, ṭa, and śa [indicate] peace (śāntam). 3. [The letters] kṣa, jha, na, ṭa, and na [indicate that something] is established as being like a treasure (nidhivat). 4. [The letters] kṣa, jha, na, ṭa, and va [indicate] "or" (vā). 5. [The letters] kṣa, jha, ma, la, jha, na, ṭa, va, and ya [indicate] "by means of wisdoms" (vayunā vayunāni). 6. [The letter] jha [indicates] "one who causes to perceive" (cetayitā). 7. [The letters] kṣa, jha, la, na, ṭa, and ta [indicate] "therein" (tatra). Ṛgveda 1.114.1–7.

I praise Agni, the three-headed, the seven-rayed, the perfect one, seated in the lap of his parents; him who has filled all the luminous realms of heaven, as he dwells within this moving and steadfast world. tri-mūrdhānam sapta-raśmim gṛṇīṣe 'nūnam agnim pitroḥ upasthe | niṣattam asya carato dhruvasya viśvā divo rocanā āpaprivāṃsam || 1 || I praise the three-headed, the seven-rayed, the flawless Agni, seated in the lap of his two parents; him who is established within this moving and firm [world], and who has filled all the radiant regions of heaven.
By this verse, Agni is praised in the form of the sacrifice. He is "three-headed," meaning endowed with three heads in the form of the three *savanas* (pressings).
According to the rule *dvitribhyāṃ pādamūrdhasu bahuvrīhau*, there is an udātta accent on the final syllable of the latter member of the compound.

Furthermore, having kindled the seven-rayed Agni— who is endowed with the seven regulating meters (*chandas*), who is unimpaired and complete in form, and who possesses qualities such as beauty (*aṅga*)— he stands firm, providing protection and preservation, in the lap of his parents, that is, in the lap of Heaven and Earth, according to the reading in the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā*.
Thus, being one who extends aid and protection, he remains established.
Or rather:
having supreme qualities, moving from here, that is, possessing the movement toward our divine people, he stands—that is, he remains.
Immediately thereafter, upon the elevated region of the wide earth, characterized by an altar, he places his feet—that is, he sets down his steps.
Furthermore, the *aruṣāsaḥ*, the ruddy ones, the illuminators (*ārocanāḥ*), lick (*rihanti*) his *ūdhaḥ*—the atmosphere, which stands in the place of a udder.
Or alternatively:

the sacrificers, being ruddy and illuminating through spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), lick his *ūdhaḥ*—the sacrifice, which stands in the place of an udder—and thereby lick the desired realms such as heaven and so forth.
Moving together toward their common course, the two all-nourishing ones wander forth, well-established;
measuring out their paths that cannot be bypassed, they bestow all perceptions upon the great one.

The same; moving together toward the place of birth; all-pervading, the two milch-cows; they move apart, well-established; measuring out paths that are not to be bypassed; bestowing all great insights upon the vast one. 3.

Moving toward the single, common calf—the fire which stands in the place of a calf and is a cause for joy like a son—the two milch-cows, characterized as the wife and the sacrificer, move about in every direction, gladdening [the fire] by performing their respective duties; that is to say, they nourish it through the offering of fuel and the sweeping [of the hearth], which are analogous to suckling at the breast and so forth.
What kind are they? *Sumeke*: those of beautiful deeds or beautiful intellects; that is to say, those skilled in service. Furthermore, *anapavṛjyān*: those free from being subject to abandonment.
By the rule "namsubhyām," the final syllable of the subsequent member [of the compound] is udātta.
Measuring out the paths—the regions at the edge of the fire—making them free from hair and impurities;
furthermore, increasing all perceptions directed toward growth, and holding fast to great things in abundance;
such two cows, whether in the form of the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer, or as husband and wife, move about everywhere.
The wise poets lead him to his station; guarding with various hearts the undecaying one, they gazed around, desiring to win him. The river became visible to them, and the Sun appeared before the men.
The wise poets lead the word in various ways; guarding with their hearts the ageless one, desiring to win it, they beheld the river on every side. The Sun became manifest to them, to these men. 4.

The wise ones—the learned and intelligent performers of rituals such as the *adhvaryu* and others—lead this undecaying (*ajuryam*), ageless Agni to his place (*padam*), that is, to the site characterized by the altar; they bring him from the place of churning or from the *gārhapatya* fire.
Alternatively, those whose characteristics will be described later, such as the sacrificer and others, cause him to go to his station (*padam*), the abode of all desires.
What are they like?

The *kavayaḥ* are those who see afar, the wise. 1. *Ārupāsaḥ*: shining; 2. *Ārocanāḥ*. 3. *Abhi saṃcarantī*: moving toward [the sacrifice], moving face-to-face; they perfectly satisfy [the gods]. 4. By means of making offerings (*abhi-huta-karaṇena*). 5. They please [the gods]. 6. Of the unexhausted ones (*akṣīṇām*). 7. From the place of churning (*manthana-deśāt*), or alternatively, those who recite the Vedas (*anucānāḥ*).

According to the Śruti text, "Or those who are learned in the Vedas (*anucānāḥ*) are the sages (*kavayaḥ*") (AiB 2.2). Furthermore, they are "protecting" or upholding [the sacrifice] with various minds—that is, with many kinds of intellects.

Moreover, being of such a nature, they "desire to win over" (*sipāsantaḥ*), that is, they desire to partake of Agni, who is like a "flowing river" (*sindhum*)—flowing toward the fruits [of action] through the gateway of the sacrifice.

In the word *saniteḥ*, the absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the optionality provided by the rule *sanīvantardha*. The substitution of *ā* for the vowel [of the root] occurs by the rule *janasanakhanām*.
The term *paryepaśyanta* means "they look around on all sides."
The meaning is "they desire to hear.

Furthermore, this Agni, the impeller (*prasavitā*) of all, being praised by the *phaṇyas* in this manner, "became manifest" (*āvir abhavat*)—that is, he became perceptible through his favor—to the "men" (*nṝn*), that is, to the leaders;
there is a change of number (*vacanavyatyaya*) in the word *nṝn*.
Or it may be construed thus: "In order to favor wise men.
He is worthy of being seen; he is preeminent in all directions, noble, and worthy of praise for the sake of great life.
Since he has become manifest in many places as a divine being, Maghavan is visible to all from his wombs.

Deserving to be seen, he has gone around the boundaries; he is the victorious one, worthy of praise, great, and approaching for the sake of life. In many places, since I became the progenitor for these embryos, Maghavan has become visible to all. ||5||
This Agni is "desirable to behold" (didṛkṣeṇya) as he moves through the ten directions, having traversed one after another among the "limits" (kāṣṭhāsu).
He becomes endowed with vision, joined with grace.
Or else:
He is the object of the desire to see for these [beings], that is, one who has become the focus of the wish to behold them.

From the root *dṛś* with the suffix *san*, the suffix *kenya* is applied according to the rule *kṛtyārthe tavaikenkenya*. For this very reason, he is called *jenya*: "one who is everywhere disposed toward manifestation, or one who is victorious."
Furthermore, at the time of the *pradhāna* offering, another [deity] becomes worthy of praise (*īḍanya*). Why is this so?
For the sake of the life of the great deity and the small one—the sacrificer—[it is for their] living.
"By carrying the oblation and by the bestowing of wealth"—this is the distinction.
He states the reasoning for this: "Since," that is, because, "in many places" (purutrā), meaning in many regions.

The suffix *tra* is applied by the rule "devamanuṣya°" and so forth. "Maghavā" means one who possesses oblations characterized as sacrificial offerings. "Viśvadarśataḥ" means this Agni is one who is to be seen by all objects of perception. "Ebhyaḥ garbhebhyaḥ"—the dative case is used here in the sense of "for the sake of" (*padyārthe*).
Of these officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who are like embryos requiring protection within, he became the *sū-*—the progenitor, the one who brings them forth.
Therefore, the connection with what precedes is: "The sages (*kavayaḥ*), protecting [him] with various intentions (*hadā*), lead him to his station.
The fifth hymn, beginning with "kathā te," is the seventh [hymn] dedicated to Agni by Dairghatamas; it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states, "kathā.
Its application (*viniyoga*) is prescribed for the *Prātaranuvāka* and the *Āśvina-śastra*, as indicated by the rule: "'trimūrdhānam'—three [verses]."
In this manner, they have offered pure oblations before you, seeking long life; with swift hands, they have presented gifts of strength.
Sustaining both their children and their progeny, the gods have brought the song of Truth into harmony.

The narrative: They, purifying themselves before the living man, have offered gifts with swift steeds, hastening with their offerings; when they establish both seed and progeny, the gods rejoice in the harmony of the Eternal Law (*ṛta*).
O Agni, your rays— shining, manifesting their brilliance everywhere, and *āśupāṇāḥ*, meaning either those who quickly (*āśu*) bestow (*pāṇāḥ*) or those who quickly consume (*āśan*);
that is to say, they are the swift consumers even of wind and other elements—
or alternatively:

1. *kṣa-ba-ṭa*: this is the essential point (*marmam*). 2. *ka-vibhāktavyatyayaḥ*: there is an inversion of case endings. 3. *kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa*: one whose nature is vision (*darśanaśīlaḥ*). 4. *kṣa-jha-jha-na-ṭa*: by means of the granting of movement (*carapradānena*). 5. *kṣa-na-ṭa*: this one is everywhere (*purutrā*);
[the word] *śoṣayitāraḥ* means "those who cause to wither."
Or rather:
"pervading everything.
[This is derived from] the root *bhū* with the suffix *kānac* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The suffix *u* occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), as do the suffixes *u* and *sic*; thus there is a double formation.
From the root *ṇup*, preceded by the prefix *āṅ* and having the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied, the suffix *śānac* is applied, with the Vedic elision (*luk*) of the *śap*.
From the root *san*, with the word *āśu* as its attendant (*upapada*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Such are the rays: "With strengths (vājebhiḥ), with Agni, together with life-force (āyoḥ)—that is, vitality (āyuṣyam).
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the object.
"In what way? By what means (kathā)?"—they bestow (dadāśuḥ), that is, they give.
The root *dāś* means "to give. This is the Vedic subjunctive (*liṭ*).
The meaning is: "favor this means."
If it is asked where the granting of boons by the rays is seen, it is said:
"Since both the aforementioned [periods of] ignorance and life, as well as the son (*toke*) and the grandson (*tanaye*)—who are the expanders of the family without interruption.
Or else:

"Toke" means sons; "tanaye" means grandsons and so forth. "Dhānāḥ" means supporting. "Devāḥ" refers to the performers of the ritual, the sacrificers. "Ṛtasya" means of the sacrifice. "Sāman" refers to the *sāmans* such as the *Rathantara* and others associated with the sacrifice. "Ramayanta" means they delight, they enjoy, or they cause [others] to delight, or indeed they utter sounds.
Since those accompanied by their sons, grandsons, and others, having sacrificed with Soma, delight in the *sāman*, it is understood from this visible purpose that the rays bestow [these things].
Such are your rays; [the meaning is: "favor me as well.
O youngest one, O self-sustaining lord, grant me understanding of this splendor—of that which is most abundant and fully presented.
One person fears you, while another sings your praise; O Agni, I laud your body, you who delight in the assembly.

O Agni, youngest one, rich in self-sustaining power, you alone perceive this my splendor that has been offered, most abundant; you alone praise it, for you are the one who delights in it. I extol your greatness, O Agni. 2.

O youngest one, O most youthful one, O you who possess self-power (*asvadhāvan*): take note of this speech—characterized by praise—which is now being performed; that is, of this word in the form of a hymn, which is offered as an oblation (*havis*), which is my food, which is most worthy of honor (*amaṃhiṣṭhasya*)—meaning most highly venerable—and which has been excellently prepared (*prabhṛtasya*).
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the object.
Understand this speech characterized by longing; that is to say, "be aware of it" or "be praised."
"O Agni, you are in this world.
Regarding this, Yāska, having stated that "atvaḥ" and "nemaḥ" have the same meaning (*Nirukta* 3.20), cited this very passage as an example:
"One person protects."
This is a killer; it harms. The meaning is that one does not honor [it] through sacrifice and so forth.
"You alone follow and speak favorably.
Between those two, O Agni, I, who am inclined to praise (*vandāru*), praise and extol your body, your form.
Those two guardians of yours, O Agni, protected Māmateya from the darkness at the boundary and from misfortune.
Protect those doers of good deeds, O you who know all things; for the enemies, though wishing to deceive, have not deceived me.

Those guardians of yours, O Agni, who dwell around Māmateya, protected the blind man from distress; protect them, O omniscient one, for the enemies, though wishing to deceive, have not deceived me. 3.
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend:
there were two sages, Ucathya and Bṛhaspati. Among them, the wife of Ucathya was named Mamatā.
She was pregnant;
Bṛhaspati took her and enjoyed her.
When the moment for the emission of semen arrived, the seed within the womb spoke: "O sage, do not discharge the semen! I am already dwelling here; do not cause a mixture of seeds."

Thus addressed, Bṛhaspati said: "By force, [he] obstructed—1. without interruption; 2. of the family of *kṣa-ha-ca-jha-jña-ja-ṭa-pha*; 3. also of me, *kṣa-ḍa-jha-jña-ja-ṭa-ma*; 4. as for Yāska, *kṣa*; 5. he utters and praises, *ḍa-kṣa-jña-a-ṭa*; 6. she was his wife, *jha-jña-na-ḍa*; she was pregnant, *tām*; 7. the emission of semen, *jha-jña*; being one who has spilled his seed (*retaskaḥ*), he cursed."

"Since you have caused the obstruction of the seed within the womb, therefore you shall enter long darkness; become blind from birth. Thus cursed, Dīrghatamas was born of Mamatā. And having been born, he praised Agni out of distress caused by that darkness.
And being pleased by that praise, he removed his blindness;
this very thing is stated here:

"O Agni, those well-known *pāyavaḥ*—protectors, namely your rays—who, seeing Māmateya, the son of Mamatā, Dīrghatamas, though blind, perceived him as one distinct from others, thinking 'this one must be protected by us,' rescued him from the evil pit of misfortune. O you who are doers of good (*sukṛtaḥ*) and possessors of all knowledge (*viśvavedāḥ*), protect them, protect them!"
The sense is: "for our protection.
The meaning is that He will protect us as well by means of them.
Thus, even though enemies such as desire (kāma) and the like—desiring to harm us, that is, wishing to deceive us—did not succeed in deceiving us who were protected in this manner.
The particle *aha* is used here for the purpose of restriction;
indeed, they are not able to deceive.

Regarding the root *dambh* in the sense of "deceiving," it is stated [in the Vārttika]: "It should be said that [the rule] applies to *śrantha*, *grantha*, *dambha*, and *svañj*" (Kāśikā 1.2.6.1). Thus, due to the substitution of *kvip* for *liṭ*, there is the elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24).

Since that [elision] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the rules for *etva* (the change of the penultimate vowel to *e*) and the elision of the reduplication do not apply; therefore, by the rule "it should be said that [the form] *dambhra* occurs" (Pāṇini 6.4.120.4), the substitution of *ra* for *bha* is prescribed.
Or rather,
Dīrghatamas, the seer of the hymn, speaks of himself in the third person as if he were another.
O Agni, whoever is hostile toward us, malicious, and seeks to harm us with duplicity—may that teacher become subject to two-fold mantras; may he destroy his own body with his evil words.

O Agni, whoever is hostile to us, who seeks to do evil, who is malevolent, and who confounds us with duplicity—may that heavy spell recoil upon him; may he destroy his own body with his own ill-spoken words. 4.

O Agni, [protect] us, who are guarded by you; "he who" is one possessing evil intent—that is, one desiring sins such as killing—and "the stingy one" (ararivān) means one who does not give, that is to say, an obstacle to us.
The suffix *kasu* is substituted for the Vedic *liṭ* (perfect) following the root *rāj*.
Or even enemies themselves may give it.
Regarding the statement "In Vedic usage, they desire the suffix *vanip*," the suffix *vanip* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).
The enemy who practices enmity does so by means of two kinds of mental incantations, distinguished as mental and verbal.
"I will not give" is the mental incantation;
the prevention of giving through the attribution of blame and the like is the verbal incantation.
Alternatively:
by means of the two kinds of mantra characterized by illusion (*māyā*) and contradictory form;

that is, [the mantra] which does not proclaim what one practices contrarily, and which does not perform what it speaks as pleasant, but rather performs something else entirely—such is the twofold nature of mantra.
The distinction is that previously [the divisions were] by way of mental and verbal [mantras], whereas now they are by way of verbal and physical [mantras].
Whatever enemy honors, reviles, or brings under control us by means of such a mantra—
may that portion of the mantra which consists of pride (māna) become, moreover, heavy for him.
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
Furthermore, it is the speaker alone who incurs the sin.
Thus, by means of ill-spoken words—harsh speech consisting of verbal insults—he should "rub" (mṛkṣīṣṭa), that is, he should wipe away or gradually destroy his own body.
Or alternatively:
May this twofold mantra be a mountain for this practitioner himself;
may other harsh words directed at me, the speaker of the syllable *ka*, exist,
and by those ill-spoken words, may that enemy destroy his own body.
The meaning is: "May it burn, having enveloped its very own self."

1. He cursed *ka-jha-taṃ*. 2. [He cursed] *ka-jha-jha-jha-ta-na-ṭa-tān* as rays (*raśmān*). 3. *Ka-jha-na-ṭa-tvaṃ*, protect, protect! 4. By *jha-tena*. 5. *Ka-jha-ṭa-°dambhasva āmiti*. 6. *Ka-jha-ṭa-°pāpecchayā*. 7. *Ka-viṣayīkaroti*. 8. May *ka-jha-jha-jha-gāritā* be the food (*bhakṣaḥ*). 9. *Ka-jha-prayogtre*. Or rather, he who, being wise, through duality causes the mind (*matīm*) to faint; O praised one, protect us from distress; do not deliver us to misfortune.

Or rather, O Victorious One, you who are wise, who by means of two [aspects] cause thought to coalesce with thought—protect him who praises you, O Agni; being praised yourself, do not deliver us to one who is difficult to cross. 5.

In the previous mantra, it was stated by means of the two types of *kuṭila* mantras that "let the performer obtain that mantra, but not us. Here, however, one requests protection from that mantra with the words "save [us] from that mantra" (*tanmantraṇāt pāhi*).
Furthermore, O *sahasya*!...

*Saha* is a name for power. In this regard, "this mortal"—a human being subject to death—"who is well-knowing," meaning one who thoroughly understands the *māyā-mantra*, "by means of the dual," that is, by the two-fold mantra according to the manner previously described, "enchants" (*mūrcayati*)—that is, renders submissive or destroys—the "intended" person. Therefore, O Agni, "being praised" (*stavamāna*), protect (*pāhi*) me, who am "praising" (*stuvantaṃ*), from such a destroyer or from the presence of that doer of harm.
Furthermore, "do not" (mā) "establish" (dhāyīḥ) "us" (naḥ) "for misfortune" (duritāya)—that is, for the suffering caused by the evil counsel [of others]—meaning:
do not subject us to misfortune.
The root *dhṛ* means "to hold.
By means of a grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*), the augment *iṭ* is applied;
there is then the *vṛddhi* strengthening in the *sic* suffix.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "na māṅ-yoge" (Pāṇini 6.4.74).
The eighth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “mathīdyat,” is addressed to the deity Agni; it belongs to the third book.
According to the *Anukramaṇikā*, the entry is “mathīdyat.
Its application was previously stated as being for the third position among the three hymns.
When Mātariśvan entered [the womb], he churned forth the Hotṛ, who belongs to all waters and all gods—
him whom they have established among the human clans, the one who fulfills his own debt, wonderful, radiant for the sake of beauty.

Mātariśvan churned him forth when he had entered [the wood]—him, the Hotṛ-priest who encompasses all waters, who belongs to all the gods, whom they have established among the human clans, shining like the sun, wondrous for his beauty, and radiant.
The *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods, who possesses all forms (*viśvāpsu*).
*Asvi* is a name for form;
it means possessing various forms through the distinctions of terrestrial, lightning, and digestive fire, or through the distinctions of the *āhavanīya* and other sacrificial fires.
Alternatively, Agni possesses a universal form (*viśvarūpatva*) because his flames assume various forms such as Kālī, Karālī, and so forth.

He is "universal" (*viśvadevyam*), meaning he is fit for the rites of all the gods. When Mātariśvan—the wind, the vital breath situated in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and the creator of rain and other elements—"entered" (*viṣṭaḥ*) into the pieces of wood and "rubbed" (*mathīt*) him, the meaning is that he caused him to grow through friction.
The root *math* means "to churn" (*viloḍana*).
By the rule "hyantakṣaṇa," the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies.
Furthermore, that very [Agni] is further specified:

"That Agni whom men—among the *viś* (clans), that is, among the subjects consisting of priests and kings who perform ritual acts with thoughtfulness—formerly established for the sake of *vapus*, i.e., for the accomplishment of the sacrificial body, and whom the sacrificers maintain.

The word *manuṣya* is explained in various ways in the *Nirukta*: "Why 'men' (*manuṣyāḥ*)? Because they sew (*sīvyanti*) human deeds; or because they were created by one who was thinking (*manasyamānena*); or because they are the offspring of Manu; or because they belong to Manu" (*Nirukta* 3.7).
Alternatively:

Formerly, the gods deposited [the fire] among men—those born as the offspring of Manu—among the *viś* (clans), among living beings, for the sake of their own form (*vapuṣe*), that is, for the manifestation of the nature of sacrifice and so forth, or for the maintenance of the body; [they did so] in the form of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Golden, golden, or easily attained through his own radiance; like the sun, wonderful, worthy of praise, and luminous.

[1. Jha₁: the composer of the mantra; 2. Kṣa₁, A, Ṭa, Vā: or else; 3. Kṣa, A, Ṭa: among the three hymns, this one; 4. Kha: the root *man* implies becoming mindful again, or the offspring of Manu; 5. Jha, Jha₁: for the sake of form; 6. Kṣa: golden, or easily accessible.]

Just as they maintain various infinite lights for the sake of achieving illumination and so forth, Yāska likewise explained the word *svaḥ*: "The sun is called *svara* because it is well-moving (*su-araṇaḥ*), well-gliding (*su-īraṇaḥ*), remembered as the essence of waters, remembered as the splendor of lights, or [it is] 'splendor' (*bhāsa*) by virtue of its light" (Nirukta 2.14).
The connection with what precedes is: "They placed that which is such; may he churn it out."
Give us, O Unassailable One; do not disregard our prayers, for you take pleasure in my protection.
May they enjoy all the deeds of this singer who brings forth praise.
They have not deceived the prayer of this giver; Agni is my protection. He has taken pleasure in that and has accepted all the works of this singer who brings forth praise.
The enemies, seeking to deceive me, have not succeeded in deceiving—that is, they are not able to harm—me as I offer to Agni a hymn worthy of thought (*manman*) or an oblation such as the *havis*.
In the case of the root *dambh*, there is the elision (*ślu*) of the suffix by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi";
furthermore, there is an irregular substitution (*vyatyaya*) of the final letter.
It is now stated: "What is my excellence?"
This Agni intensely desires (*cākan*)—that is, he greatly longs for—the *varūtha*, meaning the desirable hymn of praise and so forth, from such a giver as I am.
The root *kan* signifies longing;
here, the absence of the *yaṅ* suffix in this *yaṅ-luk* form is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Or rather, [the form] is Vedic due to the frequent occurrence of such forms; because of its inclusion in the *tujādi* group, there is lengthening of the reduplication.
Since this is so, the meaning is "they did not place.
He says that it is not only Agni who desires this, but all the gods desire it as well.
May all the gods take pleasure in all the offerings—consisting of the presentation of oblations and so forth—of this sacrificer, me, the *kārū*, who brings and offers praise.
Therefore, let them not deceive us. Indeed, those worthy of sacrifice have established him as the one most highly praised, even though he has gone to his eternal seat.
They lead him forward, exerting themselves, like well-trained horses drawing a chariot with speed.

Him indeed, who has gone to his seat, the worshipful ones have established with praises from of old; they lead him forward, exulting in the sacrifice, like well-trained horses hastening in their course.

The *yajñiyāsaḥ*—those worthy of sacrifice, either the sacrificers or the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—seize that Agni, who has been produced by friction, as soon as he has gone to his eternal seat, namely the permanent place of the Gārhapatya fire; for this purpose they take him up. In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense of the root *grah*, there is the substitution of *rebh* according to the rule *irayore*;
and *bha*-status is applied by the rule *hagrahobheḥ*.
According to the sūtra, "The *gārhapatya* fire is maintained perpetually, for its splendor has departed [from elsewhere]," the *gārhapatya* is eternal.
Because it serves as the basis for it, the sacrificial seat (*sadanam*) is also said to be eternal.
Having taken hold of it with praises—that is, with eulogies and hymns—they maintain it for the sake of the *āhavanīya* fire.

When the sacrifice, which is the means for attaining the desired goal, has become the occasion, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), being desirous of both [worlds], lead them forth; they lead them well forward.
Therein is an illustration:
like those moving with speed (*rahasā*).
The root *rah* means "to go.
This is the *kānac* suffix for the Vedic *liṭ* (perfect tense). [Variant readings:
1. kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-ma-ṭa- from the root alone.]
2. According to Kṣa, Ga, Ṭa, and Chāndasa, there is *ślu* (elision) of the suffix *śap*.

3. According to Kṣa, Ga, and Ṭa, "upastutiṃ tataṃ" means approaching that respective deity while the praise is being performed; according to Jha, "upastutiṃ taṃ devamupetya stotram" means the hymn of praise upon approaching that deity.
4. According to Kṣa, Ṅa, Jha, 1, Ma, and Ṭa, it refers to all ritual actions (*sarvāṇi karmāṇi*).
5. They enjoy or resort to [the letters] kṣa, ṅa, ja, jha, jha, la, a, ṭa, and ju.
6. They have recourse to jha and gāva. 7. Because kṣa, jha, la, ma, and ṭa are their abodes.
8. Having taken up the abode even in the sacrifice (*iṣṭau*), [it is] for the sake of seeking and accomplishment. 9. Those grasping *kṣa*, *a*, and *ṭa*:
there is an absence of the *num* augment according to the rule "the injunction of the arrival of *aniśya*."

*Vrathya*: those possessed of chariots (*rathin*) appointed there; the suffix *ī* in the word *rathī* is added in the sense of possession according to the rule *chandasi vanipau*. *Vrathāsaḥ* means "like horses."
Just as drivers lead the master of the chariot to his destination, so does the wondrous one destroy many things with his jaws. Radiant, he consumes the forest;
the wind blows after his flame, and his arrow follows the path of the falling trees.
The wondrous one destroys many things with his jaws; then, radiant, he shines within the wood. Then the wind blows along his flame, like the arrow of an archer shot from the bowstring.
Here, he is praised by means of the metaphor of a forest fire:
this Agni, the *vḍasman* (the consumer), utterly destroys (*ni vr̥ṇāti*) many (*purūṇi*) things, such as trees and the like.
[The root] *rī* [is used here] in the sense of "motion" and "impelling."
The vowel is shortened because the root belongs to the *vpvādi* class. By what means? That is stated: by means of *vjambhaiḥ*, that is, by the flames situated in place of teeth.

Then, immediately after the burning, in the forest consisting of a collection of trees and other things, he, being possessed of various kinds of light (*vibhāva*), shines—that is, he becomes radiant. Then, immediately thereafter, his *śocis* (flame) and the wind, which is favorable to the flame and has become a friend to the fire, blew through the forest.
The word *anu* is used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
Every day it blows favorably;
taking up the flames, it goes.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
He did not see Vashyā, who was going toward Vasana from the presence of Kṣemu;
for "śara" means an iron arrowhead, an instrument of violence,
or else—

*Śara* is a specific type of wood belonging to a particular species of reed; it refers to something made from that, like an arrow. Yāska states: "The *śaryās* are arrows made of *śara* grass" (Nirukta 5.4).
Or rather:
*śaryā* is simply *śara*.
Or else:
*Śara* means injury; that which causes this is *śaryā*, meaning an arrow. Just as the wind, or a velocity not produced by water, impels it favorably, so too [is it here].
Neither enemies nor those seeking to harm can injure him while he is in the womb;
though blind and sightless, they cannot deceive him with their violence, for his own eternal guardians have protected him.

No, not so! Though they are enemies seeking to cause harm, they do not injure him while he dwells within the womb. Though blind and sightless, they cannot damage him with their assaults; his own eternal guardians have protected him.

The men, the *vipas*, do not cause fear or pain to Agni who dwells within the womb—the protecting fire-drill (*araṇi*). Likewise, other harmful ones who seek to injure (*riṣaṇyavaḥ*) do not trouble him;
for the word *riṣaṇyati* is derived as a *kyac*-formation according to Pāṇini’s rule: *durasyurdaviṇasyurvṛṣaṇyati riṣaṇyati* (Pāṇ. 7.4.36).
By the rule "kyācchandasī," the suffix *u* is applied.
They do not harm.
Of what kind are they?
For they are of a nature to cause harm;
or rather,
the modes of harming performed by them do not actually harm.

Furthermore, his greatness—his splendor that shines on all sides—is not seen by the unwise, who are bound and devoid of the power of knowledge; for this very reason, they are "blind" (ava-paśyāḥ), meaning they do not see.
Or alternatively, even those who are wise [do not see it] if they are non-contemplators; that is to say, those who do not practice meditation.

Both these kinds [of causes] do not deceive, nor do they cause harm; for they do not injure. (Note 1: *tadvikāramiva* as in Kṣa; Note 2: *tāṃ karoti* as in Jha; Note 3: *nodanajanyaḥ* as in Kṣa, Jha₁, Ja, Ṭa; Note 4: *khyātiḥ* as in I, Jha₁; Note ka:
115 The sense is that [the cause] is also a motivator even through worldly assistance.)
If it is asked, "Who knows the ultimate form of Him who abides therein? it is said:
"The eternal ones" (*nityāsaḥ*) means those whose devotion is unswerving, or those devoted to the constant rites such as the *agnihotra*.
Or, because they will themselves become eternal through their grace toward others, they are figuratively called "eternal" by relying on their future eternity.

Such patrons (*yajamānāḥ*), being *pretāraḥ*—those who satisfy him alone through sacrifice and other rites—*īm enam arakṣan*, that is, they protect him; the meaning is that they honor him in the form of sacrifice and so forth.
(17) "mahaḥ saḥ" is the ninth hymn, consisting of five verses; it belongs to Dīrghatamas, is in the Vairāja meter, and is dedicated to Agni.
This is because the characteristics described in [the Anuvāka]—“The *virāj* consists of ten syllables, or rather eleven” (Anu. 6.7–8)—are present here.
Furthermore, it has been enumerated thus: “The *mahaḥ* belongs to the *vairāja*.
The application [of the mantra] is established by its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
He, the lord of great wealth, seeks the domain of the powerful one; the joyful ones attend upon him as he hastens toward the place of riches. 1.
Great is he; he comes toward us, the Lord of wealth, the Master of the house. May the pressing-stones serve him as he hastens to the place of the mighty lord of riches. 1.
He, Agni, the lord and protector of great wealth consisting of cattle and other forms, bestowing—that is, granting—what is desired;
[the form] *dan* is derived from the root *dadāti* with the suffix *śatṛ*, where the suffix *śap* is elided by Vedic license (*chāndasa*).
Because it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix by the rule "in the Veda, both ways," the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule "there is elision of *ā* before an *iṭ* augment."
He approaches (ā īpate) directly toward our sacrificial rite;
furthermore, he is the lord (inaḥ) even of the lord (inasya), meaning he is the protector of all.
Such as he is, he takes his stand (ā āśrayati) at the place of wealth (vasunaḥ pade), that is, at the altar which serves as the locus of riches.
Due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*), there is an implied verbal action [to be supplied].
Alternatively, the connection is: "of wealth (*vasunaḥ*)—that is, even of riches suitable for being stored—and of a lord (*inaḥ*)."
Or rather:
the attainment of wealth is well known.
Furthermore, the pressing-stones—the wealthy sacrificers—serve him who approaches for the sake of the Soma-pressing, as it were, with complete devotion.
The root *vidh* is used in the sense of "arranging" (*vidhāna*).
It belongs to the *tudādigaṇa*.
In the *laṅ* tense, the augment *aṭ* is absent according to the rule "it is frequent in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
The absence of the *nighāta* accent is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively,
because the word "that" (*tat*) was heard in the preceding [verse], there is no *nighāta* here since it is connected with the word "which" (*yat*) supplied by ellipsis.
Or alternatively:
the pressing-stones (*adrayaḥ*), the stones used for the extraction of soma, having approached with their own sounds, indeed honor [him] by performing worship;
that is to say, they produce delight.
He who is the bull among men, like the two worlds (heaven and earth) in his glories, whose flow is drunk by the living—he, streaming forth, has settled in his place of origin.
He is the bull of men, as [he is] of the two worlds; he possesses glory through his powers, a stream that nourishes the living. He who, flowing forth, has shone brightly in his source. 2.
That Agni, who is like a bull—the progenitor and shedder—of both Rodasī (Heaven and Earth), as he is of men;
being thus the creator of all, he exists, endowed with *śravas*, that is, with glories heard everywhere.

1. *Kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, 1, *ja*, and *ṭa* are used as designations. 2. Because the characteristics previously stated exist in *ṅa*, *jha*, 1, etc. 3. *Kṣa*, *jha*, 1, *ja*, and *ṭa* are for the sake of sacrifice (*yajñāya*). 4. *Kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, 1, *ja*, and *ṭa* indeed bring [the meaning] near; the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) is elided. 5. *Kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*: invocation (*āhvāna*). 6. *Kṣa*, *ma*, and *ṭa*: the phrase "he is such" (*sa tādṛśaḥ*) does not exist [in this version]. 7. *Kṣa*, *jha*, 1, *ma*, and *ṭa*: that fire is the producer of all (*sarvotpādaka*). It exists. Having stated that it is the "producer of all," he states the justification for that there.
For this creation is "drunk by living beings" (jīvapīta); that whose order of creation (sṛṣṭikrama) has been drunk—that is, tasted—by various kinds of living beings is thus described.
By the rule "the third [case-ending] in the sense of the object," there is the preservation of the original accent (prakṛtisvara) of the preceding member;
and in the case of *punar* and *hi*, that same accent applies.
In this regard, the process of creation is as follows:

this Agni, having received the oblation offered by himself, reaches the sun; together with its rays, in the form of lightning, it causes rain to fall through the clouds via water, thereby satisfying all living beings. Thus, by means of producing rain, he is the "Producer. Now, [the text] declares his status as the direct producer.
The fire which, having entered the womb—the seat of the embryo—carries across the emitted seed that has been infused;
the meaning is that it transforms it into the form of the body of a man, a king, or another being.
If one should cook the fire, it would indeed fill it and not cause decay.
Therefore, this [fire] is the direct producer;
the meaning is that such a fire exists as one who is illustrious.
Or alternatively:

The fire which belongs to men—that is, to those sacrificers who are endowed with enthusiasm for their rites—just as it is for them, so too is it for heaven and earth, bestowing upon them their desired rain and other blessings.
Regarding this, Yāska says: "Men are humans; they 'dance' (perform) in their rites" (Nirukta 5.1).
Just as [the fire] is for them, so it is for heaven and earth as well.
By means of a word denoting the substratum (*āśraya*), the things residing within that substratum (*āśrayin*) are indicated;
the sense is that [Agni benefits] those dwelling in the earthly realm by bestowing rain, and those dwelling in the celestial realm by delivering the oblation (*havis*).

Such an Agni, through his glories (*śravobhiḥ*)—namely, the oblations characterized as *soma*, clarified butter (*ājya*), and so forth—acting as the instrumental cause, exists as one whose nature is tasted by all without distinction by the various living beings, the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), who have drunk him into life; thus he remains preeminent.
The meaning is that, having gratified this Agni with oblations, they enjoy their desired pleasures.

Furthermore, he who, having entered the womb of Agni—that is, his own abode characterized as the sacrificial altar—and being endowed with true vital breath (*satprāṇa*), cooks the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings brought to him, is this very Agni who exists as one of great majesty.
He who has illuminated the unassailable city, like a bird of heaven flying hitherward, shining like the sun with a hundredfold soul.
He who illumined the city of Narmiṇī, like a courser, a sage, like one born from the clouds, like a steed; radiant like the sun, possessing a hundredfold life. 3.
4. Agni [approached] the *nārmiṇī*—the *uttaravedi* (high altar) belonging to the sacrificers, characterized by joy (*narma*);
or alternatively, that ground situated in the minds of men, toward which the intention for Agni’s arrival exists for the sake of the sacrificers’ sacrifice.
6. Our city is our abode. 7. A. 8. He has shone forth; he illuminates.
Of what nature is he? 9.
A steed (atyaḥ), one whose nature it is to traverse toward the desired place.
A seer (kavi) is one who has transcendent vision.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
a horse that is skilled in running.
He is like the wind (nabhasvān), which exists in the sky (nabha) without being attached to it. Furthermore, he is the "one whose self is a hundred" (śatātmā);
"a hundred" and "a thousand" are words used to denote the unlimited.
Its manifold nature arises either in relation to the various houses of different sacrificers, or in relation to the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires.

Alternatively, Agni’s form as Mitra and others is well known from Vedic texts through the distinction between Mitra, Varuṇa, and so forth, such as: “O Agni, you are born as Varuṇa” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.3.1) and “They call Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.164.46).
The meaning of the second mantra is that they declare Agni alone to be the very essence of Indra and the other deities.
Such is this hero, shining like the sun, not merely radiant like the sun.
‘Rum’ means ‘to shine.
The suffix *kasu* is used here for the Vedic perfect tense (*liṭ*).
Therefore, that such a fire exists and is preeminent—this is the connection with what precedes.

1. kṣa-na-ṭa-svādattam | 2. kṣa-ṅa-na-ṭa-udakāni | 3. kṣa-jha-na-ṭa-pāyayati | 4. kṣa-bha1-pra-ṭa-prāpayati; ka-jha-pācayati | 5. kṣa-ṅa-jha-na-ṭa-pūṃyadeva | 6. kṣa-na-ṭa-nopayeta | 7. kṣa-na-ṭa-yajñārtham | 8. kṣa-ṅa-jha-na-ṭa-mitravaruṇādirūpabhedena | 9. kṣa-jha-na-ṭa-mitrādirūpatvam |

The twice-born one, shining brightly, has taken his stand over the three luminous realms and all the regions, as the most excellent sacrificer, the Hotṛ-priest, in the gathering place of the waters. 4. abhi | dvijanmā | trī | rocanāni | viśvā | rajāṃsi | śuśucānaḥ | asthāt | hotā | yajiṣṭhaḥ | apām | sadhasthe || 4 ||
This fire is "twice-born" (dvijanmā), being produced from two kindling-sticks (araṇī);
or rather,
its first birth is from friction (mathana).
Immediately after arising, the second birth consists precisely of the form of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as *pavamāna* and so forth;
thus there is "twice-bornness" (*dvijanmatva*).
Alternatively, it is because of being born from Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*).

Such an Agni, intensely shining toward the three luminous realms—the three *rocanāni*, which are either the locations beginning with the earth or the sacrificial fires such as the *gārhapatya*—and not merely those three, but illuminating and kindling all the *rajāṃsi*, all the worlds consisting of the *rajas* element beginning with the earth; he stands, the invoker (*hotṛ*) of the gods, the most excellent sacrificer (*yajiṣṭha*), at the common dwelling place (*sadhasthe*) of the waters—the sacrificial site for sprinkling and other rites.

This is that Hotṛ priest, the twice-born, who through his desire for glory bestows all desirable things; the mortal man who, being swift in action, has offered oblations to him. 5. This is he, the Hotṛ, who, being twice-born, has established all desirable things out of a desire for renown—the mortal who, being quick in his deeds, has sacrificed to him. 5.

He who is twice-born is indeed the *hotṛ*, the performer of the oblation; for it is only he, born from the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*) through the medium of the *gārhapatya* fire, who becomes the *āhavanīya* fire—the invoker of the gods—and he, this very one, [attains] all desirable things (*viśvā vāryāṇi*).
The initial udātta accent [of *duhaḥ*] is due to the rule "dvandvavṛtraśaṃsaduhāpyataḥ."
Śravasyā, śravasyā;
"śrava" means food and sacrificial oblation, [the word is used] through the desire for that.
In the word *śravaḥ*, the suffix *ap* is added in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) after the root *śru*, which has undergone the *kyac* suffix and ends in *a*.
He bestows; he maintains. That mortal who gives to this Agni whose nature has been described becomes *sutuka*, that is, one who possesses excellent sons.
The tenth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with “puru tvā,” is addressed to Agni and is composed by Dīrghatamas.
The Anukramaṇikā states: “puru tvā... is in the Uṣṇih meter.
Its application is here in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra within the various meters.
In the section beginning with "Now, of this," it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, [I praise] thee much" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).

O Agni, as a liberal donor, I, your worshipper, shall speak much to you; for you indeed are like the protection of a great impeller. puru tvā dāśvān voce ariḥ agne tava svid ā todasyeva śaraṇe ā mahasya || 1 || O Agni, as a liberal donor, I, your worshipper, shall speak much to you; for you indeed are like the protection of a great impeller.
1. *kṣa-ṭha-jha-1-a-ṭa*: consisting of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices;
2. *kṣa-ḍa-ca-jha-ja-ṭa*: birth (*janman*);
3. *kṣa-a-ṭa-sa*: such [is it].
4. [The reading] *abhitaḥ prakāśayan* does not exist in kṣa, ḍa, ca, jha, jha, 1, a, ṭa.
5. Wealth that is to be chosen (*varaṇīya*) is found in ka, jha; actions that are to be chosen (*varaṇīya*) are found in kṣa, jha, 1, ma, ṭa.
6. He established fires or fame (*yaśas*) in kṣa, jha, 1, a, ṭa.
7. And to you, whose nature is unsurpassed [Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 21, Sūkta 150]. Second Aṣṭaka, 917: O Agni, I have spoken much to you.
Alternatively,
the connection is "I shall give much.
The meaning is that I speak such prayers as, "Give me a son," "Give me wealth," and so forth.
Why remain silent? He says "no," because since I have offered the desired oblation (*havis*), I shall speak.
One should not think, "How can it be given to one who speaks as if he were common with others?"
Since I, O Agni, am your very own servant (*ari*)—meaning one who is distressed and devoted through the offering of oblations and the like—standing directly before you;
in this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a born slave or the like remains entirely subservient within the house, that is, the shelter, of a great teacher or master, so too do I.
Since this is so, therefore the meaning is: "Speak much of what is desired; you too, give all of that.
Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "'Bahudāśu'—you indeed call upon him repeatedly; 'ari' comes from the root *ṛcchati*.
'Ari' is also [derived] from this very same [root]."

If [the word] *devayā* were something other than "those who go to the gods," then since *āmāhṛti*s are offered as oblations, the seer would have spoken thus: "In the refuge of the great striker, as in the refuge of the great striker" (*todasyeva śaraṇe ā mahasya tudasyeva śaraṇe’dhi mahataḥ*). (Nirukta 5.7)
Of the roaring, thundering, ruddy one at the libation—
never indeed has he failed to hasten toward the godless man.
Of the unassailable, the roaring one— at the offering of the libation, the ruddy one,
never at any time.
He has departed;
[he is] not devoted to the gods.
In the preceding mantra, it was stated that one should request much of what is desired from oneself;
here, however, one prays that no gift should be given to those who are unlike oneself, such as those devoid of charity and other virtues.
O Agni, I speak to you specifically.
Because of the hearing of the prefix [vi-], a suitable verb must be supplied.
Alternatively, because of its proximity, the word "vocē" (I speak) is understood;
I speak that which is contrary to what they have made known for our sake.
The meaning is: "I say that [the gift] should not be given to one whose nature is about to be described.
He states their nature:
"to an *aninas*, i.e., one who makes you masterless (*assāmin*); likewise, to a *dhunin*, i.e., one who possesses complete wealth."
This is prevented because giving by one who already possesses wealth is purposeless;
or rather,
the meaning is "one who possesses wealth that is not useful for sacrifices and the like."
Furthermore, in the case of *prahope*, it means "having excessively withheld" (*prakarṣeṇa hotum*) in the form of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Alternatively,
there is a connection with *aninasya* in the sense of "in the absence of praise" (*prahope'niṃnasya*).
The meaning is "one who is incapable of performing the duties of a *hotṛ* priest to the highest degree.
Here, by the word *ina*, his capability (*sāmarthya*) is indicated. The word *cit* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Furthermore, *kadā cana prajigataḥ* means "never indeed," that is, never at any time did they praise the gods intensely. Here, *cana* is a compound of two particles: the word *ca* signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*), and the word *na* signifies negation (*niṣedha*).
Furthermore, "to the two non-gods" (*adevayoḥ*) means those who do not desire the gods for themselves;
the meaning is that [the gift] should not be given to them.
By defining the nature of those who are censured, it is implied that since he himself is not like that, his statement "I have spoken much" is indeed appropriate.
Alternatively,
*cana* is a synonym for the word *cit*. In the manner described, even though he is wicked, whenever he might go forth or whenever he might praise you, I have spoken to him.
"I speak with particular emphasis that [the gift] should be given to such a person;
what need is there to mention [that it should be given] for my sake?"—this is the intended meaning.

1. In the manuscripts *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa*, the word “*asya*” (of him) does not exist. 2. In *kṣa*, *a*, and *ṭa*, it is said [in reference] to one who speaks out against [him]. 3. In *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa*, it is due to the influence of a prefix (*upasarga*). 4. In *kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa*, it is for the purpose of making known. 5. In *kṣa*, *a*, and *ṭa*, the phrase “*iti bravīmi*” (thus I say) does not exist. 6. In *kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa*, it is said in reference to one who does not make you his master (*svāmin*); this should be connected in every case thus: in *ṅa*, it is said in reference to one who makes you a non-master (*asvāmin*); this should be understood in every case thus; in *jha*, it is [said in reference to] one who does not make you his own master. 7. In *kṣa*, *a*, and *ṭa*, [it refers to] one possessing wealth that is not used for sacrifices and so forth; in *jha*, [it refers to] one possessing wealth suitable for the performance of sacrifices and so forth. 8. In *kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa*, it is also in the sense of "even" (*cit*) regarding the offering (*prahoṣe*). 9. In *kṣa*, *a*, and *ṭa*, [it means] in the form of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth. 10. In *jha*, furthermore: of the one who is fierce (*bharuṣaḥ*), of the non-harming one (*ahiṃsakasya*), and of the one who does not act as another's superior (*paro’ham akurvataḥ*). Furthermore: [the same applies].
O Brahmin, that moon-like splendor is most exalted in heaven;
through these [hymns], O Agni, may we be victorious over the enemy.
He is the moon, O Brahmin; by mortal men he is the most exalted greatness in heaven. May we evermore go forward, O Agni, as those who increase your vigor. 3.
O Agni, that mortal who, being wise and intelligent, worships you— that mortal sacrificer becomes like the moon, the delighter of all, in the heavenly world; or rather,
he becomes the moon itself.
The Chandogas record that the sacrificers attain the state of the moon: "From the world of the fathers to the ether, from the ether to the moon—there is King Soma" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.4);
and also, "Having experienced glory in the world of Soma" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.4).
Likewise, the attainment of the heavenly world is recorded in the Muṇḍaka as well: "'Be kindled!'—thus the resplendent oblations carry the sacrificer by means of the rays of the sun."
"The rays of the sun lead them to where the sole lord of the gods has his abode" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.5), and "This is your holy world of Brahman, earned by good deeds" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.6).
Furthermore, that very same [world] is further qualified:
"Greater than the great," meaning most exalted or most increased.
The meaning is that he is the most excellent even among the other gods.
Therefore, O Agni, may we be your *prapretaḥ*—that is, your preeminent partakers (*vanuṣaḥ*).
Or alternatively:
Having gratified [them], may we go forth;
may we indeed become preeminent.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “mitraṃ na yam,” is composed by Dīrghatamas; it is in the Jāgata meter and addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa.
The first verse, however, is addressed to Mitra alone.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “mitraṃ nava: [this] is addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa, in the Jāgata meter; the first verse is [addressed to] Mitra.”
The application is based on indicative marks.
Him whom those seeking cattle have generated with skillful labor for the sake of cows, at the sacrifice, and in the waters—him who is like a friend—they have brought forth through their devotion.
Both worlds trembled before his song as he crossed over; the worshipful one is dear from birth to all living beings.

Not [as] a friend—him whom those of good intent, seeking cattle among the cattle with their labor, have generated at the sacrifice in the waters; both worlds trembled at his far-reaching song. [They have come] toward the beloved, the worshipful one, the protector of all beings. 1.
This [Agni] is called *śimyā*; this is a name for his action, because its name exists in the statement, “*śimī* means power” (*Nirukta* 2.1.24).
Through his actions, such as bestowing light and grace, he stands as a "friend" (*mitra*), like a friend.
Alternatively,
the word "śimyā" is connected with the action:
"when many cows are present as the cause," [the phrase] "gavyavaḥ" means those desiring cows for themselves.
In this context, although the expression "gavyarvaḥ" alone would suffice without the word "gopu," nevertheless, in the phrase "gavyarvaḥ," ownership of cows is what is being established.
That [ownership] might exist with even one or two or three cows;
therefore, the word "gopu" is used to convey that many cows are desirable.
Just as in "Thou art the lord of kine" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 7.98.6) and "Thee, the Lord of hosts, of hosts" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 2.23.1), so too [here]:

"The *svādhyas*—those who meditate well, the producers of the fruit, or those of excellent meditation—at the *vidatha*, i.e., the sacrifice, [behold] thee existing in the waters, that is, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) in the form of lightning.
'Waters' (*āpas*) is a name for the intermediate space, because it occurs among its names in the statement, 'The waters are the earth' (*Nirukta* 1.3.8)."

The origin of fire from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is [attested] in other mantras such as: "O Agni, you who are born of heaven, or born of the waters" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 8.43.28), and "In the waters, O Agni, is your seat" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 8.43.9).
1. *kṣa-na-ṭa*: Therefore we, O Agni; *jha1*: Therefore we, O Agni. 2. *jha*: By two or three [mantras], etc.

The well-known [Agni], the beloved, most dear, or the one who pleases all; the worshipful (yajataṃ), the one worthy of sacrifice—sacrificers generate him, the Agni, by means of the act of friction and so forth, making him their own through the protection (avataḥ) afforded to living beings (januṣāṃ) who possess birth.
Or alternatively:
The meaning is that he generated [Agni] within the waters—which served as the instrumental cause—for the benefit of all living beings and for the sake of rain.
When Agni was thus born, both *rodasī*, heaven and earth, trembled (*arejetām*) through his *pājas*—his power—and through his *girā*—his terrifying sound.
That the trembling occurred due to Agni is well known from such Vedic texts as: "Both worlds trembled at the Hotṛ Sūrya" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.31.3).
Nor should it be said that the fire kindled at dawn for the sake of protection caused fear in both worlds; for this is merely a figure of speech involving censure and praise.
Since the conclusion of the praise is that "just as the two worlds were afraid, so did [the fire] grow," it is a eulogy.

Although it is the fire itself that is being described, while Mitra is merely used as an illustration, nevertheless, because the fire residing in heaven is indeed Mitra, there is no contradiction in the mantra being addressed to Mitra (maitra).
Alternatively:
the officiating priests manifest the deity named Mitra—who stands like a friend (*mitram*) or a companion—in the sacrifice and in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
The remainder of this [verse] should be applied in that same manner with its specific details.
Or rather, O Purumīḷha, those who possess Soma have established themselves like Mitra, being self-sustaining;
therefore, find the will and the path for the one who praises you, and hear, O Bulls, the call of him who seeks prosperity.

When those [hymns] of yours were offered by Purumīḷha, the Soma-presser—just as friends who are well-disposed have established them—the two of you, O Mitra and Varuṇa, found wisdom and a path for the singer; and hear, O Bulls, the call of the one who possesses the sacrificial seat.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, for the reason that you [two] go toward Purumīḷha—the one who pours forth many desires, the possessor of Soma, the self-sustaining, and the one whose nature is to abide in the Soma.
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
That aforementioned deed, the officiating priests—who have become like friends (mitrāsaḥ)—have placed forward and maintain with excellence, as if they were true friends;
‘ha’ is a filler particle.
Therefore, for this reason, [the singer] praises the path leading to you.
The dative case is used in the sense of the recipient of a gift.
Recognize—that is, take note of—the ritual act of the sacrificer who is singing praises and performing worship.
In the imperative (loṭ), *śa* is substituted [for *sip*] by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

Moreover, O *vṛṣaṇā*, you two showerers of desires, listen (*śrutam*) to the invocation or the hymn of the sacrificer who possesses a *pastya*—for *pastya* is a name for a house, as it is stated in the list of synonyms: "In the *pastya*, in the dwelling" (*ni. 3.4.6*)—that is, one who has a home such as the *sadas* or the *prācīnavaṃśa*. Listen!
In Vedic usage, there is elision (luk) of the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa).
Or rather:

because they have become like friends (*mitrāsaḥ*) to the Soma-offerer, to King Purumīḷha by name—being "self-existent" (*svābhuvah*), meaning having the nature of abiding in their own being and capable of their respective functions—they have [bestowed these gifts]. Therefore, for that one who praises (*arcate*), they find the mental power (*kratum*) of the one who praises, and so forth, as explained previously.
The peoples have adorned your birth from the two worlds, O Bulls, for it is to be proclaimed for great skill;
since you bring [oblations] to the immortal and to the living one, you shall enjoy the sacrifice through the office of the Hotṛ.

The people have adorned you both for the birth of Heaven and Earth, O Bulls, to be proclaimed for your great skill—when you bring [oblations] for the sake of Truth and for the steed, and when you, through the office of the Hotṛ, further the sacrifice. 3.
1. *kṣa-jha-ṭa-ajanayan* | 2. *ṅa-jha-tyat tat*.
O you two showerers of desires, O Mitra and Varuṇa, that birth, the production or origin, of you two from the two worlds, heaven and earth—[we praise].
This is because everything originates from both Heaven and Earth.
Alternatively, "Mitra" refers to Agni, who benefits all, and "Varuṇa" refers to Āditya, the dispeller of darkness; for both have their abodes in the earth and the sky respectively.
Therefore, since Agni was praised in the preceding mantra by way of the analogy of Mitra,
it is understood from this that Agni himself is Mitra;
and so it is elsewhere as well.
"Agni, like Mitra, is to be praised among the settlements" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.2.3); and "whom the Bhr̥gus established like a well-disposed Mitra" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.15.2).

Such a birth of yours two is "to be proclaimed," worthy of praise; for the sake of "great power" (*dakṣasa*)—that is, for power over all domains—the "settlements," meaning human sacrificers, "adorn" him from all sides, which means they extol him. He speaks of the praiseworthiness of that birth: [as follows].
*Yadīm*: for this very reason;
or alternatively, *īm* is a meaningless particle used here as an expletive.
Because it has been stated, "In the *Mitākṣara*, [the words] *kam* and *siddhi* are meaningless," [we understand that] you bring forth strength for the sake of *ṛtāya*, that is, for sacrifice;
and for the reason (*yat*) that you bring forth the desired fruit for the *arvate*, meaning for the one who impels you, and for the sacrificer.
Alternatively,
the dative case is used in both instances because the object functions as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*);
the meaning is that you two support both the sacrifice and the sacrificer.
And because you reach forth preeminently through *hotrā*—that is, speech in the form of praise—and through *śimī*, that is, the ritual action of offering oblations and so forth;
therefore, the meaning is that you adorn your proclaimable birth.
*Hotrā* is a name for speech, as it is listed among its synonyms in the Nirukta (1.11.35): "Hotrā is song."

That people is indeed the most excellent, O Asuras, which you two, lovers of Truth, protect with great and lofty power. From the vast heaven, you have brought forth creative skill; you yoke yourselves to the waters like a bull to the pole.

That is the dwelling place, O Asuras, which is great and dear, where you two, upholders of *ṛta*, proclaim the lofty *ṛta*. You two harness the efficient and supportive power of the vast heaven to the waters, as one yokes an ox to the pole. 4.

O Asuras—the two powerful ones—Mitra and Varuṇa, that dwelling (*kṣiti*) of yours, which consists of the host of gods, is great (*mahi*), exceedingly vast, most dear (*priyā*), or rather, one that brings delight; that dwelling has been brought forth with excellence (*pra*).
Since the prefix is heard, a suitable verb is to be supplied; the ellipsis is "sit upon it" (*tām āsīdata*).
It is well known that the sacrificial ground is "dear to the gods.

Having reached it, O you two who possess *ṛta* (truth/ritual order), you two proclaim our great, fully developed *ṛta*—that is, our sacrifice—as having been accomplished without deficiency; this is the meaning of the praise.
For you two are capable at the yoke-pole of the great heaven, in the sense of being able to carry out the satisfaction [of the gods].
Alternatively, [the phrase] "of the broad, great heaven" (bṛhato divo mahato dyulokasya) means "in order to please the gods," with "to satisfy Dakṣa" being the understood sense.
Or else,
the genitive case is used in the objective sense.
From the great and luminous heaven, you two employ—that is, you partake of—the abundant *dakṣa*, which is capable of accomplishing desired ends;
you employ the all-pervading *apah*, meaning the ritual action consisting of the Soma sacrifice, and thereby accept the oblation belonging thereto.
Regarding this employment, there is an illustration.
Like a cow—that is, like a milch-cow—for the purpose of carrying the burden of physical strength; they utilize her just as one utilizes such a cow.
Or alternatively:
The word for the material cause is used for its modification,
as in the case of milk and so forth;
therefore, you proclaim the *ṛta*.
1. The arising of *jña* and *jha*. 2. *Kṣa*, *ña*, *ṭa*, and *asura* are givers of *asu*. 3.
By the power of the prefixes *kṣa*, *ha*, *jha*, *la*, *ña*, and *ṭa*.
4. You two cause all sounds to resound everywhere with the soundless [consonants] *kṣa*, *ṭha*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*, and *ghoṣa*.

5. [The syllable] *kṣa-ña-ṭa* is capable of carrying satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*); *jha* is capable of carrying satisfaction; *jha-1* is capable of carrying both satisfaction and oblation (*havanasamartha*).
O Earth, you protect us here with your greatness; O Arēṇavas, you who possess strength, you bring together the cows at the gathering.
They move toward the sun as it sets, like women approaching their husbands.

On this great earth, by your greatness, you have won the choice prize. Free from dust, the swift ones have surged forth; the milch-cows low. They hasten toward the sun at its setting, like the fingers of the dawn that fashion [the day]. 5.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two—*vām* [is used] for the dual. *Mahī* [is used] for the singular. In the case of *sasajyā*, there is a long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*).
By the rule "And *īt* and *ūt* are *pragṛhya* when they have the sense of the locative" (Pāṇini 1.1.19), there is the status of being *pragṛhya*.
On this earth, by means of your greatness (*mahnā*), you two cause the cow to reach (*vṛṇavathaḥ*)— that is, to go to— the desirable region (*varaṃ vāram*).
This verb has a causative sense implied within it,
because the activity of going and so forth is dependent upon those two, and because Mitra and Varuṇa are the presiding deities of heaven and earth.
These cows, like milch-cows, at the time of evening, by virtue of your greatness, are desirable, blameless, unlost through the theft of thieves, and indeed swift givers of milk;
for *tuji* is a verb meaning "to give.
Being present, they come to the stall or are firmly established therein.
Because of the hearing of the prefix (*upasarga*), there is the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the action of conjunction (*yoga*).
Thus, "the cows have been made to stop" means they have ceased [moving]. There is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending.

When the atmosphere is vast with clouds and covered by them, they cry out—that is, they call out—for the sake of easy movement, directed toward the Sun (*sūrya*), the progenitor of all, who possesses excellent vigor (*suvīrya*) or beautiful power.
For another Vedic text states: "Because he is the protector of men like a hero of great strength, that is the reason for Sūrya’s name ‘Sūrya’" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 2.2.10).
They cry out toward Āditya so that there may be pleasant passage.
The root *svṛ* is used in the senses of "sound" and "affliction";
it belongs to the *bhvādi* class.
As for at what time [this occurs], that is now stated.
The dawns are free from bonds;
this applies to all times of evening and all times of dawn.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Like a thief who has committed a deed,
he is a thief;
his pursuer is a man.
It is just as he cries out;
thus, the praise of those two is that the lowing of the cows is directed toward you.
The long-maned ones have sung out to you both for the sake of immortality, O Mitra and Varuṇa, where you celebrate the path.
By your own selves, release [the waters] and cause our prayers to swell; you two rule over the thoughts of the inspired singer.

The long-maned ones have sung in praise of you both for the sake of cosmic order, O Mitra and Varuṇa, where you celebrate the path of progress. By your own power, release [the waters] and cause the prayers to swell; you two rule over the inspired thoughts of the sage.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, those with long hair—the flames at the front—have honored you both for the sake of the rite (*vṛtāya*), that is, for the purpose of sacrifice;
the meaning is that they have worshipped you by offering oblations. Where? That is now stated.
O Mitra and O Varuṇa, you two both honor—that is, accept—*gātu*, meaning either the path or the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*), at this sacrifice;
for *gātu* is a name for the earth, as stated in *Nirukta* 1.1.20: "Gātu is Pūṣan. (Note:
*gātuḥ* is used here in the sense of the sacrificial ground or the path leading to it, rather than the literal "earth" itself.)
And having come, by yourselves alone, release the rain; release it with faces turned downward.
Having done so, cause our thoughts—that is, our ritual acts—to swell, meaning to increase.
Having done this, you two take delight in the meditations—the thoughtful hymns—of the wise sacrificer.

1. O you two great ones, vast by your greatness—that is, by your magnitude—here on this earth, you two reach the cow toward the desirable region (*vāram*). By what greatness? By [your] greatness. 2. *kha-tujatiḥ*.
3. Those connected with *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *kṣa*¹, *ja*, and *ṭa*;
or alternatively, one who is quickly sinking (*sannan*).
4. Easy movement through *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *kṣa*¹, *ja*, and *ṭa*.
5. *kṣa-cha-kṣa¹-tra-ṭa-*: O Mitra and Varuṇa, [this is] yours, of you two.
6. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-*: by oneself. 7. *jha-pinvatam*: cause to swell, cause to flow; *jha¹-sevayantam* (variant).
You two are the lords, the masters.
The root *ij* has the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), as it is stated among its names: "He rules, he sees" (Nirukta 2.21.1).
Whoever honors you with sacrifices, striving and offering oblations—the sage who worships with hymns that accomplish his intent—to him do you both approach;
enjoy his sacrifice, come toward our songs and our prayer, being well-disposed and seeking us.

Whosoever, striving with sacrifices, offers gifts to you both—the sage who as the Hotṛ-priest performs the sacrifice, accomplishing the prayer—unto him indeed you two approach; you enjoy his ritual; come toward our songs and our favor, being well-disposed toward us. 7.

Whosoever indeed, as a sacrificer, for your sake—addressing you both—or for the sake of you two, performs worship (*śaśamānaḥ*) by means of sacrifices (*yajñaiḥ*) which serve as the occasion for the rite, and offers (*dāśati*) oblations and so forth, relinquishing his own ownership and establishing them as yours;
he who is a seer (*kaviḥ*), that is, one learned in the Vedas (*anūcānaḥ*), according to the Śruti: "Those who are learned in the Vedas are seers" (AiB 2.2).

Alternatively, the wise poet—the *hotṛ* priest who perfectly accomplishes the oblation, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)—being endowed with the means for meditation, namely the meditative materials such as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), performs the sacrifice, such as the Soma sacrifice.
Observing that very sacrificer, who possesses excellent wisdom (*sumati*), you two approach and reach him;
indeed.
"You two desire—that is, you long for—his *adhvara*, his sacrifice.
Furthermore, desiring us (*asmayū*), may you two come toward our songs of praise (*giraḥ*).
The meaning is: having reached such a person as me, accept these praises."

In this context, although there appears to be a general reference by the word "him" (*tam*), nevertheless, because it was stated "as for us" (*asma-yū*), it is understood that Dīrghatamas spoke of himself in the third person.
Alternatively, [it may mean]:
"Approaching him who gives and he who sacrifices, you both desire his sacrifice."
Therefore, O Ashvins, come toward me with your benevolence, directed toward my songs and praises.

O you two, the first [to receive] through sacrifices and cattle, the upholders of *ṛta*, they anoint you as if with the impulse of the mind; they bring songs to you with concentrated thought. With a fervent mind, you have attained wealth.

You two, the first [gods], they anoint with sacrifices and with milk, you who possess the cosmic order (*ṛtāvānau*), like the impulses of the mind. They bring songs to you with concentrated thought; with an unclouded mind, you have attained wealth. 8.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two who are observers of cosmic order (*ṛtāvānau*), possessors of sacrifice, and possessors of rain-water—sacrificers first of all adorn you with sacrifices, which are the means of worship, and with cows and their products such as milk;
that is, they manifest your divine portion in the sacrifices through milk and other offerings.

1. *Kṣa-kha-ca-ja-ṭa-ye vā* means "those who are learned in the Vedas (*anūcānāḥ*). 2. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa-karoti ca*. 3. *Kṣa-jha-ṭa-tameva*. 4. *Kṣa-jha-jha1-ja-ṭa-prāpnuthaḥ kāmayathaḥ*. The word *aha* is an epithet of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); the meaning is "you praise the non-injurious one. Furthermore: 5. *Kṣa-ṅa-jha1-ja-ṭa-avagamyate*. 6. *Kṣa-jha-ṭa-kāmayathaḥ*. 7. *Kṣa-jha-ṭa-stutīkṣa*.
[Ma 1. a. 21. sū. 152] Second Aṣṭaka, 923: the meaning is "they sacrifice."
Or alternatively:
they anoint with "cows" (rays of light), that is, they praise; in this regard there is an illustration:
it is not like the mind in its various applications or employments.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).
It is "like the mind" (*mana iva*);
that is to say, they first manifest it, making it primary, because all worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by it.
Furthermore, with a mind that possesses reflection (*manmanā*), being well-restrained and directed solely toward you both, people offer and accomplish hymns of praise (*giraḥ*).

Because this is so, being endowed with a mind that is unassailable (*ahṛpyatā*) and an exalted consciousness, you two have attained (*āśāthe*) our wealthy (*revat*) ritual action; that is to say, you have reached it and hold it fast.
Regarding the root *aś* (to reach), in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), the absence of the augment *iṭ* occurs according to the rule: "The teaching of augments is not mandatory."
You two have assumed two forms; you have reached out with your wondrous powers, O heroes, and thus displayed your greatness.
Neither the heavens nor the days, nor the rivers, nor the Paṇis can equal your divinity, nor can they reach your lofty source.

Richly you bestow vital strength; richly you have attained it through the wondrous powers of heroes. Your greatness extends beyond this world; neither the heavens with their days, nor the rivers, nor even the Paṇis have attained your divinity or your wealth. 9.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two bestow both wealth (*revat*)—that is, riches—and food (*vayas*); and you maintain both.
Since this is so, therefore [he is called] "wealthy" (*revat*), meaning rich;
it is understood that he has seen the food (*vayas*).

O leaders, O men, you have sought—that is, you have become—the food distinguished by wealth; what kind [of food]? That which possesses *māhinm* (greatness), which comes toward us (*itaūti*) through your *māyābhiḥ* (wisdoms), and which provides protection from here.
"This is great for me;
it is exceedingly great! From where does such power as this belong to you two? To this, he says:
Your divinity, O two of you, along with the days—
here the word *ahaḥ* denotes nights, since the day is mentioned separately by the word *ghoṣa*— those days, together with them, have not attained [it], that is, they do not reach it.
The meaning is that both day and night do not cross over [you].

Furthermore, even the rivers—those characterized by flowing—have not attained such divinity as yours; nor have the Paṇis, even though they are Asuras, attained it, nor have they attained wealth (*magham*).
The meaning is that there are no adversaries whatsoever for you two in the three worlds.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "yuvaṃ vakṣāṇi," is composed by Dairghatamas.
By the *anādeśaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding the absence of specific instruction), [the metre] is *traiṣṭubha*.
It belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, because it has been stated: "The first [verse] here is for the Maitrāvaruṇa, for it is [his]";
