thus, the application of the hymn (*sūkta*) is based on its characteristic mark (*liṅga*).

The first *vapā-yājyā* for the animal sacrifice dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa is prescribed in the section titled “Pradānānām” as follows: “You two clothe yourselves in fatness like breasts; stretch forth your arms so that we may live. [Variants:
*kṣa-ja-ṭa* read "they anoint with cows, praises, or words"; *jha* reads "they worship and praise with cows, praises, and words."]
2. *ka-kṣa-ḍa-ja-jha-ña-ṭa-ṇa-revat rayivat*.
3. *kṣa-ḍa-jha-ña-ṭa-aśruvāthe*.
Or else: [as above].
"You have partaken of distinguished food"—this means you have consumed it; "you bestow"—this means you give. (Note: *revat* is equivalent to *rayivat*). Furthermore, O leaders (*narā*), you two!
6. In the manuscripts kṣa, ja, ṭa, the phrase "of you two" (yuvayoḥ) is not present.
7. In the manuscripts kṣa, ja, ṭa, the word *antimahaṃ* is followed by the ellipsis *mahaṃ dhanam āśāthe* ("you two hope for great wealth").

8. In the manuscripts kṣa, ḍa, jha, ña, ṭa, [it is said]: "Such as this, you two, together with the days (*ahobhiḥ*) and nights (*rātribhiḥ*), the heavens (*dyāvaḥ*)—that is, the days (*divasāḥ*)—have not encompassed (*nānaśuḥ*), meaning they have not pervaded."
In this context, by the word "day" (ahaḥ), the night is meant;
for the day is mentioned separately by the word "sound" (ghoṣa).
The meaning is that one crosses over both the day and the night.

Moreover, even the rivers, whose nature it is to flow, have not failed to reach the ocean; likewise, neither you two nor the gods have failed to attain divinity—that divine state—and even the *paṇis*, the asuras, have not failed to reach their destination.
(They) move about.
(Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8). Let it not be so; this [verse] is enjoined for the wearing of new clothes during the *āvartana* ceremony.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having clothed [them] in two unwashed garments with [the verse], 'You two wear garments of fatness' (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.8.9)."
You two wear garments of fatness; your thoughts are indeed flawless streams.
You have struck down all falsehoods; O Mitra and Varuṇa, you abide by the Eternal Law (ṛta).
You two clothe yourselves in fat garments; your streams of thought are indeed flawless. You have driven away all falsehoods; O Mitra and Varuṇa, you act in accordance with the Eternal Law (ṛta).
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two are swollen with fatness;
or rather,
you two clothe yourselves in garments that are fat, flawless, and suitable for wearing.
Or rather:

with "pīvasā," meaning with thick, abundant luster, you two "dadhāthe" garments—meaning you maintain splendors that serve as the place of garments. Furthermore, your "sargāḥ," your creations, are "acchidrāḥ," flawless, and "mantavaḥ," indeed worthy of being meditated upon.
O you two such [as you are], destroy—cause to perish—all, indeed all, untruths, unpleasantries, and evils here.
In the compound *viśva* within this *saṃhitā*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) and the shortening of the vowel according to the rule "ṛtyakaḥ."
Through truth, through that fruit, through wealth, or through sacrifice, you two accompany and join with us;
the meaning is that you unite us with these.
Not even one among them has understood this: the true mantra, proclaimed by the seer, is effective.
The fierce one strikes down the three-edged and the four-edged; indeed, those who revile the gods were the first to decay.

Not even one among them has understood this: the true mantra, recited by the seers, is effective. The fierce four-edged [weapon] strikes the three-edged; indeed, the first revilers of the gods have grown old.
Between these two.
The plural number is used for the sake of honor;
or else,
it is used in the plural in view of his followers.

Between these two, only one indeed—this one about to be described—perceives (*vi ciketat*), that is, specifically understands or carries out this action in the form of efficacy (*sāmarthya*). He is further distinguished:

he alone is *satya*, uncontradicted, or existing among the good; he is *mantra*, possessed of wisdom; he is *kaviśasta*, to be praised by the wise (*kavi*) and the intelligent; and he is *ṛdhāvān*, possessing power or destruction.
By this, it has been stated that the capacity of what is about to be described is either rendered possible or established. Anticipating the question "What is that?", he says: "The three-pointed."
The weapon is endowed with three edges; it has three points, ending with that.
The possessive suffix is elided.
This is an elliptical expression;
it means "endowed with all weapons," or it may refer to one who bears this name.
He possesses four corners and even more weapons;
not only does he possess the power of his weapons, but he is also *ugra*, one who himself has raised up his strength, and he *hanti*—he strikes down—the exceedingly powerful enemy.

Furthermore, by the power of either one of you two, those who revile the gods (*devanidaḥ*)—the foremost revilers of the gods—even though they are capable, become *ajūryan*: they wither away of their own accord.
In the *śyan* [present] form of the root *jṛ*, there is the substitution of *u* by virtue of the rule "variously in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
The sense is that even one among you two possesses great strength; what then need be said regarding the power of the two joined together?
Or alternatively:
Of these two of you, one alone shall specially know (*vicitet*) this capacity—which will be described further on—characterized by truth and the rest;
the remainder is as before.

1. By *kṣa-ja-ṭa*, one causes to perceive (*cetayati*). 2. By *cha-kṣa-ja-ṭa-saḥ*, it is that very same [perception]. 3. By *kṣa-jha-jha-1-ja-ṭa-saṃbhāvanā*, there is the possibility of apprehension. 4.
It is said that by *kṣa-kha-va-kṣa1-ja-ṭa-pha*, it becomes "this" (*etād*), and by *ca-jha*, it becomes "that" (*tad*).
"Footless is the first of footed paths; who, O Mitra and Varuṇa, understands that?
The embryo bears the burden even before its birth; he fulfills the *ṛta* and sets aside the *anṛta*."
He has drunk; he comes as the first of the tracks. Who, O Mitra and Varuṇa, has understood that of yours? The embryo bears his burden; he fulfills his truth and overthrows untruth. 3.

O Mitra and Varuṇa! That well-known deed of yours—being the first among all beings possessing feet, such as humans and others, yet being "footless" (apād) and "without support" (upāt)—who comprehends it? Who understands it directly? For, day by day, like the sun and moon, because she lacks her own revolution and moves only through the movement of the sun, she is metaphorically called "footless" (apād) and "supportless" (pṛti). Who knows that such deed of yours? Who perceives it face-to-face?
‘In the act of knowing.’
The meaning is that it is worthy of praise.

Since Mitra and Varuṇa are the deities of day and night, this ritual is thus performed because the *upasads* occur precisely in the interval between day and night. Furthermore, the "burden" (*bhāra*) of this world—the maintenance [of its order]—is the "embryo" (*garbha*), namely the infant Sun who occupies the place of your own embryo.

Because it arises at the midpoint between day and night, it possesses the nature of Mitra and Varuṇa through those two alone, according to the Vedic scripture: "Day and night are indeed Mitra and Varuṇa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.10.1).
He brings forth consciousness;
he carries it away as if from all sides.
Or rather, it removes his burden of dullness.
The word "cit" is used for emphasis.
How so? That is now explained.

He fulfills the *ṛta*, which is truth consisting of the illumination, movement, and so forth of the world; he utterly submerges—that is, he destroys—the *anṛta*, which is the opposite of what has been described, consisting of darkness and the obstruction of movement and so forth. This action of bearing the burden of the world for the infant [the Sun] is due to your power.
We behold him proceeding like the lover of maidens, never falling down;
he clothes himself in the wide-spreading streams of the ocean, the beloved abode of Mitra and Varuṇa.
We behold him as he goes forth—the lover of the maidens, who does not rest; he who clothes himself in wide-spreading, ocean-like garments, the beloved abode of Mitra and Varuṇa. 4.
Of all the desirable, radiant, and maiden-like dawns.
From the root *kan*, meaning "to shine," comes the suffix *ij*. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "after a word ending in *kṛt* or *ikāra*, except for those ending in *ktin*.
Regarding the form *kanyānām* (genitive plural), the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) is Vedic.
We behold their lover, the Āditya, as he goes forth and as he returns; yet we do not behold him even for a moment as he settles down.
This too is the power of those two. Furthermore, that very point is further specified:
Wearing as garments the unceasing, unceasing, and thereby extended splendors, he clothes himself; he is dear to all, the beloved one of Mitra and Varuṇa. (Note: 1.
According to the first group of manuscripts—kṣa, ṅa, jha, ña, ṭa—he is the giver;
2. according to kṣa, ṇa, ṭa, he rises and moves even without feet.)
3. The root √kṣajñā (kṣa-jha-ña-ṭa-kit) means "to know.
It belongs to the *juhotyādi* class. There is the augment *ḍ* [before the suffix *liṭ*].

4. *Kṣa-jha-ña-ṭa-* means "in the state of being excessively praised"; *jha-jha-ataḥ* means "from that which is to be praised. 5. *Kṣa-jha-ña-ṭa-* refers precisely to the intervening period of time. 6. *Ha-vitārayāti*.

7. By the rule *ka-kṣa-jha-ṭa-in sarva-dhātubhyaḥ*, the suffix *in* [is applied]; likewise for *kha-ca-ja-pha-in*. 8. We do not see—that is, we do not perceive—such a lover (a paramour), one who moves like a lover, the winner of the night (the sun), even for a moment, as he passes by without descending and without pressing down upon them, because of their timidity; such is the sense. We do not see him.

The meaning is that everyone sees him; the sense is that because they are bashful, they do not see such a paramour—who, like the sun, does not rest even for a single moment as he moves along—but rather see the sun itself.
The meaning is that everyone sees [him].
This too is the capacity of those two,
which arises without interruption.
Furthermore, it is that very same [capacity] in the moments *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa*.
10. *Jha-vitatāni* means spread out.

*Dhāma* refers to that which is the locus of splendor (*tejas*). Alternatively, it is connected with "dear" (*priyam*), meaning the object of their love. We behold such a sun wandering by your permission.
Born without a horse, without reins, he flew forth neighing loudly, his back firm;
the youths have delighted in the unperceived prayer, praising the foundation within Mitra and Varuṇa.

Born without a horse, without reins, the courser neighing loudly flies with his back uplifted. The youths have taken pleasure in the unthought-out prayer, praising the foundation in Mitra and Varuṇa. 5.

That very Āditya, though "without a horse" (anaśva)—meaning that although he is devoid of a horse for swift travel—and likewise "without reins" (anabhīśu)—meaning that although he is devoid of reins which serve as supports and guides—nevertheless, he has become a "steed" (arvā), one endowed with swift movement.
Such is this Āditya, "neighing loudly" (kanikradat), crying out excessively.
The form *dādharti* and others are derived as irregularities (*nipātana*) from the root *kandary* (or *kandūr*) followed by the suffix *śatṛ*.

Having an upward ridge, rising higher and higher, it moves along. The unconscious Brahman, which is beyond the reach of the mind, the sovereign, the form of the overflowing ritual act— the abode of light belonging to both Mitra and Varuṇa— youths, mingling together and placing [it] upon that abode of theirs, thus praising it, extolling the origin of your two splendors,
have taken delight in it and serve it.
The meaning is that human beings praise the sun’s action—consisting of its supportless movement through the atmosphere—as being dependent upon Varuṇa and Mitra.
May the two milch-cows, the swift ones, nourish Māmateya, the lover of prayer, upon this summit.
Knowing the sacred ordinances, one should beg for food; one should not neglect the progeny of Savitṛ nor Aditi.

The milch-cows have caused Māmateya Arvanyas, the lover of prayer, to swell with nourishment at this height. May he, knowing the sacred ordinances, beg for food; may he, seeking to win her over with his mouth, protect Aditi. ||6||

May the milch-cows, protecting—that is, pleasing—me, the son of Mamatā named Dīrghatamas, who am beloved of Brahman, most dear to the sovereign ritual act, or the one who gratifies the sovereign Agni, cause me to swell with milk in this, my own udder. May they nourish me fully.
In the causative of the root *pyā*, the change to *pī* is Vedic.
The meaning is that they protect us by means of the milk flowing downwards which is to be offered by you two;
for so says the Śruti: "The *payasyā* [offering] is for Mitra and Varuṇa" (TS 7.5.22.1).

Thus, Dīrghatamas—knowing the *vayunāni*, that is, the knowledges concerning the performance of rites, and understanding that the remainder of the oblation is to be consumed—should beg (*bhikṣeta*) from you with his mouth (*āsā*) to consume such food (*pitvaḥ*), that is, the remnant of the oblation (*hutaśiṣṭa*).
Furthermore, while serving you both, may he drive away [evil] and protect this unbroken, complete, and undiminished rite;
that is to say, he should act so as to beg for what remains and to preserve the rite by its completion—this is the sense of "apīyayan."
1. The place is the abode of Ṅa-jha. 2. We do not see Ṅa-ca. 3. Nevertheless (jha).
4. *kṣa-ṅa-a-ṭa-gṛṇantaḥ*: praising, i.e., sounding forth intensely. 5. *jha-tejaḥ-prabhāvam iti*: [referring to] the power and majesty of their splendor.
6. *kṣa-jha1-a-ṭa*: "intensely" (*prakarṣeṇa*) is not present [in these versions]. 7. *kṣa-jha1-a-ṭa*: dependent upon Mitra and Varuṇa.
8. *Jha*: In this [mantra], "in oneself" (*svasmin*); *Jha-sasmin*: "in oneself" (*svasmin*). 9. *Jha*: After that, from the father (*pituḥ*), of the remnant of the oblation (*hutaśiṣṭasya*).
10. *Kṣa-ṅa-jha1-a-ṭa*: This rite (*karma*) should be protected (*uruṣyeta*) and guarded (*rakṣeta*); *Jha*: By another, this rite should be protected and guarded.
This is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal sacrifice to Mitra and Varuṇa.
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, come to the enjoyment of our oblation; O Mitra and Varuṇa, come hither" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

O Mitra and Varuṇa, O Gods, may I turn you both toward the enjoyment of our oblation with reverence and with aid. May our prayer be victorious in battles; may our divine rain be easy to cross over. 7. O Mitra and Varuṇa, O Gods, may I turn you both toward the enjoyment of our oblation with reverence and with aid. May our prayer be victorious in battles; may our divine rain be easy to cross over. 7.

O two gods, whose nature is divine, Mitra and Varuṇa— may I turn you both toward the enjoyment of the oblation with reverence, that is, with a hymn characterized by salutation, and with protection as the motive; or rather,
may I turn you toward it with salutation and with this protection.
Furthermore, O Mitra and Varuna, may our *brahma*—the strengthening ritual now being performed—be victorious in battles;

that is to say, by means of this rite, may we overcome our enemies. Moreover, may our celestial rain—that which exists in the sky—be *supārā*, meaning a perfect deliverer [from drought]. This is the sense of the remaining words.
The sense is that when there is rain, the completion of ritual actions occurs through means such as rice and other crops.
"We worship you two" (yajāmahe vām): this four-verse hymn is the fourteenth [sūkta], composed by Dīrghatamas, in the Triṣṭubh meter, dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
"We worship the fourfold"—
this is the Anukramaṇikā (index).
The application is based on internal indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
We worship you two, the great ones, with common accord through oblations and salutations, O Mitra and Varuṇa;
with clarified butter, O you who drip with ghee, especially when the Adhvaryus bring offerings to you for us with our prayers.
We worship you two, the great ones, with offerings and with reverent salutations, O Mitra and Varuṇa, who are well-pleased.
With clarified butter—O you two who drip with clarified butter! Now, when the Adhvaryu priests bring [the oblation] to you with our prayers. 1.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two who drip with ghee, the pourers of ghee—great and mighty as you are, we, the sacrificers and the officiating priests, worship and honor you. Of what sort are we?
We are *sajoṣas*, endowed with common affection.
By what means? That is stated:
by *havyebhiḥ*, such as the *puroḍāśa* cakes and so forth; and by *namobhiḥ*, characterized by acts of salutation (*namaskāra*).
Furthermore, "adha" means "api ca," and "yat" signifies "yasmāt kāraṇāt" (for which reason).
1. O you two who bring to completion (*pārayitrī*) and bring to fulfillment (*samāpayitrī*) the ritual action (*karman*).

2. O you two who cause the flowing of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and sacrificial oil (*ājya*); [variant *kṣa1*: O you two who cause the flowing of the sacrificial oil]. 3. With hymns characterized by salutations (*namaskāra*), with clarified butter as the flowing substance, and with milk, sacrificial oil, Soma, and so forth (or, according to variant *kṣa-na-ṭa*: with oblations consisting of milk, sacrificial oil, Soma, and so forth), we worship and honor you both perfectly; [variant *jha*: with hymns characterized by salutations].
O you two, the Adhvaryus— our own Adhvaryus as well (the word *na* here having the sense of "also")—
they too nourish and sustain [you] with their *dhītis*, that is, their own ritual acts; therefore, we sacrifice.
This well-fashioned hymn, like a dwelling, approaches you as an offering; O Mitra and Varuṇa, it goes forth to you.
The Hotṛ-priest anoints the two sacrifices at the assemblies, desiring to win your favor, O showerers of blessings, through his patronage.

Praise is for you; it is not a mere impulse toward your abode. O Mitra and Varuṇa, this well-fashioned hymn anoints you when the Hotar-priest anoints you at the assemblies. May the patron, seeking to win your favor, O mighty ones, desire your grace.

"O Mitra and Varuṇa, I am merely forming the intention—'I shall perform the introduction and prelude of the sacrifice pertaining to you two'—but no actual performance has taken place; no cruel application has been carried out. By that much alone, I have reached your *dhāma*, your abode of splendor. And I am a *suvṛkti*, one who offers beautiful praise, seeking your acceptance."

Whenever, in the sacrificial assemblies (*vidatha*) or at the sacrifices (*yajña*), this *hotṛ*— the officiant who performs the oblation— or this *adhvaryu* anoints you both with the offering (meaning he approaches and performs the oblation);
or alternatively, the *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods by that name, anoints you both— that is, makes you manifest— by means of the *śastra* hymns and other rites.

Then the sage, knowing your greatness and desiring to perform a sacrifice—wishing to offer it—says: "O you two showerers of desires (*vṛṣaṇau*), I [approach] *sumnam*, the happiness belonging to you, characterized by divinity; 'I approach' is the ellipsis."
The cow Aditi has overflowed for the sake of Truth and for the people, O Mitra and Varuṇa, as she offers the oblation.
The man who bestows the gift, honoring the sacrifice at the assembly, impels it like a human Hotar-priest.

The cow has swelled for the sake of the people who follow the cosmic order, O Aditi, O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who partake of the oblation. When the human priest, offering the oblation, honors you both at the assembly, he impels you like a Hotar-priest. 3.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, [I offer] this oblation for the sake of the sacrifice connected with you, for the giver of the oblation.
In the word *āmanin*, [the suffix] *vic* is applied by the rule *āto manin*. In the sense of "becoming," the elision of the vowel *ā* occurs by the rule *āto dhātoḥ*.

For the person who performs the sacrifice, the cow—the milch-cow, the nourisher, Aditi, the non-deficient, and the one rich in milk—has swelled again and again with her milk; may she continue to overflow.
The form *pyāyate* is the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) of the root *pī*, used in the sense of a Vedic prayer; the substitution of *pī* for *pā* occurs by the rule "liḍyaḍeśaśca."
The meaning is that [the gods protect] the sacrifice consisting of oblations such as *payasyā* (curd-mixture) and others, as well as the sacrificer who possesses such offerings.

If one asks "at what time?", he says: "When (*yat*)," that is, whenever "he," the famous king named Rātahavya, "honoring" (*saparyan*) you through praise, "like a human Hotṛ"—that is, like the officiant of that name belonging to a human sacrificer—"impels" (*hinoti*) you both in the assembly (*vidathe*), i.e., at the sacrifice, by means of oblations and so forth, thereby pleasing you.
Then he said, "He has drunk."
1. O Adhvaryus, our own, as well as yours—O Adhvaryu!—[we offer] to us.

2. [We worship] with ghee, clarified butter, and so forth, for us, the sacrificer. 3. We sacrifice. (Variants: kṣa, ṅa, jha, ña, ṭa; yuvām; asme; asmadīyāḥ; adhvaryavaḥ; na; adhvaryo; api; jha-te; api; ghṛtaiḥ; ājyādibhiḥ; asme; yajamānāya; yajāmahe.)
Or alternatively:

in whatever manner or by which means you two, like Adhvaryus—by means of *dhītayaḥ*, that is, by your own ritual acts—bring (*bharanti*), or rather bring (*bharathaḥ*), for us (*asme*), meaning toward us or our sacrifice;
the plural number is used for honorific purposes.
"Thus we sacrifice"—this is the meaning.

(The portion of the text beginning with "bharanti" and ending with "ityarthaḥ" does not exist. 4. Being embraced by you—this is the meaning. (In the variants kṣa, ṅa, jha, ña, ṭa, and yu, it is "yuṣmān"; in jha1, it is "yuṣmat").

Moreover, may the all-wealthy [gods] cause the soma-juice, the cows, and the divine waters to swell for you both. And may the ancient Lord of this [world] grant us a share; drink of the milk of the cow.

Moreover, may the Soma-juice, the cows, and the divine waters cause you both to swell among those who offer all wealth. And so, may the ancient Lord of this house enjoy and drink of our milk from the cow.

Moreover, O Mitra and Varuṇa, may the radiant cows and the waters—the waters that cause rice and other crops to flourish—cause you both to swell with nourishment for the sake of all subjects characterized as sacrificers, during the *maghā* constellations which are to be enjoyed by you. And furthermore, let Agni, the ancient protector and giver of this sacrifice belonging to us, be the one who bestows [the fruit].
Because all sacrificial oblations (*havis*) are offered into the fire,
the etymological explanation of that word is as follows.
And so another mantra says: "O Indra and Agni, whether you are on the lowest earth, on the middle one, or on the highest" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.108.9).
In the Taittirīya as well, beginning with "He who is on this earth by his life-span," it continues, "He who is on the second earth, on the third earth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.12.1).
Therefore, the word "earth" (pṛthivī) denotes all three worlds.

Furthermore, that Viṣṇu who "askabhāyat"—that is, propped up or established as their support—the "uttaram sadhastham," meaning the highest, most elevated, and most extensive common abode, namely the intermediate space (antarikṣa) which serves as the locus for the three worlds;
by this it is stated that he created the three worlds as well, which rest upon the intermediate space.
Or alternatively:
That Viṣṇu who measured out—that is, fashioned in various ways—the earthly *rajāṃsi*, the regions connected with the earth, namely the worlds situated beneath the earth;
for the word *rajas* denotes "worlds," as Yāska has stated: "The worlds are called *rajāṃsi*.

Furthermore, he who propped up, that is, established and created, the higher, more elevated *sadhastha*—the common dwelling place suitable for the cohabitation of the doers of meritorious deeds, consisting of the six worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
The suffix *bha*, prescribed by the rule "skambheḥ stambhu-stambhu," undergoes the substitution of *śāyac* by way of irregularity (*vyatyaya*) according to the rule "chandasi śāyaj api."

Alternatively, he measured out the worlds by means of "earthly" (*pārthivāni*)—that is, by means of particles (*rajas*) caused by the earth; the meaning is that he measured the three worlds beginning with *bhūr*.
Since the other worlds exist for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma acquired on earth, they have that [earth] as their cause.
Furthermore, that which is the "higher" (uttara), meaning most excellent, situated above all worlds,
and superior because there is no returning from it;
that "common abode" (sadhastha)— the shared dwelling place of the worshippers, namely Satyaloka— he "propped up" (askabhāyat), meaning he established it firmly.
Doing what? "Tredhā vicakramāṇaḥ": stepping out threefold, traversing in various ways the worlds created by himself.
Viṣṇu’s threefold wandering is well known from such Vedic scriptures as "This [world] Viṣṇu has stepped out" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.22.17).
Therefore, I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of that Viṣṇu, who is *urugāya*— either being praised by the vast [gods] or being praised exceedingly— and who has performed such acts.
In the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), when there is an excess of Soma, the *śastra* must be introduced.

In that case, "pra tat" is the *anurūpa*. This is prescribed in the section on "excess of Soma" (*somātireka*) in the Sūtra: "The *stotriya* and *anurūpa* are 'pra tad viṣṇuḥ stavate vīryeṇa'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.7).
In the section concerning "one desiring sovereignty through the Vājapeya," it is stated in the Sūtra: "'pra tatte adya śipiviṣṭa nāma pra tadviṣṇuḥ stavate vīryeṇa'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.9).
For that heroic deed Viṣṇu is praised, like a terrifying beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains;
in whose three wide strides all the worlds abide.
For that heroic deed Viṣṇu is praised; like a terrible beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains, in whose three wide strides all living beings abide. 2.
Since it will be stated later, "of whom," it is understood that "he" is meant.
That one of great majesty is praised—i.e., he is lauded by all—with his own heroism, that is, through heroic deeds of the nature previously described.
In the object (karman), the suffix śap is used by way of transposition (vyatyaya).
An illustration regarding being praised for one's vigor (*vīrya*):
like a "deer" (*mṛgaḥ*), that is, like a lion or similar beast;

just as a lion—who is a hunter of his own adversaries, "terrible" (*bhīmaḥ*) meaning fear-inspiring, "wandering on the earth" (*kucaraḥ*) meaning a performer of contemptible acts such as violence or one who goes to inaccessible regions, and "dwelling on mountains" (*giriṣṭhāḥ*) meaning staying in high places such as mountains—is praised by all.

Regarding this meaning, the *Nirukta* states: "Terrifying like a wild beast, roaming, dwelling in the mountains; like a wild beast, terrifying, roaming, dwelling in the mountains; 'wild beast' [is derived] from the root *mṛg* (to seek); 'terrifying' because people are afraid of him. [The commentary continues: "He is a great-souled one (*mahātman*)."

2. *kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-ja-ṭa* read thus. 3. In *kṣa-ya-ṭa*, the phrase "one desiring sovereignty by means of the Vājapeya sacrifice: ... by means of vigor" is absent. 4. In *kṣa-jha-1-la-ṭa*, it reads "that Viṣṇu, of whom... (*tad viṣṇur yasyeti*).
5. [The name] is according to the form mentioned in the previous mantra beginning with *ṅa-kṣa-jha-ṭa*.
Bhīṣma also [is derived] from this very [root].

Regarding "kucara": the action of moving (*cara*) is contemptible; furthermore, it is a designation for one who does not move about in this world, or alternatively, one who does not move about in the body (*kāya*).

“*Girikṣā*, *giristhāyī*, *giriḥ*, *parvataḥ*, *samudrorṇaḥ*—he becomes possessed of joints (*parvavān*), for a mountain (*parvata*) is so called because it fills (*pṛṇāti*) or delights (*prīṇāti*)” (Nirukta 1.20).
In the same way, this [Deity] is also a *mṛga*, a seeker after enemies; he is *bhīma*, terrifying, the source of fear for all.
His manifestation as a limb of the Supreme Lord is well known from such scriptural passages as, “From fear of Him the wind blows” (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.8.1).

Furthermore, he is a "kucara," one who performs despicable acts such as the slaying of enemies, or one who wanders through all lands (*ku*)— that is, throughout the three worlds— or likewise a "girikṣāḥ," one who dwells upon the high ground like a mountain (*giri*). Alternatively, he is one who always abides in speech (*giri*), consisting of mantras and the like.
Such is He who is praised by virtue of His own majesty.

Furthermore, that Viṣṇu is praised in whom "all beings" (viśvā bhuvanā)—that is, all classes of living creatures—dwell, resting upon His "three wide strides" (uruṣu vikramaṇeṣu), meaning His three expansive steps.
By the word "beings," His intermediate forms, such as the worlds beginning with Bhūr, are also implied.
Thus, [he pervades] the fourteen worlds, all the universes (*viśva*), and even all the classes of beings residing therein;
[and] the three realms (*tridhātu*).
*Tridhātu* is the collective term for the three realms.
He supported—that is, he sustained—[the world] in such a way that it was distinguished by the three elements of earth, water, and fire;
because [the root *dhṛ*] belongs to the *tuji*-class, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable.
The meaning is that he brought it into existence.

In the Chāndogya Āraṇyaka, after describing the creation of the three elements—“It created fire; it solidified that as food; those waters reflected”—the process of *trivṛtkaraṇa* (triplication) is established through the passage beginning: “Come, let me make each of these three deities threefold” (Chā.
U. 6.3.2–3). Alternatively, the construction may be understood as:
“He who has the three constituents (*tridhātu*) [creates] the three times (*kālatraya*) or the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) as the support (*dhāra*)”; such is the connection.
In the *Atithyā* [offering], the verse beginning with "tadasya" serves as the principal *yājyā*.
This is prescribed in the section titled "Now the *Atithyā*" in the Sūtra: "idaṃ viṣṇurvi cakrame tadasya priyambhi pātho aśyāma" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.5).
May we attain that beloved food of his, where men devoted to the gods rejoice.
For that wellspring of honey is indeed in the highest step of Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one; for he is our kinsman.

May we, O men, attain that beloved domain of his where those seeking the gods rejoice—for he is indeed the kinsman of the wide-striding one; for in the highest step of Viṣṇu is that wellspring of honey. 5. That; of him; beloved; toward; the path; may we attain; O men; where; god-seeking; they rejoice; of the wide-striding one; he; for; kinsman; thus; of Viṣṇu; in the step; supreme; of honey; the wellspring. 5.

The "path" (*pāthaḥ*)—which is dear to this great Viṣṇu, beloved by him, and renowned as that which is to be served by all—is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). For Yāska has stated: "‘Path’ is the intermediate space; it is explained by [the root] *path* (to go)" (Nirukta 6.7).
The meaning is the imperishable world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
May I attain; may I pervade.
That very state is further specified:

in that place where men who are "devayavas"—those desiring the self, Viṣṇu, whose nature is luminosity, and who seek to reach Him through sacrifice, charity, and other means—rejoice and experience satisfaction.
The syntactical connection is "I shall drink that.
That very [place] is further qualified:

in the supreme, most excellent, unsurpassed, and purely blissful station (pada) of Viṣṇu—the Supreme Lord who, as the one of wide strides (Urukrama), pervades the entire universe by assuming various forms—there exists a spring (utsa), a flow of sweetness (madhvaḥ).

"May we behold that [state] where there is no fear of hunger, thirst, old age, death, rebirth, and so forth, and where enjoyments such as streams of nectar are obtained by mere thought"— this is the meaning.
He says that there is nothing superior to this:

"In this way"—that is, in the manner thus described—he is indeed the kinsman; he is truly the benefactor and well-wisher of all meritorious deeds. His status as a kinsman is established by the Vedic scripture: "And he does not return," referring to those who have attained the state from which there is no return.
The word *hi* serves to indicate that this is well-known from all the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other sources.
"We desire to go to those abodes of yours, where there are many cattle that do not fail.
There, indeed, the supreme station of the wide-striding Bull shines forth abundantly."
We desire to go to those dwellings of yours both, where the many-horned, tireless cattle are; for there, indeed, that highest step of the wide-striding Bull shines down abundantly.

1. *Ca* signifies the three bodies (*mūrtti*) of the three realms (*tridhātu*). 2. *Kṣa*, *jha*, *ḷa*, *ja*, and *ṭa* signify the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*); alternatively, it means difficult to protect (*durūpapālana*). [Note: The variant reading *durupāṃ pālanam* for *kṣa-na-ṭa* appears to be a scribal error.]
3. *Kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa*: Of the sweet supreme bliss which is of the nature of nectar.

4. *Kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa*: Beneficial and a binder. 5. *Kṣa-na-ṭa*: Because of the non-return [to saṃsāra] upon attaining that; *kṣa-tasya padaṃ prāptānām anāvṛtteḥ*: because there is no returning for those who have attained its state.
6. The state of being a binder (*bandhakatva*) [is expressed by] *kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa*.

O you two, the wife and the sacrificer (*patnīyajamānau*), for your sake (*yuṣmadartham*), we desire (*uśmasi*)—that is, we pray to Viṣṇu—that those various well-known dwellings (*vāstūni*), places suitable for a pleasant residence, may go (*gamadhyai*)—that is, for your journey—to them. This is the meaning.
Having said "those," he asks "which ones? and says:

"In which" (yatra)—that is, in which dwellings—"the cows"—meaning the rays—are "many-horned," that is, possessed of extreme height or worthy of being resorted to by many; and "unwearied" (ayāsaḥ), meaning moving or extending very far.
Or else:
*Yāsaḥ* means those who go;
that is, those who are not like that,
meaning they are endowed with extreme radiance.

Regarding this, it is said: here, in this heavenly world which serves as the foundation for the dwelling, the supreme (*paramam*), unsurpassed (*niratiśayam*) station (*padam*) of Viṣṇu—the wide-striding (*urugāyasya*), the showerer of desires (*vṛṣṇaḥ*), who is to be praised and celebrated by many great-souled ones—is manifesting (*avabhāti*), shining forth by its own majesty, and is exceedingly abundant (*bhūri*). This station is well-known throughout the *Purāṇas* and other texts as that which is to be reached. Yāska explains that in this mantra, the word *go* signifies a ray of light.

Thus it is explained by this commentary: "We desire those abodes of yours for our journey, where there are cows with many horns—*bhūri* being a name for 'much,' as it prevails over what exists; *śṛṅga* is derived from the root *śri* (to resort), or *śru* (to hear), or *śnā* (to destroy), or it means 'shining forth from a shelter,' or 'protruding from the head'; *ayāsaḥ* means 'those who go. There, the supreme station of that wide-striding Viṣṇu, whose movement is great, shines forth abundantly, situated in the highest distance. *Pāda* is derived from the root *paṭh* (to study/to reach). (Nirukta 2.7).

The six-verse hymn beginning with “pra vaḥ pāntam” is the sixteenth; it belongs to Dīrghatamas, is composed in the Jagatī meter, and because it was stated previously that "it is indeed Vaiṣṇava," it is dedicated to Viṣṇu.
However, the first [verse] has Indra as its deity.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: "‘Pra vo jāgatam’ and ‘tvam indraś cādya stvaḥ’ [are the hymns].
Their application has been stated for the recitation of the *stomātiśaṃsana* during the *abhiplava* days of the *ukthya* sacrifices.
Sing forth with devotion to the drinking of your soma-juice for the sake of the Hero Viṣṇu, who are worthy of praise—
those two invincible ones who stand upon the ridges of the mountains like a great, well-trained steed.

Sing forth with prayer for the protection of your soma-juice; praise the heroic Viṣṇu! Those two who, invincible, have taken their stand upon the ridges of the mountains like two horses on a straight path.

O Adhvaryus and others, prepare—that is, accomplish with excellence—the *andhas* (soma-juice), which is the food in the form of soma, that belongs to you, which has the nature of protection or is worthy of being drunk.
For whom? For the great (*mahaḥ*), heroic (*śūrāya*), and valorous Indra; and for Viṣṇu, the pervasive one, who desires praise (*dhiyāyate*) through his intellect.
What is the distinction between these two? It is said:
those two, Indra and Viṣṇu, [are the lords] of the *parvatas*—meaning those that swell or those that fill.

The word *parvata* has been etymologically explained by Yāska as follows: "A *parvata* is 'possessing joints' (*parvavān*); furthermore, a joint (*parva*) is from the root *pṛṇāti* (to fill) or *prīṇāti* (to please)."
On the summit—that is, the elevated region—of the worlds characterized as previously described;
that is to say, in all worlds.
Alternatively, on the elevated region of the clouds.
The word *parvata* has been mentioned among the names of clouds. There, those two remained; they stood. Of what kind were they?
"Unassailable" means not to be deceived by others, and for that very reason "great," meaning both are vast;
or alternatively,
"in the great [light]"— the connection is with "leading along" within one's own majesty and splendor.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a noble horse (*arvan*), swift and capable of reaching a desired destination;
just as one mounts a high place by means of it, so too have they ascended to a lofty station.
Therefore, worship them with these two.
This is the optional *yājyā* verse for the third *savana*, which is outside of the *soma* [pressing].
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "Or the *yājyā* is 'veṅamithā samaraṇaṃ śimīvatoḥ'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.7).

1. *jha*: the couple, wife and husband; *patnījamānī*. 2. *ca*: as the sun; *taraṇitvena*; *jha*: as that which is to be meditated upon; *mantavyatvena*. 3. *ca*: of you two; *vāṃ yuvayoḥ*. 4. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: in all the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth. 5. *ka-kha-ja-ṇa-ta-pha-va-saṃbandhinām*: of those related to [the aforementioned]. 6. *kṣa-ṅa-ma-ṭa*: in the Satyaloka. 7. *kṣa-ṅa-ja-ṭa*: the name "Megha" (Cloud); in the list of its synonyms, it is "Parvata" (Mountain) or "Giri" (Mountain), according to *ṅa* [which reads] "nāmasu" (in the names). 8. *kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-ja-ṭa*: by means of the horse-like speed (*arvatā*) like the wind (*pavanavat*). "O Indra and Viṣṇu, your impetuous encounter, full of vigor, protects the one who presses the Soma."
That which is being fixed for a mortal—do you two protect the swift tongue of the flame.

The brilliant encounter of the two impetuous ones, Indra and Viṣṇu—O drinkers of the pressed juice, may it protect you both! You protect that which is aimed at a mortal from the bow of Kṛśānu, even as it is being released from the archer's hand. || 2 ||

O Indra and Viṣṇu, of you two who possess *śimī*—that is, who possess the performance of acts such as granting desired boons—the sacrificer, having drunk the Soma remaining after the oblation (*sutapāḥ*), protects, preserves, and honors through sacrifice this *tveṣa* (blazing) *samaraṇa* (proper movement toward the goal).
Or alternatively:

O you two who possess *śimī*—that is, who possess acts such as striking—the sacrificer protects, preserves, and praises this *tveṣa* (blazing), *samaraṇa* (proper mutual movement) of you two, which is endowed with valor and consists of the rending of clouds for the sake of bestowing rain.
What is the distinction between these two? It is said:

O Indra and Viṣṇu, for the mortal—the human sacrificer who offers oblations—you two protect (*uruṣyathaḥ*) the food and other provisions that are to be bestowed (*pratidhīyamānam*), which are of the nature of fruit, mobile (*asanām*), and characterized by being granted; [you protect them] from the presence of *kṛśānu*, the fire, which is either the desired protector or the destroyer of enemies. The meaning is that, having accepted the oblation offered into the fire, you shall grant the fruit through that very medium without interruption.

These [waters] increase his great manly power; he brings down the two mothers for the sake of seed and enjoyment. The son establishes the lower and the higher name of the father, and a third in the luminous realm of heaven.

These [waters] increase his great manly power; he brings the two parents down for the sake of seed and enjoyment. The son establishes the lower and the higher name of the father in the third luminous realm of heaven.

Those well-known oblations in the form of Soma, offered by the sacrificer, increase—indeed, they cause to grow—the great, manly deed (*pausya*) and the power of this Indra, which is of the nature to be described hereafter.
Or, *īm* may be used without specific meaning.
And that Indra brings down—that is, he causes to reach fully—the two Mothers, Heaven and Earth, with the capacity generated by the drinking of Soma.
For what purpose?
For the sake of *retas*, that is, for the capacity of living beings to produce offspring such as sons; and for *bhuje*, that is, for their enjoyment or protection.
Where [is this]? That is now stated.

In the luminous orb of the shining Āditya, above—that is, exceeding—the "name," which is the power established in heaven and earth; the "son," the protector of many, all people, [attains this] through the grace of Viṣṇu, the father and protector.
Or alternatively:

Having itself been produced from its own progenitor, the father, it assumes—relative to those two—the name "inferior" (*avara*), meaning the lowly one known as the grandson (*pautra*), and the name "superior" (*para*), meaning the excellent one known as the son (*putra*); and in relation to both of these, it bears the third name, "father" (*pitṛ*).
This is according to the Vedic revelation: "Speech has three seeds: the father, the son, and the grandson" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.6.8.4).
The meaning of this is as follows:
The oblations of Soma poured into the fire reach the solar orb and nourish Indra and Viṣṇu within the head of the twelvefold Sun; those two rain down through the medium of clouds.
By that rain, through the growth of crops and other means, they cause all creatures to increase in the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth; thus, Indra and Viṣṇu are of such great majesty.
From that fire (kṛśānu) characterized by *kṣa-ha-jha-a-ṭa-ta*, and from that fire characterized by *jha-ta*—
we celebrate the manly power of that very one, the protector of the settled, the bestower of gifts, the bountiful,
who with three strides has stepped across the earthly realms for the wide-striding one to live in abundance.

We celebrate that manly deed of his, the deed of the mighty protector who is unassailable and bountiful—the one who, with only three strides, strode across the earthly realms for wide-striding and for life. 4.
We praise—that is, we extol—the various manly deeds (*pauṣyam*), the virility, and the excellence of prowess belonging to this one of great majesty.
Of what sort is he?
He is the lord (*inaḥ*) of all, the protector (*trātṛ*), and the one who is not to be obstructed (*avṛtaka*).
A *vṛka* is a harmful beast of prey and the like;
[the term refers to] one who is free from such [beasts], a *mīḍhvuṣ*, a sprinkler, who is eternally youthful.
Among his praiseworthy exploits, he cites one as an example.
Viṣṇu, who by his power [traversed] the earthly realms— that is,
the worlds beginning with the earth (the word "earth" having been previously cited as denoting all three worlds)—
he stepped out, he strode across, so that they became *uru*, vast and extensive, by means of three strides (*idvigāma*), that is, by three various movements. This is the meaning.
To the one of wide-striding gait, to the one of wide-reaching song, for the sake of life, and for the protection of the three worlds;
or alternatively,
to the one of wide-striding gait.
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
We praise such heroic power of this wide-striding Viṣṇu;
for what purpose?
For living, for the sake of life, and for protection.
Two are the strides of this steed; having ascended them, he who possesses the light of heaven, the mortal, hastens along.
No one dares to approach his third stride, not even the winged birds as they fly through the air.
At his two strides, he of heavenly aspect, for the sake of meditation, stirs with mortal thoughts; no one dares to approach his third stride, not even the winged birds as they fly. 5.

Of this Viṣṇu—the beholder of heaven (*svardṛśaḥ*), or rather the beholder of all that belongs to heaven—there are indeed two strides, two steps. A mortal man, for the sake of attaining all prosperity and so forth, strives toward them; he goes to them, he partakes of them.
The root *bhuraṇyati* belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class and signifies motion, as it is listed among its meanings in the Nirukta (2.14.16) alongside "he moves" (*śavati*).
Because these are well-known, one understands his two strides to be the earthly realm and the intermediate space, due to his arrival through rain.

No mortal whatsoever has ever dared to reach—that is, no one is able to comprehend through their intellect—the third stride of this Viṣṇu in the heavenly world. Not only humans, but even the Maruts, who are seekers of knowledge, [cannot do so].
Of what sort are they?
Falling [from the sky], they are capable of going everywhere;
likewise, no one—neither the winged birds such as Garuḍas who are prone to flying, nor the winds—is able to overcome them.
The arrival of Chapeleṇṭi.
The meaning is that because Satyaloka is extremely remote, it is beyond the range of all [ordinary beings].
1. Viṣṇu is [denoted] by *kṣa-ma-ṭa*.
2. By *ḍa* through the praise of all and so forth.
3. Having made known *kṣa-ma-ṭa*.
With four [steeds] and ninety-nine names, he has sped across the obstacles like a rolling wheel; large-bodied, wide-ranging, and praised by hymns, the youthful son approaches the battle.

Together with four, ninety-nine, and names, he has caused the transgressors to tremble like a revolving wheel. Possessing a vast body, a wide-reaching chariot, and praised by hymns, the youth who is no longer a child comes forth to the invocation.

This Viṣṇu, whose self is the Sun, together with four— meaning ninety-four— parts of time, causes those parts of time so numbered to revolve according to their own names, that is, through his specific modes of impulsion; he causes them to turn like a wheel endowed with many spokes, which, by hurling [the enemy] upon the foe's breast, makes him tremble and whirl, even as he causes those aforementioned divisions of time to tremble and revolve.
The form [duveṣu] is derived from the root *kamp* with the suffix *yaṅ*,
followed by the *luṅ* (aorist) tense and the augment *caṅ*.
What, then, are they said to be?
One year and two solstices (ayana).
There are five seasons,
twelve months,
and twenty-four half-months.
Thirty days and nights;
eight watches (*yāma*s). The twelve ascendants (*lagna*s), beginning with Aries, revolving within a single day—these together constitute ninety-four [units]. The *navīvipat* is nine.
But surely, the sun itself revolves just like the others; how then can it be said that it causes them to revolve?
This is not a fault, because these [luminaries] are within the interior of Āmaka, Dhruva, and Viṣṇu.
Alternatively, because the wandering of others is dependent upon his own wandering, he is said to "cause [them] to wander" himself.
Thus, Viṣṇu, whose nature is time, possesses a vast body (*bṛhaccharīra*), since, in the form of the Virāj, all bodies of gods, humans, and so forth, are his own body.
He demonstrates this very fact of possessing a vast body:
Measuring out— that is, measuring himself in various ways by dividing and establishing himself as gods and animals;
or alternatively,
measuring out with *vṛk* [verses], meaning those accompanied by praise or endowed with mantras.
Although he is all-pervading (*vibhu*), nevertheless, because he is dependent upon devotion, he is measured by means of praise.

Being *vyuva*—meaning either one whose nature is to mix everywhere or who is eternally youthful—he is therefore called *vakumāra*. Such is Mahāviṣṇu, who, being *analpa* (not small), approaches or goes toward the invocation (*vāhava*) to the place of sacrifice.
The hymn beginning with “bhavā mitraḥ,” consisting of five verses and seventeen padas, belongs to Dīrghatamas.
Since it is stated that it is "Jagatī," this [hymn] is also in the Jagatī meter.
And since it is stated that it is "Vaiṣṇava," it is dedicated to Viṣṇu.
The "five existences" (bhavapañca) have been enumerated thus.
This hymn is prescribed for the Acchāvāka at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) during the *ukthya* sacrifice.
It is stated in the section beginning with “But in the *ukthya*, [the verses] of the Hotṛ-priests” (*ukthye tu hotṛkāṇām*) in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (6.1): “*bhavā mitraḥ*, *maṃ vāṃ karmaṇā*.

Regarding the *saumya-caru*, one must sacrifice with clarified butter on both sides; in that case, for the subsequent offering of clarified butter, the original *yājyā* verse is “*uru viṣṇo vikramasva*.”
On the tenth day, however, in its place, the verse "bhavā mitraḥ" is to be employed.
This is prescribed in the section on the "tenth day" in the Sūtra: "In place of the ghee-offering, 'uru viṣṇo vikramasva' and 'bhavā mitraḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.12).

1. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: "ninety-four," meaning ninety plus four. 2. *kṣa-jha-ña-ṭa*: "he causes illness for the sake of casting out"; *ca-pha*: "he causes illness for the sake of casting away. 3. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: "he causes illness."
4. *kṣa-jha-ña-ṭa*: How does this cause illness? *jha-jha*: How does it cause these to become ill? *ṅa*: How does this cause delusion? 5. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: Because of the descent of the head.

Be a friend, one not to be avoided, receiving the offering of clarified butter, possessing abundant splendor, easy to approach, and far-famed—O Viṣṇu, even for the wise man, half of this [world] is yours; your hymn of praise and sacrifice are to be accomplished by the one who possesses the oblation. 1.
"O Viṣṇu, he who is Mitra is not [so called] from non-measuring;

Similarly: "One who is fit for happiness is a *śevyaḥ*, a doer of happiness; one who offers *ghṛta* is a *ghṛtāsutiḥ*.

Or else:
He to whom clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is brought directly is such [a one].

O Viṣṇu, since you are such as you are, therefore this specific hymn (*stoma*) of praise for you is to be offered repeatedly (*adhryaḥ*) by a wise sacrificer—one who knows your majesty;
the meaning is that it is not fully satisfied by being performed only once.
Likewise, your sacrifice (*yajña*) is to be propitiated (*rādhyaḥ*) by that same sacrificer who possesses the oblation (*haviṣmat*).
Or rather:
by a learned Hotṛ priest the hymn of praise is to be perfected, and by one possessing oblations the sacrifice is to be perfected—
[he who] gives to Viṣṇu, the ancient ordainer, the most recent, and the one who possesses excellent wisdom.
He who proclaims the great birth of this Great One shall indeed surpass even his own peer in glorious renown.

Whoever offers gifts to Viṣṇu—the ancient, the ordainer, the most recent, the one who knows auspicious thoughts—whoever speaks of the great birth of this Great One, he indeed shall surpass even his equal in glories. 2.
"Whoever is the central one"—that is, for the primordial, meaning the eternal;
"for the piercer," the creator of the manifold world; "the most recent," meaning eternally new and exceedingly beautiful;
or "for the one worthy of praise," who is born of himself (*sumajjāni*).
The root *iṇ* takes the suffix *ṇādika*;

One who gladdens exceedingly is *suman*;
one whose wife (*jāyā*) is such is described as "having such a wife.
This means: to Him, the Lord of Śrī, whose nature is to gladden the entire world.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the substitution of *niṅ* [for the final syllable of *ajāyā*] occurs according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.134;
this is a compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*). [Subsequently,] there is elision [of the penultimate vowel] before a *val* sound.
"He offers"—that is, he presents oblations and other offerings—to "Viṣṇu," the pervasive one who is "of hymns" (ukthakāya).
Furthermore, may the "great birth"—the vast, worshipful origin of this "great Viṣṇu" of exalted power, appearing in forms such as Hiraṇyagarbha—"come to pass.

He too—the giver and the praiser—being endowed with *aśravobhiḥ*, that is, with food or with fame, reaches and attains *yujyam cit*, that very state which must be reached by all, *abhy asat*, approaching it directly.
1. [Variant readings: *kṣa-ṅa-ca-jha* and *1-ja-ṭa-pha* read *āsūyate*, meaning "is led toward";

O singers, nourish with your birth that ancient one, the embryo of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), just as you know him.
Knowing his very name, proclaim it; O Viṣṇu, may we partake of your great benevolence.

Him, O singers, as the ancient one, according to your knowledge—fill him with praise from his very birth, for he is the embryo of Cosmic Order (Ṛta). Knowing even his name, proclaim it! O Viṣṇu, may we enjoy the benevolent favor of you, the Great One. 3.

The worshippers [praise] that very Viṣṇu—him who is primordial (*pūrvya*), established from the beginningless past, the "embryo of Ṛta" (the embryo of sacrifice), meaning he has arisen as the very soul of the sacrifice;
for according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.1.2.13), "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice.
Or else:

The meaning is: "the embryo of *ṛta* (truth/water)," that is, the cause of the embryo, which produces water—according to the Smṛti text, "In the beginning, he created the waters alone" (Manu 1.8). Knowing Viṣṇu who is such as this, "as you know him," so "by birth"—that is, by yourselves alone and not through any external means such as gaining wealth—"satisfy him" with hymns and the like; the meaning is: satisfy him to the full extent of his majesty as you come to know it.
The form *videta* is the middle voice plural. In the *saṃhitā* reading of the phrase *vida ṛtasya*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*.

Furthermore, regarding this high-souled Viṣṇu, "knowing even his name"—that is, his designation which is to be meditated upon by all and which establishes his universal nature, namely the name "Viṣṇu"—and understanding it as the bestower of the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*), "proclaim it fully," that is, speak of it and celebrate it on all sides.
Alternatively:

"O you who understand that what is called 'sacrifice' (yajña) is indeed the bowing down (*namana*) to Viṣṇu himself—the transformation [of that bowing] into the form of the *iṣṭi* and other rites, or into the form of the sacrificial materials and deities, for the sake of securing heaven and liberation for all—do you proclaim it; speak; praise!
[In this construction, the verb *vac* takes the imperative (*loṭ*), with the Vedic substitution of *ślu* for *śap*.]
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," the substitution of *i* for the reduplication occurs.
As before, there is the substitution of *tan*.
Having now perceived it directly, he says:

O Viṣṇu, O God who is the soul of all, we—the sacrificers—worship and serve your great and nectar-like benevolent wisdom. In the ritual of leading forward Agni and Soma, this verse beginning with "tamasya rājā" should be employed. This is prescribed in the section on "Leading forward Agni and Soma" in the Sūtra: "He should begin with 'tamasya rājā varuṇastamadhinestvārtham'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.10).
King Varuṇa and the Aśvins attend to the wisdom of this Marut, the wise one; he possesses the most excellent skill for the finding of light, and Viṣṇu, accompanied by his friend, opens up the stall.
King Varuṇa, the Aśvins, and the Maruts attend to the will of this wise one. He has maintained supreme skill for the finder of light; and Viṣṇu, accompanied by his friend, opens the enclosure.
Of Māruta:
the host of the Maruts, the officiating priests, is "Māruta"; [the word] "tad-dhataḥ" means struck by that.
The possessive suffix (*matvartha*) is elided.

[The meaning is: "of the *maruts*, the gods"—belonging to them, "the *vedhasas*, the wise ones"—"of this sacrificer," "that well-known" *kratu*, the sacrifice, Viṣṇu, who is of the nature of the sacrifice;
for according to the Vedic scripture, "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice."
The king, shining as Varuṇa, serves [him];
the two Aśvins serve that very sacrifice (kratu);
other gods also serve and attend upon him.
Furthermore: "Viṣṇu [says]: 1. By the remainder of *kṣa-ma-ṭa-ba*, speak.
2. *Kṣa-jha-la-a-ṭa-te*: that greatness (*mahaḥ*) is Your name."
3. We worship you, who possess the splendor of *kṣa*, *ḍha*, *la*, *ja*, *ṭa*—or rather, we worship you, the great (*mahaḥ*) one, the possessor of excellent wisdom (*sumati*).

Pervading through the three libations (*savanatrayādhamana*), Viṣṇu, being "accompanied by friends" (*sakhivān*), that is, joined by the sacrificers and others as his friends, has "upheld" (*dādhāra*) the "supreme" (*uttamam*), most excellent "knower of days" (*aharvidam*)—meaning the producer of heaven—and "skill" (*dakṣam*), which is strength in the form of the capacity to bestow the fruit [of action].
Furthermore, "vrajaṃ ca meghaṃ ca" [he uncovers both the enclosure and the cloud].
"Vraja" is a name for a cloud, because it is listed among its names in the statement, "vrajaḥ caraḥ" (Nirukta 1.10.11).
He uncovers that [cloud] for the sake of water; he makes it free from obstruction (*apagatāvaraṇa*).
Because it is through the offering of oblations that the sacrifice itself produces rain;
or alternatively,

Varuṇa and the others attend upon the ritual act (*kratu*)— consisting of protection and other such functions— of the wise ordainer (*vedhas*), the arranger (*ṛtviṣṇu*), who is the host of the Maruts (*māruta*).
Because protection depends upon that [power],

and being "accompanied by friends"— that is, endowed with allies such as Indra and the Maruts— he maintained "skill" characterized by eagerness, which consists of the capacity for producing rain and so forth;
likewise, he uncovers the "fold."

Viṣṇu, the wise one who dwells in the three realms, having distinguished himself for the sake of companionship with the pious Indra—the most skillful among the skillful—has quickened the noble one; he has caused the sacrificer to participate in his share of the Eternal Order (ṛta). ā | yaḥ | viyārya | sacathāya | dainyaḥ | indrāya | viṣṇuḥ | sukṛtebhyaḥ | sukṛttaraḥ | vedhāḥ | ajinvat | triṣadhasthaḥ | āryam | ṛtasya | bhāge | yajamānam | ā | abhajat || 5 ||
"Viṣṇu," who is "dainyaḥ" (the protector from distress), "divibhavaḥ" (dwelling in heaven), and "sukuttaraḥ" (the most excellent among those who bestow beautiful fruits)— he "āvivāya," that is,
he comes (a form derived from the root *vī*).
For what purpose?
"For companionship, for fellowship, for assistance in the sacrifice.
For whom? For Indra."
Indra is the sacrificer because he causes *irā*—characterized as the oblation—to flow;
for Yāska has stated that this etymology also applies here, saying: "Indra is so called because he bestows *irā*, or because he performs the act of *id*" (*Nirukta* 10.8).
To him, the wide-striding sacrificer, who is a performer of good deeds—that is, a composer of beautiful hymns.

And having arrived, [he said]: "The Creator (Vedhas) is the ordainer of desired fruits; he who dwells in the three seats (Triṣadhastha), endowed with the three stations, possessing the thousandfold abode;
he who stands at the three places of libation (Savanatrayasthāna);
or Viṣṇu, whose three locations begin with the earth."
"He has come to the noble one; he quickens—that is, he pleases—the sacrificer.
The root *jiv* means "to please"; the nasal augment *num* is applied because it ends in the suffix *it*.

For that purpose, the meaning is that he "causes the sacrificer to partake" (ābhajat) in a portion of the *ṛta*— that is, the sacrifice— in the form of the sacrificial remains (*huta-śeṣa*), bringing him near to it. Alternatively,
he causes the sacrificer to partake in the portion— that is, the fruit— of the *ṛta* sacrifice, establishing him therein as its owner.

Among these, the first hymn, "abodhy agniḥ januṣā," consists of six verses; it is addressed to the Aśvins and is composed by Dairghatamas.
Because of the word "but" (*tu*) in the previous statement, "it is in the Jagatī [meter]," this hymn is also in the Jagatī meter.
The other two [verses] are in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The Anukramaṇī states: "Abodhi has six Aśvin verses; there are two Triṣṭubhs at the end.
Its application belongs to the meter produced for the Prātaranuvāka and the Ābhiplavika Śastra.
This is prescribed in the section beginning with "Now the Aśvin [Śastra]" in the Sūtra: "'Abodhyagniḥ', 'jana eṣa sya bhānuḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15).

Agni has been awakened; the Sun rises from his birthplace; the radiant and great Dawn has shone forth with her light. Because of the pervasion of *kha*, *ca*, *pha*. 2. *kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa* serve [him]. 3. *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *ña*, *jha*, *ṭa*: for the purpose of assisting in the sacrifice (*yāga*). 4. *jha*, *ña*: the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); either this ritual act is performed, or Indra is the sacrificer. 5. *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *ña*, *jha*, *ṭa*: having arrived, he is to be gratified. 6. *kṣa*, *ba*, *ṭa*: the meaning is that he brings it to completion. This Agni, being established, belonging to *jmā*—that is, Umā, the earth characterized as the altar (*vedi*)—was awakened (*abodhi*), i.e., brought to consciousness.
"Umā" is a name for the earth; for it is stated in the list of its names: "‘gmā’, ‘umā’" (Nirukta 1.1.3).
Furthermore, the sun rises;
the great earth and the vast dawn, being delightful to living beings by means of its preeminent splendor and radiance, dispels the darknesses, causing them to vanish.
Vaseluṇḍi is a Chāndasa; cheluṅ is also [a Chāndasa].
The augment *āṭ* is applied because of the rule: "It is also seen in the Veda."

From whence this Dawn rises, from whence the Sun, and from whence this Fire awakens—for that reason, O Aśvins, yoke your chariot with two female donkeys (rāsabhī) for the purpose of going to the place of sacrifice, so that it may move toward us.
Likewise, let Savitṛ, the god who authorizes all actions, impel (*prāsāvīt*) the moving world—the multitude of living beings—individually according to their respective duties.
O Aśvins, you two yoke the bull-like chariot; sprinkle our dominion with ghee and with honey. Strengthen our prayer in battles; may we share in the spoils in the contest for booty.
When you two, O Aśvins, yoke your vigorous chariot, sprinkle our dominion with ghee and honey; quicken our prayer in the battles, and may we, O Hero, share in the spoils of war. 2.

O Aśvins, when you two, the showerers of rain, yoke your chariot that rains down [blessings], then sprinkle our *kṣatra*—our power or the class of kṣatriyas—with *ghṛta*, that is, with water, and with *madhu*, that is, with the sweet; the meaning is "strengthen it. Or alternatively: sprinkle it with *ghṛta* in the form of flowing [fluid] and with *madhu*, that is, with nectar (*amṛta*); the meaning is "strengthen our power with the honey situated upon your chariot."

The fact that the chariot of the Aśvins is filled with honey is well known from such passages as “the honey-bearing chariot. Furthermore, in our battles—that is, among our subjects consisting of sons, servants, and so forth—“quicken the *brahma*,” meaning the spiritual power of the Brahmins.
*Pṛtanā* is a name for humans, because it is stated in the list of names [in the *Nighaṇṭu*]: “the *pṛtanās* of Vivasvat” (*Nighaṇṭu* 2.3.25).
Or alternatively:
in the *pṛtanās*, that is, among the enemy subjects, [O] *brahman*—the sovereign lord of them—gladden us; cause us joy.
*Brahman* is a name for food, because it is stated in the list of its names: "The splendor of *brahman*" (*brahma varcaḥ*, Nighaṇṭu 2.7.25).
And we, in battles characterized by the slaughter of heroes—battles joined by the striking down of heroes—may we share and obtain his various kinds of wealth.
May the well-praised three-wheeled chariot, carrying honey, with its two swift horses, the Aśvins, come hither;
may the three-seated, bountiful lord of all prosperity bring welfare to our bipeds and quadrupeds.

May the chariot with three wheels, carrying honey, drawn by swift horses, well-praised, with three seats, wealthy, and possessing all prosperity—may it come hither, O Aśvins, and bring welfare to our bipeds and quadrupeds. 3.

1. *kṣa-jha 1-ja-ṭa*: struck down (*vihataḥ*). 2. *kṣa-jha-ṭa*: of all living beings (*sarvaprāṇinām*). 3. *ha-jha 1*: it covered (*āvṛṇot*); it dispels the darkness (*vicāryati*). 4. *kṣa-jha 1-ja-ṭa*: in the mantra "vṛṇetu luṅi" [the form] is "ghasa," and by the rule "cheluṅ. 5. *ha*: O Aśvins, the two Aśvins (*aśvinā aśvinau*). 6. *kṣa-cha-jha 1-ja-ṭa*: "vaḥ" means belonging to you (*yuṣmatsambandhin*); *kha-va-pha*: belonging to yourself (*svasambandhin*). 7. *kṣa-jha 1-ja-ṭa*: they have joined together (*ayukṣatām*). 8. *kṣa-jha-jha 1-ja-ṭa*: sprinkle (*ukṣataṃ secayatam*). 9. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: in the form of honey (*madhurūpeṇa*); *kṣa 1*: in the form of sweetness (*madhurūpeṇa*). 10. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: many, of various kinds (*bahūni bahuvidhāni*).
May the chariot of the Aśvins come toward us, moving in our direction.

Of what nature is it? It has three wheels, is yoked with three wheels; it carries honey, being the bearer of sweetness; it is equipped with swift-moving horses; it is well-constructed, and for that very reason is praised by us; it has three seats, being provided with three wooden benches of varying heights.
The seat where the charioteer stands is the *vandhuram*.
*Maghavā* means wealthy; for that very reason, he is *viśvasaubhaga*, endowed with all auspiciousness.
May such a chariot of the Aśvins bring *śam*, happiness, to our *dvipada*, meaning offspring such as sons, and to our *catuṣpada*, meaning livestock. May it bring it to us.
The augment *aṭ* is applied at the beginning [of the suffix].
*Sip*.
O Aśvins, bring us nourishment; sprinkle us with your honeyed whip.
Prolong our life-span, wipe away our misdeeds, drive off our enemies, and be our companions.
O Aśvins, bring us strength; sprinkle us with your honeyed whip. Prolong our life-span, wipe away our blemishes, drive off our enemies, and be our companions. 4.

O Aśvins, you two, bring to us strength—either physical power or food capable of sustaining life. Furthermore, sprinkle us with your honeyed whip—that is, with speech endowed with sweetness in the form of granting desired objects—lead us forward. "Whip" (*kaśā*) is a name for speech, as it occurs in that list of names: "Kaśā, Dhiṣaṇā" (Nirukta 1.11.43).
Or rather:
with a whip (*kaśā*) that is honeyed—that is, possessing a sweet rain or endowed with sweetness—may you two sprinkle us (*mimikṣatam*).
"Honey" (*madhu*) is a name for water, because it exists as such a name in the statement, "honey is the soil" (*madhu purīṣam*, Nirukta 1.12.11).
"By striking the horse with the whip, it will quickly come and grant the fruit in the form of rain"—this is the sweetness of the whip.
Furthermore, "āyuḥ" means longevity; "pra tāriṣṭam" means "increase. The root *tṛ* preceded by *pra* has the sense of increasing.
Likewise, "wipe away" (*mr̥kṣatam*) our "stains" (*rapāṃsi*), that is, purify our evils completely;
for Yāska states: "'Rapa' and 'ripram' are names for evil" (Nirukta 4.21).
Furthermore, "drive away" (*sedhatam*) "hostility" (*dveṣaḥ*), meaning destroy the hateful enemies and so forth.
And this is to be understood:

"O you two who are co-existent (*sacābhuvā*), that is, co-arising (*sahabhuvau*) and thus sharing a simultaneous existence in our undertakings (*asmatkāryeṣu sahabhavanavantau*), may you both be; that is to say, may you maintain unanimity.
Due to the division of the sentence, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).
You two indeed place the embryo within all moving things; you two are within all worlds.
O Bulls, you two have impelled Agni from the two horses.

You two indeed place the embryo within moving creatures; you two are within all existing beings. Thus, O Ashvins, you two, the virile ones, have set in motion Agni, the waters, and the lords of the forest. 5.
O Aśvins, you two indeed place the embryo within the *jagatīs*— that is, within the cows that have the nature of moving—

and not only within the cows, but you two also place the embryo within all *bhuvanās*, that is, within all classes of living beings; for by means of growth, [the embryo] nourishes the seed situated within as its own form.

Furthermore, O *vṛṣaṇau*, you two who shower down desires: 1. [with] that which possesses a rain of sweetness (mādhurya); 2. [with] that which impels like a horse (aśvatodinī); according to the reading of jha¹, [with] that which impels (todinī).
3. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-nimṛkṣatam*.
4. From *kṣa-ja-ṭa-bhābhyām* (? [comes] *jha1-kiṃca*.
5. The meaning is: *kṣa-jha1-ja-ṭa-bhajataṃ*.
6. By means of *kṣa*, *ca*, *jha*, *jha*, *ja*, *ṭa*, [and] *bhipaprūpa*; by means of *cha*, *jha₁*, *bhipaprūpa*.
*Yuvam*—you two—*agnim ca apaś ca vanaspatīn ca airayethām*: you two should set in motion Agni, the waters, and the forest trees.

Having taken possession of Agni for the enjoyment of the oblations, and by means of the waters, you two should cause the rain-waters, the plants, the forest trees, and so forth, to flow forth for our sake.
You two indeed are physicians with your medicines; you two are charioteers with your skill in driving.
Therefore, O fierce ones, you bestow sovereign power upon that man who, possessing oblations, beholds you with his mind.

Truly, you two are physicians with your remedies; and indeed, you are charioteers with your skill in driving. And truly, O fierce ones, you bestow sovereign power upon that man who, possessing oblations, beholds you with his mind. 6.

O Aśvins, you two indeed are physicians (bhiṣajau) by means of those medicines (bheṣajaiḥ), for according to the lexicon: "bheṣaja, auṣadha, bheṣajya, agada, and jāyu" [denote] medicine, and "agada" refers to a medicinal remedy therein. By those [means], you two stand as healers.

The particle *ha* is used for the purpose of indicating well-known facts, such as "the Aśvins are indeed the physicians of the gods. Furthermore, the word *rathyebhiḥ* means "by means of those that carry chariots," i.e., by horses; and *rathyā* means "possessing chariots," i.e., having a chariot.
The particle *ha* here is for the purpose of indicating well-known facts, such as "O Aśvins, your chariot [comes hither]" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.118.1).

The specific connection between these two and the chariot is well known from other mantras, such as: "For you two, O Savitṛ and Uṣas, [the chariot] was first [yoked] for the sake of being charioteers; [the chariot] bright and rich in ghee" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.34.10). Furthermore, your *kṣatra*—your power—is indeed *adhi ha*, that is, preeminent.
The word *ha* indicates what is well known.

Since this is so, therefore, O *ugrau*, you two Aśvins of exalted power, to him who is *haviṣmān*—the sacrificer endowed with oblations such as clarified butter and sacrificial cakes—who *dadārśa* (offers) to you with a mind (*manasā*) devoted to you, him you *dhatthaḥ*, you sustain; that is to say, you favor him exceedingly. The intended meaning is: "O you two of abundant strength, having mounted your chariot and come to our place of sacrifice, sustain me, the offerer of oblations, and look upon us in this sacrifice. Thus is the essential purport.

May Vidyātīrthamaheśvara, dispelling the darkness by the illumination of the meaning of the Vedas, grant the four goals of human existence. Thus ends the second chapter of the second book in the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, who bears the burden of the command of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the supreme sovereign of kings and supreme lord who established the path of the Vedas.
1. *Kṣama-la-ṭa-tantra* is the medicine.
2. According to Jha1, there is indeed a connection between these two and a specific type of chariot.
3. According to Jha1, [the meaning is] "you two should doubt us, who have been given by us," or "doubt those who have been given to us."
4. By Kṣajhaṭasāyaṇāmātya.
|| Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa. ||
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas. Now, the third chapter begins.
‘Vasū rudrā’: this is the second hymn with respect to the section (*anuvāka*), consisting of six verses and composed by Dīrghatamas.
Since it was stated previously that "the [first] belongs to the Aśvins," this one also belongs to the Aśvins.
By the rule regarding unspecified meters, it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
The final verse, "dīrghatamā māmateyaḥ," is an anuṣṭubh.
Thus it has been enumerated: "The others are vasus; [the last is] an anuṣṭubh.
Its specific application is worldly.
O Vasus and Rudras, you of many insights, increasing in power, O bulls, grant us protection with your aids;
for when Aucathya praised your wealth, O Dasyas, you two helpers stood forth with your hymn-accompanied assistance.

O Vasus, O Rudras, you of many counsels, increasing in strength—grant us that which is most helpful, O showerers of blessings, for our protection. O wonder-workers, when Aucathya proclaimed your wealth to you with hymns and aids, you stood as his friends.

O Aśvins, you two who are showerers of desires (*vṛṣaṇau kāmānām*), destroyers of obstacles (*dastrā*), and those who ward off what is hostile to us (*asmadrirodhī upakṣapayitārau*), grant us that which is to be given—the fruit desired by us.
Of what nature are you two?
You are the *vasū*, the ones who provide dwelling for all creatures.
Or [the term] "possessing" (vān) means "endowed with wealth" (*vasu*); the possessive suffix (*matup*) is elided. Thus, *rudra* becomes *rudrau*.
It refers to physical suffering or the evil that causes it;
they are the two who melt it away,
or those who utter terrifying sounds in battle.
"Rudra is so called because he roars," says Yāska (Nirukta 10.5). *Purumantau* means "the two who know many things"; the suffix *tun* is added to the root *man* according to the Uṇādi rules.
*Vṛdhantā* means increasing; *vardhamānau* means being augmented by hymns of praise and the like; *abhiṣṭau* means either worshipped with direct intent or those who accomplish what is desired.
The particle *ha* is for the purpose of indicating the well-known nature of the aforementioned qualities.
If one asks, "For what purpose is this given?"— [the answer follows].
Because Dīrghatamas, the son of Ucathya (aucathyaḥ), seeks from you two (vām) wealth (rekṇaḥ)— that is, riches— under the pretext of praise; or rather,
because this sacrificer (ayaṃ yajamānaḥ) will give (dāsyati)— the word "gives" (dadāti) being understood— as food characterized by oblations (havir-lakṣaṇam annam) to you two.
Because you two, O friends, extend [your aid]—that is, you bestow it pre-eminently—by means of *akavābhiḥ*, i.e., by unblamable *ūtī* (instrumental plural), meaning protections;
[here the third case ending is replaced by the long vowel *ī* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*];
therefore, you have become worthy of being seen.

Because you two bestow blessings and because he either prays to you or offers the oblation, therefore the meaning is "you are to be eaten" (or enjoyed). Who shall offer to you both for this very favor? He who seeks wealth, that which is to be placed with reverence at the station of the Cow.
Awaken for us the wealthy inspirations (*purandhi*), as you two move about with a mind that fulfills desires.

Who shall worship you both for this very favor? He who seeks wealth, that he may receive it. With reverence at the station of the Cow, awaken for us riches and abundant thoughts, as you two move with a mind that fulfills every desire.
1. *kṣa-jha-jha* 1-*ja-ṭa* begins. Therein:
O *vasu*, you two who cause to dwell, regarding *vām*, belonging to you both, *asyai sumataye cit*, for this aforementioned kind of *sumati*, that is, for the beautiful intellect (*śobhanabuddhi*).
The word *cit* is used here in the sense of "even" or "also.
Regarding such an intellect—which bestows great fruit even through a very small oblation—for its gratification, who would offer (*dāśat*), who would give, or who would be able to give?
The implication is that this is because of the extreme greatness of your two powers.
The augment *aṭ* is applied to the root *dāśati* in the *leṭ* tense.
How is the excellence of the intellect [to be understood]? That is now explained:

because, in the *pada* of the *go*—that is, in the place of the earth (*bhūmi*), which is to be traversed by all or to be praised, and which takes the form of the sacrificial altar (*vedi*)—according to the Vedic scripture:
"The earth is indeed as large as the altar" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.4.3).

"Gauḥ" is a name for the earth; and thus it is explained in the Nirukta: "Gauḥ is a name of the earth because she has gone far away (*dūraṃ gatā*), or because beings go upon her (*yasyām bhūtāni gacchanti*); or else the letter 'ā' is a formative suffix of the name derived from the root *gā*" (Nirukta 2.5).

In such a place, being entreated by us with reverence (*namasā*)—that is, with an oblation characterized by grain in the measure of a barley-corn—you two maintain (*dhārayathaḥ*) a mind directed toward granting abundant gifts.

From the root *dadhāti* in the present tense (*laṭ*), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73). There is shortening of the vowel of the root. Then, by the rule "āto ḍitaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.81), the substitution of *hi* for the imperative marker occurs.

Since this is so, therefore, for us—for our sake—*revatīḥ*, [the cows] rich in milk and other wealth; *puraṃdhīḥ*, the sustainers of the body and causes of bodily growth; *gāḥ*, the cows; *jigṛtam*, call out to, meaning "give them."
The root *gṛ* means "to sound. This is Vedic; there is *bhlu* (the substitution of *śap*) for *śap*, and the *it* augment (*i*) and shortening of the reduplicated syllable.
Furthermore, those two very [terms] are qualified:
"as if by one who desires.
The word *iva* has the sense of the particle *eva*.
Moving together with a mind intent on fulfilling desires—
meaning they have formed the resolve that the desires of the sacrificer must be fulfilled.
