The root *prā* means "to fill. One who fills according to desire (*kāma*) is a *kāmapraḥ*. [This is derived] by the rule: *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3).
When you two, O sons of Tuḍī, were joined together, you placed Perū in the midst of the flood; may I go to your protection for aid, as a hero goes to battle with his swift horses.

It is fitting, indeed! O Taudhyārya, when the protector [peruḥ] was scattered in the midst of the flood, you two held him fast; may I come unto your protection and refuge, as a hero goes to the battlefield with swift, well-nourished horses. 3.
Regarding this, they relate an ancient history: having defeated King named Taudya in battle, his enemies bound him with ropes and cast him into the middle of the ocean.
Being unable to escape, he praised the Aśvins.
And those two, being pleased, quickly yoked a chariot with horses, went to the ocean, brought him out, and protected him; this is the meaning.
This matter is well-known from another mantra beginning with "The son of Tuḍi invoked the Aśvins" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.117.15), and it is stated here [in that context].
O Aśvins, your chariot—belonging to you both—is indeed yoked; it is yoked with horses.
The word *ha* is intended to indicate its well-known status from other mantras, and it has been cited [elsewhere].
For whom? For the king named Tauḍya, for the purpose of releasing him from that bond.
Where? That is now stated.
In the midst of the watery flood, in the middle of the ocean—he who was cast down, yet having crossed by means of his *pāja* (power), was established, supported, and set firm.
Since this is so, may I attain your protection and refuge; freed from the sufferings of this world, may I reach and enjoy your abode.
There is an illustration regarding the movement:
like a hero with horses that gallop like birds, he is like a hero;
just as he, having won the race, reaches his own home free from fear, so it is here.
1. By a measure of only a *yava* (barley grain) [in size].
2. Concerning the bestowing of manifold fruits.
3. Of the *śap* [suffix] belonging to the *vikaraṇa*.
4. The meaning is "kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa-da-da.
5. "Kṣa-na-ṭa" means precisely the fulfillment of desires.
6. "Kṣa-jha-ṭa" means he became joined with horses.
7. Having become worn out (*jīrṇa*), it was placed (*dhāyi*).

8. It was established (*sthāpita*) for that purpose. 9. By means of horses (*aśvaiḥ*) that fly along (*patayadbhiḥ*), i.e., those skilled in running; [variant *jha*: by means of horses that cause one to go (*gamayadbhiḥ*)].

10. Having conquered their enemies—kṣa, jha, ja, ṭa, and jit—the two [Aśvins] are praised. May the two winged ones (the Aśvins) not abandon me; may these two not consume me. May the wood, though piled high for the sight, not burn me. When you two, awakened, devour the earth within yourselves. upa'stutiḥ | aucadhyam | urupyet | mā | mām | ime iti | patatriṇī iti | vi | dugdhām | mā | mām | edhaḥ | darśa'tayaḥ | citaḥ | dhāk | pra | yat | vām | buddhaḥ | tmani | khādati | kṣām || 4 ||
Regarding this, they relate a narrative:
His limbs were withered by old age, he was blind from birth, and being extremely long-lived, the sons of Mamatā, unable to maintain him, threw their own slave-born son into the fire to be consumed.
Having been thrown there, he praised the Aśvins.
The two of them protected him;
then, when he still did not die, they threw him into the waters.
Submerged there, he again offered praise to the Aśvins.
Being satisfied, those two took him out from the water.
Thus, a certain slave named Traitana carved away his head and chest so that he would be invulnerable;
thereafter, they protected him.
This very point is expressed by two verses:
"O Aśvins, may this praise—this hymn being performed by approaching you with the intellect—protect me, Dīrghatamas, the son of Ucathya, from burning and from calamity.
Yāska [states] that "the root *urudhyati* has the sense of protecting" (Nirukta 5.23).

Having spoken thus in general, he now prays for the specific removal of each individual affliction: "May these two well-known winged ones—the day and night, which are by nature prone to flight and prone to returning—do not milk me dry; that is to say, may they not specifically drain me of my essence, nor bring about the limit [of life] conducive to the departure of the vital breaths. Furthermore, may the fuel, gathered, accumulated, and prepared ten times over, not burn me."
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with the suffix *sic*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) conditioned by the final consonant.

By the rule "optionally in the Veda," there is an absence of the augment *iṭ*. Then, the elision of the final consonant (*hal-ṅy-āp-...*) and the elision of the conjunct consonant (*saṃyogānta-lopa*) apply.
It shows the attainment of unbearable suffering:

because this person belonging to you two is bound by snares and tightly entwined, he "eats" (khādati) the earth (kṣām) with his own self (ātmanā) within himself (ātmani)—the meaning is that, being unable to move, he wallows upon the ground.
Therefore, let the praise of Upastuti extend far.

Śaunaka states the application (*viniyoga*) of this fifth [verse]: "Upon seeing an assassin (*ātatāyin*) approaching, or a tiger, or a wolf, one is liberated from them by muttering the mantra *na mā garah*. Having fasted for three nights, one should mutter it at night until the sun is seen.
Having bathed with effort, one should worship the Sun, the maker of day;
thieves do not see him, nor do others of sinful intent.
"Alone, he may overcome hundreds of thieves while traveling on the road" (Ṛgveda 1.141).

Let not the Dāsas, the most motherly [of enemies], swallow me up, since they have cast down him who was well-bound; when Traitana carved out his head, the Dāsa himself gnawed away his breast and shoulders. na | mā | garan | nadyaḥ | mātṛtamāḥ | dāsāḥ | yat | īm | su-sambaddham | avādhruḥ | śiraḥ | yat | asya | traitanaḥ | vi-takṣat | svayam | dāsaḥ | uraḥ | aṃsau | api | gdha || 5 ||

1. Kha, ca, pha: one whose body is worn out by old age; ka, jha: one whose body is shattered by old age; kṣa, ṅa, na, ṭa: one whose limbs are decayed by old age; jha: one whose limbs are decayed by old age.
2. Kṣa, ṅa, jha, na, ṭa: they caused [them] to fall down.
3. Kṣa, na, ṭa: the name Traitananāma (or Mā).
4. kṣa-jha-na-ṭa—pierced;
5. kṣa-ṅa-jha-na-ṭa—the Buddhas, having approached and reached;
6. kṣa-jha-na-ṭa—an antidote, a remedy.

7. By the specific [use of] *kṣa*, *na*, and *ṭa*, it has become exhausted and its essence is gone; by the specific [use of] *jha*, "I" have become exhausted and my essence is gone. 8. *Kṣa*, *jha*, *na*, and *ṭa* are the immeasurable portions of the wood. 9. *Kṣa*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *jha*, *jha*, *na*, and *ṭa* are perfectly accomplished.
10. *Kṣa*, *na*, and *ṭa* are the mass of blazing fuel.
11. *kṣa-ṅa-jha-na-ṭa-daha* tu. 12. *ṅa-jha-la-dṛḍham*.
13. *kṣa-na-ṭa-* is not found.
14. *kṣa-jha-1-na-ṭa-yathā* | Verse 119:

May the rivers (*nadyaḥ*), which are by nature flowing (*nadanaśīlāḥ*) and are the best of mothers (*mātṛttamāḥ*)—waters that act for the benefit of the world like mothers (*mātṛvat*)—not swallow (*vgaran*) me, Dīrghatamas; may they not cause me to sink.
The root *gṛ* means "to swallow";
in the *leṭ* mood, the suffix *śap* is optionally applied by way of substitution.
He shows the attainment of being swallowed:
because the *dāsas*—those who were my supporters, my own born slaves—have thoroughly swallowed (*susamugdham*) this Dīrghatamas, me, with all his limbs well-contracted.
In the compound *svatī*, which is a *prādi*-compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.18.4 (*svatī pūjāyām*), the original accent of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) that constitutes the first member is retained.
They cast him down with his face turned downward.
Furthermore, because that Dāsa named Vaitaraṇa, being utterly merciless, cut (*vitakṣat*) my head in various ways, that Dāsa cut off his own head.
Not only the head, but he also struck—meaning he tore apart—my chest and my shoulders.
In the *Hanteluṅ*, this form is Vedic.
Then he likewise struck his own chest and shoulders with his own weapon;
the implication is that this was due to the greatness (māhātmya) of you two.

Dīrghatamas, the son of Mamatā, having grown old in the tenth age, becomes the Brahman priest and the charioteer for the purpose of the waters’ unions. 6. Dīrghatamas; the son of Mamatā; having grown old; in the tenth; age; of the waters; for the purpose; of the unions; the Brahman; becomes; the charioteer. 6.

The great seer named Dīrghatamas was the son of Mamatā (Māmateya). By the power of the high-souled Ṛdhin, he lived for ten *yugas*—that is, until the end of the tenth *yuga*—freed from the aforementioned suffering and exceedingly happy, living together with his sons, wife, and others.
When the tenth *yuga* had passed, he became decrepit (*jūrṇavān*), aged, with his body covered in wrinkles and grey hair.

Being in such a state, [he beheld] the fruit of action being enjoyed by men, such as heaven and other realms attained by those who have crossed over, as well as by the waters and the creatures that perform their duties.

Or rather: he becomes a *brahmā*, one who is like a *brahmā*— that is, preeminent— for the sake of, or for the purpose of, those waters, which are active works, and for those progeny who are united with them.
Furthermore, the charioteer becomes their driver; that is to say, he becomes a god.
Thus the mantra repeats this account.
Or rather, it speaks of itself as its own subject through a figurative mode of expression (*parokṣeṇa*) in order to manifest the great majesty of the Aśvins.
‘Pra dyāvā’ is the third hymn, consisting of five verses; it belongs to Dīrghatamas, is composed in the Jāgata metre, and is addressed to Dyāvāpṛthivī (Heaven and Earth).
It is thus enumerated: “‘Pra dyāvā’: five [verses], addressed to Dyāvāpṛthivī, in the Jāgata [metre].”
This hymn is the *nivid*-insertion for the *dyāvāpṛthivī* [deities] at the *agniṣṭoma* and on the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭha* [sacrifice].
Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "‘pra dyāva’ is the [hymn] of Dīrghatamas" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.18).
The first two [verses] are the invitatory and offering verses for the oblation of the animal sacrifice to Heaven and Earth.

Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘May Heaven and Earth, who increase the cosmic order through sacrifices... and ‘Be gracious to us, O Rudra, and grant us happiness’—these two” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
1. *Kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-a-ṭa-na* is the throat (*garaṇ*). 2. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa* is the location of the chest (*vakṣaḥsthāna*).
3. *Kṣa-ja-ṭa* is at the tenth [digit], at the end of the pair (*yuga*).

4. [With the variants] kṣa-jha-ṭa, he becomes aged (jūrṇaḥ). 5. [With the variants] kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa, he becomes like Brahmā, or he becomes powerful, or he becomes a charioteer, or he becomes a matchmaker. 6. [With the variants] kṣa-ṅa-na-ṭa, the meaning is that he exists; or rather, living for ten yugas, he became an achiever of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) in a superior manner; [with the variant] jha1, or rather, living, he became an achiever of the goals of human life in a superior manner.
7. [The verse] with *kṣa-na-ṭa* as the *parokṣa*.
8. [The verse] composed according to the rule of *kṣa-sa-jha-1-ma-ṭa*:
"I praise with sacrifices at the assemblies of worship the two great ones, Heaven and Earth, who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and are wise in the sacrificial rites."
To him who, together with the gods, O son of the gods, through his wondrous deeds and through this excellent prayer, bestows desirable boons.

I praise with sacrifices Heaven and Earth, the two great ones who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and are wise in the assemblies; those two sons of the gods, accompanied by the gods, who perform wondrous deeds and bestow desirable boons through their wisdom. || 1 ||
Heaven and Earth; the two, Heaven and Earth.
In the word *divo dyāvā*, the substitute *dyāvā* is acute-accented on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*).
The word *pṛthivī* ends in the suffix *ṅīṣ* and is acute-accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).
By the rule “*devatādvandve ca*,” both members of the compound retain their original accentuation (*ubhayapadaprakṛtisvaratva*).
The reading of another word within the middle of a compound is a Vedic archaism.
I am the sacrificer.
I praise him preeminently with sacrifices—meaning ritual offerings serving as the instrumental cause—for the purpose of presenting the oblations.
There is a transposition of genders.
Of what nature are they?

They are the increasers of Truth (*ṛtāvṛdhā*), the augmenters of the sacrifice, the great ones (*mahī*), and those who are preeminent in wisdom (*pracetasa*) at the sacrificial assemblies (*vidatheṣu*).
Thus [says] the *Ṛgveda*.

Those sons, of noble form and wondrous deeds, brought forth two great mothers for the sake of primordial consciousness. Within the law of both the stationary and the moving, you two protect the station and the path of the non-dual Son. te | sunavaḥ | su-arpasaḥ | su-daṃsasaḥ | mahī iti | jajñuḥ | mātarā | pūrva-cittaye | sthātuḥ | ca | satyam | jagataḥ | ca | dharmaṇi | putrasya | pāthaḥ | padam | a-dvayāvinaḥ || 3 ||

Those renowned sons, born from you two, who stand in the place of sons—your offspring—are of excellent deeds (*svapasaḥ*) and of beautiful appearance (*sudaṃsasaḥ*); they have recognized you two as the great ones (*mahī*), acting like mothers (*mātarā*), and they perceive your majesty.
For what purpose?
For the sake of primordial consciousness (*pūrvacittaye*), that is, for the sake of the first awakening in the form of grace.

Furthermore, O Heaven and Earth, you protect—that is, you grant—the true, unassailable station (*padam*) and the path (*pāthaḥ*) for the sake of the support and preservation of both kinds of the world: the stationary (*stātuḥ*), which is the immobile, and the moving (*jagataḥ*), which is the mobile, acting as sons (*putrasya*) or those occupying the place of sons. This refers to one who knows nothing other than yourselves for his own livelihood; for such a person, when there is the cause for upholding and protecting, you grant that station which is real and unimpeded.
Alternatively:

those well-known rays (*sunavaḥ*), as they arise—performing excellent deeds such as illumination (*svapasaḥ*), possessing beautiful appearance (*sudaṃsasaḥ*), or thoroughly exhausting themselves for their own activity—such rays were born (*jajñuḥ*) for the sake of the great (*mahī*) heaven and earth, for the primordial cognition (*pūrvacittaye*) of living beings; that is to say, they pervade the space between heaven and earth. Furthermore, for the support (*dhāraṇe*) of both the stationary and the moving, for the sake of that [support], [they belong to] the non-dual (*advayāvinaḥ*), which is free from the two paths.
By the rule "bahulam chandasi," the suffix *vini* (which becomes *mat*) is applied after the word *dvaya*;
by the rule "anyeṣām api dṛśyate," the vowel is lengthened.
You surely protect the true path, the way of the son—of Āditya, who stands in the place of your son—and his station.

Those masters of creative power, possessed of excellent wisdom, have measured out the two sisters who share a common womb, the paired ones dwelling in the same abode. The seers of brilliant luster weave a new thread after a new thread within the sky and the ocean. 4. They, the masters of creative power (*māyinaḥ*), have measured out; they, of excellent wisdom (*supracetasaḥ*); the two sisters (*jāmī*), sharing a common womb (*sayaunī*), the paired ones (*mithunā*) dwelling in the same abode (*samaukasā*). They weave a new thread after a new thread (*navyaṃ-navyaṃ tantum ā tanvate*); within the sky (*divi*) and the ocean (*samudre*); the seers (*kavayaḥ*) of brilliant luster (*sudītayaḥ*). 4.
Those two well-known ones, Heaven and Earth, are *māyins*;
*māyā* is wisdom (*prajñā*).

They possess wisdom regarding their own domain, or rather, they possess actions characterized by knowledge; being *supracetasas*, capable of perceiving with great excellence, the rays *mamire*—that is, they measure or delimit.
What kind of sisters are they? They are *jāmī*, meaning sisters to one another.
If it is asked, "Whence is this? it is said in reply:
"Born together" (*sayaunī*) means having a common place of origin; "paired" (*mithunā*) means having become a pair for the birth of living beings, that is, being inseparable from one another.
"Sharing the same abode" (*samaukasā*) means having a common location, because Heaven and Earth both abide in the single space consisting of the void.
Or rather, in the place of assembly (*samīcana-sthāne*).

Furthermore, the *kavayaḥ*—the wise ones who possess knowledge regarding the objects of their own activity; the *sudītayaḥ*—the rays that shine excellently—[are located] within (*antaḥ*), in the midst of the *samudre*, the shining sky (*divi*).
The word *samudra* [here refers to] the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

1. The word *kṣajaṭa* means a dwelling place (*āspada*). 2. *Kṣajaṭa* refers to those who are being born (*utpadyamāna*). 3. *Kṣaḍajaṭa* refers to those who are perishing (*upakṣayanta*). 4. *Kṣajhajajaṭa* refers to those who have known (*jñātavant*). 5. *Kṣajaṭa* refers to both the stationary and the moving world (*sthātuś ca jagataś ca*). 6. *Kṣahajhajha1jajaṭa* refers to those possessing knowledge of their own respective domains (*svaviṣayaprajñānavant*). 7. *Kṣaḍajha1jajaṭa* refers to those who stand in the place of a sister (*bhaginīsthānīya*). 8. *Kṣajaṭa*: Why is that?
Because it is read among the names for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), it denotes that [space].

And it has been thus etymologically explained by Yāska: "Why 'samudra'? Because from it the waters flow forth; the waters rush toward it; beings rejoice in it; or it becomes a 'samudraka' because it swells up" (Nirukta 2.10).
"Nabhyam nabhyam" refers to the thread that is to be stretched out, that which is to be extended; it is a singular used for the class.
They stretch out the rays, spreading them in every direction.
In the two-fold bounty of that Savitṛ today, we meditate upon the most excellent [gift] at the impulse of the god.
O Heaven and Earth, being well-disposed toward us, bestow upon us wealth consisting of goods, a hundredfold.

That desirable bounty of Savitṛ we meditate upon today, at the impulse of the god. O Heaven and Earth, most wise ones, bestow upon us wealth abounding in goods and consisting of hundreds of cattle. 5.

We, the sacrificers, when there is the *prasava*—the permission—of the god Savitṛ, the impeller of all, the Āditya who exists in the form of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), we think of—that is, we beg for—that such desirable (*vareṇya*) wealth (*rādhas*), capable of accomplishing the goals of human endeavor, consisting of cattle and other riches. The root *man* has the sense of begging;
the suffix *śap* is Vedic.
Or rather:
we shall practice again and again; that is to say, "may we obtain."

The root *jñā* is used in the sense of practice (*abhyāsa*). The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Following the rule for the *śap* affix, the substitution of *man* for *jñā* is applied according to the *pā-ghrā-* rule.

Furthermore, O Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivī), you two of beautiful mind (sucetanā)—with a benevolent intention toward us—bestow upon us wealth (rayi). Of what kind? Endowed with dwellings (vasumat), distinguished by houses and such fit for habitation; endowed with hundreds (śatagvin), distinguished by cattle and the like numbering one hundred.
2 | “*te hi*” is the fourth hymn, consisting of five verses; it belongs to Dīrghatamas, is composed in the Jāgata metre, and is addressed to Dyāvāpṛthivī (Heaven and Earth).
This is indicated by the introductory formula: “*te hi*”.

On the twenty-fourth day, this hymn—beginning with “For they two, Heaven and Earth, [are the guardians]” and “Of you two, the charioteers of the sacrifice”—is the insertion for the *dyāvāpṛthivī* [duel] in the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra*, because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “The *vaiśvadeva* [śastra] is ‘te hi dyāvāpṛthivī... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).

Likewise, on the second day of both the *pṛṣṭhya* and the *abhilava* six-day periods, the *dyāvāpṛthivī* hymn is the one to be inserted as the *nivid*; for it is extended by rule to the second day of the *abhilava* period by the statement: “The third pressing belongs to the twenty-fourth [day]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.6).

The second day of the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha] is obtained from the second day of the *abhilava* [ṣaḍaha], because this hymn is prescribed by implication, as stated in the sūtra: "On the first two days of the *pṛṣṭhya*, the two days of the *abhilava* are to be applied" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.10).

The first [verse] is employed in the *āśvina-śastra*, as it is sūtrated under the rule "When the [other śastras] have been completed, for the *āśvina*": "For they are Heaven and Earth, the all-beneficent, the goddess of the entire host of gods" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.5).
For they, Heaven and Earth, are the source of all prosperity; they are the observers of cosmic order (*ṛta*), the sustainers of the realm, and the wise ones.
Between these two well-born *dhiṣaṇās* (the bowls of heaven and earth), the divine and radiant Sun moves according to the eternal law (*dharman*).

To them—Heaven and Earth, who bring all-beneficent welfare, who are observers of cosmic order (*ṛtavarī*), who sustain the seer within the realm of space; between these two well-born *dhiṣaṇās*, the divine Sun, pure and radiant, moves according to the divine law. 1.

1. *kṣa-bha-ṭa-nabhyanabhyaṃ navanavam*. 2. *kṣa-bha-ṭa-labhemahīti*. 3. *kṣa-bha-ṭa-nividvānam*. 4. *kṣa-bha-ṭa-saṃsthiteṣvāśvināya stuvate*. "For those two, namely Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), are well-known; between them, in that intermediate space, the pure (*śuciḥ*)—meaning the cleansed one or the purifier of the universe—the radiant (*devaḥ*) Sun (*sūryaḥ*), being endowed with his function (*dharmaṇā*) consisting of illumination and the bestowing of water, etc., *īyate*: he moves perpetually. [The root] *īṅ* means 'to go'."
"Such a deed [was accomplished] through your grace"—this is the praise. Of what nature are you two? "The source of all well-being (viśvaśambhuvau)."
Those two who cause the universe to experience happiness are "viśvaśambhuvā"; that is to say, they are the ones who bring joy to the entire world. "Ṛtāvarī" means "possessing the cosmic order (ṛta)."
From the word *ṛta*, the suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule *chandasi vanipau*; then, by the rule *vano ra ca*, the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *phak* are added.
[This refers to] the arising of water from the *rajas*.
"Nirukta (4.19) states: 'Water is called *rajas*'.
[The phrase] 'those two whose sustaining [powers] are unimpeded' means that their capacity to sustain, O 'Seer' (*kavi*), is such; that is to say, they are not weary in the production of water."
Alternatively,
[the two] are those who possess a supporting poet and a sage;
that is to say, they are endowed with the sun and the water of rain that supports [all things].
"Of noble birth" (*sujanmanī*) means possessing a beautiful birth; "of wisdom" (*dhiṣaṇe*) means endowed with boldness, that is, confident in their respective functions;
"divine" (*devī*) means shining.

Although the term *dhiṣaṇe* here is a name for Heaven and Earth—since it is stated among their names in the Nirukta (3.30.3) as "the two *dhiṣaṇas*, the two worlds"—nevertheless, because the term "Heaven and Earth" (*dyāvāpṛthivī*) is already present [in the compound], it should be understood here in its etymological sense.
The two vast, great, and inexhaustible ones—the Father and the Mother—protect all beings.
The two world-halves are most resolute and beautiful to behold, when the Father clothes them in various forms.
The two wide-expanding, great, and inexhaustible ones—the father and the mother—protect all beings. Most courageous, like two beautiful celestial realms, when the father clothed them in forms.

"Uruvyacasā" means possessing vast capacity for speech; "prabhūtavyacanavatī" means being exceedingly extensive. "Mahinī" means great, precisely because of that extensiveness. "Asaścatā" means not clinging together, that is to say, not separated from one another. Both "Dyaus," the Father who protects, and "Pṛthivī," the Mother who creates—these two—"rakṣataḥ" protect, that is, they preserve, "bhuvanāni," the multitudes of beings. Their nature as Mother and Father is established by such Vedic texts as, "O Father Heaven, O Mother Earth" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.51.5).
Furthermore: "sudhṛṣṭame" means exceedingly bold;
the loss of the letter *t* is Vedic. "pragalbhe" means in the two bold ones, namely heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyau*). "vapuṣye na" means as if beneficial to beauty.
The meaning is that they are like parents to living beings, protectors of the body.
He explains this very point:

"Since" (*yat*) "from all sides" (*sīm sarvataḥ*), the sky (*dyauḥ*), which stands in the place of a father (*pitā pitṛsthānīyā*), "clothes" (*avāsayat*)—that is, clothes or presides over—the world with "forms" (*rūpaiḥ*), meaning with excellent means of definition such as lights, or with rain and so forth which are being defined; therefore, both father and mother protect the worlds.
That son of the two parents, the pure and wise Agni, purifies the worlds by his creative power;
he milks from the dappled cow and the prolific bull the bright milk for all time.

He, the son of the two parents, is the purifying fire; the wise one purifies all worlds through his creative power. Day by day, he milks the dappled cow and the bull of noble seed, yielding his bright milk. 3.

1. The poet is the bearer of *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *1*, *ja*, and *ṭa*. 2. In *kṣa*, *na*, and *ṭa*, [the vowels] are effortless (*aprayatnavatī*); in *ṅa*, they are both effortful (*prayatnavatyau*); in *jha*, they are effortful (*prayatnavatī*). 3. In *kṣa*, *na*, and *ṭa*, [the compound] is "accompanied by the sun requested for rainwater" (*vṛṣṭyudakayācitāsūryopeta*); in *ṅa* and *jha-1*, it is "accompanied by the sun suitable for rainwater" (*vṛṣṭyudakayocitāsūryopeta*); in *jha-jha*, it is "accompanied by the sun that holds rainwater" (*vṛṣṭyudakadhāricatasūryopeta*).
4. A derivative word (*yaugika*) is [formed] with *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *ñ*, *ña*, *ṭa*, and *ya*. In the case of *pitroḥ* (of the two parents), that is, of the mother and father or heaven and earth:
by the rule "when [the word] *pitṛ* is combined with *mātṛ*, the former remains," *pitṛ* is retained.

‘Udāsanaḥ’: the father’s share is *udāsā*. ‘Putraḥ’: the son, who stands in the place of a son, is Āditya. ‘Pavitravān’: endowed with the means of purification; ‘dhīraḥ’: wise; ‘dhīmān’: possessed of intelligence. Being ‘vahnih’, the bearer and sustainer of the fruit, he ‘punāti’—that is, he purifies and illuminates—the ‘bhuvanāni’, the multitudes of beings, by means of his own ‘māyayā’, that is, his wisdom.

Furthermore, that very son, by means of his creative power (*māyā*), purifies— that is, illuminates— the *pṛṣṭhi*, the earth which is white in color and a nourisher, as well as the bull, the sky-world which possesses excellent seed or excellent water;
this occurs at all times, throughout every single day.
Furthermore, [it refers to] "of this" heaven;
or else,
it is the genitive case used in the sense of the object.
He milks this heavenly world;
he milks the bright milk—water resembling radiant milk.

Regarding the verb *duh*, in accordance with the Vedic rule "after a root ending in a consonant (śal), having an *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter, and being aniṭ, the suffix *kasa* is substituted for *cli*," the substitution of *kasa* for *cli* occurs.

"This Sun, of such great majesty, is the son of those two"—this is the praise of Heaven and Earth: "He is the most skillful of the skilled gods, who brought forth the two worlds that are auspicious to all; he, the wise one, who measured out the two realms with undecaying supports, establishing them together."

This one is the most skillful of the skillful gods, he who brought forth the two worlds that are auspicious to all; he who measured out the two realms with his excellent wisdom and has firmly established them with imperishable supports.
Having previously praised these [Maruts] by way of their son's greatness, he now praises them by way of praise for their own progenitor:
"Among the gods, this one is the most divine; among the performers of deeds (apasaḥ), he is the most excellent performer of deeds.
*Apaḥ* is a name for action (*karman*).
By that [quality], the possessor of it is indicated.
Among those possessing actions, he is the one with the most excellent action.
To the question "Who is this? that has been stated, he says:
The God who brought forth the two Rodasīs—the Heaven and Earth—which are of great majesty and which, being "all-beneficent" (*viśvaśambhuvā*), bring about the happiness of all beings in every way;
not merely by producing them, but that God [who also sustains] the two *rajasi*—the Heaven and Earth consisting of the quality of passion (*rajas*).
For "the two *rajasi*" is a name for Heaven and Earth, as it is listed among their names in the Nirukta (3.30.8): "the two *rajasi*, the two seats."
He measures out his own thighs, distinguishing them specifically. He says: not for his own enjoyment, but through *sukratūyā*, that is, through the desire for excellent action.
By means of such action as brings about happiness for living beings, through the desire for that kind of action— or rather, this [desire] is connected with what follows—

by means of "well-performed rites" (sukratūyayā) as the stated cause, he has properly honored and established these two, Heaven and Earth, with "unaging" (ajarebhiḥ), i.e., undecaying and most firm, "stays" (skambhanebhiḥ), i.e., pegs that serve as the means for obstructing their movement. This is the meaning.
The root *ṛc* is used in the sense of "praising.

Since there is reduplication due to the general rule regarding the letter *r* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), the augment *tuṭ* is applied to the reduplicated syllable according to the rule "tasmāddvihalaḥ. Therefore, the praise is that [the world] has been brought forth by the Supreme Lord, who possesses such great majesty as being expressed in the words, "He alone is the God; He alone is the most excellent."

When these two are praised, O Heaven and Earth, grant us great fame and vast sovereign power; bestow upon us that strength by which we may always overcome the peoples and be worthy of praise. Send down that vigor into us.

O you two who are praised by us, O enchanting ones, bestow upon us great renown and sovereign power, O Heaven and Earth—vast power, by which you may ever extend our fame and inspire within us strength worthy of praise. 5.

1. *kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa*: Āditya or Vāyu; 2. *kṣa-ha-jha-1-a-ṭa*: Or rather, the Wise One (*dhīra*) by means of the characteristics of rain; 3. *ṅa-jha-1*: Him; 4. *kha-ja-jha-ta-ba*: In his vast form; 5. *ṅa-jha-1*: Specifically, by means of the measure; 6. *kṣa-a-ṭa*: Because of the commonality of the revealed scripture (*śruti*); 7. *kṣa-i-jha-1-a-ṭa*: He is to be worshipped. Regarding the two well-known ones, heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), while they are being praised by us with their qualities—the suffix denoting the agent is used in the sense of the object.
O [Aśvins], bestow upon us (naḥ) great (maha), vast (atiprabhūtam), and renowned (śravaḥ)—that is, fame (kīrtim) heard everywhere—by means of the sacrificial food (ghāsathaḥ).
The augment aṭ is added to the root *dhā* in the leṭ mood;
the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule "sibbahulam."
Thus, you two shall bestow vast and exceedingly abundant *kṣatra*, that is, power.
That very thing is being purified.
By means of this food and strength, throughout all days (*viśvāhā*), may we spread forth (*abhivitatāna*) on every side the people (*kṛṣṭīḥ*), such as our sons and other offspring.
In the *leṭ* [subjunctive] form of the root *tan*, there is the elision (*ślu*) of the suffix by Vedic usage. The augment *āṭ* is applied according to the rule "āḍusamasya.

Since that [augment] is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix by the rule "chandasyubhayathā," the accent of the root prevails, as the quality of being *udātta* for the first syllable of an *abhyasta* [repeated] form does not apply.

*Kṛṣya* is a name for a human being, as it is listed among those names in the statement, "The *kṛṣyas* are the people" (Nirukta 2.3.7). Furthermore, *vpanāyyam* means "to be praised"; *ojaḥ* means bodily strength. The meaning is: "bestow (*vinvataṃ*) upon us (*vasme*) that which is well-distributed (*samyaṅ*), that is, increase it.
The root *invati* signifies pervasion, as it is listed among those names in the statement, "He pervades (*invati*), he has reached (*nanakṣa*)" (Nirukta 2.18.1).
3 | The fifth hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with "kim u śreṣṭhaḥ," is addressed to Agni and composed by Dīrghatamas.
The remaining verses are to be understood as *jāgata* (composed in the *jagatī* meter) according to the rule concerning the residual [verses].
And it is stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: "Is he the best, the six-naved, the three-fold?
In the *vyūḍha-daśarātra* sacrifice, on the sixth day, in the *vaiśvadeva-śastra*, this is the second *nivid-vāna* hymn beginning with "Is he the best.
Therein, "Is he the best" is the opening verse (*pratīka*), excluding the rest.

In the section titled "The Best Array" (*vyūhaśreṣṭha*), it is stated in the Sūtra: "'What indeed is the best? Has he come to us for the sake of booty?'—this consists of thirteen verses and four [others]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 8.8).

"What indeed is the best? What has the youngest come to us for? To what mission is he sent? Why do we praise him? We have not reviled the cup which belongs to the great clan; we have offered the impulse to Indra for our brothers."

1 | What? "Ūm"—is he the most excellent? What? The youngest—has he not come? Why does he go on his mission as messenger? What have we said that is to be blamed? We did not speak ill of the cup; O Agni, brother of noble lineage, we have indeed uttered a curse against one who is wicked.
The Ṛbhus were the three sons of Sudhanvan, namely Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja.
While they were still human beings, they attained divinity through their excellent deeds; once, at the time of a ritual, they set out to drink the Soma.
Agni, impelled by the gods, observed that they all possessed identical forms and, assuming that same appearance himself, began to drink among them as the fourth member.
And those Ṛbhus, seeing him arrive with a form identical to their own and being unable to distinguish him, deliberated among themselves thus:
"Is he the superior one? Or indeed is he more excellent than we, while we are the inferior ones? "He has come to us"—the root *gam* takes the suffix *laṅ*; the Vedic *śap* is elided.
Due to the elision of the *hal* and *ṅyādi* suffixes, the substitution of *na* for *am* occurs according to the rule "amo no dhātoḥ.
*Ajagat* is a word for motion, as it is listed among the names [of Agni] in the passage "agan ajagan" (Nirukta 2.14.112).
What has he come for? Is he our youngest, or is he our most youthful one who has arrived?
Or rather, what mission (*dūtyam*)—that is, the work of a messenger—is being performed or undertaken in connection with the gods?
Or has a messenger sent by the gods come to us?
[The suffix] *yat* is applied here according to the rule: "The suffix *yat* is used in the sense of the state or activity of a messenger."
"What we say here is indeed a matter of doubt; the meaning is: how is it to be determined?
We were previously only three, and now we are four of equal form; therefore, there is this uncertainty as to whether this one is merely additional or perhaps the best."

1. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-śreṣṭham* (the most excellent). 2. *kṣa-ṅa-ca-jha-jña-ja-ṭa-bṛhat* (great, vast). 3. *kṣa-ṅa-jña-ja-ṭa-ajena balena* (by means of uncreated power). 4. *cha-jña-tadākāro bhūtvā* (having assumed that form). 5. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-jyeṣṭhaḥ* (the eldest). 6. *kṣa-bha-ṭa-naḥ ājagan* (he has come to us). 7. *kṣa-preṣitaḥ* (sent forth). 8. *cha-idānīṃ tu* (but now).
Having thus somehow perceived him as distinct from himself, one attains certainty regarding him through direct intuition (*aparokṣya*).
O Agni, therefore, you must remain awake like a brother.

Just as Ātā forcibly takes his own share, so too, having assumed an identical form, he proceeded by force toward the *camasa* (the cup); thus it is said, "to the brother. O such one, we do not revile your *camasa*. Since another has arrived, we do not defile the cup by failing to drink from it.
The root *ṇidi* is used in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*).
According to the rule "it should be stated that [the substitution] is optional in the Veda," there is an absence of the dual ending.
He states the reason for the lack of enmity (*adveṣyatva*).
The cup (*camasa*) which is of noble lineage (*mahākula*), having been produced from a great family because it was fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ—
as he will say, “Tvaṣṭṛ begot me, the Māravant” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.4)— for that reason, it is *drughaṇa* (the striker).
The word *prakṛti* is used here for the modification (*vikāra*). And from that [modification], there is the word *tat*. The word *iti* is used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
We proclaim the prosperity, that is, the attainment, of the cup made of wood.
In the *videṣām* [form], there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) by the rule "vacisvapi" in the *liṭ* [perfect tense] after an *āmdas* [suffix];
the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule for roots beginning with *krī*.

"Make one chalice into four. "That is what the gods said to you; that is why I have come. "O sons of Sudhanvan, if you will do exactly this, you shall become worthy of sacrifice together with the gods.

"Make one chalice into four! That is what the gods said to you; that is why I have come to you, O sons of Sudhanvan. If you do this, you shall become worthy of sacrifice together with the gods. || 2 ||
Being thus questioned, he replied to them:

"O *Saudhanvanas*, sons of Sudhanvan, you [must] make that single cup—which was previously one and had been fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ—into four; that is, make it into the number four. [The word *caturaḥ* has its final syllable accented according to Pāṇini 6.1.167: *caturaḥ śasi*.]
As before, there is an expansion (*tanap*).
Just as, beginning with "The eldest said, 'Make two cups! and continuing with "The youngest said, 'Make four! (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.33.5), a set of four was determined;

so too, O gods, I do not speak alone, but I say to you (*vaḥ*) that those acts—the aforementioned division into four parts, as well as the subsequent acts such as the making of horse-chariots and so forth—were spoken (*abruvan*) by the gods, Indra and the others.

"I have come—that is, I have arrived—to tell you that such action is the means for attaining the state of divinity. Since this is so, if you shall do it—meaning, if you are able to act in the manner I have described—then you will become worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*) together with the gods.
This is the meaning of what was said by them.

When you spoke to Agni the messenger, you asked: "How many times has the horse come here? How many times the chariot? How many times the milch-cow? And how many times the two youths? O brother, those things we shall now declare to you. 3.

When you spoke back to Agni the messenger, saying, "With what [purpose] the horse, and with what [purpose] the chariot here? With what [purpose] the cow? With what [purpose] the two youthful ones?"—those things, O brother, we approach you according to our intent. 3.
O gods, whatever business you have spoken of concerning him— Agni— who has arrived as your messenger, distinguished by qualities such as anointing and who has attained the function of a messenger;
[that you spoke]— the middle voice [is used] by way of grammatical substitution (vyatyaya),
and the suffix *tanap* is applied as before.
Why [is it] "aśvaḥ" and "katvaiḥ"?

1. *kṣa-ma-ṭa-svānyam* (different from one's own). 2. *kṣa1-balācca somapānāya* (and by the power of *kṣa1*, for the drinking of Soma). 3. *kṣa-ma-ṭa-kāraṇāt he ame* (for the sake of *kṣa-ma-ṭa*, O *ame*). 4. *kṣa-jha1 ma-ṭa-apūrvam ekameva camasam* (unprecedented, according to *kṣa-jha1 ma-ṭa*, only a single cup). 5. *kṣa-jha1-ma-ṭa-catuṣṭayam* (a group of four, according to *kṣa-jha1-ma-ṭa*). 6. *kṣa-ma-ṭa-maduktaprakāram* (in the manner stated by me, according to *kṣa-ma-ṭa*). 7. *kṣa-ṅa-jha1-ma-ṭa-bhaviṣyatha* (you shall become; you shall become worthy of a share in the sacrifice). 8. *kṣa-devāḥ* (the gods, according to *kṣa*). 9. *kṣa-ṅa-jha1-ma-ṭa-‘karvaḥ’ ityasyānantaraṃ ‘jātāvekavacanam | aśvāḥ kartavyāḥ | kuttyarthe tavaiken iti tanpratyayaḥ | yadvā | uttaratra indro harī yuyuja iti indrāya vacoyujā tataścarita ca viniyogadarśanāt’ ityadhikam* (after the word ‘karvaḥ’, there is the addition: “The singular is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*). Horses are to be made. The suffix *-tan* is used in the sense of ‘to be done’ according to Pāṇini 3.4.14 (*tavaiken*); or rather, because in the subsequent passage ‘Indra yoked the two bay horses (*harī*)’, the application of the speech-yoked [horses] to Indra is observed”). Ṛgveda 1.120.12.
954 Ṛgveda [Aṣṭaka 2, Adhyāya 3, Varga 4]:
The meaning is that an interval of eighteen [syllables] must be made from one [unit].

Because it will be stated later, "fashioned from eighteen types of wood" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.161.7), the suffix *svan* is used here in the sense of a gerundive according to the rule "in the sense of a kṛtya-affix, [the suffixes] *tavya*, *anīya*, and *kṛtya*. Furthermore, the "chariot" (*ratha*) is "to be made" (*kartvaḥ*), that is, it is to be constructed.
The word ‘dhenu’ refers to the agent.

A dead cow devoid of its hide is called *nirandhas*; however, it should be understood here as a fresh one, because it will be stated later: "They have led forth the cow of the one who was without breath by means of their prayers" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.7).
Likewise, "two parents who have grown old must be made young again—young men endowed with excellent youth—by the agent.
O brother Agni, having performed those deeds spoken by you gods, we subsequently perform the deed; we attain it directly (*emaḥ*).
[The root] *iṇ* means "to go."
This is the end of the mantra;
or alternatively,
this is the statement of the seer (ṛṣi).

O Ṛbhus, as for what you said to the messenger who had arrived— "Whatever task is to be done, of the nature about to be described, we shall perform and accept"— all those things [the enemies] thought, "We shall slay them," just as he (the messenger) spoke;
[the plural number] is used for honor.
Because the word *etad* (this) refers back to what has been previously mentioned, and because the *Ṛbhus* are the subject under discussion, it shows the possibility of their being slain.

The meaning is: when [Indra] said, "Let us slay those *Ṛbhus* who have censured—the *Ṛbhus* who did not approve of—the cup which was to be drunk by the gods (*devapānam*), a cup fit for the gods belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, which the human-like *Ṛbhus* had taken and divided into four."
From that time forward, when the Soma has been pressed and is presented for drinking, men assume various names for one another—such as those of the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and so on.

Having concealed their former names, at the time of the invitation (*upahvāna*), they cause themselves to be addressed by these other names alone, saying, "O Adhvaryu, invite! "O Hotṛ, invite! The meaning is that they do this out of fear of Tvaṣṭṛ.
To explain how their former names had become applicable [to them] previously, he says:
The mother, who gave birth to these men, remembers and gratifies them under other names; [this is expressed by] *smarat* and *prīṇayati*,
where the suffix *śap* is used for the roots *smṛ* and *prī*,
and the augment *it* is added.
Indra yoked his two bay steeds; the Aśvins [mounted] their chariot; Bṛhaspati approached Viśvarūpā.
Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja went to the gods; O skillful ones, you have attained your share of the sacrifice.

Indra yoked his two bay horses; the Aśvins [yoked] their chariot; Bṛhaspati drove toward the one of all forms. R̥bhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja went to the gods; O skillful workers, go to your sacrificial portion.
He states the sequential application of those previously created: "Indra yoked the two bay horses";
he has joined these two horses, so named, to the chariot.
Likewise, the Aśvins—the two horsemen—yoked their chariot.
Similarly, Bṛhaspati—the protector of the great mantra, the deity so named—approached (*upa-ājata*) the cow possessed of manifold forms (*viśvarūpām*); that is to say, he accepted her.

Although the specific term "cow" is not explicitly heard here, nevertheless, because it was previously stated that she was a "milch-cow" (*dhenuḥ*) and "a doer" (*karvī*), and because it will be said later, "the milch-cow who speeds everywhere, who possesses all forms" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 4.33.8), it is determined that she was indeed a cow of manifold forms.
For this very reason, some explain the term *viśvarūpām* as "the Paṅkti [meter]," but that is incorrect.
Indra and the other gods assigned the chariot and other objects fashioned by you as their own portions;
therefore, O Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja, you went to the gods, Indra and the others.

And O you of good deeds, possessing excellent horses, chariots, and other works, do you obtain this portion worthy of sacrifice—connected with the sacrifice, consisting of Soma, and to be attained as divinity.
The meaning is: by the power of your ritual acts, become partakers of the oblation.
Thus spoke Api.
1. kṣa, jha, jha₁, a, ṭa: vārayati (he wards off).
2. kṣa, ma, ṭa: "aye" is not present. 3. kṣa, cha, jha₁, a, ṭa: those men who from this time forward have censured—that is, are performing censure.
4. The meaning is: "The Ṛbhus, who are human beings, have taken possession of the *camasa* (cup) [marked with] *kṣa-cha-jha-a-ṭa-ca*;
therefore, they would express reproach, saying, 'We must not drink the remnant,' and [Indra] said, 'Let us kill them. 5. [The name] preceded by *sva*.
6. Call [him] by the name Kṣa-a-ṭa-udgātra-rūpa.
7. [Call him] by those beginning with Kṣa-jha1-ādi.
8. The other names begin with Kṣa-ma-ṭa.
9. kṣa-jha1-a-ṭa: she who gives birth to oneself.
10. kṣa-cha-jha1-a-ṭa: by means of names such as Devadatta, Viṣṇumitra, and others.
11. kṣa-ma-ṭa: he approached, went near to, or attained the chariot (ratha).

Likewise, Bṛhaspati; [the chariot] approached, it came near, it reached, and so too did Bṛhaspati. 12. [The variants] kṣa, cha, jha₁, a, ṭa read "pūrvata. 13. [The variants] kṣa and jha₁ read "ityasyāśvapattiḥ."
14. *kṣa-cha-jha1-a-ṭa*: You ought to go.
In these [cases], such as *etair likhitam* (written by them), there is the substitution of *ta* for *ḍa-jha1-liḍi*.
15. *kṣa-cha-jha1-a-ṭa*: In the case of *somādyādiṣam* and so forth.

By means of your prayers, you caused the cow to issue from the hide; those two who were old, you made young again. O sons of Sudhanvan, you fashioned a horse from a horse; having yoked the chariot, you went toward the gods. From the hide, you caused the cow to flow forth by means of your insights; those two who were aged, you made youthful. O sons of Sudhanvan, you fashioned a horse from a horse; having harnessed the chariot, you went unto the gods.
O sons of Sudhanvan, you brought forth a cow from the skin of a dead cow—meaning, from the flayed hide of a deceased animal;
that is to say, you produced another cow covered with that very same skin, or rather, fashioned another cow resembling it.
Although the employment of horses and other animals was already mentioned previously, he speaks again in order to make known the extreme difficulty with which they were obtained.
Not only did you restore the cow-pen, but you also made those two parents who were worn out and aged young again.
Furthermore, with one horse already present, you skillfully fashioned another horse from a horse;
because you did this, having yoked your chariot with horses, you went unto the gods, Indra and the others, reaching their presence.

"Drink this water," you said; "or rather, drink this, the stirring of the *muñja* grass. O sons of Sudhanvan, if you do not take pleasure in that, then indeed exhilarate yourselves at the third libation. This water. Drink. Thus. You said. This. Or. Indeed. Drink. The stirring of the *muñja* grass. O sons of Sudhanvan. If. That. Not at all. You take pleasure in. At the third. Indeed. Libation. Exhilarate yourselves. 8.
Now the seer causes them to recite the meaning spoken by the gods, identifying them as the Ṛbhus: "It was you who spoke thus to the Ṛbhus.
O Saudhanvanas, sons of Sudhanvan, you said, "Drink this water characterized as Soma. Thus did you speak.

In the case of *bravīti*, when the middle-voice plural ending *iṅ* is replaced by *tanap*, it is treated as having the marker *p*; consequently, by Pāṇini’s rule 7.3.93 (*dhruva īt*), the vowel *u* is replaced by *ī*.
This refers to the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).
"Vā" means "or.
"Gha" is either meaningless or indicates a well-known fact.
This is the place of Muñjana; Muñjana is the name of a mountain, the source of the Soma plant.
Because it was brought from there, it has been purified by that Muñjana grass—meaning it is cleared of weeds.
"Drink this water in the form of Soma-juice," you said;
this refers to the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*). O *Ṛbhus*, you do not at all desire—that is, you do not take pleasure in—that work of drinking Soma connected with both pressings.
The root *haryati* means "to desire" (*kānti*), because it is listed among those actions in the passage: “*haryati uśika*” (Nirukta 2.6.10).
At the third pressing (*tṛtīya-savana*), however, you should rejoice (*mādayādhvai*), meaning you become exceedingly satiated;
for, as stated in “O Ṛbhus, gods, be intoxicated by the Soma,” they partake of the Soma at the third pressing.
Thus you spoke to the Ṛbhus;
or rather, this is the speech addressed to the Ṛbhus themselves:

"O sons of Sudhanvan, having attained divinity and come by chariot to the place of sacrifice for the drinking of Soma, you said, 'Drink this water characterized as Soma at the morning pressing, for we are weary.'"

In that regard, if you do not desire this, [then] "drink the *vājina* which has been purified by *muñja* grass or defiled by *muñja* grass," so he said. Later, if you two do not indeed delight in those two, O horses, then exhilarate yourselves at the third pressing (*savana*), because even there the *vājina* is present.
1. kṣa-ba-ṭa: by that; jha1: by the expanded one. 2. kṣa-ja-ṭa: but rather; ṅsa1: however. 3. kṣa-ṅa-jha1-ja-ṭa: repeats.
4. Kṣa, Ja, Ṭa: the Soma connected with both the morning and midday pressings.
5. Ṅa, Jha¹: of the mantra alone.
6. Kṣa, Ja, Ṭa: no desire.
7. Ṅa—corrected. 8. Kṣa-Ṅa-Jha¹-Na-Ta—after "vājinapracārāt," there is an addition: "because elsewhere they have a connection with the *vājina* (via the formula) 'vājibhyo vājinam' and so forth.
"Water is most abundant," said one; "Fire is most abundant," said another.
To her who was being struck down among many, one spoke; speaking thus, they set the cups in motion.
"The waters are most abundant," said one. "Fire is most abundant," said another. To many he spoke of Vadhryaṇtī. Speaking the truth, they anointed the cups. 9.
Regarding the question of why they spoke the truth when dividing the *camasa* into four parts, he says:

1. "One" refers to any one of the three [elements]. 2. "Water is the most abundant. 3. Thus 4. he said; for there is no other reality (*tattvāntara*) more praiseworthy than water that benefits the world.

"Water is most abundant," he said; "Truth," he declared. The preeminence of water is established by such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, He created water alone" (Manu Smṛti 1.8). Likewise, another said, "Fire is most abundant."
One considers that fire alone is most abundant, because it is fire itself that sustains the world through its internal and external activities such as burning, cooking, eating, and digesting.
Likewise, [the word] *vadhryantīm*:
*vadhar* is a name for the thunderbolt (*vajra*) ending in the letter *r*, since it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (2.20.7): "The thunderbolt is *arka*."
"She desires that for the sake of rain-water" refers to the row of clouds as they are about to burst.

Although she does not herself require the thunderbolt for her own destruction, she is nevertheless figuratively said to "desire it" because she is struck by Indra’s thunderbolt for the sake of bringing rain.
Or alternatively:
For the sake of those many [people], he spoke of the earth— desiring her own destruction,
which was "vadhyantīm" (a Vedic form where the letter *r* is inserted)—
as being the most excellent among the many who were in agreement. He declared that very [earth] to be the best for those many who were in accord.
Since water also has the cloud as its cause;

thus, speaking true words—that is, words that accord with reality—according to the seasons (*ṛtāḥ*), they addressed one another and *apiśata* the cups, meaning they divided them into four parts as composite wholes.
[The root] *piś* means "to divide."
The augment *num* is applied according to the rule "after *śas*, *śuci*, and so forth.

It is with reference to this very act of speaking like Ṛta that Yāska, while explaining the word *ṛbhu*, stated: "The *ṛbhavaḥ* shine widely (*uru bhānti*), or they shine by means of their work (*vartena bhānti*), or they come into being by means of their work (*vartena bhavanti*)" (Nirukta 11.15).
One [of them] brings the water, the cow, and the sheep; another carves the meat prepared through skillful guidance.
From the unloosing of the bond, the bright one alone brought them hither; the two parents approached their sons who were still warm from the womb.

One drives the female ox, the water, the cow, the sheep, and the goat; one carves the meat; one brings it with skillful guidance; one wipes it clean until it is free of blood; one carries away the refuse; and what indeed did the two parents do for their children? || 10 ||
In this context, he states that the *Ṛbhus* themselves, having assumed the form of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), carry out the sacrifice everywhere:
“*śroṇām śoṇam*.
The absence of the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) [as in *śroṇāmśoṇam*] is due to the rule “*vā chandasi*” (Pāṇini 6.1.106).
7. Water of a red color; 8. blood. Among the *ṛbhūs*, one among the priests said: "The cow. 1.
Among the three [manuscripts] kṣa, jha, ja, and ṭa, one said: "Water is the most abundant. 2. From this very reason, water is most abundant.
3. Kṣa, jha, 1, ja, ṭa—thus; ca, jha, ta, ṛta. 4.
Kṣa, ja, ṭa—the internal and the external are indeed fire.
5. Kṣa, ja, ṭa—it is thus.

6. In manuscripts Ṅa and Jha, the word ‘api’ is absent. 7. In manuscripts Ṅa and Jha, it reads ‘vatreṇa’. 8. In manuscript Ṅa, it reads ‘tāmeva ekaṃ (? bahubhyaḥ avādibhyaḥ’; in manuscripts Kṣa, Ja, and Ṭa, it reads ‘tāmeva ekaḥ bahubhyaḥ avādibhyaḥ’.
9. [The syllables] kṣa, ja, and ṭa made the whole into four parts; they divided it into four. 10.
[The syllables] kṣa, jha, and ṭa [became] "red" (śoṇam).
Or, according to the rule *vā chandasi*, there is no absence of the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) [resulting in *ābhṛtam*].
He "divides" (*vibhājati*), meaning he causes it to go toward the outer ground and establishes it as belonging to the *rakṣas* demons.

Likewise, "one" [person] "carves" (*piśati*) the "flesh" (*māṃsam*)—that which has been "brought" (*ābhṛtam*) or prepared by means of a "knife" (*sūdayā*), that is, a "cleaving instrument" (*svadhiti*). The meaning is that he carves—that is, breaks down into parts—the flesh that has been struck or prepared in the form of the heart, tongue, eyes, and other portions; he divides its various members with the knife.

Then one [of them], having completely severed the flesh, removed—that is, cast away—the excrement from within the belly, which was like withered grass and called *ubadhyā*. When they had stood in such a form, what indeed did the two parents—the husband and wife who protect the sacrifice—offer to the *Ṛbhus*, those sons in the place of sons, after all [the tasks] had been performed? What gift did they present?
The suffix *hi* is used after the root *ava*, which has the sense of throwing, in Vedic usage.
The meaning is that since everything has been accomplished by them alone, there is nothing further for those two to do.
Alternatively, this is the meaning: one among them leads a lame, crippled cow toward the water.
Another chews meat that has been brought and prepared by a butcher through the act of slaughtering.
Another carries away cow-dung—that is, dried cow-manure—from the place of the setting sun, that is, from the vicinity of sunset.
When the R̥bhus have performed [these tasks] in this manner, what else could you two expect to receive from your sons other than this service?
For him, O heroes, you made dry land out of the depths by your skillful work;
when you stayed in the house of Agohya, then you became food, and you went to the light.

For him, you made grass in the heights and water in the depths through your skillful work, O heroes, when you lay down in the house of Agohya; that indeed was a sin, for you did not follow after [the truth]. 11.

Having praised the *Ṛbhus*—the sons of Sudhanvan who, according to the *Purāṇas*, attained divinity through their deeds—the author now praises the *Ṛbhus* as the rays of the sun, as established in the Vedas.

Accordingly, Yāska, in the *Nirukta*, after providing various etymological explanations of the *Ṛbhus* as established by the method of the *Purāṇas*, and citing the verse "viṣṭī śamī" as an example, stated: "The rays of the sun are also called *Ṛbhus*" (*Nirukta* 11.16), and then cited this very *ṛc* in that sense.
O *Ṛbhus*, you who shine widely— that is, extensively— or who shine by means of *ṛta* (the sun), or who approach for the sake of water by means of *ṛta* (water);
for it is well known that the rays of light shine extensively,
and likewise the *ṛtasiras* (rays) from the sun.
It is well known that even the waters of the clouds, having taken up the essence from the earth during the time of heat through their rays, rain down again during the rainy season;
as the scripture states: "From activity arises rain" (Manu 3.76).

Such are you, O men—leaders of light, rain, and water—who have produced *tṛṇa* (grass), in the form of rice and other grains, upon those aforementioned regions such as Meru and others, for the sake of this living world and for its benefit. You have indeed made it so.
The suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule: "In the Vedic language, after a preposition, when the sense is that of the verbal root."
Likewise, in the downward-sloping regions, they created—that is, they made—waters for him alone.
Not for their own enjoyment, it is said;
rather, through *svapasyayā*, that is, with the desire for excellent action.
The meaning is that you desire what the sacrificers praise, saying, "A beautiful deed has been performed by these [Maruts].
Furthermore, for as long as you have slept—that is, remained inactive during the night—in the house, the orb, of Agohya, the one who cannot be grasped, namely the Sun (Āditya).
In *pasa svapne*:
from this [root], in the *luṅ* tense, as before, there is the substitution of *tanap* for it;
due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is the elision (*luk*) of *śap*.
For all that time during the day, you do not follow this [light] now;
that is to say, for as long as the night persists while the sun is hidden, for exactly that long you do not follow it even during the day.
Or alternatively:

Regarding that which is not to be hidden in the house, for as long as you slept in the atmosphere without seeing rain, during all that time until now, in this season of rains, you do not follow—that is, you do not pursue or attain—this activity in the form of a downpour of rain that causes the crops to flourish.
The meaning is: for exactly as long as you withhold rain, for that same length of time you should pour it forth.

1. Kha, Ca, Ja, Pha: *piśati* for the parents; Ka: *piśati* for the two parents. 2. Kṣa, Jha, Ṭa: by virtue of being well-established in the Purāṇas. 3. Kha, Pha: as examples therein; Ka, Jha: as examples of this; Ta: as examples.
4. [The phonemes] ḍa, jha, jha, and ḷ [occur] in the rainy season (varṣākāla). 5. The word "yathā" is not present in the [sections] beginning with ca and ta.
[End of] Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 22, Sūtra 161. The Second Aṣṭaka, [verse] 959.
When you crept about the worlds with eyes closed, where indeed were those two great parents of yours?
He who grasped your extended member and he who spoke of it—you spoke forth to him.
Having closed their eyes, as they crept around the worlds—where indeed were your two venerable parents? He who seized your quivering member and he who proclaimed it to you—you proclaimed it to him.
O Ṛbhus, you rays, when— having closed up, that is, having covered the worlds, the born beings, with masses of clouds— you glide around, meaning you move about or rain;
while the *tātyā* (the waters) are being extended (*tāyamāne*),
or rather:
*Tātyā* means "in those rainy seasons. The suffix *tāt* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), and there is the substitution of *ā* for the letter *d*. Alternatively, it is an adjective qualifying "father" (*pitṛ*).
Where indeed were the two parents of the world, the Sun and the Moon, who protect it, at that time? Where exactly did they abide?
[The form *āsatuḥ* is derived from the root *as* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), with the substitution of *bhū* by irregular rule (*vyatyaya*), and the absence of the augment *āṭ*.
Alternatively:]
This form [vavr̥ṣāṇā] is derived from the root *vr̥ṣ* (to rain) with the suffix *liṭ*.
The meaning is "raining by means of the division of day and night. Furthermore, whoever—be it a Rākṣasa or any other—acts as an obstructer of your rain, [him you strike] down.
This is a name for the arms, since it has been stated [in the Nirukta]: "The two arms are called *karas*" (Ni. 2.4.7).
Here, however, the form ends in *a*.
He takes—that is, he seizes or offers resistance—with your hand; destroy (*arśapat*), that is, annihilate him.
And he who spoke excessively—he restrains him with his voice; "pro" means "not at all," as in "do not speak excessively," or "do not make sounds of reproach and the like.
Alternatively, it means: "he who indeed praises—praise him excessively."
When the *Ṛbhus* saw him beautifully adorned, they asked: "O Agohya, who has awakened this for us?
The ram Basta declared him to be the awakener: "After a full year, this [sacrifice] was undertaken and ascended."

The Ṛbhus, having well adorned [the chariot], asked that [question]: "O Agohya, who has awakened us here? Who was it that woke us? The goat declared him to be the awakener: "Today, after a full year, this [chariot] has been unyoked. 13.

O *Ṛbhus*, you who consist of rays, sleeping well within the solar orb (*ādityamaṇḍala*), you asked—that is, you posed a question—to that Sun regarding that statement, for the sake of rain. [The form] *svapuṣvāṃsaḥ* is derived from the root *svap* with the suffix *kasu* in the perfect tense. You asked that Sun that question.
If it is asked what that is, it is said:

O Agohya, you who cannot be hidden by anyone, O Lord Āditya, who has awakened—meaning, who causes to be known and impels—this work of ours consisting of rain? [The form is derived from the root *budh* with the desiderative suffix *sañ*, in the *luṅ* tense, with the augment *caṅ*. Who provides assistance?
The Sun is the dweller within all; he is sufficient for everyone. The suffix *ta* is derived from the root *vas* according to the *auṇādika* rules.
The change to *ba* occurs because of the distinction between *va* and *ba*.
He spoke to the one who awakens and impels, the roaring wind in the atmosphere, saying:
"It is he who impels you.
Then, raining by means of the assistance of the wind, you have today, at the completion of a full year, caused this world to be revealed in its manifold variety.
The meaning is: "Just as previously the sun and moon were not seen, so now, having rained, when the rainy season has passed, make the entire world manifest.
The suffix *aṅ* is applied to the root *syati* in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense according to the rule "asyativaktikhyāti... [Pāṇini 3.1.52].

By day the Maruts go upon the earth, the wind goes through the mountains in the intermediate space;
Varuṇa goes by way of the sea, you who desire [us], O sons of strength.
By day the Maruts go upon the earth; this Agni goes by the wind through the mid-air; Varuṇa goes by the oceans, O sons of strength, seeking you. 14.

The Rbhus—the descendants (*napāt*) of that strength (*śavas*) which causes rain, meaning those who cause it to descend—desiring you and wishing to perform acts favorable to rain, all the gods come seeking you alone. Why is this so? It is said:
the Maruts, the gods favorable to rain, go from and come to the sky (*div*), the celestial world.
The third case ending is acute by virtue of the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.
From one stage to another, fire goes forth and returns.
This wind, the ever-moving air, goes through the intermediate space and comes from the intermediate space.
Likewise, Varuṇa, the enveloping deity presiding over the waters, comes with the oceans—that is, with the waters whose nature is that of the ocean.
Or rather, these gods who previously arrived to assist with the rain have now completed their task.
Indra is well-known;
Ṛbhukṣan is Prajāpati, the abode of the gods.
Or alternatively:
This is the great name *Ṛbhukṣāḥ*, an epithet of Indra, because it is listed among his names in the Nirukta (3.3.10): "Ṛbhukṣāḥ, Ukṣā.
[The author] shows the possibility of censure:
*yat*—because [he is the lord] of *vājinaḥ*—those who possess vigor or those who possess sacred knowledge (*brahman*)—of *devajātasya*, that which has arisen in the form of many deities.
The meaning is that the *upās* and so forth constitute its limbs, such as the head;
for there is the Vedic revelation: “Verily, the *upā* is the head of the sacrificial horse” (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.1), and so on.
Or else:
Because he was born from the gods, and because he was produced in the lineage of the Gandharvas; *sati* means one whose nature is to glide;
this is a name for a horse.

We shall proclaim—that is, we shall speak with excellence—of the heroic deeds, the valorous acts, and the powers of such a horse of great majesty; [we shall speak] regarding its *vidyās*, which are the means for attaining knowledge in the sacrifice (*yajña*).
Therefore, let them not turn away from us, but rather grant their favor; this is the meaning.

When they lead before them the seized gift of the goat, covered with a bright cloth and gold, the goat bleats facing the east; the animal of all forms, the son of Pṛthivī, goes toward that which is dear to Indra and Pūṣan. When they lead before them the seized gift of the goat, covered with a bright cloth and gold, the goat bleats facing the east; the animal of all forms, the son of Pṛthivī, goes toward that which is dear to Indra and Pūṣan. 2.
Because [he is] with a bright garment;
"nirṇij" is a name for form;
and with gold.

*Rekaṇas* is a name for wealth; for it is stated among the synonyms for that [wealth] in the *Nighaṇṭu*: “*Nirṇij*, *vatri*, *rekaṇas*, *riktha*” (*Nirukta* 3.7.1) and “*rekaṇas*, *riktha*” (*Nirukta* 2.10.2).
In both cases, the possessive suffix is elided.
The officiating priests lead before the horse—a horse adorned with gold and ornaments, covered and surrounded on all sides—an ewe that has been seized, held, and accepted as a gift to be given;
that such a goat (or ewe) goes forward well, with excellent and praiseworthy movement, even while being struck.
The root *mīñ* means "to injure.
From this root, in its *yaṅ*-lopped (*yaṅluganta*) form, the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is used in the sense of the object by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively,
his imitation of sound is "uttering the word *mema*";
*viśvarūpaḥ* means endowed with many colors, such as having a black neck or a black forehead, that is to say, possessing various colors.
Such is this [offering] for Indra and Pūṣan.
Indra is well-known;
Pūṣan is the nourishing deity Agni.
It is dear to those two:
because it is stated that "the black-necked [animal] belongs to Agni" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.5.22), it is dear to Agni;
and since all [animals] belong to Indra, it is dear to Indra.
May Pārtha obtain such food as this.

This goat, the portion for Pūṣan belonging to all the gods, is led forward along with the vigorous horse. When Tvaṣṭṛ, by means of the steed, quickens this beloved sacrificial cake for the sake of glory. eṣaḥ | chāgaḥ | puraḥ | aśvena | vājinā | puṣṇaḥ | bhāgaḥ | nīyate | viśvadaivyaḥ | abhipriyam | yat | puroḍāśam | arvata | tvaṣṭā | it | enam | sauśravasāya | jinvati ||3||
This goat, hornless and unborn, is the portion to be shared by Pūṣan— the nourisher Agni— along with the horse, the swift-moving steed.
It belongs to all the gods (viśvadaivya),
for since Agni is the self of all the gods, it is dear to all the gods by virtue of being his own.
Such a goat (*aja*) is led, that is, brought, to the front (*puras*). Since it is done in this manner, therefore [he attains] the Beloved (*priyam*), the one who causes delight.

(1) [Notes: 1. *kṣa-na-ṭa*—this name; 2. *jha1*—the goat (*ajam*); 3. *kṣa-na-ṭa*—the goat (*ajaḥ*) at each seasonal turn (*ṛtuśaḥ kṛtāvṛttau*); 4. *ṅa-jha1*—one whose movement is praiseworthy (*praśasyagamanaḥ*); 5. *jha-jha1*—of many colors (*anekavarṇaḥ*); 6. *kha-ca-pha*—the horse (*aśvaḥ*). (Ṛgveda 1.161.121)
The sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is to be offered first. *Vena* is the unborn [sacrificial animal]; or it is Tvaṣṭṛ, the god who is the progenitor of all, according to the Vedic revelation:
"Tvaṣṭṛ fashions forms" (*Tai. Saṃ. 1.5.9.2*).
Or, it is Agni, the pervader.

Because it is stated, "For the seer fears both" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.95.5), and because Yāska says in the *Nirukta* (8.15), "The two kindling woods (*araṇī*) are day and night," it is understood that the connection with the kindling woods belongs to Agni alone.

With the horse possessing the kindling wood (*araṇavat*), he brings forth—that is, he performs—the act of pleasing for the sake of beautiful food (*vsauśravasāya*) from the gods. When the men lead the horse three times around the path to the gods (*devayāna*) according to the seasons, [he does so] while desiring [the goal].
Here comes first the portion of Pūṣan; as the one who knows, he announces the sacrifice to the gods.
That which is sacrificial, offered according to the seasons, traveling by the path of the gods— this is what human beings should thrice carry around;
it is to be designated by the term "well-inspired" (*suvipra*),
and this term also indicates the unmentioned officiating priests.

All these [streams], by means of that well-known sacrifice—which is well-performed (*svarakṛta*), beautifully executed (*suṣṭukaraṇīya*), or well-adorned (*svalaṃkṛta*), and which is perfectly accomplished through excellence of pronunciation and is well-desired (*sveneṣṭa*)—fill up (*ā pṛṇadhvam*) on all sides the *vakṣaṇās*, meaning the streams of clarified butter and the like, or the well-known rivers whose nature is to flow. The sense is: "Having properly directed the sacrifice, bring about its fruit."
May the prosperity of those who prepare the sacrificial post, those who carry the post, those who carve the horse-protector for the one seeking horses,
and those who provide the cooking-vessel for the roasted grain, impel us.

May those who fashion the wooden rings for the sacrificial post, and those who carry the post, and those who carve the crest-piece for the horse-post, and those who prepare the cooking-vessel for the steed—may their overwhelming power impel us. 6.
Those who fashion the *vaṣka*— the cutters of the wood suitable for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—
and also those who carry the post,
and those who [carry] the *capāla*.
They call the portion of the sacrificial post that is to be placed at its top the *capāla*;
those who carve it for the *aśvayūpa*, the sacrificial post for binding the horse.
The expression "takṣati" (he fashions) is a grammatical anomaly (*vacanavyatyaya*).
They accomplish it well. And those who prepare for the swift, unyielding steed the cooking-vessel— the wooden implements and such that serve as the means for cooking—
they also let the victorious resolve, the thought "this must be done by all means," of those officiating priests belonging to us, pervade [the sacrifice].
The word *invati* signifies pervasion (*vyāpti*), because it is listed among those words [meaning pervasion] in the statement: "The root *inv* means to pervade (*nankṣa*)."
Or rather:
may their overcoming favor us;
that is to say, having brought the sacrifice to a successful conclusion, may it endow us with its fruit.
He has approached with a well-disposed mind; the prayer has been established for the regions of the gods, he whose back is smooth.
The wise seers rejoice after him; we have made Subandhu a kinsman among the nourishment of the gods.

He has approached; my prayer has been offered with goodwill. He of the smooth back has gone toward the regions of the gods. The inspired sages rejoice after him. We have made him a good kinsman in the prosperity of the gods. 7.
"May the *manman*—the fruit to be meditated upon—approach from the benevolent one (*sumat*).
Yāska [states]: "'Sumat' means 'of its own accord'" (Nirukta 6.22).
Or alternatively:

The most intoxicating [Soma] has been placed, indeed, within me; it is being held there. The horse, having become the fruit [of the sacrifice], has arrived, and he has been "held" by me—this is the meaning.
For what purpose?
With a back that is "smooth" (*vīta*)— meaning either well-nourished through excellent feeding or beautiful—
such as this [horse],
let him approach to fulfill the desires of the gods.
For the sake of the sacrifice, we fashion this Subandhu—the horse of beautiful construction—into a means of nourishment for the gods who are being invoked.
May the wise priests, the seers who perceive beyond the senses, and other inspired sages rejoice after him;
may they be fully satisfied, exclaiming, "Well done!"

1. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-amṛtakulyādīn* refers to those things whose nature is fluidity. 2. *kṣa-na-ṭa-karaṇīya* means "that which is to be done. 3. *kṣa-kha-ca-ja-jha-kṣa-a-ṭa-ta-pha-va-belana*. 4. *kṣa-na-ṭa-dhāryate* means "it is maintained. 5. *kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa-mayi śritaḥ* means "resorted to me. 6. *jha-prāptapārśvādbhāgaḥ* means "the side portion has been reached. 7. *kṣa-jha-1-ma-ṭa-paritoṣayantu* means "may they satisfy."

Whatever halter, whatever tethering-rope of the swift steed, whatever head-stall, or whatever cord belongs to him; or whatever fodder, or grass placed within his mouth—all that of yours, let it remain with the gods. 8.
The *vājinaḥ* is the horse possessed of speed; its *dāma* is the rope tied around its neck;
and its *saṃdāna* is the binding cord that properly restrains it, namely the foot-tether. And there is the *śīrṣaṇyā*, the bridle-rope fastened upon its head.
From the word *śiras*, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule *bhave chandasi*;
then, by the rule *ye ca taddhite*, the substitution of *śīrṣan* occurs.
[The form is] *tirasścaritaḥ*.
Or rather, there is indeed (*gha*) grass placed, struck, or cast into the mouth—the opening—of this horse;
the word *gha* is used in the sense of "indeed" (*ha*), and it carries its well-known meaning.
O horse, may all those various things belonging to you exist among the gods;
may they abide within the gods, or may they attain the state of divinity.
A change in the grammatical construction of the words.
It is said that all those employed here attain divinity; however, the attainment of that state by the horse is not to be hoped for.

Whatever of the horse’s flesh the fly has eaten, or whatever is smeared upon the sacrificial post or the axe, or whatever is on the hands and the nails of the immolator—all that of yours, indeed, shall be among the gods. 9.
Whatever limb of the raw flesh—the uncooked meat—which constitutes a part of that horse, the fly has eaten; [may that be yours].
‘Aś’ means eating;
or else,
it is the genitive case used in the sense of the object.
Or else, it is the flesh of the horse that he eats;
or rather, it is the fat (*risa*) that remains on the *svaru* at the time of anointing the animal, according to the Vedic injunction:
"He anoints the animal with the *svaru*."

Alternatively, whatever fat there is at the time of sharpening the knife, at the time of cutting, and at the time of carving; whatever fat there is on the hands of the immolator; and whatever fat there is on the nails at the time of dismembering—all those, O horse, let them belong to the gods; let them be for the sake of satisfying the gods.
Whatever is in the udder of the belly, whatever odor there is of raw flesh—let the immolators prepare that well; let them cook the sacrificial victim until it is thoroughly cooked. 10.

1. *jha-rasa* (śa) reads *kharlanarajju*. 2. *kṣa-ja-ṭa* do not have *‘gha’*. 3. *kṣa-ṅa-ja-ṭa* read *tāni*; the word *api* is used in the sense of *śa*. 4. *ṅa-jha-1* read *kim*. 5. *ṅa-jha-1* do not have *‘na’*. 6. *ṅa-jha-1* read *traśanakāle*. 7. *ca-ca*. 8. *ca* reads *saṃtoṣārthī saṃbhavantu*; *kṣa-ṅa-jha-jha-1-a-ṭa* read *santu neṣamarthāya bhavantu*. [Ma. 1. a. 22 sū. 162] Second Aṣṭaka, 965: That which belongs to the belly, namely the *ūvadhya*—the slightly undigested grass and excrement—*apacāti*, i.e., goes away.
And whatever scent of rawness there is, even a trace of uncooked meat,

whatever slight odor of undercooked flesh remains at the time of cooking— that all the *śamitāraḥ*, the preparers who perform the dismemberment, shall make well-prepared; that is, they shall render it free from the aforementioned defects.

Moreover, let them cook the sacrificial portion—the limb of the animal fit for sacrifice—so that it is prepared with a cooking suitable for the gods; the meaning is that they should not overcook it to suit the ancestors and humans, nor undercook it.

Whatever pus from your body, being heated by fire, flows out when you have been pierced by the stake—let that not cling to the ground, let it not cling to the grass; may it be offered as a pleasing oblation to the gods.

Whatever from your body, while being roasted by the fire, drips down upon the spit as you lie struck down—let that not cling to the earth, let it not cling to the grass; let that be granted to the longing gods. 11.
O horse, whatever essence or anything else flows out from your limb as it is being cooked by fire;
likewise, whatever part of your body, in the form of its essence, flows out or issues forth toward the spit when you have been completely slaughtered—
that very limb must not cling to or adhere to the earth.
The suffix *ak* is applied after the root *śriṣ* because it belongs to the *puṣādi* group.
