Likewise, let it not depart from the grass at the time of cooking, nor from the *darbha* blades at the time of slaughter. For if one asks where that which has fallen should go, it is said:
let that such [oblation] be given (*rātam*) as a complete offering to the gods who desire it.
May the approval of those who look upon the cooked horse, of those who say, "Bring forth the fragrant one," and of those who wait for a morsel of meat from the chewed— may their acclaim impel us.
Those who look upon the horse as cooked, those who say of him, "Take it out, it is fragrant," and those who wait for a portion of the horse's flesh—may even their approval further us. 12.
Those who look all around at the cooked horse, the swift steed—a limb of the sacrificial horse—with the intent to purify it;

and those who say of it, "O fragrant one, possessing a beautiful scent, take this away from here and give even a little to us"—or alternatively: [The rest of the passage follows: ...those who say, "Give us even a small portion of this," or rather, [the text continues with the ritual context].
They say, "Take it from the gods without remainder," because it is fragrant; therefore, it is fit for the gods.
Furthermore, those men who wait upon the leavings of the flesh—those who seek the remnants of the meat offered from this steed—desire them.
And furthermore, may their *abhigūrtiḥ*—their exaltation—*invatu*, that is, pervade, *naḥ*, us, by raising [us] up on all sides.

Just as [it was done] by us: 1. in the *kṣama-ṭa-supu* [mantras]; 2. in the *va-jha-darbheṣu*, let it not perish; 3. in the *cha-pāvanabuddhyā* alone; *jha*-reading: *pācanaṃ budhyā*; 4. *ṅa*-reading: "this has a beautiful fragrance"; 5. *kṣa-na-ṭa*-reading: "by which the Rākṣasas"; *ṅa-jha1*-reading: "and those who are Rākṣasas"; 6. *kṣa-ṅa-jha1-na-ṭa*-reading: "the resolve"; 7. *jha1*-reading: "they, just as..."
The *Ṛgveda* [states]: "They desire thus for what has been obtained, so that the sacrifice may be carried out"— this is the meaning.

Alternatively, the mantra may be explained as being centered on the gods: "May their approval favor us—that is, may their effort become fruitful—those gods who look upon the swift steed and wonder, 'When will he be offered? and seeing the delay, those who say, 'Carry him away with fragrant breath; offer him up entirely to us,' and those who wait for alms of the flesh of such a horse. (Note: The text contains several scribal errors. The intended reading of *mantraḥ* is likely *mantraḥ*. The term *paripaśyanti* is corrected from *paripasyanti*. The phrase *surabhirāmenaṃ nirhara* is interpreted as *surabhirāmena nirhara*; *nirhara* is understood here as a command to carry away or offer. The term *ava~to* is corrected to *avato*. The final *udyamaḥ* is corrected from *udyama*).
The inspection of the flesh-cooking cauldron, the vessels for pouring the hot broth,
the lids for the warming pots, and the carving-boards attend upon the horse.
The inspection of the flesh-cooking cauldron; the vessels for pouring the hot fat; the warming-covers; the lids of the cooking-pots; the limbs; the carving-boards—they all attend upon the horse. 13.
*māṃsaparcanyāḥ* means "those that cook meat. The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) to the root *pacati*.
By the rule *māṃsasya paci yuḍdhañoḥ* (Kāśikā 6.1.144), there is elision of the final vowel [of *māṃsa*].

The poking-stick (*nīkṣaṇa*)—the wooden instrument for testing the cooking of the cauldron (*ukhā*) and the pot (*sthālī*)—as well as those various vessels (*pātrāṇi*) for pouring the boiled broth (*yūṣṇa*), the warming-vessels (*ūṣmaṇyā*) suitable for warding off heat, the covers (*apidhānā*) for the meat-filled bowls (*caru*), and the Vetasa branches used as limbs (*aṅga*) for extracting the heart and other organs, along with the carving-knives (*sūnā*) and other tools for cutting portions—all these attend (*paribhūṣanti*) this horse, that is, they adorn the parts of the horse by means of their respective functions; the meaning is that they prepare it.
The root *bhū* in the sense of "adornment" belongs to the *bhūvādika* class.
The stepping forth, the sitting down, the rolling about,
and whatever the horse has drunk or whatever fodder he has eaten— all that of yours shall be present among the gods.

The stepping forth, the sitting down, the turning about, and whatever the swift steed has drunk from the water-trough, and whatever fodder he has eaten—all that of yours shall be present among the gods. 14.
That which is "nikramaṇa" is a place where one steps down completely;
that is, a place where one descends thoroughly. That which is "niṣadana" is a place where one sits down completely; that is, a place where one settles down thoroughly.
"Vivartana" means turning about or wandering here and there;
the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the locative (the place where such occurs).
And "padyīśam" refers to the fetter for the feet of the "arvataḥ," that is, the horse.
Alternatively,
a "place" (*pradeśa*) is that which possesses a "binding" (*bandhana*).
In all these cases, even the location itself is accepted so as not to render the horse's hair and other features— which serve the purpose of the deity— meaningless.
Alternatively,
it should be understood as referring to action;
the meaning is that those movements such as stepping forward and so forth which exist at the time of seizing and restraining [the victim].
"That which you drank, that which you drank from the vessel (yadukam),
and that which you ate— the edible grass and so forth—
O horse, may all those [acts], such as your stepping and the rest, belong to the gods; may they pervade the gods, meaning that even those [actions] should not be in vain."

1. Let it be carried out by *ṅa-jha-jha-sa1*. 2. This mantra is *cha-ca-jha-sa1*. 3. May it protect (*invatu*) by *ca-jha1*. 4. The resolve (*saṃkalpaḥ*) is *ṅa-jha1*. 5. The means for the formation of the limbs, such as the heart and so forth, are *jha1*. 6. Him (*enam*) [is indicated] by *kṣa-ja-ṭa*. 7. Rolling about (*luṭhanaṃ*) or moving about (*vartanaṃ*) is [indicated] by *kṣa-ṅa-jha1-ja-ṭa*. 8. That region ending with that is *jha-jha1*. 9. At the time of seizing the horse (*aśvālambhasamaye*), [it is indicated by] *jha1*. 10. May he obtain (*prāpnotu*) by *ca-ja*. "May the smoke-scented one not lead you away; may the pot be released, O seekers, for the slayer has struck."
The gods accept that horse which has been sacrificed, offered, praised, and consecrated with the cry of *vaṣaṭ*.

Let not the smoke-scented Agni make you roar; let not the glowing cauldron, striking against you, injure you. The gods accept that horse which has been offered, enjoyed, praised with hymns, and consecrated with the cry of *vaṣaṭ*. 15.
"O Horse! May Agni, pervaded by smoke and smelling of smoke, not make a sound;
that is, upon seeing the smoke, let him not make a noise.
For it is prescribed that an expiation must be performed for the sound of a horse."
Or rather:
O you whose parts are being cooked, may the smoke-scented heat cause you to resound;
for if there is a resonance, there would be the breaking of the vessel.
The prohibition of the *caṅ* affix is established by the rule *na nayati* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.51),
and there is an absence of *vṛddhi* strengthening by the rule *hy-antakṣaṇa*.
Furthermore, "ārjantī" means glowing intensely through extreme contact; "mā abhi vitta" means do not move toward me from all sides, that is to say, let it not destroy me by means of excessive heat.
The root *ovij* is used in the senses of fear and trembling.
The elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is according to Vedic rules (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, in the *luṅ* tense, there is the elision of the *s* by the rule *jhalo jhali*.
The pot is qualified as "jaghni," meaning it strikes or heats [the contents] with its heat.
The root *ghrā* is used in the sense of perceiving odor;
by the rule *āghrā-han-iti kiṅ-pratyayaḥ*, the suffix *kiṅ* is applied.
That such a horse—desirable, impelled by the Hotṛ, brought for the oblation, and urged forward—is presented for the sake of being offered.
Or rather:
that which has been sacrificed, gratified by the *prayāja* offerings, brought near, circumambulated with fire, and celebrated; that which is joined with the *āgū* invocation "ye yajāmahe";
that which is consecrated by the gods through the *vaṣaṭ* call—such as this, the gods (*devāsaḥ*) receive and accept it.

When they spread out a garment for the horse, an upper covering, and the golden ornaments; when they present the halter, the foot-rope, and the dear trappings to the steed among the gods—these they cause to be brought.
The garment they spread for the horse, the upper covering, the gold ornaments, the halter, the foot-rope—the dear things they bestow upon him among the gods. || 16 ||
For the horse being immolated, they spread out an upper garment—an upper covering suitable for clothing—over it, covering it on all sides.
The root *stṛñ* means "to cover";
it belongs to the *krayādi* group.
Likewise, whatever golden objects—whether made of gold, silver, or bronze—they fashion for this horse;
likewise, "the courser" (arvantam), where the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive.

The halter of the swift horse, the head-band, and the *padīṃśa*—the foot-binding that has entered into the feet—these, being dear to the gods and even more beloved, having been tied and placed in the *cātvāla*, lead them toward the gods; they cause them to reach the gods.

1. *kṣa-ha-na-ṭa-vyāsaḥ* is smoke-scented fire; *jha-vyāsaḥ* is smoke-scented wind. 2. Let *kṣa-jha-na-ṭa* resound. 3. *kṣa-ha-jha-na-ṭa* is blazing. 4. *kṣa-ha-jha-na-ṭa* is that which is intended. 5. *jha* is what is to be given.

Whatever pain was inflicted upon you while being harnessed for the draft—with great force, by the hand, or with the whip—I soothe all those [pains] of yours with a sacred prayer (*brahman*), just as one offers oblations with the ladle at the sacrifices. 17. Whatever [pain] was inflicted upon you while being harnessed for the draft—with great force, by the hand, or with the whip—I soothe all those [pains] of yours with a sacred prayer (*brahman*), just as one offers oblations with the ladle at the sacrifices. 17.
By great strength, [of] you who have made the sound "śū-kṛta"—
this is an imitation of a sound— while making that "śūka" sound, when there was a falling down (*sāda*), a collapsing, or a failure to proceed, serving as the cause [for your intervention].

The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). The word *karṣat* has its final syllable accented by virtue of the rule "karṣattvataḥ. Moving [the whip] for the sake of the goal, he *tunoda*, that is, he torments you with either his hand or with a whip, acting like a prickle.

Since that is so, therefore, *te* (of you), *tā* those, *satrā* all, *adhvareṣu* in the sacrifices, *brahmaṇā* by means of the sacred formula (*mantra*), I *sūdayāmi*—that is to say, I pour out or prepare as an oblation (*āhuti*).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as in the sacrifices, *haviṣaḥ* of the oblation, such as clarified butter (*ājya*) and the like, they "pour out" (*sūdayanti*) with the *sruca* ladle, so it is here.

The axe meets the thirty-four ribs of the horse, the steed of the gods. Make the limbs free from injury; with skill, cut along every joint, proclaiming it as you dissect it. 18. Thirty-four. Of the steed. Of the friend of the gods. The ribs. Of the horse. The axe. Together. Approaches. Without holes. The limbs. With skill. Make. Joint by joint. Having proclaimed. Dissect. 18.

Of the vigorous horse, the kinsman of the gods, the beloved of the deities, there are thirty-four ribs—these being the bones situated on both sides, which are the structural terminations. The *svadhiti* (the sacrificial knife), the instrument for moistening, comes together—that is, it approaches correctly—for the purpose of cutting.
For other animals such as goats and the like, there are only twenty-six, according to the injunction: "Twenty-six are its ribs" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 2.6).
O you who perform the dissection, [cut] the limbs—the members of the body of this horse—so that they remain without gaps, according to their respective joints and with full awareness.
*Vayuna* is a name for wisdom (*prajñā*), because it is stated in the list of its names: *vayunam abhipyā* (Nirukta 3.9.10).
*Kṛṇota* means "make" or "do"; the substitution of *ta* for *tha* follows the rule *tasanasanathanāśca*.

The meaning is: having identified the heart, tongue, chest, and so forth, do not cut them in the middle. For that purpose, having announced at every joint—that is, at each limb such as the heart and others—"This has been cut," perform the dissection (*viśasta*) with full deliberation (*saṃśaddha*). [The root] *śas* is used in the sense of "to injure."

The elision of the *śap* suffix is Vedic (*chāndasa*). This is based on the injunction: “Make every limb of his complete” (*AiB* 2.6). One is the carver of Tvaṣṭṛ’s horse; two are the joiners. Such is the proper order (*ṛtu*). Those limbs of yours which I prepare according to the proper order, those portions of the cakes I offer into the fire. One. Of Tvaṣṭṛ. Of the horse. The carver. Two. The joiners. Are. Such. The order. Which. Of yours. Of the limbs. According to the proper order. I prepare. Those. Of the cakes. Forward. I offer. Into the fire. 19.
One is the dissector of Tvaṣṭṛ’s horse; two become the joiners. Thus, according to the season, whatever of thy limbs I prepare in due order, those portions of the cakes I offer into the fire. 19.

1. *kṣa-jha₁-a-ṭa*: in the sense of going. 2. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: they make the sound "śūka" while making the horse go; *cha*: they make the horse go; *jha₁*: they make it go everywhere. 3. *kṣa-jha₁-a-ṭa*: he destroys.
The "svadhuk" (well-yielding) one is the "viśastṛ"—the performer of the dissection—of this shining horse;
he is "one," that is, indeed unique. Who is he?
"Ṛtu" refers to Time (kāla) as characterized by the seasons, since everything is ultimately contained within that alone;
or alternatively,
"ṛtu" means the immolator (śamitṛ), one who goes forth to perform the slaughter without hesitation.
Likewise, at the end of the day, the two who extend [the sacrifice], the observers of the rule, namely the deities Day and Night, or Heaven and Earth, become the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Similarly, in the word *ṛtuḥ*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) and the shortening of the vowel according to the rule "ṛtyakaḥ. O horse, among your limbs, whichever members such as the heart and so forth I fashion—that is, I cut and prepare—at the proper time (*ṛtuthā*), those very parts, from among the fragments, I offer (*pra juhomi*) into the fire with excellence, according to my discernment.
Let not your dear self burn you as you enter it; let not the axe linger upon your body. Let not the greedy, unskilled carver, seeking to please himself, mangle your limbs haphazardly with the knife.

May your dear self not cause you pain as you enter [it]; may the axe [not harm you] as you proceed by the paths—the ways characterized as the path of the gods (devayāna) which serve as the means for auspicious travel. Indeed, you reach the gods themselves;
therefore, this statement is appropriate.
Regarding the question "By what means?", he says:
those two horses of Indra named Hari shall be yoked to your chariot for you; they have been yoked and will be yoked.
This is stated as a past tense because it takes the form of an aspiration.
The Nirukta states: "The two bay horses belong to Indra" (Ni. 1.15.1).
Likewise, the two spotted mares shall become yoked—that is, they will be harnessed—as the vehicles of the Great Ones.
And the Nirukta also says: "The spotted mares [belong] to the Great Ones" (Ni. 1.15.6).
The suffix *kin* is applied by the rule "ṛtvig" etc.;
the augment *num* is added by the rule "yujerasamāse";
and the vowel *ā* is substituted by the rule "supāṃ suluk".
Likewise, a certain horse (*vājī*) standing at the pole (*dhuri*) of a donkey—that is, a horse of this name—will draw it; that is to say, he will stand ready to carry it.
Or alternatively:

a horse (*vājī*) yoked to the path (*dhuri*) of the donkey-like Sun (*bhānu*) will attend him. The meaning is that as he is departing for his divinity, Indra sends forth his respective vehicles for the journey there.
Or rather,
those various mounts carry you as you have assumed each of those respective forms.

If, at the time of the *upākaraṇa* rite, the horse does not perform the smelling or the rolling, then this following formula for the sacrificer’s recitation (*vācanā*) occurs as a contingent ritual (*naimittikī*).

Accordingly, it is stated in the Sūtra: "He should cause the sacrificer to recite: 'May the prize-winning steed bring us abundance of cattle and abundance of horses'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 10.8).
May the prize-winning steed grant us abundance of cattle, abundance of horses, heroic sons, and wealth that nourishes all;
may Aditi grant us sinlessness, and may the horse, accompanied by our oblation, win for us sovereign power.

May the Steed grant us abundance of cattle, abundance of horses, heroic sons, and wealth that nourishes all; may Aditi grant us sinlessness, and may our horse, accompanied by oblations, win for us sovereign power. 22.

May the vigorous horse, being sacrificed for us, procure for us wealth that nourishes all—wealth consisting of a beautiful multitude of cattle, accompanied by a fine herd of cows—and which sustains the universe.
[The suffix] *yat* is used here in the sense of a collection according to Pāṇini 4.2.50 (*khalagorathāt*).
The acute accent on the first syllable of the second member is a Vedic peculiarity.
Alternatively,
in this context concerning collective formations (*sāmūhika*), according to the rule *asarvatra gorajādipratyayaprasaṅge* (Pāṇini 4.3.160), the suffix *yat* is applied;
and for that which ends in *yat*, the rule *ādyudāttaṃ yacchandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.197) prescribes the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable of the final member (*uttarapada*).
Likewise, "svaśvyam" means possessed of a beautiful collection of horses; likewise, "putrān" refers to sons. The word "putra" is common to both male and female offspring.
Therefore, the meaning is "sons who are men.
Alternatively,
it means "sons such as Vadhū and others, who are men and protectors of many, born from one's own self."
The meaning is: female offspring and male offspring.
Moreover (*uta*), wealth that nourishes all (*viśvāpuṣam*)—that is, riches capable of sustaining everyone.
Furthermore, may Aditi, the unbounded, make us sinless (*anāgāstvaṃ*); may she render us entirely free from fault.
Since the aforementioned fruits are impossible to attain in the absence of the destruction of sins produced by deficiency or excess [in ritual performance], freedom from sin is prayed for.

Furthermore, may the horse—possessing oblations (*haviṣmān*), that is, accompanied by the sacrificial offerings—win for us (*naḥ*) *kṣatra*, meaning strength and the splendor of the ruling power (*kṣātra-tejas*); may it bestow them.
The seventh hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "yadakrandaḥ," is composed by Dīrghatamas; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Since the horse is being praised, it has that [horse] as its deity.
The Anukramaṇikā states: "yadakrandaḥ sasvanā."
On the middle day of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, he praises the horse standing for the ritual dedication (*upākaraṇa*) with eleven verses beginning with *ādhyai*.

Accordingly, in the section "The three pressings" (*trīṇi sutyāni*), it is stated in the Sūtra: "He praises that horse standing for the dedication with the eleven [verses] beginning with *yadakranda*, without the *praṇava* chant" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 10.8).
1. *kṣa*, *ma*, and *ṭa* were joined with *yuj*. 2.
*kṣa*, *ma*, and *ṭa* [denote] smelling and turning away.
3. *kṣa*, *ja*, and *ṭa* [denote] relatives, sons, and so forth; *ḍa*, *jha₁*, [denote] relatives, sons, and so forth; *ḍa*, *jha₁*, [denote] relatives, sons, and so forth.
4. Ḍa-jha₁: self-protection;
5. Ḍa-jha₁: offspring.
"When you first cried out at birth, rising from the ocean or from the primordial mass (purīṣa)..."
The wings of a hawk, the forelegs of a deer—with these, O steed, you were born great and worthy of praise.
When you first neighed at birth, rising from the ocean or from the primordial waters, with the wings of a falcon and the forelegs of an antelope—great was your birth, O steed worthy of praise. 1.
O you who are skilled in the forest-dwelling horse Āraṇaka, having approached your birth—your very manifestation—you are to be praised; you are to be extolled by all.
The suffix *kyap* is applied by the rule "eti-stu-śāstṛ," and then the augment *tuk* is added.
How is it that he is worthy of praise? It is said: from which ocean—this is a name for the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
Born first— meaning produced— from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), either by taking up the massing of waters or by being the cause of the joy of yakṣas, gandharvas, and others; or else,
[born] from the ocean— the sun— by means of the "massing," that is, rain.
Therefore, he is "being born":
because it will be stated later, "O Vasus, you fashioned the horse from the sun" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.163.2).
Or else, "being born as he first rises from the *purīṣa*—that is, from the water which fulfills all desires."
You are such that you cried out—that is, you made a great sound—in order to favor the sacrificer.
Furthermore, your two wings—the means of flight—are like the wings of a hawk;
the meaning is that they are like those [wings] which are the means for swift flight.
Your two arms are like the two arms of a deer;
the meaning is that they are as swift as those.
Since this is so, therefore your birth is praiseworthy—this is the meaning.
Yama gave him; Trita harnessed him; Indra was the first to mount him.
The Gandharva grasped his reins; from the Sun, O Vasus, you fashioned the horse forth.
Given by Yama, Trita harnessed him; Indra was the first to mount him. The Gandharva grasped his rein; from the Sun, the Vasus fashioned the horse. 2.

Yama, under the name Niyāmaka, gave this horse; Trita—existing in the three places beginning with the earth, or the most pervasive wind—yoked him to the chariot. Furthermore, Indra, being the first—that is, the foremost or most excellent (the word *prathama* being a synonym for "chief")—[gave him].
*Adhyatiṣṭhat* means he presided over (*adhiṣṭhitavān*).
His *gandharva* is Soma, because it will be stated later: "He was separated from Soma by agreement" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.163.3).
And he grasped—that is, took hold of—the rein, the tethering rope, of this horse.
If it is asked from where such a horse originated, it is said:
O Vasus, you rays, you have fashioned—that is, you have perfectly and completely produced—this horse of such great majesty from Sūra, the Sun.
Alternatively,
by the word *vasu*, Yama and the others who were previously mentioned are referred to. O *vasus*, you who cover everything through your respective functions!
You fashioned this horse out from the sun, Āditya; you carved it out for the sake of impulsion in the place of this [fire] which is to be kindled. The verb *takṣati* means "to make."
And that [root] expresses action in general; here,
due to the context,
it refers to "holding," meaning "they have held correctly."
In *takṣelaṅ*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
There is also the elision of *k* according to the rule "the first of a conjunct [is elided] after *sk*" (*sko: saṃyogādyo:*).
1. Because of the flooding of water; 2. Like the wings of a hawk; 3. This one of great majesty; 4. The horse pervaded.

You are Yama; you are Āditya, O steed; you are Trita by your secret vow. You are separated from Soma by an interval; they say you have three bonds in heaven. 3. You are Yama. You are Āditya. O steed, you are Trita by your secret vow. You are separated from Soma by an interval. They say you have three bonds in heaven. 3.
O horse, you are Yama, the restrainer; you are Agni.
Because he was given by him, you are designated by that term.
Likewise, you are Āditya.
Because it has been stated, "He is pleased by those who delight in heroes," likewise, [He is pleased] by the secret vow (*guha-vrata*), that is, by an action to be concealed or difficult to define;
the meaning is that He exists as the pervasive form in all places.
Therefore, you are Trita, the wind stretched out across the three stations;
for it is said, "Trita joined him," and thus you possess that nature.

Alternatively, you are the seer named Trita, so called because of his connection with *guhena vratena*—the secret vow consisting of ritual action in the form of the means for yoga and other practices.
Furthermore, O horse, you are *vipṛkta*— the prefix *vi-* here signifies "together with"— united with Soma; for you have been taken up by him.
O Horse, they who know the past say that there are three bonds—the causes of your origin—for you who exist thus in the sky, in the world of heaven, or in the sun:
namely, the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the celestial realm.

They say you have three bonds in heaven, three in the waters, and three within the ocean. O steed, Varuṇa seems to watch me closely there, where they say is your highest place of birth. trīṇi te āhur divi bandhanāni trīṇy apsu trīṇy antaḥ samudre | uteva me varuṇaś chantsy arvan yatrā ta āhuḥ paramaṃ janitram || 4 ||
Previously, it was stated that there are three bonds in heaven. Now, he says that there are likewise three bonds in the three locations:
"O Arvan, they say that you have three bonds in heaven; those were mentioned previously."
Because it is sustained by water, even the world of earth (bhūloka) is designated by the word "water" (ap). They say there are three bonds upon the earth.
Food, place, and seed—these are the three. Likewise, "within the ocean" means in the middle of the ocean;
because it flows from the ocean as its source, the ocean is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
In that regard, there are three causes for the arising of rain: the cloud, lightning, and thunder.
The word *uta* is used here; the particle *iva* has the sense of *ca* (and).

Moreover, O Arvan, horse, you who ward off evil or bring forth the fruit, Varuṇa—[that is,] you—tell me, that is, you speak to me. If it be asked what you say, it is replied: "Your supreme birth" means your unsurpassed origin.
The suffix *ina* is applied after the root *jan* to form the word *jānī*.
In which three aforementioned places they say or speak;
or rather,
in whom— that is, in which Āditya— they say the supreme birthplace is located.
Because it has been stated, "O Vasus, you fashioned the horse from the sun," the meaning is that you describe such a praiseworthy birth as having served as an instrument for sacrifice.

1. In the form of the means for [attaining] the sacrifice (yāga) and so forth, beginning with *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *yā*. 2. *Samaya* means time (*kāla*). The suffix *lu* expressing possession (*matvartha*) is elided.

Because time is dependent upon the movement of the moon, he is separated from that; he is separated for a period of six *samayas*. 3. After the phrase "because of being grasped" (*gṛhītatvāt*), some manuscripts insert: "Alternatively, because the birth of Āditya from Dakṣa has been mentioned, the horse is also called Āditya by virtue of their non-difference."
"Suchness [of yours] has been separated by time, with the moon as the intervening interval"—this is the additional portion.
4. The three places [are indicated by the variants] kṣa, jha, ḷ, ja, and ṭa.
5. "In the previous mantra" [is indicated by the variants] kṣa, ja, and ṭa.

6. In all three places, [the reading] is "cha-jha-1. 7. Because of being dependent on water, [the reading is] "cha-jha-1. 8. Since the ocean takes up the waters, [the reading is] "kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-ja-ṭa."
9. The birthplaces of *kṣa*, *jha*, and *ṭa*.
These, O steed, are the cleansings of the hooves; these are the deposits of the winner.
Here I beheld thy auspicious reins, which as guardians protect the nectar of immortality.

These, O Steed, are your places for grooming; these are the hooves, the gains, and the places where you are set down. Here I beheld your auspicious reins, which the guardians protect as the guardians of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*). || 5 ||

O steed, these aforementioned places—the celestial realm and others—are your "wiping-cloths," the spots for cleansing your limbs; moreover, these are the "hoof-resting places" of you, the winner of the sacrifice, meaning the regions where you move. Furthermore, right here among these mentioned places, I have beheld your auspicious, praiseworthy, and beautiful "reins"—the ropes fastened to your neck and other parts. Reins...

7. Here I beheld your supreme form, desiring to win the nourishment at the station of the Cow. When the mortal attained your enjoyment, then, O most voracious one, you awakened and devoured the plants. atrā te rūpamuttamamapaśyaṃ jigīṣamāṇamiṣa ā pade goḥ | yadā te marto anu bhogamānaḻādidagrasiṣṭha oṣadhīrjīgaḥ || 7 || atra | te | rūpam | utta'tamam | apaśyam | jigīṣamāṇam | iṣaḥ | ā | pade | goḥ | yadā | te | marttaḥ | anu | bhogam | ānaṭ | āt | it | grasiṣṭhaḥ | oṣadhīḥ | ajīgariti ||7||

Thus, immediately after [the horse] has gone, O horse, I have seen—and now see—your most excellent form, the most sublime form in its manifest state, here at this place of sacrifice; what kind of form?

[I see it] in the station of the earth (goḥ pade), in the place of the gods (devasthāne)—that is, the sacrificial ground—or in the place for the running race (ājidhāvana-sthāne). Of food (iṣaḥ) [I see it there].
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
Desiring food—that is, seeking to conquer all kinds of nourishment—or desiring to go;
O horse, when a mortal man has attained for you that which is to be enjoyed, namely food—then [he attains it].
The root *naś* has the sense of going as its action.
He leads [the food] gradually into his proximity;

immediately thereafter, at that very moment, by virtue of His grace, without delay, being the most voracious (*grasiṣṭhaḥ*)—that is, the greatest devourer like a great grass-eater—He has awakened (*ajīgaḥ*), meaning He consumes, the herbs, which are the foods.
The sense is: although You are of such great majesty, out of grace You accept even a tiny morsel offered by an insignificant person, just like an ordinary horse.

After you, O steed, comes the chariot; after you, the young man; after you, the cows; after you, the fortune of the clans. After you, the winds have followed your friendship; the gods have measured out their heroic power according to yours. 8. After you | thee | the chariot | after | the young man | O steed | after | the cows | after | the fortune | of the clans | after | the winds | of thee | the friendship | they have gone | after | the gods | have measured | thy heroic power || 8 ||
Now, it is demonstrated that [the horse] is indeed the foremost even of the entire world:
O *arvan*, you swift-moving horse, the chariot follows after you (*anu tvā*);
that is, it proceeds from behind because of the horse's movement ahead.
Likewise, the mortal man follows you.
The singular number is used in the sense of a genus.
The cows follow you;
even the cows follow after you.
Likewise, the fortune, good luck, and beauty of young maidens and women follow your body.

Likewise, the winds—the gusts of wind that cause agitation—and other hosts of horses, or the classes of gods beginning with Vasu, have followed after you and attained your friendship; they enter into the state of being your companions.

The gods—the shining ones—or the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having followed you, have measured out your heroic deed (*vīrya*) through praise; they contain it within themselves. Therefore, everyone follows you, but you are the most excellent of all—this is the meaning.

Golden-horned, his feet swift as thought; Indra was his follower. The gods indeed came to eat his sacrificial offering—he who first mounted the running steed. 9. Golden-horned. Noble. His. Feet. Swift as thought. Follower. Indra. Was. Gods. Indeed. His. Sacrificial-offering-eating. They went. Who. Running. First. Mounted. 9.
1. The word "devasthāne" is not found in jha-jha¹.
2. kṣa-ṅa-jha¹-ja-ṭa read "anusarati"; jha reads "anusaratu".

This horse has "hiraṇyaśruḥ"—either ears that are very pleasing, or a high head and hair on its head like ears that are pleasing to the heart. Its "pādāḥ" (feet) are "ayaḥ," meaning made of iron, resembling lumps of iron.
Likewise, they are "mind-swift," possessing the speed of thought.
Alternatively, this is an epithet of Indra:
even Indra was "inferior" (avara), that is, surpassed, in comparison to the power of such a horse whose speed is like that of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding this horse, the *havis*— meaning the eating or consumption of the oblation (the suffix *yat* being used in its own sense)—
or rather, with reference to the oblation suitable for consumption, all the gods indeed (*it*) arrived (*āyana*).
Indra, who, being the first—the foremost—mounted the courser, meaning he took possession of it or resorted to it as his own through his sacrificial offering;
for it is rightly said, "Indra was the first to mount him.
They are the divine coursers, swift as steeds, with rounded flanks and slender waists, who gather together in their heroic courses.
Like swans in a row they strive, when the horses have cast their divine course.
With smooth flanks and slender waists, these vigorous, divine coursers—like swans in a row—strive together when you, O horses, urge them toward the celestial racecourse. 10.
Here, he is praised by means of a hymn to a herd of horses.
"īrmāntāsaḥ" means those whose ends (antāḥ) are "īritāḥ," i.e., impelled; the meaning is that their extremities are widely spaced.
"Those whose middle parts are joined together and compact" means those whose central regions are thus described;
that is to say, they are dense in the middle.
Alternatively, these are adjectives qualifying the body.
*Īrma* means "driven forward" or "impelled.
Those whose broad *antaḥ*— that is, the regions of the hips— are such,
and likewise those with slender waists (*silikamadhyamāsaḥ*).
Those whose middle parts are *saṃsṛta* (joined), *saṃgata* (connected), and *saṃlagna* (adhering) are such [as described].
Because of their fullness, they have developed backs (*prauḍhapṛṣṭha*) and adhering middles; this is the meaning.
It is said that they have "adhering middles" (*silikamadhyama*) in comparison to the regions of the hips and the front.
The prefix *sam* is to be connected with the verb *yatante*. *Śūraṇāsaḥ* means those whose nature is valorous prowess;
*divyāsaḥ* means those who exist in heaven; *atyāḥ* means those whose nature is to traverse [the distance].

Even though this is the name "Aśva," nevertheless, because the word *aśva* will be explained [later], it must be understood here as being etymological (*yaugika*). Such are the horses: "in rows" (*śreṇiśas*).

A collection of many individuals engaged in a single activity is called a *śreṇi* (guild or row). For the sake of running swiftly, they strive together—forming themselves into rows—they exert themselves properly.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Like swans—just as they, being formed into rows, having the appearance described in the verse beginning with "irmāntāsaḥ," strive to travel through the atmosphere; so too [do they].
When?
It is said:

when the horses traverse the divine *ajman*—the path to be traveled or the course—then this mantra is explained by Yāska himself: “*īrmāntāḥ* means those whose ends are stirred up, or whose ends are broad; *silikamadhyamāḥ* means those with joined middles, or those with heads in the middle; or alternatively, the ‘head’ (*śiras*) is the sun, because it rests upon all beings and stands in their midst.”
This other head also arises from this very source; these senses are dependent upon it.
"The divine coursers are like arishta plants.
*Śūra* [comes] from the root *śū*, meaning "to go"; *divyāḥ* means "born of heaven" (*divijāḥ*); *atyāḥ* means "stretchers" (*atanāḥ*).
They strive in rows like swans;
"swans" (*haṃsāḥ*) are so called because they traverse the path, from the root *han* (to go).
"In rows" (*śreṇiśaḥ*): a row (*śreṇī*) is so called because it rests together, from the root *śri* (to resort to).
"When the horses cast down the divine dice upon the board" (Nirukta 4.13).
1. *kṣa-cha-ja-ṭa*: possessing a horse and possessing a chariot. 2. *ḍa*: by virtue of being one who possesses the oblation for heaven. 3. *kṣa-ja-ṭa*: those with *śilika* in the middle.

O steed, your body is winged; O steed, your mind is swift as the wind. Your horns, established in many places, move flickeringly in the forests. (11) O steed, your body is winged; O steed, your mind is swift as the wind. Your horns, established in many places, move flickeringly in the forests. (11)
O steed, your body is *patayiṣṇu*, meaning it is prone to flying or, in other words, pervasive.

Likewise, your mind (*citta*) or intellect is like the wind—like the swift-moving air; that is to say, it is conducive to rapid movement. Furthermore, your horns—those things resembling horns which have emerged from your head, namely your hair—are established in many places (*purutrā*), meaning they are situated in various locations throughout many regions.
Furthermore, those very hairs— flashing in the forests, captivating to the mind, or being filled out— move about in such a manner.
Alternatively, since a horse lacks horns, it is its radiant energies (*tejas*) that are grasped here as being like them.
On the middle day of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, during the *adhrigu-praiṣa*, after the hymn beginning with "mā no mitraḥ," two verses beginning with "upa prāgāc chasanam" are to be recited.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] beginning with 'upa prāgāc chasanam'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 10.8).

The prize-winning steed has gone forward to the place of immolation, meditating with a mind directed toward the gods. The goat, his kinsman, is led before him; behind him follow the sages and the singers. upa | pra | agāt | śasanam | vājī | arvā | devadrīcā | manasā | dīdhyānaḥ | ajaḥ | puraḥ | nīyate | nābhiḥ | asya | anu | paścāt | kavayaḥ | yanti | rebhāḥ ||12||
This swift horse, skilled in running the race-course, has approached and goes toward the place of slaughter, the site of dismemberment.
What is he doing?
Meditating—that is, reflecting—with a mind directed toward the gods, a mind that goes unto the gods.
When?
While meditating in his mind, "I shall worship the gods through my own portion; I shall attain divinity.
Furthermore, before him—in front of him—is the *nābhi*, meaning a bond or a kinsman.
Or rather:
because he is not yet liberated, this unborn one (aja) is led—meaning he is brought forward—to his place of bondage; thus situated, he is followed immediately thereafter, from behind.
In this context, although the ultimate meaning of both [words] is one and the same, two words are nevertheless used to manifest the immediate succession of both the goat and the horse.
Alternatively,
the word *anu* is connected with the verb.
The poets (*kavayaḥ*), the learned reciters (*anucānāḥ*), the singers (*rebhāḥ*), the praisers (*stotāraḥ*), and the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*) go—that is, they proceed.
For according to scripture, "Those who are learned reciters are the poets.
Alternatively:

*Kavayaḥ* is a name for the wise, because it is listed among their names in the Nirukta (3.15.10): *kaviḥ manīṣī*. *Rebhaḥ* is a name for a singer of praise, because it is read there [in the Nirukta] (3.16.1): *rebhaḥ jaritā*.
1. Because [the letters] *kṣa*, *ja*, *ṭa* are not excluded (*avimukta*).
2. To demonstrate that both [the letters] *kṣa*, *cha*, *na*, and *ṭa* follow after [the vowels] *a* and *ā*.
3. Regarding those names beginning with *ka*.
He has approached the highest dwelling place; he has come hither toward his father and mother. Today he shall go to the gods as the most beloved one; then he prays for desirable boons for the donor.

He has approached the highest dwelling place; he has come hither toward his father and mother. For today he shall go as the most beloved among the gods; then he prays for desirable boons for the donor.
This horse, skilled in the dawn-red [light], has come hither;
it approaches. What?
That which is the supreme, most excellent dwelling place—the abode known as heaven, fit for the virtuous to inhabit as a single residence—exists;
for what purpose?
To reach, with direct intent, both father and mother.
The meaning is that the horse, being most beloved and most dear at this time, is filled with joy, thinking, "I am attaining heaven.
Being thus disposed, he should go—*gamyāḥ* means he should go—to the gods.

The particle *hi* is intended to indicate that the attainment of heaven by the winged [horse] employed in the sacrifice is well-known from other mantras, such as: "With his mate, his companion, and his herd... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.4.2).
Then immediately thereafter, the sacrificer makes a prayer for whom?
For himself, the donor who has offered the oblation.
Which? The desirable riches that are to be chosen;
or rather, those which I pray for on behalf of the patron, for the sake of the man’s expenditure.

The hymn beginning with "asya vāmasya" consists of fifty-two verses and is attributed to Dīrghatamas. Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇī* states: "In 'asya' [there are] fifty-two; it is short, but there is a doubt here. It contains questions and answers concerning the removal of doubts, and for the most part, it is a praise of knowledge, liberation, and the Imperishable (Akṣara). 'pañcapādaṃ sākaṃjānām' and 'yadvāyatre'—this I consider to be [the portion on] Śaṅka. 'sasārdhagarbhā gauriḥ' are in the Jagatī meter. Up to this point, however, it is addressed to the Viśvedevas. In 'tasyāḥ samudrāḥ', the oceans are speech, the waters, and the Imperishable; that is a *Prastārapaṅkti*. 'śakyam' refers to Śakadhūma. 'ukṣāṇaṃ pṛśnim' refers to Soma."

"Three *keśins*": Agni, Sūrya, and Vāyu are the *keśins*. "Four": Speech, Vāk, Indra, and Mitra. "Twelve Sauryas": this is a description of the wheel of time (*kālacakra*) established as the year. "That which belongs to Sarasvatī," "by means of sacrifice for the Sādhyas," "the final *anuṣṭubh* is addressed to Sūrya," and "another has Parjanya as its deity, or it belongs to Sarasvant or Sūrya. Here, because the portion consisting of praise is very small due to the nature of the hymn as a *stotra*, this *sūkta* is a "short praise";
it does not possess the same abundance as other *sūktas*.
This very distinction is indicated by the word *tu* (but).
In this hymn (*sūkta*), many themes such as the arousal of doubt and so forth are generally expounded. By the verse, "The ignorant one [is] the deposer," doubt is aroused.
In the phrase “I ask you,” a question is perceived; in “This is the altar,” there is an answer;
and by the passage beginning with “He who made this,” the praise of knowledge is established.
With the verse beginning “I have seen the Herdsman,” there is praise for the direct realization of Brahman.
Because it does not perish, it is the Imperishable (akṣara), which is Brahman;
with the verse beginning “Two birds,” there is praise of that [Brahman].
The five *jagatī* verses are: “pañcapādaṃ pitaram,” “sākaṃjānāṃ sasatham,” “yadvāyatre adhi,” “ayaṃ sa śaṅke,” and “sasārdhagarbhāḥ gaurīmimāya.
The *anuṣṭubh* verse is: “samānametat.
The *prastārapaṅkti* verse is: “tasyāḥ samudrāḥ.”
Its definition is aphorized in the *Chandograntha*: “The *prastārapaṅkti* has [the first] half-verse before” (*Piṅgala 3.4.1*).
The meaning of the aphorism is that when there is a twelve-syllable *gāyatrī* in the first half, followed by a twelve-syllable *gāyatrī*, that is the *prastārapaṅkti*.
This is also stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: “If it is at the beginning, it is the *prastārapaṅkti*” (*Anuvākānukramaṇī* 8.6).
The remaining verses are *triṣṭubhs* according to the paribhāṣā rule regarding the lack of specific instruction.
For those ending with “gaurīmimāya,” the Viśvedevas are the deities.
For the first half-verse of “tasyāḥ samudrāḥ,” Vāgdevatā is the deity.
The waters are the deity of the second half-verse;
Śakadhūma is the deity of the first half-verse of the verse beginning with "śakamayam";
and Soma is the deity of the second half-verse beginning with "ukṣāṇaṃ pṛśnim."

The hymn beginning with "Three long-haired ones" (trayaḥ keśinaḥ) has the sun, fire, and wind as its deities; the verse beginning with "Speech has four" (catvāri vāk) has the goddess of speech as its deity;
and the two verses beginning with "Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa" and "The black path" (kṛṣṇaṃ niyānam) have the sun as their deity.

Regarding the verse beginning with “dvādaśa pradhayaḥ”: 1. According to Kṣa, Na, Ṭa, and Sva, [it refers to] the attainment of heaven; 2. According to Kṣa, Na, Ṭa, and Pu, [it refers to] the dissolution of the person (puruṣa); 3. According to Kṣa, Ṅa, Jha₁, Na, Ṭa, and Sū, [it refers to] the hymn being small; 4. According to Ca, [it refers to] its being large; 5. According to Kṣa₁, [it refers to] liberation in the form of the direct realization of Brahman. In Ṛk 123, Time, characterized by the year, is the deity.
Sarasvatī is the deity of the verse beginning with "yaste stanaḥ"; the Sādhyas are the deity of the verse beginning with "yajñena";
and Sūrya, Parjanya, or the fires are the deities of the verse beginning with "samānametat".
The deity of the verse beginning with "divyaṃ suparṇam" is Sarasvatī or Sūrya.

Śaunaka states the application of the entire hymn as follows: "Having committed theft through delusion, a twice-born man, having fasted for three nights and become pure, shall quickly be released from the sin by reciting the hymn addressed to the Aśvins" (Ṛgvidhāna 1.144).
In the *Mahāvrata*, during the *vaiśvadeva* recitation (*śastra*), there is a *vaiśvadeva* insertion (*nividvāna*) consisting of two sets of four verses.
Therein, the first set of four verses, beginning with "asya vāmasya," consists of forty-one *ṛc*s.
This is prescribed in the fifth *Āraṇyaka*: "‘Asya vāmasya palitasya hotuḥ’—these forty-one [verses] of Salila Dairghatamas" (*Ai. Ā. 5.3.2*).
Of this lovely, gray-haired Hotṛ-priest, the middle brother is the eater;
the third brother has ghee upon his back. Here I beheld the Lord of All, who has seven sons.
Of this lovely one,
of the grey-haired one.
And *akṣa* means all-pervasive in nature.
For the Śruti states: “By the thread of air (*vāyu*), O Gautama, this world, the other world, and all beings are strung together” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.2).
Alternatively, it may be called "middle" in relation to the Virāṭ who will be described later.
Furthermore, this Supreme Lord has a third [aspect] called *ghṛtapṛṣṭha*. "Ghṛta" is a name for water;
by that, his body, which is its effect, is designated.
He is such that his very back is a touchstone;
for the Nirukta states: "The back touches" (Nirukta 4.3).
Or alternatively, he is the back of a lamp.
The word "back" (pṛṣṭha) is an indicator for the entire body;
the meaning is that it refers to one who identifies with the manifested body.
It does not itself become an object of touch like the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra), which is identified with as the *sūtrātman*.
Among these, "the Lord of the Universe" (viśvapati) means the Lord of the people (prajā);
this is an elliptical expression,
meaning the Lord of everything.

"Lord of all, ruler of all," according to the Vedic scripture. "Possessing sons and worlds": one whose sons are the seven worlds; the meaning is that he is the creator of all worlds through his own *māyā*.
"I have seen," "I may see," and "I realize"—this is the meaning.
The sense is this:
the Supreme Lord alone is the cause of the world, having mastery over *māyā*.
The sun, whose rays are the shapers of the seven flavors (or sapids), being praised by the seven seers, carries— that is, sustains and moves— what?
The wheel with three naves.
It is that which has three joints—standing in the place of the navel—or rather, it is that to which the three seasons are connected.
What are they?
They are known as summer, the rainy season, and winter.
Alternatively:
the times known as past, future, and present are the three naves;
the wheel characterized by them is the wheel called the year, which, like a wheel, revolves again and again, and is undecaying, being free from death.
For time never dies, according to the traditional teaching that "time is without beginning or end.
It is unaging and unimpeded. This wheel called the year, endowed with various temporal parts, this Āditya causes to revolve again and again.

Since the various [units of time] beginning with the year are included within that very [cycle], and since the beginnings of the *yugas* are accomplished through its repetition, the year is described as a wheel.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is that wheel wherein all these worlds—these entire beings—[are contained].

Who has seen him first being born, when he, though boneless, supports that which has bones? Where indeed is the life-force, the blood, and the self of the earth? Who has gone to one who knows in order to ask this? Who? Has seen? First? Being born? Boneless? That which? Having bones? Supports? Of the earth? Life-force? Blood? Self? Where? Indeed? Who? One who knows? To? Went? To ask? This? 4.
Having thus established that phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is dependent upon time, he declares the transcendence of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who is its cause:
"Who has seen? Who would be able to see? When? [At the time of dissolution.]
"First" means prior to creation;
that is to say, during the state of indeterminacy (*avyākṛtāvasthā*). What [is it]?
"Being born" means having undergone the first transformation of existence;
it signifies that which is arising, namely, conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
He states the reason for its being difficult to comprehend:
5. Since [it is] "having bones," that is, possessing bones, i.e., having a body;
this is a defining characteristic.
The meaning is that it has attained the state of being an effect.

7. "Boneless" (*anasthā*) means devoid of bone, bodiless; it refers to *prakṛti* as established in the Sāṃkhya, or to *māyā*, which is dependent on the Lord (*īśvara*) as established in the Vedānta. 8. She "bears" (*bibharti*), meaning she holds [the embryo] within herself. In the state of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), being boneless and bodiless, bears [it].
When the Supreme Lord alone, variegated by *māyā*, created the differentiated world at the time of its origin—since there was no one else at that time possessed of a body and so forth—who saw [it]?

If it is argued that at that time the mind (*manas*) is of the nature of determination (*niścaya-ātmaka*) and eternal, and that some self (*ātman*) knows through its conjunction with that [mind], that too is not possible; therefore, he says:

"Earthen" (*pārthiva*) means belonging to the earth, referring to the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*); "life-breath" (*asu*) means *prāṇa*, by which the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) is indicated; "blood" (*asṛk*) means *śoṇita*.
This [term] indicates the constituent elements (*dhātu*).

Although the body consists of the five elements, it is nevertheless described in relation to two of those elements because they are perceptible. As for the self (*ātman*), which is conscious and connected with them—where (*kva*) or in what (*kvāraste*) could it possibly exist?
The meaning is that it does not exist at all.
According to the Śruti, "There was nothing else whatsoever blinking" (Ai. Ā.
2.4.1), who—being a disciple of limited intellect—would approach another, such as a teacher, who possesses knowledge regarding the cause of the world, in order to ask about that cause?
At such a time, where would that self, which consists of the aggregate of body and senses, go? It would not go anywhere.
The meaning is that both the questioner and the respondent do not exist; for the Śruti says: "But there is no second thing, nothing else distinct from it, which one might see.
Alternatively:
who has seen—that is, who directly perceives—the First Being, the cause of the world? Who realizes it?
The boneless Supreme Lord, possessing a body within a body, supports the human being who is born with bones—that is, from whom [he sustains it].
The sense is that even the Seer (the individual soul) is an effect of that [Lord].
The remainder is the same [as previously explained].

I, the simple-minded, ask with my mind, not knowing them: these hidden footsteps of the gods. Upon the young calf, the wise ones have stretched out the threads to weave the web. I, the simple-minded, ask with my mind, not knowing them: these hidden footsteps of the gods. Upon the young calf, the wise ones have stretched out the threads to weave the web. (5)

1. *jha₁*—the body (*śarīram*). 2. *kṣa*, *kṣa-a*, *ṭa*—at that time; *jha₁*—at this time. 3. *jha₁*—characterized by these constituent elements (*etatsadhātupalakṣaṇakam*). 4. *kṣa*, *ha*, *ma₁*, *ṭa*—because of the perceptibility of the three elements (*bhūtatrayapratyakṣatvāt*). 5. *ṅa*, *jha*, *jha*—the embodied one is the bodiless (*śarīramaśarīraḥ*). [The text continues: "I am being cooked" (*pākaḥ*: *paktavyaḥ*), "I am departing" (*apakramati*). With an unrefined mind (*manasā asaṃskṛtena*), not fully understanding (*adhijānan*) the extremely profound reality (*tattvam*), and being unable to know it specifically (*viśeṣeṇa jñātum aśaknuvan*), I ask—I pose a question.
He states the cause for this ignorance:
The meaning is that these words— these points of doubt— are established as truths hidden even from the gods;
or else, the words (or steps) of the gods, which are the truths, have been placed there like a treasure-store.

Therefore, I ask [this], for the purpose of attaining knowledge of reality—this is the remainder [of the thought]. As to what those [means] are, it is said: "O Child, in Vatsakaye, which is the dwelling place of all."
"Baḍit" is the name for truth; that which speaks it is "vaktṛ," namely, the Sun (āditya).
Or else: [the etymology is as follows].
A *vatkaya* is a calf one year old. Furthermore, because the word *vatsa* is mentioned separately, the word *vatkaya* indicates that specific time alone.

Upon that sun (*āditye*), the wise (*kavayaḥ*)—that is, the intelligent sacrificers—woven seven threads (*tantūn*), namely the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice (*somasaṃsthāḥ*), "in addition" (*adhi*) to it; they "stretched them out" (*vitannire*), meaning they extend the crosswise threads (*tiryaktantūn*) which constitute the form of the universe, in order to weave (*otavai*).
Or alternatively:
the seven threads are the seven meters;
they extend them.
For what purpose? For the sake of weaving the horizontal warp consisting of the seven forms of Soma-sacrifices; that is, for the purpose of constructing the sacrifice.
The sense is that the existence of sacrifices depends upon the sun;
the meaning is that I am asking about such a reality.
Not knowing, I ask the wise ones for knowledge regarding this, though I am not a knower—asking those who know about that treasure:
what indeed is that One which, being unborn, has propped apart the two worlds and the intermediate spaces?

Unaware, I ask the wise ones here about the Knower, as one who knows not asks for the sake of knowledge: Who is he who has propped apart these six worlds? What indeed is that One in the form of the Unborn? (6)

I, who am desirous of knowing but do not know the true nature of the deity, ask here— regarding this subject of reality— the wise ones (*kavīn*), those who possess special knowledge of the truth, who have seen beyond [the mundane] and attained the ultimate reality—
for what purpose? For the sake of knowing, that is, for the sake of attaining knowledge of the ultimate reality.
Knowing this, does he act for the sake of defeat? No;
he says: "I do not ask out of knowledge, but rather out of ignorance.
That Supreme Lord "stambha," meaning he has propped up, supported, or restrained [the world].
For it is stated in the Śruti: "Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1).
What [are these]? These—these six *rajas* are the worlds, consisting of the nature of coloring (*rañjana*).
"The worlds are called *rajas*," according to the *Nirukta* (4.19).
Although there are seven worlds, only six are mentioned here because the world of truth (*satyaloka*) is not common to all ritual actions (*karma*).
Now, one might ask: why is the seventh [world] not specifically indicated?
It is said:
In the form—that is, the essential nature—of the unborn Brahmā, who is devoid of birth and other such qualities, there exists a certain place called Satyaloka, which is free from rebirth;
"what indeed" (kimsvid eva) means that it cannot be attained by anyone.
The meaning is that some devotional worshippers (devopāsaka) must travel by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādimārga).
Alternatively,
the six seasons are distinct from the six colors.
He paralyzed those [rays] by means of the Reality (tattva).
Within the form—the visible orb—of the Sun, who is unborn or whose nature is motionless, being manifested and perceived...
1. [In the version] kha-pha-va-saṃhatena.
2. The *kṣa-ṇa-ṭa* principles are established; the *ṅa-kṣa¹* principles are ordained.
3. *Kṣa-jha¹-ja-ṭa* means "he performs.
4. *Kṣa-a¹-na-ṭa-vat* refers to Āditya.

In that [sacrifice] as well, the wise—the learned sacrificers—wove, and continue to weave, seven additional threads, namely the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice (*soma-saṃsthā*), for the purpose of constructing the world characterized by [divine] attributes; the sense is that these serve as a means to the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) through the purification of the mind.
Alternatively:
in which [sacrifice], the "wise" are the calves (*vatkayaḥ*); for the word *vatkayaḥ* refers to a calf one year old (*ekahāyana-vatsaḥ*), since the word *vatsa* is mentioned separately once again.
By the word *vatka*, which signifies that which sustains the year, only that specific period of time is indicated.

In the *vat*—the Sun, who is the fit abode for everything—the seers (*kavayaḥ*) extend the seven threads, that is, they perform the seven sacrifices consisting of the [seven] ritual terminuses (*saṃsthā*); they make them like the threads of a web.
For what purpose?
The Lord of the World proceeds to cut the threads of the world.
5. [In the variant] kṣa-ṭha-jha1, it refers to specific principles (tattva).
6. [In the variant] kṣa-na-ṭa, it refers to the six worlds (ṣaḍaloka).
"I ask about that Reality which exists as something unique, without a second, and which is perhaps unattainable by the mind.
This means: "That Reality established by such scriptural passages as, 'Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6)."
Alternatively, there is the Vedic mantra: "He who established the six spaces and the threefold worlds of the earth, supporting the three earths and the three heavens" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.27.8).
Regarding this Supreme Brahman, the question is: in this world consisting of various transformations—which is His form—is there perhaps anything that is of a single, unitary nature?
The question is posed with the intention of providing an answer that [the Self] exists as a non-distinct, uniform entity consisting of mere name;
for the Śruti states: "It is to be perceived simply as 'it is'" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.6.13).
Let him who indeed knows it here declare the hidden station of this lovely Bird;
his head the cows milk as milk, and wearing the thunderbolt, they have drunk the water with their feet.
Let him who indeed knows it here speak: the hidden station of this lovely bird. From its head the cows milk forth milk; wearing their covering, they have drunk the water with their feet.
O friend, let him who knows it speak now, without hesitation, of this very reality that is being perceived here.
Who is he? He who knows it.
Of what nature is it?
The *pada*—the essential form that is to be reached by all—of this *vi*, the bird who moves toward the desirable, who is seen here before us, namely the Sun, exists hidden and concealed.

Furthermore, the *gāvaḥ*—certain [rays] belonging to the time of rain, or perhaps those which are the most excellent among all, like milk from the head—milk out, that is, they flow forth as water, the milk, from the *śīrṣaḥ*, the head, of this Sun.
"Vatrim":
this refers to form and name.

Wearing—that is, clothing themselves in—form, and heating with exceedingly vast splendor, certain "rays" (gāvaḥ) of his, that is, his beams, "drank" (apuḥ)—meaning they drink—the water by the very path created by themselves; that is to say, they render the earth devoid of water.
The syntactical connection is: "Tell its true nature."

The mother, impelled by her father, has shared him out; for in the beginning she united with him in spirit. She, loathing the essence of the embryo, was pierced through; then those full of reverence approached the purifier.

The mother, apart from the father, took her part; for she had united with him in her mind at the beginning of the conception. She, shrinking away, pierced by the essence of the embryo, went forth to the recitation accompanied by those full of jests. 8.
The Earth is the mother who creates all; the Father is the protector, the world of heaven—that is, the Sun situated in the world of heaven.
She bestows [the fruit] upon him;
for what purpose?
When water or a sacrifice has become the causal condition (*nimitta*),
by what means?
By means of the ritual action consisting of the sacrifice and so forth, which is established in the intellect.
The meaning is that he satisfies [her] with his own oblations, such as clarified butter (*ājya*) and Soma.
Then, prior to that, the father indeed united with her through a mind possessed of intention; that is to say, he was joined with her and brought about rain.

Immediately thereafter, the mother—*bībhatsuḥ*, desiring the confinement of the embryo, longing for the embryo—was thoroughly pierced by *garbharasa*, the essence that is the cause of the embryo's production.

Alternatively: she whose *garbha* (womb) is *rasa*—that is, water capable of producing herbs and the like—is such that she is thoroughly saturated with water and *nividdhā*, meaning she is completely split open by means of a cleft, like a well-mouth. 1. [Variant readings: *kha-ca-ja-pha* have *ca-sthit*; *ka-pha* have *nānāvidhākārabhāji*; *kṣa-ña-ṭa* have *mantuḥ*; *kṣa-ña-ṭa* have *varṣakāle*; *jha* has *varṣākālīnāḥ*; *ca* has *tasye tacchabdaḥ*; *kṣa-ña-ṭa* have *tatrasthe tacchabdaḥ*; *ca* has *yuktā*; *kṣa-ña-ṭa* have *viddhā dāritā*.]

Regarding the sowing of seeds: here is the underlying principle. Just as any woman unites with her young husband for the sake of offspring, and he, being filled with passion for her, engages in union with her, and she, becoming pregnant, gives birth to sons—in the same way it is here as well.

Immediately thereafter, those possessing reverence— namely, those who possess *bhāvi*, *hrī*, *iya*, *priyaṅgu*, and so forth, as well as those who possess *aśva*— having approached the *upavāka* (the preliminary invocation), they attain (*īyuḥ*) the speech that correctly describes the fully ripened crops;
or alternatively, those possessing the characteristics of the oblation (*havilakṣaṇānvantaḥ*), having approached, they attain the speech consisting of the *praṣa* and other such formulas.

The meaning is that when there is rain, people may perform sacrifices by means of the crops and so forth. "The mother was joined; the pregnant one stood within the enclosures. The calf lowed as it looked toward the mother; [the embryo] of all forms was in three distances."
The Mother was yoked at the pole of the sacrificial fee; the embryo stood within the enclosures. The calf lowed; it beheld the cow of all forms in the three distances. 9.
The mother (*mātā*) is the sky (*dyauḥ*), so called because "in this [sky], beings are produced" (*nirmīyante asmin bhūtāni*).

She was "yoked" (*yuktā*) to the "task" (*dhuri*)—that is, to the fulfillment—of the "Dakṣiṇā," meaning the earth which is capable of fulfilling what is desired; the sense is that she became capable of raining down.
How so? That is explained as follows:
the *garbha*—the mass of water occupying the position of an embryo—stands (*atiṣṭhat*) within (*antaḥ*), in the midst of the *vṛjanī*s—the rows of clouds which are the best of waters.

Immediately thereafter, the *vatsa*—the mass of water occupying the position of a calf—lowed (*amīmet*) at the time of raining, making a sound when the three—clouds, rays, and winds—are joined together over the three *yojana*s.
Immediately thereafter, he beheld the multiform one; that is, he saw her in succession as she rained down.
Or alternatively:
when the three *yojanas* had been traversed, the calf—the cloud—lowed toward the earth, the cow, for the sake of raining.

Immediately thereafter, all people saw—and continue to see—the earth in its manifold forms through various crops and other things, possessing a universal form (*viśvarūpyam*). Three mothers stand erect upon the single father; they do not cause him to weary. Upon the back of that heaven, they converse in speech that knows all things and does not move toward anything partial.

Bearing three mothers and three fathers, he alone stands erect; they do not weary him. Upon the back of that very heaven, they deliberate in speech that knows all things and does not deceive anyone. 10.

The one— the preeminent or peerless son-like Āditya, or Time (*kāla*) which is the year— supports three mothers, meaning the three worlds beginning with the earth, who produce crops, rain, and so forth. Likewise,

supporting the three fathers— the protectors of the world known as Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya, who preside over the three worlds— he stands upright, elevated, and exceedingly long-lasting, existing through the nature of the past and the future.

In the solar sense, because he is higher than all, they do not cause him to wither (*vīmanam*); that is, they do not bring about his exhaustion at all. For neither Time nor the Sun is ever overcome by another.
On the back of heaven—that is, in the intermediate space above the world of heaven—the gods converse; they speak secretly among themselves. What do they speak of?

They converse regarding the speech characterized by thunder, which belongs to that Sun—speech that is all-knowing (capable of knowing everything or worthy of being known), yet not all-pervasive. This is the meaning.
For the increase of *kṣa-ma-ca-ṭa-pra-vardhana*;
2. Holding *kṣa-jha1-ja-ṭa*.
This is what is meant:
they say that this sun is dependent upon time, because states such as the intense summer heat and so forth, which consist of its southern and northern courses, are subject to time.
Others, however, say that time—consisting of the year and so on—is dependent upon it, because time is established by the sun’s movement back and forth.
While that five-spoked wheel revolves, all the worlds rest upon it;
its axle, though bearing a heavy burden, does not burn out, and its nave, being eternal, never perishes.
While that five-spoked wheel revolves, upon it all beings stand. Though its axle bears a heavy burden, it does not grow hot; from of old, its nave has never been shattered.

On the five-spoked wheel—possessing spokes in the form of the five seasons—which is the embodiment of the year and revolves by turning again and again in the forms of the *saṃvatsara*, *parivatsara*, and so forth; while that wheel of time (*kālacakra*) thus revolves, all worlds (*viśvā bhuvanāni*), meaning all classes of beings, exist within it.
Furthermore, the axle (*akṣa*) situated in the middle of that wheel, though bearing a heavy burden (*bhūribhāraḥ*) due to the carrying of the entire universe, does not [wear out].

Among the seven seasons that are born together from a single origin, arise simultaneously, [he enters] the dwelling, the seventh season.
The suffix *thaṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 5.2.50: *thaṭ ca chandasi*.
Those who know the nature of time say that a *vekaja* (intercalary) month is one produced by itself.
By the union of two each of the twelve months beginning with Caitra, there arise the six seasons beginning with spring (*vasanta*).
With an intercalary month, a seventh season is added.
Nor should it be thought that such a month does not exist at all;
for there is the Vedic revelation (śruti): "They say there is a thirteenth month" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.3.4).
That very point is now being stated.
"Six indeed. The word *eva* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). There are exactly six seasons (*ṛtu*), consisting of two months each.
The *vṛṣayaḥ* are those who go;
and they say that these are "born from the gods" (*devajāḥ*), meaning born from the primordial god. There is an absence of gods in the thirteenth month, which is the seventh support (*saptamādhāra*).
This is according to such Smṛti texts as: "The sunless intercalary month heats the orb of the sun.
Therefore, there are five gods, and the one born of the gods is the sixth.

Furthermore, the essential natures (*svarūpa*) of these seasons—which are desired by all the worlds—have been established in their respective places (*dhāmaśaḥ*), set apart individually (*pṛthak pṛthak sthāpitāni*), and manifested through their various forms (*rūpaśaḥ*), being fashioned with diverse shapes (*vividhākṛtiyuktāni*).
And that differentiation of forms is recorded by the Taittirīyas: "He gave the sap to the spring, barley to the summer," and so forth (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.2.10.1).
They "move toward" (vrajante) the Supporter (Vasthātṛ), the Sustainer;
the meaning is that they revolve again and again for the sake of worldly activity.

"They are women," yet they call them "men" to me. He who has eyes sees; the blind man does not perceive. That son who is a seer understands this; he who discerns them shall become the father of his father. They are women, yet they call them men to me. He who has eyes sees; the blind man does not perceive. That son who is a seer understands this; he who discerns them shall become the father of his father.
My rays are like women who possess fine garments, like true and virtuous wives;
they are feminine because they bear the embryo of light,
and they take the feminine gender because these rays possess feminine characteristics.

They call those men "rays" (raśmi), meaning persons who pour forth abundant rain-water; the masculine gender is used here in view of the subsequent reference. A certain great person, endowed with the vision of knowledge, beholds—that is, knows—this extremely hidden meaning.
Bondage is of a different nature [from liberation] for one of coarse vision: 1. Kṣa, Na, Ṭa—this is the single-born;
2. Kṣa, Ha, Na, Ṭa—by the union of each pair.
3. By the single syllable *kṣa-ṇa-ṭa*.
4. By the deity *kṣa-ha-jha-na-ṭa*, namely Āditya.
5. Because of the absence of being born from a deity (*devajātva*) for *kṣa-jha-na-ṭa*.

6. The desired days and nights, esteemed by all the worlds, belonging to those seasons (*ṛtu*)—namely *kṣa*, *ha*, *jha*, *na*, *ṭa*, and *ta*—have been distributed according to their respective places (*dhāmaśaḥ*) as seasonal waters (*ṛtudakāni*), and established separately (*pṛthaksthāni*) according to their forms (*rūpaśaḥ*), that is, by the distinction of their own nature as white and black.
7. [The syllables] *kṣa*, *ha*, *jha*, *na*, *ṭa* consist of essence (*rasamaya*).
8. [The syllable] *kṣa*, *ha*, *jha*, *na*, *ṭa*—behold! behold! (*paśyata paśyeta*).
He does not perceive, he does not discern, nor does he know.

Furthermore, he who is the *kavi*—the one of far-reaching vision—and the *putra*, the son-like one among the rays in the form of women and men, the protector (*pura*) of the world, characterized by the waters of creation—he alone is that son.
Or else:
He indeed perceives this matter: he knows from all sides the transition from womanhood to manhood for those who were women;
only the son knows the state of his parents, and no one else.
Whoever should know those various forms—the forms of women, men, and sons—he would be the father of his father.
The "father" (pitṛ) is the collection of rays that protects the world through rain;
his father is the Sun (āditya), and he becomes that.
The meaning is that he becomes the sun itself;
or else,
this is a common worldly expression.
He who understands these things becomes thus:
though he is himself the son of his father, he also becomes a father in relation to his own son;
accompanied by sons, grandsons, and so forth, may you live for a long time.

It goes away from the distant region;
and having come, where in what place does it produce its fruit?
Unlike other cows, this cow gives birth in the midst of her own kind;
she does not give birth anywhere at random, but rather to someone who performs the three-fold sacrifice.
Therefore, who indeed could this great being be?
Alternatively,
the collection of the sun’s rays itself is praised in the form of a cow.

The cow— characterized by her longing and consisting of rays— bearing the calf, who is like a calf in that he is to be protected, namely the sacrificer, according to the stated sequence, has emerged from her womb.

Then, having acted thus, she—having become invisible and moving toward the unknown direction (*kadrīcī*)—went away without returning to which of her own [two] halves, that is, to which portion possessing prosperity or occupying its own place, did she go to which of her own persons, the Sun?
For it is stated in the Śruti: "The rays of the Sun lead him to where the sole Lord of the Gods has his abode" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.5).
And having acted thus, in whom does she bring forth—that is, in which world such as that of Indra and so on does she generate [the fruit], and not everywhere?
The rest is the same.

Who here can declare this, as a seer, by means of the higher [breath] the father who knows this, and by means of the lower [breath] the son? Whence has such a mind been born? From where has it arisen?

Downward by the further [path], he who has discovered his father through this lower [path]—who here can declare that godly mind, which, being measured out by the seer (kavi), has been born from what? 18.

He who knows in due order that Agni—the protector of this world—who stands below (avastāt) together with his father, the Sun, who stands above (pareṇa); and likewise that Sun—his father and protector—who stands beyond (parastāt), for he too protects this very world by means of rain and other such means;
he who knows them thus, and meditates upon both the Sun and Agni in alternation (vyatihāreṇa).
Or rather:
he who perceives these two—whose *rajas* and *tamas* have been overcome and whose *sattva* has been elevated, and who are therefore masters of their own *māyā*—as one;
such a person, acting like a seer (*kavīyamānaḥ*), manifesting his own state of beautiful vision, proclaims here in this world.

Furthermore, from what cause—namely, from a particular unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*)—has the mind been produced in such abundance (*adhika*) as to be directed toward the shining deity, that is, the divine realm, or even the supramundane?
The meaning is that both [the deity and such a mind] are difficult to attain.
Those who are near, them they call far; those who are far, them they call near.
O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have fashioned carry [the world] like yokes harnessed to the pole of the firmament.

Those who are turned hitherward, them they call turned away; those who are turned away, them they call turned hitherward. O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have fashioned are carried like yoked horses at the pole through the mid-air.

The rays of the sun and moon, revolving upon their two wheels, are turned downward (*varvāñcaḥ*)—that is, facing downwards—by virtue of that rotation; yet those very same rays are called "turned away" (*parācaḥ*), meaning facing upwards, by those who know time.
