2. *kṣa-ma-ṭa-so'sumeva*]
3. And this concerns the domain of the gods.
Thus, first: those who go away, the *parāñcaḥ*—those very ones they call the *arvācaḥ*, those who come hither.
O Soma, you are Indra, the Supreme Lord; the sustainer of the earth through rain; the Āditya.
Alternatively,
among the twelve Ādityas, Indra is also one;
since it has been stated that [the others] are "joined with Vivasvat and Indra," this one too is Indra.
And those various circular revolutions which you two, O youthful ones, have performed—those [revolutions] of the *rajas*, the world whose nature is like a cord.
The sixth case ending is used for the object of the action.
They carry the world; they lead it forth.
In this regard, there is an illustration: just as horses and other animals yoked—that is, bound—to the pole (dhur) of a cart or similar vehicle carry that pole, so too [is it here].
Or alternatively:
This is the illustration in the first half [of the verse].
Those yoked to the pole are "yoked to the pole" (dhurya). Even the wheel situated on the pole is expressed by the word "pole" (dhur).

In that case, men who are engaged and absorbed therein, by virtue of revolving around it, become those facing away even when they are facing toward it, and become those facing toward it even when they are facing away; it is just like that.
Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.
Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree. Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. 20.
Here, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) are praised by means of the illustration of two birds of the mundane world.

Just as in the world there are two *suparṇau*—birds of beautiful flight, moving gracefully—who are *sayujā*, joined together; *sakhāyā*, friends; who occupy the same place; and who both *pari pasvajāte*—embrace—the very same *samānaṃ vṛkṣam*, a single tree, taking it as their support: of those two, one eats the *pippalam*, the ripe and most delicious fruit, while the other, not eating, *abhi cākaśīti*, gazes upon it. In the same way, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self, standing in the place of the two birds, are *sayujā*, joined together.
Yoga is indeed a relationship, and that is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*).

That very [Supreme Self] is the *ātman*—the essential nature—of which the individual self (*jīvātman*) is possessed; thus, it is "that-ātman" (*tadātman*). Likewise, for the other as well, that same Supreme Self is the *ātman*—the essential nature—of which the individual self is possessed.
The meaning is that they are thus of one form (*ekarūpa*).

By this, the view of the followers of Bhāskara is refuted—the view that the individual self (*jīvātman*) is non-different from the supreme self (*paramātman*) while being distinct [in its limiting adjuncts] and false, and that the supreme self is not different from the individual self because it rests upon manifold individuals.
Now, an objection is raised: "A relation is of two kinds, and that [relation] requires difference, as in the case of two birds; therefore, how can there be identity (*aikātmya*)?"
No;
it functions with reference to both adventitious difference and real difference.
For this very reason, they are "companions" (sakhāyau), meaning they share the same locus, not that they belong to another locus.
One should not say: "Since the state of one is exactly the same as that of the other, their difference is clearly apparent through such an understanding; how then can identity be asserted?
For here there is no relationship of example and exemplified between them.
Rather, whatever is the state—the manifestation—of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), that very same state belongs to the other, the individual self (*jīvātman*); thus they are called "companions."
The meaning is that there is no object distinct from the manifestation of a single form. Therefore, oneness (aikātmya) is established.
By this, even real difference (vāstavabheda) is refuted.

Just as in the verse, “They both embrace the same tree,” one must accept that both have a single substratum because no other substratum exists, so too in the case of “the two joined together, the friends,” a single substratum must be adopted for both.
That which is "cut" (vṛścyate) is the "tree" (vṛkṣa), namely the body;
and that is common to both, being indeed one and the same.

Because they exist for the sake of the individual soul's experience, because they are composed of the great elements created by the Supreme Self, and because they serve as the locus for its perception, both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self] are equal in this regard.
They embrace—that is, they resort to and take refuge in—such a common tree.

Nor should it be asked: "If the individual soul is in reality the Lord, how can it have the sorrow of transmigratory existence through the notion of being an individual soul? For those two [sorrows] are produced by delusion.

And likewise, the followers of the Atharva Veda, having recited this mantra, record the very next mantra as its answer for dispelling doubt: "Upon the same tree, two birds—[the individual soul and the Supreme Lord]—clasp each other; one of them eats the ripe fruit, while the other looks on without eating. (Note: The commentary clarifies that the two birds are the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). One is the *jīva* who experiences the results of karma, while the other is the Lord who remains a witness. They are "on the same tree" because they share a common substrate, the body. The "tree" is the body, and the "fruit" is the result of actions.)
"The person, submerged [in ignorance] and deluded, grieves because of his lack of mastery;
but when he beholds the other, the Lord who is enjoyed [by all], and His majesty, he becomes free from sorrow" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.2).
This is its meaning.

The one Supreme Person alone, the Full Self, being immersed and hidden within the body, though He Himself is the Lord, grieves as if deluded by the notion that He is not the Lord; being thus bewildered, He experiences birth and death in saṃsāra, thinking, "I am the doer," "I am happy," or "I am miserable.
But when He beholds the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara—who is eternally associated with joy and transcends the sorrow of saṃsāra—as non-different from Himself, He realizes Him directly.

Then, being free from sorrow, transcending the body, and having attained the threefold cessation of suffering through the direct realization of one's own true nature, one attains "the majesty of this"— that is,
the majesty of the Supreme Lord who is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), namely His majesty consisting of omniscience, omnipresence, and so forth.
And that majesty is not attained merely by the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of it.
Therefore, the meaning is that one becomes of that very nature. Consequently, it is established that in reality there is only one; the appearance of difference, however, is produced by delusion.
This is stated while accepting a distinction based on worldly cognition during the state of experience:
of these two, the other—the individual soul (jīvātman)—eats, that is, consumes, the pippala, which is the fruit of karma that has become savory;
for whatever is acquired by whom, that becomes savory to him.

The other is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who does not eat—that is, who does not consume—because he is free from desire due to the absence of longing; for the *Smṛti* states: "What longing can there be for one whose desires have been fulfilled? (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad Kārikā 1.9).
Therefore, relying upon their non-difference in essence (*avastvabheda*), it was said that "one of the two [is the Supreme Self]."
In reality, however, since it has been stated, "He grieves, being deluded by his lack of lordship," there is indeed non-difference.
Such a Supreme Self beholds the world superimposed upon Himself as a witness.
In this regard, the explanation of this mantra found in the Nirukta—beginning with, "Two by two are established, the well-performed doers of dharma" (Nirukta 14.30)—should be consulted.
Where the well-winged ones, partaking of the immortal, move unblinking toward the assemblies;
there the Lord, the guardian of the entire world, the wise one, has entered me, the simple-minded.

Where the well-winged ones, without blinking, hasten toward their portion of immortality at the assemblies—there the Lord, the guardian of the entire world, the wise one, has entered me, the simple-minded. 21.

"In that solar orb, the *suparṇas*—the well-flying, beautifully moving rays—having taken their share (*bhāgam*), the portion (*aṃśam*) of the nectar (*amṛtasya*) which is water, move toward and approach it without blinking, incessantly, with *vidathā*—that is, through knowledge (*vedanena*), by the thought: 'We must act in this manner.
And he who is the lord (*inaḥ*) of the entire world (*viśvasya bhuvanasya*), the collection of beings, as well as its guardian (*gopāḥ*), the protector and preserver."

"This Āditya is that Supreme Lord; being wise (dhīra), intelligent, and endowed with the intention to favor the vital breaths, He has entered—causing me, the unripe one whose wisdom is immature, to enter—into this, His own orb.
Or, in the context of the presiding deity (adhidaivata), He has entered here into our body as its controller.
Now, in the context of the self (adhyātma):

In which Self (*ātman*) the "fair-winged ones" (*suparṇāḥ*)—the senses, such as the eyes and others, which are skilled in moving for the sake of grasping their respective objects—unceasingly, that is, without blinking or interruption, approach and manifest by means of *vidathā* (knowledge), which is the consciousness delimited by the object;

for here, the consciousness conditioned by an object is called "immortality" (*amṛta*). They approach it—that which is to be enjoyed, their own respective portion—and by the removal of their veils, they cause it to shine forth through the consciousness delimited by the three [states].
Furthermore, he who is the lord (*inaḥ*), the master (*svāmī*), the protector (*gopā*)— that is, the guardian and preserver— of this body and of the entire world (*viśvasya bhuvanasya*);
or alternatively, the master of the entire world— that is, of all created beings— and the protector of this body.
By this, the identity of the referents of the terms *tattvam* and *asi* has been established.

That wise one, steadfast in the Supreme Lord and ever immutable through his commitment to *samādhi*, has entered me—me who am matured (*pāka*), whose mind is fully ripened, and whose mind is exceedingly pure and overflowing with *sattva* due to the removal of *rajas* and *tamas* through sacrifice, charity, and other means, like a mirror.
The meaning is that such an object manifests within a mind that has arisen in its true form.

Alternatively, the meaning is as follows: previously, while in a state of ignorance, my mind was unripe; I thought, "There is a Lord other than myself. Thereafter, having determined that there exists someone who is omniscient, the Lord of all, and characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, and subsequently—through the Guru and the scriptures—realizing that "I am indeed He," and having understood this through tradition, having dispelled both doubt and contrary conceptions, and having realized it directly through contemplation, I became the perfect Supreme Self. This very point is expressed by the verse: "That wise one entered me at the time of ripening."
Objection: Since the undivided Supreme Self is all-pervading, attainment (*prāpti*) itself is not possible.
Reply: In this context, attainment is of two kinds: the attainment of what has already been attained and the attainment of what has not yet been attained.

Even in the case of that which is already attained, attainment is possible through the removal of the ignorance that constitutes a veil, according to the analogy of the gold necklace around one's own neck.

Regarding this mantra, that which has been explained in the Nirukta—beginning with "Where the *suparṇas*, the well-flying ones, [are] the rays of the sun" (Nirukta 3.12)—is to be understood here as well.
On that tree whereon all the fair-winged ones who eat honey rest and breed, they say its fruit is sweet at the top; no one has reached it, nor does he know his father.
On that tree whereon all the fair-winged eaters of honey settle and breed, they say its fruit is sweet at the top; no one reaches it who does not know the Father. 22.
Here, there is a conceptualization of the tree's own nature.
He praises the sun with respect to the divine and the self with respect to the individual.
In that sun, which is like a tree—the support for all fruits—there are those who eat the honey.
"Madhvada" is a name for water;
those who eat it are "madhvadaḥ," meaning the consumers of water.
7. "Suparṇāḥ" means well-flying rays. 8. They "niviśante," that is, they enter [the sun] at night. 9. And they "suvate," meaning they produce light again at the time of sunrise from the Sun.
Where?
(10) In the eleventh chapter, "above all" (11) means above the universe.

(12) Of that tree of the sun, (13) the *pippala*—the protecting fruit—is (14) sweet, full of essence. (15) At the top, above, after the practice of meditation, (16) those who know reality say, they declare.
Or rather:
they say that he who exists above (adhi) all;
that man who does not know—that is, does not worship—such a father, the protector of the world, perishes because of him.
The root *naś* has the sense of "going.
One does not attain its fruit.
The meaning is that those who know [this] say "the pippala [fruit] is at the front" (23).
Thus, with respect to the divine aspect.
Now, regarding the internal (adhyātma) perspective:

in that Supreme Self, which is like a tree—devoid of movement and the like, and immutable—the *suparṇas* (birds), meaning the senses characterized by beautiful movement (*su-parṇāni*), who are "eaters of honey" (*madhvadaḥ*)—that is to say, possessors of knowledge through that honey of wisdom—settle down during the time of sleep; having withdrawn from their respective objects, they dissolve within the Self. Furthermore, at the time of awakening, they "fly forth over all" (*adhi viśve suvate*), meaning they emerge and regain their respective objects.
The *pippala* of that Supreme Self is knowledge—protective from the cycle of transmigration, uplifting, sweet, and worthy of being relished, characterized like nectar.
Upon tasting that fruit, hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, death, and so forth no longer occur; therefore, it is the most delicious of all.
Other fruits, such as those of heaven and the like, are not so, because they lead to rebirth and other such conditions.

1. jha₁-paripakvamanāḥ | 2. ka-ca-pha—“I am the Lord”; kha—“I am the Lord. 3. kṣa-ṅa-jha₁-a-ṭa—truth. 4. kṣa-ṅa-ja-jha₁-ja—the knower of the refuge. 5. ca—the word “adhi” is not present. 6. kṣa-ja-ṭa—of what kind? 7. ṭha-jha₁—the knowers, however. 8. kṣa-jha₁-ja-ṭa—devoid of coming and going, etc. 9. kṣa-ṅa-jha₁-ma-ṭa—they produce. 10. kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa—they perceive. 11. kṣa-ja-ṭa—such is that; [it is] sweet at first sight.
They say that "its fruit" refers to the time subsequent to the knowledge of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*).

That person who does not know—that is, does not understand through the teacher and the scriptures—either the Father, the Protector (the fruit of knowledge), or the Self which is the substratum of that fruit, does not attain—that is, does not obtain—that fruit. Therefore, the meaning is that only he who knows the Self attains that fruit of liberation.
Alternatively:
The scriptural passage beginning with "Space [is not filled] like leather" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.20) precludes the attainment of immortality through any means other than knowledge.
However, passages such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9) declare that attainment occurs through knowledge.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Having known the Supreme Lord in this manner, may I become liberated."

That which is placed upon the Gāyatrī as the Gāyatra, or from the Triṣṭubh they fashioned the Triṣṭubh, or the Jagatī-foot that is placed within the Jagatī—those who truly know this have attained immortality. || 23 ||
The Gāyatra is placed upon the Gāyatra. Because it is the first and because the earth (bhūḥ) is praised by all, the earth is the Gāyatrī;
its location is the Gāyatra.
Upon that—that is, above it—the Gāyatra, the station belonging to Agni, is placed.

Because he was created first, and because of the etymological derivation that he "sings" (*gāyati*) and "protects" (*trāyate*), Agni is also *gāyatra* due to his birth from the mouth of Prajāpati along with the Gāyatrī;
for the Śruti says, "Agni is *gāyatra*" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.5.5). Furthermore, he is *agni* because the terrestrial fire has been established [therein].

Likewise, from the *traiṣṭubha*—the intermediate space characterized by rain-born lightning and associated with the *triṣṭubh* meter—the gods "skillfully fashioned" (*niratakṣata*) the *traiṣṭubha* wind, which is endowed with the three types of *stoma* (hymns) characterized as upward, downward, and transverse; this is what Agni [says]. Or else, in the *jagat*, the highest realm to be reached by all, in the third world which is the celestial sphere (*dyuloka*), there exists that which is called the "foot" (*pada*) of the Sun, known as the *jagat* because it is prone to movement (*gamanaśīla*). This is what [Agni says].

This very laying down of the foundations for the three—fire and the others—in these three places: those men who know this, who understand it, they alone have attained immortality; they reach the state that is the form of the immortals.
Thus with reference to the worlds (*adhiloka*).
Now, with reference to the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*).

Regarding the statement that "the Gāyatrī metre was placed as a foot upon the Gāyatra morning pressing," and likewise that "they carved out the Triṣṭubh metre from the Triṣṭubh midday pressing, placing it there"—
this means that something [specific] was indeed established therein.

Regarding the statement, "In the world, at the third pressing (savana), the Jagatī meter is placed as the Jagatī step"— those men who know this, that is, the sacrificers who know the arrangement of the three meters across the three pressings, they have attained, or are attaining, immortality— that is, liberation— by means of knowledge and practice. Alternatively, [it may refer to] the Gāyatrī meter at the morning pressing.
Because the three *savanas* are measured by the three *chandases*, the *savanas* themselves are designated by the names of those respective *chandases*.
This is according to the Vedic revelation: "The morning *savana* is *gāyatra*, the midday *savana* is *traiṣṭubha*, and the third *savana* is *jāgata*" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.2.9.5–6).
Upon such a morning *savana*, the *gāyatra* foot consisting of eight syllables—in the form of the *āhāva* and *pratigara*—is placed above.
Thus, the Hotṛ [invokes] with the three-syllabled "Śaṃsāvoṃ," and the Adhvaryu responds with the five-syllabled "Śaṃsāmodevoṃ.
When these are combined, they result in eight syllables.
And those eight syllables are similar to the Gāyatrī, because a quarter-verse of that [Gāyatrī] also consists of eight syllables.
This is the first instance of establishing the *gāyatra* foot within the form of the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*).

Likewise, at the end of the libation, following the recitation, there is the phrase "The hymn (*uktha*) has been spoken," which is associated with the *triṣṭubh* meter [variant readings: *tristobhayuktam*; *padādhīnam*; *ityadhilokaṃ lokapratipādakam*, "thus regarding the world, it is that which explains the world"; *athādhiyajñaṃ yajñapratipādakam*, "then regarding the sacrifice, it is that which explains the sacrifice"; *athavā*, "or else"; *jñātvā anuṣṭhānadvāreṇa*, "having known by way of performance"; *savanantare'pi hotā svasvānantaram*, "even in another libation, the Hotṛ priest immediately after his own [portion]"]. (Ka. 125)
He speaks four syllables:
"Oṃ ukthaśāḥ," thus the Adhvaryu;
that becomes a complete word.
This alone is the supreme establishment of the *gāyatra* within the *gāyatra*.
Likewise, from the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) which belongs to the *triṣṭubh*, the priests fashioned a word consisting of the form of the call (*āhāva*) and the response (*pratigaraṇa*).
Thus, at the midday pressing, the Hotṛ calls out with the six-syllable formula, "O Adhvaryu, *śoṃsāvoṃ*," and the Adhvaryu responds with the five-syllable formula, "*śaṃsāmo daivom*."
When these are combined, they result in eleven syllables.
This is one instance of the placement of a *triṣṭubh* within a *triṣṭubh* at the beginning of the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*).
Likewise, at the end of the pressing as well, after the recitation, he utters seven syllables: "The hymn (*uktha*) has been spoken for Indra."
And the Adhvaryu responds with the four-syllable formula, "Oṃ ukthaśāḥ. Combined, these amount to eleven syllables.
This is one instance of establishing a *triṣṭubh* within a *triṣṭubh*.
Likewise, at the third pressing, the Hotṛ calls out with seven syllables, "adhvaryo śoṃsāvom," and the Adhvaryu responds with five syllables, "śaṃsāmodaivom.
This makes twelve syllables;
this is the first attainment of the Jāgata metre within the Jāgata.
Likewise, later on, after the recitation, he says: "The hymn has been spoken for Indra and for the gods.
This very [formula] consists of eleven syllables.
And the Adhvaryu responds with the single syllable "Om."
These two combined constitute the twelve-syllable [meter].
This is the supreme establishment of the *jagatī* within the *jagatī*, that is, the placement of the words of the *jagatī* meter.
Thus, in the three meters and in the three pressings (*savana*) beginning with the *gāyatrī*, there is the establishment of the words of the meters beginning with the *gāyatrī*.

All of this is clearly taught in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa*, in the section beginning "The divine subjects are to be arranged" (*Ai. Brā.* 3.12). Regarding that establishment of the meters within the meter: only those who know it—that is, those who truly understand it—attain immortality through its performance. The meaning is that those who do not know it do not obtain the fruit even by means of performance.
The meaning is that this is because of its state of being complete.

With the Gāyatrī he measures out the *arka*; with the *arka* the Sāman; with the Triṣṭubh the *vāka*. With the *vāka* he measures out the *vāka*—the two-footed and the four-footed; by means of the syllable, he measures out the seven voices. 24. With the Gāyatrī, he measures out the *arka*; with the *arka*, the Sāman; with the Triṣṭubh, the *vāka*; with the *vāka*, the *vāka*; the two-footed and the four-footed; by means of the syllable, he measures out the seven voices. 24.
With the *gāyatra* [meter], by means of the *gāyatrī* meter, he measures out—that is, he defines individually—the *arka*, which is the mantra that is the means of worship.
As the *Nirukta* states: "The *arka* is a mantra, because they worship with it" (*Nirukta* 5.4). He thus composes each mantra so that it is bound together with the *gāyatrī* meter.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of other meters; or rather, the meaning is that he measures the other meters by means of this very [meter] itself, through the addition of four syllables at each step according to their respective meters.
Or else:
The prefix *prati* has the sense of *sam* (together/with). The meaning is that he makes the mantras correspond with the meters (*chandas*).
[He makes] the *sāman* with the *arka*.
By means of the mantra whose characteristics have been stated, he measures out the *sāman* known as the *gāyatra* and *atharvaṇa*.

Now, an objection is raised: since it is prescribed that "only one *sāman* is performed" over the three verses, one should say "the *sāman* with the *arkas*"; why then is it said "with the *arka*"? It is not so.
In reality, a single *sāman* is mounted upon a single *ṛc*;
subsequently, by means of extension (*atideśa*), one sings it on the other two [verses] as well. Thus, singing on three verses is established, and therefore the singular number is not contradictory.
The *vākya* is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Here, the mention of the *triṣṭubh* is for the purpose of indicating the other meters as well;
or else, [it applies] everywhere in the absence of a specific instruction.

1. In the manuscripts kṣa, ṅa, jha₁, ña, and ṭa, the *adhvaryu* responds (*pratigṛṇāti*). 2. In the manuscript jha₁, [the response] takes the form of a *pratihāra* for the *āhāva*, consisting of a *triṣṭubh* verse.
3. In the manuscripts kṣa, jha₁, ña, and ṭa, [this occurs] even in other *savana*s.
4. When *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *n* are combined, it is the twelve-syllable [meter].

5. In the *jagatī* meter, there is the accomplishment [of the verse] through *kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*, and *ja*. 6. Because this very [meter] serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for the establishment of those various meters by means of an increase of four syllables each, it is mentioned here with primacy.
The word *arka* refers to the class [of mantras]; [it denotes] all mantras by means of the meters (*chandas*) beginning with the *gāyatrī*.
7. [The mantras] designated as *gāyatra*, *bṛhat*, *ṛc*, *sāman*, and so forth; 8.
[the mantra] called *atharvaṇa*.
9. The mention of *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha1*, *ña*, *ṭa*, and so forth is for the purpose of illustrating other meters; for previously, by the phrase "with the Gāyatrī," only the Gāyatrī was mentioned.
This statement regarding the Triṣṭubh is made with the intention of indicating its predominance.
By means of a *triṣṭubh* repeated twice or thrice, one measures out a speech-form (*vāk*) consisting of two *anuṣṭubh*s; that is, for each individual meter, he measures it out.

Alternatively, he measures out a speech-form—a hymn (*sūkta*)—thinking, "this hymn is composed of this many *triṣṭubh*s. By such a speech-form, he measures out a speech-form, whether it be a verse-group (*varga*), a section (*varga*), or a recitation-section (*anuvāka*).
He is distinguished by the question, "By what kind of speech? [The answer is:
"By that which has two feet or four feet.
This means by way of being composed in meters such as the *virāj* bound in two feet, or by way of mantra-forms such as the *anuṣṭubh* consisting of four feet.
A *varga* consists of this many two-line verses; two *vargas* consist of this many four-line verses;
an *anuvāka* is delimited by this many utterances in the form of two-line verses, and by this many utterances in the form of *anuṣṭubh* verses.
According to the view that it refers to *sūktas*, this *anuvāka* consists of this many *sūktas*.
Furthermore, by means of each syllable (*akṣara*), they measure out—that is, they fashion—the seven *vāṇīs*, which are the seven meters presided over by Speech:
the *gāyatrī* with eight syllables, the *triṣṭubh* with eleven syllables, and the *jagatī* with twelve syllables.
By means of these syllables, the feet (*pādas*) are measured; and by means of the measured feet, the meters (*chandas*) are defined.
Therefore, the syllable is the root of meters and feet;
likewise, the syllable is the root of Ṛgvedic verses, hymns, and sections—this is the praise of the syllable.
He beheld the ocean of the world and the sun within the Rathantara, which has its chariot supported by heaven;
they say there are three kindling-sticks of the Gāyatra, and from that it has surpassed all through its greatness.

He propped up the ocean of the world in heaven; he beheld the sun within the Rathantara. They say there are three kindling-sticks of the Gāyatra; from that, the Great One has surpassed all by his greatness. 25.
The *jagat* [Sāman] is the Sāman produced from a verse (*ṛc*) in the *jagatī* meter.

By means of that, at the time of creation, Brahmā supported—that is, established—the Sun in the sky, the celestial realm, as the *sindhu*, meaning that which has the nature of flowing or that which causes water to flow.
For there is a Vedic scripture stating: "He who shines yonder is indeed of the *jagatī* nature."

Prajāpati beheld the sun fixed within the *rathaṃtara*—the Sāman of that name—because he perceived the word expressing the sun, namely “*svardṛśam*,” in the Ṛc that serves as its basis (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.32.20).
For the Śruti states: “That [sun] indeed is *svardṛś*” (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 4.10).

For this very reason, the vision of the sun is prescribed therein by the Sāma-Brāhmaṇa: "While the Rathantara is being chanted, one should close one's eyes; one should look toward the 'heaven-seer' (svardṛś). Regarding the Gāyatra—the Sāman produced from the Gāyatrī—they say its "kindling-sticks" (*samidhaḥ*) are the three inflections, meaning they refer to its three feet.

Alternatively, they say there are three verses. From that, by its power and majesty—that is, its greatness—it has surpassed and excels all other Sāmans; it has fashioned them individually and separately.

Alternatively, the word *gāyatra* denotes the *chandas* (meter). They say that it has three forms, which are respectively the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī*, consisting of eight syllables, eleven syllables, and twelve syllables.

Since this is so, therefore the Gāyatrī, though being the smallest of the meters (*chandas*), excels by its greatness—that is, it surpasses all other meters—by that very power with which she brought back the Soma; they become possessed of such power.

At the time of summoning the Gharma-milker during the Pravargya rite, there are two verses beginning with "I summon" (*upa hvaye*), because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] beginning 'I summon the good milker, the flowing one'. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.7).
1. The mothers end in *kṣa*, *ṅa*, *jha*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *m*. 2. In the *sāman*, when the *triṣṭubh* origin (*triṣṭupprabhava*) is present as the cause (*nimitta*), [it is] female (*satī*).
3. They beheld; they behold all around.
The *rathaṃtara* sāman is [chanted] during the midday pressing;
and at that time of midday, the sun is seen as radiant.
And people (or "people," depending on the variant) always behold it at the time of the ritual.
4. With such power as that, in this very manner:
I call hither this well-milking cow; let the skillful milker milk her with a good hand.
May Savitṛ impel for us everything most excellent; the heated oblation has been offered—this indeed I shall proclaim to you.
I call hither this well-milking cow; let the skillful milker milk her. May Savitṛ impel for us everything most excellent. Kindled is the sacred law (Dharma); that indeed I shall proclaim clearly. 26.
I am the Hotṛ; I call upon, that is, I approach and summon her—whom?
this cow coming hither, the milch-cow who gratifies with milk, intended for the Pravargya rite.
Furthermore, of what kind?

"Sudughām," meaning one who milks well. And moreover, "enaṃ," this cow characterized as above, "suhastaḥ"—one with beautiful hands, skilled in milking—the "godhuk," the cow-milker, that is, the Adhvaryu priest, "dohat," milks her. Since this is so, the meaning is: "Therefore, I invoke her."

For that purpose, may Savitṛ—the Supreme Lord who is the authorizer of all—"sanāviṣat," i.e., authorize "naḥ," our "śreṣṭham," most excellent and praiseworthy "savam," whether it be the Soma sacrifice or milk.
How is this so?
Because of the hearing of the word *tat*, the word *yat* is to be supplied [as the correlative].

For the Taittirīyaka states: "The Pravargya is the Dharma; because that which fell as 'aghra' [the burning], that is the *dharmatva* of the Dharma" (Tait. Ā. 5.1.5). Such being the case, he is "abhīddhaḥ," meaning "kindled."
The word *tat* has the sense of the particle *eva* (indeed).
For that very reason, "I have spoken well" (*suvocam*) means "I speak well" or "I invoke. Alternatively:
I invoke—that is, I call upon—this cow seen before me, characterized by the clouds and bringing satisfaction through rain, for the purpose of milking the rain.
Furthermore, the milker of this cow—whether it be the Sun or Vāyu, who possesses a beautiful hand (su-hasta), meaning a hand skilled in milking—milks her;
for the falling of rain is dependent upon them.
Furthermore, for that purpose, may Savitṛ—the impelling Supreme Lord—impel it for our sake; that is, with regard to our enjoyment, may He grant permission.
The meaning is: "May He not create an obstacle.
If it is asked why this is said, it is replied: [as follows].
The summer season is the law; it is the withering of crops produced by the lack of rain, kindled and intensified.
Therefore indeed I shall speak clearly; for that very reason I say this.
In the *luṅ* [aorist] after the verb *brū*, there is the substitution of *vac*; by the rule "after *as*, *vac*, etc.," there is the suffix *aṅ* for the *cli*.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Muttering "hiṅ," the mistress of treasures, desiring her calf with her mind, has come hither.
O inviolable cow, yield your milk for the two Aśvins; may she increase for our great good fortune.

Muttering "hiṅ," the mistress of treasures, seeking her calf with her mind, has come hither. May she, the inviolable cow, yield milk for the two Aśvins; may she prosper for our great good fortune. 27.

Just as a cow, when called, makes the sound "hiṅ" toward her calf—making the sound "hiṅ"—she is the "mistress of wealth," the eternal protector of many riches such as milk, curds, and clarified butter.
Through both the presence and absence of sustenance, her role as the protector of wealth and her preeminence therein are established.
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
"Desiring her calf with her mind," thus she approached;
she came near.
"This inviolable cow has arrived."
This is a name for a cow:
may the cow that yields milk for those two Aśvins, for the noble one, pour forth milk;
may she, being such, increase for great prosperity—that is, for increased good fortune—and become fully grown.
Or alternatively:
for this prosperity, [he offers] milk.
(1) *kṣa-jha1-ña-ṭa* read *pravargīyām*.
2. Arising from *kṣa*, *jha¹*, *ña*, and *ṭa*.
3. For the sake of bestowing rain upon *kṣa*, *jha¹*, *ña*, and *ṭa*. 4. It is established otherwise; it occurs even with a single *vasu*.
5. *kṣa-u-jha1-ña-ṭa*—for our good fortune! May they increase it. Here too, this should be applied as appropriate according to the context of rain.

Muttering "hiṅ," making a sound for the sake of the rain-giver, the mistress of many riches—of cattle, grain, and other wealth—and their protectress, desiring with her mind the calf, the world that is to be nourished by choice, she has approached; she comes in the form of a cloud. And she is "ahyā," meaning she is not to be struck, but rather to be praised.
Milk and water, when pervaded by the two [qualities] of expansion and contraction, lead to the misfortune of both the stationary and the moving;
or alternatively,
the Aśvins are Vāyu and Āditya.
From those two, one should milk what has been milked;
for they are the ones who release the rain.
The rest remains as it was before.

This verse, "The cow has lowed after her blinking calf; homage to you; sit down near her," is recited during the *pravarya* praise at the time of milking, when the calf is being led away from its mother.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The cow has lowed after her blinking calf; homage to you; sit down near her" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.7).
The cow lowed after her blinking calf; having smelled his head, she uttered the sound *hiṅ*.
Lowing toward the heat of the sacrificial vessel, she, moving about, produces her cry with her milk.
The cow has lowed toward her blinking calf; she has made a "hiṅ" sound for the sake of suckling. Lowing toward the heat of the udder, she, being encompassed, measures out her cry with her milk. 28.
The cow, the milch-cow, having reached her lowing, blinking-eyed calf, bellows—that is, she makes the sound "mīmā.
The root *mīmayati* signifies the act of making sound.
Or else:
It is said that he casts himself after his calf;
furthermore, [he does so] in order to lick and purify the head of that calf, that is, to fashion it—
*uśan* being used here as a particle of emphasis.
She utters the *hiṅkāra* sound; she makes it.
Furthermore, directed toward the calf—the maker of foam from the mouth of the sucking one, the calf that is by nature a flow of milk—she, lowing intensely with desire, produces the sound of "māyu.
Being such, she nourishes the calf with abundant milks.
In this case as well, it should be interpreted with reference to the cloud.

Thus, the cow-like milch-cow in the form of a cloud, having been brought forth, follows after her son called the world—who is "winking," that is, whose eyes are closed due to the absence of rain-milk—and she "lowed," producing the sound of thundering which consists of the essence of rain.

Indeed, she uttered the sound in the form of a *hiṅ* (the lowing of a cow) in order to measure out—that is, to fashion—the earth, which stands in the place of the head, so as to make it endowed with crops and the like.
There is no tautology because of the difference in the mode of exposition.

Furthermore, longing for (*vāvaśānāḥ*) the son—the radiant *gharma* who is the creator of the fruit of the sacrifice—the [waters] swell (*payate*), that is, they become full (*āpyāyanaṃ karoti*) by means of their milky fluids (*payobhiḥ*).

This is that which bellows, by which the cow, having been impelled, utters her lowing while resting upon the two pressing-stones. Through her mental powers she has indeed overcome the mortal; pursuing him, she has sought out his hiding place.

This is he; he bellows, by whom the cow is encompassed. She, resting upon the two worlds, utters her lowing. For she, through her insights, has brought the mortal man under her control; becoming lightning, she has cast off her covering.
1. *kṣa-ṅa-jha1-ja-ṭa-pratyuta* is equal to *tulya*.
2. *kṣa-ha-jha1-ma-ṭa* refers to the edge of the lower lip (*adharva-danaprāntam*). 3. *jha1-āpyāyita* means "nourished" or "swollen."
4. *kṣa-jha₁-ja-ṭa*: characterized by the sign of raining;
5. *kṣa-jha₁-ma-ṭa*: the head, situated at the position of the head;
6. *kṣa-jha₁-ja-ṭa*: with waters, that is, together with milk.
"This calf here makes an indistinct sound in its mouth;
by which calf the mother cow is encompassed, having come and surrounded it on all sides. Moreover, that cow utters, that is, produces, the sound 'māyu'."
"Where is she situated?
"She is situated at the end of the path," meaning she is established in the place of the path, the dwelling-place where cattle reside.
"She," being such, "with her thoughts"—that is, with cognitions or the actions preceded by them—"has made the middle low," for she makes it downward.

The meaning is that she performs this act with even greater excellence than humans distinguished by their knowledge do when they show affection toward a child through feeding, suckling at the breast, and so forth.
Furthermore, "Vidyudvatī" means shining because of her abundant milk; "vahni" refers to her own form.
"Vahni" is a name for form.
She "revealed" (auhata) her form;
or rather,
she who possesses lightning-like vision— meaning she whose appearance is as swift as lightning— revealed her essential nature, which consists of an excess of maternal affection.
This is one meaning;
there is another meaning as well.
A teacher of Nirukta named Śākapūṇi harbored the conceit, "I know all the mantras and deities."

Thinking, "I shall cause him to be deluded," a deity possessing ambiguous characteristics appeared before him, for the purpose of concealing the true nature of reality which is difficult to comprehend.
He did not recognize her;
and desiring to know her, he asked her to reveal her own form.
And she taught [it thus]: "Then he [saw] that child; this very deity was perceived there as my own form" (Nirukta 2.8).
How is it that there is a dual gender here in reality? And if there is a dual gender, how is there a unity of the deity?
It is said in reply:
In this case, the state of having both genders occurs in two ways: through the pair of feminine and masculine genders, and through the pair of middle and supreme (or neuter) genders.
How so?
The cloud is perceived by means of two words expressing the masculine gender, namely "this" (*ayam*) and "he" (*saḥ*), as in the phrase "this is he by whom... (*ayaṃ sa yena*).

By means of the feminine gender-denoting words beginning with "adhiśritā," the speech is that of the Mādhyamikī; therefore, there is a state of possessing both genders. Likewise, up to the end of the word "vidyudvatī" is the middle gender, because therein the cloud and the thundering are perceived as belonging to the Mādhyamikī.
That being the case, in the phrase "He covers the earth with rain," the intended meaning is that he takes up the essence of the earth;
and since this is the activity of the Sun, it possesses the characteristic of the highest deity.
If so, because both characteristics are perceived in reality, both deities are [intended], according to the principle: "Whatever its characteristic, that is its deity" (Ṛgveda Anuvāka 1.139).
Therefore, how is the establishment of a single deity possible?

[The answer is: by resorting to a transposition of these words, "This is that by which..."—whether by resorting to the oneness of the presiding self of all deities, or by resorting to the oneness of the Self who is the source of all fruits—the identity of the deity is established.
By this, the identity of the deity is stated even in the view that accepts both genders, through the distinction between the intermediate and the supreme.

Therefore, having stated that "there is indeed only one great Self as deity," there is no contradiction between the factual unity of the deity and the distinction [of deities] based on the difference between the presiding agent and the locus.
This is that *śiśuṅka*.
This is that deity presiding over the intermediate speech (*mādhyamikā vāk*), who makes an indistinct sound in the *śiśuṅka*,
by which the cow is covered.
"Gauḥ" is the name for speech.
It is the central speech by which [the breath] is enveloped, encompassed, pervaded, or presided over—
this is what is meant by "in the youngling."
Alternatively, the phrase "this is that *śiśuṅka*" does not refer to the intermediate speech (*mādhyamikī vāk*) itself, but rather to the cloud.
When that [cloud] is being instructed, it is metaphorically designated as "*śiśuṅka*," just as one says "the mantras cry out.
This is that cloud which makes the sound by which the intermediate speech is manifested.
The manner of sounding is indeed being described: "He bellows" means he makes a sound characterized by thundering;
or rather, this [is the meaning].
*Luptopamā* (elliptical simile).
*Māyuḥ* refers to the sun, because it "measures" (*minoti*) or casts its rays everywhere.
The meaning is that it makes the sun exceedingly radiant.
Alternatively, by her own power, she creates for herself a form resembling the sun.
Where does she abide?
She rests upon the limit of destruction (dhvasana).
1. kṣa-jha 1-ja-ṭa-katham:
By which sound is the mother cow (gaur-mātā) covered; having come, she encircles her calf on all sides and utters (mimāti), that is, produces (nirmimāte) the lowing sound (māyu).
"In the calves" (śiśuṃke) is the intended meaning.

Where is it situated? 2. In the affection of a child for being called, for nursing at the breast, and so forth; (variant: the affection of the child for being called, for nursing at the breast, and so forth). 3. By way of its abundance.
4. Kha-pha-bha is the swift vision. 5. Kṣa-jha 1-ña-ṭa is that which has been sung.
6. Kṣa-jha 1-na-ṭa is this.

7. He taught that in the case of *kṣa-ṅa-jha 1-na-ṭa*, those which are perceived [therein] are the great deities (*mahādevatā*). 8. In the case of *kṣa-jha 1-na-ṭa*, there is no establishment of a single deity (*ekadevatā*).
9. In the case of *kṣa-ṅa-jha 1-na-ṭa*, this is "as it is" (*yathā*) when resorting to a transposition (*vyatyaya*).
10. [The section on] the nature of the presiding self (adhiṣṭhātṛ-ātmikā) regarding *kṣa-jha* and *1-na-ṭa*.
11. Regarding the hearing of unity (*ekatva-śravaṇe*) regarding *kṣa-jha-jha* and *1-na-ṭa*. 12. Regarding the hearing of unity (*ekatva-śravaṇe*) regarding *kṣa-jha* and *1-na-ṭa*.
13. *kṣa-jha 1-na-ṭa-mimāti māyum*. This is an imitative word (*anukaraṇaśabda*). He utters the sound "māyu."
Alternatively, this is an *elided simile* (*luptopamā*).
[The word] "kṣa-jha" means an exceedingly brilliant sound;
it rests upon a cloud during its dissolution.
She is such by her mental powers—this is a term for actions;
by her own deeds, she brings down the entire world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, which is subject to the law of death, even unto the rain that falls. She indeed makes it low.
He causes human beings to bow down;
he causes plants and the like to bend down by means of their fruit.
Alternatively, [he does so] by means of "thoughts" (*cittibhiḥ*), that is, by actions characterized by illumination.
"Flashing in the lightning, she has assumed a form.
"Vavri" is a name for form (*rūpa*). By implication, the root *ūhati* here signifies withdrawal or contraction.
It withdraws [the moisture] and then takes up the form characterized by water;
furthermore, through the gateway of its rays, it takes up the rainwater again during the hot season.

The state of lightning becoming the rays of the sun is established by the threefold division of that very same light, because it will be stated later [in Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.88.10]: "They fashioned him into three for the sake of existence. Regarding the state of thunder as lightning, this is intended to express the non-difference between clouds, lightning, and thunder.
This refers to the body during the state of being alive.
By this, the worthlessness of the body and the permanence of the living soul are established.

He breathes, he lies down; he moves swiftly, he lives; moving yet firm, he is in the midst of his vital powers. The living spirit of the dead moves by means of funeral offerings; immortal, yet sharing a common womb with the mortal.

While performing the act of breathing (*prāṇana*), it is "living" (*ejat*) like one who possesses life; it moves swiftly for its own activity. Afterward, following the departure of the vital breaths, being of a nature contrary to what was described, it remains "fixed" (*dhruvam*) and immovable, lying (*śaye*) or remaining like a pillar (*sthāṇuvat*) in the midst of dwellings (*paśyānām*).
The vowel *ā* may be used for metrical completion.
Now, he describes the distinction of the *jīva*:
the *jīva* is "of the same womb" (*sayoni*) with the deceased body—that is, it previously shared a common place of origin with that body characterized by death (*matyena*).
Although there is no actual birth for the *jīva*, nevertheless, because the body is similar to it, this [status] is figuratively attributed to the *jīva* through its connection with that body.

He says that very thing: "Immortal" means having the nature of being deathless, according to the Vedic scripture: "Verily, this [body] dies when abandoned by the living self; the living self does not die" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.11.3).

The soul, whose nature has been described, moves by means of the *svadhā* offerings made by its sons; that is to say, it subsists by consuming those offerings given preceded by the utterance of *svadhā*.
In the *pravargya* ritual, during the *amiṣṭava* recitation, the single verse "I beheld the herdsman" (*apaśyaṃ gopām*) is employed.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The verse 'I beheld the herdsman not resting' is used for the *ṛc* of the *drapsa*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.6).

I beheld the Herdsman, who never falters, moving hither and thither along his paths; he, clothing himself in rays that converge and rays that diverge, revolves repeatedly within the worlds. 31. I beheld. The Herdsman. Not falling. Hither. And. Thither. Along paths. Moving. He. Well-directed. He. Divergent. Clothing himself. Around. He revolves. Within. The worlds. 31.
1. *Kṣa-jha-ja-ṭa* signifies the nature of death.
2. *Kṣa-jha-jha-na-ṭa*: when lightning flashes, having dissolved [the breath], all the heads are made to bow down.
How does he cause the elements to sink low? It is said:
"The lightning, becoming manifest, flashing forth, has covered the firmament"—that is, while it is flashing.
3. The characteristics of *kṣa*, *jha*, *jha*, *na*, and *ṭa* are [as follows].
4. [The practitioner] again takes up *kṣa*, *jha*, *jha*, *na*, and *ṭa*. 5. Because the rain and the thundering of the clouds are fruitless, the water showered by the rays [is likewise ineffective].
6. Because [the letters] ka, kha, ca, jha, and pha have their place in the body.

6. kṣa, jha, ṭa, and ceṣṭ are joined with the maintenance of the vital breath (prāṇa); ḍa, jha, and ḷ are joined with movement and the maintenance of the vital breath. 7. kṣa, jha, ḷ, and ṭa—ejat, it moves.

8. This [verse] begins with *kṣa-jha-1-ṭa*. May I behold—that is, perceive in accordance with reality—the Sun, who is the protector (*gopām*) of the entire world through rain, light, and so forth; who is never falling (*anipadyamānam*), never despondent at any time; and who moves both hitherward and thitherward by various paths in the form of the atmosphere—moving toward [the zenith] from sunrise until midday, and moving away from midday until evening. May I see such a one of great majesty as he truly is.

Furthermore, that Āditya, clothing himself in all the rays of light—those converging together and those spreading in every direction, which illuminate even the enemy [regions] such as the Moon, Mars, and Sun—moves repeatedly within the worlds, that is, in certain parts of the universe such as Laṅkā and other places, performing his rising and setting.
"I saw him"—this is the meaning.
"He indeed is the protector; for he protects all this"—such is our Brāhmaṇa.
One should also consult the Taittirīyaka, which says: “‘May he protect us’—the sun, indeed, is the protector, for he protects these creatures” (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 5.6.4), and so forth.
He who made this does not know it; he who saw it is far removed from it.
Enveloped within his mother’s womb, he who has many offspring has entered into destruction.
He who made this does not know it; he who saw it is indeed separate from it. Enveloped within his mother’s womb, he who has many offspring has entered into destruction. ||32||
In this context, by demonstrating that birth is preceded by the afflictions of the embryo, it is established through implication that the Self must be known in order to avoid that [birth].

"The man who desires a son, who has produced (*cakāra*), or is producing (*karoti*), or is dispersing (*vikṣipati*) this embryo—by way of the distraction that constitutes its cause—that man does not know its true nature (*tattvam*)."
The sixth case ending is optionally used for the object of an action.
One does not know this embryo— meaning that one does not know it in its entirety, nor what it is like, nor for what purpose it exists. And he who,

by means of inference based on the swelling of the womb which would otherwise be inexplicable, points out [the embryo] while it is still within the mother’s belly— from that seer, he (the embryo) is indeed hidden.
"Hiruk" is a word meaning "hidden.
The word "iccha" has the sense of the particle "eva" (only/indeed). "Nu" signifies certainty.
It is indeed utterly hidden.
Or rather:
he who performed this—such as agriculture, trade, and the study of the Vedas—during the state of worldly existence does not know this for him in another world or in another birth.
Likewise, that which one saw during the time of life—such as mountains, rivers, the ocean, kinsmen, and so forth—is *hiruk*, indeed separate from that which was seen.
The meaning is that everything experienced here is not experienced again in another birth or in another world.

Such a person, being *parivītaḥ*—enveloped on all sides by the *ulba* (inner membrane) and the *jarāyu* (outer membrane)—within the *yoni*, the womb of the *mātṛ*, the mother, becomes *bahuprajāḥ*, one who undergoes many births.
Alternatively, having been born, he himself becomes one with many offspring through the procreation of children.
Thus, experiencing the suffering of the womb, he undergoes the great misery known as *niṛti* until the realization of the Self, which constitutes his true nature.
Therefore, for the sake of avoiding that [misunderstanding], it is said: "The Self (ātman) is to be known.
This is the intended meaning for those who know the Self.
However, according to the view of the etymologists (nairuktas), he who made this—the wind situated in the intermediate space or the cloud—makes this water visible; he is its [Self].
The word "reality" (tattvam) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Alternatively, the sense is that he does not know this action,
because those two [the body and the senses] are insentient.

But he who has seen this and sees it—even though [the rain] is hidden far away—the Supreme Lord, the showerer of rain, acts at the proper time through the power of the karma of living beings; the meaning is that He is hidden within the orb of the sun.

He who sees this which is hidden far away—he, characterized by rain, is the son in the womb of the mother, the atmosphere; that is, in the atmosphere, which like a womb is the place of origin and support.
Since both [terms] are names for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), their relationship as general and particular should be understood.
In the region of the intermediate space, within the womb, in the midst of *ṛta*, [he is] "possessing many offspring" (*bahuprajāḥ*). [Note:
kṣa-jha-1ña-ṭa read *aniṣaṇṇam* (seated)].
2. *kṣa-jha-1ña-ṭa-tathā* from the afternoon onwards;
3. *kṣa-jha-1ña-aṭa* the Supreme Self;
4. *kṣa-jha-1ña-ṭa* again.
5. In the manuscripts kṣa, jha, 1ña, and ṭa, the word "dadarśa" (he saw) is missing.
6. In the manuscripts kṣa, jha, 1ña, and aṭa, it is stated: "because of the impossibility of any other explanation for the enlargement of the belly.
7. In the manuscripts kṣa, jha, 1ña, and ṭa, the word "dadarśa" (he saw) occurs.

8. jha-sa: Therefore, from that. 9. kṣa-ka-jha-1ña-aṭa: He does not know the reality (tattva) at another time. 10. kṣa-jha-1ña-aṭa: Mountains, rivers, oceans, women, and so forth. 11. kṣa-ṭha-aṭa: From the presence of the seer; jha1: from the presence of the one who has seen.
12. The self is hidden by *kṣa*, *jha*, *1ña*, and *aṭ*.
It is like one who has many offspring and provides much assistance.
Or else:

The root *jan* here has an implied causative sense (*antarbhāvitaṇyartha*). Being the progenitor of many beings through the production of grain, he entered— that is, he pervaded and attained— the *nirṛti*, meaning the earth which is the means of subsistence.
Heaven is my father, the progenitor; my kinship is here. This great earth is my mother, my bond.
Between the two upturned bowls is the womb; there the father placed the embryo of his daughter.
Heaven is my father, the progenitor; there is my kinship. This great earth is my mother. Within the two upturned vessels is the womb; therein the father placed the seed within the daughter. 33.
Dīrghatamas says:
"The sky, the celestial world, is my father, my protector; not merely a protector, but also my progenitor, my generator, my creator."
He states the reason for its origin there:
"The navel" (*nābhi*) means that the earthly essence (*rasa*), which has become the navel, resides here; this is the implied meaning.

Consequently, from that [essence], semen is produced from food, and from semen, a human being is born; thus, because of the presence of the essence—the cause connected to birth through such a succession—it exists here.
With this very intention, she is called "the progenitor.
For this reason, she is a kinswoman (*bandhu*), a female relative (*bandhikā*).
Thus, this great, vast earth is my mother, standing in the place of a mother; the meaning is that she is the creator of her own offspring, such as plants and so forth.

Furthermore, between the two *camūs*—the heaven and earth which are spread out (*uttānayoh*) and extended upwards (*ūrdhvatānayoh*), and which are the means of enjoyment for all this—the womb (*yoniḥ*), namely the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) that is the substratum for the creation of all beings, exists; this is the sense of the ellipsis.
Here, within this intermediate space, the Father is the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).
Through the non-difference between the presiding deity and its locus, the sun is called "heaven" (*dyauḥ*).
He [does so] with his rays;

or alternatively, Indra or Parjanya has placed—the womb of the earth situated afar, characterized by rain-water which is capable of producing all things—everywhere. He bestows it; he makes it manifest on all sides.
On the middle day of the Aśvamedha, during the Brahmodya, the Hotṛ and the other priests should question the sacrificer with the verse beginning, “I ask you.
Thus it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “They question the sacrificer one by one with [the verse], ‘I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 10.9).
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask where the navel of the world is.
I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask about the highest heaven of speech.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask where the navel of the world is; I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask about the highest expanse of speech.

O Sacrificer, I ask you a question. What is it? I ask about the furthest limit, the ultimate boundary of the earth—that point where the entire earth comes to an end. Likewise, I ask you another thing. What is that? It is said: [1. the means of producing flesh; 2. the capacity for the production of the embryo].

3. [The syllables] *kṣa*, *jha*, *1*, *na*, *ṭa* do not exist in the *brahmodya*. (Kārikā 126) Here, the *nābhi* of the world—that is, the collection of living beings—is the *saṃnāha*, meaning the bond.
The meaning is: "wherein everything is fully equipped.
Furthermore, [he says] "his own, his own" regarding the stallion (*vṛṣan*), the showerer, the horse of *Vyaśva*, the Āditya.
As the Taittirīyaka states: "Yonder Āditya is indeed the stallion-horse" (TĀ 5.3.5).
I ask: what is that which is like semen (*vretaḥ*), the seminal cause?
Likewise, I ask: what is the supreme, unsurpassed space (*vyoma*) of speech, the abode and the cause of all that is uttered? I ask about these four powers.

Then, being asked thus, the sacrificer should reply, "This is the altar" (*iyaṃ vediḥ*), because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "He replies, 'This is the altar, the furthest limit of the earth'" (*iyaṃ vediḥ paro antaḥ pṛthivyāḥ*, Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 10.9).
This altar is the furthest limit of the earth; this sacrifice is the navel of the world.
This Soma is the seed of the potent horse; this Brahman is the highest heaven of speech.
This is the altar; it is the further limit of the earth. This sacrifice is the navel of the world. This Soma is the seed of the virile horse. This Brahman is the supreme expanse of speech. 35.
The farthest limit, the ultimate boundary or conclusion of the earth—that is, of the ground—is this very altar (*vedi*).
For there is no ground apart from the altar;
as the Śruti states: "So great indeed is the earth as the altar" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.4).
Thus, we are the *nābhi*—the central connecting point—of the world, that is, of the multitude of beings;
for it is therein that all fruits, such as rain and so forth, arise, and because it binds all living creatures.
Now, we are the *soma*, consisting of essence, the seed of the *vṛṣan*, the raining Aditya.
The Soma juice offered into the fire, having reached the sun, produces the fruit of rain and so forth.

We are indeed Brahmā, Prajāpati himself; he is the supreme ether (*vyoman*), the most excellent protective abode of speech in its form as mantra and the like, because it originates there and culminates there.

The seven half-embryos, the seed of the world, stand by the command of Viṣṇu in the established order; they, the wise ones, through their insights and their mind, as encompassers, encompass all things on every side.

Seven half-embryos, the seed of the world, stand by the command of Viṣṇu in the wide expanse. They, through their insights and their mind, being wise in speech and all-pervading, encompass everything on every side.
The seven rays, which have the nature of gliding or are seven in number, are "womb-bearers" (*vardhagarbhāḥ*), meaning they hold within them water that serves as a womb during half of the year;
or alternatively,
they exist like a womb in the midst of the cosmic egg, within the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

The rays of Viṣṇu—the pervasive Āditya—which are his seed (retas) in the sense of being the essence of the world through the bestowing of rain, abide and operate within the *vidharman*, the activity of sustaining the universe, by means of *pradiś*, that is, by their specific direction.
Furthermore, they exist on all sides (*viśvataḥ*) through their *dhītayaḥ*, which are their insights, and through the mind with the thought that "the welfare of the world must be accomplished."
The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the second case.
They encompass the universe; that is, they nourish and pervade the entire world.
[The variants read "supreme" (paramam) and "likewise" (tathā), while others suggest "the portion beginning with rain" (vṛṣṭyādikalam) or "the rays of the sun" (ādityaraśmayaḥ).
The meaning is that they cause the world to flourish.

Since this is so, therefore they are indeed the wise ones (*vipaścitaḥ*), those endowed with intelligence (*buddhiyuktāḥ*), the all-pervading enjoyers (*paribhuvaḥ*), and the all-encompassing ones (*vyāsāḥ*). Alternatively, they are the "seven-womb-born" (*saptādhagarbhāḥ*): namely, the seven principles (*tattvāni*) when combined, consisting of the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*).

They are "half-embryos" (*ardhagarbha*) because they possess unmodified forms. This is because they are characterized by the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), which is both cause and effect; by the indifferent self (*ātman*), which is neither cause nor effect; and by the aspect of the Person (*puruṣa*), which is unchanging. Thus, they are half-embryos insofar as they undergo transformation through the mode of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*).
The intention is that this is due to the unchangeability of the portion belonging to the Person.
For this very reason, they possess the nature of both primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikṛti*).

Since this is so, they are the seed—the cause—of the world. Being the causal agents, they abide by the command (*pradiśā*), that is, by the direction (*pradeśena*) of Viṣṇu, who is that Puruṣa, within the realm of diversity (*vidharman*).
Of the others.
I do not know what this is that I am; hidden and armored by the mind, I move about.
When the first-born of Cosmic Order have come to me, then indeed I perceive a share of this Speech for its own impelling force.

No, I do not understand this which I am; hidden and armored, I move about with my mind. When the first-born of Cosmic Order came to me, then indeed I obtained a share of this speech for its manifestation. 37.
Whether it be "I" or whether it be "this"—if I am this entire universe, then even the whole phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indeed myself.

Having abandoned name and form, which are non-ultimate, that which exists everywhere as the pervasive "Existence-Consciousness-Bliss" (*saccidānanda*)—that which is characterized by being, consciousness, and bliss—is who I am. Whether you know me or not, I do not know; having investigated, I have not found [anything other than this].
However, this knowledge "I am this" produced by the scriptures has arisen;
its meaning is that [the self] is not the non-discriminating "I.

Because of the distinction between cause and effect, when Brahman alone is understood—since the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is non-different from Brahman—the collection of phenomena also becomes one's own very nature.

This is established by such scriptural passages as “All this is what this Self is,” “Brahman alone is all this,” “The Self alone is all this,” and “He thought: May I be many, may I procreate,” because of the declaration that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all; and by logical arguments such as “Its non-difference [from Brahman] is established on account of the words concerning its being a mere beginning” (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14), the non-difference of the phenomenal world from Brahman is proven.
Alternatively, the word *iva* has the sense of a comparison: "Just as this direct knowledge— which consists of the fulfillment of all desires— is experiential, so indeed am I that very thing."
The knowledge has arisen in me that "I am all this"; however, this has not yet become realized. I do not discern, nor have I attained, that universal identity which is experiential.
The meaning is that the universal [knowledge] produced by the scriptures has arisen, but it is not experiential.
He states the reason for this:
because I am devoid of pride (*nirahaṃkāra*).

"Antarhitanāmattat" means one whose mind has disappeared; that is, one whose mind is deluded. The meaning is that [the object] is delimited by the absence of the mind's inclination toward its own nature.
Regarding that, he speaks of rebirth:

"I wander in saṃsāra, fully bound—that is, thoroughly fettered and enveloped—by ignorance, desire, and karma; for this very reason, I am joined with a mind that is intent upon external objects, distracted, and incapable of contemplation (bhāvanā).
Alternatively, I wander while armored by the mind."
"Being entirely subject to the two organs [of sense and action], I experience suffering in saṃsāra;
I do not know the universal self," he thus laments.
Yāska also cited this as an example of lamentation: "Moreover, there is lamentation: 'Because of some deficiency, I do not discern that which I am'" (Nirukta 7.3).

It is heard elsewhere that for one whose mind is directed outward, there is suffering born from the lack of knowledge of one's own true nature: "The senses are turned away [from the Self]" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.3).
[Variant readings: 1. ṅa-jha1-vyāsāradamayaḥ;
2. kṣa-ṅa-jha1-a-ṭa-puruṣasya].

3. "This is I" (asmīti) produced by the treatise (śāstra); 4. "I am" (aham iti) produced by the treatise—this is the meaning of [the variants] jha1, kha, ca, pha, and bha, namely, that it is born of non-discrimination (avivekaja).
5. The very form of itself (svasya rūpam eva)—this is the meaning of [the variants] kṣa, kṣa, jha1, a, ṭa. 6. Or else (yadi vā)—this is the meaning of [the variants] jha, kṣa, jha1, ta, and pha.

7. [The syllables] *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *bha*, *va*, and *ta* are produced by the outward-turned mind (*bahirmukhacetas*). 8. [The syllables] *kṣa*, *jha*, *a*, *ṭa*, *ba*, *ha*, *kha*, *ca*, *pha*, *bha*, and *va* are produced by the outward-turned mind through the non-recognition of one's own true nature (*svarūpāparijñāna*).
As it is said: "The Self-existent One pierced [the senses] from the primordial source; therefore, one does not see the Inner Self" (KaU 2.4.1). If so, from what does this arise? He says:
When it shall come, what is that? It is said:

it is the experience (*anubhava*) which is the first-born (*prathamaja*) of *ṛta*—the ultimate reality, the supreme Brahman; that is, the experience produced by the first inclination toward direct perception.

When he attains me—immediately and without interval—he reaches that portion of this Upanishadic speech which proclaims oneness, namely the word "I am" (*ahamasmi*), which is to be partaken of and pervaded by the Śabdabrahman, the supreme state of Brahman. By abandoning the outward-turned nature of the mind, inward-turnedness alone is established.
When that occurs, it becomes easy at that very moment to perceive one's true nature, as there is no subsequent delay.

Just as a stone falling from a mountain peak falls without delay, so too it is heard in that very [scripture] regarding the inward orientation of the mind, though it is difficult to achieve: "A certain wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inner Self with his eyes turned back" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.4.1).
Moving away and moving toward, held by the *svadhā* offering, the immortal one shares a common womb with the mortal.
These two, eternal and moving in opposite directions, go their separate ways; people perceive the one, but they do not perceive the other.
To the west, to the east—he goes, held by his own inherent power. The immortal one shares a common womb with the mortal.
These two, eternal and moving in opposite directions, go their separate ways; men perceive one, but they do not perceive the other.
This *ātman*, which is immortal—meaning its nature is not subject to death—is *sayoni* (of the same origin) with the mortal *bhūtātman*, that is, the body whose nature is subject to death.
The meaning is that wherever there is a body that acts as a limiting adjunct (*paricchedaka*), this *ātman* also exists there; it occupies the same locus.
Or alternatively:
There is a simultaneous arising. By virtue of dwelling together, even within oneself, "arising" is used figuratively.
Being thus, one is grasped by *svadhā*, which here indicates the enjoyment of that [arising].
Alternatively, by the word *svadhā*, the body composed of food (*annamaya*) is indicated.
Being seized by that, one goes downward; having performed impure action, one descends.
He goes forward; he attains the higher worlds such as heaven.

The Supreme Self itself, being conditioned by the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), performs various kinds of actions and, having assumed the designation of a "living soul" (*jīva*) for the sake of experiencing those results, wanders through other worlds bound to the three bodies. Possessing both the gross and subtle bodies, it roams about in the world endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*).
Thus it is heard in scripture: "That which is associated with the qualities, which is the agent of actions and their fruits—it is that very one which is the experiencer."
"He, the lord of the vital breaths, whose path is variegated by the three qualities and manifold forms, moves about according to his own karmas" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.7).
Now, [the author] speaks with reference to the predominance of both:
"Those two, consisting of the elements and the organs, are eternal, existing always without division."
Alternatively, in the case of the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), its constant coexistence [with the self] is established.

Even in the case of the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*), because the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*)— which are the instruments (*karaṇa*) of that [self] and belong to the *sāttvika* class— are present there, the connection with the body is established.

Moving in all directions in this world, they travel everywhere to other worlds in order to experience their respective fruits. Among them, men perceive—that is, they see and know—the one [self] as the true self of beings (*bhūtātman*); yet they do not perceive—that is, they do not know—the other, which is distinct from the shadow of the body.
Some common folk do not know that there is anything distinct from the body. Some discerning people infer that there exists someone distinct from the body who is endowed with agency and enjoyership.
Yet, no one knows the Self as being distinct from the body.
Therefore, the meaning is that self-knowledge is difficult to attain.

1. Difficult to accomplish. 2. The meaning is that it remains [fixed] like matted hair (*jaṭā*). 3. By not dwelling together with that which possesses origination. 4. "Seized" (*gṛbhīta*) is said to mean "grasped" (*gṛhīta*). 5. The gross body. 6. In this world. 7. The elemental self (*bhūtātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). 8. Dwelling together with those of equal birth; according to *jha₁*, dwelling together with those of equal sacrificial status (*samatvij*). 9. Commentary (*bhāṣya*). 10. Completely; according to *jha₁*, completely and thoroughly. 11. Or they know.
In the syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods are seated—whosoever does not know that, what will he do with the Ṛgveda? But those who know it, they sit together here.
In the syllable, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods have settled—what will he do with the Ṛg-veda who does not know that? But those who know it, they sit here together. 39.
In the preceding mantra, the body and the individual self (jīvātman) were mentioned.
Of these two, the ultimate nature of the other—the individual self—is stated here:
"in the syllable of the Ṛg-veda."
Here, by the word *ṛc*, the four Vedas—consisting of the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*) and having the *ṛc* as their primary element—are denoted.

That the *ṛgveda* and the others constitute the lower knowledge is heard in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: having made the proposition, "Two knowledges are to be known," it continues, "Therein, the lower is the *ṛgveda*, the *yajurveda*, the *sāmaveda*," and so forth.

[The term refers to] the Imperishable (*akṣara*), which possesses qualities such as being invisible (*adṛśya*), which is devoid of the perishable (*akṣara*), which is immutable (*anaśvara*), eternal, and all-pervading Brahman.

The word *akṣara* is well known in such scriptural passages as "This, O Gārgī, is indeed that under the governance of the Imperishable" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.8), "Just as that Imperishable is attained" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.5), and "By which one knows the true Person who is the Imperishable" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.2.13) as denoting Brahman.
The relationship between the *ṛk* verses and the *akṣara* is that of the signified and the signifier.
Indeed, Brahman is realized through all the Vedas, according to the scriptural passage: "I ask you about that Person who is known through the Upaniṣads" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.26).
[Objection: Granted that this may be so for the Upaniṣadic hymns;
but how can the others have Brahman as their subject matter? [Reply: It is said:

although the other portions have sacrifices and the like as their subject matter, nevertheless, by way of producing purification of the intellect, they will have Brahman as their subject matter because they are means to the Veda, according to such scriptural passages as, "By the recitation of the Vedas, the Brāhmaṇas desire to know [Brahman]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
That very [space] is further qualified:
in the supreme, most excellent, and unsurpassed *vyoman*, that is, in the sky-like [space].
It is called "sky" (*vyoma*) due to its similarity to the sky in such qualities as being untainted, formless, and all-pervasive.
Or alternatively: [the term] *viśeṣeṇa* means "especially" in the sense of protecting everything;
for it is without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna*), since it protects everything superimposed upon it by being its very substratum.
The meaning is that everything is superimposed upon such a reality. That very reality is further qualified:
in which Supreme Self all the gods are seated.
They sit down, meaning they rest or abide upon it; or rather,
the meaning is that all the Vedas, together with their auxiliary limbs, find their ultimate culmination in this entity characterized by the syllable *ut*.

Whoever—that person—who does not know that reality (*vastu*)—which is the locus for the attainment of the true nature of the gods and others, and which is established as the ultimate purport of the entire Veda—what will he do with the *ṛc*, that is, with the previously mentioned web of words such as *ṛc* and so forth? The meaning is: having failed to understand through the means of the Veda, what can he possibly accomplish?

The sense is that because there is no purpose, the entire Veda would be rendered fruitless. Alternatively, the meaning is that for one who, not knowing the Imperishable (akṣara), becomes a performer of actions and practices sacrifices and the like, no action whatsoever has truly been performed by him.
Those very ones who know—that is, understand—that reality, they alone, these knowers, "sit together" (samāsate); they remain perfectly established.
They have attained rest in their own true nature through non-return;
or rather,
"those who know" refers to those who merely understand but do not practice.
The particle *icchan* is used here for emphasis. Thus, these very same [sacrifices] are performed together;
they are practiced simultaneously, beginning with the *gavām ayana* and extending up to the *sahasrasaṃvatsara*.

1. There exists that which has the form of *kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-ja-ṭa-y*. 2. The threefold Veda (*trayī*), known as the lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) along with its auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*), is so called. 3.
[It pertains] to that which possesses qualities such as being unindicatable (*adeśya*).
4. [The reading] "vedaḥ" [is supported] by the manuscripts kṣa, ṅa, jha, 1, ja, ṭa, and ṛgādi. 5. [The reading] "brahmaparatvam" [is supported] by the manuscripts kṣa, jha, 1, ja, and ṭa.
6. [The phrase] "by means of bringing about the purification of the intellect" [is supported] by the manuscripts ṅa, jha, and 1.
7. [The section] on the subject of Brahman (jha-1-brahmaviṣaya).
8. By way of similarity such as intangibility, formlessness, pervasiveness, and so forth (kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa-asparśatvanīrūpatvavyāptitvādisādṛśyena).
9. Of the gods (kṣa-ṅa-jha-1-ja-ṭa-devānām).
The prefix *sam-* has the sense of inclusion (*saha-artham*).

Since there are no sacrifices beyond those mentioned in the mantras, the meaning is that their fruit as well is obtained through this very knowledge. The plural number is used because there are many performers (*kartṛṇām bahutvāt*).
Others, however, describe it differently:
"The *ṛcs*.
An *ṛk* is the solar orb (*ādityamaṇḍala*) which is worthy of praise (*arcanīya*), or that which consists of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth.
According to such scriptural passages as, "In the forenoon, the god [is] in heaven with the *ṛc*s," and "This sun indeed shines as that orb; therein are those *ṛc*s," [it is understood].

In that which is related to Him—the Imperishable (akṣara) characterized as being "in the highest firmament" (parame vyoman), the Brahman whose nature is described in such scriptural passages as, "That golden person who is seen within the sun"—in Him all the shining gods, the rays, abide.
He who does not know this, what will he do with the solitary *ṛc*?
Only those who understand and cultivate [this] abide as wise ones;
being free from disease and other ailments, they live for a long time on this earth as noble enjoyers of happiness.
Others explain it by way of another method.

"In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛgveda" means in the imperishable syllable consisting of the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), which is connected to all the Vedas as indicated by the Ṛgveda, or which pervades all the Vedas.
