That the *praṇava* is the essence of all the Vedas is heard in the Brāhmaṇa: "He brooded over the Vedas; from them, thus brooded upon, the syllables were born—*a*, *u*, and *m*. He combined them into one; that is this 'Om'" (Ai. Brā. 5.32).
It is "supreme," meaning unsurpassed.
Indeed, there is no collection of mantras superior to the Praṇava; for it is the expounder of Brahman, which transcends the three periods of time.

This is according to such scriptural passages as: "And whatever else transcends the three periods of time, that too is indeed the syllable Om" (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 1), and "Om is Brahman" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.8).

The relationship between the Vedas and the *praṇava* is one of the latter serving as their locus and representative; this is established by such scriptural passages as, beginning with "He who studies the *ṛc*s... and continuing, "He who studies the *praṇava* studies everything... 'Om'—this is how one enters the triple knowledge (*Ṛg*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*); speech is this supreme syllable" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.11.4). Upon which all the gods have taken their seat:
because the *praṇava* constitutes the essence of all mantras, and since all deities reside within the mantras, it is the abode of all the gods.
Or [it is called *brahmāvarta*] because it is the abode of Brahman, or because Brahman—the dwelling place of all the gods—is located there.
The remainder is not different [from what has been explained].
This mantra is explained in the *Nirukta* (13.10).
Others, however, describe it differently:
"Ṛcas" means the *ṛk*, which is the soul (*jīva*) worthy of praise (*arcanīya*).
The meaning is that it refers to the imperishable syllable related to Him, or to Vyāsa, or to the Supreme Self (paramātman).
For this very reason, [He is] in the supreme, most excellent, and unconditioned *vyoman*—which, as the specific substratum of all, is a protector (*rakṣe*), or which is like the sky (*vyomasadṛśe*).

In that Supreme Self, the gods who possess movement engage in worldly activity; or rather, all (*viśve*) those known as the senses (*indriya-saṃjñakāḥ*) have sat down (*niṣeduḥ*) upon Him—they abide having taken refuge in Him.
He who does not know this—that upon the abandonment of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that very [Self] is the true nature—such a person is gross; what then will he do?
What fruit will he obtain by means of the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, through the state of being a living being?
The sense is that he will not escape the afflictions of birth, death, and so forth.
Those who know reality—this and so forth—is established.
If a cow intended for the *agnihotra* should make a lowing sound, then one should give her fodder and the like with this verse, "sūyavasāt.

Thus it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "One should give fodder to the lowing [cow] with [the words], 'May you be blessed with good pasture' (*sūyavasādbhagavatī hi bhūyāḥ*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.11).
This same verse serves as the concluding hymn (*paridhānīyā*) in the *pravargya* ritual during the recitation of praises.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “One should conclude with the verse, ‘O Blessed One, may you indeed possess good pasture’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.7).
1. Those who are not separated from *kṣa*, *jha*, *la*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *na*.
2. Those who do not know this reality (*tattva*), namely *kṣa*, *jha*, *la*, *ja*, *ṭa*, and *ya*. 3. They will act [thus].

4. *Kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa*: The relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) consists of states such as being a delimited part (*aupādhikāṃśa*), a delimited portion (*aṃśa*), a delimited reflection (*vicchinnajñāna*), and a delimited appearance (*vicchinnābhāsa*). (*Jha-aupādhikasya vicchinnāvābhāsavimbadibhāvaḥ*): The meaning is that this relationship exists with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who is connected to the individual soul (*jīva*) which possesses limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*). 5. *Kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa*: Those who are engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavaharantaḥ*). 6. *Kṣa-jha-1-ja-ṭa*: That [body] is gross (*sthūla*).

7. By the power of the life-sustaining essence of *kṣa*, *jha*, *ṭa*, and *ja*: may you indeed be possessed of good pasture; and may we also be prosperous. Eat grass at all times, O inviolable one; drink pure water as you move about. suyavasāt | bhagavatī | hi | bhūyāḥ | atho iti | vayam | bhagavantaḥ | syāma | addhi | tṛṇam | aghnye | viśvadānīm | piba | śuddham | udakam | ācarantī || 40 ||
O *aghnyā*—
this is a name for cows—
O cow who is worthy of being honored (*ahanyate*), you, being the consumer (*attrī*) of excellent pasture (*suyavasa*) consisting of grass and the like, are *bhagavatī* (possessing fortune).
"Bhaga" is a name for wealth.
May you be "bhūyas," meaning possessed of abundant wealth such as milk and other resources that are to be produced by all; may you become so.
The particle *hi* serves as a filler or indicates well-known fact;
in the world, it is well known that the abundance of milk and such results from the consumption of fodder and the like.
*Atho*, immediately thereafter, may we sacrificers also become *bhagavantaḥ*—that is, possessors of abundant wealth.
Now, whereas it was previously said to be done once, it is now requested that it be performed at all times:
"At all times (*viśvadānīm*), at every moment, always (*sarvadā*), eat (*addhi*) the grass;
moving about (*ācarantī*), going forth in every direction, drink the pure (*śuddham*), stainless (*nirmalam*) water."

Now, the mantra has been explained by Yāska himself: "O blessed one, you who provide excellent pasture, may we indeed be blessed now; therefore, O inviolable one, always eat grass and drink pure water as you go about" (Nirukta 11.44).

Gaurī has lowed, fashioning the waters; she who is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, and nine-footed, having become thousand-syllabled in the highest heaven. 41. Gaurī. Lowed. The waters. Fashioning. One-footed. Two-footed. She. Four-footed. Eight-footed. Nine-footed. Having become. Thousand-syllabled. In the highest. Heaven. 41.
"Gaurī" means the speech of the middle region (mādhyamikā vāk), which has the nature of swallowing (garaṇaśīlā).
The absence of the suffix *su* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
She utters sounds (*mimāya*);
what is she doing?
Fashioning the waters—that is, the rainwaters—she is their perfect accomplisher.

She is *ekapadī*, possessed of one foot, having a single foundation while abiding in the cloud, or "one-footed" by virtue of the wind as her means of motion; she is *dvipadī*, having two foundations in the cloud and the intermediate space, or with the sun as her second.
Thus, she became one who is four-footed, endowed with four quarters and presiding over the four cardinal directions;

then eight-footed, endowed with eight quarters and presiding over eight directions in relation to the intermediate points; and nine-footed, endowed with nine quarters by virtue of the zenith, or with nine directions including the sun—she who has become such as this.
It would be Vedic; [the suffix] *kasu* [is used];
then, with the addition of *ṅīp*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the *vasu* [portion].
What is the use of this calculation?
It has "a thousand syllables";
this term signifies the unlimited.
The meaning is that she possesses the form of immeasurable pervasion, like water which has the nature of extensive diffusion.
Where? That is stated: "in the highest heaven" (*parame vyoman*), that is, in the exalted intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) which serves as the locus for water.
Some say thus:
"The white, possessing the nature of the *gaṇas*, speech whose essence is the *śabdabrahman*, has measured out—that is, it manifests."
The verbal root [is used] in its well-known meaning.

She who fashions substances such as pots and the like, producing them according to their respective forms, is "one-footed" (*ekapadī*) because she has a single foundation in her state of being unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), or because she is of a single form through her own nature; she is "two-footed" (*dvipadī*) because she possesses two feet in the form of the distinction between the well-trained and the untrained; and she is "four-footed" (*catuṣpadī*).
1. O Blessed Ones, may we be [thus]. 2. May we be [thus]. (Note: The variants *kṣa-jha-1-bhagavantaḥ syāma* and *kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-syāma* both mean "O Blessed Ones, may we be [thus]".)
Furthermore, it is requested for the sake of exceeding the mirror:
3. *kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-śaneḥ śarnaḥ gacchantī* (going from the slow one [Saturn] to the refuge);
4. *kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa-'sūryeṇa vā'* is not present.
5. Kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa are established in water; they are established in the elements. 6. Kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa have a single foundation.
7. Kṣa-jha-1-a-ṭa are by way of the nature of the *praṇava*.

Through the divisions of nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*), she became "eight-footed" (*aṣṭapadī*); with the eight [parts] including the vocative (*āmantrita*), she became "nine-footed" (*navapadī*) when the eight [parts] along with the *sādhya* and *ukta* [elements] are added.

Alternatively, she exists within the nine locations (*pada*) such as the chest and throat which share a common origin; subsequently, having attained manifold manifestation in the supreme firmament—the excellent space of the heart—at the *mūlādhāra*, she becomes "thousand-syllabled," meaning she is meditated upon in many forms as various types of sound.

This mantra has been explained by the Teacher himself: "Gaurī has lowed, fashioning the waters; she becomes one-footed with the middle [region], two-footed with the middle and the sun, four-footed with the quarters, eight-footed with the quarters and the intermediate directions, nine-footed with the quarters, the intermediate directions, and the syllable (akṣara); she is of a thousand syllables, possessing abundant water in the highest heaven" (Nirukta 11.40).
From her the oceans flow forth; by that the four quarters live.
From that flows the imperishable (akṣara), upon which this entire universe depends for life.
From her, the oceans flow forth; by that, the four quarters of space live. From that flows the Imperishable; upon that, the entire universe subsists. 42.
From that aforementioned cow, the oceans— the clouds which serve as the locus for the gathering of rainwater—
flow forth abundantly and in various ways;
by means of that water, the four quarters are filled.
The prefix *pra* has the sense of "vigor" (*vīrya*).
[The term refers to] the four intermediate directions (*vidiś*) and the four cardinal directions (*diś*).
Alternatively, it refers to the four principal directions (*mukhya*) as being preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*).
The desire for those [objects] is "tācchandyam. Men live by means of that [desire]. Thereafter, that syllable (akṣara) flows as water; the meaning is that it produces crops and the like.
"By that [rain], this entire world, beginning with the crops, thrives.

This too has been explained by Yāska: "From her the oceans flow forth; the clouds rain, and by that the beings dwelling in the quarters of space live. From that, the imperishable water flows; all beings subsist upon it" (Nirukta 11.41).
"I beheld the smoke of Śakra, moving forward through the midst of the enclosure."
The heroes cooked the speckled bull; those were the first ordinances.
I saw from afar the smoke made of *śakā* grass, rising straight upward before me by this lower path. The heroes cooked the dappled bull; those were the first ordinances. 43.
I saw smoke produced from dry cow-dung, consisting of *śaka* and made of *śaka*, not very far away from the rain.

Because smoke is visible at a distance during the day, it is described here as the object of vision. By means of this low-lying, dark smoke, I saw the other—the fire—which exists beyond it and is its cause.
The meaning is "I am the sacrificer.
Furthermore, he is *vṛkṣāṇam*, the sprinkler of the fruit; *vṛśnim* means white-colored.
He is called *pṛśni* because he himself attains the fruit through that [soma], or because he is the one who reaches [the goal]; *pṛśni* is Soma in the form of a drop (*drapsa*).
The *vīrāḥ*—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) skilled in various sacrificial rites—shaved him.
Here, out of regard for the root meaning, the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-pratyaya*) signifies the sense of "doing" (*karoti*).
Since that [root] expresses action in general, it means here, by virtue of contextual propriety, "they accomplished [it] by means of pressing."
These [are] 1. distinguished by case-endings together with the vocative (āmantrita) [and the consonants] kṣa, jha, ña, and ṭa;
2. the eight-pada [meter] consisting of kṣa, jha, and ṭa; and the jha₁-aṣṭāpadī.

3. [The suffix] *kṣa*, *jha*, *ṭa*, and indeclinables (*avyaya*) denote that which is colored (*rakta*); *jha* and indeclinables denote that which is colored. 4. *Kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa* are used in the sense of virility (*vīryārtha*).
5. *Kṣa*, *jha*, *ña*, and *ṭa* are used with this [instrumental case].

Therefore, his *dharmas*—the means of accomplishment, the performances, the foremost, the most excellent, the primary, and those culminating in fruit—came into being; they were fully realized. Or else: [Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka a, Sūkta 22, Verse 164] Second Aṣṭaka 1009. His *dharmas*—the means of accomplishment, the performances, the foremost, the most excellent, the primary, and those culminating in fruit—were accomplished.

In former times, Soma became a bull; the gods cooked him with dung for the sake of sacrifice. That liquid became smoke, which is said to have been the cloud.
Or rather, the mantra should be explained by the wise as referring to that [process].
Three [beings] describe Keśin according to the seasons; at the end of the year, one of them shaves him.
One gazes upon everything with his powers; the course of another is visible, but not his form.

Three [are they]. The long-haired one [keśin] speaks forth in due season. Once a year, one of them shaves [his hair]. One of them surveys the universe with his powers. Of one there is seen the course, but not his form. ||44||
The three—Agni, Āditya, and Vāyu—are endowed with preeminent rays that stand in the place of hair.
And they, "at the proper seasons" (ṛtuthā), that is, from time to time, "behold" (vi vakṣate) the earth characterized by various features.
He now states their respective functions individually.

Among these, one is Agni; when a year has passed, he "shaves" for a year—that is, through burning, he performs the work of a barber by cutting the herbs, trees, and other vegetation that stand in place of hair.
Another is Āditya (the Sun); with his powers (*śacībhiḥ*), such as light and rain, he "beholds" (*abhicaṣṭe*) the entire universe from all sides.
The "course" (*dhājiḥ*)—the movement—of the third, Vāyu, is seen by all, but his "form" (*rūpa*) is not seen because it is beyond direct perception.
"Touch, sound, support, and trembling are the signs by which [the wind] is known," so say those learned in the Nyāya.

This mantra as well has been explained by Yāska in this way: "The three long-haired ones look out in due season; at every time they behold [all things]. One of them shears the year [with his hair]; this one is Agni, for he burns the earth. Another beholds everything through his actions; [this one is] the Sun. The movement of the third is seen, but not his form; [this one is] the intermediate [wind]" (Nirukta 12.27).
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāgdevī, the verse "Four are the [steps] of speech" is the invitatory prayer (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation (*havis*), because it is so prescribed in the Sūtra:
"Four are the measured steps of speech; by means of the sacrifice they have followed the path of speech" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
There are four measured quarters of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what human beings speak.
There are four quarters of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, they do not set in motion; mortals speak only the fourth quarter of speech. 45.
The four measured steps of speech—that is, all speech—are fully delimited;
the meaning is that whatever speech exists in the world is divided into these four kinds.
These steps the Brahmins—knowers of the Vedas, seekers of the mind, and the wise—know and understand.
Among them, three, hidden in the cave—that is, established within the secret place—do not stir, do not move, and do not manifest; such is the meaning.
Humans, both the ignorant and the knowers, speak the fourth quarter of speech; they utter it clearly and employ it in worldly discourse. (Note:

Regarding the variant readings *kṣa-jha1-ña-ṭa-keśinaḥ*, this refers to those possessing excellent rays that stand in the place of hair; *jha-trayaḥ* refers to the three possessing excellent rays that stand in the place of hair.)
2. Or else, every year;
3. the cutting of hair, such as that of medicinal herbs and trees which stand in the place of hair;
4. characterized by touch, sound, support, and trembling.
5. *kṣa*, *ña*, *ṭa*, and *atha* belong to them.

Regarding the question of what those four are, many people describe them in various ways according to their own respective views. Some proponents of the Vedas maintain that all speech is encompassed within the *vyāhṛtis* together with the *praṇava*. They argue that the three *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *bhūḥ*, are the summary of the entire web of Vedic speech, while the single *praṇava* is the essence of those very *vyāhṛtis* because it constitutes the core of the three Vedas; thus, they hold that all speech is limited to these *vyāhṛtis* accompanied by the *praṇava*. Others, following the doctrine of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), [enumerate them] according to the divisions of noun (*nāman*), verb (*ākhyāta*), prefix (*upasarga*), and particle (*nipāta*).

A verb (ākhyāta) has action as its primary meaning; a noun (nāman) has substance as its primary meaning. That which is prefixed before a verbal form is a prefix (upasarga), such as those beginning with *pra*.

A *nipāta* (particle) is so called because it is fixed (*nipatana*) in specific senses such as subordination (*ubja*), excellence (*ava*), and remainder (*śeṣa*); for example, *api*, *tu*, *ca*, and so forth.
In these very particles, all speech is contained, because the entire, undivided speech has been manifested in four ways.

This is according to the Śruti: "Speech, indeed, spoke in a backward direction, unmanifested; Indra, having stepped into its midst, manifested it. Therefore, this speech is called 'the manifested' (*vyākṛtā*). (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.4.7.3).
Others, however, [define them as]: "The Mantras, the Kalpa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the fourth is the worldly [speech].
The portion of the Veda designated by the ritualists (*yājñika*) as that which illuminates the meaning of what is to be performed is the *mantra*.

The portion of the Veda that sets forth the rules for the application of the mantras is the *kalpa*, as stated in passages such as: "Thus the mantras; after this, the kalpa" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.31.2).

The portion of the Veda that illuminates the meaning of the mantras is the Brāhmaṇa. Regarding the worldly [speech] concerning objects of enjoyment, such as the form "Bring the cow," the ritualists maintain that all speech is regulated in this very manner.
The etymologists (nairuktāḥ) maintain that the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas] constitute the fourth, the conventional (vyāvahārikī).
Those who follow the historical tradition (aitihāsikāḥ) hold that the speech of serpents, birds, small reptiles, and the fourth, the conventional, belong to this category.
However, those who advocate for the Self (ātmavādinaḥ) maintain that it exists in domestic animals, in reeds, in wild beasts, and within the self.

Other Mātṛkās present it in another manner as fourfold: Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī. Speech, which is essentially of the nature of *nāda*, is called "Parā" when it has arisen from the *mūlādhāra*.
And because that very [speech], having reached the heart, is difficult to define due to the subtlety of the sound (*nāda*), it is called *paśyantī* by yogins, since it is capable of being seen.
That same [speech], having reached the intellect (*buddhi*) and attained the desire to speak, is called *madhyamā*, because it arises in the "middle" known as the heart; thus it is *madhyamā*.
Then, when that very [speech] situated in the mouth issues outward through the operation of the palate and other [articulatory organs], it is called *vaikharī*.
Thus, there are four measured steps of speech.
The wise—those Brahmins who possess mastery over their minds and are yogins who have realized their own goal, the *śabdabrahman*—know and understand these four steps, beginning with the *parā*.
Among those, the first three are hidden in the cave because they reside within the heart;
however, all humans speak the fourth state, which is known as *vaikharī*.

According to the perspective of grammar, consisting of nouns, verbs, and so forth, the wise Brahmins—those who know the division of roots and suffixes and who understand the application of speech—know those words.
Those who do not know the application of speech—common folk—speak, employ, and utilize only the fourth part, the *turīya*, of speech for the purpose of manifesting meaning.
This mantra has been explained in the *Nirukta*; it should also be considered here: "Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage:
'That speech, once created, became fourfold: three parts in the worlds, and the fourth among animals.'"
That speech which was on earth, that was in Agni, that was in the Rathantara;
that which was in the intermediate space, that was in Vāyu, that was in the Vāmadevya;
that which was in heaven, that was in Āditya, that was in the Bṛhat, and that was in the thunder; then, that speech which remained over, they placed it in the Brāhmaṇa.

"Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas speak both kinds of speech, that of the gods and that of humans" (Nirukta 13.9). "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa. Being one, the sages call him by many names; they call him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan."
They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa. The sages speak of the One Being as manifold: they call him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan. 46.
1. The *brāhmaṇa* is that portion of the Veda which, having analyzed [the mantras] in detail, elucidates their meaning on all sides.

2. Regarding the subject matter of the commentary (*bhāṣya*): according to the manuscripts *kṣa*, *jha*, and *ṭa*, it concerns the *bhāṣya*; according to *ḍa*, *jha*, and *jha1*, it concerns the language (*bhāṣā*). 3. However, others, such as those belonging to the school of Sarpapākṣin, maintain that there are four types based on distinctions such as these.
Others are the practitioners of mantra (māntrikas). Among those, three are the supreme and so forth; [in some versions] the word "four" does not appear.
This is because they are being measured.
6. Of that which is called by the letters *ḍa*, *jha*, *jha₁*, and *ga*.

7. Regarding *kṣa*, *jha*, *jha₁*, *a*, and *u*: "Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage [which says] '...thus'"; this does not exist. They call Indra—the one possessed of life-force (*asumat*) and distinguished by sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)—"this one. 1. *aiśvaryaviśiṣṭam* 2. *indram*
Likewise, they call Mitra the god who protects from *pramīti*—that is, from death—and who presides over the day;
they call Varuṇa the god who wards off evil and presides over sovereignty;
and likewise, they call Agni the god of that name, distinguished by qualities such as being the eater of food.
Moreover, this very one is also the divine (*divya*)—that which exists in heaven—the fair-winged (*suparṇa*), the well-flying, the Garuḍa, the powerful, the winged.
He who sees this is also this very one.
To the question, "How can there be multiplicity in that which is one? it is replied: [as follows].
The wise, the intelligent ones who know the true nature of the deities, speak of this very sun—which exists as a single reality—as manifold;
they call its self Indra according to its various functions and causes, because it has been stated:
"There is indeed only one Great Self, the deity; they call him Sūrya."
Furthermore, they call that very cause of rain and so forth—the Vaiśvānara, Yama the restrainer, and Mātariśvan who is praised in the intermediate space—Vāyu.
Thus, the universal nature of the Brahman as Sūrya is declared through its non-difference [from all].

Here, some, relying on such scriptural passages as "Agni is all the deities" (Ai. Brā. 2.3), maintain that since these other two lights are also Agni, this mantra establishes the universal nature of Agni alone.

In that context, the first word "ami" is the subject; with reference to it, there is the statement of its identity with Indra. This mantra is explained in the *Nirukta* as follows: "The wise speak of this very Agni, the great Self, as one and the same Self in many ways—Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and the divine Garuḍa."
"He is divine, born of heaven, the great bird, the one who possesses power, the heavy-souled, or the Great Soul" (Nirukta 7.18).
For one desiring rain, three lumps of food should be offered into the fire.
In that context, "The black path" (*kṛṣṇaṃ niyānam*) is the invitatory verse (*anuṣṭhākyā*) for the third [offering].

"The black path, the bay horses with beautiful wings, clothing themselves in the waters, fly up toward heaven."
They have returned from the seat of Truth; then indeed the earth is moistened by clarified butter. 47.

The black path, the bay-colored birds with beautiful wings, clothed in waters, fly up toward heaven; they have returned from the seat of Truth; then indeed the earth is moistened by clarified butter. 47.

The dark, black-colored cloud, moving according to its course, is accompanied by the "haris"—the "suparṇas," meaning those with beautiful flight, the rays that carry away water; they clothe themselves in the waters, that is, they cause the waters to dwell within the clouds.
The meaning is that Agni fills the clouds;
because the causative sense is implied, the verb takes two objects.
Or alternatively:
the "black path" (*kṛṣṇaṃ niyānam*) is the night,
for the night of the gods is the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
"Towards that" means during that rainy season.
Acting in this manner, they "fly up," that is, they go upwards toward heaven— the celestial world— or toward the sun which rests therein.
Those rays turn back from the seat of *ṛta*, from the place of the waters, from the solar orb; they return, coming hitherward.
Immediately upon their returning, the earth is moistened—that is, it is thoroughly drenched—by *ghṛta*, that is, by water.
One should consult the *Nirukta* (7.24), which states: "The black descent is the night of the sun; the bay-winged ones are the carriers, the rays of the sun," and so forth.

1. *Kṣa-ha-jha-1-na-ṭa*: Because of the application of sovereignty (*aiśvaryayogāt*). 2. *Kṣa-jha-1-ya-ṭa*: By means of the respective cause and effect (*tattatkāryakāraṇena*). 3. *Kṣa-jha-1-na-ṭa*: [One conceives] oneself as otherwise (*anyathātmānam*). 4. *Kṣa-jha-ṭa*: From breathing (*śvasanāt*). 5. *Kṣa-na-ṭa*: And [the breath as] wind (*vāyuṃ ca*). 6. *Kṣa-jha-1-na-ṭa*: The phrase "of the sun... becomes" (*sūryasya... bhavati*) is absent. 7. *Kṣa-jha-1-na-ṭa*: The word "who" (*ye*) is absent. 8. *Kṣa-ha-jha-1-na-ṭa*: Because it has been formulated as a sūtra (*iti sūtritatvāt*). 9. *Kṣa-na-ṭa*: They cause to revolve (*āvartayanti*). "Twelve are the spokes, one is the wheel; three are the hubs—who indeed understands that?"* *Kṣa-na-ṭa*: They cause to revolve. Twelve are the spokes, one is the wheel, three are the hubs—who indeed understands that? *Note: The verse cited is Ṛgveda 1.164.11.*
In that [chariot], three hundred spokes were fixed together with the rim, and sixty were neither moving nor unmoving.
Twelve are the spokes, one the wheel, and three the naves. Who indeed has understood that? Into it are fixed together thirty nails, sixty that are both moving and immovable. 48.
Twelve such spokes, the *paridhi* enclosures, are set forth;
they rest upon a single, unique wheel—characterized by its nature of revolution—known as the year (*saṃvatsara*).
Likewise, three hubs, which are the wooden planks resting upon the hub, represent the seasons known as summer, the rainy season, and winter.
Just as the wheel of the sun has twelve rims and three spokes joined to the hub, so too it is with the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*).
Who, whoever he may be, a great one, knows that wheel?
In that wheel, together with the pins—like pins indeed.
Here, although the word *na* is used as a prefix (*upacāra*), by virtue of its semantic force (*sāmarthya*), it has the sense of comparison (*upamā*).
In that wheel of the year (*saṃvatsaracakra*) as well, there are thirty-sixty [units] of this number;
the word *na* is used in the sense of "and" (*ca*).
Sixty spokes—the days occupying the position of spokes—are fixed; they are firmly set.
Of what nature are they?
They are "moving and unmoving."
The word *ekaścala* has undergone reduplication;
it means "moving" (*calāḥ*), that is, having the nature of motion (*calana-svabhāvāni*).
By the rule *caricali-patavadīnām acyākcābhyāsasya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.126), there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the augment *āg* [before the suffix *kvip*];
then, the suffix *asun*.
"Six hundred and thirty are indeed the days of the year," so says the *Brāhmaṇa* (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 9.1.1.43).
"Twelve spokes, one wheel—this refers to the months, for they are measured (*māna*) by the month (*māsa*)," and so forth, according to the *Nirukta* (4.27).
In the *pravargya* *abhiṣṭava*, there is one verse beginning with "yaste stanaḥ" (*That breast of yours...*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "yaste stanaḥ śaśayo yo mayobhūrgauramīmedanu vatsaṃ miṣantam" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.7*).
In this very same way, it serves as the *yājyā* for the oblation in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Sarasvatī.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'yaste stanaḥ śaśayo yo mayobhūḥ... svam soma pra cikito manīṣā'—these two [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
That breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which provides delight, and which nourishes all desirable things—
that treasure-yielding, wealth-finding, and bounteous giver— O Sarasvatī, bring that here for us to suck.

That breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is a source of joy, by which you nourish all desirable things—that treasure-yielding, wealth-bestowing, and bountiful Sarasvatī—bring her here for us to suckle. 49.

O Sarasvatī, that breast of yours— which is like a breast, providing nourishment for living beings worthy of hearing, consisting of the beautiful words of both worldly and Vedic usage— that breast lies within your body; and that breast which is *mayobhū*, the bestower of happiness upon those who taste its essence—
with that breast you nourish all desirable and cherished forms of wealth for those who enjoy it.

And the breast (*stana*) is the bestower of treasures (*vratnadhā*), the sustainer of many kinds of delightful flavors. 1. [The twelve-fold ones]—Kṣa, Jha₁, Ja, Ṭa; 2. [those situated in the navel]—Kṣa, Jha₁, Ja, Ṭa; 3. [the connecting rays]—Kṣa, Jha₁, Ja, Ṭa; 4. [the great]—Kṣa, Ū, Jha₁, Ja, Ṭa; 5. [the pins of the chariot wheel]—Kṣa, A, U; 6. [thus this]—Kṣa, Ja, Ṭa; 7. [they]—Kṣa, Jha, Ṭa. *Vasuvit*: the knower, the obtainer, or the one who makes known the *vasus*—that is, the dwellers, the riches.
Furthermore, that breast which is *sudatra*, meaning "giving beautiful gifts";
according to the *Nirukta* (6.14), " *sudatra* means giving auspicious gifts.
Here, the repeated hearing of the word *yat* ("which") is for the purpose of making known the extreme excellence of the breast.

O Goddess, who will now, in this rite (*iha*), fashion for us that breast consisting of hymns (*sūktamaya*), which is beneficial to all living beings (*sarvaprāṇyupakāraka*), for the purpose of being drunk (*dhātave*) by us?

At the churning, the verse "By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to sacrifice" (yajñena yajñam ayajanta devāḥ) is the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*), because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "He should conclude with [the verse] 'By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to sacrifice'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.16).
By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances.
Those great ones attained the height of heaven, where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. Those great ones attained the heavenly world where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide. 50.

The gods—the performers of ritual action and the sacrificers—worshipped [ayajanta] the sacrifice, that is, the Āhavanīya fire which is the means for the oblation, by means of the sacrifice produced through churning. The meaning is that they joined it together for the sake of performance.
For the Taittirīya Saṃhitā states: "Having churned the fire, he offers it; by that very act, hospitality is rendered to Agni" (TS 6.2.1.7).
Those *dharmāṇi* are the primary rites that accomplish the goal.

"Prathama" is a name for the primary [sacrifice]. The meaning is that they became "pratamāni," that is, preeminent (*prakṛṣṭamāni*), capable of producing fruit for themselves. And those sacrificers indeed [attained] *nāka*.
Because there is no suffering (*aka*) in this, it is *nāka*, the heaven.
The *māhimānaḥ*—those endowed with greatness—*sacanta*, that is, they have gathered together in that [heaven].
Of what kind is that *nāka*?
In which heaven (*nāka*) the ancient ones, the *Sādhyas*— those who possess the means for sacrifice and other rites (meaning the "deities of action" or *karmadevas*)—
reside and dwell, they attend upon that.
Therefore, the meaning is that even now humans should act in this same way.
Alternatively,

the gods who have now attained their divine state formerly worshipped— that is, honored— the sacrifice which was to be performed by means of the fire of the sacrifice, having become the sacrificial animal.
Divinity and the state of being a sacrificial animal (paśutva) are to be understood as distinct manifestations of the Supreme Lord Himself.
This is based on the Vedic scripture: "Agni was the animal; they immolated him; with him they sacrificed.
The remainder is as explained previously.
In which heaven—that is, when that heaven had become the cause—there were the ancient Sādhyas, the gods who are the performers of rites and the presiding deities of the *chandas* meters;

as well as the Ādityas and the Aṅgirasas. The Sādhyas are called "the gods who are the performers of rites. As the Brāhmaṇa states: "The Sādhyas, who are indeed the *chandas*, performed a sacrifice with Agni; they went to the heavenly world. And the Ādityas and the Aṅgirasas here also performed a sacrifice with Agni; they went to the heavenly world" (Ai. Brā. 1.16).
These gods exist in heaven; that is to say, they have attained heaven.
Or alternatively:
by means of sacrifice—namely, the sacrifice of knowledge and so forth—they worshipped, that is, they honored Viṣṇu, who is sacrifice itself.
Those of great majesty reach and unite with *nāka*, the world of Viṣṇu—
that place where the ancient gods such as the Sādhyas abide.
The *Nirukta* passage beginning with "The gods sacrificed with Agni" (*Nirukta* 12.41) should be consulted here.

1. *kṣa-jha-jha₁-jaṇṭa-yaśca vasuvit* (and those who possess wealth). 2. *kṣa-jaṭa-nivāsayitṝṇām* (of those who cause [them] to dwell). 3. *kṣa-jha-jaṭa-nirmadhyābhinā* (by that which is without middle or distinction). 4. *ḍa-jha₁- ‘sādhanāḥ’ nāsti* (the word "accomplishers" does not exist). 5. *kṣa-u-jha-jha₁-a-tra-devabhāvamāpannāḥ* (those who have attained the state of gods here). 6. *kṣa-jha₁-ja-ṭa-svargaṃ prāptāḥ* (they have reached heaven). This water is the same, both with the days and likewise with the nights; the rain-clouds quicken the earth, and the fires quicken the heavens.
The same is this water: it rises up from here and goes forth there with the days. Parjanya quickens the earth; the fires quicken the sky. 51.
This well-known water is "common," meaning it is of a single form.
By certain days belonging to the summer season, it goes upward;
likewise, by the very days belonging to the rainy season, that water goes downward, moving with its face turned downwards.
By the rule "the nominative case is used in connection with 'ca' and 'vā'," the nominative case ending is not elided.
Then, by means of the ray, he reaches the earth;
that very point is stated:

"The *parjanyas*," the clouds who are the gratifiers, "quicken" (*jinvanti*) the earth—that is, they gratify those dwelling on the earth by means of the production of crops and so forth through the bestowing of water.
Likewise, the fires—the Āhavanīya and others—when the oblation is offered into them, gladden and satisfy the gods who reside in heaven, the celestial world.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Sarasvatī, the verse “divyaṃ suparṇam” is the offering-formula for the omentum (vapā).
This is because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘divyaṃ suparṇaṃ vāyasaṃ bṛhantaṃ sa vāvṛdhe naryo yopaṇāsu’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
In the Anvārambhaṇīyā [iṣṭi], this very formula is used specifically for the sacrifice to Sarasvatī.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The divine, well-winged, great bird, like the [light] of Savitṛ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.8).

I invoke Sarasvatī for our protection— she who is divine, the well-winged, the great crow, the hidden germ of the plants, beautiful to behold, and who satisfies us from all sides with showers of rain.

The divine one, the well-winged, the crow-like, the vast, the embryo of the waters, the most beautiful among the plants; him who satisfies us from nearby with showers of rain—him, Sarasvatī, I call upon for nourishment. 52.

The divine one, existing in heaven; the fair-winged one, possessing beautiful movement; the crow-like one, characterized by constant motion; the vast and great; the embryo of the waters, the producer of the waters of rain like a fetus;
and the one who makes the herbs visible—meaning, he who causes them to be seen.
Or alternatively:
"the beautiful embryo of the plants" is a separate qualification. Furthermore, [he is] "approaching," satisfying [them] with rains in accordance [with their needs], and gladdening the world.
Or rather:
[I am] one who approaches, one who goes toward;
[I am] one who satiates the reservoirs of water, such as wells and the like; or else, I am the one who approaches.
I repeatedly invoke for protection— that is, for preservation— the god Sarasvant, who possesses water (for *sara* is a name for water), or the god Sūrya. I call upon him again and again.
In the twenty-third Anuvāka, there are fifteen hymns (*sūktas*).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with “*kayā śubhā*,” is in the *Triṣṭubh* meter.

According to the *Anvānukramaṇikā*: “The hymn beginning with ‘*kayā*’ has five fewer [verses]; it is a dialogue; the odd-numbered verses from the third onwards are the speech of the Maruts, while the last belongs to Agastya; the eleventh verse belongs to Indra; and Indra is the deity for the remaining verses.”

In this [hymn], the dialogue between Indra, Agastya, and the Maruts is set forth. Since the third, fifth, seventh, and ninth verses consist of the words of the Maruts, they alone are the seers (*ṛṣis*), according to the principle: "He whose words [are in a verse] is the seer" (Anuvāka 2.4).
Since another portion of it was recited by Agastya and others, he alone is the seer (ṛṣi). The even-numbered verses and the first verse, as well as the eleventh, are the speech of Indra;
therefore, he alone is the seer.

In this context, regarding the statement "that which is spoken by him is the deity" (Anuvāka 2.5), some [manuscripts] read "by certain days belonging to the rainy season," while others omit the word "herbs. (kṣa, jha₁, jaṭa, kaiścit; kṣa, jha₁, jaṭa).
By way of invocation (*pavāda*), Indra, characterized by the Maruts, is the deity for the entire [rite].
This hymn is placed before the *nivid* insertion in the *mahadvatīya* recitation during both the *saṃsava* and the *cāturviṃśaka* sacrifices.

It is prescribed in the two sections titled ‘yadi paryāyān’ and ‘marutvatīya’ as follows: “One should recite ‘kayā śubhā’ as the *purastātsūkta* for the *marutvatīya* [śastra]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.6; 7.3).

On the fifth day of the *ābhilāvika* period, this very hymn is used for the *marutvatīya* litany; for it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The midday [service] consists of the hymn beginning with 'pañcamasya', 'kayā śubhā', and 'yasmin marutaḥ'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.7).
In the *mahāvrata*, this hymn is likewise employed in the *marutvatīya* śastra.

In the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*, it is stated: “With what [splendor], O Indra accompanied by the Maruts, you, the bull, [come] for the joy of battle, you who are of like age and dwell in the same abode” (*Ai.

Ā. 5.1.1*). At the *Viṣuvat* day, this very [verse] is the *nivid*-placement for the *Marutvatīya* [śastra], because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘Thou art the good ram’ and ‘With what [splendor]’ constitute the *Marutvatīya*” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 8.6).
Regarding its application, Śaunaka says:
Whose—belonging to what illustrious person—mighty Vedic hymns (*brahmāṇi*) and oblations (*havīṃṣi*) do the Maruts, who are eternally youthful and of great majesty, enjoy?
And who, in his own great sacrifice (*adhvare*), turns these Maruts toward himself, diverting them from other sacrifices?
He provides an illustration regarding the difficulty of restraining [the mind]: "Like hawks—birds of that name whose flight is praiseworthy—as they fly through the atmosphere;
by what means, by what great and contemplative hymn of praise, may we cause them to rest? (may we delight them).
Then the Maruts, being addressed by Indra, reply with this third verse.
From where do you come, O Indra? Why do you go alone, O Lord of the assembly?
What is this that you ask thus as you approach with your beautiful steeds? Tell us, O Lord of the bay horses, what is in your mind.

Why? O Indra, though you are the great one and alone, you go forth, O Lord of the Good. Why do you thus question us as you come together with those who seek glory? O Lord of the Bay Steeds, tell us that which is yours among us.

O Indra, O lord of the virtuous, O protector of the good—you who are *māhin*, that is, great, worthy of praise, and to be followed by your attendants—being such as you are, why do you go alone, being without a companion? From what cause do you go?
Or alternatively:
"Where are you going?
What is this 'thus' of yours? Why are you acting like this? Is there no one at all who can follow you?"
Furthermore, you, being well-disposed and meeting with us, ask rightly;
O possessor of bay horses (Indra), that which you desire to say to us—tell that to us with beautiful words.
The Vedic hymns are my thoughts; the pressed juices are auspicious. My strength stirs, and the stone is set in motion for me.
They pray for it and long for the hymn; let the two bay steeds carry us toward that.

The sacred hymns are mine; my thoughts are for peace. The pressed juices, my vigor, and the offered stone stir me up. They call out to me; they welcome my songs of praise. These two bay steeds carry us toward them. 4.
Then, being thus questioned by them, Indra replies with this fourth verse:
"O Maruts, all *brahmāṇi*—whether ritual acts or oblations—are my own;
likewise, my *matayaḥ*—the thoughts and praises joined with reflection—are for my *śam*, bringing about my happiness."
Or rather, the ellipsis is: "my thoughts and intellects abide in them alone.
Likewise, the *sutāsaḥ*, the pressed Soma juices, are mine—belonging to me and for my sake alone.
Therefore, the meaning is that one must proceed toward the sacrifice. Furthermore, it is *śuṣma*— a name for strength— in order to ward off obstacles such as Rākṣasas along the way.
The powerful mountain is my [strength]; the thunderbolt, my devourer of enemies, having been hurled, goes forth toward its mark and does not turn back.
Not only do oblations and the like belong to me, but the sacrificers also invoke and pray to me alone.
Furthermore, the hymns—the recited praises—long for me; that is to say, they desire me and chant my praises.
Furthermore, these two bay horses of ours, these very ones, we cause to rest.
(Variant readings: 1. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-ramayāmaḥ*;
2. *kṣa-ja-ṭa-sa evameva*; *kṣa1-sarūpameva*).
3. *Kṣakṣajaṭasamaraṇaḥ* means "perfectly rushing together.

O horses, carry me—desiring to go—to those places that are to be reached, such as the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) and so forth; carry me to the desired destination. Therefore, I shall proceed with speed.
The meaning is that you too must go to one who is performing penance;
therefore, the sense is that he should be considered as being without assistance. Hence:
"Uniting with the swift ones, adorning our bodies with our own powers..."
With our great powers we harness these [steeds] for Indra; for you have become one who conforms to our own nature.

Therefore, O Indra, having yoked ourselves with our closest [companions], adorning our bodies with our own powers and great glories, we now harness these [steeds] unto you; for you have indeed come to be according to our self-nature. 5.
Thus addressed, the Maruts spoke to him in this way:
"O Indra, because you act thus, for that reason we too have made you most near to us with these abundant, worthy, and common companions— these bulls, O Hero, for our nourishment."
For we shall indeed perform many deeds, O most powerful Indra, through our will, O Maruts, whatever we may desire.

O Bull, you have performed many deeds for us with your worthy companions through these shared nourishments; indeed, O most powerful Indra, we shall accomplish many things through our resolve, O Maruts, when we so desire.
Then, having been addressed thus, they spoke again to Indra:
"O Indra, O bull, O showerer of blessings, you have indeed performed much; you have truly accomplished an abundance.
Nevertheless, with us—our equals, our companions, joined with us—you have performed manly deeds and established our strength."
But the meaning is not that there is only one;
O most powerful one (*śaviṣṭha*), *śava* is a name for strength.

O Indra, most powerful one, we have indeed performed many deeds, even more than those previously accomplished by ourselves. O Indra, whatever—such as rain and other blessings—we desire through our will (*kratu*) and action (*karman*), those [deeds] are even greater than yours; such is the meaning.
For we are the seven Maruts.
The state of being unaccented is a Vedic peculiarity.
By this, his own greatness is established;
the word *svara* is used distributively.
Alternatively, this is a statement of Indra.
"O Maruts, whatever belongs to one, let that belong to him alone.
Then, may both I and you, through our common resolve and action, desire—that is, we wish for—the work of rain; therefore, the water shall be common to us all.
This is the explanation of the *nighāta* accent in the word "marutaḥ."
O Maruts, you increased Vṛtra through your own *indriya*;
having become powerful by your own fury, I, with the thunderbolt in my arm, have made these all-glittering waters flow easily for man.
I, O Maruts, having become mighty through my own power and fury, slew Vṛtra with my *indriya*. I, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, have made these all-gladdening waters flow easily for man. 8.
Now Indra said: "O Maruts, I, Indra, have become powerful through my own *indriya* (manly vigor) and through my *bhāma* (wrath); I have come to be so endowed. For what purpose? That is now stated."

For the sake of the human being’s desire, I— being one whose arms are like thunderbolts (*vajrabāhu*)— have made these waters, which are all-delighting (*viśvaścandra*), easy to traverse (*sugā*) and flowing everywhere through rivers and other channels;
by this, it is stated that he has no need for assistants.

2. kṣa-jha₁-ña-ṭa: It was made known.

"I alone have slain Vṛtra—the cloud, or the Asura; I am the one who has struck him down."
By what means? That is stated: by the sense organ through its own capacity. And how is that [capacity] attained? That is stated:
By his own fury, born from the anger caused by the raining down of water, he became powerful and strong.
Regarding the question "in what?", both of those [factors] are now stated.

O Maghavan, nothing indeed surpasses you; no deity known to us is your equal. Neither one being born nor one already born can rival you. O exalted one, perform those deeds which you are yet to do! 9. anuttam | ā | te | maghavan | nakiḥ | nu | na | tvāvān | asti | devatā | vidānaḥ | na | jāyamānaḥ | narśate | na | jātaḥ | yāni | kariṣyā | kṛṇuhi | pravṛddha || 9 ||
Now those Maruts replied with joy:
"Ā" is used for recollection;
we have now remembered that, O Maghavan, there is nothing at all (*nakir nu*) that has not been accomplished by you.
"Nu" signifies certainty; the meaning is that what has been spoken by you is the truth.
O Lord, "tvāvān" means one like you, and "vidānaḥ" means a wise person.
The suffix śānac occurs by way of transposition.
There is no god or deity who knows the means of victory over you.

Furthermore, O mighty one, whoever—whether a god or a mortal—is being born or has already been born, whatever deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra you shall perform, must perform, or do perform, none of those reach you; none of them affect you. *Naśati* means "to reach" or "to affect."
This too is a speech of Indra:
"O Maruts, let this *stoma*—the hymn of praise—not fail to gladden (*amandat*) or delight (*modayate*) me here, in this matter of producing water.
O heroes, O friends, you have fashioned for me that *brahman* which is worthy of being heard by all—that powerful wheel consisting of the holding of clouds and so forth."

O you who are golden-hued, having fully illumined (*saṃcakṣya*) me, you have surely and certainly covered (*acchānta*) me with your glories; you cover (*chadayātha*) and continue to cover (*ācchādayatha*).
Shining constantly toward me, bestowing fame upon me alone, and being praised by my very deeds, the meaning is that you celebrate me alone.

O Maruts, which mortal indeed in this world honors you?

Furthermore, be knowers—become those who recognize—these my true words that have not yet been understood.

Let us now proclaim that ancient greatness of the impetuous host, of the bull’s banner;

For the sake of the impetuous manifestation of those [beings], meaning for their appearance or their presence.
To the question "For what purpose is that?", he says:
"For the banner (ketave) of the sacrifice—the bull, the showerer of fruit.
It is well known that the arrival of clouds occurs through the impulsion of Vāyu.

O you of mighty roar, endowed with great sound through the impetuosity of your movement, O Śakras—those capable of accomplishing everything—when each journey (yāman) is undertaken, perform (kuruta) your powers, strengths, and capabilities (taviṣāṇi), which are to be attained through your greatness, like the splendors belonging to fuel (aidhāni). Constantly bearing the sweet mead, they sport like playful children at the assemblies, O bold ones;

They do not constantly bring their son, bearing honey; the bold ones play playful games at the assemblies. The Rudras reach the one who bows with protection; they, being self-strong, do not neglect the one who has prepared the oblation.

Constantly bearing, like a beloved legitimate son, the sweet oblation (*madhu*), the Maruts—being bold against *rakṣas* demons and other foes, playful by nature—approach and sport, they play and amuse themselves at the sacrifices.
Furthermore, they are the Rudras.

The Maruts, though sons of Rudra, are also called Rudras because of the non-difference between the progenitor and the progeny. Their status as the sons of Rudra is well-known in the Purāṇas, where it is established that Pārvatī and Parameśvara, pleased by their ascetic penance, accepted the Maruts as their own sons. *Namaskṛtam* means accompanied by hymns characterized by salutation; *haviṣkṛtam* refers to the sacrificer who has prepared the oblation (*havis*). By means of *avasā*—that is, through protection or satisfaction—the Maruts *nakṣanti*, meaning they pervade or reach [the sacrificer].
Furthermore, the Maruts, whose power is self-dependent (svatavasaḥ), do not disregard the sacrificer; that is to say, they do not oppose him nor cause him distress.

To whichever sacrificer has offered oblations— that is, to one who has given the soma and other offerings— the Umās, the Maruts, who are the protectors, immortal and subject to the nature of immortality, being pleased by the oblation, have granted *rāyaspoṣam*, the increase of wealth;
and by the word "ca" (and), the increase of cattle and so forth—

Being like well-wishers who act for the benefit of this sacrificer, like friends, the Maruts—blessers who bring about happiness—sprinkle and moisten the worlds (*rajāṃsi*) with abundant water (*payas*), so that crops and other vegetation may grow.

They who have clothed the regions with their powers—your coursers, seeking the light of heaven, have sped forth. O Maruts, those coursers (*evāsas*) belonging to you—those specific horses which, by their own powers (*taviṣībhis*), that is, by their strengths consisting of the bestowing of rain and so forth, encompass (*āvṛṇvanti*) the regions (*rajāṃsi*), that is, the worlds, on all sides—your coursers, being self-yoked (*svayatāsas*), meaning harnessed by themselves without a charioteer, have sped forth (*prādhrajan*); they go forward with preeminence and pervade [the space]. Furthermore, because of your arrival, all beings (*viśvā bhuvanāni*) and all dwellings (*viśvā humyā*) tremble with fear (*bibhyati*) lest they fall.
Since this is so, therefore we go to you who are *citra*— meaning wonderful, praiseworthy, or marvelous. He states the cause of fear:
While the *ṛṣṭi* weapons stood ready for battle and were raised up with great force;

while the *ṛṣṭi*s were held in readiness.

O Maruts, when you—whose movements are dazzlingly brilliant—cause the mountains, the caves of the hills, or the clouds that fill them, to resound; or when you, who are beneficial to men (*naryāḥ*), traverse the back—the upper region—of the luminous atmosphere (*divaḥ*); then, at the occasion of your ageless journey (*ajarman*), every lord of the forest (*viśvo vanaspatiḥ*), the multitude of trees protecting the woods, trembles with fear.
Likewise, the herb—such as *priyaṅgu*, *vīhī*, and so forth—"proceeds," meaning it goes forth pre-eminently from its own place, moving here and there.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a woman desiring a chariot," that is, one who longs for a chariot for herself.
The meaning is "mounted on a chariot";

O you Maruts, who are fierce and possessed of formidable strength, being well-minded with beautiful intentions and having unharmed hosts, fulfill—make complete—the excellent understanding of us, your devotees. An illustration regarding violence:
"Just as *riṇāti* [cuts], so does the weapon (*hetiḥ*), which is well-placed, well-aimed, and well-projected, or the weapons that serve as its means."

they know—their knowledge is certain—those first, most excellent, and preeminent manly deeds (*pauṃsyāni*) of that great hero, Indra, the dispeller of various enemies, such as the slaying of Vṛtra and so forth.

As if in mutual rivalry, mighty powers (*taviṣāṇi*) characterized by mutual competition have been manifested; or rather, weapons marked by their presence have been placed upon your shoulders. Furthermore, in your *prapathas*—those resting places where paths have extended out [to them].

Not [by] nourishments (kṣā-puṣṭibhiḥ).

*Arabhasāsaḥ* means possessed of impetuosity or beautiful; likewise, *añjayaḥ* means manifest. *Aṃseṣu* refers to the shoulders, that is, the roots of the arms; *etāḥ* refers to these white-colored garlands.
In the *pavi*—the winds resembling thunderbolts—and in the *kṣura*s, which have the sharp edges of razors;

like birds [flying] with their wings, not without wings.

The Maruts are great, endowed with magnanimity;
by what?
By their greatness, that is, by their preeminent power.
Likewise, they are manifestations, pervasive, and all-encompassing.
Likewise, they possess the threefold sovereign powers (*vibhūti*).
They are far-sighted, appearing and shining even from afar.
The illustration is seen in the *Dūradarśana*:
"like the divine *stṛ*s.
*Sra* is a name for the constellations (*nakṣatra*), because of the statement in the *Nirukta*: "‘Ṛkṣāḥ’ and ‘stṛbhiḥ’ [are used] for the constellations" (Nirukta 3.20).
The gods who exist in heaven (*divi*) are like stars—masses of light consisting of their own radiant blossoms—which are visible from afar;

furthermore, they are *mandrāḥ*, meaning exhilarating; *sujihvāḥ*, meaning possessing beautiful tongues; and *svaritāraḥ* by means of their *āsabhiḥ*, that is, their mouths, meaning they are speakers, that is to say, those whose speech is pleasant.

For this very reason, they are called "fair-tongued" (*sujihvā*). Furthermore, they are "well-mingled with Indra" (*indre saṃmiśrāḥ*), meaning they are those who properly mix [with him], that is to say, the companions of Indra.

O well-born Maruts, that is your greatness; long is your bounty, like the ordinance of Aditi. That, O well-born Maruts, is your greatness; long is your bounty, like the ordinance of Aditi. O well-born ones, of auspicious birth, O great ones, your greatness is indeed such as that. To explain what is meant by "that," he says:
your gift—namely, the rain and so forth—is long, exceedingly extensive and uninterrupted.

Furthermore, O Maruts, whatever desired wealth is to be bestowed upon that well-doer, the sacrificer who performs auspicious rites such as sacrifices—that which is to be granted, even Indra does not withhold by means of his relinquishment; he does not reject it, nor does he act with crookedness.

Through these sacrifices being performed now—consisting of hymns of praise and other forms of worship—may I attain, that is, pervade, your desireless state, which is the goal sought through these rites. May I reach it directly.
This hymn for you, O Maruts, this song of the poet Māndārya, son of Māna—may it reach your bodies and grant us offspring. May we find nourishment, a secure dwelling, and life-sustaining rain.

This is your hymn, O Maruts; this is the song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Māna. May it come to us with nourishment for our bodies and progeny. May we provide food, a secure dwelling, and a life-giving rain.

This mantra has been explained at the end of the third chapter. Having offered to the Maruts the praise performed from the beginning of the hymn (*sūkta*) onwards, [the seer] prays for his own desired object:

Of the *vsumāyās*.

such rain, or a pure and specific weapon, like a row of clouds, has settled together among these Maruts.

The Maruts, far-reaching, auspicious, tireless, and youthful, have desired to bestow their common bounty like [a shared] possession. Terrifying, they do not drive away Heaven and Earth; the gods take pleasure in increasing their friendship. 4.
The Maruts, who are auspicious and possess beautiful ornaments, who are the seekers of the wind, have intensely sprinkled the clouds with their mingling lightning—
that which thoroughly drenches the mass of water—

so too these terrible ones, acting in this manner, shake the two worlds— heaven and earth— by means of their terrifying excessive rains;

1. *ka-kha-jha-pha*—these [are the examples]. 2. *jha₁*—by means of those shining intensely. 3. *jha₁*—in both (*ume*). 4. *jha₁*—as an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntatvena*). 5. *jha₁*—or in the intermediate space (*antarikṣe*). 6. *jha₁*—like a woman going toward a gathering of people during the rainy season; this is the illustration for manifestation (*āvirbhāve*). 7. *jha₁*—resplendent with beautiful ornaments and so forth. In all other cases, the accent is acute on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*); however, it should be understood that here, by way of exception, there is acute accent on the final syllable (*antodāttatva*).
Alternatively,
some say that by the word *rodasā*, Rudra— whose nature is to weep— is meant; his wife is *rodasī*.
Others, however, say that the name *rodasī* refers to the wives of the Maruts; this is indeed the preferred position because it is so used later on. In that view, *rodasī* means "the two Rodasīs."
The vowel *ī* at the end of the locative case (*saptamī*) may optionally be elided. By the rule “*īṃtau ca saptamyarthe*,” it receives the designation of a *pragṛhya*.
In that [sacrifice], they release their beloved wealth;

however, the Maruts—the gods who gladden or exhilarate—enjoy or cultivate *vṛdham*, meaning growth, for the sake of friendship (*sakhyāya*). In the case of Heaven and Earth, the meaning is that they effect the increase of those two for the sake of friendship, that is, for the state of being friends toward all living beings.

May she be pleased; when she, the divine one, to be accompanied, whose locks are loosened, [comes] to
Either Vṛṣākapi’s wife, Rodasī, or lightning—this being her name—is she who also approaches (upa-sevate) this host of Maruts.
The augment *aṭ* is added to the root *juṣ* in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood.
For what purpose?
For the sake of union with her.
Of what nature is she?
The *vāsuryāḥ* are the Asuras, the possessors of the field (*kṣetāraḥ*), the Maruts.

Belonging to them are the *viṣitastukāḥ*, meaning either distinguished masses of hair or scattered masses of hair, due to the nature of their enjoyment; likewise, they are *nṛmaṇāḥ*, possessing thought among the leaders—the Maruts—or possessing thought among men, being intent on the mind of bestowing rain; and they have *tveṣapratīkāḥ*, blazing appearances, with radiant strides or radiant limbs.

Such a goddess comes to, or pervades, the chariot of the host of Maruts as they attend upon Vidhātṛ; or, having mounted the chariot, she comes to the sacrifice to go to the place of sacrifice. Like what?
Like Sūryā, the wife of Sūrya, she ascends the chariot of the radiant Sun, whose appearance is brilliant;
or rather,
like the daughter of Sūrya who mounts the chariot of the Aśvins, so does she.
There is an illustration regarding the arrival:
"from the *nabhas*," [and] "not from the *iti*.
This word *nabhas* is common to both the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and the sky (*iti*), because it has been stated [in the Nirukta]: "The word *nabhas* is common [to both]. (Nirukta 1.4.6).
In this context, there is the mention of the sun;
its depth is like that [of the ocean],
and it is as swift as that.

The youths established the young woman, the blinking one at the assemblies, as a Pajrā for their glory—when, O Maruts, the singer possessing oblations sang a song for you, having pressed the Soma and offering his service. They established the young woman, the blinking one at the assemblies, as a Pajrā for their glory—when, O Maruts, the singer possessing oblations sang a song for you, having pressed the Soma and offering his service.

The Maruts, separating or mingling with the most youthful [clouds], or [separating] the youthful woman who mingles them—her whose form is lightning—establish her within the two worlds (Heaven and Earth).
By means of their divine voice, they sustain her upon the chariot.
Of what sort is she?
She who, by her constant rule, mingles the unblinking [gaze] with the *paja*;
*paja* means strength;
she who possesses that.
Regarding *vśubhe*: it is called *śubhadaka* because it shines and gleams;
it is for the purpose of rainwater.
Or it may be construed as "on an auspicious chariot. For what purpose?
On the occasions of the Vidyā-sacrifices which have become the instrumental causes.
When?
O Maruts, when [the singer] praises you.
The possessive suffix is elided when [the word] has the sense of possession.

The worshipper, endowed with the mantras for the means of adoration, or the sacrificer possessed of oblations—meaning one provided with the sacrificial offerings such as what is to be given—and having pressed the *soma* for the sake of the oblation, this sacrificer, while serving and performing service, sings the hymn that is to be sung; that is the meaning of "he sings."

I proclaim that which is worthy of being proclaimed: the true greatness of these Maruts which exists. When they, with their bull-like minds, are eager for battle, even the steadfast and fortunate women are carried along. 7. I proclaim that which is worthy of being proclaimed: the true greatness of these Maruts which exists. When they, with their bull-like minds, are eager for battle, even the steadfast and fortunate women are carried along. 7.
The greatness of these Maruts—their preeminent magnitude—which is to be spoken of, worthy of praise by all, true, unassailable, and unfailing—that I proclaim, I declare, and I describe.
How has this greatness of theirs been attained? It is said:
because *īm*, their own, the two worlds (*rodasī*) are *vṛṣamaṇāḥ*—possessing minds intent on pouring down rain and the like—and *ahaṃsyuḥ*—possessing self-confidence.
The egoism [of the Lord] is that there is never anyone who performs benefit for the world; consciousness (cit) is stable. The word "consciousness" (cit) is used here as a term of reverence.
Such a goddess, though utterly perishable, sustains and supports fortunate women—those endowed with auspicious fortune—and procreative offspring, or the products of rain;
for when there is rain, all living beings come into existence.
It is because of this that her greatness exists.
The meaning is: "I praise that majesty."

Mitra and Varuṇa protect from blame; they drive away those who act wickedly and are ill-reputed. Even the unshakable and firm things are moved; indeed, O Maruts, you who possess desirable wealth, have caused them to grow. 8. They protect; Mitra and Varuṇa; from blame; he acts; indeed; this one; the ill-reputed; also; they move; the unshakable; the firm; he has grown; indeed; O Maruts; you who possess desirable wealth. 8.
O Maruts, you gods who are our kinsmen; O Mitra and Varuṇa, the deities presiding over day and night—[addressing them: "ayamo" (this one).
"Ayamo" is a single word consisting of a collection of particles;
the particle "u" has the sense of the word "api" (also/even).

This one as well— these three together protect (*pānti*) this world, or the sacrifice, from reproach (*avadyāt*), from censure, from improper performance, and from the obstruction of worldly activity (*jagatyakṣe*). Likewise, they cause those things among them that are unpraiseworthy or diminished to fall away (*cyavate*), to be driven off (*cātayanti*), and to perish (*nāśayanti*).

Moreover, these [rays] are impelled by them; being *acyuta* (unfallen), they do not fall, and for that very reason they are *dhruva* (fixed) and immovable. Yet, the waters situated in the clouds do fall—that is, they cause rain—or rather, these [rays] themselves cause it to rain.
For the Śruti states: "Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed day and night; verily, through day and night, Parjanya rains.
Or else: [the verse may be interpreted as follows:]
Imperishable and stable riches fall away. When? It is said: O Maruts, when this time of yours—characterized by the giving of rain, or rather, by the breaking of the clouds—has grown or is growing.
The meaning is that at that time, the gods, beginning with Mitra, protect the world through activities favorable to you.
Or alternatively:

when the *dātīvāraḥ*—the sacrificer who possesses wealth characterized by oblations worthy of being given—O Maruts, *īm* (indeed) *enān* (these), namely you, *vavṛdhe* (strengthens or causes to increase); that is to say, "when [he does so]."

O Maruts, has not even the nearest one among you reached the limit of your power, whether from near or from afar? Having increased by their bold might, they have boldly surrounded their enemies like a surging wave. 9. Not indeed, O Maruts, has anyone among you reached the limit of your power, even from afar. Having grown strong through their bold strength, they have boldly encompassed their foes like a flood. 9.
1. Or, "they cause to fade" means they revile other matters or cause them to ripen.
O Maruts, the limit or end of your strength (*śavas*), which belongs to you—whether it be near, in the vicinity, from afar, or even from some distance;
or alternatively:
*viviti* is used in the sense of contempt.
*atyantadūrāt* means from an extreme distance.
*asme* means among us; *eke'pi* means even one; *nu* means quickly; *nahi* means indeed not; *āpuḥ* means they do not reach. [The meaning is: "Not even one among us has indeed quickly reached [it]."
The meaning is that they do not encounter [obstacles] whether in his presence or in his absence.
Now, he speaks of their power being effective even when he is out of sight:

those Maruts, indeed, increasing (*śūśuvāṃsaḥ*) by means of *dhṛṣṇu*—that is, bold—*śavas*, or strength; and for that very reason, by means of *dhṛpatā*, that is, a capacity capable of overcoming others, they *pari dhuḥ*—they surround, overcome, and bring under control—the *dveṣas*, that is, those who hate them.
In this regard, there is an illustration: "like water" (arṇaḥ) means like water;
just as water overcomes its own obstructions such as mud and the like, so it is here.
Since this is so, they did not reach the end of their strength.
One should mutter the verse beginning with “vayam agha” on the tenth day after the sun has set;
for thus says the Sūtra: “‘vayam agha indrasya preṣṭhā’—when the sun is setting” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.6.14).

May we be the most beloved of Indra; may we indeed speak forth at the assembly. May we be great from of old, and may that [glory] of ours follow us day after day; may Ṛbhukṣan favor us accordingly. We are the most beloved of Indra; we shall indeed speak forth at the assembly. We have been great from of old, and may that [glory] of ours follow us through the days; may Ṛbhukṣan favor us accordingly.
Now on this day, may we be vigilant and most beloved of the god Indra;
or rather, may we, being most beloved, proclaim the greatness of Indra— that is, may we become capable of praising him.
Furthermore, we [shall be present] tomorrow, even on the following day,
at the *samarya*— that sacrifice (*yajña*) in which there are *maryas*, i.e., officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
or [at] the battle.
Let us proclaim the greatness of Indra; moreover, let us proclaim our great strength for our sake even in the past, in former times. Likewise, day by day—that is, every single day—let us do so.
On the past day and on the future day, we shall always speak [of it].
Therefore, that is the Lord of the Rbhus;
this is great knowledge.

Because it is listed among his names in the Nirukta (3.3.10) as ‘Ṛbhukṣāḥ ukṣā,’ may the great Indra be with us— may he be favorable toward us, or rather, may he be the bestower of our desired objects among men, that is, among human beings.

This hymn for you, O Maruts, this song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Māna—may it reach your bodies with nourishment; may we find food, a stronghold, and one who bestows life-sustaining gifts. This hymn for you, O Maruts, this song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Māna—may it reach your bodies with nourishment; may we find food, a stronghold, and one who bestows life-sustaining gifts. (11)
Thus, the eleventh [verse] has been explained.

‘Yajñayajñā’ is the tenth hymn; it belongs to the fourth [maṇḍala], is composed by Agastya, and is addressed to the Maruts. Its first verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter; the remaining seven verses are Jagatīs according to the rules of metrical definition.
"‘Yajñayajñā daśa triṣṭupchandasam’ is the introductory heading;
the specific application [of these verses] is determined by their inherent indicative power (liṅga)."

Sacrifice after sacrifice, O Maruts, you are equal in your power; you hasten toward our prayer with divine zeal. May I turn you hitherward for the prosperity of both heaven and earth, for great protection, with beautiful hymns. O Maruts, in every sacrifice (*yajñā-yajñā*) you are equal (*samanā*), free from deficiency or excess. As Yāska says, "Turvaṇi means 'the one who acts swiftly'. Thus, arriving at each occasion of invocation, you accept the oblation and make it perfect by removing any defects. Furthermore, you sustain (*dadhiṣve*) every act related to you—such as the bestowing of rain—acting as the bringers (*devyāḥ*) of the gods themselves. That is to say, you cause rain to fall so that the oblations may be quickly prepared for the gods. Since you do this, I turn you toward us (*arvācaḥ*). For what purpose? For the great protection (*avase*) and gratification of both heaven and earth (*rodasyoḥ*). And why is that? For well-being (*suvitāya*), which is a state of perfect pervasion. By what means? By beautiful invocations (*suvaktibhiḥ*), that is, by excellent hymns of praise.

Like bulls, those who are self-born, possessing their own splendor, the shakers have been born toward food and heaven. Like thousandfold waves of the waters, they are to be praised with the mouth like cows, like bulls. They, the Maruts, are like *vatra*s—*vatra* being a name for form; they are as if possessed of beautiful forms, or rather, though formless, they appear as if having form. "Self-born" (*svajāḥ*) means born from themselves or from their own source; the meaning is that they have no other cause. Being "shakers" (*dhūtayaḥ*), prone to trembling, they manifest themselves toward "food" (*iṣam*)—meaning the oblation characterized by offerings or crops such as grain—and toward "heaven" (*svaḥ*). They are heard of through the medium of similes: like "thousandfold waves of the waters" (*apām ūrmayaḥ*), measured by the thousands; likewise, "to be praised" (*vandyaḥ*), worthy of hymns because of their bestowing much milk and so forth; "like cows" (*gāvo na*), like cows in their very presence; and "bulls" (*ukṣaṇaḥ*), sprinklers of the rain-water. Such are the Maruts who manifest themselves—this is the syntactical connection.

Like Soma juices pressed out, with their stalks crushed, which, when drunk, dwell within the hearts like worshippers; upon their shoulders I have taken hold as if of reins, and in their hands I have grasped both the ring and the dagger. Like Soma juices, those whose stalks are pressed, which, when drunk, dwell within the hearts like worshippers; upon their shoulders I have taken hold as if of reins, and in their hands I have grasped both the ring and the dagger.
1. Immediately after "kṣi-", there is the additional phrase: "'svatavasaḥ' means self-powerful (those whose strength is under their own control); 'avahāya' means without assistance.
"The Maruts, who are 'sutāḥ' (pressed out), 'abhiṣutāḥ' (extracted), and 'tṛpsāṃśavaḥ' (whose limbs are satisfied)—like 'somāsaḥ', that is, like Soma juices."

Just as Soma plants, which in the form of creepers possess three parts through their nourishment prior to pressing, and which later, once pressed and extracted, become juice and are drunk—having been drunk, they remain in the hearts of the drinkers like *duvas* (servants), as if performing service; in the same way, those Maruts who are invoked at the sacrifice possess three parts while being meditated upon, and they remain in the hearts, as if performing service like *duvas*.
Or rather, existing in the body in the form of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, they remain performing movements such as going and coming, like *duvas* (servants) performing service.

Among these [rays], she clings to them like a most youthful woman who is to be touched by rays; by virtue of her capacity for support, she is either a particular weapon or the splendor of the arm (*bhuja-lakṣmī*). Furthermore, in their hands, the hand-guard (*khādi*) and the cutter (*kṛti*), as well as the sword-blade and so forth, are properly joined and fixed together.

Like rain-bearing clouds that are longed for, so too do you, O Purifiers, being desired by the sacrificer who seeks manifold fruit for the attainment of food and other blessings, are invoked in many ways through hymns; this is the meaning.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Ahandya: O serpent-like being, you are like Etaśa, not like a horse.
Just as he is obtained in various ways by means of training, so it is with you.
What indeed is the further limit of this great space, O Maruts, and what its lowest depth, wherein you have come hither?
When you cause that which is joined together to fall asunder like something fragile, you fly with the mountain, creating a shimmering ocean.

What indeed is the further limit of this great space, O Maruts, and what is its lower limit, wherein you have come? When you scatter that which is compacted like fragile things, you fly with the stone through the shimmering ocean.

O Maruts, when you came—that is, when you arrived—having that water as the cause, where indeed was the further limit, the end, of this great *rajas* (the atmospheric region or the world of rain)? The meaning is: it was nowhere; it did not exist.
Likewise, "avara" means the lower part; and as for "ādi," what indeed is it? It means that no one knows where he comes from or where he goes.

Whenever you scatter the waters that were joined together as one—shaking them from their place like fragile, loose, and brittle blades of grass—then with the thunderbolt, like a mountain, you strike down the radiant, blazing, watery cloud, shattering it and casting it away.
Your destructive onset, O Maruts, is powerful, radiant, brilliant, and crushing;
your bounty is auspicious like the sacrificial fee of one who gives, born vast in its course like the divine power of Asura.

O Maruts, that formidable, swelling, and brightly shining [rain] of yours, rich in water and full of light, falls down; like the bounty of a liberal giver, your auspicious gift is wide-spreading and born of divine power, like the personification of Asurya. 7.

O Maruts, that *sāti* of yours—meaning your distribution or bounty—is like a sharing characterized by excellent qualities; likewise, your gift (*rāti*) concerning rain and other such things is *amavatī*, meaning possessed of vigor (*ama*), and accompanied by Indra and others as allies.
Just as in the passage "like a king who is *amavān*" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 4.4.1), the word *ama* there denotes vigor, so it is here.
Or alternatively:

It is a distribution that is not powerless, nor is it diseased; rather, it is resonant, full of happiness, radiant, and possesses ripened fruit. It is "pipiṣvati," meaning it is like a grinding-stone, or it is "karṣīvatī," meaning it is associated with cultivation by farmers—for it is well known that people cultivate when there is rain.
Alternatively, it is "svavirodhipeṣaṇavatī," meaning it grinds those who oppose it.
She is auspicious, worthy of praise, and laudable.
Furthermore, like the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of a liberal donor who bestows wealth, she is similarly enriching; she possesses a broad course, a wide speed, and moves swiftly.
Moreover, like the power belonging to an *asura*, she is born as one who overcomes all.
