Just as she is capable of taking water from one place and giving it to another, so too this [knowledge] is capable of taking the water residing in the clouds and giving it to the world; such is the meaning of "knowledge.
The intention is: "May such a gift be ours."
1. Bestowing abundance upon the wise.
The rivers roar toward the earth when they send forth their thunderous voice from the clouds;
the lightnings smile down upon the earth when the Maruts sprinkle the rain like clarified butter.
The rivers resound against the earth when they send forth their thunderous voice from the clouds; the lightnings smile down upon the earth when the Maruts scatter the rain. || 8 ||
The rivers—the waters characterized by flowing—resound against the paths belonging to the Maruts.
When?
At that time when they send forth, or utter, the voice of the clouds—the sound characterized by thunder—along with the thunderbolts.
Furthermore, "lightnings" refers to the flashing streaks of lightning;
they [occur] on the earth and in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
"Earth" (*pṛthivī*) is a name for the intermediate space, because it is so stated in the list of synonyms in the *Nirukta* (1.3.9): "The earth is *bhūḥ*."
There, indeed, they smile; they smile while appearing with faces turned downward—this should be connected with "on the earth" later on.
When, on the earth—that is, on the ground—the Maruts sprinkle—that is, they scatter or pour down—the dripping water, [then they smile].
The root *śru* is substituted for *mupe*, which belongs to the *kaiyādi* group, by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
When it is thus, then indeed is the meaning.
Pṛśni brought forth for the great battle the fierce, tireless host of the Maruts.
Moving together, they generated strength; they beheld the food, rich in self-power, which was to be desired.

Pṛśni gave birth to the brilliant host of the tireless Maruts for the great battle; they, moving together, brought them forth from the udder, and then they beheld their vigorous self-power all around.
Vpṛśni, the mother of the Maruts, is multicolored;
for it is seen in such passages as, “They were born from the great terror of the earth” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.11.4) and “The sons of Pṛśni are the most excellent” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.48.5).
Some, however, say that she is the deity of the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
That goddess brought forth—that is, gave birth to—the fierce and blazing host of the Maruts, the movers through the air, numbering forty-nine;
for what purpose? For the great battle.
The meaning is "for the sake of conquering the clouds.
And those Maruts, the seven-rayed ones (*saptarasāḥ*)—who are either identical in form or destroyers of the clouds—generate that cloud; they have produced it.

Immediately thereafter (*ādit*), all people behold (*paryapaśyan*, i.e., behold) the wide-reaching (*viṣirām*) *svadhā*—the food characterized by the abundance of crops and the like—which is to be desired by all.
This is your hymn, O Maruts, this is the song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Mānya. May it go forth for the strengthening of our bodies. May we find food, a secure dwelling, and life-giving rain.

This hymn for you, O Maruts, this song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Mānya—may it come to us with nourishment for the strengthening of our bodies. May we find food, a secure dwelling, and those who grant life-sustaining gifts. 10.
The tenth [verse], "This is for you," has been explained.
[Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 23, Sūkta 169] The hymn beginning with "mahaścit tvam" consists of eight verses; it is dedicated to Indra, composed by Agastya, and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.

The second verse is a four-footed Virāj, because it is not stated [in the Piṅgala-sūtra] that "the four-footed [verse] is Virāj" or "Virāj has ten syllables," and because Piṅgalanāga has sūtrified [the rule]: "The quarters are Virāj" (Piṅgala-sūtra 3.5).
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: "The eight [verses] beginning with 'mahaḥ' are the second Virāj.

Regarding this, in the section of the *Daśarātra* sacrifice during the second *Chandoma* day, specifically in the *Marutvatīya* litany under the sub-section beginning with "viśvajito'gninaraḥ," the *Sūtra* prescribes: "'dvitīyasya śaṃsā mahā mahaścitvamindram'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.7).
O Indra, you are great in power since you [overcame] these; you are indeed the great protector against violence.
O wise ordainer, as one who knows the Maruts, win for us their favors, for they are most dear to you.

Even from the great, O Indra, you [bring] these; even from the great, you are the protector against the one who seeks to harm us. Therefore, O Ordainer, mindful of the Maruts, win for us their favors, for they are indeed most dear to you. 1.
O Indra, because you do not abandon these Maruts— even though they are *mahaḥ*, that is, possessed of great power— out of affection even without [their] dependence [on you],
for this reason you are *mahaḥ* (great).
The particle *cit* is used here as a verse-filler (*pādapūraṇa*).
From the abandonment of even great injury;
or rather,
this is a name for anger.
Or from anger.
You are the one who covers, the one who chooses, the protector; that is, you exist.
Or else:
O Maruts, you shall also be a protector from abandonment or from objects such as rain.

Since this is so, O Vidhātar, ordainer of the great, you who are thus Cikittvān—possessing consciousness and endowed with the knowledge of the objects of our favor—vanuṣṣva, grant us sumnā, the joys consisting of rain and other such things dependent upon the Maruts.
For those joys are indeed preṣṭhā, your most beloved.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to indicate well-known status based on such Vedic scriptures as, "This Indra has the Maruts as his companions" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.76.2).
O Indra, the people of all tribes have joined you; you, the wise one, have settled the two boundaries among mortals.
The host of Maruts, seeking to conquer, has gathered for the winning of light and the prize of the battle-cry.

O Indra, they have yoked themselves for you, knowing all the peoples, seeking to overcome mortals as their adversaries. The host of Maruts, striving together, comes for the winning of light and the prize of the great battle.
In the preceding mantra, the assistance of the great ones (the Maruts) to Indra was mentioned;
here, the assistance of Indra to the Maruts is stated.
O Indra, those Maruts of yours "yoked" (ayuñjan)—that is to say, they become joined with you.

Of what sort are they? They are "all-pervading" (*viśvakṛṣṭīḥ*), meaning they possess all people as their domain. Furthermore, they are "those who know" (*vidvānāsaḥ*) the "obstructors" (*niṣidhaḥ*)—the clouds that completely dam up the water—for the sake of mortals among mortal beings.

Furthermore, when the onset (*pṛtsutiḥ*) of those Maruts— their army— becomes the cause for the attainment (*sātau*) of *svarmīḷha*, that is, a battle against Vṛtra and others characterized by abundant wealth (*pradhanasya sukhasetuḥ prakṛṣṭadhanavataḥ*), the army becomes joyful (*hāsamānā*), laughing with delight. Or rather, it refers to the attainment of *pradhana*— a battle whose means of wealth consists of excellent water (*prakṛṣṭodaka-ākhyadhana-sādhana*)— in which water is easily sprinkled (*sukhena mihyate*).
"Until the breaking of the clouds" means up to that point; the connection is that those Maruts who possess such an army "yoked [their steeds]."
1. By way of being known and protected; 2. Ka and Jha prefer [the reading] *amiyak*.
O Indra, that spear of yours is sharp; the Maruts impel the horse-like [chariot] from all sides.
For you, O radiant one, are unassailable; like waters [surrounding] an island, they offer up strengthening foods.

O Indra, that spear of yours has struck us; the Maruts send forth their terrifying power from all sides. For even Agni, blazing among the dry brushwood, consumes the offerings like waters breaking through to an island.
O Indra, that well-known rain of yours, [accompanied by] the thunderbolt as a specific weapon,
reaches us for the sake of our rain, having gone near the clouds;
and in this way, the Maruts also [attain it].

Because it is stated [in the Nirukta] that "sanemi ahnāya" (Nirukta 3.27.4) consists of six ancient names, *sanemi* is a name for the ancient. They release—that is, they cast forth or rain down—the ancient (*purāṇa*), meaning water accumulated over a long period of time; thus, through rain, there is the prosperity of crops and so forth, which is the excellence of the world. *Vṛṣṭyā* means by means of rain. *Sasyādi-samṛddhau* means in the abundance of crops and the like. *Rutthām* is a variant reading for *ṛddhim*. *Vam* means prosperity.
*Hi sma* is used as a filler particle. Even Agni, when the continuous ritual action has become the occasion, remains *śuśukvān*, that is, shining brightly;
subsequently, the sacrificers *dadhati*—that is, they hold or offer—the *prayāṃsi*, namely the sacrificial oblations such as the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa*.
What is it like? Like a lake with an island; for the meaning of "island" (dvīpa) is a mountain or similar landmass surrounded by water.
It is just as water supports [the earth];
or rather,
it is the weapon itself that is being described.
The term *vajrāsya* refers to a particular kind of weapon; *atase* means "in a mass of wood"; and *śuśukān* means "blazing," [referring to] fire.

The word *cit* is used in the sense of comparison (*upamā*), because Yāska stated that it has the sense of comparison in the passage: "In the sense of comparison, as in *dadhi cit* (like curd)" (Nirukta 1.4).
Thus, it functions like fire blazing in wood.
It is with reference to this very [light] being radiant that it is called "she" (sā).
This being so, the waters—the falling rains—bear and support the moving things, such as the crops and other foodstuffs, like an island.
All of this is the efficacy of Indra’s spear, which possesses great power; thus is the praise of Indra.
O Indra, you are indeed the giver of that wealth; grant us a gift with most powerful bounty, as if with a sacrificial fee.
May those praises which have pleased you cause the hymn of Vāyu to swell with sweetness and with strengths.

O Indra, grant us that wealth with your most powerful gift, like a reward bestowed by a sacrificial fee. And may those hymns which have pleased you cause the breast of Vāyu to swell with sweetness, as if with nourishing strengths.
He is indeed Indra; let him protect us—
[the word] "eva" is used for emphasis.
Do you yourself grant that very wealth which is worthy of being given by you—cattle and other riches;
since you alone are the great bestower even upon others, the meaning is: "Grant us exceedingly vast wealth.

We, however, with our most powerful (*vojiṣṭhayā*), most vigorous, and worthy-of-circumambulation dakṣiṇā—the means of prosperity consisting of cattle and so forth—glorify you, the priest and the giver, as it were. (This is the ellipsis.)
Alternatively,
the word *dakṣiṇā* denotes sacrificial gifts in general,
while the word *rāti* denotes kinsmen.

The meaning is: just as people bring a kinsman under their control by giving valuable substances such as gold, so do we bring you under our control. Furthermore, [we offer this] to you, O Vāyu, the most swift-moving, who bestows excellent boons.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object.
O Vāyu, those who are our own praisers have praised you; they have yearned for you and have offered hymns.
Indeed, these praises have yearned for you alone, as have our prayers.
This is the form in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the *caṅ* reduplication;
according to the rule "caṅy anyatarasyām," the syllable preceding the *caṅ* is acute-accented.
They caused you to swell (*vīpayanta*) through the *hotrā*s (sacrificial invocations) and through strengths (*vājaiḥ*), that is, through oblations characterized by food.
1. This [verse] consists of six ancient [verses]. Because it has been stated that "six ancient [verses] beginning with *sanemi ahnāya* are to be brought," they cause [the Soma] to swell.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
as those seeking to obtain the sweet breast [of a cow] cause it to swell with nourishing, substantial foodstuffs (vāja),
even so do we cause you to swell by means of praise and oblation for the sake of your manifold bestowal.
But you, on the other hand, must always give the wealth that is well known as being due to be given; this is the meaning.
O noble Indra, those who are most bountiful and the leaders of every living being—
may those Maruts be gracious to us, they who of old were like gods seeking a path for us.
O Indra, those who are your noble ones, most bountiful, leaders of every righteous man—may those Maruts be gracious to us, they who of old were like gods who grant us passage. 5.
O Indra, those riches of yours—those specific types of wealth—are most bountiful, being exceedingly gratifying.
*Tupyate* means satisfaction;
the substitution of *śat* for *ta* is Vedic.
Or rather:
those Maruts are givers of wealth, kinsmen who have become relatives and friends, most bountiful;
"tośati" is a term for the act of bestowing.

The thundering roar of these Maruts, who are terrible, advancing, and unwearied, is heard as they rush forward. They who, with their impetuous onsets, attack the mortal who seeks battle, like debtors rushing toward their creditors. 7. Prati | ghorāṇām | etānām | ayāsīn | marutām | śr̥ṇve | āyūtām | upabdiḥ | ye | martyam | pr̥tanāyantam | umraiḥ | r̥ṇāvānam | na | pr̥tayante | sargaiḥ || 7 ||

O Indra, the roar (*upabdiḥ*) of these Maruts—your kinsmen, who are formidable, terrifying, or possessors of sound; who are of this color (*etavarṇānām*); who are tireless (*ayāsām*), unyielding (*ayamānānām*), and ever-moving (*gamanaśīlānām*); who are approaching (*āyatām*) as they come—this roar is heard. It is heard (*śṛṇve*) that it is perceived, known, or manifested in the vicinity of the heavy [clouds] and so forth.
Truly, there is nothing today, nor tomorrow; who knows that which is wonderful?
The mind of another is to be approached with caution; otherwise, even what has been studied perishes.
Not so; indeed, it exists. "No," they say. Tomorrow—who knows that which is mysterious? The mind of another is to be approached with circumspection; even what has been meditated upon may vanish. 1.
The manner of lamentation is set forth.
Indra said:
"That which exists today will surely not exist here tomorrow."
Certainly, this is for the purpose of removing doubt.

Although the word "atha" (now) does not appear here, nevertheless, because the word "śvas" (tomorrow) is seen in the subsequent sentence, it is understood that "adya" (today) is implied here. Likewise, "śvas" also certainly implies "no" (not).
The word *u* is used for emphasis.
Even that which belongs to tomorrow does not exist at all.
Here, the sense is: "Since there is indeed nothing belonging to us that is eternal or stable, how could tomorrow be lost?"
Who knows that which is a wonder— whether it be the reversal of giving something to one after having examined it for another;
or else,
who knows that wonderful future event which is yet to come?
It is stated that one should not harbor the hope that [the goal] will be attained "today or tomorrow.
He says that very thing:
[he knows] the mind—that is, the mental state—of another, which is "to be traversed" (abhisamcareṇyam), meaning it moves everywhere; this is the ellipsis.
Moreover, even that which has been studied, meditated upon, and reflected upon is not seen; how much more so that which is merely remembered once—it utterly perishes.
Why, O Indra, do you wish to slay us? We are your own, O Marut.
Be well-disposed toward them; do not strike us down in the encounter.
Why, O Indra, do you wish to strike us? We are your own, O Maruts; with them, act rightly toward us. Do not slay us in the encounter. 2.
This is the speech of Agastya:
"O Indra, why do you wish to strike—why do you desire to kill—us who are innocent?
How is it that we are not to be slain? To this, he replies:
The Maruts are your brothers;
the meaning is that they are to be supported by you through the granting of enjoyments.
Thus, it is implied that we are not to be slain.
The Maruts' status as brothers of Indra arises from their standing together in the very same womb;
and that origin is well-known in the Purāṇas. [An objection is raised: "Let them be brothers there—what of it? To this, he says:
Together with those various Maruts, act rightly—prepare yourself or arrange the portion of the oblation together with them.
Do not slay, do not harm us in the encounter, in the battle.
Or alternatively:
The example is deficient:
"Just as you slay an adversary in battle, you do not [slay] us in such a manner."
O Atri, do you consider us two to be your friends?
For you know our minds, and thus you desire this for us.
What is this, O brother Agastya? Being our friend, do you disregard us? For we know how your mind is disposed; indeed, you do not wish to give to us. 3.
1. Who knows?
2. By the granting of a one-sixteenth portion.
This is the speech of Indra:
"O Ātaḥ! O Agastya!
You are addressed as "Āt" because of the mutual assistance provided by the offering of the oblation and the granting of the boon.
Being such a friend of ours, and even one who desires our welfare, why do you disregard us?
For what offense do you treat us with contempt and deny [our claim]?
If it is argued that this is not a denial but rather the truth itself, it is replied:
we know (*vidya*) your mind (*manaḥ*), your internal consciousness (*mānasaṃ*), exactly as it is (*yathā-yathāvastu*).
How do you know? It is explained: [as follows].
"Desire for us; you wish to give.
You do not wish to give to us that which is incapable and cast away. It is precisely for this reason.
Let them prepare the altar; let them kindle the fuel in front.
There, we two shall extend for you the sacrifice, the manifestation of immortality.
Let them prepare the altar; let them kindle the fire in front. There, we two shall extend for you the sacrifice, the manifestation of immortality. 4.
This is the speech of Indra;
others say it is the speech of Agastya:
"O officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), you [should act] so that Agastya may accept it; therefore, prepare the altar (*vedi*) well."
Let them serve [the fire] by sweeping, sprinkling water, and so forth;
likewise, let them kindle Agni—the Āhavanīya and other fires—beforehand by casting fuel upon him.
O Agastya, may both you and I extend this sacrifice, which is the indicator of the immortal Veda characterized by immortality, within that fire.
In the interpretation of Agastya’s statement, "viśiṣṭam" means distinguished.
In that regard, perform the *cetana*, which is the making known or the placing of the *vedyam*—the nectar or the oblation that is the means to that [attainment].
O Indra, we two—whether the wife and the sacrificer, or the *adhvaryu* and the sacrificer—shall extend the sacrifice for your sake.
You rule over riches, O Lord of Wealth; you are the most bountiful among friends, O Lord of Friends.
Indra, converse with the Maruts, and then consume the oblations in due season.

You rule over riches, O Lord of Wealth; you are the most bountiful giver among friends, O Indra, Lord of Friends. Now speak in harmony with the Maruts, and then consume the oblations according to the sacred seasons. 5.
This is the statement of Agastya:
"O Vasūnām vasupate, O Lord of riches—that is, O Indra, master of abundant wealth such as sacrificial cakes and clarified butter—you are the sovereign (īśiṣe) of all.
Through the presence or absence of the suffix *vṛtti*, the plurality and the constant connection [of the word with its referent] are established.
Alternatively, the construction is: "O Lord of Vasus, you rule over the vasus";
the second occurrence of the word *vasu* is either a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Thus, O Indra, Lord of friends, you who are the eternal protector of our friend and others, you are the *dheṣṭhaḥ*—the supreme sustainer of all.
O Indra, you of such greatness, speak with the Maruts; declare that they have acted rightly together with them.
Moreover, you [speak] according to the seasons (*ṛtuthā*), at the proper time.
This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of time;
thus, at that time, "consume" (prāśāna)—that is, eat with excellence—the oblations (havīṃṣi), such as clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), and so forth.
The seventh hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "prati vaḥ," belongs to Agastya; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is addressed to the Maruts.
The first two verses are dedicated exclusively to the Maruts;
the remaining verses have Indra together with the Maruts as their deity.
"‘Prati vaḥ’ [is for] the Ṣaṇmāruta [hymn], and four others are the Marutvatīya [hymns]," so says the Anukramaṇikā;
the specific application [of these verses] is based on their indicative marks (liṅga).
1. It must be considered. 2. We know it thus. 3. Of the divinity of the knower. 4. And there is an eternal connection.
With this hymn, I offer these [oblations] to you with reverence; I beg for the favor of the swift ones.
O Maruts, bestowers of gifts through your wisdom, take pleasure in us and release the stones.

Toward you I come with this homage, with a well-spoken hymn; I beg for the favor of the swift ones. O Maruts, you who are bounteous through your wise ordinances, cast away your anger and release the stones. 1.
O Maruts, I approach you; I go toward you.
By what means?
By *bhama*, that is, by salutation or by the oblation.
*Namaḥ* is a name for food.
Likewise, with a *sūkta*, which is a beautiful word in the form of praise,
I beg— that is, I entreat— your *sumati*, your auspicious mind, your benevolent intention, from you who are swift (*turāṇām*) or who are destroyers of enemies.
This is requested because of Indra’s own repeated offering of oblations.

Furthermore, O Maruts, you who are to be known through the *vidhas*—the hymns that ought to be known—and who are such as you are with a mind that delights (*vrāṇatā*) in praise, being thus praised, may you, the Maruts, grant us happiness; that is, may you make us joyful.

Moreover, Maghavan— *magha* being a name for wealth— Indra, who is praised because of his great abundance of wealth, being *śambhaviṣṭha*, the most effective bringer of happiness, may he graciously favor us.
Furthermore, O Maruts, our desire for victory—
From the root *jigāti*, which has the sense of "going," [is derived] the desire to conquer (*jigīṣā*).

May all the days—those to be conquered, those to be attained, and those being experienced hereafter—be exalted, rising higher and higher with prosperity or fame, desirable, lovely, and worthy of being cherished by all. Or rather, it may be construed as: "May they be things desired to be won and things that must be won.
Having done this, the Maruts and Indra shall bring about happiness; such is the meaning.
Envious of this powerful Indra and trembling with fear, O Maruts, we have offered these sharpened oblations to you; do not hold us at a distance, but be gracious to us.
From this one, from the powerful Indra, I am trembling in fear; O Maruts, shaking with dread, for you the oblations were prepared. We have sent them far away; be gracious to us! 4.
O Maruts, listen!
Out of fear of this well-known, powerful Indra, fleeing and unable to stand before him, I was trembling and shaking. And what followed from that? To this he says:
Those very oblations (*havyā*) which were prepared and refined for you, those we have placed far away;
we have done so swiftly out of fear of Indra.
Therefore, release us, who are innocent; favor us, make us happy.
He by whom the proud ones are stirred to thought at the dawning of the many cows,
he, the bull, the fierce one with the fierce Maruts, the steadfast giver of victory, has bestowed glory upon us.

By whom the oxen are made conscious with pride at the dawns, through the splendor of these eternal ones—O Bull, together with the Maruts, grant us renown; O fierce one, with the fierce, you who are steadfast, the giver of victory. 5.

O Indra, by that power (*śavas*) consisting of strength, being favored by you, the *mānās*—those worthy of honor or those who are esteemed by you—the *uṣtras*, meaning the rays of light, become conscious (*citayante*) at the dawning of all the eternal and numerous *uṣas*s; they perceive and bring about the wisdom for the various activities of living beings.
It is well known that in the eastern direction, the rays of the dawn, favored by him alone, rise upward.
O Bull, O Indra, you who have thus increased, being joined by the Maruts, bestow fame—that is, provide food renowned everywhere; the meaning is: establish it, give it!
Of what nature are you?
Fierce, possessing exalted strength, and a giver of power.
Strength is the power of overcoming;
the giver of that is the "Stavira," the ancient one,
together with the Maruts who are like parrots.
With fierce and cruel powers—such is his great majesty—he says: "Give me food!"
1. [The variants] jha₁-komyāni; 2. jha₁-śaśvatīnāṃ madhye. Or rather: when the dawns of such a kind have dawned, that is, while there is light, living beings become active.
"O Indra, protect the men who are more powerful; with the Maruts, be our ally here against those who strike us.
With those of good omens, may we, victorious and long-lived, find food, strength, and a life-giving abundance."

Do you, O Indra, protect our men from those who are more powerful; be with the Maruts, free from malice, accompanied by those of excellent wisdom. As a victorious one, bestowing upon us food, strength, and a life-giving domain, come hither. 6.
O Indra, do you protect and guard us—
us humans, or the Maruts— those leaders who are most powerful through your favor, possessing exceedingly increased strength.
Furthermore, together with the Maruts, be one whose wrath has departed from us; be free from anger toward us,
or likewise toward the Maruts.

Furthermore, together with the Maruts who possess excellent knowledge (*supraketebhiḥ*), being a conqueror (*sasahiḥ*)—that is, one who overcomes enemies—and being a sustainer (*dadhānaḥ*) of that which is desired by us, may you be [our protector]; this is the ellipsis.
The remainder has already been explained.

With the triplet consisting of the hymn beginning with "citro vaḥ," O Maruts, you who are "sudānavaḥ" (of beautiful bounty), quickly "parivṛṅkta"—that is, avoid or protect—the "viśaḥ" (people), such as sons, servants, and other dependents, of me, who am like "tṛṇaskanda" (one who stirs like grass) or one who is wasting away.
Or alternatively: [the meaning continues as above].
Or rather, avoid the subjects of that particular Asura who possesses the characteristics of Utkala;
furthermore, "make us" (naḥ) "upright" (ūrdhvān) "to live" (jīvase), that is, for long life.
The ninth hymn, consisting of thirteen verses, beginning with “gāyat sāma,” is addressed to Indra, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and attributed to Agastya.
It is introduced by the words “gāyat sanā.
This hymn is employed in the Marutvatīya Śastra during the third Chandoma day of the Daśarātra sacrificial session.
In the section beginning with "viśvanito'bhinaraḥ," it is sūtra-ed: "For the third [verse], Indra; svāhā; sing the Sāman" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.7).
Sing the Sāman like the celestial one; let him increase through the hymn, winning the light of heaven.
Like milch-cows, the inviolable ones have come to the sacrificial grass, as they strive together for the divine.

Sing the Sāman, the celestial one, like a bird; let us praise that which has grown strong and is full of light. The milch-cows, the inviolable ones, stand upon the sacred grass as they seek to win the heavenly seat.

O Indra, that *sāman* which is *anabhanyam*—that which is not to be shaken, situated in the sky, existing in the sky, pervading the sky, or perhaps the destroyer of Rākṣasas and others (*nabhatir* being a verb meaning "to kill," as it is enumerated among the verbs for killing in Nirukta 2.19.10:
*nabhati adati*)—O Indra, O singer, sing that *sāman* in such a way that you perceive it (*yathā veḥ*). Thus did the chanter sing.

"Therefore"—that is, for that reason because [the text] praises him—"vavṛdhānam," meaning increasing; "svarvat," meaning possessing heaven as its fruit; "śam," meaning like a bird; "arcāma," meaning we worship, which in this context means we praise. This is according to the principle that one recites what has already been praised. Or alternatively:
Let us worship that Sāman, characterized by that [power], so that it may increase everywhere.

Furthermore, let the "milch-cows"—the cows to be milked, who are "uninjured" (adabdha), meaning unharmed—serve you, O Indra, the divine one born in heaven, as you sit together upon the sacrificial grass (barhis).
The root *vivāsati* signifies the act of attending to or serving.
Having arrived, they attend upon us and likewise milk the cows; so let us worship.
Unassailable with his bulls, those for whom sweat is the oblation—like a wild beast that has been urged on, he speeds beyond the roar.
The inspired priest, joyfully minded, brings forth the exhilarating draught; the worshipful one offers the pair of delights.

Unassailable, with his bull-like steeds that carry oblations to heaven, like a wild beast he shall leap across the food. The joyous Hotṛ, praised by men, brings forth the exhilarating pair; he is the worshipful one who bears the bliss.
"The bull, the showerer [of benefits] by means of the oblation— this sacrificer [is so called] because of those who offer oblations with their own sweat,
or rather,
those for whom the oblation is kindled by themselves."

Being distinguished by "vṛṣabhaiḥ"— that is, by those who rain down [benefits], who bestow freedom from distress, such as the *adhvaryu* priests and others— he "worships" (*arcan*), meaning he causes Indra to be worshipped. Alternatively, Indra, the showerer (*vṛṣā*) of the fruit [of sacrifice], is praised by means of the *adhvaryu* priests and others characterized by their longing.

Because this Indra, like a deer such as a *hariṇa* that runs about for the sake of drinking, being "akṣaḥ" (one who eats), would "ati-juguryāt"—that is, he consumes the oblation for the purpose of eating;
just as a deer afflicted by hunger and thirst quickly devours its prey, so too does this Indra.
For this very reason, one should worship him.

1. Furthermore, because the inviolable (*adabdha*), unharmed cows—meaning the newly calved cows—are upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the sake of the sacrifice; [he approaches] the divine seat (*sānu*), the means for performing the sacrifice to the gods.
Or rather, the possessive suffix (*matup*) is elided.
I shall worship the divine one who dwells in heaven, reaching toward him.
Or rather,
the meaning is that this Indra, just as a cloud might swallow a deer, so too does he consume [the offerings] while being praised.

Furthermore, O Indra, you who are praised—being the one who delights in the *mandyu* (the hymn) of the gods who desire the *manas* (the mental worship or hymn)—the human Hotṛ priest named Marya, being a worthy sacrificer (*yajatra*) who accomplishes the sacrifice, brings forth (*prabharate*) the pairs (*mithunā*), that is, the couples consisting of the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses, or else being himself a couple in the form of wife and husband; therefore, he is called "the one who praises" (*arcati*).
The Hotṛ-priest, traversing the earth, has brought across the autumns the sacrificial offerings;
like a neighing horse, like a manly steed, he bellows loudly; like a messenger between the two worlds, the Voice moves on.

The Hotṛ has appeared; he has gone around the earth, bringing the embryo through the autumns. One half roars as it is being brought forth, the other bellows like a bull; like a messenger, the voice moves between the two worlds. 3.
This Agni, the *hotṛ* who accomplishes the oblation, moving around— that is, pervading— the seven measured (*mitā*) seats, the locations such as the *gārhapatya* and others,

reaches them; and having pervaded them, he brings— that is, accepts or gathers— the autumnal (*śaradaḥ*) offspring of the earth, the food characterized by the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), which stands in the place of an embryo.
The meaning is that it has grown for the duration of a year and has arisen from the earth;
or alternatively,
he brings the terrestrial oblation belonging to the year, which is offered during the spring and other seasons in sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma.
According to the Vedic injunction, "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣḷoma every spring," he acted accordingly;
thus the horse neighed.
This is an elliptical simile.
He neighs like a horse from the desire for the oblation;
doing what? Leading—that is, carrying—the burden of the oblation to Indra.
Furthermore, the "cow" (gauḥ) is a goer who, like a bull bellowing upward, cries out—that is, makes sound.
What is he doing?
Like a messenger (*dūta*) who carries news, [the cow] moves between the two worlds—between heaven and earth (*rodasī*). Praise-worthy or praising the gods, he travels; that is, he goes.
The meaning is that it revolves around the earth in order to receive the oblation and around the heavenly world in order to deliver it there.

In the case of the root *van*, the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule "in the sense of the agent or the object," etc.; this results in lengthening and the absence of vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
Therefore, seeking the gods, they bring forth for him deeds more effective than his own;
may Indra take pleasure in the tenfold praise, as he stands upon the chariot like the two Nāsatyas, easy to approach.

To him, the most excellent deeds are brought forward by those seeking the gods; may Indra, of wondrous luster, take pleasure [in them], like the two Nāsatyas who stand upon their easy-gliding chariot.
We prepare and accomplish for this Indra those very offerings—more abundant, more flowing, or more pervasive—for his sake; we perform the ritual act intended for him.
In the case of *kubhchandaḥ*, the suffix *luṭ* is applied in the sense of the present tense; by the rule *ghas* [is substituted] in a mantra, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix.
Because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, it is treated as an *ārṣa-dhātuka* (Vedic verbal derivative), and due to the absence of the *ḍit* designation, the substitution of *guṇa* occurs.

The *cyautnāni*—the shakers, the forceful hymns, the ritual acts, or their own inherent powers—the sacrificers, desiring the gods for themselves (*devayantaḥ*), bring forth; they accomplish them preeminently. The meaning is: "We also accomplish that oblation.
*Dasmavarcāḥ* means one of wondrous luster, or one whose power is the destruction of the enemy's side. Like the two *Nāsatyas*, [they are] like the two *Nāsatyas*. (1. ka-parimita = limited).
1. Limited by the letter *jha*.
2. Then, out of excessive joy (*kṣā*), leading the offering (*havis*) to the gods; there is no *ja* or *ta* [in this context]. 3. There is no *avā*.
"May he eat and drink; for those two are indeed Heaven and Earth, the measurers.
May he, being easy of access—easy to approach—and standing upon his chariot, thus situated, enjoy our performed work, such as hymns of praise and the like."
Milk out that Indra, who is indeed a warrior, who is the hero, the bounteous lord, and the one who stands upon the chariot;
he who, O Bull, fights even those who face him, and who destroys the darkness of the mind.

Praise him—*ūm*! Praise Indra, who is indeed a warrior, who is the hero, the bountiful one, who stands upon his chariot; who, though facing the enemy, is a more skilled combatant, possessed of strength, and the dispeller even of the obstructing darkness. (5)
Praise that very Indra, O Hotṛ; perform the hymn of praise.
What is his excellence? It is said:
he who is indeed a being of exceedingly great strength.
Or alternatively:
"satva" means a subduer of enemies;
and he who is "śūra" is one endowed with heroism.
Maghavan is the possessor of power or wealth;
he who stands upon the chariot (ratheṣṭhāḥ), remaining on the chariot;
moreover, even one who faces him directly (pratīcaścit), even though he be a more skilled warrior (yodhīyān), the best of combatants.

From the root *han* preceded by *prati*, after the suffix *kvip* (which causes the elision of the *m*), the vowel *a* is dropped by the rule *jhasi acaḥ*; then, by the rule *cī*, there is lengthening (*dīrgha*).
By the rule *aśleṣ chandasy asarvanāmasthānam*, the case-ending is acute (*udātta*).
Vṛṣaṇvān: "Possessing bulls"; *vṛṣaṇaḥ* refers to the showerers, such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and other weapons; he is the possessor of those.
"For 'A bull is your thunderbolt, and your chariot is a bull' (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.16.6)—such is the Vedic citation.
Likewise, he is the destroyer, specifically the slayer, even of the obstructing darkness such as clouds and the like.
Since he is thus possessed of such great majesty, therefore praise him."

When he thus prevails in his greatness over men, neither heaven nor earth can contain him; Indra has encompassed the world as if with a stronghold, and the self-sustaining one bears up the sky like a diadem.

When he thus prevails in greatness over men, both heaven and earth are sufficient for him to encompass; Indra has gathered the world together like a pen, and the self-dependent one bears up the sky like a diadem.

That Indra, by his greatness—that is, by his majesty and sovereignty—prevails over men, the leaders who carry out the ritual acts; he prevails for the sake of the desired [reward], such as the granting of heaven and so forth, and for the protection of this protector, Indra. For him, who desires to pervade (*kakṣayate*), the two worlds, Heaven and Earth (*rodasī*), are not sufficient (*na araṃ*) for his movement. The meaning is that Heaven and Earth are not adequate because the range of movement of Indra, the sovereign of the world, is too vast;
the sense is that they are surpassed even by the greatness of his own nature (*svadharma*).
This Indra [has taken] the earth as a stronghold, or rather, the beings as a stronghold, like a fortress.
In Vraja: this is the form of Kartanātha.

Just as that [cloud] veils the sky, so too he, by his own splendor, completely envelops the three worlds. Furthermore, this one, possessing self-power—or possessing food, meaning water characterized by rain—supports, that is, sustains, the sky. An illustration for this act of supporting is as follows:
*Opaśamiva*: "He lies down slightly" is *opaśam*; [he is] like a bull with such a garland.
Or else:
The two worlds situated near each other, known as the earth and the intermediate space (kṣi-antarikṣa), are like a crest-jewel (opaśa).
He bears the sky as if it were that [jewel];
the meaning is that he supports all three worlds.
The substitution [of *śap*] for the verbal suffix in the present indicative (*laṭ*) after the root *bhṛj* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). The elision (*luk*) of *śap* occurs.
1. Jha-1: He is raised up by everyone who is distinguished.

2. Kha-jha-pha: O Hero, for the sake of victory in battles, [we invoke] you, the protector of the pressed juice, the most renowned traveler, so that you may bestow [wealth] such as heaven and the like; the united hosts, even the wise leaders, rejoice with Indra in the exhilaration of the draught, following him with their strengths. In battles, O Hero, [we call upon] you, the protector of the pressed juice, the most renowned traveler, so that you may bestow [wealth]. The united hosts, even the wise leaders, who rejoice with strengths, [rejoice] with Indra in the exhilaration of the draught.

O Hero, O Lord of power through valor in battles! For the sake of adorning you—making you an ornament or decorating you with various signs—for the living beings who abide by taking refuge in you alone, you are the protector (*urāṇam*) who provides vast strength and other qualities; you are the most excellent traveler on the path (*prapathintamam*), the supreme path for the righteous, the Indra who shatters the enemies. [I seek you] to adorn you.

For your sake and for my sake, they are "sa-joṣasaḥ"—meaning either serving together with shared joy or having equal affection—and they strive with great effort for the earths, that is, for the lands and their inhabitants.
Of what sort are they?

They are those who "anumadanti"—that is, they rejoice along with [the king] by means of their "vājaiḥ," or forces; in battle, they intoxicate him, meaning they gladden that very master whom they have made their own.
Alternatively:

those sacrificers who delight [thee] with oblations (*vāja*)—those human *ṛtvij*s endowed with common affection, who have become sacrificers themselves—strive in the *samats*, that is, in the sacrifices which are places of shared exhilaration, to worship You alone, characterized as described above, and for their own delight in You.

Thus indeed, for you, all the waters in the ocean are a blessing, since the divine waters rejoice within them. May every cow be pleasing to you, even when you, through your inspired thought, visit the people and the patrons. 8. Thus. Indeed. To you. Peace. All. In the ocean. Waters. Since. To you. In these. They rejoice. Divine. All. To you. After. Pleasing. May it be. Cow. Even the patrons. If. With inspired thought. You visit. The people. 8.
O Indra, it is indeed thus; for when this is so, the *savanāni*—
the Soma-sacrifices, so called because the Soma is pressed (*sūyate*) therein—
belonging to you become sources of bliss (*śam*).

How is it so? If (yat) the goddesses—the shining waters—rejoice and exhilarate you within the ocean, which is the source from which the water flows out in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), while these creatures (prajāḥ) serve as the instrumental cause (nimitta).
This [verb] has the causative sense (ṇyartha) inherent within it.
When they impel you toward raining for the sake of benefiting living beings, then indeed your Soma-sacrifices become sources of happiness;

the meaning is that the sacrifices flourish by means of your bestowing the rain that is the instrument of sacrifice. Furthermore, O Indra, every voice (*viśvā gaur*)—that is, all speech in the form of hymns and liturgical recitations (*stotra-śastra*)—becomes *joṣyā*, one that delights or pleases you, in due order.
When?

If you, O Lord of the Sun, desire (*veṣi*) both the inspired sages (*sūrīn*)—those who impel the hymns—and the people who sing the praises, by means of your wisdom (*dhiṣā*, *dhiṣayā*) or by your action in the form of bestowing rain, then every hymn of praise becomes dedicated to you.

May he be for us like a good friend, most helpful through the praises of men; may Indra, established in our hymns of praise, come swiftly to us like a hero performing manly deeds. *asām* | *yathā* | *susakhāyaḥ* | *ena* | *svabhiṣṭayaḥ* | *narām* | *na* | *śaṃsaiḥ* | *asyat* | *yathā* | *naḥ* | *indraḥ* | *vandanesthāḥ* | *turaḥ* | *na* | *karma* | *naryamānaḥ* | *ukthā* || 9 || Kaṇḍikā 132.
O Indra, so that we may be well-favored— possessing excellent companions of noble form— and furthermore, well-aided— possessing excellent assistance and excellent desires;
just as men are through their praises.
Just as men become beautiful and desirable through the praises, eulogies, and hymns of kings and others, so it is here;
now he speaks by way of indirect description.

May Indra, being present in our service, act for us like one who is swift; may he, being pleased by our praise and bringing the fruit of our work through our hymns and recitations, be the one who causes us to attain the fruit of our deeds—just as it ought to be.
O priests, perform [the rite] accordingly!
Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, is like men who vie with one another in their praises.
Like those seeking a friend, they fill [the vessels] under good instruction; like those seeking the center, they strive with sacrifices.

Like men vying with one another through their praises, may Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, be ours. Like those seeking a friend, they [serve] the lord of the city under good instruction; like those seeking the center, they strive with sacrifices.

Just as friends among leaders of men (*narām*) make rivaling men (*vispardhasaḥ*) friendly toward one another, so do we, as his friends, make Indra such through our praises (*śaṃsaiḥ*). And may that Indra, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand (*vajrahastaḥ*)—always bearing the bolt to punish adversaries—be ours;
may he be favorable toward us in our rivalry.

Furthermore, like those seeking a friend—like well-wishers—in their desire for friendship, they honor with gifts the master who stands before them as he abides in good instruction; likewise, those desiring our prosperity and glory, standing in the midst of them, the Adhvaryus and others approach and worship with sacrifices, that is, with the means of sacrifice such as oblations and hymns.
The root *śikṣ* signifies the act of giving.
For indeed, some sacrifice, approaching with a focused mind, impels even the ancient Indra who is difficult to reach;
just as one who is thirsty at a watering place finds relief, so does the long path bring success to the one who strives.

For indeed, any sacrifice, even if it be crooked or approaching with a wavering mind, brings Indra to fulfillment; just as a long path leads a thirsty man to his home at the watering-place, so does it bring him to success. 11.
A certain person, being a performer of sacrifice (*yajña*)—one who possesses and carries out sacrifices—becomes *ṛndhan*, meaning he prospers;
that is to say, he causes Indra to prosper through sacrifice.
On the other hand, even one who is *juhurāṇaḥ*, moving in a crooked way, remains wandering about with his mind alone, thinking of worldly objects and the like.
Alternatively, *pari* has the sense of exclusion; thus,
one who goes while excluding this [object] incurs this [fault].
In this regard, there is an illustration:

just as one who is *tātṛṣāṇa*, possessed by thirst, quickly finds satisfaction at a *tīrtha*—a well-known path—where *okas*, such as water and a dwelling, is present *accha*, that is, directly and nearby;
the meaning is that he arrives at that very dwelling.
In the same way, a certain person approaches Indra by means of sacrifice;
this is an illustration using a crooked thing.
It is like a "long" path, which, due to its curvature, is exceedingly distant.
Just as he avoids— meaning he turns away from, keeps at a distance, or rejects— a certain fruitful object such as water, or a person seeking fruit,
so too one who knows the path of sacrifice but wanders crookedly far away does not satisfy Indra;
whereas one who is different from that [latter type] indeed avoids it.
1. Thus, O Kṣatṛ!
O Indra, protect us here in the battles with the gods, for indeed, O resplendent one, there exists for you a share of the sacrifice.
For the song of the one who possesses the oblation praises the Maruts—the youthful sons of the mighty bounteous one.

O Indra, be well-disposed toward us here in the battles along with the gods; for indeed, O resplendent one, there exists for you a great propitiation from that bountiful giver whose song of praise celebrates the Maruts—the youthful sons of the sacrificer. 12.

O Indra, here in these battles when they have arisen—these combats for the sake of growth and the conquest of clouds—do not indeed abandon us; "do not," is the remainder of the sense. Fight together with the Maruts and the other gods.
O radiant and powerful Indra, for it is truly yours; indeed, it belongs to you.
What do you have? It is said:
*avayāḥ* means that which is offered after having separated or distinguished; there is a portion of the oblation (*havirbhāga*). There is also a separate portion of the oblation for the Maruts.
The meaning is that one should not think, "Fuel is given only to the gods and not to us; therefore, how shall I fight?
Or alternatively:
*avayāḥ* means the thunderbolt (*vajra*) which goes for the purpose of excluding or destroying enemies; that [thunderbolt] is yours.
Furthermore, [the term] *haviṣmataḥ* means "possessing the oblation" to be offered; *mīḍhuṣaḥ* means "the giver of the oblation.
Alternatively, these two words are adjectives qualifying the Maruts.

For me, whose youthful speech—consisting of hymns, liturgical recitations, and the like—mingling with Indra’s fruit, praises the Maruts, the great showerers who have bestowed oblations and possess the sacrificial offerings.
Then, beginning with the first hymn of the thirteenth [section], he offers praise and prays for the fruit consisting of the Vedic revelation.
This hymn of praise is for you, O Indra; through this, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, find for us a path.
May you turn us toward prosperity, O God. May we find strengthening food that bestows long life.

This hymn, O Indra, is for you; through this, find for us a path among us, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. May you turn toward us for our well-being, O God. May we provide food and a secure dwelling that grants life-sustaining power.
O Indra, this *stoma*—this particular hymn performed at this very moment—is for you, for your sake.
O *harivaḥ*, possessor of the two bay horses, O Indra, by means of this hymn or by coming hither, find (*vidaḥ*) our path, the way to the place of sacrifice to the gods.
Having found it, O God, turn toward us, turn back to us, for our well-being (*suvitāya*), for our welfare, or for our auspicious journey.
The passage beginning with "vidyāma" has already been explained.
The tenth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “tvaṃ rājā,” is addressed to Indra, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is designated as āgneya (belonging to Agni).
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry: “tvaṃ rājā daśa.
During the increase of the Stomas in the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, this hymn is to be recited by the Hotrakas for the purpose of praising the Stoma.
"The [verses] addressed to Indra, in the Triṣṭubh metre, and with the Amaru Śakvarī metre, they should scatter," so says the Sūtra (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).
1. O you who sprinkle desires with the letters *kha*, *ca*, and *pha*.
2. With the hymn (*stoma*) consisting of the letters *kha*, *ca*, and *pha*.
O Indra among kings, and whatever gods there are, protect us; O Asura, protect us!
You are the true lord, the bounteous Maghavan, the overcomer; you are the true one, possessed of sovereign power.
You are the King, O Indra; and you, O gods, protect men. Guard us, O Asura! You are our lord of the virtuous, the bounteous one who delivers us; you are the true one, the possessor of rain. 1.
O Indra, you are the king and sovereign lord of the entire world;
moreover, you are especially so even over those gods who exist, such as the Maruts and others.
Therefore, O Asura—O dispeller of enemies—protect and preserve us, the men who lead the ritual and perform the sacrifice.

Protect us especially as well; for you are the lord of the virtuous, esteemed by the good, or the protector (*pātā*) of the fruit of our actions. You are Maghavan, the possessor of wealth, and our *tarutra*, the one who carries us across from evil. Furthermore, you are *sasya*, the invincible, or the one whose fruit is like grain; you are *vasavānaḥ*, covering all with your own splendor or bestowing riches upon those who praise you. May you be the giver of *sahas*, of strength—the remainder of the sense being that you must become so.

O Indra, you subdued the people of harsh speech when you shattered the seven autumnal fortresses that were their refuge; O blameless one, you brought the waters to the youthful Vṛtra and delivered him over to the many-conquering hero.

O Indra, when you shattered the seven autumnal fortresses—the refuge of the tribes who spoke with hostility—you released the waters, O blameless one, like a flood; you delivered Vṛtra over to the young Purukutsa.

O Indra, at the time of shattering the cities of the asuras associated with Vṛtra, you, the subduer, subdued those subjects—his progeny—who spoke with defiant words, so that they might find comfort and happiness.
This is the feminine form;
or else,
it is a transposition of syllables.
Nada means sound; anada refers to the Asura progeny who are without sound;
it is that which produces extremely terrifying sounds.
When? He says:
when they are autumnal and fresh;
or else.
The protector of this year,
you shattered these seven cities, so named, which had been firmly established for the duration of a year.
There is a transposition of genders.
In the case of the root *haṇāti* in the *laṅ* tense, there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) according to Vedic usage.
Due to the restrictive rule "rāsasya" (Pāṇini 8.2.24), there is no elision of the *t* sound.

Having done so, O blameless one, O Indra who delights in cowardice, you caused the waters—those possessing the nature of floods—to flow; you sent forth the reservoirs and other water-holding places situated in his fortresses; you made them circulate. You caused them to whirl.
Having thus attacked for the sake of Purukutsa—a king of that name who was young and eternally vigorous—you subdued, that is, you conquered and slew Vṛtra, the Asura of that name.
This is the historical interpretation.

However, from the perspective of the *Nirukta*, O Indra, you have subdued the "mṛdhavācaḥ" (those with voices of conflict), the subjects in the form of rain characterized by the sound of endurance (*marṣaṇa*).
Or rather, [the word] *aśabdya* means "did not cause to increase. When?

The meaning is: whenever you, whose nature is to glide, shattered the seven autumnal citadels— the fresh clouds that fill the world with rain— at that very moment, O blameless one, you sent forth, that is, you set in motion, the waters of the ocean-nature in the form of streams and the like.
Immediately thereafter, for the youth Purukutsa, you subdued Vṛtra, the chief cloud; that is, you slew him.
This meaning is well known from other mantras such as "O Indra, you indeed, fighting against the seven... (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.63.7).
Yāska, however, has explained it thus: "O Indra, make us humans—those whose minds are intent on giving—free from hostile speech" (Nirukta 6.31).
1. jha1—Protect;
or else, guard the people (nṝn). 2. ka-kha—Until the end of this year; ja—The protector for this year.
3. O blameless one, you who rejoice in cowardice; O blameless one, you who are delighted by the state of being a coward!
4. Explained.

O Indra, invoked by many, you have now overcome the unassailable ones who have the heroes as their lords, and with them, O much-invoked one, you have protected the tearful Tūrvayāṇa. Like a lion in his den, he has performed his deeds for the sake of the dwelling. *arja vṛtaḥ indra śūrapatnīr dyāṃ ca yebhiḥ puruhūta nūnam rakṣo agriṃ aśruṣmaṃ tūrvayāṇaṃ siṃho na dame apāṃsi vastoḥ.* 3. O Indra, invoked by many, you have now overcome those who have the heroes as their masters and the heavens, with whom [you protected] the tearful Tūrvayāṇa, the foremost protector; like a lion in his den, he has performed his deeds for the sake of the dwelling.

O Indra, those cities of the Asuras— ruled by heroic lords, protected by heroic Rakshasas, and surrounded by [guards] stationed there— are called "Vṛtāḥ" because they are situated in a state of being encompassed (vṛta).
Or alternatively:
O Hero, the sacrificers have chosen these sacrificial grounds protected by them;
go forth to conquer!
Having done so, O Unborn One, you have surely and certainly pervaded heaven;
yet why are you not alone?
O Puruhūta—O Indra, invoked by many in various ways—you are accompanied by those Maruts and others with whom you are followed; being joined with them, [you have pervaded it].

Having done so, O Indra, carry Kutsa—who is like a swift horse, a dryer-up of enemies, and one who is unappeased—on the swift-moving [chariot] that moves rapidly; for you have desired him as your own, with straight-flying steeds like the horses of Vāta.
With your great [thunderbolt], you, whose arm wields the vajra, have gone forth against the rivals in the encounter to reach the far-shining [Kutsa].

O Indra, [the hymn] which you delighted in—that of Kutsa—[was like] two straight-driving reins of the wind’s horses. In the encounter, the Sun’s wheel sped forward; he with the thunderbolt in his arm has gone forth against the adversaries.

O Indra, bring hither Kutsa, who bears that name, as well as the two Syūmanūs—*syūmaka* being a name for happiness (Nirukta 3.6.5)—those two who desire that [happiness], or who move continuously; or the two horses of Vāta, the wind, which possess equal speed and move straight: send them forth.
When that oblation has become the cause, you take pleasure in Kutsa or satisfy him with the oblation and so forth—

for that purpose, let Sūra, the impeller, the Sun, cause his own wheel, or the wheel of his chariot, to go upward or shine forth in the vicinity, in the immediate presence. Then he speaks cryptically:

This Vajrabāhu is Indra; O Indra, the wise one, the far-seeing, or the reciter or the Hotṛ priest, praises you—*vṛpat*—when the occasion for the attainment of this desirable object (*vakasāti*) has arisen.
Or else:
He, being indignant at this name, reproached him; he praised [him], that is, he praised his purpose.
The meaning is that you gave him exceedingly abundant food.
And likewise, for the *vṛtra*, the demon who oppresses living beings, you made the earth his bed, that is, his couch.
The meaning is: "having killed, cause to fall to the ground.
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense of the root *kṛ*, the suffix *cli* is elided by the rule "mantre ghasa... [Pāṇini 2.4.80].
Now, [the forms] performed in the past (*parokṣakṛta*).

This Indra, the possessor of wealth, the bountiful one, makes manifest the various worlds—whether the worlds consisting of the Dārśika, Pāśuka, and Saumika sacrifices, or the worlds consisting of the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven; or the worlds that are "dānucitrāḥ," meaning worthy of being sought after (*cāyanīya*) through their giving (*dāna*) or their vastness (*dairghya*).
Or rather: [he creates them].

He made the three cities of Aya—consisting of iron, silver, and gold, and variegated with enchantments—splendid by means of his shattering weapon. Likewise, for the sake of pleasing King Duryoṇa, he placed the Asura named Kuyava—who utters vile sounds—in a wicked womb (duṣṭayoni) during the battle;
indeed, O Indra, those ancient deeds of yours have returned anew, many victories for the sake of subduing the enemy through your power and glory.
He shattered the fortresses as if they were unbolted; the weapon of the god struck down the godless oppressor.

These ancient deeds of yours, O Indra, have become new again; many are the acts of subduing power for the sake of the one who bows in homage. He shattered the godless fortresses as if they were unbolted; the hero’s weapon increased the might of the godless oppressor.
O Indra, those *sanā*—your own eternal and perpetual deeds of valor—the *navyāḥ*, the newer ones of the present day, the *ṛṣis*, approach; that is to say, they reach them under the guise of praise.
What are these? It is said: *pūrvīḥ*, many; *narmaḥ*, acts of destruction.
The suffix *kip* is applied after a root meaning "to harm.
This is the form ending in that [suffix].

O powerful one (*sahaḥ*), you have overcome (*abhyabhavaḥ*) those who cause harm (*tā hiṃsāḥ*) for the sake of protection (*vaviraṇāya*), that is, for the sake of not fleeing (*avigataraṇāya*), for the destruction of battle.
For that purpose, you shattered the *vṛtra*—meaning the slayers who obstructed; you split apart even the *puraḥ*, meaning the cities of the Asuras.
The word *puruṣa-gati* refers to the movement of a person.
The particle *na* is used here in the sense of *ca* (and).
Thus, for the sake of the god who is beyond praise, you made the weapon—the thunderbolt—pliant and favorable against the destructive Asura.
Or alternatively:
O Indra, those various [deeds] belonging to you at each respective time are eternal (*sanā*).
There is a change of gender.
Those ancient, primordial waters—the ever-new, praiseworthy ones—come, they are arriving.
For what purpose?

For the sake of non-obstruction, non-restraint, and the non-destruction of living beings— for that purpose, you indeed showed forbearance toward the clouds, whether they were harmful or obstructive. Furthermore, you shattered the godless fortresses— those deceptive structures characterized by a lack of divine grace— and brought about their destruction.
Thus, you bent down the weapon for the slaying of Vṛtra, who was godless, devoid of the nature of a god, and hostile.
O Indra, you, the shaker, released the waters that were held back, like flowing rivers;
when you, O hero, carried across the ocean, you brought Turvaśa and Yadu safely to the further shore.

9 | O Indra, you, the shaker, have set in motion the waters that possess the power of shakers; like flowing rivers, you have released the streams. Since you, O hero, have carried us across to the ocean, ferry Turvaśa and Yadu across in safety. 9 |

O Indra, you are indeed the shaker (*v-dhuni*) who causes the enemies to tremble; therefore, [you shook] those rivers possessing *v-dhuni*, that is, those having waves characterized by trembling. Or alternatively: *dhuni* is the name of an Asura who obstructs the waters; [the rivers were] such as had him as their impediment. You chose them—*vapaḥ* means you caused them to go—you made them fall upon the earth. Therein is an illustration: *sravantīḥ* (flowing) *sīrāḥ na* (like rivers)—that is, like flowing streams; the meaning is that they were continuous.

Having done this, O Hero, when you carry across—that is, having crossed over and filled with water—the ocean, then you protected both Turvaśa and Yadu, the two royal seers, with safety and non-destruction by means of a full downpour of rain. And so says another mantra: "Thou didst quiet the waters for Yadu and Turvaśa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.31.8).

O Indra, may you always be ours—the most unyielding protector of men. As such, grant us victory over all our rivals; may we find strengthening food from you, the giver of life, within our communities.

O Indra, may you be ours at all times, the most unyielding protector of men; as such, grant us victory over all our adversaries. May we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts. 10.
O Indra, you are for us at all times, in every situation, or in every manner, the most unassailable; or rather,
the most generous giver.
Be such;
likewise, O protector of men (*narām nṛpāta*), be the eternal guardian of our many human beings, who exist in the form of sons, servants, and so forth.
The second occurrence of the word *nṛ* is a reiterative reference (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, O Vasu, be the giver of strength for the sake of all our armies—the causes of all rivalries; that is, be the bestower of power for their purpose.
The meaning has been understood.
The sixth hymn, consisting of eleven verses, beginning with “matsyapāyi,” is dedicated to Agni and Indra.
The first verse is a *skandhogrīvī bṛhatī*, because its second foot contains twelve syllables while the other three contain eight syllables each;
this is because the definition stated [in the Anuvāka]—“the second being a *cayaḍkusāriṇī*, an *uparabṛhatī*, or a *skandhogrīvī*”—is present here.
This [verse] is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
The remaining [verses] are *anuṣṭubhs*, because they are nourished by the specific rule “but that which ends in *anuṣṭubh*” within the general definition of those ending in *triṣṭubh*.
This has been enumerated [in the Anukramaṇī]: “The *matsi* [verse] is an *anuṣṭubh* ending in *triṣṭubh*; the *skandhogrīvī* [verse] is self-evident.”
In the second [agniṣṭoma], [the stotras] are by their own inherent nature; however, the first is the *stotriya* of the *tvac*.
In the section beginning with "The *abhijit* has the *apṛṣṭha*," it is sūtra-ed: "'O you who drink the fish, this is for you; come toward him' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.5)."
O impetuous one, your exhilarating intoxication flows like the draught from a large vessel;
O bull, for you the bull, the Indu is a prize-winner, most effective at winning a thousandfold.
Thou hast drunk; for thee, the exhilarating, intoxicating, and virile Soma—like the golden-hued steed at the great vessel—is poured out, O Bull, as the prize-winning Indu that bestows a thousandfold.

O Lord of the bay horses (*harivaḥ*), with your two bay steeds; likewise, O Indra, this great Soma is to be honored by you, the Great One. Just as Soma is held in a vessel by means of that very vessel—the Soma-cup—so too is it [held] by you, who are like it.
(The genitive case is used here in the sense of the instrumental.
Or alternatively:
The construction is either: "O Soma, great indeed is your greatness, which is inherent in you like that of a vessel," or "It has been drunk;
it is being drunk."
Because the sense of "expectation" (āśaṃsā) is intended to be expressed, there is the use of the suffix -vat.
Since you drink from this, therefore be exhilarated, rejoice, or take your delight;
drink exceedingly so that the Soma is filled in the vessel, and having drunk, take your delight—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, for you, the bull (*vṛṣṇe*), who are impetuous with desire.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.
*Matsaraḥ* means that which causes intoxication; *madaḥ* means the exhilarator; *vṛṣā* means the showerer; *induḥ* means the moistener, that is to say, the one who brings delight;
*vājī* means possessed of food (*anna*).
Because he possesses the state of being never satiated by horses, he is called "possessor of horses" (*aśvavān*).

He is the giver of the most abundant thousands, the supreme bestower of the immeasurable, or one who possesses the excellence of a thousand [attendants] sufficient for the service of a thousand men; such is the Soma of great majesty that has been prepared—drink it, is the meaning.
1. The operation of *kṣa* and *ajña*:
May your exhilarating, bull-like, most desirable intoxication come to us—O Indra, the victorious, the winner of spoils, the subduer of armies, the immortal one.
O Indra, may your exhilarating, bull-like, and most excellent intoxication come to us—victorious, winning booty, subduing armies, and immortal. 2.
O Indra, let this exhilarating Soma of ours, which effects satisfaction, come to you.

Of what nature is it? It is a showerer (vṛṣā), a joy (mada) that satisfies, most excellent (vareṇya), worthy of being chosen, accompanied by strength (sahāvān)—or possessing power through force (sahasā)—worthy of being honored (sānasi), a conqueror of hostile armies (pṛtanāṣāṭ), and immortal (amartya).
May such Soma come to you.
Or alternatively,
the second half-verse may be explained as referring to Indra.
O Indra, you are the victorious one who sits with us, accompanied by Soma, or you are the powerful one worthy of our worship; you are the conqueror of hostile armies and the immortal.
For you are the hero, the winner; you urge on the chariot of man. As the victorious one, burn down the lawless Dasyu with your flame as if with a protective shield.
For you are the hero, the winner; you urge on the chariot of man. Overpowering the lawless Dasyu, you have enveloped him with your flame as if with a vessel. 3.
O Indra, you are indeed a hero, endowed with valor; you are the winner and the giver.
Therefore, impel—urge forward—the chariot of me, a human being, that is swift, moving, or a mental desire, or the means for going to heaven, or the sacrificial chariot.
Furthermore, becoming possessed of Soma as your companion, or being powerful, burn up the Dasyu, the destroyer, the lawless one who performs no rites and does not practice religious observances.

Like fire with its heat, radiance, and flame [burning] a vessel—meaning a specific sacrificial vessel that serves as its own support—the sense is: "Burn him who, being entitled to perform sacrifice, does not sacrifice."
O Sage, you who rule by your might, you stole the wheel of the sun;
carry Kutsa with the steeds of Vāta as a weapon of death for Śuṣṇa.
O Sage, you who rule by your might, you stole the wheel of the sun; you bore Kutsa, the slayer of Śuṣṇa, with the horses of Vāta. 4.
O Sage, O far-seeing one, Indra, being the sovereign lord and capable, [has acted] toward Sūrya, the sun.
According to the rule "supām supo bhavanti," the sixth case singular is replaced by the second case singular.
One wheel belonging to that [being] was stolen by force—that is, by strength and by an excellence of capability—from that one.
The substitution of *śāyac* occurs according to the rule: "In the Veda, *śāyac* is also [substituted]."
There is a traditional account (*itihāsa*) stating that formerly Sūrya possessed two wheels, one of which Indra stole;
likewise, another mantra says: "You carried away one wheel of Sūrya for Kutsa" (*Ṛgveda* 5.29.10).
Furthermore, "to Śuṣṇa"—that is, for the sake of that Asura named Śuṣṇa.
Or, the dative case is used in the sense of the accusative;
the meaning is "in order to slay Śuṣṇa."

"Carrying the *kutsa*—the weapon for cutting—and the *vajra*, the bolt of destruction, with the horses of Vāta—that is, endowed with the speed and stability of the wind—bring it; you brought it; you held the *vajra* in order to slay Śuṣṇa.
Or rather, you brought the *vajra* for the slaughter of Śuṣṇa."
Having slain him, you were distinguished by his wind-like speeds; with his riches, you went to the great seer Kutsa—meaning that you gave the wealth of the Asura Śuṣṇa to Kutsa.

And so it is said elsewhere: "You protected Kutsa as if he were the slayer of Śuṣṇa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.51.6), and "To Kutsa, the strength-slaying strength" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.16.12). Thus [the meaning is established].
For most powerful indeed is your intoxication, and most resplendent is your will;
as slayer of Vṛtra and finder of room, may you consider yourself the greatest winner of horses.
For most powerful indeed is your intoxication, and most abundant is your wisdom; as the slayer of Vṛtra and the finder of wide space, may you be mindful of us as the winner of horses. 5.

O Indra, this exhilaration of yours (*madaḥ*) born from drinking the Soma is most powerful (*śuṣmintamaḥ*), that is, most mighty. And furthermore, your activity (*kratuḥ*), your performance of deeds for our sake, is most powerful, meaning it is preeminently nourishing or glorious.
In both cases, because the technical designation *bha* is applied by the rule "atha-smāt-ādīni chandasi," the elision of the final *n* is blocked.

O Indra, you who are most excellent in granting horses—that is, in bestowing abundant wealth characterized by horses; you who are the slayers of Vṛtra; you who are the finders of wide space (*varivovit*), that is, the revealers or bestowers of wealth or its enjoyment; at your exhilaration (*madakrat*), may you grant your consent (*maṃsīṣṭhāḥ*).
The meaning is that you show favor so that they may become slayers of enemies and givers of wealth.

Just as you were for the ancient singers, O Indra, like a young man, you became one who satisfies the thirsty like water; following that proclamation, I call upon you repeatedly. May we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.

As for the ancestors, O Indra, for those who sang your praises—you have become like a young man to them, like water to the thirsty. Following that very invocation, I call upon you repeatedly. May I find strengthening food and a vigorous, life-giving community. 6.
O Indra, you have become a source of joy (*maya*) for the ancient singers, for those former chanters and praisers;
*maya* means happiness—
you have become, as it were, the very embodiment of happiness.
In that same way, be pleasant toward us, your praisers.
Therein lies the illustration:
"Just as water is pleasant for one who is thirsty, so [be you] to us. Thus it is.
Therefore, "I call upon you again and again" (*anu johavīmi tvā*) with that well-known hymn of praise (*stutiṃ*) which is the *nivid* that brings me joy.
Or rather, by the rule "in the sense of the third case" (*pā. sū. 1.4.85*), these two words [tām and anu] function as *karmapravacanīya*s.
With this hymn of praise, I invoke you;
I call upon you again and again.
"May we know" has already been explained.
The twenty-second hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "masti naḥ," belongs to Agastya, is addressed to Indra, and is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
However, because the word "tu" (but) was used in the previous rule stating "it ends in Triṣṭubh," this [preceding hymn] ends in Triṣṭubh;
whereas "masti naḥ" ends in Anuṣṭubh.
The specific application [of mantras] is based on indicative marks.

Intoxicate us for the attainment of greater wealth; O Indu, as a bull, enter into Indra. Thriving, you drive away the enemy; you do not find him even when he is near. 1. Intoxicate us (matsi) for the sake of attaining greater wealth (vasya-iṣṭaye). O Indu, as a bull (vṛṣā), enter (ā viśa) [Indra]. Thriving (ṛdhāyamāṇaḥ), you drive away (invasi) the enemy; you do not find (na vindasi) him even when he is close at hand (anti). 1.
O Indu, you who have been moistened, O Soma, exhilarate Indra for our sake—that is, for the attainment of wealth more excellent (*vasyaṣṭi*), or for the sacrifice characterized by such excellence.

For that purpose, you yourself, as a bull (*vṛṣan*) who showers down desires, enter into Indra. Then, having been thus drunk and increasing in power (*ṛdhāyamāṇaḥ*), you strike down the enemies and pervade all things.
Therefore, you do not find, that is, you do not obtain, the enemy nearby;
since the enemies have fled due to their lack of capability, you do not find them.
Or alternatively:
The second half [of the verse] is to be explained as referring to Indra:
"O Indra, you...
O Indra,
crush those who belong to the one with good horses;
crush him who milks the unyoked cow.
In what manner? That is being stated:

like a *divyā*—that which exists in heaven—a *aśani*, having become a thunderbolt, slay those who hate us. Slay him who does not press the soma, the one who is difficult to overcome, he who is no man to you. Grant us his possession; the patron gains through his knowledge. 4.
Slay him who does not press [the Soma], the equal one, the evil-looking; for he is not a manly patron to us. Grant us his possession; even a wise lord takes heed of this.

O Indra, strike down him who does not press the Soma—that is, him who does not sacrifice to you—him who is difficult to overcome (*dūṇāśa*) and who is equal (*sama*). This word *sama* is entirely unaccented and is a synonym for "all. Strike down all those who do not sacrifice. Or else: strike him down with a single effort, or without distinction. To the question, "What offense has he committed?", he replies: "He who is not a source of joy (*maya*) for you. *Maya* is a name for happiness; he is not a cause of your pleasure. Strike him who is not gratified by our oblation or by our praise. Furthermore, give us his possession, his wealth. [The verb] *dada* means "to give"; here the Parasmaipada ending is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*), and the *śap* suffix is elided according to Vedic usage. O wise one (*sūri*), he indeed brings [wealth]. *Cit* has the sense of "indeed" (*eva*). O wise one, the singer alone brings—that is, he carries and obtains—wealth.
O Indu, you whose first praise was sung at the two-fold strength of the suns; O Indu, you protected the vigorous Indra in the battle for booty.
The first [verse]: For him of double strength, in the hymns, may there be continuous flow; O Indu, you have furthered Indra in the battle for booty, the prize-winner in the contests for wealth. 5.

O Indu Soma, you have protected—that is, you have guarded or satisfied—that sacrificer whose hymns and oblations possess double strength (*dvibarhas*), that is, who possesses the two kinds of exalted actions; for him, in his chants (*arkeshu*) or mantras, there shall be continuous success (*sānuṣak*) and true victory (*sātyam*).
Or else: [the text continues].
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object.
O Indu, when you were the sovereign over two stations—O Indra, when you were present among the Arka hymns—then you protected him; you guarded him or satisfied him.

In that very battle (*ājau*), in the conflict, O Soma, you thoroughly protected (*prāvaḥ*) that Indra, who is possessed of strength (*vājinam*) and swift as a horse, on account of the *vāja*s (booties of war) or the *vāja*s (powers/strengths).

At the time of drinking, having satisfied [the gods], and at the time of battle, by increasing strength or by satisfying the wealth of the conquered enemies, you were "without a foe" (arakṣas)—this is the meaning.

Just as you were for the ancient singers, O Indra, like water for a thirsty man, so do I repeatedly invoke this *nivid* after you. May we find food, a strong community, and one who bestows life-sustaining gifts.

6 | Just as for the ancient singers, O Indra, you became like a young man to one who thirsts for water; according to that proclamation, I call upon you repeatedly. May I find strengthening food and a vigorous, life-sustaining host. 6 |||
1. *Ka-jha-arakṣaḥ*.
The genitive case in the phrase “*yathā pūrvebhyaḥ*” (as from the predecessors) has been explained.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “ā carṣaṇiprāḥ,” is addressed to Indra, composed by Agastya, and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The Anukramaṇikā states: “‘ā carṣaṇiprāḥ,’ five [verses].
Its specific application is found in the *Hotraka-śāstras* during the increase of the *stoma*.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "They should scatter [the grains] that belong to Indra, are in the Triṣṭubh metre, and relate to the Maruts" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).
The bull among men, the king of the peoples, Indra, invoked by many, who fills the dwellings—
being praised by me, O seeker of glory, come hither toward me after speaking to your two vigorous bay steeds.

The filler of the people, the bull among men, the king of the tribes, Indra, invoked by many—being praised and seeking glory, come hither toward me with your protection, having yoked your two vigorous bay steeds. 1.
This is Indra,
the filler of the peoples;
"peoples" refers to human beings.
He is the one who gratifies them with wealth and other gifts;
he is the bull (*vṛṣabha*) for all people, raining down their desires,
and likewise for the tribes (*kṛṣṭīnām*).
This [is] for humans.
The king and master of humans is Puruhūta, invoked by many.
May such an Indra know us or come to us.
The latter half is spoken in an indirect manner (*parokṣavāda*).

O Indra, being praised by us, desiring glory—that is, seeking the oblation characterized by sacrificial offerings—and being endowed with *avas*, meaning our protection or satisfaction, come hither toward us (*arvāṅ*); having yoked the two vigorous, youthful, rain-bestowing bay horses (*harī*) to the chariot, approach and arrive facing us.
O Indra, those bulls of yours, the stallions yoked by prayer, the coursers with powerful chariots—mount them; come hither with them! We invoke you, O Indra, when the Soma is pressed.

Those stallions of yours, O Indra, the powerful bulls, yoked by prayer, the swift steeds of the mighty chariot—mount them! With them come hither toward us; we invoke you, O Indra, when the Soma is pressed. 2.
