O Indra, those who belong to you— your bulls (*vṛṣaṇaḥ*), meaning rainers or youthful, powerful stallions, the most excellent ones, joined by sacred prayer (*brahmayujaḥ*), being yoked by a mighty mantra, possessing rain-bearing chariots (*vṛṣarathāsaḥ*),
meaning they are harnessed to such chariots— those coursers (*atyāḥ*) that exist, mount them; take your seat upon them.
With those [means], come hither toward us; come here.
And we, O Indra, when the Soma is pressed, call upon you.
Mount the bull-like chariot; for you, O Bull, the Soma has been pressed and the sweet juices have been poured out.
Having yoked the two bay steeds, O Bull of the peoples, come toward us down the steep slope.

"Come! Mount the powerful chariot; for you, O Bull, the Soma has been pressed and the sweet juices have been poured out. Having yoked your two bay steeds, O Bull among the peoples, come down the slope toward me."
O Indra, you, mount this chariot; take hold of it for the sake of the sacrifice.
What kind of chariot?
A "vṛṣaṇam," one that showers down the fulfillment of desires.
If it is asked, "For what purpose? it is said:
for your sake, that bull, the showerer, Soma, has been pressed—that is, poured out.
Likewise, "sweet" (*madhūmi*) refers to honey, sweet substances such as clarified butter and milk, which have been sprinkled around (*pariviktā*) and prepared;
or alternatively, it refers to honey— the sweet juices of the *soma*— filled within the vessels.
The manner of their arrival is described:

O *vṛṣabha*, bull, lord of rain, having yoked the chariot with two tawny (*hari*) steeds that are bulls (*vṛṣaṇyā*) among bulls (*vṛṣabhyām*), for the sake of favoring us—the sacrificers who dwell in the ritual acts (*kṣitīnāṃ karmasu*) of men;
or alternatively, it may be construed as "the bull of the people" (*kṣitīnāṃ vṛṣabha*).
Come toward me on a swift, impetuous chariot, hastening toward me with great speed.
This sacrifice goes to the gods; this is the sacrificial food; these are the sacred prayers, O Indra, and this is the Soma.
The sacred grass is strewn; come hither, O Śakra, sit down and drink, and unyoke your two bay horses here.

This is the sacrifice; this is the path for the gods; this is the sacrificial food; these are the sacred prayers; this, O Indra, is the Soma. The sacred grass is strewn; come hither, O Śakra, drink, sit down, unyoke your two bay horses here. 4.

The *yājyā* for the *hāriyojana-graha* on the middle days among the *ahargaṇa* days is prescribed in the section beginning with "This is the *iṣṭoma*, this is the *iṣṭoma*" in the *Sūtra*: "‘This sacrifice goes to the gods, this is the sacrificial food’—this [is used] for the others" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 6.11).
O Indra, this sacrifice is god-seeking; it goes toward the gods.
Likewise, this sacrifice is the *miyedha*.
*Medha* means an animal victim.
For the Śruti says, "The sacrificial victim is indeed the oblation";
these are the sacred words (brahmāṇi), that is, the mantras;
this is the pressed Soma.
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) has been spread; the *darbha* blades have been strewn for the seat.
These items, appropriate for you, have thus been prepared.
O Śakra, O Indra—when asked "what then?", [the answer is] "come hither" (*ā pra yāhi*), meaning come forward with great speed.
Having arrived and sat down, having seated yourself upon the sacrificial grass, drink the Soma;
for that purpose, unyoke here at this place of divine sacrifice these two bay horses.
The absence of the *num* augment is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
O Indra, come hither to this well-uttered praise of the poet Mānya;
may we, singing your praises, obtain your protection at the break of dawn. May we find food, a secure dwelling, and life-sustaining rain.

O Indra, well-praised, come hither toward us; approach the sacred hymns of the poet Mānya. Praising you with our protection, may we provide for your dwelling; may we provide nourishment and a stronghold that grants quickening gifts. 5.
O Indra, being well-praised by us and properly lauded, come hither toward us;
do not delay.
With what purpose?

Observing the sacred hymns (*brahmāṇi*)—that is, the mantras—of the venerable one worthy of honor, the *kārū* (the singer), or the patron (*kartṛyajamāna*), we, praising him or uttering his desired names, being protected by your protection (*avasā*), may we easily reach our dwelling (*vastauḥ*) or be able to remain [there] throughout all the days; that is, may we obtain food and other necessities.
The word *vidhāma* and so forth has already been explained.

The fourteenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "yad syā," is addressed to Indra, composed by Agastya, and is in the Triṣṭubh meter. [This is the second Aṣṭaka, Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 23, Sūkta 108]. The letters *ka*, *kha*, and *pha* have been produced [in this section]. 1063. The second Aṣṭaka. 1063. "yad syā" is the fourteenth hymn, consisting of five verses; it belongs to Agastya, is addressed to Indra, and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
‘Yad syā’ is the table of contents. The specific application is as before:
“O Indra, may there be for you that readiness to hear, just as you have become a helper for those who praise you.”
Do not obstruct our desire as it grows; may we obtain all these things from you, the living one.

O Indra, whatever readiness to hear you have, and as you have become a helper for those who sing your praises, do not withhold from us our desire that magnifies you; may we obtain all [the blessings] of yours, even beyond the waters of the living man.

O Indra, that well-known *śruṣṭi*—the success heard of everywhere—that is yours; just as you have become capable (*babhūtha*) through your aid (*ūtī*) for the sake of protection (*ūrje*) for the singers (*jaritṛbhyas*), those who praise you, so do you remain capable for us (*naḥ*). Do not burn (*mā dhak*), do not consume (*mā dhākṣīḥ*) our desired wish (*kāmam*) which makes us great (*mahayantam*), which renders us magnificent.
All (*viśvā*) the various objects of enjoyment belonging to you (*te*) are accessible (*āpaḥ*). Or rather: [they are] like waters.
May we encompass and pervade all the waters, all the regions, and the renowned dwellings of the human being.
O Indra, King of Kings, no one can harm you when the two sisters perform their work in the womb;
even the waters, eager for him, have sped toward him. May Indra come to us with friendship and vital strength.

No; let not King Indra deceive us, he who, together with his two sisters, prepares [the place] in the womb. Even the waters, eager for him, have sped toward him. May Indra come to us with friendship and vital strength. 2.
May this king, shining like a lord or like Indra, not deceive—that is, may he not harm from all sides—our works. Which works?
Those works consisting of rain and so forth, which [the gods] perform for one another, for the two days and nights that are like sisters, being mutually sister-like and self-dying.
Now Pūraṇa:
they place [it] in their own womb, that is, in its proper place; [here] the plural is used in place of the dual.
They both perform.
The root *kṛv* belongs to both the classes meaning "to injure" and "to do.
By the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca*, there is the suffix *um*;
however, due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously"), the suffix *śap* is also applied.
Indra also permits them;
they, being well-disposed, act as sisters toward one another and toward the sacrificer.
Or rather:
The sisters are the fingers; it should be understood that they performed those acts in the sacrifice which were done at the place of generating the fruit, namely the womb.
Furthermore, for this Indra, the waters—meaning the oblations (havis) which are the causes of excellent strength—have flowed toward him, pervading him.
May Indra grant us, for our friendship, both companionships and abundant food.
Indra is the victor over men, a hero in battles; he hears the cry of the singer who implores him.
He brings gifts upon his chariot to the donor nearby, when he himself has become the one who raises up our songs of praise.

The conqueror Indra, the hero among men in battles, is the hearer of the call of the singer who implores him; he brings his chariot near to the donor and raises up our songs when he is present in person.

This Indra, being a hero (*śūra*) and one who is valiant (*vikrānta*), accompanied by men (*nṛbhiḥ*)—that is, by leaders of battle and warriors—is a victor (*jetā*) over enemies in battles (*pṛtsu*). Likewise, he becomes a listener (*śrotā*) to the invocation (*havam*) of the singer (*kārōḥ*), the praiser who is imploring for favor.

Furthermore, whenever (*yadā*) he himself (*dhamanā*), without being prompted by another, becomes the one who raises up (*udyantā*) the songs (*giraḥ*) consisting of hymns of praise or the praisers themselves, then he is near (*upāke*) to the donor (*dāśuṣaḥ*), the sacrificer who has offered the oblation.
He has come near;
indeed, right there at the place of sacrifice, he becomes one who brings forth the chariot, bringing it forth properly.
In cases such as "jeteṣu" and so forth, the prohibition of the genitive case in the sense of the object—by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām"—is applied.
The meaning is that whenever he wishes to hear praise, he himself quickly drives the chariot and arrives at the sacrifice.
Thus, with men, Indra—glorious for his renown, the devourer of nourishments—became a friend to the two who offer friendship.
In the assembly, the praise of the sacrificer, all-conquering and loud in speech, celebrates the strengthening foods.

Thus, Indra, through men, for the sake of glory, has become the enjoyer of nourishment among those who possess friends in the assembly; he is praised as the one who brings forth food in the public debate, the ever-active laud of the sacrificer. 4.

This Indra, having thoroughly devoured the food characterized by oblations offered by the *nṛbhiḥ*—the performers of the ritual through their agency—and desiring excellent food (*suśravasyā*), or being one who desires food, has thus, in this very manner, as before, overcome the enemies even of the sacrificer who possesses allies (*mitriṇaḥ*). Or alternatively: *Note: The term "nṛbhiḥ" refers to the human agents or priests who carry out the ritual acts; "pṛkṣaḥ" denotes the food consisting of sacrificial offerings; "suśravasyā" signifies the desire for glorious nourishment or the state of being a seeker of food; "prakhādaḥ" means having eaten with excellence; "eva eva" emphasizes the manner of action; "mitriṇaḥ" refers to the sacrificer who has friends or helpers; and "abhībhūt" means he overcomes or subdues.*

Accompanied by men who are leaders and wise, this Indra, being one who is well-renowned and a consumer [of offerings], has thus overcome those who possess friends—the officiating priests and the sacrificer who has Mitra as a friend—for their desired purpose.
The prefix *abhi* is here meaningless; it simply means "he becomes."
Or it occurs "facing toward" (ābhimukhyena);
the meaning is that having accepted his oblation, it becomes favorable to him.

Now, being thus, in the "contest" (vivāci)—a battle characterized by various mutual challenges and cries, or a time characterized by various sounds of hymns and liturgical recitations, or a sacrifice involving mortals—he, being the "praiser" (śaṃsaḥ) for the sacrificer on that account, the "performer of truth" (satrākaraḥ), the true maker of fruits, this Indra "praises" (stavate) the "food" (iṣaḥ), that is, the sacrificial offering.
With you, O Maghavan Indra, may we overcome our enemies who consider themselves great.
Be our protector and our strengthener; may we obtain food, a secure dwelling, and swift-giving rain.

Through you, O Maghavan, O Indra, may we overcome our enemies who consider themselves great. You are our protector; you indeed have been for our prosperity. Grant us nourishment, a stronghold, and quickening rain. 5.

O *maghavan*, O wealthy Indra, with you as our ally, may we, the sacrificers, overcome the enemies who consider themselves great—that is, those who deem themselves exceedingly powerful and invincible.
O Indra, you alone are our protector;
therefore, may you yourself be present for our prosperity, that is, for the increase of our wealth and other blessings.
The passage beginning with "vidhāma" has already been explained.
1. Having consumed *ka*, *kha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ta*, *pha*, and *khā*.
2. *Ka*, *jha*, *jha*—thus it became so.
[Maṇḍala 1, Adhyāya 23, Sūtra 179] The Second Aṣṭaka, 1065.
The hymn beginning with "pūrvīraham" consists of six verses, is in the Pañcadaśa-stoma, and is composed in the Triṣṭubh metre;
the penultimate verse is a Bṛhatī.
Here, because of the [traditional] association of the seers with the verses as Lopāmudrā, Agastya, the metres, and the deities, these are indeed the seers.
The subject matter expounded by this hymn is *rati* (sexual love) as its deity.

Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: "Having heard the conversation between the six earlier wives of Agastya and Lopāmudrā for the sake of *rati*, the disciple [Vatsaprī] perceived the final two verses in the *Bṛhatī* and other meters; [the rest] were seen by the teacher Brahmā.
The specific application (*viniyoga*) is determined by internal indication (*laiṅgika*).
Lopāmudrā said:
For many autumns have I labored, wearing away the nights and dawns;
old age diminishes the beauty of our bodies. Let husbands therefore come even unto their wives.

Through many autumns have I labored, through nights, through dwellings, and through dawns that bring old age. Old age diminishes the beauty of our bodies. Yet, may the strong ones now come even unto their wives.
He said, "O Agastya, I am Lopāmudrā; may we now come together with husbands who provide every enjoyment for many autumns.
The words *u* and *nu* are expletives.
They would have come together;
therefore, the meaning is: "How is it that you do not experience me?"
Agastya said to her:
"The gods do not speak falsely regarding that for which we have exerted ourselves; we have heard all these things from here.
Proclaim the victory here in this battle of a hundred ways, since we two, a pair of horses, have run together toward the goal."

No; it is false. We are weary. Since the gods urge us on, let us overcome all our rivals. O possessor of horses, let us both win here in this race with a hundred paths, when we two, a pair of horse-riders, drive forward together.
O husband, we two have not labored in vain; we have not been exhausted for nothing. For the gods, being pleased by our austerities, protect us.
We two have overcome all rivals; we have completely subdued them on every side.

Here, in this world, having heard the amorous conversation of another couple—a means for attaining immeasurable enjoyment—one who desires to perform an expiation for that [transgression] speaks the following verse.

The application of these two [verses] has been stated by Śaunaka: "Reciting these two verses, *imaṃ nu somam* and so forth, while being self-restrained, one attains all desires and is liberated from sins" (Ṛgvidhāna 1.147).
I now declare from my heart that this Soma has been drunk;
may it forgive whatever we have done against it, for it has many desires toward mortals.
I now address this Soma that has been drunk from nearby, dwelling within the heart: whatever offense we have committed, may he graciously forgive it; for mortals have many desires. 5.
...having approached and reached [him] with the mind, one prays.
What does he say? It is said:

"Whatever sin (*āgas*) we have committed—that is, we have transgressed—within the range of hearing the lewd talk of our elders, may that Soma, from that sin, graciously (*su*) forgive us; may he bring us happiness, meaning he shall not cause the suffering born of sin."
To the question, "How can great sin being experienced be wiped away by prayer? he says:
"For (hi) because (yasmāt) a mortal (martyaḥ), a human being, possesses many desires (pulukāmaḥ);
by means of action alone (aṣṭenaiva karmaṇā), one brings about many desires."
Since this is so, the meaning is that one should therefore avoid it. Alternatively, he says that because it is to be relinquished, it is as if it were attained [only through its abandonment].
For mortals indeed have many desires; being struck by desire, they exist as if completely obstructed by it.
Therefore, such an exultation is improper. Furthermore, the fault of hearing that word was merely accidental; the meaning is that this must be remedied by us with the Soma we have brought.
Alternatively, this mantra should be explained as referring to the Moon; for since the mind is the presiding deity [of the moon], that sin is also conceived as existing only in the mind.
In this view, "drunk in the hearts" means situated within the heart.
The remainder is clear.
Then, from among the two [hymns] thus assigned, the pupil spoke with the second hymn, the sixth [verse].
Agastya, digging with spades while desiring progeny, offspring, and strength, the fierce seer nourished both castes; his prayers went forth to the gods and were fulfilled.
Agastya, digging with spades while desiring offspring, progeny, and strength—the fierce seer nourished both castes and attained true blessings among the gods. 6.

This Agastya, the seeker of honey, digging with "diggers"—the means for producing fruit such as sacrifices and hymns—producing abundant fruit; desiring "offspring," that which is born again and again in excellence, and "progeny," the sons and others who are the means for the non-falling of the lineage, as well as "strength";
or alternatively, desiring "offspring" in the form of servants and the like.

The Ṛṣi—perceiver of that which transcends the senses, possessed of great majesty, fierce, and having shaken himself free from sin while wandering through the cycle of existence—cultivated both praiseworthy forms: desire and austerity. "I am his disciple; indeed, immediately after hearing this flow of conversation, I too became eager [to hear more]. (Note: *Satyāḥ* refers to Satyavatī. *Jha* indicates a variant reading. *Aham* is the speaker's name. *Antevāsī* means disciple. *Kṣipam* means quickly. *Saṃbhāṣaṇapravāha* means the flow of conversation.)
Thus acting, having approached, I speak to this Soma that has been accepted and drunk within the hearts—that is, in our own inner selves.
[2] Jha-Jha1: I pray; Jha1: I speak.
4. *Jha*: the sphere of lustful chatter. 5. *Kha*: the meaning is "one should take away.

6. *Ka*–*Jha*: by way of the avoidance of evil; *Ta*: by way of the non-avoidance of [the] night; *Jha*: by way of the non-avoidance of the watch; *Jha₁*: by way of the non-avoidance of the lamp; *Jha*: by way of the non-avoidance of evil.
The blessing went from among the gods to the gods; it reached them.
Since he possesses great power, the meaning is that he protects us.
Now, in the twenty-fourth section (anuvāka), there are twelve hymns (sūkta).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "yuvor rajāṃsi," is addressed to Agastya and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
According to the technical rules (paribhāṣā) regarding the word *tuhi* and others, this group of five initial hymns is [to be recited] as a single unit (*ābhīna*).
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: "‘yuvordāśvinaṃ vai’:
these five hymns, beginning with this one, excluding the third, are employed in the *Prātaranuvāka* and the *Aśvina-śastra* in the Bahvṛca [Ṛgveda].
In the section titled "Now the Aśvina [Hymns]," the Sūtra prescribes: "'yuvo rajāṃsi': one should omit the third of these five" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.15).
Your well-governed horses traverse the realms; when your chariot speeds around the curves, your golden fellies roll forward as you drink of the honeyed draught and accompany the Dawns.
O you two, when your well-guided horses traverse the realms with your chariot, as they fly around the ocean, your golden fellies move forward; drinking the sweetness, you accompany the Dawns.
O Aśvins, may your excellent chariot, which is most noble, traverse the *vrajās*—the *rañkas*, the worlds that are well-governed (*suyamāsaḥ*), meaning those that move through the three worlds. When?
He says: [when you desire].
When your chariot, O two [Aśvins], moves toward places that are more desirable— that is, when it goes toward or moves around those desired locations—
the root *dī* signifies motion, as it is listed among the verbs denoting movement in the statement: "He moves (*dīyati*), he reasons (*tarkati*)" (Nirukta 2.14.69).
Furthermore, at the time of the chariot’s arrival, your golden fellies— or the rims of the chariot wheels— proceeded forth, pr̥ṣṇan, toward the desired goal. Or rather,
the golden fellies are honey-vessels for you two, for the sake of the Ārya.
Since this is so, therefore, you two [drink] of the *madhvaḥ*, that is, of the *madhu*—the Soma juice which is like honey.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*).
Drinking—that is, tasting—the Soma juice, you two attend to, or join with, the sacrifice at the time associated with the dawn;
the sequence [of the verbal actions] is not intended to be significant here.
"Come at the very time [of the sacrifice] and drink the sweet Soma juice"—this is the meaning.
You two overcome the enemy's horse when you, O lords of men, drive around the blazing one;
for your sister, praised by all, brings [the offering] for you both, who desire strength, for the drinking of the honeyed [Soma].

You two descend upon the steed when he, the noble one, the one worthy of sacrifice, is being led forward; when the sister, praised by all, brings [the offering] for you both, seeking strength for the sake of the honey-drinker and the food-eater. 2.

O Aśvins, you two have caused that chariot—which is swift, moving continuously, traversing various paths (or possessing diverse motions), beneficial to men, and most worthy of worship—to stand still; before its rising, you two reached the place of sacrifice to go toward the deity-worship. These words ending in the genitive case function as accusatives of the object. You two caused that chariot of such a form to halt, and prior to its departure, you two reached the sacrificial ground to proceed.

Furthermore, when at all times both of you, praised by all (*viśvagūrtī*), are uplifted, then Dawn—your sister, who shares your station or moves of her own accord (*svasā*)—brings nourishment (*bharāti*); that is, she causes the break of day for your arrival. When, O drinkers of the sweet [Soma] (*madhupāu*), the sacrificer praises you two for the sake of strength (*vājāya*) or for going, or for food (*viṣe*)—that is, for abundant nourishment—then you reach the chariot; this is the meaning.
You two placed the ripe milk within the raw cow; you filled the interior of the cow with the essence of the bull.
When the one who possesses the oblation, shining like the doors of heaven, approaches the two of you—the seekers of Truth—within the dwelling.

You two placed the milk within the cow—cooked within the raw; you released the fullness of the cow. When the pure one, possessing oblations, worships you like doors at the streams of Truth (*ṛtap-sū*) that are within the wood, [then you grant this]. 3.
O Aśvins,
you two placed— that is, you established and set down— the paths upon the *ustriyā*, that is, upon the cow that bellows with joy at the prospect of enjoyment.
Likewise, when the raw [cow] was uncooked, you two held down—that is, set aside—the cooked, fully ripened milk fit for enjoyment belonging to the cow;
that which had been previously deposited right there, you two extracted from the cow for the sake of further enjoyment.
For this reason, O Ṛtapsū, you whose nature is Truth...
By these and other such passages, the animal sacrifice is also prescribed for the Aśvins.
Likewise, the "sweet flows"—the soma juices—also go toward you both; they approach you.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like wheels belonging to a chariot— just as those wheels move toward a sloping terrain, so it is here.
O Dāstros, may I turn you hither for the sake of the gift, as the aged Taugrya did with the milk of the cow;
the two great worlds come together through your majesty, O worshipful ones, as the worn-out man flees from the swift-moving razor-sharp [weapon].

O Dastrās, may I turn you toward me with gifts of cattle, as the aged son of Tugra did with his strength. Your greatness encompasses both heaven and earth; O holy ones, your ancient power delivers us from distress.

I shall cause you two, the Aśvins—the destroyers of enemies and the subduers—to turn toward the place of sacrifice in order to bestow gifts upon us and to carry [the offerings] for you both. This is derived from the root *vṛt* with the causative sense internalized (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*).
By what means? By that [means].
May he send you forth; may he satisfy;
may he pervade;
or may he desire.
The forms [of the roots] *prī* and *veti* take the suffix *keṭ*.

Immediately thereafter, as one who possesses the activity of heat (*uṣman*) and so forth—which is neither beautiful nor excessively praised—this sacrificer takes for himself, that is, appropriates, the *vāja*, meaning food, for the sake of greatness.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *āṅo do’nāsyaviharaṇe* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.20). The elision of the *ta* suffix is effected by the rule *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu*.
Alternatively:
This is a form [derived] from the Vedic *liṭ* [perfect tense].
Having accepted [this], you two alone shall satisfy me for my own greatness.
For we indeed, your singers, truly celebrate your wondrous deeds; for you are the dispeller of the stingy Pani.
And so, O blameless ones, you protect us with your wisdom; for you, O bulls, guard the path leading to the gods.

For we indeed, your truthful singers, celebrate you with hymns; even the stingy Panis, though they offer gifts, are surpassed. For verily, O blameless Ashvins, you two bulls drink the draught that is near the gods.
For we indeed—we too, as your singers and praisers—being true, that is, possessing true fruits, shall praise you manifoldly.
The Paṇi, the supporter of the Paṇi (the Soma), namely the Droṇakalaśa vessel, has been established as the container of the pressed juice;
or rather:

May this merchant, hunter, and fowler—who is unrighteous, devoid of compassion, and though possessing fixed wealth, is called "wealthy" yet remains unrighteous—be utterly separated from his possessions.
Due to the hearing of a prefix (upasarga), an appropriate verb must be supplied by ellipsis (adhyāhāra).
And furthermore, *cid* and *hi* and *dha*; these three are particles used for filling out the meter. O blameless *Aśvins*.
This is a praise [of the two].
O two praiseworthy ones, O two bulls, O you two showerers of desires, you two drink the Soma—the food—at Antideva’s, in the presence of the gods;
or alternatively: [the text continues as follows].
It should be understood that "Soma" refers to that which exists nearby and reaches the gods.
For even you two, O Aśvins, with your swift horse, aided Agastya in the winning of cattle from Rudra’s fountain;
he, the most praised among men, like a bowstring that sounds at the pull, was made conscious by thousands [of riches].

For even you two, O Aśvins, did Agastya—most renowned among men among men—follow at the winning of the flowing waters of Virudra, making himself known through his powers like two rattling chariot-bells. 8.
O Aśvins, you two—
indeed, "cit," "hi," and "dhma" are three filler particles.

When there is the acquisition (*sāti*)—that is, the obtaining—as a cause for the daily flow (*prasravaṇa*) of the rainwater from the mountain (*anu yūni*) of Viśvṛtra, who possesses the pain of a particularly hot form or whose melting is manifested in various ways, the great seer named Agastya makes known (*citayat*), that is, he awakens through praise, those among men (*nṛṣu*) who are leaders (*narām*) and executors of action, being himself most excellent among such men, by means of countless (*sahasaiḥ*) hymns of praise.
Therein lies the illustration.
Like a *kārādhunī*.
*Kārā* is a word meaning "sound. A *kārādhunī* is like a conch shell or similar instrument that causes that sound to shake or resound.
Alternatively,
this too is an epithet of Agastya:
*kāraḥ* refers to the invoker, such as the *hotṛ* priest and others.
*dhuniḥ* means a shaker or an impeller, as it were. The particle *iva* is used here in the sense of *saṃprati* (presently).
According to the Nirukta (7.31): "The particle *iva* is employed in the sense of *saṃprati* when it has the meaning of a comparison (*upamā*)."
When you two drive forth with the greatness of your chariot, you go speeding like the Hotṛ-priest of man.
O Nāsatyas, bestowers of wealth, may we be masters of riches, possessing both what is held for the patrons and that which belongs to our father-in-law.

When you two travel forth with the greatness of your chariot, you go speeding like the Hotṛ-priest of man. O Nāsatyas, may we be possessors of wealth, bestowing horses upon the liberal patrons. May we be those who follow after riches. 9.
O Aśvins, you two, by the greatness—
that is, the magnitude— of the *ratha* (chariot), the means of movement, carry forth [the sacrifice], or rather, you bear the yoke of the sacrificial chariot, the means for reaching heaven.
Likewise, O ye two swift ones, ye who have the nature of flowing, ye go;
that is, ye come to your own place at the commencement of the sacrifice, and ye go back again at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Therein is this illustration.
The *manuṣ* Hotṛ—the Hotṛ of the human sacrificer—just as he arrives at the commencement of the sacrifice and departs again once the rite is completed, so too [be it].
At the time of his arrival, bestow and maintain the fruit for the patrons (*sūri*), the singers;
or indeed, bestow a multitude of excellent horses (*śvaśrya*).
Nāsatyā:
those who exist among the good are "satyau"; those who are not "asatya" (unreal/false) are "nāsatyau."
Through your grace, may we become such as those, possessors of wealth, having a collection of riches.

O Aśvins, we invoke you today with new hymns upon your chariot for our well-being—your chariot with its uninjured fellies, which travels across the heavens. May we find this nourishing strength, a secure refuge that bestows life-giving gifts.

That chariot of yours, O Aśvins, we invoke today with hymns for our well-being—a new one, with uninjured fellies, traveling around the sky. May we find this troop of yours, which bestows quickening gifts. 10.

O Aśvins, O you two Aśvins, we who desire to reach the goal shall invoke—that is, call upon—your chariot, which is connected to you both and is worthy of praise for its swift motion, on this day of this hymn. By what means? It is said:
by means of *stomas*, that is, by hymns of praise.
For what purpose?
For *suvitāya*, that is, for the attainment of prosperity. Of what kind?
"New," meaning praiseworthy or fresh; likewise, "Ariṣṭanemi," whose wheel-rim is unharmed; "pari iyānaṃ dyām," moving all around the celestial realm, dwelling in the world of heaven.
"May we know," and so forth, is as explained previously.
‘Kadu preṣṭhau’ is the second hymn, consisting of nine verses; it belongs to Agastya, is addressed to the Tridhātu, and has the Aśvins as its deities.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry: ‘Kadu nava’.
The application of the Prātaranuvāka and the Abhīnaśastra has already been stated in the preceding hymn.
When you two, the most beloved dispensers of riches, act as Adhvaryus and lead the waters with your song—
this sacrifice has offered praise to you both, O bestowers of wealth, protectors of men.

Come hither! O most beloved ones of refreshments and riches, you who act as Adhvaryus when you have been praised. This sacrifice here has offered you glory; O bestowers of wealth, protectors of men! 1.

1. *jha1-vahathaḥ* | 2. *jha1-saṃbandhanaṃ tam*. O Aśvins, most beloved (*preṣṭhau*) ones, when will it be for you two—[the time] for *iṣām*, that is, for the desired foods, and for *rayīṇām*, that is, for riches?
The two genitives are used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).

You two, "desiring to complete the sacrifice" (*adhvaryantau*), raise up the limbs and the riches; you two raise up the waters of the rain and the rains themselves, bringing them to a superior state. When was this?
Why is it said thus? It is said [as follows].
"This sacrifice, being performed by us, offers praise—meaning it performs a laudatory hymn—unto you two alone.

The meaning is that the *śastra* recitations, which are to be praised during the sacrifice, extol you both. Since this is so, O you two who are the bestowers (*vasudhitī*) of wealth (*vasu*), the performers of desirable deeds, and the protectors (*avitārau*) of people characterized as such, when will you become the givers of food and riches?"
May your pure, water-drinking horses, swift as the wind, divine coursers,
mind-swift, vigorous, with smooth backs, and self-ruling, bring you hither, O Aśvins.
May your pure, water-drinking horses—swift as the wind, divine, coursers fleet as thought, vigorous, with smooth backs—bring you hither, O self-ruling Aśvins. 2.
O Aśvins, you two who are joined with beautiful horses—let your horses bring you here to this sacrifice; that is, let them cause you to arrive.
The remaining words are adjectives qualifying the horses. Of what kind are they?

"Pure" means clean or radiant; "water-drinkers" means drinkers of rainwater; "wind-swift" means possessing the speed of the wind; "divine" means existing in heaven; "going" means having the nature of moving; "mind-swift" means as fast as thought; "virile" means showerers of benefits, that is, young men;
"smooth-backed" means having beautiful backs, that is, handsome in form;
"self-ruling" means shining by their own power.
"May they be such as this!
"Your chariot, like a downward-flowing stream, with its wide seat, shall come for our well-being;
it is the swifter of the two bulls, more fleet than thought, the foremost, worthy of sacrifice, and full of wisdom."

Your chariot, like a downward-flowing stream, with its broad seat, is to be approached for our welfare; it is drawn by vigorous steeds, swifter than thought, self-yoked, preeminent, worthy of sacrifice, and full of wisdom. 3.
In the previous mantra, the arrival of the Aśvins was described under the guise of horses;
here it is described under the guise of a chariot.

O *adhiṣṇyā*, you who occupy elevated places, you who are the two charioteers presiding over your own chariot—may that chariot of yours, which exists for the sake of *suvitāya* (attaining auspicious results), come hither to our sacrifice.
A transposition of genders:
he is qualified by the question "What kind of chariot is it?

It is "like the earth" (*avanir-na*) in its "slopedness," meaning it is as exceedingly vast as the ground; "with a broad seat" (*saprabandhuraḥ*), meaning its front portion is wide; and it is "swifter than even the mind of a stallion" (*vṛṣṇo manaso 'pi javīyān*), meaning it possesses the speed of thought.
"May a chariot such as this come—one that is 'I-first' (eager for precedence), full of ego, spirited, or noble, and fit for sacrifice; it is worthy of being sacrificed for. 1.
jha1—The word "bhaviṣyati" (will be) is not present. 2. jha1—"yuvāṃ yat" means "when you two [act]. 3. jha-jha1—"divyāsaḥ" (those who sport/divine). 4. jha-jha1—"vahantu" (let them carry). ka. 135.
Those born here have lowered their voices together with bodies free from blemish and with their own names:
one of you, the victorious, is called the son of Sumakha; the other, the fortunate, is proclaimed as the son of Diva.

Born here, here, they have both lowed together with their stainless bodies and their own names. One of you two is the victorious patron of the noble sacrificer; the other is considered the fortunate son of Heaven. 4.
O Aśvins, you two have lowed together;
you are praised together, perfectly and repeatedly, or you desire the sacrifice.
There is a change of gender.
"What are you two like? You are born here and here.
By both instances of the word "here" (iha), the middle and the highest positions are expressed.
Regarding their origin:
it means "by the moon and the sun.
According to the *Nirukta* (12.1), some say, "the sun and the moon."
"Arepasā apāpau":
the sense is that they were free from the taint of sin due to the decapitation of their preceptor, the descendant of Atharvan, and so forth;
this is known from Vedic mantras such as, "O Aśvins, descendants of Atharvan, you restored the head to Dadhyañc" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.117.22).
By what cause? It is said:
"By means of the body"—that is, by way of the beauty of the body as the instrumental cause—"with your own names," such as "Aśvins" and "Nāsatyas," which are distinguished by their own greatness;
the meaning is that you two are praised because of your possession of beautiful bodies, your endowment with majesty, and your status as the most excellent.
Alternatively,
it should be construed as "with a stainless body.
This means that by establishing such greatness through a head that is sinless even after the severing of the preceptor's head, in the manner previously described.

Furthermore: "Of you two (*vām*), the one (*anyaḥ*)—the other—is Soma, who, like a son of the middle realm (the atmosphere), being victorious (*jiṣṇuḥ*) and the impeller (*sūriḥ*) of the beautiful sacrifice (*sumakhasya*), carries (*ūhe*) [the world]; he sustains the entire universe.
Upon the rising of that moon-mind, the plants, trees, and so forth flourish.
The other (*anyaḥ*), the second, the highest-positioned son of heaven (*divaḥ putraḥ*)—the Sun—being possessed of auspicious wealth in the form of beautiful rays (*subhagaḥ*), carries [the world]."
Thus, you two of great majesty, who sustain the entire world, are praised together.

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "Born here and there, you two are praised with bodies unstained by evil and with your own names: one is the victorious Vāmana, the most mighty impeller of strength; the other is the fortunate son of Aditi, the middle [deity] of heaven" (Nirukta 12.3).
May your swift, humped, tawny-colored bull go toward the dwellings according to our will.
May the two bay steeds of the other [Aśvin] swell with strengths, and may you, O Aśvins, traverse the mid-regions with your roars.

May your tawny-colored, preeminent steed, moving downward according to our will, come to our dwellings. May the two bay horses of the other be nourished with strengths; O Aśvins, may the fly speed through the regions with its cries.

O Aśvins, between you two, the chariot of one of you is *kakuhá*—the most excellent, of tawny form (*piśaṅgarūpa*), or golden form (*hiraṇyarūpa*)—yellow-colored, or perhaps being adorned with many parts of horses; it follows after *vaśán*, that is, according to desires, or as desired.
The meaning is: according to our desire for sacrifice.
Or else:

May the preeminent one, having brought his followers under his own control, moving lowly through the quarters and intermediate directions in due order, proceed from his own station toward the mouth of the sacrificial ground;
may he go forth with excellence, entering our sacrificial halls.
There is a transposition of genders.
Although the phrase "of another" (*anyasya*) is not explicitly stated here, it is nevertheless understood because it is so stated in the subsequent sentence. [The meaning is:
"Of another—one of you two who is more capable—the *harī* are the horses; the *rajāṃsi* are the worlds.
Here, the word *loka* denotes people.
Those people have the form of sacrificers.
1. In the form of the moon and sun;
2. by means of the body—this is the meaning.

And they cause me to swell—that is, to increase—by means of offerings such as curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) produced through churning and stirring, or by means of praises (*ghoṣaiḥ*), or by means of specific sounds characterized by invocations and the like.
Like a bull that has burst forth, the showerer of rain brings you both forward; he pours out many streams of honey.
By the movements of the other, they swell with milk; like waters from a spring, they have come to us upward like a chariot.

Like a bull that has burst forth, the arrow-showering [Soma] has come toward you both; he bestows many refreshments, streaming with sweetness. By their own movements, they cause the milk of another to swell; like men standing upright by the dwelling, they have come hither.
O Aśvins, one of you two is the middle-positioned Śarad-dhan, possessing the power of dispersal (*viśaraṇa*) of clouds, trees, leaves, and so forth;
or else, he is the one of many years, ancient, meaning eternal.
He is like Indra, the bull, who rains down.

Like him, being the one who tears apart (*niṣpāt*) and drives out the enemies, he moves forward with excellence (*pracarati*) toward many (*pūrvīḥ*), numerous, or ancient foods (*iṣaḥ*) intended for consumption.
In the view that [the subject] is the moon situated in the middle region, it refers to one possessing the autumn season (*śaradām*);
for during that season, the moon becomes full.
And by that, the grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and so forth flourish.
Why does he act in this way? It is said: "Desiring sweetness"—that is, desiring the oblation which is like honey, resembling honey.
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
Desiring the oblation,
they act in this manner for that very purpose.

Likewise, by means of those desires or movements belonging to another, namely the highest Āditya— which serve as the cause— the sacrificers cause [the gods] to swell and become satiated with oblations.
Impelled by him who was pleased, they went forth—spreading through the quarters, upward, lofty, and excellent; like those who are joyful, they have come for our sake.

The ancient song, O wise ones, has been released for you two who possess the stalk; it flows in three ways. O you who are praised, protect us as we struggle; listen indeed to my call as I approach you both on my journey.

The ancient song has been released for you two, O possessors of wisdom; may it reach you with the arrow. Moving in three ways, you who are praised, protect us; hear my call as I approach on my journey, both on the path and off the path. 7.
Those two creators, the Aśvins, have indeed released for you—the word in the form of praise—when the two firm and stable supports serve as the cause.
Of what nature is it?
It is exceedingly stable, eternal, consisting of the Veda, threefold through the divisions of mantra and so forth, and moving toward you both.
The meaning is that such a hymn has been composed.
Thus, being praised, O Nāsatyas, protect—that is, preserve—or satisfy him who is *dhamāna*, imploring his desired fruit.
Furthermore, whether in motion (*yāman*) or in non-motion (*ayāman*), hear our invocation (*havam*).

1. The lord of gods (Indra) is the rainer of *ka*, *kha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ta*, and *pha*; the bull (*vṛṣabha*) is the rainer of the *jha* sound. 2. *Ka*, *kṣa*, and *ga* are the "attached" (*prasaja*). 3. *Kha* and *pha* are the "elevated" (*unnīra*). 4. The two Aśvins are the *jha* sound. 5. It is emitted and uttered as *jha*.

And may this song of yours, radiant and beautiful, swell the men in the assembly where the triple-layered sacrificial grass is spread. O bulls, your bull-like cloud has swelled; bestowing gifts upon man, it flows like the pouring of milk for the cow. 8. And may this song of yours, radiant and beautiful, swell the men in the assembly where the triple-layered sacrificial grass is spread. O bulls, your bull-like cloud has swelled; bestowing gifts upon man, it flows like the pouring of milk for the cow. 8.

O Aśvins, may this song of praise—the speech that causes the white, radiant, and beautiful form of yours to appear—cause the leaders of men (nṛn) to swell with nourishment in the sacrificial seat where the threefold sacred grass is spread; may it cause them to swell by means of the restoration of offerings that were previously cut off. In what manner is this said?

O you two showerers (*vṛṣaṇā*), pourers of desires, your own cloud—the sprinkler, the rain-cloud, or a specific gift—is a showerer (*vṛṣā*); being such, while bestowing (*daśasyan*) gifts upon men (*manuṣaḥ*), it causes them to swell (*pīpāya*). The illustration for this swelling is: "like the sprinkling of a cow" (*gor na sekai*), that is, like the sprinkling of water during the *śāṃtana* rite.
The meaning is that it nourishes in that manner;
or alternatively,
"na" is used here in the sense of "now."
The connection is that when the sprinkling of water from the cow has become the cause, [the intention is] "may he drink."

O Aśvins, like Puṣan, the inspired singer praises you both; the one possessing oblations does not grow old as he approaches Agni. When I, praising you with my desire for wealth, invoke you, may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts. 9. O Aśvins, like Puṣan, the inspired singer praises you both; the one possessing oblations does not grow old as he approaches Agni. When I, praising you with my desire for wealth, invoke you, may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts. 9.
O Aśvins, you two, the wise Puraṃdhi— like Pūṣan, the nourisher— one endowed with oblations praises you;
or rather,
Puraṃdhi is the sustainer of many, like Pūṣan, or like the Earth.
The nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Just as he praises her, so too [praises] you both;
and just as [he praises] the Soma-pressing,
so [does he praise] you both.
The intention is that, just as in the case of the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*, the two deities Ābhīya and Upastya are also present together. When?

He says: "When"—that is, when the singer (*gṛṇānaḥ*), endowed with *varivasyā*, i.e., service (*paricaryā*), praises [them], then the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) also "sings" (*jarate*). This is the meaning.
The passage beginning with "vidyām" has already been explained.
The third hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "abhūdidam," is addressed to the Aśvins and is composed in the Jagatī meter.
The sixth verse, "avaviddham," and the eighth verse, "tadvāṃ narā nāsatyau," are both in the Triṣṭubh meter.
As stated in the Anukramaṇikā: "In this [hymn] of eight verses beginning with 'abhūdidam,' there are two Triṣṭubhs."
The application of these [verses] belonging to the *chandasya* [hymn] is in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "Three [verses] beginning with 'abhūd idaṃ' and 'yo vāṃ parijmā'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.15).

This wisdom has come forth; adorn it well! Let the chariot, drawn by stallions, be anointed; let the wise ones be gratified. O you who quicken the prayer, you who are worthy of praise, you who possess all wealth—O sons of Heaven, you whose vows are pure, [be present] for the sake of the one who performs good deeds. abhūt | idam | vayunam | o iti | su | bhūṣata | rathaḥ | vṛṣaṇvān | medata | manīṣīḥ | dhiyaṃ'jinvā | dhiṣṇyā | viśva'lāṃvas iti | divaḥ | napātā | su'kṛte | śuci'vratā ||1||
1. [The hymns] beginning with *kha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ta*, and *tri* have sacrificial grass spread upon them.
2. The first [verse] beginning with *kha* and *pha* is according to the Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). 3. [The hymns] beginning with *ka* and *jha* belong to Agastya and the Aśvins.
The wise, mindful, and intelligent officiating priests (ṛtvijas) have perceived—that is, it has arisen—our *hvam*, our wisdom (*prajñāna*).
What is that like? It is said:
The chariot belonging to the Aśvins—the means of their movement—has arrived, [it is understood]. It has come as one that possesses rainers who grant desired showers.
The two Aśvins have mounted it; they have adorned themselves. *O* is a single particle consisting of a collection of two particles.
Adorn yourselves well;
turn toward them to offer praise.
Rejoice in those two Aśvins of such great majesty!
This [root] has the causative sense (ṇyartha) inherent within it; it means "to gladden" or "to honor. The Aśvins are the object being qualified.

O you two who enliven the intellect for me who have performed good deeds well, you who are gratifiers of the mind or of ritual action; O you two who are worthy of praise, possessors of wisdom, and objects of hymns; O you two whose wealth is the swift-footed Viṣpalā, who became such through the gift of golden legs to her—she who was formerly lame and covered in wounds—as the *Ṛgveda* mantra states: "Immediately [you gave] an iron leg to Viṣpalā" (ṚV 1.116.15);
O you two grandsons of Dyu, the son of Āditya, who are destroyers of enemies or protectors of men, and whose ordinances are pure, whose actions are radiant.
Rejoice, O Aśvins, such as you are!
For you are the most Indra-like, the most worthy of hymns, the best of Maruts, the most wondrous-handed Dāstas, the most skillful in subduing, and the best of charioteers.
You drive your full chariot, adorned with pearls; with that, O Aśvins, you go toward the skillful man.

For you two are most like Indra, O wise ones; most like the Maruts, O wonder-workers; most skilled in deeds, most worthy of praise, and best of charioteers. You drive your full chariot, which is thought-swift in every way; with that, O Aśvins, you come hither to the skillful man.

O Aśvins, you two are indeed most like Indra; for with each epithet, such is the connection. Thus: *dhiṣṇyā* means worthy of praise; *maruttamā* means moving with the speed of the Maruts or possessing measured passion (or measured speech); *dastrā* means destroyers of enemies; *daṃsiṣṭhā* means those of most excellent deeds; *rathyā* means riders of chariots, possessing chariots; and *rathitamā* means those who are most excellent chariot-warriors.
They are the leaders of the chariot-warriors;
they are the best among them,
because [the term] "rathīrathavarāṇām" (Rigveda Saṃhitā 8.11.2) has been explained as referring to leaders.
Such as you two are, you carry a chariot that is full of, filled with, and laden on all sides with *madhu*—that is, water resembling honey or nectar—from the sky.
With that chariot, distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, O Aśvins, being yourselves endowed with those same qualities, you approach the sacrifice facing toward it.
What do you two, O destroyers (*dastrā*), do here? What do you sit for, regarding any person whatsoever who exalts himself without an oblation?
Pass over him, consume him who is wasting away; bestow life and light upon the sage who offers praise.

What do you two, O destroyers of foes, do here? Why do you sit there? Whosoever among people is honored though he offers no oblation—pass over him, consume him who is wasting away; bestow life and light upon the sage who offers praise. 3.
O you two destroyers (*dastrā*), who are capable of consuming, what do you two do here—among these men?
The implication is: because of the absence of sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
Why do you two remain right there? Why do you stay?
Regarding this, it was asked "Where? and he replied:

"Whosoever is a person born [into the world] who, being devoid of sacrificial offerings (*ahaviḥ*), meaning lacking the oblations intended for sacrifice, is honored—that is, worshipped by himself and not worshipping you—surpass him;
that is, remain having overcome him."
Not only did you spare him from mere transgression, but you also preserved—the word *asu* meaning "life"—the life of that greedy hunter who had become a merchant; you did not destroy it.
For the wise sage, who desires hymns of praise (*vacasyu*) from you both, create great light; that is, grant him the knowledge concerning the sacrifice to you.

Crush on all sides the barking dog; slay the assailants, O Aśvins, and provide those [remedies]. Make every word of the singer rich in treasure; O both Nāsatyas, protect my praise. 4 Crush! On all sides! Of the barking! Dog! Slay! The assailants! They provided! Those [remedies], O Aśvins! Every word! Of the singer! Rich in treasure! Make! Both! My praise! O Nāsatyas! Protect! 4
O Aśvins, crush and destroy on all sides the barking dogs that come to revile us or to kill us;
likewise, slay the adversaries who wage war against us.
You two know the means of destroying them.
Furthermore, with your very speech, make the speech of the singer—the singer who praises you—into that very speech characterized by praise, making every hymn of praise possess delightful fruit.
O Nāsatyas, you two who are truth itself, both of you, protect and preserve my *śaṃsa*, my hymn of praise.

You two fashioned for Taugrya this winged boat, endowed with life, upon the rivers—by which you two, with a godward mind, carried him forth; as well-faring ones, you traveled through the great flood. You two. This. You fashioned. Upon the rivers. A boat. Endowed with life. Winged. For Taugrya. Indeed. By which. Toward the gods. With a mind. You carried forth. Well-faring. You traveled. Through the flood. Of the great [waters]. 5.

O Aśvins, you two fashioned for Bhujyu—the son of King Tugra—that well-known boat, a means for praise, endowed with life (strength), possessed of wings (a chariot equipped with wing-like hymns of praise), and providing comfort.
King Bhujyu, the son of Tugra, dwelling by the sea, set out with his army to crush the enemy host.

The opposing forces having arrived, they struck him down; he, however, praised the Aśvins who bestow the fruit of grace, saying, "Protect yourself"—this ancient legend has been elaborated in many ways previously.
Or rather, *kam* is used as a filler (*pūraṇa*).
The meaning is that you fashioned many chariots and other vehicles as companions for that water-traversing chariot;
this matter is well known from other mantras such as *tam ahathur naubhiḥ* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.3), *catasro nāvaḥ* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.182.6), and *tribhī rathaiḥ* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.4).
By means of that boat (*plavena*) which belongs to you, and with a mind endowed with grace directed toward the gods (*devatrā deveṣu madhye manasā*), [you acted].
Or it may be construed as "with which mind.
"Nirūhathuḥ" means you two cause to go forth.
Likewise, being "suparnī," those of beautiful flight, or having excellent flight, you two [cross] the "mahaḥ kṣodasaḥ," the great flood.
This is the water;
from the water you two have emerged, O Pethathu and Tadadhahpata, following the higher path.

The son of Tugra was pierced within the waters, cast into darkness where there is no support; four ships, beloved by Jaṭhara, sent forth by the Aśvins, carry him across. 6. Pierced. The son of Tugra. Within the waters. In [the midst]. Without support. In darkness. Cast forth. Four. Ships. Of Jaṭhara. Beloved. Up. By the Aśvins. Sent forth. They carry across. 6.

Within the waters, in the midst of that which was cast down and covered by those standing upon it, in the darkness—darkness as it were—devoid of support, without a hold, and obstructing sight and so forth; [therein] they entered and thoroughly oppressed Bhujyu Taudhya, who had been plunged into the midst of the belly of Jaṭhara, the bearer of the water within the womb. Thus they were served and enjoyed.
Or alternatively:
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
Having reached the belly, they have entered into the water;
impelled by the Aśvins and striving, they carry the ships across, draw them out, and bring them forward.
What tree indeed stood firm in the midst of the flood, which the son of Tūtuji, in his distress, embraced?
Like two birds seizing the full wings of a beast, you two, O Aśvins, bore him away for the sake of his renown.

What tree indeed stood firm in the midst of the flood, which Taudhya, when he was in distress, climbed up? Like two birds grasping at the fullness of a beast, you two Aśvins bore him up for the sake of his renown. 7.
Who indeed—what benefactor—is the "tree"? A chariot, which is a modification of wood;
the word for the material cause is used here for the modification.
Or else:
This refers to the intention of familiarity;
the meaning is that the tree is called a "praise" (stotra).
What kind of chariot is it?
"Established" means existing immovably.
Where? It is said: "in the midst of the water," that is, in the middle of the fluid.
The son of Taudhyā, Bhujyu, being distressed and imploring, embraced this tree; that is, he clung to it for support. An illustration for this support is given:

like the leaves of a *pataru*—a tree prone to falling—which serve as a hold for a hunter (*mṛgasya mārjayituḥ*) who intends to clean or kill [the prey].¹ 1. Or, alternatively, *mṛgasya* may mean "of the deer," and *mārjayituḥ* "of the one who cleanses" (i.e., the groomer), referring to the act of taming or killing. 2. That is, just as leaves provide a grip for a person about to fall from a tree.

Just as those [roots] are capable of supporting their object, so too, O Aśvins, you raised him up for the sake of glory— that is, for the possession of fame. In the context of praise, the meaning is that you raised up that tree known as the hymn which had taken refuge [in you].
To you, O Nāsatyas, heroes, the sons of Pṛśnim have uttered this hymn of praise.
From this Soma-draughting assembly, may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.

To you two, O Nāsatyas, the sons of Manu, the reciters have uttered their hymn of praise following the *pyāghna* [oblation]. From this Soma-draughting assembly today, may we find nourishment and a stronghold that yields quickening rain. 8.

O *narā*, leaders of the rite, or rather, O *narākārī*, those who take human form; O *nāsatyau*, you two who are free from falsehood or whose fruit is truth—may this such hymn of praise be favorable toward you, or may it reach you. It is fitting that this be said:
may our *hotrā* and other priests, full of honor (*mānāsaḥ*), that hymn (*ucatha*) which they have uttered for you, be likewise favorable to you.
O Aśvins, on this day of the principal sacrifice, from this *sadas*— belonging to us and connected with the *somya* [Soma-sacrifice] that is being performed by us;
the particle *ā* is used in the sense of "also"—
even though it is being performed by us, O sacrificers, please take pleasure in the hymn of praise.
The knowledge has thus been explained.
The fourth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "yujāthām," is addressed to the Aśvins; it is composed by Traidhātubha Āptya and is dedicated to the Aśvins.
1. Of the belly that is like a bronze vessel;
2. Like leaves, the *ka-parṇā* leaves.
Harness that [chariot] which is swifter than thought, O Bulls (*vṛṣaṇā*), which has three seats and three wheels.
Wherewith you approach the dwelling of the righteous; with your triple-layered wings you fly through the sky.

Harness that [chariot] which is swifter than thought, O powerful ones—that which has three seats and three wheels, by which you approach the dwelling of the righteous man, traversing the paths with its triple-layered wings like a bird with its feathers. 1.
O you two showerers (*vṛṣaṇā*) of desires, yoke—that is, harness—that chariot which is distinguished by the qualities about to be described.
Regarding that which was referred to as "that," he asks: "Which?"—it is the chariot that has three seats (*trivandhura*), meaning it has three positions for the charioteer.
They say that the *vandhura* is the standing place of the charioteer,
based on other mantras such as "Come with the *vandhura*" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 3.43.1).
Furthermore, he is three-wheeled, being endowed with a triad of wheels.
Furthermore, that very chariot is further specified: by which chariot you two approach; what [is it]?
He has come to the *duroṇa*, the house— namely, the sacrificial hall— of the well-performing sacrificer, who possesses the karma of auspicious fortune.

It was asked "by what? and now it is said "by what?"—namely, by means of a chariot endowed with the three realms, that is, possessed of the three types of stations, or alternatively, endowed with the three supreme realms of gold and silver;
this is the illustration for the act of going.
Just as a bird flies swiftly with effort by means of its wings, so do you two fly—that is, go—by means of a chariot possessing the aforementioned characteristics.
The two with well-rolling chariots move about, seeking alms at the sacrifice; you two, full of wisdom, attend to the nourishment.
This beautiful song accompanies the beauty [of the rite]; you two are united with Uṣas, the daughter of Heaven.

The well-rolling chariot moves as it goes toward the earth; when you two, possessed of wisdom, stand upon the nourishment, may this song accompany you who increase every form of beauty. You two, O daughters of heaven, are accompanied by the Dawn.

O Aśvins, your chariot is well-rolling, with beautiful movement and the graceful turning of its wheels; as it goes, it approaches the earth, proceeding toward the sacrificial ground. That chariot which you two—possessing resolve or possessing ritual action—sought for nourishment when the oblation served as the occasion.
The prefix *anu* has the sense of "for the purpose of reaching.
*Adhi-tiṣṭhathaḥ* means "you two occupy" or "you two take recourse to.
The meaning is that such a chariot has arrived at the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*).
Immediately thereafter, may this speech—beneficial to your bodies, nourishing to the physical form, and consisting of praise in the manner now being performed—attend to your *vapus* (splendid forms).
And may you two, together with *Uṣas*, the daughter of Heaven (*divaḥ*) or of the Sun (*ādityasya*), who occupies the position of a daughter, attend the sacrifice;
for the meaning is that the time of *Uṣas* and that of the Aśvins is identical.
Mount your well-rolling chariot; according to your sacred laws, the oblation-bearer turns toward you, O Nāsatyas, so that by it you may come to us for our protection and for our own comfort.

Mount [your chariot]; your well-rolling chariot follows your sacred laws, O lords, as it bears the oblation. With that [chariot], O Nāsatyas, you come to provide nourishment and to protect both [us] and yourselves. 3.
1. *Ka-kha-ja-ta-pha-upāgacchathaḥ*:
O Aśvins, you two, mount the well-rolling (*suvṛtta*) chariot;
that chariot which is rich in oblations (*haviṣmān*).
The nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
It follows the *vrata*s—meaning the ritual acts—of the sacrificer who possesses the oblation (*haviṣmat*).
Or alternatively:
He is possessed of that [chariot] because the oblation has been given to the sacrificer.
And with that chariot, O *narā* (leaders), O *nāsatyā* (you two who are free from falsehood)— the sense being that you desire to reach the sacrifice (*iṣayadhyai*)—
with that chariot [comes] *vartiḥ* (the path).
This is the name for the house.
You two go to the sacrificer’s sacrificial house for the sake of offspring—that is, for the obtaining of a son—and for the sake of yourself, for your own welfare.
Let not the male wolf nor the female wolf dare to seize you; do not turn back, and do not bring us distress.
This is your portion, set down here; this is your song, O Dasyūs; these are your reservoirs of honey.
Let not the wolf nor the she-wolf dare to seize you; do not let them turn you away, nor deliver you over.
This portion is set apart for you both; this is the song, O Dāsas; these are the vessels of honey for you two. 4.
O Aśvins, you two who destroy the enemies— by your favor, it is implied— the predatory wolf,
such as a wild dog or similar beast, shall not dare to attack me; likewise, the female wolves, those other harmful creatures, shall not dare to attack me.
There is a transposition of words.
One should construe it as: "May they not commit an assault," or "May you two alone not be assailed."
Likewise, O two youths, do not "pari-vartam"—do not exclude me from all sides;
and furthermore, "uta" (also), bestow "mātim" (thought/attention) upon us, do not give it to another by passing us over. Why is this so? It is said: [as follows].
This portion, this share of the oblation worthy of being enjoyed, has been set apart for you two;
likewise, this song in the form of praise has also been set apart—this is the ellipsis.
O Dasras, O Aśvins, these repositories of honey, that is, of Soma juices, have been established for you both.
Gotama, Purumīḷha, and Atri, bearing oblations, invoke you both for protection.
Like one who points out the direction, like two who travel along a straight path, O Nāsatyas, come to my invocation. 5.
Gotama, Purumīḷha, and Atri—the possessor of oblations calls upon you, O Daśras, for his protection.
Like one who follows the appointed direction with straightness, come to my invocation, O Nāsatyas. 5.
O ye two *dastrā*, O Aśvins, Gotama, Purumīḷha, Atri, and these great seers—each one of them, being possessed of oblations, invokes you for protection or for your gratification.
Even so do I invoke you. This invocation for the sake of attaining the fruit is illustrated by this example.
Like one who goes straight: "yantā" means one who approaches, desiring to approach;
"ṛju" [is used] with the accusative case ending changed to "ā";
just as [one goes] toward a desired direction that has been pointed out by one who knows the path and travels straight, so too [is it] for him.
Just as a traveler, in order to reach his destination quickly, calls upon one who knows the way and travels straight;
or rather,
"by a straight path" (*ṛjuyā*).
The word *iva* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed).

Just as a traveler reaches his desired destination by following a straight path, so too does one attain the fruit of one's desire through the path of pleasing you. O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, having perceived my invocation (*havam*), come near; approach me.
We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; O Aśvins, this hymn of praise has been offered to you both.
Come hither by the paths traveled by the gods; may we obtain food, a dwelling, and the gift of long life.

We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness. O Aśvins, this hymn of praise has been offered to you both; come hither by the paths traveled by the gods. May we find nourishment and a dwelling-place that grants life-sustaining gifts. 6.

O Aśvins, by your grace, we have crossed over—the very limit and end—of this darkness, of that gloom which is the cause of suffering and an obstacle to our welfare. O Aśvins, this hymn of praise has been offered to you;
it has been composed. Come to this sacrifice of ours by the paths traveled by the gods.
The remainder has been explained.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.
Thus, salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa by the illustrious Vīrabukka, the King of Kings, the Supreme Lord, and the promoter of the Vedic path.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
The fourth chapter, concerning the second immovable stage, has been explained with devotion by Sāyaṇārya; the fifth shall now be explained.
In this context, “tā vām” is the fifth hymn in the twenty-fourth anuvāka of the first maṇḍala.

Since the preceding hymn was stated to have six verses, this is a ṣaṭka (a group of six) according to the technical rule (paribhāṣā) that "the number of verses follows the preceding hymn. According to the rule "the seer [is determined] from another source," it belongs to Agastya.
Likewise, because it has been stated, "This indeed belongs to the Aśvins," this [hymn] also belongs to the Aśvins according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding satisfaction and so forth.
According to the technical rule regarding the absence of a specific instruction, it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. It was introduced with the words, "Those two of you."
The application of these five hymns, beginning with "yuvo rājāṃsi" and excluding the third, has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra;
among them, this is the fifth.

We invoke you both today, and you both tomorrow, with many hymns as the dawn breaks forth—O Nāsatyas, wherever you may be, O sons of Heaven, most liberal givers for the sake of the noble patron. tā vām adya tau aparaṃ huvema ucchantyām uṣasi vahnir ukthaiḥ | nāsatyā kaha cit santāvaryo divo napātā sudāstarāya || 1 ||
"O you two who are renowned for your protective power, we invoke you both today on this day of sacrifice"—this is a prayer of benediction.
Likewise, "we invoke you both on another [day] as well.

The word *aparam* is used here in the sense of "on another [day]," because of its association with that meaning, and because it is seen so used in other mantras, such as: "May he protect us today and on the next" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 2.29.2).
Or rather, it refers even to another sacrifice.
At what time?
At dawn, when the deity Dawn (*uṣas*) is shining, that is, while she is driving away the darkness.
For at the time of dawn, the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra* are employed.

At the stated time, O Nāsatyas—those free from falsehood (*asatya*), the two sons of Heaven (*divo napātā*), or those who are like sons of the heavenly world—wherever you may be, existing in some place, we, the Hotṛ-priest, being such a bearer of praise (*vahniḥ*) and an impeller (*arthaḥ*) or master of praise, call upon you both with hymns (*ukthaiḥ*) for the sake of the sacrificer who gives most excellent oblations (*sudāstarāya*). This is the connection [of the verse].
In this case, the verb should be understood as being in the singular number;
or the word *vahiḥ* should be understood as being in the plural;
or else, there are two separate sentences.
"Since the Hotṛ priest recites you two as the two leaders of the troop (*ūrtugaṇaka*) from outside, therefore we, the sacrificers, invoke you two."

O Bull-like ones, rejoice well among us; strike down the Paṇis, crushing them with the night. Hear me through the utterances of my thoughts, O Heroes, you who are seekers and perceivers through your ears. asme | ūm | su | vṛṣaṇā | mādyethām | ut | paṇīn | hatam | ūrmyā | mardantā | śrutam | me | acchoktibhiḥ | matīnām | eṣṭā | narā | ni | caitārā | ca | karṇaiḥ || 2 ||
O Ashvins, you two who are showerers of desires, may you both rejoice well among us;
be thoroughly satisfied for our sake.
Likewise, having uprooted the Panis—the greedy traders—destroy them utterly.
Of what sort are you two? *Ūrmyā*:
this is a name for Night.
At night, they are exhilarated and gladdened;
or alternatively,
"wave" (ūrmi) is a name for Soma.
Because of such usage in passages beginning with "‘ūrmyaṃste pavitra ā’" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.64.11),
[the phrase refers to] those two who are rejoicing with our soma.
Such as you two, [I address] my thoughts (matīnām)— composed of pure Vedic utterances that bring about direct presence (acchoktibhiḥ)— unto me.
The genitive case is used for the object.

With the mind as the means, perform the praises; with the ears as the means of drawing near, hear what has been heard. O leaders (narā), you two are indeed seekers (eṣṭā) of our praises, as well as perceivers (nicetārā) and gatherers of those that have been obtained.
In place of this [verse], one should recite *nir itas*.
Because they are of such a nature, therefore [the text says]: "Listen!
"O Pūṣan, for the sake of glory, just as the gods Nāsatyas, having performed the separation, brought the bridal procession of Sūryā."

Your lofty steeds, born of the waters, are being yoked like the worn-out ages of Varuṇa’s many [deeds].
