Savitṛ, the Sun, intending to give his daughter Sūryā in marriage, summoned the gods to examine their respective merits; having arranged a contest, he decreed: "He who shall win this shall receive this maiden and a hymn composed of a thousand verses.

Agni won first; following him, the Aśvins also won, and having defeated Agni, they obtained the maiden and the thousand-verse hymn as their prize. Then Indra won by means of the *upāṃśu* [whispered] method.
And those two, being requested by those followers of the Aḍa doctrine, assigned to them various portions according to their respective capacities and maintained the Sūryā-sacrifice themselves.

This historical account is recorded in the Brāhmaṇa at *Prajāpatitvaṃ somaśca rājñe* (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 4.7), and has been elaborated upon by us in the first part of the eighth [chapter] regarding the verse *Ā vāṃ patiśvaṃ sakhyāya* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.119.5).
Here, he says:
O Pūṣan, nourisher, O Sūrya!
This [epithet] is also indicative of Candra, because the Sun and the Moon are indeed the Aśvins, as stated by Yāska: "The Sun and the Moon are the two Aśvins" (Nirukta 12.1).
Therefore, O Pūṣan-yukta— O nourishers, the Aśvins— it is said;
O nourishers, O Nāsatyas, you two gods who are free from falsehood (asatya), for the sake of glory (śriye)— that is to say, for the attainment of the hymn and the maiden—
[come] like one who has prepared an arrow (iṣukṛtā iva).

The word *iva* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed). Having already made themselves swift-moving like arrows for the sake of running the race, [they were] of *Sūryā*, the daughter of Savitṛ who bears this name.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*). "Sūryā" [is the object] "to hold onto" (*vahatum*) "the chariot," meaning they won the race.
Since this is so, therefore the *kakuhāḥ*— the praises in the form of *śastra*-recitations produced through ritual acts in the waters—

are proclaimed toward you both by the Hotṛ and other priests for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of Varuṇa, which possesses an uninterrupted flow and removes the sins that obstruct the fruit [of the rite].
The meaning is that they praise you two alone with the mantras contained in the *śastra*s at the time of the sacrifice.
*Yugā* means like worn-out ages; the word *iva* has the sense of "just as. The meaning is that just as the ancient times of sacrifice were, so too are the present ones.

The purport is that just as they praised you both in former times, so too do they now. May that delight of yours, O lovers of sweetness (*mādhvī*), be ours. Further the hymn of the poet Mānya. When, out of desire for glory, the people, O bounteous givers, rejoice in your heroic power. *asme* (for us); *sā* (that); *vām* (of you two); *mādhvī* (O lovers of sweetness); *ratiḥ* (delight); *astu* (let it be); *stomam* (the hymn); *hinotam* (further, promote); *mānyasya* (of Mānya); *kāroḥ* (the poet). *anu* (following); *yat* (when); *vām* (you two); *śravasyā* (out of desire for glory); *sudānu* (O bounteous givers); *suvīrye* (in heroic power); *carṣaṇīyaḥ* (the people); *madanti* (rejoice). || 4 ||
O Aśvins, may that well-known gift of yours—the *mādhvī*, consisting of vessels filled with honey—be ours.
For that purpose, further this hymn of praise, the song of the venerable and meditative singer Agastya; gladden it!

O you two who bestow excellent gifts (or fruits), because of your desire for glory (or fame) or for existence, the people (or human priests) rejoice in succession for the sake of the sacrificer who possesses great heroism (or beautiful strength); they rejoice either together with you both or by themselves.

This hymn has been fashioned for you both, O Aśvins, with well-turned verses by the Mānas, O bounteous lords. Come, O Nāsatyas, rejoicing for the sake of Vṛti, for her offspring, and for Agastya himself. eṣa vām stomo aśvināvakāri mānebhir maghavānā suvṛkti | yātaṃ vṛtistanayāya tmanai cāgastyai nāsatyā madantā || 5 || This hymn has been fashioned for you both, O Aśvins, with well-turned verses by the Mānas, O bounteous lords. Come, O Nāsatyas, rejoicing for the sake of Vṛti, for her offspring, and for Agastya himself.

O Aśvins, O bounteous ones, or rather, O you two who possess the horse characterized by the oblation— for you both, this hymn of praise has been well-fashioned, meaning it has been made with excellent removal of defects; or rather, it has been very carefully composed.
Of what nature is this?

Accompanied by *mānāni*, that is, by measures consisting of the offering of oblations; O Nāsatyas, you two who are free from falsehood (*asatya*), being exhilarated (*madantā*)—that is, rejoicing—in Agastya, the great seer of that name, [and likewise] in me, you have come to, or reached, the *vartiḥ*, meaning the dwelling or the sacrificial site.
For what purpose?
For the sake of obtaining a son, such as a daughter, and for one's own benefit.

We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness. O Aśvins, this hymn of praise has been offered unto you. Come hither by the broad paths traveled by the gods. May we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts. 6. We have crossed... of this... darkness... to the further shore. Unto you, O Aśvins, this hymn of praise has been offered. Come hither by the broad paths traveled by the gods. May we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts. 6.
The sixth [verse], "atāriṣma," has been explained.
‘Katarā pūrvā’ is the sixth hymn, consisting of eleven verses; it belongs to Agastya and is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
It is cataloged as ‘Kataraikādaśa dyāvāpṛthivīvyam.
On the sixth day of the Ābhiplavika rite, this hymn is recited as the insertion (nivid) in the Vaiśvadeva Śastra dedicated to Heaven and Earth.
"Of the third" [refers to] 1.
"the one worthy of honor" (ka-ja-jha-ta-mānanīya).
Thus it is formulated in the section: "'Which is the eastern one?'—this is for the Viśvedevas" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).
In the Mahāvrata as well, the Vaiśvadeva [Śastra] is this very same one containing the Dyāvāpṛthivī Nivid;
for there is an extension [of the rule] from the statement: "The third pressing begins with the last [verse] of the Abhiṣavika" (AiĀ 5.3.2).
"Which of the two is the first, which the later? How were they born? O sages, who truly knows? (RV 1.185.1).
He who by himself supports the universe—when his name unfolds like two wheels, day and night—who is the earlier, who the later?

How were the two born, O sages? Who truly knows it all? He who by himself supports the universe—when his name unfolds like two wheels, day and night. 1. Who is the earlier, who the later of the two? How were they born, O wise ones? Who truly knows it all? He who by himself supports the universe—when his name unfolds like two wheels, day and night.
Regarding their age: between these two, heaven and earth, which one was the earlier, having arisen first;
or which one was the later, occurring afterwards?
Such is the question concerning priority and posteriority.

The sense is that they exist together through an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). Likewise, "how" (*kathā*) means by what cause were they born; the meaning is: "what is the material cause of these two?

O sages (*kavayaḥ*), you who have transcendent vision and knowledge beyond the senses, speak! Who (*kaḥ*) truly knows (*veda*)—that is, who specifically understands after having discerned—the priority and sequence (*paurvāparya*) as well as the cause?
The meaning is that it is not known by anyone.
He states the reason for this ignorance:

because (vī), indeed (khalu), for that reason, he alone (nāma) supports (vibhṛtaḥ)—that is, sustains—the entire (viśvam) universe (jagat) without distinction (aviśeṣeṇa), by himself (ātmanaiva), independently of others (anyanairapekṣyeṇaiva).
Alternatively:
whatever collection of objects exists, namely the entire universe, all that is supported by the Self.
By this, even the reason for which we speak is itself withdrawn by these two; thus, the absence of a cause is established.
By the subsequent [verse], the absence of priority and posteriority is stated.
These two, heaven and earth, roll about like two wheels joined with a rim.
Here, the *Nirukta* passage beginning with "Which of these two is the earlier, which the later? (*Nirukta* 3.22) should be consulted.
The two vast, footless ones bear within themselves the moving embryo, which possesses feet;
like a son ever in the lap of his parents, O Heaven and Earth, protect us from the water.

The two [worlds], vast and moving not, bear within their lap the moving, footed embryo that is itself footless; they bear it eternally, as parents bear a son. O Heaven and Earth, protect us from the watery mist. 2.

These two, Heaven and Earth, though themselves footless (*apadī*), support and sustain the entire multitude of living beings—the vast, moving, and footed embryo—within their unshakable (*avicali*) wombs. Indeed, between these two, the whole world proceeds in safety. An illustration for this supporting is as follows:

Just as parents—meaning mother and father—sustain and nourish with affection their own son, who dwells eternally and firmly in their lap or embrace, so too [do you]. Now, he speaks directly: O Heaven and Earth, O Dyāvā-Pṛthivī!
The duality of both [the gods] exists through mutual dependence.
O Vāstoṣpati, protect us from great fear—that is, from this great danger—[and] from evil.
Or else:
*Abvat* means *abbaṃ mahat* (greatly great);
that is to say, "exceedingly. *Abba* is a name for "great."

Because the substitute [ādeśa] has been applied in the *dvandva* compound, the use of the word *rakṣatam* in the middle of the word *dyāvāpṛthivī* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Due to the non-existence of the vocative (*āmantrita*), there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent).

I invoke the blameless gift of Aditi, the peerless, sun-bright, and food-providing one, accompanied by homage. O Heaven and Earth, produce that for the singer; O Heaven and Earth, protect us from distress. anehasaḥ | dātram | aditeḥ | anarvam | huve | svar-vat | avadham | namas-vat | tat | rodasī iti | janayatam | jaritre | dyāvā | rakṣatam | pṛthivī iti | naḥ | ambāt || 3 ||
Of Aditi—
this is also an elliptical designation for the intermediate space (antarikṣa)—
I invoke, that is, I desire, the gift, the wealth, belonging to the indivisible Earth and likewise to such an intermediate space.
What kind of wealth is it?
It is *anehas*, meaning free from misfortune, calamity, and suffering, and consisting of happiness; *anarva*, meaning without conflict, without strife, and inexhaustible;
*svarvat*, meaning possessing heaven as its fruit on all sides; *avadha*, meaning unassailable; and *namasvat*, meaning possessed of food.
I invoke such wealth.
O *rodasī*, Heaven and Earth, generate—that is, produce—for the singer, the sacrificer, that wealth characterized by the desired [objects] which we long for.
The word *dyāvā* and so forth has already been explained.

May we follow after the two world-halves, Rodasī, the daughters of the gods, who do not grow weary and who protect with their aid. O both Heaven and Earth, you who belong to the gods, protect us with both your days from harm, O Mother! atapyamāne (not growing weary), avasā (with aid), avantī (protecting), anu (after), syāma (may we be), rodasī (the two world-halves), devaputre (daughters of the gods), ubhe (both), devānām (of the gods), ubhayebhiḥ (with both), ahnām (days), dyāvā (O Heaven), rakṣatam (protect), pṛthivī (O Earth), naḥ (us), ambāt (O Mother). 4.
When one who lacks mastery is tormented by decline—by some inferior state brought about by oneself that is worse than one's own previous condition—and by prosperity [of others].
This is the form of the act of austerity, which has sovereignty as its fruit.
*Atapyamāne* means not being scorched, nor being oppressed by others.
*Avasā* means with food; *avantī* means satisfying. *Devaputre* refers to the gods as the masters of discourse and humans as their sons. They are of the aforementioned nature.
Humans and gods, who abide in the two worlds, are called "sons" because they depend upon them.
Such are both these *rodasī*, heaven and earth, the days of the gods;
this is also an elliptical expression for their nights.
By means of the two kinds of diverse riches—characterized by cold, heat, and so forth—belonging to the shining days and nights;
that is to say, for the sake of obtaining them.
For that purpose, may we both follow after you and experience [them].
The remainder has been explained.

Meeting together, two young women, moving as one, sisters and kinswomen in the lap of their parents; smelling the navel of the world, O Heaven and Earth, protect us from distress. *saṃgacchamāne* (meeting together), *yuvatī* (two young women), *samante* (moving as one), *svasārā* (sisters), *jāmī* (kinswomen), *pitroḥ* (of the parents), *upasthe* (in the lap); *abhijighrantī* (smelling), *bhuvanasya* (of the world), *nābhim* (the navel); *dyāvā* (O Heaven), *rakṣatam* (protect), *pṛthivī* (O Earth), *naḥ* (us), *ambāt* (from distress). 5.
1. Or, according to Jha₁, "not being heated.
2. According to Jha₁, "by means of dharmas. *Saṃgacchamāne* means "meeting" or "being joined together" by way of mutual assistance.
The distinction between "rain" (*vṛṣṭi*) and "shower" (*vipruṣ*) is that they stand in a relationship of mutual benefit to one another.

Alternatively, it is said that although the two were previously joined together, they later separated and performed the acts of raining and showering; subsequently, having been requested by humans, the two were wedded by the gods and became united once more.
This meaning is recorded in the Brāhmaṇa texts, such as: "Heaven and Earth were together" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.3.2).

They are *vyuvatī*, meaning either eternally youthful or mutually mingling; they are *samante*, meaning in all things, or at the same limit, or at the same boundary; they are *svasārā*, being sisters to one another;
and they are *jāmī*, being kinswomen, because they were produced together from Prajāpati. Thus, there is mutual kinship (*jāmitva*) between them.

And thus there are two Vedic verses: "Heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and also the light" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.190.3), and "From whom they fashioned heaven and earth" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.31.7).

[The two goddesses] are kissing—that is, smelling or touching—the *nābhi*, the connecting bond, namely water, which is situated in the *upastha*, the lap or womb, of those two parents who stand in the place of the father of all, the protectors; [they do so] for the sake of the *bhuvana*, the multitude of beings.
From the Vedic mantra passage beginning with "This water is common" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.164.51), it is well known that both [the Aśvins] bestow water;
as such, may you two protect us.
I invoke with the Truth the two wide, flowing, great ones, the pair who are the birthplace of the gods through their favor;
they who possess beautiful countenances bestow immortality—O Heaven and Earth, protect us from the waterless waste.

The two wide ones, the flowing ones, the great ones, by means of *ṛta* I invoke with the aid of the gods. Those two who, as the progenitors of the gods, bestow immortality—O Heaven and Earth, you of beautiful countenance, protect us from evil! 6.

The two wide ones (*vurvī*), the two extensive ones (*vistīrṇe*), the two flowing ones (*vsrbanī*), the two that serve as the foundation for the seat (*sadanādhārabhūte*), the two great ones (*bṛhatī*), the two of great majesty (*mahānubhāve*) belonging to the gods—
this is an elliptical expression [meaning] belonging to gods,
humans, and so forth— the two mothers (*janitrī*) who, by means of their favor (*avasā*) as the cause, produce rain (*vr̥ṣṭi*).
I invoke you by means of rain from the gods, by the satisfaction of the gods, and by the sacrifice performed as the occasion;
that is to say, for the sake of the oblation to the gods, for our sacrifice. O you two of beautiful countenance, possessing excellent forms, who maintain the immortal water—those two of you I invoke.
The remainder is clear.
I address with reverence at this sacrifice the two vast, wide, and spacious worlds, whose ends are far away;
may those two fortunate ones, who are victorious and well-disposed, protect us, O Heaven and Earth, from the waters.

O wide one! O broad one! O vast one! O you whose ends are far! I address you with reverence at this sacrifice. May you two, who are fortunate, most auspicious, and swift in action—Heaven and Earth—protect us from misfortune. 7.
O you two who are vast, lofty, great, wide, expansive, manifoldly extending, multiform, whose ends are far distant— that is to say, boundless—
such as you two are, in this sacrifice, with reverence (namas)— meaning by means of praise that effects homage— [may you act] toward one another as mutual benefactor and beneficiary.
I address you, approaching you; that is, I praise you.
Furthermore, of what nature are you two?
O auspicious ones (*subhage*), possessing beautiful splendor; O well-crossing ones (*supratī*), possessing excellent gifts—those two of you who sustain the entire world, I address and praise.
Whatever sin we have committed against the gods, or against a friend, or against our own household lord—may this prayer be an expiation for them;
O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil speech.
Whatever offense we have committed against the gods, or against a friend, or even against our own kinsman—may this prayer be an atonement for them. O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil! 8.

Whatever offense or transgression we have committed against Heaven and Earth, or against the gods, at any time— that very act of non-sacrificing, we have done at all times; or whatever we have done against a friend or a beloved companion,
or against the lord of the household.
Those who are wicked—toward their husbands, sons-in-law, or spouses—to perpetually commit acts such as attributing faults and instigating quarrels;
in order to bring about the removal of these aforementioned sins, may this act consisting of your praise become [a means of purification]. May it be so! May it come to pass! May it exist!
The passage beginning with *cāveti* has already been explained.

Here, in every instance, the prayer "protect! protect! without a mantra in another form is entirely appropriate for those two [the Aśvins], because it is impossible for them to have many thoughts such as those of the Aśvinīs and so forth.
Therefore, they are prayed to in this way: "remain in your own place and be favorable."
May both noble praises protect me; may both assist me with their aid and protection. O gods, even though he be very liberal, may we, rejoicing in his service, find strength for our journey.

May both of you, the two who are beneficial to men, protect me; may both of you attend to me with aid and protection. Even against a wealthy enemy, let us prevail for the sake of one who gives better gifts; rejoicing in nourishment, O gods, may we enjoy long life. 9.

May both praises (*śaṃsā*)— the two domains of Heaven and Earth, both praises beneficial to men (*naryā*), such as these two praises based on both [deities]— protect me. Or rather, because they are designated in this way, there is the masculine gender for the two deities presiding over Heaven and Earth.
Likewise, may both protectors, Heaven and Earth, attend to me with their protection;
or rather, may both blessings, which bring welfare to living beings and pertain to both this world and the next, reach me.
Likewise, may both those aids belonging to the two presiding deities of those [worlds] be near us for the sake of our protection.

O gods—indeed, all the gods contained within heaven and earth—O praisers, we who are the singers, being exhilarated and gladdened by the food characterized by Soma, [may they be] exceedingly well-bestowing, for the sake of most excellent giving. *Bhūri* (much) and *cit* (even/also)—*cit* is used here for emphasis.
We desire to enjoy wealth that has been fully honored;
or alternatively,
"aryaḥ" is a form of the genitive case.
The meaning is that it is even more difficult than from a lord such as a king;
the rest is the same.

The two verses beginning with “ṛtaṃ dive” are the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the oblation (*havis*) in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivīya*).
This is stated in the *Khaṇḍa* section [of the *Śrautasūtra*] as follows: “‘ṛtaṃ dive’, ‘tad avocam pṛthivyai’—these two” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
1. [The reading] *mantramantareṇa* does not exist in manuscript Jha.
2. [This is] because it is possible by means of this [term], just as in the case of Āśvinī and so forth;
[this is stated in] Ka. 137.

I, the wise one, have first proclaimed this Truth (*ṛta*) to Heaven and Earth for their protection. May they both guard us from reproach and from misfortune in our encounter; may Father and Mother protect us with their aids.

The Truth—this I have proclaimed to Heaven and to Earth for them to hear, being most wise at the first instance. May they both protect me from reproach and from ill-will in the encounter; may Father and Mother guard me with their protections. 10.

"I, Sumedhas, possessed of beautiful wisdom, have spoken— indeed, I am speaking— the first, most excellent, and preeminent *ṛta*, the hymn of praise that is pleasing to *diva*, the deity of heaven, and to *pṛthivī*, the deity of the earth."
For what purpose?
"For renown," that is, for being heard from all sides.

Furthermore, may both—the Father, the protector, the heavenly world (dyuloka), and the Mother, the creator of crops and other things, the earth—protect us from "blame," that is, from censurable suffering and from sin.

Likewise, "in the encounter" (*abhīke*); "nearby" (*antika*) is a name for that; "in close proximity indeed," with "protections" (*avaubhiḥ*), meaning with "complete satisfactions" (*abhitatarpaṇaiḥ*), [let them] "protect," that is, preserve [us].
May this be true, O Heaven and Earth, O Father and Mother, as I address you here:
may we, through the protections of the gods, be the lowest [in sin] and yet find food, strength, and a life-giving abundance.

This is it: O Heaven and Earth! Let it be true! O Father! O Mother! Since I address you here, become the lowest of the gods with your protections; grant us a dwelling, food, and a stronghold that bestows swift life. 11.
"O Heaven and Earth"—that is, "Heaven and Earth," may this hymn being performed by us "be true," meaning let it be non-false, let it be fruitful.
Having said "this," he asks what that is; [he replies:
"O Father Heaven, O Mother Earth, may that hymn which I address to you both here in this sacrifice, speaking as I approach you, be true."
"O you two who are most near— meaning closest— to us, the praising gods; being ever-present, become endowed with protections (*avobhiḥ*), that is, with means of satisfaction."
The remainder has been explained.
The seventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "ā na iḷābhiḥ," is composed by Agastya, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to the Viśvedevas.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry: "ā no vaiśvadevam.
Its application is determined by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

May the god Savitṛ, the lord of all men, come to us with nourishing offerings for our protection and for our fair praise. And may he, like youthful exhilarating ones, bring the whole world here at the time of our arrival, through our inspired thought.

May Savitṛ, the god of all men, come with his nourishing powers for our enjoyment and for our fair praise; so that the young, exhilarating ones may be with us, and the whole world may attend to our prayer at the time of rest.

"May Savitṛ—the impeller, the Sun, who is dear to the welfare of all living beings—come (vetu) to our sacrifice with good praise (suśasti)—the *luk* elision of the case-ending [leaving us for *asmadīye*]—that is, with beautiful recitations and hymns; together with precious gifts (*pradaiyaiḥ ratnaiḥ*), or alternatively, with the *iḷās* (the offerings), by which term those residing upon the earth are designated; together with the deities situated on the earth; and Viśvānara. [From the commentary: "From censurable sin; he who is fond of performing what is beneficial for all creatures; may the impeller, the Sun, the god, come."

O you who are ever-youthful, or rather, the perpetual rejuvenators and the minglers of the sacrifice— come toward us at our arrival, that is, at our sacrificial gathering; with *manīṣā*, meaning through the power of mental vision or by your own will—
the word *api* here expressing possibility—
may you also gladden us as you dwell within our thoughts.
"Vyathā" means "the entire world"; this is also an indication of His state. Or rather, it means that just as the entire phenomenal universe rests in Me, so too do we.
Alternatively, the word *jagat* refers to human beings in the form of sacrificers; the meaning is: "Just as all sacrificers abide in me, so [do you]."
In the Vaiśvadeva animal sacrifice, the verse "ā no viśve" is the invitatory formula (*puronuvākyā*) for the oblation:
"May the praise of the gods come to us; may all the gods come to us, drawing near" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7):
"May all the gods come to us, drawing near—Mitra, Aryaman, Varuṇa, in harmony."

May all the gods come to us, the companions—Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa, well-disposed—so that they, as our all-enrichers, may make us victorious, and may their arrow not strike us like a fragile thing.
May all the gods, our kin, come to us—Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa, well-disposed—so that they, as our all-enrichers, may make us victorious, and may their arrow not strike us like a fragile thing. 2.
O all you gods, who are the strikers (*vāskrāḥ*)—those who leap upon or assail the enemies—come to our sacrifice; let them approach.
Who are they?
Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman—all three of them, being of one accord (*sajoṣaḥ*), let them come.

But let all the Viśve Devas come so that they may be our strengtheners, increasing us; let them come so that they do not make our own weapon (*śarvaḥ*) weak or deficient through their excellent overcoming of enemies.
I praise Agni, your most beloved guest, with hymns of praise, you who are abundant and united in spirit.
May Varuṇa, of good renown, and the praised patron (*sūriḥ*) grant us nourishment and carry us across [difficulties].

I praise Agni, your most beloved guest, with hymns of praise—may he be well-pleased and victorious. May Varuṇa, of glorious renown, be gracious to us; may he, the patron praised by the noble, bring us strengthening food and deliver us from the enemy. 3.

O gods, Agni is your most beloved (*vpreṣṭham*), because he delights all and is the bringer of joy to everyone; therefore, among the gods, Agni is the most beloved. Him I choose as a guest (*vatithim*); I praise him, I laud him.
The middle [verb] is used by way of transposition.
By what means?
By *vaśastibhiḥ*, that is, by recitations, praises, and hymns.
What am I like?
One who bestows quickly (*tūrviṇi*), one who wins swiftly (*tūrṇavani*), one who distributes rapidly (*śīghra-sambhaktṛ*); and one who is well-pleased in harmony with you (*sajoṣas*).
Or rather:
These are the specific epithets:
he who is swift, the sharer of the sacrifice, and well-disposed— rejoicing together with you—
I praise that Agni.

In whatever manner Varuṇa—the god of that name—dwells as one of beautiful renown (*sukīrti*) for us, so may he do. For in Vedic hymns such as "I beg the beautiful renown of the abundant Varuṇa" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 2.28.1), this very beautiful renown is to be sought from Varuṇa. May this Varuṇa, who is ever celebrated among the *arīs*—the non-givers—and who is the impeller (*sūri*) for the slaying of enemies or for the dawn, fill (*parṣat*) our dwellings with food.
The meaning is: "In that same way, we too praise him.
1. *ja-aitu*.
"May he come toward you with homage, desiring to conquer, like the night and the dawn, like a cow that yields milk well."
On the same day, measuring out the hymn of praise within the diverse garment, he has become one with wealth in this world.

I approach you with reverence, desiring to win through my devotion—Night and Dawn, like two well-milking cows—measuring out the hymn on a single day, though you are of different forms, within this same udder.
O gods, having approached you with reverence, with an oblation, or with salutation, I desire [to enter] into your service out of a desire to conquer the wicked.
This form is the first person singular of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) derived either from the root *i*, meaning "to go," or from the root *īṣ*, meaning "to move" and so forth.
I worship.
At what time?
Day and night—both by day and by night.
Or rather:
I also approach the deities of day and night;
there is an illustration for the act of going.
The cow that yields milk easily is like a cow that comes to the milker’s house for milking; acting in this way,
she pours forth diverse forms into this common udder when it has been filled.
And may Tvaṣṭṛ come toward us, well-pleased together with our patrons at the pressing;
and may Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, who fills the people and is most eminent among men, come here to us.

And may Tvaṣṭṛ come toward us, well-pleased together with the patrons at the arrival [of the sacrifice]; may Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the protector of the people, the most powerful among men, come here to us. 6.
May the divine Tvaṣṭṛ also come toward us now; may he come to this sacrifice.
And having arrived, may he take delight, or abide for the sake of our prosperity and praise.
In this context, it is used in the sense of praise.

"Praiseworthy" means in such a manner; when the sacrifice—which is to be approached—has become the occasion, let [Indra] be "in harmony" (sajoṣāḥ), meaning possessing equal delight, with the patrons (sūribhiḥ), the praisers, and the officiating priests (ṛtvigbhiḥ). This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Likewise, Vṛtrahā is the slayer of Vṛtra; Carṣaṇiprāḥ refers to the people—
the human sacrificers—
and he is the fulfiller of their desires.
Most powerful, most abundant, and greatest—endowed with vast virtues, may he come, may he approach us, the men, in this very rite.
And indeed, our thoughts, yoked like horses, lick him as cows lick their young calf;
we, embracing him—the most fragrant among men—approach him with songs like wives.
And indeed, our thoughts, yoked like horses, lick him as cows lick their young calf; our songs, like wives approaching their husbands, embrace him, the most fragrant among men.

Moreover, our hymns—our praises consisting of the yoking of horses, meaning those whose impulse is like that of horses—lick, that is, taste and praise, this very Indra, who is ever-youthful and eternally young. In this regard, there is an illustration: just as milch-cows lick their calf, even as a suckling, so do they lick him.
He says that very thing:

"Him, him indeed—this one, the most fragrant (*surabhiṣṭama*) among men (*narām*), that is, among the sacrificers (*yajamānānām*)—you, the *janayaḥ*, the producers of fruit, [and] the *giraḥ*, the hymns of praise, *nasantaḥ* pervade him.
The root *nas* has the sense of pervading."
In this regard, there is an illustration:
as wives (janayaḥ) do not produce their husbands (patyaḥ), so [the elements] do not produce the husband (pati).
And may the Maruts, with their increased hosts, sit down together with Rodasī in harmony;
they whose horses are spotted like rushing streams, who are destroyers of enemies, and who are gods allied with Mitra.

And may the Maruts, with their mighty hosts, sit down together with us, as well as Rodasī, being of one mind—like chariots with spotted horses, like steeds that are irresistible, like gods who are joined with Mitra. 8.
Moreover, O Maruts, may you now sit together with us at this very sacrifice of ours; from which place? From the two worlds, heaven and earth—or rather, let heaven and earth also come along.
1. Let them come; let them approach.
Of what nature are these Maruts?
They have a vast army, their strength is fully increased, they are of one mind, they are of uniform thought, and they have spotted horses—that is, horses with white spots on their backs.
‘The *pṛṣṭhya* [hymns] belong to the Maruts,’ says Yāska (Nirukta 1.15.6).
They are called *vranayaḥ* because they possess the nature of *vraṇa* (wounds/injury); or they are *vrathāḥ* because their nature is *vraṇa*, or they are *vrathavantaḥ* (possessors of *vratha*).
The suffix expressing possession (*matvartha*) is elided.
Or rather: the devourers, the destroyers, the violent ones, the wide-striding,
the flesh-eaters.
"Vriśāḥ" means enemies.
"Vteṣām vattāraḥ" refers to those who deal with them; "mitrayujaḥ devāḥ" means gods joined with friends—dealers who are endowed with friendliness—or alternatively, officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Or else: [the text continues].
Just as other gods go forth endowed with benevolence (*maitrī*),
so too do they proceed when their harnessed teams (*prayuj*) are yoked according to their greatness, for they are mindful of it.

O worshipful ones, may this our devotion toward you be both nourishing and a place of rest; may it strive among the gods for wealth, so that we may find strengthening food and a life-sustaining community. 11. This—your devotion—toward us, O worshipful ones, let it be both nourishing and a place of rest; it which strives among the gods, seeking wealth, may we find strengthening food and a life-sustaining community. 11.
O worshipful gods who are worthy of sacrifice, may this renowned *dīdhiti*— your own radiance— be for us a nourisher, ever-encompassing, a seat,
and a dwelling place. May that very radiance, which seeks the *vasus* and abounds in wealth, be directed toward the gods with constant effort to illuminate them as well.
The word "vidyam" has been explained.

The eighth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “*pituṃ nu*,” is addressed to Agni; it belongs to the seer Agastya and is composed in the *gāyatrī* meter. However, the first verse is in the *anuṣṭubh* and *uṣṇih* meters, because it has been stated: “In the group of five [verses], the first two are *anuṣṭubhs*” (Anuvāka 5.7).
The third, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eleventh verses constitute five *anuṣṭubh*s.
Thus says the *Anukramaṇikā*: “*Pitum nu* is a hymn of eight verses in the *gāyatrī* meter; the first verse is in *anuṣṭubh*, while the third, fifth, and the next three [verses] are *anuṣṭubh*s.
Regarding the ritual application (*viniyoga*), Śaunaka states: “One should worship with the hymn *Pitum nu*; it is prescribed for the *upasthāna* (homage) performed at dawn.”
One should always honor food and eat that which has been consecrated as an oblation.
He shall have no disease born of food, and even poison shall become nectar;
having drunk this mercury, one should recite the mantra that destroys poison.
"One should eat neither from a boat, nor while impure, nor when the food is loathsome;
rather, one should give it away, honor it, and offer it as an oblation. Then no misfortune whatsoever shall befall him, nor shall he suffer from disease" (Ṛgvidhāna 1.148–151).

I shall now praise Pitu, the possessor of great laws and power, by whose might Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb. I shall now praise Pitu, the possessor of great laws and power, by whose might Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb.

I, Agastya, now quickly praise—that is, I extol—the protector (*pitu*), the great (*mahaḥ*) upholder of all (*dharmāṇam*), and the source of power (*tarviṣīm*). Or alternatively: [the text continues].
It is the sustainer of the great world;

by whose power, strength, and capability Indra—though stretched across the three locations beginning with the earth, thus being most extensive and renowned for his fame—crushed Vṛtra so that he was "viparva," meaning his joints were severed and his connections broken. Indeed, he destroyed him.
O sweet food, O Soma-food, O honey-food, O nourishment! We choose you; be our protector. 2. "O sweet," "O food," "O honey," "O food!"—we choose you; be our protector. 2.
1. One should not eat while making a hissing sound.

O *svādo*, you who are to be tasted; o *pito*, you who protect; o *madho*, you who possess sweetness; o *pito*, you who are the food that is the means of nourishment—we, *vayam*, *tvā*, you, *svā*, well, *vadhmahe*, we serve.
In all these instances, because the preceding [syllables] are not *anudātta* and lack a specific denotation, they are subject to suppression (*abhighātatva*).
However, because the unaccented syllables have specific meanings, they possess the quality of being emphasized (abhighātatva).
The repeated hearing of the word "father" (pitṛ) is for the purpose of making known his excellence.
O Father, be our protector—that is, our satisfier.
Having drunk of us, move forward as a benefactor with your auspicious aids; be a source of delight, free from hostility, a most gracious friend, and one who is not double-tongued. 3.
Come to us, O Food, with your auspicious protections—auspicious, a source of delight, not to be hated, a friend, most kind, and free from duplicity. 3.

Since you are *śiva*, auspicious, therefore come toward us with *śivābhiḥ*—that is, with *ūtibhiḥ*, protections endowed with auspiciousness. Having arrived, be *mayobhūḥ*, the bringer of happiness; *adviṣeṇyaḥ*, one whose essence is not to be hated, meaning one whose essence is dear; a *sakhā*, acting like a friend; *suśevaḥ*, therefore very pleasant; and *advayāḥ*, free from duality—meaning remain possessed of these aforementioned qualities and do not be devoid of them.
Alternatively, this is a statement by way of illustration:
"Just as a friend who is very kind, non-dual, free from contradiction in thought and action, and a source of joy is one who is not treacherous—so may you also be.
O Father, those juices of yours are established throughout the realms, resting like the winds in heaven. (4)
These juices of yours, O Food, are spread throughout the regions, resting in heaven like the winds. 4.
Those sweet and other flavors belonging to you, O Soma, are established in accordance with the worlds—the realms and the objects situated within them—in various ways.
An illustration of this manifold establishment is as follows:
they are like the winds that rest in the sky and the intermediate space, pervading them in that manner.
These [powers] of yours, O Food, you bestow; you, O Food, are most sweet. The flavors of juices, like powerful-necked [bulls], rush forth. 5.
Thine, O Pita, are these; grant them. Thine, O most sweet Pita, are the flavors of juices; they surge forth like those with thick necks. 5.
"O *pita*, O protector—those men who seek their own welfare (*svadarthin*) become your enjoyers; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Who are those men?
O most delicious (*svādiṣṭha*), O most sweet (*svādutama*) *pita*, O protector—by your grace, they become those who give to you, who bestow [offerings] upon you."
Or rather,
[the repetition] is for the sake of showing respect;
for they consider that there is greater significance in repetition.

Furthermore, those who are the "tasters" (*svātmānaḥ*)—that is, the enjoyers or consumers—of the six flavors (*rasānām*), such as sweetness and the rest, are like those with "many necks" (*tuvigrīvāiva*), [consuming] the objects located in the world (*loka-sthānārthān*). (Note: Regarding the variants, *jha* reads *lokasthānārthān*; *khapha* reads *lokasthānārthān*.)
*tuviti* is a name for "much. Those with elongated necks indeed (*eva*) go forth—that is, they proceed or move about.
The word *iva* has the sense of *eva*, or it is a mere filler (*pūraṇa*).
It is well known that on the earth, things indeed become utterly essence-less through force;
for when one fasts, the neck hangs down.
Or rather:
The sense is that those who consume your juices come to possess as many necks as there are flavors, due to the great abundance of those juices;
thus, this is a praise of the *añja* tree as being endowed with many flavors.
O Food, you are great; within the mind of the gods, you are established.
By your beautiful banner, you have slain the serpent Ahi.
O Food, for thee indeed, the great one, the mind of the gods has been set; it has been made beautiful by thy banner. By thy protection, he slew the serpent. 6.
O Father, the mind of the great ones worthy of worship—the gods such as Indra and others—has been placed and fixed within you;
even immortality, having abandoned [all else], abides in you alone.
O Father, your beautiful and perfect banner [is manifested] through you.

Kindled today, you shine as a god among the gods, O conqueror of thousands. As the messenger and the sage, carry the oblations. Fully kindled, you now reign as a god among the gods, O conqueror of thousands. As the messenger and the sage, carry the oblations.

O Agni, kindled (*samiddha*) by the gods—the officiating deities—and being thus a god yourself, shining brightly, or indeed kindled together with the gods; being so kindled, you shine forth (*vrājasi*) today on this day of sacrifice.
O conqueror of thousands (*sahasrajit*), victor over a thousandfold wealth or enemies, you are the messenger (*dūta*) of the gods, the bearer of their oblations, or the invoker;
for it is said in the Śruti: "Agni was the messenger of the gods" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.8.5).
O Krāntadarśin, you who abide in the cause, carry our oblations (havya), that is, convey our sacrificial offerings (havīṃṣi) to the gods.

Tanūnapāt, as you proceed, the sacrifice is anointed with honey; bestowing thousandfold nourishments. (2) Tanūnapāt! As you go toward the cosmic order (*ṛta*), the sacrifice is thoroughly anointed with honey, bestowing thousandfold refreshments. (2)
*Tanūnapāt* is the one who causes the body of the sacrifice to descend;
or alternatively,
since it is stated that "the waters are here called *tanvaḥ*," he is the one who causes the waters to descend, or their offspring.
The plants are non-dual; from the plants comes fire—thus you are ours.
You are the sacrifice, worthy of worship;
or, you are the sacrifice because you are the one who brings the sacrifice to completion.
Such is this fire: it anoints— that is, it unites— the sacrificer who has performed the sacrifice, who is striving toward it, or who is engaged in its performance, with his desired object,
by means of the sweet [oblation] consisting of soma and other substances.
What is he doing?
Bestowing—that is, holding out for the sake of the sacrificers—thousandfold *iṣas*, meaning foodstuffs of that number.

Being invoked and worthy of praise, bring hither the gods who are worthy of sacrifice; O Agni, you are the winner of thousands. 3. Being invoked, worthy of praise, bring hither the gods who are worthy of sacrifice; O Agni, you are the winner of thousands. 3.
O Agni, being invoked by us, worthy of praise by us, and named *hṛp*, bring hither—the gods who partake in the sacrifice—for our sake.
O Agni, you are the giver of thousands, that is, of immeasurable wealth.

With power they have strewn the eastward-pointing sacrificial grass, which possesses a thousand heroes, where you, O Ādityas, shine forth in splendor. 4. Eastward-pointing; the sacrificial grass; with power; possessing a thousand heroes; they have strewn; where; O Ādityas; you shine forth. 4.

"Facing east" (*vprācīnam*) means having its tip directed toward the east; "possessing a thousand heroes" (*sahasravīram*) means that from which the gods—who are the specific drivers away (*vīrāḥ*) of enemies numbering in the thousands—proceed.
Alternatively, it means that by which sons and others of unlimited number (*aparimitavīrāḥ*) are produced.
Endowed with the power of the mantra's characteristics, the officiating priests (ṛtvijas) spread and covered the sacrificial grass (barhis).
Upon that sacrificial grass where you, O Ādityas—sons of Aditi—shine forth in various ways, they spread it as was fitting.
1. *Jha-1-prasiddha*: 2. *Kha-pha*: the deity named thus;
Virāṭ, Samrāṭ, Vimbvī, Prambvī, and Bahī.
Let the firm [stones] drip with clarified butter.
The wide ones, the sovereign ones, the bright ones, the lofty ones, the many and the numerous doors through which the clarified butters have flowed. || 5 ||
Virāṭ:
those who shine pre-eminently; this is a singular form with an indeclinable [prefix]. Samrāṭ: those who shine perfectly, that is, in a most venerable manner.

Here too, the singular number is used with the indeclinable [particle]. *Vimbvīḥ* means "becoming manifold"; *vimbyaḥ* means "becoming manifold"; *prambvīḥ* means "becoming preeminent"; *prambyaḥ* means "becoming preeminent. *Bahīḥ*, *vahvyaḥ*, and *bhūyasīḥ* refer to those doors—the gates of the sacrificial hall—which exist in great numbers according to world-renowned counts; these flow, or flow forth, *ghṛtāni*—that is, waters—for the benefit of living beings. Or alternatively:
The words *vahnībhūyasīḥ* and so forth are expressions of number;
the remaining terms are their names.
For they are well-adorned with fine gold and beautiful ornaments; shining with splendor, may the two Dawns sit here.
O ye two of beautiful luster, well-adorned with excellent form, shining forth with splendor—may the two Dawns sit here. 6.

Upon the two well-known deities of day and night, who possess beautiful golden ornaments (*surukme*), who are well-formed (*supeśasā*), and who thus shine exceedingly with splendor and beauty—indeed, they blaze forth preeminently—the two Dawns (*uṣasau*) [are praised]. (Note: *hi* is not subject to the rule of *anighāta* here due to its connection with *uṣasau*). Such are those two Dawns.
This is a figurative designation for the night;
the word *uṣas* is a figurative designation for the day.
Let both the night and the day sit down—that is, having arrived, let them remain or come—here, on this very day.
For the two divine Hotṛs, the sages of beautiful splendor, shall indeed perform this sacrifice of ours as the first.
