"Prathama" is a name for the primary;
"prathamau" means the two most relevant to the context;
"hi" indicates what is well-known.

With beautiful splendor and pleasant speech, may these two divine Hotṛs— the invokers of the gods or the performers of the oblation, the two sages— perform this sacrifice of ours, or go toward it. O Bhāratī, Ilā, and Sarasvatī— all of you whom I invoke— I impel you for our glory.
O Bhāratī, O Ilā, O Sarasvatī—whatever goddesses you all are, I address you; impel us toward prosperity. 8.

He is Bhārata; Bhārata is Āditya (the Sun). Bhāratī is that which is related to him. O such goddess of the heavenly world, O Ilā, goddess of the earth, O Sarasvatī! "Saras" means either speech or water; O such goddess of the intermediate space, O Goddess! These are the deities beginning with Śrī. [Note: 1. "Saras" is so called because it flows (sarati); 2.
according to Ka, Jha, Jha, Jha, Ta, it means wind or water.]
They say that these are indeed the forms of the specific power of the sun.

Those three, all of you, I approach and praise; do you impel us toward prosperity and abundance. For Tvaṣṭṛ is the lord who has fashioned all forms and all cattle; for those, pray grant us increase. Tvaṣṭṛ, for he is the lord, has fashioned all forms and all cattle; for those, pray grant us increase. 9. Tvaṣṭṛ | forms | for | lord | cattle | all | has fashioned | of them | for us | increase | hither | pray sacrifice. 9.

Tvaṣṭṛ is the deity presiding over the sacrificial vessels used as instruments of sacrifice; he is indeed capable (*prabhu*) of fashioning the forms—the seminal essences (*retas*)—created within the womb into their various forms.
The word *hi* serves to indicate what is well-known from other Vedic texts, according to the Śruti:
“As far as the emitted semen [extends], Tvaṣṭṛ fashions the forms” (Tai. Saṃ. 1.5.9.1–2).
That god thoroughly anoints—that is, clearly manifests—all our cattle, such as cows and the like;
from the root *añj* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the form is *samānaje* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), with the substitution of *nu* for *na* according to the rule "tasmānnuḍ aci.
Now, [he speaks] directly.
Sacrifice for us—that is, perform worship from all sides—for the sake of the increase and prosperity of those anointed animals; this is the intended meaning.
O Vanaspati, by your own power, release the offering to the gods; may Agni make the oblations savory. upa | tmanyā | vanaspate | pārthaḥ | devebhyaḥ | sṛja | agniḥ | havyāni | siṣvadat ||10||

O Vanaspati, O divine sacrificial post, by yourself, through your own self, bestow—produce—the food in the form of the animal for the gods, beginning with Agni. For if you do not exist, there would be no binding of the animal, and consequently, no oblation. When you have acted thus, may Agni make the offerings (*havyāni*) sweet; may he render them palatable.

Agni, the leader of the gods, is anointed with the Gāyatra; he shines amidst the utterances of Svāhā. 11 Agni, the leader, of the gods, is anointed with the Gāyatra; he shines amidst the utterances of Svāhā. 11
This Agni is the leader of the gods, going before them toward the battle with the Asuras;
or rather,
among the gods, Agni alone is the leader toward the sacrifice.
For this very reason, precisely because he is not led forward (*apraṇī*), the word *agni* is established.
The *Nirukta* states: "Why is Agni called *apraṇī*? (Nirukta 7.14).
Such a one is *samajyate*—he is properly characterized or indicated—by the *gāyatra*, that is, by the mantra indicated by that term.

During the *svāhākṛti* offerings, amidst the utterances of *svāhā*, and while the oblations (*havis*) are being presented to the serpents, he shines—indeed, he blazes intensely. According to the view of some, these deities of the progeny are the presiding deities of the constituent parts of the sacrifice; thus, by means of them, the sacrifice itself is being praised.
Others maintain that it is merely another name for Agni.
The tenth hymn, beginning with "O Agni, lead," consists of ten verses; it is situated in the eighth book, is composed in the Triṣṭubh metre, and is addressed to Agni.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: “‘agne nayādyāvādyānayam’.
Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the *Traiṣṭubha* metre for both the *Prātaranuvāka* and the *Āśvina-śastra*.

This is because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “Now, regarding this [verse]: ‘agne nayāgre...’; from among those [verses], one should extract the three highest ones from the highest” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.13).
Regarding this, Śaunaka says: "If one has set out upon a wrong path, or if one should ever encounter eight paths,
or if one should enter upon a path after performing a censurable act,
one should offer clarified butter with each verse of the hymn beginning with 'agne naya'."
"One should constantly recite [the Vāmadevya] with self-restraint, or perform the *upasthāna* [worship] of the Sun" (*Ṛgvidhāna* 1.151–153).
These [verses] beginning with *ā ghā* are prescribed for the *Śravaṇākarma* rite:
"On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa..."
Regarding this, it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having offered with the four verses beginning with *agne naya supathā rāye asmān*, verse by verse" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.1.4).
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni (*āgneya-paśu*), these two are the first two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*) and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "*agne naya supathā rāye asmān; pāhi no agne pāyubhirajasraiḥ*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).
The first [verse] is the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the cake-offering to Agni at the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice;
that same [verse] serves as the offering verse (*yājyā*) at the *udayanīya* sacrifice.

Regarding this, it is stated in the Sūtra: "'O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth... we have come upon the path of the gods'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.3). This refers to the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice on that day.
And the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are also reversed.

"O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God, you who know all ways. Drive away from us the crooked sin; we shall offer to you the most abundant word of homage. (RV 1.189.1) O Agni! Lead! By a good path! To wealth! Us! All! O God! Ways! Knowing! Drive away! From us! The crooked! Sin!...
The word *tanaya* means "son. May you be one who bestows happiness upon him. Or rather, the meaning is: "Be the pacifier of diseases and the remover of fears; act as such."
O Agni, drive away from us all sickness; may the enemy-less people come to us.
O God, grant us prosperity for our well-being; with all the immortals, be ever-present for us.
O Agni, drive away from us all diseases; let the enemy-less people overcome their adversaries. O worshipful God, grant us back a secure dwelling with all the immortals. 3.
O Agni, drive away and turn aside from us all maladies and diseases;
[ward off] those non-friends, the people and subjects who, unguarded by Agni, seek to overcome us.
The non-impingement [of the senses] occurs through the ellipsis of the word "yad" (which).
Ha! Drive them away! Or rather, those enemy-less yet wicked people (*kṛṣṭayaḥ*), the progeny, have assailed us.
They deserve to be afflicted on all sides by diseases and brought to such a state;
but we are not like that.
Therefore—

Do not deliver us, O Agni, to the malevolent, to the hungry, to the enemy, or to misfortune. Do not surrender us to one who has teeth, nor to one who is toothless; do not hand us over to the injurer, O Lord of Might! 5. mā | naḥ | agne | ava | sṛjaḥ | aghāya | aviṣyave | ripave | ducchunāyai | mā | datvate | darśate | mā | adatai | naḥ | mā | rīṣate | sahasāvan | parā | dāḥ || 5 ||
O Agni, protect us from the one who intends evil, from the injurer, from the one who seeks to overcome us; protect us from misfortune and calamity.
*Śunaṃ* means happiness.
*Duṣṭasukhakāriṇe* means "to the one who causes evil happiness"; that is to say, to the one who causes suffering.

Do not deliver us over to that enemy; do not abandon us—meaning, do not subject us to his power. Likewise, do not deliver us to one who has teeth, who bites, who sees, or who devours, such as a serpent or similar creature.

Likewise, do not deliver us (*mā avasṛjaḥ*) to the devourer—the one who does not eat [himself] but strikes with horns and the like; nor, O powerful one (*sahasvavan*), surrender us (*mā parā dāḥ*)—that is, do not let us be overcome—to the injurer, such as thieves, Rākṣasas, and so forth. The meaning is: by all means, do not give us up.

O Agni, born of Truth, may he who seeks to harm you, seeking to conceal his own body, be struck down; for you, O God, are the dispeller of every one who wishes to injure or revile us, and you are the one invoked in our sacrifice. 6. vi | ghna | tvām | ṛtajāta | yaṃsat | guṇānaḥ | agne | tanvam | varūtham | viśvāt | ririkṣoḥ | uta | vā | ninitsuḥ | abhihūtām | asi | hi | deva | viṣpaṭ || 6 ||

O Agni, born of Truth (ṛtajāta), arisen for the sake of sacrifice— praising you as such a protector (varūtha) for the nourishment of our bodies, may a person endowed with you as their deity free themselves from bondage;
indeed,
they release themselves from the presence of one who desires to harm or strike them.
Or rather,
O God, you are indeed the one who especially obstructs the enemies who wish to revile and who act crookedly against those who offer oblations;
therefore, through your grace, may this person be separated from them.

O Agni, you who know both these [classes], you go forth at the departure of men, O worshipful one; at the arrival [of the sacrifice], you become subject to the command for the sake of Manu, like a noble steed urged by eager drivers. tvaṃ tān agne ubhayān vi vidvān verṣi prapitve manuṣo yajatra | abhipitvaṃ manave śāsyo bhūrmumajenya uśigbhirnākraḥ || 7 || O Agni, you who know both these [classes], you go forth at the departure of men, O worshipful one; at the arrival [of the sacrifice], you become subject to the command for the sake of Manu, like a noble steed urged by eager drivers.

O Agni, worthy of sacrifice, you who are yourself to be sacrificed to—having distinguished those two kinds of humans, both those who are to be sacrificed to and those who are the sacrificers, you, being wise and knowing, desire to sacrifice at the very moment when the time for departure has arrived.
Acting thus, you are the one who overcomes for Manu;
here the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
For the human sacrificer, at the arrival of the time, or at the sacrifice characterized by approach, you should be one who is to be instructed—
be obedient, saying "do this, do that"—
like a purifier (murmujanya) for the sacrificer, as if for the desiring officiating priests (uśigbhiḥ).

We have uttered our prayers in this victorious Agni, the son of Māna. May we, with our hymns, win a thousandfold; may we find strengthening food and a life-giving realm. 8. We have uttered our prayers. Our prayers. In him. Of Māna. The son. In the victorious. Agni. We. A thousandfold. With hymns. May we win. May we find. Food. A realm. Life-giving. 8.
In this Agni, we have uttered—indeed, we speak—utterances consisting of hymns of praise, accompanied by restrictive observances;
he is further distinguished by these [qualities]:
the son of Māna.
*Māna* is a mantra because it is measured (*mīyate*); that is, because it arises through the *sunu-prabhṛti* mantra. The nominative case is used in the sense of the locative.
To Māna’s son, the powerful one, the conqueror of enemies, the singer—we have spoken.
With these *ṛṣis*, with these mantras that reveal supersensuous objects as our means, may we win and enjoy a thousandfold, immeasurable wealth.
"May we know"—this has been explained.
The hymn beginning with "anarvāṇam" is the eleventh hymn, consisting of eight verses; it belongs to Agastya and is addressed to Bṛhaspati.

To him, the seasonal words of praise flow together, he who has been released like a stream for those seeking the gods. He is Bṛhaspati, the powerful one; he has spread out the wide spaces and, like Mātariśvan, has brought the waters together through the cosmic order (*ṛta*). To him, the seasonal words of praise flow together, he who has been released like a stream for those seeking the gods. He is indeed Bṛhaspati, the powerful one; he has spread out the wide spaces and, like Mātariśvan, has brought the waters together through the cosmic order.

The seasonal (*vṛtviyāḥ*) voices—those belonging to the rainy season (*varṣartu*), pertaining to the intermediate region (*mādhyamikāḥ*)—attend upon (*upasacante*), that is, serve in the proximity of, Bṛhaspati. His is the release (*sargaḥ*) of water;
the word *na* is used in the sense of *api* (even/also).
The fruit was released for the sacrificers who desire the gods; or rather, it was released— that is,
having been poured forth as rainwater— for those humans who desire that very god.
Or alternatively:

the seasonal (*ṛtviyāḥ*) or timely words, impelled by the Hotṛ and other priests, attend upon him; he who is like a *sarga*, a creation such as the emission of water—that very one is Bṛhaspati, for he is indeed the manifestor (*vaṅgaḥ* = *vyañjakaḥ*).
When he rains, all things come into being.

Therefore, *vimvaḥ*—the all-pervading one, *vibhuḥ*, like the wind (*mātariśvā*) moving within the atmosphere (*mātari*) that produces rain, or like the wind itself—producing desirable fruits such as rain and the like, *sam babhūva*, he came into being when *vṛte*, water, had become the instrumental cause.
Or else:

Aṅga is the manifestor of sacrifices; Mātariśvan is the fashioner of the fruit. When the sacrifice is being performed and Bṛhaspati is present, he—being the pervasive one—became desirous of the *varāṃsi*, the desirable oblations, when the sacrifice had become the instrumental cause.

He extends his praise, his song of joy, and his rising hymn of fame, like Savitṛ stretching forth his arms. He who is worthy of invocation at the proper season—he who is formidable like a wild beast, yet free from malice and full of power. [He extends] the praise, [the song] of joy, and also the rising [hymn], and [the] fame; he shall bestow [them], like Savitṛ [stretching] forth his two arms. Of him, by his due season, there is one who is to be invoked; he who exists, formidable like a wild beast, yet devoid of demonic power and exceedingly mighty.

This Bṛhaspati, having approached the hymn of praise being performed by the sacrificer, strives with great effort to accept the offering characterized by the oblation (*namas*), the *udgāra* (the utterance), and the *śloka*—whatever other specific mantra exists.
Or rather, the sacrificer bestows all that upon him.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like Savitṛ, like Sūrya.
Just as he accepts the hymns of praise and so forth, so it is;
in the sense of being the recipient of the sacrificer's offerings, he is like Savitṛ, the impeller of all, who is like Sūrya.
Just as he bestows light and so forth from his arms, so too does the sacrificer [bestow them] by means of his two arms; this is the meaning.
He describes its greatness:

having chosen through ritual action that which is to be accomplished for Vṛhaspati—who is *varakṣas*, i.e., free from obstructing demons—the Sun, who is *vasya* (to be dwelt in) and *sādhu* (good), exists as one who is *bhīma* (terrible) like a wild beast (*mṛga*), a cause of fear like a lion, and *tuviṣmān* (mighty); the word "he wanders about" is to be supplied.

The meaning is that by his majesty—that is, through the power of Bṛhaspati, who presides over the mantras—he becomes exceedingly radiant by conquering the Asuras such as Mantra; such a one of great majesty accepts the oblations and other offerings given by the sacrificer.
1. They become manifest.
2. The manifester of objects.
[A. 24, Sū. 190] Second Aṣṭaka: 1107.

His fame is proclaimed in heaven and on earth; like a horse, he, the wise one who sustains the sacrifice, does not falter. Like the weapons of wild beasts, these [missiles] of Bṛhaspati fly toward those who possess the magic of the serpent. His fame is proclaimed in heaven and on earth; like a horse, he, the wise one who sustains the sacrifice, does not falter. Like the weapons of wild beasts, these [missiles] of Bṛhaspati fly toward those who possess the magic of the serpent. 4.
The glorious renown (*śloka*) of Bṛhaspati—consisting of praise or his thundering voice—spreads and pervades both the shining sky (*divi*) and the earth (*pṛthivyām*).

This Bṛhaspati, who is like the sun (*āditya*) in that he is expansive (*asyaḥ*) and non-transient (*atanaśīla*), sustains the honored oblations such as the *havis* (*yakṣabhṛt*); being wise (*vicetāḥ*)—that is, one who brings various things to mind or is endowed with distinguished intelligence—he bestows the fruit of action (*yaṃsat*).
Furthermore, as hunters seek weapons to slay wild beasts, so too do the missiles of this Bṛhaspati—his destructive weapons—move forward and strike.

There is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because of the rule "the first case [is used] in connection with *cavā*" (*cavāyoge prathamā*). Regarding the phrase *vāhimāyān*: those whose *māyās* (deceptive powers) consist of moving through the atmosphere—referring to Vṛtra and others—are the *asuras*.
[The word *divasān* takes the accusative ending] according to the rule *kālādhvanoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.5).
And their weapons appear clearly to those two.
Even a verb that has become a prefix is considered a verbal root (dhātu) when it is combined with its action.

Those wicked folk who, regarding you as a mere firebrand, O God, live off your auspiciousness—O Bṛhaspati, you do not grant them any desirable wealth for their ill-will; rather, you bestow it upon the one who acts righteously. 5. Those | you | O God | firebrand | regarding | wicked | auspiciousness | live off | offspring | not | for ill-will | after | you give | desirable | O Bṛhaspati | you bestow | indeed | upon the one who acts rightly | 5.

O Lord Bṛhaspati, those wretched people— sinful, evil-minded, and insignificant— who regard you, the auspicious one, as a mere *ulki* (a firebrand; *ulki* being a name for a cow), and who, thinking you to be a lowly cow, a bearer of ill-fortune, or a worn-out bullock, subsist upon you— that is, they approach you, live off you, and beg from you.
For one who has carried away [the prize], for the evil-minded one.
There is an interchange of the verbal roots *vac* and *cakṣ*.

O Bṛhaspati, you do not grant—that is, you do not bestow in a favorable manner—the desirable wealth (*vāma*) to those of evil intellect; yet, O God, you indeed go toward—that is, you favor—the one who hates the beloved, who is devoid of the habit of protecting [the gods], who sacrifices with Soma, and who desires great fruit, in order to encourage him.
This is the form of the root *ci*, meaning "to go" or "to accumulate."
Or alternatively:
O Bṛhaspati, [ward off] the malicious one, the injurer.
This is the form of the act of harming that is being drunk.
"You punish that one who harms living beings"—
that is, he indeed kills him.
"O Bṛhaspati, as you [punish] the one who offends the gods" (Nirukta 4.25)— so says the Nirukta.

Easy to traverse like the path of Sūryavasu, difficult to restrain like a well-pleased friend; those two who are irresistible have stood over us, uncovering the waters that were covered. *supraituḥ* (easy to traverse), *sūryavasoḥ* (of Sūryavasu), *na* (like), *panthāḥ* (the path), *durniyantuḥ* (difficult to restrain), *pariprītaḥ* (well-pleased), *na* (like), *mitraḥ* (a friend); *anarvāṇau* (the two irresistible ones), *abhi* (over), *ye* (who), *cakṣate* (behold), *naḥ* (us), *apīvṛtāḥ* (covered), *aporṇuvantaḥ* (uncovering), *asthuḥ* (they have stood).

O Bṛhaspati, you are *supanthas*—you ought to go well; like the excellent path of one who possesses *suvavas* (good pasture or wealth), meaning you should be as conducive to happiness as the path of one traveling on the way of sacrifice (*yajñamārga*). Furthermore, like a friend (*mitra*) or a counselor (*mantrin*) who is *parimita* (well-restrained) toward a king who is difficult to control (*durniyantuḥ*), being satisfied in every way and free from hatred—you, too, should act for us in that same manner, turning us away from misconduct just as such a friend does.

The meaning is: like a friend, having directed one who does not know the path toward the path consisting of sacrifice and so forth, may You also be the bestower of the fruit therein. Furthermore, those men who are *anarvāṇaḥ* (sinless) and who look toward us (*abhi...cakṣate*)—that is, who awaken us—even though they are *apīvṛtāḥ* (covered by ignorance), may they become *apoṇuvantaḥ*, that is, standing with their veils removed and possessed of knowledge; or alternatively: [The rest of the verse follows: May they stand as those whose darkness has been dispelled. And may we, O Agni, being well-disposed and possessing good intentions, be united with you through our own deeds. May we, O Agni, be your companions, like friends, in this world. And may we, being sinless, stand firm among the people, O Lord of the House, for the sake of prosperity. [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-verse; the translation reflects the portion supplied.]

Those who, being unassailable (*anarvāṇaḥ*), do not reach you and are our adversaries—who look upon us, speak against us, and revile us—they become *apīvṛtaḥ*, covered and protected; yet they become *apopnuvantaḥ*, deprived of that protection.
‘Saṃ yaṃ stubhaḥ’—this verse is the *yājyā* for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘Saṃ yaṃ stubho 'vanayo na yanti evā pitre’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
He to whom the praises go together like rivers, like streams flowing toward the ocean with their banks as wheels—he, Bṛhaspati, the wise and eager one, beholds both: the waters and the crossing.

Like rivers flowing toward the ocean, like streams whose banks form their wheels, the chants proceed together. Bṛhaspati, the wise one, beholds both from within; he is the vulture who watches over the waters and the crossing. 7.

Just as all the waters—the *bṛhaspati-stubh* chants, the hymns of praise, and the *avanaya*s—come together and meet with their master for the sake of the ritual work, even as men [gather] so do the *rodhacakras* come together toward the ocean;
this is a name for rivers.

Just as rivers—those flowing streams whose wheels (of whirlpools) are characterized by obstruction, and which advance toward the bank—reach their destination, so too do all hymns of praise reach Yama alone. Like a vulture, one who is greedy and longing for rain, that wise Bṛhaspati, knowing what is about to be said, stands between both the crossing—the swelling of the waters—and the waters themselves; he observes them, meaning he oversees and brings them about.

Thus has Bṛhaspati, the great, the highly born, the mighty, the bull, been established as a god. Praised by us, may he grant us that which is rich in heroes and rich in cattle; may we find strengthening food and a secure dwelling that bestows life-sustaining gifts.

Thus has the great Bṛhaspati, the many-born, the mighty, the bull-like god, been established. May he, being praised, bestow upon us that which is rich in heroes and cattle; may he, the wise one, grant us food and a secure dwelling that provides quickening gifts. 8.

Great, mighty, born with many powers, manifold, arisen, most powerful, strong, the bull, the showerer of waters—the god Bṛhaspati is established (dhāyi) in this very manner; that is to say, he is praised.
May that praised god bestow upon us a fruit endowed with heroes—sons and the like—and endowed with cattle. "May we perform" (vidhāma) has been explained.
1. May my path be like a good pasture for one who goes by the right way;
may it be similarly pleasant, unlike the journey of one who goes by the wrong way.
"Kaṅkata" is the twelfth hymn, consisting of sixteen verses.
The seer is Agastya;
the deity is the Sun, known as Asun; the meter is Triṣṭubh.

The three [verses] beginning with “*sūrye viṣam*” are great *paṅkti*s, because they possess the characteristics stated in [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka] 10.3: “The two groups of eight, the group of seven, the group of six, the group of ten, and the group of nine. This verse, “*navānām*,” is the thirteenth, a great *bṛhatī*.
It has been stated: “The four *aṣṭakas* and the *jāgata* [verse] constitute the *mahābṛhatī*” (Anuvāka 9.9).
Although the syllables here are deficient, they must nevertheless be completed by means of *vyūha* (expansion).

Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*Kaṅkata* [composed] sixteen *upaniṣad-anuṣṭubhs*; then *Atri*, *Viṣa*, *Śaṅkha*, *Vātaraśana*, and *Agastya*; and the three beginning with *Prāgbārhata* are *mahāpaṅktis* and a *mahābṛhatī*.”

"Upaniṣad" means a secret doctrine. Agastya, who was afflicted by poison, conch-shells, and so forth, spoke this for their removal. The specific application of the Vedic [mantra] is indicated by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

Regarding this, Śaunaka says: "One afflicted by poison, being self-restrained, should recite the hymn beginning with 'kaṅkataḥ na'; then the poison does not affect him, even from the venomous gaze of a serpent. Whatever poison is found in insects or spiders, and whatever comes from fanged creatures—"
"By reciting both the Mūla-mantra and the Kṛtrima-mantra, one dispels everything [inauspicious]. (Ṛgvidhāna 1.154–156)

The comb is not a comb; indeed, it is a comb of reeds. These two, called "the two gnats," unseen, have smeared themselves. 1. *kaṅkataḥ* | *na* | *kaṅkataḥ* | *atho* | *satīnakaṅkataḥ* | *dvau* | *iti* | *pluṣī* | *iti* | *ni* | *adṛṣṭāḥ* | *alipsata* || 1 ||

A *vkaṅkata* is a certain small snake; a non-*vkaṅkata* is its opposite, a large serpent and so forth with abundant venom. From the root *tak*, meaning "to go," the word *kaṅkata* arises through a transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*). Furthermore, there is also the *satīnakaṅkata*.

*Satīna* is a name for water, as it is listed among its synonyms in [the Nirukta] 1.12.59: *satīnaṃ gahanam*. A water-dweller (*udakacārī*) is some small venomous creature, such as a leech (*dhūmbubha*) or the like.
Thus, "two kinds" refers to the two types distinguished either by small and great venom, or by the distinction between aquatic and terrestrial.
"Vpluṣī" means "those that burn.
Two instances of the particle *iti* are used to indicate the two-fold nature of the two types [of snakes]:

those that have been seen and those whose forms are not seen. Thus, there are certain venomous serpents (*viṣadharāḥ*) designated by these names who exist in the manner described; they surely wish to smear me excessively (*viśeṣeṇa limpanti*).
It covers all the limbs unevenly;
the sense is that it is not known by whom this was done.
She strikes those unseen when she approaches; moreover, she strikes them as she departs. Furthermore, striking them down, she kills; moreover, pounding, she grinds them to powder. || 2 ||
By this, the anti-poisonous herb (*viṣadhyoṣadhī*) is praised:

coming toward (*vāyatī*) from the vicinity of the poison-vision (*viṣadṛṣṭi*), the herb that is the means for destroying poison kills (*hanti*) the unseen (*vadṛṣṭān*) venomous serpents (*viṣadharān*). Moreover, going away (*parāyatī*)—that is, moving backward at the time of sweeping—it kills (*hanti*), i.e., destroys, the water-dwelling venomous serpents (*jalacara-viṣadharān*).
And furthermore, Vatho and Vavaghnī.
Actions have the agent as their causal condition.
An herb being pounded destroys many kinds [of diseases] by its own fragrance;
or rather,
a certain herb indeed kills those who desire to bite it.

Moreover, the medicinal herb, being ground by the grinder, grinds—that is, it pulverizes—poisons. Alternatively, in all these statements, the destruction of all those who produce poisons is stated without distinction.
The *śarāsa*, *kuśarāsa*, *darbha*, and *sairyā* grasses,
as well as those made of *muñja* and *vairiṇa*— all these unseen [plants] have clung together.

The *śarāsa* grasses, the *kuśarāsa* grasses, the *darbha* grasses, the *sairyā* grasses, and also those made of *muñja*, the *adṛṣṭa* grasses, and the *vairiṇa* grasses—all of them together have become smeared with poison. || 3 ||
He states the causes of the excessive portion:

*śarāsaḥ* refers to arrows, or specific types of grass resembling bamboo stalks that have hollows within; *kuśarāsaḥ* refers to inferior arrows, or specific types of grass resembling arrows that have hollows within.
*Darbhāsaḥ*: *darbha*s, *kuśa*s; *sairyāḥ*: a specific kind of grass growing on the banks of ponds and similar bodies of water. [Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.24, Sūtra 191], Second Book, 1111.
For they appear just like thieves, harmful robbers;
what are they like?
Though unseen and not visible, they are seen by all—those by whom the universe has been seen—and thus they are perceived.
Therefore, O men, become awakened; indeed, become awakened.
Heaven is indeed the father, Earth the mother, Soma the brother, and Aditi the sister;
unseen yet seen by all, she stands—be gracious, O Lady! Rest here.
Heaven is your father, Earth your mother, Soma your brother, Aditi your sister. Unseen ones, all-seers, stand still and rest well. 6.
Hereafter follows the medical treatment for poison.
In that regard: O serpents, heaven is your father;
earth is your mother.
Soma is your brother;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, is your sister.

O great serpents of such majestic power, who are unpoisoned, whose forms are invisible to others, yet yourselves visible to all and the observers of everything—remain each in your own respective place.
Do not come toward me;
rather, move away, go forth, or proceed in such a way that there is supreme happiness (*kaṃ*).
By the word *soma*, the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), which is the support of Soma, is denoted.
The serpents who dwell in the places of earth, atmosphere, and heaven—may they each attain their own respective abodes; the meaning is: "Do not cause harm for our sake."
Those that are on the shoulders, those that are on the limbs, those that are needle-like, and those that are prickly—
whatever unperceived things you have here, all of you perish together!
Those that are on the shoulders, those that are on the limbs, the needle-like ones, those that are crawling about—all you who are unseen, whatever you may be here, perish together! 7.
Or those that are *aṃsyāḥ*, *aṃsāhāḥ*, and *aṃgasāḥ*—those which exist on the shoulder (*aṃsa*) or those that feed upon the shoulders;
likewise, those that are *aṅgyāḥ*, *aṅgāḥ*, or *aṅgena hantāraḥ*—those such as lice and the like that kill with the body (*aṅga*);
and *sūcikāḥ*—scorpions and the like, whose hair on the tail resembles a needle (*sūcī*).
And whatever *prakaṅkatas*— whether they be great serpents (*mahoragas*) with potent venom or those who move swiftly— who have not bitten us, who are not visible,
or whatever species of serpent exists here in this vicinity belonging to you:
therefore, all of you together, utterly release and abandon us.
The root *muc* (jasu) in the sense of "releasing" belongs to the *devādika* (divādi) class.
The sun rises in the east, seen by all, destroying the unseen;
he crushes all unseen evils and all female sorceresses.
The sun rises in the east, beheld by all; he is the slayer of the unseen, crushing all unseen beings and all female sorceresses. 8.
1. He removes great serpents and the like as if by chanting: "O serpents! 2. *ka-kha-ja-jha-sa1-ta-pha*: she is a sister (*svasā*).
3. *ka-kha-jha-sa1-pha*: our affliction (*asmadvādhām*).

This sun rises in the east, in the eastern direction. Of what nature is it? It is "seen by all" (*viśvadṛṣṭa*); that is, one by whom all things are to be seen. It is the "destroyer of the unseen" (*adṛṣṭahā*): either the destroyer of specific poisons or specific venomous serpents; or rather, the destroyer of the darkness of ignorance which consists in not seeing what is to be seen. When the sun has risen, all venomous serpents or poisons flee. If one asks what it is doing [as it does so], it is said: "crushing" (*jambhayan*)—that is, destroying—all "unseen" things, such as the faction of poison and the like; likewise, "crushing" all *yātudhānīs*—female serpents or female demons who are the sustainers (*dhātrī*) of *yātus*, i.e., those intense pains caused by moving—that it rises in the east. Therefore, the connection is: "be driven away from us."

That Sūrya, the Āditya, visible to all, rising from the mountains, has ascended, consuming all things and destroying the unseen. 9. He has risen, that Sūrya, burning away all things, the son of Aditi, visible to all, the slayer of the unseen. 9. *uda̭pa̭sat* (ud-apa-sat): has risen. *a̭sau* (asau): that. *sūryaḥ* (sūryaḥ): Sūrya. *puru* (puru): much/abundantly. *viśvāni* (viśvāni): all. *jūrvan* (jūrvan): consuming/burning. *ādityaḥ* (ādityaḥ): the son of Aditi. *parvatebhyaḥ* (parvatebhyaḥ): from the mountains. *viśvadṛṣṭaḥ* (viśvadṛṣṭaḥ): seen by all. *adṛṣṭahā* (adṛṣṭahā): the slayer of the unseen. 9. [Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 24, Sūkta 191] Second Aṣṭaka 1113.

The Sun indeed does not die; he does not perish. Nor do we die. His grace lies precisely in that the poison was administered [to him]; therefore, we too do not die. He states the reason for the immortality of both: *hariṣṭhāḥ*—those who stand upon the bay horses (*harayaḥ*). The Lord (*ādhipaḥ*) stationed among them brought about the removal (*āre*)—that is, the distant sending away—of the application of this poison. That very thing is expressed thus: "O Poison, having struck you, he made you honey (*madhu*), that is, nectar (*amṛta*). Having cast away the poisonous nature of the poison to a distance, he made it nectar. Such is the *madhuvidhā*: the giver of honey, the maker of poisonless, the fashioner of honey. This which consists of the application of poison to the Sun and the subsequent making of it into nectar—that is the *madhuvidhā*. (15)
This tiny little bird has swallowed your poison;
he will not die, nor shall we die. The one who dwells in the distance has taken it away; he has made you sweet with honey.

So small a bird, a little warbler, has swallowed your poison. Indeed, he shall not die; nor shall we die. Far away is his range, for he dwells among the tawny steeds; you have made him sweet with honey. 11.

*Iyattikā* means "making such a small amount" or "being of such a size. *Vā* has the sense of *ayara* (indeed). *Śakuntikā*: *śakunta* or *śakuna* [means] "bird"; its female is called *kapiñjalī*. "That one (*sā*) indeed (*citru*) ate (*jaghāsa*) your poison (*te viṣam*)"—she is well-known as the "poison-eater" (*viṣahatrī*). "She indeed" (*so citru*): *sā u* is a collection of particles; it is a single word. That bird (*śakuntikā*) does not die, because poison is its constant antidote. The rest has been explained previously. By this, it is stated that whatever poison is brought here for the sake of the science (*vidyā*), there is an offering of it to the birds and to the Sun (*āditya*).
Twenty-one female bees have eaten the flower of the poison;
they do not die, nor do we die. O Poison, your range is a yojana; the honeyed one has made you sweet.

Three times seven are the poison-snakes; they have eaten the flower of the poison. Yet they do not die; indeed, we do not die. Far away is its range; established upon the two bay horses, it has made you honey-sweet with honey. 12.
"Three times seven" means those numbered as seven multiplied by three.
"Various poison-tongues" means diverse poison-tongues. Those which, among the seven tongues, consist of twenty-one through the distinctions of red, white, and black.
Alternatively,
there are twenty-one varieties of poisonous insects (viṣapuliṣka), three times seven;
the *sūkṣmacaṭakikā* are the antidotes to these poisons.
May they consume—that is, eat and destroy—the nourishment and growth of the poison that obscures us;
and may they not die, nor shall we either. The rest is the same as before.

Of the ninety-nine piercing poisons, I have seized the foremost name of them all. O enemy, your range is gone; you who dwell in the sun, he has made you honey, sweet with sweetness. Of the ninety-nine. Of the piercing. Poisons. I have seized. The foremost. Name. O enemy. Of this. The range. Dwelling in the sun. You. Honey. Sweet with sweetness. He has made. 13.
Of the nine, of the ninety-nine—that is, of those rivers numbering ninety-nine.
Furthermore, of what kind?
Of those that are the destroyers (*ropaṇīnām*, *lopayitrīṇām*) and the ploughers (*kṣetrīṇām*) of all poison—of every poison that does not spread.

7. Of all those aforementioned rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, I take up and proclaim their foremost name. [The form] *gṛhṇāmi* is derived from the root *grah* with the suffix *liṭ*; [the form] *saṃkīrtayāmi* is derived from the root *kṛt* with the suffix *ṇic* followed by *liṭ*. [The form] *gṛhe* is [used] in the Vedic *luṅ* tense; it is a Vedic usage where *ghla* takes the suffix *luṅ*.
[This is according to the rule] "hy-aham-meḥ... [Pāṇini 3.4.94].
The passage beginning with "its yojana" and so forth has been explained.

The thrice-seven peahens, the seven sisters who are foremost—let them carry away your poison, as women carry water in jars. 14. Thrice-seven; peahens; seven; sisters; foremost; they; for you; poison; away; carried; water; as; women carrying jars. 14.
Seven times seven— that is, twenty-one— peacock bones (*mayūryaḥ*) are [required].
These are well known as "poison-destroyers" and "snake-averses," because they are endowed with the wings of Garuḍa, the enemy of serpents.
Likewise, there are seven such sisters, numbering seven, whose nature is to glide; they are self-moving (*svasāraḥ*) and foremost (*agravaḥ*).
This refers to the rivers.
There are seven well-known rivers that hold the celestial Gaṅgā as their source.
7. O body, let them carry away—that is, let them specifically remove—the poison from you.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like women carrying water in jars (*kumbhanīḥ*), that is, those who fetch water with jars (*kumbhavatīḥ*).
Just as they carry it away, so let the rivers and peacocks carry it away in great abundance.

So much is the *kuṣumbhaka* insect; I split its shell with a stone. From that, the poison has flowed forth, following the distant enclosures. 15. So much is the *kuṣumbhaka*. I split its shell with a stone. From that, the poison has flowed forth, following the distant enclosures. 15.
*Īyatsakaḥ*: from *kutsita-yataḥ*, meaning "one who is measured by me" (i.e., one who considers himself small).

*Kuṣumbhakaḥ*: he who "sumbhati," that is, digs or scratches the earth (*kuṃ pṛthvīm*); thus, he is the contemptible subduer or restrainer of serpents. *Kuṣumbhakaḥ* is the mongoose. The ellipsis is "may he take away your poison."

If he does not do so, I shall crush—that contemptible mongoose—with a stone; I shall split him open. In the application for extracting poison, until the poison has vanished, they who know that [method] perform it with a large stone, following the direction of the wind.
This is what is stated in the mantra:

"Therefore, when the ritual application is performed in this manner, the universe has turned away; from the body that has turned away [from poison], let the poison go forth, let it issue out. Toward what?"
It is said:

"Toward the distant quarters—those that are turned away, possessed of other women, and extending to great distances; toward those quarters characterized by distribution—let him go to the very end of the horizon, let him not come toward me. This is the meaning.
The verse beginning with "Kusumbhakaḥ tat" is prescribed for the commencement of the study of a chapter and for the creation [of the world];
for it is enjoined in the Sūtra: "Having begun with 'He offers curd and phūñj,' [he recites] 'Kusumbhakaḥ tadabravīt'" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.5.7).
The *kusumbhaka* plant, acting as a remedy for the scorpion, said to it:
"O scorpion, your poison is tasteless; your poison is indeed tasteless."
The safflower said this: "O mountain-born one, the poison of the scorpion is sapless; O scorpion, your poison is weak. (16)
While the great-souled sage Agastya was speaking thus, Kusumbhaka the mongoose, who had set out from the mountain and was arriving here with extreme speed, spoke these words, recounting that speech.
What was it? It is said:
"This venom of the scorpion is tasteless and insubstantial; it does not cause affliction"—this is the meaning.
Likewise, in the world as well, they say that even if something is seen by everyone, it is merely a perception that may be sublated; therefore, there is no contradiction.
By this statement, the snake also became free from poison.
Then the mongoose said to that scorpion:
"O scorpion, your venom is tasteless;
therefore, what will it do to that seer?
For this reason, he avoids it."
From the moment he spoke thus, the venom of the scorpion became powerless;
this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) for neutralizing poison.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth Anuvāka and the first Maṇḍala in the second Aṣṭaka of the Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa composed by Sāyaṇācārya.
